title: The Fathers on the Psalms
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Those who set themselves up as leaders without ordination are the ones the Holy Spirit points out as sitting in the chair of pestilence.
comments.comment: [There are] those who, without divine appointment, set themselves over reckless gatherings on their own initiative. They establish themselves as leaders without any law of ordination, and with no one granting them the episcopate they take the name of bishop for themselves. The Holy Spirit points them out in the Psalms as those sitting in the chair of pestilence (Psalm 1:1)—plagues and pestilences of the faith, deceiving with the serpent's mouth, contrivers of truth's corruption, vomiting deadly poisons from their pestilent tongues.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Blessing is more than avoiding evil, since even the irrational avoid it, and it begins with the will for the good in the law, which leads us step by step from the easy commands to the hard.
comments.comment:
Blessed, then, is the one who longs for the things that truly are. But how is the blessing in a taking-away of evils? For abstinence from evils is common also to the soulless and to the irrational. For this reason, then, he added: “But his will is in the law of the Lord.” For this belongs not only to a rational being, but is also the beginning of taking up the good things: the flight from evils. “Turn from evil,” he says, “and do good” (Psalm 34:14). For as on a ladder the first ascent is withdrawal from the earth, so in the progress according to God, the separation from evil.

But also in general every idleness is easier than even a chance action: such as “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not fornicate” (Exodus 20:14) and the rest, which need each person’s idleness and not-moving. But “You shall love your neighbor” (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39), and “Sell your belongings and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21), and “If anyone conscripts you one mile, go with him two” (Matthew 5:41) are already deeds of a youthful soul and of athletes.

If he had set the perfect things before you at once, you would have shrunk from the undertaking; but now he trains you beforehand with the more easily grasped, so that you may dare the things next. As deeds fitting for athletes, we already need a youthful soul toward the achievement; so wonder at the wisdom of the one who leads us through the easier and more easily grasped toward perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm says more than 'avoids evil'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'way of sinners' can be understood as the devil, and whoever does not stand in it will come to the Lord, who is the way.
comments.comment: The “way of sinners” can be said to be the devil; the one who has come to be in it must not remain, according to “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). For the one who has not stood in it will come to the Lord, who said “I am the way” (John 14:6); coming to be in it and running according to the mark, he will obtain the prizes. “Ungodly”: those who do not know God. “On a seat”: the working of evils, come about by succession. “But in the law”: the evangelical, clearly. “He will meditate”: by his counsel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blessed man has put away childish things and has his will in the law of the Lord, whereas many keep the law only for fear of punishment or for praise.
comments.comment: Therefore, 'blessed' is not simply the man, but the 'man' who has done away with 'the things of a child' (1 Cor 13:11), who has not walked 'in the counsel of the ungodly' (Ps 1:1), nor sat 'in the seat of scoffers' (Ps 1:1), nor 'in the way of sinners' (Ps 1:1), … but having 'his will in the law of the Lord' (Ps 1:2). This one has his will in the law of the Lord; for many observe the law so that they may not be punished or so that they may be honored with praise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Infants and animals could avoid the ungodly, but cannot have their will in the law.
comments.comment: [Concerning the first Psalm:] For they say that 'to be blessed in not walking in the counsel of the ungodly and not sitting in the seat of scoffers' (Psalm 1:1) would also apply to irrational animals and infants. But they are refuted by what is presented; for it is said: 'But his will was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night' (Psalm 1:2), which does not apply to infants and irrational animals.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fruit means virtuous action from the disposition, while the leaf is the outward appearance shown in form and adornment.
comments.comment: … for it is proper to attend to both the serious matters, both in rightly calculating and in displaying an outward adornment suitable to the ways, which the Psalmist, instructing, says in the first Psalm: 'Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly' (Ps 1:1), and shortly after: 'He shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, which shall bring forth its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall' (Ps 1:3). By saying 'fruit' he means virtuous action from a disposition, but 'leaf' is the outward appearance, which is shown in form, adornment, and the smiling of teeth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tree is Christ, planted beside the waters of Scripture, and its fruit is right faith while its leaves are the fulfilment of the commandments.
comments.comment:
A tree, Christ is written in the God-breathed Scripture. Aquila rendered “transplanted”: for rooted in the patriarchs’ roots, he is transplanted so that others also may partake of his image, taken according to the being-transplanted; or it is said of the Savior’s soul transplanted from here into paradise. For he said to the robber: “Today you will be with me in the paradise of God” (Luke 23:43). “Outlets of waters”: the divine scriptures, in which everywhere one can find Christ proclaimed.

The fruit of the tree you will understand as the right faith. Its leaves, the fulfillment of the commandments. And one of the saints used to say that leaves are the ascetics’ humility, covering their fruits and never falling. “It will prosper”: for there is no deed of those done according to God that is useless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the tree, its water, fruit and leaves plainly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever becomes like the tree of life is joined to it as a branch bearing divine fruit, and the fruit of the tree is the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures, with ready words as its leaves.
comments.comment:
And he who becomes like the tree of life is planted in paradise to be with it; thus it is heard of what is written in Isaiah from the face of God: 'The days of the people of my God shall be as the days of the wood of life' (Isaiah 65:22). This being true, since the wood of life is eternal, it joins and shares in the passion of Him; thus the likeness makes us grow together in the wood, so that we may be made branches and shoots to bring forth divine fruit. For the wood of life is said to be a true vine toward those becoming imitators through goodness: 'I am the true vine; you are the branches; my Father is the gardener; every branch abiding in me, he prunes it, so that it may bear more fruit' (John 15:1, 2, 5).

But also, the mystical and spiritual understanding of the Scriptures is a fruit of the wood planted by the watercourses (this is the wisdom of God), and the ready words are leaves covering the said fruit, intended to do the proper work in guarding the fruits and becoming food for the most pure men, those called simple like cattle, according to: 'You will save men and cattle, Lord' (Psalm 36:6; LXX 35:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The virtues will yield their fruit in the age to come, the fruit of eternal life, since toil goes before and blessedness follows.
comments.comment: [The best things are] the good things that are truly desired and loved by those of sound mind, which endure for ever, which gladden God and bring forth ripe fruit for those who possess them: the virtues, I mean, which will yield their fruit in their season (Psalm 1:3), that is, in the age to come, the fruit of eternal life, to those at least who have laboured worthily and offered their own toils as far as they were able. For toil goes before, and eternal blessedness follows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'fruit in its season' plainly.
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: Those who choose impiety are swept away like dust by an evil wind.
comments.comment: For if they desire to be in the deficiency of dust through impiety and to bear the image of the swine, similarly they are swept away from the face of the earth by the most meager dust, being scattered there by the evil wind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ungodly are worthless in intention rather than substance, like chaff moved by a wind of tribulation or a deceptive word.
comments.comment: 'Not so the ungodly, not so, but like the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth' (Psalm 1:4). Their worthlessness shows not so much of substance as of intention; for 'those who think on earthly things' (Philippians 3:19), having become entirely of the flesh and of the members, are chaff not having a sheaf, nor a stable seat. Thus a wind briefly moves them. And this wind is able to be either tribulation or a deceptive word. For thus some are carried away by 'every wind of doctrine' (Ephesians 4:14)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the chaff and the wind plainly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the way of the ungodly perishes, their ungodliness becomes non-existent while the people are left.
comments.comment: And having said that the way of the ungodly perishes, he corrected the suspicions of the heretics who supposed their substances are made to vanish into non-being, from what was said: “but as the chaff which the wind throws from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4). For when the way has perished, the ungodliness becomes non-existent, those to whom it happened being left.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ungodly will be raised, but not to glory or to a place among the righteous; they rise to penalty and punishment.
comments.comment: The ungodly, the profane, and those who have lived outrageously will indeed be raised, yet they will not go on to live the glorious life; they remain without any share in glory. For they will rise not “in judgment, nor in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5), but for penalty and punishment, for they will go down into the outer darkness (compare Matthew 25:30). For how can what is being punished be in glory?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'not stand in the judgment' means in a clear way.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ungodly will not rise into judgment, and 'knows' means 'honors', so the Lord knows the way of the righteous while the way of the ungodly perishes unknown.
comments.comment:
“Therefore the ungodly will not rise in judgment” (Psalm 1:5). Having said the ungodly will not rise, he says “into judgment,” not “into questioning.”

“Because the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish” (Psalm 1:6). “Knows” instead of “honors,” according to what was said by God to Moses: “I know you above all, and you have found favor with me” (Exodus 33:17). It is to be noted universally that only the good is known by the Lord; for the way of the righteous is good; but also “the Lord knew those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19) and the way of the righteous, having said “I am the way” (John 14:6).

The way of the ungodly is the one walked by those who speak evil of the Creator, becoming like chaff thrown from the wind; therefore they are not counted worthy of the resurrection in judgment, as neither are sinners of the counsel of the righteous. For the way of the righteous, being worthy of God’s knowledge, is known by him; but the way of the ungodly will perish, as not being known by the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the Lord knows the way' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The ungodly are self-condemned by their unbelief, God owns the deeds of the righteous, and no examination of the ungodly after the resurrection is spoken of.
comments.comment: The ungodly shall rise, but they shall not be judged, being self-condemned for being. For he who does not believe in me, he says, is already judged, having been shown to be condemned from his own unbelief. … The deeds of the righteous are owned by God; for by this He knows them here. … For these things have been written concerning only those sinners coming unto judgment and the righteous being raised unto eternal life; of the ungodly, there is nothing of these being raised, nor will there be an examination of them after the resurrection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations are squeezed by their own sins, and Christ calls his servants to tear off the bonds and put off the heavy yoke of the letter.
comments.comment:
“Let us burst their bonds, and throw off their yoke from us” (Psalm 2:3). For the nations are squeezed by their own sins, not being free; therefore Christ says this, either to the angels who serve him, or to the Father and the Holy Spirit, or to the apostles the servants of the gospel, calling on them to tear their bonds apart.

The peoples, being bodily under the yoke of the law — which contains ordinances that are not good and commandments that are not good — when they are brought through Christ to the spiritual law, which has the good ordinances and commandments, put off the heavy yoke of the letter that kills, the Savior saying to the fellow-workers already named: “Let us throw off their yoke from us,” that is, let us make this from ourselves, not waiting for the request of those who are burdened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bands and the yoke of the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He who dwells in the heavens laughs at the kings and rulers who have an earthly mind and do not grasp the wisdom of the Savior's becoming man.
comments.comment: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them” is toward the kings of the earth, whom the Lord in the heavens will laugh at, as having an earthly mind and not who have understoododod the wisdom about the Savior’s becoming-man. And he will mock the rulers also. And it was fitting for the Son of God to say: even if the nations have cried out and the peoples have meditated empty things, we will burst the bonds of the one and throw off the yoke of the other, since they no longer receive the healing easily. For they did not want to come inside the holy net, about which it is written: “The kingdom of the heavens is like a net thrown into the sea” (Matthew 13:47).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's anger is a chastisement for the sinner's benefit, and he speaks rather than chastises because he threatens toward salvation, as with the Ninevites.
comments.comment: “Then he will speak to them in his anger” (Psalm 2:5). Anger of God is a toilsome chastisement for the benefit of the one who has sinned. But also in the time of the judgment they will taste the anger of God, and all the enemies of the saving Word will be troubled by his wrath. He did not say “he will chastise them,” but “he will speak to them in his anger”; for when they repent he did not chastise, as with the Ninevites. For God threatens toward salvation, he said, and to the Ninevites he sent Jonah.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says he 'speaks' in his anger.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His kingship on Zion is not his eternal, innate kingship but the one he received for our sake.
comments.comment: If, therefore, he says: 'I have been established king by him upon his holy Mount Zion' (Psalm 2:6), he is not speaking about the innate and eternal kingship, but about that which he received for our sake. And teaching is a kingship upon God. Thus, there was the teaching before the advent, which they said was spoken by him as a Word like God, and there is another for the sake of some. This, therefore, has a beginning and an end.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'You are' shows the Son's eternal being, and 'Today I have begotten you' shows his new birth in the flesh from the Virgin.
comments.comment: You see the confession at the very start, that is, the declaration. For the Father has set down the words "You are" in order to show the Son's eternal being. He did not become Son in time; he always was this—that is, Son. Then the Father brought in the words "Today I have begotten you" (Psalm 2:7) in order to show his newest birth according to the flesh, which he willingly underwent through the holy Virgin. This is why she has been named Mother of God. For she gave birth not to a mere human being simply joined to God by an external connection, but rather to the very Word from God the Father, who put on human poverty and became a human being like us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two halves of the verse, 'You are' and 'Today'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though the Word became flesh, the Father still knows him as his own Son, as these words declare.
comments.comment: The one who alone knows the Father and is known by the Father alone, his wisdom and word, the angel of great counsel, makes the mystery of the plan of salvation with flesh very clear to us. For though he is Son by nature and truly, and though he has shone forth from the very essence of God the Father, he became flesh—that is, a human being—and underwent birth according to the flesh among us, even though he is eternal and always co-existing with the one who begot him. Yet even though he became flesh, the Father knows him as his own Son even in this state. For he said, "The Lord said to me: 'You are my Son; today I have begotten you'" (Psalm 2:7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The psalm speaks of the generation of Christ in the flesh, though he is always Son, and of his kingdom over those without a king.
comments.comment:
But since not to be ungodly was set first in the beginning of the blessing, the second word sets out the things that have come to be outside ungodliness, the evangelical mystery spoken beforehand; so that in a way the first psalm is an inscription of the second.

For it speaks the generation through flesh there of Christ who has been begotten “today” for us (and “today” is a part of time), but who always is Son and God from the Father and in the Father; and it speaks the kingdom over those without a king, who because they did not slave for God had been counted among the nations.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Today' is always being called, and the devil showed the Savior the kingdoms.
comments.comment:
“I have begotten you today” (Psalm 2:7). “Today” is always being called.

“Ask of me, and I will give you nations, your inheritance” (Psalm 2:8). The devil showed the Savior their kingdoms and the glory in a moment of time.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A potter's vessel, unlike an earthen one, can be reshaped after it is crushed, which he reads as the mystical washing of the faithful drawn from the nations.
comments.comment:
[On baptism:] It was this crushing and this mystical cleansing that the prophet was hinting at long ago when he said, 'You will crush them like a potter's vessel' (Psalm 2:9). That he is speaking about the faithful is shown clearly by what comes before: 'You are my Son,' he says, 'today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession' (Psalm 2:7-8). Do you see how he remembered the Church drawn from the nations, and spoke of Christ's kingdom stretching everywhere?

Then he says again, 'You will shepherd them with an iron rod'—not a burdensome one, but a strong one—'you will crush them like a potter's vessel' (Psalm 2:9). See how the washing is presented here in a more mystical way. He did not simply say 'earthen vessels,' but 'a potter's vessel.' Pay close attention. Earthen vessels, once crushed, cannot be repaired, because of the hardness the fire has produced in them once for all. But a potter's vessels are not earthenware; they are clay. So even when they are distorted, they can easily return to a second shape through the craftsman's skill. When Scripture speaks of an incurable disaster, it does not say 'a potter's vessel' but 'an earthen vessel.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'potter's vessel' image plainly.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: No one is essentially good or bad, so Israel, once God's heir, fell away while another people from many nations is brought in, and his teaching will prevail to the ends of the earth.
comments.comment: Of all men moving by choice (for they are free agents), no one is essentially good or bad; and since the one possessing virtue is owned by God alone, and every such one becomes an inheritance of God. The whole of Israel was not good; it was said concerning him, 'He became a portion of the Lord, a branch of the inheritance of Israel Jacob.' It is shown that this nation did not only become an inheritance, but through goodness was so treated from what is said concerning God by the holy men: 'He chose for us His inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom He loved.' If, however, one keeps the commandments and the faith toward God, one becomes an inheritance of God; the one transgressing the commandments of God and falling away from faith toward Him is cast out from such honor, just as he who turns from evil and does good becomes a lot of God even if he was not so before. This sequence remaining, he who formerly through godliness was an heir of God, Israel, becoming an apostate of God, fell away, not receiving the one who previously went before him in blessing, even as also for all other men, the Savior has come. It is necessary, therefore, that another, being fulfilled from many nations, should be brought in and approach… But also the saying 'The ends of the earth shall hold fast to you' is understood more simply: until the ends of the earth, his teaching shall prevail, the gospel being preached in all creation under the heaven.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word is Lord of all by nature yet is called heir and told 'Ask of me' because he became flesh.
comments.comment: The Only-begotten Word is believed to be by nature Lord of the wholes with God and Father, yet he is placed heir because he became flesh. For it was said to him, as one who appeared as a human like us for our sake: “Ask of me, and I will give you nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” (Psalm 2:8)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Serving in fear ends in progress, so that divine exultation comes with trembling, as befits the Most High and awesome.
comments.comment: 'Now receive understanding, you risen from the dead who were crucified; and you, rulers, be instructed, knowing what you honored by surrounding with death, having risen, having loosed death' … for this will turn you to serve in fear, knowing what is being plotted against you, what God is, through which you have come. This slavery in fear will cease, having produced progress, so that divine exultation may come to you with trembling; for if any joy comes reasonably, it is exultation; but it does not happen before God with mere trembling. … With this, 'Shout for joy to God with a voice of exultation, who is the Most High and awesome' … is consistent; for since the exultation is of the Most High and awesome, it is necessary to have it with trembling.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Training is a measured suffering of the passions, coming from the practical life.
comments.comment: “Take hold of training” (Psalm 2:12). Training is a measured-suffering of the passions, which is naturally apt to come about from the practical life; and the practical life is a spiritual teaching, cleansing the passionate part of the soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'Seize instruction' urge quick action lest the Lord be angry.
comments.comment: The saying 'Seize instruction' is spoken in an extraordinary way, as if to be the follower of the phrase: 'Seize instruction quickly, and what you are encountering in this life, lest, while you are being sluggish, the Lord be angry and you perish from the way of righteousness' (Ps 2:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who make progress have many afflicters, and the soul that applies itself to God's wisdom is lifted up by him as a head rises above lesser heads.
comments.comment:
“Lord, why have those who afflict me been multiplied?” (Psalm 3:1). Those who are making progress have many who afflict them.

“But you, Lord, are my helper, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (Psalm 3:3). Then the mind is lifted up, whenever it applies itself to the manifold wisdom of God (Ephesians 3:10). The glory of the holy one is God. And everyone whose glory is God is lifted up by him.

The head, that is, the rising of the soul. For just as the head of one who has been made large in body is lifted up above the heads of the lesser ones that lie below, so also, when the soul of the blessed has risen, the head is lifted up, God working with it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'lifter up of my head' and the many troublers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'head' signifies a ruler, so Christ is called the head of the holy.
comments.comment: … it must be said that his head is also raised, the God who is, or that his divinity becomes manifest to the faithful through demonstration. The name of the head in these things signifies ruler; therefore, Christ, the ruler of men, is rightly their king of those being holy, and in this way he signifies their head.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy mountain may be the Only-begotten.
comments.comment: “And he heard me from his holy mountain” (Psalm 3:4). See whether the holy mountain can be the Only-begotten, from where God will hear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The holy mountain of God, from which he hears those who pray, can be his only-begotten Son.
comments.comment: His exceedingly high mountain is able to be a holy mountain of God, from which God hears those praying, his only-begotten Son, concerning whom it was said, 'The mountain of the Lord shall be visible at the end of days' (Ps 3:5), this word indicating the manifestation of what is to come …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because Jesus voluntarily laid down his soul, he slept, and having been raised he became the firstborn from the dead.
comments.comment: To sleep signifies a reclining, after which sleep immediately follows. Since Jesus voluntarily laid down his soul, for this reason, having slept, he slumbered; for he would not have died if he had not given himself to this, and having been raised from the dead, being grasped by God, he has become the firstborn from the dead.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I laid me down and slept' as Christ's own laying down of his life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who sings the third Psalm has the courage of those told that one will pursue a thousand.
comments.comment: Having the same courage, he who sings the third Psalm also was emboldened to say: 'I will not fear from ten thousands of people surrounding me.' (Ps 3:6). To those thus arrayed, the word, encouraging them, says: 'One of you shall pursue a thousand, and two shall put ten thousand to flight' (Deuteronomy 32:30), not of men alone as warriors, but also of the invisible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enemies are 'in vain' when no cause is given for hatred, and the 'teeth' of enemies are used sinfully, but with the petition established, enemies become friends.
comments.comment: Vainly does one have enemies if he does not provide a pretext of hatred and enmity; such are all those persecuted for living piety in Christ Jesus, to whom it is said by the Savior, 'Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and lie every kind of evil against you on my account,' and the following. With this intention also David had many enemies in vain, such as Saul and Absalom and those with them; for having often shown much gentleness and goodness toward them for the holy one, they were enemies in vain. … Concerning such teeth, he often says to God, 'They have set their teeth against me,' and thanking that he was not harmed by them, he says, 'Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us into the prey of their teeth.' It is evident what he says concerning spiritual things. To those spoken of as 'biting,' who use the teeth badly, as the Galatians bite and devour one another, the teeth are called allegorically, being used vainly and sinfully with the powers of the soul. For when the petition is established, instead of enemies, friends and instead of sinners, diligent ones will be.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God saves those for whom he arises and strikes those hostile in vain, and the crushed teeth of sinners are like the 'gnashing of teeth'.
comments.comment:
“Arise, Lord, save me, my God, because you have struck all who are hostile to me in vain. You have crushed the teeth of sinners” (Psalm 3:7). To each, God has a certain state: those for whom he has arisen, those he also saves; but those who are hostile in vain he strikes.

And of those hostile in vain, such is also this: “they hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). And of what sort are the teeth of sinners crushed by the Lord, such also are these about whom it is said: “there will be the weeping and the gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 8:12); and “the teeth of the one who has eaten the unripe grape will be set on edge” (Jeremiah 31:29).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Salvation is to be sought from the Lord alone, and his good pleasure on his people is shown in the Savior who became man.
comments.comment: The salvation of the Lord; therefore, let us not seek this from another, but from Him. And your good pleasure is upon your people; but what is the good pleasure coming upon the people, is it the will of the Father concerning the epidemic? Having shown the Savior who became man, he says, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every art has an end, and the end of the rational nature is to be made alive in Christ, each in his own order.
comments.comment:
It is to be known that, just as of every art and science there is an end, toward which the one who genuinely pursues the art or the science hastens, so also of the rational nature there must be an end. And this is to be made alive in Christ, according to the things said by Paul the most wise in the first letter to the Corinthians: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive, but each in his own order” (1 Corinthians 15:22-23).

But as far as saying “in his own order,” he does not sketch one end of all; for it is likely that each will be made alive according to the worth of the things done, either coming to this without torment, or after punishments.

And Christ, having made alive in himself all who die in Adam, reigns over those who have been made alive.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: An ode is a song of the mind alone and a psalm is a hymn sung with the right actions of the practical life.
comments.comment:
An ode is a triumphal song, being uttered with a single voice, but a psalm is a hymn being struck with the instrument called the psalter or the lyre. If the ode, for the sake of leading upward, is an ode having become composed by thought alone, the psalm is a hymn with actions being performed according to the right reason, as if one having the practical life were singing …

Since now David perceives God and His truth with a pure heart, he utters a song, and he says that things are in the psalms because he has achieved much in a practical way. This song is that which they are accustomed to call the end, the most desired of his own things, while all other things are to be chosen and desired, but not for the sake of another; for it is the perfection of all things, concerning which also Paul says, 'If one has become like God, he will see Him' (1 John 3:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God enlarges in affliction by giving the magnanimity to bear circumstances bravely, not by removing the pressure or overthrowing the evildoers.
comments.comment: But God is enlarged in affliction, not ceasing the pressure, not overthrowing the evildoers, but providing magnanimity to bear the circumstances bravely (Psalm 4:1). This is the mindset that should be heard. And many afflictions of the righteous, and from all of them He will rescue them, granting endurance (Psalm 34:19). And he who also, even outside of circumstances, makes himself a magnanimous man, standing against the circumstances like Joseph and Job, but also himself standing against what lies ahead.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God heard him in the calling itself, not after it, and we are widened in affliction when we come to know the reasons for the trials.
comments.comment:
“In my calling, the God of my righteousness heard me; in affliction you widened me” (Psalm 4:1).

He did not hear me after the calling, but in the calling. When we come to know the reasons of the afflictions and of the trials, then especially we are widened.

Even if as a man the prophet calls, and because of the calling is heard by the God of his righteousness — I mean the righteousness of the one speaking — and for this reason comes to be in a widening in the times of affliction, still, as toward God, being such, he is below. For the eyes of the Lord are high, and man is low, and he needs to be pitied by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'thou hast enlarged me' in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'enlargement' in affliction is the cheerful, undaunted state of mind made by the presence of the comforting Word.
comments.comment: … the saying in the Psalms: 'In affliction thou didst enlarge me.' (Psalm 4:1) For by the co-working and presence of the comforting Word of God who saves us, the cheerful and undaunted state of our mind in the season of circumstances, made by God, was called enlargement.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Sons of men' is a figure of speech, and evil is of a heavy nature as opposed to the light cloud that is a rational nature filled with virtue.
comments.comment:
“Sons of men, how long heavy-hearted?” (Psalm 4:2). “Sons of men,” someone will suppose, has been said by periphrasis, as it is also the custom of Greeks to use such a figure, saying “sons of the Achaeans” and the like.

Here we know that evil is of a heavy nature; therefore the Lord, coming into Egypt, is said to sit upon a light cloud. And a light cloud is a rational nature, filled with every virtue and knowledge.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Sons of men' is said instead of 'men', and the heavy-hearted, who ignore everything with malice, are children of men rather than of God.
comments.comment: And many such things are borne also in the Scripture, for it is said, 'The mortal is born of a woman' (Job 14:1), and in John 'Among those born of women, none is greater than John' (Matthew 11:11). For these words are spoken instead of 'man.' The saint of God is not to be wondered at if he bears afflictions magnanimously, which seem to be beyond man, but also if he, calling upon God, should immediately have a rebuke, whereas the heavy-hearted man ignores everything, that is, having a mindset with malice; if the word was spoken concerning Christ to the Jews, because the heavy-hearted are not children of God but of men …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Prophecies, miracles and the resurrection point to the Holy One, and those who cast off the heavy heart and search the writings will know.
comments.comment: [To the Jews, concerning Christ:] For the Lord did not marvel at the Holy One in him and through him, having fulfilled the prophecies, with extraordinary powers occurring through him, and also having risen from the dead. But you will know, having cast off the heavy heart and having searched the writings concerning the Holy One; for the newness of the Spirit will be found searching for you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord has shown as wonderful the one who trusted in him, and believing is not the same as knowing, for the believer must go on to know the truth.
comments.comment:
“And know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful” (Psalm 4:3).

Know, then, you who have trusted in multitudes, that he has shown as wonderful the one who has trusted in him. David prophesies about Christ in the fifteenth psalm, that he is a true holy one, and the apostles are witnesses about him, who have understoododod: “nor will you give your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 16:10).

And it is possible also to be taught about every holy one. But to believe and to know are not the same; as neither is it the same to believe the truth and to know the truth, and to believe God and to know God. Therefore to the apostles already having believed the Savior says: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you” (John 8:31-32). For as Isaiah says: “If you do not believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9). And David: “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Psalm 116:10). And “Be still and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10) makes clear that knowing differs from believing; for this was not said to the unbelieving.

And it also shows what sort of knowledge it will be necessary to receive, and how the holy ones have been made wonderful by God, having been led to the wonders of the unspeakable mysteries and of the holy contemplations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'know' and how knowing differs from believing.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Do not assent to anger or act on it.
comments.comment:
“Be angry, and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4).

He exhorts not to assent to the appearance, nor to bring on the deed confirming the anger.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Be angry' may mean the involuntary first stirring of anger or our assent to it, and we are told to put away the assent.
comments.comment: Ephesians 4:26 "Be angry and do not sin" comes from Psalm 4. "Be angry" has two senses. One is involuntary—the pre-passion even the mature may feel when circumstances provoke anger. The other is assent that it is right to punish the person one thinks has wronged you; that assent is in our power, and the apostle commands us to put it away. So the first sense of the verse means: even if anger once entered, leave it without effect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what 'be angry and sin not' asks of us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul took up this verse in 'Let not the sun go down on your anger', so the angry man must not sin by staying angry, as the words about the heart and the bed confirm.
comments.comment: Having received this word [Be angry, and sin not], the apostle brought it to it: 'Let not the sun go down on your anger, nor give place to the devil' (Ephesians 4:26). He who has received this apostolic exhortation, being angry, does not sin by persisting in staying angry and calling it monthly anger. This thought is confirmed by what follows: 'For you say' (clearly being angry) 'in your hearts, strike upon your beds, so as to have risen from sleep and to have done or said nothing of those in the heart covered in anger' (Psalm 4:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness is impassibility offered to God, and hope is expecting true knowledge.
comments.comment:
“Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope upon the Lord” (Psalm 4:5).

Righteousness is impassibility of a rational soul, offered to God; and hope is a good expectation of true knowledge.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Angels always see the face of God, while men see the light of his face, which is a partial knowledge of what has come to be on earth.
comments.comment:
“The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord” (Psalm 4:6).

The angels always see the face of God; but men, the light of his face. For the face of the Lord is a spiritual contemplation of all things that have come to be on earth. And the light of the face is the partial knowledge of these same things, as the wise Tekoite said: “As an angel of God, knowing all things on the earth” (2 Samuel 14:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between God's face and the light of his face.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Light of God's face can be called the exact imprint of his hypostasis, and the one who shows the good things is the only-begotten Son.
comments.comment: It is possible to call the Light of the face of God the exact imprint of his hypostasis and the icon of the invisible God, through which light it was signaled toward us, having been formed according to Him (Psalm 4:6). … It should not be ignored how some read 'Who will show us the good things thus'; the good things are not of many, but it is of one to show; and he is the only-begotten Son of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To have God's eyes shine upon us we must take up the virtues, and then we can say the light of his face is marked upon us.
comments.comment: So if you too want the rays of God's spiritual eyes to reach you, take up the virtues. Then, just as we say, "Lord, your eyes are on faith," we can say, "Lord, your eyes are on" each good thing you acquire. And if you have grown so far that the Lord's eyes shine upon you, you will say, "The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord" (Psalm 4:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As soldiers need a watchword, we need the seal of the light of the Lord's face marked upon us to be recognized as God's.
comments.comment: In battle, generals distribute a watchword to their troops, so that friends can easily call to one another, and so that when they are mixed with the enemy in close combat, the separation can be clearly made. No one will recognize whether you are one of ours or one of the enemy, unless you show your allegiance through the mystical symbols, unless the light of the Lord's face is marked upon you (Psalm 4:6). How will the angel claim you? How will he snatch you from the enemy, if he does not recognize the seal? How will you say, "I belong to God," if you do not carry the marks of identification?
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The promise of wheat, wine and oil refers to intelligible rather than sensible goods, and the gladness of God gladdens the righteous.
comments.comment:
“You gave gladness into my heart, from fruit of wheat and wine and oil” (Psalm 4:7).

These things are promised in many places of the Scripture to the holy, and the deprivation of them is threatened to sinners — clearly of the intelligible and not of the sensible. Some, thinking them evils because of the smallness of the promise, wanted to worship another God fabricated by them. For when it partakes of the better things, each soul is both sanctified and in good condition toward being able to complete the works that fall to it.

And into the coming age Paul also brought these: “Let no one judge you in food or in drink, or in part of a feast, or new moon, sabbaths, which are a shadow of the things to come” (Colossians 2:16-17). Wheat and wine and oil multiply sinners; but the gladness of God gladdens the righteous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'gladness' is, and what the gifts stand for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To lie down and sleep in peace is to depart from life free of all disturbance, because God has settled the speaker on the hope of the age to come.
comments.comment: … I, expecting an age to come and the reward of upright citizenship, having become free from all disturbance through hope, 'I will sleep and lie down also' (Psalm 4:8), saying the departure from life; giving the reason for having slept and having slumbered in peace, he immediately brought to it 'You have settled me on hope' (Psalm 4:8). … God does this, proposing the hope of coming divine good things to those dwelling by Him in intellectual and practical virtue and in doctrines of truth and ecclesiastical laws.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sleep in peace as a death met in hope; the only comment on 4:8.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's inheritance is the rational nature.
comments.comment:
“Unto the end, concerning the inheriting one” (Psalm 5 inscription).

The inheritance of Christ is the rational nature.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The psalm is a prayer for an inheritance that cannot decay, the one the Savior calls the worthy to receive.
comments.comment: He prays for the soul being brought forward, that the church might be prepared for a divine inheritance for those who are healers of God; for inheritance belongs to those being healed by the Lord. But this inheritance is not corruptible and does not possess being in sensible wealth; for it is said that the heirs of this are to be brought into an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in the heavens (1 Peter 1:4). Into this, the Savior calls the worthy: 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you' (Matthew 25:34).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hears the prayers of the righteous because they are near to him, and he is King of those not ruled by sin.
comments.comment: As for 'To enlighten,' it is not used in a common way; in the Scripture, it constantly signifies receiving into the ears the words being announced by the speaker because of their nearness. It is said that the righteous are near to God, that God hearkens to the prayers of the righteous and has them in his heed for their supplication (Psalm 5:2-3). And God turns out to be a King and Creator of those who have not stretched out their hands toward a foreign god, nor are they ruled by sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what hearing the prayer means and why God is called King, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who sees the sun of righteousness rise confesses to the Lord in the morning, and his sight keeps growing.
comments.comment: According to theory, then: to whom the sun of righteousness has risen, having come into being at the beginning of an intelligible day, bringing a gift of grace to the cause of illumination. 'In the morning,' he says, 'hearkening to my voice' (Psalm 5:3); for to whom must one confess such a great good, O Lord, regarding the one who caused light to rise for me, existing as the greatest vision? For he always enters into the visions that are to be and desires to see the beauties of the truth. This is also presented from the 'And I shall see.' For just as 'I am coming' signifies unceasing approach, so 'I shall see' manifests an ever-increasing comprehension; for how can he who has obtained the promise not always see, 'The Lord shall be your eternal light, and Light to the righteous always' (Isaiah 60:19; Proverbs 13:9)?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The morning in the verse points to the time when Christ came as light, so that our prayers could be acceptable and we could stand before God.
comments.comment: Moreover, the lighting of the lamps in the morning would signify the time when he became man. For something like a day dawned, and a light perceived by the mind shone out, driving away the darkness of our ancient ignorance and scattering the mist that had fallen like night upon the hearts of all. So too the prophet called for the time of the Savior’s coming among us, when he said: ‘In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you, and I will keep watch’ (Psalm 5:3). For when would the prayers of all have become acceptable, and when would we who once wandered have stood, as it were, before God, through kinship with him (the spiritual kind, of course) and through obedience and faith, if the light from heaven, that is, Christ, had not shone upon us?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of the morning, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Evil does not come from God, who alone wills the good to be.
comments.comment: … evil is not from God, unlike those who make evil their very substance. For from the mouth of the Most High, evil shall not come out, nor the good alone. For He alone wills the good to be; it is impossible for evil to exist in any way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man is judged a liar by his intention, not by his voice alone, and likewise a man who sheds blood is not always a man of blood.
comments.comment:
One must judge the liar by his intention, but not by voice alone, lest those who once acted providentially like Rahab be under the threat; for it seemed to be lying to those searching to kill the spies, who were good men; but having been sent by Joshua son of Nun, they were praised. Since the intention of a man is very important, it is not appropriate to rank it among the being destroyed or among those speaking falsehood. Just as he who kills a man in a certain way is not a murderer, so likewise he who sheds blood is not always a man of that name …

And the deceitful is reasonably joined to this; for how is he who pours out the blood of men treacherously not loathsome to the Lord?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy temple is Christ, and in fear of the Lord the worshiper turns toward him.
comments.comment:
“I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear” (Psalm 5:8).

A holy temple of God is Christ, because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). In the fear of God everyone turns aside from evil (Proverbs 16:6); and in the fear of the Lord he worships the temple, which is Christ: for “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it” (John 2:19).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the temple means and why worship is directed toward it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The man who follows God's justice is led by God, the giver of virtue.
comments.comment: It must be examined how anyone is led by the justice of God. Lest perhaps he who progresses according to the justice of God (for that is genuine virtue) following God … is led by the one who provides virtue, namely, God himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies are the unseen ones who plot against the soul.
comments.comment:
“Lord, lead me in your righteousness, because of my enemies” (Psalm 5:9).

In the righteousness of practice, in Christ. — “Of my enemies.” The intelligible ones, clearly; for many are those who plot against the God-loving soul, begrudging its progress according to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the enemies are and what the prayer for leading asks.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The open tomb is a throat filled with dead works.
comments.comment:
“Because there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain” (Psalm 5:9). First, there is no truth except Christ; and perhaps the second clause has borne their plot.

“An opened tomb is their throat” (Psalm 5:9). Filled with dead works.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, clear meaning for the open tomb of the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God sends away only those who did not listen.
comments.comment: Concerning some it is said: 'God will cast them away, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Hosea 9:17). When they depart, they were led astray here and there, no longer having a firm purpose. And he assigns the cause to us: 'because they did not listen.' It is not God's will to cast anyone away from him. But it is his will to send away those who did not listen, so that he might not seem to hate virtue. And since they did not listen, 'according to the abundance of their lawlessness, cast them out, because they have turned aside from you, Lord' (Psalm 5:10). This is what it means to be led astray.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer asks God to thrust them not away from himself but out of their ungodliness, making them pious.
comments.comment:
“Judge them, God; cast them out from their counsels

For God does not thrust anyone out from himself; for “those who make themselves far from you,” he says, “will perish” (Psalm 73:27). Of the multitude of their ungodlinesses, then, thrust them out. For these, he says, they were making all the counsels against me, opposing my progress according to God; for those who persecute the soul that does what is dear to God embitter God, clearly fighting against God.

Thrust them out from the ungodliness, having made them pious. Blessedness is to fall out of every counsel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the harsh prayer as a prayer to remove ungodliness, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who hope in God rejoice forever because God lives in them as in his own temple.
comments.comment:
“And let all who hope on you be glad in you; they will exult forever, and you will tabernacle in them” (Psalm 5:11).

When the plotters have been dissolved, the gladness is of you tabernacling in them forever. And how is it not exultation, for the one to whom God is present, dwelling and walking as in his own temple (2 Corinthians 6:16)? As being far from God, when sin takes captive, is worthy of lamentations. And the end of the good things is to receive an inheritance and to have as a lot God dwelling in one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the joy lasts: God is present in those who hope in him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The joy lasts because God dwells in those who receive him.
comments.comment:
It is not short-lived nor temporary; rather, they will rejoice forever, because God dwells in them. For how could they not always rejoice when God is present, tabernacling as if in his own temple? For how could those who have God in themselves, dwelling and walking about, be near to joy, when the distance from God, caused by sin capturing them, is near to wails and lamentations?

The preceding words shall be said concerning the arrival of the Savior, the joy of all those waiting for his human appearance (Psalm 5:11); for the prophets and those who understand the prophecies hoped for this. For the Word of God arrived having become flesh to dwell in those believing in him; for he says, 'The Word became flesh and dwelt among us' (John 1:14). Thus, having dwelt, those who received him in themselves will rejoice forever …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Grace is a crown for our labors and fences us in like a weapon.
comments.comment:
“As with a weapon of good pleasure you crowned us” (Psalm 5:12).

A crown, he says, for us of the labors is grace, which — the end of these — as with a certain weapon fences us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cross is both a weapon and a crown.
comments.comment: The cross is both a weapon and a crown; a weapon for those warring, a crown for those conquering. And again: a weapon for the soldiers, a crown for those reigning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spiritual circumcision on the eighth day means casting every worldly thought out of the heart.
comments.comment: But he is contained in hymns having a more divine thought, and he himself is such; and he also sees toward the end the most perfect things regarding the eighth. It must be considered what the spiritual circumcision is, which one having God is circumcised, not necessarily one being circumcised according to the flesh. For the prophet says to those striving only according to the flesh: 'Be circumcised to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your uncircumcision' (Jeremiah 4:4); and the same prophet says: 'All Gentiles are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts' (Jeremiah 9:26). Therefore, he who is sensibly circumcised removes something of that which serves the generation of the member, just as he who casting out every thought friendly to the generation of the intellect circumcises the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eighth day stands for a state beyond the world, reached after the true Sabbath.
comments.comment: For circumcision is established on the eighth day; for the circumcised must overcome the world that was created in six days, and this is to become on the seventh day a true, holy, and sweet Sabbath. And since the ceasing from worldly things is not sufficient for perfect blessedness, it is necessary to receive, after the Sabbath, a super-cosmic state as the eighth. He who has been tempted by this desire will not love the world nor the things in it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Anger that disciplines can be a way of healing, and the one who endures it will be brought into the light.
comments.comment: He is reproved in anger, and his sins are not made manifest (Psalm 6:1); being led by Him according to a bitter and painful guidance, just as one who has fallen under the wraths of God, receiving the sensation of the cause of the evil having happened, is being disciplined in anger for suffering these things. … For if one, having been led into such a state, knows that the wrath has been brought upon him from God by a way of healing, he will not at all be unwilling to be subject to it, so that the judgment might be justified on account of Him who judges not thus.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wrath of God is not a passion in him but a means he uses to discipline sinners.
comments.comment: We do, then, speak of the wrath of God; but we say that it is not a passion of his. It is something employed to discipline, by sterner methods, those who have committed sins so many and of such a kind. That what is called the wrath of God, and what is named his anger, disciplines, and that this is the teaching of the Word, is clear from what is said in the sixth Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:1); and in Jeremiah: “Discipline us, Lord, but with judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few” (Jeremiah 10:24).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what God's anger means in the verse, with no ancient controversy needed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wrath is no substitute for a virtuous life, but one who deserves punishment is better rebuked by wrath, which comes before the punishing.
comments.comment: Having read the divine writings and having known how God is indignant against sinners and that he 'stirs up wrath' (Ps 7:11), which the holy man was entreating, saying: 'Do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger' (Psalm 6:1)—this wrath is not better than living with virtue; rather, if one is worthy to be punished, it is preferable for him to be rebuked through wrath or to be disciplined by that punishment. For he who is able to punish rages before the actual punishing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wrath and anger convict and discipline, and the speaker asks for a gentler healing that brings fewer labors.
comments.comment:
“Lord, do not convict me with your wrath, nor discipline me with your anger; have mercy on me, Lord, because I am weak; heal me, because my bones were troubled” (Psalm 6:2-3).

Wrath is an impulse of desire of a tame soul, pre-eminently of defense. He says then: even if the more outward wrath convicts, and the anger more quickly disciplines, I at least, because of my weakness, need your mercy, and to be convicted and disciplined by another healing, which does not bring on such great labors.

For he wants both not to be convicted by the wrath of God, and not to be disciplined in his anger, and to be shown mercy, being weak, and to be healed from the trouble of his bones and of his soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer of the first verses in clear terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Remembering God does not happen in death, for the one who remembers him is not in death.
comments.comment:
Those who imply that the upcoming words refer to common death err, but rather they act impiously. For the holy men do not have remembrance of God and the common life only then, but much more so, as they are separated from the corruptible body.

… For it is not said, 'He does not remember God in death' (Ps 6:5), but rather, 'He who remembers him is not in death,' as the Savior says, 'He who hears my word does not see death for eternity' (John 8:51).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever remembers the Life is not in death.
comments.comment:
“Because there is not in death the one who remembers you” (Psalm 6:5).

Everyone who remembers the Life, who said “I am the life” (John 11:25), is not in death.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, clear reading of the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The verse urges weeping during night prayer.
comments.comment:
“I will wash my bed every night” (Psalm 6:6).

An exhortation toward weeping in the night of one who is praying.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul is to be made new against its enemies, putting off the old man and putting on the new.
comments.comment:
Look if it is possible to be made new against all my enemies (Psalm 6:7) and to have another mind. He who lives with righteousness, always living in renewal according to the newness of the spirit and the new covenant; because, having departed from the praiseworthy life through our inattention, having become old according to the antiquity of that man, whom Paul advises to strip off (for his life is vain), that we may put on the new man created according to God in holiness and knowledge of the truth (Eph 4:22-24); such is the unblemished life.

You will understand that these things are said also regarding the invisible enemies and evil powers who have prepared a device against him, who are envious of his progress according to God …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He prays for his enemies to be ashamed, which will do them good.
comments.comment: He prays with good intention for the enemies; for he wants them to be ashamed because of what I do, since they became enemies of the righteous and of God. And this will be beneficial to them …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Demons work lawlessness always, men not always, and angels never.
comments.comment:
“Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled” (Psalm 6:10).

It belongs to demons to work lawlessness always, to men not always, to angels neither always nor not-always, which is never.

To fall from wicked counsels is not an evil for the one falling, who is not coming to their wicked end …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: David sings the psalm as practice while contemplating its meaning as theory.
comments.comment: He sings the psalm practically, while also bringing it forth theoretically. … These things being observed as an ode, it is fitting that David sings the present psalm practically while contemplating theoretically concerning each of the things being done wisely and very Godward, desiring to know what is signified by those things being accomplished in such a sensory way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father saves through the Son, who came to seek and save the lost, so the divinity of Father and Son must not be divided.
comments.comment: 'Who is it that said, Saving is not from me, he who has come to seek and to save the lost, and to give his soul as a ransom for many?' (Psalm 7:1-2). These signify that the Father God saves through the Son, the existing Word of God; therefore, even in the present matters, the divinity of Father and Son must not be divided, as some might suppose.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet calls down on himself the loss of glory and life if he is guilty, showing that seeking glory from men is forbidden in the old Scripture too.
comments.comment: Again, we say that laying claim to glory from men is forbidden not by the teaching of Jesus alone but also by the old Scripture. One of the prophets, at any rate, calling down a curse on himself if he should be guilty of those sins, says that worldly glory too would come upon him as the greatest of evils. He speaks thus: “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall away empty before my enemies; may the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and make my glory dwell in the dust” (Psalm 7:3–5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The empty man cannot say he received from Christ's fullness.
comments.comment:
“If I repaid those who repay me evils, then let me fall empty from my enemies” (Psalm 7:4).

Empty is the one who cannot say: “From his fullness we all received, and grace for grace” (John 1:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being overtaken means becoming earthy, not heavenly.
comments.comment:
“Let the enemy pursue my soul, and overtake it” (Psalm 7:5).

So that I might become earthy, instead of heavenly (1 Corinthians 15:47-49).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The enemies' ends are the pride in which they think themselves secure, and the prayer does not return evil for evil.
comments.comment:
'I beseech you, Lord, arising in wrath, appear high at the ends of the enemies; for the end of iniquity will consume those things through which my enemies occur.' (Psalm 7:6-9). It is possible to say the ends of the enemies are their arrogance and pride, upon which they have reached and consider themselves to be secure, thinking themselves to be in the best states. The prayer is not defensive; for he does not give back evil for evil.

When God, sparing the enemies who oppose Him, wishes them to know how God is exalted in their borders, He uses wrath not against their essence, but against the malicious intention they possess.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the prayer against the enemies is not a wish to repay evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations gathered around the judge are the church, and the judge then turns upward to the height.
comments.comment: When the judge arrives, he says, many nations surround him, gathered together (Psalm 7:7). He means the church, and he announces that the Lord says they will be gathered to him. When this happens, the judge will turn upward to the height, having handed over the kingdom.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who gathers around the judge and what his return on high means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's righteousness reaches to men in a lower form, and the speaker asks to be judged by it.
comments.comment: 'Bring Your judgment upon me only according to Your wickedness and my righteousness; for I shall be justified when no iniquity is found in my deeds.' Regarding 'wickedness' here, he says, one must not lack goodness according to what is written, 'The innocent believes all words,' but rather the simplicity that cleanses from deceit … In certain copies, 'Judge me, Lord, according to Your righteousness,' the word is to be explained thus: there is a righteousness of God reaching to men, being distributed toward a lower righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Human righteousness differs from the righteousness of God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
comments.comment: Paul, writing about the difference of these things concerning the Jews, says, 'For I testify to them that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; for knowing not the righteousness of God, but seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God' (Romans 10:2-3). By saying the righteousness of God, he means that which comes to all who believe through Jesus Christ, which He Himself also desired. He says all things were sent so that one might be found having the righteousness from God through faith and not his own. Wishing this to be present also for the disciples, Jesus says to them, 'If your righteousness does not exceed that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God measures human goodness to fit us, while the holy angels' goodness far exceeds our measure.
comments.comment: … they [those consecrated to God] must be pure and without blemish, at least as far as human nature allows. For somewhere the inspired David sings, and very wisely: ‘Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my innocence that is in me.’ (Psalm 7:8) For with God the standard of human goodness is in some way measured to fit us, while that of the holy angels plainly rises higher and far exceeds our measure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why David can ask to be judged by his own righteousness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: When the sinners' wickedness is completed, the righteous man is no longer warred upon.
comments.comment:
“Let the wickedness of sinners be completed, and you will direct the righteous” (Psalm 7:9).

If the wickedness of the sinners is completed, the righteous directs his own way, no longer being warred upon by them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wicked confess God with the mouth but not in the mind, while the speaker asks for just help so that he may have an upright heart.
comments.comment: They are called bodily. This is shown from many scriptures, one of which is: 'Near is their mouth, but far from their kidneys.' This is said concerning wicked men, who indeed confess that God exists by word, but do not have Him in their intellect. 'My help is just from God, who saves those upright in heart.' This teaches by power whether He saves those upright in heart. And I demand just help from Him, by which I shall be saved; that I may have an upright heart, free from all deceit …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's examining of hearts is perfect knowledge, and the kidneys are the mind's powers, not bodily organs.
comments.comment: 'To God belongs the examining and searching of hearts'; this does not signify merely seeking and tracing, but having a perfect apprehension; for He is a knower of hidden things, and every mind is revealed to Him. And one must not hear 'kidneys' as the bodily ones, but the intellectual powers of the soul …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what God's trying the hearts and reins means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God is a just judge, sin is to be feared, yet his power joins long-suffering to give time for repentance.
comments.comment:
If God is a just judge, it is to be feared to sin; for we approach the Word as a judge seeing the hidden and not being ignorant of anything being done. And just as a judge, so also He is just, bringing the judgment according to merit to those judged under Him. And a judge who is just and has power can without delay punish those stumbling.

If no one receives justice from the ungodly and sinning ones, through the long-suffering of the judge's goodness, there is an overcoming of the retribution … For He is good and does not bring wrath every single day, even though ungodliness and sins are happening constantly. But let us long-suffer not that we should persist in evil, but that we may have time and place for repentance; for He desires the repentance of the sinner so that he may live, rather than accepting death by persisting.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is powerful enough to punish at once but is long-suffering, and he whets his sword only for those who do not turn back.
comments.comment: God brings punishment upon men not as it happens by chance, but when He judges it beneficial to bring it upon them; for the Lord is a 'righteous judge, powerful and long-suffering, not bringing wrath on every single day; if they do not turn back, He will whet His sword' (Ps 7:11). Since God is a 'righteous judge,' how is it that sinning men do not fall under punishment and retribution? Is it because, through weakness, He 'did not bring it'? No; He is 'powerful' and was able to punish immediately, but with His power He is also 'long-suffering' and 'does not bring wrath on every single day' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's pairing of a just judge with long-suffering.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wrath is stored for the day of judgment for those who remain in wickedness, and the sword stands for punishment.
comments.comment:
However, even if he does not bring wrath on each day through exceeding goodness and patience, for those remaining in wickedness, wrath will be brought upon them in a day of wrath, that is, in a day of judgment. For if you do not turn back, he says, enjoying remaining in sin, he will make his sword shine (instead of being blunt).

And with it also his bow he will make ready, preparing in it instruments of death, having worked out the arrows of the punishments against those being burned from the fire of the sufferings. Often of the divine disciplines, the punishment is found being made manifest by the name of the sword. For that which is in Amos the prophet, 'All the sinners of the people shall be finished with the sword' (Amos 9:10), does not signify a physical knife …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sword and bow mean as God's discipline.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword in Scripture names the punishment coming on sinners, and if they turn, the sword itself opens the way to virtue.
comments.comment: It is being testified by many: 'By the sword' he says, 'all the people of the sinners shall perish' (Amos 9:10). And not everywhere do all perish by swords, but the name of the sword indicates the punishment that is about to be brought upon those who sin. And the saying 'You Ethiopians are wounded by my sword' (Zephaniah 2:12) presents the same thought … To this also is consistent that 'If you do not turn the sword, it will shine' (Psalm 7:12); and this sword, being turned, is said so that, having been turned from evil toward the virtue of the man, it might itself provide the entrance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword is a spiritual word that separates.
comments.comment:
“If you do not turn, he will make his sword flash” (Psalm 7:12).

The sword is intelligible, a spiritual word separating soul from body, or from vice, or from ignorance.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sword shines and the bow is ready, but the arrows of punishment are not yet released.
comments.comment: A sword, but it is shining. And the bow has been drawn and prepared to shoot the arrows of punishment, but it has not yet released the arrows, even though it has fashioned them and holds them ready to shoot. It can be said that instruments of death are prepared in a bow, those serving the punishments, often called instruments of wrath.
comments.selected_reason: Shows plainly that God's weapons are held ready but not yet used.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who burn are those who receive the devil's flaming arrows.
comments.comment:
“He prepared instruments of death, his arrows for those who are burning” (Psalm 7:14).

The burning are those who receive the flaming arrows of the devil (Ephesians 6:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who conceives pain brings forth injustice and first harms himself, for evil injures the one who shares in it.
comments.comment:
He who has labored in iniquity has conceived pain to give birth to injustice (Psalm 7:14-16). These are the offspring that the one who has conceived will bring forth in secret, he who is to be punished through iniquity and injustice which he did; and appropriately, he will seize both the pain in the punishment and the pain in the sinning. For the work of iniquity is most heavy and burdensome, compared to a talent of lead; for nothing is more inferior than evil, which always brings down the one who does it.

… And every one sinning first harms himself, if he harms others; for the evil thing is injurious and harmful, first of all to the one participating in it, harming and damaging him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of conceiving and bringing forth, as a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture often means wickedness by a pit, so blind teachers who lead others into it must be avoided.
comments.comment: Its wickedness is a pit. And often in the Scriptures, a pit is taken instead of wickedness, just as when the blind man leads the blind, both shall fall into a pit; and for this reason, blind teachers and students, who are under ignorance and other evils, must be avoided.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The crown stands for the mind.
comments.comment:
“And on his crown his injustice will come down” (Psalm 7:16).

The crown now signifies the mind, if the crown of grace, according to Solomon, which is wisdom, is bound to the crown (Proverbs 4:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
