comments.capsule: He confesses and sings according to God's righteousness to the Most High, whom only the one striving for piety approaches.
comments.comment: Having begun from hoping in the Lord his God, the Psalm settles into thanksgiving, as is fitting, having obtained the things requested or faithfully awaiting them; for 'I will confess' (Psalm 7:17) declares thanksgiving here; therefore 'I will sing' is joined to it. And he confesses not as if by chance, but according to the righteousness of God; and he sings not aimlessly, but to the name of the Lord the Most High, as he declares having called Him to himself. Therefore also it is high according to holiness and virtue; for no lowly person, but only the one striving for piety, partakes of the Most High's approach.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm ends in thanksgiving and what it means to sing to the Most High.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The winepresses are the churches, because many altars now stand through the whole earth instead of the one temple.
comments.comment:
“Unto the end, over the winepresses” (Psalm 8 inscription).

… Here “unto the end” is said because the things prophesied in the present psalm have come to pass at the completion of the ages; and “over the winepresses” because of the peoples constituted in all the earth, and the churches of God, which the word is accustomed to refer to winepresses allegorically.

Of old, then, when the people called Israel was one, this people was styled a vineyard. And the temple among them was a tower, and the altar before the temple was a fore-vat, according to the prophecy of Isaiah (Isaiah 5:1-2). But now the word mentions not one winepress but more winepresses, because of the many altars throughout the whole earth constituted through Christ in his churches.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The winepress and harvest stand for the gathering of human works and thoughts at the end.
comments.comment: The word uses winepress and harvest, as in the Gospel, to indicate the gathering of fruits at the consummation. The fruits are human works and thoughts, according to Isaiah, who says, 'I am coming to gather their works and their thoughts' (Isaiah 66:18) (Ps 8:1).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Life is the vineyard, whose fruit is brought into winepresses as the insights of truth and the works of the virtues.
comments.comment: For the life of every man is called a vineyard according to the Scriptures. … He who bears clusters of truth and brings forth grapes through such a vineyard. Since the offspring of the vineyard have a season for being plucked, it is fitting to reap them and bring them into winepresses, so that they might make wine pressing that gladdens the heart of man. And since the life turns out to be both practical and contemplative, the former are the insights of truth, and the latter the work, which is praised for bearing fruit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Each virtue has its own vintage, for the song is not for one vintage but for many.
comments.comment: Not merely fruits, but more; for the ode is not for a single vintage, but for many vintages. Again, since the practical virtues are many fruits, each will have its own particular vintage; some bear fruits upon the vintage of temperance, those who succeed in chastity and maintain a pure bed; others bear fruits upon the vintage of courage, which those are the farmers of; and concerning the other virtues, they speak of similar things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After the resurrection the name of the Lord is wonderful in all the earth because his majesty was lifted above the heavens.
comments.comment: … For it has much harmony with the resurrection day of the Lord, on which there has become a harvest of many vineyards, as the disciples of the Risen One are sent to make disciples of all nations and to testify to the Risen One to the ends of the earth, so that the proclamation of the Risen One may be spread everywhere, as it is immediately shown from the words of the psalm. 'Great is the name of the Lord in Israel' (Psalm 76:1), which was said in former times when Israel alone was holding to godliness; but now, the prophecy having been fulfilled, 'all nations shall serve him' (Psalm 72:11), (for he is the hope of the nations), 'Wonderful is your name become in all the earth' among those partaking of Christ's proclamation everywhere. For his name has been magnified over all, as it is carried in another psalm. And the cause of his name being wondered at throughout the earth is given in the following verse. For he says, 'Your majesty has been lifted up above the heavens,' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the name is wonderful in all the earth and what the lifted-up majesty means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christians everywhere are named by Christ's name, and his majesty, lifted above the heavens, is the salvation of the world.
comments.comment: Having been taken up, rising from the dead, the Christians of the whole earth are called by your designation, O Christ. The majesty of the Savior is being praised; the economy, which received its purpose for the salvation of the world, is above the heavens. … His majesty was lifted up above the heavens, having been made to sit at the right hand of Majesty in the high places after the cleansing of sins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David ascribes the praise of the children to the Lord, whose name has become wondrous in all the earth.
comments.comment: As our Savior Christ of all was going up to Jerusalem, children went before him, praising and saying: “Hosanna to the son of David.” The doxology is wholly God-befitting. The Pharisees were indignant and came saying: “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus said to them: “Yes; have you never read: From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise?” (Matthew 21:15–16) Here we must recall blessed David: “O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth, for your majesty is exalted above the heavens. From the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise.” (Psalm 8:1–2) The children praised, saying “Hosanna to the son of David,” and he accepts the doxology as one praised. Blessed David did not ascribe this to a common human, but rather to the Lord, whose name has become wondrous in all the earth; for the majesty too was exalted above the heavens.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the Gospel applies the verse to the children's praise of Jesus.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Infants are those perfected in understanding yet innocent of wickedness, and sucklings are those who still receive milk.
comments.comment: … The difference between infants and sucklings is shown from the word: those receiving milk are sucklings, while those having surpassed this age of infants are being called infants. It is appropriate, as the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians, 'I gave you milk, not food' (1 Cor 3:2). One must watch over this differently: the one being introduced, receiving milk, is a suckling; but the one having been perfected according to understanding, yet being an infant in wickedness, remains an infant. Such are all those having turned and having become like children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between infants and sucklings in the verse, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As enemy Satan forces us to sin, and as avenger he punishes those handed over to him.
comments.comment:
“Because of your enemies, to destroy enemy and avenger” (Psalm 8:2).

… As enemy, Satan forces us to sin; as avenger, he punishes those who are handed over. So Hymenaeus and Alexander, having himself made them blasphemers, he again disciplined, because of the blasphemies against God (1 Timothy 1:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the enemy and the avenger are with a plain Scripture example.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God cares for fallen, weak man, who was made a little lower than the angelic glory because of his earthly body.
comments.comment: But, he says, you, the maker of such great works, care for a human being who is altogether small, and you remembered him when he fell away from you, and you looked after him when he was brought down into weakness (Psalm 8:4). His creation was precious to you from the beginning, and he was made a little less than the angelic glory because of his earthly body.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of what the verse says about man's smallness and God's care.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God crowned man with glory and honor by making him in his image and giving him converse with himself, and the Son's coming adds to it.
comments.comment:
“You made him a little lower than angels; with glory and honor you crowned him” (Psalm 8:6).

… How the God of all crowned man with glory and honor, you will understand, because only of man it is written that God said: “Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness”; and God made the man; according to the image of God he made him (Genesis 1:27).

And he deemed him worthy of his own appearances, and to one clothed in flesh he imparted divine converse, then through angels, then also himself appearing through himself to the saints and giving oracles; and besides these he showed him a partaker of the Holy Spirit and of heavenly power, so as to foretell the future, and to heal all kinds of diseases, and already even to raise the dead; such things prophets and apostles are recorded to have done.

And if to all that was said you add the incarnate economy of the Only-begotten Son of God, you will see how it is said: “With glory and honor you crowned him,” namely, that you crowned man.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus, made a little lower than the angels, is crowned through death.
comments.comment: From here he brings in other words of the psalm. We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, being crowned with glory and honor through the suffering of death; for it was necessary for him, through whom all things and through whom all things, to lead many sons into glory, to perfect the leader of their salvation through sufferings (Hebrews 2:9-10).
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse to Jesus through the passage in Hebrews.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man was made a little lower than the angels but not less than them.
comments.comment: But most correctly he said, 'You made him a little lower than the angels,' but 'You have not made him less than the angels' (Ps 8:5). … But even if it has not happened in that way regarding him, he has nonetheless been crowned with surpassing honor and glory by you, because he has become according to your image and likeness, through which image and likeness you have exercised the rational being, having subjected all things to him as being under his feet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man's reign over the animals is by wisdom and mind, since he catches what escapes his hands.
comments.comment: For glory surrounded him as one reigning over the works on earth that you had made, holding all irrational nature under himself—not only the land creatures, easily caught, but also the creatures of the air and the water. Each of these escapes human hands, the one by its movement in the height, the other by its hiding in the deep and its passage through the waters, but they are caught by wisdom and mind, and the earthly man captures the things in heaven and in the waters. From these things it is clear that in his intellectual nature he surpasses the irrational and mindless nature of animals, and he is comparable to the intellectual and angelic nature, while sharing with the irrational animals in his bodily nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains man's dominion as the rule of mind over the animals.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Man ruled the beasts before the transgression, and the righteous rule them even after it.
comments.comment: … For before these transgressions, man ruled; and the righteous rule even after these transgressions, as Daniel, having been thrown into the den of lions and suffering no harm from any of them, and Paul, having shaken off the viper from his own hand upon the fire. For wild beasts, they say, shall make peace with you; and in addition to these, the beasts of the field are included, as we have learned in Genesis.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm ends with its opening words because the Spirit teaches that the beginning is the end.
comments.comment: It is fitting that the song spoken concerning the resurrection of the Savior should have a resemblance to the end at the beginning (Psalm 8:9); for beginning and ending use the same words, the Spirit teaching the beginning to be the end according to the subject.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm closes with its opening words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet confesses on behalf of human nature, giving his whole heart to God and recounting God's wonders to his hearers.
comments.comment:
“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders” (Psalm 9:1).

But others say the present psalm is sung to him, not about him, the prophet confessing on behalf of human nature, saying that it is proper to the perfect to dedicate the whole heart to God: “For you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Deuteronomy 6:5).

And what “with my whole heart” now indicates, and what he does: having foreseen the things to come with prophetic eyes, he recounts them, making the hearers partners of the confession, having as joy the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), and recounting the wonders of God with lifted-up contemplations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what confessing with the whole heart means in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sitting on the throne means he is judge, and the impious shall perish in their ways so that it no longer profits them.
comments.comment: … Such a sitting signifies him as a judge, but not that a certain seat has been established. Stand firm, if there is room to say, that after the nations have been rebuked, the impious shall perish in the manner of their ways, so as to no longer profit them. And this shall happen, the previously spoken thing being fulfilled thus: 'The way of the ungodly shall perish' (Psalm 1:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations were rebuked through the teaching of the apostles, and the ungodly perished as their worship died out.
comments.comment:
“You rebuked nations, and the ungodly perished; you wiped out their name to the age of the age” (Psalm 9:5).

On behalf of tyrannized human nature you laid so bitter a punishment on him. You rebuked the nations, that is, handing over to them the divine teachings through the apostles and the subsequent teachers; when they received them, the ungodly perished, no longer having those who worship according to error.

Thus also Paul and Barnabas rebuked the Lycaonians who were trying to sacrifice, saying: “Men, why do you do these things? We too are men of like passions with you, turning you from these vain things” (Acts 14:15). And Paul rebuked the Galatians: “O foolish Galatians, who bewitched you, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was portrayed as crucified among you?” (Galatians 3:1). Thus to the Corinthians: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such as is not even named among the nations” (1 Corinthians 5:1).

His name, then, was wiped out to the age. For every rite of those now men and ignorant of the mysteries of piety has been quenched, so much also as: “The way of the ungodly will perish” (Psalm 1:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The enemy's cities are the false teachings and vices, which the Savior pulls down when he arrives.
comments.comment: … But the aggressions of the enemy are, in a sense, the heretical teachings and the vices according to appearance, which some have left as if they could no longer contend super-abundantly as cities, and they themselves shall be destroyed; for cities are collections of people standing together and being governed unlawfully. For it has been written concerning the one establishing them as 'building cities in vain and preparing cities in iniquity'. For their substance is wrongdoing and the shedding of blood of those being scandalized. The Savior, having arrived, pulls these down, pulling down the enemy who wishes to rule tyrannically, having been as it were cities.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cities made dust may be Jerusalem, ruined after the Savior was crucified in it.
comments.comment: … may it be, Lord, that what you have made cities into dust, a city of the ungodly, shall never be built for ever. Stand firm, if it signifies the raised ruin of Jerusalem, of the Savior having been crucified in it, of its citizens being the remainder of the ungodly because of the killing of the Lord (Psalm 9:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God showed his power in this life and will show his fearful tribunal in the life to come.
comments.comment:
“And the Lord remains forever; he prepared his throne in judgment” (Psalm 9:8).

Not only in the present life did he show his own power, but also in the coming one he will show his fearful tribunal to all men, judging and assigning to each what is according to desert.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the Lord's throne of judgment means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The inhabited world is the church, and those who have blameworthy deeds and an ungodly mind must fear such a judge.
comments.comment:
“And he himself will judge the inhabited world in righteousness; he will judge peoples in uprightness” (Psalm 9:9).

You will understand the inhabited world as the church, inhabited by both Father and Son, according to: “I and my Father will come, and we will make a dwelling with him” (John 14:23). And peoples as the rest besides the church, or those from circumcision. For as many as sinned in the law will be judged through the law, while the lawless who sinned perish lawlessly (Romans 2:12). Therefore those who have blameworthy deeds and an ungodly mind must fear such a judge.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The petition God did not forget came through lamentations and dirges.
comments.comment:
“He did not forget the petition of the poor” (Psalm 9:12).

What sort was it? The one that came about through lamentations and dirges, having a kind of request concerning the terrible things that hold them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gates of death are the vices that lead down to Hades.
comments.comment:
“The one who lifts me from the gates of death” (Psalm 9:13).

So that the gates of Hades might not prevail against him either, which are the vices that lead down to the bottom of Hades (Matthew 16:18).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gates of death mean the sins that lead to destruction, and the gates of Zion mean good deeds.
comments.comment: … And again it is said in the ninth psalm: “You who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Psalm 9:13–14). By “gates of death” the text means the sins that lead to destruction, just as, on the other hand, by “the gates of Zion” it means good deeds.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'gates of death' and 'gates of Zion' in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To be raised from the gates of death is to come to the gates of blessed life, with excellent deeds and entries into good works.
comments.comment: … And to each of the righteous is a similar voice, by which they say: 'He who raises me from the gates of death' (Psalm 9:13). Of what death, indeed, is this, or the one that consumes the soul from blessed life? For this one, having been raised from the gates of death, comes to the gates of blessed life beyond, bringing forth: 'that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion' (Psalm 9:14). These are indeed excellent deeds and entries into good works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Awareness of one's evils leads to the prayer to be lifted from the gates of death, whose opposite is the praiseworthy deeds of the gates of the daughter of Zion.
comments.comment:
The awareness of one's own evils and the knowledge of God's goodness leads to the prayer, 'Have mercy on me and see the humiliation that has come upon me from my enemies' (Psalm 9:13). For they humiliated me by dragging me down; but You alone are able to lift me up from the gates of death through a goodness that is always present.

Regarding the daughters of Zion, those participating in this must hear in harmony with being called sons of light, peace, and wisdom. The gates of the daughter of Zion, being opposite the gates of death, are praiseworthy deeds and contemplations of God's virtue and wisdom to be fulfilled.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Vice is the opposite of virtue, which is called incorruption, and so it is called corruption and decay.
comments.comment:
“Nations were stuck in the corruption they made; in this snare which they hid, their foot was caught” (Psalm 9:15).

And indeed, against virtue, which is called incorruption, as in: “Grace be with those who love our Lord in incorruption” (Ephesians 6:24), the vice that is oppositely disposed would reasonably be called corruption and decay. It has been said, then: “If anyone corrupts, God will corrupt this one” (1 Corinthians 3:17). And in the prophet: “Because of uncleanness they have been corrupted with corruption.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Corruption means evil, and those who practise it fall into the very thing they practised, for each one dies by his own sin.
comments.comment: Concerning the incorruptible virtue, it is said: 'The grace is with those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption' (Ephesians 6:24), while the opposite, evil, will be called corruption and destruction. It is shown that corruption is called evil from the saying, 'If anyone destroys the temple of God' (1 Cor 3:17) … The word says that the mortals have fallen into that in which they practiced corruption (Ps 7:15). For no one else is seized by another's impiety and sin; for each one dies by his own sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked who prepare snares for the unsuspecting are punished by that very snare, which is God's judgment.
comments.comment: And since the wicked, having first harmed themselves and others through deceit, attempt to bring the same harm by trial, they secretly prepare snares in their treacherous wisdoms and words to catch the unsuspecting. By that very snare they are punished. For they render justice and through those whom they deceived. And to suffer thus becomes a judgment of the provident God; for how is it not His judgment that, in His works, He seizes the sinner who has used the pretext of acting wickedly to be condemned from without? … This is consistent with what was said a little earlier: 'He who digs a pit will fall into it' (Ps 7:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly how the wicked are caught in the snare they hid, and why that is God's judgment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man comes to know the Lord through his judgments.
comments.comment:
“The Lord is known as he makes judgments” (Psalm 9:16).

There is a time when man, guided also from the judgments, comes to know the Lord.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the hymn begins after the interlude, with 'Let the sinners be turned away', the words 'Hymn of the interlude' are placed between the psalm's two parts.
comments.comment: Since 'Let the sinners be turned away' follows the interlude, the name of the hymn is entwined with the interlude. For if the whole psalm is called a hymn, the preface of the hymn was always arranged in a way and with a power before it, as is demonstrated for many psalms. But since it is not so here, and since the beginning is taken after the interlude, it is fitting that 'Hymn of the interlude' be placed in between.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sinners are turned back into Hades so that they might see Jesus' soul descending and ascending.
comments.comment:
“Let sinners be turned back into Hades, all the nations that forget God” (Psalm 9:18).

Sinners are turned back into Hades, so that they might see Jesus' soul descending and ascending; those who expected it were looking as it were outside, first the sinners in us, then the nations.

Why did the nations forget the Lord? For forgetfulness is second to knowledge; therefore from this also is clear: “I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all true; How did you turn into bitterness, the alien vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners and mortals are not men only but also fleshless powers, and the poor man who is impoverished through sin is not forgotten by God.
comments.comment:
Interpreting who the sinners are, he brought forward that the things being forgotten are mortal things of God. But sinners and mortals must be understood not as men only, but also as fleshless powers. For if the sinner does not signify essence, but rather what kind of voice the sinner is—a nickname not from the sin itself—then everyone participating in sin would not be called thus. Appropriately to these things, the mortals will also be called. Just as one who is not locally in heaven, but walking upon the earth, is able to possess citizenship and thought there, so also one not dwelling locally in the abyss is able to bear signs of death and of sinning himself, as if he dwells in the abyss, even though he is among those in the life after the body.

And he is called poor, the one impoverishing through sin, and the moderate and the foolish, and the one needing to receive from God; and such a one is born wretched. According to all these ways, the one called poor is remembered by God. For through something advantageous, some forgetfulness of him might occur, but it does not remain entirely so, and for this reason he will not be forgotten unto the end. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The human race asks the Lord to come down so that the proud 'man' set against it may not be strengthened for long.
comments.comment: The human race does not bring the words of its pride as an embassy to the Savior, saying, 'Arise, O Lord, descend to us, so that the human who is proud against us may not be strengthened for long.' For the devil says that 'man' is not a mortal rational animal, but that they have fallen away from divinity just as those to whom God said, 'I am; you are gods and all are sons of the Most High, but you, as men, die' (Ps 82:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Let not man prevail' may be said of the devil, who is called a man and an enemy in the parable of the tares.
comments.comment:
… Ps 9:20: 'You, Lord, make those who stagger and those who faint fall from the lofty height, opposing the proud; let them not then be strong, but let them be judged before you; for a surpassing benefit will spring forth for them.'

Let it be interpreted that 'Let man not be strong' as it was said concerning the devil, and it is said in the parable of the tares as being an enemy of man, but also in the prophecy: 'Not man is the one provoking the earth.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God stands far from sinners because he discerns their sin, though he is always present; the afflicted righteous seem abandoned while the proud increase.
comments.comment:
The prophet asks like a man and inquires of God, saying, 'Why, Lord, have you stood far off?' (Psalm 10:1). If the Word responds to him, what is the good of God for the repentance of sinners? For God has stood far from the sinners, His presence discerning the sin itself and driving the sinners far away according to what has been said: 'Your sins divide you between me and you' (Ps 83:15). Otherwise, God is always present to all and happens to fill all things everywhere. Therefore it has been said in the prophecies: 'I am a God approaching,' says the Lord, 'and not a God from afar.'

But for the righteous who are afflicted in the present life and oppressed by the ungodly, he says, 'As if standing far off, you abandon them, O Lord, and look down from above' (Psalm 10:1). Consequently, the pride of the ungodly increases, while He burns your poor and wretched one, the God-fearing man, who zealously desires and inwardly burns the soul with zeal.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner who praises himself in his own desires provokes the Lord and stores up wrath, yet God's goodness means it will not be searched out in full on the day of judgment.
comments.comment:
And especially those who are deprived of divine wealth and wisdom and are not precise concerning the doctrines of piety; for they do not stumble upon judgments praising the sinner for that which he desires, it being manifest that the sinner reaches out not for the heretical but for the pleasant and the passionate. Along with these, they consider wealth and human, fleeting glory to be a blessing from the same error, asserting that the wrongdoers are blessed by God; but it is necessary to examine how the blessing of God is given to the righteous. … But he does not very much rage against the proud one having stumbled and, if it is said according to the scripture, having set fire to the poor man because of the bad use of the things that were to him by God's providence. For this is shown from the following words: for it is said, 'The sinner provoked the Lord.' And the one provoking is the impious one, praising himself according to his own desires. And he provoked the Lord to such an extent as for the anger to become stretched out, that he himself has stored up for himself according to what was said, 'According to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you store up for yourself wrath in a day of wrath' (Romans 2:5).

However, even if much wrath has been stored up by him, nevertheless there will not be a search according to the abundance and greatness of it on the day of judgment because of the goodness of the judging God. For if a search according to the abundance of the wrath were to happen, the wicked would immediately be lost. Having seen this very thing, they say, regarding the goodness being shown: 'If iniquity is observed, Lord, Lord, who will endure?' (Psalm 130:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner provokes the Lord by turning away from him, as Cain did, and much more the devil, whose ways are defiled at all times and who denies God's providence and judgment.
comments.comment:
The pretext for the sinner provoking the Lord is not having him before the eyes and in the presence, since he has turned away from God. For every one sinning does this; therefore God says concerning every such one, 'They turned their backs on me, and not faces' (Psalm 130:3).

Cain, having become the father of this impiety, 'Went out from the presence of the Lord God, having turned away from him' (Gen 4:16) clearly. If these things are said concerning sinful men, much more concerning the devil, having provoked God and not having him before him. For especially the following words are said concerning him: 'His ways are defiled at all times' (Psalm 10:5). For whose ways are defiled at all times, except of the impious, habitually performing many, many things? And he walks impiously, not only in single acts seizing men, but also defining unprovidence.

Indeed, he has persuaded many to dogmatize the unprotected world, having first himself fallen from the right opinion concerning God's administration and judgment. This is shown from what is said to God concerning him, 'Your judgments are overthrown from his face; he shall lord it over all his enemies' (Psalm 10:5), not as if he were going to do this always, but because this very thing is set forth …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil rules only those who practice sin, not the holy patriarchs, prophets and apostles, who set their feet on his authority.
comments.comment: He will be Lord over all his enemies. For especially his enemies are those perfect in holiness in whom no one rules. But he rules over only those practicing sin; for it is said, 'Everyone practicing sin is a slave to sin.' And the slave of sin is ruled over by the devil, who has worked sin in him. And according to the insatiable nature of his wickedness, what follows is brought forth: 'For if indeed,' he says, 'I shall never be shaken from generation to generation by evil' (Psalm 10:6). The word reveals his arrogance and impudence. By this voice, one having understood will interpret regarding only those humans who have become his enemies, to say that he will rule over all his enemies. For if indeed from generation to generation one has never been shaken in heart by evil, it is evident that the saying refers only to humans having the 'being' in succession. But even this is not entirely true; for he did not rule over the holy patriarchs, prophets, and apostles; rather, they themselves stretched this authority under the feet of Jesus.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His mouth is full of curses, bitterness and deceit, for his word itself is harmful.
comments.comment: He, having fallen away from his holiness, truth, and blessing, leading himself far away, has a mouth full of curses, through which he says, testing, making a punishment and a curse upon those being deceived. And his word has much wickedness along with the harm; therefore, along with the curse and bitterness and deceit, his word is full, being called his mouth. And since he brings forth none of these things to harm and destroy under his tongue, but the word itself is harmful, pain and toil exist; for nothing is gentle or kind, but if he brings in toil and pain, he brings it forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous bless the Lord always, but the sinner lies in ambush.
comments.comment:
“Whose mouth is full of cursing…” (Psalm 10:7).

“He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places” (Psalm 10:8).

The righteous blesses the Lord at every time, but the sinner sits in ambush.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He chooses rich men who seem wise in word, sits with them, and hides so as to kill the innocent.
comments.comment: Setting before himself harm and destruction through all things, he chooses men appearing to be rich in word (having false knowledge), and sitting with them, he tries to hide so as to remain unknown, to kill the innocent by wounding him with his burning arrows (Psalm 10:8-11); … with the stichoi we bring forward 'To kill the innocent in secret.' For the 'in secret' part causes doubt, being divided in two ways, as we have previously noted by stichoi: 'He sits in the seat with the rich in secret' (Psalm 10:8), followed by 'to kill the innocent.' However, even if he sits in a seat with the aforementioned rich, intending to look and to kill the innocent, it is necessary to oversee that no one of the God-wise may be able to wound one clothed in the panoply of God; for he, obeying the command to turn his eyes toward the poor man, has him captured, the same one acting toward the poor man being scorched by the impiety of the ungodly's pride.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like a lion looking about for prey, the sinner devises seizure and greed by night and day, but he will stoop and fall.
comments.comment:
“He lies in wait in secret, as a lion in his fold; he lies in wait to seize the poor, to seize the poor in drawing him in his snare; he will humble him, he will stoop, and he will fall in his dominating the poor” (Psalm 10:9-10).

Just as the lion transfers the eye here and there, seeking prey, so night and day he devises a device of seizure and greed; but nevertheless he will stoop, and he will fall. He draws through reasoning, but seizes through sin in act.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lion image of the verse in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like a fierce lion he snatches the poor man with deceptive words and deeds, while hiding love of money under talk of stewardship.
comments.comment: He sits in secret, a fierce lion in his den, to snatch the poor man through deceptive words (and indeed also through deeds), and he will drag him after snatching him into his trap in order to devour him. For he is a fierce beast, rather even a lion. Often indeed, sitting in a seat and seemingly speaking about stewardship, he conceals the matter concerning love of money. As one speaking about temperance, he proposes a manner of intemperance, just as the serpent deceived Eve in the paradise through the transgression of the commandment, setting up equality, and likewise Judas through love of money. The 'looking down' written there shows that, having turned the eye downward, he fell; for how could he not direct his gaze downward, he who rejects Providence, by saying 'God has forgotten' and the following things? (Psalm 10:11)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord knows of the poor.
comments.comment:
“Do not forget the poor” (Psalm 10:12).

If the Lord had forgotten the poor, the Lord knew of the poor.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even if the sinner reasons this ten thousand times, God sees.
comments.comment:
“For he said in his heart: He will not seek” (Psalm 10:13).

But even if he should reason these things ten thousand times, you see; for this is to be understood.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The poor man is not abandoned: God lets him be afflicted a while so that he may willingly place himself in God's hands, and then makes him rich with good things from heaven.
comments.comment: Being able immediately to humble the proud one who tyrannizes those being shaken by his audacity, for what is the use, being able to help them, if you allow them a certain time to be afflicted, during which you understood not only the pain upon him and through him? And this has happened, so that those who have benefited through the timely affliction may willingly deliver themselves into your hands, having a remaining desire to be disciplined and to be ruled by you. To you, then, the poor man is not abandoned; you will manage the things concerning his salvation, so that you may make him rich by providing good things from heaven. So also he helps the orphan, presiding over and rearing him into the rank of a son.  …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The arm is the soul that has worked wickedness, and breaking it makes the sins vanish, which is a benefit.
comments.comment:
“Shatter the arm of the sinner and the wicked” (Psalm 10:15).

A sinner is the one who sins from pleasure-loving and licentiousness; a wicked one is the one who is voluntarily an evildoer. And he said “arm” of the soul that has worked wickedness. The shattering of the arm makes the sins vanish; and to be delivered from sins is a benefit of someone’s arm being shattered; thus I also am persuaded that God punishes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the shattered arm means and why God's punishment is a benefit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Evil is not found when sought because it is not an essence but has being only through choice.
comments.comment: 'Crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked, his sin shall be sought; and it shall not be found through itself' (Psalm 10:15). For because it is unsubstantial, it is not found; for evil is not an essence, but has being having been produced in choice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil's arm is broken and his sin, when sought, is not found, since evil is a quality and not a substance.
comments.comment:
But who is the sinner and evil, as spoken of with the article, the devil? His arm is broken by the Lord, and his sin, being sought, is not found, having found its end in its fulfillment. For evil is not a certain substance but a quality, and thus the end will be established over all things, not because all other things have become so; for he himself is nothing, as there is no end to his kingdom. For one cannot be under two lords and kings. The one who ruled and reigned was the sin of the one doing it; God is not the lord or king of the one sinning. And since the sin that was ruling the one acting it was sought, it was not found, the Lord reigns forever and unto the age of ages.

It is said of the good heart of the earth of God (Psalm 10:16). … From this earth mortals perish, if every vain thought and evil purpose is cast out; for vain thoughts and purposes are mortal, being destroyed by the blessing of God. But if someone wishes to signify even the land of the gentle (for it also belongs to the Lord), mortals perish from this earth. For no one sinning is permitted to ascend into it; for only the saints shall inherit it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord must reign until he has heard the desire of the poor, which he does when he grants the soul its desired thing.
comments.comment:
“The Lord reigns forever and to the age of the age; you nations shall perish from his land. The Lord heard the desire of the poor” (Psalm 10:16-17).

For the Lord must reign through the ages, until the Lord heard the desire of the poor, until he put all the enemies as a footstool of his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25).

For his kingdom is the contemplation of all the ages that have come to be and that will come to be; through which contemplation the enemies also become friends. And the land of the Lord is the contemplation of the ages that have come to be. And the kingdom, we say, is this: the Lord then hearkens to the desire, whenever he grants the desired thing to the soul that has desired.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord hears the desire of the poor, paying attention to the readiness of their ruling principle.
comments.comment: Because the desire of the sinful and evil man is worn away at the arm, it is fitting that it is revealed to God, who oversees hearts and knows the hidden thing, as an active prayer. But the Lord heard them, paying attention with his ear to the readiness of their ruling principle; for how would the heart not be ready toward salvation, those having desire for the things foretold? (Psalm 10:17).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who tyrannizes cannot magnify himself while he is crushed under the feet of the saints.
comments.comment: In this way, the man must be caught out, either by boasting toward the mortal rational animal, or toward the one saying, 'I will seize the world with my hand, and no one shall escape me or answer me, the deceiver.' For he will not magnify himself while being crushed under the feet of the saints who tread upon his power, Jesus, this one having granted.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul is urged to be like a sparrow, with the wings of virtue, so as to pass over the high mountains and remain unharmed among spiritual things.
comments.comment:
And it should be read also thus: 'In the Lord I have trusted'; how do you say to my soul, 'Behold, the sinners have bent a bow, they have prepared arrows in a quiver,' and the following? (Ps 10:1-2). Upon these spoken things, the soul is urged to be poised like a sparrow with the wings of virtue, so that having passed over the high mountains, it might remain harmless among the spiritual things. And how one should bear the distinctions of the reading, it is fitting to trust in the Lord. (Ps 10:1-2).

According to theory: as if the ruling principle were held ready against many sophistically prepared visible and invisible enemies, resembling a bow drawn in readiness, and also arrows prepared, and persuasive words are used; in order that you might shoot down the enemy, you have a passage through high mountains, and having occurred there, you will not be harmed. It is said that the more divine meanings of the Scriptures are signified by the correspondence of the things seen; toward these, also the wise teachers, apostles, and prophets. It is possible through the Spirit to grasp the saying, 'Repent, go to the mountains like a sparrow,' exhorting one to withdraw, desiring to run from the venomous strike of the archers.  …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The archers are sons of darkness, and the righteous Lord will lay snares on the sinners and give them a cup of punishment.
comments.comment: Since the archers prepared to sophistize are sons of darkness and of night, those having a straight heart set themselves to shoot in the clear night. … The Lord is righteous; what will he do? Will he lay snares upon the sinners and divide to them a cup of punishment, so that while drinking them they become weak from the impulse to shoot?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eyes of the Lord look upon the poor, so we should become poor; God's dwelling in heaven is not a limited place, and his eyelids are his critical providence.
comments.comment:
“His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men” (Psalm 11:4; LXX 10:4).

If the eyes of the Lord look upon the poor, let us become poor, so that the eyes of the Lord may look upon us. And if the rich are not poor, the eyes of the Lord do not look upon the rich.

But when you hear from holy Scripture that God is in the heavens, and sojourns, or is more inward than the veil, do not understand certain limits and local dwellings, and changes, and goings-up, and goings-out; for, our nature being poor-fitting, as it is able to hear, the Holy Spirit converses with it.  …

And eyelids you will understand as his critical providence, also examining of affairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the eyes and the eyelids of the Lord mean and how to read God being in heaven.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord has his throne in heaven, and his watchful powers are his eyes while his eyelids examine men's actions and thoughts, which shows the kindness of the Judge.
comments.comment:
In His holy temple and He has the throne in heaven, reigning divinely and supernaturally. We also noted that previously the throne was taken instead of the kingdom.

But the watchful ones and the powers of God, called His eyes, become toward the sufferer, guarding him harmless from those appointed around him. The eyelids of the eyes of God examine the actions and the thoughts of men. From this, the philanthropy of the Judge is shown. For if He examined with eyes and not with eyelids, the judgment would be unendurable to men. But His examining with His own eyelids does not mean all the sins of those judged are observed, nor do these exist in magnitude.

It is also possible to say: His eyes are upon the one being benefited, if a sufferer exists, but the eyelids are upon the sons; many men's sons, if the benefits are abundantly and boldly accomplished, but the punishments hide much concerning God. And these things he will say by thought; they show no perceptible eyelid or anything of that kind, therefore these things must be thought of in a God-befitting way. Christ is not to be revealed on a step; all must be brought to each one what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who hates injustice loves his own soul.
comments.comment:
“And the one who loves injustice hates his own soul” (Psalm 11:5; LXX 10:5).

If the one who loves injustice hates his own soul, the one who hates injustice, clearly, loves his own soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who does evil makes himself subject to punishment, while the one who loves his soul and his neighbor strives toward virtue.
comments.comment:
… Having said this, under the Lord's examination being done of the righteous and the ungodly, he brings it as if he hates his own soul, the one doing evil without hating it as injustice, making it subject to punishment because of sinning; he acts contrary to the one acting justly.

He who loves his soul and his neighbor as himself strives toward virtue. The Lord does not fight, but examines the righteous and the impious by the fact that the impious do not stand up in judgment. For the former signifies those who are entirely atheistic, while the latter signifies those who despise God because of sinning. For the Scriptures declare this, especially that which says, 'The righteous shall be like the impious' in Genesis.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cup names punishment, mixed with vice and ignorance.
comments.comment:
“Fire and brimstone and a storm-wind, the portion of their cup” (Psalm 11:6; LXX 10:6).

Cup now names punishment, in which a drink of vice and ignorance has been mixed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the cup of the verse stands for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God lays snares on sinners by delivering them up to the desires of their hearts, and the cup of the verse means painful recompense, as in Isaiah and Jeremiah.
comments.comment:
He will lay snares upon sinners, that is, he will punish them by making snares and by keeping those being hunted within them, unless they are delivered up by him to the desires of their own hearts; this is also declared by the sufferings of dishonor and an unproven mind. And therefore, if not for this, it is said 'He will lay snares' rather than 'He will rain snares'; for those having been ensnared by themselves are being rained upon with snares. This is also declared from 'The Lord will lead those turning into straits with those working iniquity.'

You will apply to the latter the recompenses, as it is written in Proverbs: 'God sends toward crooked, crooked ways.' Regarding the former recompense, you will punish by sending crooked ways to those who have become crooked through wickedness; but regarding the latter, the recompenses are those being delivered up, which are shown through the sufferings of dishonor and those being reproached. 'Fire and sulfur and a spirit of tempest are the portion of their cup.'

The painful recompenses are often declared in the Scripture by the name of the cup, as in Isaiah: 'Arise, arise, Jerusalem, pouring out the cup of downfall, the bowl of your fury,' and the following; but also in Jeremiah the same is presented from the sound of that voice: 'Take the cup of the wrath of my uncontrolled anger from my hand, and you shall make all the nations drink it, whom I have sent against you.' Does not this also signify the punishment in the things set forth by the portion of the cup divided to them, especially what the fullness of this cup is: 'Fire and sulfur and a spirit of tempest'? The things written in Genesis are not symbols, if they are the punishments having come upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord; toward this fire and sulfur and spirit of tempest is the watering of the cup. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The storm indicates a storm of temptation, so we should flee impiety that the cup of wrath may be far from us.
comments.comment: … Along with these, the Spirit indicates a turning of some kind of storm of temptation. And as to what kind of temptation the storm indicates, it is clearly to be learned from that which is written in Isaiah: 'As a storm passing through the desert, coming near, its appearance is fearful and its hardness was announced to me.' Let us therefore flee from impiety, so that this cup may be far from us, and let us live in piety, so that we may drink the intoxicating cup as strongest; for perhaps even that is said: 'The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is just in essence, he watches over the poor, and he sees the straightness in those who have it.
comments.comment: For the Lord is just and loved justice, and straightness is his face. For this reason, he watches his eyes over the poor for his salvation, but also upon the sinners he sends snares. For it does not happen by chance, if it becomes of the providence and the judgment of God; for the Lord is just in essence, not merely in participation of justice. Moreover, even if he does not have it by nature, he does not love the justices that are in the many righteous, accepting the intention of each. It is also possible to say another way that he loves justices; since there is justice in the judgment of each, and the judgments of God are many, about which it is written: 'The judgments of the Lord are true and justified'; on the same basis, it is necessary that many justices also exist. And as he is just, so also seeing straightness; and straightness you say is the opinion being regulated toward the right reason; he sees this rejoicing in those who have it. It may also be said regarding straightness in harmony with the second thought concerning the justiceses existing in his unsearchable judgments, which he sees because of the utterly accepting of his face; for God appears present in the works of providence and in the results of the judgments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the gift of truth is in danger of being extinguished, the holy have failed, and the scarcity of the holy may be the cause of many heresies.
comments.comment:
“Save me, Lord, because a holy one has failed, because the truths have been diminished from humanity.

Because the gift of the truth is in danger of being extinguished, the holy ones have failed, and the truths have been diminished; the truths are not in the holy ones only, and holiness is also in those who are true.

Or because the holy ones have failed, for this reason the truths have been diminished; and perhaps the scarcity of the holy ones has become the cause of the many heresies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the failing of the holy one and of the truths means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fullness of human deceit and wickedness creates the need for the Savior's arrival to destroy the harm.
comments.comment: As the fullness of the deceit and wickedness of humanity, as if there were no mercy and truth and knowledge of God on the earth, there has become a need for the arrival of the Savior toward us, for the destruction of the existing harm (Psalm 12:1; LXX 11:1). To this end that which is in Jeremiah shall take place: 'Each will play with his neighbor, they will not speak truth; their tongue has learned to speak lies' (Jeremiah 9:5). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The deceitful use and boastful speech of the lips are the trouble, and the impious man who prospers says to the Lord that he does not wish to know his ways.
comments.comment: … For it is not necessary to consider the members of the body being destroyed, but their deceitful use and their boastful speech; for even in Proverbs it is said: 'Remove from yourself a crooked mouth and long deceitful lips from you' (Proverbs 4:24). Our lips are with us; who is our master? From this audacity the impious man, prospering in finding what he desires, utters a voice like that in Job (Job 21:14-15): 'Depart from me, I do not wish to know your ways; what is sufficient, what shall we serve him?' For indeed they do not think the prosperity coming to them is due to anything, saying to the Lord: 'Depart; do not make your ways manifest to me; for I do not wish to know them; for what more is of us sufficient, that we may serve you?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tongue often stands for the word.
comments.comment: … Often you will find the tongue used instead of the word. As if he says, 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the great-sounding tongue' (Psalm 12:3), he calls the word 'great-sounding'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord arises because of the misery of the poor, and a second reading takes the poor to be those who groan humbled while he arises by his resurrection to give salvation to all.
comments.comment:
“From the misery of the poor, and from the groaning of the needy, I will now arise, says the Lord; I will place in salvation, I will speak freely in him” (Psalm 12:5).

If from the misery of the poor I will now arise, he says, says the Lord, who has not feared the Lord arising? And: “Arise, Lord my God, be exalted”? Let us pray away such an exaltation, and not wish to see a hand being lifted against the disobedient, still more being sent upon the harder ones. And he did not forget the cry of the needy, and the poor will not be forgotten to the end.

Or also thus: the poor through me and having become needy by your spirit, always groan being humbled, attending to my word, and preserving unswerving faith; for whose sake I will arise, and according to what is fitting, by my resurrection I will place salvation for all men.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord arises at his visitation to release the poor and needy from suffering and groaning, as Jesus Christ rescued the wretched one from the body of death.
comments.comment: Regarding the impious ones thinking much of themselves as having a boastful tongue and deceitful lips, the poor suffer and the needy groan, not bearing their tyranny (Psalm 12:5). Therefore the Lord says: 'I will arise now, having placed my counsel in salvation; I will speak boldly in it against those swelling up proudly of the lowly; and I will release the poor and the needy from suffering and groaning.' You say 'the poor' and in this also 'the needy' to exhort themselves through the weakness coming to them or through the wickedness leading to such a state. Indeed, they have not become superior to suffering and groaning, because the Lord, at the time of the visitation, has arisen and has come to us so that the salvation of those who have suffered and groaned might be made manifest. It is indeed appropriate to hear the following: 'I am a wretched man; who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24). Upon which, speaking boldly thereafter, he says: 'I thank God through Jesus Christ.' For it is shown through these things how Jesus Christ, who rescued the wretched one from the body of death, is the one who said: 'I will arise now,' says the Lord. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor man is one made poor as the Savior was, and 'placed' in salvation shows being made into apostles and bishops.
comments.comment:
It is not to be the case that the poor man is not being turned away from necessity. And perhaps what has been said concerning the poor man will be constructed as an argument, for it is said in the Scripture, 'The rich became poor,' and 'We became very poor'; in agreement with these, what was said concerning the Savior will also be taken: 'As He became rich through our poverty, so that we might become rich through His poverty.'

This also agrees with that concerning the needy: the groaning of the needy, always being in distress and wailing because of the hardship of approaching the destitute. 'I will come' in salvation declares 'I will limit and I will make,' just as He also in the Being placed Himself as heir of all things, the word declaring He limited and manifested Himself as heir. Toward these things, God placed first the apostles and the following in the church, and what was said toward the presbyters of the church: 'The Holy Spirit has placed you to shepherd the church as bishops.' For the word 'placed' shows the demonstration of being limited and made into apostles and bishops.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pure words of the Lord are signified by silver, as the divine teachings and the word often are.
comments.comment: … Often, the divine teachings and the word are signified by this name: 'The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace, tested, cleansed in the earth seven times' (Ps 12:6). And again, it is said proverbially: 'The tongue of the righteous is like refined silver' (Prov 10:20). For the word is signified by the name of the tongue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord keeps us as the Savior kept his disciples, and the one praying first guards his own heart, then prays that the Lord will guard and preserve us.
comments.comment:
According to this meaning of preserving, the Savior also said to the Father concerning the disciples: 'Holy Father, keep them; though I am not with them, I kept them, and the evil one did not touch them' (John 17:11). But if this is the meaning because of what was said in Genesis concerning Adam to the serpent: 'He shall guard your head, and you shall guard his heel,' is not 'to guard' (φυλάσαι) and 'to keep' (τηρεῖν) the same thing here? For it appears from it: 'He shall guard your head,' and 'you, his heel.'

The one who is praying sends back the prayer: 'You, Lord, will guard us,' after having done all things from Himself, according to the exhortation saying, 'Keep your heart with all vigilance.' And since these things being made right are not sufficient for the things we strive for against the unforeseen (for if the Lord does not guard a city, in vain the one guarding it stays awake Ps 127:1), it is a rule to bring forward a prayer after we have been guarded by ourselves, saying, 'You, Lord, will guard us and will preserve us.'  …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ungodly walk in a circle, while the pious walk a straight path, so the Lord keeps us from those circling around us.
comments.comment:
“You, Lord, will keep us, and you will preserve us … The ungodly walk in a circle” (Psalm 12:7).

Since the circle is opposite to the straight according to crookedness and straightness, and the ungodly walk in a circle, the pious then walk a straight path. Therefore he says: You will keep us, because circling around us, the ungodly, plotting against our salvation, and these would be opposing powers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'circle' and the keeping in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The end is the fruit of the labors, eternal life and the kingdom of the heavens for those who contend genuinely; David contended and sent up the psalm unto the end.
comments.comment:
“Unto the end, a psalm to David.” …

Because of the end, the one with God, he contended manfully in all the things before the end; and the end is the fruit of the labors, procuring eternal life and the kingdom of the heavens for those who genuinely contend.

Since then David also was one of these, he sent up the psalm and the ode to God unto the end. But at the beginning, as if still contending, he put forth the first utterances.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's forgetting means that a sinner escapes his notice, and his turning away his face means he does not look on shameful deeds.
comments.comment:
“How long, Lord, will you forget me unto the end? How long will you turn your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1).

… Teaching that forgetfulness has fallen from the memory of God at a certain time (for God makes forgetfulness of those who escape his notice; and everyone who sins escapes his notice); but also since he turns his own face from those who do something shameful, unworthily of his eyes, that is of his contemplative and overseeing power …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: These words were written so that we, too, can use them as saving medicines of the soul when we need repentance and confession.
comments.comment:
“How long shall I set counsels in my soul, pains in my heart day and night?” (Psalm 13:2).

… Instead of which Symmachus interpreted saying: “Care in my mind by day.” And these things, he says, were written for our admonition, so that we too, with the mindset of the one who has said these things, if there should be need of repentance and confession for some things not rightly done by us, might use the same methods, as it were saving medicines of the soul, timely using the present words of confession.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The petition is for the light from the knowledge of God, not for sensible light, and the true light is the eyes of the heart, the noetic powers.
comments.comment:
Even if these things are spoken by the Holy Spirit in the manner of an embassy, they are not spoken by one subject to the oblivion of God, but by one receiving all things of the petition into himself; and it is clear that the things of his petition are not concerning a sensible light or sleep and death, but concerning the light from the knowledge of God.

For 'enlighten yourselves with the light of knowledge, and draw near to the Lord and be enlightened.' This enlightenment becomes not concerning the sight of the flesh (for this is the sight of the sun) nor any other sensible light of those seeing the sun of righteousness; it is the true light of the eyes of the heart, not of the body, for the noetic powers are the eyes of the inner man. To the one being enlightened, there is blessed life. 'For I am the light of the world,' says the Lord; 'he who walks in me,' he says, 'shall not remain in darkness but shall have the light of life' (John 8:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eyes of the inner man are lightened by keeping the divine commandments, not the eyes of the body.
comments.comment: The outer man has eyes, and the inner is said to have eyes: Lighten my eyes, lest I sleep unto death. He is not speaking about these eyes, nor about perceptible sleep, nor about the common death. The commandment of the Lord is bright, lighting the eyes. It is not that by keeping the Lord's commandments we become sharper-sighted according to the body, but that by keeping the divine commandments we become sharper-sighted according to the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lightened eyes and sleep of death in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who sleeps into death is the one in the darkness of ignorance, so we must flee that sleep so that the enemy cannot prevail.
comments.comment: When death comes to the one having been enlightened, it is his sleeping into death, while the one sleeping and dying is the one being in the darkness of ignorance. For he who has given up his eyes to sleep through negligence and laziness will immediately die, falling away from the life which is with virtue; therefore, one must flee from this so-called sleep and death, so that, the eyes of the soul having been enlightened, the enemy may no longer be able to prevail against him, he who formerly thought that we had sinned. (Psalm 13:3-4)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When enemies rejoice at a stumbling, we should be grieved for those who fall and look to God's salvation, in which the heart rejoices.
comments.comment: Since the enemies, those who afflict the righteous, rejoice (Psalm 13:4-5); if it happens that a stumbling occurs because of sin, it is necessary to be grieved for those falling; but even if they rejoice at someone being shaken, I, O Lord, pity my hope in you, and I will not be persuaded to see in myself the cause. For I await your salvation coming soon, on which my heart rejoices; for how can he not be glad and rejoice who is experiencing the experience of God's salvation? And if prophecy is being declared concerning the coming of the salvation of God, the Christ, visit. For he, having come for the salvation of the world, brought down those who were leaning upon the shaking ones according to the soul, casting down with them the enemy who was exalting himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the psalmist has been made upright, the gift is a victorious song, which we sing by contemplation and by practical energy.
comments.comment: He has loftily enlightened the eyes, so that no one might see the death of the soul. He, having come to visit and having looked upon, ceased the pain; but when the psalmist has been made upright, the blessed gift is a victorious song, saying: 'I will sing to the Lord who has done good to me, and I will sing to the name of the Lord Most High' (Psalm 13:6). Having truly learned what is said well by the Lord toward those who pray, while He is still speaking to you, I will say: 'Behold, I am here.' And He says these things to those who are present. Having happened to experience what I requested, therefore, through each goodness occurring to us, let us hymn, and let us also say the set hymn, not by contemplation alone but also by singing; for contemplation signifies the seeing, and singing signifies practical energy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord found no worker of goodness, and it is perhaps the very completion of a worthless thought that corrupts.
comments.comment:
“They corrupted, and became abominable in practices” (Psalm 14:1; LXX 13:1).

Coming, says the Lord, I did not find even one worker of goodness, but liable to every out-of-place deed. If they are corrupted in the practices, then perhaps it is not the worthless thought that corrupts, but the very completion of this thought.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The foolish man lacks not common concepts but the companionship of the virtues and wisdom, and he says in his own heart that there is no God.
comments.comment: The foolish one lacks not common concepts, but the companionship of skill, rather the one of the virtues, wisdom, concerning which it is written: 'He who acquires wisdom loves himself, and he who guards wisdom will find good things' (Proverbs 19:8). But what is the natural companionship? The word declares, as if he is not obeying anyone but says in his own heart, 'There is no God' (Psalm 14:1). For no one received the words concerning the denial of God. Almost all men, having an unswerving thought concerning God, the first verse has much familiarity, as has been said concerning the devil. For even he is not to anyone, but 'In his own mind': 'I will ascend to heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my throne; I will be like the Most High' (Isaiah 14:13-14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever sins does not know God, and among those who corrupt their duties no one doing goodness is found, since goodness is cut off by hardness of heart.
comments.comment:
But as he who knows God keeps His word and turns His commandments into work, not so does everyone sinning, who comes to this by not knowing God; for John writes, that everyone sinning is far from having the knowledge of God, that everyone sinning has not seen Him nor known Him (1 John 3:6). … Having space for it, one possesses virtues. But if the intellect is weak, it would be clear if it were to happen from the writings concerning the sons of Eli (1 Sam 2); for they, not knowing the Lord, proven plagues, were sinning, but rather they were impious regarding the priestly service, corrupting the duties of both the law and godliness.

The following will be taken and what is announced in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 9:3) likewise: Offspring upon offspring, deceit upon deceit; all are committing adultery, a gathering of those breaking covenants, what has come out from evil into evil; but 'me he did not fear,' says the Lord. For how will it not be that, having ignorance of God, they are transgressors of his laws? These things being considered generally, it persuades that one has God in memory, so that we may be praised in duties, pursuing them with incorruptible intention.

Among those who have been defiled by corrupting the duties, no one doing goodness is found; for all are wicked, all goodness having been cut off because of hardness of heart (Psalm 14:1-3). As wisdom will not enter into a craftily-made soul, nor does it dwell in a body guilty of sin, likewise he who works lawlessness does not receive divine knowledge; for no one sinning sees or knows God, according to that which is written in the Epistle of John (1 John). But he who desires to be a knower sows into righteousness, reaps the fruit of life, and will thus enlighten himself with the light of knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All have turned aside through the flesh and the easily led mind, so God sent his Son from heaven to save and to enlighten.
comments.comment: … For the flesh that comes from the earth has already fallen sick with the law of sin within it (Romans 7:23), and the human mind is very easily led astray, so that it turns aside toward evil from youth, as it is written (Genesis 8:21). That is why the sacred word rightly grieves over us: ‘For all,’ it says, ‘have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.’ (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:12) But since there was no turning away from evil, God the Father sent us his own Son from heaven as Savior and Redeemer, to justify by faith and set free from punishment, to make the feeble very strong, to enlighten what was darkened, to turn back what was wandering, and to draw out from the devil's greed what lay prostrate beneath him. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why all have turned aside, and God's answer in sending his Son, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: After Adam's transgression all on the earth corrupted their way and were punished, though human nature was being trained toward the knowledge of good.
comments.comment: … We must, then, open out more fully the way this sacred teaching works. David said, accordingly, “All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there was none who did good, there was not even one” (Psalm 14:3). For after the transgression in Adam all who were on the earth had corrupted their way (Genesis 6:12). That is why they were punished: all of them together underwent a common penalty, the flood, and they were also punished in particular ways, at certain times and in certain lands and cities. For even though there was no law, human nature was still being trained by God, through its inborn impulses, toward the knowledge of what is good. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The enemies of God's people are workers of lawlessness who are deprived of the knowledge of God, and if they devour his people they will suffer judgment for it.
comments.comment: And since the enemies of the people of God are workers of lawlessness, as if to devour him, they are deprived of the knowledge of God; and someone, preferring to devour and harm him, acts according to: 'Bite each other and devour each other; see that you are not consumed by one another' (Galatians 5:15). And in Isaiah (Isaiah 9:12) it is written likewise: 'Syria from the rising of the sun and the Greeks from the setting of the sun, devouring Israel with a maw of mouth.' But if ever they are able to devour the people of God delivered to them, they shall suffer judgment through sin; for Holy Israel belongs to the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who eat God's people did not call on the Lord, thinking to tyrannize by their own power.
comments.comment: Those about to eat the people of God unjustly did not call upon the Lord, thinking to carry out all things by their own power and to tyrannize the people of God. For if they had known that they received him through the judgment of God by sin, they would have feared even more, lest they should fall under the same judgment. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is in a generation of the righteous, meaning their harmony in righteous deeds, since where two or three are gathered the Lord is present.
comments.comment: 'Since God is in the generation of the righteous,' you will say, 'a generation of the righteous,' meaning the harmony of the righteous deeds in which the righteous judge is found, or the concord of righteous men and the commonality toward the same end. For if where two or three gather at his assembly, the Lord is found present, how much more would a whole generation of the righteous be found?  …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the generation of the righteous' means, with the Lord present where two or three gather.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord became poor so that we might become rich.
comments.comment:
“You shamed the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope” (Psalm 14:6; LXX 13:6).

For on our account the Lord became poor, being rich, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The captivity is that of the one who falls by laziness under the power of sin, and the Lord redeems him by repentance, so that Jacob, the mind that overcomes the passions, rejoices.
comments.comment:
… But as for the captivity of the people, it must first be viewed, so that we may subsequently see its return. He who falls away through his own laziness from the doing of good is taken captive by the law of sin, so as to have the power of death under the tyrannically devouring devil. This one, having been found having surrendered to the enemies outside the fatherland (and this is the partaking of virtue), is called back.

The Lord is submissive to the manner of repentance and to the forgiveness of those who have previously sinned; and this is the redeeming of the captives and the turning back of the captivity. When this has been fulfilled by the Lord's cross, as the people believing from the nations have been redeemed, Jacob rejoices. The same, according to the underlying meaning, is Jacob through thought alone, discerning the difference. For if one, doing good things and working according to virtue, overcomes the passions and evils and the working evil powers as a conqueror of them, he is Jacob rejoicing; but if, after the practical life, having obtained a pure heart, he sees God, he is Israel, a mind seeing God. For he does not receive into the voice of the Greeks a divine joy, being rejoiced; no one is grieved to take from a parallel passage the 'Let him rejoice and let him be glad' to be said.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who lived by the law dwells as a sojourner in the tabernacle, but the one who has hastened to Christ dwells in the holy spirit of God.
comments.comment: See if the one living according to the law, having become the pedagogue unto Christ, dwells as a sojourner in the tabernacle of the Lord, wandering around the tent of the testimony.
