But the one having hastened unto Christ, having adhered to the evangelical teaching, dwells in the holy spirit of God, not another, but of the Son of God, concerning which it was prophetically said: 'The light of the Lord shall appear.' Stand firm, if it be rightly understood: the holy light of God is the God the Word, and his tabernacle is what the man took up. And it is necessary to know beforehand according to the flesh Christ, if he is the only-begotten according to the Father. He who says, 'Even if we have known according to the flesh Christ, but now we know no longer,' who has seen his glory, the glory as the only-begotten from the Father, dwells in the tabernacle, no longer a sojourner but dwelling in the holy spirit of God. And to him it is said: 'Ascend upon a high light,' he who evangelizes Zion.  …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blameless do not reproach those nearest them.
comments.comment:
“And he did not take reproach against those nearest him” (Psalm 15:3; LXX 14:3).

The one living blamelessly does not take reproach against those nearest him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who does not accept reproach from those near him is indifferent to those who always reproach others.
comments.comment: He does not accept reproach from those approaching him, those who always reproach those who have evils approaching them as if they were praising their neighbors and having good friends. To this, the speaker is indifferent: 'Walking in an unblemished way, it did not work for my benefit; speaking righteousness, it did not direct itself before my eyes' (Psalm 101:6-7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: An oath is a word with God's witness, and the apostle used it without pretension, as a pattern.
comments.comment: And the word of an oath of a man is unsearchable, upon which the 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' are confirmed. If even at times there is a need for God to be a witness to the word toward the 'No', he does this unpretentiously, just as the prophetic apostle leaves behind a pattern and a guide in the Epistles, who says: 'God is my witness, whom I serve in the gospel of his Son' (Romans 1:9); and 'No': 'I call God as witness upon my soul' (2 Corinthians 1:23); and again: 'God, who is over all, is my witness, I do not lie' (2 Corinthians 11:31). For this is an ungraspable faith; for an oath is nothing other than a word with God's witness, a thing being confirmed by God's witness. And however an oath may be held, it does not invalidate an oath to a neighbor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Usury keeps a person from dwelling on the holy mountain.
comments.comment:
“His silver he did not give on interest” (Psalm 15:5; LXX 14:5).

This is to be said to the usurers, as something that prevents tabernacling on the holy mountain. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To lend without interest is spiritual: those who sow spiritual things receive only food, not silver according to the value of what they give.
comments.comment: And it is also to lend spiritually without offspring, as it is signified by what was said to the disciples of Jesus by the Teacher: 'And do not turn away from the one who wishes to borrow from you' (Matthew 5:42). For how could anyone say this perceptibly to those saying, 'We have left all and followed you' (Matthew 19:27), or those saying with boldness, 'Silver and gold I do not have' (Acts 3:6)? Since, therefore, to lend perceptibly to the saints (whenever it is said they do this) is described, it is necessary to take this spiritually; the one lending must take the intelligible teaching word instead of silver for the sake of gaining something corporeal. For if even those sowing spiritual things receive the fleshly things only to be fed (for worthy is the laborer of his food Luke 10:7), they do not lend in this way; for they do not receive silver according to the value of the logical spiritual things given, but the only food.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who hears the words of Jesus and does them remains unshakeable forever, founded on Christ.
comments.comment:
And he shall not be shaken forever, because he remained through life having steeled himself in virtues (Psalm 15:5; LXX 14:5ab). For this is the same as what is said here: 'I shall not eat meat forever,' and 'He shall be your slave forever.' He who has heard the words of Jesus and has done them remains unshakeable forever.

For he possesses the houses of his own citizenship, which are named as those having their foundations laid upon Christ, called a rock. They are not as firm as those concerning whom Jesus says, 'Whoever believes in me shall live forever' (John 11:25). There are some such as are standing; and what the apostle writes concerning them: 'Having been founded and rooted in love' (Ephesians 3:17). If that which is not to be shaken for eternity shows a greater endurance of an age, similarly examine the one said: 'And everyone who lives and believes in me shall live forever' (John 11:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly why the one who does these things will never be moved.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever has kept the whole way of life according to God, complete in words and deeds, will never be shaken.
comments.comment:
“The one who does these things will not be shaken forever.”

Eusebius: The one who has succeeded in all the things previously enumerated together, having become complete, and having kept the whole way of life according to God whole, as it were sound and furnished with all good things of words and of deeds — will not be shaken forever.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The saints who remain unshakeable for ever have a pillar of victory, and the psalm's 'pillar-writing' stands for the lasting life of the saints, whose teaching is written on hearts.
comments.comment: The saints, remaining unshakeable for eternity, will perfect their life, not being limited by time but remaining always; and this is a symbol of their pillar of victory (Psalm 16:1; LXX 15:1a). And this 'pillar-writing' of David is a prefiguration of the psalm to be set forth. For the deeds of those being destroyed and no longer existing do not turn out to be such; nor do the deeds of sinners have the quality of not remaining. For it is said that the enjoyment of sin is temporary, and that the sin of the sinner and the evil one will not be found. But the life of the saints is not such; for they look toward the things not seen and eternal. It is said, therefore, concerning each of them: 'His righteousness remains for the age of ages.' And since it is called a pillar in another way, as scriptures elsewhere lay down laws calling them tablets and boards, it should be called a 'pillar-writing' of the saints, who have handed down teachings written not on stone tablets but on fleshly tablets, that is, having ears and hearts favorable and well-receiving toward the writing. How he possesses the things of the prefiguration of the psalm, we shall see when God reveals it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title marks the psalm as an inscription, a trophy set up for the Savior's victory over death.
comments.comment: They likewise issued the inscription, as it contained prophecy deserving of eternal remembrance. Just as victorious athletes in stadium contests are awarded pillars, and triumphant warriors erect trophies for later remembrance, so too the great trophy of the Savior—erected after he overthrew the holder of death’s power—was established from above through prophetic writings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalm's title signifies, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He prays for protection against countless enemies, then says 'The Lord is my Lord', which only one who serves God and not sin can say, by deed and disposition.
comments.comment: Since I have put my hope in you, O Lord, protect me (Psalm 16:1; LXX 15:1b). For I will not be able to endure harmlessly, with myriads of enemies both visible and invisible attacking. Having prayed these things, he brought forth: 'The Lord is my Lord' (Ps 16:2). Who, sinning, is able to confirm this with his voice? For a slave who makes himself a sinner cannot serve God; for no one, he says, can serve two masters (Matt 6:24). Let it be said also in another way regarding the matter at hand. The apostle writes: 'No one can say, Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit' (1 Cor 12:3), meaning to say this by deed and disposition.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to call the Lord 'my Lord'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Saying 'Lord' is true only for the one who says it in diligent work and true disposition, and God receives our gifts only so as to give back far greater ones.
comments.comment:
Therefore, the one saying 'Lord Jesus' in the Holy Spirit, not in mere utterance but in diligent work and true disposition, is truly a servant, just as when you hear with the apostles, 'You call me Lord and Teacher, and you say well, for I am so.'

Thus, the one announcing the foregone things by a practical and contemplative life has established an unshakeable pillar crying out, 'If you are my Lord' (Psalm 16:2; LXX 15:2). And since you turn out to be my Lord, I offer you gifts from your own dogmas, not as to one in need; for they, as not having need of our good things, receive them in order to grant back something far more excessive and greater.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God accepts our virtues so as to give us higher things, and his holy ones on earth have their citizenship in the heavenly Jerusalem.
comments.comment: For we perform virtues, as we manage our own bodies through complete temperance. We are what God accepts, not for our own benefit, but as those who ask him to give us the good things from heaven; for for whose grace does God seek human virtue, if not so that he might grant higher things instead of those which we offer to him? The holy ones of God dwell upon his earth (Psalm 16:3; LXX 15:3a). And this heavenly Jerusalem is that in which they have a citizenship in heaven, even as they dwell on earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm does not forbid gathering assemblies or remembering names, but says they are gathered out of immortality and not out of blood, and remembered with deep insight.
comments.comment:
He never says 'not to gather their assemblies,' but 'out of blood' (Psalm 16:4; LXX 15:4bc); nor does he say 'not to remember their names,' but 'through my lips' (Psalm 16:4; LXX 15:4bc). Perhaps, when there are some gathering assemblies out of blood, pouring them out to harm those gathered, he is himself benefiting, rather vivifying those who are called, gathering them not out of blood but out of immortality, remembering their characteristics, not out of superficiality but having depth of disposition. It will also be said thus: even if many prophets and apostles were killed, their blood being poured out, it is not in these many blood-offerings that the truth lies.

I will gather the assemblies of them, but only into the one single eye of the spotless and unblemished Christ; for this honor is given, so that they might be liberated from their vain, ancestral conduct. Concerning those who have been thus liberated, he will remember not by word alone, but by deep insight.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Assemblies from the nations are gathered through praise and bloodless sacrifice, not through blood, and former names like idolater are no longer remembered.
comments.comment:
“I will not gather their assemblies from bloods, nor will I remember their names through my lips” (Psalm 16:4; LXX 15:4).

Gathering, he says, assemblies from the nations, I will not gather them through bloods, nor will I prepare them to come forward to me through the legal worship, but rather through praise and the bloodless sacrifice.

Formerly, he says, they were brought to appellations according to the worth of their deeds, being named idolaters, polytheists; but now I will no longer remember those names, calling them pious and holy, called and elect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's wording about blood and names in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The new worship has no blood, and we are now called children of God.
comments.comment: He speaks of the manner of the new worship of God, the one without blood, and he shows the change that is in the Holy Spirit, according to which we are no longer what we were before, nor do we bear the same names—no longer children of men but children of God (Psalm 16:4; LXX 15:4).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one who has given up everything has God as his only portion, and God is also a cup that gives the mind joy through the light of knowledge.
comments.comment: He who has become above all the world possesses no other portion and inheritance than God; for everyone must renounce all things, so that one might be able to say, 'My portion is God unto the age of ages.' … It is worth observing how the Lord becomes a cup for someone. Never does he provide moral instruction and thereby nourish the man in secret, becoming bread, supporting the heart of the eater; but he is also a cup according to the theory of truth, providing joy to the one drinking through the agreement of the illumination of knowledge. This cup is provided by the true vine so that the mind might be made to drink and be made glad …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'portion' and 'cup' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is the one through whom the good things given at the beginning are restored to us and made certain, as in 'you are the one restoring my inheritance to me'.
comments.comment: Who then is it that through whom the recapitulation of all things concerning us has become from God and the Father? It is evident that it is Christ, which also follows us to say, as through the lyre of the singer, "The Lord is a part of my inheritance and of my cup; you are the one restoring my inheritance to me" (Ps 16:5); for through him we have had the repetition of those good things granted in the beginning according to nature, and the certainty into possession.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The measuring line falling 'among the best' means that good things of the spiritual inheritance were divided to him, as the cord is a sign of measure and lot, like the land divided under Joshua.
comments.comment:
Regarding this spiritual inheritance, given by analogy to faith and excellent life to the heirs, it is fitting that the measuring line fell upon me among the best; for the cord is a symbol of measure and lot.

Indeed, concerning the sensible earth, into which the Hebrews were led by Joshua the son of Nun, being divided, it has been written many times … Having observed these things, he who says, 'The measuring line fell upon me among the best,' demonstrates that good things were distributed to him, having entered into the best parts of the inheritance, which his lot shows through these spiritual geometric cords.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'lines' as a measuring cord and lot, using the division of the land.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The inheritance called 'most strong' is truly the most beautiful, like the true Jerusalem an angel measures.
comments.comment: [Of the measuring line in the verse:] Such a measuring line an angel holds in his hand to the prophet Zechariah, in order to measure how much the length and width of the true Jerusalem is. Furthermore, it is said: 'For indeed my inheritance is most strong for me,' (Psalm 16:6) signifying through this that my inheritance truly becomes the most beautiful.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verses are said from Christ's person, and God's right hand is not to be taken as a place, since then the Father would also be at the Son's right hand.
comments.comment: Since the following are said from the face of Christ (Psalm 16:8; LXX 15:8), and the saying—the face from the Lord is my portion of inheritance (Psalm 16:8; LXX 15:8)—is preserved without any change, whoever takes these verses spoken by the Lord does not sin. But those not having their thoughts about God properly ordered take them locally: that the Son is at the right hand of the Father because of 'Sitting at my right hands,' and that the Savior has sat after the ascension at the right hands of majesty, which is impossible to say. For if the Son is at the right hand of the Father locally, it is impossible for the Father to be at the right hand of the Son according to that same meaning; but the Son says: 'I saw the Lord at my right hand' (Ps 16:8). Therefore, it is not otherwise, according to place, to miss the Son at the right of the Father and the Father of the Son, just as 'I am in the Father and the Father in me' (John 14:10) is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who guards virtue can say he has set the Lord always before him, for God is with the man who is with God and draws near to the one who draws near.
comments.comment: For of the one guarding virtue and being in it, this is appropriate, as to say: 'I have set the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken' (Ps 16:8), and 'But I am with you always' (Mt 28:20). And of the man being with God, and God being with him: it has been said: 'Draw near to God and he will draw near to you' (Jas 4:8); but when some turn away from him, they hear: 'They went astray from me, and I will go to them in angry wrath' (Leviticus 26:28).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verses are spoken humanly by the Word made flesh, who has God at his right hand and is not shaken by bitter things, and whose heart rejoices from understanding and not chance.
comments.comment: If these things are impossible (for the body does not see God, nor does it possess the thought of him who is at the right hand and before him), it remains, according to the economy [the Word's becoming flesh], to speak these things humanly by the Word of God having become flesh truly, perfectly, and truthfully; for he will speak all things from one person, both the God-befitting and the human, as a man indeed has become, having the God at his right hand, he will not be shaken even if bitter things surround him, or if the kings of the earth stand against him and the rulers gather together against the Lord and against his Christ. For indeed, not having been shaken in soul, he did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, having been tested in all things according to likeness without sin. Furthermore, it is brought forward how his heart rejoiced and his tongue exulted (Psalm 16:9) over having the Lord at the right hand and before himself always. It is a praiseworthy exultation and gladness, he who does not become so because of chance things, but because of understanding.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who speaks these verses and why he is not shaken.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Tongue means the Spirit's gift.
comments.comment:
“And my tongue rejoiced” (Psalm 16:9; LXX 15:9).

By tongue he now means the gift of the Spirit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's soul and flesh both remained unharmed through his death in the tomb, so that his soul was not left in Hades and his flesh did not see corruption.
comments.comment: From these syllables, it is most clearly shown that the Lord became man; for his soul, the flesh having been laid in the tomb, was in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, having risen with the flesh, having severed the soul from the body. It is said that the flesh tabernacled in hope because of the resurrection that is to come; for it was not dissolved, suffering any corruption, but having remained unharmed, it was joined again to the soul which was not abandoned to Hades. … Even if it seemed to have suffered because of the cross, it was not destroyed; the fact that both soul and flesh remained unharmed, having been joined together again, was demonstrated. Again, the holiness of God has not seen corruption, but is also the cause of the resurrection of the others, the dead …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Peter explained that David, knowing God's oath about the Christ, spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, who was not abandoned in Hades and whose flesh saw no decay.
comments.comment: Peter, recalling this within himself, added: 'Brothers, it is permitted to speak openly with you about the patriarch David, that he both died and was buried, and his tomb remains among us to this day. As a prophet who knew God had sworn an oath to him—that from the fruit of his loins He would raise up according to the flesh the Christ to sit on his throne—having foreseen this, he spoke concerning the resurrection of the Christ, that he was neither abandoned in Hades nor did his flesh see decay. This Jesus God raised up, of whom we all are witnesses.'
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the apostle Peter applied the verse to the resurrection of Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: After rising from the dead, the incarnate Word is shown the paths to eternal life and filled with perfect joy, which he gives to the saints.
comments.comment: The incarnate Word of God, having risen from the dead, sings praises (Psalm 16:11; LXX 15:11), in that he has become man without abandoning even his being as God, having revealed to him the paths leading to eternal life, so that he may be filled with perfect joy, filling the saints with all spiritual joy. … And what follows the one who has walked the known paths of life, to have divine delight in the truth and wisdom of God's right hand? And this is the only-begotten Son of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'path of life' and 'fulness of joy' as fulfilled in the risen Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David prayed that his judgment come from God's face and that his eyes see straightness, which shows he did not yet have it and was not arrogant.
comments.comment: Some people, acting with arrogance, judge the one praying as being of moderate character; no one would say, 'Hear, O Lord, my righteousness, and let my judgment come forth from your face' (Psalm 17:2). But David, not being arrogant, while doing all the will of God, but desiring to be judged with goodness, prayed that his judgment might come forth from the divine face. 'Let my eyes see straightness' (Psalm 17:2). One prays to see straightness with the eyes of a man, by which God judges, bringing the judgment forth from his own face; one prays to behold the virtue of straightness. If, however, he prays to see it, he does not yet possess it; thus he is advised not to be arrogant by the way he offers the prayer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker shows much boldness and purity, for the heart of one who endures in obscurity is tested, and 'night' is the dim state in which God visits and proves him clean.
comments.comment: And through these things, much boldness of the speaker is manifest (Psalm 17:3; LXX 16:3). For if he says these things concerning God, he manifests much of his own purity; for the heart of everyone who endures in obscurity is tested, and he who is afflicted in everything is not distressed, but enduring until the end, he is proven righteous; such as Job, to whom God said: 'If perhaps I may prove you, you shall be more righteous than I' (Job 40:8). … It is worth following to see what is meant by 'I visited in the night' (Psalm 17:3; LXX 16:3); and indeed, if he calls the state of those in obscurity 'night' because of the dimness and having nothing propitious, in which God, having visited him, left him proven and, having refined through afflictions, showed him clean from all iniquities.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Affliction works testing, and the night in which the heart is tested stands for the affliction that darkens a stumbling soul.
comments.comment:
“You tested my heart; you visited by night” (Psalm 17:3; LXX 16:3).

If affliction works patience, and patience testing, then affliction works testing. And if the testing ran its course in the night, the night here signifies the affliction, in which a stumbling rational soul is darkened.

“Enter through the narrow gate and the afflicted way”: that is, the practical life, which seems at first a bringer of pain and not of joy, but afterward giving back fruits of righteousness to those trained through it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'visited me in the night' means, in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paths toward virtue seem hard, even unto death for the truth, but kept by the words of God's lips they become light through habit.
comments.comment: The paths bearing one toward virtue seem to be hard, having much roughness; for how is the path not hard, which commands the one being struck to a place beyond the jaws, and the rest of the hand to receive insult? In addition to this, a rough path seems to be one through which someone struggles toward death for the sake of the truth. And it is, through injuries, the most bitter of threats, of fire and iron and the assault of wild beasts, the completion of this; except even if these paths and those related to them are hard, they are guarded because of the words of the lips of the protecting God, and they are made smooth as if they were no longer something hard or heavy. For John indeed writes, 'And his commandments are not heavy' (1 John 5:3), and Jesus says to those hearing his words, 'My yoke is good and my burden is light' (Matt 11:30). For from much habituation and training, approaching without interruption, the heavy things appear most light, and the bitter and joyless things are made upright with much ease.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's ways are the keeping of the commandments, made smooth by continual treading, so we should walk in them that our steps may not falter.
comments.comment: By the words of your lips, I have kept to hard paths. A model for us, and through these things the Savior gives, so that those needing God’s help do not think only of themselves. The ways of the Lord are the observances of the commandments; yet rather, the virtuous actions, smooth and level, demonstrated by continual treading from those rushing toward their goal, which is blessedness and the fulfillment of promises. Let us therefore act in accordance with them, so that our steps do not falter, if the Lord prepares them in his ways. Concerning this request, the one who gains it says: 'I ran without iniquity and I directed my course.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's paths are the keeping of the commandments, smooth and level for those who press on toward blessedness, so we are to run in them without stumbling.
comments.comment: But the paths of the Lord and of his saints happen to be the keeping of the commandments (Psalm 17:5; LXX 16:5a), rather the energies according to virtue, being shown to be smooth and even, having been developed from constantly suffering toil by those hurrying to reach their end; and their end is blessedness and the fulfillment of the promises. Let us therefore run according to them, so that we may find salvation, not wavering in our steps, that is to say, not stumbling.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'thy paths' are and how to walk in them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cry is made with an attentive mind, not a loud voice.
comments.comment: 'I have cried out' (Psalm 17:6) is to be heard spiritually; for it is not necessary to have cried out toward the invisible God with a loud voice, but with an attentive mind; this is the cry of the inner man.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how one cries to an invisible God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Remembering past answers to prayer prepares for later favors.
comments.comment: For having been heard before, he says, I ask to be heard now as well. For Paul says we pray with thanksgiving, because the remembrance of former things prepares the favors that follow (Psalm 17:6; LXX 16:6).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The hand of God that helps is the angels, whom demons oppose.
comments.comment:
“Make wonderful your mercies, you who save those who hope on you; from those who have stood against your right hand, keep me as the pupil of the eye” (Psalm 17:7; LXX 16:7).

Just as Job calls the power that struck him the hand of God: “Your hand,” he says, “let it not whirl me so much.” And David calls the enemies of the beneficent hand of God the sword of God. And the beneficent hand of God is the angels, through whom the perceptible world is provided for, to whom demons are opposed, the angels wishing all men to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's right hand is his only-begotten Son, and the devil, his angels and evil men stand against it.
comments.comment: The right hand of God will be no other than his only-begotten Son, as was said a little earlier: 'Delight is at your right hand unto the end' (Psalm 16:11). The devil and his angels, and with them sorcerers and evil men, stand against this, from whom the holy one desires to remain harmless, saying to God: 'Protect me from those standing at your right hand, according to the pupil of my eye, so that my mind may remain harmless; but also cover me in the shelter of your wings from the face of the impious who desire to surround me with misery' (Psalm 17:8; LXX 16:8). It is possible to call the impious and those opposing the right hand of God in various ways, according to the underlying subject.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only the enlightened can say 'Protect me as the pupil of the eye', and God's 'wings' are his covering powers that shield from invisible enemies.
comments.comment: But the voice 'Protect me as the pupil of the eye' does not belong to everyone, but only to the one having been enlightened according to the soul, having the eyes of the heart enlightened. And 'In the shelter of your wings you will cover me' is to be understood spiritually; for the covering powers of God are called his wings, through which he covers and for the sake of good cheer protects the one beseeching to be rescued from the impious who are planning misery against him. For indeed, there are certain invisible enemies making misery for those being caught by them, by bringing them under sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'apple of the eye' and the 'wings' as the verse's pictures of God's protection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies enclose his soul, speak with pride, and surround the one who has taken shelter in order to harm him.
comments.comment: The wild and raw nature of those standing against signifies, by saying, that his soul is being enclosed by his enemies who have shut their canopy because of the striving toward matter (Psalm 17:9; LXX 16:9). … therefore also their mouths speak pride, not steadily bearing anything friendly or appropriate. For indeed, the enemies, casting out from much arrogance, surround the one saying these things in order to harm and destroy the one who has become sheltered within. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The attackers plot murder with flattering words, are fat in body and look sideways like a lion in ambush, as Saul acted toward David.
comments.comment: He describes the work and the appearance of those who attack him. The work is murderous plotting and flattering words for an ambush. They are fattest in body, fenced about with fat, looking sideways with their eyes like a lion rushing to its prey and lying in wait secretly (Psalm 17:10-12; LXX 16:10-12). Such was Saul toward David, saying that David had found favor in his eyes, ordering him to stand by, and keeping him as an attendant, yet attempting to kill him from ambush.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the attackers are and what the verses' pictures mean.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Eyes set on the earth belong to those who think of passing, earthly things, while those who bear the image of the heavenly set their eyes on heaven.
comments.comment: That their eyes are set upon the earth, turning aside and becoming lawless; for this is shown by having set their eyes upon the earth, wanting to observe the passing things and thinking of earthly things, turning aside from not wanting to walk the straight way, but being tossed about by crooked paths. For, they say, those abandoning the straight ways of going, they go in ways of darkness, whose ways are crooked and winding. Not indeed they set their eyes upon the earth, but those bearing the image of the heavenly are setting their eyes upon heaven in order to straighten the straight way that leads up to the heavens (Psalm 17:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what eyes 'bowing down to the earth' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's rising up lets the wicked suffer and understand, so that they stop increasing their destruction, and takes from them the sword they used wrongly.
comments.comment: Since you are long-suffering, that you might sleep, you do not receive justice from them who were cutting me murderously, Arise therefore, O Lord, that you might cause them to be overshadowed (Psalm 17:13; LXX 16:13). For they will understand having suffered this, so that not always running toward evil they might increase their destruction; for surrounding my soul and doing other things, if not prevented, they harm it most greatly. Therefore overshadow them, so that they may no longer be able against me, you having rescued my soul from each one being such and therefore being named ungodly; for rescue my soul from the ungodly (Psalm 17:13). He will take his sword from their hands; for they received it given unrighteously. And they take it from them not using it as is necessary.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A hidden punishment, like that said of Judas, will enter into their belly.
comments.comment: A hidden punishment has been prepared for them, he says, which will enter into their belly, according to what is said of Judas: 'May the curse enter like water into his inward parts, and like oil into his bones' (Psalm 108 [109]:18) (Psalm 17:14; LXX 16:14c).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He will be satisfied when God's glory is seen face to face, which is to behold the glory of the Only-begotten Son, full of grace and truth.
comments.comment: They indeed are not, he says, as it is said, 'But I shall be seen in righteousness before your face' (Psalm 17:15; LXX 16:15); for the virtue of the hidden ones from you is not like their wickedness. … but I, knowing in part, shall be satiated then, when your glory shall be seen standing according to the coming perfection, to face a Person face to face. It is possible to receive the glory of God when the Only-begotten Son is seen, as it is written: 'All flesh shall see his salvation, and the glory of the Lord shall be seen' (Isaiah 40:5). This is fulfilled in this, that we might behold the glory of the Son, a glory as the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be satisfied with God's likeness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The song of victory is given to the Lord, who alone grants victory, and David offers thanks for the day he was rescued from his enemies and from Saul.
comments.comment:
It says, to the child of the Lord, David. A conclusion to be taken from these things is victory over all enemies; for on account of this both wars and everything contributing to the excellence of a king exist. And it is rightly said that it is not the other things, but this itself, that triumphs. For since victory exists, it is not necessary to give thanks to anyone else but to God who granted it. For it is said to him by Ezra: 'From you is the victory.'

David refers the song to the Lord, as his child and servant, having wisely and faithfully expressed all the words of thanksgiving on that day (that is, in that light), in which all the enemies and Saul the king of Israel were overthrown, and David was rescued unharmed from them. And these things are said as regarding the history.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalm's title and occasion mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To many the song is from the Savior's person, as a victory hymn on the resurrection from the dead and rescue from the nations and rulers who stood against him.
comments.comment: But since it seems to many of the faithful that the song is present from the face of the Savior, it must be said that the triumphal hymn refers to the resurrection from the dead, his being rescued from all the guarding nations and the empty peoples who studied to destroy him, but also from the kings who stood against him and the rulers gathered against him. And you say that he was rescued also from the hand of Saul, who was then ruling the Jews, in a certain way; for it was not an inaccurate representation of their manner, being wrathful and having with them an evil spirit, saying they did not have a god for a king; for how could they not be about to deny God, to be ruled by some base person? …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pains of death are the sins that lead to death, and the words fit the Lord's coming in the flesh, since his soul was troubled near death.
comments.comment:
'Streams of iniquity' were called, as another says, and because of entering into iniquity those who do not bravely stand against the trials. And if the preceding words concern the death that follows those who sin, and the harmony having with it slavery, then the pains of death and slavery are the sins that exist toward death. In accordance with this understanding, you will say 'streams of iniquity' referring to the currents of wickedness, and 'snares of death' referring to those which practically constitute sins toward death.

According to the previous explanation, the present passages fit the economy of the Lord according to the flesh. For 'My soul is greatly troubled, and my soul is very sorrowful near death' (Matthew 26:38) possesses much intimacy with the Now.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pains of Sheol also fit the Savior, sorrowful even unto death.
comments.comment: The pains of Sheol surrounded me; they anticipated me beforehand, like snares of death. Yet these things will also be fitting for the Savior, who has much familiarity with them. Now my soul is troubled; my soul is exceedingly sorrowful even unto death.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A pure conscience makes prayer a real cry; 'ears of God' is a figure.
comments.comment: Prayer has much boldness from a pure conscience, since to call upon the Lord is not a mere report, but to cry out to God. … It is said metaphorically that his cry enters into the ears of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the cry came 'into his ears'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God grants requests quickly to the righteous, who can say that he heard their voice from his holy temple.
comments.comment: Because he is good, he will grant the requests of those who ask, but not to all at once. To those who have excelled in righteousness, however, he holds out what they ask without any delay and lends them a most ready ear, so that over each of their requests they say with joy: “He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears” (Psalm 18:6). So the cry “Here I am,” while the righteous man is still speaking and lifting up his prayers, shows plainly the generosity that will not delay and the great readiness of God who gives.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hills that are moved are like the mountains that faith as a grain of mustard seed removes, among them the spirit of moon-sickness.
comments.comment: These oracles remove from the deceived those having faith like a grain of mustard seed (Psalm 18:7); for if Paul says that faith as a grain of mustard seed removes them [the mountains]. Among these was also the spirit of moon-sickness about which the Savior says: 'If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you say to this mountain, Move from here to there' (Matthew 17:20). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shaking earth is the people of the earth filled with the report of God's descent, the mountains are the opposing powers subdued by knowledge of God, and the fire that burned men was put out by God's own fire.
comments.comment: And it was shaken, and the earth became terrified. The foundations of the mountains were shaken and trembled, because God was angry with them. This clearly shows the descent of God through the aforementioned—that is, death and the pangs of Hades. … For every Hebrew hearing and barbarian was filled with the report about him. He said the earth, those upon the earth. But mountains, of the opposing forces; which by the wandering of the idols they allotted to men, … being subdued by the knowledge of God. The foundations, and the deep reasonings, perceiving the power of the Lord, were shaken, being burdened. Which, God having been angered, smoke went up as upon a threshing floor; and the fire being extinguished and having ceased, by which they burned men. But this fire was extinguished by its own fire. Because fire consuming has been said to be God beside Moses. And in the Psalms: Fire before him will go forth, and it will flame around his enemies. And again: God will manifestly come, our God, and he will not keep silent. Fire before him will be kindled, and around him a violent tempest. Therefore also the Savior said: Fire I came to cast upon the earth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The coals are the apostles, who received the fire of Pentecost and, with fiery tongues, lit and purified the nations.
comments.comment:
“Smoke went up in his anger, and fire from his face set ablaze, coals were kindled from him” (Psalm 18:8).

He was angry, he says, and he cast down the fire, through which again he burned the men. Coals: the chorus of the apostles; for having partaken of this fire on the day of Pentecost, and having received fiery tongues upon their heads, they were reasonably called coals, lighting the nations together and purifying …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'coals' are.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Coals mean both punishments and the piercing, hot words of God that purify the soul's thoughts, and the fire consumes sinners' deeds while purifying them.
comments.comment:
They sent up smoke, which is consumed by the coming wrath, making coals. Coals were kindled from it. These coals signify, on the one hand, punishments, and on the other hand, the piercing, hot words of God that purify the thoughts of the soul.

Punishments are signified in: 'If your enemy hungers, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for so doing you will heap coals of fire on his head' (Rom 12:20). And in: 'Coals of fire shall fall upon them, and you shall cast them down; they shall not help you' (Psalm 140:10). The piercing word is shown in Isaiah: 'And he was sent among the seraphim.' Thus, prepared for the virtue of the soul, it warms and fires the thoughts to show them bright and splendid, but it will consume the deeds of sinners while purifying them; those not receiving this fire will be consumed by the eternal fire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'coals' and the fire in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's coming down from the heavens speaks of the Lord's becoming man, with no change of place, as he took the form of a servant.
comments.comment: The phrase 'He inclined the heavens and came down' (Psalm 18:9) follows the word concerning the economy [God's plan of salvation in Christ] and the descent. Since the Savior is said to dwell in the heavens, having become man, he changes his dwelling; for he became lowly and walked among men on earth. He dwells in the heavens not locally, nor does he descend transitively (for these are things pertaining to bodies), but according to the saying 'he dwells in the heavens.' For existing in the form of God, having taken the form of a servant, he descended, without any local change occurring to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'he bowed the heavens and came down' without picturing a change of place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Cherubim' is interpreted as knowledge and understanding.
comments.comment:
“And he bent heaven, and came down, and gloom under his feet, and he mounted upon cherubim” (Psalm 18:9-10).

Cherubim is interpreted knowledge and understanding; therefore he speaks unto the righteous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'cherub'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bowing the heavens shows his humility and self-emptying, the darkness shows the hidden side of his plan, the cherub his ascension, and no one sees God unless he enters the darkness of incomprehensibility, as Moses did.
comments.comment:
These things he did by bowing and descending, not one heaven only, but all, as many as ever are; to bow.

His humility in stature and the emptying of his deity are revealed. The hidden and concealed aspect of his economy is made known through darkness and mist. Then he was taken up upon the cherub, though not descending with it. As he ascended bodily, the divine contemplative powers that had surrounded him escorted his rise, proclaiming: Lift up your gates, you rulers; be lifted up, eternal gates; so the King of glory may enter. This has come to pass as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, where they witnessed him being taken up and a cloud received him from their sight.

… He established darkness as his concealment, with his tent encircling him. Who could see the one within the tent without entering inside? Thus, no one can see God unless they enter the veil of incomprehensibility. Moses entered the darkness where God was present. Having stood firm in regard to God’s creation and providence, he came to know that God is contained within these. By slightly opening it, he who bears the image learned from the image itself; and from creation and providence, he came to know the Creator and the Provident One.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cherubim stand for a multitude of knowledge, and God, riding upon them, flies through a sharp intellect.
comments.comment: And 'He rode upon the cherubim and flew' (Ps 18:10). The cherubim are understood as a voice for a multitude of knowledge; there is much knowledge there, but more ungraspable. One ascending from there flies through an elevated and ethereal intellect. It should not be thought that the name signifies the fullness of knowledge possessed by immortal animals. And God, having ascended upon these rational animals, flies through sharp intellect.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God rides on the winds either by his providence over the sensible winds or on the lofty thoughts and true teachings of those moved by the Spirit, blowing where he wills.
comments.comment:
'He spread himself upon the wings of the winds' (Psalm 18:10). If the saying is taken regarding the sensible winds, it means God, according to His providential word, mounting the wings of the winds, that is, by their lifting up as He Himself wills; for 'He draws out the winds from His treasuries' (Psalm 135:7). But if one were to take the winds as those blowing like judgments, lifting up wise men being moved by the spirit,

God rides upon the wings of these, which are higher and more lofty thoughts. There are winds of teaching, as the Apostle Paul says regarding heretics, speaking of every wind of teaching in the cunning of men, in craftiness toward the method of error. But not as false teachers are the winds upon whose wings the wandering spirits of the people ride; rather, God, riding upon the wings of every wind of true teaching, blows where He wills. And this is to be spread upon the wings of winds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Darkness around God means his hidden, incomprehensible depth, and as a tent hides one inside, God cannot be seen unless one enters into the difficulty that covers him, as Moses entered the cloud.
comments.comment:
Previously and truly, the God who dwells is unapproachable light, the Son who is true light, and the Holy Spirit who is the possession of knowledge and wisdom, just as of this light it is said, 'And the light is with Him' (Daniel 2:22). Secondly, by reason of the incomprehensibility concerning His essence, it is said that His hiddenness is called darkness. For that which is indistinct and incomprehensible because of the depth of the matter is called darkness. In this way, it is said that He perceives a parable and a dark speech; and God, uncovering the deeps out of darkness, makes manifest and clear those things hidden under indistinctness and difficulty of comprehension.

His tabernacle is around Him. Just as he who is contained under a tabernacle cannot be seen unless he has entered into it, so also the God surrounded by indistinctness and difficulty of comprehension cannot be seen unless one has entered into the interior of the covering of that difficulty. Immediately, regarding Moses, it is said how he entered into the cloud where God was (Exodus 20:21). For having understood the thought, the creation, and the providence concerning God, he knew that God is contained by these; thus, having slightly passed through this tabernacle concerning Him, he might behold from the image (which is not the image) the one according to the image, and from the creation and providence, the Creator and Provider.

In many places of the Scripture, we find clouds being carried allegorically. For he who said 'the vineyard of Israel,' speaking of clouds receiving commands not to rain upon it, we find no others but the prophets. It is not only with them that 'Thus says the Lord' and 'The word of the Lord came to me' are found; until these clouds, the truth shines. For these clouds are souls.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hiding himself in darkness means that what can be worthily thought of him is hidden from those who cannot bear the brightness of knowing him.
comments.comment: In a Hebrew manner of speaking, then, it is said of God in the seventeenth Psalm (Psalm 18 in English Bibles) that “God made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 18:11). This is said to show that what could be worthily conceived about God is hidden and unknown, since he has hidden himself, as it were, in darkness from those who cannot bear the flashing brightness of the knowledge of him and cannot see him: partly because of the defilement of the mind, bound as it is to a human “body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21), and partly because of its too limited power to comprehend God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why God is said to hide in darkness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Darkness is set between us and God as the veil was between Moses and Israel, and this bodily gloom stands between us and God, as Paul says God dwells in unapproachable light.
comments.comment:
“And he set darkness his hiding-place, around him his tent” (Psalm 18:11).

He set the darkness his hiding-place, having placed it in the middle of himself and us, as Moses of old the veil in the middle of himself and the hardening of Israel, unless a dark nature easily sees — not easily attaining the stored-up beauty, it also easily casts it off, because of the ease of the creation. Therefore in the middle of us and God this bodily gloom stands, as the cloud of old of the Egyptians and the Hebrews; and this is perhaps “he set darkness his hiding-place.” Therefore also Paul says: “Who alone has immortality, and dwells in unapproachable light” (1 Timothy 6:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The clouds are spiritual words that become clear in Jesus, when the law and prophets are fulfilled, and the sinners have no excuse left.
comments.comment:
Flowing as a rain of spiritual words, they belong to the air, not the earth; for having detached themselves from earthly things and no longer thinking of them, they are lifted up and exalted by their own virtue and by the active spirit of the air.

The water within them, before having attained clarity and manifestation through Jesus, is said to be a dark thing, being difficult for the many to see. But when God has spoken in the Son at the end of days, the law and the prophets shall be fulfilled: they shall come together before him in a bright shining (that is to say, his illumination), visible clouds and distinct, because of the presence of what was pre-proclaimed by them (Psalm 18:11-12).

Since no apology remains for those sinning, coming out of dark clouds into light through clarity, there immediately follows the bright shining of the clouds with hail and coals of fire. This is signified by the punishments through the pre-proclamations and having attained the manifestation of what was prophesied concerning Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God thunders from heaven to lift minds toward heaven through the high words about his Son, but sends arrows to throw into confusion those united in evil.
comments.comment:
God immediately thunders from heaven, either through the loud voice of the words being fulfilled by Jesus, or by casting the highest words of theology concerning the only-begotten Son into each mind, not only having cried out this: 'This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased,' but also the Most High gives a voice to those who discourse highly concerning Christ, who did not reveal his own Son to them in flesh, but the Father in heaven revealed his own Son.

Just as for those prepared in mind for the vision of God and the hearing of the Word, the Lord thunders from heaven and the Most High gives his voice, so that, being lifted up by the thunder coming from heaven, they may fall away from earthly things and fly toward heaven, bearing the image of the heavenly, and may receive the high things of the thoughts being given by the Most High; but to those who are of contrary disposition, the Lord sends arrows sufficient to throw into confusion those who previously were of one mind concerning evil. … He will light up like lightning, and will throw into confusion those scattered by the aforementioned arrows. For those being scattered cast off their agreement toward evil, having become in turmoil and confusion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When ignorance and malice are removed, or the veil over Scripture is lifted, the springs of the waters will be seen, so that one can draw from them with joy.
comments.comment: When all the aforementioned things have happened, the springs of the waters will be seen. And if someone says that the springs of the waters are those sown among us concerning God and good thoughts, he will say that these will be seen when the ignorance and malice lying upon the soul are withdrawn. For these, having been removed, will not hide the springs of good things in us. But if someone says that every God-breathed scripture, though spiritual, is veiled by ambiguity, he says that the springs will be seen; stand firm! For if we turn now to the Lord, the veil of ignorance and ambiguity will be removed, and the springs of the waters lying within will be seen, so that it is easy to draw from each one, according to Ps 36:9 'Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation.' For this water of gladness is a part of the being of the springs of salvation, which were granted to the discerning one, and now he sees God, according to Ps 34:8 'Bless the Lord in the churches, O Israel, from the springs.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the water-springs are seen.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The foundations of the world may be the divine men, built on Christ, whose uncovering comes with the punishment of sinners.
comments.comment: And if someone says that the foundations of the inhabited world are the divine men, because of the goodness of life and the narrowness of virtue upon which those living according to Christ are built, the uncovering of these foundations too will happen, through the occurrence of a rebuke. For the uncovering and revealing of these foundations will not happen without the punishment of these sinners.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not bring wrath daily despite constant sins, but announces its punishments beforehand.
comments.comment: Because of great human-lovingness, even though a multitude of sins occurs constantly, He does not bring down wrath for every single day. This is what it means for Him to breathe His own spirit of wrath, because He pre-announces the punishments of wrath: 'For I will discipline them in the wrath of their affliction' (Hosea 7:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'breath of his nostrils' as God's patience and warning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many waters mean the turbulent matters of life and disordered opposing powers, and God delivers from strong invisible enemies and from deceivers terrible in their sophistry.
comments.comment: Out of many waters—meaning the turbulent and salty matters of life, called a sea tropically, which are the poured-out and disordered opposing powers—He stands against them; and even if the doctrines of ungodliness are many, they are not able to quench love. God delivers from powerful enemies the invisible ones, as is said, and perhaps also those in high positions and those intending to deceive through pseudonymous knowledge, who are terrible in their sophistry.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous are most attacked in affliction, but whoever takes refuge in God finds him a support, who gives breadth in affliction by letting him be stretched toward it courageously.
comments.comment: Indeed, those who hate the righteous most vehemently attack then, when a time of affliction is present. For, being ignorant of the judgment of Providence, they suppose that the righteous is being afflicted through sin for no other reason, like those conversing with Job. For when God had subjected him to afflictions, so that he might be shown to be righteous, they said that this man had fallen into these things because of impiety and sin; but even against the one stumbling, all the predatory demons and the devil are strong, as they now think sin to be an evil. … For in the day of affliction, whoever takes refuge toward God, He becomes his support (Psalm 18:18), meaning, supporting him so that he might not be shaken and fall. … For the Lord becomes a support for someone, leading him out of the narrowness of afflictions, giving him breadth according to 'In affliction he enlarged me' (Psalm 4:1). But one is enlarged in affliction not by becoming outside of the affliction entirely, but by being courageously and piously stretched toward it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Lord was his stay in the day of calamity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rescued by providence, he hopes to prevail over all enemies and not withdraw first.
comments.comment:
“He will rescue me, because he delighted in me” (Psalm 18:19).

Thus I, having been rescued by your providence, hope to prevail over all the hostile, and not to withdraw first, until I make them subject again; for this he also hinted when he said: “They will fall under my feet” (Psalm 18:38).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who speak this psalm in the Savior's presence find him tested without sin; righteousness is the general virtue of practice and clean hands are practical actions made pure.
comments.comment: Truly, the boldness of the pure and perfect is such that he condemns nothing of himself, even the shortest thing; therefore, those who wish to speak this psalm in the presence of the Savior, and who apply this word to Him, find Him having been tested in all things according to likeness, without sin. He speaks of righteousness as the general virtue of practice, and of cleanness of hands as the practical actions becoming pure and unstained by being fulfilled from the best of ways; for often hands are said to be upon the practical powers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'righteousness' and 'cleanness of hands'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He gives God the credit for his successes, and keeps the Lord's ways by walking in his commandments and thinking rightly of God.
comments.comment: And he does not say these things arrogantly, as some are, but having placed the cause of the successes upon God. He who walks in His commandments keeps the ways of the Lord, and he who has correctly grasped the doctrines of truth does not act impiously toward his own God, conceiving blamelessly concerning God, speaking holily concerning Christ, remembering piously concerning the Holy Spirit, and glorifying in the proper manner concerning the other doctrines.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'keeping the ways of the Lord' involves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even when God's judgments seem an abyss we are pleased with them, for 'judgment' means the right ordering of his rule.
comments.comment: For even if His judgments are unsearchable and seem like an abyss because of the incomprehensible, it is not possible for those having them not to be displeased with Providence, nor to act impiously toward the one who provides. For even if we do not grasp, but having resolved that these things are fulfilled by God's judgment, we are well-pleased with them. And the very name 'Judgment' signifies the rectitude of the administration; for it contains and is heard to be that which has happened according to righteousness, as opposed to judgments of the unrighteous and the perverted which are performed apart from the right. Because of this, he says, a perverted judgment will come forth. 'I hold fast to the rights of God,' he says (Psalm 18:22).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judgments can mean God's tested and examined words, and even the thoughts of the righteous are judgments, accurately examined and tested like a rule.
comments.comment:
And the rights and statutes must be spoken of which have been legislated according to equality and justice, such as 'If a Hebrew acquires a child' (Exodus 21:2), and the following. For all these things, the judgments are arranged as side-notes, and the following.

The judgments, being named with the rights, can signify the tested and examined words of God; for they are not called judgments because they are not being checked or being overturned. In this way even the thoughts of the righteous are judgments, that is, having been accurately examined and tested, and being this very thing similar to a rule.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who embrace good through God and not for other reasons are unblemished with God.
comments.comment: Perhaps those who, not through God but through glory or something else, find fault and call something unblemished, are unblemished indeed, but not with God; but those who have embraced the good through God and not for the sake of anything else, are unblemished with God; for this union toward God preserves one unblemished and good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'My iniquity' is the lawlessness of man, the mind's leaning to evil from youth or the mindset of the flesh, from which one given to God's law keeps himself.
comments.comment:
He who has accomplished all the aforementioned things, how does he speak of his own lawlessness? It is to say that he does not wish to understand at any time; this is it: 'The mind of man leans toward evil things with care from youth' (Gen 8:21), as it flows toward sin, being enticed by pleasure. He who has given himself to the law of God protects himself from the lawlessness that overshadows men.

Perhaps also that which is called among us the mindset of the flesh, which is enmity toward God and does not submit to His law, is the lawlessness of man, from which one preserves the deeds of the body of death in the spirit and abstains from the works of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'mine iniquity' is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness here is the righteousness established by faith in Jesus Christ, revealed to all who believe.
comments.comment: There he calls righteousness here, that which is established from the faith of Jesus Christ. For the righteousness of God has been revealed to all who believe (Rom 3:22); for to the one believing rightly, 'the faith is reckoned as righteousness' (Rom 4:3/5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some say these verses are spoken to God, others that they speak of men, so that whoever keeps company with the holy becomes holy and whoever keeps company with the crooked is perverted, and he then turns his face toward God.
comments.comment: Regarding the change of face in Psalm 17:26–28, someone says these upcoming verses are to be spoken toward God, because he does not say to another, 'That you will save a humble people and humble the eyes of the proud,' but to God. Another will say that these are not spoken toward God but toward a man: that the one spending time with the holy should imitate their virtue, and the one spending time with the wicked should undergo perversion, as the divine writing of Proverbs says: 'He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be destroyed' (Prov 13:20). The interpretations are thus: 'With the holy man, O Lord, he shall be made holy,' providing him the holiness supplied from you so that, having been perfected according to it, you may bring him into the fitting promise, and the others following the one before it. He also says, 'You will pervert,' for it is possible to say, 'He perverts with a crookedness'; this is not said, but 'You will pervert.' For God perverts the one running toward evil things, blocking his way with stumbling blocks and rebuilding his paths; for to be prevented from evils is the beginning of blessing. But he who wishes to be taken toward a man says that the one associating with a holy man becomes holy from the holy things being done, as Elisha with Elijah and Timothy with Paul; and the one hastening with the innocent, having seized that one's virtue, will be innocent. Likewise, the one spending time with an elect man, but the one associating with the crooked, desiring to become like him, will pervert his own life. And he, having clarified the verses thus, turns his face toward God from 'That you will save a humble people.'
comments.selected_reason: Sets out two readings of the verses on God's dealing with the holy and the crooked.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind is not light in essence but can receive it, and the darkness is the passionate and desiring part, which is enlightened when the Lord lights the mind.
comments.comment:
[The mind, called a lamp:] In essence it is not light, but it is capable of receiving light. But its darkness is the passionate and desiring part.

If the mind is now enlightened by the Lord, sharing with it His own rays, the victorious movements and the irrational movements of the soul are enlightened through knowledge being perfectly accomplished; not that the irrational parts themselves participate in light (for they are incapable of knowledge), but that which is under an enlightened mind is guided by knowledge and virtue without needing a way. If the mind, which is said to be a lamp, is now enlightened by the Lord, then the darkness we have spoken of must necessarily follow being enlightened.

And this is what the Savior says: 'If the light in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!' (Matthew 6:23). For if the eye of the body, that is, the mind, which ought to be a lamp, is deprived of light, then the other is much more so; in this way, the body of the soul becomes darkness, but it is not a human body, rather it is that which happens according to its irrational composition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God promised that light would shine out of darkness, and David speaks for those in gloom when he says the Lord will light his lamp, a promise fulfilled when the light of the mind dawned.
comments.comment: The mind of those who go astray is filled with a darkness of the mind and with demonic deceit, but God promised that light would shine out of darkness for us (2 Corinthians 4:6). For He said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, “The people that sits in darkness, see a great light; you who dwell in the land and shadow of death, a light will shine on you” (Isaiah 9:2). And the inspired David says, as if speaking for those in gloom and darkness, “For You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, You will light up my darkness” (Psalm 18:28). Since the Father’s promise has now been fulfilled in us, and the divine light, seen by the mind, has dawned on us, we have come to know His glory in the face of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'thou wilt light my candle' as God's promise of light in darkness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One is saved from temptation by being in God, not by avoiding it, and sins form a wall of separation that he leaps over by clinging to God and rising above the senses.
comments.comment:
It is not otherwise possible to be saved from the surrounding bitter things by becoming in God; for someone becomes in God partaking of Him. Just as one having come to be in knowledge is saved from ignorances, so one hastening to be in God will be saved from temptation, not by not entering into temptation, but by not being caught by its snares. … But the multitude of things being done toward us irrationally separates us from God and discerns a gap, as the prophet says: Is not the hand of the Lord able to save? Did his wrath grow because they did not listen? But your sins discern a gap between you and God. And he who now becomes in God, clinging to him and being toward him, surpasses the wall of sins by a little and casts them before and behind, so that, not being pierced through by anything, he may face God face to face.

Perhaps also the sense of bodily and sensible things, standing between our thought and God, separates us from him. But if we now, scientifically as much as possible, through the thought concerning God, grasp him above all bodies and senses, desiring to be united with him, we withdraw from the sensible and bodies as if to leap over the world and all visible things, so that we may be able to present ourselves to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'leaping over a wall' as rising above sin and the senses by clinging to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The way to God is faultless through virtue, and especially so in Christ, the way, through whom one comes to the Father.
comments.comment: Our God is faultless in the way toward him (Psalm 18:30). And this is virtue, through which, traveling by practice and discipline, we shall be shown faultless coming toward him. But especially faultless is the way of God, he who said: I am the way and the truth and the life (John 14:6). For through this way it is possible to come to the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'his way is perfect'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word of the Lord is a fire that consumes weakness and defends those who hope in him, fighting for them with his shield, and no one is truly God except the God of the Word.
comments.comment: The word of the Lord, having been made fiery, is in the one who is truthful and pure, or is a fire that consumes the weakness of the matter of those partaking. He is a defender of all who hope in him. Those who know the weakness present to them, if they make those attacking them stronger, by casting hope upon God, are worthy to have him fight for them, saying, 'Fight, those who fight against me.' And thus God fights for them with his own shield, according to: His truth shall surround you with a shield (Psalm 91:4). For no one is truly and principally God except the God of the Word, who is called the only-begotten God (Psalm 18:31).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No god exists in any way like our God, for those who are gods by participation cannot be like the Lord Jesus Christ.
comments.comment: [The psalmist,] having said that no god exists in the strict sense except the Lord, he says that no god exists in any way like our God. For none of those who are gods by participation can be like the Lord Jesus Christ, or like our God as the one of the only-begotten Father; for to us is God the Father and is Lord Jesus the Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The girding with strength points to Christ, the power of God, and the whole psalm may be read in his person.
comments.comment: 'He girded me with strength' is said. But according to Paul, the truth is that those having put on the armor of God are girded, from which it is gathered that the Christ is the power of God; for the Savior says, 'I am the truth' … And he set my way blameless, that is, he demonstrated. For to demonstrate now means to have demonstrated, just as it is said 'He has appointed him heir of all things' … It is also good from this verse to proclaim the whole psalm from the person of Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who has overcome evil has his feet prepared by God, runs his course, and is heard in the high places, where standing is a gift of God and not from himself.
comments.comment: He who says these things, having refuted the serpent-like evils and the evil powers that worked them, has the feet of his own man prepared by God (that is, the walking powers), so that he may be able to say, 'I have run without lawlessness and have directed my course' …; and having fulfilled the course, he will be heard in the high places by God: 'You yourself also stand with me' … And to stand in the high places is not something one has from himself, but from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'feet like hinds' feet' and 'high places' as gifts of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God teaches the soul's powers to fight the opposing powers, as the Savior did for us, and the bronze bow means strength to wound those set against us.
comments.comment:
For he [God] strikes the hands of the soul (I mean the active powers of it), and teaches how to skillfully hold the mental shield and the sword of the spirit and other spiritual defenses, and how one must use such things. For even the Savior, having become man, having fought on our behalf, taught us to overcome and to fight against the opposing power …

Symbolically, he set a bow called bronze upon the arms (Psalm 18:34); for because of the bronze, it represents the unpierceable or the strong, and because of the bow, the ability to release arrows from our own arms to wound those set against us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'teacheth my hands to war' and the bow of steel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sent his Son to fight with his own shield for him, and God's discipline is both teaching and strenuous training that perfects him to the end.
comments.comment: Besides these, you have given to me a shield of salvation, having sent your Son to fight for me with his own shield (Psalm 18:35). But also your discipline, he says, has perfected me to the end—that is, the disciplinary teaching and the strenuous training. He has brought me to the end, that is, unto a perfect resurrection and standing. For discipline signifies the disciplinary aspect, as in 'Take my discipline, do not let go' (Prov 3:11), but also the strenuous aspect through 'Do not despise the discipline of the Lord' (Prov 3:11). And thus, in both ways, your discipline has become a teacher of good things to me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'shield of salvation' and the word 'discipline' for the verse's 'gentleness'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Helped by God, he pursues enemies and neither toil nor fear trips him.
comments.comment: Having been aided by ten thousand through God, confidence arose to pursue the enemies; and the end of the pursuit is their falling to the end (Psalm 18:37). For neither toil nor fear caused me to stumble.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, not meaning to destroy attackers, surrounds them with tribulation so they stop hating.
comments.comment: Sparing those who were envenoming, he crushes them, so that they might become unshakeable and immovable in the enmity (Psalm 18:38). For, not intending to destroy them, he surrounds them with tribulation, so that, having perceived they are evil, they might cease from the intention of hatred.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enemies falling under the holy one's feet means submission, for one who falls from the law lies down and submits.
comments.comment: The falling of the enemies under the feet of the holy one signifies nothing other than the submission of the various kinds (Ps 17:39b). For as it is trivial to stand in the hand of the law, the beginning of salvation is to fall from it. For one falling from it does not oppose it, but lies down and submits.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since David never reigned over enemies, the one born of him fulfills it.
comments.comment:
“You shackled all who rise up against me under me” (Psalm 18:39).

And yet we do not know David as having reigned over the enemies; therefore through the one born from him according to the flesh the prophecy is fulfilled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the verse is finally about.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God stops the enemies' impulse to evil so that they fall beneath him and become friends instead of haters, for he removes the evil and not their essence.
comments.comment: You caused all those rising up against me to stumble, not permitting them to advance in the face of evil (Psalm 18:39-40). For, being hindered from the impulse toward evil, they will fall down beneath me, regarding me as nothing other than their ruler and head, so that, instead of hating, they might become friends; for such are they whom you have destroyed; for you do not destroy their essence, but only that which has happened to them.
