For it is very fitting for the goodness of God to make the evil vanish, but not the essence of that which has happened to them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God 'subdues' enemies by ending their hatred, not their being.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Gave me the back' means you turned them to flight.
comments.comment:
“And my enemies you gave me the back” (Psalm 18:40).

That is: you turned them to flight. For it is proper to those fleeing to give their backs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's wording.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those thickened by earthly thoughts are thinned into dust by exhortation and discipline, and the just one treats them as mud so that, cleansing themselves, they may become vessels of honor of gold or silver.
comments.comment:
Regarding those of whom the Word speaks, having become thickened by thinking of earthly and material things, bearing the image of the earthly, they are thinned through exhortations, admonitions, threats, and painful discipline, so that, as having become dust in the face of the Divine Spirit, which is called the tropical wind, all that is earthly, being dispersed by them by the breath of the Spirit, may become pure dust as their underlying substance, for whom it has happened to be earthly.

And if they also willingly follow this calling, the author says as if to a filthy city: 'Shake off your dust, Jerusalem' (Isaiah 52:2). But the Lord, or His imitator, the just, licks these even as mud in the streets. But this mud being licked will not be able to become an earthen vessel useful in the great house in which there are golden and silver and wooden and earthen vessels; but since the golden and silver are for honor and the wooden and earthen are for dishonor, the one cleansing himself from these becomes a vessel of honor, having been sanctified and made useful to the Master, prepared for every good work, while those who remain such mud in the streets—that is, the mire of pleasures and desires—are being freed from all roughness from the passions.

He who says these things, by instilling a uniformity through the licking, is now making them earthen vessels, if they should cleanse themselves by a spontaneous impulse as if to become vessels of honor, golden or silver. For just as some have become earthen vessels from golden and silver ones (For the precious sons of Zion, exalted with silver, how were they reckoned as earthen vessels of the work of hands? Lamentations 4:2), so from their own domestic choice they shall become golden or silver from earthen ones.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God knows only the righteous, and the people from the nations who had not been known by the Savior came to him through repentance.
comments.comment: It is said that he recognizes only the righteous. For the Lord knew those who were his, but he ignored the wicked. The Savior says to them: 'Depart from me, workers of lawlessness, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). And the people from the nations, not being known by the Savior, though he healed both demons and idols and practiced all manner of evil, having changed through repentance to serve Christ, came to him. And even the saying 'He did not know' is true. For it is not said: 'A people I do not know served me' (Psalm 18:43).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked are not known by God, but one who has ceased from sin is known now, as Paul says that those who knew God have been known by him.
comments.comment:
For he who is doing the works of wickedness is not known; but he who has ceased from sins was not known before, but is known now.

To this the apostolic word agrees, saying: 'But formerly, not knowing God, you served those which by nature are not gods; but now, having known God, and even more having been known by God' (Gal 4:8). For they did not know God, and they were unknown by him, but having known him, they were known by him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God 'knew not' a people who then served him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unbelief of the Jews was foreknown and used for the calling of the Gentiles, of whom Christ says that a people he did not know served him.
comments.comment: He did not come for this, to produce unbelief in the Jews; but knowing beforehand that it would come about, he foretold it, and he made use of the Jews’ unbelief for the calling of the Gentiles. For “through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles” (Romans 11:11). Of these Gentiles the Christ who speaks in the prophets says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 18:43–44);
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'To the hearing of an ear I obeyed' means obeying with an ear that obeys all things, a divine ear added to him.
comments.comment: Perhaps it will seem to some that the spoken thing passes by: 'To the hearing of an ear I obeyed' (Psalm 18:44), meaning to obey with an ear that obeys all things. But the ear is not intended to pass by or to be superfluous for the one obeying all things, so as to use a non-human and mortal hearing, but a divine ear added to the one approaching; for he added to me an ear for hearing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who share in evil instead of virtue grow old through their own corruption, while those who share in virtue and wisdom are constantly renewed.
comments.comment: 'Alien sons have grown old' (Psalm 18:45), and the following. God the Father, becoming the beginning and source of the good, becomes the source of those doing good works, and those who are found in doing what is necessary are truly sons of God, partakers of his only-begotten Son. But if those who did not draw near participate in the opposites (and these are the evils), they would be alienated from God, and the growing old would follow. For participating in virtue, in bright and imperishable wisdom and incorruption, they were finding constant renewal; but falling into wickedness, they would be growing old through their own corruption (if indeed it is so), being worn out.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'growing old' as corruption through sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Anyone who clings to Scripture without meditating on it as he should is said to limp in it.
comments.comment: To limp, as Elijah says: 'How long will you limp with double inclinations?' (1 Ki 18:21). 'If he is Lord, go after him.' And perhaps everyone who has clung to the divine scripture, not meditating upon it as is necessary, is said to be limping in it, because he has not accepted it, neither walking nor limping in it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God lives by giving life and is blessed because all blessing is in him, and he is exalted by those who recognize great things about him, not by moving from a low place to a high one.
comments.comment: It is said that God lives, not by taking life but by providing it. And He himself indeed often says concerning Himself, 'I the Living am, says the Lord.' … He is the living God and is blessed, having blessed the saints with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places (Eph 1:3). It is said that he is blessed if all blessing is in him. For everything said, thought, and spoken or thought blessedly is about him. … 'The God of my salvation is exalted, having taken my senses to his greatness; for great are his works, and they themselves are great.' Since the salvation of the rational animal is not a small work, it is necessary that the cause of this be great. And God is exalted, not by changing from a lowly place to a high one, but by those having recognized great things concerning him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the LORD liveth' and 'let God be exalted'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Where wrath prevails, irascibility follows, so our enemies are wrathful, with wrath like the serpent's.
comments.comment:
“My deliverer from wrathful enemies” (Psalm 18:48).

In those in whom wrath prevails, in these also is irascibility; and if our enemies are irascible, our enemies then are wrathful; for their wrath, he says, is according to the likeness of the serpent, and in his wrath being angered upon us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He gives thanks for the salvation of others, bearing their sins as an ambassador of their repentance.
comments.comment:
For he confesses thanks for this progress and salvation, having taken their sins into himself, becoming an ambassador of their repentance.

For the voice 'I will confess to you' signifies both. For the Son also sings in the name of the Father, doing all things according to the will of the Father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ gives salvation to those saved with him.
comments.comment: The Father exalts the salvation of the King Christ (Psalm 18:50); it is not that the King himself is saved, but he provides salvation to those being saved with him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If it is about the true David, God gives him and his seed eternal mercy and an indestructible priesthood.
comments.comment: The voice of Christ signifies priest and king (Psalm 18:50). … But if the word is about the true David regarding God ('For I will arise for you a shepherd like my servant David' 1 Sam 2:25/2 Sam 7:12), he provides eternal mercy to him and to his seed, and his anointing and his priesthood are to be indestructible; for the old priesthood being transferred, the priesthood of Christ is inviolable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whom 'David and his seed' finally means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heavens that declare God's glory are the powers dwelling in heaven who sing it, and the firmament announces God's works by deeds as well as by words.
comments.comment: The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1); and the glory of God is the only-begotten according to the radiance of glory, the order and the supremacy of his kingdom, according to 'And the glory of the Lord shall be seen' Isa 60:1. These the heavens declare by singing and theologizing, the powers dwelling in the heavens, named homonymously as dwelling in heavens according to the manner of metonymy. And the firmament announces the work of the active powers of God, called his hands, not only by words but by the works themselves (Psalm 19:1-4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who treasure life in heaven are the heavens narrating God's glory, and those who act become a firmament whose works announce what God's hands have made.
comments.comment: Those grasping life treasure in heaven, having their heart there; the heavens are narrating the previously spoken glory of God through the contemplation of intelligible things. But those who have accepted the practical aspect accomplish a firmament through works, that is, they become stable and immovable; they announce the making of the hands of God, working the works of God and through them crying out as works becoming the works of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The day of the resurrection tells the day of the cross that the crucified one rose as God, and the night of the betrayal shows him master of the elements.
comments.comment: And the day of the resurrection utters speech to the day of the cross, how the one crucified in that day here rose as God, and raised the dead. And the night that happened before the cross announces such knowledge to the night of Christ’s betrayal, how in that night fearing and praying, and later also being handed over, in this day he is master of the elements, so as even to bring on night in the middle of the day, he has been shown.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The day is the luminous intellect, which brings forth a word when filled with the Spirit's nourishment, and the night is the deepest discourse, which searches the mysteries of God and announces knowledge to another such night.
comments.comment:
But also the day, that is, the luminous intellect, being not in harmony with another luminous intellect, searches out a word, which is why the Old Scripture says the day is luminous: for God called the light Day (Gen 1:5). This, having been filled with the nourishments of the Spirit, being searched out from the fullness, a word is brought forth in the New Covenant; allegorically also this day is so named.

And the night, the deepest discourse of things, announces knowledge to another such night. For if anyone searches the Spirit who searches all things and has the depths of God, he searches some of the deeper mysteries of God; having known it from this, he proceeds to the similarly obscure, and will come to the knowledge of those.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Day and night, set in proportioned measures of increase and decrease, proclaim through their works the one who distinguished them, since such harmony is the offspring of wisdom and not of chance.
comments.comment:
“Day to day utters speech, and night to night announces knowledge. There are no speeches, nor words, whose voices are not heard” (Psalm 19:2-3).

… Night and day, being appointed measures of the seasonal withdrawal, both according to decrease and increase, and keeping the analogy toward one another through all, proclaim through the works the one who distinguished both; for the perpetual and unconfused is not in things according to chance, but a harmony, offspring of wisdom. And the voices of their words are not of those not heard; for everywhere of the inhabited world they are heard through the sight, both of heavens being seen, and of night and day.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul used these sayings of the apostles, and Symmachus renders the verse as a sound that went out into all the earth.
comments.comment: And Paul used these sayings upon the apostles; therefore he also spoke indefinitely, but not as he is accustomed on the preceding to say: “Isaiah cries over Israel.” And again: “As Isaiah has said before.” And again: “As it is written.” And again: “For the Scripture says.” And Symmachus rendered more clearly: “And night to night announces knowledge, not with sayings, nor with words, whose voices are not heard, but into all the earth went out a sound.” Or according to Aquila: “Their rule, for they send forth neither word nor voice; but indicating the rule and their own order, they call all earth and sea to the divine hymnody.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church can be God's tabernacle set in the sun, wherever the sun shines, and each person who holds God's glory can be set in Christ, the sun of righteousness.
comments.comment:
But according to the law of anagogy [the spiritual sense], the church can be the tabernacle of God, set in the sun—that is, wherever and as far as the sun shines; for the sound that has gone out into all the earth runs together with the sun's rays, and his words have reached the ends of the inhabited world.

And each one of those who contain the glory of God, being called his tabernacle, can be set in the sun of righteousness, that is, in Christ; for of such tabernacles the foundation and base is the true light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the tabernacle set in the sun stands for, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The chamber from which the bridegroom comes out is the Virgin, who bore Christ without a man, so that he came forth from a clean chamber clean of all defilement.
comments.comment:
“In the sun he set his tent, and he as a bridegroom going forth from his chamber will exult as a giant to run his way” (Psalm 19:4-5).

… He called the chamber the Virgin, from whom the bridegroom Christ went forth, clean of all defilement, coming forth from a clean chamber. And the holy Virgin is the chamber of Christ, since having given birth without a man, she reasonably had as bridegroom the one being born himself, who by invisible power worked the birth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The giant is the Lord, who exulted in the time of the economy and fell upon the demonic ranks, and the way he ran is his becoming man.
comments.comment: Giant is interpreted as falling-upon, and is taken for the Lord; for he himself exulted at the time of the economy [God's plan of salvation], accomplishing our salvation, and he fell upon the demonic ranks, putting out of work their domination against us. And understand the way as the Lord’s becoming-man, in which as a giant, because of the strength done in the cross and the death, he was running exulting. Recently he exulted in the gospel because of the finding of the one sheep. For he left the ninety-nine sheep that did not wander, that is the angelic powers, upon the mountains, that is in the heavens, and came upon the wandered sheep, and finding it he exulted; or he ran the way upon the heavens exulting, or from earth into the underworld he ran.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sun of righteousness goes forth from the end of heaven and returns to where he began, and no one is hidden from the fire of his heat.
comments.comment:
And this one, having the beginning of his going forth from the end of heaven, descended to the end of heaven, ascending there whence he also began his course. For he says: 'If you see the Son of man ascending where he was before' (John 6:62), and 'No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man' (John 3:13).

But also from his heat no one is able to hide; for of the fire which he came to cast upon the earth all partake, so that some become fervent in spirit (Luke 12:49).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sun's circuit and heat as the Savior's descent, ascent and fire.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law may convert souls from vice to virtue or from the perceptible to the intelligible, and it converted the souls of all the nations into the truth.
comments.comment:
“The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls” (Psalm 19:7).

… It is to be asked whether it would convert from vice to virtue, or from the perceptible to the intelligible; and perhaps the second; … as it also converted the souls of all the nations into the truth. Because of his boundless love toward us, he passes by neither a fornicator nor a robber, those who have fled his love exceedingly, and have arrived at the extremities of sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's testimony is faithful because it is worthy of belief, and it makes wise the childlike, the newborn in the gospel and the unlettered, while his commands, free of all crookedness, make straight those who receive them.
comments.comment:
The Lord's testimony, which testifies through good works and the knowledge of truth, is faithful. It is called faithful not from the act of believing, but from the worthiness of being believed, just as the Word 'Faithful' is said of the Faithful One, and concerning God it is said, 'God is faithful and there is no injustice in him' (Deuteronomy 32:4) and 'God is faithful through whom you were called' (1 Cor 1:9). For because of worthiness and the being worthy of being believed, it was so named, but also because of the certain and unchangeable nature. Thus indeed the Lord's faithful testimony makes wise those who have turned and become like children according to the will of Jesus.

And it makes wise even the newborn infants, those born through the gospel. Perhaps it also makes wise those little ones who have not been trained by disciplines and with the exercises of human words, but the unlettered and the laypeople. And the commands of the Lord, being outside of all crookedness, are straight, making straight those who receive them, so that they might cast off all sorrow and become in divine joy the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the testimony is called faithful and who it makes wise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fear of God is pure because it is the reverence of piety and not a passion that drives out love, and it lasts into the age to come, while his judgments are true as against false and unjust ones.
comments.comment: And the fear of God is said to be pure, not a passion that casts one out from perfect love, but the same one that is characterized by piety and divine reverence. It does not work out the state of those who are merely fittingly pure, but it extends even unto the age to come, not being transient and short-lived. The judgments of the Lord are true. He who performs all things according to His own truth and judges, judges truly; as the apostle says: 'For the judgment of God is according to truth upon those practicing such things' (Rom 2:2). God judges according to truth, and the judgments are true—it is said 'true' in contrast to false and unjust judgments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'clean' fear and 'true' judgments mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's judgments are fearful to sinners, but to those who keep the law they are more honorable than wealth and sweeter than pleasure.
comments.comment:
“The judgments of the Lord are true, justified together” (Psalm 19:9).

It was necessary that he added the third verse to the two former; for the judgments of God, for those who sin and transgress, have been established as fearful and to-be-sought-out; but for those who work the law of God and keep it they appear more honorable than all wealth, because of the hope of the recompense, and even sweeter than any pleasure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the judgments are called more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sweetness of these things is perceived by a divine sense and not tasted bodily, and the reward for keeping them is great because it is above the world and the heavens.
comments.comment: [Whoever turns his desire to them] … he will perceive the sweetness of these things more sweetly than the sweetness of a garden and honey in the senses. He will not taste it bodily, but by a divine sense he will perceive the sweetness of the things mentioned before. The servant of the Lord keeps these things. For indeed your servant keeps them; he is not saying this about himself alone, but also about every servant of the Lord. If one turns toward the guarding of these things something temporary and sensible, the recompense is not great; but since the recompense for the guarding of these things is supra-cosmic and supra-heavenly, it follows that it is great.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the honey comparison and why the reward is great.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who does not keep God's judgments is not his servant, and the one who desires nothing but them has a great recompense to come.
comments.comment:
“For indeed your servant keeps them; in the keeping of them there is much recompense” (Psalm 19:11).

… If your servant keeps them, the one who does not keep them is not your servant. And the one who keeps the desirable things of God is the one who desires nothing but them; therefore he has a great recompense of the things that are to come from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the servant is and why the reward is great.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Trespasses are hardly understood, so cleansing from secret parts is asked.
comments.comment: … “Who will understand trespasses? From my secret parts cleanse me” (Psalm 19:12). For in truth, someone recognizes sins, but trespasses, which in a certain way are unintentional, someone hardly understands.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Aliens' is rendered 'the proud': success can puff up the mind so that it falls, so the speaker asks to be delivered from pride, which is a great sin, and cleansed of hidden things.
comments.comment:
“Who will understand transgressions? Cleanse me from my hidden things, and spare your servant from aliens” (Psalm 19:12-13).

And Aquila rendered “aliens” as “the proud.” For upon those who succeed, this passion sometimes follows, the mind becomes puffed up by this, and in another way they are again thrown, such as the apostolic saying, “lest being puffed up he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:6). Having necessarily said beforehand “For your servant keeps them,” he entreats to be delivered from pride; having been cleansed from this sin, which is great, I will be blameless from pride, at the same time also having been cleansed of the hidden things; for now I do not yet dare.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'aliens' are and why the speaker fears them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Few see the transgressions that occur in secret in the thoughts, which even the one who has them does not know, and the righteous ask to be cleansed of them because secret sins left uncut may pass over into practical sin and give others a pretext to capture him.
comments.comment: Everyone is aware of the manifest and effective sins, but the transgressions occurring in secret in the thoughts and reasonings, the one who sees them is rare; … Furthermore, regarding the transgressions, who will understand? It lies to say, 'From my secret things cleanse me' (Psalm 19:12). This is said only by the righteous, since defilement occurs in the secret reasonings of the heart, which not only others but I myself am ignorant of; you, remove it, being a knower of those things which happen in secret. For this defilement, if it is not destroyed, becomes an increased starting-point and pretext to be captured by others; sparing your servant, do not let him be captured by others, having cleansed him from the secret things. For the sins occurring in secret, if not being cut off, may at some time pass over into practical sin, through which one might be involved with the things of God or with evil powers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of his mouth and the study of his mind are acceptable because they come from God, who cleansed him of secret faults, helps him against his adversaries and redeems him.
comments.comment: If the words exist from you, then the words of my mouth are for acceptance; for I have previously prayed to you, praising you and thanking you; and the words of acceptance are worthy. The study of my intellect, occurring in thoughts and notions, is found always before you, free from all reproach. However, the praiseworthy study is not from another but has risen from you, having cleansed me from my secret faults. With you helping, O Lord, I fall not to any who fight against me spiritually. But if, through my inattention, I should be seized by the adversaries, you redeem me from those who have seized me, as you are found to be my helper and redeemer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The afflicted learn to pour themselves out to God in prayer, and the name of the God of Jacob protects them because Jacob's many sufferings made his life a symbol of the athletic life of enduring trials.
comments.comment: … 'The Lord will hear you in a day of affliction.' Through progress, the afflicted learns not to be meager nor to cast down hopes, but to pour out himself to God through prayers; for prayer leads to hearing God. He does not urge the afflicted to pray in order to appear pious; 'The Lord will hear you in a day of affliction, and the name of the God of Jacob will protect you' (Psalm 20:1). The presence of God, which has been made to dwell in Jacob, being a shield, is from you. One should seek why, God having enriched Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the name of the God of Jacob, and not the God of Abraham and Isaac, protects the afflicted. Perhaps it is because, since Jacob has become in many sufferings and hardships as if his life were a symbol of the athletic life, the afflicted, practicing to endure tribulations and contending against them, is protected by the presence of God, which is that of Jacob, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names the God of Jacob in the day of trouble.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'all' points to a multitude, since God does not remember a small sacrifice, and the burnt offering is fattened when it is given over to the Spirit, the intelligible fire.
comments.comment:
“May he send you help from the holy place, and from Zion may he support you; may he remember all your sacrifice, and may your whole-burnt-offering be fattened” (Psalm 20:2-3).

You will be delivered, he says, bringing to him thankfully a spiritual sacrifice; “all” indicates multitude, for he does not remember a small one. And a whole-burnt-offering is fattened when it is given over to the whole intelligible fire, the Spirit; and this will be when those who offer happen to be spiritual.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Out of Zion' is read first as the heavenly Zion, and the sacrifice remembered is a spiritual one offered with thanks, while the burnt offering differs from the sacrifice in being a living victim.
comments.comment: … The first reading is understood as 'Out of the heavenly Zion of God'. 'May all your sacrifice be remembered', he prays, signifying this for the one being afflicted: that he will be released from this affliction as if he had offered a sacrifice thankfully, so that God may remember all your sacrifice, which is not such a sacrifice as is being approached, but a spiritual one. 'But also accepting your burnt offering, let it ascend'; it should be noted that a burnt offering differs from a sacrifice. For perhaps the name of sacrifice is laid upon the soulless things brought to the altar, whereas a burnt offering is a living victim.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Zion and the difference between a sacrifice and a burnt offering.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives according to the heart of the one who prays for what he rightly requests, and a counsel is fulfilled when it does not fail in its intentions.
comments.comment: … God gives according to the heart of the one praying, whatever such things he requests; and it is proper to give to God, and it is beneficial to the receiver. For the prayer concerning these things, being done rightly, satisfies God. And 'to fulfill all your counsel'; counsel, that is, to fulfill the counsel being done rightly. And a counsel is fulfilled if it does not fail in its intentions, but meets those things about which it was pre-counseled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God grants the heart's desire and fulfils the counsel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To speak of salvation is to speak of the salvation in which there will be rejoicing, and to be magnified in the name of the Lord, unlike being magnified in worldly things, signifies progress in goodness.
comments.comment: … It is said that to speak of salvation is to speak of the salvation which is being saved, to whom God hearkens in a day of affliction, in which salvation there will be rejoicing. And 'we shall be magnified in the name of the Lord our God'. Unlike those being magnified in worldly things, we 'shall be magnified in the name of the Lord our God'. 'We shall be magnified' signifies progress in such goodness. For it does not say: 'We are great'. In this way, Isaac, as he went forward, became greater, as he became very great. And someone is magnified in the name of the Lord by performing the work of a genuine and perfect servant. A great encomium regarding that about which the word is: 'all his requests shall be fulfilled by the Lord, asking nothing which God does not provide'. And the fulfillment of requests is to emerge and come into abundance regarding those things for which someone was worthy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm is spoken of Christ's human economy and perhaps of all believers, his members, who may have salvation, and 'Now I know' means we know Christ is saving now.
comments.comment: The hypothesis of the psalm is taken, and it is spoken regarding the human economy [God's plan of salvation]. Perhaps it is also for all those believing, fulfilling the body of Christ according to the teaching that not even Christ is one body, but many members; Christ is said to be saved, and those who have become his body and members may have salvation (1 Cor 12:27). And also to say 'Now I know'—for 'now' means in this present age we know Christ is saving, receiving the earnest of salvation from hereafter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's right hand, his Word, makes salvation with power.
comments.comment: He hearkens to Christ according to every foretold repayment. And the right hand of God, that is, his Word, makes salvation, not by chance, but with power, like a best general or king.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Horses and chariots are the passions, but God's approach is our defense.
comments.comment: … thinking of horses, the skittish powers of passions that ride upon them; and chariots, the concord of the rushing passions prepared against us. But even if not in these things, the unvanquishable defense of us is the approach of God.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the horses and chariots stand for and where our defense lies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who trust in horses are deceived, as the Egyptians were when they were crushed in the Red Sea, while the saints are the ones who have risen and been set upright.
comments.comment: They are being deceived, having learned through experience that 'a false horse is for salvation.' Concerning those fighting in this way, the choir of the saints says: 'These are in chariots and these are on horses, but we shall rejoice in the name of the Lord; they themselves were overthrown and fell, but we have risen and been set upright' (Psalm 20:7). Similarly to these, the tyrant of Egypt and all those marshaled with him were dejected when they were crushed in the Red Sea, as a victory hymn began to be sung against them from: 'I will sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; he has thrown horse and rider into the sea' (Ex 15:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse prays for King David now.
comments.comment: “Lord, save your king, and hear us” (Psalm 20:9). And now, for the present, save for us the king David.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The king's successes came not by the power of the man but from the power given to the man, as Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God.
comments.comment: Has the success not occurred in those things in which it is necessary to rejoice and be glad? These successes have not happened by the power of the man, but from the power to the man. Likewise, Paul says the resurrection of the Savior happens in this way: "He was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God" (2 Corinthians 13:4). We do not say the life is living by the power of God, nor the power is living by the power of God. "Having been put to death in the flesh, he was made alive in the spirit." He is put to death in the flesh, not put to death in divinity. We understand these things said about the man because: "the king shall rejoice in your power" (Psalm 21:1); for even if he has prevailed over wars and subjected them and "given authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions" (Luke 10:19), this has happened by power; for this power strengthened the existing temple and the king himself to become the "author of salvation" (Hebrews 2:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every saint is a king, and the verse says 'he shall be made glad' and not 'he rejoices', because the gladness comes when its time comes.
comments.comment: Every one of the saints, therefore, is a king. And they were saying that what is fitting for the Savior also fits the righteous, even if in a diminished and lesser way. He says therefore also concerning each saint: 'Lord, in your power the king shall be made glad.' And he did not say 'he rejoices,' but 'he shall be made glad.' When the time of gladness is, then he shall be made glad.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'shall be made glad' and applies it to each saint.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse can be said of David: having ruled well, he shall receive a reward and enter into the joy of God.
comments.comment: Therefore, this can also be said specifically concerning David and concerning his human and sensible kingship, that having ruled the kingdom well, he shall receive a reward upon it; for each one, when he has been entrusted with what, if he endures well, has a reward upon them. Becoming faithful over a little, he enters 'into the joy' (Matthew 25:21) of the neighbor and of God.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain historical reading of the verse about King David.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Power can mean the king's camp or capacity, and Christ is the power of God, so the king rejoices in that power; the king is David historically, the man from Mary, and those who imitate him.
comments.comment:
And power also signifies capacity. And the king's camp also signifies it: 'he cast Pharaoh's chariots and his power into the sea' (Exodus 15:4). 'A king is not saved by much power,' by much hand and camp. The Savior, therefore, apart from these things signified, is called the power of God; for by what word the Father is able, not having this from power, but from essence, and his essence, according to which he is able, might be called power, so also the Son. He says therefore: 'he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God' (2 Corinthians 13:4). … The power, therefore, of God is Christ, as he is God. 'In the power' therefore 'the king rejoices' (Psalm 21:1). …

Kings are to be understood historically as David, by upward leading as the man from Mary, and by imitation and following as those who imitate him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king upon Zion is truly king, rejoicing in divine joy from God's power, and the whole psalm concerns Christ the king.
comments.comment: … the one established as king upon Zion is truly and certainly king, rejoicing in divine joy from the power of God present to him. And let the whole psalm be interpreted concerning Christ the king and the one co-reigning with him, so that we are not compelled to signify this for every single word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king rejoices over salvation as over power, for salvation and power are one thing seen in two ways, since all God does in men he does for their salvation.
comments.comment: And 'he will rejoice exceedingly in your salvation' (Psalm 21:1). The king, just as he is gladdened by power, so also rejoices exceedingly over salvation. And salvation and power are the same, being understood according to one or another conception. Power is that which sustains all things and leads all things thus as it thinks. So also it is salvation; for what he does, he does for the sake of salvation—what he does in men, he does for the sake of the salvation of men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One strengthened by the Spirit receives from God the desire of his heart, and even a needy man is not denied because of the prayer of his lips.
comments.comment: He does not fulfill the desire of the flesh, but walks by the Spirit (Gal 5:16). One strengthened by the Spirit receives the desire of the heart from God. For he, having abstained from the cravings of the flesh, hungers—that is, the mind hungers—and receives from God, who implants his desire in good things. But even if someone happens to be in need, he was not denied by the Lord because of the prayer of his lips.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose heart's desire God grants and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The desire of the soul itself, with nothing bad added to it, is a desire for good things, unlike the desire of the lover of silver.
comments.comment: You gave him the desire of his soul. You know that the word 'himself' denotes authority, not merely the things adjacent. The desire of the soul is bad when, assuming a bad soul, one says 'soul'. But when I say that the soul itself has desire, I speak of its essential desire. The one using desire in this way sees nothing of the bad things, but of the good things; for he received the desiring faculty and the desire, so that he might pursue the beautiful things, so that he might enjoy the profitable things. If, therefore, it happens that he is a lover of silver of wealth, he did not receive the desire of his own soul, but the desire of the lover of silver. Great, therefore, is the happening of the desire of the soul, without adding 'the bad' to it. Indeed, in another psalm he also says: 'the one filling your desire with good things' (Psalm 103:5). He speaks to the soul. … Thus indeed it is said: 'every desire of a righteous man is good.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the verse is about the one born of Mary, his petition is his intercession for those he came to save, and for the saints, who are also kings, it is their prayer being received.
comments.comment: … And he did not withhold his lips' petition from him. If the word is about the one from Mary, it is clear that he brings a petition for those for whom he has come to save. You have indeed: 'wherefore also he is able to save to the perfection, always living to intercede for them'. … He always lives in interceding. And take 'always' thus: as much as they need, entreating and mediating. 'And if anyone sins, we have a counselor toward the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous' (1 John 2:1). … Even if we speak about the saints—for they too are called kings—and there is great praise for them, it is when their petition is well-received.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God preceded the king in blessings of goodness, as in 'while you are still speaking I will say: behold, I am here,' answering a prayer for virtue before its words are finished.
comments.comment: 'For you have preceded him in blessings of goodness' (Psalm 21:3). God has preceded the king in all interpretations in blessings of goodness. The 'you have preceded in blessings' is equal to: 'While you are still speaking I will say: behold, I am here' (Isaiah 58:9). For example, suppose a certain prayer is being sent up concerning living well, concerning having virtue; it says: 'while you are still speaking,' not yet having fulfilled the word of the prayer, because of the giving, I say I am present.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God goes before the king with blessings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One is crowned from his own works, with the crown of righteousness or of glory.
comments.comment: One is crowned from his own works and practices. Without doubt, he who has justly pursued the just shall receive the crown of righteousness (2 Tim 4:8), and he who has rightly glorified the Trinity shall bring the incorruptible crown of glory (1 Pet 5:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the crown on the head stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who has stored up precious stones of virtue is crowned with them, and those known to Christ may become a crown set on his head.
comments.comment:
But also he who has treasured precious stones with gold and silver, from which he worked precious stones, shall be crowned, God restoring to him the head of the soul with the crown of precious stones; and being adorned with divine power in every virtue, he is called, 'All a good stone you have bound.' …

And since the apostle writes to his own disciples, 'Joy and my crown' (Phil 4:1), perhaps also those who are known to Christ, being precious stones through virtuous character, having placed a crown, will be set upon the head of Christ …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the imitator of Christ asked life, God gave him eternal life, and if Christ asked, the Father gave it to make the dead alive.
comments.comment: He asked life from you and you gave it to him. If the imitator of Christ is the one concerning whom the Word is, God has given eternal life to him who asked life from him; for the gift of God is eternal life (Romans 6:23). But if he speaks concerning Christ, regarding the one who asked life from him, the Father gave, so that he might vivify the dead (Eph 2:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who asked for life and what the gift is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king asked for length of days to have them immortally, and each description of thought is a certain day.
comments.comment: He asked to have obtained the length of days, so that he might have them immortally and without end. The length of days is received also by the one who has enlightened himself with the light of knowledge, as if he had a doctrine of truth enlightened within him; for each description of thought is a certain day.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The length of days asked for is not a span of perceptible days but the life of the coming age, in which each doctrine of truth and each virtue is a shining day.
comments.comment:
They desire this long life, because they consider no other good than such a state. Just as life now is praiseworthy and forthcoming, so also 'length of days' for this age, so that each doctrine of truth may be known and illuminating, having great light. A praiseworthy day is each practical virtue being made straight. …

Thus, if you take the king, and even the holy man, and even him who has come forth from Mary, they do not pray about that life or length of perceivable days, but about those already spoken of. They receive long-age life and offer thanks concerning this. And the long-age life is not the life of one age. Appropriately, each age receives life, sometimes as beginning and introductory, sometimes as intermediate, and sometimes as complete.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The glory and magnificence laid upon the Savior are his working what is fitting in great things, and through his arrival they became an addition, as through the cross.
comments.comment: … Let us come from being led by the sensible things to the things about which the word is: the Savior worked the appropriate in great things. And the righteous man shows the appropriate in great things toward men. What is greater than saving the inhabited world, and making peace not only of the earthly things, but also of the heavenly things? What is greater than rectifying that by which the heavenly, the earthly, and the subterranean things bend the knee to the Savior for the glory of God the Father? … This glory is magnificence, and it has a kinship with propriety. … 'Glory and magnificence You will lay upon him' (Psalm 21:5). And it is good also to say 'You will lay upon.' In another text, this is also attributed to Him: for not only now when He arrived, did He begin to place this glory and this magnificence in the rational things, but always and everywhere, as He was able, He did this. And the glory and magnificence through His arrival have become an addition, such as through the cross.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The glory in God's salvation is great because that salvation reaches mind and soul, so even the seeming dishonour of the cross is a glory surpassing all.
comments.comment:
In the salvation of God, therefore, there is 'great glory'; for this salvation touches the mind and the soul. And of all that is in us, the mind differs and the soul from the body, even if it does not seem so to others. And it is possible even to call the Savior himself 'salvation', as he is found in many places: 'All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God' (Psalm 98:3). 'And all flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Isaiah 40:5), instead of 'every man' or 'every sensitive soul'. In this salvation, therefore, is 'great glory'.

Even if the death which he received seems to be without honor—for 'cursed is everyone hanging on a tree' (Gal 3:13) according to the law—yet this seeming dishonor was able to receive such glory from the purpose of salvation, because salvation has become not of food, nor of men simply, but of soul and mind and spirit, as Paul writes: 'Your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23). The seeming dishonor is therefore a glory surpassing all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's salvation brings great glory, the glory of the resurrection, to the king raised from the dead and those rising with him, and the blessing given to him for ages is the blessing by which he blesses those who approach him.
comments.comment: The salvation of God acquires great glory for the king raised from the dead and for everyone rising together with him (Psalm 21:5). You will lay glory and majesty upon him, this glory which is according to the resurrection. And 'you will lay upon' signifies that even before this glory he had another, according to 'I glorified and again I will glorify.' And majesty is that which is becoming in great things. The becoming in great things has not happened concerning the Savior alone. For what is greater than to raise the dead and to walk upon the sea and his enormous miracles among those nearby? But even from his rising from the dead, the becoming in great things has exceeded for him; for he was taken up into the heavens and sat at the right hand of the Father, 'For you will give him blessing unto the age of ages.' All these things have exceeded for him, that blessing is given to him for the age of ages from the Father, by which he blesses those approaching him; then especially the curse having been turned for our sake, he redeemed us from the curse of the law regarding becoming mortal, through the blessing of Abraham (Galatians 3:13-14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the glory and the lasting blessing mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessing that lasts unto the age of ages differs from what mortals call blessing, such as wealth that departs with material life, for what is done in truth remains while a blessing by supposition is dissolved.
comments.comment: For 'You will give him a blessing unto the age of ages' (Psalm 21:6). Thus, as we have said concerning life: not so that he himself may have it—for he has it—but that those who approach him, those who occupy themselves with his teachings, may have it. But this 'unto the age of ages' blessing is distinguished from what seems among mortals to be blessing; for this too is sometimes called blessing: 'for in his life his soul shall be blessed, unto the age he shall not see light' (Psalm 49:18). He shall not see the light, even if he seems now to see bright things. He does not have this glory as lasting. The spiritual blessings, then, given in the heavenly places, are the same as this remaining 'unto the age of ages'; for if one should consider having received wealth a blessing, he does not have it 'unto the age of ages'; for it departs together with the material life. But it is possible to say gracefully and ethically that: if the one having wealth spends it in such a way as to find glory even after these things, concerning which he says: 'Charge the rich of this age not to be high-minded' (1 Tim 6:17). Then he says: 'laying up for themselves a foundation of good works' (1 Tim 6:19); the blessing of such a one remains 'unto the age of ages'. And the things done from wealth remain indestructible. Likewise also in the case of the others: if one is glorified and blessed for temperance—true temperance—he has it remaining 'unto the age of ages'. but if one thinks he is blessed for virtue in hypocrisy, he has it being dissolved; for when the truth shines forth and things appear as they are by nature, the blessing according to supposition is dissolved. Sometimes it even causes danger.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes a blessing last for ever, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gladdens him with joy by gladdening his face, or both God and his face gladden him.
comments.comment: 'You will gladden him with joy with your face' (Psalm 21:6). The word seems ambiguous; for on the one hand is signified by it: 'You will gladden him with joy with your face'; gladdening your face, you gladden him also. or both gladden him: you gladden him with joy, and your face with you gladdens him. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The same joy from God and from his face comes to the king who hopes in God, for the face is the exact imprint of God's hypostasis [the distinct person], and the king conformed to it rejoices.
comments.comment: 'Rejoice him in joy before your face' (Psalm 21:6). Oh, the same grace and peace are given from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, the seed from God, such that the same joy from God and from his face comes to be; for the face is the exact imprint of his hypostasis. And these things shall happen concerning the king, hoping in God the Lord, finding himself being of those who hope. For having approached the expected things through experience, he rejoices before the face of God. And otherwise: since your image is a face, and this is the God the Word, the king becoming with this face makes his temple profitable and, becoming conformed to him, rejoices in joy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rejoicing in the face of God comes to the Savior and to every righteous man, in whom the face through which he became in image and likeness shall be revealed.
comments.comment: Concerning the one having taken on a face by the Savior and every righteous man, it is said: "rejoice him in joy with your face" (Psalm 21:6), for when the Son and the Father come, and someone has seen the character immediately and the one of whom the character is: "he who has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). Rejoicing happens by God and of his own face. And it is also possible to take it this way: "rejoice him in joy with your face." Therefore, this is said concerning every righteous man: for your face, through which "in image and likeness" (Gen 1:26) it has become, shall be revealed of him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Anointed by the Most High, the king possesses an impassable priesthood after the order of Melchizedek.
comments.comment: Having received oil from the Most High to be anointed with oil of exultation, he possesses an impassable priesthood from the anointing, according to the order of Melchizedek, a priest unto the age (Psalm 21:7). For that he shall not be shaken shows that he will not soon see the worthiness from which he is shaken.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king hopes in the Lord that there will be salvation for those for whom he came to suffer, and since hope is the expectation of good things from God, his hope does not fall and he is not shaken by the mercy of the Most High.
comments.comment:
For the king hopes in the Lord (Psalm 21:7; LXX 20:7). This king hopes in the Lord. He hopes that there will be salvation for those for whom he has come to suffer. The end of the one striving is not in doubt. But he hopes unchangeably; for 'in the mercy of the Most High he is not shaken' (Psalm 21:7). Therefore his hope does not fall. And I offer a paradigm, though it is perhaps a violent one: no one hopes for things present. The healthy man does not hope to be healthy, nor the rich man to be rich. It is of things to come. Hope and expectation are the same. Expectation is a genus of hope; for hope is indeed the expectation of good things from God. …

He says, therefore: 'Rejoice in him with joy; for the king hopes in the Lord' (Psalm 21:7). The king is the one hoping. And his hope and expectation are unpassable. And he says: 'In the mercy of the Most High he shall not be shaken' (Psalm 21:7). He being shown mercy by the Most High is not shaken; for then he is shaken, when the subjects are found unworthy of his kingship. And he abandons them, he turns away from them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the king's hope is and why he is not shaken.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A hand and a right hand are both named of God, and the hand is found against enemies while the right hand finds those who hate him, who may be less evil than enemies, since every enemy hates but not every hater acts as an enemy.
comments.comment:
'May your hand be found against all your enemies, and may your right hand find all those hating you' (Psalm 21:8). Just as also regarding the body there is a difference between the right and the hand; for the right hand is a hand, but not every hand is a right hand. We also have here a hand and a right named concerning God.

… for they must at some time know that He is a judge, even if not in this life, but when the time comes. Therefore it is said: 'May your hand be found.' 'May your right hand find.' But the hand is found against enemies, and the right hand finds those who hate. And those who hate may be slightly less evil than the enemies. Not every hater acts as an enemy, but every enemy hates.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between the hand and the right hand, and between enemies and those who hate.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's hand is found for all his enemies, bringing punishments, and those who do not keep his commandments hate him, so the right hand of the Savior is asked to bring them to prosperity.
comments.comment: His hand is not found for a few, but for all the enemies of God, bringing punishments upon them and warring against those set against the divine law, according to 'The Lord fights with a hidden hand against Amalek' (Exodus 17:16). And perhaps he means by enemies those bringing in thoughtlessness and embracing ungodliness. For if these do not set God before them, the hand would be found distressing them and bringing rebuke upon them, so that then they might know what God stands over of those who sin. He says 'hating God' here regarding those committing sin. For if in keeping the commandments the love of the perfect God is completed, according to 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word' (John 14:23), he who does not keep the word and the commandments of God hates God. And he who hates thus is said to be perishing. Since there is no expectation of the Savior coming, the right hand of God, to seek and save the lost, it is fittingly said: 'May your right hand bring all who hate you to prosperity' (Psalm 21:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hand is set upon punishments and the right hand upon salvation and other good things, so the hand is found punishing the enemies and the right hand is found for those who hate God.
comments.comment: But by what does the right hand differ according to the writings? One should consider the hand set upon punishments, as 'Your hand has utterly destroyed them' (Psalm 44:2), and 'Now having sent the hand, I will strike you' (Exodus 9:15) (and indeed 'The hand of the Lord has laid hold of me' Job 10:1); but the right hand is upon salvation and other good things; for 'His right hand saved him', and 'He made the right hand of the Lord a power', and 'The right hand of the Lord saved me' (Ps 18:35), and such things. It is fitting, then, that even here he says the hand is found punishing the enemies, but the right hand is found for those who hate Him, so that they might be found no longer in destruction.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Falling out of sins and wicked thoughts is a benefaction.
comments.comment:
“Let your hand be found to all your enemies; let your right hand find all who hate you” (Psalm 21:8).

It is a benefaction to fall out of sins and wicked thoughts; for a wicked reasoning is a seed of sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The furnace does not annihilate those in it: gold and silver are only burned, while wood, hay and straw are consumed as such, since the fire of punishment works upon states and qualities and not upon essence.
comments.comment: You have set them as a furnace of fire for the time of your face. Concerning the enemies alone can it be said of those being handed over to punishment. But if even concerning both, thus interpret what is written: See, those building upon the foundation, the Christ, if they are gold or silver, they are only burned, but they are not annihilated, nor are they consumed even if found by the fire (1 Cor 3:12-15). But if 'wood, hay, or straw,' they are annihilated and laid down like a furnace of fire, for they are like smoke. And the smoke is a follower of the beneficial energy of the fire. Therefore, when wood and hay and straw are 'for the time of the face' of God—for it will be a time when a judge shall be shown, as it lies—those called wood and hay and straw do not be annihilated so as to no longer exist—and it is impossible to be annihilated in this way … but as they are hay, they are annihilated; for this fire of punishment does not work upon essence, but upon states and qualities.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Teaching makes the ignorant vanish only as ignorant, and to be confounded is to begin to waver and repent, so that the fire devours them and they are no longer such.
comments.comment: … teaching does the same: it takes the ignorant and makes him vanish, not as a man, but as an ignorant person; for it makes his ignorance vanish. In this way, righteousness makes the unrighteous vanish, not so that he no longer exists, but so that he no longer exists as unrighteous. Lord, in your wrath confound them, and let fire devour them (Psalm 21:9). Someone is confounded when he begins to waver and repent. And 'let fire devour them' means so that they no longer are such.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly that the fire of 21:9 destroys ignorance and wickedness, not the person.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The furnace is not a continual punishment but belongs to the time of the shining of the divine face, and God sets punishments to meet those able to behold his face, as a furnace burns for a useful purpose like baking bread.
comments.comment: … I think it is meant that they shall be cast upon the enemies; not that anyone is handed over for punishment to be cast as a furnace of fire always and continually, but as at the time of the shining of the divine face. And there also, 'the time' signifies not a duration of time but the kind of state of those capable of receiving the face of God. And I think also that the mention of the furnace was not in vain; for just as a furnace does not burn in vain or by chance, but for some useful purpose in baking bread or something similar, so also God sets punishments at the time to encounter such people as may be able to behold His face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked are not consumed by a wholly physical fire but by one that follows the disease of the soul and consumes the quality of their wickedness, not their essence.
comments.comment:
Those being disturbed by wickedness and false glory, being agitated by the allurements of pleasure, God shall shake in His wrath, and those being disturbed by the expectation of punishment.

But these are not consumed by a fire that is entirely physical, but by that which follows the disease of the soul; rather, when the soul repents for the evils it has done, a penalty of fire pierces it, or when dissatisfaction arises in it, a fire analogous to the diseases of the body is generated. For just as bodily foods, when consumed beyond what is necessary, having a disease-causing quality, raise fevers in those who have eaten them, so too, from these foods, a fitting fire will follow the wickedness and the worthless doctrines; it consumes them not by destroying their soul's essence (for it is indestructible) but their quality, according to which wood becomes hay, stubble, or weeds, so that when the things that joined them are consumed, the pure essence that was bound remains visible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Seed' means a plant's seed when set against fruit and a man's seed when set against children.
comments.comment: 'You shall destroy their fruit from the earth and their seed from the sons of men' (Psalm 21:10). The 'seed' is a homonym. When contrasted with fruit, it denotes the seed of a plant; but when contrasted with children, it is the seed of a man; for we have in the Scripture many times the 'seed' named after children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two senses of 'seed' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fruit destroyed from the earth is the works of the flesh borne by those who clung to the earth, and the seed destroyed is their fitness for worthless fruit, so that the seed of wickedness is prevented.
comments.comment: This says: being upon the earth and having drawn near to the earth, they were stuck to it. Instead of the pure soul, the works of the flesh bore fruit. This is 'you shall destroy the fruit from the earth.' The earth is the good and beautiful thing, which, receiving the seed of Jesus that is cast, bears fruit. But the same earth, as a subject, is this one that bears thorns. And the receptive one is a rational substance of seeds. And from ourselves, this earth receives the difference. 'And their seed from the sons of men' (Psalm 21:10). He sowed into the sons of men, not into the sons of God; for they are unfit for these. 'From the sons' therefore, 'of men you shall destroy their seed,' so that also the fitness toward the worthless fruit is lost. If someone has virtue by operation, the seed of wickedness is prevented, …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Their essence is not perishing but they bore fruit badly, and God destroys the seed of those who sowed wicked teaching.
comments.comment: And here it is shown not that their essence is perishing, but that they bore fruit badly: 'for your works are weary and worthless' (Psalm 21:10). Just as plants bearing perfect fruit project seed from that fulfilled fruit to become plants similar to themselves, so those having borne the seed of teachings in wickedness and impiety are cast down to make others like them, worthless and impious. God destroys this seed from among the sons of men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Their choice turned toward evil, and the one who does right receives praise.
comments.comment: 'Because they turned to you for evil' (Psalm 21:11), to you, having made them straight. Their choice turned toward the evil. You know that regarding sensible creations and idols, the one who has worked the evil work receives mockery, but the one who has done what is right receives praise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who wished to build a tower could not stand, while God perfects counsel rightly deliberated.
comments.comment: … those who wished to build a tower, having the head up to the very limit, deliberated and were not able to stand. Indeed, they scattered. God perfects counsel when it is deliberated rightly and according to his will. He who pursues this 'does all things according to his counsel.' By this counsel, God brings a completion. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evil is accomplished by turning aside and not by straightness, and the worthless deliberate treacherously against one who will not suffer harm, so their plan cannot stand because wickedness is unstable.
comments.comment: 'They turned evil toward him' (Psalm 21:11) referring to the false doctrines concerning Him, attributing the cause of wickedness to Him; and the traitors and enemies of Him, having been proven, turned evil toward the Savior. It should be noted that evil is accomplished by turning aside, and not by straightness, as the good are seeds. For all the worthless, having turned aside, act against the incapable; for they deliberate treacherously against the one who will not suffer harm. Perhaps also every evil man, through whom one sins, deliberates a plan that is unable to stand, because wickedness is unstable and not abiding.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The things set at God's heels are put behind his body, the church, as Moses was shown the things behind, while the face is prepared in his remnants for the saints who pray for it.
comments.comment: "You shall set them at their heels." It is often said of those concerning God that his body is the church; "you are the body of Christ," and in this body eyes, ears, and hands are found. Therefore, "you shall set" "them at their heels." You shall arrange these behind your body. This can be understood thus: the preceding things are called the face of God, and these created, sensible things are behind; for they are with him. Indeed, just as Moses at the end was not able to behold the face of God, God passes by with his glory and shows him the things behind. Indeed, he immediately wrote down the generation. Therefore, he shall set them at their heels; for the face is set toward the saints according to the prayer they offer up: "let your face shine upon us and we shall be saved." "In your remnants you will prepare your face." The remnants are the other saints besides those who "hate," those who were left over in the destruction. And it is well that it is "you will prepare" and not "you will give." It holds it ready so that everyone wishing to see it is able to see it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not turn away but sets them low, and the remnants of God are the things above his sensible creations.
comments.comment: 'For you will set them low; with the remnant you will prepare their face' (Psalm 21:12). God does not turn away; He sets these low, making them capable of being a face. … Therefore he says: 'And in your remnants you prepare their face' (Psalm 21:12), for the remnants of God are those things above His sensible creations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Israel would be destroyed as killers of the Lord yet Jerusalem would not perish altogether but be set at the back, and all Israel will be saved once the flock from the nations is gathered.
comments.comment: He [the Lawgiver] knew that for this reason the people of Israel would be destroyed as killers of the Lord and as men who had savagely abused the Son; yet Jerusalem would not perish altogether, root and all. She would remain like a woman bereft of children, waiting for the last time, at the end, when she too will be saved, running behind the nations. For she has been set at the back, that is, behind, as the Psalmist’s words have it: ‘For he will put them at the back’ (Psalm 21:12). For all Israel will be saved, once the flock from the nations has first been gathered into the divine folds (Romans 11:25–26).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: To exalt God is not to lift him from low to high but to confess him, and the power that rejoices the king and does all these things is no longer thought lowly by men.
comments.comment: "Be exalted, O Lord, in your power." We shall sing and indeed chant your mighty acts. For you do all these things powerfully. And after the beginning of the chanting, the power of God is praised: "Lord, the king shall rejoice in your power." The power that rejoices the king and performs all the things spoken of is exalted, not rising from a low place to a height, but no longer being thought of by men as lowly, but high as it is. And if we say, "I will exalt you, O Lord," we do not mean that we are lifting you up from the low to the height. To exalt is to confess him; that is the height. Therefore, he sings triumphantly—for power is spoken of a king alone, and of this king there are powers—things that can be done kingly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to exalt the Lord in his power.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king took up weakness and was crucified out of weakness, and so we see and sing of his powers as a triumphal king against the devil and the opposing powers.
comments.comment: Since descending with our weakness, you took up something weak, O He who is stronger than men, having been crucified out of weakness, 'Exalt yourself in your power' (Psalm 21:13). It is terrible to take up through contemplation, but to sing is to act according to virtue. Contemplating the intelligible of the powers and acting according to them, we see and sing of your powers, you who ruled as a triumphal king against the devil and the opposing powers. It is also possible to declare the graciousness: we cry out to you, having ruled against death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title 'the morning perception' speaks of a spiritual day, in which a person lit by the true light acts decently.
comments.comment:
The morning perception; a psalm of David. It is a spiritual day being made by the 'Sun of Righteousness,' about which much is laid down in the Scriptures, and especially in the New; 'as in a day,' he says, 'let us walk decently' (Romans 13:13). You know that even according to the literal sense, those doing something shameful do so in darkness, and especially then, when many good people were present. He who is, therefore, in ignorance of the existing good, is in darkness and does many things bringing shame. But when one is illumined by the light of the true one, 'walking in the day,' that is, progressing—for walking signifies progress—he does and thinks all things decently, nothing of those bringing shame.

The prophet Isaiah also presents this state, saying: 'My spirit cries out to you, O God, in the night' (Isa 26:9). This, therefore, is the morning perception; for even if we have illumination and the beginning of the day, we beg for the light to be present, so that the day may not fail, so that it may not be unable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The whole psalm is spoken in one person, the Savior, since the New Testament takes three of its sayings as his.
comments.comment:
Listen then: this psalm is single-personed. That which says 'person' from the beginning until the end is the same. And there occur often in psalms and in prophecies shifts of persons, both of those speaking and toward what is being said and concerning what is being said; for everyone who speaks carries the person of the one announcing. And since he does not speak as it happens, but speaks to certain people, there is also a second person: the one hearing the speaker and the matter concerning which he announces. The speaking part therefore is one person here.

And many things were taken from this psalm in the New Covenant, as if spoken from the person of the Savior, the one the psalm is said to be. Entirely this is so: 'the God, my God' (Ps 22:1); the Savior, encountering the cross, said this voice. And 'they divided my garments among themselves' (John 19:24) was also said by the Savior, having been said in the Gospels. And 'I will announce your name to my brothers' (Hebrews 2:12); Paul in the Hebrews wrote that this was said from the person of the Savior. Since, therefore, three testimonies lie here from the psalm, that the speaker is the person of the Savior, the whole psalm must be received as having been announced from his person.
comments.selected_reason: Tells the reader who is speaking in the psalm and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word was not weak before the plots against him; the cry speaks of human nature, forsaken by God when Adam broke the command, and so cursed and held by death.
comments.comment: “And Jesus cried with a loud voice: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” So then — do we say that even the Word from God the Father himself needed help from above? And yet how is this not altogether silly? For he co-rules all things with God the Father, and he established the heavens by his own spirit, and he is named — and truly is — Lord of the powers. Or did he grow weak before the Jews’ plots, and was the hand of those crucifying him unmatched against him? … Know that the servants of the Jews’ synagogue were present with the cohort of soldiers, and the traitor leading; and when they sought to seize him he met them saying: “Whom do you seek?” And they said to this: “Jesus the Nazarene.” Then the Savior to them: “I am.” And they went back and fell to the ground (John 18:4–6). Then how would he have grown weak — he who by the voice alone exposed the weakness of those plotting? What then does he mean by saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1) (Matthew 27:46) We say that when the first father Adam trampled the command given him and disregarded the divine laws, human nature was somehow forsaken by God, and for this became also cursed and held by death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the cry 'why have you forsaken me' does not mean the Word needed help.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: To be forsaken is to have God turn away, which happens to those who sacrifice but not to martyrs, and the Savior asks the cause so that his body may learn it.
comments.comment:
'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). The name of the forsaking, when spoken literally, does not reveal becoming being in darkness. For the martyrs, indeed, were not forsaken, though they were cast into the boiling pot. But those who sacrifice, even if they suffer nothing, were forsaken. When someone asks not to be forsaken, he asks this so as not to fall from his purpose. It seems that falling into abandonment does not happen to one suffering nothing, but sometimes it happens to him through malice, as I said, of the sacrificers. Abandonment, therefore, is the turning away of God from the one being forsaken.

Which Saul experienced: 'You have not listened to me,' he says, 'nor even in sleep' (1 Samuel 28:6); and he went toward the medium. If ever, therefore, you see a rich Christian having everything well, but having haste toward astrologers or toward necromancers or toward such things, these were forsaken. And if you see a poor man having fallen from wealth, but possessing God, such as Job was (Job 1:1), this one was not forsaken.

Since, therefore, the Savior came to a cross, and it seems to men to be abandonment to fall by such a death, he says this toward their assumption: 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1). Perhaps he also speaks of abandonment as if of his own body; for the Hebrews were a body to him before this. Therefore, that people was forsaken. And he speaks of his own abandonment, since he was their head. 'My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?' (Psalm 22:1); he demands the cause and the end of the abandonment, for what it is.
