'For what reason have you forsaken me?'; he is demanding an end, not so that it might be known to him, but so that it might be known to the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He did not do sin but knew it as a concept, so only the words of transgressions were far from his salvation.
comments.comment: Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions. … Not "are far from my salvation"; for he did not know sin, he did not do it. But I have it by concept; I know what sin is. And therefore the words of transgressions were far from my salvation. Let my salvation not take a mixture so as to be darkened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks why he was forsaken, believing it was for something beneficial to all and not for sin.
comments.comment: The voice is inquiring about the cause of the abandonment. Since he possessed a great purity with himself (for sin was not necessary), he did not believe he was being forsaken because of sin, but because of something else that is beneficial to the whole. He does not wish this to become manifest through himself suffering, but through those seeing him; for having known what was forsaken for their sake, they will praise him as Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of transgressions are not the transgressions themselves; the Savior held them far from his salvation and triumphed over the powers behind them on the cross.
comments.comment: Therefore, let us speak the words of the transgressions, not the pronunciations concerning the transgressions. For just as we say a word of heaven by which it has become, and a word of the sun by which it has risen, so also we shall say the words of transgressions, and not that the transgressions themselves drew the Savior into his own body. But his body brought these words of transgressions before the passion, and having risen from the dead—he who is also said to have saved—he held the words of the aforementioned sins far from his salvation, having stripped off the ruling principles and powers that work the transgressions, and he triumphed over them in himself, speaking boldly upon the cross.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Human life has bright days and dark nights; God hears in both, and in the night his mercy is made known even to those being punished.
comments.comment:
O my God, I have cried days to you, and you do not listen, and night, and it does not come to my mind (Psalm 22:2). The state of the life of men is diverse. It has some profitable aspects, and it has some dark aspects. And in these human things there are days, which are called 'day', and dark things, which are named 'night'. This therefore he says: and in the pleasant and bright things toward you I cry, and you listen, and in the night I do this, and it does not come to my mind; for after your departure and the dark things no longer being unclear, it has become manifest to me. He listens to our crying in the days; and at night, that is to say, being in the dark state, we have him helping, and in the matter we have received knowledge that he helps; for this is: 'and at night, and it does not come to my mind'. … the dark things are ignorance and night; 'by day,' he says, 'the Lord commands his mercy, and by night he will make it known' (Psalm 42:8).

When we clearly and readily see men being pitied, God has commanded his mercy by day. And 'by night' he 'will make it known'; for if you know that God also punishes and hands over in order to make his mercy known—for he does not hand over men to punishments crudely—in this night, the dark one, he will establish it, and the mercy of God will be made known. And by day he commands the mercy when his mercy is manifest, and by night; it is possible to manifest it through the darkness of the state of those being punished. However, even if they also despair, he himself will make known even in the night his mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God dwells among the saints, they are not abandoned when they suffer, for he is present in those he teaches.
comments.comment:
'And not unto oblivion of me' (Psalm 22:2); I do not cry out in ignorance at night, I do not cry out in ignorance that you listen. 'But you dwell among the saints, O praise of Israel' (Psalm 22:3). See what he says: you who dwell among the saints and are the praise of all those having pure hearts and seeing you—for such people are Israel—you have not abandoned me; for if you dwell among the saints, and the saints suffer something, they were not abandoned; for how could you be in them, and not simply, but the praise of Israel?

And it is also possible that 'but you dwell among the saints' means this: even if you have surrounded some with a pitiful death and it seems to one that you have withdrawn from me, yet in the saints, in those I teach, in those I think upon, you dwell. If you are in these, I have not been abandoned. And it is possible for the holy things to be taken also upon the blessed logical beings, and upon the holy men, and upon the mysteries of the kingdom of the heavens. For God, being present everywhere, is found in such things, and all such things are his temple, a multi-purpose temple.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's dwelling among the saints means the sufferer is not forsaken.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is himself praise, and Israel praises him.
comments.comment: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel” (Psalm 22:3). From this we learn that the Lord is self-praise and is praised by Israel, or himself being praise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His ancestors by the flesh, not the patriarchs, hoped and were rescued.
comments.comment: The fathers from whom I am according to the flesh (they are not the patriarchs) have hoped in you, desiring my illumination (Psalm 22:4). But having hoped, they did not fail; they were rescued.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be rescued from oppressors means bravely enduring them without harm to the mind, not escaping them, as the witnesses of the truth were saved through their tortures.
comments.comment: For we do not say that to be rescued and saved from those standing around as oppressors means to become something outside of them, but to bravely and through toil endure them, so that the mind might not be harmed by the right intention being cast out by the pains. We say, indeed, that the witnesses of the truth, having suffered ten thousand things and having died by tortures, were rescued and were saved from the tribulations; for those having come to be outside of the tribulations through denial were not only not rescued and saved from the temptations, but were also exhausted by them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fathers who hoped and cried out were heard and saved, not by being taken out of afflictions but by overcoming through them.
comments.comment: Our fathers hoped in you (Ps 22:4). Our fathers, having hoped in you, were heard 'and were not put to shame' (Ps 22:5); for always receiving their prayers, you brought them to a state of favor, even if they should die through afflictions. For that which hears them when they cry out is not that which makes them be outside of the afflictions, but that which is outside of the harm brought by the afflictions; thus also it was interpreted: 'do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). Even if the holy ones praying seem not to be heard, all the more they are heard, because by remaining in afflictions they are proven as athletes. For what a failure it would be if one praying should turn away from the afflictions? Furthermore, 'our fathers' is in the presence of the Savior; you know that he counts himself in many ways according to the human manner. They hoped, and you saved them; they cried out to you and were saved. Not by leading them into nothingness, but by overcoming through afflictions. 'They cried out to you.' Having cried out, they were saved. And the cry we take to be the stretched-out prayer; for we do not cry out with a laughing voice, for thought is the word of the soul, and voice is the sound of the inner man.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being heard and saved means for the fathers who trusted God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He calls himself a worm because his body came not from a man's seed but from simple matter taken from the womb.
comments.comment: I am a worm and not a man (Psalm 22:6). … And this too can be understood: since his body did not come from the casting of a man's seed, but from the mere matter taken from the womb, according to this he calls himself a worm; for the worm does not come from a union, but from simple matter. And here, from the simple matter subject to the female, the body arose for him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why he calls himself a worm in terms of how his body came to be.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As the incarnate God he calls himself a worm, by the lowliness of his flesh.
comments.comment: “But I am a worm” (Psalm 22:6). He speaks as from the person of the incarnate God, even if it is not taken according to the Godhead, but according to the appearing and the lowliness of the flesh: “I am the worm.”
comments.selected_reason: Plainly says in whose person and in what sense he is a worm.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He is called a worm because he hid his divinity like a hook in the worm of his body, to draw up the dragon.
comments.comment: He was called worm: For I am a worm and not a man (Psalm 22:6, LXX 21:7), because he hid his flashing divinity like a hook in the worm of his body, let himself down into this deep of life, and like a good fisherman drew up, to fulfill what is written: You will draw the dragon with a hook (Job 41:1, LXX 40:25).
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: 'All' who saw him did not mean everyone, since the apostles did not mock him, but those who looked on him as a reproach.
comments.comment:
A reproach of men and a disgrace of a people. I am a reproach not simply of men, but of the 'men'. All those who, looking at me, mocked me.

Some wish to falsely make the universal many times; for the universal is sometimes cut and becomes universal in another way. If I say, 'All men are mortal,' I say this universally. But if I say that 'all the grammarians,' I speak of certain men, and the universal has come from the grammarian, not from the man. 'All the diligent are righteous.' I do not say this that 'all men are righteous.' So also here: not all those looking at him mocked him—for indeed the apostles, looking, did not mock him—but all those looking at him in this way as a disgrace of a people, as a reproach; for the others did not look at him in this way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'all' means in 'all they that see me laugh me to scorn'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who speak with the lips and shake the head speak without the heart, with a wavering mind.
comments.comment:
They spoke with lips, they moved the head. If they had spoken from the heart, they would not have moved the head. They spoke with lips to many. And it is not a wonder if they said these things concerning the one who suffered and was seen hanging. And God himself blames them, saying, 'This people honors me with their lips' (Isaiah 29:13). Therefore all the hypocrites, when they rejoice with the holy and the righteous, speak only with lips. And those who indeed boast grandly about the Savior were doing this: 'But he said the one destroying the temple and in three days building it up' (Mark 15:29). …

And often the head signifies the mind. When anyone thus speaks against the Savior with lips without having seen him as he ought to be, he has a shaken mind, he has a wavering mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lips and the shaken head in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's help brought Christ from the womb, and the saints draw hope from the breasts, that is the milk, of the upper Jerusalem, their mother.
comments.comment: 'For you are the one who burst me from the womb.' He said 'to burst' and according to the former probable thought that: since the place in Mary where she gave birth had no opening, she gave birth through the cooperation of God. 'My hope is from the breasts of my mother.' I did not begin to hope after completion, but from the breasts of my mother I had hope in you. If it is understood concerning the holy, we say: the upper Jerusalem is the mother of the saints. From the breasts of this one hope is taken by those who hope, from those who have been discipled by them; for often the breast does not signify the member, but the milk itself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father alone drew the Savior out of the Virgin's womb, and the child of Mary alone had hope from birth, since he was never born in wickedness.
comments.comment: For perhaps he who is conceived of seed, having been brought to completion in the womb, having been filled with the time of birth, is thrust forth from that womb to the outside. But the Father alone thrusts the Savior out from the womb of the Virgin, not having been cast into her from the outside by seed, but having been thrust out from her, from the divine offspring. To other men, hoping and expecting the things to come happens after the fulfillment of the word has come to pass with ages. But the child from Mary alone hopes for perfection; for God holds the hope; for he was never born in wickedness, unlike all men who grasp at the good through ignorance and malice. … Before the becoming-man, Jesus alone possessed intimacy toward the Father; for his Father was God, and he himself was the Son of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: From the womb means from the time he began to know, serving no other god, or, for a few such as John and Jeremiah, having God from birth.
comments.comment: From the womb of my mother, my God, you are (Psalm 22:10). As from the womb of a mother, according to the former explanation from the womb of a mother, Job guides orphans; that is to say, from the womb of a mother, that is to say, from when I began to have knowledge, I served no other god, not my own womb, nor mammon. Or if it is the other, that in this way they descended having God, possessing God. But we do not say this about everyone, but about those who are proclaimed in the Scripture that they have never almost existed in sin, such as John and Jeremiah.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was cast upon God alone from the womb, and from the time he began to know piety he perceived and served God.
comments.comment: 'Upon you I was cast from the womb, from the womb of my mother, my God, you are' (Psalm 22:9). Upon you I was cast; not toward another was I cast, and then after that toward you. This is given, that from when I began to know piety, I perceived you, I served you. And according to the deeper meaning, that in this way I came to have God with me, just as John.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words what being cast upon God from the womb means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He speaks of the coming passion and asks for God's presence, since no one else is able to help.
comments.comment: Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near (Psalm 22:11). He speaks concerning the passion. And I need your presence. … For there is no helper. No one else is able to help. It can also be understood thus: 'for there is not'—I did not cast my care upon another helper. And it can also be: 'for there is no helper to me,' since all are against me, there is no one now, as far as human reasoning goes, who helps. Therefore, do not turn away from me. And it is possible also to say: not even an angel is able to help the one so far off. He does not dare to help because you, being greater than all, that is, the divinity, are present with him, and no one else is of such a kind as to help in this matter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the cry 'be not far from me' and 'there is none to help'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer of Christ as man is addressed to God, the one divinity of Father and Son, who are one in essence though the Father is not the Son.
comments.comment: But when these things are said from the person of the one who was anthropized [made man], it is not said privately toward the Father nor toward the Son, but toward God—one divinity of Father and Son—we say. If, therefore, we say that: 'Christ is the head of every man, but the head of Christ'—he did not say 'the Father', but 'God'; for he receives Christ now as High Priest and as King. Therefore, the head is the divinity. For if 'the Father' has spoken, he excludes the Son; if 'the Son' has spoken, he overlooks the Father; for he has spoken 'God', since there is one divinity of Father and Son, and one God: indeed, God is one, but Father and Son are not one. Abraham and Isaac are one man, but one is the father and the other the son. Therefore, they are not one according to relation, but one according to essence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In trials one should not pray that God be absent, since without God there would be no helper.
comments.comment: To provide endurance as if to bring forth the one being afflicted, but in the absence of God, those surrounding him are strong. He does not rejoice, the one saying the psalm, which becomes a type for us humans and teaches us in trials not to pray that such things might happen to him, so that God might be absent, since in the presence of God he would strike down those raising up affliction. For if God were to depart from someone, there would be no helper for that person (Psalm 22:11-13).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bulls are the various factions of the Jews and the rulers who caused the Lord's crucifixion, who did not know what they were doing.
comments.comment: Many bulls have surrounded me, fattened oxen have enclosed me. Consequently, he speaks of the various factions of the Jews: Pharisees, Sadducees, and the others called Jewish Scribes; for these, in thinking greatly of these animals, are compared to them, especially since these animals are also tillers of the earth. And it is possible to call them bulls, and the fattened oxen are those acting as such, for example: 'the peoples labored in vain' (Psalm 2:1)—these are the bulls. 'The kings of the earth stood up' (Ps 2:2). But we do not always perceive kings and rulers; for even a single king, being small and no longer having a kingdom, has been overtaken by the remaining Roman authority. But Paul interpreted who the rulers are: those who became the cause of the Lord being crucified, of whom he says there are many wisdoms. And he says: 'If they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Corinthians 2:8). If they had known that they were bringing about the destruction of their own order, they would not have dared to do this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the bulls are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bulls are the evil powers, the teachers of false doctrines, the Jews and Pilate, who surround the Lord and his body the church, and the roaring lion may be the devil.
comments.comment:
And if calves and the evil powers working around earthly and bodily things (for this animal is a tiller of the earth), and those presiding over false doctrines through deceptive words and sophisms, they turn out to be fat bulls with horns, being so because of being ostensibly learned and adorned in phrasing. And it is also possible for the Jews, diving into the law from which they find calves, named as such, to surround the Lord hostily; and Pontius Pilate and if there are others existing in the pride of horned bulls, are striving to enclose him.

The Savior says these things also concerning his own body, the church, seeing men as low-dwellers and working the earth, hostily surrounding his body: 'Many calves have surrounded me.' And setting aside from them the thing awakened to evil and the preparation for affliction, he says: 'They opened their mouth against me like a lion seizing and roaring' (Psalm 22:13). For their mouth is opened to seize the deceived; the sophist is the word. Perhaps 'like a lion seizing and roaring' refers to the devil …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who seemed quiet as oxen opened their mouths like a roaring lion against him, crying 'Crucify, crucify him'.
comments.comment: Their mouth is like a roaring lion snatching and roaring. They were prepared to be like oxen. But they changed into ferocity, as if to open their mouth against me, according to the roaring lion; for then especially it harms greatly, when it roars. Therefore, their wildness and their mocking attitude against the Savior signifies—for he says, 'as a roaring lion, they opened their mouth' (Psalm 22:13)—that they are no longer quiet, no longer intending to be quiet. These then, who seemed to be quiet by meditating on the law of God, were oxen, until they desired to open their mouth against me and to say: 'Crucify, crucify him; we have no king but Caesar' (Jn 19:15), according to the lion that was not satisfied, they have done this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the roaring lion by what the crowd cried out against him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The scattering of the apostles, who are his bones, is what the verse says of him, since they hold the body together.
comments.comment: Taking upon himself the suffering, he says these things: it has happened to those who complete his body. Since the sheep did not remain scattered when the shepherd was struck, he says, as Hosea says, 'a gift was poured out' (Hosea 14:7); for the gift having been emptied is scattered. But also concerning the apostles he says, 'All my bones were scattered' (Ps 22:14); for they themselves are his bones because of the good tension and the holding together of the whole body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Poured-out water pictures the disciples scattered at his arrest, and the apostles his bones, but like water they will be gathered again.
comments.comment: Like water I was poured out, and all my bones were scattered (Ps 22:14). He speaks of the scattering of the body here, of them, of the disciples, when all were scandalized and it is filled: 'all you will be scandalized' (Matthew 26:31). And the hour will come when all you will flee, you will go to your own, and you will leave me alone (John 16:32). Just as the water that is being poured out. It always runs and does not stand still; so also here, 'as water they were poured out' (Ps 22:14). He did not say 'they are being poured out,' for they do not remain in such a state always. What he says concerning himself, he says concerning himself regarding the body which is the sum of the faithful of the church. 'My bones'—the support of my body; for the apostles were more supportive than those who believe. And these were scattered. My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly (Psalm 22:14); were his bones scattered? This occurred when the disciples were stumbled. This poured-out water, unless it becomes an obstacle, is always carried along. And the disciples, therefore, were scattered, as if they were poured-out water. When they were around him, they were gathered like river water, being a spring. But when they went out from him, it happened at a certain time, like the water that is poured out. And the water will stand one day; for it is not always carried along. So also the disturbance and the stumbling of the disciples will immediately cease, which has already happened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the poured-out water and scattered bones as the scattering of the disciples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heart of Christ's body is its believers, who melt like wax in the disturbance yet stay within his belly to be formed again.
comments.comment: My heart became like wax melting in the midst of my belly (Psalm 22:14). The heart of this body, which is composed of the sum of those having believed, is the spiritual part. And these, therefore, became like melting wax, those who are the heart of him. However, even if the wax melted, it did not happen outside of his belly; for they are within his belly, so that they may be formed again. After the disturbance, indeed, those who had experienced it were shown again to be sons of the Savior. But what kind of disturbance? It was a passion extended for a little while, not so as to remain. And the melting of the wax does not happen always, but when it melts, it changes into some vessel or some other use, and again it is gathered, not far from the belly of the one producing this heart. But for what purpose the belly? It is the very power of the Savior, through which he forms and begets. If he again produces the procreators of the body, Paul, being of the body, was saying: 'through the gospel I have begotten you' (1 Corinthians 4:15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A heart with matter mixed into its virtues melts like wax, and in this melting the matter falls away from the mind.
comments.comment:
Moreover, 'has my heart become like melting wax?' (Psalm 22:14). I said that what is said about it according to the human might be said also about everything righteous. His heart, when it is not light, but has something material mixed in, melts. But toward the beautiful, the melting happens; for the melting wax does not become outside of the one having it. 'In the midst' therefore 'of my belly.' …

If it possesses the preceding virtues, it is honey. But if, along with those, it has something of matter mixed in, it is wax. For this reason, he says that the sinners melt like wax 'from the presence of fire'. Honey, however, is praiseworthy; it is a preceding substance, and it signifies sweetness. …

Thus a man sometimes melts; the material sometimes falls away from the intellect and the heart, so that the mind no longer has anything entangled with it, but is entirely incorporeal …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His heart melts in love for his scattered disciples, his strength is dried hard by trials, his tongue is silent without hearers, and the dust of death is the mortal body.
comments.comment: Perhaps someone's heart is melting like wax in the midst of the belly (Psalm 22:14), and the soul sees those who have suffered labor pains and those bearing calamity born by it. Since, therefore, the things foretold concerning the disciples of Jesus have happened, his heart being divided toward them lovingly, he endured the passion of wax, burning in the midst of the belly, sympathizing with those he bore. But also the sweetness of the heart was like wax that was melting, and the food became and entered into the stomach; for the thoughts of the heart, having been eaten like wax, descended into the belly, melting and thinning through continuous study, in order that the substance of the eaten might be restored. But also the strength, having been brought into the furnace of life, was dried up like an earthen vessel; for after the experience of tribulations, as one coming out of a furnace, he will receive the dryness of an earthen vessel, no longer being moistened by the moisture of the clay and the flux of pleasures. Of the scattered listeners, no longer being present, the tongue is not active in teaching and conversing, being inactive if it is stuck to the throat; for the one bringing forth a word moves, not being hindered by the sticking to the throat. 'Dust of death' perhaps is to be said, the 'body of death' being named by Paul (Romans 7:24); for this is truly fashioned from the earth. And 'dust of death' is said regarding the one who is born and will die. For if the being laid up is to be entwined with the body, it is necessary also that a dissolution take place, which is death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His strength is dried up like a shell or fired clay, with all moisture and mud cast off, and perhaps all bitterness from the coming affliction.
comments.comment: 'My strength has dried up like a shell' (Psalm 22:15). My strength has cast off all moisture and all liquidity, as if it had been thrown aside like a shell. And it can be said otherwise: that which is muddy in us—and you know what that is—if it remains mud, it is dissolved by the passing of moisture. But when it takes on dryness and casts off all the moisture from without from the matter, it dries up according to the shell. Each of the examples taken is taken according to something. This is often said; for if it were taken from everything, it would not be an example, but that very thing which we wish to show. Therefore, the shell is often mocked in this way: a vessel made of shell, if broken, they say, does not receive liquid, nor can it be glued. I say in another way: that which is made from clay, when it is hardened by fire and a kiln, casts off the soft and the easily broken. Thus 'my strength' 'has dried up like a shell'. We take it in both ways: it no longer has any moisture, nor a muddy state. It can also be taken otherwise: it has cast off all bitterness from the much approaching affliction.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sticking of the tongue to the throat means silence, since the word no longer goes forth when the listeners are gone.
comments.comment: 'And my tongue is stuck to my jaws' (Psalm 22:15). It is the custom of Scripture to speak of the sticking of the tongue to the throat to mean silence. Since my sweet things are no longer present, and since those concerning me and my listeners are no longer present, lest I seem to carry the word in vain, I have been silent: 'my tongue is stuck to my throat'. But it is not stuck when we are conversing. Through the movement of the tongue, the word is carried forth. But when it is stuck to the throat, it is silence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the clinging tongue means in Scripture's usage.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He went down into mortality and Hades, the dust of death, for three days and three nights.
comments.comment: This is not the body which the Savior, having entered into the womb from the Virgin, says, 'You have brought me into the dust of death' (Ps 22:14). Perhaps he also descended into mortality and the Hades, which for us is the dust of death; for it happened in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dust of death is the mortal body that can be dissolved, which the Savior took on by God's leading without sinning, though for the flesh-loving soul it also brings death.
comments.comment:
Since He himself, for the sake of the economy [God's plan of salvation] and the salvation of all, received a body and God prepared a body for Him, He says: 'to be led by God into the dust of death.' …

Here, however, the soul was not humiliated by Jesus into the dust, but was led by God. He came to this in an economical manner; for He had by no means committed sin, even though He was receptive; for if he were not receptive, he would not be praised at all. The abstaining therefore from sins brings praise to the one who has refrained when he was by nature prone to act.

Now, is dust and death the same thing? No; for He did not say: 'and into the dust of death You have led me.' If dust and death were the same, He would have said: 'into the dust of death You have led me'; but: 'into the dust of death.' The mortal body, which is able to be dissolved from the essence carrying it, is 'the dust of death.' And perhaps also by a second sense it is the dust of death, because it brings death to the flesh-loving soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The silence of the stuck tongue comes from listeners who do not succeed, so that he no longer speaks when they have their thoughts on other things.
comments.comment:
But this silence does not come from the one being silent, but from those who are not succeeding as listeners. For he says in one of the prophets in Amos: 'Many are the fallen in every place, I will cast down silence' (Amos 8:3). If they flee, I cast down silence, so that I may not be honored to bring forth the teaching. And this indeed is one of the aids. …

Just as it no longer rains when good fruits are not being borne, so he no longer speaks nor converses when those listening have thoughts concerning other things. …

I do not only keep silent from the mystical things, but also from the ethical things; for in every place in which it was necessary to stand and be established and to be ready for a listening, a fall has occurred, and everywhere I cast down silence. Therefore, the sticking of the tongue to the palate signifies silence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Dust of death' and 'body of death' are said of the Savior differently from other men, because he took on a body able to die so as to taste death for all.
comments.comment:
And you have led me into the dust of death. Even if the voice were in the presence of Jesus, even if it were in the presence of the holy men who knew God, having become like the wicked in the place of affliction, having been humbled—"you humbled us in a place of affliction" (Psalm 44:19). For the ones saying this are holy, as the conjunction signifies of the psalm. "Body of death" (Psalm 22:15) is said of that which surrounds us, and it is also said "dust of death" (Psalm 22:15). It is not "dust of death" in essence, but because those being forced from the life outside the body come into this, the body is named death. "Into the dust" therefore "of death you have led me" (Psalm 22:15). If it were life, it would have been led upward; for to be led up is to be brought into life and blessedness and an immortal state. Even if the Savior therefore says this, this: the light "into the dust of death you have led me" (Psalm 22:15). They descended into a body so that I might die on behalf of all, so that "by the grace of God above all" (Hebrews 2:9) I might taste "death."

Differently, therefore, from other men, it is said "dust of death" and "body of death" for the Savior; for if the body becomes death when the one using it sins, and Jesus did not sin, he came into the dust of death being able to undergo death. Therefore, those who stumble, saying that he is either merely a man or a heavenly body having endured nothing, and attributing death to him, are mistaken. It is not so. Divinity, without such a thing, does not undergo death; for it is immortality.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse speaks in the past tense of what had not yet happened because a divine eye saw the future in advance.
comments.comment: But was the passion not yet? All these things are said prophetically. Things that are possible before they exist, before they come into being by energy, in a state of possibility they both may come to be and may not. And no one has the power to guarantee whether it will happen or not; for toward both sides both possibilities are equally likely. But when someone having foreknowledge, or God himself, foreknows that of the possible things this shall be, as it happens to us, when it already exists; for upon the existing and the having happened already, we have the power to say which is true and which is false, whether it has happened or has not happened. But upon the future things, we do not have the power to say this, but only to say that the other will be, but not this. Since therefore even here a divine eye saw the future in advance, it is no longer to him as possible things. Because of this he says: 'They laid hands on my hands and my feet.' If another were speaking, he would not have said this, but 'they will lay hands' or 'they will not lay hands.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the dogs and the company of fornicators surrounded him, they gripped his hands and feet, which men who remained men would not have done.
comments.comment: 'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me, they have gripped my hands and my feet' (Psalm 22:16). Thus write: 'For many dogs have surrounded me, a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' The 'for' is a causal conjunction. It is not attached to those following: 'You have led me into the pit of death,' 'for many dogs have surrounded me.' No, but: since 'many dogs have surrounded me and a company of fornicators has enclosed me,' because of this 'they have gripped my hands and my feet.' Humans remaining would not have done this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Dogs means men with a dog-like manner, base, shameless and flattering, and the people who had been sheep of God became dogs when they thought against the Savior.
comments.comment:
But he says 'dogs' here to mean men having a dog-like manner. And he slanders the movements of the dog in many ways. They are entirely base toward filth. Thus, it has become customary to call the lawless and the women 'dogs' in this sense. Indeed, even the law also, suggesting this meaning, counted the dog along with the prostitute: 'You shall not substitute a dog for a change, nor a prostitute's hire' (Deuteronomy 23:18). He did not say a change of a donkey or a horse; for these changes were being brought into the house of the Lord. And it is both shameless—'and the dogs are shameless to the soul'—and flattering. Therefore, men who have such movements are called dogs in judgment. These, then, surrounded the Savior. When they were sheep of God, they were at least outside the dog-like state. But when the people had become lost sheep, the loss did not turn them into non-existence, but into a dog-like, deficient, and scorpion-like state. And all this was said regarding the Hebrews: 'And all dogs are inward, knowing how to bark' (Psalm 22:16).

When the Israelites thought against the Savior, then they became dogs. And the being a 'company of fornicators' followed their becoming dogs; for when they were sheep, they were a divine flock. So they became dogs around me and a company of fornicators.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'dogs' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The striking of his hands and feet means the cross, and the assembly of fornicators is those who rise up against the shepherd.
comments.comment:
The striking of the hands and feet of the Savior signifies nothing other than the cross. Therefore, consider the things just mentioned: is this assembly, which is not shameless for souls that are unbridled and lustful—those who lust through insults, who hate the one who made the resurrection of the dead and the sight of the blind and the healing of lepers, and who wish to subject them to death—is this not an assembly of fornicators? But there is a praiseworthy assembly. …

So when dogs became prevalent, and even humans became dog-like in manner, life, and disposition, they were called an 'assembly of fornicators.' To be 'fornicators' means to rise up against the benefactor, to stand up against the shepherd.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The piercing of hands and feet means the cross, and the counted bones are the zealous few left when the superficial believers flee.
comments.comment: 'They pierced my hands and my feet' signifies the death of those coming to this, having their hands and feet dug out through the piercing of the nails. 'All my bones were counted.' All the bones of the body can be counted, if they are stripped of the joined flesh; and regarding the body of Christ, the apostles declare the bones, but his flesh is spoken of by those believing more superficially and more bodily. For the body is not the same thing: the bones hold the flesh together, and the flesh happens to be around the bones, covering them. If some fear should disturb those fleeing, the superficial believers, only the hard and zealous ones are left, as if they were counted as remaining having been stripped after the fleeing of the crowd. 'They understood and looked upon me; even though they did not cause my death to happen (for I took these things willingly), they divided my garments among themselves and cast lots upon my clothing' (Ps 22:18).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They measured his bones to find where to fix the nails.
comments.comment: “And they considered, and they looked upon me” (Psalm 22:17). Feeling, as is likely, his whole body and measuring each of the bones, that they might see where they must fix the nails.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'they look and stare upon me' meant.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words of Scripture are the garments of the Word, and those who hold different opinions divide them, dragging the words toward their own meaning.
comments.comment:
All my bones were numbered (Psalm 22:17). Whatever was in them, they subjected my bones to numbering, even though they were not countable. …

And the powers of his teaching can perhaps be called bones. …

I say: just as the sum of the believers was called the body of Christ according to a certain figure, as the apostolic testimonies signified, and we used to say that the joints of this body are the useful parts, so again we say that this very God-breathed Scripture is the body of the Savior, but the useful meanings of this body are the contemplations concerning the other superior meanings. And the words are garments; for the Word according to the understanding is clothed by the words. Even if, therefore, I have enumerated its bones, they were not divided; they only saw them as if they were not; for if they had seen them as they are, they would have been empowered in them and would have made them their own, as it is said: 'All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?' (Psalm 35:10). For these are not sensible bones that say this.

Therefore, the garments of the Word are divided by all those who hold different opinions, those who hold false doctrines. They drag the words toward what they want and make them their own, such as: 'The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways' (Proverbs 8:22). … The Arians drag it as they wish and consider it their own. The ecclesiastics, again, receive it as being worn by Wisdom who says this, and others receive others. And it is possible to find the same words almost by all the heterodox being handled differently and differently. So they divided them, they stripped the words of the Word and dragged them naked of the Word toward their own will. 'And upon my clothing they cast lots' (Psalm 22:18).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The garments of Jesus are the words of Scripture, which others divide, but the Church wears them whole and will clothe herself with Jesus himself.
comments.comment: Regarding the history, the words of the Scriptures are more allegorical concerning the garments and the clothing of Jesus; for the God-Word, subsisting according to spiritual meanings, both wears and is surrounded by these. The heterodox, the executioners and the spirits of the slayer, divide the garments of the Savior. For each of them receives the words of the Scriptures, and receives those not of the Scriptures, even though the seamless tunic of Jesus is seamless because it is woven; for it does not consist of joined parts but has a unified nature. And it is also from above because it is divinely inspired, woven through the Spirit; for the Scripture is from above by all power. But the Church does not divide the garments nor casts lots upon them; for she has and puts on, standing at the right hands of Jesus, a Queen clothed in golden attire, variegated. Having ascended above these garments, she will clothe herself with Jesus himself, becoming wise and powerful, possessing the wisdom and power of the Father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Gospel's account of the soldiers dividing his garments and casting lots for the woven tunic fits the verse, since the Jews had handed him over to the soldiers.
comments.comment:
It also rises up according to history, the dividing of his garments and the casting of lots around the weaver's whole cloak (John 19:23-24). In a certain way, the word in the present Gospel text struggles; for the soldiers did this. But the soldiers were not Hebrews; for altogether a Jew was not permitted to serve in the military; but since they in a certain way became the cause of him being handed over to the soldiers as well, they apply the utterance to themselves. …

'They divided my garments among themselves' (Psalm 22:18). For this reason, we no longer wish to remain here regarding the historical sense; for it has already been said that even the soldiers divided them into four parts, having made them, and cast lots upon the tunic woven from top to bottom of all.
comments.selected_reason: Ties the verse to the Gospel account of the garments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The true heir holds the whole robe of Jesus, while those who cast lots divide only the words, for a wise man shows what they think is theirs is not.
comments.comment: They come as partners, and concerning them a lot is cast. If someone leaves an only-begotten son and appoints him as successor, all the things belonging to the deceased are his, and no lot is cast. But when many come upon the true heir saying, 'We too are children of him,' a division of his garments occurs. But they are not divided, only the words; for the same word is not held in different minds by heretics. Each one drags the word toward his own mindset and will. Therefore, the diligent and truly faithful one possesses the whole robe of Jesus, not having it torn; so he does not cast a lot; the whole is his. For even if they cast a lot and use the words, they do not become his, they do not become masters of them; for a wise man according to Christ comes into the midst and shows that what he thinks is his is not his. And what about garments and clothing? The garments together are called clothing, but each one by itself is not called clothing. And just as many sheep gathered together at once are called a flock, but each one is not called a flock, and people who have come together into one are called a people, but each one is not called a people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks for help so that the plot against him may be shown vain.
comments.comment: Regarding his words: 'Do not withdraw your help from me; for if you do not help and attend to my understanding, I shall rise a third time from the dead to show the vainness of the plot against me' (Psalm 22:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though tribulation was near, God's help was not far, since the resurrection came at once and those who were scandalized turned back to him.
comments.comment: 'But You, Lord, do not delay Your help' (Psalm 70:5). If they exerted themselves in these things, even if they bring tribulation upon me, I have entreated You not to turn away, 'for tribulation is near' (Psalm 22:11). And the tribulation, if it has become near from those surrounding me like calves and bulls, from those scattering my bones, from those becoming causes to me such that my tongue is stuck to my throat, but You, do not delay Your help. Immediately then the resurrection of the Savior occurred, and immediately those who were scandalized turned back to Him. So the help has not been far.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea for help as answered by the resurrection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The help he asks is the resurrection, which Father and Son work as one act, since 'God' does not separate the Father from the Son.
comments.comment:
And these things, according to the intention of man, Jesus says: 'Do not delay Your help.' The help which is required happens from no one else but from God. And I said that, when 'God' is said, it does not always signify the Father, separating the Son, nor the Son dividing from the Father; for the divinity is one. And because it is thus, we call the help the resurrection from the dead. …

He has given life and has raised him, from which it is shown that the one resurrection and the one work being done by Father and Son happens through only one divine energy. Even if the Father does it, as God working this, he works it; even if the Son, he does this as God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If God pays attention the help is near; Christ alone was raised above death because he did not sin, and by his death he destroyed death.
comments.comment: Pay attention to my understanding. For if you pay attention to my understanding, the help is not far from me, but being near, it worked; for he says previously these things concerning the men: for he did not come so that previously he himself might die and rise, but through others. 'By the grace of God he was raised above all death' (Hebrews 2:9). All died on behalf of them. This one by the grace of God was raised above all. 'The love of God holds us together, judging this thing to be that if one died on behalf of all, then all died' (Rom 6:10), so that those having died might no longer be dead, 'but live by that one who died on behalf of them and rose' (Rom 6:10). Some human power is able to give life on behalf of another, and some reproach is able to be received on behalf of another, and a rebuke. But death, no one is able to receive on behalf of another. And behold: he was raised alone, he was not swallowed by it, nor did it consume him. But he who is being swallowed by death swallows it himself. 'Death, having prevailed, swallowed up' (1 Cor 15:55). This one swallowed death, the one having been laid under it. And since Jesus 'did not commit sin,' and through the seizing of sin death is swallowed and swallows the one sinning—therefore he was raised above all; indeed, he was raised. And he has given the reason: 'so that through death he might render powerless the one having the power of death' (Heb 2:14). In death he destroyed death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies hold a sword that wounds the soul rather than the body, perhaps the devil himself, and he asks to be kept from disturbance and cowardice.
comments.comment: Since the surrounding enemies, seeking to kill, possess a sword capable of wounding not the body but the soul, he asks to be saved from these blades, kept unharmed from disturbance and cowardice (Psalm 22:20). For even if our soul has been sufficiently prepared, seeing the devil with the whole phalanx of demons and the swarm of opposing and evil human energies acting through them, it becomes disturbed (for its nature is changeable) and calls upon the One capable of saving from the enemy's sword. Perhaps even the devil himself is allegorically called a sword, since he dares to wound every soul by pre-meditation; thus, he asks to be saved from this sword.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sword threatens and what he asks to be saved from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword is the adversary, like the sword that pierced Mary's soul; a thought he casts passes through those who refuse it, but it entered Judas, and 'save' means save me so that I may not suffer from it.
comments.comment: He sometimes reveals both an evil power and the devil himself; for when it is said regarding Mary, 'and a sword will pierce your own soul' (Luke 2:35), he speaks of the adversary. When he casts thoughts upon someone or wishes to cast them, if that soul does not receive them, they pass through it, like the fifth arrow of the Psalm (Psalm 91:5) when it is sent not at the mark, passing through the archer. He cast it into Judas; he acted against Judas. He did not secure himself, he did not guard against it: 'do not give place to the devil' (Ephesians 4:27), and he did not pass it by; for it entered into him. And he who says, 'I did not know the evil one passing away from me,' had the sword passing through. To not know here does not mean ignorance, but not having been tested. Thus, even those who despise to say something, even if it is present, even if it is, say: 'I do not know.' Regarding 'save': the 'save' certainly means all this: 'save me, having seized me and being under it.' Save me so that I may not suffer anything from it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When he says 'my soul', the whole composite man is speaking, since soul, body and spirit are each other than the composite but all together are not other than him.
comments.comment: Regarding: who is speaking? They wish to say this: 'if he speaks about the soul himself, who is the one speaking? It is a body that is speaking.' But those saying such things stumble. In composite things, each of those in the composition is said of the whole composition. 'Your whole spirit and soul and body.' Is the spirit something else from the men, and the soul something else, and the body? Therefore they posit them as separate. We often speak about a city, saying it has a bad city, a bad ruler, a bad people, bad laws, not right ones. What is the city apart from the bad rulers, the counselors, and the people? And just as we speak about the human body, saying a head of the body, a face of the body, a hand of the body, feet—is the body something other than these, while each is something else beside itself? Those who have done the logical things well understand these things easily. See: everything having sensation and soul is an animal, and I say that the animal is not a man, nor a horse, nor an ox. But I say this: that man is not the whole genus, nor is he the whole animal. And I say that the particular species are other than the animal. but all together I do not say are other than it; I say they are it. So also in the case of the body I say the hand is other than the man's body, and the foot, the head. but all are not other than the body; rather, each is other than the whole body. So it is also in the case of man. If he says: 'my soul and my body and my spirit,' each is other than the composite man. But all together are not other than him. If then he says 'my soul'—for this is not written concerning Jesus alone. And each of men says this: 'Why are you sorrowful, my soul?' (Psalm 42:5); 'my flesh has been changed because of oil'. and 'my spirit': 'and my spirit was troubled'. Each, then, is other than the composite. But all taken together I do not say are other than the composite; rather, each—if then he says 'my soul,' the composite man is the one saying these things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The many dogs are called one dog, and 'hand of the dog' means their action; the soul is only-begotten because it alone neither did nor knew sin.
comments.comment: 'and from the hand of the dog my only-begotten' (Psalm 22:20). He said: 'for many dogs surrounded me' (Psalm 22:16). These many dogs he calls, specifically, one dog. The one rescued from the individual men wishing to plot was rescued from man. And by 'hand of the dog' he means his action. 'And the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai' (Hag 1:1). But concerning the worthless it has been said: 'thorns grow in the hand of the drunkard' (Prov 26:9). From the hand, then, from the action of the dogs who surrounded me, being according to the form of one dog, rescue my soul. Some are said to be solitary: 'God settles the solitary in a house' (Psalm 68:6). And it is possible to say that all these who are settled have one manner, and in this respect are called solitary, as in: 'be perfected in the same mind and the same judgment' (1 Cor 1:10). But it is also possible thus: the one having a judgment not changing, a manner not becoming different from different, is solitary; for the wise man is not changed like the fool, but shines like the sun. And the sun has no changes of illuminations. Only-begotten, then, to him is this soul. I said that other souls also, made his own through virtue, come to be. But they do not have the steadfast, the firm. This one alone, having neither done nor known sin, is only-begotten.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He calls this one soul unique because it is unshakeable and always with him, and any disturbance in it is only a pre-passion.
comments.comment: He has souls; but this one he has as unique, for it is unshakeable. And I say unshakeable in this way: not being turned; for that which is called unshakeable in a completed sense signifies the unchangeable. When I say that the righteous man is not turned toward injustice, I say the righteous is unshakeable in the measure that he possesses righteousness; for the unshakeable does not turn. But not everything that does not turn is unshakeable. Therefore, this soul is unique to him among the others, because it alone possesses the capacity to be always with him. No reasoning, no impulse, no disturbance can separate it; for even if it is disturbed, the disturbance stands only as a pre-passion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus says this of his own soul and of every soul made his own.
comments.comment: Save my soul from the sword (Psalm 22:20). Jesus is also the one saying this verse, and he is able to say this also concerning his own soul, which he had the power to cast out and take back, and concerning every soul made his own.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He names the dogs in the singular by their race and calls his soul only-begotten because it alone knew no sin and was united with the God-Word, or perhaps the church is so called.
comments.comment: “Rescue my soul from the sword” (Psalm 22:20). And to the holy God-bearer Simeon says: “And a sword will pass through your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). “And my only-begotten from the hand of the dog.” And now in the singular he names, by the race, those whom he called dogs above. And he called his own soul only-begotten, as alone not having known sin; but also because it alone through all had the union of the God-Word. And perhaps he calls the church that stood beside him only-begotten, not having spot or wrinkle, perfectly completed from the blameless, which according to progress is divided into various ranks: “sixty are queens, and eighty concubines, and maidens of whom there is no number; but above all is a perfect dove, being only-begotten to the mother, the Jerusalem above” (Song of Songs 6:8-9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why his soul is called only-begotten.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prayer 'Save my soul from the sword' is spoken from the person of the whole Savior, whose soul was saved though his citizen fell by the sword of execution.
comments.comment: For how could he, the one affirming to God, "Save my soul from the sword" (Psalm 22:20), not remain free from all harm? This voice is carried in the twenty-first Psalm, spoken from the person of the whole Savior being brought forth. Having had the soul saved from the sword after sending up the prayer, his citizen fell by the sword of execution, according to that which was said in Amos the prophet: "Let all sinners of the people perish by the sword" (Amos 9:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks to be saved from the devil, once called a lion, and from the horns of the unicorns, an opposing power promising a kingdom.
comments.comment: He asks to be saved now from the devil, previously spoken of as a lion, but also through his own humiliation, by which he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross (Psalm 22:21). And he wishes to be saved also from the horns of the unicorns, which are an opposing power promising a kingdom; for the horn is a symbol of a kingdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lion can be the devil, who attacked at the time of the passion, or the people who turned on him, and even a perfect rational being needs God's help.
comments.comment: "Save me from the mouth of the lion" (Ps 22:20). Here he can also call the devil a "lion", for he attacked in the time of the passion. Indeed, when it was said in the forty-day temptation that "the devil departed from him", it is adjacent in the Gospel to "until a time" (Luke 4:13). Then again, it came when the passion was. And since I was saying that the attacks are brought to the man of the Savior himself and to his own, when Peter says or the Savior says to Peter, "Behold, Satan has demanded you" (Lk 22:31), in a way he wanted to devour the members of the Savior by attacking against the Savior. He says, therefore, "Save me from the mouth of the lion". He can also call that people a "lion", for "it became said my heritage is to me like a lion in the thicket" (Jeremiah 12:8). May I not suffer these things which they want to dispose me toward. He says these things because every rational essence, even if it is perfect, needs the alliance from God. "Save me from the mouth of the lion."
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the lion is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unicorns are the strong, untamed people he had planted, and the humiliation from their horns is the cross and death, from which God raises him.
comments.comment:
And 'from the horns of the unicorns my humiliation' he can say here, referring to the multitude of the Jews, the people of Israel; for he said in Jeremiah: 'I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance. My inheritance became to me like a lion in a forest' (Jeremiah 12:7). Having been a people whom I placed in Paradise, where there was much fruit, when they had turned into wildness, then consequently they nest in fruitless trees—for the forest is nothing other than a place of fruitless trees. Therefore, they encamp there. And my inheritance, which I had so that it might be a people and a portion of the Lord, was so provoked against me as to be thrown upon a lion, not a lion being tamed—for often lions come into human places being tamed—but as in a forest, as a wild beast. …

'And from the horns of the unicorns my humiliation' (Psalm 22:21). The unicorn is a strong animal. It is not subject to man, it is not tamed by man. 'From the horns' therefore, 'the humiliation of the unicorns,' the cross and death saying his own humiliation. 'He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross' (Philippians 2:8). My humiliation, therefore, then, flows from these unicorns—and these are also some evil enemies—then, when I rise from the dead; for 'the kings of the earth and the rulers were gathered together' to surround him with death. Then God delivers him from his humiliation; he rises from the dead. And all these things are spoken concerning the man.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unusual phrase about the horns of the unicorns.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unicorn, a strong one-horned animal, praises the Savior's kingdom, which is simple and single like the presence of God.
comments.comment: 'And from the horns of the unicorns.' It is also called a rhinoceros. And in the eighteenth Psalm this is so: 'And the beloved as a son of unicorns' (Psalm 29:6). This animal is said to have a size not less than a large calf. But it is very coiled, it is thick, and it has a horn above the nose, and the animal is very strong, and when it is angry, its horn becomes so much the strongest as to be harder than an elephant's. But when it is not angry, it is soft as flesh. And sometimes, when there is heat, it throws large stones so that it may place itself in that place, being cool. This animal, then, as I have said, when having become angry, has the horn very hard. But when being calm, it does not have it. Therefore they are tested to take its horn; for it is precious. Since, then, they want such a thing, they do not shoot at it without foresight; it does not fall to a beast, nor is it wounded by a polecat or any other. But they throw at it with a bow. So when it is angry, then they shoot at it with the dart. But: toward what kind of person do we take it? Toward Christ? —if it be taken praiseworthily. And it is taken praiseworthily in the eighteenth Psalm: 'And the beloved as a son of unicorns' (Psalm 29:6). It signifies having an only-begotten kingdom. The kingdom of the Savior, therefore, does not have duality, but is simple, like the presence of God. And because of this, it is called one-horned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The horns of the unicorns are the upper ends of the cross, and one who sings to God in the midst of the assembly must himself be righteous.
comments.comment: The phrase 'from the horns of the single-horned ones' is a mystery, for the upper ends of the cross had the shape of horns. … 'I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the assembly I will sing your praise' (Ps 22:22). He who sings to God in the midst of the assembly is one who offers hymns with boldness and decorum. It is necessary for the one singing to God to be righteous; for 'praise is fitting for the upright' (Ps 33:1), and 'there is no beautiful praise in the mouth of a sinner' (Sirach 15:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He says 'my brothers' as one made like his brothers in all things, not according to his divinity, since the only-begotten has no brothers.
comments.comment: Therefore, without delay he immediately brought forward: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' (Hebrews 2:12). 'I will proclaim your name to my brothers; and again: behold, I will be trusting in him, behold, I and the children whom God has given to me.' And again: 'Wherefore he ought to have been made like his brothers in all things' (Hebrews 2:17). Not only according to the body, but according to all things. According to his divinity, the only-begotten Son of God does not have a brother; for if he had a brother, he would not be only-begotten. But to have brothers is opposed to being an only-begotten one. The only-begotten has no brothers. The one having brothers is not only-begotten.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the brothers are and in what sense.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hebrews says the words are spoken by Christ, who declares the Father's name to his brothers and sings praise in the midst of the gathering.
comments.comment: The Epistle to the Hebrews says that this word is spoken from the person of Christ, as he says to the Father: 'O Father, your own name, that is, your own property and peculiarity, I will declare, making it manifest to my brothers who were born of me, to whom you sent my spirit; to whom it will be said, What you are, God sent the spirit of his Son into your hearts. For they are not those who have received the spirit of adoption from God, so as to be sons of God and brothers of the only-begotten. And having indeed risen from the dead, having appeared to the women, he says, "I have gone to my brothers." And in the midst of this gathering assembly, he will sing praise to the Father, sending up theological thoughts and songs.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To sing to God in the midst of the assembly is to do so with boldness, living what one teaches, as the Savior does.
comments.comment: Just as we say that the divine Word is spoken 'in authority'—when someone teaches about temperance while being temperate, he has the Word in authority; but if he is uncontrolled and filthy, he does not bring it forth fully. His conscience trips him up. … Just as the one who carries out appropriate works and has the practical life conforming to the contemplative life has the Word in authority, so the one who sings to God in the midst of the assembly is one who lacks no hesitation. For example, if one teaches about temperance so that he may be temperate, then he sings to God in the midst of the assembly; likewise, one teaching about almsgiving should be such, and one speaking about courage should be such. Therefore, when you see someone speaking about courage while being a coward, he is not doing this in the midst of the assembly. For the 'midst' signifies boldness, and this is to be learned from another psalm: 'He did not dwell in the midst of my house, practicing arrogance' (Psalm 101:7). … Thus, the Savior sings to the Father in the midst of the assembly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in the midst of the congregation' as praise given with boldness and an upright life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The name of the Father is not syllables or sounds but what makes his identity manifest, so declaring the name is giving understanding of God.
comments.comment: So also is the name of the Father, but a name not that which is composed of syllables nor signified in sounds, but that which makes manifest the identity of the Father. According to this is the understanding of the name of God and that which is said in the Psalm: 'I will declare your name to my brothers' (Psalm 22:22); for how else is a declaration of the name understanding of God?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'declare your name' means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jacob is named in many ways, so 'the seed of Jacob' means not all who descend from him but the seed of Jesus who came from teaching and will glorify God.
comments.comment:
In many ways he is called Jacob (for the typology signifies this: when he is the divine man, the son of Isaac, the father of the twelve patriarchs; when he is the twelve-tribed people proceeding from him; when he is the ten tribes alone having split from David and having followed Jeroboam; when he is the savior himself, 'Jacob my servant, I will take hold of him'; 'Israel my chosen one, my soul has received him'; for Matthew wrote this prophecy concerning the Savior), it should be sought why it is said, 'O all the seed of Jacob, glorify him' (Psalm 22:23). And one might say: the twelve-tribed seed of the patriarch Jacob, having been immersed in the reading of the law and the prophets, wishes to glorify God also through thoughts and words and good works. But perhaps, since this is a falsehood, many of those descended from Jacob being unfaithful and traitors to Jesus, someone will say: what is said of the seed of Jacob the 'plucked-up' and 'beaten-down' by death and the opposing power (and Jesus is that seed), his seed who came from teaching, will be able to glorify God. And since Israel is also the one whom the soul of God has received, the chosen seed of his, Israel will fear God. …

If Jesus has a struggle against the principalities, powers, and rulers of this darkness, Jacob is one who beats back the opponents; but if he has a pure heart and a clear mind, he will see God, Israel being such a person. No seed of such a person will fail to fear God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who fears God should praise him, and this fear is not the fear of punishment, since love casts out fear.
comments.comment: 'You who fear the Lord, praise Him' (Psalm 22:23). It is not the one who happens to praise God, but the one having fear toward Him. But not every fear is of God; for there is a fear of punishment. This is not of God. Furthermore, regarding 'perfection' toward God, 'love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). The one having love toward God from all heart and all mind does not have a passive fear. In this way, the disciples of Jesus were called by the Savior to be outside of passive fear, saying, 'Do not fear those who kill the body' (Matt 10:28). And those saying, 'The Lord is my helper, I will not fear; what can man do to me?' (Ps 118:6). They cast out the passive fear; for the fear of God is not passive, it is not of punishment …
comments.selected_reason: Tells what fearing the Lord means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seed of Jacob called to glorify God are those outside all wickedness who wrestle against evil powers as Jacob did, and the Savior is also called Jacob.
comments.comment:
'All the seed of Jacob, glorify him' (Psalm 22:23). It can also be said explicitly that: since that people from the patriarchs was called to hymn and to serve God, it appropriately stands over all to do this.

For since many have become sinners from them, we take 'all the seed of Jacob' not to mean the evil one—for it was said concerning him: 'evil seed'—but when it is outside of all wickedness, as he himself is whose seed it is. And we take here Jacob the patriarch and say that: since this one has become a wrestler and from this deed he received the appellation, all those wrestling, being surrounded by evil, of the opposing powers, of the evil adversaries, these are Jacob; for in his exploits Hosea arranged this, saying: 'In the womb he wrestled with his brother and prevailed with God and was able' (Hos 12:4). To prevail with God and to be able is a great exploit. Thus indeed he counted the one who wrestled with his brother in the womb.

And the Savior was also said in Isaiah: 'Jacob my servant, I will take hold of him' (Isaiah 42:1). And Matthew said that this word is fulfilled by Christ. 'Let all the seed of Israel fear him' (Psalm 22:23). Not passive fear is glory, but the fear of God, which after much effort comes to those who have strived to have it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the seed of Jacob' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He did not disregard the prayer of the poor Savior who became poor for us.
comments.comment: All the seed of Jacob, glorify him (Psalm 22:23), because he did not make nothing of nor disregarded the prayer of the poor. Here he calls the Savior who came among us 'poor' because he became poor for our sake.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the prayer of the poor man was heard, you should praise, glorify and fear God, knowing that the one who prayed is rich and became poor to make you rich.
comments.comment: [Christ speaking:] Since he did not reject the prayer of me the poor man nor crush it (Psalm 22:24), for this reason, becoming thankful that the prayer for us was heard by the Lord, you praised, glorified, and feared him. For even though I prayed to him as a poor man, but you ought to know what I am: a rich man, a treasure of the fullness of goods; through you I became poor so that through my poverty I might make you rich; for those who are surrounded by the flesh did not receive my wealth, knowing and prophesying only a part of it. Having become poor for you, I cried out to the Lord on your behalf, and he heard me, giving you those things by which you were found rich. For in my interceding for you, he did not turn his face away from me, but rather he shone it upon me; therefore he also applied his attention to my cry.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God hears the poor one's prayer and who the poor one is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ, being rich, became poor for others without losing his wealth, and he did not disregard the prayer of the poor, for he was interceding for the salvation of all.
comments.comment: And behold the difference: “know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that being rich he became poor for your sakes” (2 Cor 8:9). To become poor for us, is not to be rich for us; for it has not been said to become rich just as it has been said to become poor, but “being rich he became poor for your sakes.” And just as having the form of God and being in the form of God, having taken the form of a slave of God, he did not cast away the form of God, so he, becoming poor for the sake of others, did not cast away the wealth; for we do not say of his wealth as if it were the virtues of holy men; for he himself is the provider of the virtues, he is the one in whose participation the virtues exist. Thus, remaining rich, he became poor. But he became poor for the sake of others, so that they might become rich. And when we remain in the prior poverty and do not hasten to take up that wealth which his poverty grants, that which is for us, he remains poor; for if for the sake of others, so that they might become rich, he became poor, when they become rich, he is no longer poor. He became poor by becoming flesh. When we behold “his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), we have become rich from the poor, and he himself was shown to be rich from the poor, he did not become rich. For his glory has become manifest, that “as an only-begotten” he is “from the Father, full of grace and truth.” “He did not disregard nor make void the prayer of the poor”; for he was interceding for the salvation of all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ pleads for sinners as a Paraclete and then for their keeping, and God turns his face from prayer only when it does not match his will, as with Jeremiah and Samuel.
comments.comment:
… Truly, insofar as we are in sins, we have him as a Paraclete. But when we cease from having sins, he no longer pleads at all concerning this. Therefore also he is able to save to the full those who approach God through him, always living to intercede for them.

If he intercedes for them so that they may live, when they live, he no longer brings up this prayer concerning them, but rather pleads concerning its preservation, concerning its remaining. This, therefore, the prayer of the poor, he neither despised nor disregarded the one bringing it. 'Nor did he turn his face away.' A person turns his face away from one praying when God is not favorable, but also when he prevents the prayer from being sent up. He prevented Jeremiah at one time from praying for the people. Why? For ambassadors and Paracletes ought to bring an embassy for those having repented and no longer sinning. …

So also the face of Samuel was turned away, when he heard: 'How long will you grieve over Saul, while I have rejected him?' (1 Samuel 16:1). But the face has boldness for those interceding, if those for whom they intercede run together with his will. For he neither despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor, nor did he turn his face away from me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He says 'he heard me' by showing that what he prayed for exists, and his praise in the great congregation is that he accomplished it, a church without blemish or wrinkle.
comments.comment:
The poor man himself says concerning himself. A change of face has occurred. The writing Spirit says: 'He neither despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor.' Then that same poor man, whose prayer was not loathed, did not turn away, says: 'Nor did he turn his face away from me, and in my crying out to him, he heard me.' And in my crying out to him, he heard me. Great is it to say this. This is not said in mere words, but when it is shown that the thing for which he prayed exists.

And so this happened: 'My praise shall be in you in a great congregation' (Psalms 22:25). Behold, the work of the cry I have accomplished; I have established it as a congregation of peace for me, 'glorious, having neither blemish nor wrinkle or anything of this kind' (Eph 5:27).
