My praise, therefore, is this, that he accomplished this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men praise for visible works, but God, who sees what is hidden, praises for perfect virtue and surpassing knowledge.
comments.comment: Men indeed praise based on visible works and conveniences, but God, seeing the hidden, praises based on perfect virtue and surpassing knowledge (Psalm 22:25). It is not for anyone to say with boldness: 'O God, my praise is from you, not based on chance things, but on a great assembly'; for a great assembly is the one gathered from the great according to their kind, just as a great assembly is the one gathered from many (Psalm 22:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what praise 'in the great congregation' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Vows are paid by those who are thankful for what they asked, and he pays them before those who fear God so that they may learn from it.
comments.comment: "My praise is from you; in a great church I will confess to you; I will pay my vows in the presence of those who fear him" (Psalm 22:25). Vows are paid regarding those who are thankful and who have already acted. A prayer sent up to God is called a petition. But when it is sent up with a confession, saying, "if these things shall be to me, I will pay these," this prayer is a supplication and a vow. Even Jacob said: "If God will give me bread to eat, of all that he gives me, I will give a tenth." This is a vow. No one, having prayed for something and not having received it in due time, will say, "I will pay my vows," or "in the presence of those who fear him"; rather, he says it so that they may be benefited, for they themselves will also learn the vows which they pray to pay. And it is possible to do it "in the presence of those who fear," not in addition to those sacrificing—for those sacrificing cannot know which thanksgiving has been fulfilled or which vow has been paid—but in addition to those who fear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the vow in the verse is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer is a confession in thanksgiving, and the Scriptures speak of two kinds of wealth, each with a contrary poverty.
comments.comment: A prayer is a confession made in thanksgiving, if one should obtain these things from God (Psalm 22:26). Concerning the two kinds of wealth, as the Scriptures say, to be the one rich in good works and in every word and in all knowledge, and the other to be rich from false-glorious dogmas and unpleasant deeds, being a poverty contrary to each kind of wealth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor become rich through Christ's poverty and eat the bread of life and are satisfied, yet they always desire it again, and this desire is being filled.
comments.comment:
"The poor shall eat and be satisfied" (Psalm 22:26). "Being rich," he has become poor because of our poverty. Therefore, he not only freed these poor people for whose sake he suffered what he has said, but he also showed them being satisfied from those who were starving; for he is indeed the "bread of life," and his flesh is incorruptible food and his blood is a divine drink. When therefore the rich, having become from the poor through his poverty, partake of these, they eat and are satisfied. Similar to this is: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied" (Matt 5:6); not ceasing to eat the bread of life, but in chewing and having it sensuously. …

The one eating wisdom is never satisfied, but is always in a state of hunger. And the one drinking it as a divine water or wine harvested from the true vine thirsts again; that is, he always desires. Therefore, the desire to place it again and to crave it is to be filled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the poor are and what eating and being satisfied mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A pauper has come from wealth into poverty, while a needy person is among the needy and toils to provide the necessities.
comments.comment: The difference between a pauper and a needy person has been said many times: he who has come from wealth into poverty, that one is called a pauper. And you have this from the Scripture: 'the rich have become poor and have gone hungry' (Ps 34:10). But a needy person is one among the needy, who always provides the necessities while toiling. Thus they differ by another and another thought, since they are alike insofar as they are left behind from the abundance of those who crave.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who seek the Lord will praise him, for God is always being sought, and to be entirely in the state of seeking him is perfection.
comments.comment: And those who seek Him will praise the Lord, as it was said concerning wisdom, because being drunk, it prepares those who have drunk to thirst again; and divine food—for food is also the breathing of air. When we live, we breathe; we do not live by having been breathed into. Thus it is with the divine food and the holy drink: in being approached and being supplied, it prepares the benefit. And those who seek Him will praise the Lord. I say: God is always in the state of being sought; for even if someone finds Him, it has been said: 'He is found by those seeking Him' (Ps 105:4). There is, therefore, a certain way of being always in the state of seeking. Even if Eunomius rages, it is possible to find Him according to partial knowledge and according to partial prophecy, and again, He is in the state of being sought. And the seeking of God itself is beneficial. To be entirely in the state of seeking God is perfection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Their hearts shall live' speaks of the life of the believer, which rests on the essential life every soul has, since no one could live by faith unless he were immortal.
comments.comment: He does not speak now about this natural life saying: 'their hearts shall live' (Psalm 22:26)—but according to that life which the believer has and the one knowing God has. If the hearts live unto the age of ages according to the blessed life, it is evident that they also remain always according to the essential life, which is common to sinners and to the diligent. And just as I say that everyone has sight when animals have sight, I say that the one seeing well previously had sight; for he would not have seen well if he did not have the seeing, and again he would not have seen badly if he did not have the seeing. Therefore both the soul and the heart have life forever, whether it be wicked or diligent. And natural life anticipates; for he would not have been able to live according to God and to live according to faith, if he were not immortal, if he did not have essential life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor are those from the nations who had no hope and now come to faith and eat and are filled, and they worship in spirit and truth where they are, not at one temple.
comments.comment:
Concerning those who labor not in a praiseworthy way, the saying 'The poor shall eat and be filled' is spoken. But you say 'the poor' according to the saying, meaning those from the nations who previously had no hope and were atheists in the world, who are coming to faith and shall eat and be filled (Psalm 22:26). Remembering God at the ends of the earth and turning from the nations, those who have passed from the earth shall have their citizenship in heaven. And all the families of the nations shall worship before Him.

The Jews also seemed to worship before God coming to Jerusalem and the temple which Solomon built. This typical worship in a place, however, is not what the nations dwelling even unto the ends of the earth are to perform; rather, they were taught to worship in spirit and truth, remaining where they are, performing worship before God, as God wills them to live as citizens. With this, the prophecy also agrees, saying: 'And all the islands of the nations shall worship before Him, every place from its own place,' as Zephaniah says (Zephaniah 2:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the poor are and why the nations worship from every place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations turning to the Lord was foretold as fulfilled through Christ, and the same psalm that speaks of his passion goes on to foretell it.
comments.comment: … the prophets of God foretold that the nations would worship him after the false gods they once served had been exterminated. “The Lord will prevail against them,” he says, “and will exterminate all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zephaniah 2:11). And not only the islands, but all the nations—so much so that even all the islands of the nations are included—since elsewhere he does not name islands but speaks of the whole world: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship before him, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule over the nations” (Psalm 22:27, Septuagint Psalm 21:27). … That these things were to be fulfilled through Christ is clear enough both from many other testimonies and from the very psalm from which I quoted this. For when a little earlier he himself spoke through the prophet about his coming passion, saying, “They dug my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They looked and stared at me. They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Psalm 22:16-18, Septuagint Psalm 21:16-18), a little later he brings in what I cited: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord,” and the rest.
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the verse foretells all nations coming to the Lord through Christ.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Those on the earth who turn from earthly things or from worldly wisdom, wealth and rule come to worship God, and his own soul lives for him while the seed serves him.
comments.comment:
Those nourished in the earth can be 'poor of the earth' (Psalm 22:29), those who, having been called to repentance in spirit, are killing the deeds of the body so as to no longer think of earthly things, having eaten the spiritual food offered by Jesus, worshipped God in spirit and truth. And it is possible to call 'poor of the earth' those on earth who are departing from worldly wisdom, those becoming rich and ruling sensually; for these, having eaten the food from Jesus, being not a remedy for those foreseeing evils, shall worship God, finding Him above all wisdom, wealth, and rule. …

But he said well that his own soul lives for him, and not that it serves him; but that the seed shall serve him. For the nature that was taken was united to the divinity that took hold of it, and partook of the same glory and honor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'A generation goes and a generation comes' is taken of the two peoples, the departing one that turned away and the coming one called from the nations, to which God's righteousness is announced.
comments.comment: 'A generation goes and a generation comes' (Eccl 1:4)—some take it of the two peoples: they have called those of the circumcision the departing generation, because they have turned away from the Lord, having become 'a crooked and perverse generation' (Deut 32:5). And the coming generation is the calling from the nations, hastening to the very Savior who calls. This one, then, will be announced to the Lord by the ambassadors on her behalf, saying: 'To you nations shall come from the end of the earth' (Jer 16:19), and 'All the nations, as many as you have made, shall come and worship before you' (Psalm 86:9; LXX 85:9). For the Savior who says, 'The one coming to me I will not cast out' (John 6:37), does not cast out this coming generation. And it is well said 'the one coming' and not 'the one who has come'; for he does not cast out the one who is always effecting his coming to him by practicing the things of virtue. And the generation of which the discourse speaks has not come but is coming to him, cherishing the things of faith. And these same ones who announce to the Lord the coming generation also announce God's righteousness through faith in Jesus, effected in all who believe, to the people to be born, a divine offspring, whom the Lord made, having acquired it through his own blood, calling the not-people his people (Hosea 2:23; Rom 9:25).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul that is still a sheep grazes on spiritual herbs, and in its gentle, steady state it says the Lord is its shepherd and it will not want, as a baby says its nurse feeds it.
comments.comment: Sometimes the soul is called, as I have already said, a sheep. When it is a sheep, it grazes on pasture, not on flesh, not on the flesh of Jesus, nor on bread. It is not yet able to have desire for these foods or to manage them, even if they are presented to it. It grazes on herbs; and herbs are spiritual. Sometimes it is also called a plant and needs rain; it grazes on the art of agriculture, so that having grown, it may bring forth perfect fruit somehow; 'but I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God'. And here, therefore, the sheep-like state, which is as it were more irrational, along with gentleness and stability, signifies through the saying: 'The Lord is my shepherd, and I shall not want' (Ps 23:1). I am without wandering, and without wandering as a sheep. Just as even a baby says: 'The nurse feeds me, and I shall not want', making it clear that it is of infantile foods.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one still progressing is a sheep, shepherded by the Lord, fed on the gospel and given water, while for the perfect the Lord is king.
comments.comment: The perfect one, known according to the image of God and likeness, for whom the Lord is called also king, not shepherd; but the one progressing in introduction would be called a sheep of God, and is shepherded by him, and feeds on the gospel, and drinks water of which he who drinks will not thirst; but not yet the wine of the true vine, and he rests through the ransom of regeneration, putting off the burden of sins. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one named a sheep of Christ is led by the good shepherd to saving pasture, where ethical teaching is the green grass, and the water of rest cures thirst and releases from sins.
comments.comment:
The one who, through attaining the meek and well-ordered, has been named a sheep of Christ will say concerning the good shepherd: 'The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing' (Ps 22:1).

For he leads me to the saving pasture, where there are divine grasses, concerning which the shepherd himself says of his own sheep: 'He shall go in and go out and find pasture' (John 10:9).

And the place of green grass can be the divine instruction, where spiritual grass is found, being ethical teaching.

In this place, then, 'he made me dwell'—not 'he settled me'; for he wants me, as far as I progress, to use such pasture perfectly.

For having become from a sheep a man, I shall be tried no longer by a shepherd but by a trainer and teacher.

'He nourished me by water of rest' (Psalm 23:2; LXX 22:2). For the ethical lesson is not only a cure for thirst, but also provides release from sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shepherd, the green pasture and the water of rest in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm speaks first as a sheep given pasture and water, then of a table, where the bread of life and Wisdom's cup are given to the one who has progressed.
comments.comment:
… 'The Lord,' he says, 'shepherds me, and nothing shall I lack. Into a place of pasture he has led me; upon waters of rest he has nourished me' (Psalm 23:1-2; LXX 22:1-2). He speaks as a sheep; he reports what exists with the shepherd gratefully. Then he says: 'He has restored my soul. He has led me' (Psalm 23:3; LXX 22:3). And shortly after he brings forth: 'You have prepared a table before me' (Psalm 23:5; LXX 22:5).

It is no longer a place of pasture, no longer a meadow, no longer grazing land, but a table, upon which lies 'the bread of life,' 'the bread which came down from heaven' (John 6:35, 51), the flesh of Jesus, the true nourishment. And after the progress of the table, he partakes also of the cup, of which wisdom 'who has mixed wine for herself' (Proverbs 9:2) offers. It is your cup, if you pour it for me; and my cup, if you have measured it for me, which I am able to drink.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Water goes with pasture for the sheep, as wine goes with bread, and the sheep-like state is helped by pasture and water.
comments.comment: Water is appropriate for the sheep. Those who are being led to pasture and are being fed are watered, not with wine; for where there is bread, there also the wine is named. 'Bread sustains the heart of man'—and a perfect food is indicated through the bread—'and wine gladdens the heart of man' (Psalm 104:15). Therefore, where there is pasture, there is also water, and where there is bread, wine is also found. And the perfect Eucharist is fulfilled from bread and wine; for the sheep-like state is aided by pasture and water.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The water of rest does not tire the drinker: it leaps up toward him as a spring, and it feeds, cleanses and casts out thirst and filth.
comments.comment: The 'water of rest' can be said because the one drinking it does not grow weary; for 'the one drinking' (John 4:14) 'from the water which I will give' (John 4:14) will have 'a spring leaping into eternal life' (John 4:14). The water is not moving downward, but it comes toward the drinker by leaping itself. Hence it is 'water of rest.' This water serves for nourishing and for cleansing. And since the soul being cleansed casts out sin—for this was compared to a 'talent of lead'—the water provides rest. It casts out both thirst and filth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the water is called water of rest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Restoring the soul marks a change: it is no longer a sheep under a shepherd, and God leads it on the paths of righteousness, which are virtues or the acts of virtues.
comments.comment: Furthermore, since he remembers about shepherding and pasture and water, he immediately moves to the inner man, the Word, and says: 'He restored my soul' (Psalm 23:3). In the restoration, the change is indicated. I no longer remain a sheep, I am no longer under a shepherd, I do not have a craving for water. 'He restored my soul' (Psalm 23:3). And what has happened by my soul having been restored? God 'led' it (Psalm 23:3) 'upon paths of righteousness' (Psalm 23:3). The paths of righteousness are, in appearance, virtues or the acts of virtues. Often in the divine teachings, the name of righteousness signifies virtue in general; for there is also a specific virtue called so, justice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The paths of righteousness are the well-trodden practical works of justice, in which every kind of virtue is gathered, and the soul's return is the journey onto them, so that it is no longer a sheep.
comments.comment:
Thus, the paths of justice that are well-trodden, walked upon by many, are the paths of justice. And the practical activities of justice can also be paths of justice; for justice is most especially suffered and worn down when it is practiced. Since practical virtue is signified by this name of justice, this is confirmed by this: 'walking blamelessly and working justice, speaking truth in his heart, who did not deceive with his tongue and did not do evil to his neighbor' (Ps 15:2-3). And with a little more: 'he who does these things shall never be shaken for ever' (Psalm 15:5).

You see that having gathered all the kinds of virtue together, he spoke of it generally as justice. 'Lead me therefore' (Ps 23:3) 'upon the paths of justice'. And those before the written law observed this justice. Concerning Abraham, it is said that 'he kept all the judgments and commands' of the Lord. Even though they had not yet been given, but he kept them, and lived according to them. And Abel, therefore, is testified to be upon justice. The return, therefore, of the soul is the journey that leads onto the paths of justice, so that it may no longer be a sheep.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shepherd goes ahead and wears the paths so that his sheep may follow, and he turns back the soul that has wandered and guides it on the paths of righteousness, which are the virtues.
comments.comment:
For he mounted as the shepherd, and wore paths beforehand, so that his own sheep might follow in the tracks. Righteousness then is the practical habit of the just, whose paths are according to the activity. And if someone should call righteousness the generic virtue, he will say that its paths are the virtues according to species, upon which he guides the one who inscribes his appellation.

“He turned back my soul,” he says, that had wandered from its own or had fallen down; or the Lord turns back the soul that has fallen out, and restores it after the shepherding, and it is encamped into a place of green grass; then having turned it back he guides upon paths of righteousness and virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shepherd leading the soul back and onto the paths of righteousness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God leads on the paths of righteousness for his name's sake and not for the worth of the one led, because without God's mercy the good a man runs after is not reached.
comments.comment:
He led me on the paths of righteousness because of his name (Ps 23:3). This was not so much because of my own worth, but because of his own designation he provided this for me; for even if someone runs toward good things and has a desire for them, if God does not show mercy, the things being striven for are not achieved.

Likewise also in the 118th Psalm it is said: 'I have run the path of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Psalm 119:32; LXX 118:32). Because you enlarged my heart and gave breadth to my understanding, I have run the path of the way of your commandments. Therefore, through God, the things being striven for are always achieved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says God leads 'for his name's sake'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A name is not a string of syllables but a designation showing the specific quality of the one named, as 'wise' comes from wisdom, and a physician's disciple who knows no medicine lacks that quality.
comments.comment:
[on 'for his name's sake':] And by designation I mean not a collection of syllables joined together, but a designation showing the quality of the one named; here is how a name is defined: 'A name is a principal designation representing the specific quality of the one named.' And this is especially true of a nickname. One is called 'wise' from wisdom, and it does not have a mere designation, not one consisting of syllables joined together, but one declaring the quality which wisdom provided to the soul. A principal designation is therefore the name that is primarily representing the quality of the one named.

So if you say 'man,' it is representing the quality of a man—and by quality here I mean the specific identity—for you have said the specific quality of the one named. And the specific quality of a man is manliness; for if you were to say another quality, others would share in it; it would not be specific. Let it be said that someone is a disciple of a physician, but he knows nothing of medicine; he does not have the quality of medicine, and he is a reproach to the one who taught him medicine when he knows nothing of it nor practices it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shepherd turns back the straying soul, for no one is inherently bad who is open to returning.
comments.comment: It has happened through wandering to sin, but the shepherd turned my soul back to the strayed. It should be noted that no one is inherently bad if they are open to returning. One returns to where they began. Since sin has happened to those turning away from God, it should be abolished.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God is with him and drives away every evil, not even the shadow of death comes near; and 'evils' can mean wickedness or merely harmful things, as when God brings hardships so that his word is not set aside.
comments.comment:
For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will not fear evils, because you are with me (Ps 23:4). Since 'because of his name' he 'restored my soul' (Ps 23:3), he is with me. And since he is with me, driving away every evil, not even the shadow of death approaches me.

But 'evils' is said in two ways in Scripture, and perhaps also in common usage. The opposites of virtue, the kinds of wickedness, are called evils; as if one says: 'In the laughter of a fool, he does wrong,' and: 'Turn away from evil and do good.' But they also call unpleasant things evils, since men call pleasant things good.

… But it appears most clearly from Isaiah, the prophet saying thus concerning God: 'And he himself was wise to bring evils upon them' (Isaiah 31:2). Even for a wise man it is not easy to bring the kinds of evils … how much less for God. Indeed, even the wicked, when they pretend virtue, do not say: 'we are bringing evil to someone.' But it is said concerning God that as a wise one he brings evils. He speaks of things that are harmful. And he views the end of the bringing of evils: 'and his word shall by no means be set aside.'

On account of his word not being set aside, he brings difficult things; for they heard by a commanding word what they must do and what they must abstain from, but they despised this word, and as much as reached their misery, was set aside; so he brings evils, so that his word might not be set aside. And medical surgery and cauterization, bringing health to the one suffering these things, are not evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shadow of death is sin, which stands in the way of death as a painter's shadow-sketch begins an image, and one in the midst of it, like Joseph, need not fear.
comments.comment:
But he speaks here of a shadow, not that one which we say the law has—'for the law has a shadow of the things that are to come' (Hebrews 10:1)—but here he speaks of a shadow standing in the way of death. And sin stands in the way of death. And now I say death, not the common one. See: the painters, before the images and the forms, draw in shadow. And that shadow is the beginning of the image. Therefore death has a shadow, namely sin. And this prefigures and demonstrates death.

For if I become in the midst of the shadow of death, I do not fear it. Such as Joseph, how much, at the exhortation desiring to seduce him into immorality, he became in the midst of the shadow of death, and he did not fear evil, and that did not seize him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shadow of death is the dread and cowardice that affliction can bring and not the affliction itself; the martyrs were in its midst without being in death, and with God present he fears no harm.
comments.comment:
'If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death' (Ps 23:4). … I do not say the shadow of death is the act of being afflicted, but rather the sense of dread and cowardice arising from affliction. For the martyrs were in the midst of the shadow of death, but not in death itself. They were afflicted, but they did not succumb to the tribulation that was promised to follow. A similar thought is expressed in: 'Do not bring us into temptation' (Matt 6:13). For they do not say: 'Do not let us be afflicted.' If that were the case, the apostles would never have spoken, saying: 'In all things being afflicted' (2 Cor 4:8). Therefore, not entering into temptation means not being seized by the will of the one testing.

'I will fear no evil, for you are with me' (Ps 23:4). Having you with me, I fear nothing of those intending to harm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's staff supports and his rod disciplines, and both comforted the speaker and brought him out of death, even when he was inside its shadow.
comments.comment: 'Your rod and your staff, these have comforted me' (Ps 23:4). You see that he was not inexperienced with the shadow of death. Your staff, becoming my support, and your rod, disciplining me, comforted me; they brought me out of death, even if I have become within its shadow, even if I have entered into the midst of its shadow. The rod and the staff of God are taken both for discipline and for support: 'He who brings wisdom from the lips, strikes a heartless man with a rod' (Proverbs 10:13). He named the disciplinary and corrective word a rod. And Paul writes to the Corinthians: 'What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?' (1 Corinthians 4:21). And it is taken for support: 'The staffs are in your hands; and you received it with haste; it is the Lord's Passover' (Exodus 12:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shadow of death is the common bodily death, distinct from the soul's death, which those who believe in the Son of God do not undergo.
comments.comment: You might also say that the shadow of death is the physical and common death, distinguished from the death of the soul; according as it has been said that the soul that sins shall die, as the one who believes in the Son of God will not die unto the age, having passed from death into life; for they do not undergo a shadow of death, or dangers, or dissolution of the body.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the shadow of death is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: With God present nothing harmful can harm, and the evils meant are painful things like poverty, sickness and distress; the rod rebukes and disciplines, while the staff supports through counsel.
comments.comment:
When God is with one, nothing harmful can harm or injure, as the prophet says: 'Behold, the Lord will help me; who will harm me?' (Isaiah 50:9). If indeed one has walked in tribulations and pains, which is called the shadow of death (Psalm 23:4; LXX 22:4c), I will not fear the harmful things, having God with me. The evils here are not the strictly evil things, but the painful ones: poverty, sickness, distress, and the like, concerning which Job says: 'We shall not suffer evils' (Job 2:10). For no one having God with himself encounters evils that are the opposite of the strictly good; for sin is far from all that is in union with God.

He speaks of the rod to rebuke and to discipline, according to the question 'What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?'; and the staff to support through counsel, exhortation, and advice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'evils', the rod and the staff in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After the milk of the sheep-like state, solid food is given: Wisdom prepares her own table of wise teachings and mixes her own wine with the Incarnation, giving each the mixture he can contain.
comments.comment:
He prepared a table before me in the presence of those afflicting me (Ps 23:5). We connect the present things to the prelude; for because of them it has happened, when we said that after the drinking of milk, 'solid food' is given, being the wisdom of God spoken of in the perfect (1 Cor 3:2).

… We had the condition of a sheep; we had need of feasts resembling lessons and having the power of water. But when I advanced, my soul being turned back by you toward the paths of righteousness (Psalm 23:3) so that I might be comforted by your rod and your staff, I have become a man. For this reason we did not prepare a feast, but a table, and you revealed to me before me its beauty, its nourishment, its deliciousness. Your wisdom has prepared this table for me.

She has laid upon it 'having slaughtered her own victims' (Prov 9:2). And she has laid upon it 'her own wine' (Proverbs 9:2), 'mixing' it with this table, and she calls all to eat and drink from this table. And we call here the table of wisdom the divine one for children. And sacrifices are laid upon this; for when we perform the sacred rites and slaughter the doctrines of piety, so that we may make them ready for food, then the sacrifices are laid upon the table. And no one else offered them except Wisdom herself, who 'prepared her own table' (Prov 9:2); for she did not simply say, 'she prepared a table,' but 'her own.' And the table of Wisdom does not have other delicacies laid upon it except the wise teachings.

Furthermore, she 'mixed her own wine' (Proverbs 9:2). She took water to it, so that we, being unable to receive it unmixed, might take wine already mixed. There are certain unspeakable words, which are not let to be called wine. When anyone is able to lead these into explicit teaching, she mixed, adding to them a perceptible gift: the examples of the Scripture, the words announced in parables. Again, since God is the Word and Wisdom is the Word, but we were not able to take the Word unmixed, she mixed it with the Incarnation, and we received, moreover, mixed wine from both the Word of the Incarnation and the majesty of the Only-begotten. 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory' (John 1:14). Behold the mixture. This was not the mixing of anyone else but of her own Wisdom. You know that the one mixing sometimes makes the mixture according to the capacity of the drinker. And so Wisdom mixed her own wine and does not give the same mixture to all, but what each can contain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Applying the mind lavishly is the priestly anointing, the ointment Aaron bore as a symbol.
comments.comment: [on the anointing of the head:] This is to say, applying the mind lavishly to it; and this is the priestly anointing, the ointment which Aaron bore as a symbol; for he says, 'Like ointment which descends upon the head, upon the beard, the beard of Aaron' (Ps 133:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Each affliction sets a spiritual table, and the Lord prepared the table before the speaker so that, filled with solid food, he could stand nobly against those who afflict him.
comments.comment:
What does “opposite those who afflict me” want? It has some unspeakable mystery, that someone may pray to be afflicted. Think for me, just as in the great contests prizes lie upon each contest, so according to each affliction: whenever an afflicting is present, and the afflicting powers, the opposing ones, think for me a spiritual and intelligible table prepared through this affliction. As often, then, as you are afflicted, so often also a spiritual table is set beside you. Only have eyes that see my tables, that giving thanks you may say with the apostle: “And not only so, but also boasting in the afflictions” (Romans 5:3).

… And the Lord, wishing me through these who afflict me to rise strongly toward them, prepared a table before me, on which solid food lies, that having been filled with this athletically I may be able to stand against the afflicting nobly. For when we happen upon perfect good things, we have the opposing strong and more, as the apostle says: “For a great door has opened to me, and the opposing are many” (1 Corinthians 16:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a table is prepared in the presence of those who afflict.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: While he lives the believer sees the truth through a mirror and is a sheep led by a shepherd, but in the age to come he sees it face to face and comes to the Father's spiritual table, prepared for him from now.
comments.comment: And in the beginnings we were saying that the one from progress encamps into a place of green grass; since then the one progressing, even if he should arrive at the end, no longer remaining a sheep, but having been shown rational, has a table of rational foods, made ready by the Lord … And give heed, whether also as long as one lives, seeing the truth through a mirror and a riddle, he is a sheep led under a shepherd; but having passed upon the coming age, gazing face to face at the truth, he applies to a spiritual table, according to: “And I will covenant a covenant to you, to eat and to drink upon the table of the Father in the truth.” Whence also “you prepared” has been said, for from here God prepared the things which the eye has not seen, and so on. And “before me” shows that the table has been manifested to me and known to me, opposite those who afflict me, many wishing to be hostile to me.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Anointed from the Lord with Christ, the oil of gladness, he can refuse the oil of a sinner.
comments.comment: And the one whose head is anointed with oil from the Lord will say: “Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head” (Psalm 141:5; LXX 140:5), as being anointed from God with the oil of gladness, Christ. And I think that also when fasting he is thus anointed on the head, and the face is washed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The table is set neither near nor far but before him, in front of those distressing him, as when a strong and effective door of the word brings many opponents, among them the devil.
comments.comment:
Therefore, he prepared this table not near the one being called, nor far from him, but before him and in front of those distressing him.

The apostle, turning this enigma to something clearer, writes: 'For a large and effective door has been opened to me, and many are standing against me' (1 Cor 16:9).

When someone has a word and a door of a word strong and effective, he has many standing against him.

And the devil himself stands against, wishing to prevent the benefit from the effectiveness of the word, as do sophist men and other evil men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The oil points to Christ, in whom the saints are anointed beyond their fellows, and the one who is anointed is not to be touched.
comments.comment:
You showed me Christ; according to what is signified it is said:

'Touch not my anointed ones' (Psalm 105:15; LXX 104:15).

And this holy one was one of the anointed, of those anointed 'with oil of gladness beyond his fellows' (Psalm 45:7)—of Christ.

The man himself was anointed beyond his fellows, beyond the other anointed ones, concerning whom it has been said:

'You went forth for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones' (Hab 3:13).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The head signifies the mind, which rules and leads our whole composition, and the words are 'with oil' because there is also worthless oil, the oil of the sinner.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the head and the oil stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since not everyone can drink the whole mixing-bowl Wisdom mixed, each is given a cup, and 'intoxicating' means gladdening, an excellent, sober intoxication.
comments.comment:
'And your cup intoxicating, as excellent' (Psalm 23:5; LXX 22:5).

Since not everyone can drink the whole mixing-bowl which wisdom mixed (Prov 9:2), he distributes to each a cup, which receiving, he can be gladdened.

Some copies have:

'and my cup';

which you have given me.

However, it is said either way.

'Intoxicating,' then, is 'as excellent'.

It brings the drinker excellent intoxication—sober intoxication.

And 'intoxicating' is instead of 'gladdening'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unusual word 'intoxicating' for the cup.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who drink in darkness and ignorance drink intoxicatingly, but those who take the divine drink are made glad and drink soberly.
comments.comment: "They drink intoxicatingly by night." In darkness and ignorance, these people drink. But those who drink, having taken a divine drink—that is, having been made glad—drink in a sober way. "Eat, drink, be intoxicated, brothers," the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 5:1). The "be intoxicated" does not mean this, not "be strengthened" from wine, but "be made glad."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Holy Spirit divides from the mixed vessel a cup to each, the strongest and most precious for the one who receives it, and the mixture of wisdom is not human.
comments.comment: The Holy Spirit, having mixed divine decrees with human words, divides from this vessel a cup to each; and the cup that is strongest for the one is the most precious and exceptional to the one receiving it, for it is said that the Holy Spirit makes this a matter of profit. To the one who has received, He says, 'And my cup' (Ps 23:5). If your cup were to carry such a thought, it would be the cup of you, the Lord, 'whom you have given me to drink' (Ps 23:5). For the aforementioned mixture proposed toward wisdom is not human.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The oil signifies the gladness in the saints' hope or the visitation from above, and the head is a type of the mind.
comments.comment: David too sings somewhere: ‘You anointed my head with oil’ (Psalm 23:5), the oil signifying the gladness in hope of this voice of the saints, or else the visitation from above that makes us glad. For we who have believed have received mercy, and we are blessed by the Lord, our mind richly fed by the supply of the Spirit; and the head is a type of the mind.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: God's mercy anoints the head not for a little while but always, staying close so that it pursues him all the days of his life and does not let him grow distant.
comments.comment: And "your mercy shall pursue me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Your mercy is as if "I have anointed my head" (Psalm 23:5); it does not anoint my head for a little while, but always; since it is near to me, and thus every one of the anointed ones becomes a Christ eternally. Therefore "all the days of my life" pursues me; it does not allow me to become distant from it; for it is close by, since it is present to me … It no longer dwells for a day or two, but for "all the days of my life." And "all the days of life" takes in the illuminations of the soul having come from the sun of righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Salvation comes not from works but from God's mercy, which pursues the speaker always and not at times, and he dwells in the Lord's house all the days of immortal life.
comments.comment:
No one reaps such a salvation from works, but from the grace of God being merciful (Psalm 23:6; LXX 22:6a). For God, being rich in mercy, through the great love approaching Him toward men, has made alive in Christ the dead who had come to be through sins and trespasses; therefore the Holy One says: 'And your mercy shall pursue me, always coming and overflowing for me' (Ps 23:6). Not indeed at times or sometimes, but all the days of my life it pursues me (Ps 23:6). And all the days of life are the various illuminations of the truth through which we happen to be made alive, namely the Christ who is present with us through life.

He settles in a place of pasture, and in the house of the Lord he dwells (Psalm 23:6; LXX 22:6b), not for a certain time but all the days of immortal life, being illuminated unceasingly and repeatedly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mercy that pursues is Christ, who overtakes those who flee less and leads them into the church, that they may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days.
comments.comment:
Who is the mercy that pursues? I learned Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God from the apostle, and that he was born for us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption. He himself says: “I am the way and life and truth” (John 14:6). Learn that he himself is also the mercy that pursues; living mercy pursues you.

Those who flee less it overtakes and holds, and leads them into the church, that he may have mercy and they may dwell in the house of the Lord, unto length of days, and into the holy church in the heavens, and become long-lived.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the pursuing mercy is and where it leads.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The title is fitting because the first of the Sabbath is also the eighth day, which begins a second week, the new Sabbath of the Gospel.
comments.comment: A Psalm to David; of the first Sabbath. The superscription is appropriate; for it is for the one day of the Sabbaths. "One of the Sabbath"; the eighth following. This also is the first of the Sabbath. For since it is a beginning of a cycle of a week, it is also called the eighth; for the week is circumscribed up to the seventh, the seventh being an addition, that is, a day or a unit. The second begins again from a unit. This is called at one time the first of the Sabbath, that is, after the Sabbath, and at another time the eighth, so that the two weeks may be gathered together. In the giving of the holy part to the seven and the eight, the Jew alone has the Sabbath. They have neither the first of the Sabbath nor the eighth, having not at all considered the former week. Therefore, he alone, having the ecclesiastical opinion, who brings forth from his treasure new and old according to another comparison of the Gospel (Matthew 13:52), has the new of the Sabbath. Transcending the first week, he began the second, which is according to the Gospel. And this also is called the eighth in relation to the first week and the first of the Sabbaths.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fullness of the earth is its fruits and animals, the inhabited world and its inhabitants are the Lord's too, and God made both, so the verse speaks in a general sense.
comments.comment:
The first verses of the Psalm can be understood both according to the word and the sense. … We take this literally: that fruits and animals are the fullness of the earth. The apostle instructs, advising those from the Gentiles and the Jews not to be superstitious about foods, saying: 'Whatever is sold in the market, eat, without examining anything (1 Cor 10:25); for the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Ps 24:1).' Meat is especially sold in the markets, but also other things contributing to nourishment.

'The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' (Ps 24:1) means the inhabited world and all who dwell in it. I said earlier that the earth was divided into its part for farming and its part for habitation. That which has the preparation for habitation is called the inhabited world, but that for farming and other things is called earth. God is the maker of both; for how could these be his, if he himself had not made them? Therefore, 'the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' takes it in a general sense.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the earth', 'its fullness' and 'the world' mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth is the Lord's because he descended and freed it from the demons who held it, its fullness is all the mortal things on it, and the inhabited world is his church, founded on the seas, which are the storms of trials.
comments.comment: The earth has become more mystical of the Lord; how greatly he descended and liberated it from those who tyrannically hold it, the demons, destroying all the deceits being performed upon it: magic, sorcery, the divinations of the demons upon the earth along with the laws concerning idols and sacrifices. But also its fullness is of the Lord, namely all the mortal things dwelling upon it; the fullness of goods He cast upon it according to the Psalm, 'The earth is full of the Lord's mercy, and full of His praise' (Psalm 33:5). But also the inhabited world; and this is His church under the sun, apart from those dwelling in it. But this inhabited world is inhabited by those who think and live ecclesiastically. He himself established it upon the seas, and the seas being understood as the many storms and salt-spray of the trials that occur.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Read upward, the earth is the good heart that bears fruit: with the practical virtues it is an earth having fullness, and with the gifts of the Spirit it is an inhabited world having inhabitants.
comments.comment:
And for an upward leading: the following words force even the preceding verses to be led upward. 'The Lord' is that 'earth,' that 'good and noble heart' which received the one whom Jesus cast seed, and bore fruit a hundredfold, or a hundred and sixty and thirty (Matthew 13:8). Often I have said that the intelligible things can be taken in the same way through more various thoughts, when they were saying the soul is a sheep and a plant. Here, therefore, the same earth is both earth and inhabited world. When, therefore, it bears the practical virtues, it is an earth having fullness. But when it has the divine gifts of the Spirit, it is an inhabited world having inhabitants. It is not a desert; for He has not said, 'Come, and let us abandon it,' as it is said to the doomed inhabited world. And this is the assembly of the Jews.

And he extends this also to every soul having, at first, a dwelling, but leaving it by its own fault. Therefore, this is connected to: 'He himself founded it upon the seas' (Psalm 24:2). Sea and seas is the name given to the place of earth and the condition of those dwelling there. Having being in billows and in saltiness, I call the dwelling; upon these seas He founded it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth, established upon the seas and prepared upon rivers, has no hard and solid foundation but hangs in the waters, as Job says it hangs upon nothing.
comments.comment: He established it upon the seas and prepared it upon rivers—that is, the earth or the inhabited world. The inhabited world is also the earth. What is said here is equal to what is said: 'He who made the earth stand upon the water,' and by Job: 'hanging the earth upon nothing' (Job 26:7); for if it is established in the sea, it does not have a hard and solid foundation, but in the waters it has the hanging. And every water has a ground beneath it. Since the sea has a ground beneath it, it must certainly have something underlying it. But nothing else is found except the liquid. For this reason, he says the earth is established upon the seas.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth holds itself by turning around itself and not by resting on hard ground, which is what hanging it upon nothing means, by the will of God.
comments.comment: It holds itself by turning upon itself. It is not a hard ground supporting it as if so arranged, but it turns around itself. Indeed, even the Greeks say in their accounts that straight lines sent from a circle—and straight lines are not perceptible, but are considered by reason—hold it in the very center. And this is the hanging it upon nothing. This is the will of God; for 'you established the earth for its stability, it shall not be moved for ever and ever' (Ps 104:5). For how could the seat received by such a word of God be prone to falling?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth founded upon the seas shows water poured around it on every side, yet the earth hanging by itself presents the same or greater difficulty.
comments.comment: For what does “He founded it upon the seas” (Psalm 23:2 (LXX)) indicate, except that the nature of water is poured around the earth on every side? How then, since water is flowing and naturally falls downward, does it remain suspended and never flow away? But do you not consider that the earth hanging by itself, being heavier in nature, presents the same or even greater difficulty for reasoning?
comments.selected_reason: Explains what founding the earth upon the seas means.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The earth is founded upon the sea and prepared for the rivers so that it may be benefited by them, since bodies without water sprinkled through them become fragments.
comments.comment: It has been founded, and a part of the earth is the inhabited world, and it itself appropriately has this seat by its moist nature. And he says regarding the rivers that it is prepared for them; not to be founded upon rivers, but to be prepared; for it is not possible to say that it is founded both in the sea and in the rivers, but it has been founded upon the sea, having been prepared for the rivers, so that it might be benefited by them, just as certain springs and channels flowing through it. Such bodies, if they do not have water sprinkled throughout them by which they can be held together, become fragments. And these things are to be understood regarding the literal sense.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between 'founded upon the sea' and 'prepared for the rivers'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rivers on which they are prepared are those flowing from the belly of each believer, and the various gifts of the Spirit are the rivers.
comments.comment: … for here they are established so that they may appear 'having been rooted and built up in love' (Eph 3:17). And 'upon the rivers' (Psalm 24:2) of those flowing from the belly of the one having the Spirit, they are prepared, so that they may receive these rivers flowing from the belly of each believer. And the various gifts of the Spirit are the rivers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who ascends the Lord's mountain is the one who makes progress, and standing in the holy place is perfection, being perfect as the Father in heaven.
comments.comment: 'Who is he that ascends into the mountain of the Lord and stands in the holy place?' (Ps 24:3). An answer is brought: 'You seek who is ascending and standing? He who is innocent with his hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain' (Ps 24:4).' This is the one ascending through progress. And progress is the ascent. And the standing is in the perfection. When someone becomes 'perfect as the Father in heaven' (Matt 5:48), he has stood in the holy place, unless indeed he surpasses the whole such state and takes the beginning of another; therefore also in the psalms it is said: 'I have seen the end of every completion' (Psalm 119:96).
comments.selected_reason: Explains ascending and standing as progress and perfection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question of who ascends and stands cannot be taken historically, and the answer is not a place but a character: innocent in hands and pure in heart.
comments.comment: But since the following things can no longer be taken historically: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place?' (Ps 24:3), it is necessary to say that the way of the ascent and the seat of the standing were not mentioned, but the answer is made to the one asking: 'Who is the one ascending and who is the one standing?' Thus: 'innocent of hands and pure in heart.' That being innocent refers to the hands, and that being pure refers to the actions. Then he says 'a divine character': 'innocent of hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain may be read as the temple, and the words about not swearing recall the commandment against taking the Lord's name in vain, which the young man keeps by not swearing at all.
comments.comment:
The Jews, therefore, perhaps say that 'to ascend to the mountain' means to ascend into the temple and to stand in it. … It lies in the Decalogue: 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not cleanse him who takes his name in vain' (Ex 20:7).

… The young man, being ready to receive the laws of God, 'does not swear at all' (Matthew 5:34); therefore he does not take the name of the Lord in vain. He receives it not in vain, being satisfied with 'yes, yes' and 'no, no' (Matt 5:37).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The generation of the righteous is likeness: 'the generation of those seeking him' names those adorned with the same virtue, as the sons of this age are a generation of similar way of life.
comments.comment: It might also be said thus: the generation of the righteous is similarity, and this is signified from 'This is the generation of those seeking him' (Psalm 24:6); for having said, 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who has innocent hands and is pure in heart' (Psalm 24:3-4) and the following, he brought forward: 'This is the generation of those seeking him,' having spoken of one generation of those adorned with the same virtue. By this, in the opposite way, similarly, it is the thing said: 'Sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation'; for the generation of such things is the similar state and way of life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question is about every person with clean hands and a pure heart, and the generation of such people seeks God's face in order to be enlightened by it.
comments.comment: The inquiry has become directed toward a holy place, not as an answer concerning a single person, but concerning every pure person with clean hands and a pure heart. Therefore, the text also brings forth the generation of those seeking him, instead of saying 'All such are'; and the generation having possessed the virtue of the aforementioned are seeking the Lord. They seek in order to find the face of God, as Jacob, whom they wish to behold, might be improved by the understanding and the illumination of it in some way: 'The light of your face has been signaled to us, Lord' (Psalm 4:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As the answer to who shall stand names no number but the one innocent in hands and pure in heart, so the answer to who is the King is given by his deed: the Lord strong in war, who destroyed the power of death.
comments.comment: The mountain of the Lord: 'and who shall stand' (Psalm 24:3). And 'how many' was not used—not that Abraham or John were meant—but 'if anyone is innocent in hands and pure in heart', so also here he did not say 'how many', but by deed he showed the matter: 'the Lord is mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:7, 8). As it began, these things were pre-proclaimed. But when he rose and was ascended, it is no longer said that 'he will come out' (Ps 24:8), the one who transformed the kingdom upon the earth, the one who destroyed the power of death, the devil; but he is 'mighty and strong, the Lord is strong in war' (Ps 24:8). Comparing that prophecy which has it thus: 'the Lord of powers will come out and will crush the war'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To take one's soul 'in vain' is to spend its deliberating and acting on transitory things or on sins like drunkenness and injustice, and to exhaust the mind's strength on vain things.
comments.comment:
This is understood in two ways. 'In vain' refers to the foolish person taking his own soul, deliberating, choosing, and acting; for often these things—the unseemly, the sensible, the transitory—are signified by the name 'vain'; as if he were saying, 'and you will know where you were, when you were trusting in vain things,' meaning the transitory things. It can also refer to the sins themselves. 'In vain' he took it, the one rising in the morning and drinking wine and staying late so as to be consumed by the wine; for 'woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink and stay late; for the wine will consume them' (Isa 5:11). Again, they have haste to rise from dawn and hurry to the courts, in which injustice follows; this one 'has taken his soul in vain.' This is also consistent with what is said in Isaiah to certain people: 'Vain is the strength of your spirit' (Isaiah 33:11). Here, 'spirit' is the opinion.

… His mind is also worn out by 'worldly cares' toward vain things; his strength is in vain. They exhaust the power of reasoning toward vain things. Indeed, one can see such people and even more wicked ones. They exhaust the whole strength of the mind toward these things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In a second reading, God made man rational so that he might receive virtue and exercise it, so one who takes his soul in vain has it unused, like a man who has feet and never walks.
comments.comment: A second explanation for: 'who has not received his soul in vain' (Psalm 24:4). God prepared man as a rational being, not merely so that he might possess reasoning and do nothing according to it; for this He made the rational being, so that he might receive virtue and exercise it. 'He has received his soul in vain' does not mean God gave it thus, but that he himself has taken it thus. As one might say, for example: He made man from soul and body, and there are certain movements of the soul, and there are also movements of the body. We have the activity of members: walking, doing something with the hands, seeing. If anyone, then, for instance, having feet, never walks, he has his feet 'in vain' in a certain way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in vain' with a plain comparison.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After the ascent of the mountain the one who has ascended receives a spiritual blessing in the heavens, which the Lawgiver gives to those who turn to the law in deed, and its cause is the fear of the Lord.
comments.comment: This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord. … And after the ascent of the mountain, so that the summit of the mountain may be the holy place, he says that 'this one shall receive a blessing from the Lord', 'a spiritual blessing, the one in the heavens'; for it is said: 'for indeed the Lawgiver will give blessing'. And the Lawgiver gives not to those transgressing the law, but to those turning toward it in deed. And again: 'Behold, thus', he says, 'shall be blessed the man who fears the Lord' (Psalm 128:4). The cause of the blessing is reverence, the fear toward the Lord; therefore it is said: 'The Lord shall bless you out of Zion' (Ps 128:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who receives the blessing and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those with the same desires are one generation, and to seek the face of God, as Jacob did, is to pray sincerely for his appearing.
comments.comment: Again, those having the same desires are one generation. It is thus also with: 'The generation of the upright shall be blessed' (Ps 112:3). Jacob was seeking the face of God. Everyone praying sincerely for the appearance of God prays to receive it, and this is to seek the face of God. The saints indeed send up a prayer saying: 'Let your face shine upon us and we shall be saved' (Psalm 80:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'generation' and 'seek thy face'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who seek the face of the one about to arrive have heard that he will descend and that a Savior is coming, so that they may learn to strike down the adversaries.
comments.comment: They 'seek the face' of the one about to arrive, having heard that 'bending the heavens, he shall descend' (Psalm 18:9), because 'a Savior is coming' (Isaiah 62:11). For the heralds of the truth, those running ahead of the one arriving, hear: 'Say to the daughter of Zion: behold, a Savior is coming to you' (Isaiah 62:11), and: 'Say to the cities of Judah: behold, our God comes with might' (Isaiah 40:9), to shake off evil, so that we may learn to strike down the adversaries, those working evil, 'the one working in the sons of disobedience' (Ephesians 2:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lower creation lifts the gates at his incarnation, and the upper at his ascension.
comments.comment: And in the twenty-third Psalm: 'Lift up your gates, O rulers, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter in' (Ps 24:7). He exhorts the lower creation to lift up the gates in his incarnation, and the upper in his ascension.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The powers ask who the King of Glory is, as Isaiah asks about the one coming from Edom, and the risen Lord's body kept the marks of the wounds so that he would be recognized as the one who rose.
comments.comment:
Taking these things up, they speak to the heavenly powers, to those dividing the heavenly gates. Then they inquire, 'Who is this King of Glory, whom you announce is coming, to whom the gates must be lifted and the eternal ones—not the temporary ones—the immortal ones, must be raised up?' Near to this is what is brought forward in Isaiah: 'Who is this coming from Edom, with garments stained red from Bozrah? Why are your garments red?' (Isa 63:1). And they inquire again.

Even if this body, being raised from the dead, and especially the one of the Savior previously, does not possess the characteristics of flesh having been transformed into spiritual, yet by the grace of the one ascending, traces were preserved for the recognition of where the one ascending comes from. And because of this: 'Garments stained red from Bozrah' (Isa 63:1). And just as having risen from the dead and appearing to the disciples, desiring to confirm to them that the body which he had has risen, he showed the marks of the wounds, he showed the side, not that the body possesses a side—for to have a side is difficult and unusual—but so that he might be fully known as the one who rose, so that they might not think badly concerning the resurrection from the sign of the fullness of the resurrection, as if after the resurrection the raised body carries the characteristics of the corruptible, 'he entered through closed doors' (John 20:26); so also here, being taken up, immediately after the ascension, he showed the characteristics of the flesh, not so that they might remain; nor did those things which he showed, such as having eaten and the marks of the wounds and the others, remain with him having them. Not so that we might eat, for he ate after the resurrection, but so that they might see that he, whom he said, was himself the one who rose. This indeed Luke says: 'To whom he also proved himself alive after his suffering, by showing many proofs and by eating and touching' (Acts 1:3). Observe that he also proved himself alive after his suffering by eating.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The powers ask for whom the gates are to be lifted, and the answer, 'the Lord, strong and mighty, mighty in war', is given from his works.
comments.comment: Lift up your heads, O gates, and be lifted up, O ancient gates, and the King of Glory shall enter (Ps 24:7). Who is this King of Glory? They inquire: concerning whom is this said that he shall enter, so that we may open the doors for him and lift them up? He says: 'The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord, mighty in war' (Ps 24:8). He makes the answer from His works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who asks the question and how it is answered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Angels running ahead tell the heavenly gates to be lifted up for the King of Glory, and the powers above marvel to see him ascend surrounded by flesh.
comments.comment:
Running forward, divine angels were addressing those standing at the heavenly gates: 'Lift up your gates, O rulers; you are leaders and you are guards.' For just as he, bowing, bent the heaven and did not open it, so having been taken up, he did not enter through opened gates, but through those being lifted up. Since these gates also are spiritual, and the angels say toward them: 'Be lifted up, eternal gates.' But these spiritual gates are not temporary, because they are not bodily, but eternal because of the incorporeal and unblemished nature; yet they say that the gates should be lifted and be lifted up, not so that the glorious ones might enter, but that the King of Glory might enter.

And it is said that the Savior is the King of Glory to rule over all the glorious ones according to God, and as one bringing glory from all and possessing the true and lasting kingdom. Providing this to the worthy, and he is its Lord, it is said according to: 'For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of Glory' (1 Cor 2:8). But since not God the Word alone ascended, but coming forth he was taken up in flesh, being animated by a spiritual soul, the powers above were astonished, asking: 'Who is this King of Glory?' For seeing the one spoken of as the King of Glory surrounding himself with flesh, they marveled.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After the Savior's arrival his ascent is signified by the call to lift up the gates, which the rulers guard, and the heralds, angels, announce him.
comments.comment: Finally, having enjoyed the economy [God's plan of salvation]—for 'still' 'it shall say of your word: I am present' (Isaiah 58:9)—immediately the ascent of the Savior is signified after the arrival; for the word says through the psalms: 'Lift up your gates, O rulers of yours' (Ps 24:7). Your rulers, lift up the gates. Or thus: your gates, O rulers, lift up, which you preside over, which you guard. 'And be lifted up, O eternal gates' (Ps 24:9). The word says 'and be lifted up', presenting the greatness of the one about to descend and enter through the gates. If you remain here, you will not be able to contain his ascent. To lift up and to lift up further can also mean to make them through the middle; for he who is the very distant King does not need an entrance. And again: 'And the King of glory shall enter' (Psalm 24:9). The heralds, angels, announce the Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the Lord is mighty and strong in war, the rulers are told not to delay in lifting up the gates, which are themselves rational, and the answer comes that the Lord of powers is the King of glory.
comments.comment: The Lord is strong in war: 'lift up your gates, O rulers of you' (Ps 24:7). Since they asked who it is, and having said it, they asked 'which are the gates' and to open them, they say: since the Lord is mighty and strong and strong also in war, do not hesitate, do not delay. And behold: to those in charge he says: 'lift up the gates' (Ps 24:7). And since the gates also are rational, and toward them he stretches out, saying: 'and be lifted up, eternal gates' (Ps 24:9). And 'be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will come in' (Ps 24:10). Therefore he says: 'the Lord of powers, this is the King of glory'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question is asked twice; the first answer, 'strong and mighty in war', might fit one of the powers chosen by God, so the second answer names him 'the Lord of powers', Lord and not himself a power.
comments.comment:
Thus they are arrayed for battle. Who is this king of glory? The Lord of powers, He is this king of glory. Do not seek who He is regarding what we say; for the Lord of powers, He is. And you also are powers, and each of you a power according to the second meaning. 'Lord' therefore; because with authority He said that 'He is the king of glory.'

… But previously they inquired: 'Who is this king of glory?' (Ps 24:8) and they heard an answer; then, since the king of glory is not a random person, they inquired with greater precision and a second time, and moreover they received another answer, no longer 'the Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord is mighty in war' (Ps 24:8); for perhaps it was possible to suppose that one of the powers had been chosen by God; and he says: 'The Lord of powers, he is the king' (Ps 24:10). Thus I call him the Lord of powers, not as a power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the question 'Who is this King of glory?' is asked twice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angels answer that the King of Glory is the Lord mighty in war who has defeated the fallen powers, and they call him 'Lord of Powers' as commander of armies.
comments.comment:
Again, those running forward said, 'Lord, mighty and powerful,' shouting contrary to this: 'Not the one surrounding himself with a body, but the one having excelled against those who fell from us and having taken on a tyrannical power, the Lord who is mighty in war,' having seen that he had utterly defeated all, to contradict and to wish to stand against them. …

They were not satisfied with doing only what was commanded, but they also stood over the higher powers and the gates of the higher heavens, as they reported, proclaiming the gates of the Most High, your rulers, and so on. And when they were questioned again, the angels answered them, and this was their answer, saying, 'Lord of Powers,' He is the King of Glory. But they call Him 'Lord of Powers' as a commander of armies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Powers' can mean the heavenly armies or each rational being who shares in Christ the power of God, and the Lord is the Lord of these powers.
comments.comment: Often the armies are signified by the name of power. The Lord is of these powers, of the heavenly armies; for such powers appeared to the shepherds praising God when Christ was born. And altogether the Lord is of all these powers, of the thousands and myriads praising and ministering. And it is possible to take the powers thus: each rational substance acting as a power of holiness. Just as we say a musical woman and a grammatical woman, when she possesses these things, so the one participating in 'Christ, the power of God' (1 Cor 1:24), each is a power. Therefore, the Lord is of these powers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one taken up in glory, as Paul writes, is the Lord of glory, the king of glory.
comments.comment: Concerning this power and this manifestation, Paul also writes: 'The mystery of godliness is great, for He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit' (1 Tim 3:16), and 'taken up in glory' (1 Timothy 3:16). The one taken up in glory is the Lord of glory, He is the king of glory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Lord of Powers' renders the name Sabaoth, which is also rendered 'Pantokrator', and that title fits the Son, through whom all things came to be and hold together.
comments.comment: It should be noted that those who have been precise regarding the Hebrews say that the voice of Sabaoth is lying in the Hebrew. The Seventy translate into Greek either 'Lord of Powers,' 'Lord of Armies,' or 'the Pantokrator.' They say, indeed, that in this place where Sabaoth is located, the translation into 'Lord of Powers' has occurred. But if Sabaoth lies concerning the Savior, it is also translated into 'the Pantokrator,' so that it is fitting the voice of the Pantokrator should be attributed to the Savior; for if all things came into being through Him, and He is before all things, and all things consist in Him, and He holds providentially all things having come into being through Him, and He is before all things consisting in Him, it follows that He is called Pantokrator. For it is His face speaking in Zechariah: 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have been sent after glory' (Zechariah 2:8), and 'You shall know what the Lord of hosts has sent me to you' (Zechariah 2:11). For the Son is the Pantokrator being sent by the Pantokrator, being sent by the Father. And most clearly in the Apocalypse of John, the Savior is called Pantokrator: 'These things says the Lord, the faithful and true witness, the one who was and the one who is and the one who is coming, the Lord God the Pantokrator' (Rev 1:8). For these things have been said about the Son without dispute.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who lives to God alone can say he has lifted up his soul to God, tearing it away from the things below, from the devil and the causes of evil.
comments.comment: 'To you, Lord, I have lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1). It is not for everyone to say: 'To you I have lifted up my soul, O God.' But he who is able to say: 'My soul lives to him' alone lifts up his soul to God. God is in highness; I do not speak according to a place—and often these things have been made clear to us—but in a highness of surpassing nothingness. When someone therefore tears away from the things below his own soul, from the devil and the causes of evil and of evil itself, he lifts it up to God, so that it may live to him alone, so that it may dwell with him, so that 'having been joined as one spirit' it may become to him. It is a great thing to say this voice, having an unknowable soul. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to lift up one's soul to the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A psalm 'to David' is brought to the one who does all God's will, so it may be said of everyone who does the will of God.
comments.comment: A Psalm of David. The psalm is said to be 'to David'; for it is one thing to be 'of David' and another to be 'to David'. 'Of David' is said when he himself has composed or is singing. But 'to him' is said when it is brought to him. If, therefore, I say that this triumphal hymn is to the athlete, to the victor, then David has set a subscript. And the things said do not stand only regarding his own person, but also if another should be found according to him. Who then is this David? 'Who will do,' he says, 'all my will' (Acts 13:22). Let the psalm be said concerning everyone who does the will of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Few can truly lift up their soul to the Lord, for that takes a heart made pure by the truth and a life free from sin, and to say it is easy but to do it is hard.
comments.comment:
One is able to say such things about oneself. But such a person is rare, and because of the difficulty of finding them, they are perhaps thought by some not to exist at all. Furthermore, the rarity is shown by the proverbist saying: 'Who shall boast having a pure heart and shall speak boldly as being free from sin?' (Proverbs 20:9). By saying pure, he means the heart being rightly disposed and thinking concerning piety. He who is persuaded according to the truth, that one has a pure heart. And he who is outside of practical sin speaks boldly as being free from sin.

Because the truth and those things thought truly purify the soul and the heart, Peter the apostle writes: 'having purified your souls in the obedience of the truth' (1 Peter 1:22). And James writes: 'Cleanse your hands, sinners, and purify your hearts, double-minded' (James 4:8). They cleanse hands, those making their actions crooked, and they purify their soul, those casting away all double-mindedness; 'and purify' indeed, he says, 'hearts, double-minded.' Most of all, those thinking wrongly are double-minded.
