Sometimes they are seized by glory and held by it, but when they look at things otherwise, they find them to be having something else, and how they once remain in the grasping bad-glory.

Thus, one is presented as free from sin who has lived a life according to the right way. He has a pure heart, the one thinking the things of the truth, having taken 'the mysteries of the kingdom' (Matthew 13:11) in soul and having been initiated according to them. This one, therefore, lifts up the soul toward the Lord. It is not one who happens to do so who lifts it. To say it is perhaps easy for everyone, but to do it is either difficult or has reached the point of being nearly impossible, not because of his own nature.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who call God Lord in deed as well as voice are truly his slaves and are not put to shame, while those who commit sin feel shame and perish in that state.
comments.comment:
… And these men themselves, when they call the God Lord, do not say it with voice alone, but with deed and disposition. When they act thus, disposed as toward a master, doing what he wills and commands, they are truly slaves; and since what is turned toward him is that of a truly slave, he is truly a master. 'My God, in you I have trusted; let me not be put to shame' (Psalm 25:2). Happy is the one having precise knowledge, having trusted in it, who converses with all and is not put to shame. …

They act wickedly; therefore, they are not ashamed. For those committing sin are the ones undergoing shame. Some say, 'they shall rise up for reproach and eternal shame.' Thus the word prays for the unfeeling that shame may come to be for them: 'fill their faces with dishonor'—speaking regarding faults—'and let them be ashamed and perish and know that you are the Lord' (Psalm 83:16-18). When they feel shame, being such wicked people, they perish according to that state in which they are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He prays with trust in God not to be shamed or made a laughingstock by his enemies, who are the devil, the evil powers and all men except the God-fearing.
comments.comment: Let me not be put to shame, as those who trust in others are put to shame; for he who trusts in wealth shall not fall (Psalm 25:1-3; LXX 24:1-3). This is to be said synecdochically concerning all temporal things. For I pray, having trust toward You, not to contend with those who are striving, lest I should be made a laughingstock by the enemies; and my enemies are the devil and the other evil powers and men except the God-fearing. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enemies mock when trust in God seems to end in shame, yet they are his enemies, not he theirs.
comments.comment: … Let my enemies not mock me. Then my enemies will mock me, when saying that having trusted in you, shameful things are being worked out. They are enemies to me, not I to them. For this reason also the Savior says: 'Love your enemies' (Matt 5:44). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who endure and hope in God will see their mockers' laughter come to an end, while the way of those who work iniquity brings shame.
comments.comment:
Enduring you. Perhaps these things suit the saints before the arrival. They await him and endure his coming descent. For when he has come, the laughter of the enemies will reach its end, those who mocked against those hoping in God.

The way through emptiness, the vain and empty, signifies this (Psalm 25:3; LXX 24:3b). Such is that in Proverbs 14:12: 'The way of all those who work iniquity, bringing shame to those who sin in vain'; for they do not perform the things of iniquity toward any perfection like the guardians of the law. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'All' here means 'no one', so none of those who wait on God is shamed, and those who act lawlessly do so for nothing, since wickedness has no being of its own.
comments.comment: … For indeed all those waiting for you will not be shamed (Psalm 25:3). The 'all' is often in the Scripture taken instead of the universal decision; for we do not even say this, that of those waiting, some are shamed and others are not, as the particular decision teaches, saying: not all men are just. Here therefore instead of 'no one': no one of those waiting for you is shamed. And continuously in the Scripture the universal decision is signified through the universal affirmation taken from transposition. And you know that the affirmation from transposition often follows the simple decision. … Let all those acting lawlessly be shamed for nothing. Hear 'to act lawlessly for nothing' thus: wickedness is worked out for nothing, not to bring glory, not for the promise. It is unstable, its being is in something else. If therefore the one having wickedness wishes to cast it away, it no longer exists. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must be taught the Lord's paths step by step, the practical life first and then the contemplative life, and be led finally by Christ, who is the truth.
comments.comment: … The paths of the Lord, his commandments one must speak (Psalm 25:4-5; LXX 24:4-5). But he also says that one must teach them as paths worn by foot-traffic, so that having trodden the tracks, I may make my course unerring. And since the practical life alone is not sufficient for perfect salvation, so that with this I might also perfect the contemplative life, 'Guide me pedagogically upon your truth.' And furthermore, according to the place, it will be said: of the law and the prophets, encountering the paths of the Lord, no one else will make them known to the one desiring to be tested by them, who is the Lord himself. For having made known to his paths and having taught the foot-traffic, through having spoken to the fathers in the prophets, 'Guide me upon the one who said: I am the truth' (John 14:6), having spoken in the Son at the end of days. And indeed you, O God, are my savior; for through whom you taught me, you will provide salvation to me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To learn the Lord's ways one follows those who have worn the path, and to know comes before to teach, since the learner must already hold some common concepts.
comments.comment:
Therefore make known to me your ways; for in this manner I shall learn your paths, following those who have worn them down, those who have proceeded in the good things or those who have proceeded because you proceeded, having a subscript and a pattern, 'that we may follow your footsteps' (1 Peter 2:21). Therefore, to know precedes to teach. Thus it is said that demonstrations and teachings come from things already known. It can be understood in this way: that common concepts are pre-known. And indeed, when we test a teaching, we say we are testing it in reference to common concepts.

For indeed, at times a teacher says something, and the common concept of the learner pre-perceives and knows whether he speaks well or not. You will find even in these human, scientific demonstrations, that sciences are not being led well if those listening do not pre-perceive what it is necessary to pre-perceive. For indeed, this has often been said to us: that when someone learns something that must be foreknown before the instruction, it is not right to speak to him through obscure words, since it is not familiar to him. 'Guide me into the truth' (Psalm 25:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks the Lord, who is his Creator and Savior, to be his teacher and guide him into the truth, which is Christ, and 'all the day' means the whole of the saints' life, lit by the truth.
comments.comment:
After the practical virtues and the guidance according to disposition, the guidance into the truth occurs; for, he says, 'desiring wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will supply it to you' (Sirach 1:26). And wisdom and truth are the same. The Savior, indeed, is said to be both: 'Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24). And he himself said: 'I am the truth' (John 14:6).

And teach me, that you are my God and Savior. You are my God, having created me; you are my Savior, willing that I should improve. Therefore, become my teacher. As Creator, so also become teacher. And I waited for you all the day. I waited for you all the time of my life, so that I might have you as teacher and Savior; for 'toward you' I 'lifted up my soul' (Ps 25:1), not toward another. I did not entreat another, so that you might make known to me your ways and teach me your paths, but I deemed you worthy to become teacher of these things to me.

Often the whole of our life's time is called 'a day', according to what has been said: 'for your sake we are dying all the day' (Psalm 44:22), instead of what the apostle has made 'every day' (1 Corinthians 15:31). And 'a day' can be said to be the whole time of the life of the saints, because they are always in light, being illuminated by the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the psalmist asks to teach him and what 'all the day' means, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's ways are of two kinds, those leading toward him, which are the virtues, and those he himself walks in his providence, and he must make both known.
comments.comment: 'Make known to me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths. Lead me into your truth' (Ps 25:4-5). The ways of God are said to be twofold: either those leading toward Him, or those which He Himself walks, proceeding through all things, as is necessary according to the word of providence or according to benefiting and being in His receptive ones. For he says: 'I will dwell in them and walk about' (2 Corinthians 6:16). But he who walks about has paths, which He Himself walks. Thus, we call the ways of God either those leading toward Him—and these are the virtues—or those which He Himself treads according to His providence and judgment and administration and gift. It is therefore necessary to know the ways of God by Him making them known. 'And teach me your paths' (Ps 25:4). That is, those which those hurrying toward You tread, or those which You tread, proceeding through the works of Your grace. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'your ways' and 'your paths' mean in a way a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy belongs to God's nature as shining belongs to light, so he is asked to remember mercies that are from the age.
comments.comment: As the proper energy of light is to illuminate and of knowledge is to know (Psalm 25:6; LXX 24:6), so it is the proper energy of God to have mercy and to show mercy, and 'God and Father of mercies' is said. The saint does not wish to say it is such a thing; being a Father who is a source and beginning of them, he says 'Remember these, your offspring.' For even if you were angry for a little while with those who sinned, but the anger is not according to your nature, but having come into being usefully for destroying evil, let it cease, taking memory of your mercies which are according to your nature. And we also have become accustomed, being indignant at our own, and to speak to weak men, 'Remember your goodness and imitate yourself, reconciling with those under indignation.' Just as the mercies fittingly belong to God, so also his mercies, present to him according to nature, are 'from the age' (Psalm 25:6), whence they also remain unto the age according to 'For his mercy is unto the age'; and to someone God says, 'With eternal mercy I have had mercy on you' (Isa 54:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks for mercy not as something his merit has earned but as the gift of the God who has always been merciful and good.
comments.comment: Remember your mercies, O Lord, and your compassions, because they are from eternity. For even if I have entreated and lifted my soul to you and desired other things to be present to me from you, I do not ask these things according to merit. You provide these things mercifully and compassionately in accordance with the one: 'not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16); for even if we have done all things from ourselves, by the mercy of God we strive to attain their end. Hear me as a merciful one, and as a compassionate one receive my prayers. 'And your compassions, because they are from eternity'. For it is not yesterday and the morning that I began to be compassionate. You are eternal, you are eternally good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist appeals to God's mercies rather than his own merit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks forgiveness for past sins and ignorance, 'youth' can mean the newness of a person's conduct and not only his age, and 'remember me' means 'know me'.
comments.comment: Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances (Ps 25:7). You see that concerning former ignorances and sins one prays for mercy and the compassion of God; for there is no longer repentance sending back a prayer upon committed sins. Repentances happen upon things passed away. For it says: 'do not remember the sins and the ignorances of me' (Ps 25:7) which I have, and now I do not have, but those of youth. And it is possible even thus: whatever the age of the one ignoring and sinning may be, he is young in the youth of his mind, in the newness of his conduct. … According to your mercy, remember me. What about 'remember me'? It is a personal idiom of the Scripture instead of 'know me' (Ps 139:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sins of youth are and what 'remember me' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Confession is made over sins that have ceased, and God, merciful and straight by nature, remembers the repentant with mercy and lays down law for those who sin.
comments.comment: … No one confesses upon those present and actively committing sins, but upon those having ceased and those no longer being sinners. This indeed he says even now, asserting, 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance.' For those having sinned and acted ignorantly in youth are no longer actively committing them to the one having passed through youth. Perhaps the term 'youth' does not signify age here, but the unstable and uncertain state of that period. For anyone who is in such a condition, he is ignorant and sins, as the Scripture says, 'That I might give cunning to the guileless,' whereas a young child is given perception and understanding. Having deemed it worthy that he should not remember the sins and ignorances of his youth, he immediately brought forward: 'According to your mercy, remember me' (Psalm 25:7; LXX 24:7c). For according to mercy, God remembers; he does not recall the faults. By nature, being merciful and God being good, he possesses kindness by nature; he remembers the one repenting with mercy (Psalm 25:8; LXX 24:8). And he is straight because he is not disposed toward sin, and because he requires the sinners to be straight; therefore, he will legislate for those sinning in the way (Psalm 25:8; LXX 24:8). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord remembers him for his goodness and not for his virtue, and because he is good he gives laws to those still sinning so that they may reach salvation.
comments.comment:
Because of your goodness, Lord, not because of my own virtue do you remember me. The Lord is good and upright; he who lives with uprightness is good. For often 'good' is taken in a sense of deception: 'bad associations corrupt good morals' (1 Corinthians 15:33). Thus, 'good' is not taken here in a praiseworthy sense, but in a sense of being easy or indulgent. Similarly with 'innocent': 'the innocent believes every word,' instead of meaning 'the well-disposed.' And regarding heretics, Paul writes: 'by flattering speech and blessing they deceive the hearts of the innocent' (Romans 16:18). Because of this, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way.

If he were abrupt, if he were not good, he would not establish laws in the way of salvation for those sinning, but would hand them over to be punished. Therefore, he establishes laws for those sinning in the way, so that having traveled this way, they may possess salvation. And observe: he does not say 'those who have sinned,' but 'those sinning.' And those still sinning, through exhortations, admonitions, and laws, he leads into the way. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God remembers the psalmist and why a good God teaches sinners.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God puts sinners under law so that they stop sinning and walk the way of salvation, and he guides the gentle, who have turned from the way of death, and teaches them his own ways.
comments.comment:
… For he subjects those actively committing evil to law, so that, having been prevented from sinning, they might walk the way of salvation (Psalm 25:9; LXX 24:9).

The God who legislates will guide those having gentleness and stability in judgment—that is, having been examined and scrutinized (Psalm 25:9; LXX 24:9). For having learned the two ways before the face of man, the way of life and the way of death, and having turned away from the way of death and walking the way of life, he walks in judgment, being led by the Lord, because of the calmness and stability of the mind; for the gentle possess tranquility of thoughts. The Lord himself, after having led the gentle in judgment, will teach them and his own ways, which are the ways leading toward him; for he himself travels them; for one traveling behind the Lord learns his ways (Psalm 25:10; LXX 24:10). All the ways leading toward the Lord, he himself walks in the manner having been said (Psalm 25:9-10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gentle are guided after being judged, and their gentleness is the perfect virtue Christ taught when he said he was gentle and lowly in heart.
comments.comment: He will guide the gentle in judgment. Having judged, he guides the gentle; for again, gentleness often signifies indulgence. But when they are guided having been judged, they possess a perfect virtue, which the Savior taught them to have, saying: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart' (Matt 11:29). And 'in judgment' can also be understood thus: judging these gentle ones to be capable of being benefited, he guides them. And the first interpretation is most in harmony with the text: that having been judged, they come upon the way having God as a guide. Or does he not guide, he who says: 'Learn from me, for I am gentle' (Matt 11:29)?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, and mercy comes first, since we need mercy in order to know the truth.
comments.comment: All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. In many places of the Scriptures, mercy is joined with truth. How great is the truth, so that I might say, it is above men. And observe that all things rational, and all things transcendent, and all things above, require truth. Here, however, we require mercy, so that we may be able to know the truth. It has been said in the previous sections: 'Guide me in your truth, O Lord, and in your paths' (Ps 25:5). Therefore, the beginning of walking these blessed ways is from mercy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why mercy and truth are joined in the Lord's ways.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's testimonies are the words testified by him, so they are irrefutable, and witnesses to the truth confirm themselves and not the truth.
comments.comment:
"And His testimonies": His testimonies are the words testified by Him. You know that what has been testified is irrefutable. Therefore, the irrefutable is often signified by the name of 'testimonies' regarding the divine instructions. What? That which He Himself testified? That which He Himself confirmed. And it is possible to call things irrefutable and unshakeable testimonies, not because they were testified by someone, but because their nature is such that they testify by the truth.

"And the witness," He says, "is faithful in heaven." Concerning God, if it is said that God testifies, we do not mean that the one testifying establishes Him. John came "that he might testify about the light" (John 1:7); for John, the one testifying about the light, did not provide faith and standing to the light. The one testifying shows himself to be knowing by his knowledge, and the one testifying is shown to be diligent by his virtue. So also those who have been well-pleasing and have struggled in persecutions are called witnesses as is fitting. They showed themselves to be lovers of truth, they showed themselves to be knowers of the truth. They did not confirm the truth, but they confirmed themselves. Therefore, those things worthy of the one testifying are often called testimonies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's ways are seen as mercy and truth only by those who seek his covenant and testimonies, which are the covenant with the fathers, the new covenant Jesus confirmed by his death, and the words God inspired.
comments.comment:
Those things established according to truth and becoming present with goodness are mercy and truth. For it is necessary to be shown mercy first, lest anyone fall upon them and, through this, outpace the one traveling upon the truth. But the ways of the Lord are not viewed as mercy and truth by all, but by those seeking His covenant and His testimonies; for he who is outside the covenant and the testimonies is a stranger to the goodness and the beauty of the Lord's ways.

One must seek the covenant which God set forth for the fathers, leading them out of the spiritual Egypt … For having sought and having searched it, we shall enter into it and also the new covenant which Jesus confirmed with His own eyes; for every covenant is powerless if death has not overtaken the one establishing it, as the apostle says; for a covenant is established upon the dead, lest perhaps the one establishing it were not living. Therefore, to fulfill His own covenant, Jesus, willing, accepted death. And one must seek in the covenant also the testimonies of God, those having testified and having been inspired by Him with words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks pardon for the sake of God's name and not for his own diligence or life, and calls his sin great because even a small stain is a great sin to one wholly cleansed.
comments.comment: "For your name's sake, O Lord. Not for the sake of our diligence or our life, but because of your name. This indeed is said in another psalm: 'Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory' (Psalm 115:1); for we are enriched by you and you were named our God, so do it for your name's sake. "And atone for my sin; for it is great." … It has been said before the next part: "Cleanse me from my secret sins" (Psalm 19:12), because even a small stain is a great sin to the one who is entirely cleansed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks pardon for God's name's sake and why his sin is 'great'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: For God's forgiveness the servant seeks his covenant, hoping for a son's inheritance, and asks pardon for his sin as it ceases.
comments.comment: For the sake of Your forgiveness, O Lord, I, Your servant, will seek Your covenant, expecting freedom from it and the inheritance which You appointed as if I had become a son (Psalm 25:11; LXX 24:11). But also, be propitiated toward my sin, not toward the sin being worked, but toward it being ceased. For the required purity is great, not according to quantity but according to the comparison of that which is owed to be offered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fearing God is not something to claim lightly, for the one who truly fears him lacks nothing and is completely full.
comments.comment: … It is not a random person who fears the Lord. Many of us think this way, and many times we say, 'I simply want to fear God.' But we do not know what we are saying; for 'the fear of God surpassed all things,' as the Scripture says. And further: 'there is no lack for those fearing him.' If the one fearing God has no lack, he is most full. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be the man who fears the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Either God or the man can be the one chosen in this way, and virtue is called 'choosable' whether or not anyone chooses it.
comments.comment: He will lay down law for him in the way in which he was chosen. God himself is chosen. But it is possible for the man to be chosen; for virtue is primarily called 'choosable.' Just as that which is worthy of being loved is lovable, even if no one loves it; and likewise that which is worthy of being hated is hateful, even if no one hates it; so the 'choosable' is choosable, even if no one chooses it. For even bad things are chosen, but they are not choosable. Rather, the opinion regarding these things is mistaken. 'He will lay down law for him in the way in which he was chosen.' That is, either the one laying down law or the one receiving law. Both are true.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who fears God is rare but can be found, and the land his seed inherits is not the ground underfoot but that of the gentle ones.
comments.comment: He who fears God is indeed rare, but is not unfindable (Psalm 25:12; LXX 24:12). By this, the Lord does not legislate a way which He Himself preferred, but the one who fears Him. The soul of the devout, if it does not go further into the good things, is satisfied in them, always working them (Psalm 25:13; LXX 24:13). Therefore, the seed will generally obtain the inheritance of the land, not the one under the feet, but that of the gentle ones (Psalm 25:13). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who fears the Lord has a soul delighted in good things, and his seed means those begotten by instruction in virtue.
comments.comment: His soul shall be delighted in good things. This man who fears the Lord has his soul being delighted in good things. And his seed shall inherit the land. 'His seed' is not necessarily the physical—for the bad sons of many holy men were shown to exist—but the seed being generated through instruction and the imitation of virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'his seed' means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who fear God have no other stronghold than the one they fear, and his covenant is like a sealed will written for heirs, which will one day be released so that they receive the inheritance.
comments.comment:
The Lord is a stronghold to those fearing him. Therefore, he speaks of the magnitude of the one fearing God. Those fearing God have no other stronghold than Him whom they fear. He is their strength, he is their king, he holds them. 'And the name' of Him has become a particular possession of 'those fearing him.' It is not a particular possession of men, but of those fearing; for indeed He gave it to all, but it has become the property of those fearing. And His covenant is to make it manifest to them. Covenants, when they are sealed, are not yet manifest...

It is written to the heirs. Therefore, this testament does not remain forever sealed, but it shall one day be released, so that the inheritance may be given to those written down. Thus he will make it known to them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The divine word is called a testament, old and new, which is released when what was foretold is fulfilled and the things promised are handed to those who are worthy.
comments.comment: And since he often calls the divine word a testament, both the old and the new, the one before the visitation and the one after it, this testament must be made known; it must be released. It is released then when the things foretold are fulfilled by the outcome, according to: 'so that what was said might be fulfilled'. For it becomes valid when the one who made the arrangement has died; for the release happens then. Even if it is not released in the sense of a contradiction, it is released by power; for when the things commanded are being handed over to those who have received them, the testament is released. … And what about 'and his testament'?—the testament of God is made known when someone is proven worthy to receive the things promised.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who always keeps his eyes toward the Lord has no sin and a pure heart, and so he is able to see God.
comments.comment: … My eyes are toward the Lord always, because he himself will drag my feet out of the snare (Ps 25:15). Observe that, if we do not attend precisely to the words, opposites are found. It is no longer according to the one saying, 'Great is my sin' (Psalm 25:11), but rather, 'My eyes are toward the Lord always' (Ps 25:15); for he who always keeps his eyes toward the Lord has no sin at all, he has a pure heart. In this way, he is also able to see God himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'mine eyes are ever toward the LORD' means for sin and for seeing God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who keeps his eyes toward the Lord is with him always and does not sin unless he becomes outside God.
comments.comment: Therefore, when he does not see at one time, and perhaps not at another, yet having his eyes toward the Lord always, he says, 'But I am with you always' (Ps 73:23). And being with you, he does not sin. Unless someone becomes outside of God, he does not sin. 'Those who prolong' therefore 'will separate themselves from you' (Psalm 73:27). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous must keep their eyes always toward the Lord, as his eyes are on them, and one who sees God does not sin and so escapes the snare that sin prepares.
comments.comment:
… 'My eyes are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). Since 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Ps 34:15), it is necessary that the righteous also have their eyes continually toward Him.

They do not see Him at all times, but sometimes they see one of the forbidden things; for just as 'no one can serve two masters' (Matt 6:24), so no one can have his eyes toward God and toward evil or the maker of evil first. God is a spiritual essence seen by the eyes of the intellect. When the eyes of the intellect are stretched toward Him alone, they see nothing else. And the physical hands are not able to see when we see God, just as one serving God is not able to serve Mammon.

And regarding 'is not able' I say this: he is not able to do justice while he is doing injustice; for I do not say as I say 'it is not possible for a man to fly,' but rather that as far as he is righteous, he is not able toward sin, and when he is a sinner, he is not able toward virtue. 'My eyes' therefore 'are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). I always see Him. And he who sees God does not sin; 'everyone who sins has not seen Him nor known Him' (1 John 3:6). And behold the piety of the saints; even if he himself chooses to direct his eyes toward the Lord, it is evident that he is not sinning; the achievement of sinlessness is inscribed by God: 'since my eyes are continually toward Him' (Ps 25:15), because of this I escape the snare which sin prepares; for 'He Himself will rescue my feet from the snare' (Psalm 25:15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: There are eyes of the heart and eyes of the senses, and the invisible things of God are rightly seen when we look through his visible works to the one who made them, not when we take the sun for God.
comments.comment:
… And 'having been enlightened the eyes of the heart' (Eph 1:18). We have a twofold knowledge; for then it is knowledge of truth, when the form of each thing being known is received into itself.

The works of God are both visible and invisible; and from the greatness of these and from their beauty, the one who constructed them is perceived. And our mind is an eye seeing the invisible, the pure heart, which also sees God. And we also have the sense of eyes. And if it applies to the visible works of God in this way, as they were constructed and possess nature, it is healthy. But when, I say, seeing the sun we think it is God himself, seeing the heavenly arrangement we regard as mere idle chatter, this eye does not see correctly; for it was necessary 'that the invisible things of God be seen through the works of the creation of the world' (Rom 1:20).

The invisible things of God are seen then, when we apply our sight to the visible creations of God and thus from the creation of this sensible world we see clearly the invisible things of God. We are not able to see the arts and the sciences in the minds of men except when the mind is invisible. And from the constructed works or scientific contemplations we receive the sense of the mind, according to what science or art has made it. Primarily, therefore, one perceives the science of the mechanic; he who is able to receive the principles of mechanical constructions into his own intellect. Similarly also regarding others; we call that one a physician who knows medical matters as they ought to be, as the science dictates.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God keeps the one whose eyes are on him from the traps of the wicked, who are caught in their own snares as Haman was hanged on the wood he prepared, if not in this life then in the next.
comments.comment: Even if the trappers and hunters seek to catch my foot, as if to throw it into a trap, I do not suffer this because I keep my eyes toward the Lord at all times. For often the settings of the wicked snares are called the disciplines of the Divine: 'the foot was caught in that trap which they hid' (Psalm 9:15). Frequently the enemies of truth prepare traps, and by catching others in these traps, they themselves are snared. And there is such a thing in history: Haman prepared wood in order to crucify the righteous Mordecai, and he himself was crucified upon it. And concerning this great man it is said: 'He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the pit which he made' (Psalm 7:15). Even if these things do not happen in this life, they certainly happen in the life to come, caught in the trap which he prepared.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how the Lord plucks the feet of the one who looks to him out of the net.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Only-begotten' here means alone and poor, as the saint who has no support from those of like mind, and it differs from the sense of the only-begotten Son.
comments.comment: He says according to the one saying: 'I also was left alone, and they seek my soul.' Therefore also I am poor, for I do not have the support of those of the same mind. And it is to be known what the 'monogenes' means: the only, just as you would say the only sun; it is not the same as the 'monogenes' Son. For what pertains to the monogenes Son, the only-begotten from the Father, is said to be the only one from Him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sin takes a person from the eyes and face of God, as Adam hid and Cain went out, since God's gaze enlightens those it looks upon.
comments.comment: By sinning, one is distanced from the eyes of God and from His face. Adam, indeed, when he sinned along with Eve, 'was hidden from the face of the Lord God' (Gen 3:8). They do not endure being seen by the face of God when they most clearly realize to themselves that they have sinned. But Cain, acting impudently, led himself away from the face of God; for 'Cain went out.' And the one going out does so by choice. Concerning Adam and Eve, it is said: 'the Lord cast them out.' While they were still inside, He cast them out; for it was no longer permitted for them to be inside. Nevertheless, they were surrounded by desire. They are not as evil as the one who went out from the face of the Lord. These are those about whom it is written: 'lawless ones do not abide before your eyes' (Psalm 5:5). But they go outside the eyes of God voluntarily; for the eyes of God, beholding, enlighten those who are looked upon. 'For I am poor and only-begotten' (Psalm 25:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to ask the Lord to turn to him and look upon him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Only-begotten' said of the Son carries the addition 'from the Father', unlike the sun, which is only an only-begotten sun, as a child is called only-begotten by being the only one to his parent.
comments.comment: Aetius, the leader of the Eunomian heresy, says to some: 'How great a thing you grant by saying that the Christ is the only-begotten of God. And many other creatures are only-begotten. The sun, indeed, is only-begotten.' I say to him: it is not the same thing to be something 'only-begotten' and to be an only-begotten offspring or an only-begotten Son. Therefore, these things said to others as 'only-begotten' are not said with the addition of 'Son,' or 'from the Father,' or 'offspring.' But the Savior, if He is ever so named, is called with such an addition: 'and we beheld His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). And the one who is the only-begotten Son from the Father is the Father's only. And again: 'so God loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son' (John 3:16). I say: since there is an only-begotten Son, it is impossible for there to be another son belonging to that only-begotten Son. And nothing of the creatures is only-begotten; for even if the sun were only-begotten, it is not an only-begotten creature, nor an only-begotten work, but an only-begotten sun. So also among humans we say 'only-begotten child,' not because he is the only one that exists, but because he is the only one to that parent. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Only-begotten' can mean one made solitary and set apart from others by life and contemplation, poor before God though rich in knowledge, or one who has only one soul that God draws out of the snare.
comments.comment:
By what logic they say the sun is only-begotten, by the fact that there is no other sun; so when the saint is made solitary and separated from other men by life and contemplation, he is only-begotten. 'Only-begotten' therefore means 'I am and I am poor.'

Yet he who is thus poor is rich; for he 'is rich' in every sense and in all knowledge. But toward the God who looks upon him and bestows gifts, he is poor; just as Abraham said: 'Since I have begun to speak to the Lord, I am indeed dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27)—for he did not say 'dust and ashes' all at once, but 'since I have begun to speak to the Lord'—so also Moses, though trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and possessing sufficiency regarding speech, called himself 'heavy-tongued and slow of speech' (Ex 4:10) from the time he began to speak to your servant. And this man, therefore, even if he is rich—for nothing is richer than he who has his eyes always toward the Lord—yet toward the one looking upon him and showing mercy, he saw himself as poor.

And it is also possible to say 'only-begotten' meaning 'I have only one soul.' This soul, having been caught, you will draw out from the snare; for to me it is only-begotten.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Tribulation 'widens' the heart only for one who bears it bravely, afflicted but not in anguish, as Paul, Job, the apostles and the martyrs did.
comments.comment:
The tribulations of my heart have widened. Not in every case, I say, do tribulations widen, but for the one bearing them bravely. The apostle writes this: 'In all things being afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Cor 4:8).

Those knowing the Hebrew dialect say that to be in anguish, when it is named after tribulation, signifies the intention of being afflicted, the being in anguish from not bravely bearing the afflictions, such as Job, who 'in all things being afflicted was not in anguish' (Job 1:21); for how could he be in anguish, he who says: 'As it pleased the Lord, so it happened; let the name of the Lord be blessed'? And the apostles coming out from the council, because they were dishonored for the name (Acts 5:41), were not being afflicted according to the disposition, but were rejoicing.

And regarding sensible things, the one contending for the crown of expectation, seeing it lying before his eyes, bravely bears the wounds, and rejoices that, being struck, he does not falter. Therefore the name of tribulation, when one is afflicted but not in anguish, signifies the brave bearing. The martyrs of the truth, being afflicted, were not in anguish.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'enlarged' in a way a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Necessities' here means afflictions, as elsewhere in the Psalms, and he does not mean the fate that astrologers say apportions things to men.
comments.comment:
'and bring me out of my necessities' (Psalm 25:17; LXX 24:17). Here he calls the afflictions necessities. And in other places: 'and they cried to the Lord, and he delivered them from their necessities' (Psalm 107:6; LXX 106:6).

For we must not attend to those who introduce nativity-astrology; for those say this: that fate apportions something to men. But if one is godly and becomes wise according to God, he becomes outside the things suspended by fate. … Some of those occupied with nativity-astrology thus hear such sayings, namely: 'There are fateful crises to which I am subject. Make me outside these; loose fate.'

We do not take the saying thus; rather, he calls the demonstrations necessities.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever is held by the world lives under necessity, but one who rises above it, as to the seventh day, becomes blameless, and he prays to be brought out of necessities by the forgiveness of sins.
comments.comment: The world came into being in six days. He who does not surpass it is under necessity. This number is perfect. What he says is this: he who is contained by the world and its parts and thus lives is necessarily under necessity. But when he surpasses the world and ascends above it, in the seventh he sabbaths from the works of the world. And becoming in the seventh—which is led, pure, and left to the people of God—he becomes blameless. … 'Bring me out of my necessities' (Psalm 25:17). Since we have given to your judgment, look at what appears to me; I say, 'Bring me out of my necessities,' so that I may not be compelled by sin and become loose toward virtue. Then you bring me out of these, if you will give me forgiveness of sins. This too can be understood: the coming punishments, the additional and distressing necessities.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks to be brought out of the pressures that force his purpose off course, and one who sees his own sins, humbled and suffering the fruits of repentance, prays for forgiveness.
comments.comment: And you will perceive the tribulations of the heart and those driving through with opposing thoughts. 'Bring me out of my necessities' (Psalm 25:17); from those surrounding, forcing and necessitating the departure of my intention, just as 'bring me out of great necessities' (Psalm 25:17). One, having taken the perceptions of his own sins, humbling himself because of the lack of boldness and suffering because of the fruits of repentance, says: 'See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins' (Psalm 25:18).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Affliction is called humbling, and the righteous man who always sees the Lord then sees himself as humble, as Abraham did when he began to speak to the Lord.
comments.comment: He labors in this world, having reached a peak, 'the body of lowliness.' Along with this evil, it happens to be humbled; for often affliction is called humbling according to: 'You humbled us in a place of affliction' (Psalm 44:19). When we have come into the place of affliction, we were humbled. … He always had the Lord before him, seeing Him, and then he saw himself humble, even if he is righteous, just as they say concerning Abraham: not always did he see himself as 'earth and ash' (Gen 18:27), but when 'he began to speak toward the Lord.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the psalmist's words about affliction and lowliness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Unjust hatred has no cause other than the hater's zeal, as the disciples of Jesus were hated, and we are taught to pray for those who hate us and not to hate anyone.
comments.comment: 'Behold my enemies, for they have multiplied and unjust hatred has hated me' (Psalm 25:19). Unjust hatred is hated by one who hates for no other reason than that he is zealous. In this way, indeed, the disciples of Jesus were hated. Concerning these things he teaches to send up a prayer: 'Pray for those hating you, love those hating you' (Matt 5:44). It is not we who hate anyone; for it has been said: 'Do not hate any man, love every man' (Lev 19:18). But they hate.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is not our sin to be hated by some when we give no pretext, so those who hate us do so unjustly.
comments.comment: And it is not our sin to be hated by some, but rather an accident, when we provide no pretext of hatred. Therefore he says: 'Behold my enemies, for they have multiplied and unjust hatred has hated me' (Psalm 25:19). They do not hate me with righteous hatred. They hated me as an unrighteous man, as a covetous man. And since they hate me having nothing of these things, they hate me unjustly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what hatred 'without cause' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked hate the righteous in many ways, since one righteous man holds all the virtues while wickedness is divided, and Joseph, Naboth and John were hated unjustly.
comments.comment:
And such people multiply; for if the righteous man is hated because of virtue, he possesses all the virtues according to the many things said concerning the sequence of virtues. The unrighteous hate the righteous, the intemperate the self-controlled, the arrogant the humble, and in every way those in wickedness hate the righteous. The righteous man, therefore, is one, even if he has all the virtues; for wickedness divides those having them, for it is not possible to have all the wickednesses at once. Therefore the coward cannot be bold, the superstitious cannot be impious, the rogue cannot be foolish.

In one way, Egypt hated Joseph, making him a prisoner and a captive to be tested as an evildoer. This hatred was unjust. Jezebel against Naboth worked out death, and it was this hatred that was unjust. And Herodias, the wife of Herod, worked out death against John, showing pity, as much as was in her. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who has ceased sinning hates the demons at work in sins, and many hate him unjustly, so he asks to be kept from falling to those who hate without cause.
comments.comment: When someone ceases to have previously been active in sins, he will hate the demons who are active in them. And indeed many, becoming against the one being plotted against, hate him unjustly; but unjust hatred is that which happens against those doing things not worthy of hatred, while justly hating the evil things. 'Preserve the soul, lest it fall to those who hate unjustly' (Psalm 25:20); but also to rescue it from deeds such as those which they will be able to hold onto.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If God guards his soul he will be rescued or crowned for his affliction, and the guileless and the upright who clung to him are the same people seen in two ways, as turned from evil and as taking up virtue.
comments.comment: … Guard my soul and rescue me; let me not be put to shame, for I have hoped in you (Psalm 25:20). If you guard my soul without harm or injury, I know that I shall be rescued; for indeed I am rescued from the evildoers or I receive a crown because of having been afflicted. The guileless and the upright clung to me, because I endured you, Lord. Not only did I profit myself by enduring, endurance which brings salvation—for 'the one who endures will be saved unto the end' (Matthew 10:22)—but I profited many because I endured you, and I had many friends. But he speaks of the guileless here as those being crushed by malice, not the well-behaved. Thus the upright were joined with them. According to the reception of malice they are guileless, but according to the taking up of virtue they are upright. For example, one who turns away from evil so as to no longer practice it has become guileless. And since after the turning away from evil he receives the doing of good, the one who turns away from evil becomes upright. It is therefore possible to call the same people guileless and upright according to one thought and another. And it is also possible thus: those who are guileless according to practice being outside of malice, while the upright are those who think the things of piety.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the psalm's 'integrity and uprightness' and what the psalmist gains by waiting on the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Guiltless' means those free of malice, and 'upright' those who have reached perfect virtue, or perhaps the angels.
comments.comment: 'Guiltless' he says, either referring to those being deprived of malice or the more simple, and 'upright' to those having accomplished perfect virtue. 'Not clinging to me (through unanimity), what I endured, O Lord' (Psalm 25:21). Perhaps also 'guiltless' refers to the diligent among men, and 'upright' to the divine angels clinging to Him and becoming of divine powers concerning the diligent. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who has obtained his own petition wills the same deliverance for Israel, and what is said of the man of the Lord is common to all the righteous.
comments.comment: Redeem, O God, Israel from all his afflictions. Since He Himself has attained the petition concerning Himself, He wills also for Israel—for every discerning one and possessing mind—to have the same salvation, to become outside of the afflictions through God having redeemed. It is not out of place, then, to take these things also concerning the man of the Lord. Beginning from where we began the psalm, if we have spoken, it is because the things said concerning the man according to the Savior are common to all the righteous, only His being His own in the theological sense. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist can speak boldly to God because his heart does not condemn him, and he says he has already walked in guilelessness.
comments.comment:
Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my guilelessness. The voice is very bold toward God. But he has boldness toward God, whose heart does not condemn, as the great disciple and evangelist John writes in the epistle: …

"Our heart does not condemn us; we have boldness toward God." Thus the whole psalm is sent up from much boldness. He speaks of some things as if already accomplished, and of others as present and active, and some things signify a prayer of the speaker; for he says: "Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in iniquity" (Psalm 26:1). He did not say "I shall walk," but "I have walked." And here "iniquity" means guilelessness. He who has turned according to the instruction of Jesus and has become as children, he has become in guilelessness, and such a person is perfect in mind, but a child in wickedness, as the apostle writes: "Be perfect in mind, and a child in wickedness" (1 Cor 14:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bold opening of the psalm and what "walked" and guilelessness mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be guileless is to know evil and still not act on it, by choice, which an infant's ignorance cannot be.
comments.comment: He who is a child in wickedness does not ignore it—for how could he be a child in it if he ignored it?—but he does not act upon it. This is indeed what he says: "In my iniquity I have walked." Thus, here it is different. In both cases the guileful means what was previously said, "turned according to the children." Therefore, he who has turned according to the teaching of Jesus and has become as children does not lack sense. He does not mean the foolishness of infants, but the immobility toward evils. It was said, therefore, that a child sleeping with a woman does not accept her desire. So when someone, having become perfect, has such a state of being without desire for debauchery, he is a child in guilelessness and has become as children having turned. For observe that these children, according to their age, are not such as to be foolish or easy-going. But the perfect one has become such that it is a matter of choice to be thus a child and thus without guile. Regarding infants, this does not appear; it is not a matter of choice, but of an age that does not permit having a perfect intellect.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words "I have walked" speak of a way of life begun long ago, and hope in God keeps the one who hopes from being weak.
comments.comment:
The "I have walked" here does not speak of an interruption or a stopping, but that I began this way from a long time ago, or I began this way from the womb; for he says: "Upon you I have been leaned from the womb, from my mother's womb you are my covering" (Ps 71:6). …

And hoping in God, I shall not be weak. He no longer says "having hoped," as with "I have walked." But the hope toward God makes one strong and very capable. Since, therefore, I hope in you, "I am not weak."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's training does not leave the one who hopes in him weak or sick in soul, for the one who keeps the commandment is healthy.
comments.comment:
Weakness is often produced by the divine disciplines. 'He brought them'—he says—'them'—evidently the Hebrews—'in gold and silver, and there was no weakness in their tribes.' For when God leads anyone in gold, that is to say, in a pure mind, and in silver—a tested word—there is no weakness. Those led thus do not suffer weakness, but are strong 'in the one strengthening' them. And as the apostle says, 'I can do all things' (Phil 4:13), he who is able to do all things does not suffer weakness; so also each of the wise men who is strong does not suffer weakness. For how could he who says to God in Psalm 92, 'I will love you, O Lord, my strength' (Psalm 18:1), suffer weakness? He who hopes in wealth will surely suffer weakness.

And even if the name of weakness signifies sickness—for it does mean—this is what it says: hoping in the Lord, I shall not be sick according to the soul, I am always being healthy; for 'the one keeping the commandment, this one is healthy.' This is not spoken concerning physical health; for many keeping a commandment suffer sickness, and many transgressing commandments are healthy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope in God gives something firm and immovable, and God tests and tries the righteous so that their endurance is proven, as gold is.
comments.comment:
Hoping, I shall not be weak; for I am contained by the hope toward God, being strengthened by it, I shall not be weak. Scripture is carried forth saying: 'I shall not be shaken.' And through this it is not made manifest: because the hope toward God provides for me something firm and immovable, 'Hoping in the Lord, I shall not be shaken' (Psalm 26:1).

Since it is not the one recommending himself who is proven, but the Lord establishes, having testified to himself that one should walk in integrity and desiring that one should not be weak, he wants one to be tested and tried by struggles, so that the righteous may be revealed, and one may be tried so that, having received a trial, he might have endurance that is proven. And previously, having an analogy between the kidneys and the heart, it is said. That these two things should be purified through painful struggle, so that they might be shown as proven gold (Psalm 26:2).

I would not have been worthy to suffer the aforementioned painful things, unless your mercy had considered me, coinciding with me so as to enable me to endure them. Your mercy, which has been seen by me in front of my eyes, works together to please in your truth; for God's mercy makes one please according to truth and not by affectation (Psalm 26:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist's boldness in asking God to test him is like that of an athlete who asks the judge of the contest to try him.
comments.comment: Test me, O Lord, and try me (Ps 26:2). Behold the boldness; 'refine my kidneys' and see if there is injustice in me. No one is called to examine such hidden things, knowing the marrow, unless he has much boldness. Therefore, some people, because of the excess of the boldness of the one speaking boldly, take the psalm for the man of the Savior. And it has been said to us already many times, that the achievements of the Savior touch the man and all perfect men. 'Test me, O Lord, and try me.' Bring me into the contest. Just as a capable athlete might say to the contest-setter: 'Test me and try me, if I am such a man as I promise.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the request to be tested and tried is so bold.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture often joins the kidneys and the heart, and neither means a part of the body, since the heart here is the intellect.
comments.comment: The kidneys and the heart are joined together in many places in Scripture: “God tests hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:9). “And even until night my kidneys instructed me” (Psalm 16:7). And just as when we hear 'heart', it does not mean the part of the body, but rather the one who has it sees God; again: “Hear me, you who have lost your heart”, no one loses this bodily part in such a way—if not, if God casts out a stony heart and places a fleshy one in its stead, we understand the intellect. Along with this heart, the so-called kidneys are not parts of the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist trusts in his purity, yet knows that without God's mercy he would not be made perfect, so he has God's mercy before his eyes.
comments.comment: “Purify my kidneys and my heart. For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 26:2-3). Behold that through all things he trusts in his own purity. Since these things seem to be beyond human power, he immediately says: “for your mercy is before me” (Psalm 26:3). I know that even if I propose good things, even if I hasten to run after them, if you do not show mercy, I will not be perfected. Therefore, “I have rejoiced in your truth” (Psalm 26:3). One need not be self-deprecating here when the subject is truth. … He who rejoices in the truth of God has the mercy of God before his eyes. Having the one who cooperates and perfects before his eyes, he will speak boldly toward those who have already been made upright by him. Therefore I say: “Purify my kidneys and my heart, for your mercy is before my eyes” (Psalm 26:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the psalmist can claim purity and still rely on God's mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The kidneys are what the soul brings forth, and the psalmist has no such offspring as Judas, father of all traitors of the truth, while one who rejoices in God's truth is not ashamed of his words.
comments.comment:
Therefore there are also wombs, according to that which the soul or the mind brings forth; those he calls kidneys along with the named heart. 'You are near,' he says, 'to their mouth, but far from their kidneys' (Jeremiah 12:2). From these kidneys you are far, O God, not from the physical parts. Therefore I have directed my kidneys and my heart, test me (Psalm 26:2). I do not have seeds capable of bearing offspring, such as to become exalted children, destructive children, like those Judas had … He calls all the traitors of the truth his children. … Through this eagerness, he became the father of all the traitors of the truth.

'And I rejoiced in your truth'. The one rejoicing in the truth of God is not ashamed of his words; for Jesus said: 'Whoever is ashamed of me and my words' (Mark 8:38). But if he himself is ashamed of the one being ashamed, the one speaking boldly and remaining in the truth and preferring it above all, he himself is a weakling; let him remain in him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To sit in the council of the vain is to have dealings with the ungodly who harm rather than help, even if one does not sit with them in the same place.
comments.comment: …To play and to counsel in vain are the same thing; for here the playing is not praiseworthy, but it turns out to be like that which the butchers had; for they “sat down,” he says, “to eat and to drink, and they rose up to play.” This way of playing turns out to be forbidden. “I did not sit” therefore “among those playing at the council.” And it has been shown many times that the superficial things of life, those who harm rather than help, the ungodly, are called vain. He who has concern with such people, even if he does not sit with them locally, is sitting in the council of vanity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "sitting with vain persons" means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist's walking in integrity and hope in God is what keeps him from the seat of futility, and he not only does not sit but does not even enter.
comments.comment:
I did not sit with a seat of futility and with law-breakers, I will by no means enter. The evil and the good are not co-existing. The one having the good cannot partake of evil. The one having been set upon evil, insofar as he is evil, is unfit for virtue. And since abstaining from evil—when one, having a nature toward them, abstains from them by choice—the children do not have intemperance, but I do not say they abstain from intemperance. The soulless and the irrational do not have impiety; and I do not say they abstain from impiety; for abstaining is a volitional movement. …

Just as he does not previously say that the perfect man abstains from evils by having his own will in the law of the Lord, and having said the appropriate good things here, he then says what is forbidden and says: because I walked in integrity (Psalm 26:1) and hoped in you, not having my mercy weak before your eyes, since I am such a person, "I did not sit with a seat of futility" (Psalm 26:4). He did not distinguish the futility of the seat by anything other than being in such a life; for life is divided among men, not a place. Diligence divides the serious man from the base men, and knowledge separates the one who has it from the ignorant. So also here, the one who walked in integrity and having hope in God, and because of this being strong and not weak, "did not sit with a seat of futility" (Psalm 26:4).

And here one might say: "the child and the irrational and the soulless did not sit with a seat of futility." But they did not sit with a seat of futility because of not being by nature, but because of walking in integrity and hoping in God. "And after those who transgress, I shall by no means enter" (Psalm 26:4). I never consented with those who consult in vain and sit in council to do such things, nor did I enter after transgressors. I did not only not sit, but I did not even enter; for after the entrance, the sitting is that which is in the council. Jeremiah also was attaining to this choice and virtue, saying: "I did not sit with those playing, but I was reverent from the face of God" (Ps 26:6-7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law-breakers are those who transgress a law they have, and to enter with them is to act as they do, as to enter into virtue is to act according to virtue.
comments.comment: “And with law-breakers I will by no means enter” (Psalm 26:4). He says “law-breakers” here to mean those transgressing the law, not those who have no law at all—for those are lawless and law-breaking—since he was far from such people. And what about: “I will by no means enter”?—instead of: I did not enter into lawlessness; for to enter with law-breakers, that is, to transgress the law, is just as to enter into virtue means to act according to virtue. I hated the assembly of adulterers and I will not sit with the ungodly. The adulterers are either the same as those sitting in vain, or they are not far from them. And perhaps those sinning in practical matters sit in vain, while those thinking false things and having heretical opinions are the assembly of adulterers. And it is good even to say “adulterers.” No one is said to be adulterating according to his nature, but rather he who is disposed toward acting thus, yet is able to be outside of that action.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Washing one's hands in innocence means that, having a pure disposition, the speaker also cleanses his actions, since disposition alone does not satisfy him.
comments.comment:
“I will wash my hands in innocence” (Ps 26:6). He who says: “In my innocence I walked” (Psalm 26:1), and saying: “Test me and try me, refine my reins and my heart” (Ps 26:2), says: “I will wash my hands in innocence.” We say this: the former achievements are spiritual.

They were a disposition signifying the one speaking boldly that he has no injustice in kidneys and heart, to walk in innocence, to hope in God, to speak boldly and say, 'test me and try me' (Psalm 26:2). Since therefore I am thus according to the opinion, and I have pure actions. The disposition has washed my actions. 'I will wash' (Psalm 26:6) therefore 'my hands among the innocent'; for I am not satisfied with disposition alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Priests washed and circled the altar to teach that one who serves must have pure actions, and the basin made from mirrors shows he must reflect on himself.
comments.comment: And I will circle your altar, Lord (Psalm 26:6). And the priests according to the law, washing, circled the altar. And such a regulation teaches that the one officiating must have pure actions. Therefore, without fail, a basin was constructed for washing 'the feet and the hands' not from any other material but from mirrors. Moses took much gold and other vessels from the Hebrews to construct many of the temple's vessels, a lampstand, a table. And the silver ones, and the gold ones, but the basin he made from the mirrors of the women (Ex 38:8), teaching that someone, having washed his actions and the moving powers of the soul, ought to reflect himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the washing of hands and the circling of the altar from the law's practice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like the hearer in James who looks in a mirror and goes away, one who hears the law and does not do it forgets himself.
comments.comment: For such a way is called a mirror, and James writes: the 'one having become a hearer of the word' (James 1:23) and not a 'doer of the work' says: 'he perceived his face in a mirror and immediately went away and forgot what he was' (Jas 1:24). He did not blame the perceiving of the face in the mirror, but the departing immediately. Just as the one looking in the mirror, when he turns away from the mirror, no longer sees himself, so the one returning to the law, if he is not a doer of the law, passes away according to the one departing from the mirror …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hands are the practical powers of the soul, washed in innocence with good works, and the one who has done this goes around the spiritual altar where pure prayers are offered.
comments.comment: One washes the practical powers of the soul, called hands tropically, in innocence, doing nothing trivial but something significant in them. Perhaps also the one who stains them in the work of evils washes and cleanses them, using good works instead of water. Having become outside of all the aforementioned evils and having washed my hands in innocence, I shall surround with the justice of an innocent priest the spiritual altar of the Lord, upon which someone offers up spiritual sacrifices, namely the pure prayers or the lawful acts. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what washing the hands and compassing the altar mean in the psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Going around the altar and the tent, as Israel was commanded, teaches that we should stand near God with no sin or pleasure between.
comments.comment: God prescribed that the sons of Israel must break camp, and also halt, that is, encamp together, in fitting order, and he expressly commanded them to go around the tent, in keeping, I think, with what the blessed David sings so gracefully: ‘And I will go around your altar, O Lord, that I may hear the voice of your praise’ (Psalm 26:6–7), or again: ‘I went around and offered in his tent a sacrifice of joyful shouting’ (Psalm 27:6). But what they were commanded to do as in a type hints at something else as well. For we must not keep ourselves apart from God, but be seen, so to speak, standing near and all around him, with no sin coming between, no worldly pleasure setting us apart, while an upright steadiness of mind and a readiness for every admirable thing gather us into spiritual unity. For those who have chosen to win approval in this way, it is above all fitting that they bear fruit. For it is written: ‘All who are around him shall bring gifts’ (Psalm 76:11). So he commanded them to set out together with the tent and to march around it, and again in an order: not one that matched their ages and kept strict sequence from the first to the last, but with them joined together as they were, group by group, just as in the bringing of the gifts.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: After the washing of hands come the seeing of wonders and the hearing of the voice of praise, and the one who does this is a priest who always encircles God's altar.
comments.comment:
For after the washing of hands, there comes also the seeing of wonders and the hearing of the voice of praise. For virtue must not stand only up to practice, but also up to contemplation and praise, up to the knowing of that very good thing, the truth, and to narrating all your wonders. The hearing of the voice of praise happens toward the narrating of all the wonders of God. He does not have in his own word any other narration or that concerning the wonders of God.

Thus, the one saying these things is a priest, not one who priesthoods by succession according to the daily shifts of the law, but just as Samuel was always in the house. And each of the saints is able to say, 'I also am with you always.' And here it is said, 'My eyes are toward the Lord always' (Psalm 25:15). He who has his eyes toward God always encircles the altar of God, remaining with Him always, always performing the sacred rites.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verses follow one another: washing, the altar, then praise and telling God's wonders.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To love the house of God is to love the truth of its teachings and the order of the church, and the tabernacle stands for progress while the temple stands for perfection.
comments.comment:
He who loves the Lord from his whole soul and all the things of God, to whom also the decency of his house belongs, loves; and the decency of God's house is the truth of the dogmas and the command of the canons of the church, being considered his house. …

And he says that even the tabernacle of the glory of God is loved. Perhaps the tent of witness which Moses constructed in the wilderness is the tabernacle of the glory of God; this is a symbol of progress. But that which Solomon built after the journey to Jerusalem is the temple, bearing a type of the beauty of perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what loving the house of God and the dwelling of his glory means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tabernacle is a portable house for travellers and stands for progress, while the house is fixed in one place and stands for perfection.
comments.comment: Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the tabernacle of your glory (Ps 26:8). What is the difference between a tabernacle and a house? It has often been said that the tabernacle signifies progress; for it is a house of travelers, a portable house. But the house is established in one place. It signifies perfection. 'And the place of the tabernacle of your glory I have loved,' when it was progressing. The glory of the tabernacle, that is, of progress, becomes virtue both in the practical and in the contemplative. Magnificent is this one who is able to say, 'All that we were useful to do, we have done.' This one is magnificent. Primarily, the fitting is well when it becomes virtue and godliness. He is beautiful who, through chastity, achieves 'how to please the Lord.' He who is 'holy in body and spirit' (1 Cor 6:19) has beauty. Therefore, I loved the beauty of your house, the perfection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not to be destroyed with the ungodly means to be kept in piety, and not to have life with men of blood means to be dead to the life they live.
comments.comment:
Do not destroy my soul with the ungodly, nor my life with men of blood (Psalm 26:9). He does not say, 'Being righteous, do not condemn me with the ungodly, do not draw me toward them.' Rather, you do not join with me with the ungodly if you prevent me from entering into ungodliness. I am prevented from entering into ungodliness if there remain to me achievements of what I have confessed, if I remain walking in innocence, if hoping in you so as not to grow weak. I am perfect. And being perfect, I do not perish with the ungodly. …

The type of destruction is twofold: do not punish me with the ungodly, and do not number me among those punished because of ungodliness. And second: guard me in piety, in pleasing with 'your truth'; for 'ungodliness does not save' those who are by it. Not saving him, it destroys him.

And 'with men of blood my life' (Psalm 26:9). Let me not have such a life as those murderous men have. By an analogy: those who are arrogant, being great men, yet stumbling the little ones in the church, are 'men of blood'. Do not let such things happen to me so that I have life with them. 'This life and the length of days is to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). He having this life does not have life with men of blood; he is dead toward the men of blood, but dead because he does not have the life which they have.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He does not want his soul destroyed with the ungodly or his life with men of blood, whose ways are total wickedness.
comments.comment: However, he does not wish for the ungodly to possess it, lest his soul be destroyed along with them; for one possessing a pious intention will not be persuaded by this. He also exhorts one not to become a murderer, so that his life may not be destroyed along with men of blood; for in the practice of these things there is injustice and total wickedness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those with lawlessness in their hands and a right hand full of gifts include those who show partiality, who bribe themselves with what pleases them.
comments.comment: Of whom lawlessness is in their hands. Still in their own practices they have lawlessness. They do not possess it, but they have it. And their right hand was filled with gifts. It is possible also to slander judges as bribe-takers. And even those who do not judge, many times we bribe when we show partiality to someone. And if he acquires pleasant things for himself, he bribes; he receives gifts from himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hands full of mischief and bribes mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Conscious of his best deeds, he still needs redemption and mercy because of hidden sins.
comments.comment: Even if he is conscious of the most beautiful things foretold to him, fearing to sin, he is not justified by this alone, through many hidden sins; he deserves to be redeemed and to receive mercy (Psalm 26:11; LXX 25:11b). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist who says he walks in integrity still asks to be redeemed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who walks in innocence can say "I went my way in innocence", and even one whose virtue is lifted up still asks God to deliver him, for his foot stands in uprightness.
comments.comment:
But I, in my innocence, went my way. No one of those bribing and having the right hand filled with gifts, no one of the lawless and men of blood, went in innocence. Such was Elymas the sorcerer, ungodly and walking in lawlessness and having the right hand full of gifts; for it seemed to be excellent at deceiving, and it is said concerning him: 'O full of all deceit and all trickery, son of the devil' (Acts 13:10). But he, being full of all trickery, is not able to say: 'In my innocence I went my way'.

Deliver me, O God, and have mercy on me (Ps 51:1). He who walks in iniquities, existing in the iniquities previously mentioned, says 'deliver me'. Even if I am in the most distant iniquities, and with your cooperation all the things of virtue are lifted up for me, yet you have still touched me, the 'body of humiliation', yet 'in the place of my affliction' I am; therefore 'deliver me'. For my foot has stood in uprightness. The same thing as standing in uprightness is the foot of the inner man and that in the rock according to what was said: 'You stood upon a rock' (Exodus 33:21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Standing in uprightness is like standing on an unbroken rock, and standing in faith, which does not happen without Jesus, and the psalmist will bless the Lord in the churches.
comments.comment:
… for straightness is like an uncracked and continuous rock. My foot is therefore firm in my straightness. Standing in straightness is the same as standing in faith; for it says, "for indeed you have stood in faith" (2 Corinthians 1:24). Such a standing does not happen without Jesus. Those having this standing stand by him, as he says, "there are some standing here," meaning, here by me.

"I will bless you in the churches, Lord" (Psalm 26:12). In the church I will offer thanksgiving hymns, not outside anywhere. He who promises to give thanks to God outside, contrary to the ecclesiastical opinion, does not bless in the churches.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the standing foot and the blessing of the Lord in the congregations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
