comments.capsule: Standing on level ground means walking in righteousness and uprightness.
comments.comment: …David also sings somewhere: ‘For my foot has stood on level ground’ (Psalm 26:12), that is, I have walked in righteousness and uprightness, and I have hated what is crooked.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: If God gives light and salvation, no man or power need be feared, for the one who has the light of life has God's truth as his shield.
comments.comment: "The Lord is my light and my savior" (Psalm 27:1); whom shall I fear? If God enlightens me and saves me, whom do I fear? Neither man, nor an evil power, nor even the devil himself. And the "who" here is instead of "no one"; for this usage lies here continuously. … Therefore, the word is not about sensible life and some sensible illumination; for by the divine light the mind and the soul are illumined. And life is always joined to salvation. … He who has the light of life is not defeated by anything, especially since the truth of God itself becomes a shield fighting for him; for 'his truth shall surround you as a weapon' (Psalm 91:4). Therefore, it immediately reaches: 'The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I dread?' (Psalm 27:1). The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I dread? Who is able to make me afraid? I am clothed in 'the armor of God' (Ephesians 6:13), I 'have the shield' (Ephesians 6:16) of faith, extinguishing 'all the flaming arrows of the evil one' (Ephesians 6:16). If the shield of faith extinguishes the arrows of the evil one, it does much more for those of inferior archers; for there are also other worthless archers. For indeed, 'behold, the sinners have bent a bow, they have prepared arrows in a quiver to shoot at those upright in heart' (Psalm 11:2). I am not defeated by anything. The armor of God is unhurt and unstriking. His shield is truth. And no one is able against the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'whom shall I fear?' means and why the speaker is unafraid.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: These words belong to the whole company of the righteous, who share in them by participation and not in equal measure.
comments.comment: It is not the Lord's man who says these things, but the race of the righteous, the collection of the saints; for even the Son of God does not say according to man, 'The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?' (Ps 27:1). Many times I have said that the things said about the righteous men and about the Lord's man are said in common; but they are common not according to equality, for he surpasses all others even in these things. I say these things are common according to participation, just as I say the medical art is common to the one who has been perfected and holds it without lack, and to those still progressing. I do not say common according to quantity, but according to quality.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This psalm is 'of David', composed by him through the Spirit, and 'before being anointed' most likely means before the first of his three anointings.
comments.comment: Of David; before being anointed. The psalms before this were "to David"; this one is written "of David." He himself brought it forth by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. He sent it forth "before being anointed." Thirdly, David appears anointed; first, when he went to Samuel and was anointed, and Samuel to Jesse. Second, after Saul had finished; the beginning was preserved; for some were seeking David as king, while others sought Mephibosheth the son of Saul. After the son of Saul was betrayed by Abner because of the appearance of a woman, David was anointed over all the people in Hebron. Therefore, he was anointed a third time. Previously, the peak clearly belongs to a private person. Second, in order that he might rule a part of the people. After the death of the son of Saul, in order that he might also rule the rest of the people, he has been anointed again and again by all. We seek, therefore, regarding what kind of anointing he speaks here. One says that it is generally regarding every anointing; he says the psalm was spoken before being wholly anointed, and quite so; if before the first anointing, it is clearly also before the second and the third. If before the second, not necessarily before the first. If before the third, not necessarily before the first and second. But the psalm seems to have been spoken especially before the first anointing, which is before every anointing. Therefore, the psalm is "before being anointed."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being united to the Lord as light and defender, he fears neither visible nor invisible enemies, and he seeks above all to dwell in the church.
comments.comment: God our Savior is the one rescuing us from sins and from death, and a light that dissolves the darkness of wickedness and ignorance, and illuminating with the light of knowledge (Psalm 27:1; LXX 26:1bc). He who has thus been united and enlightened by the Lord, whom shall he fear? For no one is able to harm such good ones who have attained security. The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I dread? (Psalm 27:3-4; LXX 26:3,4). These things shall be said, and concerning perceptible enemies and concerning a phalanx of invisible enemies; for if he says, 'war rises up against me,' in this heart which does not fear them, I hope, having become bold, in a God who fights for me. It is also requested and sought to dwell in the house of the Lord, that is, in the church, through thinking on ecclesiastical matters all the days of his enlightened life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not everyone who afflicts is an enemy, since parents and masters afflict to discipline, but those who afflict without exhorting are enemies.
comments.comment:
"My enemies themselves have grown weak and fallen." Not every one who afflicts is an enemy; the good person also afflicts. For many enemies, intending to afflict and surround those against whom they are hostile, are not able to do this unless God permits it. But many also afflict without being enemies. For instance, parents afflict while disciplining children, and masters afflict slaves, and they are not enemies at all.

It can indeed be said that both groups—the afflicters and the enemies—have grown weak and fallen. And this is possible: the afflicters themselves are also enemies, for they do not afflict for the sake of exhortation and instruction. They are not such as it is said of: "He who brings forth wisdom from his lips, strikes a man without heart with a rod" (Proverbs 10:13), and: "What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod or with love?" (1 Cor 4:21); these afflicters are not enemies.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes enemies from those who afflict for discipline, which clarifies 'mine enemies and my foes'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who come to eat his flesh find nothing to feed on, since the one who has put the flesh to death is not in it, and so they fall.
comments.comment:
In the approaching of those intending to harm me to eat my flesh. Those intending to harm the soul eat flesh. If anyone is found having flesh, he has strong enemies against him. The flesh is his food. And the flesh, about which Paul says: 'for the mindset of the flesh is enmity toward God' (Rom 8:7), and: 'we are not in the flesh' (Romans 8:9); if he were speaking about the sensory flesh, his word would be false; for all the saints, being in the flesh, pleased God while still surrounded by flesh, and they are not able to say: 'we are not in the flesh.' But when someone kills the flesh and casts down its works, he is not in the flesh. …

2 Those distressing me and my enemies, they themselves grew weak and fell (Psalm 27:2). They had come to tear me into weakness, to treat me badly. But for them the passion has happened which they intended to inflict on me; for if they had found 'flesh,' they would have devoured me into weakness and consumed me into sickness. But since they did not find 'flesh,' 'they themselves grew weak and fell' (Ps 27:2), having been subjected to famine.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even if a whole army of evil men and powers is set against him, and even if the body is killed, his heart and mind stay unshaken.
comments.comment: If an ambush is set against me, my heart shall not fear. Therefore, how it does not fear nor tremble is explained by saying: "Whom shall I fear?" and: "From whom shall I tremble?" (Psalm 27:1), since the expression "whom" seems to exceed the scope of the question. Even if a whole ambush of evil men and powers is set against me, my heart does not fear; even if they kill the body, the heart remains unshaken, my mind is not struck. If a whole camp with great generals comes against me, I have a fearless heart, my mind does not fear.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what 'my heart shall not fear' means when an army encamps against the speaker.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His heart is not afraid when war rises, because it is strengthened by the fear of the Lord and armed with virtues and the doctrines of truth.
comments.comment: If war rises up against me, in this I hope (Psalm 27:3). There is even more of an encampment if war rises up against me; in my heart I hope, which does not fear, being strengthened by divine fear; 'fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Psalm 34:9), and 'there is no loss to those fearing him' (Psalm 34:9). 'In this I hope.' I am confident that this heart becomes everything to me. The virtues are the weapons of piety. 'Let us put on the weapons of light, let us cast off the works of the flesh' (Romans 13:12). The weapons of light are the virtues, the pious thoughts, the mysteries and doctrines of the truth. In these secure fortunes, no one is shaken, but has unashamed hope. 'In this,' therefore, 'I hope,' not simply in my thought, but in that which is thus secured.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the ground of the speaker's confidence in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one request is for all virtue and for God himself, and the one who still says 'I seek' shows that he has not yet reached it.
comments.comment:
One thing I asked of the Lord, this I will seek (Psalms 27:4). God the Giver is of many good things; for He 'will give good things to those asking Him' (Matthew 7:11), and He fills the desire with His own good things; for He is 'the one filling your desire with good things' (Psalm 103:5). Therefore, it is reasonable to say that these good things are, in essence, virtues and in essence, the mysteries of the truth. When someone—so that I may say it this way—possesses the genus of the virtues, he possesses all. Therefore, he asks for one request, all virtue. … Therefore, the one having come to perfection asks one request. 'One' then, 'I asked from the Lord' (Psalm 27:4). And this is also possible: their help—so that, having been prepared for the wars and the encampments that arise, they are able—does not ask one request. They seek much help: a military encirclement, the strength of walls, constructions. But he who has God himself as a helper and asks for this one thing, asks one request. 'All in all' happens, as each of those having been perfected has Him as all things: as bread, as light, as teacher, as shepherd.

'One' then, 'I asked, this I seek out'. He who says 'I seek out' and 'I asked' shows that the one seeking does not yet have it, and longs to find. For no one has perfection unless even if he reaches the very goal and the end of virtue and of union with God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of 'one thing' and what that one thing is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He began asking for the sake of the end, those who reach it dwell in God's house, and whoever begins to long for that life comes out of the night.
comments.comment: I did not begin to ask now, but because of the beginning of the end I began; for the one beginning an art begins because of the end of the art. Those having reached this dwell. 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 84:4). He who has the blessed life is in the days; it does not happen in nights. Even if ever it becomes in night, but he takes up the beginning of longing for life, he comes out of the night.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever desires to behold the Lord's dwelling rejoices to become a dwelling himself, more than one who only holds the established teachings of the church.
comments.comment: Regarding the dwelling of the Lord, he who desires to behold this rejoices in becoming a dwelling, approaching it closely and genuinely, not only approaching but also surpassing, as if the Lord visits and surrounds his temple, perhaps not even wishing to depart, imitating Samuel. He who simply, having grasped the established dogmas of the church, beholds the delight of the Lord, differs from one who approaches the Lord by surrounding his temple regarding the Trinity (Psalm 27:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lover of God is stirred toward God by a house and a vessel dedicated to him, as one is stirred to remember a friend by his garment or book.
comments.comment: Again he sets apart love for God through love for the temple dedicated to him (Psalm 27:4; LXX 26:4). For the one who loves God rejoices in the places dedicated to him, not enjoying his desire in the sight of these things—for it is a small thing to take pleasure in handmade works—but just as someone gladly looks at a garment or a book of the beloved, being stirred through these things to the memory of that person, so the God-loving person is stirred toward God through a house and a vessel dedicated to God (Psalm 27:4; LXX 26:4). This one thing alone I have asked: to dwell in the temple of God, which Hannah does, and to rejoice in the beauty of the building as I look toward it. Now a house of God had not yet been built when David sang these things, but he brought the word up to the tabernacle and left it to those able to hear spiritually to raise the word up to the spiritual house (Psalm 27:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the speaker asks to dwell in the Lord's house and behold its beauty.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: David asked to live in the holy tent, which is the firm and unshaken state of a holy way of life, and in it the passions could not take him.
comments.comment: But the divine David was never found wanting to go outside the holy tent; rather, he made it one of the chief things in his prayers to linger there and live close by, saying: ‘One thing I have asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of the Lord and to visit his holy temple. For he hid me in his tent in the day of my troubles; he sheltered me in the secret place of his tent’ (Psalm 27:4–5). By the divine and holy tent, I think, he means here the firm and unshaken state of a holy way of life; having, as it were, entered into it, he could not be taken by the passions that wished to ravage him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what dwelling in the Lord's house and being hidden in his tent mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: God hides the one who is progressing in the mysteries of his tabernacle, and lifts him up on the rock, which is Christ, when he reaches perfection.
comments.comment: 'He covered me in the secrecy of his tabernacle' (Psalm 27:5; LXX 26:5), which is the instruction by which we progress. The manifest things are the former, but the secret and withdrawn things are the mysteries. In progressing, God does not cover in the obvious things, but in the secrecy of his tabernacle. His action is set forth as a representation that not every tabernacle is, that is to say, progress according to God. 'He lifted me up on a rock' (Psalm 27:5), having reached progress, me upon the narrowest and most unyielding word of perfection, a rock called allegorically; 'the Lord himself lifted me up.' It is appropriate for progress to be 'He hid me,' and for perfection to be 'He lifted me up.' It is also possible to call the guidance through law and prophets a tabernacle; in the secrecy, that is, in the mystical way, God hides the one being instructed, lifting him up on a spiritual rock, not another, but one that is Christ's.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The body is a tent, and the secret of the Lord's tent covers and protects, while the exposed part of it does harm.
comments.comment: And the body is a tent; for it is said, 'the earth is a tent for the prudent' (Wisdom 9:15), and, 'we groan being in the tent' (2 Cor 5:4). Often, while we are still dwelling in the tent, the body hides us so that we are not harmed by it when someone, as I said previously, surrounds the death of Jesus in the body and strikes the body and enslaves it. 'He covered me in the secrecy of his tent.' For the secrecy of his tent is not harmful, but a covering. But the accessible part of the tent, which is already laid bare, harms rather. In this way, I am a body dwelling as if not being in a body, being swallowed up of the mortal 'by life.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be covered in the secrecy of his tent is to perceive the mystery of the Savior's coming, which the Jews did not perceive.
comments.comment:
One who has become in the body is also able, if he perceives the cause and the mystery through which it has happened in him, to be hidden in the secrecy of it; for having immediately known the mystery and the cause, he will harm himself and will not be swallowed up. And this can be said about the Savior or toward the Savior. If regarding him it is said: 'in the secrecy of his tent he hid me,' he had a tent, he became man. The descent of the Savior has a hidden mystery.

He who is able, after the one who became flesh has tabernacled in him, to say: 'we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14), was covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.' His covering has become the perceiving of the mystery of the Savior's coming. The Jews, indeed, did not perceive, and as many as are such, and they were not covered 'in the secrecy of his tent.'
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of the 'tent' in the verse as the Savior's coming in the flesh.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rock is the unshakeable Word of God, which defeats those who come near it and lets the one standing on it send up songs of victory.
comments.comment:
'You have raised me in a rock' (Psalm 27:5). It is not a great thing to be raised in a sensible rock so as to send up grateful praises. All things happening by God, on which it is fitting to give thanks, which must be praised, are not at hand, nor are they able to be present to everyone. The rock, therefore, is the unshakeable Word of God himself, who, becoming the one around, is not cast down. For it has been said also in others: 'The judges laid hold of a moving rock' or 'their strong ones'; and indeed, rulers being outside the rock seem to be strong and to prevail over the uncertain. But when they become near the rock, they are immediately defeated. … Those who advocate the things of the heterodox, thinking to construct the heretical arguments as strong and mighty, when the rock, the truth, draws near them, are swallowed up and proved nothing. …

'In a rock you have exalted me' (Psalm 27:5; LXX 26:5). The one having his feet standing on this rock sends up thankful praises: 'He put a new song into my mouth' (Psalm 40:3). When the feet stand upon the rock and the steps of the one thus helped are directed, then he shall say: 'He put a new song into my mouth', a victory song. The one exalted on the rock, then, sends up victory praises, having his progressive impulses secured.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the rock is and why standing on it brings praise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lifted head means that the mind has been made ruler over its enemies, and the sacrifice of victory is offered with both contemplation and virtuous action.
comments.comment:
And now, after having passed through progress and having reached the goal of truth, to lift up the head, to understand my Christ having become the ruler of my mind, over my enemies, so that I may see them under my feet and having been made subject (Ps 27:6). 'I encircled and offered a sacrifice of praise in his tabernacle' (Ps 27:6). …

A victory being completed is offered as a sacrifice, having encircled the enemy in his tent. To shout aloud is to cry out amidst the defeated enemies. He who, being surrounded by the enemies, rightly offers a gracious sacrifice of victory in the tent, that is to say, in progress. I will sing and I will praise the Lord. Not only will I contemplate the things of truth which are clearly manifested through the 'Singing', but also I will act according to virtue which is presented through the 'Praising', doing both in a pleasing manner to God. For this is what it means, 'I will sing and I will praise the Lord' (Psalm 27:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Head' means the mind, and 'and now' shows that the head has often been raised above various enemies, always with God's help.
comments.comment: 'And now, behold, he has exalted my head above my enemies' (Psalm 27:6; LXX 26:6). The one saying 'and now' shows that his head was often exalted above enemies. And by 'head' he means the mind, as has often been shown. Indeed, concerning it, it is also said in Ecclesiastes: 'The wise man's eyes are in his head' (Eccl 2:14). The wise man has a discerning mind. 'And now,' then, 'he exalted my head'. And always wrestling and prevailing over the enemies—and the attacking enemies are various—he says at each victory: 'and now he exalted my head above my enemies'. Some rose up inciting to licentiousness, such as the elders against Susanna, the brothers against Joseph, and she herself who later boasted to have become his mistress. At the same time, speaking thankfully, he shows that he did not have these achievements by his own power, but with God helping.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'head' and 'and now' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shout is a cry of victory over fallen enemies, as at Jericho, and the one who encircles the tent proves himself a conqueror.
comments.comment: A shout of victory is offered at his tent. The shout signifies victory, for it is a loud cry made against fallen enemies. For instance, when they encircled Jericho and blew the horns and shouted, the walls of Jericho fell at their shout. … Therefore, when he encircles his tent according to all interpretations—the progress was called a tent—the one progressing and succeeding truly becomes a circle of it. And again, the body was called a tent. When the inner man resolutely sets himself against the body, he becomes a circle around it and conquers. When anyone encircles the tent, the body of Jesus, through faith, he is proved a conqueror.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He sings who contemplates the truth, and he plays who uses his body as an instrument for the moral virtues.
comments.comment: I will sing and I will play to the Lord (Psalm 27:6). It was said to us in the earlier psalms that to sing means to have contemplation, to send up praises and songs without an instrument. It was said that to play means to practically pour out the song of triumph. Both, then, he says, are sufficient for me: I will play and I will sing. I sing by contemplating the truth. He who takes in the dogmas of piety and having contemplation of their scientific and wise nature, sings. But he who, taking the body as an instrument, both a lyre and a psaltery, striking its strings which are all the impulses and the senses, being able to bring forth a psalm harmoniously, that one plays. This, then, is the holy man who is promised to do the two: to sing and to play. He who subdues his body and disciplines it and performs the moral virtues, such as one doing almsgiving, one establishing gentleness, one advancing in courage, he plays. But he who contemplates each mystery of the truth and is able to penetrate with knowledge every dogma of piety, he sings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between singing and playing in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who asks only for small things speaks calmly to God, but one who asks for the great heavenly things cries out, since the thought is the cry.
comments.comment: 'Ask,' he says, 'the great things, and the small things will be added to you.' Thus, the one asking for small things says to God, but not with a shouting voice. 'Ask,' he says, 'the heavenly things, and the earthly things will be added to you.' Therefore, the one sending up a prayer concerning sensible things previously does not cry out to God; he speaks to Him calmly. But the one asking for those truly great and heavenly things and those making one god-like cries out to God. For thought is the cry.
comments.selected_reason: Says what it means to cry to God with the voice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being shown mercy and being heard go together, and the heart, having sought God's face, does not stop seeking it.
comments.comment:
'Have mercy on me and hear me,' my heart has said to you (Psalm 27:7-8). My mind has said to you: 'from you I ask mercy.' My heart expects mercy from you and says to you, 'hear me.' These things turn back toward themselves: the one being shown mercy by God is heard, and the one being heard is shown mercy. It is not possible, then, to say one before the other. But to hear precedes to show mercy. Yet not in time before. And just as it is not possible to say appearance before color, nor color before appearance. If there is color, there is appearance. If there is appearance, it has been colored. Appearance is pre-conceived. It is necessary for there to be an appearance, so that there may be such color. And the 'it is necessary' I do not take according to time, but according to thought.

'My heart has said to you.' It signifies persons. According to every word, the three persons are signified: the one speaking, and that toward which he speaks, and that concerning which he speaks. Therefore, the person of the one praying is the one now announcing. And he announces the petition to no one other than God. 8 'I sought your face' (Psalm 27:8). My heart saying, 'have mercy and hear me.' I did not seek your face before now. Your face, I did not entreat only now: 'let your face shine upon me and we shall be saved' (Psalm 80:3). And 'I sought' signifies a seeking that was not raised. 8 'Your face, Lord, I will seek.' My heart, Lord, will seek your face. Even if 'I sought' and I had it grasping me, I do not cease until this. Again I seek it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hears the voice of the heart more than the spoken voice, and the heart's face seeks God's face as the image made like his.
comments.comment: Knowing these things, he who says these things, hearing God through the prayers of the righteous, from the same disposition, having cried out to the righteous, deems it worthy that he will be heard. If you, Lord, were to consider according to merit, you would not hear a mortal; for no one would send up such a cry as to reach you. Having looked toward your goodness, have mercy on me; for you will also hear me. Both to be shown mercy and to be heard then happen not from the superficiality of lips, but from the heart toward you. Through this, it is presented that God hears not entirely the spoken voice, but above all the voice of the heart. 'Seek my face'; and this, if my heart is toward you, the face of my heart, which is nothing other than the mind, will seek you. And I will find, after the seeking, the face, approaching you face to face, the vision through a mirror and in a riddle having been done away. 'Having understood, I knew the face of your servant, imprinted according to the image and likeness of yours; therefore I seek to see your face.' For having understood it, I shall perceive a greater light. Then I am able to seek, if you appear, your face; for if this does not happen, I will not be able to approach it. Therefore I say: 'Do not turn your face away from me' (Psalm 27:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eye of the inner man is never filled by the face of God, whose light stays marked on the one it has illuminated and increases the desire.
comments.comment: 'Do not turn your face away from me' (Psalm 27:9). The eye which is healthy and preserves the virtue of sight, when light is present, has a desire for it, and it is never satisfied; for light is insatiable for the eyes: 'sweet to the eyes,' as the Preacher says (Ecclesiastes 11:7). … But that which comes from the light has no satiety, especially when the vision possesses its own inherent virtue. Therefore, moving from the sensible to the intelligible: the eye of the inner man, or the eyes, are never filled and never receive satiety from the face of God; for it is always appearing, illuminating and increasing the desire. 'The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord' (Ps 4:6); it remains. But that of the sun, or generally of the sensible light, does not remain. For if anyone withdraws from seeing the light or closes the eyes, he does not have it marked. But the intelligible light appears to remain to the one having been illuminated; it is not cast away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the speaker keeps asking God not to hide his face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God may seem to turn away without anger, as he did from Job, and he prays that neither should happen to him through his own sluggishness.
comments.comment: Do not turn away in anger from your servant (Psalm 27:9). It is possible for one to seem as if God is turning away, but not in anger. Some thought that He turned away from Job when his possessions, his children, and his body were delivered to the one asking; but this did not happen in anger. May it not happen so concerning me, from our own sluggishness, so that you should turn your face away from me in anger. Both are therefore possible; may such a thing not be done to me, so that having been angered, you turn away from me. Or thus: may you not be angered in such a way that I am deprived of your presence.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes God's turning away from turning away in anger, which the verse names.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To hate one's parents for the Savior's sake means not preferring them to God, and whoever does so is abandoned by them.
comments.comment: Since God is to be loved most in a time of struggle, in a time of persecution, the love of God must be preferred above all. If one pulls away from parents or the old age of a parent, 'honor God, since you are not able to follow me' (Exodus 20:12). Therefore, to hate the father and the mother does not mean that kind of hatred by which we are provoked and loathe, but rather according to not preferring them to God. In this same way, one treats the wife and the children, and in this same way, the brothers. 'And he will hate even his own soul' (Luke 14:26), he says. He hates his own soul while enduring death for the sake of a witness, but on account of the Savior; for see what he says: he who hates a father 'because of me' (Matthew 10:37), not completely. The Savior is to be preferred above all. Just as if someone hates a mother because of the Savior. This hatred does not bring slander. He who thus has hated the parents for the sake of the Savior is abandoned by them. Therefore he says: 'for my father and my mother have abandoned me' (Psalm 27:10). The abandonment is unto the end.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a father and mother could forsake the speaker.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks God to teach him a law to walk in and to lead him on the straight way, keeping the mean between excess and deficiency, away from his enemies.
comments.comment: Instruct me, Lord, so that having received such a law from you, I may walk in the word spoken (Psalm 27:11). And guide me in the straight and unbending way of yours, escaping the enemies lying in wait, those placing stumbling blocks for me. For what is the virtue of the mean, of not being an excess or a deficiency, but keeping the proportion; you, Master, guide me, bringing me to the end of it, escaping my enemies who are working evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The straight way is the way of true doctrines, and he prays to be led on it by the Lord.
comments.comment: Acting excessively, standing by the door, they receive through deception those who do not stand by the distinction of moderation and excess. If you say that the path of true dogmas is a straight way, be careful that, not being led by God, the adjacent false dogmas are enemies of this age, who are its rulers; so that we may not fall into their deception, we pray to be led by the Lord on the straight way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He chose the straight way and prays not to be handed over to those who trouble him.
comments.comment: Since I have chosen to walk the straight way, all the wicked have set to trouble me (Psalm 27:12; LXX 26:12); but You, Lord, my guardian, do not deliver me into their hands. He prays not to be delivered to them or to be numbered with their souls; those troubling him are witnesses that they are unrighteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Injustice lies about itself, as the earth is said to lie, so as to no longer exist.
comments.comment: And furthermore: 'and injustice lied about itself' (Psalm 27:12). Here, to lie, we say in this way, as we often say the earth lies. Injustice therefore lies about itself, so as to no longer exist. It lied about itself because of its own nature.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The land of the living is the land of promise and eternal life, where there is no death of sin, and the good things of the Lord are seen by contemplation.
comments.comment: The land of promises was called the land of the living, according to eternal life (Psalm 27:13; LXX 26:13), since no one in it participates in the following death of sin. But this land is in the unseen and eternal things, and upon it are the truly and properly good things of God. Therefore the saint says such a thing: I believe to participate in eternal life, so that by it, living, I may be transplanted into the land of the living, to see the Lord's good things which lie according to the promises for those living holily. And it is possible to say both to see and not to eat or taste something else; for the whole benefit is provided in contemplating the divine good things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the land of the living' is and what 'to see' the Lord's goodness means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The exhortation to wait for the Lord may come from the Spirit, so that he may ascend to the vision of the good things.
comments.comment: He says this, reasoning with himself, or to everyone hearing him (Psalm 27:14; LXX 26:14). And such an exhortation may be brought to him from above by the Spirit, since, having believed to see the good things in the coming age, wait for the Lord, or wait for the descent of the Savior here; for through it he will be able to ascend to the vision of the good things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He cries to God alone because no one else can supply what he lacks, and the temple of God is the heavenly place where God's presence is hosted.
comments.comment: Since you are not lacking in many things, that you might be able to have these things replenished toward you (Psalm 28:2; LXX 27:2a), I am worthy to cry out to you, that you might hear the voice of my prayer when I am praying to no one else; for no one else is able to replenish what I lack. The temple of God is the one, and the super-heavenly space and the powers within it, hosting the presence of God as much as is possible (Psalm 28:2; LXX 27:2b). And the Word of God is also the one who declares: 'The Father who dwells in me performs the works.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He prays not to become unrighteous and perish with those who practice it.
comments.comment: He prays, not saying: 'Since destruction certainly comes to the wrongdoer (Psalm 28:3; LXX 27:3b), do not let me, providing justice to me, fall into becoming an unrighteous one, lest I perish with those practicing it.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The foolish man does evil because pleasure entices him, and the saint prays that he be repaid with pains that make him turn away from evils.
comments.comment: The discerning one, approaching things with scientific knowledge, turns away from the harmful useless things, choosing the good and profitable ones (Psalm 28:4-5; LXX 27:4). But the foolish one, being enticed by pleasure, performs evils, not seeing their harmfulness. Since he does not rationally perceive the harmful things, the saint prays that the foolish one might be repaid according to his painful works, so that through those pains he might turn away from the evils having become causes of punishment for him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'give them according to their deeds' asks for, namely a repayment meant to turn the foolish from evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who do not comprehend the works of the Lord and the works of his hands receive punishment that follows what they chose.
comments.comment: A man does, his works indeed, but they are the works of his hands; for he works according to a disposition (Psalm 28:5; LXX 27:5). And the active powers, being called his hands, perform the practical aspects of sins. They deserve to receive a retribution in kind, because they did not comprehend the works of the Lord and the works of his hands; they turn out to be the visible works and the invisible works of God. For those who do not comprehend the works of God and the works of his hands, he wishes to receive the retribution of them; for they themselves having chosen the non-comprehending, the punishment followed them to fall into it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His heart is helped when it agrees with what is necessary and holds no foolish opinion.
comments.comment: Hoping in the Lord, the helper and defender, my heart was helped (Psalm 28:7; LXX 27:7), so that there is nothing in it of a shameful remembrance or a foolish opinion. For the helping of the heart is to agree with what is necessary and to renew toward the opposites.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flesh that sprouts now holds the word of a seed toward the resurrection, as Paul shows with the example of what is sown.
comments.comment: My flesh has sprouted in doing these things, aiding my heart. Perhaps also the hoping heart will be aided, the flesh having risen according to the time of the resurrection, enjoying it. Near to this, even our bones sprout like herbs. For our body now holds the word of a seed toward the resurrection; for this very thing, having been sown in corruption, sprouts in incorruption, being sown. Paul also used the example of that which is sown regarding the things of the resurrection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He confesses and gives thanks of his own will, for all things that happen, and not only when pleasure drives him.
comments.comment: And I will confess to him according to my will. Many, through fear of punishment or shame, or because they are being reproached by men, forbid sins by disposition, enjoying them. But the critical man, having seen the mystery and the harm of sins, voluntarily turns away from them, confessing them to God of his own will. And if 'I will confess to him' signifies thanksgiving, someone does it according to his will, being thankful for all things that happen, even if something seems unpleasant. For those thanking only in things that please, they do not do it of their own will, but are driven to this by pleasure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to praise or confess to God willingly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's people have no stronghold except the Lord himself, who is the defender of the salvations of Christ.
comments.comment: The people of God have nothing else as a stronghold except the Lord himself being their refuge and fortress (Psalm 28:8; LXX 27:8). He himself is the Lord and the defender of the salvations of Christ. And every partaker of Christ is called 'Christ' homonymously with him. He who is not saved of the salvations, his Christ is not a defender; but if he is a defender of the salvations of Christ, the Son of the one who is, then salvation is heard through him by which he saves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks that God bless his people with every spiritual blessing, lift them up through virtue and shepherd them for all this age.
comments.comment: Save this your people, for you are a stronghold, blessing your inheritance; not like any other people (Psalm 28:9; LXX 27:9). Bless it with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly things, lifting them up and suspending them through virtue, but also shepherding them into all this age. For in the future, having surpassed the state of being fed, they will be a pupil and a teacher to you.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the writer's reading of 'bless thine inheritance, feed them also, and lift them up'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who rightly receive the Trinity bring glory to the Lord, those who keep his commandments bring honor, and he who follows the church's doctrines and canons worships in his holy court.
comments.comment: Protect then those who have the spirit of adoption by the angels, to bring upon the tent those things for healing (Ps 28,1b–2); and they carry glory, and they are also sons of the lambs. Lambs ought to be considered those who return to a life of godliness according to piety, without logically contemplating the truth. Therefore they are also sufficient to rule, and sons of lambs are those born of the imitation of their way of life. Those having correctly and justly and piously received the Trinity carry glory, but those guarding the commandments of the Lord carry honor. For he who transgresses the law, by transgressing, dishonors God; honor he offers to Him, the one who is contained by the divine law. Bring glory to the Lord in His name; likewise to Him before Him. Worship the Lord in His holy court. He who worships God according to the ecclesiastical doctrines and the blameless canons of it, worships the Lord in His holy court.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must worship within the Lord's holy court, which is the Church, and whoever makes a god of anything besides God does not worship in it.
comments.comment: Worship the Lord in his holy court (Psalm 28:2 LXX; Psalm 29:2 in Hebrew numbering). One must not worship the Lord outside his holy court, but only after entering within it. That is, the person who owes true service to God must not step outside the body of the Church and start a rival assembly and schisms on his own. For that was not fitting. Just as a person makes himself a house of the Lord, so as to become a temple of God, so he can also surround himself with a court, walling himself around with his way of life, his reason, and divine thoughts, and worship God within himself. He has sufficient grounds for worship in what already exists in him, since the Creator is understood both from his bodily frame and from the ordering of his soul. The Lord also called the court of the Jews a court when he said, "I have other sheep that are not of this court" (John 10:16), showing clearly that there is also another court, the truly holy one, which was to gather Christ's sheep—those from the nations predestined for salvation. That is, this Church, in which true worshipers worship in spirit and truth. No one who makes a god of anything besides God can worship God in his holy court. Some make a god of their belly—their god is the belly (Philippians 3:19). Others make a god of silver—those devoted to greed, which is idolatry (Colossians 3:5). And each person, whatever he has honored above all else, to that he assigns the glory of God. Such a person is not in the holy court, nor does he worship God, even if he seems inseparable from the visible gatherings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'his holy court' is and who worships in it.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The voice of the Lord upon the waters is John, the voice crying in the desert, baptizing in the Jordan and at Aenon.
comments.comment: “The voice of the Lord is upon the waters” (Psalm 28:3 LXX). What voice? Upon what waters? Let us take the saying as prophecy. Remember John, who, when asked by the Jews, “Who are you? What answer shall we give to those who sent us?” replied, “I am the voice of the Lord crying in the desert” (John 1:22-23). So John is the voice of the Lord, an angel sent from God before the face of the Lord, to make ready for the Lord a prepared people. This voice, then, was upon the waters—upon the Jordan, in which he baptized, preaching the baptism of repentance. And not only in the Jordan, but also in Aenon near Salim, because there were many waters there. So “the voice of the Lord upon the waters” is John at the baptism.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of 'the voice of the LORD is upon the waters'.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The God of glory thundered when the Father's voice came from heaven at Jesus' baptism, and the Lord was then upon many waters.
comments.comment: There also the God of glory thundered. For a voice came from heaven saying, “This is my Son, the beloved, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Then also the Lord was upon many waters, when he deemed it worthy to come down to John’s baptism, in order to fulfill all righteousness that is in the law (Matthew 3:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the thunder of the God of glory and the 'many waters' of the verse.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The voice upon the waters may be John baptizing, who by his austere life cuts the flame of fire.
comments.comment: Someone, imposing a more superficial interpretation, will say of John baptizing in the Jordan river, 'A voice of the Lord upon the waters' (Ps 28,3a). Yet John, having taken up a more pleasant and austere life, making the flame of the pleasures of life manageable, is a voice of the Lord cutting the flame of fire (Psalm 29:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The voice is 'in strength' because it removes the people's weaknesses by the baptism of repentance, or because John bears witness to the strong Lord.
comments.comment: “The voice of the Lord in strength” (Psalm 28:4 LXX). For it takes away the weaknesses of the people through the baptism of repentance, since through it he baptizes in water for repentance. “In strength” means the voice that says, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3:2), and “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8). Or perhaps the voice is “in strength” because John bears witness to the one who truly is the strong Lord, saying, “I baptize in water; but the one coming after me is stronger than I.” So this voice bore witness to his strength.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what way the voice is powerful.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The voice is 'in majesty' because John speaks great mysteries about Jesus and nothing lowly about him.
comments.comment: “The voice of the Lord in majesty” (Psalm 28:4 LXX). John speaks the great mysteries about Jesus, saying, “I saw the Holy Spirit as a dove coming down and remaining upon him” (John 1:32), and again, “From his fullness we all received, and grace in place of grace” (John 1:16). For these waters are high and display the greatness of the glory surrounding the Only-Begotten. Therefore, “the voice of the Lord in majesty.” And it is also majestic to say, “No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known” (John 1:18). And he clearly speaks many things majestically about the Lord when he says, “A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the voice is called majestic.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: John crushed the impieties raised against the knowledge of God, and the Lord by his coming crushes the opposing powers, called cedars of Lebanon.
comments.comment: “The voice of the Lord crushing cedars” (Psalm 28:5 LXX, Psalm 29:5). It is possible to say that, in preparing a people made ready for the Lord, John was crushing and pulling down the impieties that were lifted up and exalted against the knowledge of God, and he was making the crooked ways straight. For the one who humbles every hill and every mountain was the one crushing the cedars and smoothing the way for the Lord’s coming, by leading the people’s high and exalted and un-humbled heart into repentance. Therefore, receiving his preparation, the Lord crushes through his own coming the opposing powers, which are figuratively called cedars of Lebanon. For the Lord must reign until he places his enemies under his feet. And he will make these cedars fine, like the calf of Lebanon.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who or what the cedars are.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: After the opposing powers are destroyed the Lord's invincible strength appears, and he is likened to the unicorn for his rule over all and his single origin in the Father.
comments.comment: “And the beloved is like a son of unicorns” (Psalm 28:6 LXX, Psalm 29:6). After the opposing powers have been destroyed, then love for the Lord will appear, and his strength will become manifest, with none of the adversaries casting a shadow over it. Therefore, after the making fine, he says: “The beloved will be like a son of unicorns.” The unicorn is a ruling animal, not subject to man, with unconquerable strength, always dwelling in deserts, trusting in its single horn. For this reason the Lord’s invincible nature is compared to a unicorn, both because of his rule over all things and because he has one origin of himself, the Father. For “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Lord is compared to a unicorn.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The opposing powers will be ground fine and destroyed like a calf of frankincense melted by fire, or like the golden calf Moses ground to powder.
comments.comment: What, then, is the calf of Lebanon? They say that those who worship idols, with excessive idle curiosity, form images of calves out of frankincense and then bring them near to the fire. In this way, then, he says that the opposing powers will be made to disappear into destruction, as they deserve. Or the calf is the one made of frankincense and melted by the fire, according to what is said: “As wax melts before the face of fire, so sinners will perish” (Psalm 68:3 LXX, Psalm 68:2 Hebrew). And it is also possible to understand the cedars being made fine, and Lebanon itself, the originator of the cedars’ exaltation, being made fine. The calf was once made fine at the Exodus through Aaron, when the people, having rebelled against God and turned aside into idolatry, fashioned it. Moses took it, ground it to powder, and threw it into the water. So the Lord will make all Lebanon fine—that is, the first origin of evil—just as that calf was made fine by Moses. “And he will make them fine like the calf of Lebanon.”
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: John cut through the fire of sin spreading over Israel by preaching repentance and the eternal fire of judgment.
comments.comment: “The voice of the Lord cutting through a flame of fire” (Psalm 28:7 LXX, Psalm 29:7). John was cutting through sin, which was spreading like fire over Israel, when he said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (Matthew 3:2). The flame of the passions, then, which arises in souls from sin, he was cutting through as he told the Jews about the eternal fire, speaking the severe things of judgment: that “the winnowing fork is in the Lord’s hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor; and he will gather the wheat into his barns, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the voice does to the flame of fire.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Whoever has the voice of God passes through fire unharmed, as Israel crossed the Red Sea when the flame of the fire was divided.
comments.comment: When, then, does anyone pass through fire and remain unharmed, unless he has possessed the voice of God, concerning which it was said: 'The voice of the Lord breaking a flaming fire' (Ps 29:7)? Just as the people crossed the Red Sea with the holy rod without any loss, as the flame of the fire was broken and divided, so the crossing proceeds without being consumed by the flame.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The voice of the Lord prepares souls, called deer, to kill the acts of the body by the spirit.
comments.comment: It has not become a desert the inhabited world (Psalm 29:8; LXX 28:8). The previously mentioned voice of the Lord prepares the allegorically called deer. And these are souls, to kill the acts of the body by the spirit and to strip the impious one by the spirit through the lips by imitation of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: John shook the desert as peoples came to repent there, and his voice makes holy souls like deer and uncovers the hidden sins like forests.
comments.comment: “The Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh” (Psalm 28:8 LXX). For John was baptizing in the desert. He shook that desert by the arrival of peoples from every direction, which, because those who came repented, was called holy desert. For Kadesh means “holy.” This voice also perfects the deer—the holy souls who seek the heights, who destroy serpents, who make their dwelling on the high mountains. These would be great-souled souls, running up from lowly things to the heights of the heavenly way of life, light and lifted up, waging war against the opposing powers just as deer wage war against serpents. But it also reveals forests, so that the serpents hidden by the shade of the forests become visible, and the deer can consume them with less labor. Perhaps, then, the one who exposes the evils done in secret reveals forests—that is, he brings into the open the sins lurking in material nature, which are called serpents because of the many-colored character of pleasure. And he will reveal them in the day when he will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and the purposes of their hearts. Perhaps John too, being the voice of the Lord, spoke to Israel in a riddle: “Already the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9). He was revealing the forests—that is, he was exposing the uselessness of fruits, for a forest is fruitless timber. By showing them its harmful character, he was summoning them to the fruit-bearing that was required of them, saying, “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wilderness of Kadesh, the hinds and the forests of the verses.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The voice reveals the woods when the fruitless trees in them are cut down by the axe of the Word and thrown into fire.
comments.comment: And the voice of the Lord will work for her and a revelation of woods (Psalm 29:9; LXX 28:9), so that the beasts lurking in them might be made manifest, they are lifted up as deer. And a wood is a natural place of fruitless trees; and the wood is revealed when the fruitless trees in it are being cut down by the axe of the Word and are being thrown into fire.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When what overshadows men is removed, all will speak of God's glory in his temple, and his sitting shows the lasting strength of a kingdom without end.
comments.comment: When that which overshadows the progress of men is removed, then everyone, having ceased from the manifold error, will speak glory in the temple of God (Psalm 29:10; LXX 28:10). The sitting of God signifies his strength to remain unshakeable and incorruptible forever (Psalm 29:10; LXX 28:10). For indeed he distributes it to those perishing through turning: 'You sitting for the age, and we perishing for the age.' And here the permanence of his kingdom is presented. For this reason, 'And the Lord King is established for the age' (Psalm 29:10; LXX 28:10), having no end to his kingdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in his temple doth every one speak of his glory' and 'sitteth King for ever'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: John's work builds the temple of the Lord, where all can truly give him glory, and the Lord dwells in the soul washed in baptism as in a flood.
comments.comment: From all these things there is one result: the building of the temple of the Lord, where everyone who is constituted there can truly bring glory to the Lord. But also, “the Lord will inhabit the flood.” For through baptism the Lord comes to dwell in the souls of his sanctified ones. God inhabits the soul that is being washed clean of sin. For this reason it is said that he inhabits the flood. That Scripture calls the forgiveness that comes from baptism a flood we have also learned from the thirty-first psalm, where it says, “Surely in a flood of many waters they will not draw near to him” (Psalm 31:6 LXX). For the sins of sinners, in the redemption that comes through baptism, will no longer be permitted to approach him. “And the Lord will sit as king forever” (Psalm 28:10 LXX).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in his temple' and 'the LORD sitteth upon the flood'.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The Master gives strength to his people and peace to those worthy of him.
comments.comment: After all these things, it remains for us to acknowledge the rule of the Master over all things, who gives strength to his people, so that having conquered the evil one, we may receive the blessing given by the Lord in peace to those who are worthy of him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace'.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: To exalt God is to share in his power and to give him a house in oneself, as the psalm's own title speaks of a house being dedicated.
comments.comment: … in the Psalms 'Let us exalt his name together' is said … For this is exalting God's 'name' 'together': when one, having received of divinity's effluence by conceiving from God and getting mastery over his enemies, gladdened at a fall they cannot effect, exalts the very power of God of which he has shared. Which is declared in the twenty-ninth Psalm through 'I will exalt thee, O Lord, for thou hast upheld me, and hast not gladdened my enemies over me.' (Psalm 30:1) And one exalts God by consecrating him a house in oneself — since even the psalm's title runs thus: 'A Psalm of a song, for the dedication of the house, of David.' (Psalm 44:18 (LXX))
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words of the psalm, said of the man the Savior took up, can be said by everyone who imitates him, and to exalt God here means to give thanks.
comments.comment:
He began saying in the Psalms that what is said about the man whom the Savior took up, might be said about every imitator of him, not only what is said about him as the only-begotten Son and the Word of God; it might be said—I do not speak about humans, nor even about rulers, but about no created thing at all. What is now being said fits the man of the Savior; therefore also others are able to do these things. 'I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up' (Psalm 30:1). What I have said many times, and now I say: what is said about God, is understood as being about God; but what is said about humans, is understood as being about humans.

… When therefore the saint says: 'I will exalt you', this he says: I will give thanks to you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To exalt God is to see his height, and a person who has been taken up by him comes to know how high he is.
comments.comment:
Not according to the flesh, but when one no longer perceives according to the flesh, but beholds 'his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (cf. John 1:14), and knows that he who has seen the Son sees the Father, and this is to exalt him.

Therefore, because he says this graciously, the following is brought forward: 'because you have taken me up' (Psalm 30:1); having taken me up, you exalted me. When I was exalted, then I knew your height.

And this can also be seen from things held in the hands; one approaches by skill; not yet the magnitude, not yet the beauty, not yet the height of it he sees. But if he begins to grasp it and is improved by considering each part in light of what has already been made known, then seeing the magnitude and the height of the skill and the art, he exalts it, that is, he confesses its height.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to exalt God, with an everyday comparison.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Had God not taken him up, his enemies would have rejoiced over him, and he would not have exalted God.
comments.comment: And therefore, in the person of Jesus, it is said according to the man and of every imitator and of his member becoming so: 'because you have taken me up' (Psalm 30:1); for if you had not taken me up, my enemies would have rejoiced having taken me in hand, and would not have exalted you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, forbidden to build the temple, prepared its materials and left this psalm to be sung when the temple was built and dedicated.
comments.comment: But he who speaks according to the history says that David the king, having been eager to build something tangible for the Lord, was forbidden by God speaking to him (1 Chronicles 28:3): 'Not you shall build for me something, because you are a man of war from your youth, but he who comes out of your loins shall build for me something.' Having been persuaded by the oracle, David ceased from building, but he pre-arranged the materials for the building. As he says, he prepared the materials, and also having composed the psalm, he left it as one of the necessary things, and how, after the temple having been built and dedicated, it might be struck with singing and chanting by those appointed to this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dedication of the house is the rebuilding of the fallen house, the church or the soul, and its renewal comes when those once outside dwell in it again.
comments.comment: Thus, it is the building up of the fallen house and the return from captivity. According to a former principle, we say that the inhabitant and the house are the same thing. But it can also be taken more universally: the sum of the faithful, the church, is the house; 'that you may know how one must conduct oneself in the house of God' (1 Timothy 3:15); and 'I have loved the beauty of your house' (Psalm 26:8). And those who inhabit it are these faithful ones, those living according to virtue. But if the soul is the house, the earnest thoughts which are connatural with it are the inhabitants. Then both the building up and the dedication happen at once. And renovation occurs when those who were previously outside of it take up habitation within it again.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A 'psalm of song' begins from practice and leads to contemplation, while a 'song of a psalm' begins from contemplation and leads to a life of virtue.
comments.comment:
But he who both sings and practices, and sings and contemplates: if he begins from practicing, it is a psalm of song; but if from contemplating, it is a song of a psalm. We see these things happening: often some, wishing to contemplate, stand at the virtues and their works, and taking from the standing itself the possibility to succeed, they come to the practicing. It has become a song of a psalm. The song led, the contemplation.

'Having desired wisdom, he kept the commandments' (Sirach 1:26); the one desiring saw; he kept the commandments, he sang; and again he has songs being provided to him. Sometimes it begins with the song and receives the psalm, and then, with the psalm having made a way for the soul, it brings a song again. If therefore the beginning and the thought of the beginning arise from work as a craft, it is a psalm of song; but when someone, having begun from contemplation, receives the desire to live according to virtue, it is a song of a psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer for healing is answered at once: the one who prays already has what he asked, as the leper and the sick man in the Gospels were healed without delay.
comments.comment: Lord my God, I cried to you, and heal me (Psalm 30:2). The voice has been heard; for if he cried concerning healing, he already received what he desired. … 'While you are still speaking, I will say, Behold, I am here.' … for your prayer does not delay my gift, but it happens at once; you have prayed, you have the thing. Let us take examples from the Scriptures; a leper came to the Savior saying, 'If you wish, you are able to cleanse me' (Matthew 8:2). He says, 'I will, be cleansed'; and the cleansing happened as if there were no delay. … Again: 'Do you wish to be well?' Immediately: 'Rise, take up your bed and walk' (John 5:8). And the work of Jesus's command did not happen a second later.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist can say 'thou hast healed me': God answers prayer at once, with Gospel examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cry is Christ's, and in these words he referred Adam's condition to himself.
comments.comment: … Such was also the cry in Psalm 29 (30): “I cried to you, and you healed me; you brought up my soul from Hades; you saved me from those going down to the pit” (Psalm 29:3-4 [30:3-4]), … In these words he clearly referred Adam’s condition to himself.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ went down into Hades unforced, freed the souls held there, and the dead mocked death for its defeat.
comments.comment: For I, without even being urged on, rescued the souls held down in Hades. “Lord,” it says, “you brought up my soul from Hades” (Psalm 30:3). … The devil did not see this, and so he dragged me down, intending to swallow me, not knowing that he would have to vomit up even those he had already swallowed. For the moment I stood in Hades, I stripped his tombs and laid bare his graves. I laid them bare not by fighting openly, but by invisibly providing the resurrection. I was releasing no one, and yet all were being released. I was saying nothing, and yet freedom was being proclaimed. I was calling no one, and yet all were running together. For the moment I stood there as king, the tyrant was despised. I shone as light, and the darkness was dissolved. You could see every prisoner looking at freedom, every captive dancing at the resurrection—so much so that the dead themselves were marveling at me for the victory and mocking death for its defeat, saying: “Where, death, is your sting? Where, Hades, is your victory?” (Hosea 13:14).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the verse as Christ bringing souls up out of Hades, in vivid language a general reader can follow.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: He went down into Hades not for his own sake but to lead up those held there, and so he says he is ascending.
comments.comment: … May he heal them. For the healing is the bringing up of my soul from there. I became there not to remain myself, but neither to simply depart and return, but to lead up those there. 'Having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, in which he also preached the message to the spirits in prison' (1 Peter 3:19), he led them up. And because of these things he went down there, and because of these things he says he is ascending; for he went down to lead up. If he were not ascending them, he would not have gone up there; for he did not descend or ascend for his own sake.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls Hades the pit, and Christ, having accepted death for men, says he was numbered among those going down into it.
comments.comment: In the places of Scripture, Hades is named the 'pit'. For see what it says: 'Lord, you brought my soul up from Hades, you saved me from those descending into the pit' (Psalm 30:3). And the Savior, having become man and having accepted death on behalf of men, says: 'I was numbered among those descending into the pit, since I became as a helpless man'. He was crucified and his hands and his feet were as 'helpless'; 'he was heard like a sheep toward slaughter' (Isaiah 53:7), as 'helpless'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words are said as from the face of Christ, who gave his soul for us, went down and rose again, and was not abandoned to the pit.
comments.comment:
He says that he will be saved (Psalm 30:3) if God does not let him descend to him, or after descending, having brought him up. These things are said economically and as from the face of Christ, who having descended his soul on our behalf and having given it and having risen from the dead by the good pleasure of God and Father …

"For You did not abandon my soul to the pit, a pit called by name; I say with confidence: You saved me from those descending into the pit" (Psalm 30:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was not held in the pit as those who fall into Hades are, and he calls the saints he led up to join him in praise.
comments.comment:
'You saved me from those descending into the pit' (Psalm 30:3). For even if I descended into Hades, I was not seized in the pit like the falling waters, but I was saved, so that what happens to those falling into Hades does not exceed my harm. 'Praise the Lord, you saints of his' (Psalm 149:5). Therefore, while praising and extolling because he was received, he intends to fall upon the hymn even those whom he led up from Hades, the saints having been shown; for those around Abraham and the other saints were there.

And other souls were there too, but some were shown to be the souls of saints, and others were not; for we do not say that the Savior sanctified all, but those souls which were awaiting him there. … Just as therefore I sing a psalm, you also praise; you join in with instruments to our song, which I send up on behalf of you …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To confess here is to give thanks, and the holiness to remember is one the singer has received and must reclaim.
comments.comment: … And you confess the memory of His holiness. Confession here is not called the disclosure of sins; for this too is called confession, as if one says, “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5:16). But most often in Scripture, confession is signified by the word thanksgiving: “We will confess to You, O God, we will confess to You” (Psalm 75:1). … If anyone is sanctified, having shared in the holy, he has obtained holiness. And so it has happened, so that one might be holy not by essence, but by choice, having received the holy and the good in advance. Therefore, do not neglect, while confessing and singing, that holiness is your own; because you have become it, take hold of it; you have become it so that you might be holy, not profane; yet you have become in filth and profanity. Reclaim your holiness, and thus desire to become it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'confess' here means giving thanks, and what remembering his holiness asks of the singer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Life lies in God's will, so a person must follow and do that will, asking to know it, with his own will cooperating.
comments.comment: … For wrath is in His mind and life is in His will (Ps 30:5). … And just as it becomes like wrath in the mind, so also “life is in His will” (Ps 30:5). He who follows His will and works it, asking to know it from Him—indeed, someone sends a prayer saying, “Teach me to do Your will” (Psalm 143:10). … And our own will must also cooperate, so that He does not say, “How often I willed, and you did not will.” Therefore, “life” is “in Your will.” … In the will, therefore, of Him who brought you into existence, life lies. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'in his favour is life': life lies in following God's will.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evening and morning are taken as the end of the letter and shadow and the beginning of the day the Spirit brings, which gives rejoicing.
comments.comment:
… The evening is the end of the day and the beginning of the night, just as in the morning the end is of the night and the beginning is of the day. But many times it has been said that the opposites, the good and the evil, are co-existing. It is possible to receive in the evening the end of the shadow, the end of the letter.

But when someone wishes to be among them having received the end of the letter and of the shadow, he weeps rather, no longer seeing the pleasantness of the letter, no longer beholding the flower of the Scripture. But when the life-giving Spirit has risen and the New Covenant has been revealed, it is a beginning of the day bringing rejoicing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Weeping in the evening and joy in the morning point to the rising of the sun of righteousness, a weeping for the circumcised and a joy for the Gentiles.
comments.comment: The end of the day prepares the true light; they weep in the evening—that is, having come into being at the beginning of the night—while the beginning of the day rejoices, having occurred for them with the rising of the sun of righteousness (Ps 29:6d). This applies to both: the weeping of the circumcised when the sun of righteousness rises for them, and the joy of the Gentiles when the saving word shines upon them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse can be read two ways, as spoken when he prospers or as meaning that in his prosperity he will never be shaken, and both have meaning.
comments.comment:
… 'And I said in my prosperity, I shall never be shaken for ever' (Psalm 30:6). The expression is ambiguous. It can be read thus: 'And I said in my prosperity, I shall never be shaken for ever.' When I am prospering, I said this: I shall never be shaken for ever. But it can also be thus: 'I said, In my prosperity I shall never be shaken for ever.' Both markings have meaning. …

… And it is also possible thus: to verse differently, 'I said in my uprightness'; when they were being upright and seemed to be resting, he said 'I shall by no means be shaken for ever.' If indeed help had not come quickly, he would have been cut down, because he had encouraged himself, having great confidence in the fruitfulness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two ways the verse can be read.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prosperity is spiritual fruitfulness, the seed of Jesus multiplied a hundredfold, and in it he stands firm and is never shaken.
comments.comment: One must hear prosperity through spiritual fruitfulness, so that the seed of Jesus becomes a hundredfold and the other generations of virtue are multiplied (Psalm 30:6). In this prosperity, having been evidenced through these things, I will say that I remain firm and immovable, never to be shaken for ever. And one must cry out thus: "In my prosperity, I shall not be shaken for ever" (Psalm 30:6); for through his works he cries out, "If I were in the aforementioned prosperity, I would be unshakeable, not being turned aside by the adversary."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The beauty he asks God to strengthen is spiritual, the inner man, made of virtues in proportion with one another, as the bride's beauty is without flaw.
comments.comment: … Lord, in your will, grant power to my beauty. That is, he says, either gracefully or thankfully. Let us see what kind of beauty he speaks of. He does not speak of bodily beauty, but of spiritual beauty and of the inner man. This beauty, which is perceptible, which is manifested in the face and in the form, has its constitution from the proportion of the members, if the members of the man were proportional to themselves, and not to be such that some exceed and others fail; for the beauty is distorted. It is necessary to have a fitting eye for the nose and this for the mouth; for if the members were disproportionate, even if it might seem beautiful in itself, it does not make beauty for the face. This indeed he says: those virtues which follow your will, the individual ones, so that my thoughts, having been proportioned, are the actions. And in the song of songs, he who praises the bride: 'All beautiful is my beloved, and there is no flaw in you' (Song 4:7). Because of this, 'all beautiful are you,' because there is no flaw and nothing in you is outside of proportion or shame.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'beauty' as the inner beauty of proportioned virtues, with a clear comparison.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The beauty of the soul lies in the harmony of all the perfected virtues, as bodily beauty lies in the proportion of the limbs, and God gives it to those who do his will.
comments.comment: Bodily beauty appears through the symmetry and proportion of the limbs (Psalm 30:7), but the beauty of the soul is in the harmony and symphony of all perfected virtues, having symmetry and proportion in all activities according to reason, and the harmony of the soul's powers in proportion. "Grant this beauty to me, O Lord, according to your will." For having done your will and that of the Father in heaven, he took it up, since everyone having become conformed to the image of the Son of God has received beauty from God, having been united with the Lord's will.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blood of Christ did profit those it redeemed, but those who still remain as dust do not confess or declare God's truth, and he came to suffer to change them.
comments.comment:
