What profit is there in my blood, in my descending into corruption? I descended into corruption; what profit has occurred? Behold, they remain in their own evils. But he does not say this at all. Rather it is said: 'you were bought' with the blood of Christ, and that: 'not with corruptible things, silver and gold, were you redeemed from your vain manner of life, but in precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and spotless, Christ' (1 Pet 1:18-19). And this is possible: the whole sum of the saved is called the Body of Christ.

Since, therefore, the Savior arrived and received all that we previously mentioned—the darkness and the cross and the descent into Hades—not all returned, not all took up virtue and faith, but some and others; according to this he says: 'he turned my face away' (Psalm 30:7) from certain things being members of me, being my body, 'and I became troubled.' If, therefore, he saved and redeemed and set free by his own blood, how does he say: 'what profit is there in my blood, in my descending into corruption?' Much profit has occurred—but toward those who remain in evils. …

For this reason he has said: 'shall dust confess to you or announce your truth?' (Psalm 30:9) Behold, there are some being dust. But I have come to suffer, so that I might transform them and make them heavenly from being swine. Since, therefore, they remain still wearing the image of the swine, they do not confess to you, nor do they even announce your truth. But I have come so that I might also make the truth manifest, exposing the wandering and the falsehood, and so that I might grant confession, so that someone might cast off the image of the swine and take up that of the heavenly. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To cry out to the Lord is to cry out to the Trinity, without dividing the Father from the Son.
comments.comment: I have cried out to the High Priest as a physician, and I will help toward my God, without dividing the Father from the Son. He who cries out to God cries out toward the Trinity; for the Trinity is one God, not the same as the numerical identity, if it is necessary to speak of numbers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saying belongs to the Savior as man and as soul: when he sees the sins of men, he asks the Father what profit his blood has brought.
comments.comment: … For it is not alien to the divinity of our Savior, when he beholds the sins of men, that the saying 'Woe is me' should now belong to the Savior—not as God but as man, not as Wisdom but as soul. … The blessed soul came upon human life; it took a body for the sake of men. If it sees the sins, it says to the Father: 'What profit is there in my blood, in my going down into corruption? Will dust confess to you?' (Psalm 30:9)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One who persists in sin is dust and will not confess to God.
comments.comment: He who, through doing material things and thinking of earthly things, being as dust and persisting in sin, will not confess to God, nor announce the truth to Him, being led astray through morals and knowledge (Ps 29:10c-d).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'became' shows the Lord was not their helper before, and mercy shown to him is salvation for them.
comments.comment: The Lord heard and had mercy on me (Ps 117:2). By showing the mercy of the Lord, he speaks of their salvation, that they might receive mercy. … The Lord became a helper to me. The verb 'became' signifies that they were not previously so: 'A helper and a protector became to me for salvation.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Became' marks a relation and not permanent being, and the weeping turned to joy shows the emotion, as hands laid on the chest show it.
comments.comment: It is to be noted that "became" does not mean "always being," but also signifies a relationship toward someone. If such a voice were ever to occur regarding the Savior, it signifies a relationship toward Him and not merely being (Psalm 30:10-12). "You turned my weeping into joy for me." The voice of weeping signifies the emotion, just as the very act of the hands placing them on the chest demonstrates it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sackcloth stands for the severe, bitter and cleansing life of one in mourning, and God changes it into gladness.
comments.comment: You turned my mourning into joy for me (Ps 30:11). … Having torn my sackcloth, you girded me with gladness. I was carrying a sackcloth of mourning, a severe life, rough, but he changed it into gladness. … We say that the name of the sackcloth signifies the severe, bitter, and cleansing life of the one lamenting.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sackcloth in the verse stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the Assyrians fell, the people of Jerusalem could say that their mourning was turned into joy, for the great mourning was matched by great joy.
comments.comment: … So the war is ended, and the threats flee along with the dangers; and so from then on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, rejoicing greatly at the help that came from God, could say: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me” (Psalm 30:11). See how things are reversed; consider carefully what he says: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me.” Great was the mourning because of the multitude of those making war; great has the joy become because of the multitude of those who have fallen.
comments.selected_reason: Shows the verse's reversal of mourning into joy with a concrete example from Israel's history.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Laughter is of two kinds, and the true kind is the gift of the Spirit given in the life to come to those who weep now, which the psalmist foretastes.
comments.comment: For laughter is twofold: the one being false, occurring with pleasure, which is followed by weeping; the other being the gift of the Spirit, being joy, which shall be given to those weeping now in the life to come. For 'blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh' (Luke 6:21), they have the harvest of this from afar because of virtue; the holy one, having received the experience of this from afar, as I said, said: 'You have turned my mourning into joy for me, you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness' (Psalm 30:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'You have turned' mark a change from grief to joy, and the one who sings glory to God has right conduct and sincere knowledge.
comments.comment: One who has not become aware in the consciousness of his own sins, and who has not actively awakened his sensation through spiritual hands, changing from being consumed by grief, will receive the fruit of the Spirit as joy. The phrase 'You have turned' signifies a change from cutting and grieving into joy; and 'I shall not be confounded' (Psalm 30:12) is said instead of 'I shall not know'. He who sings glory while saying these things to God possesses a right conduct and sincere knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He finds the common reading, 'while my glory sings, I am not dejected', unsatisfying, since 'dejection' often means repentance.
comments.comment: … So that my glory may sing to you and I may not be dejected (Psalm 30:12). Some say a hint: 'I shall not be dejected'; while my glory sings to you, I am not dejected. But this reading does not satisfy me. Many in the church read it this way. The term 'dejection' (katanyxis) often signifies a repentance. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: My glory sings to you and I act according to your will, so I do not repent and am not brought low by sorrow, and I will give thanks forever.
comments.comment: … This is therefore what he says: my glory sings to you, I act according to your will, and I do not repent, I am not brought low by sorrow. He is not brought low as if by evil, so as to no longer be active. Therefore he connects the thought and says: "Lord, my God, I will give thanks to you forever" (Psalm 30:12). "Lord, my God, I will give thanks to you forever." Since, therefore, I will give thanks to you forever, singing to your glory, I am not brought low, nor do I repent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'ecstasy' in the psalm's title can mean madness, or it can mean wonder at the greatness of God's works.
comments.comment: The name of ecstasy is homonymous; for it means many things, one of which is deviation or folly; the one who wanders is in ecstasy (stands outside himself). But the name of ecstasy also signifies wonder; for he who wonders is said to be in ecstasy (standing outside himself): "I perceived your works and was amazed" (Habakkuk 3:2) having seen their greatness, the art by which they came to be.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To hope in the Lord and not be put to shame means getting what one asks of him, for the whole span of life and beyond.
comments.comment: Upon you, Lord, I have hoped, that I might not be put to shame for ever (Psalm 31:1). For I am not put to shame when the things of the petition exist; for then the one praying suffers shame when he does not happen to get what he expected. And if we take 'the age' more simply, this says: in the time of my life, let me not be put to shame, always attaining those things which I entreat to receive from you; for it has been said many times that the time extending the life of man is called 'an age', just as: 'I will not eat meat for ever'. And it is possible also to say thus: since you are eternal and your existence and your kingdom extend through all the ages, and I too am immortal according to the soul, 'let me not be put to shame for ever'; for I am always with you. Now I know in part and I prophesy, but the one who is perfect will receive that which is in part, so that my hope becomes greater, having a greater remainder of expectation. Therefore, the one who hopes in the Lord is without shame.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'let me never be ashamed' asks for, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness came down from heaven to loose the injustice that filled the earth, and when it is revealed and those who ask it are saved, all injustice is dissolved.
comments.comment: Save me in your righteousness and bring me out (Psalm 71:2). The beginning of this seventieth psalm has a certain kinship and likeness. And in the seventieth lies the 'bring me out' itself, concerning which it is said: 'righteousness bowed down', when having bent the heaven, it came down. It has come to loose injustice; for the world having come about on earth was full of injustice; for 'the earth was filled' with iniquities (Genesis 6:13), just as before the flood, when 'all turned aside, at the same time they sinned, there is no one doing goodness' (Psalm 14:3). Just as the light rises and becomes there where the darkness is, and the darkness is made manifest by the presence of light, and when virtue shines forth, evil is driven away—so, when righteousness is revealed and those entreating it are saved, all injustice is dissolved.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The opening words belong to everyone who hopes in God and seeks an end without shame, not to one man only.
comments.comment: … For indeed the beginning of the psalm has become thus: 'In you, Lord, I have hoped, let me not be put to shame for ever' (Psalm 31:1), regarding everyone who has hoped and is seeking an unashamed end of expectation; all the words take hold of this. For he who speaks in praise does not speak of this one or that one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who hopes in the Lord is not put to shame, and because our cry cannot reach God's height, we ask him to bend down to us.
comments.comment: He who has hoped to reach the end of what is laid up for the saints, and who will not be put to shame for ever, has placed such an expectation upon the Lord. … And since our cry may not reach your height, 'Incline your ear to me' (Psalm 31:2) so that you may descend to accompany me; for the existence of this means that, having received my prayer, you will immediately deliver me by your wills.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Our voice is too small to reach God unless he stoops to hear it.
comments.comment: Incline your ear toward me, hasten to bring me out (Psalm 31:2). Even if I cry out to you, I am small-voiced as toward your majesty. If you do not incline your ear toward me, my cry is not able to ascend to you. If you do not descend with me, you will not receive my voice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks God to bow down his ear.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer does not rise to God unless he inclines to it, and so the psalmist asks for quick deliverance.
comments.comment: The prayer remains, and does not ascend to him if it does not incline toward him; but it inclines by descending together. When you incline your ear to me, receive me and quickly take me out from those holding me, from those attacking me. Even if enemies are, 'quickly let me be delivered' (Psalm 31:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks God to be his fortress, wall and shield so that no enemy can harm him.
comments.comment: Become for me, O God, a protector and a house of refuge to save me (Psalm 31:2). Become for me an invincible fortress, an unpierceable wall; become for me also a protector, your shield, your weapon. When you become my protector, none of my enemies can harm me. A beast cannot overcome me, the very one snatching, about whom we were sending a prayer: 'never snatch my soul like a lion' (Psalm 7:2). 'And into a house of refuge' (Psalm 31:2). Become for me that which is called a stronghold, where one fleeing enters within walls; for a building is a guard by means of salvation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'rock' and 'house of defence' as a walled place of refuge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A hiding place means God as protector, sheltering us as a fortress does, and he guides and feeds us with heavenly bread though we are unworthy.
comments.comment: And here 'Make me a hiding place' (Psalm 31:2-3) signifies a protector for the one being protected. It is also worthy that those near a refuge should have God become a salvation for them, just as one is saved unharmed while remaining enclosed by an impregnable and unassailable fortress. This I have often and always attempted, as the Psalmist says, 'You are my strength and my refuge, since your name is my stronghold; for I am your man and your servant' (Psalm 31:3; LXX 30:3). Even if I am not worthy to receive what I ask, because of your goodness you will guide me toward salvation and sustain me, providing me with your heavenly bread (Psalm 31:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist flees to God alone, and asks to be led and fed for the sake of the name he bears, since God's Son is both the way and the bread.
comments.comment: For you are my strength and my refuge (Psalm 31:3). You are everything to me, both strength and refuge. I flee to no one, not to a ruler, nor to wealth. And my strength: from you I have the power to hold fast, participating in you, just as a king holds fast. For the sake of your name, you will guide me and nourish me (Psalm 31:3). He says this because since your name is called upon me, because of this name of yours which I wear, grant both to me; and guide me, so that I may finish the race without fault and be able to say: 'I have run without lawlessness and I have directed my course' (Psalm 59:4), and: 'I have run the path of your commandments' (Psalm 119:32). And let me be nourished by you. Your way and bread is your Son. 'Way' is he saying, 'I am the way' (John 14:6). He himself is both way and bread. Therefore, 'for the sake of your name,' which you granted to me, so that I may have salvation; for I grew and said: 'O God, in your name save me.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be led and guided 'for thy name's sake'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Deceitful enemies have laid a snare to catch the psalmist.
comments.comment: Bring me out of this snare which you hid for me (Psalm 31:4), because you are my protector. Enemies are many, some deceivers, they have prepared a snare for me, so that they may hunt me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In committing his spirit to God, the psalmist entrusts him with his soul, so that the enemies cannot strike or destroy it.
comments.comment: 'for you are my protector, into your hands I will commit my spirit' (Psalm 31:5). I do not commit my spirit to another, but into your hands. … And if a holy man is the one saying these things, his spirit is that which is joined to the soul, concerning which it is said: 'your whole spirit and soul and body.' Some say the spirit is something other than the soul, others say it is its mind, and others say its will. But in all these interpretations, God preserves the spirit. If it is the soul, it is committed into the hands of God so that, being covered, it might remain unharmed, not being struck by enemies, not being destroyed. … Because it is sometimes said that the soul is spirit, Stephen teaches; for as he was about to die, and he exhorted them not to let the sin of those murdering him stand, he says: 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), instead of 'my soul.' And James writes: 'just as the body without spirit is dead' (James 2:26), calling the soul spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the spirit is that is committed into God's hands, with Stephen's prayer as proof.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The spirit may be the soul or the will, and the hands of God into which it is committed may be the two covenants.
comments.comment: And since this belongs to the soul when it possesses God, he says this: 'may such a thing not happen to me, so that my spirit might be outside your hands, but may all virtue be made straight for me, so that my spirit might be in your hands.' It is also possible to call one's will 'spirit,' so that he also wants it to be guarded in the hands of God. … Therefore, also the interpretative points: the two covenants can be the hands of God. Into these, then, I commit my spirit, wanting to understand both the old, that is, those things protected there, and the new. May both your hands contain my spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Spirit' is used in several senses in Scripture, including the intellect, the soul, and the conscience.
comments.comment: It should be noted that the spirit of man is spoken of in many ways. For in the prophecy of the Virgin, where it is said she is to be holy in spirit and body, spirit refers to the intellect. But according to James (as the body without spirit is dead), the designation of 'spirit' signifies nothing other than the soul. And in the passage 'For what are the things of man, except the spirit of man which is in him?', it is shown to be nothing other than the spirit joined to the soul or being part of it, which is also called conscience; for the conscience of man is the inward thoughts, which are something other than the soul; for the soul is the man, not the inward thoughts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior on the cross committed himself into the hands of God, which are his providential and protective powers.
comments.comment: And the Savior, having been hung upon the stake, his hands and feet having been pierced according to the prophecy, 'Into your hands I shall commit myself' (Psalm 31:5), has used the hands of God, which are none other than his providential and protective powers, to be exercised.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The God of truth rescues from deception, as the God of righteousness rescues from unrighteousness and the God of self-control from incontinence.
comments.comment: He is ransomed by God, being made outside of all disturbance. Thus the God of truth ransoms from deception; since God is the God of truth, He ransoms from deception and false glory. When someone has mistaken and false opinions, he cries out to God, so that by His truth He might make him outside of all deception. Again, the God of righteousness rescues from unrighteousnesses; for it is said: 'Hear me, O God of my righteousness' (Psalm 4:1), so that you might make me outside of all unrighteousness, so that you might bring low those who work unrighteousness against me. And so it is for each one: Joseph called upon the God of self-control, so that he would not fall into the snares of the rebellious toward incontinence; and Susanna, so that she would not fall to the elders toward adultery.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist calls God 'God of truth' when saying he has been redeemed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Into your hands I commit my spirit' is true in three ways, God of truth redeems the captive, and whoever guards vanity for nothing is hateful to God.
comments.comment: Regarding the Psalm 'the spirit of man having been set in your hands', stand firm to grasp in what way it is meant: 'Into your hands I commit my spirit' (Ps 31:5). And it pleases me that the present text is true according to the three ways. 'Having been seized by enemies, as having become a captive, I will redeem, O Lord, you who are the God of truth and of the truth shared by each of those participating in the truth of the Only-Begotten' (Psalm 31:5). In general, everyone guarding vanity for no reason does this, making the uncertain to be, or making vanity to happen emptily and superfluously. And he who hates this makes those guarding it hateful to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God is the God of truth he hates empty vanities, which have no substance, while the psalmist hopes in the Lord as his servant.
comments.comment:
You hated those who guard vanities for nothing. Since you are the God of truth, and you hated those who guard vanities for nothing. But vanities are not true. And he said 'for nothing' because in a certain way they do not exist. Every falsehood is unsubstantial. … Every evil happens for nothing, it has no end. Therefore he says: You, O God, hated those who guard vanities for nothing. …

But I have hoped in the Lord (Psalm 31:6). You, O Master, did not 'hate those who guard vanities for nothing,' but I have hoped in you as my Lord; for it was possible to say, 'But I have hoped in you.' Instead he says, 'I have hoped in the Lord.' He speaks these things as a slave. From the disposition of a slave and the work of a slave he speaks these things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the 'lying vanities' are worthless, and why the psalmist hopes in the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even a man who confesses God as Lord is saved by God's mercy, which brings him out of his necessities, meaning his tribulations.
comments.comment: I will rejoice and be glad in your mercy (Psalm 31:7). Upon your mercy; for even if I confess you as Lord and I have hoped in you, it is not by my own power that the end is achieved, but by your mercy. For you have seen my lowliness (Psalm 31:7). You have seen my lowliness which is about to receive mercy. Forgiving, you will not let me fall into it. You saved my soul from necessities. … For it is said, 'he will be brought out from necessity,' and, 'they cried to the Lord, and he heard them, and from their necessities he saved them.' He has brought me out from all tribulation, making it evident by his answering the plea; for a prayer was sent up, so that I might be rescued from enemies, from the impending wars.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that rescue comes by mercy, and what 'adversities' means here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sees his humiliation, rescues his soul from its necessities and gives it firm standing on slippery ground, so that the passions do not carry it away.
comments.comment: The humiliation, on one hand, shows blindness, when it calls for humility, and on the other hand, the harm by enemies. And it is good to see God in both kinds of humiliation. What follows, he considers to be the harm following the humiliation: 'For you have compressed my soul by necessity' (Psalm 31:7), saying 'necessities' regarding the circumstances from which the soul, having been rescued, is not enclosed into the hands of the harming enemy. If the 'spaciousness' were to say the same regarding the wide and spacious way (which is the love of pleasure), it would thank it for its stability and for desiring a standing in this life. For it says something like this: being in the place of the earth, where living is slippery and unsafe because of the sliding pleasures, you have given a standing to my soul, so that I might not be carried away there by the passions. But if it were to praise the spaciousness, it would say: 'Since being afflicted, I am not constricted, being more strengthened by pains' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being shut up in the enemy's hands means being defeated by tribulations, and standing firm in a broad place is God's gift.
comments.comment:
'And you did not shut me up in the hands of an enemy.' I am shut up in the hands of those attacking, when I am defeated by necessities and tribulations. But when I am saved from them, I am not shut up in their hands, nor do I do what they want to bring upon me. 'You have set my feet in a broad place.' …

It is a great thing having happened in this broad place and spaciousness: not to be dragged under, but to stand. And standing comes from God. Therefore he says gratefully: 'You have set my feet in a broad place.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being shut up in the enemy's hand and set in a broad place means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The troubled eye is the mind disturbed by anger and passion, and the stomach is the part that receives heavenly bread or harmful food.
comments.comment:
My eye was greatly troubled in anger (Psalm 31:9). My mind was troubled not in my own anger, but in the anger of the enemies or in your anger; for thinking against those committing sin, having sinned, I fell to the anger and my mind was troubled. My soul and my stomach (Psalm 31:9). Not alone, he says, my eye—that is, the mind—was troubled by anger. And this is also possible: 'in anger my eye was troubled.' When I rage, my mind is disturbed; for the passions are disturbances of the mind. And my soul was troubled, of which the eye is the one troubled by the anger.

And 'my stomach'; he does not mean here the stomach of the body, but that which was receiving from the bridegroom and bringing forth: 'from your fear we have taken in the stomach and labored' (Isaiah 26:18), so as to no longer save what was received, but to cast it away as small things. And this is also possible: because making the stomach calm, I did not receive the bread of heaven, but I received some other food, harmful, a poison, and my stomach has been disturbed. Therefore, he does not cast away salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eye is the mind, which steers the whole soul, so when it is troubled the soul is troubled too.
comments.comment:
Thus, when speaking about his own intellect or his own mind, saying that it is troubled by passion, the soul also says this. You know that when the helmsman is badly dragged, the whole vessel is damaged, and when the pilot is overturned, the ship is overturned. Therefore, the one called 'eye' is a certain intellectual power that steers the whole soul. If this is troubled, the soul is also disturbed. …

Therefore, if he says 'eye' and 'womb', it is possible to speak of both regarding the same power; because the mind is called an eye because it sees, and the womb is called a womb because it can generate and bring thoughts into the midst.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist's life is spent in pain and lament because he always toils for virtue, and he asks God to ease the labor.
comments.comment: 'For my life has wasted away in pain, and my years in lamentation' (Psalm 31:10). Since my life has wasted away in pain—for I always had it painful—I sometimes lament and sometimes not; I always lament, desiring virtue; I always toil, I always sweat for the sake of the acquisition of the good. Since I suffer this through life, in a way my life has wasted away in pain and my years in lamentation; therefore I beseech you, so that I may no longer endure so much toil; for if I toil again guarding it, it is not the same toil as that of acquiring something and guarding what already exists.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poverty is a lack of virtue and knowledge, not of money, and the bones are the powers of the soul that hold it together.
comments.comment: And my strength has grown weak in poverty, and my bones have been shaken. Here, poverty does not mean the deprivation of material goods. Strength here is spoken of in distinction of weakness. The strength which consists according to the soul is from wealth, but the sensory and bodily strength is not necessarily so; there are strong ones possessing nothing, and weak ones being masters of many goods. Just as if someone were to speak also concerning virtue or knowledge: 'Since I have fallen into poverty from virtue and knowledge, my strength, which I ought to have had from the presence of these qualities, has become weak.' 'My bones have been shaken.' Bones are parts of the body that hold the other parts together. While bones exist, nerves, veins, and the others can also be. Therefore, when the strong powers of the soul, called bones, become weak, the whole soul becomes in weakness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the 'poverty' and 'bones' are of the soul, not the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bones in the psalm are not those of the body, since they speak and confess; they are the soul's well-proportioned powers.
comments.comment: And that he speaks of bones, not those of the body: 'All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?' (Psalm 35:10); for the bones of the body do not have any concept of God, so that they might be able to say, whether there is anyone like Him or not. For it is necessary first to know God, and then thus to say. If therefore he says, 'All my bones shall say,' he means the powers of the soul which are well-proportioned and hold the other powers of it together, the sensory, the phantasic, the mnemonic.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In spiritual things strength is the same as wealth, so one who has turned from the wealth that is not divine says his strength has grown weak.
comments.comment: … Not every poor person is weak (for many poor people are strong), nor is one lacking in strength poor; but in spiritual matters, since strength is the same as wealth, the one who is wealthy has strength in good works. He does not wish to say 'I am such a thing'; since, having turned away from the visible wealth (which is not the divine), he says, 'My strength has grown weak.' It is to be noted what it means to say 'is' instead of 'has'; for it is not strength that is weak, but the one who has it, just as we do not say one is ignorant of knowledge, but that one is ignorant. This is in agreement with what was said by Paul concerning Christ: 'That we might become the righteousness of God in him' (2 Cor 5:21). For in these things, he called those having righteousness 'righteousness.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm says 'to my enemies' and not 'to all men', for enemies are those with an opposing disposition, and not all the Israelites were such.
comments.comment: Furthermore: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies' (Psalm 31:11); he did not say 'to all men,' but 'to my enemies.' And enemies are not just bad men who justify, but enemies by disposition; for he himself is an enemy to no one, but many are enemies to him. 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word; say, brothers, to those who hate you' (Isaiah 66:5). They hate and are enemies. And you, he says, call them 'brothers' not by voice, nor by utterance, but by disposition, or you demonstrate toward brothers by a disposition of brotherly love. And this is enmity: to have an opposing disposition. If even the Savior says this—let us say that it can be said from the person of the Savior as a man—he says the Jews have become his enemies. But not all have become his enemies; for the apostles also were Jews, they were Israelites. He did not therefore say 'to all the Hebrews, to all the Israelites,' but 'I have become a reproach to my enemies.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'enemies' are by what the verse does and does not say.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The neighbors are those who promise to know his Scripture, and their reproach is greater than that of the Gentiles.
comments.comment: 'And greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 31:11). His neighbors are those promising to know his Scripture and calling themselves his partakers. Therefore, 'greatly': for example, let the Gentiles be enemies; for they sin and act impiously. I have become a reproach among all those, as having endured the cross, as having descended into death. 'And greatly to my neighbors.' But when those owing to me and promising to have their own buildings near me do the same things to enemies, the reproach among these has become great.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse points to the cross, where reproaches meant for God fell on the speaker, and the sinner is God's enemy, not God the sinner's.
comments.comment: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies and greatly to my neighbors' (Psalm 31:11). This psalm was said both before and in the presence of the Savior according to the man: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies.' It alludes to the cross; for he says in another psalm, which Paul took to be from the presence of the Savior: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Psalm 69:9). I have received them. Some reproach you, O Father or O God, and these reproaches have fallen upon me. And it is nothing wonderful; often even a learned man, when he sees others mocking the learning, draws the reproaches upon himself. Those sinning are his enemies. This is said: 'For being enemies, we were estranged' (Colossians 1:21). The one sinning is an enemy of God, not God is an enemy of him; for God is an enemy to no one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the Savior speaks here, the reproach is the cross, which he despised, and it comes from enemies, not from friends.
comments.comment: And if the Savior says this, he calls the cross a reproach; for this is what the apostle taught: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Romans 15:3). Again: 'Who, despising the shame, endured the cross instead of the joy set before him' (Hebrews 12:2). Reproach and shame are the same thing. And see how much it reached him, that joy was set before him, a man not having sin. Therefore he despised the shame, he trampled it. … Reproach does not happen from friends and those having the same virtue, but from enemies. Consider, therefore, the reproaches which they bring against the Lordly Man: 'Do we not speak well, saying, You are a Samaritan and have a demon?' (John 8:48).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'reproach' as the shame of the cross endured by the Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lovers of pleasure feel no shame for their evil and boast over those reproached, while he confesses his own poverty and accepts reproach.
comments.comment: Those enemies who are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, not only do not feel shame nor seem to suffer reproach for the evil they do, but on the contrary, they take pride, as it has been said concerning them: 'The glory is in their shame.' And they boast over those who become objects of reproach. Therefore, turn away from your boasting and reproach against the Lord; otherwise, they shall rise to reproach and eternal shame. But he who perceives himself to have become in the aforementioned poverty confesses that he is to be reproached. Therefore he says: 'I have become a reproach to all my enemies, but also to all those who draw near to me according to the proverb—that is, to those who hold the same opinion.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who knew him fled when they saw him suffer, and the dead are quickly forgotten by those who grieve.
comments.comment: And a fear to those known to me. Those knowing me, having seen me suffering these things, had either a similar reverence, or had a fear of not suffering the same things. Those seeing me fled away from me. Those seeing me, having seen these things happening concerning me before, were seeing from outside me, not having departed from me, but they fled outside. Everyone fleeing Jesus becomes outside of him, outside of salvation. I was cast out as if dead from the heart. … And of the dead, a quick forgetting happens. For those undergoing afflictions say thus: 'From where the dead was placed, it is blotted out,' it says, 'the sorrow is blotted out from the soul.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who feared his fall fled from him, he seemed a lost vessel, and he heard the slander of many who only dwell around his teaching without abiding in it.
comments.comment: Those who attack me with persistence, perceiving that they have fallen from wealth into poverty, fearing that they might suffer the same, hasten to be outside of my stability. But also, a vessel which formerly was precious and very useful to the master, seemed to have been lost. Because the ear hears the slander of many dwelling around. If a teacher is called a liar by those who seem to be his disciples because of the necessity of learning, yet they dwell around and do not remain in the lessons, they do not abide in them. And it is possible to not be so; since the ear hears the slander of many around me, because they do not abide but merely dwell around our things, for this reason I have become a lost vessel. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be forgotten does not mean he is not known, but that others cast him out of their heart, as we say to friends 'you have already forgotten me'.
comments.comment: 'I was forgotten' therefore 'from the heart.' They cast me out from their own heart; for he did not have me purely as the apostle says, 'but Christ lives in me' (Galatians 2:20). I no longer lived in them. When anyone having the word in himself no longer works according to it, he rejects the amount of the word in him, and it becomes in his forgetfulness. But hear about forgetfulness thus: not as not knowing that he once had it; for many such things are said both in common usage and in the Scripture. For many times indeed we say to friends, 'You have already forgotten me,' not saying this, that 'you have no memory at all.' But the Scripture says: 'The evil of a time causes forgetfulness of pleasure.' Now the one, having been harmed by pleasure, forgets the time. And again: 'and they shall forget,' he says, 'their former tribulation, and it shall not ascend again upon their heart.' Thus you think, that the one having come out of tribulation forgets it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those in whom Christ lives never forget him, but those who do not work according to Christ forget him as if dead.
comments.comment: He became as if dead from the heart. The one understanding Jesus as being life—for he says: 'I am the life' (John 14:6)—and living, is the son of a living Father; for he says 'I live' because of the Father—they never forget him; for being present in their intellect, he always enlightens them, so that each one says: 'But Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20). Such a person is in Christ and has Christ in himself, living and working. But when someone perceives him not as living nor working, he forgets him as if dead; for Christ does not live in all, but in those working according to him. And those who consider themselves to be Christians, but do not work according to Christ, do not have him living in them. … See: the foolish man lives according to wickedness, being 'more a lover of pleasure than a lover of God' (2 Timothy 3:4), doing all things hedonistically. He considers the righteous man to be dead, because he is stripped of his own foolish life and does not receive it in his intellect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being 'forgotten as a dead man' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He became only like a lost vessel, made like sin and a curse, so that he might bring blessing to all who believe.
comments.comment: 'I became as a lost vessel' (Psalm 31:12). I have not become a lost vessel, but like the lost vessel. And take for me the example: the other men being crucified beside the Savior seem to have become useless vessels, vessels of destruction. This one saying these things as if he has become the lost vessel, but not lost. Just as sin became not the same thing to others as being sin, but so that they might become the righteousness of God in him, he was made like sin (2 Cor 5:21), he was made like the lost vessel. For that men are called vessels is not unknown, and these indeed are for honor, but those for dishonor. This vessel according to Jesus is not of destruction; for he did not know sin. But it has become like the lost vessel. It has become a curse, so that it might bring blessing. … For he was a blessed man, though cursed. This one, having become a curse, has become a cause of blessing, and not for one man, but for all who believe.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'broken vessel' as being like, but not truly, a lost vessel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who slandered Jesus were Israelites dwelling around him, who encircled him like bees.
comments.comment: I heard the slandering of many dwelling around. I heard many slandering me, not having set themselves apart at all. The Israelites were dwelling around Jesus. They slandered him: 'He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons' (Matt 12:24). 'He is a sinner because he does not keep the Sabbath' (John 9:16). They were around. If those saying these things were Gentiles, they would not have been his circle. These have become a circle. For he says: 'And they encircled me like bees, Lord' (Psalm 118:12). They encircled me aggressively.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'the many' who slandered are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: That all gathered at once to take his soul shows the greatness of the attack, yet they could not do it unless he gave himself.
comments.comment:
In the gathering of them all at once against me. He mentioned enemies, neighbors greatly reviling him; he mentioned those attacking him from the heart; he says those dwelling around and slandering. These were gathered together at once 'to take his soul,' especially when 'nations and peoples raged and labored in vain' (Psalm 2:1); for here also nations having raged were not yet entirely set apart from him or separated. 'Why did they rage?' They attacked the Hebrews more arrogantly. And the Hebrews in vain and emptily labored over the prophecies concerning me. All the things said: the hosts 'were gathered together at once, they deliberated to take my soul.' The magnitude of the attack is shown, that 'at once all were gathered together to take his soul.' … Not one, nor two, nor ten, nor a thousand, but all at once. The unshakeable and the irresistible, or the not being overturned, of the soul of Jesus is signified. They hardly gathered at once to take my soul or deliberated, and they did not seize it. 'No one takes my soul from me; I lay it down from myself, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18).

They deliberated to take my soul. They have gone as far as deliberating to kill him. If he himself does not give himself, they were not able to do this. For they came greedily to seize him, he says: 'Whom are you seeking?' (John 18:4) and he says: 'Jesus the Nazarene' (John 18:5). 'I am,' as he said, 'they went backward and fell to the ground' (John 18:6). And again a second time: 'Whom are you seeking?' and he said the same to them, and they fell to the ground again.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even when they gathered against him to take his soul, the speaker did not cease to hope in God.
comments.comment: But I hoped in you, Lord; I said: You are my God. In your hands are my lots. Even if those did thus and were gathered together against me, having counseled to take my soul and having done the other things, yet I did not cease from hoping in you.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly that the psalmist kept hoping in God despite the plot.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lots in God's hands are the ministries God has assigned, and one holding such a lot is safe from plots.
comments.comment: The papal explanations say this, that the lots are in the hands of God, such as the ministry, the presbyter, the episcopate. And it is blessed to have in the hands of God the lots which one has been allotted. Such a one is unplotted against; for 'no one' snatches 'from the hand of the Father' (John 10:29). 'In your hands are my lots,' says the Savior.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the lots in God's hands are, with the promise that no one snatches from his hand.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those whom God has allotted to him, such as the nations and each believer, are in God's hands, and only by going out of them is one lost, as Judas did.
comments.comment: And that we may agree with the given interpretation, we say: those whom I allotted to serve me, whom I set in the Church as apostles and prophets and teachers, are in your hands. And it is possible — and Israel, when it was called 'my people,' was called his portion and inheritance —; all the nations have been given as inheritance to the Son. Many lots are the nations. These lots are in your hands, secured by your active and covering powers, so that no one is able to snatch from your hand; for 'no one' 'is able to snatch from the hand of the Father.' He did not say: unless someone makes himself outside the hand, he cannot be snatched by anyone. For some will say: and yet the diligent later were dragged into impiety. And that I may not speak from mere images, as Judas himself made himself outside the hand; for when it was night when he was considering the betrayal, he says: 'he went out; for it was night' (John 13:30). 'My lots,' then; each of those believing in me is my lot. He is in your hands, equal to inheritance; for the lot follows the inheritance when it is reckoned among many. We speak this also more amply: the hands of God are the two covenants. If someone is his lot, he is in his hands.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Everything allotted to him, whether to suffer or to profit from, comes by God's judgment and not by chance.
comments.comment: My lots fall into those things which are covering and guarding by your hands, being profited by them; that is, all things allotted to me according to your judgment, either to flow from them or to suffer; for it does not happen to them by chance. … Others clarify the word not thus: the powers given, they say, are called their lots, as if they have superiority over teachers or others. They are not in the hands of God. For just as He establishes, so also He distributes kings. Therefore, because some are coming to move this superiority which is present to me, wanting to do so, they will not be able, since all things concerning me are in your hands.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who persecute are enemies, and the persecution may be a hunt to ambush, or the evil action itself from which he asks to be delivered.
comments.comment: Not all enemies persecute; but all who persecute are enemies. That the not persecuting here is not for taking, but for ambushing: 'The enemy said: Having pursued I will overtake' (Exodus 15:9). This persecution is not done for the sake of imitation. But one must love those persecuting righteousness. Those persecuting righteousness persecute it for the sake of sharing in it and becoming according to it, as if someone should pursue knowledge in order to contemplate according to knowledge. So also 'seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14) must be taken. It can be taken more ethically thus: since the hand of the enemies and of those persecuting me is wickedness, a forbidden action, deliver me from this action, lest I fall under their evils, their action.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's face shining on his servant means raising him from those who persecute, for the servant bears God's own likeness.
comments.comment: If you raise me and make me outside those persecuting, you made your face shine. And I am your face, the 'exact imprint of your hypostasis' (Hebrews 1:3), your 'image' 'of the invisible God' (Colossians 1:15). But since I took 'the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7), 'make your face shine upon your servant.' Show that this servant has your form, your face dwelt in this servant, that the 'deliver me' may be said according to the thought of the servant, but the 'face' according to the thought of the truth, of the imprint of the divine hypostasis. 'In your mercy,' then, 'save me.' Raise me from the dead. And perhaps he also calls his own salvation the salvation for those for whom he came, that he might become to them 'a cause of eternal salvation' (Hebrews 5:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker is God become man, so some words are said as from the man and others as from the Word, and 'your slave' is said of himself as man.
comments.comment:
And something else concerning the bare man: just as each of us, frequently narrating about a man, sometimes indicates him from the soul, and sometimes from the body. If I say that he is a beautiful man, 'pyrakis'—so that I may speak from the Scripture, 'with beauty of eyes'—it is immense; then I say that he is a learned man, a slave of God, he is subject to the Lord; for the change of persons is not outside of all things. When it is spoken concerning a composite, the changes of persons are carried from part to part.

Since, therefore, also the one saying these things is not a man alone, nor is he God alone, but God having become man, some things are said as from the man, and others as from the Word of God or concerning the God Word. 'And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14).; for he does not say: 'Let your face shine upon your slave,' the other to me; me, your slave.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ungodly are brought down into Hades against their will, so that, knowing where they are going, they are put to shame.
comments.comment:
I have called upon you. Then I am not ashamed, if the things of the calling exist. …

The ungodly were shamed and were brought down into Hades. The 'were brought down into Hades' again has a certain power. He did not say 'they descended into Hades.' But for those descending voluntarily, there is the descending. These, however, are not being brought down into Hades voluntarily. Also, concerning Capernaum, it is said: 'And you, Capernaum, which shall be exalted to heaven, shall be brought down to Hades' (Luke 10:15). It is being brought down by others. Then they are ashamed when they know that they are ungodly and do not have the impulse of readiness to descend into Hades. Because of this, they are brought down so that, having received the understanding of where they are about to descend, they might be shamed. Furthermore, they will do even more evil to themselves because they have become ungodly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist does not curse the lying lips but prays that they will fall silent by ceasing to speak unjustly.
comments.comment: Being a fellow-laborer, the saint prays that no one should fall and be delighted or find pleasure in this. For often, seeing someone hastening toward evil deeds, we pray, saying: 'May he not happen to be the one striving.' With this same mind, the saint, while praying, sings, not cursing: 'Let the deceitful lips that speak lawlessness against the righteous with pride be made silent, and let them be brought to nothing' (Psalm 31:18). And for the deceitful lips to become silent, what would it be other than to cease speaking unjustly, once the speaker recognizes how improper such a thing is?
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the prayer for silence is a prayer that liars will stop, not a curse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer that the lying lips be silenced is a blessing: they fall silent when they lose the deceitful word and then speak God's word with boldness and truth.
comments.comment:
Let the lips be without sound.

The deceitful ones speak lawlessness against the righteous. He does not cast them down; rather, he blesses them; for he did not say, 'Let their lips become silent.' The 'deceitful ones' become silent when they are deprived of devilish words. Their lips are not entirely silenced, but rather 'the deceitful ones'. Having cast away the deceitful word, they otherwise speak with boldness and truth. Thus it is said: 'The Lord will destroy all deceitful lips and the loud-sounding tongue' (Psalm 12:3). When the loud-sounding tongue—that is, the word—is destroyed, that from which it is destroyed, the person then speaks the remaining word of God.

… In pride and contempt. Since 'of the righteous' lies absolutely, it can mean both of a righteous man and of a righteous matter, concerning which it is said: 'Rightly the just' (Deuteronomy 16:20). But he who speaks against the righteous and against him who possesses it and is convinced by it, speaks in pride and contempt; for then their lips become silent when they know what kind of lowliness they are, when they know that the one whom they will despise is not worthy of contempt.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hides the abundance of his kindness from those who fear him, since knowing the threat is only in form would make them despise it.
comments.comment:
He hides the abundance of the wealth of his kindness because of those who fear, because of the small ones, because of those who refrain from evil through the fear of punishment. 'How much indeed is the abundance of your kindness, Lord' (Psalm 31:19). He hid it; for the knowledge of it was making them stumble into evils. If anyone should bring forth words of indignation even unto the point of causing amazement, and hide the kindness as if he were about to punish, if the son had known that the threat is only in form, he would have despised his kindness and would have been lost and become responsible for wrath. In truth, much kindness is his, a great abundance.

For the apostle also says to some: 'Or do you despise the wealth of his kindness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?' (Rom 2:4). And the one not knowing this thinks that he is not being unyielding to evils, and therefore does not come forward. And Peter, the foremost of the apostles, writes the epistle and has said such words: 'The Lord is not slow concerning the promise, which some count as slowness, but is patient, not wishing anyone to perish but all to come to repentance' (2 Pet 3:9). Behold the kindness. It was not necessary for it to be made known to the many; for they would have despised it even more. You have therefore hidden from those who fear you the abundance of your kindness. 'I have worked for those who hope in you, against the sons of men' (Psalm 31:19). Those who hope are those who are watching for the divine rewards and the promises which God promised to those living well. 'I have worked' therefore this, 'for those who hope in you.' I have worked this, to hide the abundance of your kindness, so that even those who hope in you might not see this, that for a certain reason you do not bring forth wrath.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God would keep his goodness 'laid up', so that it is not despised.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sons of men are those who imitate men, and what is hidden from the face of God is what cannot yet be known, though he is known now through his works.
comments.comment: Regarding 'Against the sons of men': You say 'men' regarding those having preserved the rational and incorruptible image, but 'their sons' regarding those having become their rational disciples and imitators. And 'hidden from the face of God' you say, meaning that which is not attainable now to knowledge, but will be revealed then, when we shall see Him as He is. With this 'hidden' thing, that which is said by Paul is contrasted: 'made known to men,' that is, His creative and providential nature. For after the 'God revealed' it is said: 'For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the works.' (Rom 1:20)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fear is cast out by perfect love, and 'sons of men' is sometimes praise and sometimes reproach, as they are lifted toward God or fallen from being sons of the Most High.
comments.comment:
To those who love: for here we receive the fear that is being set aside for the sake of love—'perfect love casts out fear' (1 John 4:18). And love is perfect when we do not love for the sake of another. Therefore, 'perfect love casts out fear because fear has punishment'—not that which is said concerning it: 'it is no loss to those who fear him.'

I have worked for those who hope in you against the sons of men. I have worked this concealment. Some are sons of men who are not reproached. But men and sons are often reproached when it is said: 'Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted?' (Psalm 4:2) But when it is said: 'The Lord looked down from heaven, he saw all the sons of men' (Psalm 33:13), these sons of men are praised.

And I say a paradox: when they are lifted up toward God, they are righteous men and sons of men; but when they are toward the righteous, the sinners are sons of men, being vile, concerning whom Paul writes: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not human?' (1 Corinthians 3:3) and concerning whom: 'But you, indeed, as men, are dying' (Psalm 82:7), having fallen from being the sons of the Most High. Toward the holy men called or named gods, the vile are called sons of men; but toward the sons who are the cause for God, those whom he looks upon, they are diligent.

And again: 'You will save men and cattle, Lord. As you have multiplied your mercy, O God; and the sons of men hope in the shadow of your wings' (Ps 36:7). 'A great man and a precious man is the merciful one.' Here the man who is 'according to the image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of God is praised in greatness. But when someone, having fallen from being the son of the Most High, becomes a son of man, this man is vile.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God often hides his goodness from the small ones who keep from evil only for fear of punishment, and does not punish at once but brings goodness.
comments.comment: God often hides His own goodness from the small ones who fear Him. We examined yesterday those who fear, abstaining from evil through the fear of punishment, if it must be called this abstention from evil. 'Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment' (1 John 4:18). The disposition of knowledge of good and evil, and desiring the good and, having bowed to it, abstaining from evil lust, stays away from evil not by the fear of punishment, but turns away from evil. If, however, some word persuades him that there is no punishment, he practices what he chooses as evil. God, therefore, often does not bring punishment immediately, but brings goodness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hid the abundance of his goodness from those who fear punishment, because the careless would have been harmed by knowing it.
comments.comment: How great is the multitude of your goodness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you. Since it seemed to someone to speak in a strange way, but looking into the intention of the speaker, we say that they are not curses, but rather blessings. And you wish for them to be found good. Since it happened that those not ignoring the goodness and the end of the saved were being rubbed, you hid it from those who fear you. But he says 'fearing' here to mean those having the punishing fear, not the righteous, nor those having that fear which has no deficiency, nor those surpassing all. He says: since your goodness is inborn with your goodness, and you do all for the salvation of all, and you make the dark things and the falling of someone dark to be dark, but because those being rubbed through carelessness were going to be harmed, you hid it from those who fear you …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hides only the abundance of his goodness from those who fear him, and reveals it so that perfect love may cast out their fear.
comments.comment: He does not merely hide his goodness from those fearing him (for they see much of it), but the abundance, so that they may not be harmed. (Psalm 31:19-20) And it is also good to say: To those fearing you, it is stored up for them. Reveal it to them, so that those having become in perfect love might cast out fear. 'You have made it known to those fearing you' means you have revealed it by energy, so that those having more hope than fear possess it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hides those who hope in him from the disturbance of men, from teachings that trouble the uninstructed, until they reach perfection.
comments.comment:
The manifest works of providence can serve as his face, for through them we perceive God; but his secret, private words are the basis of all things, though we do not perceive them in the perfection of reality.

From the disturbance of men—those human doctrines promising things to men while causing disturbance, through which they trouble the uninstructed—God, making those who hope in him outside of this disturbance, hides them in the secrecy of his face in all the ways mentioned. He will cover them in a tent from the opposition of tongues. He who has reached the perfection of all progress, having withdrawn from it, understands the truth through which it is un-deceivable; but he who encounters it while still progressing needs the covering of God in a tent, that is, of various tongues, or rather various false doctrines. For it is said toward the perfect: 'And every voice that shall rise up against you for judgment shall defeat them all' (Isaiah 54:17). For every heterodox word rises up desiring to be judged alongside the ecclesiastical opinion. But he who thinks the things of the church will defeat them all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's creation is his manifest face, but his hidden face is seen when we grasp the reason behind his works, as a physician's skill shows in his work.
comments.comment: You will hide them in the secret of your face (Psalm 31:20). The creation of God is sometimes said to be his face; 'in proportion to the greatness of the beauty of the creatures, the Creator is perceived'. They are not in his hidden face, but in his manifest one. If you see a physician working, performing skillfully, you see his face; for the works of medicine demonstrate the physician. But when we are able to see the analogy of the word of the skilled ones and the disposition of the one doing the work, we no longer see his manifest face, but the hidden one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the secret of thy presence' means by the difference between God's works and his hidden face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those still progressing are covered from the disturbance of men and the quarrel of tongues, for tongues are words, and they become disciples of God's tongue.
comments.comment: You will cover them from the disturbance of men in a tent, and from the contention of tongues. Those who are now being saved and delivered from the disturbance of men are covered in progress; for he who turns away from evil in order to do good does not at the same time as the turning away from evil have the good perfectly within himself. He becomes a disciple of the unique tongue, the tongue of God. For tongues signify words, and this has often been demonstrated: 'They bent their tongue like a bow' (Jeremiah 9:3), their word; and: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). The sensory tongue does not have a hand at all. But it has energy, the Word being called a tongue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The divinity of the Savior is the hidden face of God, and the part according to the economy is what is manifest.
comments.comment: Perhaps also the Savior has the face of God hidden, all that is according to the divinity, but that which is according to the economy is manifest. And since now the Word having become flesh dwells among us, we are being hidden in the mystery of His face, so that we may see Him as we shall see His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be hidden from God's face is the lot of the sinner, but to be hidden by God, as in the psalm, is protection from human disturbances.
comments.comment: 'For every one who sins, working unworthily, is hidden from the face of God,' just as Adam was hidden from the face of God. Contrary to this is being hidden by God according to what is said: 'You will hide them in the secrecy of your face from the disturbance of men' (Psalm 31:20). This too covers the earnest one with God's protection, so that he may not fall by human disturbances.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be hidden in God's presence: his protection, unlike Adam hiding from God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever knows God only from the order of the world sees his manifest face, but whoever sees the Father through the Son, the creative Word, is hidden in the secret of his face.
comments.comment:
'I have worked for those who hope in you against the sons of men'—the diligent ones—and let those know the work: the concealment of the wealth of your goodness. You will hide them in the secrecy of your face, the sons of men for whom I have worked your mercy. And someone is hidden in the secrecy of God thus: God has a face appearing through his own creatures; for it is said: 'Analogously, the Creator is seen from the greatness and beauty of the creatures.' He is seen from the analogy of creation; for just as if someone sees a ship, …

And he who sees a ship sailing straight from afar immediately comes to the understanding that there is one steering it. And a chariot being carried in order from afar, even if the one seeing does not see the driver, he remembers him. In this way, as the cosmos is being carried in order and having a beautiful nature, a vision of the beauty and greatness of God is known; for if the things created are great, much greater is the Maker.

Therefore, when someone takes a vision of God from the cosmos, the order, the concept, and the judgments of providence, he has not been hidden into the secrecy of His person. Such also are those who have philosophized among the Greeks; for from the greatness of the created things and the beauty, they took a vision of God. But he who, receiving a vision of God without the creation, has seen the Son and through the Son the Father—for 'he who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9)—this one is hidden in the secrecy of the person of God. And the creative Word is a secret.

Again, so that I may speak more popularly: Jesus had two persons, of man and of God. Those who know Him according to the flesh, receive Him in the manifestation of the person. But those who, turning away from knowing Him according to the flesh, have come to knowing Him as the Divine Word, these have been hidden in the secrecy of the person of God. And furthermore, since we were saying that the outward vision of the cosmos is a person, the Word through whom the things created came to be, and through whom they are provided for and governed, is the secret of the person of God; and the creative Word is a secret.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is most blessed because he is praised by those rescued from the greatest troubles.
comments.comment: Not such a great wonder is worthy of being shown by the mercy of God in the hostile and smoothed-over cities, which would be wondered at if it occurred in a city of dominion; just as for this reason God is most blessed, being praised by those who have been rescued from greater disturbance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist blesses God for hiding his kindness for mercy's sake, and the 'city of protection' is this life, a fortress in which we are enclosed.
comments.comment: Blessed is the Lord, because His mercy has marveled in a city of protection (Psalm 31:21). Having understood those who were speaking and having become in their knowledge, He sends back praises in a manner of thanks for the remainder of blessing and says: 'His mercy has marveled in a city of protection' (Psalm 31:21). They were saying that He hid the abundance of His kindness for the sake of mercy, in order that He might show mercy. Having known the reason why the abundance of kindness was hidden, he blesses Him who did this and says that 'in the city of protection' we have done this. We are able to call the life there, the sojourn in this world, a 'city of protection'; for in a certain way we are enclosed as if in a fortress. And since in the Kingdoms Zion is also called a 'city of protection'—'who will take me into a city of protection?'—this protection is to be praised; it is an invincible fortress, an unassailable stronghold. Therefore, 'His mercy has marveled in the city of protection' (Psalm 31:21). If anyone is outside this city, he is ignorant of why God hides the abundance of His kindness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'strong city' is and why the psalmist blesses God for it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Ecstasy' means wonder as well as madness, and the psalmist says he was cast far from God's eyes and asks to see the Lord's face.
comments.comment: And the name of ecstasy signifies madness, and also denotes the wonder occurring with astonishment; the present word signifies the second of these meanings. For he says such a thing: 'In ecstasy,' that is, having occurred in astonishment, 'I have been cast away far from the presence of your eyes' (Psalm 31:22), that is, far from the glory of your supervisory and inspecting powers; and since I have thus arranged, I pleaded not to remain cast away but that the face of the Lord might appear to me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'ecstasy' used here, and what the psalmist asks.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: There is one truth, and each soul has a share of it, so the Lord seeks and rewards those who have it.
comments.comment:
Since the truth that said 'I am the truth' (John 14:6) is one, many truths come to be in those who partake of the one, each soul having the truth, the type of which it received from the only-begotten truth. … Since, then, the Lord seeks out all these truths, he wishes to honor those who have them for these truths.

For this reason, his holy ones, seek him out, not without reward, resting upon the truth you have.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints are to love the Lord because he seeks truth, and the proud act in excess and in vain, since they can do nothing unless God gives it.
comments.comment: 'Love the Lord, all you his saints' (Psalm 31:23). He gave a reason; since 'the Lord seeks truth', 'love the Lord', the provider of truths. Thus we also hear righteousness being spoken of in the plural: 'The Lord is righteous and he loved righteousness' (Psalm 11:7). But when he speaks concerning universal righteousness, the essence, 'righteousness descended from heaven' (Psalm 85:11), he calls the Savior righteousness here. And just as it has become to us as wisdom, so also righteousness. … And they repay those who practice pride excessively. Since he showed the smallness of those who fear, for he also said there are men who trouble them, certain sophists and deceivers, he called these proud. But they practice pride excessively. And it is possible even thus: all evil becomes superfluous instead of being in vain. … And these therefore the proud do pridefully in excess; for not all those of whom they boast will be subordinates to them, unless God gives it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who share in the one truth are many truths now, but at the end all will be one, so each should strive to receive some truth, for God seeks it.
comments.comment:
Those participating in the truth are as many truths as there are participants. I say these things before the end, for there will not be many truths, nor many people who are true, nor many experts, nor many knowings at the end; because if from the believing ones there comes 'one heart and one soul' (Acts 4:32) and 'being completed in the same mind and the same judgment' (Phil 2:2)—even if not from all, but rather according to a certain measure—at the final desired end, there will be no difference between one expert and another.

Just as, even if by hypothesis all doctors possessed medicine in an unsurpassed way in all its parts, there were not many doctors; there were many men, but not many doctors. Since therefore the truth is one—for 'grace and truth' (John 1:17) come 'through Jesus Christ'—one truth becomes through itself, not truths as individuals through it. They become through the one, just as partial virtues become through the universal and individual knowings through the universal.

Therefore the Lord seeks these; so strive as far as you are able to receive some truth, for God seeks these. Even if you receive truth regarding practical virtues, the truth of practical virtues is judged from the disposition, if one participates in justice through that very thing. Since 'let the righteous pursue justice rightly' (Deuteronomy 16:20), pursue that very justice rightly, pursue the practice of the righteous with a disposition of righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Courage is endurance, and the Spirit commands in the psalm that we have both.
comments.comment: The mark of courage is endurance. For by this each of the saints, bearing the painful and grievous things that happen in life, prevailed against the devil. And the Spirit, wanting us to possess both of these, commands in the psalm: “Be strong, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 31:24). For the one who endures is courageous, and the courageous one would be enduring.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'be of good courage' asks for: endurance under trial.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The psalm urges those who hope, not those who only fear, to be manly and to cling to God, and clinging to him they become one spirit with him.
comments.comment: Be men, and let your heart be strong, all you who hope in the Lord (Psalm 31:24). Having said this, he anoints all the struggles for endurance, for manliness. And he does not speak of those who fear, but of those who hope. And we say that these are those working for the good of the promises with desire. These therefore are ready to become manly and to be strengthened and to draw near to God. And each one, clinging to Him, becomes one spirit with Him. And if each one of those clinging to the Lord becomes one with Him, when many are the ones clinging to Him, by a way of communion all become one spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm holds hidden mysteries, and divine things cannot be understood without divine understanding.
comments.comment: And since he speaks about hidden things here, there lies that which is according to knowledge, that which is kindred to wisdom; for the psalm contains mysteries. And this must be said: it is impossible to understand grammatical words if one does not have understanding of letters, and it is not possible to understand the arguments of philosophers unless one has knowledge of their previously proposed thesis. So also the things of God are impossible to understand without divine understanding.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lawlessness is the sinful practice of one who has no law.
comments.comment: Blessed are they whose lawlessnesses have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered (Psalm 32:1). Sin differs from lawlessness. Lawlessness is the sinful practice of one not having law; for the transgressor of law is called lawless.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Forgiving applies to sins done without any law, covering to sins done against the law and later repented of.
comments.comment:
And since the psalm has many hidden things, the one encountering it needs understanding, that he may be able to understand each of the things said obscurely.

… They say the difference between iniquities and sins is this: the sins of those who have not received any law at all are called iniquities, while those committed by transgression of the law are named sins.

Blessed, then, are those whose iniquities are forgiven, those now coming to the divine word; and blessed are those whose sins are covered, whenever, having disobeyed the law, they afterward repent.

For 'forgiveness' is said of iniquities, but 'covering' of sins, because iniquities are forgiven altogether.

For those who sin without law are pardonable; the hidden sins are not forgiven altogether but are overshadowed from love: 'For love covers a multitude of sins' (1 Pet 4:8).

And some apply the 'Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven' (Psalm 32:1; LXX 31:1) to those who have received the bath unto forgiveness of sins, and the 'And whose sins are covered' to those who from repentance have covered their sins.

And there are those who take the first of the believing nations, and the second of those of the circumcision who have received the Savior.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two verbs, forgiven and covered, in plain terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Forgiveness of sins is a new beginning upon the first, called regeneration.
