comments.comment: … The forgiveness of sins is a new genesis, a genesis upon genesis. Because of this it is called regeneration. Just as the repetition denotes song upon song, so also the regeneration is another genesis being added upon a genesis that has arrived.…
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, clear picture of what being forgiven means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sin is the larger class and lawlessness a kind within it, though both names point to the same wrongdoing.
comments.comment: "Sin is lawlessness." If, therefore, one has sinned, he has in a certain way lawlessness; but he speaks of two things. For by a connective conjunction, he has shown that there are two. Then: "and sin is lawlessness." Sin is a genus of lawlessness; for he was saying that lawlessness is a species, when the one doing evil does not have law. And this is also called sin: the transgression or violation of the law, which I called lawlessness. It is like saying: "everyone having a horse has an animal"; the animal is a genus. Not everyone having an animal has a horse, but he having a horse has an animal. He who has the species has the genus. Thus also here he speaks, as if he were speaking of the same lawlessness and sin. But in thought there is a difference, because one is general and the other is in part; one is genus and the other is species; for he said that the name of sin lies both against transgression and against lawlessness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lawlessness is forgiven when the divine law of the gospel takes hold of a person, and sins are covered through works of repentance.
comments.comment:
Therefore both kinds sin: "for as many as sinned lawlessly" (Romans 2:12). Behold, these who are without law, they sin. "And as many as sinned in law": these are those having wisdom, having transgressions of the law. Both "sinned." But the forgiveness of lawlessness happens when the divine law, the spiritual one, the one "turning back souls," holds the lawless ones. Then the lawlessnesses are forgiven. And I say thus, the forgiveness of sins does not happen immediately. Jesus forgives if he says: "the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins" (Matt 9:6). And: "Child, your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5); for he does not say: "Behold, your sins have been forgiven I." He has given a power that is making new. And the energy having come to pass destroyed the evil. Therefore those whose sins were forgiven are blessed. Consequently, they return to the blameless law of God which turns back souls.

Thus the forgiveness of sins happens when the divine law according to the gospel comes; for this is the "spiritual law" by which souls are turned back, as I said. And those sins which come to pass through transgression of the law and are added, have a covering. The sins are covered. But it is impossible for those baptized once to again find the bath. They are covered through works of repentance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When love arrives, sin stops being active but the potential for it remains, and that potential is still examined.
comments.comment:
All these things are examined not as being currently active, not because they are hidden as if they were destined, but because the arriving love has hidden those things, that is, it has departed from them, it has cast them out. And if one must speak briefly, the arriving love stops the sin in its active state, leaving the potential for sin remaining. If anything is examined, it is the activity; for example, the repentant robber had sin in activity; he had repentance; the Savior gave him remission; the activities according to which he had lived were cast away. But the potentials remain, and they are examined.

… Therefore, sins are examined in the way I have said; they pass into potentiality; for it is blessed to have the potential for evil. Opposites do not coexist. He who has virtue in activity has the potential for evil, and this is a blessed thing. Therefore, one must not have virtue in potential, but in activity. For this reason also, God from the beginning, having made man 'in image and likeness' (Gen 1:26) of himself and 'upright,' just as the good was in potential, immediately also gave a law to prevent sin, so that sin might always remain in potential.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Forgiveness of sins is the source of gladness, and prophets, apostles and evangelists all drew from it.
comments.comment: Nothing rouses the soul to gladness like the fear of God, turning away from evil, the course of repentance, and the way of confession. That is why David today blessed those who had received forgiveness of sins, showing at once Christ's love for humanity and preparing sinners to run to repentance. “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven,” he says, “and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1 LXX; Psalm 32:1 in the Hebrew numbering). So let every prostitute and tax collector run to the inexhaustible springs of Christ's salvation. Without it there is no release from evils and no attaining the blessing, whether you speak of prophets, apostles, or evangelists. For all drew from the same spring.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Those outside the faith are forgiven, while believers who sin can only cover their sin with good works.
comments.comment: And that one [the outsider], whenever he wishes, repents and has forgiveness of sins; but the one who fornicates after the faith, even if he later repents, does not have forgiveness of sins in the same way, though he can cover the sin. For he says: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven”—of those who came over from the nations—“and whose sins are covered”—of those who sin after the faith yet cover them with good works, for example covering license with abundant self-control (Psalm 32:1).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blessing reaches both the circumcised and the Gentiles, now made one new man whose lawlessness is forgiven and whose sins are covered.
comments.comment:
This existed before the gospel when the human race was divided into two kinds of men, circumcised and uncircumcised. But when our Lord pleased to come, he joined both ranks into one new man, having created him. The new man is not a Gentile, the new man is not from circumcision, but one new just as one man had become in the beginning; for there was no difference of circumcision and uncircumcision then.

… Thus, the life of the lawless and of the sinners has also been inherited; for the lawlessness of the former has been forgiven, and the sins of the latter have been covered up, and moreover, he has become a man. He no longer speaks concerning a lawless person or a sinner, and he says: 'Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin' (Ps 32:2). Pay attention to what they were saying: sin is a kind of lawlessness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word, being true, has no deceit in his mouth.
comments.comment: … that there is no deceit in his mouth is likewise to be understood as the fact that he has not possessed deceit. For there is no deceit in the mouth of the Word, being true and unsearchable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who speaks truth in his heart has no deceit in his mouth, but a cunning person can have a clean mouth and deceit in the heart.
comments.comment:
Blessed is this one [the Lord's man]; for sin is not imputed to him, for he did not know it nor did he do it. 'Nor is there deceit in his mouth.' The one 'speaking truth in his heart' according to the psalm that says this: 'Walking blamelessly and working righteousness, speaking truth in his heart' (Ps 15:2), the one speaking truth in his heart does not have deceit in his mouth, he does not have a deceitful word.

… Some do not have deceit in their mouth, but they have it in their heart; for 'your heart' is said to someone, is 'full of deceit.' And toward Elymas the magician the apostle said: 'O full of all deceit' (Acts 13:10). Therefore, it is a great thing not to have deceit in the mouth when the heart does not have deceit; for a cunning person can say all such things as to seem to have no deceit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'no deceit' means: truth in the heart, not only an honest-sounding mouth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinless one is called a man, and God does not reckon sin to him.
comments.comment:
… The sinless one is called not simply a human being but a man, on account of perfection.

Thus, then, God does not reckon sin to him, either by forgiving it or by its not having happened at all. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His bones, which stand for the strong and soft parts of his teachings, are said to grow old as a falling away, not by nature.
comments.comment: Glancing from the true light in the day, I ran and in this day I cried out to you, praying Ps 31:3. Since I did not fall silent from this cry due to inattention, my bones were struck, both the strong and the soft of the dogmas, which are called my bones. And he means by saying these things the falling away, that his bones are becoming old, but are not old by nature.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His bones grew old because he fell silent in the crying out that had kept him in the day God gives.
comments.comment:
Not 'my bones have grown worn out from crying out all day long,' but 'because I was silent from crying out all day long'; for before this they had the day which 'the sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) makes. And he was crying out, this indeed praying, and that indeed glorifying God who grants me the day. Since therefore I was silent from crying out all day long, my bones have grown worn out. It has been said to us also before that 'bones' refers to the vigorous powers of the soul and the doctrines of piety.

… When it was united to God, then it cried out all day long.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While he spoke of God all day nothing in him grew old, but once he fell silent, age reached his bones and God's heavy hand turned to his misery.
comments.comment:
An example from the Psalms, from Psalm 32: Because I was silent, my bones grew old, and what follows.

… It is enough to clarify the psalm saying somehow. As long as I cried out hymning God and spoke of God all day, nothing in me grew old; I was being made new. But when I fell idle from theology and was silent, oldness sank as far as my bones and what seemed firmest in me. Then followed Your hand heavy on me night and day, and so from earlier oversight your weighted hand was turned into my misery. I deserved it: a thorn was fixed in me when cares, or wealth, or life pleasures held me. That the prophet meant this is clear from what follows: I made known my sin, and so on.
comments.selected_reason: Reads the verses as one plain story: speaking of God keeps a person young, silence brings aging, then confession.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's hand means his punishing power, which presses day and night as discipline and turns a person to misery through the thorns of life's cares.
comments.comment: And in those things that lead forward it is said, as in many places of the Scripture, that the punishing power of God is called his hand Ps 31:4. That this lies heavily upon him day and night—that is, he says continuously—is because of the change that comes upon the hand. The Savior interpreted the cares of life, both the pleasure and the thorns of deceit of this age. And if one is pierced by such a thorn, he is immediately turned into misery. It must be understood what one becomes miserable through change and turning, not being such by nature. The word means the wretched and the pitiable. And to be pierced by a thorn signifies not being such by nature, but it approaching from without. 'I was turned into misery' through repentance and through the instructive admonishment of the Lord; for the Lord loves whom he disciplines, but he scourges every son whom he does not receive Heb 12:6.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who hates his sin brings it into the open by confession, and God forgives even the impiety of the heart.
comments.comment:
He who has fallen into sin, if he wishes to work it, provides a cover and hides it; but he who has hated it makes it manifest to the one who is able to heal through confession, declaring it Ps 31:5.… But having spoken truly, 'I confessed my sin against myself' Ps 32:5 which I have done…

I did not ask for more lawlessness than what I had; for God has forgiven not only this but also the impiety of the heart. And impiety of the heart is able to be the dissatisfaction of providence occurring to many through the irregularity of things as they seem.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why confessing sin, rather than hiding it, brings forgiveness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even the righteous, free of wicked deeds, still pray for forgiveness of the heart's impurity in a favorable time, and the waters of life keep sin from approaching them.
comments.comment:
If even the righteous cleanse themselves from practical lawlessness (Psalm 32:6; LXX 31:6a), they still often have impure thoughts from the aforementioned impiety of the heart. Even if those who pray do not have thoughts concerning lawlessness, they will pray concerning impiety, asking for its forgiveness in a favorable time. And a favorable time of prayer concerning the aforementioned forgiveness is when one cleanses himself from practical filthiness. And just as one who is wounded in a small scratch will not demand a physician's treatment, but having the whole body intact, only suffering in that single scratch, so no one filled with the guilt of actions will pray concerning the purity of thoughts, but only every righteous person.

When a flood of many spiritual waters comes (Psalm 32:6; LXX 31:6b), having had a spring of water within himself changing into eternal life—that is, the waters vanishing all sins and the impiety of the heart upon them—impiety and lawlessness will not approach the one who has prayed for them.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who prays and what the great waters stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He finds deliverance from continuing affliction only by fleeing to Christ, who is our joy.
comments.comment: He who says these things thinks he finds deliverance from the standing affliction in no other way than by fleeing to Christ (Psalm 32:7; LXX 31:7). Just as righteousness and wisdom are, so also is the joy of the diligent Jesus. For he says to Him as our joy: 'Deliver me from those pursuing me; for lawless demons and evil men pursue me; for I will be persuaded that nothing evil can happen, You saving me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Holding to reason keeps a person from falling into the headstrong, unreasoning state of a mule.
comments.comment: That is, not having cast away acting logically, you do not fall into an irrational state (Psalm 32:9; LXX 31:9), such that through being headstrong you become like a mule because of being deficient toward evils; for such an impulse does not have understanding. The prophet says toward God: He brings those who have become like horses because of being skittish and unruly, and a mule, hard-mouthed, subduing their bits with nails and drawing them with Your suitable bridle, with which You lead them under Your yoke. The compliant and gentle ones approach God by a voluntary impulse …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous who flee false doctrine are the upright with whom God is fittingly praised.
comments.comment: … Those who have accomplished an ethical life are righteous, rejoicing in the Lord, and it is necessary that those who flee from all the crookedness of false doctrine be upright. For it is fitting to praise God with these, since praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Sirach 15:9).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who the righteous and upright are and why praise belongs to them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the body or the soul is a lyre, the senses or the soul's powers are its strings, and the spirit that sings to God is the psaltery.
comments.comment: Confession and here thanksgiving are expressed. This ought not to be made on a lyre. And if the body is a lyre, the stretched strings are none other than the senses; for being struck by divine hearing, they perceive the hearing and the heavens and those in them, seeing them as to marvel at the Creator, and using the other senses praiseworthy, we confess to the Lord rhythmically and harmoniously with this lyre. But if one should conceive the soul as a lyre, its powers—which are the mnemonic, the assentive, the productive, and others according to reason—being struck like strings by the mind musically, will confess to the Lord. Musicians say there is a difference between the psalmtery and the lyre, such as this: they say the lyre is composed of the lower parts, while the psalmtery is from the upper parts with the strings, and it is more straight through strings. Since the soul is given as lyres, the spirit of man, which is in it, is perhaps something other than the mind, is a psalmtery, singing not to anyone else but to God. For we use right thoughts and with our own spirit we receive the Holy Spirit, and we sing victoriously in a ten-stringed psalmtery. And perhaps from the ten strings its perfection is shown.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who praises God with instruments and with voice sings a new song fitting the new covenant.
comments.comment: He who hastens to praise God through all things and through voice will sing to God a new song (Psalm 33:3; LXX 32:3), saying an anthem kindred to the new covenant and the newness of the Spirit, so that he might praise God not only with lyre and psalmtery but also with voice. And he wishes to sing praiseworthy with a shout of triumph; for the shout is a voice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the new song is and why the psalm asks for voice as well as instruments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's word is straight and not crooked, and the works done in it are firm and fulfilled according to the faith of those who receive them.
comments.comment:
… The word of the Lord, which he gives to those pursuing knowledge, is straight and not a crooked deception (Psalm 33:4; LXX 32:4). Moreover, the workers perform the appropriate things for this word, being fulfilled in faith; and the works which the word of God performs are in faith, that is, they are firm and unshakeable, and the word by which he governs and provides is straight.

If someone were to call the word of God a straight word, the works he performed in this word, being fulfilled in faith, would be easy; for the paradoxical works of Jesus are his works according to the faith of those, becoming things for them: 'Let it be done to you according to your faith' (Matthew 9:29).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because he judges and also loves mercy, God helps those led to judgment by his goodness, since otherwise all would be lost.
comments.comment: He himself is God, or his straight word, accepting judgment in that he must avenge the virtues being insulted by the wicked, but loving mercy, helping those being led to judgment by his own goodness. For if he were to observe all their works, no one would be able to endure. Therefore, even before judgment, he loves mercy. For if it were not so, all would suddenly be lost.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's judging goes with his love of mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the earth is full of the Lord's mercy, and God makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, we are taught to extend our good deeds to all.
comments.comment: We have found that in our prayers we must speak as people convinced that “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 33:5), and that “the mercy of the Lord is upon all flesh” (Sirach 18:13); and that God, being good, “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). He urges us to do the like, so that we may become his sons (Matthew 5:44–45), and teaches us to extend our good deeds to all people as far as we can.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Taken allegorically, the heavens' firm stability comes through the word of the Lord and the power of the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: The heavens were made thin, having the most corruptible nature (Psalm 33:6; LXX 32:6); for such is the nature of the heavens. But when taken allegorically, of all those who think upon the image of the so-called heavenly, their firm grip and stability becomes theirs through the word of the Lord, and their power, by which they are able, is not produced by anything else but by the Holy Spirit. And by this spoken word, pious men discourse that the Holy Spirit is the creative force.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'breath' of the Lord's mouth is not a human breath that disperses but the Spirit, who stands and abides as the Word does.
comments.comment: The old Scripture is also full of the glorification of the Spirit. “By the word of the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6 (Hebrew 33:6)). And in the book of Job it is written: “The Spirit that made me is divine” (Job 33:4). Just as it is not possible to suppose another Word besides the Son, through whom the heavens were made—for then they would no longer have come into being through the Lord, if they had come into being through another word—so also it is not possible to suppose another Spirit, who with the Word makes firm the powers of the heavens. When we hear “Spirit of his mouth,” we do not hear it in a human way, but as is fitting in the case of God, just as with the Word. For the Word is not a word that dissolves away, but as the Psalmist says: “Forever, O Lord, your Word endures in heaven” (Psalm 118:89 (Hebrew 119:89)). Nor is the Spirit a breath that is dispersed, but a standing and abiding one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the breath of his mouth' means.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: In the verse 'Lord' names the Father, 'Word' the Son, and 'Spirit' the Holy Spirit, through whom the heavens were empowered.
comments.comment: Thus presenting that creation is triadically ordered, he sings: 'By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the spirit of his mouth all their strength' (Psalm 33:6). For he said 'Lord' regarding God the Father, 'Word' regarding the Only-begotten Son, through whom also they were created, and 'Spirit' regarding the hypostatic Holy Spirit of God, through whom, having been sanctified, they were empowered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Word and Spirit from God's mouth are human words understood of God's bodiless nature, and the heavens and their powers are not divided between them, for the works of the Trinity are undivided.
comments.comment: Then God is spoken of in divine terms as the Creator, and the creation is the work of the Word and the Spirit. It is clear that the words are human, since a mouth is mentioned from which word and spirit come, but they are understood differently when applied to God, according to his uncompounded and entirely bodiless nature. That is, the Word exists with God who exists, and the Spirit exists. The Word is the manifestation of the Father, and for this reason he is named Word. The Spirit is the participation in the Word, as Spirit from the mouth. When he says heavens and powers of the heavens, he does not divide the creation, assigning the heavens to the Word and the powers to the Spirit, for the works of the Trinity are undivided. Rather, he expresses the same thing in different ways. As in the verse, Jacob entered into Egypt and Israel sojourned in the land of Ham, the entrance does not refer to one person, Jacob, and the dwelling to another, Israel. The parallel expresses the same thing, and we would find this custom in many places.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sea's waters are held within a boundary as in a skin, and by God's command they would otherwise flood the earth.
comments.comment: Just as water held in a skin or in another vessel is not permitted to pour out outside of the container holding it, so the vastness of the sea's water is limited by a certain boundary, not being allowed to exceed the appointed rivers. For if it did not hold back by the command of God, it would have overflowed the whole earth. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear picture of the sea held back by God's command.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gathers the waters into the sea as into a skin and stores them in treasuries, and he likewise keeps his unsearchable judgments in hidden treasuries.
comments.comment:
Because of the still and salty nature of the waters upon the earth, the sea, which is called the abyss, gathers them together—not as if they were scattered by a storm—as if in a skin, so that the Savior might take up the body to become calm and drinkable. He places them in the abysses of treasuries.

Nothing in creation is carried out disordered; for as a seed is held in its own treasuries by its own will, so it is released and held as it seems fit to it. It is said, moreover, that He brings the winds out of the treasuries, not by their own impulse, these being carried, but by the will of the Creator, sometimes closing them and sometimes bringing them out. But He also opens the treasury of the good heaven and gives rain to the seed of the earth, just as a seed is held, and He holds the rain by closing the heaven, as regarding the prophet Elijah. And the abysses, because they are not able to harm through the unlimited multitude of the waters, are placed in treasuries, enclosing them, so that if anyone wishes to use them, it is as is profitable according to the season (Psalm 33:7; LXX 32:7).

It is also possible for the ungraspable of His thoughts and the unsearchable of His judgments, which happen to be abysses, to be placed in the hidden treasuries of knowledge and of wisdom, so that no one might attain to this from himself unless God should grant it (Psalm 33:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All things came into being by God's speaking and commanding, so only the creative Word, the Son of God, spoke and commanded.
comments.comment: Since they [the inhabitants of the world] came into being by His speaking and were created by His commanding, let them be shaken by Him; for it belongs to the Creator to change things toward the good (Psalm 33:8). 'They came into being' signifies the essence of those things regarded as being, and 'they were created' signifies the adornment having come into being after the essence. If all things came into being and were created by the speaking and commanding of God, then no one other than the creative Word spoke and commanded; and this is the Son of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who it is that 'spoke' and 'commanded' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's command in creation, 'he spoke, and they came into being,' was given to the living Word, who carried it out.
comments.comment: For we say that it was to him [the Word] that the Father gave the command in the creation of the world recorded by Moses, saying “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3) and “Let there be a firmament” (Genesis 1:6), and all the rest that God commanded to come into being; and that it was to him he said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26); and that the Word, so commanded, made all that the Father enjoined on him. We say this not as our own conjecture, but because we believe the prophecies current among the Jews, in which these very words are said about God and the things he made: “For he spoke, and they came into being; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). For if God commanded and the things made were created, who, in the mind of the prophetic Spirit, could be the one able to carry out so great a command of the Father, except he who is, if I may so name him, the living Word and “the Truth” (John 14:6)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'he commanded' addresses and who carried out the command.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's heart means his deliberative and intellectual energy, whose thoughts are certain and last through all generations.
comments.comment:
… Just as in other places it is said of God in a human way—as having hands and eyes and other things—so also He speaks of His heart, meaning His deliberative and intellectual energy. The thoughts of this energy, being unlifted and certain, extend from generation to generation, that is, through all the generations.

Divine thoughts remain as a conviction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for God to have a 'heart' and thoughts that last.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A person with a prepared heart is a temple of God, a ready dwelling-place for him.
comments.comment:
And I have already said that the unceasing one saw all the sons of men (Psalm 33:13; LXX 32:13), having been cast as 'to the foolish beasts' (Psalm 49:12). These, therefore, he saw, the sons of men, from his ready dwelling-place (Psalm 33:14).

… It is said that the good thing itself is ready, as if one says, 'My heart is ready, O God'; for he who has a prepared heart is a temple of God, a ready dwelling-place for Him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's sun rises on good and evil, and his care takes in the sons of men, those dwelling on earth, and even irrational animals.
comments.comment:
He looked upon all who dwell in the earth (Psalm 33:14).

Others are those dwelling in the earth, apart from the sons of men; for those who have not kept the image, nor have become earthly, dwell.

But the sons of this kind of men do not dwell, but they reside.

For He 'causes the sun to rise' (Matthew 5:45) as it is 'upon the good,' and so also 'upon the evil,' He surveys all the sons of men, and those dwelling in the earth, even irrational animals; for He gives 'food to all flesh' (Psalm 136:25).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's care reaches everyone on earth, spirits and animals as well as people, and he understands both the deeds and the intention behind them.
comments.comment:
They inhabit the earth, not humans alone, but also invisible spirits and the other mortal animals (Psalm 33:14; LXX 32:14b). The care of God, overseeing all, extends to everyone upon the earth, bringing them out from his aforementioned dwelling-place.

Since God understands not only the things accomplished but also the intention from which these things are activated (Psalm 33:15; LXX 32:15b), it is said that he sees not, but understands all their works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who God looks on and what his looking means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture distinguishes making from forming: God made the inner man in his image and formed the outer man from dust.
comments.comment:
He who formed man alone formed their hearts.

In the Scripture, the doing is distinguished from the fashioning; for God made man 'according to His image and likeness' (Genesis 1:26), but He formed the man from the 'dust from the ground' (Genesis 2:7).

And Job indeed says both these things: 'Your hands have formed me and made me' (Job 10:8).

If he says this word strictly, the inner man becomes the result, but the outer is fashioned.

And as it has been said: 'Remember that you formed me of clay' (Job 10:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's word 'fashioneth' by the difference between making and forming.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A king is not saved by great strength, as history shows in Pharaoh's army cast into the sea.
comments.comment:
For that a king is not saved by much strength, you shall learn from history (Psalm 33:16-17; LXX 32:16-17a); Pharaoh did not have a great array, but God cast his armor and his strength into the sea. And all history is full of such things.

… And he says that the one who is exceedingly strong will not be saved in the strength present to him; but having understood this, he speaks concerning Goliath.

… A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the help is by the Lord (Prov 21:31).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Neither a giant's strength nor a horse brings salvation unless it comes from the Lord, as Goliath and the Amalekite show.
comments.comment:
Everything comes to an end. And a great giant will not be saved by the abundance of his own strength. This also contains a history: Goliath was a great giant and had an abundance of strength, and he believed in nothing other than in his own luck and his own strength and greatness. And he was also arrogant; therefore he was not saved; … And we find many in the Scriptures being cast down great, because they cast great confidence upon themselves.

The Amalekite was prepared for war and seemed to be stronger than Israel; for Israel was not fully prepared for military matters, and yet, as the hands of Moses were being lifted up, the Amalekite was being subdued and humbled, and the lifting of the hands was happening to him, and he was not saved because of his own strength. We say again: if anyone, having a god-fighter's attitude, 'building up lofty things against the knowledge of God,' falls by the strength which he had and is swallowed up, he is by no means saved. Sometimes the God-wise one contends with him and casts him down from where he has conceit.

A false horse for salvation. Again, many think greatly upon a horse, but the God-Word shows that even the conceit of horses is easily broken; for 'these are in chariots and these in horses, but we in the name of the Lord our God shall be magnified' (Ps 20:7). See, 'a false horse for salvation.' To many it was promised that Pharaoh would capture the Hebrews with horses. But they did not even possess one horse, and their salvation has become false, having sinned and having failed. And also in Proverbs: 'A horse is prepared for the day of battle, but salvation is by the Lord' (Prov 21:31). You see that it is false for salvation, if this does not exist from the Lord, even if it is according to a spoken word.

… And in the multitude of his power he shall not be saved. That is, either the one using horses or the power of many horses; for both are true: 'a false horse for salvation,' even if it be many; for it is not upon one horse alone. Often the whole cavalry is a horse. That is, therefore, the multitude of the power of the cavalry used by the riders does not save him, nor the multitude and power of the horses.
comments.selected_reason: Shows with Goliath, the Amalekite and the horse why strength cannot save apart from the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fear of God is not a passive fear but surpasses all, and those who have it are righteous and worthy of being watched over by God.
comments.comment: Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him (Ps 33:18). It is equal to: 'the eyes of the Lord upon the righteous' (Psalm 34:15). And this again in the twelfth psalm says: 'Look, hear my prayer, O Lord my God' (Psalm 13:3). Therefore, 'the eyes of the Lord upon those who fear him' is not a fear of passivity, but 'him'; for there is also a passive fear, which perfect love casts out from those having the fear of God. There is fearing and fearing God; for the fear toward God is not passive, but signifies the surpassing of all. Thus indeed it says: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Sirach 25:11), and: 'there is no deficiency to those fearing him' (Psalm 34:9). Being righteous, they are worthy of being watched over by God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who fear God hope in his mercy, because after doing all things they still expect mercy from him.
comments.comment: Those hoping in his mercy. Behold, those fearing God hope in his mercy; for having done all things, they expect to be shown mercy by him, as it was said a little earlier: 'not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of the God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16). And no one is able to keep himself unblemished.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why those who fear God still hope in his mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God rescues souls from the death of sin, not ordinary death, and feeds those who fear him in famine.
comments.comment:
… 'Those hoping in his mercy' Ps 33:18; he has mercy on those fearing him, to rescue their souls from death. For this reason, 'his eyes' are 'upon those fearing him' Ps 33:18-19 and 'those hoping in his mercy', so that he may rescue 'their souls from death' Ps 33:19. Death here we do not take to be the common death which the pious and the impious, the righteous and the unjust, all undergo, but it is a death of the soul which consumes the soul from the blessed life.

From this death we are turned away to avoid it; concerning this it is said: 'this soul that sins shall die' Ezek 18:4. And again: 'sin, when completed, brings forth death' Gal 6:8. And since this death follows sins, God, giving the forgiveness of sins, will rescue those who have received grace beforehand from the following death. And he will nourish them in famine, those fearing him and hoping in his mercy. Just as he rescues souls from death, so also he nourishes them in famine.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what death and famine mean in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Life is the light from God's eyes, and by famine he means the lack of divine teaching, not of food.
comments.comment: Since the departing light from the eyes of God is life (Psalm 33:19; LXX 32:19), the pious, participating in this and having hope upon the lion, would be saved from the death that follows wickedness, as if their souls were being made alive; but participating in the heavenly bread (and the word of God is not bread), they are nourished in famine. For famine he speaks of not the scarcity of edible foods, but the deprivation of divine teachings. Accompanying this is the saying, 'I will send famine upon the earth' (Amos 8:11), not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God has nourished his people in famine in history, and now gives the bread of life to those whose soul's eyes are open.
comments.comment:
Indeed, such things have happened many times in history. He nourished the people of the Hebrews during a long journey in the wilderness, providing manna every day by himself. And you will find this in various instances: for example, Elijah was nourished by the widow and by the angel shown to him through bread and the jar of water. And also, while Jezebel was persecuting Elijah and all the prophets of the Lord, Obadiah, the commander of the household of King Ahab, nourished fifty men in two caves, God having prepared him for this. Indeed, he said this without neglect to Elijah when he met him: 'and your servant fearing the Lord' 1 Kings 18:3. And he who feared the Lord nourished them because of the Lord.

If, therefore, he has restorations—these other things have happened according to history—he again nourishes those fearing his fear and hoping in his mercy, providing for them the bread of life, descending from heaven, which partakes of his flesh as 'true food' [John 6:51]. Being the savior of all, he holds them. …

… The one having opened the eyes of the soul and having been filled by the manner of chewing the bread of the divine logos does not suffer from famine; for 'the Lord will not let the soul of the righteous starve' (Proverbs 10:3). Whoever is in desire for bread but is not opening his eyes to his own bread, lives in famine; for the soul has many foods from God within itself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Knowing that God rescued and fed his people before, we wait for him to be our helper and defender.
comments.comment: Our soul waits upon the Lord. This is what is said: since we have known these things, that the eyes of the Lord are watching those who fear him (Ps 33:18)—even if they have at some time been in death, he rescued them; even if they have at some time been in famine, he nourished them; even if we should at some time be in any lack, we wait knowing that we too shall enjoy these things; and our soul, if it should be in death, shall be saved. For he is a helper and a defender of us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is our helper and shield, and without his help and mercy we cannot complete even the good things we begin.
comments.comment: Since he is a help and a protector for us, because of this our soul waits for him. We know that even if we propose some good things, even if we wish to run toward the beautiful things and wish to bring them to an end, unless he himself cooperates and has mercy, we are not able to establish these things. He is a helper of the needs of which we are in need; he is a protector, throwing forward his own shield so that the adversaries may not be able to wound us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'help' and 'shield' mean in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Others rejoice in strength or status or praise, but our joy is the helper and protector himself, in whose name we hope.
comments.comment:
For in him our heart shall rejoice (Psalm 33:21). Others rejoice in strength, in beginning, in status, or in praises, but for us, the cause of joy is the helper and protector himself. And in his holy name we have hoped (Psalm 33:21). We hoped in the one who was called upon for us.

… But no one hopes in what is present, but in what is coming and expected; for 'hope is a thing not seen' (Romans 8:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains where the psalm's joy and hope are placed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praying 'Hallowed be thy name' asks that it be shown holy, which happens when he helps us.
comments.comment: Even if they sometimes say in the manner of a prayer, 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:9), they do not say let that which is not holy be hallowed, but let it be shown, let it appear holy. Then indeed it appears holy, when he also helps us and protects us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer asks for mercy not as already held but in proportion to our hope, and God gives gifts according to the measure of faith received.
comments.comment:
May it be, Lord, your mercy upon us, just as we have hoped in you. 'May your mercy be upon us.' This prayer is sent up not because they already possess the mercy; for he did not say, 'Let your mercy be preserved,' but 'May it be, just as we have hoped in you.' For this reason we hoped in you.

Observe how, according to the proportion of faith, he gives gifts, and not to all everything, nor in the same measure, but according to the measure of the faith received; and so also here: 'just as we have hoped.' Some have hoped perfectly, and some not so, but according to a certain progress, or in another way according to an introduction. 'According to the proportion' of our faith, may your mercy be upon us, Lord; for thus we hoped.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'according as we hope in thee' asks for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, pursued by King Saul, feigned madness before a foreign king and was released, and the change in his appearance was voluntary, not forced on him.
comments.comment:
Thus the history is clear: he saw that King Saul was positioned with military power against his one man, David, and they were armed without armor. He fled there; and since it was not safe to enter a foreign city or land—for then suspicion of spies was greatest because the city-dwellers always had war against themselves—he feigned madness and let his saliva flow and acted foolishly, beating the doors of the gate, so that he might seem to be possessed by demons. Thus, those of Anchos slandered him. … And they released him and he departed.

He named such a state of affairs a 'change of countenance'; for change signifies a change of quality. Thus a change of quality happened voluntarily, not involuntarily; for it happens to change involuntarily, such as when someone, having been frightened, becomes pale, or having been struck, or from some disturbance, seems to be flushed. Thus this change happened voluntarily even unto form.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the story behind the psalm's title in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Read of the Savior, the change of countenance is his taking the form of a slave, a concealment of his form, not a change.
comments.comment: And since David is often drawn up, as has been said in the preceding sections, to the Savior, you will say that the change of the countenance of the Savior is the taking on of the form of a slave. And here it has not happened as a change from one form into another form, but a concealment of form from another apparent form; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To bless God at all times is to give thanks in everything that happens, the unpleasant as well as the pleasant, as Job did and as a patient does toward his physician.
comments.comment:
'I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is continually in my mouth' (Psalm 34:1). He who blesses God at all times is the one who is giving thanks in all things falling upon him. And the apostle also writes: 'giving thanks in all things' (1 Thessalonians 5:18). He who gives thanks to God does not do so only for pleasant things; he does this, but also for unpleasant things. Job, indeed, does not bless God only in prosperity and the salvation of children and the other surrounding wealth, but also when all was taken from him at once. When indeed all his ordered things, the existing things, were taken from him, he gives thanks to God, and 'he did not sin,' he says, 'Job did not act foolishly toward the Lord, nor did he give unfaithfulness to God' (Job 1:21-22). … Since therefore both times and seasons are different, and it is fitting to give thanks in everything, he rightly says: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Ps 34:1). There is no time when I do not bless the Lord. Even if the things coming upon me are unpleasant, I receive them as good.

Another word said: 'Whatever comes to you from the Lord, receive it as good.' You would not say, seeing one who is sick and being treated by a skilled physician, that he is thankful to the physician desiring salvation; for when the physician treats him, even if he divides him with a sword so that he may be saved, he accepts it, not only when the physician gives him pleasant helps. He looks not to the pleasant or the unpleasant of the things coming, but to the profitable and the effective. Therefore every time is a time to bless God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'at all times' means with Job and the physician as examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who rejoices always, like an athlete awaiting the prize, keeps God's praise in his mouth by thanking him in everything he does.
comments.comment:
If the saint rejoices always, he is never submerged or cast down when grim things are present; for even at these things he rejoices, he rejoices as if at athletic contests. He who follows the victory sees the contests and expects the crowns and the prizes, and rejoices, even if the surrounding circumstances are unpleasant. …

But we do not say this so that something impossible might follow, that the praise is in the spoken word continually. But this is impossible; for while sleeping one does not do this, while eating at times one does not do this; but thus it must be praised: all that I do, even if I eat and drink and sleep, I undergo these things thanking God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king called Abimelech in the title is Achish of Gath, for a person may bear two names, or Achish may be his title and Abimelech his own name.
comments.comment:
Regarding David, when he changed his face before Abimelech (1 Samuel 21:13), and released him, and departed. To those who read the royal histories, the present narrative is clear. How intensely David was being pursued by Saul and was about to be captured, he departed to Gath toward King Achish. It is here that Abimelech is named. The word is a double name; for double names are also found in the Scripture, such as regarding Moses' father-in-law; and Jethro is called also Reuel. And Thomas is called also Didymus. And many such double names exist; Matthew seems to name Levi in Luke (Luke 5:27). But he is not he, but Matthias who was established in place of Judas, and Levi are two double names. This is evident in the Gospel according to the Hebrews.

Therefore, it is possible both the king of Gath, Achish, and Abimelech to be said. And it is possible also to impose it otherwise; many of the kings are named by a common name and a personal name, just as all those who ruled Egypt are so named Pharaoh. And their names are found, such as Sumach, Necho, as it is a name of the office, Pharaoh, while among the Romans it is Caesar. Therefore, it is possible also this: that Achish has the name of the office, and Abimelech is his personal name. So that if he has it, the mind does not struggle. You wish, then, the one to be the name of the office, and the other the personal. This is what the grammarians say, distinguishing for the sake of the personal name; for the personal name is also spoken of as being divided; it is divided for the sake of the personal name.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saint wants his soul praised only for sharing in God, since any other praise, such as for knowledge or honor, is nothing beside it.
comments.comment: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Psalm 34:2). My soul is not praised upon anything else previously than upon participating in God; for just as another seeks to be praised upon a skill, or upon knowledge, or upon a dignity or honor, so the saint wants his soul to be praised in the Lord. He knew no other praise of the soul except this; for even if, as I have said, someone is praised upon knowledge, this praise, being compared to another occurring upon God, is not praise at all. … We say often: “Nothing is as sweet as honey.” There are indeed other sweet things, but they are not sweet as compared to honey.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist boasts in the Lord alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Just as the foolish man hides what he says and does, the diligent man wants his words and deeds known to all, so he calls the meek to imitate him and become such.
comments.comment: Listen, O meek, and be glad. Just as the foolish man wants to hide what he says and does when he is not known, so the diligent, reclining with God, wants what he says and does to be known by all. He wants his light to shine before men, so that they, seeing, might glorify God. He wants his words to go to others; for it has been said, 'talk in your perambulations' (Deuteronomy 6:7). He who talks to others talks, not to himself previously. Since therefore I have set before myself to praise the Lord at all times and to have his praise continually in my mouth, so that my soul may be praised in him, 'listen, O meek, and be glad' (Psalm 34:2). Imitate me, and you also become such.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To magnify God adds nothing to his greatness: as the sun at its rising is seen a little greater only because the viewer sees it better, to magnify God means to think great things about him.
comments.comment: Magnify the Lord with me. Having spoken about the meek to them, he turns the word further: 'and upon me magnify the Lord with me.' For someone magnifies God not by adding greatness to him from something small, but when he is able to take in his greatness. For the sun, rising, is not viewed as being of its actual size. Rather, it is seen as slightly greater; for it does not himself receive an increase, but the one viewing is improved, seeing him more clearly. 'Magnify God,' think great things about God, 'with me'; for 'magnify God' means to think great things about him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'magnify' can and cannot mean, with the image of the sun.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Magnifying God does not enlarge him, and his name is exalted and hallowed in us when we think and act holily.
comments.comment:
Just as those cast into the furnace in Babylon, praising God for not being burned by the fire, received all creation into this, knowing they were not sufficient for something so far off (for great is the praising of God); so also he who says 'Magnify the Lord with me' (Ps 34:3) wants all creation to join in this with the gentle ones. But to magnify God is not to increase his magnitude (for he is immeasurable; this is a matter of bodies, but God is incorporeal), but to think of the great things not as being toward him, but toward us, and to speak about him.

And those prepared with the same mind and the same purpose exalt his name. And the approach of God is exalted toward the created things, not rising from the lowly, but rather those who think of it do not fall to the ground, but contemplate high and heavenly things. For as they profane the name of God, not by the name itself becoming unholy, but by those surrounding it acting and thinking profanely, so also it is sanctified from our actions; for God the Savior says this also, teaching in the prayer 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:9), not of his name itself becoming holy by itself from being not holy. For it is necessary that it be hallowed in us by those who think and act holily.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's name is exalted and hallowed when our actions and thoughts suit it, when we call nothing but the Creator God, and when we do nothing profane.
comments.comment:
The appellation of God is called upon the diligent; for they are profiting from Him. Therefore, when we have actions and thoughts appropriate to His name, then His name is elevated, not divided, but 'upon the same,' as those who are complete in the same mind and the same judgment. It is also possible to say in another way that the name of God is elevated upon the same: that some might scatter the appellation of God upon lifeless matter, as if calling idols gods. In a certain way, they debase the name of God. And others carry the name from their own bellies, making God, according to their teaching, to be gluttonous and all-devouring. Therefore, when we consider nothing that is not God to be God, but only Him who created all things, we have elevated His name upon the same.

We all in the Gospel are instructed in prayer to say: 'Hallowed be thy name' (Matt 6:9). And even if the voice is imperative, since we say it in prayer, it is a prayer. Therefore, in all ways of the elevation of the name and its being hallowed, we take this: do nothing profane, nothing wretched and lowly, so that the name of God may be elevated, so that it may be hallowed; turn the appellation of God away from every base thing, from every earthly matter; for then the appellation of God is hallowed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to exalt God's name, through the prayer 'Hallowed be thy name'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeking God happens through prayer, and being heard means finding him, which is why the psalmist says both 'I sought' and 'He heard me'.
comments.comment:
He did not simply say 'I sought,' but emphatically 'I have done this.' 'And He heard me.' This shows that the seeking now being spoken of happens through prayer; for this has been confirmed: 'And He heard me.' … To be heard is quickly to find, to be perfected. …

Here, then, the 'he heard' says this, meaning that the seeking happened through prayers. Praying unceasingly, one seeks God and he heard him, finding what was sought.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being rescued from tribulation does not mean having none, since the apostles say that believers are afflicted in all things and enter the kingdom through many tribulations.
comments.comment: Many times we have spoken about these things, that God's rescuing from tribulation does not mean the becoming of an absence of tribulation; for if the apostles are telling the truth, saying: 'in all things we are being afflicted' (2 Cor 4:8), and again: 'through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter the kingdom of God' (Acts 14:22), it is never necessary to be outside of being afflicted. If someone does not take 'to be rescued' in this way, the saints were never heard; always being afflicted, they passed their lives lacking until the last breath.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be delivered from troubles.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeking the Lord means praying with a right mind and a pure life, and 'troubles' is also read as 'wanderings'.
comments.comment:
Since 'I sought and He answered me' (Psalm 34:4) is given, it is clear what seeking and calling implies; since not only in name does one fulfill the things of a prayer, but also having sought the Lord with right mind and pure life through all these things, He found him answering.

'And from all my troubles He rescued me' (Psalm 34:4) is carried as 'And from all my wanderings He rescued me.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The call to come and be enlightened is to those still far off, and once enlightened they are freed from shame, which will be wholly destroyed when the Lord is their eternal light.
comments.comment: 'Come to him and be enlightened, and your faces shall never be put to shame.' … he exhorts either all or many and says: 'Come to him and be enlightened.' Not to those already enlightened and able to say: 'The light of your face, Lord, has been marked upon us' (Ps 4:6), 'come'; for those having already come are light. Immediately, indeed, the apostles, having come, heard: 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14). And they enlighten others. 'Come' therefore, those far off, 'to him and be enlightened', and from your being enlightened, the unashamedness is urged. And 'your faces' 'shall never be put to shame'; for they become enlightened, as those who say thankfully have said: 'The light of your face has been marked upon us'. When that is fulfilled: 'The Lord will be to you an eternal light' (Isa 60:20), every shame will be destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the call to look to the Lord and why faces are not ashamed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Approaching the light frees the face from shame and gives boldness toward God, whereas sin covers the soul's face so that it cannot reflect his glory.
comments.comment:
If therefore we approach the light, by which we ceased sinning, our faces are not being shamed, and we have much boldness; for he says: 'if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God' (1 John 3:20). …

We say that when sin exists, the face of the soul is covered by shame so that its beauty and the proportion of its melodies can no longer be seen.

But when illumination comes, the remaining 'with an unveiled face, the glory of the Lord is reflected' (2 Cor 3:18).

No one having a covered face reflects the glory of God, but rather if someone has cast off the coverings that came upon him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever approaches the Lord, the true light, shares his light and so gains boldness and an unashamed face.
comments.comment: Since 'The Lord is true light, he who approaches Him partakes of His light' (Psalm 34:5), having been enlightened, having taken on much boldness, he possesses an unashamed face. The Spirit commands one to approach the Lord volitionally, so that having been enlightened, we may cast away all shame from the face of the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor man's poverty brings wealth: the Son, rich in the form of God, took the form of a servant and bore sin, curse and death so that we might receive righteousness, blessing and life.
comments.comment:
[This poor man has] a poverty that produces wealth; for a poverty productive of wealth is not truly poverty.

And as he becomes 'a curse for us' (Gal 3:13), that we may receive blessing—and a curse productive of blessing is not simply a curse, but this very curse is productive of blessing—so also the poor one:

'who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' (Phil 2:6-7).

Behold the poverty which he became poor with:

being truly rich, always existing in the form of God and being 'the exact imprint of God's hypostasis' (Heb 1:3), 'having taken the form of the servant,' he underwent all the things of poverty.

He became 'sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God' (2 Cor 5:21), a curse, that we might inherit blessing, he underwent death and was put to death, that we might receive eternal life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'poor man' is and why his poverty is productive.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who has cast off evil and cries to God is heard, including the Gentiles who had no hope, and the saints are pictured as leaping into the deep to lift up those who cannot swim.
comments.comment:
If someone, having become without evil, having cast off the wealth of ignorance, cries to God from this evil, he has Him listening. …

And it is possible also to say this concerning the people from among the Gentiles, that: the people 'not having hope and being godless in the world' (Ephesians 2:12) approached and cried and had Him listening to them. …

As some have said, such an example concerning the saints:

sailing in the skiff of this life, they saw many fallen from the skiff and, being unable to swim, carried down into the deep; and they leapt into the deep and seemed to suffer the same as those sunk, but they did this for the help of those, that they might bring up those unable to ascend by themselves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor man cannot save himself from his troubles, a poverty we all share.
comments.comment: Here he calls 'poor' the one not able to save himself from the present troubles (Psalm 34:6). And all of us possess this poverty, so that he speaks very much about one needing salvation from God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David escaped his flight by God's will, since the scheme of madness could not otherwise have prevailed.
comments.comment: David, showing himself, says that he became poor, that he was in anguish in his flight, and that he escaped this danger by the will of God, since the scheme of madness would not otherwise have prevailed if not for God's will (Psalm 34:6).
comments.selected_reason: Ties the verse to David's own escape in the story of the title.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Deliverance from all afflictions means not being defeated by them, and the angel around those who fear God delivers them from every enemy.
comments.comment:
'and delivered him from all his afflictions' (Psalm 34:6).

That 'to be delivered from all afflictions' has already often been rendered to us as not being defeated, not becoming outside the afflictive things.

'The angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him, and shall deliver them' (Psalm 34:7).

An angel encamping around those who fear God delivers them from every enemy, from every affliction, from every wound.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The single 'angel' stands for the whole kind, as 'man' stands for the whole species, so that all who fear the Lord have angels around them, and one angel is named because no one is excluded.
comments.comment:
[The verse speaks of one angel encamping around those who fear God.] If the explanation seems violent to anyone, not so: just as it is said, 'God made man' (Gen 1:26), to be the ruler of irrational animals, and we are not speaking of the individual kind, nor of this specific one, but the whole species. 'I made earth and man upon it' (Isaiah 45:12); thus he named the whole species. Even so, the angel here may signify the general, that those fearing the Lord have angels intervening and surrounding them, saving them from every tribulation.

You have this in the Gospel: 'See that you do not cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble; for their angels always see the face of our Father in heaven' (Matt 18:10). They stand before God, we see His face, they see the invisible one invisibly. Behold, therefore, of the many little ones, many angels are spoken of, but of those fearing the Lord, one angel is said. It is said singularly, for not even one is excluded.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'the angel' and what it means for those who fear God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one angel who saves from all evils is the Savior himself, called 'Angel of Great Counsel', since only he can save from every evil and forgive all sin.
comments.comment: Therefore, these who fear the Lord can have one angel intervening and saving them, the Savior himself, about whom it is said: 'His name is called Angel of Great Counsel' (Isa 9:6); for in many writings an angel is mentioned not applying to any single person. Jacob also says of him: 'the angel who saves me from all evils' (Gen 48:16). But no one is able to save from all evils except the Savior who has the authority to forgive all sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why one 'angel of the LORD' can save from all evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even those who fear the Lord with a servile fear have angels around them, as the little ones of believers do, and for the perfect the angel placed around them is the Savior.
comments.comment: If he here denotes those fearing the Lord who have the spirit of slavery (Psalm 34:7), we shall not say that angels are not surrounding them to rescue them from those intending to harm, just as even the little ones of those believing upon the Savior have angels, seeing the face of the Father in the heavens, having God, the perfect, in communion. If we take the perfect ones who fear God to have an angel placed around them to rescue them, we shall say nothing other than the angel of the great purpose of God the Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the angel of the Lord encamps round those who fear him, each person's angel likely encamps round him, so that where believers gather there is a church of men and of angels.
comments.comment: And concerning angels, reckon thus: if 'the angel of the Lord encamps round them that fear him, and shall deliver them,' (Psalm 34:7) and Jacob speaks truth — not of himself only but of all devoted to the understanding God — saying, 'The angel who delivers me from all evils' (Genesis 48:16) — it is likely, with more genuinely gathered to Christ's glory, that each one's angel encamps 'round' each 'of them that fear,' with that man whom he is trusted to guard and dispense. So that over the saints gathering there is a double church — one of men, one of angels.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Taste' means the incorporeal taste of the inner man, for the Lord is called light, spring, bread and true nourishment, so we are to taste and know him as nourishment and the spring of goodness.
comments.comment: Many times it has been said to us that the sensible and bodily things are like this: each thing is only what it is; for example, a stream is nothing other than a stream, or bread. But the thing that nourishes the inner man is called food according to various thoughts. It is indeed called light, it is called a spring, it is called bread and flesh, true nourishment. It says, therefore, 'taste' by the incorporeal taste of the inner man, 'and see that the Lord is good' (Ps 34:8), because He is good. Just taste, know that He is nourishment, see the spring of goodness, the spring of kindness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who hopes in the good Lord tastes his sweetness and is made strong, and the sick soul is to taste him as the food that gives health and casts out harm.
comments.comment: Blessed is the man who hopes in Him (Psalm 34:8). The one hoping in the good Lord—for he tastes Him—and he will experience His sweetness, and from this food he will have all things, … 'Taste and see that He is good' (Ps 34:8). If anyone is weary and sick according to the soul, let him taste Him as nourishment, as one preparing health, as one removing harm. And this food not only satisfies, but also removes, casting out the harmful things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the Lord is the bread of life, we are told only to taste him, since tasting is enough to make us desire to know him and gives the soul enjoyment beyond human things.
comments.comment: … Regarding God, the good means the same as the good. Since he is also the bread of life, the Spirit commands those who do not have desire for it not to be overwhelmed by it, but only to taste it. For the tasting is sufficient to make them desirous and to make them desire to experience it. And to taste signifies, as if by a little, to know and to examine concerning God. For he says that a pure tasting imparts to the souls an incomparable enjoyment of those things which are above human and wonderful (Psalm 34:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Taste' here means experience: what God's goodness did for David, saving him from two powerful enemies, is set before everyone who joins himself to God through hope.
comments.comment: He uses taste metaphorically for the experience of things, which was present to him at that time (Psalm 34:8). What happened to him through God's goodness, that he was not overlooked while being pursued by a foreign king but was saved from two most severe and powerful enemies, this he sets before all in common, as something that did not happen only to him but would also happen to others, as many as join themselves to God through hope in God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'taste' means in the verse.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Like honey's sweetness, the Lord's goodness is proved by tasting, not by words.
comments.comment: “Taste and see that the Lord is good” (Psalm 34:8). How can I announce the sweetness of honey to those who do not know it? Taste and see. Experience is clearer than any word for making a proof.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The man who hopes in God completely is blessed, and the fear that begins one's coming to God to keep his commandments is followed by a higher fear in the saints who have hurried toward holiness.
comments.comment: Blessed is the man who hopes in him (Psalm 34:8). The man who exists by hoping in God completely and without fail is blessed (Psalm 34:9). We say that fear is twofold. For immediately, someone coming to God, having taken up fear toward him, makes straight all his commandments. For it is said: Fear God and keep his commandments (Psalm 34:9). But in the present verse, concerning a fear that has ascended above, he speaks of that on which he calls the saints to have become; for having taken on the introductory fear, they hurried toward holiness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fear of God that frees the saints from want is reverence and piety toward what is supremely venerable, not terror of a bogeyman, and it makes them unshakable and unabandoned.
comments.comment: 'Fear the Lord, all his saints' (Psalm 34:9), for there is no lack for those fearing him. I urge all the saints to fear him, the Lord. It has been said in Isaiah: 'He himself shall be your fear' (Isaiah 8:13). Let him himself become your fear. … The fear of God makes them unshakable and unabandoned. … And the fear of God is not passive, as I have said, but equal to reverence, equal to piety. When we take up a conception of God, fear immediately increases and piety arises; for we do not fear him as if we were terrified of him, not as if he were some bogeyman, but as something supremely venerable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'fear the Lord' means and why those who fear him lack nothing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those once rich who lost the kingdom of God and the understanding of the divine writings went hungry, while those who seek the Lord, whose seeking implies longing, are filled with all good things.
comments.comment:
'The rich have fallen away and are hungry, but those seeking the Lord shall not lack any good thing' (Ps 34:10). The former, those completing the assembly before the arrival, were rich …

Being rich, they fell into poverty. The rich became impoverished and hungered, but those seeking the Lord shall not be diminished from every good thing. When the kingdom of God was taken from them, when the understanding of the divine writings departed from them, when they turned away from the old writing and from themselves, they became poor from being rich; for indeed this wealth fully benefits the possessor—for it becomes for him both food, and a covering, and a garment—so he says that these rich ones, having become poor, hungered. They cast away the spiritual food, they turned away from the 'bread of life'. They became poor; yet even if they themselves became poor, those seeking the Lord are not diminished from the good things, but they become full of them, they shall partake of them perfectly; for just as the kingdom of the heavens was taken from them—this also the mother of Jesus says: 'He has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty' (Luke 1:53).

Those formerly rich were sent away empty; for even if they possess the books of Moses and the prophets, they are empty of their divine fullness. Fullness, therefore, of the divine writing is not the shadow, but the truth and the Spirit. 'Those seeking' therefore 'the Lord'—the seeking implies a longing—are filled with all good things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The children called to come are not children by flesh but those hurrying toward wisdom, holiness and truth, who as yet have the fear that avoids evil from fear of punishment, not the perfect fear.
comments.comment:
Not according to any flesh. Those rushing toward wisdom are children of the wise; those desiring to be sanctified are children of the holy; those establishing righteousness are children of the first righteous one. For it has been said to us at the beginning of the psalm that even from the face of the Savior, according to the human, it is possible to be proclaimed. But those attending to virtue, those rushing to take up the knowledge of the truth, are children of the Savior.

Therefore he calls them 'forward-moving,' not so that, having moved transitively from place to place, they might come, but from disposition to disposition, from a lesser state to the greater and more perfect. 'I will teach you the fear of the Lord' (Ps 34:11). And these children, toward whom the word is addressed, 'infants in Christ,' are able to have a fear—not the perfect fear, nor the one making one unshakeable, but the one producing an avoidance of practical evil, the fear of punishment; for such people are children found imperfect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'children' are and what fear they are taught.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The teaching on the fear of the Lord is for all who become God's children, and tells how some fell from riches into need.
comments.comment: Come, children, listen to me. I will teach you the fear of the Lord calmly, concerning the necessity of taking up fear toward God, and how some, having fallen away from him, have become poor and needy from being rich, and that those seeking the Lord whom they fear, are filled with all good things; therefore, toward all those becoming his children, he composes the teaching, saying: 'Come, children, listen'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fear of God is taught, and is not the natural, passion-driven fear found in animals.
comments.comment: It is to be noted that, just as other good things are taught, so also the divine fear is taught, from which we learn not to signify a passion-driven fear; for an undidactic fear exists by nature not only in humans but also in irrational animals (Psalm 34:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what kind of fear the verse says will be taught.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Learning the fear of God brings the desire for life and good days, which are not bodily well-being and wealth.
comments.comment: Do you love to see good days? (Psalm 34:12) Stop your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Immediately there follows the desire of life and the learning of the godly fear, to become in good days; for we are not as sincere as some think, to consider the well-being of the body and the surrounding wealth to be good days; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Virtue unites and evil divides, so those who receive virtue perfectly are one and become one toward God, which is why the question 'Who is the man?' is put to a single hearer.
comments.comment: When they were in the lesser fear, being those who bring on punishment and fearing the punishment so that no one might sin, they were a multitude. But when they henceforth rush to approach the one calling so that they might be taught the fear of God, the things being proclaimed are announced as if to a single one; … And this multitude is not one of opposition. But when they also possess opposing perceptions, many become divided because of the present evil; for evil is not unifying, but rather dividing. Therefore, we speak of a following of virtues, not of vices. It is impossible for vices to follow themselves; for they are excesses and deficiencies. And excesses and deficiencies are oppositions. Therefore, all those receiving virtue perfectly are one, and they become one toward God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To 'see' good days means to enjoy them.
comments.comment: 'Loving to see good days' (Psalm 34:12). The 'to see' here means to be tested, and 'to be tested of good days' means to enjoy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who learn the fear of the Lord are called to stop the tongue of the inner man from evil, so that it brings forth the good and the lips cease to speak deceit.
comments.comment: He calls you to learn the fear of the Lord, so that having learned, you may become holy, undefiled, lacking no virtue. Therefore come, so that you may stop your tongue from evil.
