Let the tongue of the inner man no longer have evil. Then indeed it becomes all outward, when it has and brings forth the good. And it follows the stopping of the tongue from evil and the lips no longer speaking deceit, and it also calms the hypocrisy; for one who acts deceitfully is to do evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what keeping the tongue from evil involves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Turning from evil is a matter of choice and is not enough: one must also do the good, since avoiding evil only from fear of punishment is not doing good by choice.
comments.comment: Turn away from evil and do good (Psalm 37:27). This says: if you are already in evil, having settled in it and acting according to it, since I call you to the doing of the good, turn away from the evil. It is impossible to be outside both. … He who is not in good is in evil; he who happens to be outside of evil participates in the good. Therefore, 'turn away from evil.' And the turning is a matter of choice, for it protects and advises. But no one protects or advises one who does not have choice. I call you to do the good. You cannot do it otherwise and act according to it, unless you turn away from the evil. … It is not sufficient to turn away from evil unless one also does the good; for it is possible to turn away from evil being prevented by fear of punishment from going toward this, but this one does not do the good by choice; for if you bypass the good by will, it is no longer at all good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'depart from evil' must be joined with 'do good'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Peace is to be pursued as righteousness is pursued, and 'pursuing' has two senses, for evil men sought wisdom or Jesus to destroy them while the disciples sought him to be benefited.
comments.comment:
Seek peace and pursue it (Ps 34:14). Evil is a crowding thing and works turmoil in the soul; … One must pursue peace; for to pursue it in this way does not mean that one has driven it away. You have this also in the Proverbs: 'those pursuing,' it is said, 'love righteousness' (Proverbs 15:9), meaning that God clearly loves them, that is, those who pursue. The righteousness that is pursued is all virtue. For Wisdom says: 'Evil men will seek me and will not find me' (Proverbs 1:28). The evil men seek wisdom only to hide it and make it vanish, as much as it reaches them. But those eager to become wise do not seek wisdom in this way, but they pursue it.

And I say, since you love these interpretive things: Herod sought Jesus in order to kill him. Often the Jews sought him in order to kill him. But the disciples sought him in order to be benefited, in order to partake of him. For someone said to him: 'The crowds seek to see you,' because they wanted to believe and see paradoxical works and hear words and chance upon healings. Therefore, 'pursuing' is a homonym.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's powers, called eyes figuratively, look on the righteous, so whoever wishes this should turn from evil.
comments.comment: Since those looking upon the whole of God—powers called eyes in a figurative sense—look upon the righteous, but also his ears are ready to receive their petition, for this reason he says: if you wish to enjoy these, turning away from evil, do the good (Psalm 34:14-15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eyes of God are ready to see and save and his ears to obey, so whoever turns from evil, does good and pursues righteousness at once has God as supporter.
comments.comment: For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous (Psalm 34:15). Much exhortation again, much instruction. This is what it says: the eyes of God are ready to see and save, and his ears are ready to obey. 'Turn away' therefore 'from evil and do good, and seek peace and pursue it' (Psalm 34:14); for immediately you will have God as a supporter. Only desire to be righteous, to pursue righteousness, and you have the eyes of God lying upon you and his ears ready to receive the requests which you make to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the eyes and ears of the Lord promise the righteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What is said of humans regarding God, such as a face, is not to be taken literally, since if the body made man God's image, God would also have wings.
comments.comment: [On the 'eyes' and 'ears' of the Lord:] Often it has been said that what is spoken of humans regarding God must not be taken literally, as they think it is anthropomorphic; for they want there to be a human face concerning God, and they say that the man made according to the image and likeness of God has become so according to the construction of the body. But such a thing has been overturned by wise men; for they say: 'If by this the man is according to the image of God, because he imitates God physically and his body has a likeness to God, how then is God said to have wings: "In the shelter of your wings you will protect me" (Psalm 17:8)?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man is not God's image in body, but has intellectual wings that lift him up, and his eyes, lifted above the sensible, keep the likeness to God.
comments.comment: Man is such that he is not, according to the body, 'in image and likeness' of God. But if you reflect upon what the wings of God are, you will see that man also possesses such wings, intellectual ones, suspending him. Again, the eyes: since they take in all things according to history, the man having two eyes is not 'in image and likeness' of the One having seven, so that those things being lifted up from the sensible, the things concerning man being lifted up from the sensible, they preserve the likeness toward God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those doing evil do not remain unseen: when calamity falls and they see that it came from their evil, they receive a vision of God, as Pharaoh's army did when it was drowned.
comments.comment: And the face of the Lord is upon those doing evil (Psalm 34:16). This he says because those doing evil are not righteous. … However, they do not remain invisible to him. But when they fall into certain calamities and come to a realization that because of the evil things being done and thought they have come to these, they receive a vision of him. For Moses also pursued Pharaoh and his whole army with great speed, and he said he heard of God saying: 'I shall be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord'; for how did they know? Having become submerged, no longer being able to escape, they received a vision of God. And it is set forth in the Psalms: 'Let them be ashamed and be confounded and perish, and let them know that your name, O Lord' (Psalm 83:17-18). After the perishing, after the being ashamed, they knew God, and this is to be the appearing of him to be and to have a face upon those doing evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the face of the Lord is against them that do evil' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who do evil, thinking God not watching, will meet punishment.
comments.comment: Those placing all this thoughtlessly and doing evils as if God were not watching, will encounter punishment, receiving a reminder that God is present to exact judgment upon them (Psalm 34:16).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The memory of the wicked is destroyed 'from the earth' so that they no longer belong to it, and the Lord's punishing face works like cautery and surgery, while the righteous who cry out find him listening.
comments.comment: It is not merely 'their memory', but 'from the earth', so that they are no longer counted as belonging to the earth, no longer thinking of earthly things. … The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them. And rightly so, since he has ears toward them; having cried out, they happened to find him listening. … it is praiseworthy that the eyes of the Lord and the ears are toward the righteous, but the face of the Lord is punishing 'to destroy the memory from the earth'; for even if the end is not a decrease, but happens through evil, it is like through cauteries and surgeries and very sharp draughts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be lowly in spirit is to be poor in judgment, humble in opinion and heart, like the Savior, and not rich in arrogance.
comments.comment: 'And he will save the lowly in spirit.' Spirit here means the judgment. This is equivalent to that said in the beatitudes of the Gospel: 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3), those poor in judgment. … "I am also humble in heart." But opinion and heart are the same. Just as the Savior is humble in heart, so also those learning from him become humble in opinion. And these are the poor in spirit (Matt 5:3), those who do not wish to be rich in arrogance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be 'of a contrite spirit'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God delivers us from afflictions not by sparing us them but by helping us not to be straitened, which is yielding to them.
comments.comment: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from them all he shall deliver them.' (Psalms 34:19) For God delivers from afflictions — not when afflictions no longer occur (if even Paul says 'afflicted in all things,' as though never 'not afflicted') — but when, 'afflicted,' we 'are not straitened' by God's help. Of being afflicted — after a certain Hebrew idiom — the involuntary circumstantial is signified; of being straitened, the voluntary: overcome by affliction, yielding to it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense God delivers the righteous from all their afflictions.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul must be prepared not to avoid suffering but not to be defeated by it, looking to the release at the end.
comments.comment: He commands us to look to the end and to take courage in the release from afflictions, not to be distressed at the beginning itself whenever affliction happens to occur (Psalm 34:19). For the soul must be prepared in this way, not as one that will not suffer, but as one that will not be defeated by its sufferings.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The afflictions of the righteous are many and last through life, yet from all of them he rescues them.
comments.comment: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and from all their afflictions he will rescue them. It has already been said to us many times that from all of them he rescues (Ps 34:19). 'Many' are 'the afflictions of the righteous'; he said that through life and until a later breath.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bones God guards are the soul's sustaining powers, such as memory, contemplation and sight, which he keeps unbroken so that the righteous are not conquered by desire or led into worshiping creation.
comments.comment:
The Lord guards all their bones. If they are rescued from all the afflictions so as not to fall and be crushed, all their sustaining powers, called bones, are guarded by God. And it was said before this that the powers of the soul are called its bones; for they are the sustaining powers of the whole soul, while the bones are the sensible powers of the whole body. It was impossible for the flesh or the others to stand; the things sustaining the members of the body are bones.

And the sustaining powers of the soul, such as the mnemonic or the contemplative or the aesthetic of the beautiful, when they are unbending and perfect, are held by God in this, not by their own power. Therefore, they come by preconception toward this willing, but they are perfected according to this, God having cooperated.

Not one of them shall be broken (Ps 34:20). If they are righteous and have cried out to God and were rescued from all the afflictions, 'one' of their bones 'shall not be broken', instead of 'one power'. And that I may begin from the more aesthetic of the powers: there is a certain visual power. When one does not see, so that he may desire the beauty of women and not be conquered by the desire of beauty, this bone was not crushed by the Lord, but is guarded by him harmlessly.

When, having looked into the heaven, one sees the sun and the moon and does not prostrate himself and worship, but from the seen creation understands Him who showed all things, and by analogously contemplating the greatness of His creatures and their beauty, this bone of the sight is strengthened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'bones' the Lord keeps are, with examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God keeps the righteous's bones from breaking, and their doctrines from being overturned.
comments.comment: The Lord will preserve the bones of the righteous (Psalm 34:20), not allowing even by chance for them to be broken, nor for the doctrines of the righteous nor for his own powers to be overturned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who sins is deprived of life and falls into an evil death, and those who hate the righteous harm only themselves.
comments.comment: He who sins is deprived of life (Psalm 34:21) as he approaches the keeping of the commandments, falling into evil death. And evil death is that which is contrary to the good life, which inflicts pain upon the subject; … Those who hate what is loved harm not others but themselves (Psalm 34:21). And indeed, the one who hates the diligent righteous man errs and falls into punishment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not every death is evil, only the death of sinners, for sin when completed brings forth death within those who do it, so the death that follows them is evil.
comments.comment: And toward the other: 'the face of the Lord toward those doing evil', in the following he says: 'but the death of sinners is evil'. Not every death is evil, but the death of the sinners. And the word is not now about the common man; for that is of a living being, not of one doing, not of a sinner, not of a righteous man. Even if you call him common, when he dies as a sinner, he has an evil death—for he will receive punishment—and if the other, that which is truly appropriate to the sinner, 'sin', he says, 'having been completed, brings forth death'. But sin is completed not from outside those doing it, but in the men doing it. Therefore the death following them is evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse calls the death of sinners evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The death that follows sin is evil because it tears one from the blessed life, unlike the precious death of the saints, and those who hate the righteous hate virtue itself and will be punished.
comments.comment: The death of sinners is evil, and those hating the righteous shall suffer lack. For the bones of the righteous are kept by the Lord, and not one of them shall be crushed, but the death of the sinners is evil. It has already been said to us that 'evil' is spoken in two ways. If death, which follows sin, tears one away from the blessed life—according to: 'sin, when completed, brings forth death'—then this death is evil. Again, since they are handed over to punishment having escaped from life, they have died again in order that they might be punished. For it is said: 'Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints'; for how could this be evil, or death be evil, being planted together with the death of Christ? 'For if we are of the same kind,' he says, 'we have become indeed by the likeness of his death, but also of his resurrection.' And: 'If we died with him, we shall also live with him.' 'And those hating the righteous shall suffer lack.' The sinner, if he receives remission of sin, hates the righteous. But hating the righteous, he hates virtue. For the sinners hate the righteous not as a man—for they do not hate the sinners—but as being righteous. But he who hates a physician as a physician, hates the medical art. Because of this they shall suffer lack, they shall be punished.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Redemption truly frees souls from captivity, and those who hope in the Lord are not disappointed of what they hoped for.
comments.comment: It is to be noted what the redemption truly is: it frees souls from captivity; for if bodies are ever redeemed, it is not beforehand but this happens by consequence (Psalm 34:22); and souls are saved, not of others, but of his slaves. Those who hope in the Lord will not be disappointed of the things hoped for and expected (Psalm 34:22).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord redeems the souls of his servants from sin and so from punishment, and those who hope in him will not suffer the lack that is punishment.
comments.comment: The Lord shall redeem the souls of his servants. Therefore he says: even if an evil death touches the sinners and for those hating the righteous there shall be lack, yet he redeems the good souls of his servants. He redeems the souls from those who previously held them in a painful grip. Again you take it both ways: he is redeemed from punishment and he is redeemed from sin; for if he is redeemed from sin, it follows that he is to be redeemed from punishment. … And all those hoping in him shall not suffer lack. All those hoping in God shall not suffer lack like those who suffer lack, namely those hating the righteous; for if for those hating the righteous the lack signifies punishment and penalty, then for those hoping in the Lord, the not suffering lack signifies not being punished, not being penalized, and not falling to those who cause pain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist speaks as one who is wronged and not as one doing wrong, and he does not fight back but calls even those who hate him brothers.
comments.comment:
He demands a judge, having thoughts as if he were being wronged. It is not the voice of one committing injustice, but rather of one being wronged, rather than one committing injustice. And no one at all prefers being wronged; rather, when both committing injustice and being wronged are set forth, if it is not possible for both to exist—for it is not possible—one chooses rather to be wronged than to commit injustice; for the one committing injustice undergoes punishment, and unrighteous ones are not able to inherit the kingdom of God. But the one being wronged is not tested by these things; for he is being wronged voluntarily. Let us add that even if he is not able to defend himself, he does not exhaust himself in struggle because he cannot take vengeance, but observing what has happened, he sees that the one being wronged is more sympathetic and has many who pity him.

And the unrighteous man, even if no one punishes him, is worthy of punishment. This whole matter of examining injustice and desiring to defend oneself as if one were not committing injustice—his conscience condemns him. There is much boldness for the one saying the psalm: 'Judge, O Lord, those who wrong me, fight against those who fight against me' (Psalm 35:1). I do not fight them. And I am 'peaceable among those who hate peace' (Psalm 120:7). I am persuaded by the Holy Spirit saying: 'Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: say "our brothers" to those who hate you, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified, but they shall be ashamed' (Isaiah 66:5).
comments.selected_reason: Shows who is speaking in the verse: the one wronged, who would rather suffer wrong than do it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord judges those who do injustice by destroying the injustice in them, and fights those who fight the righteous for their own good.
comments.comment: …The righteous, trusting in his own righteousness, says, 'Judge me, Lord, and judge my case' (Ps 34:1d). The Lord is therefore judging those who do injustice, destroying the injustice within them. And he also fights against those who fight against the righteous, doing this for the good of those being fought against, as if they might at some time cease by practicing righteousness (Psalm 35:1; LXX 34:1b).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why God is asked to fight against the psalmist's enemies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who prays does not ask to harm his attackers but asks God to fight for him, so that he may remain unharmed while being wronged.
comments.comment:
'Fight those who fight me' (Psalm 35:1). There was still in the act of doing wrong to him and in the act of fighting. So that they might no longer do wrong or fight, he asks God for an ally, not so that he might wrong them or fight, but so that he might remain unharmed while being wronged and fought. And the nature of the rational being, if it does not suffer perversion, possesses this as its own characteristic.

'Fight,' therefore, meaning prevent them from surrounding me with destruction. Take the weapon and the shield and stand up for my help (Psalm 35:2). The shield of God extinguishes the flaming arrows of the enemy, of the evil one. Take therefore this shield, place it around me. I do not say this: 'You shall shield yourself with the shield.' Rather, take it in order to grant it to me, in order to make me secure. The weapon and the shield can be parallel. Perhaps also the kinds of weapons signify something.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist is asking when he calls on God to fight and take up the shield.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many have set out to fight him through false doctrine and other evils, and he asks God to fight them and to become his champion.
comments.comment:
…Since many have set out to fight me through false doctrine and other evils, fight them instead on my behalf; for they shall be irrefutably destroyed, since you are the Lord who crushes wars (Psalm 35:1).

Taking hold of your companion's shield and the wealth of truth, 'Arise to my help' (Psalm 35:2), that is, become my champion. In the same way, you will think of the sword.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer speaks of God in the likeness of a human being, armed with shield and spear, to show that what is impossible for the speaker is possible for God.
comments.comment: …He shapes the speech about God into complete likeness of a human being, as Isaiah also does, in order to show that what is impossible in him is possible for God, asking him to wage war and to be armed with shield and spear and to shut off the attacks of enemies with a middle wall. Isaiah also shows this in Christ, foreseeing him coming from the punishment of the unjust with his garment reddened from the slaughter of the foreigners: Who is this who has come from Edom, redness of garments from Bozrah, and the rest? (Isaiah 63:1). So the things that are referred to the Father in divine terms clearly belong to the Son and are fulfilled in the Son.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is pictured with shield, spear and battle.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God takes up the weapon and shield and rises to help by coming down to fight and suffer on our behalf.
comments.comment: One may pray that the incarnation might happen; for when he takes hold of a man who is able to secure us and fight on our behalf, he took hold of a weapon and a shield and rose for our help. He rose from the bosom of the Father, so that, bending the heavens, he might descend, so that he might be seen fighting on our behalf; for he has come not to fight himself, but to fight on our behalf, and he has come not to suffer simply, but to suffer on our behalf. And behold: 'By the grace of God he has overcome death' (Hebrews 2:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked are driven out like dust by angels and not by a human hand, and their way is dark and slippery since nothing in injustice has firmness.
comments.comment:
…That they become invisible is turned against them, like dust driven by the wind. They are driven out not by a human hand, for the righteous suffer this rather at the hands of the unjust, but this happens through angels, as the Lord says: The holy ones will go out and will choose the unjust from the midst of the righteous and will separate them (Matthew 13:49). For now the discordant elements are mixed together, but then they will be divided according to the difference of their manner, according to what was said again by the Savior: And many dwelling places are with my Father (John 14:2).…

…The ways of the impious, he says, are dark; they do not know how they advance (Psalm 35:6; LXX 34:6). He asks that this be accomplished, praying that the deed of the unjust be held in darkness, since it belongs to darkness, and that they fall after slipping, because they walk a slippery road, for nothing in injustice has firmness, and that they become invisible, pursued by angels, which is what they themselves do against the righteous (Psalm 35:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the chaff, the angel and the dark slippery way in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The verses that follow use commands for wishes, and the wicked fall in the snare because each is punished by his own actions.
comments.comment: …It is noteworthy that in the upcoming verses he used imperative words instead of optative ones; for 'Let their way be made' (Psalm 35:6) instead of 'May their way be made,' and 'Let him come' instead of 'May he come,' and the rest similarly. And 'he shall fall in the snare' (Psalm 35:8; LXX 34:8); for according to their actions, each one is punished.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'In vain' means they attack him with no cause from him, as Susanna, Joseph and persecuted Christians could say.
comments.comment:
…Therefore, 'they hid it from me in vain' (Psalm 35:7), wanting to corrupt me to bring me down to wickedness, or even to attack and lead me into harm.

But each of these is doing in vain—for 'in vain' here means 'vainly'—that is, that because I did not provide a cause. The one previously set to act unjustly and to suffer evil rather than to do the opposite will say: 'those surrounding me do this in vain, as God becomes my helper' (Psalm 59:9), or: 'they do it in vain because I did not provide a cause.' For example, if Susanna had been condemned by the elders through slander, she would have said: 'they decided against me in vain, since I provided no cause.' Joseph would have said this too, as would the disciples of Christ being persecuted, being denied, and being reviled for the sake of the name of Christ; for if any of the Christians is attacked not for any other reason but because he is a Christian, those attacking him attack him in vain; for sometimes some act against Christians, wanting to harm them, and they find a cause from within them. In vain they reviled my soul. For I did not do anything to cause reviling.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'without cause' with examples a reader knows.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They reproach him for nothing, since he gave no cause, and the trap they set for others is the one into which they themselves fall, by an entanglement of providence.
comments.comment:
By another meaning, it is signified that I suffered for nothing, because no cause was provided for me to suffer for the sake of the name of Christ and for no other thing. And again: 'He shall not take the reproach of evil men' (Psalm 15:3). 'He shall not take,' since it is up to us to acquire. But if, even though we have not acquired it, some surround us with reproaches, 'vainly they reproach our soul.' Do you not say that Jezebel and those who breathed with her vainly reproached Naboth, to hide from him for nothing the corruption of their trap? Furthermore: the 'trap of them'; he says 'traps' not in which they are being trapped, but in which they wish to trap. The drama prepared against Susanna by the elders was a trap of theirs, not in the way that they themselves are being trapped, but in the way they intended to trap her and subject her to punishment and shame.

Let a trap come upon them, which they do not know. This he says: those who are powerful against some, devising machines and attacking them, vainly are never placed before their eyes, that they are able to ensnare those whom they themselves prepared; for example, 'he who digs a pit' (Psalm 7:15) for his neighbor, 'he shall fall into it.' They do not quite consider that they themselves fall into the pit, since they did not dig it. Therefore he did not know that the trap was coming upon them, which they were preparing for another in order to surround him and catch him. 'Which they do not know,' therefore, which they did not have before their eyes, since they were not even preparing it.

And the hunt, which they hid, let him catch them, in order that they might hide from others and without warning hunt those. 'Let him catch them.' 'They dug a pit before my face and fell into it' (Psalm 57:6). And in the trap they shall fall in it. In this one which they prepared for others, they shall fall. Upon the fall of others they themselves have fallen in such devices as some make, and they come against themselves. It happens in some entanglement of providence. The discourse concerning providence has a great entanglement, even if it is ignored by many, lest I say by all. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul rejoices in the Lord not over the enemies' fall but because it was not overtaken, as Susanna rejoiced at her release, for the saints pray not to be taken by trial, not that their tempters be struck.
comments.comment:
She will rejoice in the Lord. Moses says, 'Do to him the way he has done evil to his neighbor' (Leviticus 24:19). Having these things happen, she will rejoice, knowing that she has suffered nothing.

Is she rejoicing over them? No, but marveling at the providence and rejoicing that she was not overtaken. For example, the soul of Susanna rejoiced, not because the elders were judged, but because she was released from the indictment. And it happened according to what was destined.

And indeed, when the saints are in tribulation, they pray, praying only this: 'Let us not be taken by the tribulation' (Matthew 6:13), not rather against those surrounding them with tribulation; for they receive it as a contest, not as a punishment. And he who receives it as a contest is not so against the opponents, as to wish them no longer to exist. 'Bring us not into temptation'; for he has not said, 'Strike those who tempt us.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the soul rejoices over: its own rescue, not the enemies' ruin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His soul rejoices at God's salvation, and 'all my bones' stands for his thoughts and true doctrines, through which he knows that nothing created is like the Lord.
comments.comment: When these things happen to them, my soul shall rejoice (Psalm 35:9; LXX 34:9), seeing by providence the wicked being punished and the diligent being benefited; but it will also experience delights, having gained experience of his salvation, of God. Let those who desire to take everything from the bare word and nothing allegorically be rebuked, even from the context of the verse. For it is not foolish to think that the bones possess the thought of God, so as to praise him and know that no one is like him. For concerning the bones of man (and his powers and true doctrines are these), it is said, 'All my bones' (Psalm 35:10; LXX 34:10); for through every thought and true doctrine, I was established that nothing of the created is like the Lord; for he himself is the image of the invisible God…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bones that speak and perceive God are not the bodily bones, which have no sensation, but the bones of the inner man.
comments.comment: …All my bones will say: Lord, who is like you? These bones speak, converse, say, perceive God — and these bodily bones are without sensation, as physicians' pupils show when they saw bones of one who does not perceive in the sawing. All my bones, then, will say: Lord, who is like you? Bones the inner man has, all of them…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the strange phrase 'all my bones shall say' simply.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God alone rescues the poor and needy from those stronger than they, whether rulers or the devil, and the poor is anyone unable to help himself.
comments.comment: …Rescuing the poor from the hands of those stronger than he. If the similarity is taken regarding this action, the verse signifies: God rescues the poor and the needy from the hands of those stronger than him. And this is over men, such as rulers, powerful in strength, and also the devil himself. Therefore, only God rescues from these.…And this is to be understood: everyone who is of some lesser strength is poor according to this, the one unable to benefit himself, the one not able to help himself and to make himself out of the surrounding circumstance.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unjust witnesses question him about things he has not been tested in, for 'not to know' can mean not to have had experience of something.
comments.comment: Unjust witnesses arose, things which they did not know, they questioned me. The unjust witnesses question him about things which the one whom they wish to testify against does not know. Here, 'things which they did not know', is 'things which they were not tested'. Not knowing sometimes means ignorance; 'but at that time not knowing God', it declares ignorance. It also signifies not having been tested, as if I say: 'the one who does not know sin', the one not having been tested by sin. Therefore, he knows her according to something; he understands her nature. But he does not know her without having used her. Thus also regarding wives and women in general, it is said that: 'he did not know her', 'he knew her'. He signifies the experience here.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Will not know' means 'has not trusted' or 'has not been tested' regarding an evil word, since the keeper of the commandment still discerns good from evil.
comments.comment:
… For the diligent knows nothing of the wicked, that is, he has not been mixed with any of the evil ones; and a testimony: 'He who keeps the commandment shall not know an evil word' (Ecclesiastes 8:5). …

For here the 'will not know' stands instead of 'has not trusted' or 'has not been tested' regarding an evil word. For it is a falsehood to think that one who guards the divine commandment does not know an evil word; for having a discernment of evil and good, he has turned away from all other things to keep the commandment. He does not say such a thing: 'They, interrogating me, seeking to distinguish my lack of experience or knowledge or intention regarding evils, questioned me about them, just as the Egyptians did to Joseph, and the elders to Susanna.' (Psalm 35:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Barrenness of soul means lacking right thoughts and excellent deeds.
comments.comment: …The 'they repaid me' is common; just as they repaid me evil instead of good, so also they repaid my soul with barrenness. And what about the offspring of the soul? Right thoughts, excellent deeds.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'spoiling of my soul' means in practice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He wished to live blamelessly and in peace with all, yet they returned evil for good and tried to make his soul barren.
comments.comment: When I, desiring to perform my duties toward all people blamelessly, wishing to live in peace with all men if possible, they instead returned evil to me for these good things, enemies and ill-wishers appearing through all things; and they attempted to annul in themselves the good fruitfulness of my soul. If, indeed, being persuaded by their questions, I had become such as they wished to make me, my soul would have been rendered barren, no longer receiving the divine marriages of the Bridegroom.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer 'turns into the bosom' when the good things asked of God are obtained, for the bosom stands for the mind and ruling part of the one who prays.
comments.comment: …'And my prayer shall turn into my bosom' (Psalm 35:13). By the name of the bosom, in many writings, the mind and governing principle are meant…The holy man prays that good things might come to be. And there is no other prayer than a 'petition for good things from God.' When someone obtains the good things for which he prayed, his prayer was turned into his own bosom. It was not cast away and remained outside, whose voice was sent up and was scattered into the air, but it brought what he had asked. And this means that his prayer is not sent up in vain, but is received into the heart of the one praying, into what he asked…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'my prayer returned into mine own bosom'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fasting cuts down the passions and cleanses sins, and the prayer of one who prays well returns to him with good things into his bosom, meaning his ruling principle.
comments.comment: Because luxury, stirring up irrational pleasures, irrationally exalts the soul, while fasting, doing the opposite, cuts down the passions; but also praiseworthy fasting effects a cleansing of sins, truly working blindness and humbling the soul. For him who has prayed well, the prayer returns to him, bringing back the good things for his sake, and having turned back, it is drawn into the bosom of the one who sent it. And 'the bosom' signifies their ruling principle; for their humiliation was into their bosom in the land of Egypt, and all things come into the bosom of the innocent; and in this way all the righteous go into the bosom of Abraham, that is, into the same mind and promise as he. (Psalm 35:13; LXX 34:13).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While they troubled him he put on sackcloth and fasted, a strict life bearing a sign of repentance, so that he would not be harmed and they would not be emboldened.
comments.comment: And I, while they were bothering me, was putting on sackcloth.…However, I was putting on sackcloth so that, not being abandoned, I would not be captured by them, and on their behalf so that they would cease their insolence toward me; I was putting on a certain strict life, bearing in some way a sign of repentance, so that I might not be harmed by the bothering, and on the other hand, so that they might not be emboldened. And it is much more for the good, if they should cease.…And they humbled my soul in fasting (Psalm 35:13). I was not putting on sackcloth alone, that is, strictness of life, but also 'they humbled my soul in fasting,' both according to the literal sense and according to the original sense, no longer being nourished by those painful things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeking God through fasting and humility turns the whole soul to prayer, which settles into the soul's bosom.
comments.comment: …He flees, he says, to his own strength, which is God. For a person seeks God with fastings and humiliations, turning the whole soul to invocations of God through freedom from bodily pleasures, when the invocations linger in the mind during prayer and slip into the bosom of the soul.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He treated his enemies as neighbors and brothers and so he mourned for them, like a father who is humbled to see a beloved son suffering evil.
comments.comment:
…Those whom it seemed to be neighbors and brothers were gathered against me; they waged war against me, as in the beginning of this psalm: 'Judge, O Lord, those doing wrong to me, fight those fighting against me' (Psalm 35:1). Again he says: 'To me they spoke peace, but they were plotting deceit in anger' (Psalm 35:20). Because of this, as one mourning them and as one being gloomy toward them, thus I was humbled; for if I were providing them with things that gladden, I would be exalted, rejoice, and be glad from cheerfulness.

But what about 'thus I was humbled'?—if someone has a son whom he loves and desires, and sees him burning, he is humbled, because not as he wished him to live, thus he sees him suffering evil. Since therefore I was providing opportunities for virtue as toward neighbors and brothers, but they themselves were proving to be enemies and foes, I was humbled toward them, though it was necessary for me to rejoice toward them.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's mourning for those who turned on him, with an image a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He mourned and humbled himself over those who were dying in their deeds, while they gathered in joy against him as if to seize him.
comments.comment:
Seeing them through whom they act as if dying, I humbled myself by mourning them and frowning upon them, seeking to preserve the one able to keep me harmless from them (Psalm 35:14).

The present text is explanatory if it is possible for God to repay me evil for good. For while I mourn and frown over them, through which they possess death, they gather together in joy against me, as if they were to take me by the hand; and they have plotted against me, so that they might gather and rejoice (Psalm 35:15; LXX 34:15c).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was kind toward them, but they gathered against him and rejoiced, eager to bring him more evil.
comments.comment: …'And they rejoiced against me and were gathered together.' But I was thus toward them from most private compassion; but they, from the opposite, having been gathered against me, rejoiced or, having rejoiced against me, were gathered together, in order that they might bring more evil and misery to me. Scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know. The eagerness is to do evil.…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who gathered against him were scattered by providence, and since they could not catch him they mocked him and bared their teeth like wild beasts.
comments.comment: Having gathered and rejoiced against me, they were split apart by divine providence; having been dissolved and scattered in such a way, they did not repent, that is, they did not recognize for whom they had advised wickedly, but instead they attempted the same against others. Because of all those who were striving to make an attempt upon me, they were not able to see or take hold of me; therefore, they turned to mocking and sneering at me. Watching like wild beasts, they bared their teeth, that is, their angry and wrathful power, against me; for wanting to devour me, they failed (Psalm 35:15-16).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The teeth can be read as the soul's chewing powers, used badly when turned against others, so those who gnashed their teeth will themselves be destroyed.
comments.comment:
The teeth are often called the masticatory powers of the soul. And with these masticatory powers which mince the foods, if one were to use them properly, he eats the 'bread of life', the fruit of the 'tree of life', the flesh of Jesus. But if he were to use them badly, he eats the flesh of the dragon.…

…If we take that the masticatory powers of the soul are the teeth, we say something true, but not regarding the immediate context. But if you also take this, that some use these masticatory powers treacherously against that: 'if you bite and devour one another' (Gal 5:15), and: 'those devouring Israel with the whole mouth' (Isaiah 9:12), and these refer to punishments, it is also possible to think thus: 'they gnashed their teeth against me'; they gnashed these teeth, and because of this they will undergo destruction; for 'you crushed the teeth of the sinners' (Psalm 3:7).…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks how long God will look on, since God's long-suffering is shown by passing by, and asks that his soul be restored from their malice by suffering nothing from them.
comments.comment:
…Lord, how long will you look on?

When you visit so as to forbid them, and to make me outside of the harms? For regarding 'to turn away' and 'to look away', we have often said that to pass by signifies long-suffering. 'Lord, when will you have pity?' For if you have pity, you will also do good to me, looking upon me and having mercy on me, and you will set even them outside of their haste toward evil, so that they do not harm me, nor do they remain any longer in that beastly malice which they are still practicing.

Restore my soul from their malice. He says this because lying enemies are present, many and having much planned maliciously against him.…He says therefore: make my soul outside of them; for indeed it was outside of them; for this is what the name of 'restoration' remembers. No one enters into a place where it never was, it is said to be restored, but one having come from one fatherland to another fatherland, or from one place to another place. He says therefore: they wished to ensnare my soul, being holy, to subject it to corruption. Then it is restored from the malice of the wicked, when it suffers nothing from them, when it does not act against them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'how long wilt thou look on' as God's patience and what being rescued means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Only-begotten' here means 'alone': he calls his soul his only one and asks God to save it from the cruel enemies.
comments.comment:
"Restore my only-begotten from the lions" (Psalm 35:17). He says that he has his soul as only-begotten. He had it as only-begotten; he had it as alone. It is not possible for more than one soul to be tested, since therefore it is only-begotten to me.…

…Therefore, when the saint says: 'Look upon me and have mercy on me, for I am alone and poor', he means 'I am alone'. And Elijah, saying: 'I alone am left, and they seek my life to take it from me' (1 Kings 19:10), it would have been said 'alone', not 'son' or 'child'. And here he says: 'my only one from the lions', the cruel ones, those having risen up against me. Save and redeem my soul, which is mine alone; for this one alone did not know sin, this one alone 'has been tested in all things without sin' (Hebrews 4:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unusual word 'only one' (the KJV's 'darling') in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evils will be gathered with those who did them, and the soul is his alone.
comments.comment: The holy one says: 'Lord, how long will you look?' (Psalm 35:17; LXX 34:17). For when you look, all the aforementioned things will be gathered together with those doing them.…And he says 'only begotten' because his soul has it alone…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His only soul, rescued from the lions, the malicious powers, by hope in God, was freed from dread, and being shaken by such turmoil is only pre-passion, which is not sin.
comments.comment:
To be freed from the fever. 'Hope in God, for I will confess to him' (Psalm 42:5). Once she [the soul] persuaded herself to hope in God, she was restored from dread and turmoil, which dread and which turmoil arose from the malice of evil powers and from the devil himself. 'From lions, my only-begotten one' (Psalm 35:17). He named these malicious ones and lions those who wish to fight, those who attack and come like whips against him.

Since 'he has been tested in all things, yet without sin, according to the likeness' (Heb 4:15), we grant her a pre-passion. But pre-passion is not sin; for if you do not grant this, you bring something foreign into the soul, and it would have neither glory nor worthiness of praise and crowns if it were not shaken. For you have in the Gospel that: 'she began to be terrified and to be in distress' (Mark 14:33); for is not the 'beginning' something other than the pre-passion? This beginning is only the beginning itself; it has nothing with it. This alone, before the choosing of evils, chose the good. This has often been said.

The essence of the rational soul is receptive of those things it is naturally disposed to receive. It is receptive of passion, desire, grief, turmoil, and fear. When something presents itself that moves fear, the rational essence is certainly troubled. Sometimes, however, it establishes the turmoil immediately as if nothing were with it. This they call pre-passion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A 'great church' is one filled with people great in soul and mind, and a 'heavy people' is a precious and honorable people, a holy nation made of those who work good.
comments.comment:
'I will confess to you in a great church, in a heavy people I will praise you' (Psalm 35:18). Then a great and many church is called, when it is filled from each side by many; for it is not called a great and many church if it is from small and lowly men. 'He speaks wisdom among the perfect,' says the apostle. These, becoming the same and 'being completed by the same mind and the same judgment,' are a many and great church. And just as I say a wise church when those filling it from each side are wise, and I say a stable and knowledgeable city when the citizens filling it from each side are stable and knowledgeable, so I say a many and great church of those filling it having greatness—but greatness of soul and of mind, not of the body.…

…For they have become accustomed to call things that are honorable and most precious 'heavy'. This too the Scripture witnesses; for how much the Queen of Sheba came to Solomon, it says, 'in great power' (1 Kings 10:1). And it says the 'heavy power' is her possession, which she had brought. She brought many precious stones, many delicacies, gold, silver, and other accompaniments of wealth. And that power of wealth was called 'heavy' instead of 'precious' or 'valuable'.

Therefore he says that when each of those who complete the people—as I have said concerning the church—is most precious and honorable, for 'glory and honor and peace to everyone who works the good' (Romans 2:10), if the one working the good possesses glory and honor, the people are an honor. Moreover, it is said about it that it was a 'royal priesthood, a holy nation' (Exod 19:6). The 'holy nation' is completed from all those who are holy, and the 'royal priesthood' is composed of many healers of God. Therefore, 'in a people, I will praise you greatly' (Psalm 35:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the great congregation' and 'much people' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He boldly says they hate him without cause and asks not to fall into evils over which they would rejoice, and they roll their eyes at him as well as speak against him.
comments.comment:
…May those who hate me unjustly not rejoice over me (Psalm 35:19). Great boldness is in saying these things. They hate me unjustly. They do this, though I provide no pretext or cause for them to lie hostile toward me. Since, therefore, the enemies rejoice when I fall into evils, let me not fall into evils so that they might rejoice over me or assail me; for he who wishes to lead someone into lawlessness rejoices over him, being evil, when he falls into what he strove to surround him with. Let this, therefore, not be to me, so as to make those who hate me unjustly rejoice.

Those who hate me without cause and roll their eyes (Ps 35:19). The 'unjustly' and 'without cause' are the same, 'without reason', and 'rolling eyes' against me; they do not only speak against me with words, but they also roll their eyes.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the plea 'let not them rejoice over me' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who spoke peaceably to him while plotting deceit in anger acted unjustly, for the truly peaceful man does not hold another intention against the one he greets.
comments.comment:
They were speaking and calculating deceits in anger. This is a kind of impiety; while speaking peaceably, they were not acting peaceably. This is an injustice. One speaks peaceably to friends and companions as a lover of peace, but calculates deceits in anger. Anyone who approaches a neighbor with any deceit and is angry with him does this. And I say: anger is a desire for punishment. For anyone approaching with deceit wants to harm that person, so that the deceitful one is also an angry one. And many times, appearing not to be, he seems to be speaking peaceably.

This indeed is also said in Jeremiah concerning someone: 'He speaks peaceably to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself' (Jeremiah 9:8). 'To me,' he says, 'they spoke peaceably.' They did not simply speak 'peaceably,' but 'to me'; wanting to deceive me, they spoke peaceably; for the truly peaceful man does not speak peaceably to someone while holding another intention against him.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it is to speak peace with deceit in the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They opened their word against him while speaking peaceably, and their cry of 'Well done' came from thinking they had caught the prey they wanted.
comments.comment:
…They opened their word against me, speaking peaceably. But their mind was groaning under the deceit.…

…'Well done, well done, our eyes have seen' (Psalm 35:21). Those who think they have obtained the hand they wanted, thus they speak: 'Well done, well done, what we wanted, our eyes have not seen; we no longer see you as you were supposed to be, but as we desired. We have found you easy to capture.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Do not remain silent' means 'do not long-suffer any longer', for God's patience does not last forever and his threats come from much goodness.
comments.comment: 'You have seen, Lord, do not remain silent' (Psalm 35:22). The 'do not remain silent' is the 'do not long-suffer any longer' (Psalm 35:22); for from many words we showed this: 'I was silent from eternity, shall I also be silent forever?' (Isaiah 42:14). I was long-suffering, I did not go out against the evils being done. This shall not be forever. Goodness is again known by the one threatening the one already being punished, so that through the threat he may be stirred up and be brought to repentance. And in another psalm he says: 'To the sinner God said: Why do you declare my judgments and take up my words through your lips? But you hated instruction' (Psalm 50:16). Then at the end: 'Having done these things, and I was silent'—not going out—'you assumed lawlessness, that I would be like you' (Psalms 50:21). But long-suffering does not remain always; for 'I will convict' 'you and present against your face' your sins. And therefore the threats of God happen out of much goodness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks God not to keep silence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks God to stay near so the enemies stay far, and he reads 'Arise, Lord' as a call for God to stand up in power so his case is examined.
comments.comment:
…Since you are present with me, the enemies are far; do not depart from me, lest they come upon me alone (Psalm 35:22; LXX 34:22b).

Because God's long-suffering is often called his breath (Psalm 35:23; LXX 34:23), the Lord is driven to indignation by the pressing of enemies, saying: 'Arise, Lord, and take up my judgment,' that is, stand up with the power of your strength, so that the things concerning me against my enemies may be examined. For this is for good, since they hate me unjustly and those who hate me without cause shall certainly be condemned (Ps 34:27-28).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is God of all by creation, but he is God of the saints by their worship and doing his will.
comments.comment: The saints call God 'God' not by mere voice, but having been made intimate with Him and serving Him like priests, becoming healers. But they also serve Him by doing His will … He is called 'God' in the sense that He is Creator … But otherwise He is called 'God' of the saints, according to worship. In this way, God of the patriarchs has been said. And according to creation, as was being signified, He was God of all, of all things which He has made. … But in another way, He is Lord of those doing His will, of those practicing what was commanded, and as a master to slaves. 'Judge me, Lord, according to Your righteousness' (Psalm 7:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'According to your righteousness' means the righteousness by which God judges human affairs.
comments.comment: … Therefore, this 'according to your righteousness' does not at all mean: not according to your unapproachable righteousness, but according to your righteousness, in which you judge human things. Do not judge me according to their enmity, but according to your righteousness; for your righteousness hates the unrighteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks that they not even say in their hearts that they have overcome him, for in Scripture a downfall can mean a victory.
comments.comment: Let them not say in their hearts, 'Well done, well done to our soul.' Even if they do not say it with words, let them not even say to our soul in their hearts, 'Well done, well done.' 25 Let them not say, 'We have overcome him.' Let them not say that we have surrounded him and conquered him; for often this too has been made clear, that according to the Scripture, downfall signifies victory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praying that his enemies be put to shame brings them salvation, for once ashamed they stop lying in wait and doing evil, and shame clothes them like a garment.
comments.comment:
May those rejoicing in my evils be shamed and put to shame. It brings salvation to those being shamed and being put to shame because of what they are doing badly; for since they want to surround me with evils and rejoice having seen what they strive to complete, let them be shamed; for having been shamed, they will no longer lie in wait for me, having been put to shame, they will no longer do these things bearing mockery and accusation. Moreover: he says 'evil things', not 'wickednesses'? For he who says, 'Judge me, Lord, according to your righteousness,' truly had no wickednesses; he who says, 'those rejoicing in me unjustly.'

… Let those boasting against me be clothed in shame and confusion. The great ones speaking against me arrogantly and rejoicing, may they be shamed and put to shame, and may they know themselves. But this happens as a call to them, and I no longer have them lying in wait like that. Previously he prays for them, but secondly also for himself. Moreover: the 'to clothe oneself'? As we say to clothe oneself in a virtue, or to clothe oneself in a wickedness, or to clothe oneself in a 'garment of salvation': 'Let my soul rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and a robe of gladness' (Isaiah 61:10). The quality becomes like a garment of the thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist prays that his enemies be ashamed: shame turns them from doing evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the enemies are shamed the friends who desire his righteousness and peace rejoice, and they magnify the Lord continually when he remains in righteousness.
comments.comment:
May those desiring my righteousness rejoice and be glad. … When 'those boasting' are said to 'clothe themselves in confusion and shame', 'those desiring my righteousness and my peace' rejoice and are glad. When the enemies are shamed and put to shame, the friends rejoice and are glad.

They are those who desire my salvation, my virtue, and my righteousness. And let them say continually, 'Magnified be the Lord.' Then they magnify the Lord continually, when I remain continually in righteousness, in not falling to the evil ones.

They are those who desire the peace of his servant—me, his servant. 'Let them say continually, Magnified be the Lord,' seeing me making peace, seeing me not having fallen to trouble or confusion or uprising or war. …

Being therefore inferior, when he speaks of achievements, he says 'to the servants of God,' but when of failings, 'to himself.' Some say that those approaching God are sons of God, but those who have reached them are these servants; for from servants they become friends and sons. The greater, then, are 'those who desire,' those who are like sons, those 'perfect as their father' who is the 'perfect one in heaven'; they desire to be the peace of also those who are lower. Or thus, that all desire the peace of each individual servant.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When his request is granted his tongue meditates on God's righteousness in hymns all the day, meaning the whole of human life.
comments.comment: And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness, all the day your praise. It shall meditate thankfully. When that which I requested exists, my tongue meditates on your righteousness. This I always recount, in hymns I bring it forth, in narrative words I name it. 'Day' here he says, the whole time of human life, just as in others he says: 'Because of you we are being killed all the day' (Rom 8:36), that is, because of strife. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who is lawless in himself is confessing that he sins, since a person first agrees in thought and then sins in practice.
comments.comment: He who considers himself lawless in himself says nothing other than that he sins. For someone, having first agreed in thought, proceeds to sin in practice.… 'If fear is held before the eyes of a man, he abstained from every sin,' but since he does not have it in himself, he says, 'to sin.' A testimony of not sinning for one who has fear is 'That how your fear may come upon you, so that you may not sin' (Exodus 20:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The servant of the Lord, knowing virtue, also knows lawlessness, as a physician knows harmful remedies as well as healthful ones.
comments.comment: Therefore, the servant of the Lord, having known the end, which is virtue over all things, also knew lawlessness; for of the contrary things, there is the same knowledge. He who possesses medical skill knows not only the healthful things among the remedies, but also the harmful ones, so that he may use the former and reject the latter. Thus the servant of the Lord, being lifted up toward the end, says in the song: 'The lawless one says that he sins in himself' (Psalm 36:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a few clear lines why the wicked man's saying is worded as it is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who sins and says in his mind that he will ascend into heaven receives the rebuke within himself and cannot escape it.
comments.comment: Because the devil thus works malice, and many born according to wickedness by him, God says toward him in Isaiah: 'But you have said in your mind, I will ascend into heaven,' and the following until: 'I shall be like the Most High' (Isa 14:14). This is consistent with what is said in the Psalms: 'The transgressor says that he sins in himself' (Psalm 36:1). For sinning in himself and saying in his mind, 'I will ascend into heaven,' he receives the rebuke in himself without escaping.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'To the end' means perfect virtue, the last thing desired for its own sake, which every servant of God pursues, so the title fits every servant of God and not David alone.
comments.comment:
… Much has been said about the end, that it is that end for the sake of which all other things happen, but it is not for the sake of anything else, which is called the last desirable thing. We desire certain things for the sake of something else. None of those is the end, but they are makers of the end. But the end is that which does not happen for the sake of something else, but for its own sake all other things happen.

Someone wants to learn grammar; he learns, he meditates, he listens to a teacher, and none of these is the end. But the very attainment of perfect knowledge is the end. Therefore, perfect virtue is the last desirable thing, with which there is no other thing to seek as a completion. We use laws for the sake of virtue; the giving of the laws is not the end. We are persuaded by exhortations, by teachings approaching moral training; but all these things happen for the sake of something else. But perfect virtue, the unsurpassed, established after all progress, is the end. Every servant of God pursues this end. Because of this: 'to the servant of the Lord, David'.

If it says 'to the servant', it is not only the end of this David, the son of Jesse, but of every one who has served God. If, indeed, we praise someone in grammar and say that he is able to write as is necessary, and to read as is fitting, and to explain as it is, the harmonies, we do not speak only about him, but about every grammarian. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words can be read as the lawless man first agreeing with sin within himself before doing it, or as his knowing he has no boldness in sin and so hiding it.
comments.comment: The wording is ambiguous. It signifies one thing thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. 'He says in himself that he sins'. First, he joins himself to lawlessness and sin, and thus comes to practicing it. It is impossible not to sin if one has not been pre-disposed toward sin. Thus 'he says' 'the lawless one that he sins in himself'. 'He says in himself'. For it is to be read thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'. But it is also possible to take the other part of the ambiguity thus: 'The lawless one says in himself that he sins'; for he knows that he has no boldness regarding sinning. Everyone who sins while following it hides the evil; for no one indeed makes himself manifest as he is. Even if he were a fornicator and wished to lie with someone, he does not want the one describing him to say he is a fornicator. Therefore, they are even more condemned, because they wish to hide what they are doing. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lawless man, knowing his lawlessness is hateful, would deceive to keep its shame from being found.
comments.comment: He who has become lawless, knowing his lawlessness to be hateful; if he were to be observed, he would deceive before Him, so that the shame of the lawlessness might not be found, lest he should hate it. This is what those who reason sophistically do, agreeing with sin as if it were a duty and not something contrary to reason.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lawless one is not so by nature, since not willing to understand in order to do good is his own choice.
comments.comment: Saying: the words of his mouth are lawlessness and toil, that is, prideful as to bringing toil upon those who attend to them. He did not will to have understanding to do good. It is clear from the things said that the lawless one is not such by nature; for not willing understanding upon doing good is by his own choice.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly that the wicked man's refusal to be wise and do good is his own choice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night has the law on his bed, not lawlessness.
comments.comment: He is considered to be practicing lawlessness, yet it is necessary to imitate that man who is blessed, the one meditating on the law of the Lord day and night: 'But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night' (Psalm 1:2). The one meditating on the law of the Lord day and night is not considered to have lawlessness upon his bed, but the law.… It is possible even to call the body a bed of the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'bed' by setting the man who meditates on the law against the man who devises lawlessness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A soul in a body can already meditate on being outside it, and one who has reckoned lawlessness on his bed should repent and be convicted so that the devil finds no place.
comments.comment:
Even if the soul is in a body, it already meditates on becoming outside of it, subduing the body and leading it as a slave. Thus indeed it is said concerning those having such a mindset: 'You are not in the flesh' (Romans 8:9). Even though they had flesh, they were not in the mindset of the flesh. And again: 'The mindset of the flesh is enmity against God' (Romans 8:7). And again: 'Those who, being in the flesh, seek to please God, are unable' (Romans 8:8).

If he speaks concerning this flesh, all the saints, being in it, pleased God. But the mindset of thinking according to the flesh, being entirely lifted up by the flesh, and consequently becoming fleshly—who is this fleshly person, or he who sells himself to sin? 'But I am fleshly, having been mastered by sin' (Romans 7:14). 'He considered lawlessness upon his bed.' According to the ascent: just as he considered lawlessness in the bed of the body. But it was necessary, while remaining upon this bed, to strip himself and to be pitied, because in the considering there is lawlessness, so as to say: 'With my tears I will wet my bed' (Ps 6:6). The voice of one repenting: but he who repents is not considered to be practicing lawlessness. And concerning others it is said in the prophet Micah: 'He was considered to be thinking of evils upon his bed, and at once with the day he completed them' (Micah 2:1).

They are often covered in the night by lawless things and at the same time complete them with the day. It is necessary, therefore, if an injustice has ever occurred upon the bed, to be convicted of it; for this is what the word protects: 'Be angry and do not sin; what you say in your hearts, be convicted upon your bed' (Ps 4:4). For if you are convicted, the devil finds no place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse says 'not good', not 'evil', for what is not good is not therefore evil.
comments.comment: He stood in every way not good, but he did not approach wickedness. He turned away every good way.… And it is also good to say 'not good'; for he did not say 'evil.' Not every thing that is not good is evil.… 'He did not approach wickedness' (Psalm 36:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'not good' and not 'evil'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who has reckoned lawlessness on his bed, accepting wickedness as his own hand, begins in practice to walk every way not good.
comments.comment: And in addition to this: He stood in every way not good, but did not attend to wickedness. Such is the 'Woe to those working evil on their bed and completing them by day' (Micah 2:1). Thus, one standing in every way not good, having reckoned lawlessness while on his bed, that is, in every evil practice; not attending to his wickedness, accepting it as if it were his own hand, he begins practically to walk every way not good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy is in heaven, for it is not of the things below, and those pitied by it are lifted up into heaven.
comments.comment: … His 'mercy' is therefore 'in heaven'; for he 'makes mercy unto thousands for those loving him' (Exodus 20:6). Just as one ascends a ladder of mercy into heaven; for the nature of the mercy of God is not of the things below, but is above. And if ever it happens in the earth, that is to say, in men—for it has been said: 'the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord' (Ps 33:5)—those being pitied by this mercy are lifted up into heaven.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's truth reaches to the clouds, which are the prophets who give a spiritual rain, and one able to pour out that rain has God's truth.
comments.comment: 'And even unto the clouds', he says, 'is your truth' (Ps 36:5). One must not pay attention to those who remove providence from the earth and say it is limited even to the mountains of the moon because of the saying: 'your truth is even unto the clouds'. The prophets are clouds ministering to us a spiritual rain, from which the paradise of God is watered, the seed that fell into good earth, which Jesus cast so that it might become a hundredfold, and a hundred and sixty and thirty (Matt 13:8). Therefore, until these clouds which minister the spiritual rain, concerning which it has been said: 'let the clouds rain down righteousness' (Isaiah 45:8), the truth of God is. If anyone is a cloud able to pour out spiritual rain and righteousness, he has God's truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'clouds' are in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The clouds that rain righteousness are divine men pouring out the word according to virtue, and the Lord's truth is in them.
comments.comment:
And in Isaiah, among the clouds, it is remembered thus: 'Let the heaven rejoice anew and let the clouds rain down righteousness' (Isaiah 45:8). But perceptible clouds do not rain down righteousness or truth, but rain down water.… The clouds raining not righteousness are divine men, pouring forth the spiritual rain, that is, the word according to virtue. And above these, a heaven rejoicing, meaning the blessed natures inhabiting the heaven, or the Savior is allegorically so named; for the heaven above is, that is, above every generated nature, and it rejoices for the benefit of all.

And here, not in the heaven, I say, but in the Savior, is the mercy of the Lord, pitying all; and his truth, which is set in opposition to wickedness and types, is in the aforementioned clouds.

For even if the prophets lived according to a shadow, they did not fail to know the truth which is this symbol. It is no wonder that those who keep the image and the rational movement find salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who think of earthly things are blamed by God, who says they have sunk into the earth and have no citizenship in the heavens.
comments.comment: Lord, in heaven is your mercy, and your truth unto the clouds (Ps 36:6). Concerning those dwelling on the earth according to the mindset, we say, 'those thinking of things on earth,' whom the God-Word, blaming, says in the prophet Jeremiah: 'You have sunk down into the earth in sitting' (Jer 48:10), if it is possible, and you want to be lower than the earth, thinking of nothing rising, not having 'your citizenship in the heavens' (Phil 3:20), not having your heart there toward those saying: 'Let us lift up our heart to the high one in heaven.' And it is said again concerning some this: 'But they sought my soul in vain, they shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth' (Psalm 63:9). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Human mercy is of the earth, but God's mercy lifts those who are lifted up so as to carry them into heaven.
comments.comment: God is merciful in one way and humans in another. The mercy that happens among men and the benefit toward the neighbor is human; for they know how to help and nourish and do other things in a human way, and this mercy is that which draws near to the earth, that is, to human things. But the God who shows mercy lifts up those who are being lifted up so as to carry them into heaven. 'In heaven' indeed 'is your mercy'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between human mercy and the mercy that is 'in heaven'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Gifts that reach the wicked and the irrational alike are not heavenly, but only what is truly good leads into heaven.
comments.comment: And this too is possible because: when showing mercy, you do not show mercy humanly; for even if you 'give food to all flesh' (Psalm 136:25), and even if you provide health to the sick, this righteousness is not touching the heaven. And so that I may express it more clearly: the things touched by the gifts of God are not only of the righteous, but also of the wicked, and of the rational and the irrational; they are not heavenly. But those alone are of heaven and lead into heaven, which are truly good and heavenly. And in another psalm you have: 'the earth is full of your mercy' (Ps 33:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteousness of God is as the mountains of God, and righteousness in humans makes those who have it like them.
comments.comment: 'Your righteousness is like the mountains of God' (Ps 36:6). The mountains of God are interpreted in many ways according to the Scripture. When it says: 'you shine wondrously from eternal mountains' (Psalm 76:4), 'eternal mountains' refers to the saints who no longer look at the things seen as being temporary, but at the things unseen which are eternal.… Therefore, 'approach eternal mountains' means approach through disposition; take up that same high mindset for them. 'The righteousness' which is 'as the mountains' is 'of God'. The righteousness in humans, when it grows those who possess it, makes them like the mountains of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'mountains of God' are, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those the Savior saved, having become the righteousness of God in him, are like the mountains of God, like the angels and archangels.
comments.comment: It is possible to call the righteousness of the descended Savior, according to another sense, those whom he saved. For 'he who did not know sin made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him' (2 Cor 5:21). Those having become the righteousness of God in him who became sin for us are like the mountains of God, like the angels, like the archangels; for they were perfected in the upper creation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whatever God has ordered, such as his word to Noah that no flood would come again, has a solid and unshaken permanence forever.
comments.comment: … For the things ordered by God are firm and unshaken, such as what was said to Noah, that he would no longer bring a flood for the destruction of living creatures, which agrees with the word about God's forbearance (Psalm 36:6; LXX 35:6). For the firmness of the word has been fixed forever, being great and manifest. So also whatever else has been ordered and fixed according to the righteousness and goodness of God has a solid and unshaken permanence forever (Psalm 36:6). Such is also the verse, Once I swore in my holy one, if I will lie to David (Psalm 88:36 (89:35)). To this also tends the saying, For the gifts of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the firmness of God's righteousness with the example of his word to Noah.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
