comments.capsule: God's judgments are unsearchable: we see that he judges and ordains each thing, but cannot say why one is strong and another weak.
comments.comment:
… Likewise, regarding health and the movements of the soul, we say that the difference of these things happens by the judgment of God. And that it happens by the judgment of God, let us take the word from the Gospel and clarify it, if it is possible, having been led into this history; in the Gospel the Savior says: 'Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if in Tyre and Sidon the powers that occurred in you had occurred, long ago they would have sat in sackcloth and ashes and repented' (Matt 11:21). If the tremendous powers had occurred to the Sidonians and Tyrians, they were called to repentance. But these spoken cities, Bethsaida and Chorazin, having been tested—why did the tremendous powers occur there, where they did not repent? It is a word resembling an abyss.

'Unsearchable' said the apostle, the judgments of God (Rom 11:33). No one searches them, no one is able to grasp their depth. But barely perceiving the things being done and as if being judged, we take a mental image that God is the one judging and ordaining each thing. But the 'why' we are not able to say, why this one, for instance, is strong and another is weak. We do not have the 'whys' to say.… 'Your judgments' therefore are not simply 'an abyss,' but 'deep.' And the simply 'abyss' is very deep.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain examples why God's judgments are called a great deep.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He governs and saves all, the rational and the irrational, and saves all men though differently.
comments.comment:
You will save men and cattle, Lord (Psalm 36:6). He saves men and cattle. And if we take cattle according to what is at hand, we also take men in sense perception. But he governs all, both the rational and the irrational animals; the rational according to themselves, and the irrational as things having come to be through the rational; for the irrational fulfill the needs of the rational.… Since even these he is able to let fall into harm and death, he saves even these. He saves also the man.

'Men and cattle you will save, Lord' (Psalm 36:6).

The same unsearchable quality of the judgments is found in these also, that he saves all men, though differently: some with much suffering, others with some rest and pleasure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says both man and beast are saved.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In true salvation the cattle are to be allegorized: those who come to godliness and the Gospel's teaching are called sheep, who hear a single voice.
comments.comment: … But if he speaks of true salvation, of saving men, and prays concerning that which has been said, that 'the Savior became the cause of eternal salvation to all those who obey', the saint, referring to what is signified, said: 'Our God, the God of saving' (Psalm 68:20); here the cattle are to be allegorized; for those who have come to godliness and to the teaching of the Gospel itself, some are called disciples, and others sheep: 'my sheep hear my voice' (John 10:27). They hear a single voice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior, wishing to save and improve all, calls some to his voice and others to his word, and saves the sheep so that they may become men.
comments.comment: There is another condescending intention of the Savior, that he be a shepherd. Since he wishes to save and improve all, then salvation and improvement ascend when, toward the capacity of being benefited in what is possible, he calls some listeners up to his voice, and others to his word, to his teaching. Thus he saves men and cattle so called. And he saves the sheep so that they may no longer be sheep, but that from sheep men may become.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not only men but also cattle are saved, since great sins require greater mercy.
comments.comment: If anyone is coming toward salvation, being astonished at the goodness of God, he will say: 'Since you have filled your lion, O God, not only men but also cattle are being saved; for great sins require greater mercy' (Psalm 36:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God brings pains medically, for the health of the soul, and we know his judgments are accomplished toward what is beneficial even if we do not grasp it.
comments.comment: It is indeed true, when God brings on pains through sin, that one capable of understanding must see the induction through His wisdom and in the bitter things, that He is not defending the sinner, but is bringing the tribulations medically and toward the health of the soul; which one of the saints, knowing this, said: 'I will bless You, Lord, because You were angry with me for the sake of salvation.' To receive the knowledge of the judgments of God is a gift of God, concerning which it has been said: 'Abyss is the multitude of Your judgments.' (Psalm 36:6) We know this much: that they are being accomplished toward what is beneficial, even if we do not grasp it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness oversees all that happens, so those who escape punishment now will certainly receive it later, and this is unchangeable with God.
comments.comment: This carries a threat of retributions, because it is impossible for anything to happen contrary to what is just when righteousness is the overseer of what takes place. So even those who now escape the punishing retributions, or who do not receive their retributions, will certainly receive them later. And this is unchangeable with God, as Paul said with confidence that God, the righteous judge, will give him the crown of righteousness on that day (2 Timothy 4:8) (Ps 35:10a).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's mercy is multiplied and his abundance shown when he also saves cattle.
comments.comment: … O God, how you have multiplied your mercy. By the mercy of God, men are saved. Then the mercy of God is multiplied and his abundance is shown, when he also saves cattle.…
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a few clear lines how God's mercy is multiplied.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wings of God are intellectual, lifting the mind upward, and are to be understood as virtue, understanding and wisdom.
comments.comment:
… But the sons of men hope in the shelter of your wings (Psalm 36:7).

The sons of these men.

If, according to the previous explanation, 'men' are said to be mortal rational animals and 'cattle' are those serving them, then the sons of these men have hope in the shelter of God's wings.

These wings are intellectual, lifting the mind upward.

Thus the saint says: 'Who will give me wings like a dove?'

(Ps 55:6).

We do not say that he prays to be given wings of a sensible animal; for this is impossible.

And that which is impossible is neither love nor prayer.

'As an eagle upon its young ones has hovered' (Deuteronomy 32:11).

Then they were winged, they were able to be taken up 'upon the transforming ones' of God.

And what is it for us to be thus winged?

Listen to what the prophet Isaiah says: 'Those who wait upon God shall renew strength, they shall fly up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary' (Isa 40:31).

And another prays saying: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's' (Ps 103:5).

When the saint says of being winged, his wings are to be understood as virtue, understanding, and wisdom; for these things, as a catapult, lift man upward.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wings are in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who enjoy God's or the Savior's instruction will be intoxicated from the power of his teaching.
comments.comment: Since the Church's doctrine participates in God, it participates in His potency; those contained by it will be intoxicated with a sober drunkenness. If the Church is God or the Savior, those enjoying His instruction will be intoxicated from the potency of His teaching (Psalm 36:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fountain of life is the Savior, who gives himself to all who live, and the torrent of luxury is the Holy Spirit, who gives his various gifts.
comments.comment: 'Since with you is the fountain of life' (Ps 36:9), and He is the one who said 'I am the Being', it is fitting that you also water the torrent of your luxury coming from the fountain of life, those who have been intoxicated from the potency of your goodness. The fountain of life is the Savior, who does not have it outside but provides himself to all living, not only to men but also to those who have ascended above, the same divine life, just as he is called the fountain of wisdom; and the torrent of luxury is the Holy Spirit, to luxury-drench those who have received from Him the various gifts of Him (Psalm 36:8).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the fountain of life and the river of pleasures are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The torrent of delight is the provision of teaching, and those made to drink from it come to the life from which the river flows.
comments.comment: The flowing liquid is able toward quenching thirst and leading into a sober drunkenness. He names it a 'torrent of delight,' just as it is said, 'a river of delight issues forth from Eden and waters the paradise' (Gen 2:10). And the provision of teaching, the participation of instruction, is called 'torrents' of 'delight.' 'You make them drink upon it.' And it is well also to say, 'you make them drink upon it,' since after this torrent they come to be and are in that very spring. As infants they are being made to drink, and so that I may speak from apostolic wording: to those being led in, Paul writes, 'I gave you milk' (1 Cor 3:2). And those unable to drink for themselves are being made to drink; those being instructed are being made to drink. When they are made to drink from this river of delight, they consequently come to that life from which this river flows, 'for with you is the spring of life' (Ps 36:9). Since with you is the spring of life. He did not say, 'for with you the spring of life has become' or 'a spring of life shall exist,' but 'with you is the spring of life.' This spring of life is always. But when those being made to drink approach, a stream also flows and becomes from the spring, called the 'torrent of delight.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The things that lead to life are supplied abundantly by God, and the light from heaven is common to the righteous and the unrighteous.
comments.comment: … The things that lead to life are supplied abundantly by God, and if they were not supplied, life would be destroyed (Psalm 36:9).… He is illuminated, he says, by the light from heaven, by the one who set the sun as the light of day. But these things are common to the righteous and the unrighteous, and in them he marveled at God's philanthropy, since the ungrateful are not excluded from enjoying what comes from God. But what is exceptional and proper to God's own is something else.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fountain of life and the light as God's gifts, in plain terms.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The true light is the light of God, and in it we shall see light.
comments.comment: 'In your light we shall see light' (Psalm 36:9); the true light is the light of God, the radiance of the eternal light. In this light we shall see light, regarding you as the eternal light, it is said: 'God is light' (1 John 1:5). He who has seen me has seen the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the light is in which we see light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A spring does not receive the life-giving thing from elsewhere but has it within itself, so life itself is the spring of life.
comments.comment: … If, therefore, the good things flow from it and it does not receive them from elsewhere like a pit or a head, it is a spring of life. And what am I saying? He himself was saying, 'I am the life' (John 14:6). It is the same to say 'life' and 'spring of life.' Life, indeed, because it vivifies and leads into immortality; but a spring, because it does not receive the vivifying thing from elsewhere, but has it itself within itself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is called a fountain of life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In God's light we shall see him as light, since he who saw the Son saw the Father.
comments.comment: If this voice speaks to the Father, it says: since he who saw the Son, being true light, sees you as existing in light, in your own light we shall see you as existing in light; for 'he who saw the Son saw the Father' (John 14:9). And 'he is the image of the invisible God' (Col 1:15) indicating the one of whom he is the image, and 'he is the character of the divine hypostasis' (Heb 1:3) revealing the hypostasis of God. Therefore, 'in your light we shall see light'. And if this is also spoken to the Son, in your luminous instruction and teaching we shall see you existing as light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Holy Spirit is light, and in him we are enlightened, as David sings that in your light we shall see light.
comments.comment: The Holy Spirit was praised and is light, in whom also we are enlightened, just as the apostle writes: 'that he might give you a spirit of wisdom and of revelation, in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your heart enlightened' (Ephesians 1:17-18), and as David sings: 'for with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light' (Psalm 36:9); that is to say, in your Son, the radiance of your glory, your Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David says there is a spring with God because the Son, who is with God the Father, is the spring of the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: In the Gospel the Son promises to give water to those who walk in thirst, saying to the Samaritan woman about the Holy Spirit: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10). And after a little while he says to her: “Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst forever. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up to eternal life” (John 4:13-14). And for this reason David, singing to God, says: “For with you is the spring of life; in your light we will see light” (Psalm 36:9). For he knows that the Son, who is with God the Father, is the spring of the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: God's mercy to those who know him is for their being established and ascending to what is above all things, and the pure in heart shall see God.
comments.comment:
Where he says: 'extend, O God, your mercy to those who know you' (Psalm 36:10), he speaks of that knowledge concerning which it is said: 'this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God' (1 John 5:20). These ones, having this knowledge, are loved by God.… Otherwise, he shows mercy to those coming in a manner of repentance, those asking for the forgiveness of sins.

He shows mercy to those knowing him so that they may be established and ascend to that which is above all things unto the end. And your righteousness to the upright in heart. And upright in heart and pure in heart are the same. It is therefore good for the pure in heart to see God; for 'blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matt 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what knowing God means and what God's lovingkindness to them is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Feet of folly lead into Hades and there are likewise feet of pride, so he prays that pride not walk in his soul nor the hand of sinners, meaning their practice, shake him.
comments.comment:
The feet of folly lead those who use it after death into Hades. Those who walk according to folly, using the feet of folly, are brought down into Hades. Just as there are feet of folly, so there are feet of pride.

Therefore, 'let not come to me the feet of pride' (Psalm 36:11), meaning let there not be a walking of pride in my soul and in my mind. 'Nor let the hand of sinners shake me' (Psalm 36:11). For hand is often said to mean practice, as if saying: 'Thorns grow in the hand of the drunkard,' meaning the shameful desires, the unrestrained pleasures.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the foot of pride and the hand of the wicked.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hand is practice, and practising what sinners do would shake him from virtue.
comments.comment: … For 'do not let pride take place in my soul to deceive me' (Psalm 36:11), but also let not the hand, that is, practice, shake me as a sinner; for if I should practice the things of sinners, I shall be shaken from virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The workers of iniquity fall not by nature or an outside force but by their own work, and God drives them out so that they may not stand in evil.
comments.comment: There the workers of iniquity fell (Psalm 36:12).… 13 They were driven out and are not able to stand. For since they themselves brought themselves down to the foot of pride, and are handed over to the hand of the sinner, which they chose to have, and this handing over is called their expulsion. And God, being a benefactor, drives them out so that they may not be able to stand in the evil. It is not, therefore, a nature or some external force casting him out, but his own work being iniquity and wickedness. He drives him out so that he may not remain, so that he may not hold a fixed stand in it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the workers of iniquity fall and cannot rise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The workers of iniquity fall in the future life, spoken of as already done because the prophet sees it as certain, and they are driven out, hindered from acting though their powers are not destroyed.
comments.comment:
Those imprisoned in the body will be released there, and if something like that. He says not where, but in the future life, for all those working in lawlessness have fallen. For even if they seemed to stand and act in lawlessness, they no longer fall there, no longer permitted to act as they previously acted.

One should not be surprised if he speaks of what will be as if it has already happened; for many such things are spoken, such as 'They stretched out my hands and my feet, and they divided my garments' (Psalm 22:16); because the one prophetically foreseeing what is to come does not see the things to come as if they were certainly happening, but for this reason, he speaks of them as if they had already happened.

They were driven out, that is, they were forced to become outcasts, or they became outcasts through their own actions; because they can no longer stand, having been actively hindered, but not having had their practical powers destroyed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Do not envy sinners their present success, because a lover of good does not desire temporary things, and those pass away.
comments.comment: 'Do not be envious of those committing adultery, nor be envious of those practicing lawlessness' (Psalm 37:1). God fashioned a lover of good as a creature. To be a lover of good is not to desire the temporary and present things; for the temporary and present things belong even to sinners. Therefore, do not be envious of them, whether they prosper or whether they are healthy; for they do not remain always.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm says not to envy evildoers: their prosperity does not last.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Goodness leads the believer to the true Shepherd and his pasture, and the Lord himself is the food that satisfies the heart's longings.
comments.comment:
Surely goodness will bring you to dwell upon the holy land, to be a shepherd upon its wealth (Psalm 37:3; LXX 36:3), for you will find the true Shepherd leading you to a divine pasture, which is named the wealth of that land. …

The Lord, providing himself for us in all things, is found to be both food and drink for us (Psalm 37:4; LXX 36:4). We do not feed him, finding him to be the bread of life, and let us be filled with his flesh and his blood, being true food and drink; Having feasted upon him, we will find him satisfying all the longings of the heart, that is, of the mind, not the sensible things but the spiritual and intelligible ones.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A righteous person should make his way plain to God and hope in him, and God will bring his hidden righteousness out as light.
comments.comment: Feast upon the Lord, and having attained the things spoken, make your way, which you practically walk, manifest (Psalm 37:4-7; LXX 36:4–7a). But what are you doing? For those things which you do, God looks upon. For the one sinning hides God, hastening to cover his way. But making your way manifest to God, place hope in Him, and He will do the things hoped for you and expected for you, so that your righteousness, which was worked in secret, may emerge as light, like that of Job and Joseph. For the likeness of their light, having shone forth, was distributed throughout the whole inhabited world to all generations, but also your judgment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to commit one's way to the Lord and have righteousness brought out as light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Submitting to the Lord is done by keeping his commands, entreating him and asking forgiveness of sins already committed.
comments.comment: You have tested in yourself that at noon, having a bright and sharp light, it will be equal to the same. For all those revealed in you will become as a star in the world. But now the end is: 'Submit to the Lord' (Ps 37:7). How will this happen? Through guarding the divine commands, entreating Him, asking Him for the forgiveness of sins already committed, and through obtaining the things spoken.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm commands us to be still and wait for God, hoping for future things rather than being disturbed by present ones.
comments.comment: He commands to be still and wait for God, not being disturbed by present things but hoping for future things, according to the apostolic word: Rejoicing in hope, enduring in affliction (Romans 12:12), and Jeremiah's word: It is good for a man when he bears a yoke in his youth (Lamentations 3:27). He will sit alone and be silent; he will give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he will be filled with reproaches.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what waiting on the Lord means: patience in present trouble and hope for what is to come.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Anger destroys even the wise and hinders virtue, so one must give it up and pursue gentleness.
comments.comment: Anger is a destructive passion, even as it destroys the wise (Ps 37:8). For anger destroys the wise, and it is also an obstacle to the activity of virtue; for the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God. Therefore, stop from anger and leave behind wrath, becoming a zealot of meekness and gentleness.
comments.selected_reason: Plain explanation of why the psalm says to cease from anger.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We are told to look far ahead at the end of the wicked and the safety of the good, because the present age does not show these outcomes.
comments.comment: He commands us to look far off and not be astounded by present things, and to foresee the destruction of the wicked and the preservation of the good (Psalm 37:9). These things clearly reach their end in another age, since the present age does not have the outcomes of these things, but rather the wicked prevail over the things on earth. Therefore he says, The whole world lies in the evil one (1 John 5:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm points us to the future destruction of the wicked rather than to what we see now.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The wicked are destroyed in being made no longer wicked, and those who wait on the Lord inherit a heavenly land through endurance, which is itself a gift.
comments.comment:
That those committing adultery will be destroyed (Psalm 37:9)—to be destroyed, but they are being destroyed in the way that they are evil, so that they may no longer be such. And it also signifies the punishment. And the punishment is again an impediment to wickedness. …

They shall inherit the Lord a land. Those waiting on the Lord inherit the land already interpreted as being in highness, lying in the heaven. And this David said: 'I believe to see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living' (Psalm 27:13). He was a king. And to be a king is to have the good things of one's own land and to rule over it. But no one believes to receive what he already has, but believes to have received.

And this one says: 'I believe to see,' not 'I have seen' those good things, which God gives 'to those asking him,' when they pray sincerely concerning them. 'Those waiting' therefore 'on the Lord shall inherit the land' (Psalm 37:34). Endurance is a greatest contest of virtue: 'the tribulation works out endurance' (Romans 5:3). You see that after tribulation comes endurance. He therefore waits on the Lord as is necessary, having no endurance other than Him. And just as wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become to some, so also endurance.

This David himself in another psalm says: 'And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 39:7). This endurance they always strive to have, those contending for virtue and piety. The hymnodist himself again says: 'Waiting, I waited on the Lord' (Psalm 39:7). Not simply 'I waited,' but 'waiting,' as in: 'to pursue the just thing justly.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner's place is the sin in which he stands, so when he is no longer a sinner his place is not found.
comments.comment: The place of the sinner seems to be the place concerning the earth; for here lawlessness happens, here sins are completed. Therefore the earth will pass away along with the heaven. 'And you will seek his place and will not find' (Ps 9:10). Place is mainly called the position of each. … The place of the sinner will not be found if he is no longer a sinner; his place was sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the wicked 'shall not be' and his place cannot be found.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When wickedness is done away there is no longer a place for the sinner, since places are orders of difference, such as teacher and student.
comments.comment: Since the things of wickedness will be done away with after a short passing of time (Ps 37:10), the sinner will not exist, for in the time when such a thing is not found, he will not be. Therefore, even having searched for his place, you will not find it. But a place is to be heard of as being in a certain order, where a difference exists between teacher and student. There is a place for the teacher and a place for the student; if the student should be filled with knowledge, just as the teacher having become so will leave the place of the student as if it were no longer there. Since even among logical things there has been a difference by its own nature, such as the place of the righteous exceeding that of the sinners, when wickedness is vanishing, there will not be a place for the sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The meek, who are free of anger, inherit an eternal place and delight in a peace that the present land of wars cannot give.
comments.comment:
'But the meek shall inherit the earth' (Ps 37:11). Shortly, the sinner will neither be seen nor his place found, even if searched for; the place of the meek remains for ever; for it is eternal, it is immortal. …

Therefore the meek, that is, those having gentleness, those perfecting themselves in lack of anger, shall inherit the earth; for the one without anger is gentle; for one should not say of others that he is gentle if he becomes angry at those whom it is necessary to be angry with. …

And they shall delight in abundance of peace. When does this abundance of peace occur? When the prayer of those saying, 'grace to you and peace be multiplied' is heard. He who is able to say, 'among those hating peace I was peaceful,' has an abundance of peace, and delights in this abundance of peace. It is possible to say that, having been relocated from this land, where wars and disturbances occur, they become in the land of the meek, where peace is lived out.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the meek are and what the abundance of peace is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner watches the righteous like an archer looking for a bare spot, but the righteous man wears the armor of God and is fully protected.
comments.comment: The sinner will watch the righteous man and gnash his teeth at him (Psalm 37:12). This says that the sinner always wants to be an enemy of the righteous, and not only an enemy, but wants to be a murderer against him. And see how 'will watch' lies; primarily this watching means to observe how one might harm someone. What kind of person is armed? He who wants to shoot him with an arrow watches which part of him is naked, and where he sends the arrow. Since therefore the righteous is protected, he is not naked, but has put on 'the armor of God' (Eph 6:11) and 'has taken up the breastplate of faith' (1 Thessalonians 5:8) and is entirely secured.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sinner's plotting and why the righteous are safe.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner who watched the righteous man failed to strike him, and grinding the teeth often signifies repentance.
comments.comment: But the truly perfect righteous one is not subject to reproof. For having watched, he [the sinner] did not seize him, did not strike, did not wound; and thus, at the failure, he grinds the teeth. And the grinding of teeth often signifies repentance, as also in the Gospel concerning the one bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness 'prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matt 25:41); 'there shall be the weeping and the grinding of teeth' (Matt 8:12). And the 'there' here again signifies such a condition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God laughs at the sinner because he foresees the day of his condemnation, and this language is not to be understood as human passion.
comments.comment: 'But the Lord shall laugh at him, for he foresees that his day is coming' (Psalm 37:13; LXX 36:13). the sinner who shall grind the teeth against the righteous; for 'he foresees' 'that his day is coming'. The Lord, foreseeing that his day shall come in which he shall be condemned, shall laugh at the sinner. But such sayings spoken of God must not be heard in a human-passioned way. But we take their meaning in a God-befitting way; for indeed it has been said: 'He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall sneer at them' (Ps 2:4). This is not spoken humanly; we do not take it of God in a human-passioned way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God can 'laugh' without human passions.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinners bend the bow and draw the sword to strike the poor and needy and the upright in heart.
comments.comment: It is possible for the devil to raise these things up with a breath, the one called a sinner (Ps 37:14). And the sinners themselves break the sword and bend the bow, so that with bows they may strike the poor and needy, and with the sword they may slaughter those who are upright in heart;
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword of the wicked is the guileful word, and whoever tries to harm another with sword, mind or tongue falls under the same harm.
comments.comment: 'The sinners drew the sword and bent their bow, to cast down the poor and needy' (Psalm 37:14; LXX 36:14). They prepared a sword, that they might cast down the poor and needy. It is turned back and comes into their own heart, as it is said: 'he who digs a pit for his neighbor shall fall into it' (Prov 26:27). … The sword can be the word with guile; for they draw it, that through it they may strike. You have it said in Proverbs: 'there are those who, speaking, wound as with a sword, but the tongues of the wise heal' (Prov 12:18). There are those who in speaking wound as with a sword. But it is to be read with the dative: there are those who in speaking wound with a sword. Those who corrupt good manners with evil conversations (1 Cor 15:33) wound with a sword in speaking. 'and their tongue is a sharp sword'; their word, like a sword, harms and wounds. … A bow being bent is the ruling faculty thus prepared so that arrows are loosed from it. And let these be evil reasonings, harmful words. … everyone who brings punishment upon someone shall fall under punishment; everyone wishing to harm someone with a sword—with his own sharpened mind, or tongue and word—shall fall under the same things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked suffer the very things they prepare against the righteous, as a man is slain by the sword he drew.
comments.comment: He says that the wicked set in motion against themselves the very things they prepare against the righteous, as if someone drew a sword and was slain by it, and the plot too will be futile, like a bow shattered in the hand of an archer (Psalm 37:15). In David's case this was also fulfilled bodily: David struck with their own sword, the one they had drawn against David (cf (Psalm 37:15). 1 Samuel 17:51).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse plainly: the wicked are hurt by their own weapons.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sword of the wicked turns back on them, a little knowledge with piety beats wealth with impiety, and the arms meant are powers of the soul.
comments.comment: Thoughts are evil, but the tongue having been unsharpened, indeed their word is destructive in its differences. Since therefore the one sinning by his own sin dies, and of these the sword which has been dulled against others will harm them into their heart (Psalm 37:15). Regarding understanding: it is better for the righteous to have a little knowledge with piety than wealth with impiety of the sinners, who are some coming from the things of false knowledge (Psalm 37:16). Regarding arms, now it is not to be said of the arms of the body but of the practical powers of the soul (Psalm 37:17; LXX 36:17a).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord knows the blameless by their blamelessness, and since they are always in light and day, he knows all their days.
comments.comment: The Lord knows the way of the righteous and the ways of the blameless (Psalm 37:18; LXX 36:18a). … for the Lord knows all the ways of the blameless, judging them by their blamelessness. And it is also carried forward that the Lord knows the days of the blameless. Since the blameless are never in darkness but are always in light and day, for this reason the Lord knows such days of theirs, and all the days of their life, as they work always without reproach and blamelessness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Lord knows the days of the upright.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The famine meant is a famine of hearing the divine word, and sinners who feel shame may leave their sin and so perish as sinners.
comments.comment:
In the prophet, indeed, it is said, where it is written: 'I will bring a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of the Lord' (Amos 8:11), it is applied: 'Many have fallen in every place, I will cast down silence' (Amos 8:3). To the fallen, the famine is. To these, however, the silence of the divine word is brought. Thus, 'in days of famine they shall be satisfied.' Because the sinners shall perish.

Twice again we perceive the destruction of the sinners: namely, in the way they are sinners, they perish having experienced the oppressors. The righteous 'are not ashamed in evil time' (Psalm 37:19), but the sinners are ashamed. When they are ashamed, knowing how evil they are, and they blush because of sinning, sometimes they despise the sin and become free from it, and thus they perish in such a way that they are no longer sinners.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In an evil time the blameless are not ashamed, and the sinners are destroyed by ceasing to be sinners.
comments.comment: An evil time is, or some hardship, when one enjoys the fruits of sins (Psalm 37:19; LXX 36:19a). In this, in this time, the blameless will not be ashamed, not having deeds for which it is to suffer (Psalm 37:20; LXX 36:20a). For the sinners will be destroyed, not by the dissolution of their constitution from the outside, but by no longer being sinners (Psalm 37:20; LXX 36:20a).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies of the Lord, those who think impiously, vanish like smoke at the very moment they are being exalted.
comments.comment: But the enemies of the Lord, at the same time as they are to be glorified and exalted, having vanished like smoke, they vanished. Sinners are able to be enemies of the Lord. And it is possible also to call sinners those who sin according to ethics, those who transgress the divine commandments, and enemies of the Lord those who think impiously, those outside godliness, those who falsely glorify. These, therefore, are the enemies of the Lord, who at the same time as being to be glorified and exalted immediately vanished like smoke. And behold, always he likens sinners to smoke. And in another psalm it is said: 'As smoke vanishes, so they vanished; as wax melts from before the fire, so the sinners shall perish from before the face of God' (Psalm 68:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the enemies of the Lord are and why they are likened to smoke.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sin follows the capacity for virtue as smoke follows fire, so sinners who seem great are extinguished like smoke.
comments.comment: Sin is a follower of virtue. The rational animal has become capable of virtue. Yet this capability is not an essence of any kind. Humans are not good by essence; for they were created so that they might become good through participation in the truly good. But the capacity for evil follows the capacity for virtue. Just as the bad always follows the good, bad art follows art, and mishearing follows hearing. Sin, therefore, is a follower of virtue; the sinning animal would not exist if it were not capable of virtue. Similarly, wax is a follower. For this substance does not turn into non-existence, but changes into something better. And sinners become smoke because of this very evil; for lawlessness is in a certain way like a harmful eye or smoke to the eyes. You see that lawlessness becomes to those using it like smoke to the eyes. Smoke does not need great force to be overturned, for it is quickly overturned. Therefore, sinners are 'as wax melts from the presence of fire,' and 'as smoke vanishes, so let them vanish.' Smoke is, as I have said, a follower of fire; for it exists because fire exists or comes to be. Thus the enemies of the Lord, even if they blaze brightly and are praised as capable or promising, are extinguished like smoke at the very moment they are exalted. It is ours to see their vanishing; for even if they remain for a time, being glorified and praised and thinking great things, those able to see that which they think great find them instantly vanishing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous man shows mercy and gives to others, while the sinner borrows from God what he was given and does not repay.
comments.comment: The sinner borrows and does not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and gives. He not only returns what he borrowed, but also becomes a benefactor to others. By showing mercy, he gains. 'He who shows mercy to the poor lends to God' (Prov 19:17). The one borrowing from God is righteous, having gathered a multitude of works and of reasonable silver, and he benefits another; for the evil ones harm those who are with them, but the righteous ones benefit. And that the evil one is harmful is manifest. For it has been said in proverbs that the wise man benefits and improves: 'Rebuke a wise man and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). Being rebuked, he receives the rebukes well as to love the one rebuking him. But having loved the one rebuking him, he no longer works the things upon which the rebuke occurred. Just as 'he is a brother to the one who loathes himself' (Proverbs 18:9), the one doing evil. Therefore, the evil one harms himself above all. The righteous, therefore, shows mercy and gives, and he is full of grace and simply participates in good things toward his neighbor. Those saying that, 'if a brother or sister are naked and lacking of the daily food' (James 2:15), that is: 'Go in peace, be satisfied,' but do not give to them the necessities, did not benefit them, since they do not 'show mercy and give.' And it is possible also to take it thus: the sinner, borrowing from God the common concepts given to him and the commandments, 'does not repay.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the borrowing and the giving of mercy in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What God gives is a loan to be worked with and repaid with interest in works of righteousness, not a debt that can be ignored.
comments.comment: 'The borrower does not repay' (Psalm 37:21). What God gives for the benefit of humans and the soul, those receiving do not take as a debt; for no one receives anything in this age as a debt, but giving as a gift, the good man gives a loan so that, having worked with it, he may gain and give interest. I take the word concerning righteousness. If I give back and also provide interest, I offer the works of righteousness to God. But if, having received the word concerning righteousness, I do nothing according to righteousness, having borrowed from God, I have not repaid; for God gives so that we may act, and God provides so that we may turn words into deeds. His divine silver is lent, concerning which it is said, 'silver refined is a test for the earth' (Psalm 12:6). The borrower therefore pays back interest and also that which he received. But the righteous man shows mercy and gives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God shows mercy even to the ungrateful, and the one who buries what he received, like the servant with one talent, loses it.
comments.comment:
'But the righteous' Ps 112:5 God even more 'shows mercy and gives.' He who receives does not give back, but he himself even more 'shows mercy and gives.' And I say: then the mercy and the benevolence appear, if the receiver is ungrateful. 'He is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil,' Luke 6:35 he gives. Those receiving are ungrateful—for by not giving back what is necessary to give back, they are found ungrateful and evil—but God is still kind even to these. Therefore the righteous even more shows mercy and provides. The imitator, therefore, of God, 'who shows mercy to the poor and lends to God' Ps 112:4, even if the one being lent to does not provide what he owes to provide, he is still merciful, he still provides. And take for me the parable of the Gospel concerning the talents: 'to each according to his own ability' Matt 25:15 he gave the rational things belonging to him, not to each according to his nature, but according to the ability which he himself had prepared by choice. 'And to the one he gave five, to the other two, to the other one' Matt 25:15. 'The one having received five talents worked with them' Matt 25:16 and doubled them. Having borrowed, he paid back. The one with two likewise. The one having received the one and having buried it in the earth, neither worked with it nor gave interest, he hid it in the earth Matt 25:18.

When you see a man having the ability to do good or to be a philanthropist and not doing it, he has buried what he received into the earth, he has buried it into his own material choice. And being asked for it, when the time remained to 'gather' Matt 25:19 to those who had received the rational silver, he says: 'See, you have the sponge' Matt 25:24. And he accused God, wanting to write his own slowness upon another: 'I knew,' Matt 25:24 he says, 'I knew that you are a hard man, removing what you did not set, reaping where you did not sow; and having been afraid, you hid your silver in the earth' Matt 25:22-23 and to no one did you give it. From which things he said, he had the rebuke and the condemnation: 'Man, wicked slave, you knew that I remove what I did not set' Matt 25:26, if I remove not what is mine, I overstepped my own, not what was received; if 'I reap where I did not sow' Matt 25:23? In any case, they were taking mine, if you had given it on a table so that it might be multiplied. Therefore, even this was deprived.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who bless the righteous inherit the land, and those who curse him, by speaking falsely of the benefits they received, are destroyed.
comments.comment:
For those blessing him shall inherit the land. Those blessing the righteous. One must receive both kinds of returns: namely, the righteous man or God. He who does those things which God requires of him blesses God, so as to say: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Psalm 34:1). And the righteous man is blessed: 'for the blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous' (Proverbs 10:6), and: 'this one shall receive blessing from the Lord' (Psalm 24:5). 'The land,' that land, concerning which it was said: 'and he will lift you up to inherit the land' (Psalm 37:34). …

But those cursing him shall be destroyed. Therefore the impious one curses the righteous by speaking about him, or toward those whom he speaks to: 'Woe to them, because they have departed from me; they are wretched, because they have done evils against me; I redeemed them, but they spoke lies against me.' 'I,' he says, 'redeemed them,' meaning he led them into the bath of regeneration, having freely granted the complete forgiveness of sins, having wiped out their lawlessness. But they speak lies against me, not doing those things for which they were called. And they had the forgiveness of sins; for not for this purpose did I redeem them, so that they might sin, but so that they might become outside of sin. If, therefore, after the ransoms and the means, someone does something absurd, he speaks lies by saying in a certain way: 'He did not benefit me,' he says lies against him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man chooses to walk from bad to good, and the Lord directs his steps without forcing him.
comments.comment: The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way (Ps 37:23). The man walks volitionally from the inferior to the superior, from the temporal to the eternal. And to him belongs the willing of the good, since it is 'not of him who runs nor of him who wills, but of the God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16) to successfully complete the way. 'The steps of a man are directed by the Lord.' The steps are not given; for it is ours to will to walk from the bad to the good. Immediately, indeed, in the epistle of John, he writes: 'We know that we have passed from death to life' (1 John 3:14). 'We have passed,' not 'we were led.' God, directing the steps, did not force us into this by violence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God directs a man's steps while the man still chooses to walk.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God directs the way by enlarging the heart, but the man must intend to run it, and he who sets out with the Lord is not made to stumble.
comments.comment: By making these things happen, they are set on right steps. And you have many such things in the Scripture: 'I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart' (Psalm 119:32). Because God enlarges the heart and has given breadth to the understanding, someone runs the way of the commandments. Not that he ran and his heart was enlarged, but that God was enlarging it, casting out all narrowness from faulty thoughts and afflictions; because of this, we ran the way of God. Again, if it is said in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 10:23), do not think it as an opposition: 'I know that the way of man is not his own, nor does a man direct his steps.' The prophet's meaning is twofold. Nebuchadnezzar threatens the destruction of Jerusalem and the deportation of the whole Hebrew race. The prophet said that, even if the threat existed and we ourselves provided the causes for this to be suffered, 'I know that the way of man is not his own' (Jeremiah 10:23). You are able to prevent his way against us; for even if a man is thought to be great, his course is not made straight if you prevent it. It is also possible to take it according to the meaning already assigned to: 'not by the willer or the runner, but by the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16). Set your intention to run the saving way. It is not within our power to run the way, but to will to arrive at the end of the way, so as to say: 'I have finished the race' (2 Timothy 4:7). From Him is the directing, from Him is the guiding. 'Lead me in your truth' (Psalm 25:5). The one being led by God does not make himself straight. But he intends to be made straight and has given himself to the One who is able to lead him into perfection. Such things as are according to God, I say, and seeing toward Him, are richly fulfilled, and it is not possible for each to be divided from each other. If someone has set before him the good, he strives to be an imitator of God, to set and to take up virtue; having set it before him, he does not stand still until the setting, but acts, meditates, strives, and disciplines himself. To aim at good things. 'Has it not been announced to you, O man, what the Lord requires from you: except to love mercy, to do judgment, and to be ready to go with the Lord your God?' (Micah 6:8). He who prepares himself to always go with the Lord your God is entirely unstumbling. Only let him prepare himself for this, saying: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.' And no one among those who are stumbled by shameful thoughts or some impulse can say: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready'; for he has bonds, 'he is constricted by the chains of his own sins.' God desires the path of the one being directed in his steps. And he who has spoken, 'I am the way' (John 14:6), walks willingly, running the way of life. He treads and runs upon it. 'And he shall desire his way' (Psalm 37:23). It is also possible to say this: he whose steps are directed by God desires the way of God, into which He leads him, upon which He guides and escorts him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like a skilled runner who only briefly feels a stumble, the righteous man who falls is not destroyed and gives the devil no place.
comments.comment: And even if it should ever happen that he falls, he is not destroyed. 24 When he falls, he shall not be shattered (Psalm 37:24). Take for me such an example: let a runner be excellent, having by nature swift feet and having the art of running most prepared. This one, having sharpness regarding the running and having trained the feet of the inner man, if ever he should stumble while running, receives in some way a brief sensation of the stumbling; for he is neither turned over nor, as if struck by a blow, does he stop from the race. And even if it should ever happen to be some slipping, he is not destroyed. Judas slipped from the way of truth and fell; for it has been said: 'Becoming headstrong, he fell in the midst' (Acts 1:18). But he would not have become headstrong if he had not been shattered. And good is also this: 'When he falls, he shall not be shattered' (Psalm 37:24). And even if some stumbling should occur, it does not provide 'a place for the devil' (Ephesians 4:27), so as to turn him and shatter him entirely.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse with the image of a runner who stumbles but does not fall out of the race.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God feeds the righteous in famine as he fed Elijah and Daniel, and the righteous in turn lend divine lessons to others.
comments.comment: When much scarcity of food comes because of a great famine, according to the commandment of God, ravens feed them as they did Elijah with foods, and as they did Daniel in the den of lions, the best being carried to him by the meteor of Abamuk (Psalm 37:25; LXX 36:25ab). And this toward the literal, but toward the thought: from a young and uncertain mind, as one being younger than a youth, having changed into an old age, having come to a life without blemish and having acquired much prudence, such one, having progressed thus, is not a righteous man left abandoned. … but he is a sharer with God, lending divine lessons to those who listen, just as one lends to God according to the saying 'He lends to the poor,' in order to gain salvific interest and so that their seed may be blessed with every spiritual blessing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We should flee evil and do good, hoping for eternal rest from a righteous overseer.
comments.comment: Such an exhortation again comes from the prediction: to flee from evil and practice the doing of good in hope of eternal rest, and the reasoning about the matter is that the overseer is righteous and does not overlook his own.
comments.selected_reason: A plain statement of why the psalm urges leaving evil and doing good.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To turn from evil and do good is to guard innocence and be outside all evil.
comments.comment: Therefore he says these things: 'Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell for an age of ages' (Psalms 37:27). He says: 'Guard innocence, see uprightness,' having become outside of all evil. But he is innocent according to the present.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The land that the righteous inherit is not the earth we plough but the heavenly land, the most perfect knowledge of God.
comments.comment: It is also promised to the seed that he will give the land, that land about which the Savior said, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth' (Matt 5:5), and in the Psalms, 'Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land' (Ps 37:35), and it is clear that not this land which we plow and sow—of which he was king—but the heavenly one, which is the most perfect knowledge of God; this 'the righteous shall inherit and dwell upon it for an age of ages' (Psalm 37:29), but it shall not be upon the sensible land.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous speaks wisdom because his word meditates only on contemplation, and he speaks or is silent as he has judged.
comments.comment: The righteous, having perfected all moral virtue, has arrived at contemplation (Psalm 37:30; LXX 36:30); therefore, his word, which is figuratively called 'mouth,' meditates on nothing other than the wisdom found in contemplation. To this end, the discourse of the pious possesses wisdom throughout, while the fool changes like the moon. And the tongue of the righteous does not speak haphazardly or by chance. For having judged and examined the difference between words to be spoken and words not to be spoken, he will say some things and keep others silent. Such is the lip of the wise, bound by perception, to both speak and be silent; for he uses the perception of the lips as a restraint.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the righteous man's mouth speaks wisdom and his tongue does not speak at random.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God's law is in the righteous man's heart, he meditates on wisdom and his steps, the walking powers of the soul, do not slip.
comments.comment: "His steps will not be made to slip." (Psalm 37:31). For the law of God is in the heart of the righteous; he meditates on wisdom and his steps are not made to slip, which are "the walking powers of the soul." Such a thing also the saying of Proverbs means, "the judgments of the thoughts of the righteous" (Proverbs 12:5). And when such thoughts exist, the word follows to be like this: "for the good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart" (Luke 6:45).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: the law in the heart keeps the righteous man's steps from slipping.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The divine commandment must be written in mind and heart, and whoever has the law there will be firmly fixed in virtue.
comments.comment: Therefore the divine commandment must be written down unto mind and heart, and making the benefit of the matter clear the divine David said concerning every just one: ‘The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be tripped.’ (Psalm 37:31) For it is, I think, also very clear that for whomever the divine law is present unto mind, there will also altogether be present the having been well fixed, and the lying in the firm of virtue.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: With the law as leader we pass without stumbling, and even when many seek to kill, we are to wait on the Lord and keep his commandments to inherit the land.
comments.comment: We do not possess by nature a law in the heart by which we discern what is to be done and what is not to be done, but it is not other than that of the Creator, who made us according to His own image of God (Psalm 37:31; LXX 36:31). Let us take care that we save our thoughts from being unswerving, avoiding the evil and imitating the better. Using this law as the leader of the way, we pass without stumbling toward the goal toward which we hasten. And it is possible for the evangelical law to be made manifest through the present word. The sinner, understanding the righteous man and seeking to kill him, is told: 'Wait upon the Lord' (Psalm 37:34; LXX 36:34). Even if you have many who kill against you, receive salvation from God. But wait upon Him and keep His way, observing His commandments. For in this way, being prepared, you will follow the one who is exalted, so as to inherit the land often spoken of.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be not abandoned into the hands of the wicked does not mean being spared their seizure, as the martyrs and Susanna show; it means they do not achieve what they intended.
comments.comment: Even if he is laid upon, he will not abandon him into their hands. We speak of a difference in the meaning of the word 'abandon'. Even if Naboth (1 Kings 21) was taken by those who attacked him not abandoned into their hands; for then, it was called abandonment if they achieved what they intended. The martyrs were taken by some, but they were not abandoned into their hands. For then, they were being abandoned if they were being sacrificed. When a sinner is judged by a righteous man, the righteous man is not condemned. The elders were judging with Sosannas, and she was not condemned in the judging of them; for they were shown to be false informers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: However many enemies trouble us, we are to wait on the Lord and keep his way, and he will lift us up to inherit the land and let us see the sinners destroyed.
comments.comment:
'Wait for the Lord and keep his way, and he will lift you up to inherit the land' (Psalm 37:34). Therefore he exhorts: even if there are many things troubling, even if many are the enemies wanting to harm and take away, but 'wait for the Lord and keep his way', so as to say: 'I have finished the race'; for then he will lift you up and you will inherit the land. The contest of endurance showed that: he will make you high, he will take you up, he will lead you into heaven.

You shall see the sinners being destroyed (Psalm 37:34). This says: you shall see the sinners being destroyed and you will know yourself that you have inherited the land, because you waited for the Lord and kept his way, you did not fall with them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what waiting on the Lord and being exalted to inherit the land mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ungodly man exalted like a cedar of Lebanon is found not to exist when one looks to the life after this, because ungodliness has ceased.
comments.comment:
'I saw the ungodly being lifted up and exalting himself like the cedars of Lebanon; and they passed by, and behold, he was not, and I sought him, and the place of him was not found' (Psalm 37:35-36). Often the ungodly think themselves great and elevate themselves like the cedar in Lebanon. …

I passed through in thought into the life after these things, into the account of providence, and I no longer saw him, nor was his place found even when sought. Ungodliness has ceased; there is no longer ungodliness. He is not among the immortals, just as concerning righteousness he says: 'Righteousness is immortal.'

For, 'like the cedars of Lebanon' (Ps 92:12)? Often he signifies the haughty ones by this wood: 'And the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.' There are also praiseworthy cedars. But concerning the great ones in this life, he signifies by this name: 'Open, O Lebanon, your gates; fire consumes your cedars' (Zechariah 11:1). Then he interprets: 'Because the giants have greatly afflicted me.' He said the giants are the cedars. So there are also praiseworthy cedars, but the word is not concerning these now.

'And they passed by, and behold, he was not.' They passed by in thought, and I saw him not existing. I saw him acting insolently because of wealth, because of human rule. They passed by in thought, and I saw that the ungodly is not among those existing. He is still highly exalted according to Lebanon and its cedars; for I searched among the existing things for his place and I did not find it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wicked man's greatness and why he cannot be found.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ungodly are not found in the coming life, not because their being vanishes but because the evil that was their place is gone.
comments.comment:
Having passed by, he says, in thought toward the coming life, the ungodly is not found, just as seeking his place and not finding it. It has been said that the worthless ones are not found after these things, not by the vanishing of their essence, but by the quality according to which they are such; and regarding the not finding of their place in order, it has been demonstrated. If one were to say these things about Satan, since he is called the ruler of this world (and this world passes away), having searched, someone in the coming age will not find the place of this ruler.

And if even sin is a place of the devil according to 'Give no place to the devil' (Eph 4:27), the place of the ungodly was not found with the vanishing of evil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God made all things very good and does not delight in destruction, so there is no place for the evil among the things that exist.
comments.comment: God has made all things 'very good' (Gen 1:31). 'From the mouth of the Lord neither the good nor the evil shall come forth' (Lamentations 3:38). He does not say that neither the good nor the evil, but rather that the good shall come forth from the mouth of the Lord, and the evil not. Thus, the good are in the plural. For this reason, there is no place for the evil among the existing things; for God has made all things 'very good.' And 'He does not delight in the destruction of living things' (Wisdom 1:13). 'The generations of the world are salvific; there is no medicine of destruction nor a kingdom of Hades upon the earth' (Wisdom 1:14). Guard innocence and see uprightness, for it is a remnant for a peaceful man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peaceful man cannot be utterly destroyed and keeps a remnant, while the remnants of the ungodly fall into destruction together.
comments.comment:
This is what is meant. The one possessing virtue sees and perceives the uprightness. 'For there is a remnant for man, peaceful' (Psalm 37:37). This says that it is impossible for the peaceful man to be utterly destroyed. Even if he is left behind, he possesses a remnant. …

At the same time the lawless are being destroyed; for this is to fall upon the same destruction. 38 The remnants of the ungodly shall be destroyed. But there is a remnant for the peaceful. The remnants of the ungodly shall fall into destruction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the remnant of the peaceful man and the destruction of the lawless.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peaceful man has a legacy for the coming life, and the Lord saves the righteous in the time of tribulation and brings them out from sinners because they hoped in him.
comments.comment:
If you wish to understand according to the word the difference between iniquity and uprightness, if there is such a difference: if iniquity is the non-practice of the evil, uprightness is the state according to which we perform all things impassively; but if iniquity means the achievement of character, uprightness is the unbending contemplation of the dogmas of truth.

Either way, it commands to guard iniquity and to see uprightness as a remaining legacy for the coming life for the peaceful man, the hope that is not being shamed, of the ungodly being destroyed altogether at the same time according to the time of judgment. But the salvation of the righteous becomes by the Lord protecting them in the time of tribulation. To this is joined: 'But our salvation in the time of tribulation shall be' (Psalm 37:39). And there shall be for them also the finding of help from the Lord and to be rescued from enemies, but also to be taken out of the hand of sinners, that is, the practice of evil powers; because they hoped in Him (Psalm 37:40).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous receive their salvation from the Lord, not from men, and in trouble he shields them so they remain unhurt in the soul.
comments.comment: But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord. This says that even if the righteous should ever think they have not received salvation from men—such as Abel and how many others were targeted, righteous ones—their salvation is from the Lord, the eternal salvation, not the temporary. 39 And He is a defender of them in a time of tribulation. If a time of tribulation overtakes, He is a defender of them. He puts forth His own shield over them, so that they might remain unhurt, not at all in the body, but in the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains where the righteous find salvation and how the Lord is their defender.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By helping them the Lord rescues the righteous, and if not at once then at some time.
comments.comment: And the Lord will help them and will rescue them. By helping them, He rescues them. If not in this manner, then they shall be rescued at some time; for if they are targeted through piety and think they will die, but not by punishment. This is truly to be helped by God, to be rescued by God. And it has both: helping and rescuing. He rescues them from the surrounding pains.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Keeping the Sabbath means spending time in virtue and living pleasingly to God, and the one who becomes good is remembered.
comments.comment: For this reason, therefore, it is 'for the remembrance in the Sabbath' (Psalm 38:1). And since keeping the Sabbath is to spend time in virtue and to live pleasingly to God and to serve by doing what God wills, human life began from virtue; … Therefore, the one becoming in the good is remembered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He does not shun rebuke or discipline as such, but rebuke in anger and wrath, since discipline can come through instruction.
comments.comment:
'Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath' (Psalm 38:1). One does not avoid being rebuked or disciplined at all, but in anger and wrath. Yet it is possible for someone to be disciplined logically and systematically, according to what is signified by the holy one praying—or rather praising and blessing—saying: 'Blessed is the man whom you will discipline, Lord, and from your law you will teach him' (Psalm 94:12). He showed that this discipline happens through instruction.

And often there is also rebuke and discipline through anger and wrath, through harsh things, through bitter things. And often there is rebuke when the one in whom the error is, is shown by word to the responsible party; for it says: 'Rebuke the wise, and he will love you' (Prov 9:8). … But God sent a proclamation of repentance. They approached the proclamation. They were instructed and reproved, not in wrath or anger. For example, the Sodomites were reproved and instructed in wrath and anger. Therefore, He does not want to be reproved in this way …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist is asking: correction through instruction, not anger.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Anger and plague that fall on someone often show his sin, as Israel was handed over because of sins already committed.
comments.comment: often an anger and a plague that comes upon someone shows that person's sin. He endured much impiety, and was delivered to the Assyrians, and to the Babylonians into their hand; for it did not happen that the handing over of Israel occurred by chance, but because of sins previously committed; 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin' (Lamentations 1:8), and it became a reproach.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A memorial for the Sabbath means taking the beginning of some good, and the true Sabbath is kept by the one who lives beyond this six-day world with his mind in heaven.
comments.comment:
Remembrance differs from recollection; for one is reminded when another recalls the first things to him. Thus some have said that those desiring to be saved come 'into the knowledge of truth' (1 Tim 2:4). This is the same as 'into remembrance'. For one is reminded of what he knows. No one is said to be reminded of what he already says. … To take a memorial for the Sabbath is to have the beginning of some good.

The Sabbath means rest. To keep the Sabbath is not to keep it in the six days, but when one goes beyond these. This, in which we spend our time, the visible and the immediate, was brought about in six days. But when one goes beyond these and lives super-cosmically and super-heavenly in the heaven, he keeps the Sabbath in such a way. This is the true Sabbath of the Lord.

And for the one walking on earth but having his citizenship in the heavens, he has his mind keeping the Sabbath in the world while in heaven. And there they will one day have their heart and are already keeping the Sabbath, 'the sweet, holy Sabbath to God', to him who says: 'Come to me, all you who are weary and low in heart, and you will find rest for your souls' (Matt 11:28).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker confesses and asks to be reproved by word and taught by instruction, not struck in anger.
comments.comment:
A confessing person is introduced in this Psalm (Psalm 38:1). For he says, 'If they have struck me, what kind of thing is it that I should be reproved by passion and instructed by anger, but having repented, I ask to be reproved by word and not by passion, and to be instructed by teaching and not by anger.'

The metaphor of the arrows and the beatings sometimes makes clear, as it is said in those things that lead forward (Psalm 38:2). He says therefore: 'Since I have committed sins, punishment follows: Your arrows have pierced me' (Psalm 38:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Arrows stand for the punishments that divine instruction brings, as Job says the arrows of the Lord are in his body.
comments.comment: 'For your arrows have struck me' (Psalm 38:2). Because of this, I avoid the reproof that is in wrath and the instruction that is in anger, since 'your arrows have struck into me' (Psalm 38:2). … Often, the arrows of divine instruction signify the punishments; as if Job, having become in many afflictions, says: 'The arrows of the Lord are in my body' (Job 6:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the arrows in the verse stand for, with a parallel from Job.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His great suffering is like a body wounded all over, and these are signs of wrath whose cause is sin and which make a soul aware of its sins.
comments.comment: He compares his great suffering and many afflictions to a body entirely afflicted, as in Isaiah: From the soles of the feet to the head there is no soundness in it, but wounds and bruises, the burning inflammation of a threat (Isaiah 1:6) (Psalm 38:3). These are signs of wrath, and the cause of the wrath is sins, so that the sufferings bring awareness of sins, and in this way they benefit souls, just as bodies are brought from insensibility to sensation (Ps 37:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the body is pictured as afflicted and what the sufferings are for.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Only the one who repents sees the face of his sins; the sinner who does not know he sins does not.
comments.comment:
There is no peace to my bones from the face of my sins (Psalm 38:3), because I see my sins present.

But not everyone takes understanding of the face of them, but he who repents and wishes to flee them.

The one sinning and being ignorant of this very thing that he sins, does not see the face of his sins, nor does he see their shame.

But the one perceiving those things which he does, and seeing that he performs them according to the transgression of divine commands, has the face of the sins appearing to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'face of my sins': who sees it and who does not.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bones here mean the firm beliefs and powers of the soul, which have peace when they follow one another in order.
comments.comment: He does not say 'bones' of the body in every way, … so that he does not speak concerning the bones of the body, but concerning the solid beliefs of the soul and its powers; … Where is it said: 'There is no peace to my bones?'—when the powers of the soul follow one another, they are at peace. When the soul does not divide, when the powers of the soul follow one another in order, there is peace to the bones.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sins laid bare show that they are present, and iniquities press down the ruling principle like a weight that only the repenting person feels.
comments.comment:
'My sins being laid bare' (Psalm 38:3); for it is a sign that they are present that their face is seen.

He says that iniquities have raised their head above his own (Psalm 38:4), so as to press and weigh down his ruling principle, which is called the head, and that these have also, in a way, burdened him like a weight; for since the nature of evil is inferior and most heavy, it is compared to a talent of lead, only the one repenting perceives the weight of it, supposing it to be lighter when it is acting with pleasure. But Jesus calls those who toil and are burdened toward himself through repentance, those having felt the heaviness of sin and having toiled from it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The burden of evil weighs a person down, while Jesus' burden lifts him, and only one who feels evil's weight comes to Jesus.
comments.comment: They have become a heavy burden; they drag me down, though I ought to bear that burden which Jesus lays on and the yoke which he imposes; for there is a worthless burden, as this very saying says: 'my iniquities as a heavy burden were heavy upon me' (Psalm 38:4). 'Come,' then, he says, 'to me, for I will give you rest' (Matt 11:28); I take the burdens from you and the lying loads; 'for my yoke is kind and my burden is light' (Matt 11:30). This burden lifts up the bearer; it carries him upward; this burden is winged. But that of evil weighs down; it casts down. Indeed, concerning the worthless he says: 'you shall sink as lead in mighty water' (Ex 15:10). … And this too—to know that evil is a heavy burden—belongs not to everyone, but to the one who has perceived its burdensomeness. Then, indeed, one of those bearing this burden labors, when he perceives the weight of evil. And then he comes to Jesus.
comments.selected_reason: Sets the heavy burden of sin against the light burden Jesus offers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sores come from the stings of thoughts and desires, and they swell and rot when they are not healed quickly.
comments.comment:
'They swelled and my sores decayed from the face of my folly' (Psalm 38:5). I had sores from the arrows of punishment or from the burning arrows of the evil one; for it has also been said to have burning arrows. When someone receives impressions, that is, thoughts and memories of evils and impieties, he is in a sore. But when these have increased and having become unburdened they swell, then they also undergo putrefaction. 'They swelled' therefore 'and my sores decayed.' But from where did I have the sores, from where has their putrefaction happened? — 'from the face of my folly.' It is necessary to expose my folly and to turn away from it. Someone undergoes folly when he does not possess prudence.

The stings of thoughts and of desires, these make sores. It is necessary to heal these quickly. Someone saw a woman toward desire; he had a sore. Let him heal, and until the passion, let him set the anger in order; for in this way neither desire shall swell nor bring putrefaction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wounds of the verse as the sores that thoughts and desires leave in the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wretchedness comes to the soul from the body of death, which is the body used to sin and which can stop being such.
comments.comment:
I was wretched and was bowed down to the end. The unseemly and burdensome things often bring wretchedness. And the body itself indeed makes the one burdened wretched. This concept is submitted by the apostolic word which has it thus: 'Wretched am I, man; who will rescue me from the body of this death?' (Romans 7:24).
