Since indeed I am in the body of death, I am wretched, … We say, therefore, that wretchedness comes to the soul from the body of death.

We do not at once take the body of death to be any body, but a body of this kind. When someone uses this body as if to do sins toward death, a body of death remains surrounding him. But it is possible to make it not a body of death; for when I separate from it those things making it a body of death, it is no longer a body of death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wickedness bows down the one who has it, as sorrow presses on a person and as the sinner bends down and looks below.
comments.comment: Lowly wickedness is, it bows down the one possessing it; for always the great sorrows lie upon one, crushing and bowing down the one carrying them. Immediately, indeed, regarding her who had that 'spirit of infirmity' for eighteen years, it says: 'she was bent over and could not raise herself to the full.' She never raised herself up. The one sinning, therefore, bends down and looks below. It says, therefore: 'they set their eyes to bend down toward the earth' (Psalm 17:11); …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being bowed down means for the sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His mourning is the godly sorrow that leads to repentance, and he walks on and does not stay cast down.
comments.comment: I was walking, mourning all the day. Even if 'I was bowed down to the end' because of the approaching misery, I did not become insensitive to this. Mourning, therefore, I walk, 'working the godliness according to God, the sorrow leading to repentance unto salvation without regret' (2 Cor 7:10). And so mourning I walk all the day. And the 'I walk' is good. It does not remain cast down, but it walks. … 'Mourning,' therefore, 'I was walking.' Those things were working which were transferring me out of the misery. Then, however, I am transferred out of the misery, if I cast off the causes of the misery.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mourning of the verse as repentance that keeps moving.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While the soul is filled with the lessons of sin, the flesh cannot be healed or made peaceful.
comments.comment:
For my soul was filled with instructions. My soul was filled with sins. … Regarding sins: the deceiver plays with the deceived, and thus the soul is filled with lessons. In some copies, it says 'my loins.' It is said concerning these that the seeds consist. When someone is thus drawn into lawlessness and hastens more toward lust or toward being a lover of God, he has the loins filled with lessons.

“And there is no healing in my flesh” (Psalm 38:7). As long as I am filled with these lessons, not only is my flesh not healthy, but having become diseased and thus disposed, it does not receive healing. Just as it is impossible for a sensory person, while still in the state of being sick, to recover health, so the one filled with lessons is not able to make the flesh peaceful, that is, sober, or not divided against itself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flesh is weak and lacks self-control, and the soul is played with by present mockeries.
comments.comment: For they say that it is not possible to be in my flesh, because my soul has been played with by the mockeries of the present; for the flesh, flowing and lacking self-control, is very weak, and so he who commits fornication in the body sins (Psalm 38:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He humbled himself willingly so that he might be exalted, and he cried out from a heart that knows what to sigh for.
comments.comment:
“I was afflicted and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 38:8). It is possible to say 'I was afflicted and humbled' voluntarily. Since I have become in sensation of the swelling of evil and harm and blindness, I led myself volitionally toward humiliation so that I might be exalted; for “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Mt 23:12). …

“I cried out from the sighing of my heart” (Psalm 38:8). Not mockingly wailing about the evils surrounding me, but “from the sighing of my heart”; understanding in what kind of sighing one must sigh, a sigh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains his humbling as willing humility and his cry as coming from true sighing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous person always longs for virtue, and so all his desire can be placed before God.
comments.comment: “And all my desire is against you” (Ps 38:9). The righteous man always has love and longing for the virtues and for things done praiseworthily. It is indeed said concerning the righteous: “All the desire of the righteous is good” (Proverbs 11:23). … “Against you,” therefore, that is, before you, is “all my desire.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why all his desire can lie open before God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His groaning comes from the depth of repentance and a good desire to pass from wickedness into virtue.
comments.comment: From the depth of repentance, bringing forth groans through repentance, not from superficiality or pretension like the hypocrites of repentance; therefore also, daring, he says: 'To you, Lord, as truly the desire of my heart is before you' (Psalm 38:9; LXX 37:9b,10); for indeed all the vile impulse is far from you and is hidden from you, but the desire of my heart, desiring to pass from wickedness into genuine virtue, possesses a good desire, which one does not find in dreams. He may also speak concerning the vile desire: since the evil desire lying within me has not eluded you, confessing concerning this I groan, as if the groan concerning it, being bold, would not be hidden from you; for it is praiseworthy to groan over evils (Psalm 38:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not overlook a groaning that comes from a desire for goodness, unlike the groaning of one who only mourns not getting what he wants.
comments.comment: And my groaning was not hidden from you. Having a good desire and longing to be in goodness and virtue, I groan as much as I see myself failing. This groaning, however, comes from a desire for beauty, from the expectation of something better. Even if I often hide my groaning from many, so that I might not seem to be self-indulgent and appear to be repenting only outwardly, my groaning is 'moreover' to you; it was not hidden from you. The Egyptians indeed oppressed the Hebrews. When the 'sons of Israel' (Exodus 2:23) rejoiced in the works of the Egyptians, their groaning was hidden from the face of God. But when they began to groan over the works, when they perceived that the Pharaonic works were destroying both the land and, even more, were doing evil outside of God, then they groaned, and the groaning was not hidden from God; for He immediately set them free. When they were rejoicing, they were held there, and they did not attain freedom. This groaning corresponds to 'the sorrow that works repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10). This sorrow is another from that of the world, which works death. If, indeed, you see a man groaning because he does not attain what he desires, even if they are bad things, this groaning is destructive.
comments.selected_reason: Shows which groaning God hears, using Israel in Egypt as the example.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the heart is troubled, strength leaves, but whoever imitates the gentle and humble Jesus is outside all such trouble and keeps his strength.
comments.comment: My heart was troubled, and my strength left me. When the heart is troubled, that is, the mind, then strength becomes distant. Strength is that which is appropriate to the peace and stability of the heart. He who learned from Jesus 'that He is gentle and humble in heart' (Matthew 11:29) does not have a troubled heart; for he imitates Jesus. And he who imitates Jesus is outside of all trouble. Until he does not have this trouble, strength remains with him, so as to say: 'I can do all things in Him who strengthens me' (Philippians 4:13), and: 'I will love you, Lord, my strength' (Psalm 18:1).
comments.selected_reason: Connects a troubled heart with lost strength, and strength with the peace of imitating Jesus.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The light of the eyes is the knowledge that comes from keeping the Lord's commandment, and it leaves the one who does not guard it.
comments.comment:
For those seeing sharply, the knowledge of truth is present; for it has been said: 'light up for yourselves a light of knowledge' (Hosea 10:12). For the word is not about these eyes nor about sensible light; listen to the one saying: 'the commandment of the Lord is far-reaching, enlightening eyes' (Psalm 19:8). Indeed, the keeping of the far-reaching commandment enlightens the eyes of the inner man; …

It is not, therefore, at all about the eyes that it is said: 'and the light of my eyes is not with me' (Psalm 38:10). He has left me, because I turned away from it, because I myself did not guard it to remain with me.
comments.selected_reason: Says that the light of the eyes is not bodily light but knowledge that obeying the commandment gives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His heart is in turmoil, and strength and the light of the mind have left him so that he cannot think clearly.
comments.comment: Of my heart—that is, of my intellectual power—undergoing turmoil, my strength according to common understandings has abandoned me, but also the knowledge of the truths, the light of my eyes—that is, being the mind—is not with me; for having determined according to reason, I will not be able to conceive clearly or to think strongly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Friends stand against a man in times of trouble, as Job also said.
comments.comment: 'My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood opposite me' (Psalm 38:11). Such things happen in circumstantial times. And Job, having been born in distress, said such things: 'My friends have become merciless, they have known others as three times more than I' (Job 19:13). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man who falls is abandoned by friends and neighbors and accused by those he loved, while his enemies argue against him with deceit.
comments.comment: One should speak thus: if anyone falls by various circumstances, he is abandoned by all those who were previously near him, both friends and neighbors, just as he is also accused by the one he formerly loved. These images are found in Job. And those who, seeking my soul harmfully and through strife, came forward and wished to surround me with violence, thought they were leading me down with coercive words as if they were proofs; but they hurried to subject me to the investigation of evils, through which vanity spoke to me. For the argument was not as a proof, but as a vain and deceptive sophistry. And the vanity through which they sophistically argue all day long, that is, through life, they practice deceit, not bringing proofs to the things, but deciding to seize the mind sophistically.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Friends deserting and enemies rising were seen in the Savior's sufferings, where he kept the silence foretold.
comments.comment: He laments the desertion of friends and the uprising of enemies, which are also seen in the Savior's sufferings, when the disciples were scattered in fear, and the wicked used every bitterness and malice against him, toward whom he also fulfilled the silence predicted here.
comments.selected_reason: Short and clear: reads the psalm's friends, enemies and silence in the Savior's sufferings.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He had just grounds to answer his slanderers but bore the accusations in silence, knowing that speech would do them no good.
comments.comment: Having, he says, just grounds to answer those who slandered him, but knowing that speech would not be for their benefit, I bore the false accusations without resentment (Psalm 38:13). And as one who does not hear, I was silent, and as one who has no reproof. For what would I say and answer? It was for nothing, as the Lord also said: If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask you, you will not answer (Luke 22:67-68). When people do not listen, speech is useless toward them, but useful toward God who hears.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason for the silence in the verse: speech is useless toward those who do not listen.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To be deaf to bad conversation is sometimes right, when one cannot rebuke it or knows that rebuking it would do no good.
comments.comment: Regarding 'rebuke'—it is said in a double sense; often one is unable to rebuke. One lacks such boldness or such power of speech as to rebuke, and so pretends not to hear. For example, a heretic is present, speaking atheistic doctrines and heretical opinions. If we are unable to rebuke the things said by him, we are called 'men who do not hear,' for rather than benefiting, hearing such conversations causes agitation. For it has been said: 'Bad conversations corrupt good morals.' If anyone possessing a good character knows this—that he cannot stand against bad conversations—he is not obliged to provide his hearing, but rather to become as if deaf. Another, possessing the ability to rebuke the most shameful conversations, does not do this when he knows that it is not at all effective to rebuke him in that way; for it was said that just as foods are administered medically at the right time, so also are the aids to the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Deafness toward impious words is fair when there is no hope of correcting those who speak them.
comments.comment: We must expect impiety's prophet too — perhaps not one but more — speaking to us as the Lord's 'word' what the Lord 'commanded not,' or a wisdom-word foreign to wisdom, to kill us with his mouth's word. But even then, when the sinner stands against us, let us say: 'But I as one deaf heard not, and as one dumb who opens not his mouth. And I became as a man who hears not.' For deafness toward impious words is fair, when we despair of correcting those who say the worse (Psalm 38:13-14).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like a deaf and dumb man, the one guarding himself neither hears nor answers deceitful words, since even hearing them is dangerous.
comments.comment: He who judges to guard himself will be deafened, not receiving vain hearing toward the deceitful and deceptive words, not wishing to have their sense from hearing (Psalm 38:13-14); and much more, he would not wish to answer or to refute such words, like a senseless person. For it is said in other places that it is foolish to refute very gentle words. 'I became, he says, toward such men as if not hearing and not having reproaches in my mouth.' For there is much danger in hearing defamatory words and in conversing about proposed problems which lead to punishment. Therefore, it is blessed to be deaf to such things and to be considered as if one were not refuting them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He stays deaf to the reproaches and does not answer them, leaving vengeance to the Lord so as not to lose his readiness to repent.
comments.comment: Having been tested and having experienced the despair of salvation, I myself am being subjected to such thoughts, being deaf and unable to hear, not wishing to refute them, lest by being found guilty of this, I should lose the brief readiness for repentance. For, O Lord, not hoping, I do not dare to assume I will be heard. For, being unable to defend myself, I endure the defense, knowing: 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for the wrath, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord' (Romans 12:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because he hoped in God, who will hear him, he kept silent as if deaf and cried out to God in his mind.
comments.comment: 'For in you, Lord, I have hoped; You will hear me, Lord my God' (Psalm 38:15). Since I hoped in You, You will hear me. I am confident that all things that are possible for him to be present with me, shall be present. Therefore, being confident in You, the Greater One, and the One who knows how to rebuke and whom it is necessary to rebuke, I kept silent, as if I had become deaf, not having rebukes in my mouth. And thus it must be said: 'Since I hoped in You, You will hear me'; for having become deaf and mute toward him and not having rebukes in my mouth, I cried out toward You in my mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the silence of the verse as confidence in God, who hears.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He hopes in God alone and prays, since others bring up his past deeds to hinder his repentance.
comments.comment: Since, having despised all others, I hoped in you alone, O Lord, and You being God, will hear me; having prayed, I began, O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger (Psalm 38:15). For often those who associate with me, even if they sinned, bring the past deeds as insults, as if through this to hinder my repentance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He kept silent so that the enemy would not rejoice over him, for the one who falls will rise and the mockery will turn to lamentation.
comments.comment: For this reason I was silent and became as deaf and as having no reproofs, lest, if I dared these things, becoming stronger, they rejoice over me; they shall mock against me. For this reason the apostle also says: do not do this, 'lest Satan rejoice over you because of your guilelessness'. He then rejoices over the one being harmed. 'I will exalt you, O Lord, for you upheld me, and did not gladden my enemies over me' (Psalm 30:1). For if you had not upheld me, they would have rejoiced, not rightly nor in the fitting manner exalting you. And in other places he says: 'Rejoice not over me, my enemy, for I have fallen' (Mic 7:8); 'and I shall rise'. You rejoice over my fall, but know that I shall rise. When then I stand, your joy turns into mourning, and the mocking songs turn into lamentations. 'And when my feet were shaken, they boasted against me' (Psalm 38:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fear that enemies will rejoice, and answers it: the one who falls will rise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man whose feet are only shaken has not fallen, and that is a stronger position than the one who rises after falling.
comments.comment: They magnified me as if I were a fallen corpse, speaking words of pride. One might say in another way: 'Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; I shall stand up.' But he who speaks now says I did not fall at all, but only my feet were shaken; for if one who falls stands up and leaves the enemy's triumph, he is much more than one who never fell. It is easier to stand and steady the feet when one is shaken than to rise up having fallen. Therefore, if the difficult thing happens, the easy thing is much more quickly established.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He is ready to be lashed by God, as a beloved son is disciplined, though he refuses to be treated as one overturned.
comments.comment: For I am ready for lashes. Even if I am in motion and my strength has left me and the light of my eyes is not with me and my feet were shaken, I am ready for lashes; for I do not refuse to be lashed by you, as one whom you discipline as a beloved son. 'Do not slight the Lord's discipline; for whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and He lashes every son whom He receives' (Heb 12:5-6). Since therefore I am a son, even if I have shared in the cause of lashes myself, I refuse to be magnified by them, that is, their treating me as one being overturned. But I am ready to be lashed by you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the readiness for lashes as the discipline a father gives a son.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His pain stays before him as long as he has its causes, like the mourner who weeps as long as he sees the dead.
comments.comment: And my pain is before me always. I suffer because I have become entirely among those who bring rebukes, those who bring lashes. He who grieves the 'godly sorrow that brings repentance unto salvation' (2 Cor 7:10) has this pain added to himself always. Just as one who has a dead person and wails over him, weeping as much as he sees him, so the one who has come into the bringing of lashes wails and weeps as much as he sees them, and has this pain added to himself always.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pain stays while its causes remain, but once healed he will suffer no more.
comments.comment: As far as I have the causes of the pain, I have it continually added to me. If, therefore, you, having heard, offer a helpful secondary remedy like the lashes in a useful way, once healed, I will no longer suffer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He is ready to be struck for his past sins, since the pain always before him is what turns him back.
comments.comment: I am ready and well-disposed toward the lashes of the senses. Indeed, even my pain, through which I suffer for past deeds, is before me, wounding and scourging me. And it can be so; since my pain is such that, while I suffer for the evils I have done, it is necessary to receive lashes besides the sins, I am ready for these, that is, I am ready to be struck for the sake of returning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He declares his lawlessness without hiding it and does not wait to be accused, since one must accuse himself first.
comments.comment: For I will proclaim my lawlessness. He says this: by proclaiming my lawlessness, I do not hide the pain; for always remembering and going through it, having the pain, that I have become in it. And I do not proclaim it only so much as to want to find the one healing it. … For I proclaim it, I do not hide it, I do not wait for what is from without to convict me, I do not wait for another to say to me: 'You are in sin and lawlessness.' … 'say you the sins first, so that you may be justified.' Do not wait for the accuser. One must be an accuser in his own first instance; for if this happens, then he is ashamed, since you cared about your sin, how you might no longer act it.
comments.selected_reason: Teaches that a repenting person declares his own sin first and does not wait for an accuser.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be sorry for one's sin is to remember it and hurry to make the work of repentance right.
comments.comment: The clear sympathy toward us is the memory of the one's own suffering throughout. For, as Paul says, since he himself has suffered, he is able to help those being tempted. Just as according to the law, he who commits sin was mindful of those being offered as a sacrifice for it, so it is to care for one's own sin, hurrying to make the work of repentance right.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks God to strike him with strong remedies so that he may be healed, since the sins that live in him feed his wickedness until Jesus crushes Satan.
comments.comment: And my enemies live and are prevailing against me. For this reason I call upon you as a helper; for this reason I have made myself compliant toward being scourged by you. … To sin and to have lawlessness—'they live and are held fast against me' (Psalm 38:19)—for they nourish my wickedness; therefore, do what I ask of me: 'I am anxious' (Psalm 38:18) 'concerning my sin.' Therefore, strike me, bring near strenuous helps, so that I may be healed; for then the rest become weaker than me, they are crushed under my feet; for Jesus alone is able to crush Satan under the feet of the saints. And again: 'And the God of peace will crush Satan under your feet quickly' (Rom 16:20). As long as neither he nor those after him is being crushed, they live.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be hated unjustly means to be hated without fault, as the elders hated Susanna and Egypt hated Joseph.
comments.comment: And those hating me unjustly were multiplied (Psalm 38:19). However, great is the praise that he hated not justly. For instance, if someone were to hate someone as if he were proud when he is not proud, but also entirely blind, he hates him unjustly. The elders who rose up against Susanna hated her because they did not find her fault. This hatred is unjust. Egypt hated Joseph. This hatred is unjust.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'hating unjustly' with examples from Susanna and Joseph.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who hate him for repenting are strong in their bad life, but when God is present the enemies are weak.
comments.comment: While I care for my own sin, those who hate me because I have repented live according to the bad life, being strong and powerful to make me weak according to this life. If even they cast me off as a dead thing to be loathed, but You cover me under Your mighty hand; for when You are present, the enemies are weak and feeble.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word persecute here means to pursue after righteousness, as in 'Seek peace and pursue it'.
comments.comment: They beset me, because they persecuted righteousness. I did not harm them; for no one is 'justly pursuing the righteous' (Deuteronomy 16:20) and persecuting righteousness—the 'persecuted' here does not mean to pursue in a hating way, but to pursue after, as it signifies. Just as if one says: 'Seek peace and pursue it' (Ps 34:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He did them good and they gave him evil in return, rejecting him as a loathsome dead thing though he loved them.
comments.comment: I worked good things for them, and it was necessary for them to receive good from me instead of good. But 'evils' 'instead of good' they provide to me, being unfeeling, as they are of the evil ones; and in what disposition I am toward them, I am such as not rejoicing in their evils, but loving them and desiring to make them outside of the evils. The beloved of me, whom it was necessary to love, they rejected as a dead thing to be loathed, as if they were fleeing from me, a stinking corpse.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the evil rendered for good: he worked good for them and loved them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ speaks these words in place of human beings, asking for their salvation as his own, for he is never alone since the Father is with him.
comments.comment: Human beings would not say these things about themselves, but Christ, in place of human beings and for human beings, suffering as a righteous one at the hands of the unrighteous and taking what is theirs upon himself, would say them: in one place, Why have you forsaken me? (Psalm 22:1) in another, Do not forsake me, and Do not depart from me, since this is impossible for him (Psalm 38:21). For I am not alone, he says, because my Father is with me. He asks for the salvation of human beings as his own, having something proper to the request as far as the human element in the mixture with divinity is concerned—this was the passible element naturally united to the flesh—and also having the dignity of the nature that transcends, by which he fulfilled the things of the request.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He needs help against evil men and unseen powers, and seeks it from the Lord alone.
comments.comment: Since I am surrounded by enemies, both evil men and invisible powers, I need help; I do not require help from another, but from You, Lord; for You also are found to be the God of my salvation, and the cause of this salvation is God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the closing plea for help: the psalmist looks to no helper but the Lord, the God of his salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David set singers over the ark, and the speaker of this psalm is shown passing from repentance into virtue.
comments.comment: King David, having brought the ark of God into Jerusalem, arranged certain men as singers for its liturgy and order, so that the hymns of God might be heard. Regarding these, even Jeduthun, as in the list and numbering of the previously mentioned songs in the Chronicles, carries something like this. He who composed the present psalm himself on behalf of David, or having received it from David, proclaimed it. And in the present psalm, the one proclaiming is introduced from repentance into virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm is a victory song, sung after the enemy is conquered, as Moses and Israel sang only when Pharaoh was drowned.
comments.comment:
This is one of the Psalms. In Ezra and in the Book of the Remaining, there is a memory of each name of those being submitted. And this, then, is one of them, or perhaps he himself composed the psalm, or received it from David and proclaimed it. And it is the work of the Psalms to say their psalms, both those they themselves composed and those others arranged.

This, then, is a victory song. Often the sinner is troubled by these things, but after conquering and trampling him and taking him under hand, the psalmist sends back the song; for no one sings a victory song while still warring and being warred against, but in the having conquered. Likewise, Moses and all the Jewish multitude did not say a victory song when they were against Pharaoh, but when they saw him become a drowning man: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously He has been glorified; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' Ex 15:1. …

And David says in the seventy-first psalm: 'In the day when he rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, then he said: I will love you, O Lord my strength' (Psalm 18:1), and all the rest which the song contains. It is a prayer before the war and in the war, but a victorious hymn and song after the destruction of the war, after capturing the enemies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Almost every sin begins in speech, so whoever does not sin with the tongue guards all his ways well.
comments.comment:
I said: 'I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue' (Psalm 39:1). For almost every practical sin has its beginning in the word. …

If, therefore, someone does not sin in the tongue, he guards the ways well; for he said that the beginning of these ways is the word. And from the opposite of all good works, the word is the beginning. But he does not speak only about those ways; he added, 'so as not to sin in my tongue' (Psalm 39:1). Yet sinning in the tongue is not the same as saying, 'My tongue will meditate on your righteousness' (Psalm 35:28). 'The beginning of your words is truth' (Ps 119:160). The cause of saying your words is your truth; I will make this manifest if I know it. Therefore, upon the virtues and the well-flowing ways, truth is the beginning, the cause. But upon the forbidden ways, from which it is necessary to guard oneself and from which it is proper to turn away, the word is the beginning, as has already been said.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist guards his tongue in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because a man is justified or condemned by his words, the mouth needs a guard so that it speaks what is good and keeps silent about what is harmful.
comments.comment: I set a guard upon my mouth (Psalm 39:1). Remember how he said 'not to sin in the tongue': 'I set a guard upon my mouth.' Since 'from the words someone is justified and from his words he is condemned' (Matt 12:37), it is necessary for the mouth to place a guard, so that I may say the good things and not the bad, that we may speak the profitable things and be silent about the harmful ones; for no one is able at once to bring forth words that both justify and condemn. Something like this is said with an enigma in the proverbs: 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). And the 'hand' of the 'tongue' is the word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Life or death is in the tongue, so one must weigh words and open the lips only for what is beneficial.
comments.comment: The activity of the tongue. He who speaks what is beneficial and leads into the kingdom of life has life in the tongue. But he who speaks the opposite and the forbidden things has death in his own word called a 'tongue'. And in another scripture it says: 'With your words make a balance and a weight' (Sirach 28:25). It is necessary to speak having weighed; it is necessary to have a balance and to cast the words upon each scale. And if the upright words are found to be balanced, it is proper to choose those and to proclaim them, but to turn away from the bad ones. Again it is said: 'The lips of the wise are taught by perception' (Proverbs 15:7). When someone speaks having perceived, the lips are taught, not opening them to every word, but to what is beneficial. 'I will open my lips and my mouth shall proclaim your praise' (Ps 51:14). He who has the taught lips, having perceived that what he intends to speak is beneficial, opened them. But when they harm what is being uttered, he closes and binds the lips with perception; he binds the word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because almost every sin begins in speech, the speaker binds himself to keep from sinning with the tongue, so that cleansing from sins of action may follow.
comments.comment: Since almost every beginning of sin occurs through speech, he intending to guard his ways through actions sets covenants with himself, so that he might not sin with the tongue. For if the sinless state regarding speech is kept by him, the cleansing from sins according to action will follow; 'For by your words you shall be justified,' he says, 'and by your words you shall be condemned' (Matthew 12:37); and 'Amen I say to you: regarding every idle word you shall give an account on the day of judgment' (Matthew 12:36).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the penitent guards his mouth, the sinner stands against him, reminding him of his former deeds to mock him and drag him back into sin.
comments.comment: After the verse, the sinner and there the devil and the evil angel present with the man are called. If anyone, intending to guard his ways for himself so as not to sin in tongue, sets a guard for his mouth, the sinner, representing himself as such in opposition to the one repenting, reminds him of former things, bringing them into the midst as a reproach, wishing to mock through the reminder, so as to drag back into the former sin the one who has turned away from it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the sinner stands against him to provoke him, he keeps silent out of good judgment, which is wisdom and not a refusal to speak good things.
comments.comment:
'In the standing of the sinner against me, I was made deaf and humbled, and I kept silence for the sake of good things' (Psalm 39:1-2). Often appearing, the sinner provokes and is called out to the things pleasing to him. If, therefore, he ever stands against us, it is our part to make him stand; for if we do not give him a place, he is not able to stand. But to stand in this way is to stand in battle. It is necessary to be silent; for he often provokes; because the serpent, having stood against Eve, provoked her word and harmed her. It was necessary to be silent, having received perception of her own weakness or of the sin that had come before, not to speak anything to her, but to keep silence for the sake of good things.

And the 'keeping silence for the sake of good things' does not say 'not to speak the good things', but to have a silence made wise from the good things. For example, having taken up virtue, a prudent man knew that he must not respond out of the good, that is, out of prudence. I kept silence toward the standing revealed and provoking toward sin. If, therefore, that young man had been responding to nothing from right understanding toward the harlot, he would not have 'been led astray by much association' (Proverbs 7:21) nor 'been enticed by the morsels of his lips' (Proverbs 7:21). I kept silence, therefore, when the good things had come upon me, persuading me not to respond to him. He does not say: 'I kept silence so as not to speak the good things', but 'so as not to speak the provoking things'. …

He who thus remains silent is found wise. And it is indeed wisdom to know to whom one must speak and to whom one must not, and when to bring forward words and when not. "He is therefore found wise while being silent, and he is silent, for he has no answer." And this man possesses a certain quietness of mind; for having known that he has no answer, he keeps peace. "And he is wise, being silent, knowing the right time." This man is perfect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist kept silent before the sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sorrow is renewed when the sinner looks again at what he has done, and it is blessed for the sinner to renew sorrow and not pleasure.
comments.comment: And "my sorrow was renewed" (Psalm 39:2). Then the sorrow is renewed when the sinner stands in reflection upon what he has done, upon which it is necessary to grieve. And just as the sorrow received a renewal, renewal is to dwell in a house at first. A renewal, therefore, is to lead that which has already withered and is silent into flowering. "My sorrow" therefore "was renewed." Having said, "I kept my ways not to sin with my tongue" (Psalm 39:1), I knew that I had sinned. Therefore "my sorrow was renewed." And it is blessed for one who has sinned to experience a renewal of sorrow and not of pleasure; for he who rejoices over what he has done and brings those things back into the midst again, renews the sin. But he who grieves, having perceived that it is necessary to guard the ways and not to sin with the tongue, renews the sorrow, weeping and grieving, "working the sorrow according to God, which is repentance."
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the renewing of sorrow means for a penitent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was silent toward the sinner but spoke in his own tongue to God, as one speaking from genuine desire and not deceitfully in a foreign tongue.
comments.comment: With the verse set before him, the fire of such study consumes the pre-existing exhaustion. Regarding the sinner he says: 'I was deaf and humbled and was silent' (Psalm 39:3); but regarding God: 'I spoke in my tongue' (Psalm 39:3). He who brings forth words in his own tongue from genuine desire and intention is different from him who speaks deceitfully in a foreign tongue. And since we have a tongue even within the human being, which is strictly our own tongue, by which it is possible to speak from a disposition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A heart that burns within from meditation, without bursting out in word or deed, has a fire that is to be praised, since fire can reshape as well as destroy.
comments.comment: Having experienced a disturbance in thought or in reasoning, and having done nothing according to that disturbance of thoughts, nor even having spoken, he possesses the state of having been disturbed and not having spoken. Such a person has within him a heart having been warmed. 'And in my meditation fire shall be kindled' (Psalm 39:3). My inner self. And thus for each of us, two men have stood, One is outside, the other inside. Therefore, when a disturbance arises in the soul and does not transfer the disturbance to the outer man, but keeps it within so as to recognize it and weep over it, he has within him a heart having been warmed, not in order to act, but in order not to act. 'In my meditation the fire burns.' In others, by voice and by action and by thought, a fire burns, consuming them, burning them. 'Their heart was warmed like a fiery furnace.' Here the meditation is like a fire that has burned, with something to burn beneath. And the meditation and the heat of the Holy Spirit is the all-consuming, which comes to pass by the blowing Spirit. Therefore the fire burns in order that it may act, not in order that it may harm and consume. 'Was not our heart burning within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Lk 24:32). This burning is to be praised. And observe also regarding manufactured things: some are heated in order that they may be reshaped and become a vessel, gold or silver. But if wood or something else is set on fire, the heat is harmful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fire in the heart and why such burning can be good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heart grows hot from the renewal of sorrow and from intense self-scrutiny, and the heat stays within rather than spreading outside as it does in those burning with passion.
comments.comment: "My heart was warmed within me" (Psalm 39:3). One may say: my heart has received heat just as warmth, and from the renewal of sorrow. And one may also say this: because I seized myself intensely and I am being consumed and I weep aloud the sorrow, "my heart was warmed," it has become fiery. "In" indeed "my practice, a fire burned up" (Psalm 39:3), consuming and making me ash; for they were hay and wood and other things. I have this consuming fire not only in the being perfected, but also in my practicing the sorrow. And the "within me" is also good. The heart becomes hot so that the heat spreads even to the outside. Those, indeed, who are burning with passion do not have a heart warmed within, but, having spread to the outside, they have the state of one being pressed. It is as if it were said: "I was troubled and I did not speak."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heat was kept within, and fire burned in his meditation.
comments.comment: From the words of the one standing as a sinner before me, my heart was heated, being consumed by fire. But since I said nothing from such thoughts within me, the heating was guarded, and 'In my meditation fire shall be burned' (Psalm 39:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hearing the enemy's bold and abusive words, he was kindled with indignation for the righteousness being dishonored.
comments.comment: And hearing, he says, and reckoning up the bold and abusive words of the enemy, and seeing how great an authority of speech he used, to whom it was not fitting even to speak, I was kindled with indignation on behalf of the righteousness that was being dishonored (Psalm 39:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what stirred the heat in the heart.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist spoke in his own tongue, a true word from one who really desires to know his end, and not in the counterfeit tongue of a hypocrite.
comments.comment: 'I spoke in a tongue.' Even if I did not let it become outward, but it remained within me, through a burning from meditation it made itself for me, and so I spoke in a tongue: 'Make known to me, Lord, my end' (Psalm 39:4). From my own tongue I said this; for the tongue as shaped by its owner is this: for example, the temperate man, speaking the things of temperance, speaks in his own tongue, the tongue of the temperate man, not that of a human deceiver. And the one desiring to learn his own end and to offer his life to God, in my tongue, not in the tongue of a deceitful man, but I, desiring to know my end, spoke in a tongue. This my word is not a counterfeit. When a hypocrite speaks concerning temperance while not being temperate, he does not speak in his own tongue. But the temperate man, when he delivers discourses concerning temperance, speaks in the tongue of the temperate man. No hypocrite, therefore, speaks in the natural tongue, but in the counterfeit tongue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that he spoke in his own tongue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeing how much he lacks, the psalmist asks to know his end so that he may know whether the time left is enough to reach completion.
comments.comment: This is therefore what I say; since I saw myself lacking much—for I had only just begun to progress—'Make known to me, Lord, my end,' so that I might know how much time of life remains to me, if it is sufficient for completion and fulfillment. Thus also another was saying: 'Declare to me the brevity of my days; do not bring me back in the midst of my days' (Psalm 102:24). In a certain way, I am in the midst of the days that come from the Holy Light. Do not then bring me back in such a way. Therefore, fulfill my days.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'The number of my days' can mean the number of his enlightenments, since each enlightenment is a day, so that he may know what he lacks.
comments.comment: But God fulfills the days of some not by providing an increase of them; for when it is said, 'I will fill him with length of days' concerning the righteous, we do not say that he makes him many-years. There are also impious people who have lived many years. 'And the number of my days' (Psalm 39:4). It is also possible to say 'the number of my days' meaning: you have enlightened me much, I have become composed of days; for each enlightenment is a day. Therefore, reveal to me the number of my enlightenments, so that I might know what I lack.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'the number of my days'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As a student of any science asks to learn its principles so as to know what he lacks, so the psalmist asks for his end and the number of his days.
comments.comment: As if someone, having taken up a desire for art or science, lest he should have a perfect knowledge of his education, says: 'Reveal to me what are the luminous things of science, so that I might know what I have and what I lack.' It is blessed to have things, works, and thoughts that are countable, those worthy of being numbered. … So that I might know what I lack. If I learn the number of my days and my end, until when it is reached, I recognize in what things I lack, which are the things I have not yet learned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since a wise man works toward a goal, the psalmist asks to know the end set for his life and what he still lacks for perfection.
comments.comment: Since I have begun to live according to human life and expect its end, this is not clear to me; make known to me my end, so that having learned the multitude of the years of life in the flesh, I may know whom I must aim for (Psalm 39:4). What have I accomplished, and what is lacking to me for the completion of perfection? And so it is: since every wise man acts and works toward a certain perfection and goal, it is necessary to have knowledge of this, to know what the end is set for living and what is the number of the days according to the decrees of truth. For one is not wise if he does not know what he lacks for the fulfillment of the goal; just as one intending to take up a certain science asks the teacher: 'Show me how many the decrees of the science are, so that I may know which they are, and by which I lack the peak.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David asks to know his end like a conscientious steward who foresees the judgment and wants to make up what is lacking before he departs.
comments.comment: If you wish, listener, to see the fear of a steward managing what was entrusted with sober piety, unfold the book of David; seek those words where the man of many deeds says to God concerning his own end: 'O Lord, make known to me my end, and who is the number of my days, so that I may know what I am lacking' (Psalm 39:4). See how the disposition of the one who has made a vow is viewed through the word as if in an image: that he is bound, and he foresees the future and awaits the judgment, and he examines the appointed time, so that the unexpected arrangement might not seize him at the moment of departure; and having calculated, he seeks to see what the deficiency of his sojourn is, so that having hurried, he might make up for it before the one leading out comes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer to know one's end through the picture of a steward.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: He calls his days wrestling matches, both because the old days have grown old and passed and because we always have those who fight against us, men and evil powers.
comments.comment:
"Behold, I have made my days into wrestling matches." The former reading, this more common one, is: "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." I am not young or a newborn, not having begun to live just now, but "I have made my days into old wrestling matches." And this must be said: that which approaches always makes old that which has passed. Thus also laws grow old. Therefore he says: the old days which I had, when I lived as a man of old, have grown old and have departed; I have clothed myself in the new. …

Since the name "wrestler" is homonymous—meaning also the one contending in the arena, and also indicating a certain measure—it is possible to take it both ways. He says: "I have made my days into wrestling in the arena"; for we always have those who fight against us. At times human temptation comes and fights and wears out human passions, and at other times evil powers; for "our wrestling is not against blood and flesh"—for us, but for others, yes—"but against the principalities, against the powers" (Ephesians 6:12). In order that this may be, "I have made my days into wrestling matches."
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the days are called wrestling matches.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Hypostasis' means both a being's essence and its endurance under hardship, so in saying his is as nothing before God the psalmist speaks of both.
comments.comment: And my hypostasis is as nothing before you (Psalm 39:5). The name of hypostasis signifies many things. Regarding the present, there is a need for two meanings. Sometimes essence is called hypostasis; for instance, when the Son is called the 'character of the divine hypostasis' (cf. Heb 1:3), meaning the divine essence and existence. Hypostasis is also called perfect endurance, by which someone stands firm against hardships. Thus he speaks in both senses: 'the essence of my soul is nothing before you' (Psalm 39:5), as if toward you a certain great essence. And saying that it ought to be perfect according to you, the Father, I diminished it. … And since it also signifies endurance, he says: even if I endured desiring to see my end and I entreat you that you make this known to me, yet my endurance is not something brief in this way toward you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Other mortal things are vanity, but man alone is living, and yet the man who lives only by the human standard is himself vain.
comments.comment: Moreover, all things are vanity, every living man (Psalm 39:5). This must be known in two ways: all things are vanity through man, as the Preacher has clearly interpreted. Regarding the things that have ascended above and are perfect and truly eternal, the hypostasis is vain, except 'every living man.' Thus it is possible to say: even if all other things apart from man are vanity, such as mortal animals, the transient things, even if they are soulless, man alone is living, living according to that life which they live according to Abraham; for 'God is not of the dead, but of the living' (Mk 12:27). And the man who lives according to the human standard is himself vain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even a living man who lives well is nothing beside the divine life of God, the fountain of life, for small and great are said only in comparison.
comments.comment:
They are no longer. But the man is living. Even if he should die, he still lives. Or in this way: a man living who does not become outside of human life is himself vanity; so that it is thus: 'except all things are vanity and every living man' (Psalm 39:5). Or in this way: 'except all things are vanity, but the man is living'. Beyond this: the essence? Even if the man lives differently than a mortal would live, in view of the excellence and the greatness of the divine life and of God himself, the fountain of life, he is nothing.

The small things and the things no smaller than small are said in relation to something. And the small does not have a limited amount; for it is said in reference to the greater. We say, for instance, that the wrestler is greater than the boxer. Indeed, you have in categories a small mountain and a large gulf.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was enrolled to contend, first against blood and flesh and then against the rulers of this darkness, and his existence compared with God's seems to be nothing.
comments.comment: Having passed from life into the struggle, I was enrolled to contend, as at the beginning having the wrestling match against blood and flesh, but having surpassed the child and becoming a man, I am at the beginning against the rulers of the powers of this darkness, so that the struggle may be mine (Psalm 39:5). This signifies that the Wrestler is the same as 'In the struggle, set my days' (Psalm 39:5). Now it is possible for hypostasis to be said instead of Essence, such that the saying is this: my existence, being compared to yours, does not seem to be anything.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the images in which men walk are many and mostly false and deceptive, many are disturbed.
comments.comment: When he signifies the life of man, he says, 'every man lives' (Psalm 39:5), and 'yet a man wanders in an image'—not in the same one, but because the images are diverse, and especially because many are false and deceptive, many are being disturbed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every man walks in some image, heavenly or earthly, and that he can walk in either shows that he governs himself and is not good or evil by his make.
comments.comment:
However, even if he is living, he does not always have this motion; 'but indeed', for he says, 'a man wanders in an image' (Psalm 39:6). He did not say whether he wanders in praise or in mockery; but however anyone wanders, however he acts, he is in some image. Taking it more generally, it is to be said that it is either of the heavenly or of the earthly. And it is shown from such a word that the man is self-determining; for if he were good by construction, he would always wander in the heavenly, if he were evil by essence, in the earthly.

And it is possible to divide these general images into kinds. And I say that one is in the image of a fox, another in the image of a lion, … and another in the image of a dove, except 'in an image every man wanders'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that man walks in an image.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man who stores up wealth on earth does not know who will gain it, so he should store up righteousness in heaven, where the heart and mind will be.
comments.comment:
And he therefore speaks of the vain trouble, because this striving concerning human things is such. For instance, he 'stores up' 'and does not know to whom he gathers them' (Psalm 39:6). He stores up and does not know to whom he gathers them. …

And often what one has treasured, he leaves behind. Sometimes, as a year passes, he falls away into other things. Therefore, it is not necessary to be anxious about treasuring in this way; for 'lawless treasures will not profit, but righteousness rescues from death' (Proverbs 10:2). Therefore, the righteousness that rescues from death and from every other evil is to be treasured. This wealth is treasured in heaven.

'Do not treasure for yourselves treasures on earth, but treasure treasures in heaven' (Matt 6:19-21); because where the treasure is, there also the mind is, which is called the 'heart'. It is to be treasured in heaven so that we may have the mind there, and one should refrain from treasuring on earth, so that we may not have the intellect there. …

The man, therefore, wandering in an image, treasuring, did not know to whom he was bringing them; for it is unclear to him what he will bequeath. Therefore, the diligent one hears to treasure in the heavens. He has wealth set aside in good works. This is also what Paul writes to Timothy: 'command the rich of this age not to be high-minded concerning wealth, but in God, who provides all things' (1 Tim 6:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a man who stores up wealth does not know who will gather it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man lives, but not without transgression, since had he kept the first image in which he was created he would not be troubled or store up in vain.
comments.comment:
And what about 'only in an image'?—even if every man is living, he is not living without transgression in the praiseworthy living. For if he had remained in the true image, the first, according to which he was created, he would not have been troubled, nor would he have treasured in vain. But indeed, even if he has become living, he wanders in an image; and not altogether in the first, but rather wandering in an image; for never can the rational animal be able to act outside of acting according to reason. And acting, he acts either praiseworthily or falsely, thinking and doing certain things and certain others.

And what about 'but in vain they are troubled'?—it has often already been said to us that these changes occur in such a way. When they do not guard this image according to which they have become, they are a multitude of the vain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every man lives led by an image, either that of God or that of some animal, and in his striving for mortal things he does not know who will inherit what he stores up, while the one who stores up in heaven stores up for himself.
comments.comment:
But indeed every man lives being led through an image, either through that of God, observing what is according to the image, or through that of some other animal, becoming female or irrational according to its nature. And indeed the sensible and apparent world is an image of the intelligible and invisible. Man is not led through this world, which is an image, by his own will.

Having said these things concerning the common man, he says concerning each individual that they are in vain, being tossed about in the strivings concerning mortal things. For regarding each one, he says, 'He stores up and does not know for whom he gathers them' (Psalm 39:6). For the one storing up upon the earth does not know who will inherit the wealth for which he himself labored; but the one storing up in heaven, having stored up for himself and not for another, knows the wealth that is inexpressible and unremovable from him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man who gathers wealth wrongly leaves its enjoyment to those he does not know, so, as David says, he stores up and does not know to whom he will gather it.
comments.comment: If you have wealth justly, use it properly, like the blessed Job; if unjustly, distribute it to those who were plundered, like a prisoner of war; or take what you received along with an addition, like Zacchaeus. If you do not have it, do not acquire it wickedly. For sin will follow you as a bitter provision on a necessary journey, and the enjoyment of what was acquired will be left to those you do not know. Then you will marvel at David saying, 'He stores up, but does not know to whom he will gather it' (Psalm 39:6).
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: For himself the psalmist says that his stability and strength to stand against all things is the Lord, so he waits for no other.
comments.comment:
And now, what is my stability? Is it not the Lord? Regarding others, the things spoken have been said. But as for myself, I say: 'What is my stability? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 40:17; LXX 39:17) I do not wait for another. And just as 'wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification become' those who participate, so also stability becomes to the one waiting, the Lord himself.

And my hypostasis is with you. Concerning the Lord, he says that his stability is. But toward the Lord, who is, he says his hypostasis is: 'and my hypostasis is with you' (Psalm 39:7). It is possible to call hypostasis here the strength by which one is able to stand, because, with you cooperating and being my stability, I stand against all things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His hypostasis, meaning his being as a rational soul, is from God, who gave him the soul, and it does not begin from seeds.
comments.comment: And the 'hypostasis from you' is a praise to me. And it is possible to say hypostasis instead of essence. And my hypostasis of the rational soul, of the rational animal, is with you; for you have given me a soul; from you I have the soul, not beginning from seeds, not being composed according to an opinion like the Stoic school, but 'my hypostasis is from you' (Psalm 39:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He waits for what is God's, enduring present labors in hope of good.
comments.comment: I do not, he says, have anything in myself worthy of expectation, but I wait, expecting what is with you and what is yours, enduring in present labors in hope of future good things (Psalm 39:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist is waiting for.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He asks to be freed from all his lawlessness, and a reproach from the foolish is to be fled, though reproach for good things is to be welcomed.
comments.comment:
Save me from all my lawlessness (Psalm 39:8). Not from some, but 'from all,' so that I may become outside of every false image.

A reproach of foolishness you have given me (Psalm 39:8). … For the fool indeed reproaches regarding good works and with zeal. For this reason, even in proverbs, as if there were no difference, reproaches are mentioned: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Proverbs 3:31); for he did not say at all, 'Do not acquire reproach,' but 'of evil men.' Do not reproach regarding triviality; for there are those being reproached regarding good things. To the well-known, Jesus says: 'Rejoice and be glad when they reproach you' (Matt 5:11). This kind of reproach is not to be rejected; for it is good and will lead into the kingdom of heaven. But the reproaches of evil men are to be fled from.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer to be saved from all transgression and from the reproach of fools.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He hoped to be delivered from all his iniquities and was not, and the strong hand that lashes him is God's discipline, by which man is reproved and freed from fleshly thickness.
comments.comment:
Since, having hoped to be delivered from all my iniquities, I have not attained this (Psalm 39:8), the fool reproaches, as if holding your handiwork in his hand: 'From the strength of the power of your hand I have been cut off' (Psalm 39:10). For if the striking hand lashes strongly, the one being lashed is cut off by such a thing.

And from the present word we learn that the things being said are not other than the lashes of God, not rebuking us. For after saying, 'Remove your lashes from me,' they have come to be in reproofs concerning iniquity. For man is disciplined by reproofs offered concerning iniquity, his soul having been stretched out to cast away all fleshy thickness. Then indeed he is able to weave according to the spider, not having matter lying outside him, but bringing forth this from where and from himself. The word is able also to make manifest the unsubstantial nature of the evil thoughts of the soul, just as it is said in Isaiah concerning the sinners, 'They weave a spider's web' (Isa 59:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist stays mute and does not answer the one who reproaches him, in line with the apostle's teaching on how to deal with a contentious man.
comments.comment: I was made mute and I did not open my mouth (Psalm 39:9). … And here again the same thing is signified: "I became mute and did not open my mouth." He did not answer him regarding what he reproaches. This is often said by another power, as the apostle teaches this, saying: "Reprove not a contentious man for one exhortation" (Titus 3:10). Do not open the mouth to him at all. But so that you may have a defense and a word to say about yourself, "I have done this by myself," exhort him. If he does not submit to the exhortation, or "and a second"—for some manuscripts have "and a second"—overthrow him, "knowing that he sins." One who is "self-condemning" should not be set against.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He bears reproach without answering back, knowing God wills him to be trained by it.
comments.comment: I bear, he says, being reproached now and not answering back, knowing in some such way that God wills me to be trained by reproaches (Psalm 39:9; LXX 38:9). So David himself bore being reviled by Shimei, saying that the Lord had told him to curse David (2 Samuel 16:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist did not open his mouth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He asks that the whips be turned away because he is God's handiwork, since God lashes every son he receives, and once delivered from his iniquities he will no longer be liable for punishment.
comments.comment: For you are the one who made me, turn away your whips from me. Do not lash me; for I am your handiwork. "But he lashes every son whom he receives" (Heb 12:6), having it clear through which he is lashed. Therefore, leave these things to me; grant me a remission, for in this way I shall no longer be lashed. Now I am still liable for the lashings. … Therefore, he who has placed the Most High as his refuge (Psalm 91:9) has no approaching evils nor a whip approaching his tent. Make me therefore such that I am no longer liable for the lashings; turn away the thing that punishes me. Since therefore I say, "Deliver me from all my iniquities" (Psalm 39:8), when you deliver me, I am no longer liable for punishment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea to remove the whips as God's training of a son.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The strong, correcting hand of God presses on him so that he fails, giving up his former state, and one may fail either praiseworthily or shamefully.
comments.comment:
From the strength of your hand I have failed (Ps 31:9). The strength of your hand, the educational one, the striking one, the one subjecting to pains, presses upon me. Since therefore it has become strong against me, I have failed. I cast away my former life, I left my former state; for I did not fail so as to no longer exist, or to become weak, but so as to fail the state preparing to punish me. "I have failed." I, saying these things, confessing, saying, "You have given me reproach through thoughtlessness," have failed, having become outside of my former state. It is possible to fail praiseworthily, and it is possible to fail shamefully.

"And Esau came from the field, leaving behind" (Gen 25:29), when he desired to eat a meal. The "leaving behind" here is instead of "having grown weak" and "longing for food."
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to fail under the strength of God's hand.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul of the man reproved for lawlessness is stretched out like a spider, for its own benefit.
comments.comment: Regarding the one called a spider, he says there is an extension of the soul. When the soul is stretched out, this extension occurs for its own benefit; for the spider-like quality is weak in it, and moreover it is shown to be an external evil. Therefore, you have examined the soul of this man as a spider, he who is being reproved under accusations for lawlessness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men outside God's instruction and reproofs are tossed about in vain, but one who is reproved and stretched like a spider suffers it for a change toward better things.
comments.comment: Moreover, every man is tossed about in vain. All men who are outside the instruction of God and the reproofs are tossed about in vain. But this one, even if he is tossed about while being reproved, even if his soul is stretched out like a spider, he does not suffer this in vain; for he receives a change toward better things. But if anyone were such a bare man, not being under instruction, not being under reproofs, he is tossed about in vain according to what was said previously: 'Indeed, man wanders in an image, but they are tossed about in vain' (Psalm 39:6). He who does not wish to be tossed about, but has tranquility, becomes God, having received the word of God; for 'he called those gods, those to whom the word of God came' (John 10:35). And these are not tossed about in vain, but even if it happens that they slip or a passion occurs, they say: 'I was tossed about and I did not speak.' Their tossing stands only until passion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the man under reproof is not tossed about in vain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man whose soul is searched out like a spider is a psychic man, who thinks himself self-sufficient and does not receive the things of the Spirit.
comments.comment: "And you searched out his soul like a spider" (Psalm 39:11). You searched out his soul like a spider, his soul according to which he is psychic. Concerning someone bad it is said, "he was carried by the desires of his soul." When someone reshapes things from the soul, let it be said, as if they were prophecies or as if they were doctrines of piety, "he is carried by the desires of the soul"; he is not carried by the Holy Spirit. In another book I have stated the difference: that man is fleshly, he who fights in the flesh, he who follows the desires of the flesh, he who is driven by the flesh, he who has become fleshly and is driven by sin. But a man is spiritual who has ascended above the psychic state, when he carries everything by the Holy Spirit and by God-bearing, doing and practicing them. And psychic is he who is neither fleshly nor spiritual. And perhaps all the wise of the world are such. They think themselves self-sufficient according to the movements and thoughts of their own souls. And because of this they do not receive the things of the Spirit; for they prefer their own and think their own understanding to be great, they do not receive the foolishness of the Spirit, regarding it as such. And indeed there are certain heresies established in their entirety, both among the Greeks and among the Christians, which say that allegories are foolishnesses, they are mere fabrications. And they say that the theorems concerning the intelligible are false, since they think all things to be bodies and sensible. These, therefore, are psychic men, not receiving the things of the Spirit, regarding themselves as self-sufficient and capable of contemplating all things by themselves. His soul, then, such a soul—not the essence, but the state according to which it is a soul—you searched out like a spider. And the spider is very weak, as it is said, "they weave a spider's web; their web shall not be a garment" (Isaiah 59:5-6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The reproached soul is spun like a spider's web.
comments.comment: Let the spider-like webs of the reproaches against lawlessness be destroyed; the soul of the one reproached is spun like a spider's web (Psalm 39:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A sojourner may pray and ask, while the inhabitants of the land are those responsible for wickedness, and all the fathers who pleased God through faith were strangers and sojourners.
comments.comment: 'Do not disregard me, for I am a sojourner in this land.' Do not disregard me while I am praying, entreating, weeping, and bearing tears—such things as 'those who sow in joy shall reap.' Therefore, 'do not disregard me,' but having responded, give what I have requested; for disregard sometimes signifies delay and patience, and sometimes indeed patience, when it occurs regarding sins: 'having done these things, I remained silent' (Psalm 50:21), instead of 'I have not repaid you.' If I were an inhabitant, I would not have dared to ask and to pray. For the inhabitants are those responsible for wickedness and impiety. For it is said in Jeremiah: 'from the face of the north shall the evils be burned upon those inhabiting the land' (Jeremiah 1:14), not 'upon those sojourning.' And in the Revelation of John, it is said three times: 'woe, woe, woe upon those inhabiting the land' (Revelation 8:13). If I were, therefore, an inhabitant, I would not have said, 'do not disregard me.' And I am a stranger just as all my fathers were. The sojourner and the stranger are one and the same. For Paul, having made a list of all those who were well-pleasing through faith in the Epistle to the Hebrews, called them sojourners and strangers (Hebrews 11:13). None of them is an inhabitant, none is a native, but a stranger. He has come from elsewhere into this place; he was not born here. Therefore, all the fathers according to virtue were sojourners in the land and strangers, such as the patriarchs and others who produced according to divine instruction, such as prophets, teachers, and lawgivers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be a stranger and sojourner, with the Bible's own examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A petition asks for what one lacks, while prayer in the full sense asks for greater, heavenly things, as one who has been filled.
comments.comment:
Hear, O Lord, my prayer and my supplication. It seems there is something else that is the supplication of the prayer. He sends up a supplication, the one who has known himself to be begging and lacking, so that he may be filled. But the one praying has this form as well, yet at times asks for the existence of good things from above. The one asking from God to receive something, that is, what he does not have, asks to receive it, or what he has, so that it may remain with him. Primarily this is prayer; it is a request sent up along with the one theologizing, the one wishing, to whom the prayer is sent up. …

When one asks for only those things which he lacks while being in need, it is a petition, being sent back like a wish. It is also possible to take it this way: those asking for more bodily things petition, such as health, wealth, and the others, as being in need, and many times they are worthy to receive these. …

Since even as one lacking, I ask that something might be given to me—for I am still at the peak of childhood—listen to my petition. But since I am about to come by chance to those things of which I am lacking, having become full, I ask for greater things; I ask for heavenly things and I say: 'Our Father who is in the heavens, hallowed be your name' (Matthew 6:9)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeing himself lacking, he weeps with godly sorrow that works repentance, and those who weep now are promised laughter.
comments.comment: Unite them with my tears. Seeing myself lacking, I weep, making that 'godly sorrow working repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10), regarding which I say: 'I will wash my bed every night, with my tears I will wet my couch.' And since he who is lacking perfection and the extremity of virtue—again he pours himself out saying: 'We who dwell in the tent groan' (2 Corinthians 5:4), and again: 'I have poured out my tears before you according to your promise'—you see: 'as in the promise I have poured out my tears.' What tears are these, or those of the ones weeping so that they might laugh? For 'blessed' are 'those who weep now, that they may laugh' (Luke 6:21). These placed the tears as in the promise, so that they might laugh, so that they might be filled with joy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To 'no longer exist' does not mean passing into non-existence, since the soul does not, but no longer being as he desired to be.
comments.comment:
Refresh me, so that I may find refreshment before I depart and no longer exist. Here, refreshment is called praiseworthy, being equivalent to 'delighting in the Lord.' 'I found refreshment for myself,' says Ephrem. And that refreshment is a slight thing. One refreshes praiseworthily when he enjoys virtue, when he 'delights in the Lord,' when he perceives and receives the understanding of the 'paradise of delight.' Since, therefore, much is lacking to me—for this is why I send up a petition, so that I may be filled of the things lacking—for this also he said at the beginning of the Psalm: 'Lord, make known to me my end and the number of my days, what it is, so that I may know what I lack' (Psalm 39:4). When he knows the things that are lacking and acquires these, he finds refreshment through such possessions. …

I shall refresh myself before I depart from this life and no longer exist. He does not say, 'I shall not begin to be,' but rather, 'I shall be such a person as I desire to be'; for the soul does not move into non-existence. …

He who says this is immortal. Therefore, if he says, 'I shall no longer be,' he does not say, 'I move into complete destruction, I turn into non-existence,' but rather, 'I shall no longer be in the way that I desired to have been.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'be no more' means for the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He prays for time to find refreshment after being worn out, so that he does not depart as one lacking and no longer share in Being.
comments.comment: Since he is not himself asking for much, he prays that he might be granted something to spend his life in, so that he might find refreshment after being worn out by perfect goods. For if he departs not as he should but as one lacking, he shall no longer exist—not in the sense of being destroyed into non-existence (for the soul is both immortal and indestructible), but in the sense of no longer being in participation of Being. For this is what truly is being: to participate in the One who says, 'I am the Being,' meaning that those not having this participation do not exist according to what was said in prayer to God: 'Do not give your scepter to those who are not' (Esther 14:11). Longing to participate in this existence, he prays that time might be given to him to find refreshment in the participation of Being, so that he may truly exist.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm has one speaker from start to finish, and 'waiting, I waited' is a way of speaking like 'I healed medically.'
