comments.comment: The preceding Psalm [the psalm before us] could have been spoken by any saint who has lived his life with patience and magnanimity, and by the Lord's man; for the Apostle, taking words from it, has set forth in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning Christ those things having been said. … And the Psalm is single-personed. The same person who began announces and sings until the end of the Psalm. He therefore says thankfully to God: 'Waiting, I waited upon the Lord, and He heard my prayer.' The 'waiting, I waited' has such a meaning as if someone were to say, 'I healed medically, I wrote grammatically.'
comments.selected_reason: Says who is speaking and how to read 'waiting, I waited'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To wait patiently is to endure with knowledge and not for praise, for the Lord himself is the endurance of the holy, and he hears those who endure to the end.
comments.comment:
He does not merely say 'having endured, I remained' as if to please the body and soul; rather, he endured with knowledge and as was necessary, not to receive a prize, glory, or praise from men. To endure thus is to say, as I might say, 'I acted wisely according to wisdom.' It was said in the preceding psalm that God is the endurance of the righteous: 'And now, what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 39:7). He who bears the heavy things falling upon him through this endurance says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord.' He bore the heavy things with an enduring disposition, for many, as I have said, bear the heavy things for some other reason. God is therefore the endurance of the holy. … He who is therefore established according to this endurance and is named from it says, 'Having endured, I remained with the Lord,' speaking as a slave. …

And he heard my prayer. Being in distress, I cried out, and God, attending to my prayer, has fulfilled these things. For I 'having endured, I remained' obeyed the commandment concerning which the Savior said, 'He who endures to the end, this one will be saved' (Matthew 24:13). The 'I remained' is a state of having come to rest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Read as the Savior's words, the waiting points to his distress before the passion, which his soul, unlike the Trinity, could feel and overcome.
comments.comment:
And what kind of face did the Lord have? For we have not spoken out of necessity. If, then, you take it from the face of the Savior—for it has become a matter of pre-passion, it has not become a matter of passions—Jesus 'began to be amazed and distressed' (Mark 14:33). Such things happened to him until the beginning. We do not say that pre-passion occurs without disturbance; for we do not say that anyone other than the Trinity is without disturbance.

For the soul, which Jesus took up, is something other than the Trinity; it is of a nature to receive passion and the beginning of being terrified and distressed. And I say according to the apostles: 'Instead of the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising shame' (Heb 12:2). If it had not become a victor in passion, it would not have been a feat or a contest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous man's long waiting ends in being brought up from Hades into a secure and joyful life with God.
comments.comment: He speaks of the eternal waiting of the righteous as his own, and of the prayers through which they will hear God accomplish the ascent from Hades, the life made secure forever, and the firm standing in that life amid gladness, brightness, and hymns to God (Psalm 40:1; Psalm 40:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the waiting and the rescue from the pit lead to.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The pit of misery is idolatry and the mud of clay is pleasure, and Christ saved mortals from them.
comments.comment: He calls idolatry a pit of misery, as those drawing from it are being miserable; for they draw nothing from that which is useful for life, just as Jeremiah, reproaching the Jews, said: 'They have dug for themselves broken pits, in which no water can be held' (Jer 2:13). Pleasures are a mud of clay, since they are dust and corruption of bodies and mere pits; whereas on the other hand, Christ saved the mortals through the faith in him and through the preaching.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the pit and the mud stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rock on which the feet are set is Christ, the unbroken Word, and standing on him gives a firm and God-directed course.
comments.comment:
When this corruptible body is changed into incorruption, it is no longer held by the surrounding mud and distress, but has been rescued from these things. 'And he set my feet upon a rock.' Let this be said generally concerning the righteous. Regarding 'rock,' let the unbroken and indivisible Word of God be heard in these matters, which no storm or tempest moves. Often, indeed, the memory of a rock becomes a memorial of the holy words, not capable of being grasped by sensation; for when the saint says thankfully to God, 'Lift me up on a rock,' he does not say, 'He placed me suspended on a sensible rock,' but upon the unbroken and indivisible Word.

Paul interpreted this rock and said who it is, that it is Christ: 'for they drank from a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). … Upon this rock, Christ, … the feet of the one being benefited stand, to be saved from shaking and tempest and having enemies. … 'And he directed my steps' (Psalm 40:2). And see how the Word leads us far into the history. No one standing walks, no one walking stands. When someone is therefore made firm according to Christ so as to be able to say, 'Who shall separate us from the love of God?' (Rom 8:35), his steps have directed paths; for he always hastens toward the higher things, toward the heavenly, being directed by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rock and the firm footing in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rock is not a rock of sense but the unshakeable perfection of virtue, on which the Lord directs a man's steps from mortal things to immortal.
comments.comment: Those who think that nothing is made manifest in the Scripture apart from the Word say: 'As one having attained a small good, he set the feet of the body upon the sensible rock, and thus he thanks the one who gifted this.' But we say that he who, having been freed from the aforementioned pit and mud, has been established upon the unshakeable and immovable perfection according to virtue, proclaims the things to come; for he follows the one standing on the rock, and his steps are directed by the passing Lord from evil to virtue and from mortal things to immortal things, and indeed according to every progress (Psalm 40:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pit of misery is the earthly place and Hades, into which Christ counted himself so as to lift people out of the clay of matter.
comments.comment:
And he brought me up out of the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. If each of the saints says this, 'the pit of misery' refers to the place concerning the earth; for a pit is a place where the waters falling from above gather. Often, in the divine writings, both the place concerning the earth and Hades are signified by this name; for when in the twenty-ninth Psalm it is said according to the man: 'You have saved me from those going down into the pit' (Psalm 30:3), I do not myself go down into a pit. Because of others, I have been there. No one else brought me down.

Moreover, this appears more clearly from: 'I was counted among those going down into the pit; I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Psalm 88:4). I am not one of those being led into the pit, but I 'was counted'. I counted myself among those. …

Therefore, he 'brought me up' 'from the pit of misery'. He who humbled his own body and enslaved it, and while still walking upon the earth, having acquired his citizenship in the heavens, he was lifted up from the pit of misery and from the clay of matter. … And Jesus will also say this according to the man: I have become into the pit of misery, I was counted, so that I might free them from misery and from the clay of matter; for because of them, I have become into the clay of matter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A new song is an unbroken one, the thankful hymn of a man raised from misery, and those who see him come to fear and hope.
comments.comment: And he cast into my mouth a new song (Psalm 40:3). 'Into the mouth' of the inner man, that is, into my word. … That which is uninterrupted is always new, while that which has been succeeded is old. … A hymn to our God. He who was lifted up from the aforementioned circumstances of the pit of misery and the mire of matter obtained an uninterrupted victory. The victory of the uninterrupted is a new triumph. What is this new song? It explains: it is a 'hymn' 'to our God.' When we hymn God, when we receive His praise, as far as possible, becoming in perfection, we sing a new song; for that which is in perfection is uninterrupted. Therefore also the hymn which is sent up to God thankfully within it is a new song. … Many shall see and shall be afraid and shall hope in the Lord (Psalm 40:3). 'Many shall see,' having seen me lifted up from the pit of misery and from the mire of matter, and having my feet established upon the rock, and my steps being directed, and me singing and hymning; 'and they shall be afraid' so that they too might come into such a guidance, 'and they shall hope' so that they too might attain these things which already exist for me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the song is called new and what the many who see it do.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessed man has the Lord's name itself as his hope and looks to nothing that can fail, such as wealth, bodily size or military might.
comments.comment:
Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord (Psalm 40:4). David once had a single combat against Goliath and did not hope in a shield. You see that the name of the Lord has become his hope. And it is said regarding the Lord being signified by hope—and there is no other hope than the expectation of good things—that often some say of things already existing, 'my hope.' The wealthy indeed say 'my hope,' not regarding what is expected, but what is already present. And therefore, those who already possess the name of the Lord consider it to be hope.

And he did not look toward vanities and false delusions. He who looks toward the Lord does not look toward vanities and false delusions. He does not look toward wealth, nor toward greatness of body, nor toward military might, nor toward any other of those things which are able to fail.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what trusting the Lord and not looking to vanities means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some madness is true, as with those who receive God, which is why the verse can speak of false madness.
comments.comment:
And indeed these manias are not false; for instance, those receiving God or those receiving Christ are god-bearers, and these manias are not false but true, instead of being 'repressed.' For if they were not also true manias, he would not have said: 'he who has had a false hope regarding madness' (Psalm 40:4).

The Phrygian party, not having been ignorant of how these things are said, understanding both the meaning of madness and of ecstasy, call the spirit-bearing men as having spoken in ecstasy or having prophesied.

And they speak truly regarding ecstasy, but not regarding derangement or insanity. If indeed Paul says: 'whether we have gone out of our minds, it is to God' (2 Corinthians 5:13), he is not speaking of madness, but of standing outside of human limits and having given.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessed person hopes in God and seeks eternal things, because whatever people procure by themselves is falsehood and only what comes from God is true.
comments.comment: In this, he says, the blessed person places hope in God and seeks eternal things, not being enticed by what appears for a short time nor turning aside from the true good to falsehood. For everything that people think they procure by themselves is falsehood; only what comes from God is true. And he demonstrated this through the whole ordering of human affairs, refuting all human things and bringing in the perfect good that comes from himself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the blessed man trusts and what he turns from.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Vanities are life's pursuits, and false madnesses are false teachings, unlike the true madness of prophets.
comments.comment:
He says that life's pursuits are to be called vanity, and false teachings and false prophecies are to be called madness. …

He added 'false' to 'madnesses' in contrast to true madnesses; for perhaps those seized prophetically possess a true madness, while false diviners possess a false madness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one can do God's wonders, and God's thoughts differ from ours as the heavens from the earth, since he knows all things at once.
comments.comment: Many and great things are, 'and with Your thoughts' (Psalm 40:5), according to which You do wonders, 'no one shall be like You.' No one is able to do such wonders; no one is able to bring someone out of the pit of misery and from the filth of material things and set his feet upon a rock and direct his steps and the other things. … God, therefore, has such thoughts that He knows all things at once, yet in a different way than men; for in Isaiah He said: 'As the heavens are far from the earth, so are your thoughts from my thought' (Isaiah 55:9). He wished to show the superiority of His own intellect through a sensory example; for His intellect has not stayed away from the intellect of men locally, but by a greatness of superiority.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how God's thoughts and wonders differ from ours.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's thoughts are his providential plans, and nothing made can be found like the mind of the Lord.
comments.comment: he speaks of the thoughts of God, meaning the deliberations occurring according to God's providence. To these, he says, no created thing shall be found resembling the mind of the Lord which knows all. Regarding Ps 39:6c, 'Your wonderful works and your thoughts'; for if anyone wished to examine something regarding depth, he would find it even more obscure than before: 'If I said, I will act wisely, but it has escaped from me far away, and a deep depth, who can find it?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God no longer wanted shadowy animal sacrifices, since a body was prepared that is offered as a bloodless, spiritual sacrifice.
comments.comment: But you did not desire the perceptible burnt offerings, the bodily sacrifices from the slaughter of animals and others, the shadowy ones. 'A body he has prepared for me' (Ps 40:6). Instead of these, the apostle has interpreted that this body is the logical and bloodless sacrifice. When therefore a greater sacrifice is found, then he no longer wants the former; they are no longer desired by him. … You did not desire a physical sacrifice and offering, since I have prepared for us a body, which we are able to perform as a sacred rite and sacrifice to you; 'I urge you through mercies to present your bodies as a logical sacrifice' (Rom 12:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Other interpreters read 'you have prepared ears for me', meaning ears opened by God to hear what the outward sacrifices pointed to.
comments.comment: In other interpretations it is said: 'And you have prepared ears for me.' One interpreter says this: since you did not desire a sensory sacrifice and offering, 'you have prepared ears for me,' through which I hear those things concerning the things made manifest by the sensory, such as the intellectual sacrifice of understanding: 'sacrifice to God a sacrifice of understanding.' Furthermore, if you call me to a lecture, you no longer seek sensory things being performed, so that what is said might be like: 'The Lord's instruction opens my ears' (Isaiah 50:5). An unmusical man does not have ears for hearing musical words. And another of the interpreters said: 'You have dug out ears for me,' since you removed their dullness, you removed that which obstructs hearing.
comments.selected_reason: Gives another reading of the verse and what it means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hebrews gives these verses as the Savior's own words: the time of the shadow has passed, and God prepared a body for him so that sin offerings would no longer please.
comments.comment: the Epistle to the Hebrews says that these upcoming verses are spoken from the face of the Savior concerning the Savior: 'Therefore, entering into the world, you said, a sacrifice and an offering you did not desire,' and the rest. This provided an occasion for him to speak the whole psalm, maintaining the same person until the end of what is said. Now, having passed the time of the shadow, according to which sacrifice and offering were brought, God, not wishing for worship through these things, perfected a body from the Virgin for the Son, so that whole burnt offerings and sacrifices concerning sin would no longer be pleasing. When the Savior said to the Father, 'Behold, I have come to do your will,' according to the will by which He removes the sin of the world, He himself, having been taken and brought forward for the sin of all, so that once remission has occurred, there is no longer a need for the sacrifice concerning sins.
comments.selected_reason: Says who is speaking and why sacrifice gives way to the prepared body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Now that Christ has come it is sin to cling to shadow worship, because the Son says God prepared him a body and he ended the law's offerings.
comments.comment: So it is sin and defilement, now that Christ has been revealed and the time of the law and the prophets has gone by, to cling to worship as in shadows, and to attempt to bring to God a sheep, or fat, or frankincense, even though the Son says plainly to God the Father: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you took no pleasure. Then I said: See, I have come, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book, to do your will, O God’ (Hebrews 10:5–7; Psalm 40:6–8). For the Son, offering himself up for us as a spotless victim (Hebrews 9:14), put a stop to the things of the law, which could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:11); for Christ is the end of the law and the prophets (Romans 10:4).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: 'I have come' means coming to end the shadow by becoming the offering, and the book's heading is all Scripture.
comments.comment: Then he said: 'Behold, I have come' (Psalm 40:7). Then I, for whom a body was prepared, said: 'Behold, I have come,' instead of saying: since the purpose of his coming is this, to receive the end of the shadow, so that sacrifices and burnt offerings are no longer brought, I have come, in order to fulfill the sacrifice by becoming a burnt offering. … It has been written in a heading of a book concerning me. The heading of a book is called 'all inspired Scripture'; for the main point of the Scripture is the life rule of life concerning Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'I come' and 'the volume of the book' mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'heading of the book' means all God-breathed Scripture, which sums up the Savior's becoming man to do the Lord's will.
comments.comment: the heading of the book calls all the God-breathed writing both legal and prophetic: 'For in this it is written concerning the coming conduct of the Savior.' And it is a heading because it summarizes all into one. And it is the becoming of the Savior a man, so that the will of the Lord might be done.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The spiritual law lives in the heart, meaning one's own disposition.
comments.comment: 'You have written it upon my leading principle.' And everyone who does according to the spiritual law has the law in his heart, that is, in his own disposition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law within him is spiritual food held in the inner man, and it takes the place of sacrifices.
comments.comment: 'To do, O God, your will I have desired' (Ps 40:8). Therefore 'I said: behold, I have come' (Heb 10:7), since the will was desired to do your will after you did not desire me for sacrifice and offering. … And 'your law in the midst of my belly' (Psalm 40:8). It is spiritual food containing itself in the belly of the inner man. And the law, which is evident everywhere, is spiritual food; for it is not sensible food. … No longer desiring your sacrifice or offering or burnt offerings, having the spiritual law as food.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the law within him is and why it replaces sacrifice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteousness preached to the 'great church' is not that of the law but one that exceeds it, and we should not be ignorant of it but preach it.
comments.comment: This is not the righteousness according to the law, about which the apostle says, 'having become blameless in the righteousness of the law' (Philippians 3:6). This then righteousness I preached to the great church; for if the letter and the shadow were not preached to the great ones, but to infants. … But what kind of righteousness? —about which the Savior was saying, 'unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees' (Matt 5:20), is this not according to the shadow? Therefore yours—of the disciples—the Savior says, let the righteousness exceed theirs. And he says that theirs was with ignorance. Because of this, let us not be ignorant of the righteousness of God, but let us preach it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Lips' means the word: with imperfect hearers the speaker holds back and speaks in riddles, but before the perfect he holds nothing back.
comments.comment: Behold, my lips I will not restrain. 'Lips' here means the word. Often when he is called to say something to small and imperfect men, we restrain our lips; we do not have them released, but we descend with them, we speak cryptically, we speak proverbially, and our lips are restrained. But when to the perfect and a great church, since he does not restrain his lips, since he does not hinder them from speaking anything. … He never restrains his lips, always bringing forth the words of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what restraining the lips means and why he does not.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He can say to God 'you have known my righteousness', for he practices what he announces, and God knows it even if others speak blasphemy against him.
comments.comment: Lord, you have known my righteousness (Psalm 40:9). Since much of what is said has testified to himself—for 'to preach righteousness in a great church' is great and, so that I may say this, beyond man—he says to God: 'you have known my righteousness' (Psalm 40:9). This righteousness, which I announce, I possess and have practiced according to it. … And this is also possible: even if some, being ignorant, speak blasphemy against me, but you know my righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'thou knowest' claims and why he can say it to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The great assembly is filled from many perfect ones, to whom the righteousness established through faith in Jesus is preached without restraint.
comments.comment: A great assembly is being filled from many and perfect ones. In this, the righteousness established through the faith of Jesus is being preached. Proclaiming this unceasingly and continuously, he says: 'My lips I shall by no means restrain.' He himself says: 'I knew my righteousness, having accepted this and being at home in it.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever knows God's righteousness keeps truth with it in his heart, mercy goes with truth, and the salvation spoken of is Christ, declared to a great assembly of believing Gentiles.
comments.comment: I have not hidden your truth in my heart. He who has known the righteousness of God does not hide the truth joined to it in his heart. … But truth has the mercy of God; for if God does not show mercy, no one is able to know the truth, how much and what it is. Therefore 'mercy and truth met.' … 'And I have spoken my salvation' (Psalm 40:10). The confession of the truth is my salvation. If he also says the truth concerning Christ, he again says Christ is the salvation, and 'I have spoken my salvation and revealed your truth.' I speak of the salvation being the Christ whom I make manifest. 'I have not hidden your mercy and your truth from a great assembly' (Psalm 40:10). We say that mercy is joined to the truth. And 'a great assembly' means those from the Gentiles who have believed, having been gathered from all the Gentiles.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how righteousness, truth, mercy and salvation belong together in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks that God keep his mercies near.
comments.comment: 'And you, Lord, do not distance your mercies from me' (Psalm 40:10). I have come to your mercies, blamelessly and as is necessary. Do not therefore distance them, so that I may remain such.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy and truth have taken hold of him, and he asks that they stay.
comments.comment: “Your mercy and your truth have taken hold of me continually” (Psalm 40:11). Your mercy and your truth have taken hold of me, the one in need. “Do not lengthen” therefore “your mercies” (Psalm 40:11), so that your truth, being taken hold of, and the mercy joined with it, might remain thus.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea that mercy and truth keep him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While he does what was foretold he asks that God's mercies stay near, since mercy and truth together keep a man from error.
comments.comment: While I am doing the things foretold, You, O Lord, do not let Your mercies be far from me; have mercy on those who benefit through me. For the greater part of salvation does not arise solely from the working of God's mercy, but also the truth, taking hold, preserves one lest they be caught in a deception or some other error. … And they have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head; that is, the evils surrounding us are multiplying unperceived. With these many things having happened, being deprived of thinking rightly, we have been left abandoned from the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The church needs mercy and has no weapons, money or walls, yet it survives and grows, which shows that its power comes from God.
comments.comment:
By speaking of himself he reveals the church, and he presents us as needing mercy so that we may remain in grace. The request for mercy is powerful, because it is said to go not to human beings but to him. For in this way we human beings obtain what comes from God: Christ, on our behalf, is the one who receives the good meant for us, as he says: “And I make a covenant with you, as my Father made with me” (Luke 22:29).

For there is no power for salvation in the church of Christ except what comes from God, since we have neither weapons nor money nor surrounding walls nor control of land nor anything of the kind that the Jews had (Psalm 40:13). So it is a wonder, and no less than any of the other wonders, that people warred upon by countless nations, unarmed, unprepared, and non-resisting, remain and increase Such was the wonder of the bush that burned and was not consumed, and this was a figure of Christ conquering through suffering. For the church that suffers and is not destroyed bears in itself all the proofs of wisdom and the clear marks of help from above.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The evils around him are beyond counting, and his iniquities, taking hold of the mind's eyes, leave him unable to see.
comments.comment: “For evils surround me, of which there is no number” (Psalm 40:12). For this reason, “do not lengthen your mercies from me” (Psalm 40:11), because many evils surround me, not falling under number, that is, because of multitude—if the heavy things are signified, because of multitude they do not have a number. But if the other evils, the practical ones about which it is said, “a fool does evils in laughter” (Proverbs 10:23), they are not in any word or number; for they are not of things that exist, they are thoughts of men, transgressions of divine laws. Therefore, take the double meaning of the evils. … “My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was not able to see” (Psalm 40:12). … for they are harmful to the eyes of the mind, providing blindness to the inner eye of man. Since, therefore, they have overtaken me, I am not able to see.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When iniquities seize him his heart forsakes him, so he asks God to save him, and the hairs of his head are a figure of speech.
comments.comment:
“And my heart has forsaken me” (Psalm 40:12). Since the lawlessnesses that seized me and removed my sight “were multiplied beyond the hairs of my head” (Psalm 40:12), “my heart has forsaken me” (Psalm 40:12), I no longer have the heart of a wise man; for the heart of the one saying these things is fleshy. When therefore the fleshy heart forsakes someone, it becomes stony.

“Be pleased, Lord, to save me” (Psalm 40:13). Since the lawlessnesses seized me and I am not able to see and they were multiplied beyond the hairs of my head (Ps 51:11), “be pleased to save me” (Ps 51:11), so that the heart may not remain forsaken.

If the word was about these hairs of this head, he has spoken hyperbolically; for if lawlessnesses occur, they are not able to exceed the number of the hairs of the head. Therefore it is spoken hyperbolically.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Let those who cry 'Well indeed' be shamed at once, for the one who accepts sinlessness wishes no one to fall into sin.
comments.comment: As evils rush upon them, let them hasten to turn back to the things behind, setting aside the bad intention; for then they are able to be shamed even in the sense of perception. Let those saying to me 'Well indeed, well indeed' immediately bring upon themselves shame. He who accepts sinlessness desires that no one should come into sin. But if anyone should go astray, 'well indeed', how he is immediately shamed for the bad and arrogant things he is doing, saying 'Well indeed, well indeed' (Psalm 40:15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who seek the Lord find him and rejoice, love his salvation always, and entrust their care to him as weak, poor and needy.
comments.comment: Those seeking the Lord have an end to the seeking, which is to find him; and upon having found him, they rejoice and are glad with rejoicings and gladness. For someone having sought and having found God, and desiring to magnify him, wants to love the salvation of God, either the salvation from him or the Savior himself. And he loves him through all things and not for a little while. Toward the possession of good things, having confessed himself to God as weak, poor, and needy, he entrusts the care concerning himself to God, casting his care upon the Lord as upon a guardian (Psalm 40:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what seeking, rejoicing and being poor and needy lead to.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The church, poor in the world, will be enriched and glorified by God's help, which it asks not to delay, and the request will be granted.
comments.comment: To these ends, he says, the church will advance, having first become poor and come through great poverty in the world, and having been enriched by the power that comes from you and glorified by the help that comes from you, which she asks not to delay (Psalm 40:17). And because of the request it will not delay, as it is said: “The one who is coming will come and will not delay” (Habakkuk 2:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'make no tarrying' asks and promises.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In Scripture 'the day' means what happens in it, so an evil day is a time of evil events, not a stretch of time.
comments.comment: He [Job] curses not the day, which is a chronological interval, but the things happening in it. For by custom, in the Scripture, the things happening are called the day. This the Psalmist teaches, saying: "In a evil day the Lord will deliver him" (Psalm 41:1), not calling the evil day a chronological interval, but the evil things happening in them; and what is said by Paul: "for the days are evil" (Ephesians 5:16), refers to the mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'a day of trouble' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm presents the Savior's person, and the blessed man is the one who understands the truly rich one who became poor for our sake.
comments.comment:
This psalm is also joined to the same theme. For it presents the person of the Savior, the remembrance of the passion, the prediction of the resurrection, and the return to heaven (Psalm 41:1; LXX 40:1). Just now, then, he was saying: “I am poor and needy,” and it would fittingly be brought in as spoken especially by him concerning himself (Psalm 41:1; LXX 40:1).

Even if understanding is good concerning all who are poor in the world for the sake of righteousness—and understanding consists in considering such poor people rich—yet the one who knows and understands the truly rich one who became poor for our sake is truly blessed (Psalm 41:1). And all blessedness follows the knowledge of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the poor man is and why understanding him brings blessing.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The evil day is the day of judgment, or perhaps the whole of this present life, when the Lord saves the one he pities.
comments.comment: An evil day is the day of judgment, in which the God who pitied may pity the one pitied, and he is saved from every punishment; and perhaps even the whole existing life is an evil day, in which the Lord himself saves from those standing around (Psalm 41:1-2). Let the evil day and the day of punishment be understood.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord helps the sick man and turns his whole bed, giving health of soul.
comments.comment: For the Lord will help him at his bed of pain, and will turn his whole bed in his sickness, delivering him from human sickness, also granting him the health of the soul, even if there should happen to him some sickness of the soul
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God did not give a brief healing but turned the sick man's whole bed away from sickness, as when Lazarus was carried to Abraham's bosom.
comments.comment: 'You turned his whole bed in his sickness' (Psalm 41:3). This says: he did not give a brief healing to the one greatly sickened, but 'turned his whole bed' (Psalm 41:3) away from the sickness, so that he might no longer be sick, but might be healthy, as I said concerning the paralytic. And you also say concerning Lazarus, the one being drawn out having a body, that, when he was taken up from thence by the angels, his whole bed was turned, his whole sickness. He was no longer laid down in sickness. Instead, he was being carried into the bosom of Abraham.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that his whole bed is changed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who suffers for human beings speaks their sins as his own and seeks mercy for them, dispelling contempt by revealing his glory.
comments.comment: Again the one who suffers on behalf of human beings speaks of human sins as his own, and he seeks for himself the mercy upon them that comes to us (Psalm 41:4). He dissolves the contempt of those who do not know him by revealing his glory—upon himself according to his own power, and upon us according to the grace of Christ (Psalm 41:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the speaker confesses sin that is not his own.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He sinned and so lay on a sickbed, and having said 'Lord, have mercy' he already holds what he asked.
comments.comment: You see that, when he sinned, then he was in trouble and then he was laid upon a bed and a couch. When therefore anyone knows Him who is able to rescue, he will attain to the one who is striving, similarly to him: 'I want, be cleansed' (Mark 1:41), 'Rise, take up your bed and walk' (Mark 2:11). … I have sinned against you, I have sinned against you. In this way, almost all of us sin toward God, knowing much about Him through ignorance and doing much contrary to His laws. 'I have sinned' is thus 'against you'; but having said, 'Lord, have mercy on me,' he possesses the petition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The invisible powers, then the Jews, sought to cast the true king from his rule and seize an inheritance that was not theirs.
comments.comment: For this was eagerly pursued, he says, first by the invisible powers, then by the visible Jews, to cast out the true king from his natural rule, thinking to take possession of an inheritance that did not belong to them (Psalm 41:5). Therefore they said: “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The enemies are the Jews and Judas, who thought Jesus' name would perish with his death, but it shone no less after he was crucified.
comments.comment: My enemies said evil things to me: 'When will he die, and will his name be destroyed?' (Ps 54:1). I say that this psalm is to be spoken from the person of the Savior according to man. And since the Jews have become His enemies, like traitors to the truth, having not understood the one who came among them, and since Judas also became one of the disciples, regarding the enemies he speaks singularly of those having risen up against him—once in reference to Judas as the beginning of the betrayal, and once plurally because of those following him and having overthrown Jesus. … And thus he says: 'My enemies said.' This they said: the evil things which they think are evil, they said against me: 'When will he die, and will his name be destroyed?' (Ps 54:1). For they thought that after the death of Jesus his teaching and his fame would be extinguished, and they said: 'When will he die?' On the contrary, it went the opposite of what they thought. His name did not shine forth less when he lived and was alive than when he was crucified and taken up.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the enemies are and how their hope was reversed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judas, having had much time with Jesus, came in to see him many times, as one of the fellowship.
comments.comment: Regarding the remnant of Judas, he says: if ever 'he went in to see, but in vain he ran' (Psalm 41:6); just as we said recently, that he who possesses something more has more words concerning others than other men, so also Judas had something more than the other traitors; for he benefited from much time and had the legacy and the spark of his instruction. Therefore he entered many times toward Jesus, as also in the fellowship he was found.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies whispered in secret instead of speaking boldly, and the lawless word they set against Jesus was their charge that he worked by Beelzebub.
comments.comment: All my enemies were whispering against me; none of them spoke against me with boldness. And you find the Jews seeking how they might take him secretly; they were whispering to Judas, and he to them; for he did not enter a synagogue and shout this: 'What do you want to give me, and I will hand him over to you?' (Matt 26:14-15). … This is what Jesus himself says: 'I teach every day' (Matthew 26:55) in the synagogue, and now 'as if I had come to a robber.' … They set a lawless word against me. They were reading the Scriptures 'every Sabbath' so that they might learn the things of the law. And from the opposite, it was necessary for those reading with the law to know who is the one prophesied and testified to by the Scriptures; they set a lawless word against me, saying: 'This one does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub.' 'If this man were from God, he would not have loosed the Sabbath' (John 9:16). 'Is it not bad that we say, "You are a Samaritan and have a demon"?' This is the one against whom they set a lawless word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the whispering and the evil devised against him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls death sleep because of the hope of resurrection, since one who sleeps unharmed wakes and the dying man will be raised.
comments.comment: Does he who is sleeping not add to rising? Rather, he himself says: since death surrounded me, I slept; for in the Scriptures the name of sleep sometimes signifies death. Sleep is also called slumber, and the union of a man with a woman is called sleep. And death is also called sleep according to the Scripture because of the expectation of the resurrection; for just as he who sleeps, if he suffers no harm to nature, might be raised, so the dying man will be raised.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why death is called sleep and what follows it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies do not know the righteous man's death is a sleep leading to resurrection.
comments.comment: They hurry, he says, to put the righteous man to death, not knowing that his death is a sleep, becoming toward a resurrection, and not a removal of life but a transition introducing him into heaven, according to the saying, “His life was taken from the earth” (Isaiah 53:8) (Psalm 41:8; Psalm 41:9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The betrayer is a disciple who shared the speaker's food and sought to seize his heel, as the Lord himself recalled in John, and the resurrection will undo the plot.
comments.comment: The resurrection, he says, will dissolve the conspiracy of the enemies against us and the betrayal of friends (Psalm 41:9). For already a disciple has risen up against me—one deemed worthy of peace from me, counted among those entrusted to me, and sharing my food—but he was exposed as a serpent, wanting to seize my heel. The Lord himself remembered this as spoken about him, saying, “But so that the Scripture may be fulfilled, the one who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me” (John 13:18) (Psalm 41:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the betrayal by the friend who shared his bread, with the Lord's own use of the verse in John 13:18.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Eats my bread' marks the betrayer as the table-mate who dipped his hand with him in the bowl, and John makes this clearer.
comments.comment: We will not surely understand from this that none of the other disciples, but only Judas, dipped the morsel in the bowl with him. I think what was said has some such sense: he wants to say, as is likely, that the betrayer will be the one who dipped his hand with me in the bowl (Matthew 26:23) — that is, the fellow diner and table-mate, sharer and participant of table and of salt. For thus he also was accusing him through the voice of blessed David, saying, “But you, man of equal soul, who sweetened foods for me at the same table.” (Psalm 55:13) And again, “He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.” (Psalm 41:9) John made this very point more clearly; for he said the Lord had said, “It is that one to whom I will give the morsel when I have dipped it.” (John 13:26)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one who ate his bread raised a 'wing' against him, a word for setting on someone with deceit, as Jacob 'winged' Esau.
comments.comment: The one eating my bread magnified a winging against me. 'The man of my peace, in whom I hoped' (Psalm 41:9), 'he raised up his wing against me', he wished to wing me. … and Jacob is called a winger; for he winged Esau when he took the blessing of the elder. To set upon someone with deceit is called a winging.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'I will repay them' means that the risen Jesus will judge them, as those who crucified him will look on him and learn their due retribution.
comments.comment: But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I will repay them. … These things again are said more humanly concerning the man Jesus. 'But you, Lord, have mercy, and I will repay them.' I shall be their judge. The one who rises to repay and to judge, as he finds the dispositions, gives back. Many, having experienced harm or seeing that they once condemned him, himself is about to judge them, according to: 'they shall look upon him whom they crucified' (Jn 19:37), they come into knowledge and they know how the due retribution persists toward them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'that I may requite them' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'In this I knew' is less his own knowledge than the proof, to enemies and acquaintances alike, that God wills him, so his enemy will not rejoice over him.
comments.comment: In this I knew that you willed me. This is knowledge and proof that it is your will to have me; for in this they shall know me. The 'in this I knew' does not refer so much to his own knowledge, but rather that those of mine shall be known in this. Above all, having been condemned, will they know him?—all having received a perception of his greatness, whether they were enemies before or acquaintances. Because my enemy shall by no means be pleased with me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At his resurrection the enemies who rejoiced at his death feel shame.
comments.comment: To make them rejoice, he surrounded him with death; but upon his resurrection they do not rejoice, but rather they experience shame and stand in fear, having seen the one they had betrayed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was upheld through innocence: he did not know sin yet became sin and a curse in order to loose the curse and give blessing.
comments.comment: But you took hold of me through my innocence. For I did not know sin, even though I have become sin; even though I have become a curse, I was not shown to be a curse because of a preceding sin, but so that I might loose the curse and provide a blessing. And just as it has become sin so that God might make righteous those for whom sin has become, so it has become a curse, not so that it might be held by the curse. This very thing, then, has become a curse upon a blessing, sin upon righteousness, death received for life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the integrity is that upholds him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Innocence can mean freedom from sin or complete virtue, and 'established before you for ever' means he remained simple and was made firm by God.
comments.comment: Innocence, then, often signifies the absence of something, and it is when there is complete purity from sin. But when it says, 'the simple believes every word' (Proverbs 14:15), and also, 'bad associations corrupt good morals' (1 Corinthians 15:33), it speaks of the surrounding good morals. And complete virtue is also called innocence, concerning which he says, 'the simple and upright cling to me' (Psalm 25:21). And you have established me before you for ever. Not for a little time, then, did I not slip, being simple before falling to enemies, but I remained simple; for 'you have established me' indeed 'for ever.' Not simply, then, but 'before you.' And not everyone who is being established is additionally established by God, but he who has the perfection established.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Innocence is found in Christ alone, and the permanence before God is the heavenly life promised after the resurrection.
comments.comment:
We hear of innocence especially in the case of Christ—the purity from all evil that the Creator sought among human beings, who were made for this purpose: to be worthy of their Maker and to remain in what is good, since all the works of God are exceedingly good (Sirach 39:16). Yet when he sought it, he found it in none of Adam’s descendants, but only in the one who was from Adam according to the flesh and had not displayed the marks of Adam’s transgression, but possessed the divine form remaining even with the fleshly covering. This is what the heavenly voice testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

The permanence and eternal confirmation before God is that which is in heaven, which was also foretold in the fifteenth psalm after the resurrection in the words, “You will fill me with joy in your presence” (Psalm 15 [16]) (Psalm 41:12).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'May it become' is a prayer and not a blessing given to God, just as 'Hallowed be thy name' does not make his name holy.
comments.comment: Blessed indeed is the one whom the Lord blesses, and blessed means that which is worthy of being blessed eternally. Since the one is being blessed by the God of Israel, the 'may it become' prays 'may it become'; not that the prayer makes God blessed, just as neither the name of God is sanctified by the prayer of those saying, 'Hallowed be thy name.' This was said concerning these things in the previous parts.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the closing 'Amen' asks and does not ask.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The grace and the victory are credited to God, not to the speaker's own innocence or power.
comments.comment: Blessed is the Lord God of Israel from ever and to ever (Psalm 41:13). Let it be, let it be. … To him I write the grace and the victory, not by our power; for even if I am simple, I do not give the whole by my innocence, but by the cooperation of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The deer, which kills serpents and then hurries to a spring to be cleansed, pictures the soul that longs for God, who is the spring of wisdom, life and the Spirit.
comments.comment:
As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God (Psalm 42:1).

This animal is said to be a destroyer of serpents.

And when it has killed the serpents, it becomes thirsty from their venom and hastens to find a spring of water, so that it may wash away the thirst and be cleansed; for it is said that as the serpents are torn apart by this animal, they cover the face of the deer with blood and other things, and so it goes away to wash itself,

so that the impurity brought upon it from the destruction of the serpents may be washed away. … The other thing of those signified here is shown by the saying: 'In the same way that a deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, my God' (Psalm 42:1); he compared the longing toward God to the longing of the deer for the springs; for God is a spring, and His word is a spring: 'You have left the spring of wisdom' (Baruch 3:12). 'For with you is the spring of life' (Psalm 36:9).

And again: 'You have left me, a spring of living water,' God says (Jeremiah 2:13).

And the Holy Spirit is a spring, if indeed all the gifts flow from Him and from Him they have their beginning. … In the same way that the sensible deer longs for the springs of water, so our soul, becoming a deer and a destroyer of harmful things, longs for you, O God.

Those who 'are ready to avenge all disobedience' (2 Corinthians 10:6) are deer, destroying the serpents of injustice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of the deer and the springs in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The serpents are pleasures, and the many deer led by various pleasures do not seek the one desire, which is the Savior himself.
comments.comment:
Therefore, it must be said and it is morally right: the serpents are pleasures; for pleasure is diverse.

And 'being led by various pleasures and desires'.

He speaks concerning the faults of women whom the heterodox capture as captives.

These therefore diverse deer do not long to find God; they do not seek one single desire.

But one desire is the Savior and our Lord himself.

Just as he is called wisdom and truth and light and righteousness, so also he is desire.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title 'for understanding' marks a psalm full of mysteries, sung in unison by the sons of Korah, which must be understood and practiced, not only voiced.
comments.comment:
To the end; for understanding, to the sons of Korah, a psalm. Three sons of Korah became temple singers. And their names are brought forward in Exodus and in the Chronicles. These, just as some take from faith one soul and one heart, so also these, having received one soul from the uniting spirit which grants the singing, because of this they bring forth the verses of the psalm in unison.

And this psalm is not one filled by chance with mysteries. Because of this, "for understanding" is inscribed. … And here, therefore, many riddles lie. Therefore, understanding is needed by the one encountering such psalms which are so inscribed. … He says, therefore, that this psalm ought not to be spoken by voice alone, but also to be understood by the mind and to practice the works appropriate to it …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sons of Korah, united in one mind and judgment, sing the whole psalm together as one.
comments.comment: But the three sons of Kore were arranged with others to sing the awesome psalms, which the Scripture also calls hymns, in which also the names are carried in Chronicles. So not the three, being equipped with the same mind and the same judgment, having been united in that which agrees concerning all things, in a unified way pronounce all things in the present psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The deer's haste to the water pictures the holy one's search for the springs of God, and the diligent pray for the time when they will appear before God's face.
comments.comment: The deer, a creature warring against the eyes and eating them, if ever, having eaten, were to burn from the approaching venom of the serpent, seeks with haste the springs of water to quench the thirst. But those saying that she who wishes to see herself in the waters traces the springs, so that she might know the pollution having happened to her from the blood of the eyes, so that she might cleanse it; for in the scattering of the eyes, they sprinkle the divine blood into it. And the holy one, not lifting up the eyes against serpents and scorpions by which he received authority from Jesus, but also avenging every disobedience, being a spiritual deer, hastens to track out divine springs of water, since the God says, 'You abandoned me, a spring of living water' (Jer 2:13), and concerning the savior it is said to someone, 'You abandoned the spring of wisdom' (Baruch 3:12), and the Holy Spirit concerning whom the Word announced, 'I will cause him to drink from the water, I will give to him; there shall be made in him a spring of water springing up unto eternal life' (John 4:14). Perhaps also every inspired Scripture proves to be a saving spring. … The intention of the diligent toward God is like that of the deer toward the springs of water with longing. And since they, in the present life, through a mirror, present him to God, having the face to face set aside for the things after this, pray that a time may be established through which, having come, he might appear before the face of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those still in this life thirst for God because they feel far from him, though nothing is far from God in place, since he fills heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
Men who are still in life thirst for God as the deer thirsts for the springs of the waters (Ps 42:1).

Yet they do not say that their desire stands at this point; for they are still far from God in some way of relation and disposition, not in place; nor is anything locally far from God, for he 'fills the heaven and the earth' (Jer 23:24).

Therefore he who approaches him says: 'Where shall I go from your spirit and from your face, where shall I flee?

If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into Hades, you are there' (Ps 139:7-8).

Thus those in this life having received a vision of the coming age thirst courageously for God, as if they see themselves far off while the evil of the world and the weight of the world and the corruptible are still pressing upon them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist thirsts for a God who is not far away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To thirst for God is to love him, and the one who hopes to see his face prays that he may not appear before God empty, as the feasts required.
comments.comment:
My soul thirsted toward God, the strong and living one (Psalm 42:2).

To thirst is often to take hold of love.

Thus indeed in another psalm he says: 'O God, my God, toward you I cry out; my soul thirsted for you' (Psalm 63:1); for he who longs for something and asks in order to receive it, thirsts for it. … And this is so, since in the feasts of the Hebrews it was customary to see three times of the year; for 'three times of the year all your male shall be seen before me' (Exodus 23:17), and 'he shall not be seen before me empty' (Exodus 23:15).

No one shall be seen before him empty.

Since therefore even this one aims for the springs of the waters, he prays to be fulfilled, so that he may arrive and see the face of God not as a ruler but no longer empty.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ ascended to appear before God's face on our behalf, since humanity had come to be outside God's face and seeks the strong one to restore it.
comments.comment: For he [Christ] ascended into heaven to appear before the face of God on our behalf, bringing in himself what had been separated and alienated from the beginning (Psalm 42:2). … From this the discerning person—whom the inscription summons—can understand that humanity came to be outside the face of God, so that through God it might seek restoration to the face of God. Rightly, then, does he seek the strong one, having fallen into weakness according to the words, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:2) (Psalm 42:2). Hence it is necessary to have fallen into the present weakness. For not loving to endure by his own small strength, nor being able to do so, he seeks not to be left without true strength (Psalm 42:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist longs to appear before God, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whoever finds it hard to be freed from the body has not thirsted for the living God as the hind longs for water, nor poured out his soul in hope of reaching God's house.
comments.comment: But if this [being freed from the body] seems hard to anyone, he has not 'thirsted toward' God the strong, 'the living,' nor longed for God as the hind longs 'for the springs of waters' (Psalm 42:2–5); nor said, 'When shall I come and appear before God's face?'; nor reckoned with himself what the prophet, reckoning — when 'Where is thy God?' was said to him 'daily' — poured 'his soul' over himself, rebuking her if ever she became faint through weakness and troubled, and saying: 'I shall pass through to the place of the wondrous tent, unto God's house, with voice of exultation and confession, the sound of feasting.' (Psalms 42:4)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His tears became his food as he repented, shed in measure and in dark times, and he drank them because he knew that tears and labor are followed by joy.
comments.comment:
Therefore he says: 'My tears became to me bread of days and of night' (Ps 42:3).

I do not weep casually, nor in pleasures, so that at times I might occupy myself with luxury and at times with the weeping of repentance, but also in the dark times; for the dark times are called night.

You also find a voice in another psalm that says this: 'You feed us bread of tears and you give me to drink in tears in measure' (Psalm 80:5).

It is necessary to bring forth the tears of repentance in a measured way, so that they may become bread and drink. … And besides, there will be other things that succeed the labor, the offspring produced from the tears. … In that which is said to me every day, 'Where is your God?'; for this reason also I offered so many tears to become food for me, because I heard them saying: 'Where is your God?'

(2 Kings 18:33); this also Sennacherib and Rapsakes said: 'Where is the God your God?'

And you, Israelite, 'Where is the God your God, that he may save you?'

Tears therefore became food for me, but 'in measure,' and I drank them and I ate them; for I knew that the tears and the labor of these things succeed something making joy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the psalmist's tears are called his bread.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Tears shed for virtue become the mourner's food by day and night, while those deceived mock him as though God were in a place.
comments.comment: He who does not toil in vain with tears but from a disposition for the sake of virtue, his own tears shall be fed as a just reward; he calls the day not only in the bearable circumstances but also names the night in the accidental circumstances (Ps 41:4a-b). Those deceived in all things stumble, and concerning the thinking that God is in a place; mocking indeed they say, 'Where is your God?' (Psalm 42:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who have forgotten God mock the seeker, and the tears he sheds from this grief bring blessing and comfort, since he grieves because righteousness is reproached.
comments.comment: Those who have utterly forgotten the return to God, he says, consider the seeking of God to be vain and reproach those who do it. I was brought to tears, living with the most unpleasant grief instead of sweet food, according to what is said in Lamentations: “He fed me with ashes” (Lamentations 3:16). I did not abandon my desire because of the separation and the reproach, but I was grieved because righteousness was being reproached. Necessarily, then, the harassment of the wicked and the reproaches come, since the tears that come from these are not harmful to the righteous. For upon these rests the blessing: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). And immediately comes the comfort (Psalm 42:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the tears and the mockery in the verses and the comfort that follows.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Remembering the insults, he did not pour out his soul outside but upon himself, like the one who says 'I was troubled and I did not speak'.
comments.comment:
These things I remembered and I poured out upon myself my soul.

When in recollection and memory I became of the insults of these ones who were speaking, these my enemies, I did not go out, I did not pour my soul out outside, but upon myself I poured it out.

It is like the words: 'I was troubled and I did not speak' (Psalm 77:4), and what Paul says: 'But we have received the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we may not be trusting in ourselves' (2 Corinthians 1:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fleshly festivals were shadows of spiritual ones, and the tabernacle stands for progress toward the perfection in which we dwell in God, in rejoicing and holy confession.
comments.comment: As it is said that the law contains the things of the future, the festivals according to the flesh were seen as shadows and symbols of future festivals; one longs to enter the spiritual festivals, so that the face of God may be seen perfectly, being nothing other than the icon of the invisible God. … Since I am progressing and not yet perfect, and the tabernacle is a symbol of progress as it is often said, for this reason I am troubled; but the tabernacle according to God wonderfully bears upon His own dwelling, that is, the perfection through which we dwell in God (Psalm 42:4). I shall pass through a wonderful place of tabernacling, as the dwelling of God, in a voice of rejoicing and holy confession according to the manner of those celebrating spiritually; for those celebrating spiritually hear themselves rejoicing and confessing (Psalm 42:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tent stands for progress in virtue and wisdom, and the one who passes through a place of wonderful tabernacle toward the house of God has not yet reached the end.
comments.comment: The tent is described as progress according to virtue and wisdom, being a shelter for those wandering. The theory is made clear in the first and fortieth Psalm, of the one hurrying toward the house of God, saying: 'I will pass through a place of a wonderful tabernacle until the house of God' (Psalm 42:4). For a place of a tabernacle and a wonderful progress is necessary for the one passing toward the house of God, dwelling but not yet tabernacling, until having reached the end with much progress, as one might say, in a joyful disposition.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the tent and the passing toward the house of God stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who rejoices at the presence of the Spirit celebrates the great feast of virtue, and 'confession' here means thanksgiving rather than confessing sin.
comments.comment: For the great feast is the perfection of virtue. For this is also what the psalmist says: 'Hear the voice of rejoicing and confession of those celebrating' (Psalm 42:4); for he who rejoices at the presence of the Spirit and confesses, not as one sinning and repenting, but as one giving thanks, celebrates—for the name of confession lies in place of thanksgiving, as in 'We confess to You, O Lord Father of the heavens...'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul's disturbance is turned toward himself rather than shown to others, and since the soul is disturbed he needs the cleansing bath of baptism.
comments.comment: My soul was disturbed toward myself; this is the kind of disturbance. And this was also said, when he says, 'I poured out my soul upon myself' (Psalm 42:4) toward the outside; I did not appear to them being disordered. The one being disturbed by these things, his disturbance is turned toward himself. … Therefore I will remember you from the land of Jordan and Hermon (Psalm 42:6). Since my soul is disturbed, even if the disturbance is toward myself, I need a cleansing bath, I have need of baptism. 'I remembered you' therefore 'from the land of Jordan and Hermon'. Hermon is interpreted as 'way of the lamp' or 'offering'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul is told to hope because God is present to free it from sorrow, and God saves the face by freeing it from ignorance and wickedness.
comments.comment: As if even while laboring you say, and while sick: 'Why have you despaired of health? Behold, the physician is present.' Hope in God, because I will confess to him; salvation of my face and my God. God is present; expect from him to be freed from sorrow and trouble. … Where the face is revealed from ignorance and sin; for 'the wisdom of man brightens his face' (Ecclesiastes 8:1). This bright face does not have a covering of ignorance, nor an overlay of wickedness, but is pure; you are the salvation of the face, O God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul should not be grieved by present things, since hope in God will console it with the good things and the salvation to be obtained at his appearing.
comments.comment: Do not let present things grieve you, he says, O soul, nor let them trouble you. But let hope in God console you, because we will obtain the good things worthy of thanksgiving and will have salvation at his appearing—which, according to Paul, is to await the appearing of the Lord and his kingdom. These things are intelligible concerning the future and the promises according to the law, and they reach higher, to what was said afterward by Paul … the better thing is to depart and be with Christ (Psalm 42:5). What follows is a narrative of the things that still grieve.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain reading of 'hope in God' as a comfort for the grieving soul.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Confession' in Scripture means either disclosing one's sins or giving thanks, and the one who confesses by recounting God's wonders is praising God.
comments.comment: The name of confession in the Scriptures signifies two things, so I will not speak of a third meaning. The public disclosure regarding sins is called confession, as if one says: 'having been gathered to confess concerning your sins.' This is found in the Epistle of Barnabas, in the epistle according to him: 'having been gathered to confess concerning your sins.' And again: 'confess your sins to one another' (James 5:16). 'I made my sin known to you, and my lawlessness I did not cover; I said, I will disclose my lawlessness to myself before the Lord' (Psalm 32:5). One confesses while wailing and stripping off his former sins. … It also signifies thanksgiving, as if the Savior says: 'I will confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden the divine things from the wise and understanding, and have revealed them to infants' (Matthew 11:25). … Thanksgiving, therefore, is manifested through confession. And: 'Let us confess to you, O God; let us confess to you, all peoples. I will recount all your wonders when I take my portion' (Psalm 75:1-2). The one who confesses by recounting the wonders is praising God, not regarding his own sins.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'confess' that the writer reads in the verse, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture often names the whole person by one part, so that 'Why are you sorrowful, my soul?' speaks of the more honorable part.
comments.comment:
Often the composite is signified by one of the things in the composition.

When the holy one says:

'Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?' (Psalm 42:5); then he makes the signification concerning the more honorable part.

When again he says that:

'I discipline my body and bring it into subjection' (1 Cor 9:27).

For he does not speak of it as separated from the soul, but since the body is subject and the soul is ruling, when the body is subject to the soul, being ruled, and ruled indeed with the word and with the law of God, it is disciplined and brought into subjection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even saints who endure much suffer in soul, as David did when he sang of being troubled, yet they do not fall from the divine purpose.
comments.comment: the saints, having endured much, suffer in soul under the opposing power, indeed as participating in human nature, but they do not fall from the divine purpose. And David, having become in such a war, sings: 'I was troubled and I did not speak' (Psalm 77:4); and again: 'Why are you dejected, my soul, and why are you disturbed within me?' (Psalm 42:5); and just as his own intellect is being shaken, he encourages them, saying: 'Hope in God, for I shall confess to Him' (Psalm 42:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the soul shrinks, the mind of Christ in us says 'Why art thou downcast' to it, and if it is still troubled the trouble is kept from outsiders and told to God.
comments.comment: And if ever you perceive a shrinking about your soul, let the mind of Christ in us say to her, who wills, so far as she can, to confound him too: 'Why art thou downcast, O soul? And why troublest thou me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him.' (Psalm 42:5) And again — would that the soul be nowise troubled, but even before the tribunals and bare swords borne against the neck be guarded by God's peace that surpasses 'all mind,' and calm, reckoning that those absent 'from the body' go home to the Lord of all himself! But if we are not so great as to keep untroubled always — though the soul's trouble be not poured out nor shown to outsiders, that we may have room for defense before God, saying to him, 'My God, my soul is troubled toward myself.' (Psalm 42:5–6,11)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Jordan stands for holy baptism, and Hermon for a way of light into the mind and heart.
comments.comment: If I were in the land of the Jordan, that is, if I were made worthy of the holy baptism, I will remember your victories (Psalm 42:6). And they also interpret 'Hermon' as the way of the lamp, as the holy baptism opening for them a way of light and radiance into the mind and heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Jordan and Hermon stand for, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Separated from God, the soul that desires him melts, and dwells in the small land of Jordan and Hermon amid storms and waves of calamity.
comments.comment: Separation from the one desired melts the soul that desires. I am separated from God, he says as long as he does not yet see paradise, his own foundation from the beginning, but still dwells in the land of Jordan and Mount Hermon—very small compared to that one—and is troubled as if by storms of winds and crashing waves, with calamities rushing upon him one after another like torrents (Psalm 42:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the longing, the place names and the waves in the verses as one picture.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The waterfalls of God are the deepest words about him or the divine prophets, and the one who sails uprightly through life's storms reaches the harbor of salvation.
comments.comment:
The deepest words about Him are the waterfalls of God, or the divine prophets (Psalm 42:7). The teaching of this Jesus calls upon the abyss, calling upon the abyss from the Old Scripture. Perhaps also, since the judgments of God are a great abyss, it is presented what is said of the judgments of others as judgments, and even those of all others are from the word of God, which is said to be a small stream (Psalm 42:7).

Having the cause; for the God Word is a great sea, but a small sea through which he voluntarily remained in a state of emptying for our sake. All your billows and your waves have passed over me. The sea, which is tropical to human life, not shipwrecked in it but sailing uprightly, having experienced storms and the swellings from the winter of the sea, having arrived at the harbor of salvation, will say the verse: 'For they did not pass over me, but they passed over' (Psalm 42:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As day calls to day in shining speech, the deep things of God are hidden like night, and we come to know deep things from other deep things.
comments.comment:
Listen: in the eighty-tenth Psalm it is said that 'day calls unto day the word, and night declares knowledge to night' (Psalm 19:2). During the day, that which is shining. The word of God, when it is luminous and shining and demonstrated, calls out in a manner of harmony, and we understand luminous things from such things; but the deep things are hidden, for the depth is darkness and night. 'Uncovering the deep out of darkness'.

This darkness is not the essence, but from that which 'He set as a hidden thing'. Wishing to make clear, we find something else unclear, rather it is for the one being instructed, and from that one the knowledge, from night indeed, and also here, since the 'judgments' of God are 'abyss' by 'much' in name it is signified. For it is said that 'the abyss is as a garment, his covering' (Psalm 104:6). We know the deep things from the deep.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good things belong to the coming age of God's mercy, while the present night is for gladness in hymns and prayer.
comments.comment: He teaches that the good things belong to the coming age, calling it the day in which God has promised to establish his mercy, according to what is said in Psalm 89: “Fill us in the morning with your mercy” (Psalm 89:14 [90:14]) (Psalm 42:8). But the present time, he says, is for gladness, when it is night and darkness, the conversation with God through hymns and the stretching out in prayer.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the day and the night of the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Thanksgiving in song comes before prayer, and 'Why have you forgotten me?' means not that God forgets but that he seems to neglect one unworthy of his care.
comments.comment: The words of supplication are also spoken in songs. But since supplication must be offered with thanksgiving, the song is placed before the prayer. For no one who has been ungrateful for what came before is strong in asking for what is to come. And the request seeks divine remembrance from God. For if I were in remembrance with you, the psalmist says, I would not be going about in gloom and being oppressed by the unjust. It is clear that forgetfulness does not touch the divine nature, since forgetfulness is a change in memory, and the divine is unchangeable. For this reason he also asks, “Why have you forgotten me?” No one says “Why?” about an involuntary experience of forgetfulness; rather, it presents voluntary forgetfulness as neglect of one unworthy of God’s care.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's mercy often comes painfully, so we do not see it, but the one who has deeply sought him knows that whatever God brings is for his good.
comments.comment: We have all deeply sought God manifestly as merciful, but not all of us see how he shows mercy; for often, those things occurring according to his mercy, those experiencing them painfully and not sweetly, we think they are not mercy. But he who has deeply sought, whatever God brings, he brings advantageously, that one will not say such a thing as 'Why have you forgotten me?' (Psalm 42:9), unless he is discussing his own repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'Why have you forgotten me?' is a question the seeker should not ask.
