comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bones are the soul's sound doctrines, crushed by deceivers' reproaches, and the soul is told to hope in the Lord, whose truth undoes their deceits.
comments.comment: Through the advancing bones of the soul, its pleasant doctrines and powers are said to be. Since it often happens to be crushed by terrible sophists, the deceivers reproach, not saying 'Where is your God upon whom you prosper?', but saying to his wisdom that it has been educated, and also concerning this suffering he reasons with his own soul, saying 'Why are you dejected? (Ps 42:5/11) For you hoped to confess upon the Lord; for certainly his face will shine upon you (Psalm 42:5/12)', nothing other than the truth, as you are able to loose the deceits of those crushing your set-before bones through the truth from God. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This psalm can be spoken from the presence of the Savior.
comments.comment: Psalm to David. Judge me, O God, and judge my cause from a nation of the unrighteous (Psalm 43:1). This psalm can be proclaimed from the presence of the Savior. Both the sacred and the profitable lie here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nation he asks to judge him has nothing to charge against him, yet it says he is not from God because he does not keep the Sabbath.
comments.comment: 'Judge me, O God, and plead my cause from an unrighteous nation' (Psalm 43:1). A holy nation he calls, whereas it says, 'Woe to a sinful nation, a people full of iniquities' (Isaiah 1:4). Since therefore he wishes to be judged by this, for they do not have that which I might charge against him; there are no indictments against them. They say, 'This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath'. And what is it to keep the Sabbath? Is it not necessary in the Sabbath not to raise the dead? How does it become a matter of bringing the 'blind from birth' into sight?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This psalm continues the last one without a title, and in asking the righteous Judge to plead his cause it adds the guidance of the light that has come into the world.
comments.comment: This psalm is inseparable from the previous one, not divided even by a title, and it holds to the same power of the return to God. It adds also the guidance through the light that shone forth, which says, “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who follows me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46) (Psalm 43:3). By this shining it prepares comfort for the one who grieves, just as the psalm before it made comfort for sorrows through the expectation of things to come. Since, then, the portion of the righteous is attacked both nation by nation and man by man, and they cannot obtain what they deserve unless they receive the heavenly judge and advocate—as if the case against their adversaries were a concern to him who judges all justly—he calls upon him, since he judges not from hearsay but brings forth what is just from knowledge. For this reason he asks for escape both from the nation and from the unjust man.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Psalm 43 continues Psalm 42 and why the psalmist asks God to judge his cause and send his light.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His only strength is God, so not being strengthened feels like rejection, and his 'why' asks that the trial end in mercy.
comments.comment:
The psalmist says this as one who has nothing else for strength, and he obtains God—as it is also said, “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:2 (18:1)) (Psalm 43:2; LXX 42:2a). Then he speaks here also about those who oppose him.

If strength comes from God, it is reasonable that not being strengthened is a rejection from God, most grievous to the one who puts forward this help alone. The “why” is not as if God does something without cause or in vain—for this happens for our contest—but as if the contest ought to have an end through mercy, and comfort ought to be given to those who mourn by the one who comforts those who mourn (Psalm 43:2; LXX 42:2). For it makes no sense that God would overlook the righteous. Therefore, seeking what comes from God, he says “why” as if to say: It is fitting for you to take hold of your own and not to permit pleasure to your adversaries (Psalm 43:2). Why then is what is yours not accomplished, but what comes from us abounds? As it is also said, “How long, Lord, will you forget me to the end?” (Psalm 12:2 (13:1)) and “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to destruction?” (Psalm 30:9) (Psalm 29:10 (30:9)). For even if affliction is necessary for some time, it is not forever; and even if we are justly afflicted on our own account, we ought at least to obtain help according to God’s mercy, so that discipline may give back a peaceful fruit through God’s love for humanity to those who have been trained by it (Hebrews 12:11). But in the case of the Lord, the “why have you forsaken me” is said in a complete sense, since what concerns him is not worthy of forsaking. Therefore the appearance of heavenly help is swift for the suffering body, because of that which concerns us.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Since his requests for light, truth and entry to God's altar have been granted by God, he gives thanks, striking the senses like lyres tuned toward virtue.
comments.comment: Speech signifies thanksgiving, for the requests have come to pass. He desired to know the reason for being driven away and for walking in darkness; he desired that the light and the truth be sent to him, since they led him; he desired to enter the altar of God and to experience the tabernacles of God and the holy mountain. Since, therefore, of these good requests it has come to pass through experience by God having given them to him, and not by himself having found them, because of this he may gratefully confess to him, striking the senses, which are nerves or lyres, and various thoughts or members; for when each of the members is tuned toward virtue, it is a stretched nerve, so that it may be struck musically by the striker of truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist ends in thanks, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Light and truth are the Word of God, who calls himself the light of the world.
comments.comment: But light and truth the Word of God is; for he himself says: 'I am the light of the world', 'I have come as light into the world', and 'was the true light'. 'Send out' therefore 'your light and your truth'.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the light and the truth are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The altar of God is an inner altar patterned on another, and the one who passes from the shadow of the law to the newness of the spirit comes to it and praises God with the harp of practical virtue.
comments.comment: And this altar, into which someone enters, is an interior one. … It is according to the imitation of another altar; for all things have been made according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain (Ex 25:40). A sacrifice of praise and that of righteousness is set forth; for 'sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God' (Ps 50:14) and 'sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness' (Psalm 4:5). 'I will come' (Psalm 43:4) therefore 'to the altar of God', then 'to the God who rejoices my youth' (Psalm 43:4); for the one turning away from the shadow of the law and the exterior altar says: 'What multitude of your sacrifices to me? I am full' (Isaiah 1:11), he enters, 'according to the order of Melchizedek priest' (Ps 110:4) saying: 'I will come to the altar of God, better than the visible things'. … 'I will come' therefore away from the sensible, from the literal, 'into the altar of God'. The one surpassing the 'oldness of the letter' which had preserved the shadow of the law and the old covenant, knowing these things, says: 'I will praise you, O God, with a harp' (Ps 108:2). Because I will enter into your altar having youth from the 'newness of the spirit' having been brought near, through this I will praise you gratefully with a harp. And the harp I have said many times that it signifies practical virtue or the body being struck by the inspired soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The harp shows brightness and the double address love, and we should give thanks for what is coming as we await God.
comments.comment:
He has shown the brightness by the addition of the lyre, and the love in the address repeated twice.

This is the reminder of comfort. For even if we are weighed down by present things, he says, let us give thanks for the things to come, and already by expectation let the sorrow depart, as we await God, the salvation of the person who looks to him (Ps 43:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the closing verses plainly: praise on the harp, and hope in God that lets sorrow depart before help arrives.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because he has already decided to give thanks, he rouses his soul to hope, and God is the salvation of the inner face when it is lit by wisdom.
comments.comment: “Why are you dejected, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess to him” (Ps 42:5). He asked if something belonged to him, and while he was still speaking of it, he sighed; moreover, before he receives, he has thus faithfully determined as if he had already received. Therefore he rouses his soul and says: “Why are you dejected, my soul?” Since, therefore, I have pre-decided to confess to him, hope in Him; accept that the things of thanksgiving shall belong to you. And the confession here signifies thanksgiving. … “God is the salvation of my face” (Psalm 42:11). “You are the salvation of my true face” (Psalm 42:11). The light is the salvation of your inner man, concerning which it is said: “The wisdom of a man makes his face shine” (Ecclesiastes 8:1). And again the saint says to have “the eyes of the heart” (Eph 1:18) enlightened, and “with an unveiled face to reflect the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor 3:18). When the face is reflected by the appropriate and divine glory and is enlightened by wisdom, God is my salvation. Others, having been rescued from sickness, said: “My salvation is the physician”; and another, having been rescued from storm and sea, let him say: “My salvation is the pilot.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints say 'our ears' to set their hearing apart from common hearing, and their fathers in instruction announced the divine things to them.
comments.comment:
They are not the ears of God but the ears of men themselves, just as musicians are said to be men. Musical instructions are heard by the ears of musical men. Therefore, when they say 'to our ears' (Psalm 44:1), they are not saying it for any other reason but by distinguishing the common things, they say 'to our ears.' The command 'let the one who hears, let him hear' agrees with this.

Our fathers announced to us; those fathers according to instruction announced the divine things, and the ancestors announced what was done through them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints' hearing is not ordinary hearing, because God adds an intellectual ear that hears his words in a way worthy of him, and this is what 'in our ears' means.
comments.comment:
It is therefore necessary to understand: 'God, in our ears we have heard, our fathers have declared to us' (Psalm 44:1). In their own ears, the saints say, we heard the words of God. An addition of ears occurs at the common hearing, when someone is able to hear intellectual words. The physician hearing medical words has a medical ear, but another does not. The one powerful enough to say, 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears' (Isaiah 50:5), does not speak about sensory hearing, but about that which is able to hear the intellectual words of God.

Thus, therefore, 'in our ears' must be heard, and it is not passing by; for it does not signify what is existing, but what is being added. And behold, how the saint says: 'The instruction of the Lord opens my ears.' He says: 'The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction to know when it is necessary to speak a word; He has placed for me first, He has added to me an ear for hearing; and the instruction of the Lord opens my ears.' The ear given according to addition is intellectual; it hears the words in a God-befitting way. And when this is added, His instruction then opens the ears—this thing which was added, the other ear, the intellectual one, the one hearing God-befittingly, the one able to say: 'I have heard unspeakable words'; for it is not possible for everyone to say this, but for the one having received the addition of an ear from God.

These things were in the mind of the Savior, having them, He was saying: 'Let him who has ears to hear, hear' (Matthew 13:9). But not all had the hearing of the words of Jesus, the words being announced in parables. … In our own ears, not the common ones toward irrational animals, but in those joined toward the intellectual words of God.

… 'Our fathers informed us' (Psalm 44:1). Our fathers according to instruction. Wise are those who say this. In what way, then, are they wise, having been born from them? Not as men; for many are wise from the unwise, and many are not wise from the wise.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what hearing 'with our ears' means for those taught by God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'work' is one of kind, not number, that came to be in the light of the fathers' lives, which they shared with us.
comments.comment: If he says 'work', he does not mean it by number, but by kind or even by genus. In their light—for we take the fathers to be wise—we say that in the days they lived, dazzled by the true light of the sun of righteousness—a work came to be in the light of their life, which they were not envious to share with us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God brought down the nations and hid his people in the holy land, as Moses prayed, but no one who stays outside merely hearing can enter the holy mountain.
comments.comment: He said, and he remembers: seven nations under the later called holy land he brought down (Psalm 44:2). They were hidden, having been led in by God into that land. Moses, therefore, without neglect, prays to repeat the mystery: 'Having led them in, hide them in the mountain of your inheritance, O holiness, Lord, which your hands prepared' (Exodus 15:17). See that no one living externally and hearing is able to enter into the holy mountain. The crowds in the parables, therefore, hearing and being outside, did not enter into the holy mountain, where the parables were made clear. It is necessary, therefore, to be led in first, and then thus to be hidden.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's 'hand' is his punishing power, carried out by angels and other ministers, just as we say the hand of a king.
comments.comment:
'Your hand' therefore 'destroyed nations'. Your punishing power. Those who serve with punishments, angels, are able to be called hands of God, just as we say the hand of a king, and we do not mean the limb of the body of a hand. …

This therefore he says: 'your hand', that is, the punishing power, or the active power of the persecutors, or your ministering power, 'destroyed nations'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'your hand' means when God is said to have driven out the nations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Read as about the Church, those from the nations were planted by God's instruction and saved by grace through his right hand and arm, not by their own work.
comments.comment: 'Your hand has destroyed and planted them' (Psalm 44:2). Regarding the thought of Israel, after the betraying of the Savior from the hand of God, those from the nations, having been destroyed, were planted by divine instruction in the God-breathed writings. God, having maltreated the people of the circumcision, cast them out from the holy training of the law. But the ones from the nations, having conquered not by a law of war, inherited the land spoken of as peaceful. Nor did their own arm save them, that is, their own work. For they have obtained salvation by grace under your right hand and the arm, that is, of the only-begotten Son. 'And the light that finds your face is illumination' (Psalm 44:3); what you have been pleased to save in them by grace, not by their work, so that they should not boast.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God harmed the nations for their discipline, and when they would not heed it they were driven out; the fathers took the land not by their own sword but by his right hand and arm.
comments.comment: You harmed the people and drove them out; for they did not inherit the land by their sword, and their arm did not save them. Those whom you drove out, you drove out having harmed them. But you brought harm upon them so that they might be disciplined. Often harm disciplines; for we do not speak here of harm from sin, but of harm from corrective discipline. Since, therefore, they did not attend to the corrective discipline as is necessary, they were moreover driven out and rejected. 'For they did not inherit the land by their sword' (Psalm 44:3). Our fathers, having taken the history of those driven from the land, did not possess the land taken from them by their own war, nor by their own power; 'for not by their sword, nor their arm' prevailed over them, 'but your right and your arm and the light of your face' (Psalm 44:3). There is the light, and the salvation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God drove out the nations and gives the credit for the land to God, not to the fathers' arm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The land was won not by the people's own hand but by God's arm, right hand and the light of his face, which on a higher reading is the Savior.
comments.comment:
But your right hand and your arm and the light of your face. … You did not inherit the land by your own hand or by your own arm, but the arm of God and the right hand and the light of his own face provided this to you.

In one way, this is for tropology: that you were not liberated and became in the holy land by your own power or by your own deed. But if you take it with a higher allegory, both his arm and his right hand and the light of his own face are the Savior. Therefore, not in themselves, but in this you were saved, you were migrated from the land of bondage into the good one.

Having prepared, he triumphed, but with God having fought alongside, as the scripture says: 'not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16). For you were pleased in them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The right hand means the practical power of the good, and the left is the power that opposes it.
comments.comment: One hand and the right hand: for the right is always a hand, but not every hand is right; for we have things to say that are performed by the right hand in a praiseworthy manner. Thus it is said in the Psalms: 'You held the right hand of me' (Psalm 73:23). The right is the practical power of the good, but the left is the opposing one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is both Creator and king, and as king he commands salvations for Jacob through his ministering spirits.
comments.comment:
You are yourself my king and my God (Psalm 44:4). For you are not only my God being my Creator and leading me toward my being, but also king, because by providence I rule, no longer being entangled in 'the affairs of life.' And indeed you are my God, I am a creation of God—and every creation has God as God—but as you rule.

He who commands the salvations of Jacob (Psalm 44:4). To Jacob, who is fleeing from evil, the king and being God commands the salvations. And salvations are commanded to the spirits who minister the salvations, concerning which the apostle says: 'Are not all of them ministering spirits sent for the service of those who are about to inherit salvation?' (Hebrews 1:14). Not so that they might confirm and give it, but so that, having heard it, they might proclaim it beforehand.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to call God both 'my king' and 'my God'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is the people's king and their strength, so that those who rise against them will be trampled.
comments.comment:
You, he says, we have as king—God, who provides for the salvation of our people—and we know that you will accomplish this, and we take courage in your will (Psalm 44:4-5).

You, he says, we have as a horn to ward off all enemies, and your name upon us will make those who rise up against us and hope to overpower us a thing to be trampled (Psalm 44:5).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God commands salvation to the ministering spirits for the saints, and as certain animals are given horns for protection, the saints have the powers of Jesus to gore their enemies.
comments.comment: The salvation of Jacob, which shakes off the worthless things, is commanded by God to the holy spirits sent for ministry, for those intending to inherit salvation, so that they may quickly arrive at understanding and give help through themselves. Just as God has granted a horn of protection to certain irrational animals so that they may escape those able to harm them, so the horns of Jesus are powers for the saints, goring their enemies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God himself is the saints' horn and defense, and his name upon them is an invincible weapon against those who rise up against them.
comments.comment: "We strike with horns our enemies in you" (Psalm 44:5). You see, we do not strike our enemies using physical horns; you are our horn and our defense. Therefore, you have that which is said in one of the Psalms by all the saints: "And in your favor our horn shall be exalted" (Psalm 89:17). It is not the physical horn; for the horn of those possessing it is again a defense. Through it, they will repel the approaching evils. Thus, those who have you as king and God do not have any other horn besides you. For instance, the word attributes something in one of the Twelve: "Those who say, 'We do not have horns in our strength'" (Amos 6:13). Having a horn and having power, we strike our enemies with horns. Because of this, the horns of these are also crushed: "and all the horns of the sinner I will break" (Amos 6:13). It is also possible for a king and a kingdom to receive a horn, as it is presented in Daniel: "the ten horns, ten kingdoms" (Daniel 7:24). Therefore, having you as king, we have you as a horn, and "we strike our enemies in you." And "in your name," since we have your designation upon ourselves, "we render powerless" all "those who rise up against us," having an invincible weapon: your designation. However, one must possess a designation, and not merely a hollow one. Not everyone who calls himself a Christian truly possesses the name of Christ, but rather he who is a Christian. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the 'horn' is and what it means to push down enemies in God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He may have a bow and a sword, but he does not place his whole expectation in them.
comments.comment: "For I do not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me" (Psalm 44:6). I indeed have a bow and a sword, since I am clothed in "the full armor of God," but I do not hope in these; not the whole of my expectation is in these, using them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A sword can be the speech of those who have the word.
comments.comment: Often the sword of those possessing the word is said: 'who have sharpened their tongues like a sword' (Psalm 64:3); and 'sons of men, their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp knife' (Psalm 57:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because God saved them from those who afflict and shamed those who hate them, they learned not to put their hope in the bow.
comments.comment:
For you saved us from those who afflict us.

Since you saved us also from those who afflict us, we knew that 'in you we gore our enemies' (Psalm 44:5).

Because of this, then, since this has surpassed us from you, we knew that one must not hope in the bow—to use it, indeed, but not as having shot through it irretrievably.

And you turn those who hate us to shame.

Those who hate have a difference again from those who afflict …

Often the same ones both afflict and hate …

Sometimes, however, the one hating is not able to be an enemy when he is weak; for the weak one is able to hate, but he is not able to act as an enemy from the manifest action, for it would harm him.

… God delivers and saves from these and puts them to shame.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because success never came from the people's own weapons, they boast in God and thank his name for all time.
comments.comment:
For I do not prepare myself, he says, with bow and spear (Psalm 44:6). Therefore I do not trust in weapons, since these did not suffice even for our fathers, nor was the success accomplished according to their strength, but the work is beyond all human preparation (Psalm 44:7).

He says the earlier teachings correspond to the later events. We have been taught that our salvation from adversaries has always come from you, and we have seen their power turned to shame.

For this reason, he says, we boast altogether in you through all time, and we offer thanks to your name by which we are saved—as it is also said through Ezekiel: “It is not for your sake that I act, O house of Israel … but for the sake of my name” (Ezekiel 36:22) (Psalm 44:8; Ps 43:10.11).
comments.selected_reason: Shows why the psalmist refuses to trust his bow and gives the glory to God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The saints have no ground for praise except God, and confessing in his name means giving thanks, since his name has become the cause of their salvation.
comments.comment:
'In God we shall be praised all the day long' (Psalm 44:8).

Of those being praised, some are praised for the beauty of the body, others because of strength.

The stout ones are praised in strength, others in another skill, and others because of wealth, because of nobility; but in you we shall be praised.

We have no cause for praise other than you; for even if we have hardship, since through you we have attained these things and 'in God we do power' (Psalm 60:12), in you we have the praise. …

And we shall confess in your name forever.

This calling of yours provides much power to us.

For in it indeed we 'despise' all 'those who rise up against us'.

Therefore 'in your name we shall confess forever'.

The name of the confession here signifies thanksgiving: 'I will confess to you, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and have revealed them to infants' (Matt 11:25).

In order that it may be a gift, it is possible to say thus: 'in your name we shall confess', because it has become to us a cause of salvation.

And it is also possible to say this: in your name which has been invoked upon us, as if you are saying: in knowledge or in virtue I shall confess.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to boast in God and to confess his name, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's holy men were sent into captivity not for their own sins but to help and heal those condemned there.
comments.comment:
And he says: 'But now you have saved and protected us, and you will not let go in the powers of our own'.

When he went out in the powers of our own, his military power or by the power of our strength, we always prevailed.

And everything contrary exists here for us.

And since I was saying … Israel, sinning, was driven from Jerusalem to Babylon in the manner of captivity.

And Daniel and those three and Joshua the son of Nun and Ezekiel and the others of the Twelve Prophets were there, Haggai and Zechariah.

These were not taken into Babylon in the manner of captivity, but for the sake of being a participant, helping and healing those condemned there.

God condemns someone with mercy, that is, he does not leave him without help.

And he sends angels and makes holy men to fall and be harmed and in captivity, not because of their own sins, but for the sake of the salvation of others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good are left among sinners and put to shame by God so that they may help others, and this shame is beneficial and brings them glory.
comments.comment:
Regarding the good being abandoned to the bad, it is not to provide help or to have a supporter so as to be left alone; rather, in some way they were left abandoned, having become helpers to others, not so that they might be destroyed, but so that they might be useful and not allow the sins of the condemned to increase. …

Not everyone of the people was saying, 'God, in our ears we have heard, our fathers announced to us' (Psalm 44:1). And with a few, 'But your right hand and your arm... and the light of your face' (Ps 44:3). Not all the people said this. … These, therefore, did not stretch out hands toward a foreign god. 'Now I will send away and shame us' (Psalm 44:9). No one sinning is shamed by God.

But by himself. And God is shamed in a certain way when the one not sinning is with the sinners; and the shame is beneficial and brings glory to the one being shamed. …

'And you will not go out in our powers.' Formerly you used to go out in our powers; you used to run ahead of us into the wars, and we were surrounded by those attacking. But this thing of not going out in the powers, he says: you help, but you do not help. You help us so that we may be shown to be athletes through being left behind and we may benefit others; for he did not say: 'You destroyed our powers,' but 'you will not go out in our powers.' You turned us back to the rear before our enemies. The enemies were behind them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Their hopes stay firm though the opposite has happened: they are left behind by God, shamed and plundered by those they once mastered.
comments.comment: But these hopes, he says, are firm and unshakable, and we will not abandon them because of what has happened. Yet what has happened now is the opposite of them. For we have been left behind by you, he says, having been thrust away, and you are not present with our armies. The shame that then seized the battles has come around upon us, and we have been diminished before those whom we formerly mastered, and we have been plundered by those whom we plundered. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms the people's complaint that God has left them to defeat.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's turning away from his people is not always because of sin, since there are other causes for which he is not responsible.
comments.comment: 'God has turned away from himself' (Psalm 44:10; LXX 43:10), not entirely because of sin, but also because of other things for which He is not the cause. And not everyone turning toward the things behind experiences this; for if someone, leaving the worthless things, flees far away by withdrawing from them, not everyone having turned toward the things behind has left what he left behind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turned his people back before their enemies for a useful purpose, since they came to an earthly place for the sake of others.
comments.comment: They say: 'You turned us backward among our enemies' (Psalm 44:10). And those hating us seized us for themselves (Psalm 44:10). They would not have been able to take us by hand, if you had not turned us back among them for the sake of usefulness. They are enemies and haters; for to hate is to be an enemy. But we are neither enemies nor haters. … Lord, you turned us back among them, you have made us to be with those who are condemned. Therefore, those who were formerly in the form of God, having taken the form of a slave through compassion, say such a thing: that we have come to an earthly place not for ourselves, but for the sake of others, because you did not go out in our powers; for formerly you used to go out in our powers to bring us the victory against our enemies, and guarding us in the land of our fathers where we descended. Since therefore you did not go out in our powers, we were turned backward among those hating us. … Again Judas betrayed the Savior, and the betrayal became useful for the removal of 'the sin of the world' (John 1:29). Again, those crucifying did not crucify him with this intention.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who leave Zion, which is virtue, and turn back toward Babylon fall among the enemies.
comments.comment: … If someone, having left Zion, that is to say, virtue, rushes toward the evil called Babylon, turning back to the things behind, he receives a blessed thing; but those saying the things set forth, since they have become among the enemies, having turned back to the things behind, fell into filth (Psalm 44:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even when devoured by enemies like lions and wolves, God's people remain sheep.
comments.comment:
For it is not, as some suppose, that they blame that day. Instead, they move toward other sayings: 'You have given us as sheep for food' (Psalm 44:11). We were handed over for our own eating; lions and wolves are devouring us. However, even if we are being devoured, we do not cease to be sheep: 'Israel was a wandering sheep; lions drove him out; the first devoured him, the King of Assyria' (Hos 11:7, 10:6). It is a bad thing for what has happened to be praised, not to remain as it is, but to be resolved into another quality. The one eating bread, if he sends it down into the stomach, the bread does not remain. And those who have been cast down and have become the food of enemies have not ceased to be sheep. …

These therefore say: 'You gave us as sheep for food.' Having been eaten as sheep, they remained sheep.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people scattered among the nations are like seeds sown in the earth, which change the earth into their own nature and bear many grains for the benefit of others.
comments.comment: They seem to say this: 'We have been sown among the nations, we have been dispersed in many places.' But they seem to have suffered this in Babylon and Assyria alone. Therefore, what he says is this: the sowing of these seeds, such as wheat or barley, is first useful in a Gospel-like way if they are sown in the earth; for this earth receives them into its own substance through a change and transformation. For from the earth, having changed, many came from one grain; they changed from the earth into harvests. … And he says 'seeds' regarding those saying these things, the saints, saying: 'In you we shall be praised and in your name we shall confess for ever' (Psalm 44:8). Behold, those saying: 'With you we horn our enemies' and the others, let them say: 'You have sown us among the nations' by way of seeds, so that the nations, in a certain way, if we are sown among them in a foreign land, we might change into ourselves, and one of us might become an ear of corn bearing many grains, benefiting many souls. And those being benefited are said to be different: sometimes children of those benefiting, when those are named fathers, sometimes sheep, when those have the state and conduct of a shepherd. These therefore, as seeds having been cast down, took into themselves those being benefited from being placed before them. Having been placed, the seeds changed the earth. The nations therefore are the earth, but the seeds are those cast down for the benefit of others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints, given like sheep to be food, were scattered among the Gentiles like seed, to change the Gentiles into their own likeness.
comments.comment: Those saying these things are like certain sons who, similarly to a sheep being led to slaughter, are given to be food for those approaching them for their own benefit with words and life; but even among the Gentiles they were scattered by God, sowing the seed like farming, so as to change the Gentiles into the same quality as themselves. For one must not pay attention to those saying that God's portion was scattered among the Gentiles in the manner of captivity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Israel is devoured like sheep and scattered among the nations, and being sold means losing honor and falling under human masters instead of God.
comments.comment:
We have been gripped by cowardice, he says, a cowardice unable to defend us against those who devour us like sheep. This is the cowardice that Moses also threatened would seize them for their transgressions, because the sound of a driven leaf would pursue them. And we have become captives, he says, and we have been scattered among the nations—we who were formerly brought out from the nations and possessed the holy land. This is a dissolution of honor, just as for man the dissolution of his formation is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). So also Isaiah says about the people: “We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your mercy was not called upon us” (Isaiah 63:19) (Psalm 44:12).

Freely they were sold, as Isaiah also says. And he says they were sold for their sins, just as Paul says about man: “I am fleshly, sold under sin” (Romans 7:14). The sale is the alienation and the coming to be under human masters instead of God. This is what he also threatened Jeroboam and the people with him through Shemaiah the prophet: that they would become slaves to the Egyptian king Shishak, and they would know the slavery of God and the slavery of the kings of the earth (2 Chronicles 12:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being given as sheep, scattered and sold means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Being devoured like sheep, sold and mocked comes most justly upon them, since they led Christ like a sheep to slaughter, bought the Lord for silver and mocked him on the cross.
comments.comment: For such a thing is a parable—that they are remembered in the curses. Just as Jeremiah says against the false prophets: “They will take up a curse against him in the exile, O Judah, in Babylon, saying, ‘May the Lord do to you as he did to Zedekiah and as to Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in fire because of the lawlessness they committed in Israel’”. Grant these things now, and most justly: they are devoured like sheep, when they led Christ like a sheep to slaughter; they are sold to the nations, just as they bought the Lord, betrayed for silver and in some way handed over to death; they are mocked, just as they made mockery and shaking of heads at the crucified Lord (Psalm 44:11-14).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Being led into captivity was dishonor, yet it was endured so that God might gather his people to himself.
comments.comment: You sent away your people without honor (Psalm 44:12). … for having been led into captivity, we were not led there with honor, but having been led by the law of captivity; for nothing is more dishonorable than this. 'Without honor' therefore is 'you sent away your people'. … And for this reason we have endured these things, to come into captivity and to be scattered among the nations, so that you might gather to yourself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Under the law a sheep is put in place of a firstborn donkey, so that substitutions stand in for what is owed.
comments.comment: And there was not a multitude in our substitutions. Often, for the sake of certain things, safe and redeeming substitutions are given. For instance, it says: 'It is holy everything that opens a male womb.' And it says that, if it is a firstborn sheep or an ox or a goat, among those brought to the altar, it is necessary to perform the sacrifice itself. But if it is a firstborn donkey or something else of the priests, it is not even brought to the altar; 'you shall change a sheep in its place.' Through a sheep its value is changed and it enters into the temple. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not for honor but for their sins God handed his people over to their enemies.
comments.comment: Not for honor, he says, having taken the people, he sent them away, but because of their sins they have been made submissive to enemies (Psalm 44:12); for through their sins they were given over according to the prophet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people's reproach in captivity is likened to the reproach of Christ, which is a greater wealth than treasure, unlike the reproach of evil men or fallen angels.
comments.comment: A reproach has become to us from our neighbors. Regarding the history, the neighbors are the nearby ones... since therefore we were carried off into captivity, 'a reproach we have become to our neighbors' (Psalm 44:13). They themselves have not suffered nor have they prevailed with the rising of wars, but we. And as for the thought of this: just as the cross of the Savior has become a reproach for the sake of salvation—for it has been said: 'counting the reproach of Christ a greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt' (Hebrews 11:26)—so also these have in a way fallen into reproaches, having been seized and having been led into captivity. 'Angels,' he says, 'who did not keep their own beginning, but having left their own habitation, fell into everlasting chains' (Jude 1:6). This reproach of the angels is not praiseworthy, because having been granted to dwell in heaven and being able to stand and remain beside God always praising, they became in wickedness so as to fall from heaven. This reproach is trivial. Behold, indeed, the reproach of Christ is not only praiseworthy, but is greater than treasures. And if there were no difference between these, the proverbist would not have said: 'Do not acquire the reproach of evil men' (Proverbs 3:31). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A parable compares one thing to another, as the Gospel compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, humble and small in its wording.
comments.comment: He made us a parable among the nations. Something hidden by a word is compared to something similar. That it may become clear, let us see from the Gospel (Matt 13:31): he compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed, not saying 'it is like a mustard seed' while being a seed itself; for it was no longer a similarity, but an identity. He says 'hyper' [beyond/exceeding]. Therefore, the mustard seed has a power smaller in size than the seeds, capable of transforming and becoming such a plant. And the kingdom of heaven, thus revealing the teaching of the Scriptures, is something humble and small in its wording. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: People point to the captives as a parable among the nations, who cannot tell good from evil, because the saints stand above other ranks of men.
comments.comment:
The Greek word is an evangelical word. For this reason, therefore, this parable was spoken: 'for a parable' thus 'us as a nation among the nations'. If anyone wishes to interpret the captives, they use us, saying: 'Behold, these ones having been led away well before... God, when the right hand of God and the light of his face were protecting them, they fell into a most evil leading away'. If anyone therefore wishes to show a falling away, they refer to us. And 'made us a parable' is not in Israel, not in Israel, not in the Hebrew multitude, but 'among the nations'.

Those who are truly nations do not know the difference between good and evil, but they consider all pleasant things and all appropriate things to be good, and the opposites of these to be evil. And the name of the parable may be this: the rank of the saints has a certain superiority compared to the other ranks of men. Because of this, they have become a parable. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While we have works of shame we wear a veil, as 'the shame of my face covered me' shows, whereas Paul, who had none, had an unveiled face.
comments.comment: As long as we have 'the works of shame,' it is clear that we have the veil, according to what is said somewhere in the forty-third Psalm: 'And the shame of my face covered me.' (Psalm 44:15; LXX 43:15) I have set beside this that the one who has no works of shame has no veil—as Paul was, saying, 'We all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 3:18) Paul has an unveiled face; he does not have works of shame. The one who is not like Paul has a veiled face.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'All the day' means the whole span of a life, and the face covered by shame is covered rather than destroyed, while those who reproach are straying into idle words.
comments.comment:
He says 'all the day' and 'through life'. A man's life is called that which is from birth until death, sometimes called one day, sometimes an age. Thus it is said: 'I will not eat meat for ever' (1 Corinthians 8:13), and: 'he shall be thy servant for ever' (Deuteronomy 15:17). I had trouble against me all this day which I endured for the sake of others (Psalm 44:15); and the shame of my face covered me. The shame of the inner man covered me. For my face was not destroyed, but it was covered. And it is possible, having cast off the single covering, to bear his face naked, illuminated, as it is according to nature. And, so that I may phrase it this way, the ignorance that happens to other men destroys their face; for others become from others, from men serpents and wolves and foxes. But the holy man, even if he does not bear his own face naked, has it covered. … When someone becomes foolish among the thoughtless, having cast folly upon himself, he has his face covered; when he becomes lawless among the lawless, he has his face covered.

From a voice reproaching and speaking idly. He says this: those are reproaching me and speaking idly. And those speaking idly are straying. … To speak idly is to say superfluous things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fallen from virtue, they bear their own disgrace, the shame covering the face of the soul that should reflect the Lord's glory.
comments.comment:
Since we have fallen away from the aforementioned things through a life fearing destruction, we face our own disgrace (Psalm 44:15), the shame of our face covering us so that we no longer have boldness, with the face of the soul uncovered to reflect the glory of the Lord.

From the voice of the one reviling and acting unjustly and speaking wrongly, he sees that the day of ruin is before him (Psalm 44:16). And from the one displaying his terrible face, driving out an enemy, the shame of it covered his face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many forget God in pleasant times as well as in affliction, and those who abandon the divine laws are resettled from the Jerusalem above into an earthly place, which is captivity in allegory.
comments.comment:
Because the voice is of holy ones. Many many times also from the pleasant things they forget God, not only from the unpleasant ones. For he says: 'take care of yourself lest, having eaten and being filled and having built fine houses... the Lord your God you forget' (Deut 8:12). Sometimes, having come into afflictions, it is said they forget God. All these things came upon us, and we did not remember you, and we did not act wickedly against your covenant. …

There is also a Jerusalem above. Those living according to the divine laws dwell in God. If they become apostates from the divine laws, they are resettled into the place concerning the earth, and this is the captivity according to allegory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The noble bear affliction bravely, knowing that it is necessary to enter the kingdom through many tribulations, and they do not wrong God's covenant by questioning his decrees.
comments.comment:
And just as if someone is a father, when he sees his son suffering from fever and weakness, he strikes him, he is grieved, not because he strikes him, but because he has come into such a state; so also these, being noble and knowing that 'through many tribulations it is necessary to enter the kingdom of God' (Acts 14:22), they do not sink entirely into the afflicted. For they say: 'In all things we are afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Corinthians 4:8).

Not being distressed is to bear the afflictions bravely. 'And we have not acted unjustly toward your covenant' (Psalm 44:17). What has been decreed according to your will remains for ever, and all things according to your judgments, and therefore we have not acted unjustly. If anyone says, 'Why is this one a child and that one a child, and this one rich and that one poor?' he acts unjustly toward the covenant of God. Just as with these covenants which men establish, if anyone wishes to contradict and fight against one of those written, he unjustly acts against the covenant in vain. His own injustice seems to be an injustice against the covenant. If anyone handles the God-breathed Scripture differently, as the heretics do, they act unjustly toward the Gospel, toward the Divine Scripture.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The exiles' one hope was that they never turned to idols or left the one God, as Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael showed, but the Jews of his own day lack this, since their impiety toward Christ enslaves them as never before.
comments.comment: This alone remains to Israel as a hope for the recall of those who are left, which the prophecy foreseeing says: that they did not turn aside to the customs of the Greeks according to the idolatry they had agreed upon, nor did they swerve from the path of piety toward the one God that had been commanded them, even though they were so humbled and exiled and placed under the authority of those who kill. This was preserved especially by those around Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, who endured fire rather than accept worship of idols. And indeed, this is not present as something pious among the remaining Jews at the present time. For while they do not entirely abandon the practice of not going to idols or the Greek sickness of incantations, their impiety toward Christ is shown to be most harmful in this way: because, not worshiping idols as before, they are enslaved as never before.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Under many afflictions and pressure to forget God, they remembered him; the place of affliction is the earth and the underworld.
comments.comment:
The voice, having taken up perfect courage (Psalm 44:17): for having heard many and various afflictions upon them and being coerced into forgetting God, they say, as it were, 'In the affliction of the Lord I remembered' (Psalm 44:18). …

He abandons his own way, handing himself over to the desires of his own heart and to an unproven mind (Psalm 44:18). The earth and the underworld are a place of affliction; thus those having experienced the body of death are humbled (Psalm 44:19). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Their hearts and paths did not turn from God's way even when he handed them over to captivity.
comments.comment: And our heart has not turned backward (Psalm 44:18). You see that there is a remaining straightness of following. 'Has not turned backward' means we have not become others, having a heart that is right and straight and looking straightly. And this thing of the unsettled and the uncertain happens to us; many, having come into affliction, turned their mind so as to grumble against providence. 'And you have turned our paths from your way' (Psalm 44:18). This says that we ran your way well before we descended into this condition and conduct. 'You have turned our paths from your way,' because you have transferred us into another life and a way suitable to life. However, even if 'you have turned our paths' by handing us over to captivity, nevertheless our paths did not turn away from your way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The place of affliction is the earth, or the land of captivity, and the shadow of death lay on them without consuming them, like a stone held up on high that has not fallen.
comments.comment: For you have humbled us in a place of affliction (Psalm 44:19). Take the place of your humbling according to both the consequences of the deportation from Jerusalem to Babylon. Primarily this place is the earth, where the souls that are brought low are humbled, 'the body of humiliation.' It can also be handed over to the afflicted to bear the shame and the place of affliction, namely the land of Assyria or the land of Babylon. 'And you have covered us with the shadow of death' (Psalm 44:19). Even if the death of affliction lay upon us, it did not consume us. His shadow covered us. Let it be like a heavy stone lifted up on high. Let someone be under this, but not necessarily fallen upon it.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain picture of being under the shadow of death without being crushed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Place of affliction' means the region about the earth, where man was cast from paradise.
comments.comment: He too is a prophet who said, “You brought us low in a place of affliction” (Psalm 44:19), calling the region about the earth a “place of affliction,” the place to which Adam, that is, man, came when he was cast out of paradise because of wickedness (Genesis 3:23–24).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: These words are no longer said to God himself but to others, and every falsely named god of the nations counts as a foreign god.
comments.comment: If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god, then these things are no longer said toward God himself. Previously, it was said toward God himself: 'You turned our paths from your way; you humbled us in a place of affliction' (Psalm 44:18-19). Therefore, they say to others that they have become in these things through sin and lawlessness, and they say: 'If we have forgotten the name of our God and if we have stretched out our hands toward a foreign god,' that is to say, if we have worshipped a foreign god. But all those called gods according to the Scripture who are falsely named should be considered foreign gods; for it has been said: 'All the gods of the nations are demons' (Psalm 96:5; LXX 95:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Forgetting God's name or stretching out hands to a foreign god is no small matter, and God seeks it out because he knows the secrets of the heart, which men do not.
comments.comment:
He says: do not think it a small thing to forget the name of God or to stretch out hands toward a foreign god. For God also seeks these things. And you know that some, especially in persecutions, were saying this: that it is possible to do things without acting with the heart. Indeed, many died saying this, and they silenced the name of God as if forgetting Him. He says, not even this is enough to hide God, who is invisible, and He seeks these things. For does He not seek? The following text does not permit this way of thinking. For He himself knows the secrets of the heart.

Let him who is ignorant of the secrets of the heart seek first whether he acted thus or like that. For instance, if someone, pretending to be wise, says: 'I did not stretch out my hands toward a foreign god,' I say: 'I, who am ignorant of the secrets of the heart, am examining these things.' But God does not seek; for He knows them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist can appeal to God, who alone knows the secrets of the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul is crowned in secret too, because the testimony of a clear conscience is martyrdom before God, who knows the secrets of the heart.
comments.comment: But not the open martyrdom alone: secretly too the soul is crowned that denies itself through love toward God. 'The testimony of our conscience' (2 Corinthians 1:12) — this too is martyrdom before God, who 'knoweth the secrets of the heart.' (Psalm 44:21) For 'for thy sake we are killed all the day' (2 Corinthians 1:12) — the daily death of the self-denied. Blessed then are the pure in conscience, whether before tribunals or in secret, for God seeth in secret and rewardeth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who die every day for God and are counted as sheep for slaughter can be offered to him as a pleasing sacrifice, like the souls under the altar in Revelation.
comments.comment: "Because of you we die all day, we were counted as sheep for slaughter" (Psalm 44:22). … Those dying all day for God and counted as sheep for slaughter have no doubt whether they have come to the name of God or stretched hands toward a foreign god. Therefore, one does not seek these things from a heart that is manifest. "We were counted" then "as sheep for slaughter." Everyone who wishes to slaughter us can do so. And this is possible; even if some fight us, we consider ourselves as sheep being ritualized, as being sacrificed to God for a "pleasing sacrifice" (Ps 50:5). Indeed, in the Revelation of John, "the souls of those being persecuted for the testimony of Jesus" (Rev 6:9) appeared dancing under the altar of the heavenly God, clearly as victims having come there.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be counted as sheep for slaughter for God's sake.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sleep ascribed to God in this verse is figurative speech, so the wrath ascribed to him can be read figuratively too.
comments.comment: That what is said about the wrath of God is meant figuratively is clear also from the fact that sleep is recorded of him. As if waking him from it, the prophet says: “Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). And again he says: “And the Lord awoke like one who sleeps, like a mighty man reeling from wine” (Psalm 78:65). If, then, sleep means something else, and not what the obvious reading of the words shows, why should wrath not be understood in a similar way too?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God seems to sleep when he is patient with the wrongs done to his holy men, and in Babylon those around Daniel were cast away only in place, not to the end.
comments.comment:
"Arise; why, Lord, do you sleep? Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). It seems that God sleeps when He is long-suffering toward the wrongdoing of His own holy men and the groaning of those made according to Him. Indeed, they send up a prayer saying: "Cast the hands toward their pride to the end" (Psalm 74:3), and: "May the pride of those hating you ascend to you always" (Psalm 74:23). And it seems God sleeps when He is long-suffering, when He overlooks His own being afflicted. "Arise and do not cast us away to the end" (Ps 44:23). For if even we have become captives and are being afflicted in the place of ill-treatment, being human, mortal, and liable to fall, we fear being cast away to the end. Israel was cast away in Babylon, when they worshiped Bel and had made the image of Nebuchadnezzar and other things of the Babylonians; they were cast away to the end. But those around Daniel, even if they were cast away locally, they were not cast away to the end; for they remained in the same godliness. It seems they were cast away, but they were not cast away to the end, the lions being silenced and him ascending unhurt.

"Why do you turn your face away, forgetting our poverty and our affliction? For our soul has been humbled into dust" (Psalm 44:24-25). This is the same as sleeping and seeming to turn the face away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is said to sleep and what being 'cast off for ever' does and does not mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The body of humiliation surrounds the saints without humbling them inwardly, and the belly cleaves to the earth when the soul feeds on earthly things instead of heavenly bread.
comments.comment:
Why then do you turn away? Will you then forget our poverty and our affliction? Because of you we are afflicted, because of you we are poor. But you do not forget these things. In which things one conquers, even if he is gloomy or even if he is joyless. It was said that the dust is more bodily. 'Our soul was humbled' therefore, of those saying these things, 'into the dust'. 'The body of humiliation' surrounds us, but we were not humbled by it. As if someone, for instance, receives a blow from a certain tyrant, he seems to have been humbled, but he was not humbled; for he still has the same pride, he still has the same joy. Because of this we are poor and are afflicted, because our soul, having been humbled into the dust, does not clearly possess its own resurrection, and 'our belly was stuck to the earth' (Psalm 44:25).

But they do not say this about them in truth, but about their own members, about their own people. And there are two ways for the belly to have been humbled to the earth: when someone thinks of earthly things and seeks lower things, he does not produce heavenly offspring, he does not produce God-fearing thoughts, but all human things; and the soul saying these things becomes a mother, 'because our belly was stuck to the earth' (Psalm 44:25). And according to a second meaning, the one being nourished by the heavenly bread, the belly receiving heavenly nourishment, was stuck to heaven. But those who eat the flesh of the dragon and carry the same food to the serpent, being earth, have the belly stuck to the earth. And just as it is said concerning the sensible things: 'the foods to the belly, and the belly to the foods; and God will destroy both this and these' (1 Corinthians 6:13), so also the belly and the stomach of the soul, when it is not nourished by heavenly things, when it does not receive from its divine bridegroom, has the belly stuck to the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul is humbled to the dust and the belly cleaves to the earth when it feeds on nothing heavenly but only on earthly things.
comments.comment: If one speaks these things tropically, what is meant is this: since we are currently surrounded by the composite of pleasure and other passions, because of this, 'Our soul was humbled to the earth, having become low-minded, and also our belly was stuck to the earth, feeding on nothing heavenly but eating all things according to the nature of earth all the days of their lives.' But if the present text is explained allegorically, the soul stepping into the body says, 'Our soul was humbled to the earth.' Having fallen away from itself and from the blessed life of the heavenly, while thinking of the lower things, it says, 'Our belly was stuck to the earth,' for it feeds on nothing other than earthly things (Psalm 44:25).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The people ask to be helped and redeemed for God's name's sake, not trusting in their own righteousness, because they are God's own and were sent into hardship to help others.
comments.comment:
Arise, Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name. We ask for help, lest the afflictions remaining for a long time might harm our soul which is turning. …

And then, so that they may not boast in their own righteousness, trusting in it, he says: 'Arise, O Lord, help us and redeem us for the sake of your name' (Psalm 44:26). We are enriched by you. For this reason we have come into these afflictions, because we are yours, and for the sake of help you have sent us into this hardship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm ends by asking for rescue for God's name's sake rather than for the people's own merit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They ask for help by God's own name, and the words also fit the Savior, who rose to give deliverance and his soul as a ransom for many.
comments.comment: These say that they are worthy to receive help and deliverance, not by the grace of another but by His name. And these things are also said regarding the Savior, being worn down in the heart of the earth according to the season of passion, so that having risen, He might provide help and giving deliverance, giving His soul as a ransom for many. And He does these things for the glory of His name.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The song is assigned to the beloved because he became the cause of the change in us, as a victory song is credited to the king or general.
comments.comment: 'Unto the end,' therefore, 'for those who shall be altered; to the sons of Kore for understanding.' And since the inscription itself and the whole psalm have mysteries hidden within them, for this reason understanding is needed for the one bringing this song; for it is 'for understanding.' … This very triumphal song became for the beloved; for he himself became the cause of the alteration; for he said that 'being rich, he became poor,' so that he might work us to be rich … He said that having become cursed, he established a blessing. Therefore, the beloved has become the cause of this best of transformations. For this reason, the song is assigned to him; just as a victory song is sent to a general or a king, even though others, spear-bearers and soldiers, are accompanying him, yet the essence of the victory is inscribed to the king or the general.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A person fed on the bread of life and the flesh of Jesus brings forth a good word, as one who eats an apple breathes out its scent.
comments.comment:
"My heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 45:1). Some take this psalm to be spoken from the presence of the Father and from the presence of the perfect man, the wise one. And you know that the eructation of previously eaten food brings forth its fragrance; for there is no eructation other than a proceeding of spirit from the stomach declaring the quality of the things previously eaten. If indeed anyone eats an apple, he has the eructation bringing forth the quality and fragrance of the apple.

When therefore a holy person eats the "bread of life" (John 6:35) and having Jesus' flesh as true food and the fruits of the "tree of life" (Genesis 2:9) and drinks the wine being harvested from the "true vine" (John 15:1), he has an eructation suitable to the foods previously eaten. He who has thus been fed and has eructated signifies: "the good man out of the good treasure of the heart brings forth the good" (Luke 6:45). And since it is concerning spiritual things, he was not hesitant to speak of a treasure instead of stomachs, namely the heart.

He who therefore has been fed on the blessed food and has enjoyed the flesh of Jesus and the "bread of life" (John 6:35), the bread of heaven, brings forth words suitable to that which he was fed and eructated: "my heart searched out a good word" (Psalm 45:1). We have therefore spoken fully concerning the man.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of the heart bringing forth a good word: what a person is fed on shows in what he says.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God has a heart, which means his mind, and the Son, the Word, is the offspring of that mind and not of another essence.
comments.comment: And here, therefore, again, the Word, desiring to show that the Savior is not of another essence than the Father's, says that he himself has drawn a word from the heart: 'for my heart has drawn out a good word' (Psalm 45:1). For God has a heart, and no other heart of his own; for the heart signifies the mind. And he is that very mind. And just as it is said that he has immortality not from another beside him and has life in himself not being another existing of his, so also he has a heart not being another of his; for he is mind, and the Son is the offspring of mind. And the Word is the offspring of mind. Therefore, 'my heart has drawn out a good word'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good word is in the Father's heart as an offspring is in the womb, and the Word speaks of his works in agreement with the Father.
comments.comment: 'My heart drew out a good word' (Psalm 45:1). Just as an offspring comes from the womb, so also the good word is in the heart. And a heart toward God and a womb are not one thing and another. 'I declare my works to the king.' A change of person has occurred here. The good word himself, being begotten and in agreement with the Father, says, 'I declare my works to the king'; for just as when we hear, 'God said, Let there be' (Genesis 1:3), and, 'He said, and they came into being; He commanded, and they were created,' we do not hear these things in a human way; for He is not ignorant of the Son what must come to be and how; He commanded and said, but because of us, so that the agreement of the Father and the Son might be shown, that all things came to be by a single will and all things are provided for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good word concerns the king's coming, who fulfills what is not truly fulfilled among human beings, and the tongue that declares it is like a swift scribe's pen.
comments.comment: He [the psalmist] announces a good word about the coming of the king, who oversees the works of the righteous for his contemplation, and which are brought up by them as a kind of hearing for him, and who gives to them the divine fulfillment. For he has come as the fulfiller of what is not truly fulfilled among human beings, lawful by divine purity and by the sanctifying participation that comes from him. And he indicates that he will say many things quickly, comparing the tongue that declares these things to the pen of a very swift scribe.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Father writes the knowledge of his will in us with the Son as his pen, which is why David calls the tongue a pen of a swift-writing scribe.
comments.comment: For the Master God of all writes, as it were, in us the knowledge of his own will, using the Son in the Spirit as a pen. For he named him so through David, saying: 'My tongue is a pen of a swift-writing scribe.' (Psalm 45:1) For the Father's pen — that is, the Son — engraved on the hearts of all the knowledge of every good, using the Spirit of the Father and his own as a kind of finger of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the pen picture: the Son is the Father's pen that writes God's will on the heart.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: God did not beget his Son as men do; the Son, the Word of truth, came forth from the heart of God.
comments.comment: Martianus said, "What I have always wanted to learn, you have suddenly confessed: the error of your belief and law. So God has a Son, as you say?" Achatius answered, "He has." Martianus said, "Who is the Son of God?" Achatius answered, "The Word of truth and grace." Martianus said, "Does he have this as his name?" Achatius answered, "You had asked not about his name, but about the power of the Son himself." Martianus said, "Make the name plain." Saint Achatius answered, "He is called Jesus Christ." Martianus said, "From which wife of God was he conceived?" Saint Achatius answered, "God did not beget his Son by intercourse with a woman, in the manner of men. He formed Adam first, with his right hand fashioning him. Far be it from you to ascribe the touch of a mortal girl to the divine majesty. He put together the limbs of the first man from mud, and when he had already completed the whole figure, he granted him soul and spirit. In the same way the Son of God, the Word of truth, came forth from the heart of God. For this reason it is written: My heart pours out a good word (Psalms 45:1).
comments.author: Acts of the Martyrs

comments.capsule: The Son is called Word to show that his begetting involves no flowing, loss or passion, as our word is begotten from the mind.
comments.comment: Since some heretics, hearing that the Father begot the Son, take offense and think a flowing or passion happens to the Father—such as naturally sometimes happens with thick bodies—the evangelist, anticipating their folly, from the preface called the Son Word once and twice and thrice, to present the passionlessness of the begetting; for as our word is begotten from the mind without flowing, without diminishment, and without passion (likewise also our spirit), so also is the begetting of the Son. Therefore it was also said: “My heart has belched forth a good word” (Psalm 45:1), which is God, who alone “is good.”
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'For those who are being changed' means change in quality, as from unbelief to faith, which reaches its end when God becomes all in all.
comments.comment:
Toward the end, for those who are being changed; to the sons of Kore for understanding; a song for the beloved. Change is a movement and a transformation of something according to quality. Not every movement and transformation is a change. For there is a change according to becoming. I say, for instance, an egg becoming a bird and a grain of wheat a stalk. This movement and transformation is according to becoming. And there is another occurring according to corruption; when the body of a human decays and is dissolved into fluids and worms and the like, it is not said to be changed, but to have decayed. And there is also another movement and transformation according to increase, when an addition to the previous amount occurs; for when I am extended from a smaller to a greater size, I am said to have increased, but to have diminished when the amount is contracted and becomes less. Change, therefore, is a movement according to quality, such as from sickness to health and from health to sickness, from ignorance to knowledge and likewise, from unbelief to faith.

'Toward the end,' therefore, 'for those who are being changed.' We have often explained regarding the end, that it is that which is after all things, the last thing to be desired. Thus, 'toward the end, for those who are being changed.' When change reaches such a limit that it is no longer possible for it to be further extended, in the perfection of things, when 'God becomes all in all' (1 Cor 15:28), the quality can no longer be extended.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title speaks of those changing from evil, and the sons of Korah sing of the beloved, the only-begotten Son, who gives incorruption for corruption.
comments.comment: A goal for those making progress and changing from quality to quality is that the one at the summit of qualities should hasten (Psalm 45:1; LXX 44:1), by which the corruptible and the immortal might be proven. Concerning this, the end being attained. Concerning those who shall be transformed, that is, those who are changed and have become eager from evil, sons of Kore turning all things into a song concerning the beloved, bringing forth and shouting. And the beloved here is the only-begotten Son of God. Concerning this, the triumphal song is sung, through whom He transformed, having given incorruption instead of corruption.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The grace poured on his lips appears in Luke, where all marveled at his words of grace, which hold those who hear with understanding.
comments.comment: 'My tongue is like a scribe's sharp pen. He beautifies with grace among the sons of men' (Psalm 45:1-2). The evangelical word is among all these human words. … Grace was poured out on your lips (Luke 4:22). This is interpreted in the Gospel according to Luke; for how he entered the synagogue in Capernaum, 'and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him' (Luke 4:17), so that it might be read, he said: 'and all were marveling at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth' (Luke 4:22). In this way his words are grace-filled as to hold those who hear. He says 'hearing' according to understanding, not according to mere hearing; for all hear the gospel, and 'Greeks and Jews' (Rom 1:16), but they are not possessing the grace of the words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'because of this' name a cause, yet the word of God has no cause for his blessing, since he himself is the blessing.
comments.comment: 'Because of this, may God your God bless you forever' (Psalm 45:2). And this is said also concerning the man; for to be blessed with a cause is not of the word of God. He himself is the blessing, the source of blessing. The 'cause' lies here in the 'because of this,' just as also in: 'because of this God your God has anointed you' (Psalm 45:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse points to the unspeakable beauty of the invisible one, shown through his words and deeds.
comments.comment: This points to the ineffable glory and beauty of the invisible one, and he foretells the manifestation of that beauty through words and deeds, saying that grace has been poured out on his lips, just as the Gospels also make clear that everyone marveled at the words of grace that came from his mouth (cf (Psalm 45:2). Luke 4:22).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse about grace on his lips was read from the Gospels, where all marveled at his words.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Grace poured out on his lips is the same abundance as the Spirit poured on all flesh and the love of God poured into hearts.
comments.comment: Those hearing the words of Jesus, being full of grace (Psalm 45:2), will say the upcoming text: 'He has poured out abundance' shows the grace; this agrees with 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Acts 2:17) and 'The love of God is poured out in our hearts' (Rom 5:5); for in these the abundance of the spirit and the wealth of the love from God is shown. Because of this poured-out grace, 'God has blessed you with your lips' (Psalm 45:2), testifying of blessedness to you for all eternity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah sees his outward appearance failing beside the sons of men, while David tells of his divine beauty.
comments.comment: Isaiah foresees his outward appearance failing compared to the sons of men, prophesying his dishonor according to the flesh (Psalm 45:2). But David interprets the divine beauty, which is also made clear in Isaiah through the words that the king will be seen with glory.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The thigh names the things of generation, and Abraham's oath 'under my thigh' may point to the Savior who was to come from his line.
comments.comment:
