Therefore he says: if he proposes to help me as God, the help is superior. Having become a man, help me. And he says to Him: "Gird your sword upon your thigh, O Mighty One, with your beauty and your splendor" (Ps 45:3). You have beauty and splendor; for you did not commit sin, nor did you know it. "Gird" therefore "the sword upon your thigh." Often the name of the thigh signifies the things of generation, as if saying: "every thigh shall be moistened," meaning euphemistically and decorously through the thigh the functional organs of generation. …

Abraham, sending his son for the marriage of Rebekah, says: 'Put your hand under my thigh, and I swear you' (Genesis 24:2); for since he was about to receive a virgin and lead her from a far place to a far place, he necessarily secured his prudence. And it is also possible in this way: since the one coming for the salvation of all is to come from my thighs, there 'put your hand, and I swear you'. And the Scripture very solemnly names many such things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword girded on the thigh is the Word of God that cuts away excess desires, and the king's beauty and loveliness are his sinlessness.
comments.comment:
Your thigh, powerful one.

Therefore we say: the faithful man, the self-controlled one, the imitator of God, girds the unyielding Word of God, which is being wielded above every sword, around his thigh, so that he may cut away superfluous desires.

For he who has grasped the honorable marriage and keeps the bed undefiled, has the sword of the Word of God cutting them away.

If 'powerful' here refers to the God-Word or the soul joined to Him, 'thigh' refers to the incarnation, the birth from a woman.

Therefore, preserve this sword while your beauty and your loveliness remain.

And beauty and loveliness are sinlessness, when spoken of the soul; for it did not know sin.

But if spoken of the God-Word, this he says: the beauty and the loveliness of God remain to you, having become man; for you did not change from being the Word and God-Word.

And to each of the rest of the temperate it is said: put on beauty and loveliness from the other virtues, take also temperance, the Word that cuts.

But what kind of sword should we take?

The Word concerning temperance, the Word in general, the one that cuts.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sword girded on the king's thigh and his beauty and majesty in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sword is the word of God, and those struck by it fall under Jesus's feet, confessing his kingdom.
comments.comment: And you would say a sword and a dagger is also the word of God; for Paul says: “and the sword of the spirit, which is a saying of God,” (Ephesians 6:17) by which, the bride says, “I am wounded with love.” (Song of Songs 2:5) And David also says: “gird your sword upon your thigh, O powerful one, in your beauty and your comeliness.” (Psalm 45:3) Those struck by such a sword fall under Jesus’s feet according to “peoples will fall under you,” (Psalm 45:3) having confessed his kingdom …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He reigns for truth, gentleness and justice, and whoever acts according to God is guided marvelously by the right hand of good practice.
comments.comment: As for Psalm 44:5, the archer directs his best bow, wounding those who are thrown into divine arrows. It must also be read that he directs them to provide joy; and along with these, 'reign, O King, among the wounded' (Psalm 45:4-5). The reason for your reigning is the perfection of virtue, not in practice alone but also in knowledge, because of truth, gentleness, and justice; for he says, 'reign, because it is necessary for the truth, gentleness, and justice to be known and established by those under your rule.' And 'your right hand shall guide you marvelously' (Psalm 45:4). He who does all things according to God is marvelously guided by the right hand of good practice, using that path toward the Savior. And the Savior, performing paradoxical powers by his right hand, is marvelously guided.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the king reigns (truth, gentleness, justice) and what his guiding right hand does.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of Christ strike hearers like arrows, so that the apostles and the peoples fall under him.
comments.comment: As for Psalm 44:6ab, the words of the mighty Christ are like arrows that strike those who hear, so that they may judge the following of those toward Him. The apostles, being wounded by these arrows, having sent all things into the world, fell well to judge Him. And the peoples, who previously held a bad position, were struck by these arrows to be established in good, falling under Him; that is, they were made subject to Him and have become His.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior's arrows instill divine love in those they strike, and the same Savior is the bow, the archer and the chosen arrow.
comments.comment: 'Your arrows are sharp, mighty' (Psalm 45:5), which instills divine love in those struck by them, as if speaking like a blessed bride possessing divine love: 'I am pierced by love.' And behold the paradox: the same Savior is the bow, the archer, and the arrow. For in the present prophetic word spoken to Him by God, it is said: 'I have bent you, Judah, as my bow' (Zechariah 9:13); but in the Psalm, those praising Him say: 'Your arrows are sharp, mighty' (Psalm 45:5); and He Himself says about Himself in Isaiah: 'He has made me like a chosen arrow; He has hidden me in His quiver' (Isa 49:2). For how could the one fashioning those who are being pierced as chosen not be a chosen arrow, hidden in the quiver which He possessed from the flesh of Mary?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the king's sharp arrows as the Savior's words that wound with divine love.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The arrows are praiseworthy when the words shot toward love pierce the soul, as the Church says she is pierced by love.
comments.comment: But it is also taken as praiseworthy: 'Your arrows, having been shot, O Mighty One, shall cause peoples under you to fall' (Psalm 45:5). Your words, having been shot, are directed toward passion and love; for you are powerful and you powerfully send out your words, and you direct those who are being cast by them toward love. Likewise, the soul undergoing this—that is, the Church—says: 'Pierced by love am I' (Song 8:6). Thus, the arrows are both praiseworthy and piercing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A throne often means a kingdom, but it can also mean a teaching office, as with the seat of Moses.
comments.comment: For a throne is often taken to mean a kingdom, even if it is used instead of a teaching office, as is clear from 'The Lord King is established forever' (Psalm 29:10), and again: 'Your throne, O God, is unto the ages of ages' (Ps 45:6), and even more: 'A throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' (Proverbs 16:12). But it is also said to the disciples: 'You also shall sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28). When it is said, 'The scribes sat upon the seat of Moses' (Matthew 23:2), this seat is one of teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The anointing belongs to Christ by nature, as in a pure vessel, and the one who anoints him is his God.
comments.comment: So, he says, as in a pure vessel the divine ointment has been anointed upon him, joined by nature and not by participation because of kinship—not given by grace as it is also to your partakers. And he addresses Christ as God, and says that the one who anoints him is his God, not abolishing the human constitution and the Word's relation to the flesh, according to which there is also an anointing of the Spirit, since the flesh was sanctified beforehand and sanctified again through the Spirit who was present from the beginning and came again. For from the beginning, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35); and again, 'Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power' (Acts 10:38).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He who holds the throne of deity is anointed as human, not into the nature of deity.
comments.comment: If the one who holds a throne forever is the maker of angels — having loved righteousness and hated lawlessness, and for that reason said to be anointed with the oil of gladness by God the Father — what thoughts should we form about him? If he makes his angels spirits and holds a throne of deity, how is he anointed with the oil of gladness? So he creates angels as God, and is anointed as human — not into the nature of deity, but into the skilled economy of the anointing (Psalm 45:6–7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The Lord needed no anointing, being holy by nature, but the Spirit came upon Christ so that we might be led to share in the Spirit.
comments.comment: By saying 'partakers,' he also showed the reason for the anointing: so that the anointing by participation might go forward, for this reason the anointing by participation also came. For as far as the Lord himself was concerned, there was no need of anointing, since he was holy by nature and became holy, and placed holiness as something innate in his body, and by this brought the human form to maturity. But since this was not in us, nor was it possible among human beings to be holy by nature, but there is need of gift and heavenly grace, for this reason the Spirit came upon Christ, so that he might show us as led from him to participation in the Spirit through kinship according to the body (Psalm 45:7).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ loved righteousness most and received the whole anointing with the oil of gladness, while his companions share in it each according to capacity.
comments.comment: … Like him, they [those who teach the word of Jesus soundly] have “loved righteousness and hated injustice; and therefore God, the God” of Christ, “has anointed” them too “with the oil of gladness” (Psalm 45:7; Hebrews 1:9). But he, who loved “righteousness” and hated “lawlessness” more than his “companions” (Psalm 45:7), received the firstfruits of the anointing and, if one may so name it, the whole anointing with the oil of “gladness”; while his companions, each according to his capacity, shared in his anointing too.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'above thy fellows': Christ received the whole anointing and his companions share it according to their capacity.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The oil of gladness is the Holy Spirit, and the garments of Christ breathe the scent of kingship through his death.
comments.comment: Having loved iniquity, but having been granted righteousness through faith which comes from his presence by a paternal good pleasure, a man becomes and is anointed with the oil of gladness, that is, with the Holy Spirit. The garments of Christ breathe the scent of kingship and hierarchy through the death he undertook (for this is the fragrance imposed upon the buried dead), but also a continuous, unceasing scent of myrrh because of having something more than Christ's death for the salvation of others and the destruction of the devil, and of cassia because of his word being fiery; for this ointment is warming. The garments of Christ are those which are reasonably theologized about him. Since he did not take up along with the others that which is praised as being like a corpse, it is fitting that from his garments the aforementioned things breathe; with this, 'The fragrance of your myrrh is above all ointments' (Psalm 45:8) accords.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The kings reign with Christ, and their daughters, who teach souls, have glorified him from the high things of theology that ivory stands for.
comments.comment: Kings are spoken of here as those co-reigning with Christ, while he himself is King reigning over them. Their daughters have become, according to teaching, educators of souls, or rather of the church; these daughters, in honor of the one being praised, have glorified the King, Christ. From ivory. But 'ivory' you say, meaning the high things of theology; for ivory, it happens, is a symbol of the Word, since the musical instruments and the teeth are vocal; and the great houses are heavy. Since they did not magnify their own word as the greatest of contemplations concerning God, many of the kings' daughters, from the aforementioned rich ivory, have glorified Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul that has become Christ's bride is the church, named queen and standing at his right hand in golden garments.
comments.comment: The soul, having truly become a spouse to the true King Christ, is the church, and is named queen because it is the bride of the king, standing at his right hand to hold the right position, possessing its foundation in virtue and faith. And she also holds golden garments, having wrapped herself in Christ; and she is also draped and variegated, embracing the manifold wisdom of God. And one should not stumble because he himself is both bridegroom and clothed; for in one relation and another, and in one thought and another, these things exist, just as shepherd and lamb, and ten thousand other things are found in the Gospels.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The queen at Christ's right hand is the Church, dressed in gold for what is honorable and in embroidery for the many kinds of virtue.
comments.comment: And so divine David, in the forty-fourth psalm, sets beside Christ a pure virgin, the Church, as in the rank of a queen, and puts on her a robe woven with gold and embroidered, saying thus: 'The queen stood at your right hand, in clothing shot with gold, wrapped about and embroidered.' (Psalm 45:9) The gold, as I judge, marks well what is honorable and conspicuous, and the embroidered, the many kinds of virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the queen's gold and embroidered robe as the honor and the many virtues of the Church.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Garments are the virtues, their actions and the doctrines of piety, and with them the Church, Christ's bride and queen, is covered.
comments.comment: For clothing and garments, according to divine analogy, are the virtues according to kind and the actions performed according to them, and the doctrines of piety and the mysteries of the truth. With these garments she is covered: the bride of Christ, being the Church, and a queen, as it is sung in the forty-fourth and fourth Psalm: 'The queen stood at your right hand, arrayed and adorned in gold' (Psalm 45:9) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As a royal garment takes the sun's ray and gleams in many colors, so the Church shines in a heavenly, variegated array.
comments.comment: For just as the flowery and brightly-colored royal garment receives a solar ray and produces diverse gleamings, and as the beauty is of the dye, so it achieves such splendor; and just as by the present dye it is re-dyed and the beauty of the air is turned into gold, or into purple, or into green, or into some other of the colors, not by the ray being divided, but by the garment, the ray's effect being shaped by the light: in such ways the beauty of the Church always shines with blossoms, having a royal garment and being adorned with a heavenly and variegated array; as also the psalmist says: 'Daughters of kings in your honor; the queen stands at your right hand, arrayed in gold of various colors' (Psalm 45:9).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The prophecy is about the whole Church but applies properly to each soul.
comments.comment: So that the God-inspired prophecy may be confirmed by deeds, and what was said may apply to your soul: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in gold-woven garments, richly adorned. Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and the king will desire your beauty” (Psalm 45:9-11). For the Psalmist proclaimed these things in general, announcing beforehand the beauty of the whole body; but it will apply properly to each individual soul, since the Church is made up of individuals.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily in Time of Famine and Drought

comments.capsule: God, calling the church from the Gentiles his daughter, bids her hear his words and forget her kin and her father's house.
comments.comment: A change of face appears to have happened (Psalm 45:10); for God is the one calling the church from the Gentiles and naming her his daughter. He says: 'Having received my words, O daughter, listen and see their mind, having understood it for them; for what more will you desire to incline your will more fully toward them and to hear and long for them more effectively? And the forgetting of your kin will follow you, no longer desiring to restrain those same things and your fatherland; and the memory of your father who begot you according to the malice of the devil will also come upon you.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is addressed as 'daughter' and what hearing and forgetting her people means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To forget one's people and father's house is the same as Abraham's departure from his kin, the earth being the body and the father's house the word of the mind.
comments.comment: This sword of use is given by way of a judgment to Abraham, so that he might depart from the earth and from his kin and from the father's house, the earth being understood as the body in which he was surrounded, and kin as those who are of the same kind and were brought up together, and the father's house is the spoken word of the mind, as one of the wise interpreted concerning the Mosaic education. What was said to the divine bride, or rather to his father, is equivalent to what was said to Abraham: 'Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house, for the King of your beauty has desired you, and He is your Lord' (Psalm 45:10). For it is the same thing to forget one's own people and the father's house as to depart from the kin and the father's house for the one driven to this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations' turning from evil makes the bride beautiful and desirable to the king.
comments.comment: The departure of the nations from evil things makes the bride beautiful and desirable to the king. For this is our beauty, and by this we are adorned, and by this we are made close to God, and so greatly do we become sought after by God that he speaks according to his desire, the kind of things a lover would say about the beauty of his beloved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the king desires the bride's beauty: it is her turning from evil.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The daughter of Tyre has become God's daughter, and the rich of the people, Jews who repent, come to her as suppliants.
comments.comment: Because of this I call you, daughter, says God to her, on account of the doing of the things commanded to you; since my son the king has desired the beauty existing in you according to the image and according to likeness having been made mine, and he, the king desiring your beauty, is not among your equals (Psalm 45:11-13). For he is your Lord; for he is not an angel or an archangel or any other created being; for all worship him. Since it is not of God to be worshiped, be a god, the king desiring your beauty, who is also your Lord. Toward this also you undergo much change. For you, daughter of Tyre, because of which you had fear, have been made my daughter, so as to bring all the rich of the people as suppliants to your face. For all of the people from circumcision are becoming rich for you according to faith and are coming to you the truth of the gospel, beseeching your face to become a spouse to the king. For just as formerly those from the Gentiles, coming to the Godly service of Israel, were adhering to his face entreating him, so now those from the Jews, repenting, flee to the church of the Gentiles, deeming themselves worthy to be received by it. All the glory of the daughter of kings is Asbos. Asbos is interpreted as 'thoughts'. And the king of the thoughts being righteous is the Lord. The glory of the daughter of Tyre, which is being praised, is not other than that from the king of the thoughts. And it is to be understood that often in the Scriptures instead of the intelligible essence, gold is taken, as it will be timely shown.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bride's garments are the varied teaching of Christ, and the souls that come to him are made perfect and taken up into the one perfect bride, the Church.
comments.comment:
Virtues are not merely found in the garments of the bride, nor is the discourse concerning the intelligible realities, especially that concerning the Trinity, adorned with golden embroideries; rather, it is made diverse through the varied and multifaceted teaching of Christ. … It is made manifest from these words that the souls approaching Christ are such that some, having not yet the time for marriage, are maidens; but those coming to him after having been restored, some are noble and have ascended far above the world that became existent in six days. … but the one surpassing them all according to the Spirit, having been perfected, to be a perfect dove of the Word, is the glorious Church, which has no nest, no wrinkle, or anything of that kind. …

The psalmist, in the verses preceding this, says that he hymns this Church, that she shall be brought to her bride with those others being embraced by him, the queens being the maidens who formerly did not have the time for cohabitation, but now, because they have been perfected, are being led into the bridal chamber, so that, having slept with the king, they might be taken up to become members of the one perfect bride, no longer being such as they happened to be when they were imperfect.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many souls are called virgins, but only those near the perfect bride are brought to the king, led by those who give them preliminary teaching.
comments.comment: Regarding Psalm 44:15b, even if many are incorruptible, it is a custom to call souls virgins, but not all are brought to the king, but only those having become near and close by the disposition of the perfect bride. And also 'they shall be brought'; for those not having experience of the Word of the bride are not such as they are to go to him by themselves; but those handing the preliminary educations to them bring them to him; for they are not law and prophets.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bride is near the king and the virgins follow her, so that through her they are made close to the king.
comments.comment: The bride is near the king, and virgins are near her and follow her, and through her they are made close to the king, like attendants accompanying a bride, young maidens (Psalm 45:14). To her, according to the Song of Solomon, the synagogues of the Jews would most fittingly be second and following, according to 'The first will be last and the last first' (Matthew 20:16), and 'The proselyte among you will rise above you as head, and you will be as the tail' (Deuteronomy 28:43-44). For those who long ago became proselytes of the law in order to be made close to God now themselves lead the assembly that draws near to God, and this is clear from what follows.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The queen stands beside Christ and gives the inheritance promised to Abraham to his bodily descendants.
comments.comment: For this queen stands beside Christ and enters with him into his holy temple, and she gives the inheritance of the world and the kingdom promised to Abraham to those descended from him according to bodily lineage, with the king willing it and the queen consenting (Psalm 45:15). Therefore those young maidens whom he said were fathers he now calls sons, since they have received the rank of sons and being deemed worthy of inheritance from their mother as sons (Psalm 45:16).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In place of the fathers of the circumcision the church has sons of the same race who resemble the gospel word, made rulers over all the earth.
comments.comment: Since almost everything of the psalm is said toward Christ, this verse says that although you have children according to the flesh from fathers, that is, those from circumcision, there have been born to you from the same race sons resembling the evangelical word. And these you also have established as rulers over all the earth, saying to them, 'Having gone, make disciples of all the nations' (Matt 28:19), they are his witnesses, having become the beginning of the king, even to the end of the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the children and princes of the verse are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Peoples will confess with thanksgiving unto the age of ages, while only in this age can one repent and confess.
comments.comment: Because of this, peoples will confess with thanksgiving (Psalm 45:17), not for the sake of the second age, but even unto the age of ages. For we do not permit the confession concerning sins to be named now. For it never happens even unto the age of ages; only in this age is it possible to repent and to confess. But if they shall be remembered, according to another writing, instead of 'Those having been bequeathed to rule with you,' they shall be remembered by your name in all generations and generations, by extending your kingdom unto all the ages.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who flee to God have all safety and power to share in him, and his help is in the tribulations that find us.
comments.comment: For those fleeing toward God have all safety and power to partake of him, as the apostle says: 'I am able through him who strengthens me to do all things' (Phil 4:13). A help in the tribulations that find us intensely. The 'intensely' lies uncertainly; for the help is intensely in the tribulations that find us, or it is a help in the intensely finding tribulations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountains moved are evil powers entering disturbed souls, not parts of the earth.
comments.comment: Mountains being moved in the hearts of seas (Psalm 46:2), one should not consider the sensible parts of the earth being moved, but evil powers being moved into the souls disturbed by storms, a salty drink of wickedness and bitterness of character. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's picture of mountains and sea as evil powers troubling souls.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The streams of the river are God-bearing men filled with the Spirit's grace, who gladden the Church, the city of God.
comments.comment: … the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is at work in the feast, fills “the streams of the river”, by which I mean the God-bearing men who possess “teaching in teaching” (Romans 12:7). They in turn visit the earth of mankind, an earth of mind and reason, and gladden the holy Church, which is “the city of the great King” (Psalm 48:2), Jesus Christ, as it is written: “The streams of the river make glad the city of God” (Psalm 46:4). And the Church, gladdened and delighted out of the richness of her heart, praises and glorifies the Lord who reigns in her.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the river's streams are and what gladdening the city of God means.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The Most High dwells in the midst of the city whose tabernacle he sanctified, never outside it.
comments.comment: It is also said in the forty-fifth and fifty-first Psalms regarding the royal city and those receiving gifts near the one ruling it royally: 'The streams of the river gladden the city of God; the Most High has sanctified its tabernacle, God is in its midst, it shall not be shaken' (Psalm 46:4-5). For the Most High, having sanctified its tabernacle, dwells in the midst of the peaceful city being spoken of, never becoming outside of it, but remaining unshakeable within it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is in the midst of her and preserves her beauty, and when the soul holds faith as unassailable, Christ is revealed to it.
comments.comment: The Lord is in the midst of her, in the midst of threats (Psalm 46:5). There is another scripture saying, 'God will help her with His face.' For He preserves her beauty, which is both vulnerable and incorruptible, the intelligible beauty; clearly, the intellect will receive disturbance from opposing things. For when the soul holds faith within itself as unassailable and assigns to itself the refinements of all virtue, the intellect possesses beauty and Christ Himself is revealed to it. Since the immediate, visible, and unchangeable is set aside, the Church, he says, will not be persuaded by this; for He preserves her beauty.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The city is indestructible, with God in it, when the present night ceases at early dawn.
comments.comment: He says the city will be indestructible, so that God will be in it, when the present night ceases at early dawn. For it is night as long as the darkness has not been entirely removed nor every authority and power abolished, but they still stir up warlike attempts against the righteous (Psalm 46:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'right early' as the dawn that ends the present night.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The nations are hordes of demons warring against the Church, who are filled with dread when they see the Savior's incarnate appearance.
comments.comment: He calls the nations the hordes of demons warring against her (Psalm 46:6). And when these see the incarnate appearance of the Savior, they are troubled against His Church and are filled with dread. Furthermore, the falling of the seven kingdoms over which death and sin reigned will follow. Even if you call those reigning 'kingdoms,' they too have fallen, flowing from error into the knowledge of truth and from wickedness into virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God gave his voice by the Gospel the earth was shaken and customs, laws and deception changed, so that we are courageous with the Lord of powers with us.
comments.comment: Regarding the silence of God, the earthly and material things seem to have stability and standing, being shaken by God's having given a voice (Psalm 46:6). For if God assists the intellect, immediately everything earthly is moved. And upon God having given the voice according to the Gospel, the earth has been shaken, with all customs, local laws, useful things, and even the impious deception being changed; the nations are troubled and the kingdoms are falling. While the earth is shaken, we are courageous, having the Lord of powers with us, the God of Jacob taking hold of us (Psalm 46:7). Just as he who does the works of Abraham is His child, so he who imitates the asceticism of Jacob becomes His son, having an understanding from the God of Jacob.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shaking earth and the troubled nations as the world changed by the Gospel, with the Lord of powers on our side.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The apostles filled the world with wonders, and Christ, having destroyed the devil, has abolished wars to the ends of the earth.
comments.comment:
The apostles also filled the inhabited world, running everywhere and recounting what had happened through him and performing wonders in his name. The Word is able also to call the nations to know the Creator of this world from the wonders seen concerning creation. …

Having come and having destroyed the devil, the holder of the power of death, and the other evil powers, he has abolished wars even to the ends of the earth, that is, those passing from the lands; smashing the bow, the burning arrows of the evil one which were being shot, but also consuming with fire the door of unbelief opposite the door of faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'he maketh wars to cease' as Christ's victory over the devil and the arrows of the evil one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who renounces every occupation can know God, which is why the tyrant of Egypt burdened the Hebrews with work.
comments.comment: No one sinning and being occupied with wandering is able to know God; for everyone sinning has not seen him, nor has he known him. He who desires to know God, having renounced every occupation, will know who God is, as the present saying says: 'Be at leisure and know.' This, therefore, the tyrant of Egypt, having perceived, subjects the Hebrews to occupations so that they may not attend to God, saying, 'Be at leisure' [as in, 'you are mere laborers']: for this reason they say, 'Let us go forth and serve our God.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Be still, and know' as freeing oneself from every occupation in order to know God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Israel was handed over to the nations not in vain, but so that it might know God's power, since through its transgression salvation has come to the nations.
comments.comment: Not even when you were handed over to the nations, he says, abandoned by God, were you handed over in vain, but so that you might know the power of God, who acquired all the nations for your reproof, and who acquired every land instead of one land under his own worship, because by the same transgression, according to the apostle, salvation has come to the nations to provoke Israel to jealousy (Ps 46).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Hands stand for deeds, and the nations are to join a right mind and a shout of rejoicing to the harmony of their deeds.
comments.comment:
Since hands are often said to be instead of deeds, and the nations perform various things according to diverse customs before the visitation, the Savior, having visited men, commands a tumult to occur, that is, a harmony of the practical powers of the nations, tropically called hands. …

Not only is a harmony of deeds sufficient for salvation, but also a right mind with these things. Therefore, he commands the nations to shout aloud in a voice of rejoicing along with the tumult.
comments.selected_reason: Explains clapping hands and shouting as deeds joined to a right mind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This psalm is addressed to the nations, announcing joy and shouts of triumph because of the Lord's manifestation from on high.
comments.comment: The psalm before this one is addressed to Israel, but this one is addressed to the nations who go up together to Jerusalem and are joined to those descended from Abraham. So it announces joy to the nations, victory applause, and shouts of triumphant praise because of the manifestation of the Lord from on high, which will come with great fear.
comments.selected_reason: Says whom the psalm addresses and why the nations are told to rejoice.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He is fearsome and worthy of reverence to the pious, and he reigns over the super-celestial beings.
comments.comment:
And he is fearsome and worthy of reverence to those who hold piety toward him. …

It is not doubtful that he reigns over the super-celestial beings. Concerning those wavering about the earth, even if he holds even it, the preceding verse is spoken, and especially because those describing providence even unto the lunar sphere do not wish to admit those under the earth to be under providence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He hands the kingdom to his holy ones, taking none for himself, and gives it to his people through the chosen bride, the queen.
comments.comment: For he [the Lord] will take hold of the earth, according to the vision of Daniel, handing over the kingdom to his holy ones. As one of the successors of the apostles has said, he will appear to the king of the world in Jesus—not taking any kingdom of his own into glory for himself, but for his own people, who are established in the kingdom through the chosen bride, the queen (Psalm 47:3-4). As it was said beforehand in David: “You will make them rulers over all the earth” (Psalm 44:17 (45:16)).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He set the apostles over all peoples and chose Jacob's inheritance, showing God's impartiality, since anyone who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable.
comments.comment: He ordained the holy apostles as rulers and teachers of all peoples, both the circumcised and the Gentiles, under their feet, having chosen for himself an inheritance not other than that of Israel; he himself chose the election of Jacob. And he says of the whole people of the Hebrews, Jacob. From this the impartiality of God is known, that he loved nothing other than the beauty of Jacob; for in every way the one fearing him and working righteousness is acceptable to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whom the Lord subdues and chooses as inheritance, and why: God shows no partiality.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God loved the land of Israel not because it differs from other land but because of its inhabitants, the firstfruits of piety in the world.
comments.comment: “You have shown us to be a kingdom over all the nations,” he says, “and he has given us back our inheritance from our fathers, the land of Israel, which is precious in his eyes.” The prophets and apostles from Israel call the land of Israel their own inheritance, and it is given back to them according to their lineage, just as the Lord himself was not outside the succession of his fleshly descent. They say that land was loved, not because it could differ from any other land in God’s sight—for nothing is precious or beautiful to him, nor is one thing more precious or more beautiful than another—but because he loved its inhabitants, who were the firstfruits of piety in the world (Psalm 47:4). And he keeps his love toward them and toward the land where they dwelt, having nothing that ceases, but all things eternal.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the excellency of Jacob whom he loved' means: God loved the people who first showed piety.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The voice of the trumpet means the loud voice and piercing of the dogmas, and a trumpet in the Gospel means making something manifest.
comments.comment:
A voice is made significant by the shout of falling enemies, in which he rejoices (Psalm 47:5); and it rises above our understanding when it is found. …

The loud voice and the piercing of the dogmas are called the voice of a trumpet; for in the manifest and in the Gospel, a trumpet is taken up, as in the saying, 'When you do alms, do not sound a trumpet before you' (Matt 6:2), which is, do not make it manifest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who ascends, reigns and sits on the throne is the divinity in the Son.
comments.comment: Without distinction he signifies the divinity in the Son. For this is surely the one who ascends, the one who reigns, the one who sits on the heavenly throne. And having seated himself on earth before his ascension, gathering around himself the rulers of the nations and all that is strongest among humanity, and lifting them up to heavenly glory (Psalm 47:9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Singing is to be spiritual and not only sensual, and doubled and unceasing to Christ, who is Creator, God and King.
comments.comment: Sing not only sensually according to the shadow of the law, but also spiritually according to the Gospel (Psalm 47:6). Perhaps it commands doing this unceasingly and continuously through doubling. And this same doubling of singing must be raised up to the King Christ; for he is indeed Creator, God, and indeed Providential, King. Therefore, it is necessary to sing unceasingly to the same God and King.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse repeats 'sing praises': singing is to be doubled and unceasing, in spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who sings must understand what is sung, since what counts is understanding the song rather than rhythm and tone.
comments.comment: He who sings must also understand the things being brought forth in the song (Psalm 47:7). It is not necessary that the thing happen primarily concerning the rhythm and the tone of the voice, but concerning the understanding of the things being sung. For God spares those who do not sing thus, but only make a noise, saying, 'Turn away from me the noise of your songs, and I will not hear the sound of your instruments.' But he sings intelligently, the one practicing according to the divine teachings and understanding them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'sing ye praises with understanding': what matters is understanding what is sung.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The colt is the nations, on which God mounts to reign, and the apostles untied them from darkness and brought them to their Creator.
comments.comment: They [the apostles] were sent “to bring the colt to Him” (Luke 19:35), and the colt is the nations, so that He might mount them and reign over them, as the psalmist says: “God has become King over the nations; the Lord sits on His holy throne” (Psalm 47:8). “On which no one has ever sat” (Mark 11:2; Luke 19:30): for the nations had neither God mounting and ruling over them, nor law, nor prophets. “Untie it,” He says, “and bring it to Me” (Matthew 21:2; Luke 19:30). For the apostles untied the nations from darkness, that is, from ignorance of God; from error, from sin, from slavery to an alien master, from “the power of darkness” (Colossians 1:13), from “the ruler of this age” (John 12:31). And they brought them to the Lord, their Creator and Maker.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'God reigneth over the heathen' through the colt that Christ mounts, which stands for the nations.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The rulers of the peoples are the apostles or church leaders, or perhaps angels, gathered with the God of Abraham.
comments.comment: The rulers of the peoples are the apostles or the leaders of the churches, gathered with God Abraham, so that they might bring in the peoples who benefit through him; for their God is the God of children having become of Abraham. But stand firm, if the rulers of the peoples can be angels, concerning whom it has been said, 'He set the bounds of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God' (Deuteronomy 32:8), who also are gathered with God Abraham, since through faith they were made children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the princes of the people are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mighty ones of the earth are those who have lived rightly and exalted themselves by thinking of things above.
comments.comment: The mighty ones of the earth are men who have lived rightly, exalting themselves by thinking of the things above and seeking the things above. For they, having been greatly exalted, being suspended by divine knowledge and virtue, have become of God; for the mighty ones of the earth, having become the possession of God, were exalted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the shields of the earth': the mighty ones are those who lived rightly and sought the things above.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In Christ we are lifted high, minding things above.
comments.comment: For in Christ we have been freed from minding the things of flesh, and from rolling in earthly evils; and we are lifted as it were high through him, minding things above, and citizenshiping in heaven. For it is written that ‘The mighty ones of God of the earth have been raised up exceedingly.’ (Psalm 47:9)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The joy of all the earth is Christ, and the 'sides of the north' are people once on the devil's side who were changed into the mountain of Zion, whose great dwellings belong to those who hear Jesus and do his words.
comments.comment:
The joy of all the earth is a deep-rooted and good-rooted thing (Psalm 48:2); perhaps there is no other one of him who said, 'I am the true vine' (John 15:1). For he himself is the joy of all the earth, being also the provider of joy.

It does not seem that some, having moved from wherever, were heard to have suffered, to signify from the appointed word; for they say that the Savior was crucified on the northern sides of Zion, there being the place of the skull (Psalm 48:2).

But we say, following many writings, that the north is not anything other than the devil, according to the 'Exert yourself, O North, and come' (Song of Solomon 4:16). This side is wicked men, just as they say the retainers of a ruler are his side. The wicked men who serve the devil, having previously been his side, transformed so much in virtue that they did not merely plunder Zion, but became its mountain (Psalm 48:2). Paul, then, being a traitor, being a side of the north, plundered the body of the church which is Zion as it was transforming. And since the woman is called the side of the man, and the souls that became spouses to the devil, being his side through fellowship with him, became the mountain of Zion through transformation, just as the city of the great King Christ was plundered. For this word intends this, saying Zion is the mountain, which was formerly the side of the north or of the great king, we understanding it again as a great king by excellence of power but not of size. And in this city there are certain heavy and great dwellings in which God is known and the care of the city is grasped. These dwellings are of the same kind as the house which he builds upon the rock, he who heard the words of Jesus and did them (Psalm 48:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The kings marvel at the sight of Zion's changed souls, and the sight troubles even the virtuous, who fear that they too might fall.
comments.comment:
Having been gathered together, having become the same, prepared by the same mind and the same judgment; but the kings are not those ruling according to God, such as Abraham was to someone, although not perceptibly ruling: 'You are a king from God in our midst' (Genesis 23:6).

Not having seen the ancient ones who rose to such height from the north side, they marveled at the sight of Zion, being struck by the change occurring in the rational nature. And if one sees the bad becoming diligent and wise, marveling at the change, if he considers what might happen again—that those able to fall might be the diligent and wise—having thought this, he will cause trouble and shaking even to those who have greatly progressed in virtue, as if they were to seize the terror of dread.

Accompanying this is: 'The righteous groan in the places of the ungodly' (Proverbs 28:28), for when they fall, they become terrified. There are pains like those of a woman in childbirth. In the city of the great king, it is likely that souls have become pregnant from the bridegroom, and they have a time for delivery to form the offspring cast upon him, as if to labor to bring forth the mother's offspring.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ships of Tarshish are bodies, which the Spirit breaks so that at the resurrection incorruptible, strong bodies might come from corruptible ones, and those near may find divine joy.
comments.comment:
The name of pains may signify those who are troubled and shaken, whom terror has seized. 'A mighty wind shall break the ships of Tarshish' (Psalm 48:7). The bodies are often called the ships of the souls in the Scripture, as also in 'Those going down into the sea in ships' (Ps 107:23). These bodies are not being crushed by the Divine Spirit striking them violently in essence, that is, being dissolved, so that at the time of the resurrection, incorruptible, strong, and promising spiritual things might come forth from corruptible, weak, and dishonorable, psychic kinds.

But these ships are not simply so, but are 'Tarshish,' changing the voice of Tarshish into the joy of discovery. For then the bodies, being crushed and dying, are praiseworthily broken, so that those nearby may discover the divine joy. While experiencing this in this life, we hear much concerning the heavenly city of God and the spiritual goods in it from prophetic words and other inspired Scripture. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The believers who rise to the upper Jerusalem will see the city of God that they heard of, which God himself established for eternity.
comments.comment: Let us become from the earth in the upper Jerusalem, weighing together the things seen in it which we have heard of long ago, saying: Just as we heard, so also we shall see. For it is also the city of our God, since He Himself established it for eternity (Ps 47:9c-d). And the Savior is not spoken of in these things; for the Father shows Him, saying: I will build my city. He is the artisan and creator, while God is the one having the foundations of the city which all the righteous receive.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's praise reaches the ends of the earth, and the daughters of Judah, souls devoted to confession, will rejoice at the Lord's judgments when they see the truth face to face.
comments.comment: Just as your name is wonderful in all the land, so is your praise, since the earth is full of His praise (Psalm 48:10). One must consider the ends and the borders of the earth, those who have passed from the earth into heaven, upon which the name of God and the praise have reached. Of the assembly named Zion, its Lord is the one whom those trusting in the Lord resemble (Psalm 48:11). 'Judah' is interpreted as confession, and the souls participating in the exercise of confession are the daughters of Judah. … The daughters, not of the Judah being given on either side, but approaching as much as possible the judgments of the Lord, are true and justified, and they will rejoice in the same way. And since the judgments of the Lord are unsearchable, they do not rejoice at the present, but they will rejoice face to face, approaching the truth then.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's righteousness shows no partiality, so when Israel sees the nations brought in it will rejoice in God's judgment, as Peter and the apostles did.
comments.comment: “This is your righteousness,” he says, “which has no partiality.” And Peter, perceiving the calling of the nations, says: “In truth I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). When the wise Israel sees the nations brought in and understands the mercy, he will not envy, but will rejoice in God’s judgment, just as Peter and the apostles did then (Psalm 48:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's joy in God's judgments in terms a general reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Zion stands for the Church's careful study of the truth, whose teachers must describe it in a circle, divide its teaching into parts, and so tell the next generation who God is.
comments.comment:
Regarding the ecclesiastical opinion, being a scrutiny of the truth and for this reason called Zion, it is fitting to take it up with wisdom, so that having reflected upon the doctrines of the truth, we may describe them in a circle to their own intellect. And since the city of God is surrounded on every side by the approaching enemies, and has towers constructed from which the approaching enemies can be scouted. And since the enemies of the city are now warring, it is necessary also for those in its towers to give guidance. It also agrees: 'Upon your walls I have set guards by day and by night, who will never be silent until the end' (Ps 47:12bc/13-15). … Set therefore your heart, that is to say your mind, having scientifically attending to the power of Zion (this is the ecclesiastical teaching), and divide out analytically to each one attending to it.

For just as it is logical to divide things into essence and what has become, and genera into being, so also to divide the power of Zion into its weighty parts as much as possible; and its weighty parts are the individual contemplations in which the doctrines of piety dwell. Do this, so that you may narrate to another generation what our God himself is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever studies the city of God learns that the God who called the Gentiles is the same God as before, who will shepherd his people for ever.
comments.comment: Since the former generation, having received the city and its power, was reproved as evil, adulterous, crooked, and perverted by its own heresy, having attended to the power of the city and dividing its weighty matters, you shall know the things concerning the calling of the Gentiles, which is another generation besides the former, in which you shall also narrate that this is not the God who, having done the aforementioned paradoxical things, cast away the former generation and called another and others. But this God, concerning whom the proposed theology is always the same and likewise has, unto the age and unto the age of ages; and He himself will shepherd us unto the ages according to what has been said: 'And the Lord shall shepherd his flock in strength' (Isaiah 40:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The call to hear goes out to all the Gentiles, the dull and the prudent alike, for teachers are debtors to the wise and the foolish, and one speaks wisely only after meditating understanding in the heart.
comments.comment:
Prepare your hearing, not the common one toward other animals, but the one of the inner man through which we comprehend what is heard, as the Savior says: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (Matthew 11:15).

Since among the called Gentiles, some are dull of the matter and of the earthly mindset, but having been born sons of men, they rise up through knowledge and instruction, through lessons and examined words; and He calls not only the herd-like and grazing ones, but also the prudent, saying: 'Hear these, you who are born in the Gentiles and are sons of men.' For teachers are debtors not only to the wise but also to the foolish.

I bring forth wisdom from my mouth, having previously meditated understanding in my heart (Psalm 49:3). For then one will be able to speak wisely.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is called to hear and why teachers owe their words to wise and foolish alike.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who can bring forward the word is the one who has trained his mind in understanding and learned divine things well enough to hand them on.
comments.comment: To bring forward a word, one who has trained the mind according to understanding. He who has learned the divine things and is able to hand them over well (Psalm 49:4). Therefore, even after falling into a parable, he promises to open his own riddle in the Psalter; for he set forth for himself, proclaiming in a rhythmic and patterned way according to theory, he opens his own riddle in the Psalter. And the word is patterned as one who must speak the truths. Perhaps also he who shows the divine words as being riddles, opening each of the riddles in a Psalter composed of sensation and power.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By saying he inclines his ear rather than opens his mouth, the psalmist may be showing himself as a hearer of the Spirit, who speaks the wise and hidden word through him.
comments.comment: “I will touch upon a wise and hidden word,” he says, “mixing the riddle with song.” Why did he not say he opens his mouth for a parable, but that he inclines his ear? Is it because he wants to show himself as a hearer of the Spirit speaking rather than as the interpreter himself—or that the Spirit speaks the words through his mouth? For it is also said in Psalm 84 (85): “I will hear what God will speak in me.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says the psalmist inclines his ear to a parable.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: All born of Adam are brothers and none can redeem a sinning brother, but the one man who did not know sin, sent to save them, will live forever.
comments.comment: If iniquity should surround me with its wing (Psalm 49:5), no other vision of the ancestral tradition has reached the wing of Adam. All the born are of one kind and brothers, but no one is able to redeem his own brother who is sinning. For that one man alone shall be redeemed, concerning whom it is said, 'I will send a man to them who will save them' (Isaiah 19:20), who also says concerning himself, 'Now you seek to kill a man whom I have spoken the truth to you' (John 8:40). But that man, since he did not know sin nor did he do sin, will not give to God an expiation of himself which is given for the sake of those sinning, nor will he even attain the price of his own soul's redemption; but having lived according to virtue, he will live forever.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: None can give God a price for his own soul, since Christ gave his soul as a ransom for all.
comments.comment: And it can also be said concerning the one being redeemed, 'He will not give to God an expiation of himself.' For not everyone is one who is able to give an expiation, Christ propitiating all in his own blood, nor is anyone able to give a price sufficient for the redemption of his soul, Christ having given his soul as a ransom for all. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one can pay for his own redemption, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He willingly undergoes death to this age yet lives to God.
comments.comment: But he says he will undergo death willingly, as far as this age is concerned, dying to the world and being taken from the earth of his life, yet living to God (Psalm 49:9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A person freed by Christ will not be shaken at the sight of wise men dying, since the stumbling belongs to those thought wise.
comments.comment: He who has been set free by Christ will not possess salvation so unsteadily as to be unstable and unmovable, even if he sees those considered wise dying (Psalm 49:10; LXX 48:10b), since he is not so scandalized as to see corruption. For the stumbling over seeing is not to be placed upon this one, but upon those considered wise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mindless who rely on this life alone, expecting no resurrection, leave their wealth to strangers and make tombs their eternal houses.
comments.comment: He says that they do not know the one who is entirely cut off, but the evil-willed and the bad-minded (Psalm 49:10-11); and indeed we are accustomed to call the ill-faced one faceless and the ill-skilled one unskilled. Not so, for the evil-willed and bad-minded shall undergo no punishment; for indeed their destruction is such that they will leave the wealth they did not treasure well to strangers. For no one is an heir of the rich man of mind and understanding through these things. Not so, the foolish and mindless, having not known who they are, have glorified what, according to irrational animals, their soul does not abide in. For they say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (Isa 22:13). Therefore, the tombs in which they are buried become their houses for an age, not expecting a resurrection of the dead; but also their tents are in every generation and generation (Psalm 49:11), they shall be tombs, hoping pitifully in this only life. Perhaps also, doing nothing vital but being dead through which they sin, they are casting the tomb down as an eternal house.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those the psalm describes call on their own names upon their own earths, whereas the names of the apostles are written in the heavens.
comments.comment: And they did not even call upon their names upon the earth. For the names of the apostles through whom they act or think are written in the heavens, but those concerning whom the word speaks called upon their own names upon their own earths, through whom they act, being urbanized upon the earth; for having departed from the earth, they shall be written.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though made rational in God's image, man acts without reason.
comments.comment: Man has become in image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26), and having been shown to be rational, he will have the greatest honor (Psalm 49:12). But this not understanding, but acting with irrationality.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Death was not part of man as he was made but came from dishonor, so that having fallen from the likeness of God he is made like the beasts in death.
comments.comment: The suffering of death, he says, was not attached to man as he was made, but came upon him from dishonor. For though he was honored with growth toward immortality, he did not perceive it, having a good from honor greater than his nature (Psalm 49:12). And so, having fallen away from the likeness of God that consists in immortality, he is made like the beasts in death. For as Ecclesiastes says: “As the death of this one, so the death of that one, and one spirit is in them all; and what advantage does man have over the beast? Nothing, for all is vanity. All things go to one place; all things came from the dust, and all things return to the dust” (Ecclesiastes 3:19-20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says about man's honor and his likeness to the beasts, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A person compared to irrational cattle has imitated the impulses of irrational animals, yet was not made like them and has hope if he wishes to become like God.
comments.comment: He is compared to irrational cattle, like a female horse having become so and having imitated the impulses of all other irrational animals. He was not made like irrational cattle, having hope if he wishes to be made like God. For there shall be five above the cities and ten the upright in the time to come (Psalm 49:14). And Solomon in the Proverbs says the same thing: A wealthy man hastens to be rich, and he does not know that mercy will hold him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At the coming age's morning, human power ceases and God's power prevails.
comments.comment: But when the coming age arrives, he says—which is the early morning of the coming day—the kingdom of good things will be present, when every human power has ceased and the power from God prevails (Psalm 49:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'morning' of the verse means for a reader.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God will take the psalmist's soul from the slave that holds it, and the forgiven sinner thanks him.
comments.comment: If even the aforementioned things have happened to the majority of men, nevertheless God will take my soul from the hand of the slave holding it and desiring to swallow it (Psalm 49:15). And since the sinner is in slavery according to his condition, the one forgiving those holding him in sins thanks God having received his soul from the hand of the slave.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the age to come the good will reign and the rest obey, since the strength of wealth has passed.
comments.comment: Then the race of the good will be glorious and royal, and the race of the not-good will be subject and enslaved, since the strength that comes from wealth has passed away, but the strength that comes from virtue remains (Psalm 49:16-17). And all that is left of humanity on earth will obey the good, who reign according to God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: What cannot depart with its owner is nothing great, unlike righteousness, which does.
comments.comment: So let wealth and glory be reckoned as nothing great—at least, the things that do not depart together with the one who acquired them, as righteousness does depart with him and brings back those who have been brought low.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Dying, a man takes either nothing or only the good he has done with his money and glory, so that what he gathers does not remain.
comments.comment: But concerning sensible and human things it is said: “Do not fear when a man grows rich and the glory of his house is multiplied, for when he dies he will not take all things” (Psalm 49:16-17). Here the pretext that says “he will not take all things” is not a partial denial but a universal one — instead of “nothing.” And if you wish to take it literally as a partial privative denial, it says this: that there are things one does take — if, having money, he does good; if, having glory and office, he reaches out to the helpless and tries to help — from his zealous labors he takes these with him: beneficence […] just as he was born until death. If, then, “in his abundance he toils for the wind” (Ecclesiastes 5:16), what he gathers does not remain. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor man should not envy the rich, since wealth does not travel with its owner or stand by him in judgment but is cut off by death.
comments.comment: The rich man here [in church] cannot look down on the poor man, because he hears from the divine Scriptures: 'All flesh is grass, and all human glory is like the flower of the grass' (Isaiah 40:6). Nor will the poor man, seeing another grow rich, be seized by envy, because he too hears another prophet say: 'Do not fear when a man becomes rich, or when the glory of his house increases; for when he dies he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory go down with him' (Psalm 49:17-18 (LXX 48:18-19)). Such is the nature of this abundance: it does not move with those who have it, it does not travel with those who possess it, it does not stand by them when they are judged there and called to account, but it is cut off entirely by death. Many it has abandoned even before death. Its use is untrustworthy, its enjoyment unstable, its possession dangerous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means for a poor man tempted to envy the rich.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: The rich man who knows no other life thinks to bless his soul by indulging his desires and, like his fathers, will enter the same abyss of ignorance and not see the light.
comments.comment: The one lying before us rich, not knowing another life in his life, thinks by this to bless his soul; and only then does he confess that it is good to him through the giving of material desires (Psalm 49:18). A father having begotten him through evil works and a clumsy intellect (Psalm 49:19). Likewise, acting toward them, he imitated the parents, and as being similar to the generation of the fathers, he will enter into the same deep abyss of ignorance as they. For having accepted only the present life, he did not hasten to see the light; therefore it has been said regarding the age not to approach it; for perhaps, having been condemned in outer darkness, he will not be permitted to behold the eternal light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man was first made upright and honored, and fell to the beasts from the human state and not the other way round, for the good always comes before the false.
comments.comment: But if, as it is the truth, virtue is before wickedness—for 'God has made man upright, but they sought out evil counsels' (Wis 1:13)—and see that the seeking of evil counsels is after the uprightness. And virtue prepares the uprightness. 'A man being in honor did not understand, he was cast down with the irrational animals' (Ps 49:20). It did not come from a beastly manner to the man, but from the human to the beastly it came. And in every way the beautiful things are always before the false things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gods are men who share God's word, and the psalm shows both of Christ's comings, the first from Zion and the second in glory with his angels, when each is judged by his works.
comments.comment:
He says the gods are not the idols and the demons, but the men partaking of the words of God; for those are gods to whom the word of God came. God the Lord is of these gods, just as he is king of kings. And again, from the rising of the sun even unto the settings, he says, … From Zion the splendor of his beauty has come. For the one according to the flesh was shown from the seed of David. The God of the gods himself, having called all the earth to partake of him, will not hide nor be forgotten, but will manifest clearly according to the second presence in glory with his angels; and he will not be silent.

Thus, each one is judged according to his works and his practice. It should be noted that in this present word, both presences of Christ are shown: the first through the 'Out of Zion' glory, and the second through 'God has appeared manifestly' (Psalm 50:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'gods' are and how the verses speak of Christ's two comings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the law was given before heaven and earth as witnesses, God calls them to examine the people who received it and did not keep it.
comments.comment: Since the giving of the law is given upon witnesses, heaven and earth, as it is written in Deuteronomy, it is necessary that the people, being distinguished upon the witnesses through whom they received the law, be examined having stood upon the divine laws. He calls not the heaven above, that is, the divine powers, and the earth, I say, the inhabitants upon it, so that those made his children upon it might be exposed: 'Hear, O heaven, and pay attention, O earth, for the children of God are being proclaimed; for they, having received the law upon you, did not keep it' (Psalm 50:4; LXX 49:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse calls heaven and earth to the judgment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gathers his holy ones to establish his covenant on spiritual sacrifices such as the sacrifice of praise, and the heavens that announce righteousness are holy men bearing the image of the heavenly.
comments.comment:
Perhaps he commands angels to holy men, so that he might gather his pious ones to prepare and establish his covenant of God upon spiritual sacrifices: namely, the sacrifice of praise and if anyone else similar. He commands the pious ones to be gathered to him, receiving the spiritual covenant upon which they are to offer the sacrifices, so that they might fulfill the things foretold.

'The heavens announce so-called righteousness' (Psalm 50:6; LXX 49:6a), being men who are holy, bearing the image of the heavenly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The perfect heavenly ones will sing God's righteousness, saying that he is gladdened by judgment and not by sacrifices.
comments.comment: The heavenly perfect races, he says, will sing in praise of God's righteousness, applauding with perfect words that possess what is most just and most discerning: that God is gladdened not by sacrifices but by judgment, and holds this as his everlasting covenant (Psalm 50:6; LXX 49:6; Psalm 50:13; LXX 49:13).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God judges not the things offered but the disposition of those who offer, as he exposed Cain for not dividing the offering rightly.
comments.comment: 'God examines not the things themselves offered to those approaching, but the disposition according to which they approach' (Psalm 50:8; LXX 49:8); and indeed, he exposes Cain for not having divided the offering rightly. If someone offers a spiritual sacrifice as whole burnt offerings through his whole body, let him do this with right intention; for one is not praised for the things being done, but one is examined for the intention not being rightly fulfilled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God looks at in an offering, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those in the land called bulls turned against the Savior, so God will not receive them or their rams, but takes instead the men from the Gentiles who were once beasts of the forest.
comments.comment: 'Since those in your land, figuratively called bulls, have become hostile to the Savior, concerning whom it is said, "Many bulls have surrounded me, wild oxen have enclosed me"' (Psalm 50:9; LXX 49:9-11a); for this reason, I will not receive them, nor the rams associated with them. For they, offering themselves on behalf of sin, are no better than those who sin. Know then what those who were once beasts of the forest, men awakened from the Gentiles, are to me, being made subject to the divine teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cattle and oxen are those who belong to Christ and trample the law's shadow, and souls winged by right thoughts are called things of heaven, for God knows those who are his.
comments.comment: They have become previously unfruitful, for the grove is a symbol of this. But also the cattle, being like the sheep of Christ, and the oxen who have gone up over your fence—that is, trampling the shadow of the law in the dogmas of the gospel (because of the height they do not reach)—are our own possession. Does Paul say that the care of the oxen matters to God, he who sets forth the law concerning the ox in the books? Or is he speaking certainly about us? But also the souls that have become lofty, being winged by right thoughts and activities, are being called things of the heaven; for I know them, for I know those who belong to me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God needs none of the sacrifices offered to him, for all the beasts are his, so the offerings are to be used symbolically, as virtue practised perfectly and not carelessly.
comments.comment: For all sin as they bring to God as a needy person, ignoring what was said in the Psalms toward Him, the God: 'Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?' (Psalm 50:13) and also: 'Mine are all the beasts of the field, cattle on the mountains and oxen' (Psalm 50:10). For all that you have in abundance from me, I also have all things, so that one not in need did not command, but rather from these, using them symbolically, it is fitting to use virtue not carelessly, but perfectly and completely.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A right heart that receives Jesus's seed and bears fruit is the beauty of the field, which stays near the sower.
comments.comment: The good land that has received the seed, that is, a right heart, having cast the seed thrown by Jesus and having borne fruit, a hundred and sixty, thirty, possessing a full and ripe fruit, is the beauty of the field, not far from the sower; for he says, 'The beauty of the field is with me' (Psalm 50:11; LXX 49:11b).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ hungers for people's salvation and not for shadow-worship, so those who want the God who heals by the Spirit should offer him a sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving.
comments.comment: The Savior hungers for the salvation of some; as for the lack of concern for the salvation of the Samaritan woman, he says to the disciples, 'I have food to eat which you do not know' (John 4:32), and 'My food is to do the will of him who sent me' (John 4:34). Since those coming from circumcision approach him with the sensible worship of the shadow as one starving, he says, 'If I hunger, it is not for you'; for the glorious church, which has become mine, is inhabiting the world and its fullness. And the fullness of it is the gospel, not the type, the shadow. Being nourished by the fullness of the Gentiles, I will not demand from you food according to the shadow; but if you wish to have me as your God who heals with the Spirit, sacrifice to me a sacrifice of praise, of thanksgivings and theologizing; for these I receive as offerings; for I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings (Psalm 50:14; LXX 49:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God needs no food or drink, so the true sacrifice is awareness of his benefits, confession from the heart, and prayers fulfilled as a debt owed to him.
comments.comment:
For God is not in need of food and drink, he says, that he should attend to meats as food and to blood as drink. Then, introducing the true honor of God in place of the name of sacrifice, he adds what follows.

Consider this to be sacrifice, he says: the awareness of benefits, the confession from the heart, and the fulfillment of prayers as a debt owed by human beings to God (Psalm 50:14; LXX 49:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God wants in place of sacrifices of meat and blood, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is both the Most High and the deliverer from distress, asking thanksgiving for praise and promises for prayers.
comments.comment: He is the same God who is both Most High and a deliverer from distress (Psalm 50:14-15; LXX 49:14). Regarding praise, he says to offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving that befit you, and regarding prayers, the promises; for he says both in the first and twentieth Psalm, 'I will render my thanksgivings in the presence of those who fear him' (Psalm 22:25). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope for God's help in affliction, then glorify him by giving thanks without ceasing.
comments.comment: And if you do these things, he says, be of good hope that you will obtain God as your helper in afflictions, so that you may also glorify him when you are benefited, offering thanks without ceasing (Psalm 50:15; LXX 49:15; Ps 49:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the promise of help in trouble asks of the one who prays.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A sinner's praise is unfitting, since God's covenant must be received in the heart before it is spoken, and to agree with those who steal the truth or lead Christ's bride astray is to take their part.
comments.comment:
Since praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Psalm 50:16; LXX 49:16), God strikes the one sinning, saying, 'Why do you not recount my righteous decrees, so that you may fulfill them, and why do you take up the...'
