Did you receive my covenant in your mouth? For it is necessary that, having received it in your heart and having imprinted the thoughts according to it upon yourself, you would not utter the words of my covenant in this way. To this, the one proclaiming 'do you steal?' agrees, and the following (Psalm 50:16-21).

And regarding the mind, 'you will think and not thus'; if ever you were observing someone stealing the will of the truth with heterodox opinion, you were agreeing and running together with him; but also those attempting to commit adultery with the bride of Christ, to draw the ecclesiastical souls toward them, by being of like mind with them or not turning away from those committing adultery, you are placing your part with them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Approving of those who sin harms the soul and mind, and the one who consents becomes a partner in their sin and is not blameless.
comments.comment: To such a one [who carelessly lets himself be filled with other people's offenses] the divine David also said somewhere: ‘If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you took your share with the adulterer’ (Psalm 50:18). For just as doing what is not permitted harms and deadens both soul and mind, so does approving of those who do such things; and the one who consents would be a partner with those who commit the sin themselves, for he is in no way blameless. That is why Paul too says: ‘Keep yourself pure, and do not share in other people’s sins’ (1 Timothy 5:22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Running with a thief, joining adulterers, and speaking deceit against a neighbor each paralyze a commandment of the law.
comments.comment: These things are a paralysis of the law: the commandment “You shall not steal” is paralyzed by running together with a thief; “You shall not commit adultery” by being arrayed with adulterers; “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” and “You shall not go about in deceit among your nation” by speaking conspiratorial and deceitful words, by accusing, and by devising stumbling blocks for a neighbor (Psalm 50:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the sins listed in the verses break the commandments, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sinning in ignorance is sin, but sinning after knowing the good is rebuked for wickedness.
comments.comment: 'Your mouth has increased wickedness.' He who is ignorant of the good but does the evil, he sins; but he who, after knowing the good, sins, is rebuked for wickedness; therefore also the servant who knew the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten much. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference in guilt between sinning in ignorance and sinning knowingly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse names a brother and a mother's son, and asks whom a man can love who is not so toward his brothers.
comments.comment: 'Sitting against your brother you have spoken, and against the son of your mother you have set a stumbling block.' Regarding the word 'brother', one can be of like mind and of the same fatherland; but regarding 'son of a mother', one is of the same womb and not from the father. He who is not thus toward brothers, what other can he be able to love?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spoken to a Jew who offers sacrifices by the letter, the verse charges him with speaking against the brother who lives by the spirit of the law and with setting circumcision as a stumbling block to the son of the mother.
comments.comment: And regarding the mind: since the word is toward a Jew, perceptibly offering burnt offerings and sacrifices to God, regarding this it must be said to be spoken in the presence of God, 'Sitting'. O you, regarding the letter of the law, you speak against your brother who is according to the spirit of the law and living by it; and you are also against the one who is the son of your mother; for from the same intention the spirit and the letter of the law were issued. And you scandalize the son of the mother, having set a stumbling block and a scandal, the circumcision which is a way of shadow and flesh. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's silence is his longsuffering toward sinners, meant to benefit them, though they wrongly imagine him to be like themselves.
comments.comment: I was silent. The silence of God is called the longsuffering toward sinners; for if He were to punish them immediately by those things, He would not be silent, deciding against them, whereas they ought to suffer. … It is necessary to be benefited by such silence; from the opposite, you received lawlessness toward the wicked, by which you imagine me to be like you; for you, having glorified me, rejoice that I do not come forth against you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God's silence means in the verse, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At the judgment God will make each person visible to himself, as hearts are uncovered and his deeds are gathered suddenly before his eyes.
comments.comment: But the judgment will reveal the knowledge, because I will make you yourself visible to yourself. For each person will see himself, when hearts are uncovered, as he was formed from his heart. And Theodotion, rendering “I will add, I will heap up,” indicated the sudden gathering of deeds that comes before the eyes of the one who did them (Psalm 50:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God will set the sins before the sinner's eyes.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To think one can win God's closeness by doing what offends him is to suppose him like ourselves, for even a mortal's friendship is won by pleasing him.
comments.comment: Does God not see what happens? Does He not understand your thoughts? Does He cooperate with you in your lawless deeds? You supposed a lawlessness, He says—that I would be like you (Psalm 50:21). When you seek the friendship of a mortal man, you win him over with good deeds, saying and doing the things you know please him. But when you are drawing near to God and hoping to be received into the rank of a son, you do what is hostile to God and dishonor Him by breaking the law—and from the very things that most offend Him, you hope for closeness?
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: God's longsuffering is an occasion for repentance, and if a man will not understand, lawlessness seizes him with no one to rescue him, though God rescues those who understand and repent.
comments.comment: Those who, having taken up the forgetfulness of God through sluggishness, take hold of understanding, stand upon the spoken words: 'What I longsuffer toward sins, I do not rejoice in, nor do I do this as an evil man, but as an occasion for repentance through goodness and innate kindness, by setting aside punishment' (Psalm 50:21). For if you will not choose to understand, the law or the lawlessness seizes, and there is no one rescuing; for God will rescue those who understand and have repented from evil. Let those who confess not care about those who have ceased and are no longer acting, confessing, saying: 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have been ungodly' (Psalm 106:6). For it is not the one currently doing these things who confesses.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praising and theologizing the beauty of God glorifies him, and 'the salvation of God' can mean either the salvation or the Savior Christ.
comments.comment: That is, the one praising and theologizing the beauty of God glorifies Him; for the sensory worship rather dishonors, bringing God in by making Him manifest and in need of movement. The way is not there in sensory worship, but there in the truth which encounters beauty, which God shows by illuminating His own salvation, the only-begotten Son the Savior, who is the salvation itself; for the salvation of God at times signifies the salvation, and at times the Savior Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm of repentance stands fiftieth, the number of forgiveness, as in the Lord's fifty debtors, the fifty days to the outpouring of the Spirit and the Jubilee year when debts are cut.
comments.comment:
The history was preserved, not because the fiftieth was arranged with them. But what analogy the number has to a lion, the Savior, teaching about forgiveness, took fifty debtors and with five hundred denarii of forgiveness, and to each side it had happened through the fifty and the related number to owe; but the five hundredth is not. Regardless, the Passover of the slaughter of the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, having risen from the dead, who has made the forgiveness, the people for fifty days pass through rejoicing the fiftieth day of the outpouring of the Spirit, being worthy.

And called by the Hebrews Jubilee, the year through fifty years is a feast in which the cutting of debts and the restoration of the properties of the Hebrews' freedom are confirmed; therefore it is also following the psalm of David concerning repentance to be placed as fiftieth. And it is composed also of seven weeks and a unit, as if it were a week of weeks in number. It is necessary for there to be in weeks one who casts away the filth and the work of sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Repentance needs God's mercy and God's mercy needs our recognition of sin, and as stubborn dyes need many washings, great lawless acts need many mercies to be erased.
comments.comment: He who intensely repents and loves the fruits fitting for repentance asks for the great mercy from God to come to him (Ps 50,3a), for repentance is not sufficient without the mercy of God, nor the mercy of God without the recognition from us toward salvation. Just as the hard-to-wash dyes are removed not by one washing but by many, so also the great things of the lawless acts are erased by many mercies of God (Ps 50,3b).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks for great mercy and many mercies, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one should rise up against David, for when God has justified there is no one to condemn, and he fell into only this one sin besides counting the people.
comments.comment: But let this not become an occasion to rise up against David; for when God has justified, there is no one condemning. But he will be pious toward the man, having understood that the man is long-lived and has spent most of his years in powers and in kingship, introducing only this one sin, having done it, and in addition to this, having counted the people contrary to the will of God, but not even persistently...
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sins of the saints are written down so that, as they are teachers of virtue, they are also teachers of repentance, and the grace of God is seen when they slip.
comments.comment: For such a great and far-reaching king was rebuked in sin, that when he was rebuked by a private man, he not only did not feel indignation, but even made himself worse, as the rebuking prophet says: 'And the Lord showed your sin' (2 Samuel 12:13). For to say that the Lord showed it is to say that David himself, having led himself to most intense repentance, was led to his sin. We say that what other men fall into when sinning, the saints, running the race of salvation, if ever they should stumble as men inattentive, do not fall but persist in the race, as if the instability of the race had not seemed to them likely to trip them up. And for many other ineffective things the sins of the saints were written down in this regard; for since they are called to imitate an exceeding virtue, being hesitant, they made a pretext for having a divine portion and for the saints being unendurable in sin, but not being such, they were unable to imitate the far-reaching saints. Thus Providence granted a pretext for sin to have occurred concerning them, so that just as they are teachers of virtue, so also they are teachers of repentance for those being instructed then, having done such things. Perhaps also those far-reaching saints, having reached the height of virtue, did not arrive at this by their own power but by the cooperation of God. If they were not to fall, the divine grace would have been little, so that, having slipped, they might seek the helper of their own weakness, having come to be through consciousness (Psalm 51:1; LXX 50:1,2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm's place among the Pentecosts of the Psalter fits mercy and forgiveness, and the story of Bathsheba took place while David was reigning, later than the histories in earlier titles.
comments.comment: And this psalm was not written in vain for Pentecost. For the number has a harmony toward mercy and forgiveness, since, if the writing spirit maintained the sequence of history, it arranged the first Pentecost and the hundredth and those following. For the first Pentecost has an inscription containing the slander of Doeg the Edomite; but that history is before the kingship of David. And the third Pentecost, the slander of the Ziphites against Saul concerning David as being hidden among them, contains this; and this narrative happened before the kingship of David, but the encounter with Bathsheba happened while David was reigning. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lawlessness and sin differ by intention, but God can wash and cleanse each.
comments.comment: The same energy calls lawlessness and sin, differing by the intention: the one consisting as lawlessness without law, the other consisting as sin according to the transgression of law (Psalm 51:2); however, each is worthy to be washed and to be cleansed by God who is able to wash and cleanse it from the aforementioned defilement. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two words for wrong in the verse, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David accuses himself, seeing his offense always yet not despairing of healing, because of mercy.
comments.comment: This was the “righteous accuser of himself.” For I do not wait, he says, for the reproof of another, even though the prophet did reprove me. He did so once, but I see my offense continually—yet I do not despair of healing, because of mercy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist means by his sin being always before him.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: David was a king subject not to human law but to God, so he did evil before God alone and God alone is his witness.
comments.comment: As for being a king, he was not subject to human law, but to God; nor did any of the lawgivers or a witness testify that he did evil before any of them; but since he wishes to be a king and God-fearing, he was subject to the law of God; therefore he did evil before God alone, and the witness is to God alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why David says he sinned against God alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since men lean toward evil and no one is without sin, God is justified in his words and conquers when judged, for to claim sinlessness is to make him a liar.
comments.comment: And again: since you are God, and the mind of men leans more toward evil things (Psalm 51:4), and there is no man who will not sin, God is justified in His own words, in which He says that all who have strayed ought to sin; by this also He conquers when being judged against men, proving them to be sinners. Accompanying this, if we say 'We have not sinned' (1 John 1:10), we make Him a liar; for if it had been declared that all lean toward sin, he who claims sinlessness proves God to be a liar.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sin has grown together with us from our origin and passes to us from the mothers who conceive us, since evil was rooted in the first woman and we come into the light through childbirth.
comments.comment: This is a request for pardon, because sin has grown together with us from our first origin, passed on to us from the mothers who conceive us (Psalm 51:5). For “through one man sin entered the world” (Romans 5:12), and evil was rooted in the first woman, and from her it passes through childbirth to those who are born. This is said more fittingly of the mother, even though sin also comes through the father, because we are brought forth from the father in seed, but from mothers completely, and we come into the light through childbirth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says about sin in the mother who conceives, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Nature is unclean because, after the transgression and the curse, it endures corruption, and those born are sown in the love of bodily pleasure, though God created all things that they might exist.
comments.comment: And nature is defiled in another way too: those who are born are sown, as it were, in the love of bodily pleasure. And the inspired David seems to hint at something like this when he sings and says: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me’ (Psalm 51:5). So nature is unclean, since as a result of the transgression and of the curse it endures corruption, contrary to what God willed. For ‘he created all things that they might exist’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:14); the saying is true.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: The psalmist was brought forth in iniquity by accepting its deeds, and God, who loves truth, leads us through earthly means to truth and cleanses us until we are whiter than snow, with the Spirit like hyssop.
comments.comment: Psalm 51, verse 7: I was brought forth in iniquity—not only in the womb, but because I accepted the deeds of iniquity, including murder and the illicit acts of a bed I violently seized. Verse 8: I have loved truth. This is the understanding: You, Lord, being true and loving truth, desire to lead us into truth through earthly means, and you cleanse us from ancient sin. You will cleanse us until we are whiter than snow; yet this cleansing for us comes through hyssop, and the energy of the Holy Spirit is likened to hyssop—it warms and removes all the filth within us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Born in sins, we cannot be glorified before a judge whose pleasure is the truly good.
comments.comment: We, he says, have been rooted in lawlessness and are born in sins, but what pleases you is what is truly good and in no way distorted. How then can human beings be glorified before such a judge, rather than carry away shame by being condemned? (Psalm 51:6)
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those trained in the skill of arguments, like Moses and Daniel, come to love the truth and are made wise by God, who makes known the hidden things of his wisdom.
comments.comment: He who has been trained in the skill of sophistry upon the prey of truth, having known its greatness, possessed a perfect love toward it. For those not having been trained in falsehoods, having become more discerning, see the priceless beauty of the truth, namely Moses and Daniel. For after having been tested by the sophistical arguments, having ascended to the true wisdom, they received testimony from God as being perfect wise men, God having made known to them the unmanifest and the hidden things of His wisdom, so that nothing was unclear to them or overshadowed. David, by chance having this skill, spoke the coming verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David asks for pardon on the strength of grace already shown, thanks God for the gift of wisdom, and asks him to remove the defilement that has come on him.
comments.comment: From the grace that already existed toward him, he asks that sparing may also now come about. For God brings what follows upon the beginnings that come from himself, for the sake of his own purpose and steadfastness, even if what comes from us is not entirely worthy—just as, for the sake of the covenant with Abraham, he has mercy on the race descended from him when it suffers harm, bringing what follows upon the beginning and guarding the certainty of the promise above the equality of authority. Since, then, he knows he has obtained wisdom from God and has been honored by it, so as to understand even the hidden things about which he prays—“Open my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118:18 [119:18])—for this reason he acknowledges gratitude for the gift of wisdom, and asks that God remove the defilement that has come upon him, adding this also to grace.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one who approaches the Passover by the lamb's blood is purified.
comments.comment: He who has truly approached the typical Passover by the blood of the lamb in us is purified, being led in with hyssop as it is written in Exodus (Ex 12:22); …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David will hear in Hades the coming of the Savior as great gladness, and his bones in the tombs will rejoice with him.
comments.comment: The Savior said that Abraham, expecting his day, rejoiced beforehand, and when it came he saw it and rejoiced—Abraham, as he says, “your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). But David speaks of hearing instead of sight, saying that he will hear in Hades the cause of great gladness—the coming of the Savior signified to him by the Spirit—and that he will rejoice in Hades in spirit, and his bones within the tombs, humbled by sin and death, will also rejoice together with him, since the body that is the cause of resurrection was buried with them (Psalm 51:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist says 'make me to hear' and what the rejoicing bones are, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The soul's doctrines and powers are like bones, humbled by sin but rejoicing at God's gladness, and sins are erased as virtue comes in.
comments.comment: … The doctrines and powers of the soul are like bones; they are humbled by sin and by deceptive influence. But having heard the joy and gladness of God, the humbled bones will rejoice (Psalm 51:8). And sins are erased from the transformation of virtues (Psalm 51:9); for just as knowledge coming into the soul erases and makes the ignorance vanish, so also every sin is erased by the presence of perfect virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the bones are and why sins are blotted out, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God erases the sins written in the heart, creates a pure heart and kindles a steadfast spirit, which is the Holy Spirit or the upright conscience.
comments.comment: If you will erase all my sins, the ones written through the impressions in my heart, you create a pure heart in me, lacking all evil (Psalm 51:10), but also kindle a steadfast spirit within my indwellings. And the upright thoughts and earnest perceptions dwelling in the soul are those about which he says: 'And all that is within me, bless his name.' And the steadfast spirit is the Holy Spirit or the conscience, the upright one, which the spirit of a man within him says. It is to be noted that what the voice has created does not signify essential beings, but a certain relationship being established which has been produced.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Free choice alone cannot make the heart pure, so the one who prays asks God to create it.
comments.comment: And what sees God is a pure heart, from which there no longer “come forth evil thoughts,” no “murders,” no “adulteries,” no “fornications,” no “thefts,” no “false witness,” no “blasphemies” (Matthew 15:19), no “evil eye” (Mark 7:22), nor anything else that is wrong. That is why it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). But since our own free choice is not enough for us to have a heart wholly “pure,” and we need God to create it so, the one who prays with understanding says: “Create in me a pure heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks God to create a clean heart, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Create in me a clean heart' means sanctify me so that I may be renewed after being corrupted by sin, and a steadfast spirit is a spirit of God's reverence that makes him worthy of God's temple.
comments.comment: Because that it is to create and to sanctify, which the divine Spirit is accustomed to do, David testifies, singing: 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Ps 51:10), that is: sanctify me, so that I might be renewed, having been corrupted by sin; for how else could another heart be created for him? And he confirms this with: 'And a steadfast spirit establish within my innermost parts' (Psalm 51:10), instead of: 'Provide me a spirit of your exceeding reverence, so that,' he says, 'being revealed pure through its sanctification, I might become worthy of your temple. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Create' need not mean bringing into being; David asks as one who cast his heart away.
comments.comment: That 'created' does not always signify subsistence, is shown by David saying, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God' (Psalm 51:10). For he asks not as one not possessing, to receive, but as one having cast it away, to receive it again having been cleansed. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only the sinner is cast out from those who stand before God, so David asks not to be rejected nor stripped of the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: Among those who constantly stand before God, only the one who sins is cast out and rejected. (Psalm 51:11). But do not judge me, being contained by your divine comprehension, to be such a one as to be rejected from your face; but also do not take away the Holy Spirit whom you made to dwell in me, lest I be made naked of it (Psalm 51:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist fears when he asks not to be cast away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Expecting the Savior's descent, which brings perfect joy, David asks the Father to restore the joy of salvation and to support him with a ruling and perfect spirit.
comments.comment: Expecting this descent of the Savior, by which it happens that he possesses perfect joy, he entreats the Father, saying: 'Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and with a ruling and perfect spirit support me.' And in these things, the Holy Spirit says 'ruling and leading' is either the man's internal principle or the soul of the man. And this ruling spirit desires support and confirmation according to the former interpretation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Confessing to God brings the lawless God's teaching, so that even the impious may return to him.
comments.comment: Behold, indeed, even here what has been said is confirmed: for through the confession toward God, He promises to teach the lawless the ways of God himself, so that having stepped upon these, even if they were once impious, they might return to Him in a little while.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the psalmist's confession leads him to teach transgressors.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who erred should imitate the repentant, and David, from the sins of blood against Uriah, is worthy to be saved by the God of his salvation.
comments.comment: For those who have accomplished righteousness have the imitation and pattern of a good life, so also those who have erred concerning knowledge have to imitate the one coming into repentance, being impious ones returning toward God. 'Since by which I have done toward death, I am full of sins of blood' (Psalm 51:14), 'save me from these, the God who is once and our own.' Perhaps also David, from the sins of Uriah and if any others died with him, is worthy to be saved by God, being the God of his salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God opens the lips of the one who has received the word, so that his mouth praises him always.
comments.comment: 'My tongue, called my own, in the always speaking concerning your righteousness, will rejoice in your righteousness' (Psalm 51:14). From that, God opens the lips of the one having received the word in the opening of his mouth, so that his mouth shall proclaim the praises of God, always praising and giving thanks to Him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praying for the communion of the Holy Spirit, David asks that Zion be made and the walls of Jerusalem built, which are guards of angels.
comments.comment: 'He who confesses concerning his own sin, what do you wish to discuss concerning Zion and Jerusalem?' (Psalm 51:18/20). But since we hope that he has not been entirely harmed by having stumbled in the short race, for this reason, possessing a prophetic thing and praying for and prophesying the communion of the Holy Spirit, he says: 'Doing good, saying that Zion was brought into being in your good pleasure for your son and approaching the Spirit'; but also the walls of Jerusalem are being built up. And these are guards of angels, a rooting out of incorruptible decrees.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sacrifice of righteousness is the righteousness that stands through faith in Jesus Christ, and the oxen on the heavenly altar are the souls of martyrs.
comments.comment: He says righteousness, which is standing together through the faith of Jesus Christ for all those believing. But this righteousness turns out to be a lifting up and spiritual holocausts, and 'sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness' (Ps 51:19); but also upon the spiritual altar, they bring up oxen like tillers, not other souls, but having been seen as the souls of martyrs, being brought up upon the heavenly altar.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A leader of beasts is no shepherd, so David speaks the psalm as if to the devil who moved the wicked man.
comments.comment: Who then would justify such a tragedy, when the one who leads irrational animals is supposed to be a shepherd? For we are without a leader. David, having realized his own great wickedness, spoke the words of the psalm (Psalm 52; LXX 51) as if to the one moving him through envy, the devil, as if he were present.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse compares things of the same kind and not opposites, as when Sodom is said to be justified because of Jerusalem.
comments.comment: Or, is this comparative? Pay attention to what you say. The things said to be comparative are said as being of the same kind, not as being opposed; just as when I say, 'Sodom was justified because of you' (Ezekiel 16:51), it is not that Sodom has been justified. 'Because of your own sins, O Jerusalem', because a prophet was killed and has become a traitor to the Savior. That Sodom incited one man, Lot. 'That Sodom was justified because of you.' Not simply was it justified—for it has not been justified—but 'because of you.' And if it says again: 'He loved wickedness rather than goodness, and deceitful lips rather than to speak righteousness' (Ps 52:3), these things are said comparatively, not oppositely; for this is said because, once one is decided, the other is immediately placed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Edomite loved a deceitful tongue and words of drowning, that is, words that bring punishment, like the millstone the Gospel threatens.
comments.comment:
Words of drowning are those bringing punishment, the drowning signifying chastisement, just as the lips of the unthinking drown him.

And the Edomite is not truly interpreted as earthly, always shaking because of being uncertain; for he is interpreted as being in a state of instability, he who, having worked slander against the healers of God, loved a deceitful tongue and with it words drowning him. And the Gospel signifies drowning to be the punishment, saying to the one causing scandal among the little ones in the church: 'It is better to be drowned in the depths of the sea' (Matt 18:6), with a millstone hung around his neck.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because he loved evil, the one badly planted is uprooted and driven from the holy tent and the land of the living, as are all who fall from piety.
comments.comment: Because he loved evil to the end, he falls completely, as one not well built but also as one badly planted; 'Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted' (Matt 15:13); but he will be made to migrate from the holy tent, casting out and driving you away from that tent, whom you have slandered and into whom you have led to death, even the root of the living. For even if you were an Edomite, if you had attached yourself to Israel through the instruction of the law, you were planted in the tent and in the land of the living; for if you did not have reverence toward the God of Israel, you would not have even begun to disturb the sanctuary. And the things said against this man will apply to all those falling away from piety.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God will pluck the wicked out of his dwelling place and root him out of the land of the living.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who dwell in God's house, nourished by the divine light, bear fruit by doing what is needed and thinking pious doctrines.
comments.comment: Such was the one to whom the holy one cries: 'Therefore God brings you to an end, to uproot you and to transplant you from a dwelling, and your root from the land of the living' (Psalm 52:8), while everyone remaining in the house of God says thankfully: 'I am like an olive tree flourishing in the house of God' (Psalm 52:8). For how can the one dwelling in the house of God, nourished by the divine light, not bear fruit, in doing what is necessary and thinking the pious doctrines? Thus the man blessed in the first Psalm was a fruitful tree; for it has been said concerning him: 'He shall be like the tree planted by the streams of water, which brings forth its fruit...'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeing the fall, the pious fear the same for themselves and dare not mock.
comments.comment: The very pious, those falling away from virtue into wickedness, receive a fear lest they themselves suffer the same. Nor will they dare to mock the fallen, as if saying they would laugh at him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the righteous 'see and fear': they take the fall of the wicked as a warning to themselves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thanksgiving shows that God has done what David set out to do, his flight from Saul, and God's name is full of goodness before his holy things.
comments.comment:
Thanksgiving through confessing to God shows that he has done it, perhaps what he had previously set forth. For he had set forth to flee from Saul.

But also, 'what shall I do?' he says, 'your name is such that I might encounter whatever is good and full of goodness in the presence of your holy things'; Ps 52:2a for those having been made steadfast by the holiness of your goodness perceive it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fool who says there is no God has cast out piety and with it all virtue, and so has corrupted his own mind and become abominable.
comments.comment:
One is called foolish if he is lacking divine wisdom. …

For he who has thought badly concerning God enters into wickedness; for casting out the piety of his own soul, he has also cast out with it all virtue following it like a royal garment of piety. Therefore, those saying through foolishness that God does not exist have corrupted their own mind by practicing lawlessness, from which they became loathsome, that is, they have become abominable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the fool is and why denying God ruins the mind, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's providence looks down on the sons of men and sees not only the body but the hidden part of the heart.
comments.comment: The present verse introduces providence, of not only those in heaven but also those on earth; Ps 52:3 for it has been said to look down providently from heaven upon the sons of men, not looking upon them from without only according to the body, but also according to the hidden part of the heart. He looks upon the sons of men, so that I might know if he is one who understands by doing the good and seeking God by examining the truth. And it has been said in a human way that he stoops from heaven to see if he understands; for great, if not in this way, is the impact.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what God looking down from heaven means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All have turned aside from the straight way, and this turning aside is sin, so that of them it is said that none does good.
comments.comment: … And from the present word we learn that sin consists in a transgression of the law by one who follows, if he is by nature evil. For all have turned aside; and this turning aside is sin, a failure not of the straight way. And those who turned aside were useless; saying it is useless, either according to the dominance of passions or according to the ignorance of one who, not thinking, is swept away into other things, does not have the knowledge of one thing. Of all those turning aside, it is rightly said, 'He does not do good' (Psalm 53:3). According to each of the aforementioned, the 'until one' limit shows that neither is there one doing good, nor one not doing good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who acted the part of virtue to please men will fear what God reveals about them, and their hypocrisy will put them to shame.
comments.comment: There they will fear a fear that no fear can be brought up to the coming age; in that, fleeing from pain and sighing and grief, one must have courage. In this, not being in a state of fear, those approaching the things by which they will be punished will fear. Therefore, they will fear what God revealed there regarding those who became hypocrites, having the aim of pleasing men, scattering their bones, the doctrines and conveniences of laziness and greed, and the impulses of a vile soul. For if even there they were thought to be pleasing to men, deceiving them, but being nullified by God as if they were nothing, they were shamed. And perhaps those doing evil will encounter the previously spoken-of punishments. But those hypocritically acting the part of virtue will not be tried by another punishment, their hypocrisy having been exposed; for he who does almsgiving to be glorified by men will not be punished by fire or anything of that kind (for he did not show mercy), but will be shamed, having been shown to have shared in the poverty of existing things not through God but through men (Psalm 53:5-6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Forgiveness given as a gift frees those held captive by sin.
comments.comment:
For sin is that which takes captive those who do it. But the forgiveness of sins being given as a gift, the Lord rejoices.

Israel and Jacob rejoice with those rejoicing in the heavens, similarly with one sinner repenting.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the bringing back of captives means: forgiveness given as a gift.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ, the Father's power, judges hidden things and asks for examination by God's power.
comments.comment: Christ is the power of the Father. Since He judges the hidden things of men, He entreats that they be handed over for examination not to other judges, but by the power of the good God; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who asks God to enlighten his words must speak only what is true and pious.
comments.comment: It is necessary that his prayer become well-pleasing and that he receive the things for which he prayed. But also, having become near to God through good works, 'Enlighten with the words of my mouth' (Ps 52:9). For no one, uttering a word that is idle, shameful, or some other evil, wants God to enlighten his words, but only everyone speaking the true and pious.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist can ask God to hear the words of his mouth: only true and pious words are fit for it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The strangers are those opposed to the earnest, and the strong are demons that turned from God.
comments.comment: He says that those having an opposing disposition to the earnest ones are strangers, and the wicked demons are strong. And he says: because they did not set God before them, turning away from Him and having given their backs to Him, they rose up against the righteous and sought his soul.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the strangers and the strong are and why they attack.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is confessed as helper and sustains the soul, turning the enemies' evils back on them, and his truth destroys liars.
comments.comment: He confesses God as a helper, perhaps the Father and Lord sustaining his soul, so that He might somehow turn the Son; 'He will turn the evils toward my enemies; for they desire to bring evil upon me' (Psalm 54:5), these things He turns toward them, this being judged by the Lord in this way. 'Do to him as he has done to his neighbor' (Leviticus 24:19) agrees with this. And the truth of God, reproving those who are liars, destroys them if they are such; for they are not to be refuted at all, but rather they are such as the holy one prays.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer 'In your truth destroy them' asks that arguments opposed to the truth be destroyed, so that all may offer God a rational sacrifice.
comments.comment: As we begin, we say to God in prayer that prophetic word: “In your truth destroy them” (Psalm 54:5). Plainly this means the arguments opposed “to the truth.” For these are destroyed by the truth of God, so that, once they are destroyed, everyone, set free from distraction, may say the words that follow: “Willingly I will sacrifice to you” (Psalm 54:6), and may offer to the God of the universe a rational sacrifice that sends up no smoke.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what destroying the enemies 'in your truth' means, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The voluntary sacrifice is offered freely, not by necessity or force.
comments.comment: Having these things happened, coming to thanksgiving with a self-willed mind, 'I will offer to You a voluntary sacrifice, not by necessity or force, but by a self-commanded readiness' (Ps 54:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the freely offered sacrifice means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saint is grieved and troubled at seeing the enemy speak proudly and the sinner fall, as a father grieves for a son who stays behind.
comments.comment: The same enemy can be to the sinner, differing only in the lack of distinction. When the sinner is distressed by those through whom he acts wickedly, and when the enemy speaks the truth, 'I was grieved in my iniquity and was troubled' (Psalm 55:2). Here iniquity signifies prayer, as also in the first of the Kingdoms, Anna says, 'Out of the multitude of my iniquity I have stretched out to you until now'; for concerning prayer itself she says this. The saint says: seeing the enemy speaking proudly and seeing the sinner distressed, he was grieved toward God through a prayer of iniquity; seeing those of the same kind and of the same race fallen into the depth of wickedness, he was also troubled by the instability of nature, lest even I should undergo this same turn. Perhaps he is also most caretaking-ly grieved and troubled seeing the wicked going astray, just as a father grieves for a son who remains behind. For some say that this psalm is reported to have been spoken from the face of Christ according to the human nature, and it is fitting to be grieved concerning those being harmed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A thought of sin kept within brings trouble and fear of death, and the passive part of human nature, stirred up, brings fear, trembling and the darkness of perplexity.
comments.comment:
Every serious person understands that to sin in thoughts is neither tolerable nor so, and in deed and word it is both dangerous and heavy. Therefore, if it ever happens in thoughts to cause a stumbling block and harm, guarding these within oneself and not uttering a word, according to the sin committed in secret, and not acting effectively, knowing that the thought is both healing and yet incurable; therefore he says, 'My heart was troubled within me' (Psalm 55:4). For I did not interpret the trouble as having done something through it, but also, as the fear of death was falling upon me following the sin, I seized it within myself. For it happens that fear appears from the outside and becomes a stumbling block to others for the one who has been revealed. Fear and trembling came (Psalm 55:5).

Human nature has inherent the passive, which some also call the irascible and the desiring. And even if one progresses in virtue, since the passive is not destroyed, it happens to be in what is called pre-passion. Indeed, then, also the person set before us, pushed by the voices of the enemy and the affliction of the sinner, had the inherent passive stirred up, so as to fear and fall under trembling and be covered by the darkness of perplexity; for the word 'darkness' here signifies dizziness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Afflicted, he asks for the Spirit's uplifting, the wings of a dove, to fly up and live free from care.
comments.comment:
And since many afflicting things surround him, he prays that there be given to him the upliftings and raisings of the Spirit, more allegorically called the wings of a dove.

These wings make him fly to a height, so that the one who has flown up, resting there, may henceforth live free from care, keeping the delicate and blessed sabbaths of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wings of a dove stand for and why he wants them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Going far off and lodging in the desert is read as putting enemies to flight and resting in peace, or as the righteous leaving the circumcised for the desert of the church, as Christ withdrew to a desert place.
comments.comment:
The word 'putting to flight' signifies pursuing and turning to flight those being driven.

For the one saying the psalm says: 'Behold, I went far away'—that is, putting the enemy and the sinner to flight for a long time, so that, with those driven away, I may lodge in the desert, that is, rest in a peaceful condition.

But if 'putting to flight' here properly signifies fleeing, the righteous one will say, fleeing and going far from those of the circumcision on account of the arrogance present in them: 'And I lodged in the desert'—the church of the law and the prophets.

And these things fit especially Christ according to the economy.

For doing these things symbolically, he was recorded in the Gospels: 'For having heard, he says, that John was handed over, he withdrew from there into a desert place' (Matt 14:13).

Concerning this desert are also the 'Rejoice, thirsty desert' (Isa 35:1) and the 'Voice of one crying in the desert' (Isa 40:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker flees the city full of lawlessness and deceit to rest in the wilderness, the Church from the Gentiles, among the believers.
comments.comment:
This can be referred to the Psalm 54:10b, 'Behold, I fled away and was distressed in the wilderness,' through the middle of the two verses from 'I waited for God who saves me,' as the 'He divided their tongues' is such a thing: since in the so-called city of God, Jerusalem, they were committing lawlessness and speaking against the truth, committing lawlessness and speaking against the truth, I fled away from it, so as having become in the wilderness called the Church from the Gentiles, to be distressed in it, resting and spending the night among the believers (Psalm 55:10-11).

Since all night and with the day they commit lawlessness and speak against the truth in the city, as the city would be surrounded by lawlessness and speaking against the truth and by the camp coming upon it because of these, lawlessness and speaking against the truth reached and upon its walls, the holy apostles guarding it. For they did not leave it, seeing it committing lawlessness and speaking against the truth, because lawlessness and toil have come against the praiseworthy pleasure in its midst with injustice, as the birth and deceit of those dwelling in it do not cease from its streets, those acting craftily through whom they think wickedly, toiling by taking upon themselves the burden of evil, with lead being thrown against it.

And its streets were to be considered as souls widening themselves for the sake of pleasure, to walk a wide and spacious road, this being a glorious and passive life. And for always remaining in these, the toil concerning evils and the deceit concerning frauds, it makes it so that 'It did not fail from its streets'...
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Breaking up agreement in evil is good.
comments.comment: Agreement for evil is terrible, and on the contrary the dissolution of those who agreed for evil is a great good.
comments.selected_reason: A one-line statement of why the psalmist asks that the tongues be divided.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At Babel one voice and one lip were joined in impiety, so the psalmist asks that the tongues of those who agree against him be divided, as Paul divided Pharisees and Sadducees.
comments.comment: Regarding the building of towers, they were assigned one voice and one lip, but through great impiety, having been joined together, they no longer had concord. For those who were making something from harmony, intending to be impious, they did not do this, their tongues having been divided. And here, indeed, the one praying desires the tongues of those who have voiced concord against him to be divided, the tongues being submerged, that is, becoming invisible. And before this, if it is said, 'to punish' means 'to submerge.' And Paul, knowing that sometimes it is advantageous to have disagreement against the wicked ones, defending himself on the steps, struck against Pharisees and Sadducees.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who descend into Hades are those who received the instruction of the divine teachings yet only sojourned in them, with wickedness in their midst.
comments.comment: Someone of the ancients said that those descending into Hades alone are those having received the instruction of the divine teachings. For the taste of the words of life is dead; those living thus descend into Hades. For those living without the common life do not descend into Hades as becoming a body there, for no one has the common life there. Since neither Judas nor all the people of the Jews had received the instruction of the law and the prophets, they descend into Hades with death coming upon them, living according to sin. Consequently, the one approaching is also said in the verse: 'That wickedness is in their sojournings, in their midst.' For even if they had experience of the life-giving writings, they did not dwell but sojourned in them, having wickedness in their midst, that is, in the ruling principle; for it is said that the wickedness is in the midst of the animal.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who cries to God is heard by the Lord; the outcry of Sodom was not a cry to God.
comments.comment: 'I cried to God and had my voice heard by the Lord.' For only he who has cried to God is heard by the Lord. For not everyone crying to God shouts; concerning the Sodomites it is written, 'The voice of Sodom and Gomorrah has been filled up,' not having cried to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it takes to be heard by the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pious man narrates wisdom through the evening of wickedness, the morning of the sun of righteousness, and the noon, and God hears his voice.
comments.comment: Since the narration of a pious man is wisdom throughout, a pious man and narrating wisdom throughout, the psalmist says: 'The evening sets for me the things of wickedness and the extinguished light of the ungodly, but the sun of righteousness rises for me as to make it in the morning; having become one having reached its noon, I will narrate the things of the aforementioned evening and of the previously foretold morning and of the aforementioned noon; and my announcing, God hears the voice of me, accepting and—if so—rejoicing at my voice which has narrated everything.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior is eternal and before the ages, since the ages came to be through him, as in 'I am,' not 'I was.'
comments.comment: … And the Savior is eternal, being from eternity, before the ages, so that even the ages themselves have come to be through him. And Paul says, 'And he himself is before all things' (Colossians 1:17). The one existing is the same as the one before all things; for it is not that he has come to be before all things. And regarding the Savior, 'Before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58), not 'I was' or 'I have been', but 'I am'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some sins are curable and have an exchange, such as sacrifice, almsgiving and fasting with prayer, but for incurable sins there is no exchange to lay down as a ransom.
comments.comment: Regarding sins, some are difficult and incurable, others are curable (Psalm 55:19). Concerning the curable, there is found an exchange: the sacrifice brought up for sins, but also almsgiving and fasting with prayer (for these things rescue from death). But for the incurable of those who have sinned, there is no exchange to lay down as a ransom and a savior. For if a man sins against a man and they pray for him, there is an exchange for these; but if he sins against the Lord God, who will pray for him? For there is no exchange for such things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'no changes' as the lack of any exchange or ransom for the incurable sin against God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The stretched-out hand of God repays those who profaned his covenant by rejecting the one prophesied under it, and they were scattered because they did not receive his shining face.
comments.comment: He stretched out his hand to repay those who worked what was deserved (Psalm 55:20). Since traitors and murderers of Christ have become unchangeable and madmen, they are worthy to fall under punishment as those who failed. They were captured by the Romans so that they might be stripped of their manhood and driven out of the nurtured land which they had never belonged to any other. Nor were they accepted back to their fatherland. For they profaned the covenant of God, not only by not adhering to it but also by rejecting the one prophesied under it. Perhaps also, even though the covenant was destined to be kept according to the sensible until the time came when it had to pass from the one according to the flesh to the one according to the spirit, by remaining in the typical worship, they profaned his covenant. Therefore, also, stretching out his punishing hand, he repaid them so that his wrath might reach them to the end, by which they were divided, no longer gathered together in his land, but scattered in every land. These things the wrath of the face of God brought upon them, since when his face shone and appeared, they did not receive it (Psalm 55:21). For they were considered to be smooth and without fault because of their hypocrisy...
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's words are like oil loosening the pains of sufferers, but to those who despise them they become missiles that strike.
comments.comment: … For those interpreting even concerning God do not do so correctly; God has drawn near to their own heart, coming down with men, bringing forth words like oil being poured out and loosening the pains of those who suffer. But for those who despise them, the words concerning oil are found to be missiles, striking those who despise them. Often, regarding the striking, there is the metaphor of the arrow, and arrow and missile are the same according to the subject.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God casts those who profaned his covenant into a pit of destruction, the abyss into which those corrupted in mind are brought down.
comments.comment: God does not give a stable place to the righteous, but those who have profaned his covenant he casts into a pit of destruction, contrary to the wells from which the Word protects life and incorruption from drinking. Perhaps 'pit of destruction' means the abyss into which those having been corrupted in their mind are brought down by his vote and are handed over by his judgment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one praying asks that men of blood and guile not reach half their days, so that they are punished for a few sins and not many.
comments.comment: He does not wish that the Jews, who exist from before the ages, should be humbled by God. For they fell against the will of the Only-begotten, not fearing God but also profaning his covenant. And he says 'men of blood' concerning those saying, 'His blood is upon us and upon our children,' being guilty of all the blood of the righteous poured out upon the earth. And they themselves are men of guile, always approaching the Savior and the saints deceitfully. He does not wish that for these, even for half of their days, they should overtake death. For after they turned away from the day consisting for themselves from the brightness of the true light, having conceived a day of illumination through mythical traditions, it is evil that in this their days be filled; he intercedes that, in the intervening of their days, lest they should reach even half of their days, the sun of righteousness should set for them, so that they might become in the day of the Lord. And regarding the word 'let him force such things'; since in life the impious, dwelling in unrepentant resolve, do many evils, fearing them, it is worthy that, as human life is in the middle, they snatch away life so that for a few sins and not many they might be punished. Of these, he says, not being divided, 'I lay my expectation and hope upon you, O Lord.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being trampled by men is set beside trampling the Son of God, and the enemy who wars daily crushes the righteous man's day of life without wanting peace.
comments.comment: The scripture arranges the idea of being trampled with contempt, just as it is said of the chaff on the threshing floor, 'They throw it out' (Psalm 56:1). To be trampled by men and concerning the one devaluing Christ, it has been written: 'How severe a punishment do you think the one who has trampled the Son of God will deserve?' (Hebrews 10:29). And the holy one, being devalued by a man through foolishness, according to the scripture 'Where is your jealousy and zeal among you, and do you walk according to man?' (1 Corinthians 3:3), deserves to be shown mercy by God. But this man is an unceasing, murderous enemy who crushes the day of life of the righteous by warring, not desiring to be peaceful in any measure. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flesh-minded man is an enemy to God and cannot please him, and he fears the man of the spirit.
comments.comment: Regarding the flesh, he says that the man who has the mindset of the flesh is an enemy to God, not being subject to the law of God. For he who becomes one in this flesh is not able to please God. He fears lest he who becomes one in the spirit should do to him, as having killed the works of the flesh; for he has not truly hoped in God (Psalm 56:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God saves the fallen freely, by grace and not by works.
comments.comment: God saves those who have fallen into wickedness freely, receiving nothing from them (Psalm 56:7). For he says, 'Behold, you were struck by your sins and you shall not be redeemed with silver' (Psalm 56:7), being saved not by works but by grace. Indeed, 'above nothing' signifies that they are not given salvation above anything else.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The living man makes his life known to God through disposition and practice.
comments.comment: The voice growing bold before God (Psalm 56:8). For the living one, not by sin but by God, through these works, makes his life manifest to God, announcing it through disposition and practice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praising God begins with a partial word and grows to the full discourse, as those who know in part now receive the perfect knowledge.
comments.comment:
The word brought forth upon God and through God is praiseworthy, likewise also the discourse. But he argues from a parallel against the same word and the discourse, or sets such comparisons one upon another. Since the word is a part of the discourse, the one being led into godliness, if perhaps unable to participate in the most full discourse, begins from a word, that is, a partial discourse. Care not; first the word of the Lord comes upon Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1-2), and after this, the discourse of the Lord comes to him; and in Isaiah, he says, 'Hear, O word of the Lord, you who tremble at his discourse' (Isaiah 66:5). But the word of the Lord is heard in the one occurring through him in the introduction. …

With much power, those who know and prophesy partially now receive a word toward the coming knowledge and teaching, as the perfect word is being given to them and the perfect knowledge is shining upon them as if the partial were being abolished. He who accepts both the introduction and the full bestowal of the word praises God with word and discourse (Psalm 56:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man may pray to do or render something to God, and he may also pray to praise God; these are prayers of praise.
comments.comment: He who prays does not stand in harmony with those to whom he is promised through prayer, but holds within himself the prayers of praise to render to God. And prayers of praise are those concerning praise; for just as someone prays to do or to render this or that to God, so someone prays to praise God (Psalm 56:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul snatched from the death of ignorance of God has its feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel and lifted above the earth, so that it pleases God and lives in the light.
comments.comment:
And since mourning and the falling of tears follow the one dying, no one mourns the one dead according to the soul except himself, fittingly after the soul has been snatched from the death of the intellect of ignorance concerning God and his eyes have been freed from tears. He snatched his feet from slipping, having shod them with a shoe that lifts up and makes them above the earth. For God says, 'I have shod you with hyacinth.' And the hyacinth, imitating the body of the heaven, shows the soul being colored with the heavenly, with a shoe not being any other than the preparation of the Gospel. Since the one shod is being lifted up, there follows the being snatched from slipping, concerning the feet being snatched from the matter (Psalm 56:13).

Someone is snatched from the aforementioned harmful things in order to please God, living and having been enlightened. For he who pleases God does this while living in light; and he lives and has been enlightened, everyone partaking of God; for he himself, being life, is the light of men, according to the scripture: 'And the life was the light of men' (John 1:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains being delivered from death to walk before God in the light of the living.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We need God's mercy both now and hereafter.
comments.comment: The doubling shows that both in this life and in the future we need the mercy of God (Ps 56:2a–c). And he calls the divine protection the shadow of wings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why mercy is asked twice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shadow of God's wings is this life's shelter on the way to the wings themselves, and lawlessness is shown to be temporary.
comments.comment:
The shadow is pre-ordained to distinguish itself from the truth; it means this: in this life, finding myself in the shadow of the wings, I hope to come upon those very wings, being carried on wings by virtue and spiritual intellect. But the wings of God are His sheltering powers, or the lofty thoughts about Him.

The passing away of lawlessness shows that it is temporary (Psalm 57:1). And Paul indeed writes in Hebrews that the enjoyment of sin is temporary (Hebrews 11:25). It is not as if lawlessness were passing away having begun from a certain time; for he says something about it: it shall be neither from the beginning nor unto the age (Ps 56:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He cries to the Most High to be lifted far from the harmful beast.
comments.comment: But the Most High is not in vain (Psalm 57:2). For since lawlessness is clinging and low-lying, the one being delivered from it cries out toward the Most High, so that by lifting himself up with the cry, he might become far from the harmful beast.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's sending from heaven is not a local descent but the Word of God becoming flesh and walking among men.
comments.comment: The Lord, sent from heaven to save, says: 'I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will' (John 6:38). For God sent this word of His and healed those wounded by their corruptions, as David himself says elsewhere. If anyone seeks to ask whether the one sent from heaven signifies a local emission from the physical heaven, it would seem absurd to attribute a local descent to God. For does the voice of heaven not signify the incorporeal and intellectual essence, according to 'Store up in the heavens' (Matt 6:20) and 'God is in the heaven above' (Psalm 115:3)? Therefore, the one being in the form of God … having taken the form of a servant, came to men (Phil 2:6-7). And this is the sending from heaven, so that the Word of God might become flesh and, having appeared upon the earth, might walk among men (John 1:14). Peter also writes, initiating mysteries concerning the Holy Spirit: 'Now it has been announced to you through those who preached to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven' (1 Peter 1:12)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'he shall send from heaven' means: the Word becoming flesh.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy and truth are not different in essence, for both are the Savior, who rescues the soul from enemies like wild and wrathful dogs.
comments.comment: In the preceding verse, having said, 'He sent from heaven' (Psalm 57:3), not having said what was sent from heaven, he now interprets what mercy is and truth, the one rescuing his soul having become among enemies of those who trampled; for these are wild and wrathful dogs. Mercy is not otherwise according to the essence of truth; for both are the Savior (Psalm 57:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sleep here means rest: troubled among enemies and dogs, he slept and cast the trouble away instead of lying awake in it.
comments.comment: Sleep often signifies rest, as in, 'In peace I will lie down and sleep.' He does not wish to say this, that is, even if I was troubled being trampled by enemies and terrified by the dogs having taken me in the midst, but the trouble did not remain. For I slept having been troubled, not remaining awake being troubled, but I slept having cast away the trouble (Psalm 57:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what lying down among enemies means: sleeping the trouble off in rest.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A bowed-down soul is like the woman Jesus freed from Satan's snares, and like all who think only of things below.
comments.comment: This is a symbol of the woman continually weakened by the spirit, collapsing and not able to rise up completely, whom Jesus released from the snares of Satan, the daughter of Abraham (Psalm 57:6). Perhaps also everyone who thinks of the things below has a soul having become fallen, not able to contemplate the things above, is such a thing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bowed-down soul by the woman Jesus released in the Gospel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Circumcised and repentant idolaters become one church.
comments.comment: And you will perceive the people and those from circumcision, but the mortals from the idols having repented, as to become one church (Psalm 57:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever does good may be said to set up a pillar as a sign of his struggles.
comments.comment: They say the law: 'You shall not make for yourself a pillar' (Deuteronomy 16:22), signifying that everyone who practices forbidden things raises up a life like a pillar. Therefore, one may also rightly say that the one doing good things is setting up a pillar, as a symbol of the contests through which he has struggled.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Injustice binds a man's sins in a knot, and iniquity worked in the heart is worked in the land, that is, in material things.
comments.comment: For such is the fruit of righteousness (Psalm 58:2), and in Proverbs: 'To perceive true justice and to direct judgment' (Proverbs 1:3). But injustice entangles, joining sin by acting without distinction in evil. This is equal to the binding of one's own sins in a knot. It is not in vain that you work iniquity in the land (Psalm 58:2); for if someone makes iniquity in the heart, he works it in the land, that is, concerning material things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what working iniquity in the heart and in the land means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A newborn infant is receptive in power to both virtue and wickedness and learns good and evil by what it meets.
comments.comment: Those daring to slander the Scriptures and dragging this word into error, saying that those who are led astray from the stomach and speak lies are not true, say that the fulfillment of the word is sinning. It is not right to say that those who have not perceived the habit of the Scripture have thought these things; the newborn infant is receptive to virtue and to wickedness in power, then receiving by operation whichever of these two it encounters, it will know good and evil. For then also the word is fulfilled, when it begins to act according to virtue. It is said that the good has been made from the mother's womb. Such is what Job says: 'Even if I ate my morsel alone and did not share with the orphan' (Job 31:17); for from the mother's womb they guided them and I nourished them as a father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The asp stops its ears so as not to hear the charmer, as these stop the ears of understanding so as not to hear the prophetic and apostolic words.
comments.comment: They say that the ears of an asp, the so-called 'palms,' stop up its ears. For if ever an incantator according to his own wisdom were to utter some incantation capable of lulling it to sleep, if it should hear, it stops up its ears so as not to hear the voice of the incantator, as if a medicine being prepared by a wise man. And these also stop up, not the ears of sense but the ears of understanding, lest they hear those who utter the wise prophetic and apostolic incantations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the deaf adder image: the asp stops its ears, and so do these in their understanding.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God breaks their molars as a benefactor, so that they cannot devour the men they have deceived and earn excessive punishment.
comments.comment:
And God does this to them as a benefactor, lest, devouring the men deceived by them, they become liable to excessive punishment, and so he crushed their molars, that they might neither bite nor devour.

And it should be noted that according to Scripture molars differ from teeth; for the cutting teeth divide the food, while the molars chew and grind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God breaking the teeth is a kindness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like water scattered in a channel they come to nothing, and God's bow and arrows are his judicial power, which weakens them for their good by destroying their strength for evil.
comments.comment:
And just as water passing through some channel, not remaining but being scattered, is brought to nothing and becomes contemptible, so also these shall be despised, having nothing firm and permanent but having received temporarily a watery and moist life. …

And we said before that his arrows signify his punishments, and the bow is that from which the arrows are sent; these are God's judicial power.

He stretches this bow, then, not slackening it until those struck grow weak; and their growing weak is for their good, since the strength they had concerning evil is being destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of water, bow and arrows: punishment that weakens them for their good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Punishment melts away the thickness of a wicked disposition as fire melts wax, but those who fall under it no longer see the sun of righteousness.
comments.comment:
And just as melting wax is destroyed insofar as it is meltable, having the thickness of the first subject changed into fire, so the worthless, having experienced punishment, melting, cast off the thickness from the wicked disposition.

But before punishment is the true light, which is the sun of righteousness; for after punishment it is not possible to approach the radiance of the intelligible sun.

Hence it is said here: when the punishing light fell, those who fell under punishment did not see the sun.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who understand their passions, the thorns, are spared punishing wrath, and those who do not are swallowed up by it, for to swallow up means to master and conquer.
comments.comment:
But those who have understood their own passions, more allegorically called thorns, shall not be tried by punishing wrath, but before understanding the thorns and bramble spoken of spiritually, as if living, they shall be swallowed up by wrath; for not living but being like the living, they shall be seized by wrath.

For 'to swallow up' according to Scripture signifies to master and conquer, with the one swallowed already mastered and conquered.

For the mortal is swallowed up by life, with life mastering and conquering death (2 Cor 5:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous rejoice by purifying their own deeds.
comments.comment: He does not rejoice exultantly, but, lest he himself be subject to punishment, he purifies his own deeds, becoming more secure (Psalm 58:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the righteous man rejoices when he sees vengeance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David prays to be rescued from the many enemies who stand behind the one Saul, wishing perhaps to give his own soul as a ransom for many.
comments.comment: When one Saul is pursuing him, he prays to be rescued from many enemies (Psalm 59:1). He prays not to be rescued from the spear-bearers sleeping with Saul, or from the predatory demons acting against him, saying 'many enemies' to be rescued from them. And he prays to be liberated from these rising up against him, wishing perhaps that the ransom of the one being liberated might be to give his own soul instead of many.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The workers of lawlessness are those who do what the law forbids, and the man under God's protection is rescued from them and from murderous men.
comments.comment: But workers of lawlessness are those doing what the law forbids, and since among the forbidden things is murder, men are men of blood, preferring to kill men because of the coming brutishness. But he who is not bothered by those working lawlessness is rescued, being under the protection of God, and also he who is not handed over into the hands of those willing to shed his blood is saved from murderous men.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the workers of lawlessness are and how one is rescued from them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He is also rescued from the disposition to lawless acts and from the devil and those with him who work lawlessness in men, as in Judas.
comments.comment:
And in another way: one is rescued from these; for he who does not work lawlessness but is disposed contrary to those doing it is rescued from the disposition of practical lawless acts, just as he who exists outside of murderous intent is saved, not being associated with murderous men.

The verses are to be interpreted thus: since men commit the work of lawlessness while the devil and his angels are working in men, he prays to be rescued from the devil and those with him who precede in the work of lawlessness. The testimony of this thought is: from the beginning the devil sins. For following that, others fall into sin in whom he works. Having cast betrayal into the heart of Judas, he became a traitor, following the thought of betrayal because of the one who incited him to this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blood of a man is poured out by one strong in evils, as Saul and his men sought David's soul, yet by God's power he would be saved.
comments.comment: And also to add 'men' to the murderers; for it is not by chance, but the blood of a man is poured out by one strong and perfect in evils. Regarding the intention and brutishness of Saul and those sent by him to take him from his own people and to kill him (Psalm 59:3), he says, 'They have sought my soul, though by the power of God I shall be saved,' by a paradoxical art of his wife.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David asks God to rise and help him, since their envy and not his sin roused them.
comments.comment:
