With the aforementioned enemies persisting in their zeal against me, having been roused, meet me to help me, no longer being patient with them.

And I beseech him, roused to meet me, to see that they do not murder against me on any pretext of mine, as though I had sinned against them.

For neither my iniquity nor my sin provoked them, but their envious passion, grieved at our good repute.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'without my fault' means: it was their envy, not his sin, that roused them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God of the powers and of Israel visits the nations to heal them of idolatry and demon-worship, sending the Word as physician of souls.
comments.comment: He is Lord, the God of the divine powers, but also the God of Israel, attending to visit the nations so that He might heal them as they are being badly consumed by idolatry and the service of demons. The visitation of the nations occurs because the divine Word has been sent to heal all and to save them from the corruptions that take hold beforehand. Indeed, He is a physician of souls, healing those who are crushed in heart. He is called God of powers and Lord of the rational, holy animals and heavenly hosts. Just as He is God of these powers, so also, by the voice of the discerning men called Hebrews of Israel, He is God (Psalm 59:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the visiting of the nations as a healing visit of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His prayer takes in all the nations as well.
comments.comment: With the prayer concerning himself he takes up together the petition concerning all the nations, being at once loving to men and a prophet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, anointed but not yet king, would not seize the kingdom by violence but waited to receive it from God.
comments.comment: While David was being pursued by Saul because of the aforementioned envy, he knew what the successor of the kingdom would be. And having prophetically seen what was to come, and having been anointed for this by Samuel—though he was not yet fully filled with the knowledge of it—he did not repeatedly rush into his hands, wanting to legally receive the kingdom from God, but not to seize it by assault and murder. From this intention he says, 'God is my strength, I will guard myself toward You' (Psalm 59:9), not intending to strike, but waiting to receive it from You; and I am confident in this assurance, having known through experience many times that You are both God and my perceiver. For it is not by our power that we are worthy to reign, but rather Your mercy, having foretold me, will show itself to me among my enemies, in which they shall be disciplined by falling under punishment, but I shall receive the kingdom from You.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why David says he will wait upon God for his strength.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David asks that his enemies be scattered rather than killed, so that they are punished moderately and may repent and be gathered again, and that their proud speech be stopped.
comments.comment:
As a matter of history: the enemies lying in wait are worthy to be rebuked by God, but not to die. For it is not right that, if they remained wicked, they should die, for they would bring an end to the divine law; but being scattered by the power of God and being handed over to captivity, …

For complete punishment prepares and turns one toward recognition. But David, sparing them from this, pleaded that they might be disciplined by a more moderate punishment so that they might be sober; he adds the following: for if they are scattered, they are punished at once, and they will be able to be gathered together again having repented. Likewise, He also wills that they be brought low, that is, humbled: to stop the sin of their mouth, the word of their lips, which is beneficial both to those being humbled and to the majority, so that they may not be provoked to zeal against those speaking and saying things in pride and unrighteousness. For those having spoken with pride, having lied against the righteous, receiving the condemnation in the pride of their own words contrary to their works, they receive it as if being caught as lawless men being reproved.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This verse answers those who think ill of the Creator: God's anger aims at salvation and mercy, so it is no passion.
comments.comment: It is to be reproved also from the present word those who think with a defensive mindset that the Creator is a heretic (Psalm 60:1). God is angry not to destroy, but to have mercy. By this, 'I will bless You, Lord, what You were angry with me for, toward salvation' (Psalm 60:1). For if He is angry toward salvation and toward mercy, His anger is not a passion, but is received usefully.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: For those who think earthly things stable, being shaken by God's mercy is useful, turning them from entanglement in material things to the Lord who heals.
comments.comment: Those striving for material things and thinking of earthly things (Psalm 60:2), regarding them as being stable and imperturbable, this such a state brings harm to them; it is better to be shaken and troubled by the mercy of God in a useful way. For having known that to be entangled in material things and to think of them causes trouble and shaking, turning away from the former bad life toward a serious one, without care and having been crushed, having received the realization of the existing destructions from the demons, she will call upon the Lord who is able to heal these things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's shaking of the earth can be a mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hard circumstances taken as a call to recognize former sins become the wine of compunction and lead to repentance.
comments.comment: Hard things are shown to someone if he falls into painful circumstances (Ps 59:5); but if anyone receives them toward the recognition of former sins, he drinks the wine of compunction, taking from the drinking the cause of being moved to repentance. Often the Scripture unreservedly calls the hard circumstances 'hard things'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hard things and the wine to drink mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'hard things' share a name with the 'hard ways' of virtue, but here they are the afflictions that test the people.
comments.comment: As in the Cup in the hand of the Lord, the mind is uncontrolled. But the hard things are homonymous with the hard ways spoken of; in the Psalm it says: 'Through the words of your lips I have kept hard ways' (Psalm 17:4). For indeed, hard ways are those called according to virtue because they are made straight through much sweat and toil, but here it is when the people, having been tested by hard things, are afflicted.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sign God gives is the illumination to discern spirits and good from evil.
comments.comment: What is the sign that God gives, which is the illumination by which it is possible to discern spirits and good and evil? For having this knowledge existing, we flee from the malicious, becoming far from the evil of work and the evil spirit. But the sign is given not to those who happen to be, but to the God-fearing pious.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the sign given to those who fear God is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those loved by God are saved by his right hand from unseen enemies, and once saved they ask for divine goods, the gifts of the Spirit.
comments.comment:
'That your beloveds, remaining unhurt, may be washed away from the face of the bow, you gave the said sign' (Psalm 60:4-5). It must be said also: then they will be washed away from unseen enemies, whom your only-begotten Son shall save with your right hand. For the right of God has been interpreted many times, especially where it was foretold: 'I have strengthened you with my right, just, and with my right I have established the heavens' (Isaiah 41:10).

One must supervise how the order of thought precedes the order of utterance. For previously, having heard, God saves, and thus the unharmonious harmony, the word having the sequence 'Save' then 'Hear my' after it, unless it is thought otherwise: 'Having saved by the right, hear my prayer,' the prayer of the one being saved is not about being saved (for that is what is said) but about asking for divine goods, for the gifts of the divine Spirit are such.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men made in God's image remain his beloved even when deeply fallen into sin.
comments.comment: But those who through goodness-and-beauty become gods' beloveds are worthy to be loved by him; men made according to the image of God, even if they have fallen most deeply into sin, yet they are nonetheless, because of the soul's spiritual and rational essence, his beloveds.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the beloved are, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God speaks to all who share in holiness, and Christ spoke in Paul and in every prophet, since the Father who abides in him does the works.
comments.comment:
God speaks to everyone participating in holiness.

Indeed, Christ spoke also in the holy Paul and in every prophet. But if the voice is seized regarding the Father, the holy one in whom the Savior speaks is he who is in agreement with the one: 'The Father who abides in me does the works,' and 'The Father has given me a commandment, what I must say and what I shall speak'; these things fit the economy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one praying from the ends of the earth knows God is above in honor and essence, and the man below in the earth, having come from non-being into being.
comments.comment: He who prays here, knowing himself to be far off, sends up his prayer from the ends of the earth and says that he has cried out to God in his distress; for as it is said in Ecclesiastes: 'God is in the heaven above and you are in the earth below.' And it is signified by the word not a local distinction but a difference of uncreated essence and created things, of the existence of God being said to be above in heaven through the superiority of honor, and of the man being below in the earth by having come from non-being into being.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what praying from the end of the earth means: man below, God above.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Rock is Christ, the spiritual drink, who lifts up and guides those who follow him, and he is a tower of strength against the enemy.
comments.comment: We shall accept 'Rock' to signify the Christ, the flowing spiritual drink. He who becomes in this rock to partake of it (for wisdom and righteousness and holiness exist) is lifted up according to the mind, being raised by God. And those intending to fall toward the Savior, according to his exhortations saying, 'Come after me,' and again to Philip, 'Follow me,' using him as a guide, partake of that same lifting up, not hoping to find any other leader of the way which rushes toward the cause of all. Having obtained this gift, David also says with his mouth to the Lord: 'You have guided me to what became my hope'; and not only a guide but you have become a tower for me from the face of the enemy. For I remained unharmed, having you as a tower of strength and power, even though the enemy was an adversary and wished to fight me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rock higher than I and the tower as Christ who lifts and guards.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever begins to build the tower must finish it or be shamed.
comments.comment: He who begins to build this tower, as if starting with the foundation, should complete the building as if placing a crown upon the roof, lest he suffer shame before those passing by, who are accustomed to mocking those who have not completed the citizenship they undertook.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints' hope is the Savior, a tower of strength, and whoever dwells in his holy tabernacle for the ages is covered under the shelter of God's wings.
comments.comment: A connection can be made to 'Lead me from the face of the enemy' (Psalm 61:3) and 'You have led me in a straight path thus'; 'You have led me from the face of the enemy' has become my hope, but also a tower of strength in leading me from the face of the enemy. The hope of the saints is the true and unshakeable Savior, as Paul says, 'Jesus Christ of our hope' (1 Tim 1:1), and the prophecy upon him is that they hope in him; for he himself, having been foretold, shall be the expectation of the Nations. Someone, having been perfected in holiness for the ages in that dwelling, signifies 'Who shall dwell in your holy habitation?' (Psalm 61:4); for this is the same eternal one in the tabernacle, the Lord, and not man. Although such a tabernacle does not possess the perfection of the Holy of Holies, there is no state with it surpassing the rational ones in which they shall be in Father and Son, but rather in the Trinity. Therefore, it is said to dwell for the ages, but not to reside in the dwelling. He who has become in this dwelling shall be covered under the shelter of the wings of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God freely gives perfect men the inheritance of his sons, and what is given to those who fear his name is given much more to those who have ascended above.
comments.comment: For he says, 'You are very rich, and you provide great gifts' (Psalm 61:5), rather, by freely giving to perfect men the becoming of your sons, you have given them an inheritance. For although it is expected to be given according to the resurrection in the future age, it is nonetheless being given in a favorable way to those who are being led according to the time what is necessary. And to those who fear his name, God has given an inheritance (Psalm 61:5). If there is a difference between those fearing God and his name, and those believing in him and in his name—since it is often said that those made intimate by the approach of God, those united to him, the God, are inferior—it is seen that the inheritance is given also to those fearing God; for if grace has been increased to the inferior, much more to those who have ascended far above. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Reigning with the Lord is added day by day, so that the eternal things are fulfilled and life is extended as generations before God.
comments.comment: … By this signified thing to reign, and the apostles, expecting, say to the Corinthians, 'You reigned without us, let us also reign with you.' To the reigning which has happened, there is added by the Lord, 'day by day occurring.' For it is necessary from a preceding state of light to a transition into another likewise, so that the eternal things, concerning which it is said, 'And I remembered the eternal and meditated upon them' (Psalm 77:5), might be fulfilled from that which is named of the days. And the life of the days is extended by taking them day by day, as generations of generations before God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy is joined to his truth because weak men cannot know his truth clearly unless his mercy first saves them.
comments.comment: Who will seek out His mercy and truth? Often, of the divine teachings, His mercy is joined with the truth of God. For since to know clearly and purely the truth of God is not possible for one surrounded by human weakness, from this there is a need of the mercy of God in order to understand the truth. This contributes to the fore-set purpose, that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. For first, it is necessary to be saved by the mercy of God, so that subsequently the knowledge of the truth may exist. For the salvation of men is the work of the mercy of God. 'For God sent His mercy and His truth,' and the following.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why mercy is named with truth: mercy saves first, so that the truth can be known.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The singer will praise God's name through works, thoughts and good words, repaying his vows day by day as Jacob vowed to tithe to God.
comments.comment: Since in whom I have found a thankful reception from You, I will sing in Your name, praising through works, thoughts, and good words the prophecy of You called upon me (Psalm 61:8; LXX 60:8); and with this I will repay day by day, just as Jacob says, 'If God gives me bread to eat,' and the following, 'all things to me shall be mine if I tithe them to You' (Gen 28:20-22). For before these words it is brought forward, 'Jacob made a vow,' saying, 'If the Lord be with me,' as 'I will tithe them.' And also to say 'repaying prayers day by day' and 'singing in the name of God unto the age of ages,' for the one singing in the name is the one being praised, to extend into the coming age; but the one repaying the prayers, it is as if the time being fulfilled of the days is being completed; it is not that which is delayed by each individual's life. Since we are not in this life, we shall repay the prayers, so that we also may sing unto the age of ages in the name of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who fall from virtue to vice are first shaken in their thoughts through the passions, and a pious thought must intervene to prevent a greater shaking.
comments.comment:
Everyone shifting from virtue into vice is shaken (Psalm 62:2), but this does not happen abruptly; a disturbance first occurs in the thoughts through the passions, so that if appropriate action is taken, the shaken thoughts do not become a collapse and a fall.

For when an ugly desire or some other irrational movement begins, the pious thought must intervene, grasping God, to direct the impulse toward action, so that a greater shaking does not occur. The Savior clearly teaches this in the Gospel, uprooting the beginnings of sins so that their remaining does not result in a greater practical shaking.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a person comes to be moved, and how to stop it early.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man rooted in love is an unshakable wall with a hedge of guarding angels, true teachings and virtuous actions, but bad fruit lets God remove it.
comments.comment: He who is established and rooted in love is an unshakable wall and has a firmly set hedge (Psalm 62:3); how then could those passing by the way, wicked men and evil powers, not strike it? God surrounds him with such a secure hedge, saying, 'I have plowed and set a hedge.' For this hedge consists of angels guarding, and of truths of dogmas, and of actions being performed according to virtue. While this remains, no one will be able to harm the divine fruits of the spiritual plant. But if the one guarding the vineyard should ever bring forth thorns instead of grapes, God, abandoning him, says, 'I will take away his hedge and it shall be for plunder, and I will pull down his wall and it shall be for trampling.' If this happens because of the production of bad fruit from us, the wall is leaned and the hedge is pushed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wall and the hedge through the Gospel image of the vineyard.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The honor the wicked plot to cast away is virtue and piety; since deceivers cannot draw one into vice by force, they flatter, blessing with the mouth while cursing in the heart.
comments.comment:
The honor of the wise, which the wicked plot to cast away, is virtue and piety (Psalm 62:4), according to 'Glory and honor and peace to everyone working the good' (1 Clem 1:1). Therefore, vice is a dishonor, in which those who have fallen, feeling they have suffered, say, 'Our dishonor has uncovered us unto tribulation' (Psalm 62:4). To this, man also takes part, not understanding the value of being in honor. Since the deceivers lying in wait cannot draw one into vice by force, they say, 'They did not drive away my honor, but they plotted to cast it away'; for they are not those who can overcome the one standing strongly against them. Related to these are those about whom Paul writes, 'Deceiving through flattering speech and lying words the hearts of the innocent' (Romans 16:18).

It is of the same mind: 'If your enemy entreats you with a great voice, do not be persuaded Ps 61:7; for seven evils are in his soul, perhaps coming from the seven spirits, as the unclean spirit receives from more evil spirits than himself.' … for blessing with the mouth, he curses the heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the excellency they plot to cast down is, and why they bless and curse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Salvation and glory rest on God alone, not on the speaker's own power or art, and he hopes in the one who has often saved him even when thrust back into error.
comments.comment: I will not repent, becoming a repentant one by sinning and being distanced from God Ps 61:8, according to what is written concerning Jacob, who was overwhelmed and turned away from God his savior. Grasping God, I have not become a repentant one, they attain salvation and glory upon God; for I was not saved by my own power or art. And he says 'glory upon God' because it is that which the only God gives to those seeking him, and 'salvation' not of the flesh but of the rational soul, which the one having believed into the Trinity possesses, according to what is said, 'Finishing the faith, the salvation of souls.' Therefore, even if he is violently thrust back into error, I make hope upon him, who has often saved me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peoples who believe are told to pour out their hearts before God, which means to love him with the whole soul and heart, for 'pour out' often means rich abundance.
comments.comment: All the assemblies of the peoples of the nations who have believed Ps 61:9, who no longer have God and hope, hope in him against all craftiness, making your hearts manifest before him; for God will become a helper to you. The same is meant by to pour out before him the heart, to love him from the whole soul and the whole heart. For often to pour out has been arranged instead of a rich abundance and a lavish supply, as in 'the love of God is poured out in the hearts of you through the Holy Spirit' Rom 5:5.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what pouring out the heart before God means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Justice is wanted in every dealing, and those who run together toward vanity strive in vain.
comments.comment: To such people it was said Ps 61:10, 'Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood, even though you are commanded not to have a small and a great weight, but a true scale, since a double weight is an abomination to the Lord.' It must be said whether these things are intended, and also toward those who have dealings and fellowship; for in every matter, justice is desired; for those running together toward vanity vainly strive, always having a vain agreement and zeal. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One cannot hope in injustice and in God, and the heart should not grieve if honest wealth flows away.
comments.comment: For it is not possible to serve God and mammon, nor indeed to hope for injustice and God (Matthew 6:24). If it seems that the wealth of one who does not seize and does not act unjustly is flowing and diminishing, it is not necessary to add to the heart, so that the heart might not be grieved by the diminishing of the money.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'trust not in oppression' and 'set not your heart upon' riches in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, who is simple, speaks once and all at once, but we hear doubly, as we hear his command on sacrifice or circumcision both bodily and spiritually.
comments.comment:
God is incorporeal, rather existing beyond all generated being, both material and intellectual, having nothing entangled with himself; thus, when God speaks, He speaks once, that is, monoidly and uncomposedly, not as I hear Him thus anymore. For what is spoken once, you hear as two, according to the manifestation; for this voice is a pointing voice. …

And it must be said otherwise: we use vocal organs, and we are unable to say many things at once. Of God, speaking once and all at once, we hear doubly. Stop, lest it be possible to say a third. Of God, commanding once concerning sacrifice, we hear the command both sensuously and spiritually.

Just as we understand circumcision in two ways, once spoken by God: the bodily and the spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God speaks once and the psalmist hears twice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's rendering to each according to his works is measured by quality, not quantity: the reward of the righteous exceeds their works and the punishment is lessened.
comments.comment: It is necessary to seek how he gives to each according to his works. For if the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that is about to be revealed (Rom 8:18), and he who has worked only trifles is not punished worthily. For if one observes iniquities, 'Lord, Lord, who will endure?' (Psalm 130:3), how must one take judgment by equality? One must oversee lest it becomes not according to quantity but according to quality; and quantity is indicated by the word, the greater things of value being given praiseworthily to the righteous and the punishment being diminished. For equality is not according to corrective justice, but according to distributive justice, the equal and the unequal.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Calling out to God at dawn does not mean going to him in a place, for God is not in a place, and only the saint can say to him, 'God, the God of mine.'
comments.comment: … This is accomplished for the one who has come out of ignorance and malice, as 'The night has passed, and the day has approached' (Romans 13:12). To this, 'Out of the night my spirit watches for you, O God' (Isaiah 26:9) is conjoined. But if someone does the works of the night and darkness, how can he say 'I watch at dawn' without the dawn standing before him? And 'I watch toward you' is not to be heard locally. For God is not in a place, but in a disposition, becoming a relationship toward God by having leaped over the sensible things; for to this follows coming toward God. And also the saying, 'God, the God of mine.' For the God of the saints worshipping him is God once and for all, not of all those who have the 'is', but of some who have been set free. Therefore, the belly of those having desire for luxury is not simply called God; nor even the demons are strictly gods of the Gentiles, though called gods. God alone, and every truly wise man will say by nature and truly to God, 'God, the God of mine.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the early seeking and the phrase 'my God' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'desert' and 'waterless' land is a person who lacks knowledge and the Spirit only in small measure, or one free of wickedness and the moisture of the passions, where no evil spirit finds a place.
comments.comment:
And indeed the place concerning the earth is not made manifest through the word 'desert' by means of perfection, nor 'waterless' by the not having abundantly the gifts of the Spirit. As in 'Rivers of living water were said to flow out of the spring of the one having believed' (John 7:38); therefore also it is uninhabitable, of no one passing over it, of those imitating God as much as possible. For how could the interpreted place not be desert by reason of the lack of knowledge in it, and waterless by the becoming of the pledge of the Spirit in it? For it is not desert and waterless by a complete deprivation of those dwelling and treading, and water is said, but because these things happen in it sparsely and briefly.

And it must also be understood otherwise: the one outside of wickedness and ignorance is a desert of these things, and the one who is also outside the moisture of the passions is waterless, just as being uninhabitable means being manifest to the evil, because a place of the devil or of some other evil spirit is not found in him. Never will the unclean spirit permit itself to approach such waterless places; it passes through them without finding rest among them …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm can be heard of a soul that thirsts for God while the flesh, drawn to the passions, is weak.
comments.comment:
Someone happens to see the vision in a desert, interpreted on both sides as an inaccessible and waterless land, while a soul thirsts in holy desire for God, with the flesh also following as much as is possible.

And another scripture is brought forward, 'And my flesh was weakened,' concerning which it must be said thus: not that my soul thirsts for God, but the flesh, enjoying thickness, being composed of shameful desires and other passions. To this, one should take the evangelical saying: 'The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak' (Matt 26:41).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A desert land is a virtue in which no deceiving desires dwell, so the devil finds no rest there.
comments.comment: … and David says, 'In a desert land and uncultivated and waterless, so I appeared to you in holiness' (Psalm 63:1). A desert land is therefore the virtue which does not have the old men dwelling in it, those decaying according to the desires of deception; therefore the devil does not even find rest in it, if he passes through waterless places seeking rest and does not find it; for he himself is king of all those in the waters.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'dry and thirsty land' as a soul where the devil finds no rest.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The Son is the Father's power and glory, shown in his healing works and in the glory he had with the Father before the world.
comments.comment:
… And if the Father is the one who does not thirst, the only-begotten is His power and glory. For Christ is the power of God, He himself being also the glory concerning whom it is said, 'The glory of the Lord shall be seen' (Isa 60:1). And if the Son is His glory and power, the theology concerning Him and the performing of wondrous works exists according to that which is written in the Gospel, 'Power went out from him and healed all' (Luke 6:19), and again, 'And the power of God for the healing of him' (Acts 10:38).

Correspondingly, with this power and also the things concerning His glory were taken from Him, as in 'We have seen His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten' (John 1:14), and 'Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world was' (John 17:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy is greater than both the present life and the life to come, because one is brought into those lives by God's goodness and not by the merit of works.
comments.comment:
The apostle has written that piety is useful for everything, possessing the promise of life, both of the present and of the one to come (1 Tim 4:8). Regarding the present, he does not speak of the common life of living creatures, but of that which exists in life, concerning which the Savior says, 'He who believes in me has eternal life, and this is eternal life, that he may know you, the only true God, and whom you have sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3).

Of this present life and of the one to come, whoever becomes according to perfection, those who approach the truth face to face, the mercy of God is greater, for through it and by it one becomes in these lives, being lifted up into them. For one does not come to live both lives according to the merit of works and contemplation, but by the goodness and mercy of God.

And it is said that mercy is better than them as the cause of the agent. See then, lest the mercy spoken of here be something other than the Word of God, concerning which it is written, 'God has sent His mercy and His truth' (Psalm 57:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist says God's lovingkindness is better than life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind that has tasted the divine banquet is filled in soul, not in body, and never stops desiring, and it praises God with lips of gladness.
comments.comment:
The mind is the true vine and the true drinking of wisdom. For having been called to partake of the table prepared by wisdom, having slaughtered her own victims and having mixed her own wine, the mind, being filled with the desire of the divine banquet and expecting to be filled, says: 'Oh that my soul might be filled with satiety and drinkability' (Ps 63:5). And since, always partaking of this liturgy, it hungers because the desire of the mind is insatiable, it says 'Oh that it might be filled' and yet 'my soul has not been filled,' even though it has abundantly partaken of the food and the drink.

Let those who, after the resurrection, dream of sensible food and drink be put to shame. For it is not the flesh or the body, but the soul that is to be filled with satiety and drinkability, the desire of the soul being filled with God in good things, as it is said in another psalm. And having been filled with gladness, it rejoices gratefully toward the one who has desired the food, saying: 'And lips of gladness shall praise your name' (Psalm 63:5), concerning which it is said: 'My lips shall praise you' (Psalm 63:3). And virtue is the lips of gladness. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the satisfaction and joyful lips of the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Following behind God is a journey whose end is union with him, and the soul that has cleaved to him is held by his right hand.
comments.comment:
… Just as for the one running toward virtue and piety to reach the goal, it is said: 'I have finished the race' (2 Tim 4:7), and 'I have run without law and have directed my course' (Gal 5:4) (for the one who finished is the one who ran the race), so does the one following God, according to Jeremiah: 'But I have not been weary in following behind you' (Jeremiah 17:16), and according to Hosea: 'I will go after the Lord' (Hosea 11:10), and as Moses says: 'You shall go after the Lord your God' (Deuteronomy 13:4); let him finish at last the journey after God, having reached the goal of blessedness.

… Regarding this state, having arrived after traveling behind, as if to be joined behind, he says, 'My soul has cleaved behind you,' (Ps 63:8) signifying the voice of 'It has cleaved' is 'It has been united.' For it is not to be heard that those shunning the evil are being joined to the good. He shows union towards God, and 'He who is joined to the Lord is in the spirit.' … For the end of traveling behind the Lord is the joining of the soul of the one traveling behind him; however, even if reaching union behind is also an end of a journey, there is nothing more perfect than the joining to the Lord in the spirit to become with him.

As he receives the things of the vision, he confesses that his soul has been cleaved behind God, grasping the right hand of God. And this is the only-begotten power of God …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul's clinging to God after him is not a bodily going, since God is greater than every place and nothing contains him.
comments.comment: But neither shall we ask anyone, as though God were in a place, and say: “How are we to go to him?” For God is greater than every place and contains all things whatever, and there is nothing that contains God. So the command given us, “You shall walk after the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 13:4), does not tell us to go to God in a bodily way; nor is it in a bodily way that the prophet, who clung to God, says in his prayer: “My soul has clung close after you” (Psalm 63:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to follow or cling to God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wicked who enter the lowest parts of the earth do so in the sense of the soul that thinks only earthly things, not under this earth.
comments.comment: … The sinning soul, under the influence of earthly passions, happens to bear the image of the swine and, being entirely earthly in its thinking, is described as such; for it is said concerning the wicked, 'They shall enter into the lowest parts of the earth' (Psalm 63:9), not of this earth, but of that which is understood tropologically, according to which it is said concerning certain things, 'And you have sunk down into the seat', and, 'You stretched out your right hand and the earth devoured them' (Exodus 15:12), and not having been placed under the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Held by the mighty hand of God, the psalmist cannot be snatched away by his enemies, and those who sink to the earth by their own choice are given over to punishment.
comments.comment:
… the nearby visible and invisible enemies sought in vain the soul of him saying these things, unable to snatch away the one being guarded by the mighty hand of God (Psalm 63:9-10). 'Let the sinners be turned away into Sheol, all the Gentiles who forget God' (Psalm 9:17) is in agreement with the entering of the wicked into the lowest parts of the earth. And having entered, they shall be delivered to punishment, the sword being signified by the name. The hands of this sword, or rather, it works pains and bitterness to those serving it, being called vessels of wrath in others. And it calls the evil powers a 'fox-catcher,' because of the cunning, deceitful, and malicious nature of those called fox-catchers.

And the present things are to be interpreted otherwise: since it is commanded to become material and fleshly such a one, you will say he has sunk himself down to the earth as if to have entered into its lowest parts by choice. And those who are delivered to dishonorable sufferings undergo this, having desired it with the desires of their hearts toward impurity. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Pharaoh and his men were swallowed, in the historical sense, under the depths, and given over to the devil's swords to become portions of foxes.
comments.comment: In the same manner, both Pharaoh and those around him were swallowed up under the earth, and Moses, as in a triumphal hymn Ps 118:12b: 'Stretch out your right hand, O God', says the earth swallowed them. And indeed, in the historical sense, they were not swallowed under the earth, but under the depths; those having been swallowed thus under the earth and having descended into the lowest parts of the earth, they were delivered into the hands of the devil's swords, allegorically so-called. And his hands are either his angels or his skillful actions. They, having been delivered thus, shall become portions of foxes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives courage to the one praying, who asks to be kept unharmed from two armies of the wicked, those who corrupt teaching and those who do wrong.
comments.comment:
… God works fear, not necessarily overturning or casting down the opponent, but granting courage to the one praying. …

… Regarding the double harm of evil, both in thought and in deed, there are two phalanxes attacking the righteous, from whom the one praying asks God to be saved unharmed from the things set before him, saying, "Protect me from the distortion of the truth of the dogmas" (for they are those wishing to corrupt the truth of the dogmas), but also from those performing practical injustice and wishing to drag me into it. For both these camps have sharpened their tongues like swords, as if having a word, the ones committing adultery gathering together with a pseudonymous knowledge, and the others with practical wickedness. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God warns those who fear him to flee the bow, while the wicked boast that no one can grasp their polished teaching and hide their snares in their narratives.
comments.comment:
… Moreover, even if they are not prepared wickedly, the benefactor God gives signs to those fearing him to flee from the face of the bow. … It is said that finding a bitter thing (and such is every evil and impious dogma), they, having aimed this, shoot the bow from it, having an analogy of arrows to the burning arrows of the enemy.

… And the heterodox say that no one is able to grasp their embellished and sophistically-made teaching. …

… When the wicked are failing, you will search; you will search out because they have searched out lawlessness very much, so as to strengthen an evil word for themselves and to hide snares in their narratives, which they have striven to produce with much elegance and take pride in as if they were unassailable words, so that no one may see them. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man of deep understanding comes to expose the deception, as Paul did with Elymas and Moses with the sorcerers of Egypt, and God is exalted through him.
comments.comment: To expose the deception, a true man comes to them, preserving the image and the being, being a learned person with a deep heart—that is, possessing deep understanding—as one who exalts God by seizing the wise in their craftiness. Likewise, through the Apostle Paul, He revealed the guile and craftiness of Elymas the sorcerer (Acts 13:6-12). For how will not God be exalted through holy men, as the error of the deceivers is being loosed? The pharmacists and flatterers of Egypt thought much of sorcery and sophistry, but Moses, the theophany of God, possessing in himself a deep heart, having approached, overturned the deception upon which they thought much. And thus God was exalted, being remembered by all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'deep heart' as deep understanding that exposes deceit, with examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Stephen laughed at the slanderers' arrows because whatever the slanderer shoots cannot wound the worker of truth.
comments.comment: He laughed when he saw the slanderers circling him; and seeing the false witnesses standing by, he said these words to himself from David’s songs to the harp: “Their blows have become children’s arrows” (Psalm 64:7). For whatever the slanderer shoots, the worker of truth is not wounded; whatever arrows the evil one lets fly are set in motion and sent in vain. For he does not pierce the upright, does not strike the guileless, does not bite the innocent.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The arrows of the wicked do not wound the prudent, their words grow weak, and those who watched them learn that God is maker and provider.
comments.comment:
And he who possesses this deep understanding receives it from the Spirit who searches all things. Just as the arrows sent of the prudent do not strike even to a speck, wounding anything (Psalm 64:7-9), so also the capture has left a bitter thing upon the prepared sophists, their matter being overturned; and their tongues grew weak, that is, their words, as if they were unable to strike even in quantity the door of faith being taken up. The men, observing the things foretold, having formerly testified to their own skill, were troubled, no longer remaining in the false opinions of the sophists, having received fear because of being associated with such impious doctrines.

For having learned from them that providence is not, that all things are carried by necessity, and having been snatched away along with other deceivers, they received both naturally good and bad men, and added that fate is presiding. These false opinions being shaken, they were troubled, and they revealed the truth: that God is the maker of all things and the provider. For they reported the works of providence and understood His creatures, and they came to know the one who provides, having observed the Creator in proportion to their greatness and beauty.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous rejoice when error is exposed and those who wandered now announce God's works.
comments.comment: When the error is being reproved, the righteous man will rejoice in God (Psalm 64:10), seeing the men who formerly wandered now announcing the works of God and having understanding of His works. And because of this, he will much more hope in the Lord …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the righteous are glad, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm stands for practical life and the hymn for contemplation of God, and in Zion the hymn is offered first and the prayer of thanksgiving follows.
comments.comment:
… it was said previously that the psalm denotes practice, while the hymn denotes contemplation. The practical life, being perfected by the contemplative life, demonstrates a perfect man.

From the spoken word one must move toward the church's understanding. Because of the aim of the truth, being called Zion, hymn and prayer are appropriately offered to the Source of all things. The hymn signifies the contemplation of God and of the truth, and the prayer signifies thanksgiving. Therefore, let him who is giving thanks in everything in Zion do this, beginning from the hymn; the prayer gives its due.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the praise and the vow of the verse as hymn and thanksgiving.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All flesh comes to God as the Gentiles come from the ends of the earth and as the well-disposed soul is drawn by the law written on the heart, not on stone.
comments.comment: … All flesh comes to God, the Gentiles having the power to come from the ends of the earth toward you, and all the Gentiles whom you made are before you (Psalm 65:2). It is also to be understood that all flesh comes to God, the soul that is well-disposed being drawn toward the easiest path by divine law and the truth; as it is signified, it has been said that the spiritual law is written on the heart, not on stone. This is also presented from the prophecy of Ezekiel, God saying concerning the hard-hearted, spoken in foolishness: I will remove from them the stony hearts and I will put in them hearts of flesh, so that they may walk according to my commands (Ezekiel 36:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'all flesh' is and how they come.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'All flesh' here means men, the rational humanity that is made worthy of the gift of the Holy Spirit and stands in awe before the Lord.
comments.comment: But there is also when only men are revealed by the designation of flesh, as in: 'Hearken to prayer, to you all flesh shall come' (Psalm 65:2). And it comes to God in relation and disposition, not the irrational, but the humanity, being made worthy of the bountiful gift of the Holy Spirit by the one saying: 'I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy' (Joel 2:28). … This so-called flesh, being rational, is receptive of divine awe; for indeed, 'to stand in awe from the face' of the one appearing to it is commanded …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one chosen by God is relocated from the earth to dwell in his courts, and being chosen and then received by the one who chose is the most perfect state.
comments.comment:
… the one chosen by holiness, if he remains in the election, is received by God, as having been relocated by him from the place of the earth to dwell in the courts of the chosen one, concerning whom it has been said: Enter into his courts with hymns; and one having desire from there places it upon him, and my soul is enclosed in the courts of the Lord (Psalm 65:4). And since the end of blessedness is not in the courts, he who is received there dwells, so as to progress and having come to the home, he may dwell being blessed; for he says, Blessed are those who dwell in your house, they shall praise you forever and ever (Ps 84:4).

What is more perfect than to be chosen and then to be received by the one who chose? It is evident from: 'In your counsel you guided me and received me with glory' (Psalm 73:24). For the one chosen does all things according to the will of God, and then receives the promises with glory. These words are brought forth by those who, having been delivered from life, give glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the blessedness of being chosen and brought near.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's house is the living church, from which the gifts of the Spirit come, and the believer filled with them becomes a holy temple in whom the Lord dwells.
comments.comment:
Paul, sending the church of God to Timothy, calls it: 'If you delay, see how you ought to conduct yourself in the household of God, which is the living church of God' (1 Tim 3:15). From this household come the good gifts of the Spirit, as well as the things concerning the Trinity and the rest of the doctrines, which are the statutes and canons handed down by the apostles. …

Virtue, signified by the name of righteousness, is marvelously fulfilled in Him. The one believing and working good things, having been filled, has the Lord within himself; for it is said through faith that Christ dwells in the inner man. Thus the Lord, coming to the one keeping His word, makes a dwelling for Himself, so that the man is a holy temple; for it is written, 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (1 Cor 3:16) and also, 'For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple' (1 Cor 3:17). It is also marvelous, and he is made upright in righteousness through the standing of Jesus Christ, full of the good divine gifts of the Spirit, of which those expecting to share say, 'We shall be filled.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peoples at the borders were afraid because the signs wrought showed that God exists, abolishing charms and magic and leaving Satan powerless.
comments.comment: … For how could those dwelling at the borders not have been afraid and the Gentiles been stirred, when the charms were abolished, so that the prophetic demons could no longer boast, and with these magic and drugs were being abolished, and he, Satan himself, having the power of death, was being rendered powerless? For the signs that were accomplished were sufficient, showing that God exists. Knowing His divinity from the things happening, they know moreover how He also provides for the things in heaven, as the stars rise and set by His laws. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fear of those in the uttermost parts at God's signs.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The faithful of the nations, watching the stars rise and set, know the God who became man.
comments.comment: The sunrises are delights, and the sunsets are delights; the remaining faithful of the nations, having observed what he does—causing the sun, the moon, and the other stars to rise and to set—is the one who became man and freed them from deception and death (Psalm 65:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The river of God is the Word of God, full of the fullness of the divine, watering all rational creation and giving drink to those who cultivate the earth.
comments.comment:
The Word of God is a river of God, being life and a fountain itself. And perhaps, if it is toward God, a fountain exists; for it is said, 'From you is the fountain of life' (Ps 36:9). A river is then found which waters the rational creation. The impulses of this, that is, the partial teachings, gladden the city of God, that is, the church. And since the fullness of deity dwells in him, he is filled with waters, as it is said concerning him, 'We have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14).

Therefore, not only is the river full of these waters, watering all the rational creation, but it also has food being prepared from God, sowing the seed of Jesus, bearing fruit a hundredfold. From this river, the cultivators of the earth, upon which the spiritual plow has been cast, get drunk, drinking with joy, as the offspring of righteousness growing in it are being multiplied, concerning which it is said, 'Sow for yourselves for righteousness, reap for the fruit of life' (Hos 10:12); and 'Seek the Lord as he comes, let the offspring of righteousness come to you' (Hosea 10:12). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the river of God is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'river of God' full of waters is the Son, so his Spirit must be understood as life-giving water and drink.
comments.comment: Do not be surprised. For if he himself is “the river of God,” in the words of the Psalmist, the one “full of waters” (Psalm 65:9), the torrent of delight whom God the Father is said to give as drink to those who love him (Psalm 36:8), how could his Spirit not have to be understood as the life-giving drink and water? Since, then, we have been called into unity through the Spirit and have become one body with Christ, let us keep the bond of love unbroken (Ephesians 4:3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God waters the soul with spiritual rain, through the old law and then the new covenant, enriching it in knowledge and good works.
comments.comment: You visited the earth and watered it, you filled it to make it rich, giving spiritual rain; first through the old law and then through the new covenant, through which the allegorized earth (which is the soul of man) was made rich in every way and in all knowledge and good works, as God increases it (Psalm 65:9-10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the watering of the earth as God's care for the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rain from the clouds is the words of Scripture, and souls that open their eyes to knowledge are filled with the bread of the practical virtues.
comments.comment:
The clouds, according to what was said, 'And the clouds rained down righteousness,' cause the earth to rejoice, rising in the drops coming upon it (Psalm 65:12-13). These are the words and the meanings of the God-breathed writings.

It is possible to say that the rams are clothed in joy, as it is commonly said, 'The mountains shall be girded,' where the rams are the sheep and the joy is the clothing, while the girdle is the belt. All those bearing fruit of the aforementioned things, and the hollow souls—which we call hollows because they lack thought—are filled with that grain which someone makes into bread to be eaten, according to the command, 'Open your eyes and be filled with bread' (Proverbs 20:13); but it is not the eyes of the heart, but to open them so that they may receive the light of knowledge. For when this happens, the breads, which are the practical virtues, multiply, feeding the inner man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ, the judge of the hollows, became a grain of wheat that fell into the earth through the cross and made much fruit.
comments.comment: … 'I am the flower of the field, the judge of the hollows' (Song of Solomon 2:1). He means such a thing: I have become a flower of the field in the place of the earth called low, so that men may receive the beginning of fruit; and I have become a judge for the hollows (the souls in Hades), having taken up death. He who has become thus the judge of the hollows shall be a grain of wheat, as he himself says, 'Amen, amen I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls and dies, it remains alone; but if it falls and dies, it bears much fruit' (John 12:24). Because the grain, having fallen through the cross into the earth until it reached its heart, made more fruit, and in those places he has become a reason for the hollows to have a multitude of grain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because the devil is destroyed and the dead are raised, the whole earth is commanded to shout and sing to God, and the singer must make the praise fitting.
comments.comment:
… The shout is a voice of those having triumphed over those having been conquered, being sent up insignificantly so that the sound of the voice might be passed on to the utmost extent. For since, by the grace of God, through Jesus having tasted every death, the dead are raised, the devil having been destroyed—he who held the power of death—it is commanded not just a part of the earth but the whole earth to shout to God, as the righteous and unrighteous dead are being raised everywhere.

And regarding the resurrection of repentance, it is fitting for the whole earth to shout, the place being called the place of repentance for the men of the whole earth. … When the shout of the voice has occurred on behalf of those defeated, those having been freed from the enemies are commanded to confess to God the cause of the victory, praising Him and singing in His name; but not as they happened to be, but gloriously; for He says, 'He shall praise His glory.' And this happens when the one singing makes the praise a fitting practice; for it is fitting for the well-disposed to praise. Therefore, the unworthy is forbidden from doing this, as it is not beautiful for a beautiful mind to be in the mouth of a sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies of God lied, for the works of Jesus showed a power greater than any creature, yet they thought him a mere man.
comments.comment: It is not always necessary to take falsehood upon word and glory (Psalm 66:3; LXX 65:3). For the voice itself lies even regarding the protesting of the purpose. By this meaning, the enemies of God lied, even though they were not able to withstand Him in any measure. For through the multitude of divine works being done by Jesus, a divine power being manifested in the things occurring, the Jews, wishing to hate, thought Jesus to be a mere man and were lying, saying, 'By Beelzebul, ruler of the demons, He casts out the demons,' even though the works were demonstrating that these are greater than any created thing; therefore, for their understanding, the Savior said to them: 'Do not believe me; believe the works, so that you may know what I am in the Father and the Father is in me.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the Savior came, worship in spirit and truth may be offered in any place, and not only in the temple at Jerusalem.
comments.comment:
With the Savior having arrived, the shadow of the Law finally took its leave (Ps 65:4); therefore, nothing is hastened to be performed in the temple in Jerusalem regarding the rites of God.

Worship, being done in spirit and truth, does not prevent a worshiper of God from doing this in any place. For they shall worship Him, and whoever does appropriate things for worshiping God from that place, for the word says: 'Worship Him and sing praises to Him' (Psalm 66:4). And they do this blamelessly, when Your presence is called upon them; for God has necessarily brought the 'Sing praises to Your name' (Psalm 66:4) to pass.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'all the earth shall worship' as worship in spirit and truth, not tied to one place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's works are done in faithful men by his will and not their own, and he turns the troubled sea into dry land so that they pass from wickedness to virtue.
comments.comment: Come, O lovers of learning, and see the works of God accomplished in faithful men, being carried out not by human will but by the will of God. For how is it possible to accomplish poverty and lack, unless the will of God is working them? And what God is He, who provides the power to endure these things? He, whose life is tossed and troubled, changed the unruffled into dry land, casting the word of fire upon the earth, all moisture drying up, so that those coming from wickedness into virtue and from unbelief into faith might have the sea turned into a path to walk upon. The symbol of this is iconographically depicted by the faith of the apostle Peter, walking upon the sea toward the Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sea and river are turned into dry land so that one may cross unhindered from wickedness to virtue, and God reigns over the age and delivers believers from it.
comments.comment:
But the river is the word, strengthened by Greek wisdom and art, blocking the way to the land leading to holiness. But He also turned this one, mocking the wise in their craftiness, and made a firm footing for those traveling toward holiness. And the things said against those who interrupt the divinity are a refutation. For no other god divided the Red Sea and performed the tremendous powers in the Gospels. For Jesus saved the people in Egypt, as it says in an apostolic epistle.

Having become by work and disposition, the sea and the river were turned into dry land so that one might cross as a path, traveling unhindered from wickedness and impiety toward virtue and piety. We rejoice in Him who made the difficult easy, God reigning kingly over the age and those in it, as He separates from the evil in it those who have believed, according to what was said: 'How He shall deliver us from the present evil age' (Galatians 1:4). And it is possible to take the age that is testing, from the spoken word, in agreement with the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crossing of the sea as the believer's passage from wickedness to virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fire is the soul's burning and water its drowning, and God helps the believer pass through both, as Isaiah says.
comments.comment: To burn and to move the soul hotly, it is called fire; but by another thought, it is called water because of its drowning and suffocating those who do not bear these things bravely. This, having been passed through by the cooperation of God, comes forth for the refreshment of life, hoping for rewards upon them. And since the beginnings and the progress belong to our practical efforts, while the ends belong to the gift of God—giving to themselves the passing through fire and water, while writing the cause of the end to God—what are the circumstances of fire and water? It is shown by the prophet Isaiah saying from the face of God: 'Fear not, for I am with you; and if you pass through fire, flame shall not burn you; and if you pass through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isa 43:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'fire and water' as trials the soul passes through with God's help.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Now one enters the church, God's house, offering perfect virtues as the burnt offering and paying the vows.
comments.comment: … 'I will enter into your house with burnt offerings, and I will pay my vows' (Psalm 66:13-14; LXX 65:13-14). Before the arrival of the Savior, the sacrifices according to the law were offered; but entering into the house of God (which is the church) spiritually, one performs perfect and complete virtues through burnt offerings, giving to this burnt offering compatible virtues and paying the vows his lips sent.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the burnt offerings and the house of God as spiritual in the church.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The incense is prayer, the rams the impulses of the soul's anger, the ox the body offered to God, and the goats the works and words of repentance.
comments.comment: The previously interpreted spiritual burnt offerings are found to be flourishing and marrow-filled, which are offered up not for the sake of another but for God. These things, indeed, are offered up in the manner that is necessary, with supplications; and this is signified by the very name of incense. 'Let my prayer be directed as incense before you' (Ps 141:2). And the offering is not made by incense alone, but also by rams. The rams are movements and impulses, having their origin from the irascible part of the soul. Along with the marrow-filled burnt offerings, of the incense and of the rams, he promises to offer up oxen with goats, with the one offering his own body as a living sacrifice to God perhaps ministering as an ox; for the animal is a tiller of the earth, whence it has an analogy to the body, which has its formation from earth. And the goats are the works and words of repentance; for the goat is offered concerning sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sacrificial animals as parts of the believer's spiritual offering.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whether God hears a person is a sign of whether iniquity is in his heart, since not knowing any fault in oneself does not prove one righteous.
comments.comment: It has become a matter of truth, he says: 'I do not know anything to myself, but not in this have I been justified.' For it enters into me, that I do not truly possess righteousness, and not because of this—that I have known nothing to myself of those things that harm—am I justified. And again the holy David says: 'If I saw iniquity in my heart, let not the Lord hear' (Psalm 66:18). A sign of having or not having iniquity is whether one is heard by God or not heard.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's condition for being heard.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Few can ask with the boldness of a pure heart, but David was heard because he saw no injustice in his heart, and he did not rely on this alone since Paul says one is not justified by it.
comments.comment: … Such boldness approaches one living a life beyond understanding; but such a person is rare; 'for who shall boast of having a pure heart?' (Proverbs 20:9); for few are those existing thus in virtue, as it is said: 'if I had seen injustice in my heart, Lord, do not listen to me; because of this, he listened to me' (Psalm 66:18-19), since he did not see injustice; but he desisted from fear that he might be judged according to the one saying: 'I do not know myself; but not in this am I justified' (1 Corinthians 4:4); he takes up what is set forth and also: 'if our heart does not condemn us, we have boldness toward God' (1 John 3:21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy did not depart from the speaker, not because he was sinless, but because he asked for good things and not only things pleasant to men.
comments.comment: This is what is taken by Paul: 'I do no favors to myself, but I am not justified by this; for God sees the injustice in me, and my heart does not perceive it.' To this, who will understand the transgressions? 'Cleanse me from my secret sins' (Psalm 66:20; LXX 65:20). This has happened to me, not so much because of my sinlessness, but because of His mercy, which did not depart from me, the divine mercy not withdrawing because of not asking good things, but things pleasant and sweet to men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm needs little interpretation, for it proclaims the Word becoming man, his saving appearance and the salvation of the Gentiles, and it is a hymn because the deeds are God's.
comments.comment: The Psalm (Psalm 67; LXX 66) is not in need of much interpretation because it has a clear mind. For it proclaims the becoming-man of the Word of God, and the saving appearance, and the salvation of all the Gentiles; 'Unto the end it is written.' And since the accomplished things are not human works, it is not written in panegyrics or praises, but in hymns; for to hymn is God's, but to panegyrize through praise is of men. …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what the whole psalm is about.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The face of God shines on us when the Word, the exact imprint of his being, becomes man, and those who see him with a pure mind see the Father.
comments.comment: Men are filled with mercies and blessings when the face of Him shines upon those wishing to experience this (Psalm 67:1). And the face of the Creator of all shines when the exact imprint of his hypostasis, having become man, arrives and manifests Himself to those worthy, as He says, 'I will manifest myself to him.' Since this exists, the one saying these things is an image of the invisible God; the one approaching Him with a pure mind sees the Father; for He says, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). In this way, the divine face having appeared, those being benefited are pitied and are blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for God's face to shine upon us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God's face has appeared the way to the Father is known, for Christ is the way, and it is made known among all the nations, with salvation in harmony with it.
comments.comment:
Your face having appeared, the way leading to You toward the Father is known (Psalm 67:2). And who is this who said, 'I am the way and no one comes to the Father except through me' (John 14:6)? …

The way of the Lord will be known among all the nations when all flesh is filled with the sight of the salvation of God. It is possible, when the way of God is made known in the land, to receive his commandments, according to 'I have run according to your commandments' (Psalm 119:32).

Salvation, being in harmony with this way, is what has come to be known by all the nations and is what has come to provide. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'way' and 'saving health' as Christ made known to all nations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Once the face of God has appeared, all the peoples are called to confess their sins to God and be forgiven, as the Hebrew people once did.
comments.comment: … in ancient times, a people of the Hebrews was confessing to the one saying to God, 'I am the one who blots out your sins; therefore first confess your sins (uttering them in a manner of repentance) so that you may be justified'—the holy one, bearing the face of this people, says, 'I made my lawlessness known and I did not cover my sin'. But since the arrival of the Savior, all the peoples from the believing nations, being fulfilled, are called to repentance in order to obtain the forgiveness of sins by having confessed to God. How then could it not be a willing following for all the peoples to confess, when the face of God has appeared to them?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the peoples' praise as confession that brings forgiveness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The nations rejoice, freed from evil and deceit, when they learn that the Lord judges peoples in uprightness, the peoples being the circumcision and the nations the Gentiles.
comments.comment: … when the way is known in the land and the salvation of God among all the nations, the nations rejoice, having been freed from all evil and the deceit of the many-minded, as they establish moral virtue, and they exult having received the knowledge of God, having learned how the Lord will judge peoples in uprightness and will guide the nations in the land. 'Peoples' and 'nations' are used in a parallel sense: the peoples are those of the circumcision, and the nations are those from the Gentiles.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the nations are glad and who 'peoples' and 'nations' are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The humans on earth are to be filled with praise and the fruit of piety, offering incense and pure sacrifice in every place.
comments.comment: … for how is it not destined that all the earth, that is, the humans upon it, should be filled with praise and bear the fruit of piety, in every place offering incense and pure sacrifice among the nations, as the name of the Lord is magnified, according to what is carried forth in one of the twelve prophets?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'Let God arise' are a prayer to the Father that the one who went down into death may rise, so that those gathered against him are scattered.
comments.comment: These things should be said in the manner of a prayer to the Father: that God—who descended into death because of Christ's suffering, while his body lay in the tomb being despoiled by the Jews, who were gathered together with those filled with deceitful demons and other evil powers—may rise up; for man has become one who has descended into death, so that those gathered against him might be scattered. For then even those who hate him, being unable to look upon him when he rises from the dead, will flee from his face (Psalm 68:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who rises in the verse and why his enemies flee.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Let him arise' and 'let them flee' are a prayer in the form of a command, and the scattered enemies are the impious, those who hate God and those who flee his face by wicked deeds.
comments.comment: … prayer is a word sent forth through imperative words; for instead of 'let him arise' (ἀνασταίη) and 'let them flee' (φύγοιεν), it was written (as 'let him arise' and 'let them flee' in the imperative). For this form is found most continuously in the Scriptures; I mean instead of what is said in a merely direct imperative way. It is possible to say that enemies will be scattered: those who are impious concerning the knowledge of truth, those who hate God, and those who flee from his face having practical wickedness. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sinners flee from God's face because they hate him, yet they are not utterly destroyed, while the righteous have a joy before God that is a fruit of the Spirit.
comments.comment: It must also be seen that the sinners are not utterly destroyed nor excluded from the presence of God, since, having become such, they flee from his face because they hate him, and the lawless do not remain before his eyes. There is a joy, according to which the righteous rejoice before God; joy is one of the fruits of the Spirit (Gal 5:22): love, joy, peace, and gladness, which is the flowing of the soul's thinking, rightly called well-being.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Smoke and melting wax show that the quality that makes a man a sinner is removed, while his essence is not destroyed.
comments.comment: A testimony of wickedness being smoke is this: just as a harmful path is called a way and smoke harms the eyes, so lawlessness, used by those, harms the powers of the soul in the same way, which are figuratively called teeth, cutting and devouring the spiritual foods, and also the thoughts of the soul, which are called the mind. It is to be understood that the melting wax does not destroy itself into nothingness from his presence, but its essence is given over to the fire. Thus, even if the quality by which someone is a sinner is removed, his essence remains incorruptible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one whose way is prepared brings Adam, cast out of the eastern paradise, back into it, as he promised the repentant thief.
comments.comment: Prepare the way for the one coming with the Lord's approach, according to Moses and the prophets, to mount upon enemies. Adam has been cast out from the paradise planted toward the east, to bring him again into the east, which even he has done, saying to the repentant thief, 'Today you shall be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is a father to those who leave their former father in wickedness, and his holy place is the church made holy by Christ.
comments.comment:
The Word gladdens those who are afflicted by Satan, exhorting them to rejoicings through the showing of their protector and helper, who is the father of orphans and judge of widows. Let there be a haste for you to rejoice before him, especially those having left the former father who begot according to wickedness and the first man living lawlessly with him; become orphans from him, for you shall have a father. But also the souls having separated themselves from the unlawful mixture will attempt to become slaves of the indwelling of God.

His holy place is found to be the church sanctified by Christ, which is each of the ones having believed…
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms who the fatherless are and what God's holy place is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God brings the dead out of their tombs, as Isaiah and the Gospel say, to a resurrection of life for those who did good and of judgment for those who did evil.
comments.comment: But also he brings out the dead from the tombs according to 'The dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised' (Isaiah 26:19); for the dew from you is life to them. This is like that in the Gospel, 'All those in the tombs shall hear his voice' (John 5:28), (meaning clearly the Son), and the ones having done good things shall go forth into a resurrection of life, but the ones having doing evil things into a resurrection of judgment.
comments.selected_reason: A clear reading of what bringing out the bound means, with Scripture cited.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Church is the one house in which, as the Psalm says, God makes the unanimous dwell, as the Passover lamb had to be eaten in one house.
comments.comment: Likewise, the sacred sign of the Passover in the law of Exodus contains nothing other than that the lamb, which is killed as a figure of Christ, is eaten in one house. God speaks, saying: "It will be eaten in one house; you will not throw the flesh outside the house" (Exodus 12:46). The flesh of Christ and the holy thing of the Lord cannot be thrown outside, and there is no other house for believers except the one Church. This house, this lodging of unanimity, the Holy Spirit designates and declares in the Psalms, saying: "God, who makes the unanimous dwell in a house" (Psalm 68:6). In the house of God, in the Church of Christ, the unanimous dwell, and the harmonious and simple persevere.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'house' as the one Church, with a clear Old Testament parallel.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: The shaking earth is the letter and shadow of the law, and the dew from heaven is the life-giving teaching of Moses and the prophets and later of the apostles and evangelists.
comments.comment: …as he passes through the desert in the church of the nations, the earth was shaken—that is, the letter and the shadow of the law—because it was not called thick. And the earthquake of this happened, the divine dew having poured down from the heavens according to the life-giving spirit of the divine writings. And the heavens shall be spoken of in these things, namely Moses and the prophets, or the mystical theorems; and heaven and clouds mean the same thing for this. Oh, indeed the heavens poured, but elsewhere the clouds rained down righteousness (Psalm 68:8-9).
