But also for the nations having been transferred from idolatry, the earth was shaken, while the spiritual dew-drops of the apostles, evangelists, and the rest of the teachers of the evangelical dispensation were remaining.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rain is the life-giving Spirit of the Lord, and the poor people from the nations who bless God are those once oppressed by Satan.
comments.comment: The spoken rain, having received the life-giving spirit of the Lord through weakness and desiring the cross, perfected the flesh, living by the power of God. For the divine Word gave life to his own body, having been crucified through weakness. And indeed the believer, a poor people from among the nations, is able to be, because God is, and without false hope. Concerning him the prophecy of Isaiah says: 'For this reason the poor people shall bless you, and cities of unjust men shall bless you' (Isaiah 25:3); for those being oppressed by Satan were acting unjustly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A message, however true and persuasive, does not reach the soul unless God also gives the speaker power, as the prophet says the Lord gives a word to those who bring good news with great power.
comments.comment: The divine word says that what is spoken, even if it is true in itself and most persuasive, is not enough to reach a human soul unless some power is also given from God to the speaker and grace blooms upon what is said; and this grace too does not come without God to those who speak to good effect. So the prophet says in the sixty-seventh Psalm (Psalm 68 in English Bibles): “The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power” (Psalm 68:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Lord giving the word means for those who preach.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Resting among the lots is resting between the Old and New Testaments, which water the mind, and gold stands for the sharpness of the mind.
comments.comment:
…For it is said in Genesis concerning Issachar, that having been called a farmer man, he rested among the lots (Gen 49:14); so one must now turn toward the old and the new covenant. For these indeed provide a watering for the intellect for spiritual fruitfulness. One sleeps among these two lots, placing them together in the midst of one God, as a way to distinguish the spirit from the letter. One having slept thus between the lots flies, perceiving according to the Holy Spirit.…

Gold is taken for the sharpness of the mind. Greenness signifies the life of the gold; for this color is a symbol of living plants.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The knowledge of scripture shines like gold, and the snow stands for the virtues that water the mind and cool the passions, since being made white as snow is not about physical snow.
comments.comment: And the knowledge of divine scripture shines out like gold (Psalm 68:13). 'They shall be covered with snow in Selom,' meaning they shall be filled with snows (Psalm 68:14). These are the virtues, watering the mind with springs and cooling the flame of the passions. For 'Wash me, and I shall be white as snow' (Ps 51:7) is not about physical snow. For it is an ineffable thing toward the brightness of a purified soul. Such also is 'If your sins are as scarlet, I will make them white as snow' (Isa 1:18) and 'The Nazarenes were cleansed of it through snow' (Psalm 68:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of gold and snow in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who kept the law under its shadow, and even the disciples, who have not yet reached their heavenly portion, live in the shadow of their portion, so a life covered with unstained snow is a great thing.
comments.comment: Solomon is interpreted as a shadow of a portion. Therefore, since the kings (not the apostles) who once kept the law according to the shadow are a portion of shadows, having indeed a spiritual portion but having also been tested by the shadow. Such is the one saying 'I am a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee according to the law.' And since the portion of Christ's disciples in the heavens is according to 'He has made us sufficient for the portion of the saints in light' (Col 1:12), but we have not yet reached it, as if the citizenship were in the heavens while walking upon earth, knowing in part and prophesying in part and having the earnest of the Spirit, they are in the shadow of their own portion. Therefore, it is a great thing that a life experiencing this finds itself being covered with snow unstained.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountain of God is the one incarnate Lord, in whom God dwells permanently and who nourishes both before and after he is matured, not one of many such mountains.
comments.comment: The high mountain ascends, the one being evangelized to Zion. And this ascent is through progress. Therefore, the God who is the Word, Wisdom, Life, and Sanctification, is nourishing, not receiving potency from without, but providing it to those who partake of Him. This mountain is both nourishing and matured, giving milk to some and imparting solid food to others, and nothing other than this besides milk; for it has become a food that is solid. It will be spoken of as being matured, and thus: the nourishing mountain, God, became man, having taken flesh from a virgin, through whom He is called matured, the human generation being made manifest by this expression, just as it is clearly said in Job to God, 'Remember that you formed me from clay' (Job 10:9), and furthermore: 'Did you not milk me as with milk and knead me with curds?' (Job 10:10), and 'You clothed me with skin and flesh' (Job 10:11). Since the matured one preserves the divinity harmlessly, and continues to nourish after being matured, the very words establish it, saying: a matured mountain, a nourishing mountain. For it is nourishing both before and after being matured. If you suppose the mountain is matured, did God not delight in it? (Psalm 68:16). The argument fits better against the Valentinians. For the Savior is called by many names in the Scripture, and according to each, a different essence is shown, such as calling the Lord apart from Jesus and Wisdom, and the others. Now the mountain is that in which the Lord dwells, according to 'what God was in Christ' and 'the Father who abides in me'. Therefore, demand the reason by which you supposed many mountains to be matured, but rather the one incarnate is a single matured mountain, in whom the Lord, having been born of the Theotokos virgin, dwells permanently without moving from one to another as He did with the holy men; but teachers became men—Moses and the prophets and the apostles—and even angels. For if the word spoken through angels became firm, how much more was the one being nourished as if being struck from God and being matured? Do not think such things are many by nature, like polytheism.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's army is countless, the saints and angels are yoked with Christ, and God came down on Sinai to command Moses to ascend, since no created thing can reach divine height unless God first descends with it.
comments.comment:
The army of God is not single but is myriads.

The voices of the choir of the saints are yoked together with him: Moses and the prophets, the apostles, the evangelists, the angels, the archangels, the principalities, the powers, the dominions, and those simply receiving God and having the Holy Spirit, who in the psalm says, 'Ride upon the horses, O Lord, and thy chariot is salvation' (Habakkuk 3:8). For through them the saving gospel was stretched out into the inhabited world. For more ranks appear yoked to the yoke of Christ. For this reason it has approached like an army of tens of thousands making straight their path, for no one among them is without fruit.

Just as an army and a chariot compose the unit in those whom God holds, so also the hosts having come to Sinai have the Lord within themselves, the lawgiver. And this is a high thing, in which God, having descended, commands Moses to ascend. For it is impossible for a created thing to ascend to divine height, unless God first descends with it. And Sinai is interpreted as temptation, not synonymous with a storm, but a trial, through which one, being tested by much experience, will be high, as the lawgiver ascending upon it and being revealed as a hierophant by the favor of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints' voices greet the one who ascends through the cross, takes captive those whom Satan tyrannized, and frees them as a ransom for many, drawing even the disobedient to dwell with him.
comments.comment: These preceding voices from the choir of the saints are spoken to the one ascending through the cross to the height, and there having taken captive those who are being tyrannized by Satan and freeing them from his bitterness, his tyranny, having given a ransom for his soul instead of many (Ps 68:18). In this way he redeemed all. For since not all come to him willingly and of their own accord, he takes even those who disobey to dwell with him. For many, disobeying the call of the gospel, are drawn away by sickness and other distraction. And some even came through visions to dwell with Jesus.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what ascending on high and leading captivity captive mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ, having ascended on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men, namely apostles, prophets, teachers and the words of wisdom and knowledge, enriching the souls of those who love him.
comments.comment: And the inspired Singer sings somewhere that, having ascended on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men (Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8). For some he placed in the Church, first apostles, second prophets, third teachers (1 Corinthians 12:28); and to one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge (1 Corinthians 12:8), and the gifts akin to these. In a word, he enriches the souls of those who love him with his own good things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the gifts the verse says were given.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Because of the many benefits from the Lord, we should bless him every day with prayer, and he is blessed not by receiving blessing but by giving it.
comments.comment: Of so many benefits occurring from the Lord, how could I not intend to bless the cause of such great blessings, and to bless—not perhaps never, nor perhaps always—but mixing prayer with blessing every day, asking that they may be guided by God, who grants the desire for salvation? And he is blessed, not by receiving blessing, but by giving these. For as a man is good, not by becoming so but by doing good things.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain reason for blessing the Lord daily.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is the God of saving, and he always provides exits from the death that follows sin, through which one comes out by repentance.
comments.comment: Therefore also he is blessed, the fountain of all blessing to us (Psalm 68:20-21). If the preceding things are said concerning common death, there are myriad ways known to all toward the common death; but if concerning living according to God and the death opposing this is also signified here, our God, the Savior, is the God of saving. For he becomes the cause of eternal salvation. Indeed he says concerning himself, 'The Savior does not stand away from me.' Just as God is of saving, so also the exits of death do not possess him as lord, providing always exits through which one comes out through repentance from the death following sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the issues from death' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'heads' are the enemies, the rulers or dominating powers, and God deals with them so that they might not live wickedly.
comments.comment: And the heads are the enemies, or the rulers, or the dominating things, as in 'From the heads of the rulers of nations'; and the dominating thing in 'I gave their paths into their heads' (Ezekiel 22:31), and 'Your hands are upon my head' (Ps 139:10). Both perhaps are shown by 'You cast death into the heads of the lawless' (Habakkuk 3:13), the God doing good so that they might not live wickedly, being described as the life according to sin. But these enemies, being such, wander in their transgressions.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's ways are not grasped but are pious and rightly understood, and those singing who accomplish the practical life are overtaken by the apostles who teach.
comments.comment: …For the ways of God are not grasped, but are pious and with right understanding (Psalm 68:25). Let us say 'those singing who accomplish the practical life,' and let us omit the young women playing the timbrel, having deadened the members upon the earth and carrying the death of Jesus in their bodies, souls wandering. These singers were overtaken by the rulers according to teaching, so that they themselves might begin from practical virtue. But they are also in the midst of young women, those who because of having the beginning of playing the timbrel—that is, deadening the members upon the earth of the young women spoken of—are the rulers overtaking the singers, which are the apostles.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The springs of Israel are the Law and the Prophets, from which the Lord is blessed by those who draw the water of salvation, and this refutes those who sever the old Scripture from the new.
comments.comment:
The springs of Israel are the legal and prophetic writings.

For from these springs the Lord is blessed by those able to draw from them, since they are saving springs, water with gladness.

And this is concerning what Jesus said: 'Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall have in himself a spring of water welling up unto eternal life' (John 4:14).

And by this those who sever the old Scripture from the new are to be refuted, as though they cannot bless God in the churches, not having the springs of Israel nor their Lord—as if daring to divide the Godhead itself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'fountain of Israel' and why the Old and New Testaments belong together.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The disciples, chosen from almost every tribe of Israel, became lights of the world though they were unlearned fishermen and craftsmen.
comments.comment: I hear the prophet David singing about them: “There Benjamin the younger in ecstasy, rulers of Judah their leaders, rulers of Zebulun, rulers of Naphtali.” (Psalm 68:27) For the divine disciples were chosen from almost every tribe of Israel and became worldwide luminaries holding a word of life — men who had been craftsmen, seafarers, and fishers, without a stock of polished words, “unlearned in speech” yet rich “in knowledge.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the named tribal leaders stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The weakness of men is loosed by God's power, the Word, at the birth of Emmanuel, and the kings bring gifts to the church, as Peter offered his brother Andrew and Philip offered Nathanael.
comments.comment:
'Command with your power over all things, O Creator, that having sojourned it may loose the weakness of men.'

And coming to us from your temple, it shall loose it, with what was wrought for our sake having been strengthened.

And this is the birth of Emmanuel, by your Word becoming flesh.

To this power, which is God the Word, God said that all things should come to be, and he commanded that diverse things be created.

With the weakness loosed by the presence of God's power, the kings bring gifts to God to the spiritual Jerusalem, that is, the church.

And if those kings whom the heavenly one distinguished in his inheritance are those bearing the gifts to Jerusalem, those benefited by them are the ones being led forward.

Thus the apostle Peter offered as a gift his brother Andrew, and Philip offered Nathanael, and the other apostles many others, and others offered as gifts serious thoughts and words and praiseworthy works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who brings the gifts and what they are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'beasts of the reed' are those who advocate the falsely-named knowledge.
comments.comment:
Understand as 'beasts of the reed' those who advocate the falsely-named knowledge (1 Tim 6:20).

The prophecy which runs thus can be said concerning these: 'Woe to those who write wickedness; for writing wickedness, they write.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Egypt stands for the whole earth, and Ethiopia for the dark and unsightly state of souls in sins.
comments.comment: By Egypt he signified the whole earth, over which the intelligible Pharaoh ruled, and by Ethiopia the dark and unsightly state of the souls in sins; as he also says in one of the psalms: 'And behold, aliens and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians; these were born there' (Psalm 87:4; LXX 86:4)—clearly, in the spiritual Zion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Egypt and Ethiopia stand for in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Ethiopia, made spiritual by repentance, says 'I am black and beautiful', black from idolatry and beautiful from leaving it, and becomes luminous when she reaches out her hand to God.
comments.comment: A people whose tongue is to proclaim that all shall serve the Lord under a yoke. From the ends of the rivers of Ethiopia come sacrifices to me. It agrees with the filling of Ethiopia from the kingdoms and in what is said. She herself, the one from nearby, and Ethiopia, having become spiritual and having embraced genuine repentance, says about herself: 'I am black and beautiful'; black indeed because of idolatry and practical wickedness, but beautiful because of the withdrawal from those things. … And it happened to her to become luminous after having reached out her hand to God, as those seeing her with the benefactor say: 'Who is she, the one ascending, having become white?' (Song of Solomon 8:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's voice is the divine scripture, which gives spiritual power as the prophecies are fulfilled in Christ, who ascended to the heaven of heavens, a state befitting God rather than a created place.
comments.comment:
His voice is the divine scripture. By this he will give a voice to receive spiritual power. And even in these things, his voice, John, must be taken, saying: 'I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness' (Matt 3:3), to be spoken as the Savior having ascended to the heaven of heavens, having fulfilled the prophecies that pre-proclaimed his incarnation, death, and resurrection, and his ascension, he gave voice to them. For those speaking about the things to come seem to be weak because of the lack of clarity of the outcome, then receiving the voice of power they will be fulfilled.

And also the saying that God has set himself upon the heaven of heavens: for only He reclines for the Lord according to 'The heaven of heavens is the Lord' (Psalm 115:16), and 'Behold, the heaven of your God, the heaven of heavens' (Deut 10:14), into which no one has been born.

But to ascend to the things of the mind. For the place to which God ascended into heaven is not any created thing, but a state befitting God, which is not manifest, not declared by a master word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Giving thanks in deed and word and singing hymns makes one true Israel, able to contain God's majesty.
comments.comment: Being made thankful in deed and word, glorify Him with hymns and theologies, so that you may be able to contain His majesty, having become true Israel by purity of heart, seeing God. For the superlative knowledge of God possesses what is fitting in greatness only to the one having sanctification and peace.
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms how to honor God's greatness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title 'Concerning those who shall be transformed' fits the Lord's turning unbelievers into believers, the Jews who did not believe, and those changed at the resurrection.
comments.comment: Since from beginning to end he preserves the same face speaking, one should take up the same rhythm of thought following him. Since therefore the Psalm signifies the Lord who has come among us, transforming men by life and teaching as to become from unbelievers and sinners faithful and righteous, the inscription 'Concerning those who shall be transformed' lies most fittingly. But also those having believed from circumcision were transformed, living according to the Spirit rather than the law. And if even through the change occurring from the better to the inferior quality, I say even so: nothing will be more fitting than 'Concerning those who shall be transformed' than the inscription for the Jews who did not believe in Him. And if even those transformed according to the resurrection from the dead, as in 'We also shall be changed' 1 Cor 15:52, are to be visited. For if the Psalm is from the person of Christ, and His passion is signified in it, concerning His dying and rising and all being raised, it is not lacking to take the inscription 'Concerning those thus transformed' to be for them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord was sunk by a storm of trials not because of sin but because he accepted death for us, laying down his life of himself in obedience to the Father.
comments.comment: Since therefore the Lord did not reach that place because of sin, but accepted death on our behalf, he says: 'A storm sank me into the depths of the sea' (Ps 69:2). A storm signifies the trials, just as the 'Storm passed through the wilderness,' and 'I waited for God who saves me from despair and from the storm.' You may consider the present text to be like 'No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself' (John 10:18), having voluntarily accepted death. Because it is not said that he gave his life through sickness or simply by the usual end, but having endured the cross, he is said to be sunk by a storm, even if he endured this not consciously, becoming obedient to the Father unto death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the deep waters of the verse as the Lord's trials and voluntary death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His failing eyes are the eyes of the heart, and the benefactor is hated, as the Savior was.
comments.comment: And he who turns all his expectation toward God will say, 'My eyes have failed' (Psalm 69:3), clearly as those of the heart. But the benefactor doing these things is pursued and hated, just as the Savior, healing all infirmity among the Jews and raising the dead, became a city of scrutiny through these things. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because Jesus does not confess sins of his own, the confessions spoken in this psalm in our person are made on our behalf.
comments.comment: It is necessary to consider what the most frequent things in the Psalm are said from our person by Jesus, bearing our infirmities and suffering on our behalf Ps 68:2-3. For certainly He does not confess sins, nor has He done anything at all. If therefore He does not confess on His own behalf, it is evident that He does this on our behalf.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why Christ can speak of sins in this psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's 'folly' is not literal but a teacher's accommodation to his hearers, since he who was rich in wisdom became poor for us so that we might become rich.
comments.comment: No one is indeed a sinner who has folly or shortcomings added to him by God, remaining in lawlessness before His eyes (Psalm 69:5). Why is someone disturbed hearing of folly? For the word is not far from him to have him confess ignorance when he says to someone, 'Never did I know you'; and he asserts as if he does not know anything concerning the day and the hour of the judgment. How these things are piously understood, and the things concerning his folly will find clarity when piously understood. For a teacher possessing perfect knowledge appears to be knowing through accommodation to those to whom these things are introduced, as if he were of the kind who are capable, in a way, resembling them; everyone accepted such an accommodation, as if possessing ignorance or folly. For since he was rich in wisdom, he became poor through us, as if some thought wisdom was not present, so that through his folly we might become rich.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ did not please himself; the reproaches fell upon him.
comments.comment: For Christ did not please himself, just as it is written: 'The reproaches of those reproaching you have fallen upon me' (Psalm 69:9; LXX 68:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus was maligned for eating and drinking though he fasted forty days, and the sackcloth points to the harsh life he bore on our behalf.
comments.comment:
Against those who maligned him. For it is said against him that Jesus and the disciples were always eating and drinking, even if they did so when called to a feast for the sake of benefit and to perform signs. They were not called to a feast to eat and drink, but they were called to a feast. For indeed he fasted for forty days.

Since fasting is not a preventative against the lifting up of the soul from irrational passions, 'I said, I will veil my soul with fasting,' he says. But the worthless are accustomed to reproach the good because of their virtues; for piety is an abomination to a sinner. Since the Savior confesses and is reviled on our behalf, he is alluded to through the sackcloth regarding the harsh and miserable lifestyle.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prayer asks that the Father hear the Son's voice and save, through the resurrection of him who died, those for whom he is worthy.
comments.comment: Therefore hear my voice in a multitude of your mercy, providing the salvation in truth for those for whom I am worthy Ps 68:14. And this will be, that you will save him who died through his resurrection. For not such life and salvation will be for them as I receive. Salvation in truth is that which is according to God, not in truth but in type and image of that which happens to the weary by physicians and generals. Even if you once demonstrated to them, you say, Father, 'This is my beloved Son in whom I am well-pleased' Matt 3:17, raise him crucified on their behalf. For that is the time, that is, the end of the good pleasure of your will for the sake of salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son prays that those dead through sin may be made alive with him and not be entangled in the body through the mud called passion.
comments.comment: Therefore also hear me, so that those dead through sin may be made alive with me as I am being made alive. The apostle is initiating this mystery: that God, who is rich in mercy because of his great love, loved us being dead through trespasses and sins, and made us alive together with Christ. And he presents this prayer for us, so that we may not be entangled in the body through the mud called passion Ps 68:15.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'deep mire' as passion and the prayer as made for us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Having been tested, he is able to help those tested, and since he became both a worm and a man he endures sufferings and the hatred of demons and men.
comments.comment:
Having been tested, he is able to help those being tested. And the depth of the interpreted waters is this: that those who do not bear the trials bravely cannot be saved from God alone, as it is said, 'Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord' (Psalm 130:1), and the following things exist for him, as he cries out, 'how can I be saved?' For nothing from those who harm him will terrify or frighten him.

Therefore, having outrun him through death, he begins to be terrified and to be distressed; first, indeed, he cries out for us, and since he has truly become both a worm and a man, he endures these sufferings. He is hated by the demons and by the men who hate him, such as those saying, 'Aron, Aron, crucify him' (Psalm 69:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son speaks in figures, and having been submerged and to rise again, he prays not to receive a second trial.
comments.comment: The misfortunes do not close in like a cistern; oh, how for me these have become completely inescapable (Psalm 69:15). For he sets these things tropically, clinging to the original hypothesis. For there also, 'Because water has entered,' he said, 'as to my soul,' and how, having said, 'And a storm has overwhelmed me,' now he says, 'Not so.' Since, having been submerged, he is to rise up again, he prays to the one who tested him, that he might not receive a second trial.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Son asks to be heard in the abundance of the Father's mercies, interceding for all, since he was sent not to judge but to save the world.
comments.comment:
Since out of much goodness your mercy will be useful, I entreat that it become upon those for whom I am worthy (for you will loose their sins), hear me; as you will look upon me interceding for all, not according to the second judgment but according to the abundance of your mercies, and they will receive much benefit (Psalm 69:16). For desiring to manage these things for me, you sent me; for I was sent not to judge but to save the world by your mercies toward those being benefited and by your good mercy.

The addition that presents the good mercy is that not all mercy is such; for God says concerning the criminals, 'Your eye shall not spare him, nor will you have mercy on him.' But it is not probable that these things are said from the face of the Only-begotten being stripped of humanity, as sometimes the child-like address signifies some son; but rather, he said these things clearly, having emptied himself and having taken the form of a slave and having become like us in all things, apart from sin, and having inhabited our daily sufferings—the natural and blameless ones, I say.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Redeeming the soul means not being held among the dead in Hades and redeeming those there, as Jesus gave his whole self on behalf of all.
comments.comment:
And the redeeming of it is not to be held in Hades having become among the dead, but also to redeem those there.

No one having sense would say these things concerning an irrational soul, which has no life and hypostasis of its own.

And how would it be redeemed? Let those who think thus say; for being redeemed belongs to a human soul, that is, a rational one.

And it is possible and plausible to say that the soul of the ambassador is all that has been made his own, so that just as one is called a man of God, such as Moses and Elijah, so also his soul might be called that which has clung to him and become one spirit with him.

For he redeems all this, giving on its behalf what he took up; for just as the body of Jesus was given on behalf of human bodies, so his soul on behalf of their souls, that the whole man might be given on behalf of all by the one who took him up. … On account, then, of my enemies who delight in the destruction of men, rescue me, raising me from the dead, that they and the devil who has the power of death may be destroyed, and that men may rise, falling asleep unto salvation; and I pray against enemies afflicting me, not unknown; for they are before you.

And my affliction is that men are worn down, on whose behalf you sent me, that I might redeem them from the devil who tyrannizes them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sympathy missing among the Jews is found in the calling of the Gentiles.
comments.comment: Moreover, even if it is not found among the treacherous Jews sympathizing and encouraging, it is found in the calling of the Gentiles. For they indeed, not having the same mind, say, 'If we died with him, we shall live with him,' and 'If we have become partakers of his death, we shall also be of his resurrection.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who had planted God's vine turned it to bitterness, so that gall and vinegar became their fruit, which they brought to him who thirsted for their salvation.
comments.comment: … they nourished him with gall and gave him vinegar to drink. For how could it be that gall and vinegar did not become their fruit, since they did not guard the planting from the beginning? For the whole true Jewish multitude having planted a fruitful vine of God, having turned by their own impulse toward bitterness, the vine has become an alien vine. For it is indeed said concerning them, having become enemies and fools: For their vine is a vine of Sodom and their branch is from Gomorrah, their cluster is a cluster of gall, its fruit a fruit of bitterness; their mind is the wrath of dragons and their wrath is the unyielding wrath of asps. I brought this drink of the gall of the cluster and the bitterness of the fruit to him, even though he was thirsting for their salvation. For the transgression of the mind is vinegar.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the gall and vinegar of the verse from the vine of Sodom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Their table became accursed through the cruel welcome they gave Christ at the crucifixion, offering vinegar mixed with gall when he was thirsty.
comments.comment: For their table has become accursed, and quite rightly: that is, the cruel welcome and the savagery that they showed toward Christ at the time of his crucifixion; for when he was thirsty, they brought him vinegar mixed with gall (Psalm 69:21; Matthew 27:34). For this reason they were also darkened in mind (Romans 11:10) and are bent down, picturing only the things on the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the table is called a snare in terms of the crucifixion.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter applied this verse to Judas, and in the plural it applies to all the betrayers of Jesus, whose city became desolate.
comments.comment: Let their habitation become a desert, and Peter, the leader of the apostles, took the sixth verse concerning Judah to be prophesied. And since it has been driven out in the plural, it must be applied to all the betrayers of Jesus, their city having become desolate and its habitation having become a shelter because of their beastly manner. For in a shelter the scraps have the bed; and otherwise, not having God within herself but rather the angels who formerly watched over her.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus takes our sins into his own body to heal the wounds, and if we persist in sinning and persecute him, we add to his suffering.
comments.comment: Jesus, taking our sins into his own body, through which indeed the wounds were struck by robbers while descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, making them his own in order to heal the wounds himself; but he has these pains if we persist in sinning. And if in addition to this we stir up persecution against him, we add a portion of suffering to him who no longer suffers simply on behalf of sinners, but also on behalf of those persecuting him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father struck the shepherd in that he allowed his Son, who chose to suffer, to suffer when the Jews would not receive him.
comments.comment: This was the one who had said through the prophet, “I will strike the shepherd.” (Zechariah 13:7) (Matthew 26:31) That is why David also says to the Father, “For the one whom you struck, they themselves pursued.” (Psalm 69:26) Yet this did not happen entirely and wholly by the Father’s will; he wanted him not to suffer, if the Jews had accepted him. But since they did not receive him, the Father consented to the Son who chose to suffer this. That is why it is also said that the Father struck “the shepherd,” since he allowed him to suffer though able to prevent his suffering. The word said to Pilate by Christ is also to be understood thus: “You would have no authority at all against me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11) — instead of “the Father did not consent to me who chose to suffer.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Father striking the Son means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God hands them over to the desires they loved, an addition of lawlessness upon their lawlessness, so that they do not enter the righteousness that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.
comments.comment:
By their own desires and by being handed over to passions, they are the cause of enduring these things, not having God as the cause, since they are handed over to those whom they loved. For He sent them away according to the desires of their hearts, so that they might walk in their own desires, an addition of lawlessness upon their lawlessness.

Since, therefore, they did not receive the truth when it came, but wished to live lawlessly within the shadow of the law, they were also driven out from the place of typical worship, so that I might add to the former lawlessness another, by wanting to keep this outside of Judea. Therefore they do not enter into the righteousness which is through the faith of Jesus Christ, concerning which it is written: 'But now the righteousness of God without law has been revealed, being witnessed by the law and the prophets' (Rom 3:21). For how could those who were always about external things and possessing the shadow, enter into the righteousness which they did not know as God, in order to establish their own?…
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'add iniquity unto their iniquity' is God handing people over to their desires.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The book of the living is the knowledge of God, in which those who have virtue and faith are written.
comments.comment: For those having virtue and faith and knowledge of God live: 'Hear, O my life, your life and the length of your days, to love you, Lord your God, with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5); but also, 'he who believes in me has eternal life' (John 3:36). It is a book in which those living thus are written: it is the knowledge of God, of him who knows those who are His, to whom it is promised that those not falling under the remembrance of God shall be blotted out.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Names written through piety can be erased by negligence, as David says of the Jews, while the faithful are written in the book of life.
comments.comment: Do not fear the proverb; even if your evil works are recorded, they can be erased through good works; just as if someone's name is written through piety, but he denies it by his ways, the proverb does not make the writing stay; for it is erased. So that you may learn that the one written through piety and cast out through negligence is erased, David says concerning the Jews who were once written and later erased: 'Let them be blotted out from the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous' (Psalm 69:28). Just as the unfaithful are blotted out, so the faithful are written. Listen to Paul saying: 'Greet the brothers whom we love, and Clement and the other fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life' (Phil 4:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being blotted out of the book means.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Christ, rich, became poor so that the poor might become rich, and having risen he cast away the wounds and poverty he bore for men and sang a triumphal song over his enemies.
comments.comment:
Rich and being outside of wounds, I have become poor, so that the poor might become rich through my poverty, and having grieved, having been wounded on behalf of wounds made by the burning arrows of the evil one (Ps 69:29).…

A poor and suffering one, as if a reproach were added to my wounds, and I am by nature a poor man, but salvation from the face of God has taken hold of me (Psalm 69:29). For having risen from the dead and having been taken up, he cast away the wounds and the poverty which he had on behalf of men. And when the enemies had been destroyed, and especially the devil, it followed that a triumphal song should be shouted by him, having conquered in the name of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'poor and sorrowful' speaker as Christ who became poor for us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To praise God with song and magnify him is a sacrifice, and God desires this and mercy more than animal offerings.
comments.comment: … And since to praise God is a sacrifice, according to 'Sacrifice of praise, you will glorify him' (Psalm 50:23), having praised the name of God with song and having magnified him in praise, he is encouraged as 'It pleases God that one brings a young bull with horns and weapons, being brought for a sacrifice.' Therefore also, to those who do not sacrifice thus, he says, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, a knowledge of God or burnt offerings' (Ps 50:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why praise pleases God more than an ox or bullock.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The poor in spirit will see this and rejoice forever, and the servants are the prophets and ministers of the gospel.
comments.comment: Let these things be seen by the poor in spirit, whom Jesus strengthened against every evil phalanx; for seeing such courage in them, to be rejoiced eternally according to 'Eternal joy shall take hold of them.' … Those formerly called prophets and God-beloved men, and after these, servants and ministers of the gospel (Psalm 69:36).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Remembrance saves those who have lost the knowledge of the good through forgetfulness, since sin enters through negligence and the one who repents remembers the good.
comments.comment:
It is possible to fail to remember those things which were previously described as having precise and complete knowledge, following the command: 'To the end, into remembrance, to save me, Lord, you are' (Psalm 70:1). This is the saving of everyone who has cast away the use and knowledge of the good through forgetfulness.

For all, having been made straight according to the image and likeness of God, have the thoughts concerning God scattered within them. For sin always enters through negligence; if it happens that after its practice one repents, he remembers the good, for his thought is rational and having become according to the image of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what remembrance does for a sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sin is led by insensitivity to the good, so those who run toward evil without feeling would be ashamed if they came to feel it.
comments.comment:
Since sin is led by insensitivity and ignorance of the good, and because of this one acts with pleasure and boldness, it is said concerning some that they have glory upon which they ought to be ashamed; for he says, 'The glory is in their shame' (Philippians 3:19). And the prophet says, 'Be ashamed of your boasting' (Philippians 3:19), for it brings mockery and destruction.

Those running toward evil without feeling, if they were to receive feeling and thought of it, would cease to desire to do it; the good turns them from the evil to do the good. He says that this very thing happens to those destined for various things: 'They would have been ashamed, knowing they are evil, having been ensnared and having failed to remember what they did; for they sought to lead my soul into the same wickedness as theirs, or to kill me, because I do not run with them into the apostasy in which they are outside of God'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who plot against the soul cannot bring about evil unless God delivers them.
comments.comment:
One must watch those who desire evil toward me; until they have the power to intend to do evil and harm, they will not be able to bring about evil, unless God delivers them (Ps 51:16). Not those who plot against money, but those who plot against the soul.

But the assault on the soul from God is alienation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who repents turns back and is ashamed of what he did, though before repenting he spoke arrogantly against the one he persecuted.
comments.comment: Saying this, he reproaches them, saying, 'They would have turned back, no longer desiring to hasten toward evil, and they would have been ashamed, regarding those things on which they acted wickedly, desiring that which harms me to be for me' (Psalm 70:2). The one repenting turns back, running again toward what he left, desiring to be with the good and to be ashamed, even though before the repentance he spoke arrogantly against the one being persecuted, saying, 'Well done, well done,' that is, 'Let us prevail, as you flee from us' (Psalm 70:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains being put to shame and turned back as repentance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope is held toward the Lord, and God saves in righteousness those who hasten to be free of iniquities, as He takes to Himself in wisdom those who desire wisdom.
comments.comment: Hope is held toward a person. One must strive, for the Lord holds hope; for blessed is the man who has trusted in the Lord (Ps 40:4), and he will be the Lord's hope. For this hope is living; therefore it is written, 'Born again into a living hope' (1 Pet 1:3). It has been said by the one possessing it, 'Not to be put to shame through the ages; and in your righteousness save me and bring me out' (Psalm 71:1-2). God saves in righteousness those who hasten to be outside of iniquities, just as in wisdom He takes to Himself those who desire to possess it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that hope rests on a person and that God saves by righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker asks God to bend down to his weak prayer, to be his defender and shield, and to be a fortress and refuge from every fear of enemies.
comments.comment:
O Lord, not of much superiority toward the creatures, but especially toward us humans, we are not strong enough to reach your ears with the prayers we offer; therefore I entreat you by much goodness to incline your way of condescension toward me, so that you might save me, receiving the prayer concerning salvation. Of many desiring to fight me, become my defender; cover me with your shield, concerning which it is said, 'His truth shall surround you with a shield' (Psalm 91:4). And since I want you to be for me all things, to become for me an invincible fortress and an unshakeable bulwark, most fortified.

You are a place where I remain outside of all fear from enemies, my refuge and my stronghold.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner's hand is a sinful practice from which God rescues, and the one rescued under God's mighty hand is snatched from it by nothing.
comments.comment: Regarding Ps 70:4, the hand of a sinner is a sinful practice from which it is worthy to be rescued, so that he may not act according to it to any extent. Likewise, when one transgresses and acts wickedly, the effective energies of his actions are placed outside of him, having been rescued by God. Whether the sinner himself or another is the subject of the transgressing and acting wickedly, examine this. For it seems to incline toward the two, if a sinner who transgresses and acts wickedly exists. But if the devil is meant by these names, his hand must be seized and his military-like power must be arranged against every evil and unclean spirit. He who is rescued from the hand of those things, having become under the mighty hand of God, is snatched by nothing from it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is the hope of the one who endures, and hope in Him from youth means a life raised up toward God or a renewed life in the new man.
comments.comment: Just as God is the wisdom and power of the holy one, so also He is the endurance and hope of the one enduring unto salvation and hoping in Him. For it is said about these things in the 70th Psalm, 'But now where is my hope? Is it not the Lord?' (Psalm 71:5; LXX 70:5) and in the 71st, 'My hope is in God, the hope of all the ends of the earth' (Psalm 65:5). One must oversee 'My hope' from youth, being able to demonstrate how one, having been brought up according to God from infancy, has never possessed any hope other than God. And in addition to this, you will say that from youth there is some hope in God, from which, having stripped off the old man, you put on the new and fresh man, created according to God in holiness and knowledge of the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'my hope from my youth' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'From the womb' means from the time a person can begin to reason, not from the moment of birth.
comments.comment: Regarding Ps 70:6ab, 'From the womb from my mother's belly' must be understood wisely, not meaning from the time of birth, but rather then moving logically and God-fearingly regarding the one being born; for it is written, 'Even Samuel, before knowing God' (1 Sam 3:7), although he was brought up God-fearingly from tender nails by God-fearing parents. For the children of men have a time from which they are able to move logically. The great Moses says in the wilderness, 'And all the children with us today will not enter into the land of promise, if indeed they do not enter good or evil' (Deuteronomy 1:39).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: While others praise rulers and teachers of human lessons, the speaker keeps his remembrance in God alone, always and without a break.
comments.comment: While others are praising rulers, teachers of human lessons, and those very lessons which are indeed glorious and constitute an honorable wealth, our remembrance is in you and not in any other. A scripture is brought forward saying: 'My remembrance is in you always' (Psalm 71:6). Regarding both types of scriptures, one must choose 'always' over 'throughout,' to have the remembrance and the recollection continually and without interruption in God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'continually' as constant remembrance of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who despise virtue call piety a terror and flee it, but God protects the speaker from them, as the apostles likewise became a spectacle to the world.
comments.comment: Those who despise virtue and consider piety an abomination, sinners, are defiling the diligent and the lowly, calling it a terror. For they say among themselves, 'Let us give up the righteous one, since he is troublesome to us.' And since those who think and speak such things are vile to us, they say, 'It is not at all a terror, but it has happened to the many, that is, to the most vulgar,' and they flee from virtue. But even if they speak to me in that same manner, you, being stronger, protect me without harm from them. With this same thought the apostle also says that we have become a cleansing for the world and a reproach to all men (1 Cor 4:10-13). In agreement with this is also: 'We are fools for Christ, but you are wise' (1 Cor 4:10). From the same disposition is also written: 'For I think that what God has shown us the apostles to be, we are last, as if marked for execution' (1 Corinthians 4:9), and 'That we became a spectacle to the world' (1 Cor 4:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, the champion of righteousness, is strong, and unceasing hope in him grows stronger when it is set against painful things.
comments.comment: Sin is weak and a cause of weakness, but righteousness is strong, and so is God, its champion. Such also is hope in God, and especially the unceasing hope. And just as hope is understood from the first origin as something that could not have existed without God, so when it stands against the opposition of painful things, it is trained all the more (Psalm 71:7; LXX 70:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is called a strong refuge: hope in him is strengthened by hardship.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A mouth filled with praise speaks of God's glory, which is His only-begotten Son.
comments.comment: Worthy is his word, the mouth having been named, to be filled with praise (Psalm 71:8; LXX 70:8). But the glory of God is the discourse concerning him, his only-begotten Son; for it is said concerning Christ, as the glory of God was to be revealed upon his appearing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Old age is precious for divine wisdom and a blameless life, not length, so the speaker asks not to be rejected.
comments.comment: And let it be considered also toward thought; since old age is precious not because of long duration, but because of much divine wisdom of the inward man and old age of an unblemished life through supreme virtue; since I am at the peak of progressing, I beseech you not to reject me but to cooperate by your goodness, so that I may reach the time of unblemished life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what makes old age precious, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker asks that God's strength, not bodily vigor, stay with him in old age, as it did for David, who still ruled and chose Solomon as successor.
comments.comment: Since in the season of youth I took your help, not bodily vigor, as my strength, let this strength remain with me even as youth fades, and when human strength has passed away entirely, let the power that comes from you stand by me—as it did for David himself in old age (Psalm 71:9; LXX 70:9). For when he was young, his son rose up against him, but when he was old, no one did. Chilled already by old age and lying helpless on his bed, he still ruled Israel and gave orders to the nation. He ruled Israel and appointed Solomon as his successor, after casting out Adonijah, who had tried to reign against his will.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer about old age with David's own example.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The enemies' words fit Absalom's rebellion and the Lord's own suffering, and the speaker asks that the wicked fail and that God hasten His help so that his hope and hymns grow.
comments.comment:
These words [of the enemies] would fit the time of Absalom's rebellion, the time about which those other words were spoken in Psalm 3: “Many say of my soul, ‘There is no salvation for him in his God’” (Psalm 3:2). And by his fellowship with the righteous, the Lord also suffered this kind of rebellion from his enemies, who said, “Let him be delivered, since he delights in him” (Psalm 22:8), and who thought that the one suffering according to the Father's will had been abandoned. So let the wicked, he says, fail in their purpose, and let the matter turn out according to my hope, not according to their supposition.

Do not be far from me, but hasten your help and turn their boasting into shame, so that my hope may increase all the more, and my hymns to you as well (Psalm 71:12; LXX 70:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the setting of the enemies' taunt and the prayer for help.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The greatest slander against a forsaken man is 'God has forsaken him', and he answers it by saying that through all things he hopes.
comments.comment: And those saying, 'God has forsaken him,' were casting into his soul. For the greatest slander against the one forsaken is declared by the phrase 'God has forsaken him,' but 'I, however, through all things, hope,' he says, showing that he will not leave any place available. Toward 'God has forsaken him' and 'I, however, through all things, hope' is the contrast.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because he promised to recount God's righteousness, beyond human power, he says he cannot count it out.
comments.comment: Symmachus says, “I do not know how to count them out.” For since he had promised to recount God's righteousness and the salvation that had come to him, and the promise was greater than what belongs to a human being, he added these words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the speaker says he cannot number God's righteousness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To remember God's righteousness alone is to care nothing for righteousness by the shadow of the law, as Paul counted his former gains as refuse.
comments.comment: God has given the power to rule the mind of the written scriptures in a kingly way. Therefore I say, I will remember your righteousness alone, not being one who cares for the righteousness according to the shadow of the law, having become according to the righteousness in the law; Paul, blameless, writes that all those shadowy things, which previously were his gains, are to be counted as refuse because of the excellence of knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hymn cries out the height of God's wonders: humans brought through many afflictions attain good things in eternal life after rising from the dead.
comments.comment: He begins the hymn at the very point where he had promised, doing it immediately, crying out with a loud voice the height of God's wonders: that human beings who had been brought through many afflictions attain good things in eternal life, having risen from the dead. This is the chief point of the divine hymns and the clearest demonstration of God, since none of those who are called gods could rival it. For God is the one who gives life to all things, and in him Christ is known, being the Son of God, saying that he himself is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25) and showing this in deed. So even if these words are spoken by Christ as a human being to the Father, it is fitting that they be spoken to him as well by human beings, as to the Son and image of God. For he is the firstborn from the dead, having descended in the manner of a human being, but having ascended by the power of God, being himself the author of the ascent, as he says to the Jews, in which the excellence of his divinity is shown.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The great works of the Most High have been lifted up because a Savior has been born, bringing glory in the highest, peace on earth and the ascent of the saved.
comments.comment: These things, as the great works of the Most High, and with them the wonders, have been lifted up, because a Savior man has come into being. For having been born of the virgin, a multitude of the heavenly host cried out, 'Glory to God in the highest,' say, 'and peace on earth, in men goodwill' (Luke 2:14). For because of the goodwill having come into being in men, much peace prevailed, the enemies of all those on earth having been destroyed; but also glory has become in the highest, of the saved men having the ascent unto the highest. For how will not those having become perfect, just as the heavenly Father is perfect, having become in unsurpassable holiness, have God within themselves, all in all becoming? And the Lord himself says in the Gospels to his own Father, 'I will, Father, that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory' (John 17:24).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God allows afflictions for some benefit and then gives life, lifting up the one who was driven down out of the depths of his circumstances.
comments.comment: Since God, through goodness, permitted to be tested by afflictions and evil things for the sake of some benefit, turning back again to himself, he gives life, imparting life to those who have seen through trials and evils, just as one is lifted up from the abysses, that is, from the depth of circumstances, the one being driven down. And since we have received the evil things, the painful and evil ones, as appropriate to the afflictions, following this, life-giving will be called according to the common life, and the ascent from the abyss; for since the evil things, having been stretched out, seem to kill and to bring down into Hades, if one receives the end of these things, he is being made alive by God and is brought up from the abysses of the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the speaker is brought up from the depths after God sent troubles.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words are spoken for the human race, tried by evils until the Lord gave his own soul as a ransom and brought up from Hades those cast down by sin.
comments.comment: The holy one does not speak these things from his own person, but concerning the human race having been tested by many evils and tribulation before the arrival of the Savior. After the trial, the Lord, having turned back toward us, came and gave life, having given instead of us his own soul as a ransom; so that everyone believing in him and receiving his teaching possesses eternal life. He brought up me from the abysses of the earth, that is, from Hades, having become there after the shedding of the body, and no one else resurrected me except him, to bring up those having been cast down there through their own sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gave a blessed new life to one despaired of by men.
comments.comment: Even if you made your great power manifest by handing human nature over to death, yet to the one despaired of among human beings you gave back a new and blessed life.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The word 'again' is not idle: the speaker was raised first by being given life and having God's righteousness increased, and then raised again from the lower parts.
comments.comment: Regarding 'You have brought me up again from the abysses of the earth' (Psalm 71:20): if the abyss signifies a sinking in circumstantial matters (as it is interpreted), it follows to take it as being often raised up from there by God, always doing good (the testimony of this is the saying: 'Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and from all of them the Lord will rescue them'); but if instead of Hades the abyss is understood, it is difficult to say how someone is raised up there again; for just as there is one entrance into life and one exit from it, it is necessary that those being separated from the body also become one in Hades. Therefore, the 'again' does not pass by, but will find consolation; yet it is not passing by the divine and is not superfluous. His thought will be such: 'Having given me life by your goodness, and also having increased your righteousness upon me, you have brought me up again from the abysses of the earth, not only by having given me life and having increased your righteousness upon me, but also by bringing me up from the lower parts.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalter is the vessel through which the speaker thankfully confesses the truth to the Holy One of Israel, and Christ is made wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption for us.
comments.comment:
The Psalter is a vessel of the psalm, through which he says 'I will confess to you,' bringing forth the truth thankfully, according to which no one is like God after having made bad things life-giving and having completed every following goodness. Regarding the confessing of the truth in a vessel of a psalm and in a harp, he promises to the God existing, the Holy of Israel. And 'Holy of Israel' is said as one sanctifying him; for just as if we say 'they are holy of God' we present those being sanctified by him, so we do not say 'Holy of him' without signifying what is being sanctified. …

Wisdom was revealed to us from God, along with righteousness, sanctification, and redemption; for wisdom became for the wise, righteousness for those being justified, and sanctification and redemption for those being sanctified and redeemed. It is not only said that the Holy One of Israel is God, but also in the Parousia, the Holy One of Israel is revealed, making manifest what the sinners do.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rational soul is redeemed because Jesus gave his own rational soul as its ransom.
comments.comment: The rational soul is redeemed, because Jesus gave his own soul as a ransom for it, and it is clearly a rational soul. For just as he redeemed the bodies of men by giving a body of the same essence for them, so he redeemed rational souls by placing a rational soul for them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'my soul, which thou hast redeemed' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm is not about Solomon but about the spiritual Solomon, Jesus, whose name means peace and who made one people of Greeks and Hebrews.
comments.comment: Regarding Psalm 71, the psalm does not pertain to the father of Rehoboam, Solomon, but to the one called spiritual, through the participation in the name; for it is interpreted with a Greek voice of peace. For who is he who says, 'Jesus, I give you my peace'? Concerning this, the theologian writes: 'For He is our peace' (Eph 2:14), and 'He preached peace to you who are far off, and peace to those who are near' (Eph 2:17), having dissolved the enmity that divided Greeks from Hebrews, as one flock and establishing one people from the nations and Jews. Thus, being shown to be peaceful through his works, he who was born according to the flesh from a virgin is from David. Indeed, it is written concerning him, 'The Book of the generation of Jesus Christ, Son of David' (Matt 1:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy men, seeking salvation, prayed unceasingly to the Father, and at the start of this psalm they asked that He give His judgment to the king.
comments.comment: Wishing to be saved from the hand of the powerful and becoming a cause of eternal salvation, they were continually and unceasingly sending prayer to the Father, at times saying, 'Show us, Lord, your mercy and grant us your salvation,' and at other times, 'Send out your light and your truth.' Concerning his sending and at the beginning of the present Psalm 71, they prayed saying, 'O God, give your judgment to the king and your righteousness to the son of the king' (Psalm 72:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Solomon is only a type, for Christ alone is the king who applies the exactness of righteousness so that his subjects are not wronged.
comments.comment:
The glory of Christ after the passion is hymned. Solomon is a type: the peace of his kingdom, the protection of the righteous, the glory of his wisdom, and the honor he received from all people. But beyond the type is this: that the days of the king endure to the consummation, and his peace and his fruit become most brilliant. For these things in no way fit Solomon, who lived only a short time, had opponents, and left no fruit from himself except one son—and that son did not preserve the kingdom handed down to him. But Christ's power is perpetual and unshaken, and his fruit is most glorious: those who believe. And the other things that came to pass in a typical way in Solomon are more perfectly fulfilled in him, as the discourse will explain point by point.

“O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king's son, to judge your people in righteousness and your poor in judgment” (Psalm 72:1-2; LXX 71:1,2). The Lord Christ is both king and son of King David according to the flesh, and for this reason he arose from the royal line, so that he might set right the ancestral kingdom according to Isaiah's prophecy, make it divine instead of human, and—what did not exist in any human kingdom—apply the exactness of righteousness to his subjects and grant to the wronged that they not be wronged. For not even in David himself was this preserved. Even though he was most righteous and pleasing to God beyond others, he still became the perpetrator of injustice against Uriah. And Solomon's case was even greater injustice, stretching into impiety through the making of idols. But this is the king foretold through Isaiah and Jeremiah: a righteous king seated on a throne established with mercy, judging and seeking judgment and hastening righteousness, as Isaiah says (Isaiah 16:5), and understanding and doing judgment and righteousness, as Jeremiah says (Jeremiah 23:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains whom the psalm is about and how the king's righteousness differs from David's and Solomon's.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The people judged in righteousness are those of the circumcision, the poor are the moderate in mind, and princes and angels bring peace to the whole human race through the blood of the cross.
comments.comment: Regarding Psalm 71:2, 'To judge your people in righteousness (clearly those of the circumcision) and your poor in judgment' (Ps 72:2); for those coming to the gospel from the nations are not called poor because of a poverty of unbelief and wickedness. But if the poor of God can be the moderate in mind, according to 'Blessed are the poor in spirit' (Matt 5:3), then He visits them. Regarding Psalm 71:3, He protects the great-minded through virtue, the high-born and those called princes, to take up peace toward the people. And even if the high-born and princes turn out to be archangels and angels, the whole human race is a people toward whom they are called to bring peace, since Jesus, through the blood of the cross, made peace between those in the heavens and those on the earth, who previously were at odds on the earth because of wickedness toward those in the heavens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Through the Lamb's sacrifice the world's sin is released and peace is made between heaven and earth, with Moses and the prophets as mountains and the more advanced believers as the higher mountains above the lower hills.
comments.comment: The Lamb of God is sacrificed, and by this the sin of the world is released, the sin of those upon the earth; peace is being made between those in the heavens and those upon the earth, joy being made in the heavens before the angels for those repenting from sin. And if Moses and the prophets are signified by mountains and hills, let them take up peace toward the people from the nations who disbelieved, knowing what they themselves had previously spoken concerning this calling. And since even among those possessing virtue, some more so and others having it less, it must be said of those who possess it more that they are increased in greater measure through practice and knowledge of the truth, that they are the higher mountains compared to the lower hills. Ps 71:4 For it is the work of him who received from God judgment and righteousness, to judge the poor of the people.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'mountains and hills' that bring peace to the people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saying about remaining before the moon is said of the anointed, since the church, composed of all generations, is established through him and in him.
comments.comment: The same is said to the one remaining with the anointed, what was said to him: 'You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,' Ps 110:4 and 'Before the moon, generations of generations, the same one established me before the age.' Psalm 72:5 It is said 'He remains with the anointed' concerning the flesh which he clothed himself with, the soul being breathed into it, being both rational and spiritual; for he remains with the anointed of righteousness because of the indivisible union. But even before the moon, which has the analogy to the sun, there exists a generation of generations, for the church is established through him and in him, composed of all the generations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sun's endurance agrees with Gabriel's promise of a reign forever.
comments.comment: Symmachus rendered it, “And they will fear him as long as the sun endures” (Ps 72:5), in agreement with what Gabriel said to the holy virgin: “The Lord will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever” (Psalm 71 [72]) (Luke 1:32).
comments.selected_reason: Links the verse to the angel's promise of an everlasting kingdom.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The moon, which has only borrowed light from the sun, stands for the church, which knows in part now and will be made perfect when the sun of righteousness comes.
comments.comment: We say that the moon signifies the church. For the moon receives light as a derivative from the sun and does not possess it from itself; so the church, being upon the earth, knows in part and has not been truly illuminated, destined one day to be according to the sun … For by the Word, knowing in part is abolished, and the surpassing knowledge will be established. Thus the lunar condition of the church will be abolished when the sun of righteousness comes, shining like the sun, completing the church of the righteous in the kingdom of their own Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the moon as an image of the church receiving its light from Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fleece on which the Son came down like rain is the Mother of God.
comments.comment: For what is David's fleece, on which the Son of the God and King of all, who is without beginning together with his own Begetter and reigns with him, came down like rain (Psalm 72:6)? Is it not, most clearly, you [the Mother of God]?
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: As rain brings fertility to the earth, the Savior's visit brought righteousness, and since the cloud is Israel and the earth the Gentiles, the rain fell on the Gentiles and peace spreads to all.
comments.comment:
Just as the rain comes upon the earth bringing fertility, so the visitation of the Savior to men has become the generation of righteousness.

It must be said that the cloud signifies Israel, and the earth signifies the Gentiles. Since previously it descended upon the cloud, and then from there upon the earth. For because Israel disobeyed and did not receive the one who had come, there was a transition to the rain upon the earth, so that all the men upon it might be moistened, rather being watered from the drops to bear spiritual fruits. (Psalm 72:7; LXX 71:7) In the days of the Savior's visitation, the light of practical virtue of righteousness rises, and with it the evangelical standing through the faith of Jesus among the living, and the appropriate peace, possessing a great multitude, so as to extend until the completion of the world. For this is what the reflection of the moon signifies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rain coming down on the earth and the peace that follows.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness dawned and peace abounded from Christ's birth, as God prepared the nations to come under one emperor so the apostles could teach all nations.
comments.comment:
For “in his days righteousness dawned, and abundance of peace” (Psalm 72:7) came about, beginning from his birth. God was preparing the nations for his teaching, so that they would come under one Roman emperor, and so that the nations’ lack of contact with one another, owing to the many kingdoms, would not make it harder for Jesus’ apostles to do what Jesus commanded them when he said: “Go and make disciples of all the nations” (Matthew 28:19).

It is clear that Jesus was born in the reign of Augustus, who, if I may put it so, brought the many peoples of the earth to one level under a single kingdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'abundance of peace' in his days.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Falling down before the king, who sees hidden things, shows genuine submission.
comments.comment: Regarding those called through their existence out of impiety, falling down before the king in a manner of recognition, the Jews, who are the king's enemies, will indeed be lacking. And it also seems that the Ethiopians fall down before him; the falling down before the king, who sees the hidden things, demonstrates genuine submission.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The islands are souls that stay firm when the sea storms, and the Savior calls them to himself.
comments.comment: And islands are brought forward. But these are souls, possessing themselves firmly and unmovably, even when the sea stirs up a gale and a storm. To these, the Savior says: 'Dedicate yourselves, islands, to me, being renewed by the newness of the Spirit, bearing the new human being created according to God.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gift-bringing kings can be taken as the apostles and teachers of the nations, and any believer who brings good deeds brings his gift to the All-King.
comments.comment: It is possible to take as those worshiping him and offering gifts the teachers of all the nations, the apostles and disciples and the successors of these; for they offer gifts to God from the men who are profited by them. And if even one of the faithful brings gifts of praiseworthy deeds and true mindset, it is as if kings bring their own gifts to the only and one All-King.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the gift-bringing kings are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Isaiah and Haggai foretell that the wealth and chosen things of the nations will come and fill the house with glory.
comments.comment: Isaiah also says these things to Jerusalem: “The wealth of the sea and of nations and peoples will turn to you; herds of camels will come, and the camels of Midian will cover you; elephants will come from Sheba bearing gold, and they will bring frankincense, and they will proclaim the salvation of God.” And through Haggai it is said: “Once more I will shake heaven and earth and sea and dry land, and I will shake all the nations; and the chosen things of all the nations will come, and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord Almighty” (Haggai 2:6-7) (Psalm 72:16; LXX 71:16).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's name is honored for deliverance.
comments.comment: It is also written that his name is honored, having delivered them from so many evils (Ps 72:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Magi bring frankincense for the child's divinity and gold for his kingship, as the psalm says gold will be given to him.
