comments.comment: It has been said to wise men that the divinity which the Magi brought to the child born of Mary, with gold and myrrh and frankincense, is shown by such a thought: since the one born of the virgin is simultaneously God and man, but also is a king, according to the one confessing his divinity, it is fitting to bring frankincense as a gift, and to present gold along with this frankincense because he confesses him as king. For it is said in the seventy-first Psalm, and that the one who has arrived is king and gold is presented to him, thus: 'Give the king his due judgment' (Psalm 72:1), and with other things: 'And he shall live and gold shall be given to him from the Arabia' (Psalm 72:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why gold is given to the king.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The grass is those who are flesh in their wisdom and seek glory from one another and so wither, while those who stay within the spiritual city are never shaken.
comments.comment:
They glorify him through all the days of this present age or of the enlightened life of those blessing (Psalm 72:16; LXX 71:16a). The outcomes of the anticipatory proclamations are more extreme than these mountains, for the one prophesied has become a support in the land (Psalm 72:16; LXX 71:16a). …

'the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree, and like a cedar in Lebanon he shall multiply' (Psalm 92:12). For when the fruit of the support has been multiplied and exceeded, the Jews who were unfaithful to the Savior shall spring up from the city of Jerusalem like grass from the earth, because of the parched state and the rapid drying up, so named and most justly.

Since they have become flesh in their wisdom, having been unfaithful to the Savior and seeking glory from one another rather than that which is given by God alone, they shall spring up from the earth as grass; for all flesh is grass and all the glory of man is like the flower of the grass. For they shall not merely bloom, but shall spring up and wither.

And also those of the grass, whether out of the city or not in the city, shall spring up, those of whom the word is. For those who hastened toward life and wisdom outside the spiritual city, Jerusalem, were dried up like the parched and rapidly drying grass; but of the one remaining within the city, nothing of this sort was experienced; for 'he who dwells in Jerusalem shall never be shaken' (Psalm 125:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's children appear in every city like grass from the earth.
comments.comment: For the whole inhabited world is luxuriant and has blossomed with the fruit of Christ, and an uncountable multitude of Christ’s children appears in every city like grass from the earth (Psalm 72:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the grass springing from the earth as the multitude of believers.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The nations blessed in him call the Lord blessed because He alone has done wonders.
comments.comment: The nations, which are to be blessed in him, make happy the one who blessed them, saying, 'Blessed is the Lord, the God of the discerning race, who alone has done wondrous things, having freed us from idolatry and the treatment of wandering demons; for truly it is a wonder.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is blessed and why the Lord is blessed for His wonders.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Blessed' stands for 'glorified': God is blessed by His works and blesses creatures by sanctifying them.
comments.comment: 'Blessed is the Lord God of Israel' (Psalm 72:18) he said, instead of 'being glorified' or 'being praised'. For God is blessed by his works, that is, he is glorified; but he himself blesses the resident creatures, that is, he sanctifies them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'Blessed'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'Only One' who does wonders is the Son together with the Father, and his glory, for which his name is blessed unto the age, is the glory to come of which Paul and Peter speak.
comments.comment: Regarding what concerns the calling of the Gentiles. The 'Only One' should not be troubled, for the Son cannot do anything contrary to the Father, unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. For the 'Only One' and such things taken regarding divinity declare a Father and a Son, as it is presented from the prophet; for, as is said to the Father: 'Tall Sabaean men shall cross over to you, and worship you, and pray in you, for God is in you and there is no god besides you; for you are God, and we knew it not, O God of Israel, Savior' (Isa 45:14). Who is the glory whose name is blessed, who has made the worthless and gloryless glorious and honorable—those who are repentant? … If indeed his glory is that which his name is blessed for unto the age, concerning which Paul writes: 'Not worthy are the sufferings of the present time compared to the glory that is about to be revealed to us, stand fast' (Rom 8:18). For especially this and the proclamation concerning it we find to be eternally hymned, as Peter said; this is what the witness of his sufferings and the glory to come declares: 'And a companion of that glory' (1 Peter 5:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The second book of psalms, like the first, ends with a blessing that sounds out the 'Amen', and this psalm closes it.
comments.comment: The second book of psalms also ended with a blessing that sounds out the “Amen,” just as the first book’s “May it be” makes clear, as has been said. For the end of that first book was Psalm 40, spoken in reference to Christ, and the end of this second book is the one just mentioned, Psalm 71.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Here David's prayers for the throne's eternal permanence are fulfilled, so this psalm is the end of the collection.
comments.comment: Here, then, David’s prayers are fulfilled—the prayers he made for the eternal permanence of the throne when he said: “Lord, the word you spoke concerning the house of your servant and concerning your servant, let it be made faithful forever; and do as you have spoken, and let your name be exalted forever, while they say, ‘The Lord Almighty is the God of Israel,’ and the house of David your servant is raised up.” Unreasonably, then, was the heading written on the next psalm: “The hymns of David son of Jesse are ended.” For this psalm is the end of that collection, and part of the thanksgiving for the fulfillment of David’s prayers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm closes with 'the prayers of David are ended'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'As' expresses intensity, not likeness, so 'as good is God' means very good.
comments.comment: The word “as” does not express likeness but intensity. It is like the phrase “as good is God to Israel” (Psalm 73:1, LXX 72:1), and “as I have loved your law, O Lord” (Psalm 119:97, LXX 118:97), meaning “I have loved it very much.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'as good is God to Israel'.
comments.author: Oecumenius
comments.work: Fragments on the Letter to the Philippians

comments.capsule: The words 'but a little' show that the speaker did not fall at all, for his steps were spilled out only a little, as when a runner is startled and turns back.
comments.comment: And here: 'How good is God to Israel, to those of an upright heart. But my feet were shaken but a little' (Psalm 73:1-2), makes the soul manifest. And this 'but a little' shows that he is not entirely slipped. For he who says: 'I was slaughtered but a little,' shows that he was not slaughtered. 'My steps were spilled out a little' (Psalm 73:2). I was running well, I was walking as was necessary, I was taking steps straightly. But these were spilled out only a little. And it is spilled out when the runner is startled and turns toward the rear.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'almost slipped' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked, clothed in injustice, are held by impiety as well as wickedness, and their sin passes from thought into act and into the heart's disposition.
comments.comment:
Since those about whom the word is are held not only by wickedness but also by impiety, they are clothed in injustice.

And there is the moral wickedness according to the soul, and with this impiety, they think impiously concerning all dogmas. And also to say that their injustice will come forth as from a cloud; then, when it comes forth, the sin is practically fulfilled, no longer remaining only in the thoughts. It has passed into a disposition of the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked refuse to act on their natural thoughts of the good, so that virtue is a joke to them and blasphemy against God is ready at hand.
comments.comment: Instead of “They passed through into the disposition of the heart,” Aquila rendered, “They passed by the watchtowers of the heart.” This means they are unwilling to carry out any of their natural thoughts, nor do they practice what they understand to be good, but they turn away from these things. Virtue is a joke to them; slander against their inferiors comes easily; blasphemy against God is ready at hand; their tongue is quick against human beings. And this is what “their tongue passed through upon the earth” means (Psalm 73:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wicked do with their hearts and tongues.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The wicked first plan evil in their thoughts, then speak deceitfully and lift their mouths against God, slandering His justice, His creation and His providence.
comments.comment: Having previously disposed themselves according to wickedness, they not only established the evil to themselves but also desired to be harmful to others. Then, after passing into a disposition of wickedness, having thought in malice, they spoke deceitfully as if of good things. They were lifted up, he says, as if to speak even against God, slandering His justice, His creation, and His providence; such as are those who, at the time of the stars, having set their preconceptions, and those who, making the heavens and the creation themselves instead of the Creator, lift up their mouth to heaven. They were torn apart, rather they were consumed, as if their tongue had passed through the earth against the Most High, so that all who hear might know what vain and impious things are being philosophized against God and His providence (Psalm 73:8-9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The impious boast loudly, and God's people take Him as the starting point of a good return.
comments.comment: Of the impious boasting loudly (Psalm 73:10; LXX 72:10), the people of God calls as a starting point for a good return, desiring to enjoy the contemplations of the light of day. And the 'Here' referring to the one saying this is God, such as what was said to Moses: 'And you shall stand with me' (Deuteronomy 5:31).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who want to cast out providence ask how God can be known through human things, confessing that they know God while ignorant of the manner of knowing.
comments.comment: Those wanting to cast out providence and injustice, having spoken toward the height (Psalm 73:11; LXX 72:11-13), bring forth such words; how can one know God through human things? For does the intellect not have a sensory, organic power? For his understanding does not receive the forms of the seen and the heard, so that, having known, he might also know providential and royal things as he wishes? And having said before, 'How will God be known?', they confess to knowing God, but they are ignorant of the manner of knowing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thought that God does not govern is the difficulty of human reasoning, but those who suffer now are more blessed in the future than the impious who prosper.
comments.comment: This [“How does God know?”] is the voice of those who have lost their natural reasoning because of the good things that came to them unprofitably, leading them into injustices. For prospering contrary to reason produces thoughts that the world is not governed according to reason … This is the difficulty of human reasoning: to repent of zeal for virtue as though it were not good or profitable. Such thoughts often enter many people’s minds, and he intends to heal them by his word. To destroy the impious reasoning, he confirms the more pious reasoning through the person of God. For what is said truly requires God as guarantor: that the pious who now suffer hardship are more blessed in the future state than the impious who prosper to the end.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the wicked's prosperity tempts the righteous and how the question is answered.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist speaks for men's ignorance of God's judgments, seeing sinners prosper.
comments.comment: By personifying the ignorance of men regarding judgments, happy David says: 'Behold, these sinners, though they prosper, possess wealth for eternity (Psalm 73:12). And I said: Therefore I justified my heart in vain, and washed my hands among the innocent (Psalm 73:13), and became whipped all day long.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He calls himself beast-like only in comparison with God's knowledge.
comments.comment: And after these things he says: 'I became beast-like beside You (Psalm 73:22).' And the 'beside You' is good; for as regarding the knowledge of God, he says, 'I became beast-like.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'before thee' in 'I was as a beast before thee'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Like Moses and Abraham, who confessed weakness only after beginning to speak to God, the speaker is a beast before Him, and only one with virtue and piety can say 'I am always with you'.
comments.comment: … 'I have become like a beast in your sight.' … In this way it is said again by Moses: 'I am not able to speak from before I began to speak to your servant; heavy of mouth and slow of tongue am I.' … In this way, Abraham spoke to the Creator: 'Since I began to speak to the Lord, I myself am earth and ashes,' he who was ignorant before speaking to God. … And it is not by chance to say, 'I am always with you,' but only to the one possessing virtue and piety in an orderly and consistent manner, which is made straight through the intervals.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'I am with You always' means that the speaker knows through God's participation and communion.
comments.comment: Then, in order to show that he was assuming the face of men, he says: 'But I am with You always (Psalm 73:23),' indicating that: by Your participation and communion, I know. Similar to 'I became beast-like beside You' is 'But I am irrational' and 'I am earth and ash.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's taking hold of the right hand shows that He does not only exhort but actively helps, since man's nature is too weak to swim out of evil alone.
comments.comment: This is a sign for you, and a very clear one, that we are not whetted by words only, and leave sin by exhortations into the mind, but that the Savior God of all has come even to this gentleness toward us, as to make the help active, according at least to the, 'You took hold of my right hand, and in your counsel you guided me.' (Psalm 73:23–24) For since man's nature is not very strong, nor sufficiently able to swim out of the evil, God somehow contends along with it toward this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God holds the speaker by the right hand.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The speaker rests and trusts the one who governs well, and is brought to blessed glory.
comments.comment: Symmachus later said, “Honor received me.” And in another sense: I rested, knowing to be silent and to trust you as the one who governs our affairs well, and so to be with you always; therefore you took hold of me; you placed good glory in me, you brought me to blessed glory (Psalm 73:24).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is not in a place, so no one is separated from Him locally, but He is far from the thought of the wicked and near to the righteous, and the good is to be joined to God.
comments.comment: … 'Since God is not in a place, locally no one is separated from him, but he is far from the thought of the unrighteous and evil, and near to the righteous and good and the cause of all things; and since the approaching of virtue takes hold of him and saves, the standing away from him having badness and impiety brings destruction.' The same applies to how sin causes God to distance himself. It is fitting that it is said: 'Behold, those who distance themselves shall perish,' … Having moved many to long distances and many words about the essence of the good, the wise man revealed himself through brevity, saying that the good is strictly to be joined to God and to place hope upon him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being 'far from' and near to God means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turns from the sinner only after the sinner has first distanced himself, His wrath is not a human passion, and His pasture is the words of the Spirit, the law and the prophets.
comments.comment: God rejects the sinner, after he has first distanced himself. For he says, 'He who comes to me I will by no means cast out' (John 6:37). Do not think the wrath and anger of God is against us; it is far from senselessness. For regarding God, no human passion is indicated, but rather the exceeding turning away through the words spoken, for he says he endures the sheep of his pasture. The pasture of God is the words of the Spirit, the law and the prophets, in which as a shepherd pastures the righteous sheep.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'In the midst of the earth' fits Christ, who did not bring His flesh down from heaven but was born of a woman who was one of those on the earth.
comments.comment: If the earth is commanded to make righteousness spring up, let no one be annoyed, when he considers that the Psalmist too says somewhere, of God the Father and of Emmanuel Himself: “He worked righteousness in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74:12). For Christ did not bring His own flesh down to us from above, out of heaven; rather, He was born according to the flesh of a woman (Galatians 4:4), who was herself one of those on the earth. So when He is said to have become the fruit and shoot of the earth, you will understand, as I said, that He was born according to the flesh of a woman taken for this service, though she was one of those from the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why salvation is worked 'in the midst of the earth'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His kingship, like his divinity, comes through no other and is before the age.
comments.comment: Just as divinity does not come to him through another, so neither does the kingship nor the holiness. 'God is our king before the age' (Psalm 74:12). And the kingship before the age is through him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sea is the turbulence and wickedness of life, the dragons' heads are the rulers of this age, demons, sorcery and idolatry, and only the Savior can crush them.
comments.comment:
The whole life of man is taken as a sea raised for contemplation. God strengthened this by his power to lead it from more abundant snow and more intense storm into happiness and serenity, as it is said, 'He who turns the sea into dry land' (Psalm 66:6). The Savior crushed not the many heads of many dragons, but also the many heads of one upon the water, the water being understood as the wickedness of the unstable and disordered affairs of life. For in such water the dragons work harmfully, and he who excels them is written about as king over all those in the waters and how he dwells in the sea.

For this great and spacious sea shows the turbulence of affairs and the wickedness, saying, 'In this small animals are tossed with large ones, and ships are driven about by playing with the dragon within it' (Psalm 104:25-26). Many heads of dragons are crushed; these are the rulers of this age who promise wisdom, and with them principalities and powers, cosmic rulers of this world, and also spiritual evils and the whole host of demons and opposing powers. And the heads of these dragons are divinations, sorceries, superstitions, and all that contributes to idolatry, but also false doctrines and deceptive practices. The work of the Savior alone is to crush the heads of the said dragons. It did not seem to be possible from any other than him to be strong.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sea and the dragons' heads that God breaks.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As the flesh of Jesus nourishes the sons of light, the sons of darkness are fed with fleshly things of wickedness and false glory.
comments.comment: And he provided all of it, this food, for the Ethiopian peoples. For he did not need others to be carried away by the flesh and parts of it, nor the Ethiopian peoples, being sons of darkness and night through ignorance. Just as the flesh of Jesus is true food, since all the sons of light are nourished from its use and eating, being enlightened beyond a white snow, so the Ethiopian children of the inner man will be fed with the fleshly parts (that is, the things of wickedness and false glory), which will be handed over to the desires of their hearts into uncleanness, and additionally into passions of dishonor and an unproven mind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Drying up the ancient rivers shows God's power to divert waters, and hints that the nations will be watered from the rock, which is Christ.
comments.comment: Symmachus puts it this way: “You dried up the ancient rivers” (Psalm 74:15) … For the fact that springs gush up and rivers pour out from them, while elsewhere the streams of ancient rivers are dried up—this displays the power that works wonders. He says the same in another psalm: “He turned rivers into a desert, and streams of water into thirst” (Psalm 107:33). For it is easy for him to divert the flow of waters wherever he wishes. Through this, however, the word also hints at something else: that to the Jews, because of their lawlessness, he will not bring the streams of the prophetic rivers, but the nations that were long a desert he will water with the torrents from the rock. “And the rock,” says the divine apostle, “is Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the drying up of rivers shows.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The enemy who mocks the Lord is the devil, and Caiaphas the high priest also mocked the Savior.
comments.comment: An enemy mocking the Lord, the devil, but the people is a flock of the other invisible and evil powers (Psalm 74:18; LXX 73:18). The high priest Caiaphas, the enemy, mocked the Savior Christ, and the people, having cried out the Jews, provoked his name: 'Aaron, Aaron, crucify him' (Psalm 74:18; LXX 73:18–21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The beasts to which the confessing soul is not handed over are the devil and his lions, and the poor of God are those who have given up wealth or the wealth of wickedness.
comments.comment: It is not true the preceding text regarding the taking of sensible beasts. For many perfect men, witnesses of the truth, were eaten by beasts. Let it be said, therefore, that a soul confessing its faith will not be handed over to those beasts, concerning whom it is written, 'A wandering sheep of Israel; lions drove him out.' The Lord crushed the teeth of these lions. Satan is among these, as the apostle Peter writes, 'Your adversary the devil walks like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour' (1 Peter 5:8). But the poor of God are those who are able, having left his possessions having been deprived of wealth, according to those saying, 'Behold, we have left all and have followed you,' whereas others become differently poor, having cast away the wealth of wickedness in false glory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The beasts to which the confessing soul is not to be delivered are the opposing energies or evil thoughts.
comments.comment: And since we say that the mind of man is man according to another understanding, having been commanded to become according to the image and likeness of God, we appropriately receive that he rules those beasts about which the saint says he sends up a prayer, 'Do not deliver to the beasts a soul confessing to you' (Psalm 74:19), which were the opposing energies, outside of which he prays for the confessing soul to be, or evil thoughts being subjected by them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks God to look upon the covenant made with the fathers.
comments.comment: After these things, he entreats God to look upon the covenant which he established with the fathers around Abraham, so that he may not leave the ones from his seed incomplete.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Earthly people, whose minds are darkened by ignorance, do not walk as citizens of heaven.
comments.comment: It must be said that the clouds of iniquity have filled those who are darkened in the earth; for they do not walk upon the earth as citizens of heaven, but because of this they have an earthly veil of life, their intellect being darkened by ignorance. (Psalm 74:20)
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'dark places of the earth' as minds darkened by ignorance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is asked to bring back those led into dark places so they sing with gladness.
comments.comment: Remember your covenant, and bring back those who have been led away into dark places to dwell in your enlightened land again, receiving the prayer of those humbled by evils and put to shame, and granting them to sing hymns with gladness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer to remember the covenant and bring the oppressed back.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Having reached incorruption, we thank God as the cause of the good achieved, and still ask for more because we are not yet perfect.
comments.comment: If to corrupt and to be corrupted is often, according to the Divine Scripture, to sin, then incorruption and to possess it signifies virtue; for it is said, 'The grace is with those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption.' And since it is necessary for Him who began the good work to bring it to completion, that is to say, to lead it to an end, 'Lest you be corrupted' is said, fleeing corruption until the end, so that no one remains in it but remains in incorruption. And this achievement is great, so a Psalm of song is sent up regarding its fulfillment. Having reached the end so as not to be corrupted, with incorruption having been achieved, we shall thankfully confess to you, God, as the cause of the good things that have existed and are being achieved; for with you and from you these are made firm. And we desire to receive even more upon the good things having been achieved; for we are not yet perfect. We shall indeed confess concerning the things that have existed, but we shall call upon your favor in order to receive more.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ gives thanks for salvation as a man, and judges between those who dissolve with the earth and those who stand as pillars.
comments.comment: Christ, the cause and maker of incorruption, speaks now to the prophet the words that are spoken—he who saves as God and offers thanks for salvation as a human being to the Father (Psalm 75:1). “To you, then,” he says, “we will offer confessions and thanksgivings for salvation; we will recount your wonders, Father. When the church assembled from all humanity,” he says, “can hear the things concerning you, and all people are brought near to serve you.” “Mine also,” he says, “is the discernment over all things, saving those worthy of salvation from those who are perishing: those who have set their minds on earthly things dissolve together with the earth, but those who have set their minds on heavenly things remain like pillars for the establishment of the new creation.”
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who dwell in the earth set their minds on earthly things and grow fat toward God, and the Savior's fire is cast on such.
comments.comment:
But to dwell on the earth is from above as if being received in praise, whereas to reside as a sojourner is as if being received in mockery. For he says, 'Woe to all those dwelling on the earth' (Revelation 8:13), and 'From the face of the north shall the evils be burned upon those dwelling on the earth' (Jeremiah 1:14).

For the one thinking of the things on the earth and doing the works of the flesh, his mindset is made fat toward God because of dwelling on the earth, according to the saying: 'He was made fat, enlarged, and left empty.' Such were those whose covering they closed up in the earth, concerning whom it has been said, 'Their iniquity shall come out like the scent of a covering.' The piercing teaching of the Savior, having said, 'Fire has come to be cast upon the earth' (Luke 12:49), has stretched out such a fatness of wickedness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pillars of the earth are the heralds of truth and the church, and the Savior sets them firmly in God's house.
comments.comment: The Savior strengthens the pillars of this ordered earth, those having a well-tuned life and a true mindset; rather, regarding the heralds of truth, it has been said, 'Pillars of heaven were stretched out,' having been winged with heavenly wings, as it is said concerning them, 'He who is heavenly, such also are the heavenly ones.' It has also been written concerning all of the glorious church, to which Christ presented himself as a 'pillar and foundation of the truth' (1 Tim 3:15). The Savior, establishing all these pillars in the house of God, does not make them unsteady, saying, 'I will lay the foundation of my holy house' (Ps 74:7b).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pillars of the earth are the holy apostles, made firm by the grace of the Spirit.
comments.comment: And Christ also said somewhere through David’s voice concerning both the earth and the holy apostles: ‘I have made firm her pillars.’ (Psalm 75:3) For the holy disciples who hold up the earth were made firm, having put on the power from on high—that is, the grace through the Holy Spirit. And they themselves were pillars, according to conformation as toward Christ, and according to likeness in grace through Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the pillars as the apostles who hold up the earth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: The 'pillars' are the power that holds the earth together.
comments.comment: But if you ever hear in the Psalms, “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:3 (LXX)), consider the power that holds it together to be called pillars. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'pillars' of the earth are.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Christ keeps the pillars of the church steady, and the apostles told all the world not to deviate or speak injustice against God.
comments.comment: Having strengthened the pillars of the church, he grants to the rest not to deviate. He says this regarding the established order and the completed work of Christ, through whom the earth and all who dwell in it were ordered. Furthermore, to the inhabitants of the whole inhabited world, it was testified through the apostles not to deviate nor to speak injustice against God, paying heed to the many errors.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must not speak against God as if he did not provide: human fortunes are ruled not by the stars or demons but by his righteous judgment.
comments.comment: One must not dare against God, nor be made bold by a conceit of wisdom, nor exalt oneself, saying terrible and unjust things against God—as though he does not provide, nor judge each one righteously, but hands over affairs to the risings and settings of the stars, and as though the stars dispose human affairs either well or badly, and not only the stars but also the demons worshiped in the high places. For these things are not so, not even close; rather, all things are encompassed by the righteous judgment of God, concerning both the humbling and the exalting of human beings—some being cast down, others raised up.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that promotion and humbling come from God's judgment, not from the stars.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Promotion comes from God alone, who sets up and removes kings and raises the poor.
comments.comment: The faithful, being pious, are such that the works of providence come not from the east or the west, nor from wicked caretakers, but from God. He himself establishes kings and removes them; he raises the poor from the earth and from poverty lifts up the needy (Psalm 75:6-7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God humbles the circumcised and lifts up the Gentiles.
comments.comment: Regarding the verse about receiving from the Gentiles and from the circumcised people, one must also stand regarding the humbling of the circumcised and the lifting up of the Gentiles (Psalm 75:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cup in God's hand is tilted from one sinner to another so that punishment leads to repentance.
comments.comment: … This cup in the hand of God is tilted from one to another, many a time for the one being punished, so that through the evils he did, he might be justified by repentance, and the one who was glorifying himself for a little while might fall into being good. However, even if it tilts from this to that, the reaper does not pour out upon men, but upon the sinners of the earth, and upon the devil and the robbers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cup is tipped from one sinner to the next until all drink, and the lees are left for the worst.
comments.comment: “he trampled a winepress” clarifies what is said in the Psalms about the punishment of sinners: “a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed mixture,” (Psalm 75:8) being tipped from this one being punished upon that one being punished, until “all the sinners of the earth” drink, the lees being left for those still more sinful than these, into whom last “the lees” will be emptied.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the cup of wrath and who drinks the dregs.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He sings to Jacob's God, who strengthens him to break the horns sinners used against the weak.
comments.comment: I give thanks that I am not found responsible for any of those accused; I rejoice and sing for ever to the God of the patriarch Jacob, who has given me strength, as if to break all the horns of the sinners, which they used against the weaker ones, being like horned bulls.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the breaking of the sinners' horns means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked perish with their wickedness, and the horns of the righteous are exalted with a power that cannot be cut down.
comments.comment: At such an end, he says, in which the wicked perish together with their wickedness, I will make the recounting of God's wonders, and I will cut down the strong things of the impious as if lopping off horns; but the horns of the righteous will be exalted, since they have received from God a power that cannot be cut down. Then they will be exalted when they reign together with their own king.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The horns of sinners are many and are broken, but the righteous has one horn, and it is exalted.
comments.comment: Having said this, he did not bring forth 'And my horns shall be exalted,' but 'of the righteous.' This is customary for the saints through approaching blindness; and they teach that it is for every man to exist in Christ, so that the righteous, having broken the horns of the sinners, may have his horn exalted. And also to say it in a plural way: the horns of the sinners are being broken, but in a singular way: the horn of the righteous is exalted.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The horn stands for the rulers, in whom a nation's strength lies, and for the arrogance of the leading part.
comments.comment: Like the word in David: “he will crush all the horns of the sinners.” (Psalm 75:10) And he means now the rulers, in whom is the strength of the nation just as in the horn-bearing among animals, and because they stand out from the body as rulers from the subjects. And Daniel also likened the kingdoms to horns. And horn also shows the arrogance of the leading part, as in: “do not lift your horn unto height.” (Psalm 75:5)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a 'horn' means in the verse: strength and arrogance of rulers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Of old God was known only in Judea, but his praise must now rise through all the earth.
comments.comment: And this song, that is, the praise fitting for him, had to arise not only in the land of the Jews but from one end of the earth to the other, that is, through all that is under heaven. For of old God was known in Judea, and his name was great in Israel alone (Psalm 76:1). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: God was known in Judea alone, but now through Christ all nations are called to know him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing and being known differ: God is known in Judea, and his name is great in Israel.
comments.comment: … It is not the same to be the knowing and the known, so that the known, being known, might be able to be known even of the unknown. For in this way, according to what was said in Judea, that God is known, and following that, in the one inhabiting Judea, Israel, great is His name, I say, of the known.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm foretells the victory of the righteous.
comments.comment: A good end and a victory of the righteous according to God is prophesied, the prophecy previously declared in the preceding psalm having been brought forward to greater clarity and brightness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To become God's dwelling we must drive out passions and evils and have peace, and this is said of the holy church.
comments.comment: In every way the disturbance of passions and the war of evils must be driven away, so that having the peace which surpasses all understanding, we may become a place of God. For we shall not only be His habitation, but also intending to be observers of truth and virtue; for His habitation is found in the given Zion. The things said will be applied to the holy church, as a place of God established in peace and the …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for God to have his dwelling in Zion: a peaceful soul and the church.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, not we, brings peace to his dwelling by crushing the bows, shield, sword and war from which the evil one sent afflictions.
comments.comment: His dwelling-place. For he says, 'Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion.' And since these things are established not by our power but by the grace of God, the word attributes to Him the cause of peace, saying: 'There He crushed the powers of bows, the shield and the sword and war' (Psalm 76:3). For peace prevails in the place of God once the rulers of bows are crushed, from whom the evil one, sending his flaming arrows, was making afflictions and disordered movements, of which he was the cause. Along with the aforementioned bows, the related shield and sword are also crushed, and along with them, those called war are crushed; for the Lord is the one crushing wars (Psalm 76:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the dwelling of God is made peaceful: the Lord crushes the weapons of the evil one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'mountains of prey' are the sanctified things, meaning mountains of food, since the psalms use 'prey' for food.
comments.comment: He calls the sanctified things “mountains of prey,” that is, mountains of food. For he called food “prey” also in Psalm 131 (132), saying, “Blessing I will bless her prey,” which Symmachus rendered there as “provision.” And in “He gave food to those who fear him” in Psalm 110 (111), Aquila and Symmachus said “prey.”
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The 'eternal mountains' are the prophets and saints, from whom God illuminates the knowledge of the truth.
comments.comment: Regarding his [God's] mountains, the prophets have said in accordance with the subject that there is a height belonging to them not only of knowledge and wisdom, but also of the application of practical life. For concerning these things, the hymn-singer spoke of the origin of all: 'You shine wondrously from eternal mountains' (Psalm 76:4). How could they not be eternal mountains, from which God wondrously illuminates the knowledge of the truth and broadly the knowledge concerning the Trinity, those who gaze upon unseeing eternal things according to the apostolic exhortation (2 Cor 4:18)?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountains of prey are the land of milk and honey, and the proud are left with hands unable to act, carried down in a stupor.
comments.comment: So he calls the mountains of the land flowing with milk and honey mountains of prey and food, from which he says God will be seen in a manner surpassing all greatness. Then the proud will suffer what has been set before them, finding their hands unable to do anything, as if they were being carried down in drowsiness. For you struck them with terror while defending your people and the places consecrated to you, so that the words fit: “A horse is a false hope for salvation”, and “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will call on the name of the Lord our God; they were hobbled and fell, but we rose and stood upright” (Psalm 19:8-9 (20:7-8)) (Ps 20:8). The same thing as the hobbling and the fall is indicated here through the being carried down and the stupefaction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'mountains of prey' and the overthrow of the mighty.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In Scripture horse and rider are mostly struck by God, though some riders are praised.
comments.comment: Indeed, one sees in the Scripture the rider as being mostly falsely named, as also in Zechariah the prophet there is a threat of God: 'And I will strike every horse in ecstasy and the rider in thoughtlessness' (Zechariah 12:4); and according to Moses, a horse and a rider was thrown into the sea—and riders being praised. For instance, toward Elijah, Father Elisha, the army of Israel and his rider; and toward the Savior it is announced: 'Ride upon your horses, and your riding is salvation' (Habakkuk 3:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one can stand against God when he is angry, yet he judges through mercy, so that fear keeps men from overlooking the One who knows the heart.
comments.comment: No one among the wretched is able to stand against God when He is angry, creating fear for those being judged, so that they might not overlook the One who knows the heart (Psalm 76:7; LXX 75:7). For those having the word toward Him as toward a judge say: 'Lord, Lord, if He observes iniquity, who will stand?' Moreover, even if no one will be able to stand against His wrath, being terrible, yet He Himself, through the coming goodness with mercy, judges. For mercy and judgment are yours, Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fear of God's anger: no one can stand, yet he judges with mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hears and sends judgment from heaven according to providence for each one's good, and sets righteousness on earth as its end.
comments.comment: Judgment listens from heaven, making everything happen according to the word of providence for the benefit of each. This agrees with what is in the prophecy of Amos: 'The Lord doing judgment, He has set high judgment and righteousness in the earth' (Amos 5:7). For as it is in heaven, He does all judgment in the high place; and as He listens from heaven, sending judgment from it to those on earth, He has set righteousness in the earth as the end of judgments (Psalm 76:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that judgment is 'heard from heaven'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who do earthly things fall still and take up quietude when the fear of judgment brings them to repentance.
comments.comment: And now a symbol is interpreted as the soul dwelling in the earth: 'The earth was afraid and was still when God arose for judgment' (Psalm 76:8). For when those doing earthly things become through the fear of judgment in repentance, they take up quietude instead of disturbance, hearing: 'And you will be still, without fear of every evil' (Proverbs 1:33), and salvation will remain for them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the earth that is afraid and still as the soul turned to repentance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who cleanses the hidden thing in his mind confesses to God with gladness, and confession may also mean disclosing one's sins.
comments.comment: The hidden thing of man is in the mind. He who cleanses this will confess to God with gladness. Then he will celebrate in doing what is profitable, and he will be able to think the truths. If, however, 'He will confess' denotes the disclosure of sins, the understanding of the matter will be this: since the one desiring to be perfectly holy must not cleanse himself in solitary acts and words alone, he must confess while rebuking himself regarding a very brief thought. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The remnant of a man's inner mind is celebrated when it is found free of evil, and the saint celebrates steadily, in sincerity and truth.
comments.comment: If one does not even imply something regarding the non-existence of sin, a confession might not occur; consequently, the remnant of the man's inner mind is celebrated having been found outside of all evil. Or, when the doubt concerning him is taken away by the manifestation of purity, the saint celebrates—not sometimes and sometimes not, but steadily and always knowing the truth and acting according to righteousness. For this is truly the feast according to the apostle who said, 'Let us celebrate, not in leaven of malice and wickedness, but in unleavened bread of sincerity and truth' (1 Cor 5:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: An angry person acts against what is right, and so his wrath leads afterward to confession and repentance.
comments.comment: Symmachus rendered it this way: “For the wrath of a human being will confess to you, a remnant of wrath girded on” (Psalm 76:10). Since the wrathful and angry person who does everything in anger and not according to what is right is subject to confession and changes of mind concerning the sins he commits. For wrath is quick to lead to sin, bold even to the point of murder itself, so that the reasoning left behind in the soul after wrath brings strong repentances that wrap around the whole soul for what was wrongly done and said through wrath.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the wrath of man ends in confession and change of mind.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is terrible to kings: he struck down Pharaoh, turned Nebuchadnezzar's mind to a beast's, and took the Spirit from Saul.
comments.comment: He is terrible before the kings of the earth, who struck down Pharaoh, and pursued Nebuchadnezzar of men, altering his thinking as if his life were among beasts (Psalm 76:12); he deprived Saul of the spirit, who, despising the covenant of God, was rejected by Samuel; for it is said, 'The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul' (1 Sam 16:14), and he was oppressed by an evil spirit from the Lord, sent upon him by judgment and vote.
comments.selected_reason: Gives examples of how God is terrible to the kings of the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one far from God must cry with the mind to him who is called God because he made all things and Lord because he rules them.
comments.comment: When the one speaking has departed far off, speaking with a strained voice (Psalm 77:1). Since, therefore, the begotten essence is separated from the One who made all, a cry according to the intellect is necessary. He is called God because He made all things, and Lord because He rules over those things which come from Him. And it is said, God indeed the Father, and Lord the Son.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He voices the weak reasonings of long affliction, first thanking God for hearing his prayer.
comments.comment: So indeed, having spoken piously in Psalm 72 (73), he now introduces the weak reasonings that come upon people in prolonged afflictions. And now he first gives thanks to God who received his supplications, describing his persistent prayer and the stretching out of his hands through whole nights.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In his whole life of affliction the saint seeks God as one seeks a physician, through deed and disposition, and is not deceived as Saul was.
comments.comment: But to the one speaking, the day is one of affliction, his whole life, indeed, the age which has come upon him, in which he seeks God as one would seek a physician for a disease, calling out. He seeks Him through deed and disposition, not being deceived like those who are ignorant of the end regarding circumstances, just as Saul went to a medium and was deceived.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: the day of trouble is the whole life, in which God is sought as a physician.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm tells of a long time of the nation's contempt, enough to remove hope of help unless one remembers the former things.
comments.comment: From the present psalm up to Psalm 82 (83), the discourse goes through the harsh and painful things concerning the people, and then in what follows it turns to brighter things (Ps 76 argument). In the present psalm he says that there is a long time in which the nation has been despised, sufficient to take away even the hope of help from God, unless someone remembers the former things and is strengthened in hope of the good things to come (Psalm 77:2-3; LXX 76:2,3).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the setting of the psalm: long affliction, and hope kept alive by remembering the former things.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The wandering voice and the spirit that does not faint are praised in Scripture, as in Hannah, Isaac and Stephen.
comments.comment:
According to Isaiah, my soul became attached to a mortal, not being self-sufficient for all the consolation of the memory concerning God. To this, what is in Isaiah also applies: 'In trouble of the Lord I remembered' (Isaiah 26:16). According to the common habit of many, a wandering voice indicates something superficial, but according to the Scripture and being placed upon one who is praised, it is authentic. …

For Anna, praying genuinely toward God, being called by the priest's child to persist in prayer, answers: 'From a multitude of wanderings I have wasted away until now.' And concerning Isaac, that which says: 'He went out to wander in the field.' …

Now, therefore, both the person and the word are praised; the spirit did not faint, which indicates the soul. For even Stephen did not say, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), but, having been faint-souled because of the enemies lying in wait, he gave himself to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enemies came before the guards of his heart, but he foresaw the trouble and uttered nothing troubling.
comments.comment:
My eyes preceded the guards (Psalm 77:4). Another scripture is brought forward, not saying: 'I have preceded the guards,' but: 'All my enemies preceded the guards.' Concerning many guards happening against me, he was guarding the saying: 'With all vigilance, keep your heart.' They preceded them, those which were about to make me faint-souled, all my enemies; for they were not few, but rather all, and they were filled against me.

Therefore, also, they having become more dominant, I have seen in a certain foreknowledge that I would undergo trouble, but I did not utter anything troubling, nor in any disposition have I become disturbed; for the things of judgment and foreknowledge were not at all heavy upon me, nor had I been made in a passionate fear. For indeed I uttered nothing, whereas those who have shrunk in courage love to speak.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Remembering past rescues gave him cheer to endure to the end, for God provided abundance even in helplessness.
comments.comment: Having these things happen to me, he says, I awoke myself to remember the former and many anticipating circumstances (not only me but also my virtuous fathers) from which all the Lord rescued me and them; by which reason I have become more cheerful to endure unto the end, so that I might happen to have salvation from the struggles of such things; for he who endures unto the end, he shall be saved. For having conversed with the ancient days and the eternal ages, having remembered and having meditated, I found many times both myself and the rest of men falling into such a state of helplessness, as to leave behind salvation and all hope; but, having been established in confidence toward God, every helplessness in those who grasp the truth is overcome. You shall remember when the Hebrew multitude comes toward the things laid before you by the valleys of the sea; for no good hope remaining there, suddenly God provided abundance in narrowness and in remote helplessness (Psalm 77:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist recalls the days of old: remembered deliverance gives strength to endure.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the night of this life's ignorance he stirred himself to sobriety, tilling his spirit so as to reap eternal life.
comments.comment: Throughout all this life, because of the encroaching ignorance of things, being called night, I did not deliver myself to sleep and heart like other men, but toward sobriety and alertness I stirred myself up; for those sleeping at night sleep and at night they get drunk. With my heart, that is, with my mind, I was conversing with myself about the actions and natures of things (for know what the present things are approaching), I learned what the end of the surrounding evils will be. And I was tilling my spirit with the art of farming, desiring to sow into it, so that from it I might reap eternal life; for he who sows into the spirit, from the spirit he will reap eternal life (Galatians 6:8). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the night and the searching of the spirit as sober self-examination in the ignorance of this life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul gathered in the quiet of the night is commanded to meditate on God's commandments.
comments.comment: The night is attentive, the soul being gathered together in it in the quiet of the senses. Then he commands to meditate in the commandments of God and to say with David: “by night I was meditating with my heart, and my spirit was searching.” (Psalm 77:6) And the night being divided into four watches, say with David: “my eyes anticipated the watches,” (Psalm 119:148) and with Habakkuk: “upon my watch I will stand, and I will look out what the Lord God will speak in me.” (Habakkuk 2:1) For then you will say: “for he will speak peace upon his people.” (Psalm 85:8) Meditate, then, in the night of the present age …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's mercy does not fail from one generation to the next, as fire and light do not stop warming and shining; his anger is only temporary.
comments.comment: Previously, he was willing to help and was favorable to those asking of him, as I reasoned: 'I remembered the days of old.' Was his goodness not present until those times, and no longer being added to, he was willing to be favorable? No, by no means. For his mercy is not cut off from the former generation, nor does it fail regarding the coming one. For they think that the end of his mercy is this: that he might do good and show mercy to one generation, and not to another. Nor will he fail to have compassion, just as neither fire nor light fails to shine and to warm. For his mercies are held in check by a temporary anger arising from sin, but they are not joined in a way that lasts forever.
comments.selected_reason: Answers the questions of the verses: God's mercy is not cut off, and his anger is temporary.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Having endured many troubles, he sees that God is not thrust away for the ages, and that the change in him is God's work, not his own.
comments.comment: Even though many troubles have come upon me, they cast a disturbance into me (Psalm 77:7). What has been recounted followed in all the appointed words, but also, having understood things, I observed that God is not being thrust away for the ages, nor has He chosen to do other things, as if in some way to cast down a different beginning of a kind of life. For through all those things I have passed through, I have begun the Now, changing all those things that disturbed and frightened me, so that I might become courageous for the rest. This change is not a change of quality (for I have passed from one disposition to another), but an alteration, not caused by another, but by the right hand of the Most High. For He also provided these thoughts and brought them together so that I might be altered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'alteration of the right hand of the Most High' is the Savior taking flesh, an assumption and not a change.
comments.comment: The alteration of the right hand of the Most High. The right hand of the Father—and especially according to the intention of the Psalmist—is often said to be the Savior. But having become flesh, he was altered, a curse. He endured becoming sin, so that the sinners might become the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor 5:21). Therefore, the alteration is an assumption in this way, not a change; for no one would seek a change regarding the unchangeable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'right hand of the most High' and its 'alteration' mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After speaking darkly of his trouble, the psalmist says 'Now I have begun' and turns to remember God's wonders.
comments.comment: He says little about glorifying and praising: ‘For I will remember from the beginning of your wonders’ (Psalm 77:11). ‘And I said, Now I have begun’ (Psalm 77:10). I said all things darkly, that having been troubled I did not speak, that the watchmen had come upon me, but rather: ‘Now I have begun.’ I will now narrate other things after those, those following the dark things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God walks among the saints, with his own way in each.
comments.comment: Since God dwells and walks among the saints (Psalm 77:13), He has in each of the saints his own way, traveling according to the intellect of each of them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'way ... in the sanctuary': God's way in each of the saints.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Greatness is said of God's nature by excellence of power, not size, and no god is as great as ours.
comments.comment:
But His word is in nothing trivial, for it is a way; rather, it is rightly said that the indwelling voice is in the saints alone. Regarding Psalm 76:14b, greatness is said of the intelligible substance by excellence of power, not by quantity. No god is found as great as ours.

He does not say that the gods are the idols or the demons (for these are called gods), but rather those who, having become toward us through the word of God, were made divine. For they are not partakers of divinity, but merely partakers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior is called God as the Only-begotten, with the same divinity as the Father.
comments.comment: Regarding Psalm 76:15a, after the article, the Savior is called God, so that he might be shown as different from those to whom it is said, 'You are gods' (Ps 82:6). None of them is as one who excels. After the article, it is said, 'God.' Such is also the Only-begotten God who is in the bosom of the Father, to be God by being alone in essence; for none of the others is only-begotten, but with the only-begotten is God. According to the same divinity, the only-begotten God and the Father God are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior made his power known among both peoples and redeemed the two joined into one, the sons of Jacob and of Joseph.
comments.comment: He performed many paradoxical wonders among the nations and the circumcised; for power went out from him and healed everyone. But also by his arm (I mean by his energy and action) he redeemed his people, the two united, having tasted death above all things by the grace of God, giving his soul as a ransom for many; for by his precious blood we were redeemed from our vain, ancestral conduct. The peoples are those in whom he made his power known, whom he also joined together into one people, whom he redeemed: the sons of Jacob and Joseph, the sons of Jacob who are circumcised and believe, and the sons of Joseph who are from the nations. For Joseph is interpreted as 'Addition of the Lord'; for God truly added to those being saved from the circumcised, those from the nations who believe. And 'He made known' does not signify the beginning of knowing, but that which is come to be known and recognized; for saying 'He who works wonders,' he recognizes these things through these words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verses: the sons of Jacob and Joseph are the circumcised and the nations, joined into one redeemed people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The waters that feared God are not sensible waters, which neither see nor fear.
comments.comment: 'God saw the waters, and they saw and were afraid' (Psalm 77:16). It is evident, however, that it is not about sensible waters, for he neither fears nor sees, for they are inanimate; for God sees not with eyes but understands with unmixed and pure intellect.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God's power appeared, the waters, the clouds and the earth were shaken, recalling the wonders in Egypt, the wilderness and Judea.
comments.comment: When your power appeared, he says, everything was set in motion: the waters writhed in fear, and a turbulent struggle gripped the depths (Psalm 77:16-18). Waters were also released from above out of the clouds, and the clouds ran through the sky with a great sound, and the arrows from heaven were hurled down. The sounds of thunder rolled around the circle of the sky as the clouds raced through, and lightning flashed across the inhabited world and shook the earth with an earthquake. These things point to the fearful wonders that appeared in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in Judea. For Egypt was struck with hail that came down with fire, and the waters of the Red Sea gave way as if shrinking back in fear. Thunder crashed in the sky and hail came down also upon the Canaanites in the war against the Jews. It is clear that lightning also flashed together with it. As for saying that the thunder sounded in a wheel, another passage says it was when he bound the axles of the chariots and brought them down into the sea with their commanders.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the storm imagery as the fearful wonders done in Egypt, the wilderness and Judea.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The circle of the sky along which the stars turn is not a sphere but, in Scripture, a heaven founded and standing.
comments.comment: He presents to us the circle of the sky along which the stars revolve, like oxen going around a threshing floor (Psalm 77:18). For a spherical heaven, according to the Greek account, is not to be found in the divine oracles, so that we should not imagine a wheel-like circuit above the earth and below the earth. For the divine Scriptures present water under the earth, not heaven, and waters above the heaven set as a boundary. For he says, “He stretches out the heaven like a curtain, he who roofs his upper chambers with waters” (Psalm 104:2). And the sun is said to run from one end to the other, from east to west, and not to run back from the west for even the smallest part of the day. And he says, “He established the heaven” (not “he who leads it around in a circle”) “and stretched it out like a tent to dwell in” (not “to be whirled around like a circle”). And Isaiah says that those who come from a far land come “from the end of the foundation of heaven”, so that the heaven is founded and standing, not running around in a circle. But these things are said for the sake of a brief reminder, so that we are not carried away to the fictions of the Greeks while neglecting the divine Scriptures.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When the Savior appeared on earth, the earth and its people were shaken and turned toward the Word of Christ.
comments.comment: When the Savior appeared on earth, the earth endured confusion and trembling (Psalm 77:18-20)—that is, the things on earth, which are above all laws and are fearful of all gods, through whose ordinances the demons are overturned; but also the earth endured confusion and trembling because of men, who are bound by passions and are being turned toward the Word of Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one can make out God's ways, as no one can see a track in water.
comments.comment: Nor could anyone know his footsteps and his ways. For it is written, ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!’ (Romans 11:33) Blessed David, too, sings and strikes up a wise song: ‘Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps will not be known’ (Psalm 77:19). For just as no one could see a track in water, whether of a man, perhaps, or of a ship, or of the creatures that swim in it, so no one could make out the divine and ineffable ways. The feet would be a type of these ways.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: God's footsteps are unknown as a track in water cannot be seen.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: God's way leaves no visible trace, and his journey is not a movement; the people were led through a short sea and a long land.
comments.comment: He says that the divine way has no visible trace, unlike the human way. Therefore he called it a journey “in the sea and in the waters,” since Solomon says that not even the paths of a ship sailing the sea can be recognized, so that what is said is figurative (Psalm 77:19-20). And it is no longer a journey of movement for God. For the Hebrews did not walk through the sea so that he might lead them through it, but the stretch of the Red Sea was brief for them in their journey, while the stretch through the land was long and lengthy. “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Psalm 76:21 (77:20)).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus alone bound the sea of this life and left traces of his way, and Christ's sheep are led by the spiritual law.
comments.comment: And the sea, the present life, Jesus God alone bound, so as to leave behind traces and proofs of the way, so that those wishing to follow him might follow; for he says, 'Your paths are in many waters, and your tracks shall not be known' (Psalm 77:19), because the word of his journey is incomprehensible. And the sheep of Christ were led by God in practice (symbolically called by the hand) of the spiritual law …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Moses stands for the law and Aaron for the high priest, brothers born of God's providence.
comments.comment: … He signifies Moses as the law, and Aaron as the high priest; therefore they are brothers, being sons of the divine providence which brought forth this law and the appropriate high-priestly word for it; for by its will these good things have been raised up to men (Psalm 77:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Moses and Aaron stand for in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Law' here can mean all the old Scripture, which teaches how to choose good and flee evil.
comments.comment: He is able to call all the old scripture 'the law' present here. If the commanding and forbidding word were to signify the voice of the law according to the preceding verse, it commands the law to take heed how those having received the command, choosing the good and fleeing the bad, might act rightly (Psalm 78:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Asaph shows that the histories of Exodus and Numbers are riddles and parables, which Paul read spiritually.
comments.comment: Then, interpreting the story of the manna (Exodus 16:14–15) and the account of the water that is recorded to have come miraculously out of a rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11), he [Paul] says this: “And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:3–4). And Asaph, showing that the histories in Exodus and Numbers are “riddles” and “parables,” as is written in the book of Psalms, begins in this way when he is about to recall them: “Pay attention, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from of old, such things as we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:1–3).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophets do not let their meaning rest in the plain narrative, and when about to recount history they speak in parables and riddles.
comments.comment: For the prophets themselves do not let the meaning of what they say come to rest in the plain narrative, nor in the legislation that follows the words and the letter. In one place, when they are supposedly about to recount history, they say: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from the beginning” (Psalm 78:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist calls his history a parable.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who have the mind of Christ understood these things spiritually, for they were explained to them with knowledge.
comments.comment: These things those having the mind of Christ understood and perceived spiritually; for it was not hidden from them, having been explained to them according to knowledge. And they themselves did not reveal to their own children born of them through instruction the matters from the beginning, so that they might be known and not hidden even to their next generation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be with God in spirit is to be confirmed in understanding, and 'spirit' here means the intellect.
comments.comment: For he who becomes with God in spirit, coming from Him, is trusted to understand and is confirmed according to the spirit (Ps 77:8d). It is to be thought that 'spirit' here refers to the intellect, according to what was said concerning the Virgin, how she conceived by the Holy Spirit and body; for in these things 'spirit' calls her opinion and her disposition, and from which having been sanctified, the body also comes to be sanctified, being served by sanctifying energies. And if the soul itself is spirit and is called so here, it is to be noted.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The water that flowed like rivers from the rock is the rivers of living water, drawn from the rock that is Christ.
comments.comment: For the water sent forth from this rock flowed like rivers (Psalm 78:16). And regarding these rivers, the Savior says: 'He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, from his spiritual belly (that which is according to the inner man) will flow rivers of living water' (John 7:38). … For the water of these rivers is drawn out from a rock, about which Paul says: 'From a spiritual rock that follows' (1 Cor 10:4); and the rock is Christ. Christ himself, since he is a rock, says concerning the water of the rivers: 'For from me he will take and will declare to you all things' (John 16:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rock and the rivers of water with the New Testament sayings about the Spirit and Christ the rock.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who sin against God are those who know his will and do not do it, and so they are left in a dry place without the spiritual waters.
comments.comment: And they added to this: sinning against him—not all who sin against God are sinning against him, but only those who have known his will and are not doing it. Certainly even David, not being ignorant of God's will, says: 'Against you only have I sinned' (Ps 51:4). Perhaps for those sinning in ethical matters, the sin becomes toward men; but for those blaspheming God and providence, the sin, being a certain impiety, rises up against God. For if someone sins against a man, and prays for him; but if he sins against the Lord God, who will pray for him? Certainly, what they overthrew the Most High with, they were lacking in a dry place, being deprived of the spiritual waters; for they turned away from the water from the aforementioned rock. And finding themselves in a dry place, they did not experience the goodness of God which is sweet.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm joins together events of different times, bringing one rebellion under one cause.
comments.comment: Regarding the manna given before the rebellion, the psalm says after the rebellion that both the manna and the meat were given (Psalm 78:17-22; LXX 77:17–22). But this is not the question. For the psalm joins together things in different times, bringing together one rebellion having occurred in different times under one cause. For if someone should interpret the first rebellion as that before the making of the Tabernacle in the second month of the Exodus, he does not place that history in its proper time in the psalm; for not then did the water from the rock happen to be given, nor did the punishment of fire follow, and indeed the firstlings were not slain and they did not unrighteously disbelieve regarding the paradoxical gift of food …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They tested God from the depth of their hearts, doubting his power and desiring pleasant, harmful food instead of food fit for souls made in his image.
comments.comment: They tested Him not in their hearts superficially, but from the depth of their own ruling principle, thinking against God and doubting His power to request food for their souls—not the souls made in the image and likeness of God (for they feed on the bread of life and the fruit of the tree of life), but the souls being transformed into flesh because they have succumbed to material things, desiring not beneficial and healthy foods, but pleasant and disease-causing ones.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to tempt God in the heart: doubting his power and desiring harmful food.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The desiring part of the soul is a power in us, and those who spoke against God had in fact been given bread from heaven and a table.
comments.comment:
The soul that desires food, the desiring and appetitive one, is a rational power in us. For concerning this, it is said, 'And let your soul desire meat'. The irrational animals also participate in this, desiring and being appetitive for food.

And they spoke against God, saying, 'Will God not be able to prepare a table in the wilderness?' and the following things; but He has indeed given bread having come down from heaven and prepared a table before His people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Moses bore the people's small-spiritedness with difficulty, and the punishment of fire fell on those who did not believe in God's power.
comments.comment: You act with small-spiritedness because you do not immediately find abundance. Therefore, even Moses did not yield to the small-spiritedness of the people. In the second dispute concerning meats, Moses also bears it with difficulty; and it is fitting that the punishment from God was somewhat sent to them, and they were being consumed by fire. It is necessary to believe from those who were previously warned, not believing in the divine power, and it is necessary to hope for salvation from Him, not hoping.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fire kindled on Jacob may be the fire of desires, or a fire from God that consumes their worldly choice.
comments.comment: Because of this, the Lord was angry and cast down, as if to pay attention to them. This was followed by the fire of desires being kindled upon Jacob; or rather, the fire decided and laboring for the sake of virtue, or the fire kindled from God, which is able to consume by their blessing their material choice and their disposition. Consequently, by this fire, wrath ascended upon Israel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who did not hope in Jesus Christ, the salvation of God, did not believe in God himself.
comments.comment: And since they did not believe in God, they did not hope for His salvation. For those who did not hope in Jesus Christ, the salvation of God, did not even believe in God Himself. To the apostles, it was said by Christ: 'Believe in me, and believe in God' (cf. John 14:1). It is possible, then, for wrath to have ascended upon Israel because they did not believe in God nor hope for His salvation, being overtaken by a force, concerning which Paul said: 'And wrath reached them to the end' (1 Thessalonians 2:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: not believing in God and not trusting his salvation go together.
