comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Heaven signifies the intelligible realms, and the opened doors of heaven are the outpourings through which God's gifts flow.
comments.comment: And bread of heaven He gave them (Psalm 78:24). The voice of heaven signifies the essence of the intelligible realms, just as we have also learned in the previous passages; and the opening doors of the heavens are the outpourings and manifestations of the patriarchs, through these doors the gifts of God flow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The manna was a type of the Word who comes from the Father, the true food of angels.
comments.comment: God sent the manna down like rain on the people of Israel in the wilderness; for this was their food and bread from above, from heaven (Exodus 16:4). But what was done did not stop at things of sense. As through a type and a shadow, it leads us up to understand that in due time the Word would come to us from above and from the Father, as bread from heaven, just as the divine David hints to us when he says: ‘He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels’ (Psalm 78:24–25). We certainly do not say that the physical manna was the bread from heaven and of angels. For a spirit is fed spiritually, and a body according to its own nature, that is, bodily. The food of angels, the bread fit for the heavens and for the spirits above, is the Word who is from God the Father. So the manna signified Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'bread of heaven' and 'angels' food' as the manna that pictured Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Calling the eater 'man' shows the man made in God's image, a table-guest of angels who receives the true manna.
comments.comment: Bread of angels man has eaten, to signify how a man is in the hiddenness of the heart. Therefore, having passed over all the other names, even though he frequently remembered them—of Jacob and of Israel and of Ephraim—he remembers the human appellation here to show the man who is truly made according to the image and likeness of God, having become a fellow-table-guest and a host to angels, receiving the true manna (Psalm 78:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'man' ate angels' food.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not destroy in the sense of handing men over to dishonor, but propitiates their sins with much mercy and compassion.
comments.comment: To corrupt signifies sometimes to fall into punishment, just as 'If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him' (1 Cor 3:17), instead of punishment. But since to corrupt also signifies being handed over to a condition of dishonor as a recompense for error and other sins being committed, God does not corrupt in this sense; rather, He finds those worthy of being seen by Him, so that they might be propitiated for their sins by much mercy and compassion. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'evil angels' are those who bring harm through their labors.
comments.comment: … He does not say He will produce evil angels such as these, but those who bring harm through their labors. He did not spare their souls from death, bringing them to the dissolution of a weary life (Psalm 78:49-51; LXX 77:49c–51).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The cattle stand for irrational powers, and God does not spare the soulish so as to lead them into a spiritual state.
comments.comment:
… having enclosed into this death and their irrational powers, which are tropically named cattle. For it will be for their good to cast away both themselves and their cattle, that is, their base life, namely, the passionate movement.

And understand more deeply: since the psychic man lives according to soul but not according to spirit, he does not spare these so-called souls of theirs, in order to, having destroyed their psychic state, lead them into a spiritual one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tenth plague killed the firstborn, and spiritually Egypt is life on earth, whose firstborn offspring, ignorance and malice, God takes away.
comments.comment:
And the tenth plague brought upon the Egyptians was death, the death of the firstborn among them from man to cattle. …

Toward those not being disciplined nor repenting of such god-fearing things, 'I struck your children,' it is said (Jeremiah 2:30), 'because you did not receive discipline.' …

For the purpose of leading upward: since every place concerning the earth is called Egypt spiritually, those dwelling in it are called Egyptians. Therefore, by the grace of God, the firstborn offspring of their souls among these Egyptians is taken away, being ignorance and malice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plague on the firstborn, and reads Egypt as life on earth whose firstborn, ignorance and malice, are taken away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Bodies are the tabernacles of souls, and holiness, the right hand of God's power, is Jesus, whose possessions are those who acquire it.
comments.comment: And that which lies in their tabernacles reveals what is to be said concerning souls when they are entwined with bodies; for bodies are tabernacles of souls (Psalm 78:54-55; LXX 77:54). Holiness is the divided and most high virtue, not the intellectual alone but also the practical. And only the one perfect Teacher, Jesus, introduces one genuinely into this. Then those who are in heaven are not sanctified, but they are carried into it by the Lord. This very holiness is not a matter of chance, but it is called the right hand of God's power, not being anything other than the only-begotten Jesus. For every excellence and theoretical vision of the truth is truly a possession of Jesus, and therefore those acquiring these dispositions are called possessions of the Lord (Psalm 78:54).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God struck them from behind to sever them from their evil state, and sinners are reproached also by their own shame.
comments.comment: He struck them from behind, so that they might not be diminished by a face of coarseness in front, but might be severed from their inhuman and evil state; for God does not desire anyone to progress in evils, but, caring for them, provided them with eternal reproach. And sinners are reproached, not only by others but also by themselves, when they are ashamed of the evils they have committed. For God says to certain ones: 'Be ashamed of your boasting and from reproach, mourn the day.' For those boasting over trivial things are benefited, if they are ashamed and reproached for the things they were vaunting of (Psalm 78:66).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: the blow from behind and the lasting reproach are for the sinner's benefit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Innocence' here means the absence of evil and simplicity, not gentleness.
comments.comment: The name of 'innocence' does not signify gentleness here, but the absence of evil and simplicity. The sheep do not imitate the innocence of the Teacher, but are shepherded by it. And lest the one practicing evil be thought to be doing so deceptively, but rather from the best state, it is said of him that he is completing the innocence of the heart. And he also guided others by the wisdom of his hands.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'integrity' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Pious faith does not fear that beasts or lack of burial can harm the bodies to be raised; the psalm exaggerates the cruelty of the killers, not the misery of the slain.
comments.comment: Pious faith does not fear this too much, holding to what was foretold: that the beasts that consume them will not harm the bodies that are about to rise, whose hair of the head will not perish. The Truth would never have said, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28), if anything that enemies might choose to do with the bodies of the slain could harm the life to come. Unless someone is so absurd as to argue that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, but should be feared after death, lest they not allow the slain body to be buried. Is it false, then, what the Truth says: "those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do" (Luke 12:4), if they have so much they can do with the corpses? Far be it that what the Truth said should be false. For it says they do something when they kill, because there is sensation in the body while it is being killed; but after that they have nothing they can do, because there is no sensation in a slain body. So the earth did not cover many bodies of Christians, but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which he fills entirely with his presence—he who knows from where he will raise up what he created. It is said in the psalm: "They gave the bodies of your servants as food to the birds of the air, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth; they poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them" (Psalm 79:2-3). But this was said to exaggerate the cruelty of those who did these things, not the misery of those who suffered them. For though these things seem hard and dreadful in human sight, yet "precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones" (Psalm 116:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verses: the lack of burial cannot harm the faithful, and the verse stresses the cruelty of the killers.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: A righteous man who suffers death with sinners has better things stored up after it, and God's name is reproached along with the people.
comments.comment:
But if a righteous man shares with sinners even to the point of death, then after death good things are already stored up for him, to mark him off from the wicked. This was the case with King Josiah. For indeed this man also, being most righteous, died in war while the Egyptian prevailed, because Israelite impiety had been great beforehand and did not receive pardon. So for the righteous themselves, if they suffer along with sinners, better things from God are stored up after the suffering (Ps 78:4). And for the brothers and kinsmen who suffer because of sins, there is great help through them, so that on account of their destruction some turning of God toward the nation comes about. This is also what the prophet now asks.

These words depend on a defense acceptable before God. For even if we deserve what we have suffered, he says, yet your name is reproached together with us, just as God himself says through Isaiah: "Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations" (Isaiah 52:5).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Neighbors who hold the same writings, and Greeks, mock believers as foolish, and the people ask that God turn his wrath upon the impious.
comments.comment:
By analogy, you call the heretics neighbors; for their dwellings are near us because they hold to the same writings. They do not reproach us, saying we are heretics, but they call us as slaves, well-behaved and foolish. Around us, if there are wise men among the Greeks, they sneer and mock us as believing without examination and foolishly (Psalm 79:4).

'You have disciplined the Jews sufficiently,' they say; 'surely, at some time, turn your wrath upon the impious mortals and upon the kingdom of your reverence that is alien' (Psalm 79:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They ravaged the God-fearing nation like wild beasts.
comments.comment: Because, he says, they ravaged the God-fearing nation like wild beasts and laid waste a holy land (Psalm 79:7; LXX 78:7).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A person's place is his station of life, and if enemies devour those who hold it, their order and place are laid waste.
comments.comment: The place of each is his own station of life; for the prudent man in some way inhabits prudence. We say that the prudent man inhabits the place of the prudent, and others the order of the righteous. If it happens that those possessing these things of yours are devoured by enemies, their order and their place will be laid waste. We say, for example, the place of a bishop and a presbyter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who repents asks that his ancient iniquities not be remembered, since it is contrary to repentance to keep sinning.
comments.comment: 'Do not remember our ancient iniquities' (Psalm 79:8). And in other places, if no one confesses what he does evilly, but rather what he acted upon of old, 'Do not remember the sin of my youth and my ignorance' (Ps 25:7). And now, those who repent of their ceased iniquities are not worthy that their ancient sins not be remembered by God. For indeed, the sensual ones always call upon God not concerning youthful sins but concerning past deeds, saying: 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have transgressed' (Psalm 106:6). For it is contrary to the one repenting to be sinning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fallen from the wealth of virtue and knowledge, we ask for mercy now, for God's mercies can enrich us again.
comments.comment: 'We have become exceedingly impoverished, having fallen from the wealth of virtue and knowledge, Lord; therefore we beseech you to grant us mercy, not in the future, but surely even now and quickly (Psalm 79:8). For you are the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, and your mercies are sufficient to make us rich again.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be 'brought very low' and to ask for mercy to come speedily.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since God's name is called upon his people, he is asked to forgive their sins so that the nations cannot reproach his name as defeated.
comments.comment: We experience the salvation of the Lord. Even if we are not worthy to suffer well because of the sins that are among us, but since your name has been called upon us (for we are your inheritance and your people), be propitiated toward our sins, so that your name may be glorified. For we do not bear the reproach of the nations saying, 'Where is their God?' (Psalm 79:10; LXX 78:10). For they hold us in subjection because we have sinned, and they reproach even your name, thinking that you have been defeated by those who are beneath us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea for God's name's sake and the nations' taunt 'Where is their God?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those pressed by the chains of their sins pray that their groan may be known to God, who looses the bound.
comments.comment: And toward a turning point of discourse: those being squeezed by the chains of their own sins have been brought low, but having become aware of the weight, they are overcome by the plains, through which they are hindered from running toward salvation and from working out those things that contribute to happiness, groaning thus, being utterly exhausted. Therefore they also pray that their groan may be known to God and enter before him. For he will move his own goodness to intervene to break their bonds; for the Lord looses the bound (Psalm 146:7). And he will set them apart for blessed life, according to the greatness of the God Word, his arm, so that, even if they appeared as sons of men having been dead, they might be shown to be children becoming living ones. For their fathers, having been killed by the enemies, are living before the Lord, and they are found to be his sons and his servants.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The number seven symbolizes rest, and as God's people and sheep they ask him to act so that they may thank him throughout life.
comments.comment: Since the number seven holds a symbol of rest, they desire the retribution to be upon the description of their impiety, through which they reproached God and were roughly brought to his servants, to be led away. For those knowing the good God will not lift up the reproaches of the scourged, but they want the scourgings to be brought upon them, so that the workers of that laziness, to whom punishment follows by necessity, may be idle. But the Sabbath number is a symbol of laziness. Since we are being enriched as your people and sheep grazing your pasture, concerning which it has been said, 'He shall enter and go out and shall find pasture' (John 10:9) (clearly meaning the sheep of Christ), we asked for blessings; do according to your greatness, so that, as you are clearly present, we may gratefully acknowledge you throughout life; for this clearly signifies 'unto the age' regarding the present. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Unto generation and generation' may mean all the generations of men, the present and the coming life, or the circumcision and the Gentiles.
comments.comment: … The phrase 'unto generation and generation' can be said more simply instead of 'and unto the generations and the many successors of men.' Or you may say more mystically, 'in the present and in the coming life,' or 'in both generations, the one of circumcision and the one of the calling of the Gentiles,' so that they may learn to praise God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'to all generations' in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Shepherd of Israel is Christ the good shepherd, and Joseph, 'addition of the Lord,' stands for the Gentiles added to the circumcised.
comments.comment: The Shepherd of Israel is none other than the one who said, 'I am the good shepherd' (John 10:11), who grazes those who have understanding and see God. He also guides those being added from the Gentiles like sheep, that is, as his own sheep, the Israelites; for Joseph, being interpreted as 'addition of the Lord,' signifies those from the Gentiles being added to those of the circumcision. …
comments.selected_reason: Names the Shepherd and explains the name Joseph.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David pleads with God as Shepherd of Israel and Leader of Joseph because the names of the beloved fathers soften him toward a sinning people.
comments.comment: … Therefore also David, entreating God to be propitious and favorable to the people, and exhausting him with myriads of supplications, so that having stilled the continuous and recurring plague of misfortunes, he might again govern Jerusalem with good foresight as before, thus says: 'O Shepherd of Israel, pay attention, O Leader of Joseph like a sheep' (Psalm 80:1). For he is appeased by the names of the beloved and friends, and most gracefully handles the entreaty of the transgressing multitude of sins, as if concealing and covering them with the titles of the holy fathers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm calls on God by these names.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh mean fruitfulness, the right hand and forgetfulness, and the saints ask the enthroned Lord to rouse his power and save them.
comments.comment: The Lord is seated upon the cherubim, as he is presented in Ezekiel (Ezek. 10). … For Ephraim is fruitfulness, Benjamin is the son of the right hand, and Manasseh is interpreted from forgetfulness. They say therefore: 'Since you are a king, having awakened a greatest power and having roused it, O Lord, so as to save us; for there is no other way to attain salvation than for you, having come to us, to turn us back from sins. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one enthroned on the cherubim is asked to rouse his silent power and come in saving action, and the people ask first to be turned back to him, since his appearing is their salvation.
comments.comment: By naming the one who sits upon the cherubim, he reveals the heavenly authority through which all things are subject to him and nothing can resist him, if only he would appear. And he calls upon the power to be roused, because it has been silent and still and has looked on while the people suffered. Such were the things they suffered from the Assyrians; and he asks that the one who for the present is not with them, because of their abandonment, should come to them. But how would he come except in his working? For this reason he says, "Come to save us," as if he were saying, "Come by way of saving." And the words "Turn us and show your face" are because the one who has turned away from God cannot obtain the appearing unless he first turns back to him (Psalm 80:3). For he says, "Turn to me, and I will turn to you" (Malachi 3:7). He asks this from the guidance and cooperation of God, as also in the words, "Incline my heart to your testimonies" (Psalm 118:36 (119:36)). For the pious attribute everything to God. And if your face appears, he says, we shall be saved; for the appearing of God is salvation (Psalm 80:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the plea to the one on the cherubim and the plea to be turned back mean.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Weeping and toil for virtue are the bread of tears, eaten and drunk in measure, and those who sow in tears will reap in joy.
comments.comment: And because you are angry at the prayer which we sent up, having turned it into weeping and lamentation, we bear such a multitude of tears at the time of food, as if to eat bread of tears and to drink with tears a little and measured drink. … Since the toil and weeping for the sake of virtue is nourishment, we eat the tears of this very weeping as bread, and also drink them in measure. And the 'in measure' prevents one from always weeping and weeping through trial. For he will receive as rest and a propitiatory state those who undergo labors for the sake of good things. To this end, 'Blessed are those who weep now, they shall laugh' Matt 5:4, and 'Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy' Ps 126:5. For those who sow virtue with sweat and tears, they are able to measure the weeping, reaping in joy; for with it they shall laugh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bread of tears and why the drink is measured.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Neighbours who are enemies mock those who cry to God, and the people ask him to end their captivity and show his face for their salvation.
comments.comment: … For the neighbors are enemies; they mock them, sneering and dragging away their wise words. … But they will also mock those crying out to God. But they themselves, rather, say they are entreating: 'Lord God of powers, turn back now, redeeming our captivity from those who tyrannize.' … And we shall desire this good thing: if you show your eternal face to us, you will grant us salvation. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Jews, bound under a heavy law, cried out for God's face to shine, and received mercy when Christ shone on them, as all have.
comments.comment: In another way too, if we turn the force of the passage toward the Jews, they truly received mercy when the Only-begotten shone upon them. For the law lay on them like a burden hard to bear and fit only to be cast off, the law that condemns and punishes sinners without pity (Hebrews 10:28). But they received mercy, gaining through Christ, late and with difficulty, the grace that justifies. Longing to see his coming, they had cried out to the God of all: ‘O God of hosts, bring us back, and make your face shine, and we shall be saved’ (Psalm 80:7). So we have all received mercy in the shining forth of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: Egypt stands for the soul's life among material things, and God moves it out.
comments.comment: For allegory: the soul is then said to dwell in Egypt, as it spends time with the sensible things and the works of the flesh. But God moves it from Egypt, tearing it away from material things.
comments.selected_reason: Short and clear: Egypt as the soul's attachment to material things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God moved the soul out of Egypt into a heavenly land by giving the God-breathed Scriptures, and the vine's shadow, branches and shoots are the righteous, the prosperous and those joined to the Jewish worship.
comments.comment: And he sang before it, having given a saving law and luminous commands before it, in order to travel to the good land; and that land is perfect virtue. If it seems well to you, Egypt, to take the land as a spiritual world in which the soul, struggling with the sensible and temporal things, is planted, you would take a transplantation into the heavenly and intelligible realms of it, with God being the cause of this so great good for it, because he has prepared the way before it by giving the spiritual discourse of the God-breathed Scriptures (2 Tim 3:16). Its shadow covered them. For those called the righteous, who were high and possessed a lasting citizenship, were sheltered by what was well spread out under it. But also those who have become wealthy and well-toned through a more prosperous life, as if to profit from God's gain, were covered by its leafy branches in a certain way, being supported by them. And the vine extends its branches to the greatest extent, as if approaching the seas without suffering harm from the trials and surges of life called seas, to bear fruit metaphorically. And it also extends its shoots, just as the rivers that water it, in order to yield the proper fruit. And its branches are those joined to the Jewish worship, who, because of remaining in the law, happen to bear fruit like the shoots of those proselytizing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David sings of Israel as a vine brought out of Egypt, whose reach to the sea and the rivers marks the borders of the land under the law.
comments.comment: Seeing this, the prophet David sings a psalm and speaks concerning those from Israel, saying, 'A vine you brought up out of Egypt; you expelled the nations and uprooted her' (Psalm 80:8). He applies this to the borders reaching the Euphrates river, and indeed even to the sea toward the south and to India, limiting the territory of the Jews: 'He stretched out its camps even to the sea, and its branches even to the rivers' (Psalm 80:11). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The vine is the soul cultivated by God, rooted in the Word who is the true vine, and its shoots are the drinkable waters of the divine words.
comments.comment:
If the vine is such a soul cultivated by God, having its beginning and its root in the Word, according to which it is logical for the one saying, 'I am the true vine' (John 15:1), God will transplant its various branches and powers, its roots metaphorically being shoots, into the various thoughts of the Only-begotten. For the vine, being raised up because it is well cultivated, will cover the high doctrines of truth, called shadows, with itself. And this citizenship and knowledge existing here are able to bear a shadow and a type of its true state hereafter.

And its side-shoots, which have branched out from its powers and virtues, are also extended, being called rivers as they are the drinkable waters of the divine words. And in another way, its side-shoots may be called such, as that which branches out from it for the benefit of the other instruction. For just as the side-shoots drink and are transformed into drinkability from the plant upon which they have branched, so also those branching out from the other learning drink from its preceding teaching, with every name being taken captive into the obedience of Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The vine covered the mountains and the cedars and reached the sea and the river, so the psalmist asks why God let it be stripped and plundered.
comments.comment: The vine mentioned earlier covered the mountains with its shadow, because it surpassed every height and every power upon the earth, and with the spreading of its branches it covered the cedars of God, because it was supported by the divine powers and reached as far as the sea and the river. For this is also how the boundaries of the Judean land are named by God: "From the wilderness to the Euphrates, and from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines" (Exodus 23:31). Therefore the vine which you yourself, he says, brought out of Egypt and transplanted, which you made so conspicuous and extended so far—why did you look on while it was stripped of its protection and plundered by passersby?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the vine's shadow, cedars, sea and river as the extent of Israel's land.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who trample the unfruitful vine are false teachers and spirits of error, and the beasts that lay it waste are the irrational passions and evil powers.
comments.comment:
Why would you remove its hedge? For if the vine does not bear fruit, the keeper of the cluster is found in the tent. But when fruitlessness exists, he abandons the tent. And those passing by the road trample it, not those walking the path. But these are false teachers and the spirits of error. They trample it, possessing a cluster of gall and a grape of bitterness; for such a settlement has become. And one bears passions instead of moral virtues, having produced thorns instead of grapes; and another errs concerning knowledge, bearing a cluster of gall and a grape of bitterness.

God desolated it from the thicket. Those desolating it are either the irrational passions and its wild passions, or the exposed and most evil powers. … But the savage beast is the irrational mind, as if someone were to mount its passion (Psalm 80:13).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sharing in God brings life and the calling on his name that saves.
comments.comment: To depart from you. For if we are not partakers of you, we shall not be made alive, and we shall not call upon your name. For from this salvation will also follow us; for everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved (Joel 2:32).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm is for the presses, where the fruit of the true vine is pressed out, and its number symbolizes the resurrection.
comments.comment:
Since the commands of those being improved by Christ are many, and his stages have been spoken of as the true vine, there are various presses—that is, promises—in which the fruit is being pressed out, making the name of God and gladdening the heart of man. …

Fittingly, the eighty-first psalm is arranged according to its title, this number containing eights and tens as a symbol of the resurrection of the Lord being accomplished on the eighth Lord's day. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We shout aloud because Jesus, by his death, has overthrown the devil.
comments.comment: Since Jesus, helping us through his death, dissolved the one having dominion over death, the devil, we shout aloud, triumphing against the abolished tyrant, rejoicing in the one providing the help (Psalm 81:1).
comments.selected_reason: States simply why the psalm calls for a shout of joy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The timbrel is the body, the harp the spirit and the lyre the soul, all made active in virtue as we take the divine word as our psalm.
comments.comment:
Since the timbrel is made of the skin of a dead animal, he wants us, having killed the members upon the earth and carrying the death of Jesus in the body, to construct a timbrel for ourselves, which we shall give instead of a psalm. …

The word commands not only to strike a timbrel for the psalm, but also a harp and a lyre. As it is said in other psalms, the harp is called so because it is straight and unbending, and because it gives back the sound from above; the spirit is the human spirit within him, the soul being signified by the lyre, with the senses stretched out and the powers of the soul composing the sound through well-ordered and musical activities.

If, then, the harp is the spirit, the lyre the soul, and the body the timbrel, it is being allegorized: we take the divine word as a psalm, in order to make the spirit, the soul, and the body active through the contemplation and actions according to virtue. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the instruments in terms of body, spirit and soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trumpet at the new moon belongs to the feast of tabernacles, which marks the gathering of the fruits and points to the end when God gives the eternal tabernacles.
comments.comment: Trumpets begin the winepresses according to the law. On the new moon of the seventh month he commanded a trumpet blast, and on the fifteenth day the feast of tabernacles. This was the gathering of fruits at the end of the year, in the collection of the works of the field, as is made clear in Exodus. And for the one who views the law spiritually, the trumpet blast would be a revelation of the trumpets that come from heaven, while the fast appointed for atonement on the tenth of the same month is a sign of that saying of the Lord: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4). For the law made the fast preparatory for the rest of the tabernacles and the joy in it, and by introducing beforehand the trumpets which signify the fear of the coming of the judge from heaven—since these announce beforehand the coming judgment, the humility for atonement follows, and so the feast for rest comes about. Let the psalm sung at the winepresses indeed correspond to the season of the feast according to the custom of the law, and for this reason let it mention trumpets at the beginning as a prelude to the feast of tabernacles. … But let it signify the end about which it is sung, as the inscription reveals: when God gathers all fruits and gives the eternal tabernacles to his own. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm opens with trumpets and what the feast signifies.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The command for the feast is a testimony to the Gentiles added by the Gospel, who left Egypt not knowing the language they heard, as the tongues of fire in Acts show.
comments.comment: … According to an upward leading, it is thus: the command which declares the spiritual will of the shadowy feast is set as a testimony by the Lord to those who were added to the Gentiles by the Gospel. For the name of Joseph and what was said before signify these. For they did not leave behind the passions and the evils and the very place of the earth by wisdom, fleeing out of tropical Egypt, but in leaving it, they previously did not know the language, that is, the dialect they heard. The symbols of this paradox are carried into the Acts of the Apostles, where, having appeared as tongues of fire, they sat upon each of the believers, so that each one might suddenly speak the greatness of God in his own dialect heard in various voices. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the people left Egypt they all at once took up the Hebrew language as a gift from God.
comments.comment: Moreover, if one examines the matter more deeply, one may say of those who came out of the land of Egypt that the whole people, beyond all expectation, took up all at once the language called Hebrew, as though it were a gift from God. As one of their own prophets said, “When they came out of the land of Egypt, he heard a language he did not know” (Psalm 81:5).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of the verse about the unknown language.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The burdens were the loads the Israelites carried in brickmaking, and God freed them from them.
comments.comment: "Burdens," that is, the loads of lifting. For those who served in the labors of brickmaking carried the clay on their backs, throwing it out with a basket. So he removed their back, he says, from burdens—that is, he freed them from the loads (Psalm 81:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'burden' from the brickmaking in Egypt.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A storm may be a trial in which God is present unseen, so one must call on him.
comments.comment: … A storm is often taken for a trial. Since God is not present with those being tempted openly but rather hiddenly, it is necessary for the one being tempted to call upon Him, so that how having heard him, God will rescue him from his present distress.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To hear God's voice means more than sensing it: it means being persuaded and understanding.
comments.comment: 'And my people will not hear my voice' (Psalm 81:11). To hear signifies not only the sensing of a voice, but also to be persuaded by the one speaking, according to the Psalm: 'You do not heed the voice of my disciplining,' that is, I did not consent to the commands of the discipliner. And hearing the voice signifies also to understand and to think. For he says, 'Whoever has ears, let him hear'; that is, whoever has understanding, let him understand. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'hearken to my voice' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paying attention to God means both hearing his voice and seeing his form; against those who say the Jews heard and saw God, the Savior says they did neither.
comments.comment: And not only 'my people will not hear my voice,' but also 'they will not pay attention to me,' even though they are capable of understanding, seeing me. For even if he despises the voice, it is good to make clear through the one approaching me with my authority, that the timely evangelical word is not understood by the heterodox, who are interrupting these things, as seen in the Savior saying to the Jews concerning the Father, 'Nor have you ever heard his voice, nor have you seen his form' (John 5:37). The heretics, not having understood what was said, say that the Jews, having heard the voice of God and having seen his form, according to the appearances written by them. But the Savior rebukes them, showing that they have never heard the voice of God nor seen his form, and that to pay attention to God involves both hearing the voice and seeing the form. And those of differing opinions were deceived, having ignored the great significance of hearing the voice. For if even the Jews, having heard the voice of God and having received the law from him, did not understand it nor were persuaded by it, they are justly rebuked for not hearing his voice; but they also did not see his form, not having conformed to the character.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God brings enemies low through lowly means, as Egypt's tyrant was beaten by small creatures.
comments.comment: In 'the nothing' of Psalm 80:15a, it signifies that they humbled their enemies through lowly things, just as even the greatest tyrant of Egypt was not opposed by great and strong armed men, but by lowly and small creatures. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God stands in the assembly of the gods and judges them in their midst, and a judge must show no partiality.
comments.comment: He will show no partiality in judgment; you will judge both the great and the small (Psalm 82:1); one will not show partiality, for such is the judgment of God. For it is necessary for the judge to know what he serves in the judgment of God. Therefore it is also well said, that God stands in the assembly of these gods and judges them in their midst (Deuteronomy 1:17), as those knowing Him in them and in their midst, according to His own purpose.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judges are called gods, and God stands in their midst, not abandoning them but nourishing their divinity through their sharing in him.
comments.comment: … they say that men set over the judging of the people are called gods, as Moses himself demonstrates, saying, 'You shall not do evil to gods, nor shall you speak evil of rulers of your people' (Exodus 22:28). For those being appointed as gods to the people of God are not further from the judges. But since hereafter in this same Psalm God says, 'I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High' (Psalm 82:6; LXX 81:6) (not having been placed there, but because the word of God came to them), it is evident that even now 'God stands in the assembly of gods' (Psalm 82:1) will be brought against them. For all those who are such gods—men and angels—are divine in the same way, for God stands in their midst, unmoving and not abandoning them; such are they. … But God, standing in the assembly of the gods, preserves their divinity, rather nourishing and increasing it through the participation they have in him. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'gods' are and why God stands among them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: There are beings more honourable than man, called gods in this verse, though not the gods of the nations, which are demons.
comments.comment: … For we know that there are many beings more honourable than man. We have read that “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Psalm 82:1), gods who are not those worshipped by the rest of mankind (for “all the gods of the nations are demons,” Psalm 96:5); and we have read that “God,” standing “in the assembly of gods, judges gods in their midst” (Psalm 82:1). We know too that “although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are for him, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:5–6).
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the 'gods' of the verse are not the idols of the nations.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gods meant here are not those of the nations, which are demons, but an assembly among whom the God over all judges and assigns each his work.
comments.comment: For the divine Scripture knows that the Lord is great above “all the gods” (Psalm 135:5). By “gods” here we do not understand those worshipped among the nations, since we have learned that “all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5). We understand “gods” of whom the prophetic word knows a certain assembly, with the God over all judging between them and assigning to each the work proper to him. For “God stood in the assembly of gods; in their midst He will judge between gods” (Psalm 82:1). For He is also “the God of gods, the Lord,” who through the Son “called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Psalm 50:1). And we are commanded to give thanks “to the God of gods” (Psalm 136:2), having also learned that “God is not the God of the dead but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). These things are said not only through the passages set out here but through countless others.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If the judges of Israel are gods, the rebuke falls on them, since judging unjustly and accepting faces perverts a judge, as when gifts corrupt the right.
comments.comment: … But even being in their midst, he distinguishes them in the manner spoken: 'How long will you judge injustice and accept the faces of sinners?' (Psalm 82:2). If the judges of Israel are gods, what is written will fall upon them. For it is a perversion of a judge to judge injustice and to accept the faces of sinners. Just as they corrupt the right through the greed for gifts, so too they judge contrary to the law by accepting faces. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rebuke 'How long will you judge unjustly' charges.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The divine lawgiver demands judgment without partiality, since the law counts works and deeds and not wealth, poverty, rank or dishonor.
comments.comment: The power of the one being observed is known from the opposite; for just as he who has his disposition and his practice established according to justice pursues the just, so he who is regulated according to inequality and malice pursues the unjust. All such people existed toward whom the word says: 'How long do you judge unjustly and receive the person of sinners?' (Psalm 82:2) of the divine lawgiver saying: 'You will judge the great and the small, not receiving a person' (Deuteronomy 1:17), even if the one being judged is rich, even if he has honor and rank. For the law of those being judged does not count the abundance of wealth and poverty, nor rank and dishonor, but works and deeds having been performed according to virtue or malice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord forbids judges who take bribes and grant favors out of friendship, as Isaiah also condemns those who justify the ungodly for gifts.
comments.comment: The word of the Lord, having appeared many times already in Zechariah and now appearing in it, forbids these things. "These things," he says, "says the Lord of Hosts" to each of the rulers of the people: "Judge a just judgment" (Zech 7:9), as there is one who judges unjustly through bribery and grants favors through friendship, and even when there is a bribe toward someone being judged. To such complaints the divine word cries out to those: "How long will you judge injustice and accept the faces of sinners? Judge the orphan and the poor, justify the lowly and the needy" (Psalms 82:3). Such are also those concerning whom the prophet Isaiah speaks: "Those justifying the ungodly because of gifts and removing the right of the righteous" (Isaiah 5:23).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Gods who turn from the good judge injustice and hide their God-like faces, and those made divine by virtue are told to defend the orphan, the poor and the laborer.
comments.comment:
If indeed they are gods who change their divinity, since they prove to be turnable, how can one judge injustice? For having an intermediate law by which it is possible to know the good to be chosen and the evil to be avoided, if they come to things in a way that turns away from the good and embraces the evil, you judge injustice; therefore you also take the faces of sinners, hiding your own faces which are according to the image of God. Judge the orphan, who has been left desolate by the father entrusted to guardianship, but also the poor man who does not wish to contend with his own righteous ones; but also bring out the laborer and the poor, being oppressed, rescuing them from the grasping sinners.

But it is also said to those who have been made divine according to virtue, how they judge worthily the one who has cast off the worthless father and the wealth of wickedness, in protection through discipline toward them. And let them also justify the one made lowly and poor through blindness, because he has come to toil for the sake of piety, excluding those who are not truly poor and needy, on account of making them do the work of a sinner by a hand outside of them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Divine knowledge enlightens those who have it, while the ignorant wander in darkness and keep progressing in evils.
comments.comment: The divine knowledge, being wisdom of God, shines and enlightens the one having it; for the wisdom of man enlightens his face (Ecclesiastes 8:1), and those called toward divine knowledge have the command to enlighten for themselves the light of knowledge. If then the wise according to God happen to be enlightened, those who are contrary, being filled with ignorance and unreasonableness, wander in darkness, always progressing in evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those used to evil want the foundations of the earth to stay fixed in their worthless opinion, but the word that loves humankind shakes them from it.
comments.comment: But since, having become accustomed to evils and having embedded the first things of wickedness, they have not only become earthly due to their material existence, but they also wished the foundations of the earth to be, remaining firmly and immovably in the worthless opinion. … They did not love, but rather the human-loving word causes them to be shaken and moved from the very bad position they hold, and to fall from the position they built with a clumsy hand (Psalm 82:6; LXX 81:6-7). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As light is upon bodies, so the Word of God is upon souls, and ignorance is the darkness in which wandering souls walk.
comments.comment: Just as this sensible light is upon the bodies, so the spiritual Word of God is upon the souls; and just as darkness is in the night, so ignorance is in the wandering souls. Therefore also the blessed David writes concerning such things, saying: They did not know, nor did they understand; they wander in darkness (Psalm 82:5). …
comments.selected_reason: Compares the Word of God to light and ignorance to darkness.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God gives men what he is, making them gods and sons of the Most High, yet they turned to the opposite and died as humans.
comments.comment: … The good God is not all envious of his own, giving to men what he is, just as he accepted the word of the gods. But the God who makes them gods is God, and he will make them sons of the Most High, participating with them, the only-begotten Son of the Most High. But although God granted to them the being to be gods and sons of the Most High, they ran toward the opposite, to become humans and to die the death that follows humans.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'you are gods' as a gift from God that was turned away from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Human beings, being made and created, are not gods by nature.
comments.comment: … while being very careful not to take this the way it was said of human beings: "You are gods" (Psalm 82:6). For those who are made and created by the Father through the Son in the gift of the Holy Spirit are not gods by nature. …
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Though there is one God and one true Son, all of us were called gods and sons through his goodness without being gods in truth.
comments.comment: For just as being one God and one Father and one true Son, all of us were called gods and sons through his goodness and abundance—not being gods in truth—according to: 'I said: You are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High' (Psalm 82:6), so just as there is one and only Holy Spirit of truth, many spirits are called, not being in nature spirits of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil was not evil by nature but became so by personal change, and the psalm shows him as a ruler and a god by god-making, not by essence, who fell.
comments.comment: The devil is not by nature evil or in essence, but he became good and well, having become devil, satan, and evil through a personal change; but then he was good and well when he held a place in the rank of angels, but he departed from them, cast down to earth because of the pride he conceived for himself. Thus he did not say to Adam: 'Behold, you have become like one of us,' but 'like one of us'; for from the heavenly ones this one fell, just as the psalmist teaches, saying: 'I said, you are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High, but you die like men and fall like one of the rulers' (Ps 82:6). For he too is a ruler and a god, not by essence, but by god-making, and he fell like those about whom it is said: 'I said, I begot sons and raised them, but they rejected me. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The children are those on earth, who were God's children by his kindness but die as humans and fall as one of the rulers, dragging the mind down with the passions of the flesh.
comments.comment: By “children” here he clearly means us who are on the earth, according to what is sung in the Psalms as in God’s person: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.” (Psalm 82:6) As far as what seems good to God and the gentleness in him by nature, we would all be children… but as David says we die as humans and fall as one of the rulers, dragging down our own mind by the passions of the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: They die not the common death but the death that follows sin, falling as the devil did, who was a ruler and fell from heaven.
comments.comment: For they did not become humans by falling from divinity (for this is how both gods and sons of the Most High happened), but according to how they loved, mortal and human. And they die not as humans do, not the common death, but the death that follows sin, falling similarly to the one who fell among the rulers. For such is the devil; for he himself was a ruler and fell in the heavens. For it is said concerning him, 'How did the Morning Star, rising in the morning, fall from heaven?' (Isaiah 14:12). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains dying 'like men' and falling 'like one of the princes' as the death of sin and the fall of the devil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To die as men is to walk by the flesh, on earth in heart as well as body.
comments.comment: The man on earth is the one 'walking according to the flesh' (Rom 8:4), according to 'you indeed die as men' (Psalm 82:7). This one is on earth not only in body, but also in heart. He 'sets his mind on earthly things' (Philippians 3:19), and 'sinks himself into his seat'. No one of such people is righteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God will judge the earth, destroying all the nations but not all the mortals.
comments.comment: … 'Rise, O God, judge the earth; you shall destroy all the nations' (Psalm 82:8; LXX 81:8). God will judge all those on the earth, for the earth was made because of those who think of earthly things. And God will judge the earth, destroying all the nations, but not all the mortals. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who become perfect are made like God in quality, but no one can be like God in essence.
comments.comment: Likeness is understood in two ways. For when there is identity in essence, it is called similarity and even strictly identity; but when it is according to quality, it is called simply similarity. According to the second meaning, those becoming perfect are said to be made like God, just as the heavenly Father is perfect; therefore it is said, 'When he is revealed, we shall be like him' (1 John 3:2), meaning, like God. And the Creator of all, according to the first meaning, which I say is according to essence, fashioned man not according to an image and his own likeness, for no one is becoming like God. For 'Who shall be like God?' (Psalm 83:1) does not declare something rare but rather something impossible, that no one is able to be like God in essence. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A created, changeable thing cannot be like the unchangeable God, and what shares in the Word cannot be the same as, or like, the Word.
comments.comment: But a changeable thing cannot be like the unchangeable God, any more than a created thing can be like its creator. That is why the holy man, considering our condition, said, 'O God, who will be made like you?' (Psalm 82:2 (83:2)), and, 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' (Exodus 15:11). He calls 'gods' those who were created but became partakers of the Word, as the Lord himself said: 'If he called them gods to whom the Word of God came' (John 10:35). But things that partake cannot be the same as, or like, the thing they partake of. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no creature can be like God.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
comments.work: Synodal Letter to the Bishops of Africa

comments.capsule: The wicked are to be set like an unstable wheel and a reed driven by wind and storm and consumed by fire, for though they began as a good planting they bore no fruit.
comments.comment: He wills them to be placed by God like an unstable and unwatered wheel (Psalm 83:13). For it will be a misfortune to them not to be made stable and to remain motionless, having pursued wickedness. Therefore also He wills them to be placed like a reed being scattered and being driven about by a fierce wind before the face of the one pursuing them, a punishing spirit, allegorically a wind (Psalm 83:13). And the fire of punishments shall consume them, having cut off the grove which had become fruit. And using another punishment against them, He will pursue them with His own storm, from which there is no escape; therefore they shall be troubled in the wrath of God being brought upon them. Since indeed their sins were diverse, a multi-faceted punishment has necessarily risen over them. … It should be noted, however, that He loved them, though they were a good planting, becoming unfruitful. For the reed has its beginning from a good seed, not beforehand, but deviating by accident. For if they had borne fruit beforehand, it was necessary for them to become wheat, if they were to be brought into the granaries of the Word. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God alone is Most High in himself, making others high through virtue without receiving it, as he alone is wise and true.
comments.comment: For even if others are high and have become Most High through virtue, being lifted up, none of them is such from himself or in essence. For God alone is Most High, making others Most High but not becoming so himself; just as He alone is wise and alone is true, providing wisdom and truth but not participating in them as a recipient, so the Most High is unique …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God alone is called Most High over all the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'As' names the beloved dwellings of God as real, not a likeness, and they are the eternal, heavenly dwellings.
comments.comment: Regarding the word 'As' (Psalm 84:1), it does not signify a likeness or a parable here, but the beloved thing itself, just as in Moses, where he is 'as' a servant, and Christ is 'as' a son. For 'as a son' signifies a true Son and not a likeness; and Moses was not a likeness of a servant of God, but was a servant of Him. Therefore, regarding the word present, the beloved dwellings of God are not according to a parable but according to truth. And if we have meditated on what kind of things they are, we will more certainly understand them as beloved things, rather than finding them to be merely like beloved things. These things are therefore eternal and heavenly, concerning which the Savior says to those present, 'Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings' (Luke 16:9). My soul longs and faints, to cast off the psychic state and become spiritual, as is appropriate for the dwelling in the heavenly courts, as they have been spoken of in parallel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist longs for the dwellings above, as all who mind heavenly things do.
comments.comment: … And he [David] was very much accepting the dwellings above, saying thus: ‘How beloved are your tents, Lord of the powers! My soul longs and fails unto the Lord’s courts (Psalm 84:1-2).’ Such ones therefore mind the things above, and thirst for the dwellings in the heavens, …
comments.selected_reason: Shows why the psalmist longs for God's tents and courts as heavenly dwellings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 5

comments.capsule: Some read the psalm as spoken by exiles in Babylon, others took the temple literally.
comments.comment:
It should be known that some have taken the psalm to be spoken from the person of those in Babylon, longing to see Jerusalem and the temple in it and the altar (Psalm 84; LXX 83).

The rest have taken the temple in Jerusalem literally, according to the history (Psalm 84:4).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The song of praise lasts to the ages of ages for those who, after all their progress, reach the house God has established.
comments.comment: This agrees with the thought previously said and with those things beginning from the 83rd and 3rd Psalms: “How beloved are your dwellings, Lord of powers. My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Psalm 84:1-2), and after a little: “Blessed are all those dwelling in your house, they shall praise you unto the ages of ages” (Psalm 84:4). For the hymn-singing is fulfilled unto the ages of ages by those who, having attained all progress, shall come unto the house which God has established.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tent is a sign of progress and the house the end of virtue and knowledge, so the psalmist blesses those who have risen through the stages to dwell with God.
comments.comment: For the dwelling of God is perfect virtue and the highest knowledge of the truth (Psalm 84:4). It is said that in the presence of God the tent is a symbol of progress; for those traveling, it is a home. But the end of blessedness is made manifest by the dwelling of God's voice. And according to the history, the people traveling had a tent of witness (the dwelling of theology) and they had various tents for their own virtues in which all the people dwelt. Having reached the holy land, they had the dwelling in houses, no longer progressing; for they had reached the end of virtue and knowledge. But they were no longer approaching the tent of witness but the dwelling established, completing the things of worship. And there, therefore, after desiring and loving their progresses through the tabernacles, he began, saying, 'How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord' (Psalm 84:1), blessing those who have ascended through the progresses to the summit, as dwelling while bearing the state according to God, when the fullness is fulfilled upon them and the Son is revealed, we shall be like him, seeing him as he is (Psalm 84:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those still in tents love and advance toward completion, while those who reach God's house dwell there, blessed and praising him.
comments.comment: For he who has not yet reached the courts, while in the tents, has love advancing and expects completion in saying: 'My heart and my flesh shall rejoice in a living God' (Psalm 84:2), when it occurs in that establishment, with which there is no other, into which those who have reached are called blessed, the psalmist saying: 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 84:4), not as sojourners but as dwellers; for this belongs to those in tents and advancements, but to dwell is to come into the house of God, in which they are blessed, as it were 'unto the ages of ages,' praising him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between sojourning in tents and dwelling in God's house.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The altars here are not perceptible ones.
comments.comment: The altars are not perceptible. For the altar was not a multitude, according to the history. Unless even the altar is called so, Lord of hosts of the heavens (Psalm 84:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The altars of the heavenly things are better than the sacrifices of shadow and type, for on them praise, righteousness and our own bodies are offered.
comments.comment: The altars upon which sacrifices are brought up are better than the sacrifices of shadow and type. The apostle says that the types of those in the heavens are linked to these sacrifices, but the heavenly things are better sacrifices than these. For the sacrifices of praise and righteousness are brought up upon these altars, and those offering the living sacrifice, presenting their own bodies pleasing to God, they offer them not upon something else but upon these altars.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God made covenants so that we receive blessings by living by their will, and those who go from power to power, the virtues and contemplations of truth, become more able.
comments.comment: He makes covenants for men. Let us not weep, nor let us praise the blameless weeping, learning from the fact that God established covenants for those who are here. For we shall also receive the blessings, living according to the will of the covenant given here. And we shall know the magnitude of the blessings given, understanding who the possessors of them are. And not such is the God who legislated. And they shall proceed from power to power. The virtues and contemplations of the truth are powers. Therefore, those having these are also more able.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Going from strength to strength is passing from the law's shadow into its truth.
comments.comment: In this way, concerning those being migrated, the hymnist says: 'They shall go from strength to strength' (Psalm 84:7). And they are also migrated from the shadow of the law into its truth, those having ascended above the killing letter (2 Corinthians 3:6) and becoming in the life-giving Spirit. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'from strength to strength' as passing from the law's shadow to its truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ brings this merit to the saints, priests and kings, who are called 'my Christs'.
comments.comment: … And more pure and more holy of the saints, but rather also of priests and kings, he is able to bring this merit to, Christ, the Son of God. For it is said, 'Do not be afraid of my Christs concerning all the saints,' and priests and kings were approaching as Christs in Hebrew. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist appeals to God's constant hearing of prayers, which we enjoy when the Father sees Christ in us.
comments.comment: He brings forward the favor of God and the perpetual hearing of prayers, about which it is said in the prophecy of Isaiah: “While they are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah 65:24) (Psalm 84:9). This will happen when we enjoy the honor that comes through Christ, with the Father looking on us as on the face of the Son, because Christ will be in us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea to look on the face of the anointed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A day in God's courts surpasses a multitude of days outside them, as the least in the kingdom is greater than John.
comments.comment: … Better it is to be in your courts for one day than a multitude of thousands of days outside your courts. For the perfection among men exceeds that which seems little in the courts of God. Such also is that which was said concerning John by the Savior: 'Among those born of women no one is greater than John, but the least in the kingdom is greater than him.' Matthew 11:11 Let it also be said thus here: men living are under time, but those in eternity are time unto a multitude.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse by the Savior's saying about John and the kingdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unceasing day in God's courts is greater than the life of many days here.
comments.comment: The days are divided, one day being an eternal and unceasing one, because of having been created in the divine courts of the Lord. For the Lord has become to him an eternal light, like the sun of righteousness, which is not able to be overcome by it. The unceasing day is greater than the life of many days occurring here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives grace to those saved by grace, and glory to those worthy of it, as he promised to those who glorify him.
comments.comment: … God gives grace to those being saved by grace, according to 'By grace you have been saved' (Eph 2:8), a gift of the grace able to be given here. For 'grace' and 'gift' signify the same thing, as one is found to be 'having been graced.' … And He also gives glory to those worthy of receiving this, because He has promised the one saying, 'Those who glorify me I will glorify' (1 Samuel 2:30), clearly through good works and true dogmas. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'grace and glory' with 'by grace you have been saved'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope, the expectation of good things, belongs especially to piety, and the faithful are reborn into a living hope.
comments.comment: And since hope is the expectation of good things, and only the rational appetite for truly good things is the proper virtue of man, to hope is especially the substitute for piety; for it is written, 'Hope is to the pious one.' For the faithful are reborn into a living and abiding hope because the expectation of good things is pure.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is pleased with a heart that becomes his land, forgives its transgressions and covers the rest of its sins by virtue, which destroys them as knowledge destroys ignorance.
comments.comment: … For contemplation: the Lord is pleased with a good and eager heart becoming His land, because it receives the seed from Him and bears fruit a hundredfold. But He turns away from it also the multitude of captives brought by evil powers, the thoughts of Jacob, because of standing against the passions. These things, having worked them, He grants as a remission of transgressions, removing and loosening their lawlessness. And if even after a remission there is error, He covers these sins, entering into virtue; for virtue covers sins, not hiding them, but utterly destroying and making them vanish. For in this way love covers a multitude of sins. Just as knowledge covers ignorance, utterly destroying it in the soul that it was generated in, so also the love of God, being the same as virtue, covers the sins of those it benefits.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God was pleased with his earth by sending his Son to live among men, which teaches that his wrath is not a passion but is managed so that sins are destroyed.
comments.comment: God was pleased with his earth, having sent his Son to appear on the earth and to associate with men; thus it is said, 'Glory in the highest to God, and on earth peace among men of good pleasure' (Luke 2:14). From these things said, we learn that what is called God's wrath is not a passion. For because of sins, wrath is sustained, but it is managed such that they are destroyed and vanished, and it approaches them as a consequence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'favourable unto thy land' and why God's wrath is not a passion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turns us back by giving us room to repent, and once we recognize our sins and turn, his fury fades like a fire when its fuel fails.
comments.comment: … Since you are God, who gives us the salvations, turn us back, providing us opportunities for repentance and receiving us as we turn toward you (Psalm 85:4). For it will be possible for your fury to turn away from us. Since we have removed that wrath through which we sinned, once we have recognized and turned back, it will no longer act against us, vanishing. Just as fire, when the combustible fuel through which it acts is failing, is no longer, so too, once our sins are vanished, your fury will no longer be sustained against us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea 'turn us' with the picture of a fire dying without fuel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives life to those who turn to him, and the people rejoice in the God who granted it.
comments.comment: God lives, providing life to those who turn to him, having departed from him and turned away from him; he himself, having turned his face, turned away from them through which they practiced evil. It is possible to understand 'having turned' in both ways, most certainly said. For it is not made clear whether he himself turned toward them or they themselves turned toward him. When life was granted to the living ones, the people of God rejoiced over him, the God who granted life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because salvation comes by God's grace and mercy and not from works, the people ask him to show mercy, and Jesus is the mercy and salvation of God.
comments.comment: Since they require salvation not from works but by the grace and mercy of God, they say, 'O Lord, show us through whom you show mercy and compassion to your people' (Psalm 85:7); for so also your salvation, that is, the salvation from you, might be given to us. It is possible to call Jesus the cause of mercy and salvation. For he is the mercy and the salvation of God, according to how he shows mercy and saves.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the people ask for mercy and salvation as a gift.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God speaks by placing his will within the mind, not by sound from outside.
comments.comment: God does not speak striking the hearing of those listening from the outside, but placing his will within that mind, he desires to reveal to the intellect without utterance, which is why it is said, 'I will listen to what he speaks in me' (Psalm 85:8). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to hear what God speaks.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God speaks within the one who hears, giving a peace that surpasses the mind to those who return to him from the depth of the mind.
comments.comment: I will aim to see what the Lord God will speak in me. … But the Lord God will speak in him, interpreting, whether it be peace or whether it be upon his people, the God of all, against all enemies of the people, clearly those subverting them, or the peace having possessed a mind surpassing all things of the people, by which all disturbance and noise are excluded, bringing tranquility. … This peace is given from God and Father and Lord Jesus by grace, as the Savior says concerning it: 'My peace I give to you' (John 14:27). And this peace is given also to those who give back the things of God to God, guarding the righteousness toward him, who are rightly called his own. And he gives it also to those who through repentance turn their heart toward him, making the turning not crooked toward him nor superficial, but from the depth of the mind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Salvation is near those who fear God and far from sinners, and his glory dwells in their land, which is the good heart that bears fruit and the body that glorifies him.
comments.comment: Then indeed he truly dwelt and brought glory in the earth, performing many and great things paradoxically: the Savior's resurrections of the dead, sight to the blind, cleansings of the lepers, and other wondrous things he did (Psalm 85:9). … For just as salvation is far from sinners, working the things of destruction, so the salvation of God is near to the opposite, to those fearing him. Therefore also he dwells, glory in the earth, of those saying these things. And you will say their earth: the good heart of theirs which has yielded a hundredfold fruit of the seed cast upon it. … But what dwells in the heart as the glory of God, the word establishes, which says: 'The God who said light should shine out of darkness' (2 Cor 4:6); He shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of Christ. And it dwells also in the body of those persuaded by the exhortation being said: 'Glorify then God in the body' (1 Cor 6:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'glory dwelling in our land' as God's glory in the heart and body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy and truth go together, since true salvation cannot be received without God's mercy, and the just is peaceful and the peaceful just.
comments.comment:
Regarding those who achieve perfect prudence (Psalm 85:10-11). From this, the following of virtues can be shown: that the merciful is true and the true is merciful, and that the just is peaceful and the peaceful is just.

In other words, truth is named along with mercy, as it is said in the Psalm: 'Thy mercy and thy truth have encompassed me' (Psalm 85:10), and 'God sent His mercy and His truth' (Psalm 57:3). I stand by saying these things because the truth of matters is difficult for men, and even more unreachable unless they happen to be granted it by the grace of God. Perhaps one cannot receive true salvation without the mercy of God, and thus they were named by righteousness. He says that mercy has met with truth. For if mercy and truth come to the same place, we shall know it and be in it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy, which called the nations, and truth, which will bring Israel back, come together, and then unrighteousness falls and righteousness and peace are united as by a kiss.
comments.comment: Mercy and truth met, when the mercy through which the nations have been called comes together with the truth through which Israel will be brought back (Psalm 85:10). For the nations have been called for the sake of mercy, as the apostle says, but Israel for the sake of God’s truth, so that the promises to the fathers might be confirmed. Now, then, their rejection, he says, is reconciliation of the world, but later their acceptance will be life from the dead, when the perfect favor of God is shown to humanity, when he fulfills the promises made to the fathers, bringing in the race descended from them not because of their worthiness but because of his own truth. For until now those called for the sake of truth have spoken against it and have not obeyed the call, but those called through mercy have come first. Then, however, both will run together—mercy and truth—and then unrighteousness will fall completely, and the unrighteous will be driven out from their power over the righteous, so that the righteous one enjoys peace, and righteousness and peace are united to one another as if by a kiss (Psalm 85:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'mercy and truth are met together' as the calling of the nations and of Israel.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Truth rose from the earth when the Savior, who is truth, overcame the earth's falsehood, and he came down from heaven as justice, bringing peace and mercy.
comments.comment: Moreover, justice loves peace and peace loves justice. For where there is justice, there is certainly peace, without it being a mere sprout. You can also grasp these things regarding the Savior, spoken through His various thoughts, as has been clearly stated before. The truth of the Savior, having become man, has risen from the earth. For there is much deception and much falsehood among men. For there is no truth and mercy nor knowledge of God upon the earth; therefore, falsehood, murder, and adultery are poured out upon the earth, says the prophet (Hosea 4:1).
