This is not the falsehood of the whole earth that prevailed, but the one overcome by Him who said, 'I am the truth' (John 14:6), having caused the truth from the earth (that is, from men) to rise. But also, becoming justice according to the Word of God and Wisdom, He descended from heaven, bowing the heavens and coming down. He brought to us peace according to justice and mercy according to truth; for all these things are thought of in Him, as has been clearly said.
comments.selected_reason: Reads 'truth from the earth' and 'righteousness from heaven' as Christ's coming.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When truth rises from the earth, righteousness appears from heaven and all good comes from God, because Christ was born among humanity to set things right.
comments.comment: When truth rises from the earth, righteousness will appear from heaven, and all good things will come from God, and everything from the earth will be good (Psalm 85:11-12). For the Lord brought in God’s righteousness on behalf of humanity, since the heavenly judgment that is to judge and rightly order human affairs could not come about otherwise unless Christ was born among humanity for the setting right of things and took upon himself the whole matter of human nature.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The earth moistened by God's goodness bears fruit, which is virtue in the soul.
comments.comment: As the manner of rain being given, the soil bears the goodness of the Lord's gift; the intelligent earth gives fruit, having been moistened by the goodness from God. And the fruit of it is the general virtue, whereby the soul, being as a fruit-bearing earth, happens to be presented as described. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The justice that goes before the people is the Lord himself, setting their steps on the way to blessedness, and the justice of the law came before him, crying 'Prepare the ways of the Lord'.
comments.comment:
… Since the Lord spoke peace upon his people, the justice of the people going before him will set his steps upon the way leading to blessedness; and the Lord himself, who is justice, goes before the people and will set his steps into a way. To whom, indeed, is it said, 'Before you I will go and I will make the level places'?

And likewise: the justice operating according to the law in Moses and the prophets, having come forward before the end of John from the Savior, having been placed into the way of his crossings in us, to dwell and walk among us, has cried out: 'Prepare the ways of the Lord straight, make his paths'; for he alone cries: 'Make straight for him who is stepping upon the mountains, the Lord, his name.' Care also regarding John, it is said: 'He will go before the Lord in spirit and in power like Elijah,' and 'Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.'

If even the Savior is justice going before the Father into the minds of the God-bearers, consider with understanding in what way it was said: 'He who receives you receives me, and he who receives me receives him who sent me' (Matt 10:40).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be called God's servant is an honor, which Jonah and the apostles claim for themselves, as men of the world put their honors at the head of their writings.
comments.comment:
'All the saints cry out as if upon a great command concerning the servant of God.' Jonah, indeed, when asked from what land he is and from what people, said: 'I am a servant of God, and I fear the God of heaven.'

And the apostles, indeed, are testified by the Savior well through works and words, confessing him as Lord: 'For you call me Lord and Teacher, and you say well: for I am both your Lord and Teacher always, learning from me and serving me sincerely' (John 13:13). And concerning their own letters, they set forward this significance, as if being refreshed by a greatest command: 'James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ,' and 'Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ.' Just as the men of the world in the writings of life-transactions wish to be designated by the honors concerning them, so the apostles in the beginnings of their writings are worthy to be designated servants of God and of Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'gods' here include the saints, who become gods only by sharing in the Word, so none of them is equal to the Lord or does his works.
comments.comment:
And 'gods' is said not only there to be taken for idols and demons, but also for the saints (Psalm 86:8; LXX 85:8). For in these no one is entirely and unchangeably the equal of the Lord. For He himself alone is likewise God to the Father; but each of these has become a god by participation, having received the Word of God according to 'They shall be gods' (Ps 82:6) and 'The Word of God became' (John 10:35).

For even if they have become the image and likeness of God, none of them is in essence the equal of the Lord, being those who shall be made like Him but not being Him. 'You shall be holy because I am holy' (Lev 11:44), He who is holy, so that they may become holy. To speak the truth concerning those who shall become holy: 'Who is holy like you, Lord?'. For it has not been written, 'Who shall be equal to you among the gods, Lord?', but 'Who is your equal?'. For they shall be like, according to what was said: 'We shall be like him, what we shall see him to be.'

No one is the equal of the Lord among the gods mentioned, nor does anyone among them attain it according to His works. Therefore also in the Gospel it is said, 'If I have not done the works which I did in them, no other man has done; he has no sin' (John 15:24). For even if the saints once did the same things as the Savior, it differs greatly in the manner: some working by prayer and faith toward God, others by exercising authority; therefore it is said that none of the gods are gods according to the works of the Savior. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the 'gods' are and why none is like the Lord, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David foretold that all nations would worship the Lord, which is fulfilled now that the nations have been called and worship him who became as we are.
comments.comment: For every knee will bow to him, and every tribe and tongue will confess him and serve him, as it is written (Isaiah 45:23; Philippians 2:10–11; Daniel 7:14). Blessed David also cried this out beforehand in the Spirit, for he said: “All the nations you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord” (Psalm 86:9). This has been fulfilled now that the multitude from the nations has been called, and all worship him who for our sake became as we are, yet in himself remained above all.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse about all nations worshipping was fulfilled, in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God made rational beings to honor him, so his purpose that all the nations he has made will worship him must prevail over their choice to sin.
comments.comment: He [the psalmist] prophesies concerning the salvation of all mankind; for it is necessary that that which is spoken of be brought to pass, about which this holy one says again in another psalm: 'all the nations, all whom you have made, shall come and worship before you' (Psalm 86:9). For God did not make the rational beings so that they might sin, by standing up against Him to worship these things, but so that they might honor God. And since this is the purpose of the Creator, but a purpose of those who have come to be has intervened, the purpose of God must prevail. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Knowing the truth comes first from being led by God in prayer, then from practical progress, which begins with doing what is just.
comments.comment: To partake blamelessly of the knowledge of the truth is impossible not through moral instruction and active deeds having been passed through (Psalm 86:11; LXX 85:11ab). For one is first led by God through prayer in the way; but this second way is that of practical progress. For the beginning of a good way is doing what is just, and so on.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever chooses these good things rejoices in them, fears God's name, and glorifies him for ever, having been rescued by great mercy from the lowest pit of sin.
comments.comment:
To be able to walk in the truth of God, one must progress in it and pass through to the end. …

He who chooses these very good things rejoices in the possession of them (Psalm 86:11-13; LXX 85:11c–13). It is also to fear the name of God; the one desiring to have it with joy prays to be made glad in heart by God through fearing His name. Having obtained this, he confesses thankfully to the Lord God with his whole heart, which was made glad by the attainment of his requests. He also glorifies the name of God for eternity—that is, all the time of his life—it having become upon him great divine mercy, by which he was also rescued from the pit of slavery. For he named the lowest pit. For those sinning many and great things fall into the lowest pit, and in order that they might be rescued, they beg for great mercy, as one of them can easily say, 'Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.' It is therefore fitting for one rescued from such great evil to glorify the name of God for eternity and to confess to Him with his whole heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains walking in God's truth, fearing his name and being rescued from the lowest pit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spoken in Christ's person, the psalm asks the Father to lead us in his truth with an undivided heart, and gives thanks for the resurrection from the lowest parts of the earth.
comments.comment: Another, saying that the psalm is spoken from the person of the Son, says: For he asks from the Father the surpassing and divine virtue for us, saying from himself the things he wishes to happen for us—so that God is the one who leads us, according to what Paul says: “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Romans 8:14), and so that we walk in the truth of God, serving the true and real worship, the worship of the Spirit, and keeping our heart undivided around the divine fear alone, with no other concern, whole in seeking the true good (Psalm 86:11-13; LXX 85:11-13). Then he offers the hymn and thanksgiving for the resurrection to God—the Lord himself, since he went down to the lowest parts of the earth, as it is written, and from there ascended by the will of the Father and by the authority of his divinity—and we likewise find our ascent by the grace that comes from him.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The words 'Visit me' ask God to look on the speaker in order to heal him and show mercy, and if the prophecy is about Christ, the kingdom God gave him is to be guarded.
comments.comment: One should not receive unthinkingly the saying that these things are spoken by our Lord Jesus Christ, with the kings of the earth and the rulers standing and gathered together against him (Ps 85:14.15). 'Visit me' (Psalm 86:16; LXX 85:16). For you visit, you look, not at another, but to make well and to have mercy. Therefore also in the following things, the king is worthy to be given and to be guarded the kingdom, which God himself has given to him. For with this will follow his salvation as a child of God. If the prophecy is that concerning Christ, the promised things, then in this manner the upcoming things are smoothed out: David says, 'Looking upon me, as God, have mercy on me.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The handmaid is Mary, the mother of the Lord, and the people of the circumcision can also be called a son of the handmaid.
comments.comment: And regarding your giving your power to your child in becoming human and taking the form of a servant. And since he follows the one who became man and died, God will save him, the son of your handmaid who said, 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word' (Luke 1:38). For truly, the handmaid and mother of the Lord is she who bore him. And he thought it to be said in parallel, the Lord as child and the son of the handmaid. And the people from the circumcision can also be a son of the handmaid. For Paul, writing to the Galatians, clearly says concerning these things, 'But he who is born of the handmaid according to the flesh has been born'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sign for good is the virgin giving birth and remaining a virgin, a help to the human race and a consolation, since we have God as helper.
comments.comment: 'Let a sign be made to me for good of the prophecy being taken up, which forbids among us humans, of a virgin giving birth before the trial of a man and remaining a virgin even after the birth' (Psalm 86:17; LXX 85:17). This is a sign for good, a help to our race. Therefore also we were comforted; for how could we not have been about to have the most complete consolation, having had God as a helper?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy apostles and evangelists are the holy mountains, whose knowledge is laid as a foundation for those who came after and keeps them from a counterfeit faith.
comments.comment: For somewhere He said to the godly Peter, when Peter was wisely and blamelessly confessing his faith in Him and saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16): “You are Peter, and on this rock I will found My Church” (Matthew 16:18). By the rock, I think, He means the disciple’s unshakable firmness in faith. It is also said somewhere through the voice of the Psalmist: “His foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 87:1). The holy apostles and evangelists may very fitly be compared to holy mountains; their knowledge has been laid like a foundation for those who came after them, and it does not let those whom they gathered in their net fall away into what is counterfeit in faith.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the foundation and the holy mountains stand for.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The city of God is the Church, made rich by gifts from above, with a firm foundation that the gates of Hades will not prevail against.
comments.comment: For the Church is the city of God, which the inspired David also spoke of when he said: ‘Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God’ (Psalm 87:3). For she is rich, made splendid with gifts from above and from heaven, and her foundation and her permanence stand firm and cannot be broken. For ‘the gates of Hades will not prevail against her,’ as the Savior said (Matthew 16:18).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the city of God is and why it is glorious.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The city of God of which glorious things are spoken is the Mother of God, who alone contained the uncircumscribed Word of God.
comments.comment: For the dwelling-place of God has no need of glory from us: she is the city of God, of which glorious things were spoken, as the divine David says to her, "Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God" (Psalm 87:3). For what city of the invisible and uncircumscribed God, who holds all things in his own hand, shall we understand, if not her who alone, truly beyond nature and beyond being, contained without circumscription the Word of God who is beyond all being, she of whom glorious things have been spoken by the Lord himself? For what is more glorious than to receive the counsel of God, ancient and true (Isaiah 25:1)?
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: Those who pass from disordered affections to a steady mind and know God are remembered by him.
comments.comment: Having come into the tranquility and stability of the mind from poured-out and disordered affections, they have entered Babylon having known God, whom God remembers, deserving of His remembrance when judged. The expansion may signify those coming from the east and west toward the kingdom (Psalm 87:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God remembers Rahab, the wide way, and Babylon, meaning confusion, in the sense that he remembers those who have known him, and forgets those who forget him.
comments.comment:
'God says he will remember Rahab and Babylon' (Psalm 87:4; LXX 86:4a), for those knowing him. Consenting to this, now having known God, but rather having been known by God. For having taken up the knowledge of him, we shall know him more, and most especially we shall be known by him: 'For if anyone does not know, he is unknown.' And to someone God says, 'Because you cast away knowledge, I will cast you away from ministering to me; you forgot the law of your God, and I will forget you, your children' (Hos 4:6).

Therefore, regarding those who are ignorant of him through faults, God has forgotten them, even though they knew him. Behold, therefore, of Rahab, who takes upon herself the wide way, and of Babylon, being interpreted as confusion, God is said to remember those who have known him. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's registration of the peoples in the heavenly city rests on the quality of each soul, which only he knows, so those who bear the heavenly image are written in the book of God.
comments.comment: Regarding the Church, not only the rulers but also the peoples have been inscribed into the citizenship of the heavenly city of the living God, having a registration upon the church of the firstborn who are written down in heaven, which only God is able to recount. For their registration has not happened from the mere collection of their names, but from that which reveals the quality of their soul, which only He Himself bears. And it is possible to learn from the opposite by the observer: in Jeremiah it has been written, 'Those having departed from the earth shall be written' (Jeremiah 17:13). Just as those having departed and having become far from God are written upon the earth as the image of the worldly, surrounding themselves with earthly and material things and thinking of them, so those bearing the image of the heavenly and having citizenship in the heavens, being enregistered there, have been enrolled in the book of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being 'written up' among the people of God's city means, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Heman, a descendant of Korah, sings a song of the Savior's world-saving sufferings in the person of the Lord, and the title says 'For the dance'.
comments.comment: We have said before that Heman was a descendant of Korah, and Korah was the grandson of Kohath, the most honored of the sons of Levi, and the leader of the order of the Levites. He sings a most lordly song. For he dances for Christ, as the song is also inscribed “For the dance.” He sings the world-saving sufferings of the Savior, bringing forward the very person of the Lord in the word, as becomes clear from what is said.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The title 'For Ma'elah' means a dance or choir of the sons of Korah, for the wise answering of one who fears God.
comments.comment: Regarding 'For Ma'elah,' that is, for the dance or the chorale of the sons of Korah, for the understanding and for answering wisely to him who fears God and because of this truly becomes an Israelite. For their fear is interpreted as having all the divine fear and reverence, and to answer with understanding is proper for a wise listener while announcing the song with the dance and the divine chorale of the psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He cries to God in the bright and the gloomy times of life, by day so that he keeps his share in good things and by night to rouse his spirit toward God.
comments.comment: 'I have cried to You not only by day but also by night' (Psalm 88:1), not occurring in solitude among the bright and pleasant things of life (it is impossible to be so by day), but also having been in the gloomy ones, containing a nocturnal state; having cried out in the day, so that the participation in the good things might remain for me, and in the night, so that when its end is coming out of the night, I might be able to rouse my spirit toward You. And it is possible to say more simply, similarly to what was said by the Savior: 'The Father will avenge His children who cry to Him day and night' (Luke 18:7). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist cries both day and night.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ tells the Father that, though he came as Savior of the world, the Father is the God of the salvation he provides, and he will intercede to save sinners.
comments.comment: The Savior therefore says to his own Father: 'Even if I have come to be a Savior of the world, having come to seek and to save the lost, being made worthy of eternal salvation for all, but rather, O Father, you are the God of this salvation which I provide for the being saved; for I grant it by your will; therefore, becoming a Paraclete toward you on behalf of those who have sinned, I will save them, interceding for them.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He cries day and night, sometimes asking for salvation and sometimes for it to be kept, and boldly asks for what is truly good, believing he is heard.
comments.comment: With works and disposition, he cries out to the God of his salvation day and night, at times asking for salvation, at others entreating that it might be preserved, which already exists. And the voice saying, 'Let my prayer enter before you' (Psalm 88:2), speaks with much boldness toward God. For I ask such things as are profitable for me and appropriate for you and good to give (for I ask for the truly good things); let our prayer become in your hearing; for in this way you will also grant the responses I have requested, descending and inclining toward my cry; for in this way I have believed to be heard; therefore, O Lord, I cry out to you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the boldness of the prayer and what the psalmist asks for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When evils surround us we should take God as our only refuge, as constant prayers at the passion show.
comments.comment: And he [the psalmist] describes a heavenly way of life for the salvation of humanity and teaches that when evils surround us, we should consider God our only refuge—just as we were also taught from the Gospels, when the passion was already approaching and he was making constant supplications and prayers (Psalm 88:2; LXX 87:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The pit and the grave are the same place in Scripture, and the Savior, who was no sinner, came to give a ransom and was counted among those going down into the pit.
comments.comment: For many are the enemies lying in wait to tear my life into the pit (Ps 88:4), by whom my soul has been filled with despondency and evil struggles, that is, the indulgence of evil circumstances. The Holy Scripture calls the same place both the pit and the grave (Ps 88:5). The Savior himself, having become not a sinner, came for the salvation of those being slain to give a ransom, by the grace of God, having tasted death above all. For he alone died on behalf of all, and in this way he was counted among those descending into the pit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ was numbered with those going down into the pit not by his own works but by the Father's good pleasure and his own will, becoming a truly helpless man.
comments.comment: For as each one rightly descends into the pit because of what he has done or thought, I was counted and numbered with them; not being led to this by the works of following, but by the Father's good pleasure and our will to be counted among those descending into the pit and being judged; not that I became arbitrarily and voluntarily as a helpless man, the likeness of which is not being raised to the man. 'Depart'; for he has become a man according to truth, and he says that to be like a man is not simply to be a man, but a helpless man. For being able not to suffer, not to be seized, and not to be bound, he gave himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though Christ became helpless voluntarily and was cast into death, he is free among the dead, for he alone says that no one takes his soul from him.
comments.comment: But even if he has become a helpless man voluntarily, as also to be cast into death, yet he is free among the dead. For among all those departing to the place of the dead, being led by some, not only the wicked but also the distinguished, Jesus alone has been emboldened to say, 'No one takes my soul from me; I lay it down from myself, so that I may take it again' (John 10:18). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'free among the dead' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Of all the dead led by others to the place of the dead, only Jesus, who laid down his own soul and never sinned, was free there, and he freed the souls held by death.
comments.comment:
It will be clear to one who has studied the Gospels. For concerning Lazarus, a distinguished man, it is said: 'And it came to pass that the poor man died and was carried to the bosom of Abraham' (Luke 16:22); and toward something trivial he says, 'In this night they demand your soul from you'; and toward another face he says, 'Until you are brought down.' For the one being brought down by others is brought down there.

Therefore, no one among the dead is free, whether they are those being pulled toward others or those being led to the place of the dead; but Jesus alone, having placed his soul by himself, receiving it from no one, has become free among the dead. And why? Because although all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), being delivered from life with bonds, having difference in what is more and what is less having occurred in Hades, he alone, not having committed sin and not having known sin, has become free among the dead, as also to loose the bonds of death of the other dead in order to raise and vivify them.

For just as he alone on earth is the liberator of sins being given as a gift, he says, 'If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free' (John 8:36); so also, having become in Hades with freedom, he liberated the held souls, making fear work in those holding them; for even the gatekeepers of those places flew away, having seen his authority and his freedom. It follows then that you should interpret the following verses as having been spoken by Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since no one took his soul but he laid it down himself, Jesus, who never sinned, was free among the dead, unlike those held by the chains of their sins.
comments.comment: And if no one took the soul, but he himself laid it down from himself so that he might take it again, in this way, as it is said in one of the psalms: 'I became like a man helpless among the free dead' (Psalm 88:4), it has happened. And according to the immediate sense, we say that those being delivered from sins while 'being constricted by the chains of their own sins' are not free dead. Since, therefore, Jesus did not commit sin nor even knew it, he was free among the dead. Only this soul was seen to be free there. For certainly the gatekeepers of Hades flew it away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As a man the Savior was not subject to being in Hades but was free among the dead, needing no angels to lead him because he is their master.
comments.comment: … For the Savior, according to the human, was not subject to being in Hades, even if it happened there through others. For it has been said of himself: 'I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Psalm 88:4-5). And indeed, angels lead the holy ones, but the wicked ones, the shadows. But the Savior, being free, did not need angels, being master of them and being ministered to and led by them. For he said: 'No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down myself'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ's body, unlike the slain, stayed full of God's power after death, as the flowing of blood and water shows.
comments.comment: … he [Christ] says, "I have become like those who have been slain and lie in a tomb" (Psalm 87:6 (88:5)). They suffer this because they were separated from your life-giving power. For it is clear that this was not true of him. The body of Christ was full of the power of God even after death. That is why blood and water flowed from him, something that never comes from dead bodies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Lord's body differed from the slain in the grave.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whoever is guarded by God's hand cannot be snatched away, but one made worthless through whom sin occurs is cast away and no longer held or remembered by God.
comments.comment:
The Savior says: 'For no one will be able to snatch him who is guarded by the mighty hand of God' (John 10:29); for he is contained by God, invincible to those desiring to attack and snatch him.

He remains. But someone having become worthless through whom sin occurs, is unworthy to be made a part of the hand, and is cast away, no longer worthy to be held and remembered by God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ did not enter Hades by his own work but, having tasted death for others, he raises those in the depth and leads them into the paradise of God.
comments.comment: Since he says, 'Because I did not come into Hades and death according to my own work, but having tasted death on behalf of others, I bring the cause of falling into the lowest pit and into the very heart of the earth' (Psalm 88:6) instead of 'You made me to go into the lowest parts of the pit,' just as having resurrected those in the depth of this, he leads them away from there to bring them into the paradise of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is victorious in the shadow of death, not death itself, and turns those in darkness from it to live in him, the light.
comments.comment: 'You laid me in the dark and in the shadows of death' (Psalm 88:6). For if he says he has become victorious even in death, it is not in death strictly speaking, but in its shadow (for he reached the third day having risen), and in the same way, having placed them in the darkness under them, he turned them away, so that they might no longer live in darkness but in me, the light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'darkness and the shadows of death' and what Christ did there.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's wrath is like a fire that feeds on sin, and the Savior submitted himself to it so that it would find no more fuel, since he was tested in all things without sin.
comments.comment: The wrath of God is like fire, which takes sin as food (Psalm 88:7). Because of these things he underwent, and he himself acts; and as they are being consumed, he also approaches (Psalm 88:9). When many human abominations were occurring, the wrath of God was being carried against them, but the benefactor Savior submitted himself to the wrath of God, so that he might be fixed upon it, no longer moving or acting to find fuel, and so that God might be extinguished, not having been fed by him; because he was not known to sin, having been tested in all things without sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior took on himself every wavering temptation and trial to be proven in all things, while those who knew him but turned away were cast out from the Father.
comments.comment: And he brought upon himself all those wavering temptations and tribulations, so that having struggled and having been tested in all things, he might be shown proven, so that we are no longer subject to wavering. For he dispelled them; and it is said of God, 'They are not for you,' because they are brought upon them for His judgment. Those of the circumcision who knew him and were known by him were fortunate, but those who responded to the law and the prophets had become far from him, having turned away and having been shown to be traitors, having been cast out from the Father and having been made far from His own Son …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who became sinners counted piety an abomination, and so made it an abomination to themselves and were driven away.
comments.comment: He drove them away according to the psalm: 'They drove You from my hand' (Ps 52:11). And he says that the pretext for them being distanced from Him is that they made an abomination for themselves. For the Jews, having become sinners, considered piety to be an abomination; for piety is an abomination to a sinner. Therefore, they also made the mystery-initiating abomination of this piety an abomination to themselves, not being of such a kind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The disciples were ashamed at his sufferings and no longer hoped for a Savior, and he was held fast by his enemies, willingly handed over, bearing all that is heavy to a body.
comments.comment: Another, explaining the words "You have made me an abomination to them" (Psalm 87:9 (88:8)), says: Just as the disciples were ashamed at his sufferings, no longer hoping for a Savior or redeemer—they even said, "The rulers handed him over to a sentence of death, but we had hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21). It is clear that he was also held fast in the hands of his enemies, handed over willingly, yet still held. There he came into affliction for our sake. For he bore everything that is heavy and afflicting to a body.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The eyes that grew weak are the perceptive ones of Israel, whose poverty is spiritual because they took everything according to the letter.
comments.comment:
'I was handed over and was not delivered away.' For the Savior was not immediately handed over by them unto death and departed, leaving them nothing remaining to them in the providing of a way for repentance. For it was necessary for them to be perceptive, just as His eyes are said to be, and they grew weak as if to see Him no longer. Because of this he says, 'My eyes have grown weak from poverty' (Psalm 88:9). For the cause of the weakness is that spiritual poverty has come upon them, for they desired the flesh and, taking everything written according to the letter, they grasped it.

How then can His eyes, the perceptive ones of Israel, be able? This will become clear to you once you understand: 'You are the body of Christ and members in part' (1 Cor 12:27). Just as those who believed according to the Gospel fulfill the body of Christ—just as the perceptive ones are the eyes, the understanding ones are the hearers, and the practical ones are called the hands—so also, before the manifestation, those holding to the Scriptures were the body of the Word of God according to the stated analogy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wonders and the resurrection the psalm asks about are for those who perceive and confess, not for the impious who fight against God and stay unrepentant.
comments.comment:
… 'Can a voice be read thus: Will you not do wonders for the unfeeling ones, and will you not perform wonders for the dead who have lost the power to grasp?' For these things happen to those who perceive and are able to marvel, not to those who fight against God, the impious, and because of this they remain unrepentant. For no one will pray for them.

'There shall be a resurrection upon your confession.' For those who happen to be God-fighters are not of a nature to confess. And regarding 'resurrection' here, he is not speaking of the most common sense (for all shall partake of this), but of the one occurring through repentance, as it is said: 'Does not he who falls not rise again?' (Jeremiah 8:4). It is possible to decide: 'Will you not do wonders for the dead?' Only, he is not saying, 'Will you not do wonders for those who have been deadened by other gods,' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy is recounted to those whose nature is to be shown mercy, and his truth to those who have passed beyond perishing to salvation, not to those who make a work of perishing.
comments.comment: For no one says that to those who have despaired and to those hidden in tombs, the announced mercy of you will be recounted to the living who desire to be shown mercy, but nor will your truth be recounted to those who are making a work of perishing and because of this are named perishing. For the Word recounts the mercy to those whose nature is to be shown mercy (for they are not those who show mercy to neighbors; for they say, 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall be shown mercy'), but also the truth is not recounted in perishing, but to those who have passed over it and have reached salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wonders of truth cannot be known in the darkness of wickedness and ignorance, or in a land choked with thorns.
comments.comment: The wonderful things are not to be known in darkness. Those held by superfluous wickedness and ignorance are darkness. For darkness is said of some, but also a land forgotten and a heart unremembered, being filled with thorns of pleasures and worldly cares. The wonderful things of the truth are not to be known in this, nor is practical justice and moral virtue in the land forgotten because of the thorns.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the dark' and 'the land of forgetfulness' stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks God to save the race he made and lead back to life those fallen into death, so that they may see his wonders and not be left in forgetfulness.
comments.comment: Save, then, the race you have made, by your own knowledge, and lead back to life the human beings who have fallen into death in each way (Psalm 88:12). They must be spectators of your wonders and interpreters of your power. Let them not remain overlooked in forgetfulness, but let them be remembered again by you and led back to life. This is what the champion of human beings says, interceding for the common race of all and working out the life of the world by the will of the Father.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea about wonders and forgetfulness as a prayer for human beings.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ presents himself for us unceasingly, appeasing the wrath he took upon himself.
comments.comment: The ambassador and priest presents himself on our behalf with unceasing presentation, from dawn and through the night, and he appeases the wrath of God against us, which he himself took upon himself in his sufferings (Psalm 88:13).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Jesus asks why his prayer is rejected, not because he has sinned, but so that all for whom he intercedes may be saved, and the rich one who became poor for us is lifted up again.
comments.comment: It is fitting for Jesus to speak with boldness, 'Why, Lord, have you rejected my prayer?' (Psalm 88:14), for it is not that you have rejected my prayer and turned your face away from me because I have sinned at all; therefore, having received my petition, lead all into salvation, for whom I intercede, shining upon them with your face. When the rich one, who labored for us, became poor for our sake, toiling for our salvation, the text says, not saying at all that he is poor, but from youth. For being rich and existing in the form of God, having emptied himself in this present age, he became poor, from the time he was born and had age; and having been lifted up to the cross and having been humbled, and his body having been laid into the tomb, it seemed to be vanishing, causing many who believed in him to stumble, but having risen from the dead, he was lifted up again into the heavens, having been taken up so as to draw to himself those who are able no longer to see him as poor and toiling because of the humanization, but as rich and the icon of the invisible God (Psalm 88:15). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the cry 'why castest thou off my soul' and the words about youth as spoken by Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The exaltation in wonders and signs was changed into humiliation when he came to suffer.
comments.comment: He calls "exaltation" the exaltation in wonders and signs, about which the Father says to him, "I have glorified it" (John 12:28), while the Son says, "Glorify your Son" (John 17:1) (Psalm 88:15). He says this was changed into humiliation when he came to suffer, suffering for human beings and abandoned by them, the ones for whom he suffered.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The terrors and the waters of evil powers passed over the Savior and troubled him, but since he knew no sin they could not harm him, for much water cannot quench love.
comments.comment:
Regarding all sin into his own body, all impulses according to various sins and his terrors passed over him as to disturb him, but they are not able to work against him, since he has not known or experienced sin. And it is said that the impulses and terrors of God, which are powers serving through punishments, turn out to be vessels of wrath.

These, having passed over the Savior, disturbed him, saying, 'Now my soul is troubled' (John 12:27). For even if he possesses a most perfect soul, yet seeing such a multitude of enemies, he experiences a fore-passion, especially since the water of the day surrounded him all at once, rushing against him and drowning him, if he had not been an excellent diver. For just as perceptible water surrounding someone drowns him, especially if he does not know how to swim, so the evil powers kill the one crushed by them.

But if they have become as water around Jesus, surrounding him all at once during the day, they are not even able to harm him; for much water will not quench the love (Song 8:7). For the perfection which is placed toward God through love is unquenchable. And this existed according to the human nature of Jesus, so that the shield of the hands cannot harm him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy is built up like a building from the many who are shown mercy, and God's truth is prepared in the heavens for those who will see it face to face.
comments.comment:
For just as a building is composed of many and various things being fitted together, so a building of many being benefited by the mercy of God takes place. … For its humanization is the foundation and the end of the building of mercy, the removal of the pre-occupying sin of all those being shown mercy. …

From these things follows: 'In the heavens your truth shall be prepared' (Psalm 89:2). For since we, those on earth, are imagined to be able to perceive divine things not yet with a clear face, but through a mirror and in a riddle (1 Cor 13:12), in the heavens the truth of God is being prepared for those having been prepared from there as if they are about to face it. For then they face to face the beauty of the truth, having seized the end of knowledge and understanding, the partial reaching of things having been abolished for them. And the truth of God is being prepared in those not thinking of earthly things but having their citizenship in the heavens, by wearing the image of the heavenly through which the heavens are used.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God swore to David so that no one would think the promise of an everlasting throne came by chance or favoritism, and the oath makes the promise stable.
comments.comment: By this God gives to David his father the throne to reign over these people forever, Jacob, into the ages (Psalm 89:4; LXX 88:4), as if there is no end to his kingdom. … And so that no one might think that David attained this blessing by chance according to favoritism, God says, 'I have sworn to David my servant'; … And the 'I have sworn' spoken by God establishes the stability of the promise toward David.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly why God swore his promise to David.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one is a son of God by essence except the Savior alone, and the rest are made like him in quality, as they become merciful and holy as the Father is.
comments.comment: This very thought is confirmed by the set-forth word: 'For who shall be like the Lord among the sons of God?' (Psalm 89:6). No one is, according to essence, a son of God, except the Savior alone, who is the only one consubstantial with the Father; but those who are not according to essence, but according to quality, shall be made like him, just as they become merciful like the Father and perfect as the Father becomes: 'You shall be holy, because I am holy' (Lev 11:44).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is fearful to those near him who disobey his commands, for being near him is like being near fire.
comments.comment: He is also fearful to those who are opposed, threatening punishments and bringing them down against those who fall away from His divine commands. For you, being near Him in receiving His divine teaching, while sinning, are near the fire, as the words of the Savior say: 'He who is near me is near the fire, and he who is far from me is far from the kingdom.' Thus, in the present word, He is fearful to those around Him who, through having believed in Him, disobey His commandments; how great is He to those held by His virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The truth around God is the Son who says 'I am the truth', and God has truth around him by generating it, not by sharing in it.
comments.comment: The truth about God is none other than the one saying, 'I am the truth' (John 14:6). If it is around God, it can never not be, lest God should descend from not being once surrounded by truth to this. But it is surrounded by this, generating it, and He alone is the true God. For just as He alone is wise, not participating in wisdom but generating wisdom, so He alone is true and has truth around Him, not taking part in it but being with others and giving it to them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jesus shows whose sea it is by calming it, and if the sea stands for the troubled life of men, he gives those who walk with him a firm footing upon it.
comments.comment:
And Jesus, demonstrating by word what kind of son he is of the master of the dominion of the sea, rebukes it while it is being agitated and stirring up a storm, and immediately calms it.

But if the sea's allegory signifies the life of men, its dominion may be the evil one in whom the whole world lies, that is, the mortal and perilous state. By this, the master of the sea, providing weakness to its dominion, grants authority to the travelers to suffer against all his power, calming the unstable and irregular surges of its waves, which are called upon it, making it also a firm footing for those receiving authority to walk upon it with Jesus, of whom Peter bears the image.

For no one, apart from Jesus, is able to suffer the sea of life, becoming subject to anxieties and pleasant passions, unless he walks along with Jesus. For he is the one walking as if on dry land upon the sea, as it was said to him: 'Your ways, O God, are in the sea, and your paths in many waters' (Psalm 77:19). For Jesus has trodden paths in the strong waters; the passions are also life-related anxieties that those following his tracks are able to mount.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm's words about ruling the sea and founding the world fit Christ, who calms the sea and winds with authority and so is truly God.
comments.comment: The disciples, he says, were being storm-tossed on the lake; then “coming they woke him saying: Master, we are perishing. And having been woken he rebuked the wind and the surge of the water, and it ceased and there was a calm.” (Luke 8:24) It has been said about Christ through the voice of the blessed David: “You rule the might of the sea; you calm the tossing of its waves; the heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the inhabited world and its fullness.” (Psalm 89:9–12) So what would fit the one who calms the sea if not also to rule all things? And to have the heavens as his own, and to be able to found the inhabited world and its fullness — how would Christ not be understood to be truly God, the one who rebukes sea and winds, and that with authority?
comments.selected_reason: Plainly applies the verses on ruling the sea to Christ calming the storm.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The world God founded upon its fullness is the church, where souls and sacred powers dwell, built on Christ as its one foundation.
comments.comment:
And he established the inhabited world upon its fullness, being no other than the church, in which souls dwell having adhered to the right reason and the truth. But sacred powers also dwell in it, intervening around those fearing him.

And the foundation upon which it was established is not other than that about which Paul writes, for no one else is able to lay a foundation other than the one laid, which is Jesus Christ. And the fullness of this spiritual inhabited world, being founded upon the same foundation, is the fullness of virtues and of the dogmas of piety, along with the divine gifts of the Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is to be praised for his works around both Tabor and Hermon.
comments.comment: Mount Tabor lies in the region of the Galileans, and Hermon in the desert near Sinai (Psalm 89:12). God must be hymned, he says, not only for his works around Tabor but also for the manifestation that took place around Hermon.
comments.selected_reason: Short, plain explanation of the two mountains the verse names.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's one perfect power is his true image, and the prayer asks that it appear among men.
comments.comment: "Your power," he says, "prevails" (Psalm 89:13). Let your strength appear, let it become manifest and glorious among human beings. … For the one true power is not like that, but is uniquely the true image and mark of God, God accomplishing all things through it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Scripture's arm, hand and right hand of God all name the Son, who is the Father's creative power and goes before his face as mercy and truth.
comments.comment:
The poetic power of God (but this is His creative power, His only-begotten Son) is signified to all those who are within by name. For 'arms' is said in the Psalms: 'And the arm of the Lord, to whom was it revealed? And your arm, O Most High, and you shall not be afraid.' But also the 'hand of the Lord' is confessed in: 'My high hand has done all these things'; and 'right hand' in: 'Exalt me with the right hand of the Lord.' For the holy one says to God: 'Yours is the arm with might, reigning and holding all things.' And it also says: 'Let your hand be strengthened, performing wonders and accomplishing great powers.' …

In thought, the power of the Father is not different; Christ is called these things. For if He is the Son of God and Wisdom and the Word of God and Truth, He is the right hand being lifted up by God, suspending and lifting up all, and He goes forth before your presence as mercy and truth; for no one who is to approach your face has been previously pitied and has conversed with the truth. It is possible, then, as in other places and here, that mercy and truth are not other than the Only-begotten, as in 'God sent forth His mercy and His truth.' It is not other than the Only-begotten Son of God, who is the same.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy and truth go before God's face, mercy through moral virtue and truth through knowledge of the mysteries of piety.
comments.comment:
With the mercy and the truth of God pre-sojourning, he manifests to the minds the Father joined to him; … this face must go before among those who through purity of heart are able to look upon the face of God—mercy through ethical virtues and truth through knowledge of the mysteries of piety.

For since we are shown mercy according to ethical activity, and according to knowledge we approach the truth; for this reason mercy is named in many places together with truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The king's throne rests on righteousness, and mercy abounds first as the forerunner of judgment, with truth beside it because nothing untrue occurs in God's patience.
comments.comment: He foretold the judgment from then on, when the king comes and sits on the throne of his glory. For that throne has righteousness as its foundation … Before that manifestation, mercy was abundant on the earth, like a forerunner of the critical coming, as the fearful judge who is about to appear prepares human beings for salvation by mercy. And with mercy comes truth, because it is not possible for anything untrue or not upright to occur in God's good patience, even if it seems to those who do not know the future that the wicked are wrongly allowed to prosper, nor is it reasonable that the good are overlooked when they suffer loss.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why mercy and truth are named together with judgment.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Our horn is exalted by God's good pleasure, since it pleased him to bring about our salvation through his own Son.
comments.comment: If we effect power, then our horn shall be exalted in your good pleasure. For our horn was exalted by the good pleasure of God, who says, 'This is my beloved Son in whom I have been well pleased' (Matt 3:17). For He was well pleased to effect our salvation through His own Son.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God speaks to his sons in vision, and the prophets saw with the mind rather than hearing or looking with the senses.
comments.comment:
He who perceives a spoken word, if he only senses it, it is through hearing, if he hears the one speaking; but if he understands the things being announced, he does not perceive by hearing, but by vision of the mind he perceives the speech of the one offering it. Since God was showing things rather than merely announcing them, He speaks to His sons who are being enriched through progress and perfection, not in hearing but in vision. So also it has been written concerning Israel: 'And the people saw the voice of the Lord' (Exodus 20:18). It is necessary to say, 'Heard the voice of the Lord,' but if it is said instead 'Saw the voice,' that is to say, he perceived it with the mind. …

The prophets were seers of visions; for they did not say they were perceiving by sensing some things or by grasping them with the eyes, but they were striking with the mind at the beauty of intelligible things. 'You spoke in vision to your sons': 'I made help as far as possible,' saying this regarding the Savior who has come from the root of Jesse. For truly in this He set help to help all creation that is able. And the one on whom He set help is the chosen one from the people, exalted not according to divinity but according to the flesh.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse recounts Nathan's promise, naming one prophet as God's sons or holy ones.
comments.comment: He now explicitly recounts the promise made through Nathan the prophet, indicating prophets in the plural from one, whom he also calls sons of God, or as the other interpreters render it, holy ones of God (Psalm 89:19-24).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one chosen and exalted is Christ, of David's seed according to the flesh, anointed with the Holy Spirit and upheld by the divine arm so that no enemy or son of lawlessness can harm him.
comments.comment:
For he was chosen from myriads, as in the selection of the elect. And because of this the Father exalted him, granting to him the name which is above every name. 'I have found David my servant' (Ps 89:20); and since the one according to the flesh is of the seed of David, it is possible and sufficient for him to be held by the hand over all the rational creation so that he might teach me in this way; therefore he anointed him with holy oil, proving him priest and king in all things (In holy oil, by the Holy Spirit, clearly meaning anointed, as it is said: 'God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness among your companions' Ps 45:7), because my hand shall take hold of him, his arm being strong.

And the arm and hand of God, the divinity of the Only-begotten; and it takes hold of him, performing strange and great works through him. An enemy will not benefit in him; instead of the devil (for he does not know sin, nor is there deceit in his mouth), thinking he can benefit, while he is able to instill deception and other wickedness. But no son of lawlessness, having come to break the law, will be able to harm him by surrounding him with sin. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's arm and hand, his Son, take hold of the man born of the virgin and work great things through him, so that the enemy gains nothing.
comments.comment: He found and with holy oil anointed him, since my hand shall take hold of him, strengthening him by my arm (Psalm 89:20-21). And the arm and hand of God, the Son of God, has been said. For he overcomes the man, taking hold of him, the one born from the virgin. And the hand overcomes him and takes hold, performing extraordinary works through him. And the enemy will not profit; the devil is in the man who is the Lord's; for he did not know sin, nor was there deceit in his mouth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God chose David from the sheepfold, anointed him, and was with him so that his enemies' uprisings failed.
comments.comment: He says that God declared he had shared his power with David and brought him forward into glory, choosing him according to the words, "I took you from the sheepfold, from behind the flocks, to be leader over my people Israel" (2 Samuel 7:8). And when he found him pleasing, he anointed him with holy oil for the kingdom. God was present with him, working together with him in everything, making the uprisings of his enemies ineffective, shattering their armies, and putting them to flight, according to the words, "I was with you in all that you undertook, and I destroyed all your enemies before your face" (2 Samuel 7:9) (Psalm 89:20). These things were spoken through Nathan the prophet. He says that David was exalted by the mercy that is from God and by the care that is fitting toward the righteous man, just as he also won victories in wars beyond all expectation and was undefeated.
comments.selected_reason: Plain account of what the verses say about David's anointing and help from God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one anointed calls God 'my Father', and the Father sets him as firstborn, a supporter of the salvation of those who flee to him.
comments.comment: He himself (clearly the one anointed with holy oil) will call upon me; 'You are my Father, God,' he says (Psalm 89:26). For since having been born from the virgin he has been called the Son of God, he will call upon me, saying 'You are my Father,' the only-begotten Son of God (for he is Son according to essence), but not only calling but confessing God as Father. And he took upon himself man, and was called the Son of God, and calls God his Father and the supporter of his salvation; for he raised him and into the heavens he took him up. And he has become a supporter also of his own salvation, not that he himself is saved, but that he saves those fleeing to him. And having thus called upon the Father, the cause of all, the Father himself sets him as firstborn, bearing the first things of all those who have been called sons of God, not in the same way as he was raised up with the only-begotten; for he alone is the genuine instrument and temple of the God Word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God swears by himself because he has no one greater by whom to swear.
comments.comment: God swears by himself, since he has no one greater by whom to swear, as Paul says. … For he says, "I swore by my holiness," or as the Fifth Edition renders it, "By my sanctification," instead of "By my holiness" (Psalm 88:36 (89:35)) (Psalm 89:35).
comments.selected_reason: Short, clear answer to why God swears 'by his holiness'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God does not change his mind after swearing, as with Abraham's oath, and the throne he promised is as lasting as sun and moon.
comments.comment: Since He does not change His mind after swearing, giving an unpassable priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek, He remains constant; and having promised to Abraham with an oath that in his seed all the nations of the earth would be blessed, He shows the immovability of the blessing. If indeed He gives something by chance, He does not swear upon it; for indeed, having handed the kingdom to Saul without an oath, He did not change His mind. … And the moon remains most fully illuminated as the gathering of those being enlightened by Christ for ever, when the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the righteous shall shine forth like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Psalm 89:35-37).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hedges and strongholds that were broken are the apostles who scattered at the betrayal, and the neighbors who reproach him are those who claim to be near his church.
comments.comment: And you demolished all his enclosures from his sons, every most fortified help, so that those attempting to plot against them might be able to act against them. For enclosures, according to the Scripture, are diversely becoming guards from God; and it is possible to call the apostles the enclosures of the Christ's vineyard, whom those seeing them scattered say are being removed by God, having been scandalized in the night of the betrayal of Jesus (Matt 26:56). You reproached his strongholds with cowardice. It has been said that the true disciples of Christ are his strongholds, having been placed in cowardice at the time of the betrayal of Jesus. … For those who seem to be gathered as neighbors of him through a pseudonymous knowledge, thinking that they contain his Scripture and are near his church, are those through whom they think and act badly, reproaching him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The throne of Christ is not overturned by the cross, since after making cleansing of sins he sits at the right hand and the throne stands firm.
comments.comment: But nothing of this sort will happen concerning his throne, since God has established him as the days of heaven, not as the things that are earthly. But also God remains in opposition to himself if the throne of Christ is as the sun and the completed moon for the age. For having seen him having been crucified and having suffered, they saw him having received the kingdom at the end, his throne having been diminished and overturned, and having taken upon himself the shame upon the cross, concerning which the apostle says: He endured the cross, despising the shame, instead of the joy set before him, having risen from the dead, no longer being abolished by the cleansing but perfecting and working, him removing the sin of the world, according to the said thing: having made a cleansing of sins, he sat at the right hand of majesty in the high places, being raised up and having firmly established the throne, remaining for a long time and an eternal age (Psalm 89:46-47).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks to be rescued from vanity and corruption, which only the heavenly king who is stronger than death can do.
comments.comment: He appears to be seeking something greater and beyond human capacity, belittling the life we now live as being nothing (Psalm 89:48). He says that human beings pass into something vain—not that they came into being for vanity—and he asks that they not be handed over to corruption, since clearly the kingdom will also be restored then, when corruption is dissolved and life for the ages is given. From where could escape from death come to us? From where, except from you? For this could not come to a human being from himself. No one exists who will live and not die, nor will anyone be able to rescue himself from death. These words plainly seek the heavenly king, the redeemer from vanity, the one who is stronger than death and the Savior of human beings from death, who changes the vanity of the present life into truth and establishes an eternal kingdom upon eternal life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the plea about vain life and death asks for.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Who is the man that shall live and not see death?' means that no one does, since death has passed upon all men.
comments.comment: Here it is possible to grasp the upcoming passage regarding 'no one': 'For who is the man that shall live and not see death?' (Psalm 89:48) instead of 'No one'. And if the discourse is about common death, no one truly lives and does not see death, according to what is said, 'For death passed upon all men, of whom all sinned' (Rom 5:12), and 'For it is appointed unto men once to die' (Heb 9:27). For 'who' is equivalent to 'all men'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist still hopes for the promise, calls on God's righteousness against those who reproach, and so he blesses.
comments.comment: He did not despair of mercy, but he seeks the promise and calls upon the righteousness of God against the impious nations who reproach the righteous man for having suffered misfortune in his offspring and having fallen (Psalm 89:50-51). He says these are enemies of God, and they reproach the footprint of the righteous king as if it had been wiped out. After making these appeals, he blesses. The blessing belongs to one who hopes. And what does he hope for, except that the prayers will be fulfilled, that the promise will be accomplished and not fail, as he appears to have believed from the beginning? As Paul also says, "It is not as though the word of God has failed" (cf. Romans 9:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm ends in blessing after complaint.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is the same, unchangeable one in every age, from everlasting to everlasting.
comments.comment: And the phrase 'And from the age and as of the age you are' signifies the movement of God from infinity to infinity. For you are the same one remaining forever, not one in one age and another in another age; for you are the same one, unchangeable and immutable, from infinity to infinity.
comments.selected_reason: Plain explanation of 'from everlasting to everlasting'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is asked not to return the raised man to lowliness.
comments.comment: Having raised man from things of lowliness and debasement to height, guarding him in that suspension and height, do not turn him back to become such as the low things
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A thousand years are like yesterday to God, so the whole age has the measure of one day for us, or even less.
comments.comment: And if 'today' is this whole age, perhaps 'yesterday' is the age gone by. … in the Psalms thus — 'A thousand years in thy sight are as the day of yesterday, which is past' (Psalms 90:4) (whatever the famed millennium is, likened to the 'yesterday' day, differing from the 'today'); … And it is no wonder that to God the whole age has the ratio of one day with us — I suppose, of even less.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the thousand-years-as-a-day verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Our whole age is plain to God, in every deed and also in our thoughts.
comments.comment: Place our iniquities before you, to punish us for them, as all our age—and time is that which extends our day with bodily life—is manifest and enlightened to you, not only of every transgression in practice but also of that which is manifest and enlightened to you in thoughts
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Against a thousand years, a human life is the thinnest span, bounded by about seventy years and filled with hardship from infancy to old age.
comments.comment:
If he has spoken this way about a thousand years, it is clear that the span of a human life will be the thinnest possible, as if indivisible (Psalm 90:10; LXX 89:10).

The whole of human life, he says, is bounded by about seventy years. He says this from the greater part. And not even this is given in ease, but almost entirely in hardship. For either we are disciplined as infants, or we labor as young men, or we suffer hardship as old men. So he rightly said, "And the greater part of them is labor and pain" (Psalm 89:10 (90:10)) (Psalm 90:10). For since the order of life follows age in this way, very little time is found that is stolen away for gladness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the length and toil of life in the verse.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The prayer asks God to reveal his providence through his right hand, who is the Word made flesh, so that we may know those taught wisdom in the heart.
comments.comment: As those standing say: O Lord God, reveal the providence of the world which you created through your right hand, so that we may grasp not how it does and works through it, but let us know it as it approaches us. The petition of those calling upon the presence of Christ is able, for He himself is the right hand of God. … For then the right hand of God became known, who is the Word having become flesh who dwelt among us; for we beheld his glory as of the only-begotten from the Father. … And having known the right hand of God, let us know with it those who have been instructed in wisdom in the heart, who are not merely those who claim to be. But we speak of Wisdom in the perfect ones.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's turning away lasts a little while but seems long to the longing.
comments.comment: 'Turn back, O Lord; how long will you turn your face and your right hand away from us?' (Psalm 90:13). For you do this to us for only a little while, yet a long time appears to those exhausted by the longing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'how long' of the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's right hand has risen on us like the sun of righteousness, and his light fills us with mercy so that we may rejoice.
comments.comment: 'We have been filled in the morning with your mercy' (Psalm 90:14). For your right hand, which we were worthy to be made known, having shone upon us, prepared the beginning of a spiritual day, like the sun of righteousness (Mal 4:2). In the beginning, occurring in the morning, we were filled with the mercy from you, as your true light enlightened us in all those days so that we might rejoice and be glad (Psalm 90:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The whole present time is night, and the morning is the coming of the Lord, when lasting gladness replaces the days of affliction.
comments.comment: He fittingly called this entire time "night," in which a human being sleeps while being put to death, and "morning" the time that is coming, in which we will live when the Lord appears and mercy comes down from heaven. He asks that the sun come and the day shine forth, and that enduring gladness be given to the righteous in place of the days in which we were afflicted, falling into countless evils. These were the times of refreshing that Peter also foretells, into which he says the appointed Jesus our Lord will be sent (Acts 3:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the morning and the gladness for afflicted days.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The morning rises on us in many ways, so we are filled in many days, and we rejoice over the days in which we were humbled.
comments.comment: But since it rises to us not in one way but diversely according to various actions and thoughts, we come to be filled in many days; in all those days let us rejoice and be glad, so much as to be able to loose the dark and evil exterior of the days, in which you humbled us by captivity and delivered us to enemies through ignorance and malice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is asked to guide his servants and their works onto the path of salvation.
comments.comment: Guide your servants and the works of your hands, and those born to us through teaching and the imitation of virtue, being pure and harmonious, onto the path of salvation. For so shall your brightness as God shine upon us, as the sun in your kingdom. Therefore we pray, direct the works of our hands upon us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The snares are laid by deceivers and sophists, by evil powers that catch souls through harmful desires, and above all by the devil.
comments.comment: Hunters are in these things, and deceivers and sophists, men attempting to trap people, so that they might go through wisdom into false doctrines. Therefore, he who interprets their trap is a confused speaker; for nothing stirs up and agitates the mind like an argumentative speech. The evil powers are also hunting through a snare, catching souls through harmful desires and other passions; for he says, 'The eye of a prostitute is a snare to the sinner,' and 'For a woman hunts the precious souls of men.' And they hunt through wealth and through those nearby. But the leader of these hunters is the devil, who himself is a snare.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the fowler and his snare stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God covers those who have grown wings like eagles, as an eagle covers its young.
comments.comment:
This is in accord with the song of Deuteronomy regarding God: 'As an eagle will cover his nest and upon his young ones he has hovered, spreading his wings he received them and carried them upon his feathers.' All those who, through endurance and the other strength of approaching virtue, soar like eagles, are high-flying, being suspended by the wings of understanding and practical virtue. It is from God that they have come to possess such things; therefore they also are his young ones, as it is said in the prophet, 'But those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength.'

They shall grow wings like eagles, running and not growing weary. God will cover those who have grown wings like eagles with the young ones of an eagle; for as an eagle covers its young, so God, having desired his young ones, takes them upon his wings to cover them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the picture of God's feathers and wings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God shelters his people like an eagle over its nest, bearing them upon his shoulders, as Moses and David both say.
comments.comment: The divine Moses said something like this when he adorned Israel with the tender care that comes from God: ‘As an eagle would shelter its nest, and yearned over its young, spreading its wings it received them, and took them up on its back’ (Deuteronomy 32:11). David too sings to every holy one who has made his dwelling in the help of the Most High (Psalm 91:1): ‘He will overshadow you upon his back,’ he says (Psalm 91:4). By ‘back’ I take him to mean the parts just below the neck, the region, as it were, of the shoulders, and not the back as a whole. So, in the words of the prophet, they will be lifted up on shoulders (Isaiah 60:4; Isaiah 66:12), and, as with Ephraim of old, they will be taken up on the arm (Hosea 11:3)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: God surrounds the one he guards as a shield with his truth, so that he does not fear even the night, since he has the light.
comments.comment:
The defender God, as a shield, and with the side of his truth surrounds all the one guarded by him, so that he may remain unhurt by all those plotting to cast him down, and especially by the one sending out burning arrows. But the one surrounded by the truth of God, having put on the armor of God and having taken up in all things the shield of faith, will not fear even if it becomes night, being illuminated by the circling truth and light that reaches him. …

Just as the one in the night does not fear, because he has light and there are those watching the night, so also the one having the one who said: 'Do not fear, for I am with you,' will fear nothing of the aforementioned nightly things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the shield of truth and the fearless night.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who uses the truth does not fear sin and error in the darkness, nor the midday demon who comes disguised as light.
comments.comment:
But he who uses the truth does not fear being led astray by a deed in the darkness. A deed led astray in the darkness is every sin and every ignorance and the working of those evil spirits of error. … He who is found in so many uprightnesses does not even fear the devil transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). A midday demon is promised a full-strength light through philosophy and empty deception; this very thing is entirely a midday demon.

Not he alone, but also his servants, transforming themselves into servants of righteousness, are midday demons.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thousands fall before they can come near the righteous, as those who came to seize Jesus went backward and fell when he said 'I am'.
comments.comment: And the falling thousand and ten thousand do not approach the righteous to harm him; for it is written, 'They shall not approach you' (Ps 91:7). For when the zealous one intends to approach, the phalanx of the adversaries falls. For it is said, 'As they approach to devour my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies themselves have stumbled and fallen' (Ps 27:2). … These things are fulfilled symbolically in the Gospels; for how closely did those who had come to seize Him dare to approach Jesus, when He said, 'Whom are you seeking?' and they answered, 'Jesus of Nazareth,' and He, Jesus, said, 'I am,' and they went backward and fell to the ground (John 18:4-6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
