comments.capsule: The thousands fall before they can harm him, as at Jehoshaphat's deliverance, though the righteous also often win through battle.
comments.comment: Next he says that a thousand will fall on the left and ten thousand on the right, before they can even draw near and inflict any harm, so that he will look without fear, by the recompense from God, upon those falling and being destroyed (Psalm 91:8; LXX 90:8). … This is what happened to Jehoshaphat according to the promise, so that without fighting—but singing and praising God through one another—he saw the enemies destroyed. For it says, "They came to the watchtower of the wilderness and looked and saw the multitude, and behold, all were dead, fallen on the ground, and there was no one saved" (2 Chronicles 20:24). … But one must not always suppose that victories come to the righteous without battle. For they often won by going through battle as well, but he speaks here of the most manifest help, in which God the helper is especially seen (Psalm 91:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verses promise and how they came true.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Kept safe while his enemies fall, the righteous man sees the punishment of sinners and at once confesses God as the cause of all his goods and his only hope.
comments.comment: Besides these things being fulfilled (I am indeed saying regarding the falling thousand and ten thousand of the enemies not approaching the righteous), he will understand with the eyes of his mind, being guarded by that which has been made upright for him by the truth, the things that have been made upright for him, and he will see also the retribution of sinners; having said these things about them, he immediately confesses Him, the Cause of all existing goods. Because of this he says: 'O Lord, all these things have been made upright for me, since no one else but You have established my hope.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who has made the Most High his refuge will be mastered by no evil, and his house will not be struck.
comments.comment: He introduced the person of the one who hopes, saying from himself to God that he has made him his hope. And again he declares to such a person: "Since you have chosen the Most High like a house of security, you will be mastered by no evil, nor will your house be struck by divinely sent blows" (Psalm 91:10; LXX 90:10).
comments.selected_reason: Plain statement of the promise to the one who trusts.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The same hardships are a scourge to the sinner but a testing to the righteous, as with Job, so no evil comes near the dwelling of the one who trusts God.
comments.comment: But since the aforementioned evils do not approach the one who makes the Most High his refuge, neither does the scourge brought upon them approach his dwelling, since he is not a sinner; for only the sinner is scourged in this way. For many are the lashes of the sinner; and it has been said to us in other places that the same circumstances are lashes to the sinners, but contests to the righteous. Never do the burdensome and evil things come upon the pious as a scourge, but as a testing … just as it happened to Job, that the righteous might be revealed (Job 40:8). And also it is said: 'No evil shall come near you' (Psalm 91:10; LXX 90:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the promise squares with the righteous suffering.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God commands his angels to guard the righteous and lift them so that they do not stumble on the stone of foolishness and sin.
comments.comment:
These words, spoken as if concerning the Savior, the devil took, as it is carried in the Gospel; but the Psalm is said from the perspective of every righteous person being helped and covered by the Most High, being the God of heaven (Psalm 91:11-12; LXX 90:11-12). And even if it is said concerning Christ, it is manifest that he is not God but is a man; for all things concerning him are announced to him as a man, and this will also apply to every holy person who imitates him and follows him. …

God gives a command to his angels, that they may guard and protect the righteous, who are ministering spirits sent for service for those about to inherit salvation (Heb 1:14).

Do not worry, for angels intervene around those who fear Him, to rescue them from unseen enemies and foes. Indeed, do not worry, even Jacob the patriarch, when about to face greatest enemies, sees the intervention of God being fulfilled by angels fighting for him, and thus he thanks: 'For God is the one nourishing me from my youth, the angel who rescues me from all my evils.' Likewise also Elisha saw a multitude of angels surrounding him, seen by him, but not by his servant; thus he prays for the eyes of the child to be revealed to see what is greater than those fighting against them. …

Having received a command from the Lord, the angels guard the diligent from all deeds and activities, and they lift him up so that his ways may not stumble on a stone (these are the angelic energies) so that the foot of his soul may not trip on a stone. For he who is carried by angels meets the blessing of that which is said: 'He shall not stumble at any stone' (Psalm 91:12). For when the light of the true one has risen and the intelligent day has dawned, he who walks in this day will not stumble on what the light sees. But the stone upon which those not lifted up by angels stumble is foolishness and most hard sin. And they also stumble upon the cornerstone, an elect one, through unfaithfulness, as if it were a stone of stumbling to them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the angels do for the righteous, with Jacob and Elisha as examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who tramples lion and dragon has received authority from Jesus, and the lion and dragon are our adversary the devil.
comments.comment: And he who now praises excellence, riding on a shield and a basilisk, having received authority from Jesus to tread upon the lion and the scorpion (Luke 10:19); and trampling, he will also trample all the power of the enemy, the lion and the dragon. And even from a parallel passage, the lion and the dragon are our adversary, the devil; for as a lion he walks seeking someone to devour; he himself is the serpent and the dragon, the ancient Satan (Rev 12:9) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Faith gives authority to tread on beasts, as Paul was unharmed by the viper, and the faithless should fear their own faithlessness more than the beast.
comments.comment: The wild beasts are a demonstration of faith. Have you trusted in the Lord? Upon asp and basilisk you will tread, and you will trample lion and dragon (Psalm 90:13 (LXX; Hebrew 91:13)). And you have through faith the authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions (Luke 10:19). Or do you not see that when Paul was gathering sticks, the viper fastened on him and caused him no harm, because the holy man was found to be full of faith (Acts 28:3-5)? But if you are faithless, fear not so much the wild beast as your own faithlessness, through which you have made yourself easy prey to every corruption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise to tread on lion and dragon as a matter of faith.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: God will answer and be with the one who loves him, and show him his salvation, which is Jesus, as Simeon saw it.
comments.comment: Since he has set his love upon me, says the Lord, the one who has fled and hoped in me, the one who has said, 'But You, Lord, are my hope' (Psalm 91:14; LXX 90:14) … Having cried out with the great voice of the soul toward me, he will find me hearing and answering him. For I am always present for him, even when he encounters distress; for I am with him in tribulation (especially then is it necessary to be with him, when the painful and distressing things are around us). Not only will I free him from the painful things, but I will also work by watching over him. And I will grant to him also eternal life, upon the long-lasting and long-enduring, the eternal light (for light is for the righteous always). And I will show him my salvation, the salvation from me, the Jesus who is the cause of this, just as the blessed Simeon, having seen, rejoiced saying, 'Now You release your servant, Lord, in peace, since my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared in the presence of all peoples' (Luke 2:29-30). … It is not to be thought that the psalm is spoken only concerning the Lord, as the Arian ones and Eusebius desire, but it is also concerning a righteous man and one having trusted in God, to see the best end of hope, Christ Jesus the salvation of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the promise of rescue, answer and salvation at the end of the psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who confesses his sins to the Lord and is forgiven proclaims God's mercy with his works, from the first light of the day.
comments.comment: The one confessing and accusing himself toward the Lord, asking for forgiveness and remission, testing by experience the benefit from confessing, proclaims with his works the mercy of God, having been shown mercy upon those things for which he repented. And he proclaims the mercy of God having become upon him, having been enlightened and having become established at the beginning of the day by the sun of righteousness standing, he proclaims first of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the psalmist gives thanks and proclaims God's mercy in the morning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Singing to the Most High begins in theology and contemplation, and the truth about God is proclaimed from deep and hidden things, which the text calls night.
comments.comment: And the singing in the name of the Lord the Most High is a premise of theology and theoria; the end has the truth which it is fitting to proclaim, not from the surface or from manifest things, but from deep and hidden things through an excess of knowledge. The obscurity which is named in such things is called night; for by nature the things said concerning the pious and the correct manifest the knowledge of many through the greatness of power. And night is that which is hard to grasp. And this night has a reference to the darkness which God has set as His own hiddenness. The morning proclaims the mercy of God and His truth according to the night (Psalm 92:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's works are so deep that no one finds the bottom, but the wise person who has the Spirit of God searches and understands them, while the one without understanding does not.
comments.comment: And as much as the greatness of them appears to us, so much do I see the reflections concerning their God, which He has made and enlarged. To this is conjoined what is said by the Preacher: 'I said, I will be wise, but wisdom was removed from me; a great and deep depth, who will find it?' (Ecclesiastes 7:23-24). How its depth seems to have appeared incomprehensible to me. But having said 'Your reflections have become very heavy,' he gladdens the lovers of wisdom, saying that a man without understanding and without insight does not know and does not comprehend them, clearly showing that the wise man and the one having the Spirit of God investigates all things and comprehends the depths of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the deep thoughts of God and the man without understanding mean, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: On the day of judgment men are humbled and the Lord alone is lifted up as King.
comments.comment: On the day of judgment, of all men being humbled, from which they were exulting in pride over temporary things, the Lord alone is lifted up as King of all, being shown blameless of all and having provided for and arranged all things (Psalm 92:8) …
comments.selected_reason: States plainly when and how the Lord is shown most high.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A mind blinded by evil overlooks God's greatness, but the purified mind finds the God who is victor for ever.
comments.comment: The height and greatness of God is overlooked when the eye of the mind, which is able to approach the Lord, is blinded by evil; and the destruction of sin occurs as if those who have become enemies of God through sinning were to perish, and to perish such are they, but the God who is the victor for all eternity will be found by the purified mind (Psalm 92:8-9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Old age here is the perfection of the soul, which wisdom and a blameless life give, not length of years; Abraham reached it, and the true olive tree anoints it with oil that heals.
comments.comment:
… Not only shall my horn be exalted like a one-horned beast, but also my old age shall be anointed with the oil of gladness; old age not the bodily one, but the age presenting the perfection of the human soul, for it has been written: for old age is precious, not the long-lived, nor is it measured by number of years, but wisdom is a thing for men and an unblemished life is old age.

Having surpassed this, Abraham was said to be nourished in good old age; for it has been written about him: 'And Abraham died in a good old age, full of days, departing' (Gen 25:8). …

This is interpreted as old age being anointed with oil, from that true olive tree speaking in the temple of God: 'I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God' (Ps 52:8). This olive tree not only anoints the light of knowledge, but also heals and looses pains, anointing the aforementioned old age.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the horn, the old age and the fresh oil mean, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies now present are cast down by sight, but he will hear of those still to rise; evil powers lose their strength.
comments.comment: And my eye has looked upon my enemies, and my ear shall hear of those rising up against me, committing iniquity (Psalm 92:11). Perhaps the present enemies are cast down by sight, but his ear shall hear concerning those who are to rise up against him. Just as their strength is dissolved, all these things must be expected concerning evil powers. For strictly these are hating us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Scripture does not mean the senses of the whole man, because we have a mortal and an immortal kind of sense, and only the immortal is our own.
comments.comment: Who, hearing something or about someone, sees and hears with his own eye and ear? In answer to these things, it is not said wickedly, but that there is a twofold genus of sensations in us, mortal and immortal; and specifically for us rational beings, the immortal part is found to be intelligible. For the mortal is not our own essence, but is common and belongs to the irrational animals. The Scripture does not mean the sensations of the whole man, but says 'my eye and my ear see and hear' as in the things set forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The palm is taken as divine teachings, fertile and protective of the fruits, and its branches and the victors' symbols come from it.
comments.comment: Those who interpret his palm as being divine teachings receive it as a fertile and protective thing for the fruits. And the bride who says these things, not being like the flowering of the righteous according to the palm, says, 'I will be made like the palm.' From this palm, one takes ornaments made from the branches of palms when celebrating the feast of the Tabernacles, and the victors carry from this the symbols of victory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous man is likened to the fruitful phoenix and the strong, thick cedar of Lebanon, for his many fruits and his firm hold on the good, and like the female palms he takes from the male the means to keep his fruit.
comments.comment: Since the phoenix bears much fruit, and the cedar in Lebanon is very fruitful and many-rooted (Ps 92:12), it is fitting that the righteous man was compared to such much-fruitful things in the virtues according to their kinds and the various doctrines of the truth. For according to these things his blossom is compared to the phoenix, but also because of the firm and strong nature regarding the good, he is likened to the cedar in Lebanon; for the cedar is indeed dense and very thick, and the phoenix is ever-living and possessing a heart upward-stretching, to which the one who has treasured in heaven and therefore has his heart there is fittingly made similar. And since in the Song of Songs the bridegroom (and he is not the God Word) is said to be a phoenix, upon whom it is promised that he shall ascend and hold his heights, the bride (the perfect soul and the church) saying, 'I will ascend in the phoenix and hold his heights,' see, in this way the righteous man will blossom similarly, receiving from it the power to save the blossoming fruit. For those called female palms by the farmers receive from the male palm the occasion for preserving the fruit. Such is that upon whom the bride says she will ascend.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The palm branches teach us to carry right faith instead of their whiteness, patient hope instead of their sharpness, and sweet love instead of their sweetness, so that the righteous may flourish like a palm.
comments.comment: Instead of their [the palm branches'] whiteness, let us carry right, undefiled, and simple faith; instead of their sharpness, patient hope, which pierces and slays every thought that rises up to take us captive away from the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5); and instead of the sweetness of the palm, sweet love, which is made up of the faith and hope already named and the rest, so that what was said may be fulfilled in us: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: Putting on glory and girding on power is better said of Christ's first coming and human weakness, through whom the world is made firm.
comments.comment: It is possible, then, to speak of putting on glory and girding on power with reference to what is known among human beings, but it is more fitting to speak of it with reference to the dishonor that came to Christ in his first coming and to his human weakness. He himself leads the world, made firm in him for secure good things, which it is no longer possible to move in any way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Lord's clothing of majesty and the unmovable world mean.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The rivers are the divinely inspired writings, which give life and make fruitful, and those who drink from them are lifted up out of the tossing of arrogance and vainglory, so that even temptations become causes of salvation.
comments.comment: Those who imitate the rivers lift up the river that gladdens the city of God (Psalm 93:3-4; LXX 92:3–4b), first by raising their mind, if they use the voices that interpret the things understood by them, so that from the waters of these many rivers they may become wonderful and worthy of acceptance through repentance and the taking up of virtue, whereas formerly, through arrogance, wealth, self-will, and vainglory, they were tossed about like the waves of the sea of human life. And it is possible also for these words of the divinely inspired writings of both the New and Old Testaments to be rivers, because they are drinkable and life-giving and cause fruitfulness. Indeed, the rivers lift up and toss about those who drink from them through the contemplation of the truth, making the tossings of the sea wonderful, as they are ready to be awakened, lifting up their voices from the voices of the rivers by thinking things in a God-befitting and sublime way. Regarding the tossings of the sea, according to the present thought, the so-called temptations will also be wonderful causes of salvation, appearing from the voices of the many drinkable waters …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is marvelous in the high things, so that his testimonies and he himself are to be believed as high, and men and angels are raised to them by faith and virtue.
comments.comment: In the high and exalted words, the Lord is marvelous (Psalm 93:4), so that his testimonies, which are kindred to the spoken rights and laws, and he himself, God, are to be believed as high in which he is marvelous. It is possible to say that men are raised to divine things through faith and the rest of virtue, and even the angels and archangels in heaven are high, in whom the Lord is marvelous, having testimonies and sayings established and examined because he has spoken them with certain stability (Psalm 93:5; LXX 92:5bc).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who have approached God become his dwelling-place, so holiness is needed in them for a length of days, since the temple of God is holy and they are it.
comments.comment: All those who have approached God become his dwelling-place, and it is truly fitting to be holy for the saints, not for one or two days, but for a length of days; thus The One who initiates, desiring the dwelling-place of God to be a sanctification for a length of days, says: Do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone destroys the temple of God, God destroys this one; for the temple of God is holy, and you indeed are it. For holiness and sanctification are truly necessary for everyone who becomes God's dwelling-place, just as the temple of God is holy and just as the holy place is holy and of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why holiness belongs to God's house, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God avenges boldly because he knows exactly the deeds and intentions of those judged, whereas other judges may err and be shamed by punishing wrongly.
comments.comment: The God of avenges, being in his avenging, has spoken boldly (Psalm 94:1; LXX 93:1). For because he accurately knows the things of those being judged and even the intention of those doing them, he brings the avenges with boldness; whereas other judges might err by not bringing the punishment in proportion to the quantity and quality of those sinning, wherefore it happens that the judge is shamed as not having rightly punished those caught in wickedness, while he alone is bold in avenging, he who says: 'Measure with a measure, it shall be measured to you' (Luke 6:38); for he gives to each according to his works.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God can avenge boldly, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At Christ's appearing a sinless man spoke boldly and judged the earth, proving it full of sin, and repaid the Pharisees and the unseen enemies who crucified him.
comments.comment: All these things shall be raised up toward the appearance of Christ (Psalm 94:2; LXX 93:2). For then a sinless man having become man spoke boldly, although he is Lord of avenges, but also he judged the earth, proving it full of sin, himself having not done sin nor known sin; therefore also he repaid the Pharisees who had been prominent above him and the invisible enemies who were puffed up in crucifying him.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how Christ is the judge of the earth in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God cannot be ignorant of anything, for the one who planted the ear and shaped the eyes must hear and understand; it is silly to say the giver of knowledge does not know.
comments.comment: For nothing would escape the one who is truly God by nature. … And let blessed David mystagogue saying: ‘Understand already, senseless ones among the people, and fools, sometime be thoughtful; the one who planted the ear, will he not hear? and the one who shaped eyes, will he not understand?’ (Psalm 94:8-9) Some were saying, I think, from ununderstanding: ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’ (Psalm 94:7) Or is it not altogether silly to say that the supplier of knowledge neither knows, nor to think that the one giving the matter to those come to be from beside him does not hear (Psalm 94:7)?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The pit means punishment, and the sinner digs it for himself, as other Scriptures show, so that punishments fall on those who sin through foolishness.
comments.comment: Often the pit is used to mean punishment, as it has been said: 'And he shall fall into the pit which he himself worked' (Psalm 7:15). And since it has been said unchangeably 'unto the abyss' (for it is not said by whom), it is shown from other writings that the pit which is being dug for the sinner is not dug by another, nor by the one falling into it; for 'they dug a pit before my face and I fell into it' (Psalm 57:6); and 'he who digs a pit for his neighbor shall fall into it' (Prov 26:27); and since the fool digs evils for himself, saying evils, the punishments fall upon those sinning through foolishness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the pit dug for the wicked means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil's tyrannical rule is a throne of unrighteousness that hunts the soul of the righteous and condemns the innocent, and demons and evil men who practice evil act cunningly against them.
comments.comment: He says that the tyrannical rule of the devil is a throne of unrighteousness, by which they cruelly hunt the soul of the righteous, even as judges and arbitrators happen to condemn the innocent. For the devil's lust for evil is so great that it is equal to this wretchedness. For the Scripture calls him destruction instead of the Law-giver and perdition instead of the one who was lost; one place saying concerning him, 'Destruction came' (in this way also Judas was branded a son of perdition, having become a son of Satan), and another place calling him lawlessness; for it says his children have become sons of lawlessness, as it says concerning Christ, 'And son of lawlessness he shall not add to harm him.' Those who practice evil are his retainers, concerning whom it is said, 'Who shall rise up against me against evildoers?' or 'Who shall stand with me against those working lawlessness?' Both demons and evil men are such, acting through cunning the things foretold against the innocent and the righteous (Psalm 94:16).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A throne of lawlessness is the tyrannical rule of the devil, who has fallen away from God's commands and weakly commands heavy, burdensome things, and it will not happen to God.
comments.comment: What these things are accomplished against your servants will not happen to you, but a throne of lawlessness will not happen to you; for you have revealed the king of the law of all things, by whom the whole is governed. If, therefore, the devil, having become an apostate from your commands, attempts to rule lawlessly, he does not understand, nor will it happen to you; but having become a distant robber, he tyrannizes against those who happen to fall under his weakness. For a throne of lawlessness is a rule characterized by tyranny; for there is no other tyrant than a lawless rule. Therefore, he is most weak and contemptible, commanding heavy and burdensome things, weaving toil through his commands.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's commandments are not heavy, but the throne of lawlessness weaves toil upon them by casting fear and cowardice into the mind, such as fear of lacking necessities, so that they seem heavy.
comments.comment: But your commandments, O God, are not heavy according to John, and they are also useful, lifting up and elevating the one being transformed (Psalm 94:20-21; LXX 93:20-21). It is possible also to take the word thus: Lord, the throne of lawlessness weaves toil upon your commands, despite your light and easy commanding, casting cowardice and opposing things to the minds of those seated. For, while the right word exhorts to righteousness as beneficial, it sets against injustice gains and supplies, proposing those from this; again, while the word calls to temperance and freedom from care, he weaves toil upon such a command, entering into a thought of cowardice and fear of not being deprived of the necessities, overtaken by sickness and old age. Likewise, regarding the other commands of God, not being heavy, he weaves toil by casting a fantasy of weight.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Unjust kingdoms cannot share in God's power, and what the wicked planned against the righteous will turn back on themselves, so that injustice is overthrown by the righteousness of God.
comments.comment: It is not possible, he says, for unjust kingdoms to share in your power, which bring toil on those who keep the law, by whom the righteous person is hunted for arrest and the one who does no wrong is murdered (Psalm 94:20-21; LXX 93:20). In these words he shows altogether the overthrow of injustice, which is established by the righteousness of God. You will not give power to the wicked, he said, but you will place security around the righteous person, standing as a stronghold for him and strengthening his hopes in you. And what the wicked thought would succeed for them against the righteous, these things will turn back and come upon themselves; and as they plotted to make the righteous invisible, so they will go away into invisibility. This is the end of the vengeance that comes from you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how God overthrows unjust rule that hunts the righteous.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To rejoice in the Lord means holding fast to the life in Christ in good cheer, so that Christ's glory shines out and he welcomes the fruits the saints bring.
comments.comment: … but in good cheer and gladness that we ought to hold fast to the life in Christ. For this, I think, is the meaning of ‘Come, let us rejoice in the Lord’ (Psalm 95:1). For so the glory of Christ will shine out purely and clearly, welcoming most gladly the fruits the saints bring, just as then, too, God came down visibly in the form of fire and consumed the sacrifices (Leviticus 9:24). He all but counts the approved life of those sanctified in faith as his food and delight.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: They give thanks to the God who appeared and shone on them, and they shout for joy to their Savior in psalms, which they do through the deeds that please him.
comments.comment: They urge confession concerning those on whom they have acted wickedly, or concerning those who have suffered well from God, thanking Him who appeared and shone upon them, his countenance being the exact imprint of his hypostasis. For He is the image of the invisible God. It is possible for the third verse to correspond to the first and the fourth to the second, regarding those who rejoice in the Lord: 'We have seen your face in confession, but also we shout for joy to our Savior God in psalms.' For through psalms they shout for joy to the Lord, through which deeds they perform such things as are pleasing to Him; for the voice of the psalm submits such a thing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word reigns over those who have become gods and holds the ends of the earth in his hand, as Lord of both heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
The Scripture calls angels 'gods' (Psalm 95:3; LXX 94:3b). But the Word of God has come to reign over those who have become gods. Wandering over all the earth, the Word, according to the account of providence, holds the things said of the ends of the earth in his hand; for his grasping is the ends of the earth, as he holds the ends of the earth. …

He sees providence. For it is said that He does not merely hold the ends of the earth there, but also in many places, indeed, as if He is Lord of both heaven and earth: 'I will confess to You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whatever holds the earth up, we should confess that the power of the Creator holds all things together.
comments.comment: But it is necessary, whether we grant that the earth exists by itself or say that it rests upon the water, never to depart from devout thinking, but to confess that all things are held together by the power of the Creator. So we must say to ourselves, and to those who ask us on what this immense and unbearable weight of the earth is supported, that “In the hand of God are the ends of the earth” (Psalm 94:4 (LXX)). This is safest for our understanding and beneficial for our hearers.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain meaning of God holding the earth in his hand.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Those who are beyond the ends of the earth in wisdom and citizenship are in the hand of the Father and the Son, and no one can snatch them away; they are Christ's sheep, with their hearts in heaven.
comments.comment: Regarding thought, they come into the hand of God, for only those who are further than the ends of the earth by wisdom and citizenship are under His protective and almighty hand; thus no one is able to snatch them away, those who are in the hand of the Father and in the hand of the Son. These ends, by way of thought, are the sheep of Christ, concerning whom the Lord says: 'My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life' (John 10:27), and furthermore: 'and no one shall snatch them from my hand' (John 10:28); and no one is able to snatch them from the hand of my Father (John 10:29). Since the interpreted ends of the earth are in the hand of God, it is fitting that He also attains the heights of the mountains, seeing those men who are separated by life and godly wisdom. But they are exceptional, surpassing even the heights of the mountains which He spoke of; perhaps they are the ends of the earth, the men walking upon the earth, yet having their citizenship and their heart in heaven because they have stored up treasure there, seeing the high angels as their wealth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dry land is said to be formed by hands, not one hand, and the creative hands of God are the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit, as Irenaeus held.
comments.comment: It is to be noted that the dry land is said to be formed not by one hand but by hands, just as 'the heavens are the work of your hands' (Psalm 102:25) and 'your hands made me and fashioned me' (Psalm 119:73). But as to what these creative hands are, it is a matter of perplexity; for one is, as we confess, the active hand of God, the Word of God, but with this hand another is also coordinated through many Scriptures, being itself creative. And it is pleasing to say, having become a follower of divine men and the apostles, that the creative hands of God are the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit. This was the opinion of Irenaeus most especially, from which it is evident that the position being set forth is an ancient glory, not merely a passive one, but a creative one, and the Holy Spirit is creative.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Worship is no longer local, as when Jerusalem and the temple were established.
comments.comment: They call upon one another to worship God, not by going from one place to another. For it is no longer a local worship, as was the case when Jerusalem and the temple there were established. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who worship come by disposition, not by change of place, and a blameless weeping of repentance gives confidence before the Lord.
comments.comment: Each one comes from his own place, not sensorially and bodily but in spirit and truth. Therefore, those who worship and fall down to him, bowing the knee to him and confessing him, come according to a disposition rather than a change of place; not only those on earth but also those in heavens and under the earth, weeping before him the weeping of repentance, and how much some weep and suffer. But a blameless weeping, escaping every stain, becomes one who is confident before the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to come and bow down, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand, with God our shepherd, so no one shall snatch us from his hand.
comments.comment: And they say the reason by which the things written are fulfilled, asserting that he himself is our God and we are sheep of his pasture, a relationship of the people to God being shown through this word. Because of this he says: We become the people of his pasture, which he himself granted to make himself our God; for since he himself is our God, and we become the people of his pasture, and since we are the people of his pasture, he is our God. And being the people of his pasture, we are also sheep of his hand, he being our shepherd. Therefore no one shall snatch us from his right hand; for I myself give them eternal life, and no one shall snatch them from my hand (Psalm 95:7; LXX 94:7c–9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being his people and the sheep of his hand means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemy tells us to sin today and keep righteousness for tomorrow, but the Lord answers, 'Today, hear my voice'; stealing today leaves us only the hopes of tomorrow.
comments.comment: For does he not suggest that we commit sin today, and persuade us to store up righteousness for tomorrow? This is why the Lord, dismantling his wicked counsels, says, 'Today, if you hear my voice' (Psalm 94:7 (95:7)). That one says: 'Give today to me, and tomorrow to God.' The Lord cries out in answer: 'Today, hear my voice.' Understand the enemy: he does not dare to advise abandoning God altogether—he knows that is hard for Christians to hear—but with deceptive arts he carries out his own attempt. He is clever at doing evil. He observes that we human beings live in the present, and every action is carried out in the present moment. So by stealing our today through his scheming, he leaves us the hopes of tomorrow. Then, when tomorrow comes, the wicked divider comes again, claiming today for himself and tomorrow for the Lord. And so, always snatching away the present through pleasure and attaching the future to our hopes, he secretly leads us astray from life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'Today' is urgent, in plain terms.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Scripture often calls the whole age 'today', as in 'unto this day' and in the Psalms, 'Today, if you hear his voice'.
comments.comment: It is the custom in many places of Scripture to call the whole age 'today' — as 'this is the father of the Moabites unto this day,' (Genesis 19:37) and 'this is the father of the Ammonites unto this day,' (Genesis 19:38) and 'this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this day,' (Matthew 28:15) and in the Psalms, 'Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.' (Psalm 95:7) …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Today' means each day of the age; sin hardens the heart as it did Pharaoh's, so let us listen to God.
comments.comment: … But he interpreted 'today', referring to the age that has fully come; for each day of the age is signified by 'today'. But the heart is hardened, appearing hard and contrary through all sin, bowing down to wickedness like that of Pharaoh. Therefore, abandoning this hardness, let us bow our hearing to the shouting God in order to become righteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even the very negligent can recover all the lost time if they now use zeal, so 'Today' exhorts us never to despair but to press on toward what lies ahead.
comments.comment: For it is possible—it is possible—for one who has been extremely negligent, if he afterward uses zeal, to recover all the loss of the time that has passed. Therefore it says, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion" (Psalm 95:7-8). It says this to exhort and counsel us never to despair, but as long as we are here, to have good hopes, to press on toward what lies ahead, and to pursue the prize of the upward call of God (Philippians 3:13-14).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain, encouraging meaning of 'Today' in the verse.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: God, angered at that generation that always erred and would not know him, swore it would not enter his rest.
comments.comment: Another says 'I said, I provided food' (Psalm 95:10-11; LXX 94:10-11), referring to not every generation, but that generation always associating with error because of not wanting the knowledge of God; he says that God, having been angered, swore not to enter into his rest, saying these things in Psalm 95:11.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner is taken captive and ceases to be God's temple, but the one who returns through repentance is ransomed and built up again as a temple, and the opening of the psalm declares this, with a song of thanksgiving at the dedication.
comments.comment:
Being sinful, the one sinning is taken captive and is disgraced, so that he is no longer a temple of God. For if God says concerning some, 'My spirit shall by no means remain in these men because they are flesh' (cf. Genesis 6:3), for formerly, when the temple of the divine Spirit was dwelling in them, it was like His own; but those sinning have become flesh, subject to passion and material, having taken it on, the one dwelling in them has departed as a conqueror, and they remained under destruction by the evil spirits who captured them.

Therefore, just as the one sinning, having become a captive, ceases to be a temple of God through the destruction of his edifice built of virtues, so also the one returning to God through repentance is not only ransomed from captivity, but is also founded and built up as a temple of God through correctness of mind and excellent deeds. And this is what the introductory part of the psalm declares. For after the captivity, once the temple is built, a gracious song of thanksgiving is sent up for the forgiveness of the captivity and the dedication of the temple.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Literally, the temple was built after the captivity in Ezra's time, and David foresaw its restoration and made the song for its dedication, which those renewed in Christ now sing.
comments.comment: And regarding the literal sense, one will be able to take what is according to the place. For it appears that the temple was built in the times of Ezra after the captivity. It must be said that concerning such a thing, David, having seen more prophetically the ancient restoration of the temple, has made the song for the dedication of the temple. But the singers, having put off the old man and having put on the new, being renewed into becoming according to the image of the one who created him, and being made suitable to the new discipleship of the new covenant, conforming to the newness of the teaching of Christ, sing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All the earth is commanded to obey and to bless God's name through good works and knowledge of the truth, that men may see them and glorify the Father.
comments.comment: Here indeed all the earth is commanded to obey, and in the heavens to worship: 'Let all the earth worship you and sing to you' (Psalm 66:4); and it is said in Isaiah, 'The whole earth is full of His greatness' (Isaiah 6:3), and in others, 'The whole earth is full of His glory.' Not all who sing to God are commanded to obey Him and to bless His name. For through good works and knowledge of the truth, one blesses and glorifies the name of God. For it is said in the Gospel, 'Let your light shine before men' (Matthew 5:16), so that they may see your good works and glorify the Father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wonders to be announced to all peoples are Christ's work of freeing souls from the devil and restoring God's ancient purpose for man.
comments.comment: Moreover, they are commanded to announce his wonders to all peoples, concerning which it is said to God in Psalm 76: 'You have done many things, Lord my God, your wonderful works' (Psalm 40:5). The prophet Isaiah says that the cause of these wonders is: 'Lord my God, I will glorify you, I will sing praise to your name, for you have done wonderful things, a true ancient purpose' (Isa 25:1). For Christ the Savior has done wonderful things, having freed every soul suffering under the devil, establishing the ancient purpose of God, according to which man existed as being straight, having come to be in the image and likeness of the Creator.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gods of the nations are demons greedy for sacrifices, who deceive those not sheltered in God.
comments.comment: They have learned too “that all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 96:5), greedy demons that wallow about the sacrifices, the blood, and the portions taken from the sacrifices, to deceive those who have not fled for refuge to the God who is over all …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the gods of the nations are, according to the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Holiness and magnificence belong to those who have God within as a temple and share in his holiness, and magnificence means seeking what is fitting in great things, not in human honors, strength and wealth.
comments.comment:
Confessing and receiving beauty, having God within himself as a temple and becoming a sanctification, it is fitting that holiness and magnificence are said of such a thing; indeed, partaking in the holiness of the present God and Christ, the sanctification of God, and also of the Holy Spirit, and seeking that which is becoming and appropriate in great and superior things; for magnificence is that which is becoming in great things, but smallness is that which is in small things.

For you, indeed, if you wish to be well-appearing in human honors and dignities and in perceptible strength and wealth, you are small if you are in the sanctification of God through the one who has enriched according to those things assigned in the intelligible and spiritual virtues and piety, but he who seeks to excel in all great things and by this possesses magnificence, is a companion not unequal to the holiness which he has acquired (Psalm 96:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's beauty, power and majesty belong to him in secret; costly temples were a type of the invisible things, and even Solomon said heaven cannot contain God's glory.
comments.comment: Let the God whom we worship be known, the one who has heaven and the glory above heaven, to whom beauty is present, to whom power and majesty belong in secret—according to his incorporeal and divine excellence, since the bodily sizes and beauties of temples have been produced with technical precision and lavish wealth, and for the nations they are for demons (Psalm 96:6; LXX 95:6). But in Israel, even if these things were present, they had come into being from the beginning as a type of the invisible things, and it was said through Moses, and they yield to the invisible things—especially now in the present proclamation of the gospel, when spiritual majesty is sought and contemplated, but also in ancient times among the wise, as with Solomon, who said that he was building a temple for God as the greatest and most lavish, since God is the greatest, yet also said that not even heaven can contain the glory of God (2 Chronicles 2:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why honor and majesty before God are not measured by the splendor of temples.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because we bear Christ's name we should act wisely and justly and raise our thought of sacrifices to the spiritual and heavenly sacrifices, of which the physical ones are types and shadows.
comments.comment: Since we are servants of Christ, having his name called upon us, let us perform all things wisely and rationally, justly and holily, and let us bring glory to the name of Christ which is upon us. And also let the appearance of sacrifices be excellent; that is, elevate the concept concerning sacrifices, not plunging down low and slaughtering animals, but thinking highly of those things signified by them, the spiritual and heavenly sacrifices, of which the perceptible sacrifices are types and shadows (Psalm 96:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what bringing an offering means for a Bible reader.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A mind with a worldly quality casts off its earthly disposition to take up the heavenly nature.
comments.comment: And every intellect having possessed a worldly quality, shaken by sympathy toward matter, casts off the former and earthly disposition in order to take up the spiritual and heavenly nature. For truly, this is to have the earth shaken in order to pass into heaven and to put on the image of the heavenly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord reigned among the nations after he suffered and rose, saying all authority was given him, and the whole earth is shaken so that virtue may become steadfast.
comments.comment: Following this are the things brought about: 'The Lord has reigned among the nations' (Psalm 96:10). For having suffered and having risen from the dead, He reigned among the nations, having said, 'All authority was given to me in heaven and on earth' (Mt 28:18). As it becomes the will of God as in heaven and on earth, and the Lord reigning in all the nations, the whole earth is shaken in the said manner from His face, so that the nature of virtue, having been made steadfast by the Lord, might take up the inhabited world instead of the earth, having become steadfast …
comments.selected_reason: Explains when and how the Lord reigns among the nations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's domain is an inhabited world where Father, Son and Spirit dwell; he will judge the peoples with uprightness, examining works and dispositions, at his second coming.
comments.comment: For the Lord's domain is not merely earth but an inhabited world, with Father and Son and Holy Spirit dwelling in it and through divine gifts. He who ruled over all living things will judge the peoples with uprightness, judging according to his own order, since his wonders were announced to all, not only to Israel. He will judge them in uprightness, examining not only their works but also their dispositions. These things will happen according to his second coming, when the heavens will rejoice and the earth will exult (Psalm 96:11-12; LXX 95:11-12a).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Lord's judging of the peoples with uprightness means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who bear the heavenly image and have citizenship in heaven are the heavens, and some of them inherit the earth through meekness, rejoicing in the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: For the purpose of ascent, those bearing the image of the heavenly one and having citizenship in the heavens are heavens themselves, rejoicing in being laden with fruit coming from the Unconquerable from the true vine; wisdom poured it into the vessel. Some of these heavens are to inherit the high and above-lying earth through meekness, being called earth by a homonymous metonymy, rejoicing in the joy produced by the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A mind stirred by passions is like a storm-tossed sea and must be changed into calm through repentance, and those souls then rejoice in glorified joy.
comments.comment: If any mind is awakened by passions, as if by saltiness and bitterness, and the soul is treating the sea as a storm-tossed sea due to disordered movements, it is fitting for this to be shaken by a blessing, so that it might change from tossing and waves into stability and calm, according to its fullness, from the bitter and disordered. For the first blessing is for those who repent, to die to disordered and disturbed impulses. And those souls, because they have received the seed of Jesus, rejoice in unspeakable and glorified joy as they reap a harvest in tears amidst the exultation (Psalm 96:12; LXX 95:12b-13b).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The joy foretold by David is fulfilled; he speaks of trees, but the Forerunner speaks of fruit worthy of repentance, and Christ announces everlasting joy to all who believe.
comments.comment: Today the oracle of David is fulfilled, which says: Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth exult. The fields will be glad, and all the trees of the forest, before the Lord, for He comes (Psalm 96:11-13). David, for his part, speaks of trees; but the Forerunner of the Lord speaks of trees that bear fruit worthy of repentance (Matthew 3:8-10), or rather worthy of the Lord's coming. Yet our Lord Jesus Christ announces everlasting joy to all who believe in Him. For He says: I will see you, and you will rejoice; and your joy no one will take from you (John 16:22).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The trees of the forest bear edible fruit only when the Lord shines on them, as he is like an apple among the trees of the grove, sharing his fruit-bearing with those near him.
comments.comment: For they are indeed woods of a grove, but unless the Lord shines upon them to bear edible fruit and to make one like an apple, as he says, in the midst of the brothers among the limbs: 'Like an apple in the trees of the grove, so is my brother among the sons' (Song of Solomon 2:3). For he himself from the beginning was bearing fruit in virtue, not knowing nor doing sin; therefore he also shares his own fruit-bearing quality with those who accompany the woods of the grove, being one who happens to be an apple in the midst.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'then' refers to the inhabited world made upright by the Lord and to the heavens' rejoicing; the trees of the forest, not fruit-bearing, exult as the Lord comes to judge.
comments.comment: The 'then' refers to the inhabited world being made upright by the Lord. The 'then' also refers to 'Let the heavens rejoice.' For the heavens shall rejoice and the earth shall exult; then the trees of the forest shall exult (Psalm 96:12; LXX 95:12b). The 'trees of the forest' are those not bearing fruit; but rather the former fruits bearing fruit exult, running ahead as the Lord comes down, 'Come!' For the Lord is coming to judge the earth, then the trees of the forest exult, always rejoicing like the trees of paradise in luxury. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord has made the world firm so it shall not be shaken, and he will judge in righteousness and truth, so the peoples receive perfect knowledge and face the truth fully.
comments.comment: He has established the inhabited world so that it shall no longer be shaken, in righteousness the coming Lord will judge (Psalm 96:13; LXX 95:13c). And he will judge in truth, and the peoples, in whom his wonders have become manifest, just as the inhabited world receives a reward of holiness according to the righteousness by which it is judged, so the peoples shall receive a perfect knowledge, so that they might no longer know by parts but might face the truth personally and fully, receiving and contemplating it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what judging the world with righteousness and the people with truth means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The islands are the Churches of Christ, surrounded by the waves of persecution, and when Christ became King of the whole world and took it from the demons' tyranny, the Churches rejoiced.
comments.comment: He addresses the islands, which we say are the Churches of Christ. They lie as if in a sea, that is, in the surge of the present life, and are surrounded by the unbearable onset of waves, that is, by persecutions and troubles, which the enemies of the truth, who fight against God’s calling, bring upon them. Of such islands the God-inspired Scripture speaks in very many places. Blessed David too sings somewhere and says: “The Lord has become King; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad” (Psalm 97:1). For when Christ became King over the whole world under heaven, taking it all into His hand and wrenching it from the tyranny of the demons, then the Churches throughout the whole earth rejoiced, that is, were filled with gladness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the isles are and why they are glad, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The earth is established when war-like noise is destroyed, and the Lord reigns because sinners have repented and turned to the kingdom, so all the earth rejoices.
comments.comment: By the sufficient hand (but the spiritual David is not he who was born of his seed according to the flesh) the earth is established, all war-like noise and disturbance having been destroyed by him (Psalm 97:1; LXX 96:1) … Therefore also the Lord reigns, not from not reigning at all, but having come to reign from the fact that those sinning have repented and turned toward the kingdom. All the earth rejoices, doing this, being protected in the fact that the Lord has reigned over all of it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The islands that are glad are the men and churches dwelling in them, and steadfast souls tossed by the passions but not overcome.
comments.comment: And regarding the rejoicing, the assigned land and islands shall be glad, that is, the men and the churches dwelling in them. And it is possible also to call the souls of the steadfast according to virtue 'islands,' being tossed about by the storm and the surge of the passions, yet suffering nothing of the whole from them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord reigned from his first coming, condemning sin in his flesh and abolishing death, and will reign in his second coming through those who share in him; the saints rejoice, the proud mountains melt, the ungodly meet cloud and fire, and the throne is a kingdom, not a bodily seat.
comments.comment: The words "The Lord reigned" must be heard in one way just now and in another way now. For from his first coming he reigned, as in a summary, condemning sin in his holy flesh and abolishing death; and in his second coming he will reign through each one of those who share in him, having destroyed evil and corruption, when people will come to behold the steward of eternal life, being already able to be filled with life from him and to behold the glory of his kingdom, which is manifested in them as in a royal house, and which makes the opponents invisible as fire melts wax (Psalm 97:5). So he says again that the earth rejoices and the many islands are glad—that is, the nations—and then next that the earth is in labor and the mountains melt. In one place he speaks of the saints, and in another of the opponents, whose height through pride he likens to mountains, and he compares the overthrow of their pride to the melting of mountains. And to those who are alien he shows cloud and darkness meeting them before the sight of the Lord, signifying fear and distress; but to those who are receptive to light he says his lightnings flash and his glory is seen, and also that the fire of judgment will consume the ungodly, when the righteousness of the Lord is revealed from heaven, as the apostle says. And the psalmist says that the revelation from heaven is announced by the heavens, calling the manifestation an announcement, and he says that heaven itself is established by righteousness and judgment as on some support. He makes it clear that the throne is not bodily, but that the kingdom is called a throne.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The cloud and thick darkness are not bodily but show God's incomprehensibility: the cloud perhaps the words flowing from him, the darkness the obscurity of what the created mind cannot grasp.
comments.comment: A cloud and thick darkness are around him—not bodily; for if the circling things were bodies, and the one being circled were a body or using a body; but incorporeal, rather exceeding bodies, are God and his only-begotten Son as God the Word is. And he says now, to present his incomprehensibility around him, 'there is a cloud and thick darkness'; and perhaps the cloud signifies the words flowing from him, and the thick darkness the obscurity of his incomprehensibility. For it is said also previously, 'He inclines the heavens and comes down' (Psalm 18:9), and 'thick darkness is under his feet' (Psalm 18:9); for that which is hard to see, rather incomprehensible to the mind of created beings, is presented through the thick darkness under his feet as he travels creatively and providentially.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the clouds and darkness around God mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Concerning the incarnation, the cloud is the assumed human nature, upon which the Lord sat kingly as the prophet says, and a thick darkness goes with it because his descent is hard to see.
comments.comment: If it is possible to take these things well concerning the Savior according to the incarnation, examine whether it can be said that there is a cloud around him, the assumed human nature being indivisible in its modes, fulfilling the prophecy saying, 'Behold, the Lord sits upon a cloud of mist' (Isaiah 19:1) and he goes into Egypt. For he came into the so-called allegorically Egypt, the inhabited world, and, if it is said so, sitting kingly upon a cloud of mist, he by no means has the weight of sin; for he did not commit sin by watering the whole world through this cloud. But since the descent of the Lord into the aforementioned cloud is much hard to see, it is fitting that a thick darkness also coincides with the cloud around him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteousness and judgment are the strength of his throne because as king he is a righteous judge, and fire goes before him against his enemies.
comments.comment: 'Righteousness and judgment are the strength of his throne; fire goes before him and blazes around his enemies' (Psalm 97:2-3). The strength of the throne of his kingdom is righteousness and judgment, since he, as king, is a righteous judge. This is agreed with what is found in Proverbs: 'By righteousness a throne is prepared' (Prov 16:12). Therefore, since he is found to be a righteous judge, fire going before him blazes at all his enemies. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the throne's foundation and the fire before him mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fire going before the Lord does not consume the souls of his enemies, which are immortal, but annihilates the works of the flesh and material thoughts; it is a different fire from ours.
comments.comment: Those who profess false doctrine and lie are enemies of the truth; and the friendship of the world makes one an enemy to God, as it is said. If one does not wish to be a friend of the world, he is established as an enemy of God, those being shown as enemies of God who embrace the worldly and more cosmic intercourse. These enemies are not consumed by the fire going before the Lord, which does not consume or corrupt their essence (for the hypostasis of their soul is immortal), but it annihilates the works of the flesh and the material thoughts surrounding them; therefore the Savior prays that the fire which he came to cast upon the earth might be kindled, so that all earthly things might be consumed. This fire should not be considered the same as that which consumes burning substances, but it is of a different nature, differing greatly from the flame among us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His teaching flashed like lightning over the world, and the shaken earth cast off the earthly for the heavenly image.
comments.comment: The bright words of his divine teaching flashed like lightning throughout the whole inhabited world (Psalm 97:4; LXX 96:4), illuminating and lighting it with the light of knowledge, but the earth, seeing these lightnings, being shaken, changed, casting off its earthly quality in order to take up the image of the heavenly. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the lightnings that light the world are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heavens are those who announce the righteousness of God, bearing the image of the heavenly, and all the peoples who imitate them see the glory that follows that righteousness.
comments.comment:
Those who preannounce the presence of the Savior here, who is the righteousness of God, are heavens (Psalm 97:6; LXX 96:6), bearing the image of the heavenly and having citizenship in heaven, having announced the righteousness of God being released from heaven. When these things were brought to an end, the people followed to behold the glory of the Lord, which was not other than his righteousness. But since practical virtue is often called righteousness, only those who are righteous men can announce this practically, being heavens.

The righteous one proclaims faith, their faith being reckoned toward righteousness. And all the peoples, having become imitators of them, see the glory following this righteousness of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the heavens declare his righteousness and the peoples see his glory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who worship carved images should be put to shame and given perception, which will turn them from their foolish opinion.
comments.comment: He prays that those who through great insensibility and foolishness worship the images which they themselves carved may be put to shame, having received perception. For such a thing will be for their good. For being put to shame, they will depart from this foolish opinion which they held as if about gods.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the psalm wishes shame on idol worshippers.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Zion is the contemplative soul, gladdened by hearing the divine words with understanding, and the daughters of Judah are the souls that confess and praise God, who rejoice as they are judged.
comments.comment: And likewise Zion will be thought of as entirely contemplative and theoretical regarding the truth, and the daughters of Judah, the souls confessing and praising God with thanksgiving for the wonderful things done through them. For Judah is interpreted as confession. And it is possible also to call all those things placed together with the Divine Scripture 'daughters of Judah'. Regarding 'Hear and be glad, O Zion' (Psalm 97:8), such things are to be said: he who hears the divine words with understanding is always gladdened, seeing the beauties of the theorems made manifest by the teaching. Since Zion has been gladdened by having heard thus, the lesser daughters of Judah, being called to the judgments of God, will experience divine rejoicing according to how they will be judged, their minds being reasonably uplifted by the presence of the Holy Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Zion and the daughters of Judah are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even if a holy person is attacked unto death, the Lord guards the souls of his saints and rescues one who falls, so that the sinner's hands are under God's hand.
comments.comment: If ever someone, intending harm to a holy person even unto bodily injury or death, strengthened the attacks, while the blameless and irreproachable soul remained, who would not confess the witnesses of the truth being guarded according to the souls by the Lord confessed by them? And if ever it should happen through inattention or slight oversight for the soul of a holy person to fall into the hand of a sinful devil or one of his kind, and the Lord rescues this one as having been set free from sins, the hands of the sinner are said to become under the hand of God. And concerning his holy disciples, he says to the Father, 'Father, keep them' (Jn 17:11); the same thing as 'to keep' is 'to guard'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Lord preserves the souls of his saints.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evil is not a nature that could be known and hated; we recognize every evil as a work of wickedness, and we hate that equally.
comments.comment: For what is contrary to nature is not divided off against the good nature as an evil thing, nor is it possible to conceive of any nature that is pointed to and called evil (Psalm 97:10; LXX 96:10). We do not have any such thing in our knowledge, so that knowing it we might hate it. Rather, we recognize every evil as a work according to wickedness, and the hatred of this—if we think rightly—we practice equally, considering it the same as that saying, “Cease from your wicked deeds.”
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: A light of knowledge rises for the one who has perfected practical virtue, and the heart becomes straight and God raises gladness in it.
comments.comment: To the one who has perfected practical virtue, a light of knowledge has risen, called righteousness, which is nothing other than the light of the True One, concerning whom the Father is (Jn 1:1). To those who fear my name, the sun of righteousness rises (Malachi 4:2). And when this light has shone upon the righteous, the heart has become straight; and God has caused gladness to rise to him having a straight heart …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what light for the righteous and gladness for the upright in heart mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture shows the Savior as God's right hand and arm, his righteous and strong action, and as the salvation all people will see.
comments.comment:
The Savior has been shown through many things to be the right hand and arm of God, according to the placement of the right hand and the arm Ps 97:1. …

And the arm of God is holy, not by participating in holiness, but as the arm of the Holy Spirit. And perhaps the right hand is called the active power of God, not being the Word of God, because it does so righteously—that is, holily, wisely, praiseworthily, and blamelessly doing all things—and the arm because of the strength and the surpassing power. As the right hand and arm of God Ps 97:1, so also Christ is his salvation and his righteousness. Indeed, 'all flesh shall see' Ps 98:4 intends to make manifest that all men, through being saved, shall see the salvation of God, namely Christ, the one providing the salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sent his Savior among the nations and revealed his righteousness, which is Christ, so that the nations are justified by faith.
comments.comment:
Since it is not naturally contained in the understanding of men as God's conception—just as His Word alone is the provider of perfect virtue and the setter of the laws of nature—God sent this understanding of the Word into the visible world, having sent His own Son the Savior into the world at the end of days, so it is rightly said that God has made known His own Savior among the nations. Having made known His own Savior according to the intention of saving, God revealed also His righteousness, which is the same as the Savior, as if it were one; for it has become for us, from God, righteousness and sanctification. For these things were simply hidden from us; but when it became possible for us to approach Him, the righteousness was revealed to us.

If someone says the righteousness through the faith of Jesus Christ, and there is something proposed concerning it, he will say that this righteousness has been revealed iconically and according to a shadow, which Paul called righteousness according to the law, having ceased, clearly showing the shadow; for apart from the law the righteousness of God has been manifested (Rom 3:21), being witnessed by the law and the prophets. And it has been manifested and revealed to those among whom God made known His Savior to the nations; therefore not Jesus alone will be made a covenant in every nation, but the one fearing the Lord and working righteousness becomes acceptable to God. Thus the nations are justified by faith and not by the works of the law (Rom 4:3), according to Abraham, their faith being reckoned for righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jacob and Israel differ in thought but are one man.
comments.comment: Israel differs from Jacob in thought but not in hypostasis (Psalm 98:3; LXX 97:3); for he is the same, at times Jacob and at times Israel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mercy belongs to those beginning in virtue and truth to those with insight, as the Savior's promise of knowing the truth shows.
comments.comment:
… Since he who struggles against the mentioned opponents has need of God's mercy, but he who is unhearing of the truth is said to remember God in harmony with the things foretold, mentioning His mercy to Jacob and His truth to Israel.

And in Jeremiah, he who is beginning in the virtue of mercy, it is necessary, as the one speaking of God says to the God-fearing: 'Remember the mercy of your youth and the perfection of your love' (Jeremiah 2:2); for he who is beginning in mercy, as also he who is led toward perfection in love, is able to say, 'There is the truth of Christ in me.' And as truth is appropriate for those with insight, the Savior says to the two hundred Jews who had believed in him: 'If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free' (John 8:31-32).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All the ends of the earth see Christ, God's salvation, not by sight alone but by faith and by minds lifted above earthly things.
comments.comment:
From the occurrence of the prophecy saying, 'All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him' (Psalm 22:27), it shall be said, 'All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.' For the gospel having been preached in all that is under heaven and in all the inhabited world as a testimony to all the nations, according to the oracle of Christ, all the ends of the earth shall see Christ, the salvation of God.

And those who do not see him by mere sight, but with faithful assent to his teaching through which a vision is present; but also toward the intellect, those having passed through the earth and having become higher than it, not thinking of material and earthly things, but seeking and caring for the things above—the ends of the earth—those see salvation and the God who is the cause of it, the salvation of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that all the ends of the earth see God's salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All people are called to sing to the Lord with the lyre, which means working virtue through all the powers of the soul.
comments.comment:
All the earth, that is to say, all people upon the earth, commands a triumphal hymn to be sent up to the Lord, who brings down the invisible enemies of men, the devil and his attendants (Psalm 98:4-5; LXX 97:4-5). And all those upon the earth, shouting to him, let them sing to him and with the lyre. But what is the lyre, as I have often said, and what is to sing in it, what it is in practice through the body...

To work the things of virtue through all the powers of the soul. And those who, plucking with this harp and uttering a song, receive a command, it is not the voice of a psalm, but rather the contemplation concerning the practical matters, instead of that which is struck upon the psalm through the instrument and some voice singing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trumpet of elm teaches the truth with instruction and proof, while the horn is used to restrain those who oppose it.
comments.comment: They blow trumpets in elms, brightly and with fire proclaiming the word of truth (Psalm 98:6; LXX 97:6a). For they are not sufficient to truly awaken for a spiritual feast, saying, 'Our sufficiency is from God,' who also made us sufficient as ministers of the new covenant, who alone are able to utter this, enriching with every word and all knowledge. But those who fight against the word blow with the horn, being able against sophisms and deceptive words. And if an interpreter of divine instruction stands, he uses a trumpet of elm to utter words pedagogically and demonstratively, but he constrains the opponents of the truth with a horn.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who have profited through faith rejoice at the coming judgment because they are not guilty, and he will judge the peoples with uprightness.
comments.comment: And those divided by wisdom and by conduct, who having profited through the height of faith, rejoice, not being guilty of the judgment which the Lord came to perform (Psalm 98:8; LXX 97:8b). For the Lord says, 'He who believes in me shall not be judged' (cf. John 3:18), that is, he is not subject to accusations, but stands at the step of Christ to receive the promised good things. And judging the inhabited world in righteousness, he will judge with uprightness those who have been made his own as his people, since the peoples have a straight heart and straight deeds; for he will render to each according to his deed (Psalm 98:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Prayer that the earth be shaken before God means the earth no longer stays earth but is made heavenly.
comments.comment: … such also is a prayer sent up, saying by the Psalmist: "Let the whole earth be shaken from before his face" (Psalm 96:9); for this happening, the earth no longer remains earth, because the Face has seized those upon the earth to become heavenly. Of the same thought is also "He who sits upon the cherubim, let the earth be shaken" (Psalm 99:1), so that a change may occur around him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is great in Zion through the law and the prophets, but higher than all peoples who come to him through faith.
comments.comment: Previously in Zion, according to the gift of the law and the prophets, the Lord is great, but he is so much higher than all the peoples coming from the nations through faith (Psalm 99:2).
