For glory and honor and peace belong to everyone who works the good, first to the Jew and also to the Greek; for having been lifted up from the earth, he has drawn all to himself. Both the high and the great exist according to his nature. For he dwells in the high places, and he is great and exceedingly praiseworthy, while the generated nature is lowly and brief, and rather nothing in comparison to him. We have a vision of his highness, we who think of the things above; but also, proclaiming great things about him, we contemplate his magnitude.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse: the Lord is great in Zion and high above all peoples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture uses the word 'confess' to mean giving thanks or glorifying, as in confessing God's great name.
comments.comment: “I confess,” he says, in the human custom, for “I give thanks” or “I glorify you.” God-inspired scripture is accustomed to take the name “confession” in such a sense. It is written, “Let them confess, Lord, your great name, for it is fearful and holy,” (Psalm 99:3)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judgment examines doctrines to tell what to think and do, and the activity of virtue is called justice.
comments.comment: … Indeed, the law of justice may reveal the virtue of practical action, and the judgment may be the examination of dogmas; and what is called judgment, by which it is distinguished what is to be thought and not to be thought, and what is to be done and not to be done, he himself called justice, namely the activity according to virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls uprightness and just judgment 'judgment', so a king's honor is splendid when it loves righteousness.
comments.comment: It is the custom of the divinely inspired Scripture to call uprightness and just judgment ‘judgment’. So the divine David sings: ‘Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times’ (Psalm 106:3). And again he said somewhere: ‘And the honor of the king loves judgment’ (Psalm 99:4). For the honor and glory of a king is splendid when it loves righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse means by a king loving judgment.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 11

comments.capsule: To exalt God is to think high thoughts of him, not to lift him up in space, and the flesh he received is his footstool that we worship.
comments.comment: You make him high, not by lifting him from below into the above (for this is a matter of bodies) Ps 98:5, but having high and super-abundant thoughts concerning him. But the flesh received may be his footstool. Since we do not take up the things concerning the Word of God as concerning the only-begotten Son of God, we exalt the Lord God; but also considering the economy [God's plan of salvation] according to his sojourn, we worship the footstool of his feet, on account of him who rested upon it his motive powers, more allegorically called feet. And the ancient temple is also called his footstool, as it is written in Jeremiah: 'How the Lord in his wrath darkened the daughter of Zion! He cast down to the earth her sanctuary; he did not remember his footstool' (Lam 2:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to exalt God and to worship at his footstool.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: True worship belongs to the Trinity alone, and in that sense Jesus too is worshipped, while men are said to worship those of high rank out of honor.
comments.comment: To worship truly and principally it is fitting for the Trinity alone; for 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve' Deut 6:13. According to this meaning of worship, the Lord Jesus is also worshipped: 'For all the angels of God shall worship him' Matt 4:10. But in another way, for the sake of honor, men are said to worship those in eminence according to this Scripture. For it is often recorded that many worshiped king David, and also the other kings of Israel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The footstool stands for God's authority over the whole earth, so we worship the authority over the earth, not the earth itself.
comments.comment: He says to worship the footstool, the worldwide authority that will then appear, which rules not only the sanctified race but all things (Psalm 99:5; LXX 98:5). It is allegorized as God’s footstool, occupying the whole inhabited earth, which is also called a footstool by the same name, just as Israel is also called an authority. The throne that is above the authority would be allegorized as God’s kinship with the sanctified—especially with the heavenly things, but already also with the things on earth. By the same name, according to Isaiah, heaven is allegorized as a throne, and Jerusalem is also a throne because of the saints in her, in the manner of heaven. This is proof that heaven is not called a throne in a bodily sense, nor the earth a footstool in a bodily sense, since we say Jerusalem, a small part of the earth, is a throne, and the authority that is upon those being ruled is a footstool. Just as God’s throne in heaven is said to be the kinship that attends the heavenly beings as holy—heaven itself being called God’s throne by the same name—so also the Lord calls those who received the good seed of the kingdom “seed,” calling them by the same name. Therefore he commands us to worship not the earth that is under authority, but the authority over it, when we perceive it in his works. And by adding “Holy is he,” he attacks the falsely named gods of the unholy. He also shows that it is right to remove the unclean from the kingdom, so that it may become receptive of holiness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The verse covers all who share these men's virtue.
comments.comment: These things are said not only concerning these men [Moses, Aaron and Samuel], but also concerning all those who have the same virtue as they Ps 98:6.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Noah, Job and Daniel are named for others of like virtue, so all faithful servants are counted with Moses.
comments.comment: [In Ezekiel's threat against Israel:] Noah, Job, and Daniel: the sword shall not enter upon them, even though the memory of men was made many thousands of years before. For Noah existed before the flood, and Job was the fifth from Abraham, many years before the prophecy. Do we not have something to say about these, or how he named those having the same virtues homonymously with them? If it is not so, it is clear that all the faithful servants also become according to Moses, and similarly regarding the others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though God spoke from the cloud to Moses alone, the verse says 'them', the collective way Scripture speaks of all through one.
comments.comment: In a pillar of cloud he spoke to them (Psalm 99:7; LXX 98:7). And from this we learn according to the writing the so-called collective manner, which names many things by the thing approaching in part, as he announces concerning all. Only to Moses, having spoken in a pillar of cloud, does he now speak concerning all. And you will find also in the Epistle to the Hebrews a pattern of such a narrative. For having enumerated all those who were well-pleasing through faith, he tells the deeds or passions of each in a collective way concerning all: 'They were struck, they were stoned,' and the following.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word of God is called a pillar because it is firm, and a cloud because it comes like rain on the minds of men.
comments.comment: But what does it mean to speak of God in a pillar of cloud? This is clearly to be understood. Not because, since the word of God is firm and unswerving, it is rightly called a pillar as the church that received him is a pillar and foundation of truth; but because it is also a drinkable and fruit-bearing thing, coming like a rain unto the minds of men, it is a pillar of cloud.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is said to speak in a pillar of cloud.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Worship on the holy mountain symbolizes honoring God's sanctifying power.
comments.comment: He now urges us to worship not only the authoritative power of God but also, more intimately, his sanctifying power, giving as a symbol of this the worship on the sanctified mountain (Psalm 99:9; LXX 98:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of worship at his holy hill.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To enter before the Lord is to consider him present in thought, as the world does by seeing the Creator in his works.
comments.comment:
To go out from the presence of the Lord God is contrary to entering before Him (Ps 99:2b). So then, having gone out from the presence of the Lord God, Cain did not leave a place in which the face of God was, but having become a desert of right notions concerning God in another place, he departed from His face, having embraced carelessness and atheism, as if he no longer had a vision or a thought of the appearance of God; so then, to enter before the Lord is to consider Him present through thought.

For having observed the Creator through the greatness and beauty of creations, the whole world has ascended into the thought concerning God, as if to stand before the Lord at all times, according to the saying, 'The Lord of powers lives; I stood before him' (1 Kings 18:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to come before the Lord's presence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gates of the Lord are the virtues, through which hymns lead into his courts.
comments.comment: The gates of the Lord are the virtues through which, and in other things it is said, 'Open to me the gates of righteousness' (Psalm 118:19), so that having surpassed his gates, having entered into the courts of God through theological hymns, they will gratefully confess to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the gates of the Lord stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The singer's hymn softens the passions of the hearers by praising God as a judge who shows mercy before his judgment.
comments.comment: Now he [the psalmist] softens and restrains the passions of the listeners through the hymn, praising God the judge of men through deeds; and since his judgment is precise, examining not only the manifest things but also the hidden things of the heart, he brings it along with a kind intention. For if he were to observe according to the worth of our works, words, and intentions, we would perish utterly; but if this does not happen, he shows mercy before the judgment; for if you, Lord, should observe iniquity, who could stand? But since atonement is with you (for you are a source of goodness and mercy), we take courage that we shall obtain salvation from you, who examine what concerns us with mercy and judgment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the singer joins mercy and judgment: God's precise judgment is met with mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Joining mercy with judgment shows God's love for humanity, since even his rebukes lead toward what is profitable.
comments.comment: David also sings this, saying, 'I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, Lord' (Psalm 101:1); for by joining the act of showing mercy with the act of judging, he shows a pattern of philanthropy. For even while rebuking, He shows mercy; for He leads the chastisements toward what is profitable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist sings of mercy and judgment together.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A blameless life needs blameless understanding too, and its goal is to receive God's presence, hence 'When will you come to me?'
comments.comment: But for the one living rightly and desiring to have an unblemished path, it is not only the practice that ought to be blameless, but also the understanding and the knowledge regarding the doctrines, having been made precise. … And he takes up understanding, thinking about those who are prudent. And since the end of acting unblemished and thinking is to receive the presence of God into the mind and the intellect, the 'When will you come to me?' (Psalm 101:2; LXX 100:2) immediately led the soul there; for your 'coming to me and dwelling as in a holy temple' (Psalm 101:2; LXX 100:2) makes the aforementioned things established for me.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the perfect way and the cry 'When will you come to me?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one moved by virtue turns inward and guides his own household, and sets nothing unlawful before his eyes.
comments.comment:
But he who is moved with innocence—that is, with virtue—concerning things to be done and things to be thought about, turns toward himself, having gathered his mind and his inner care, becoming a guide, better through wisdom, in the midst of his own household. And the houses of each of the diligent ones accomplish virtue.

In this way also James [Jacob] is remembered dwelling in a house, and the souls seeking the contemplations of the unseen and the hidden—which the word calls the wise women of the Hebrews—build houses inherited from virtues; after another word calling them wise women, women built the houses. 'I did not set before my eyes an unlawful thing' (Psalm 101:3), nor did I aim or have a goal to act unlawfully.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Transgressors are to be hated for what they are and do, not because they are human, as Paul's rule on eating with an idolatrous brother shows.
comments.comment:
And regarding what is written, Susanna, the three youths in the furnace, and the others are gathered into the rank of these; for they say to those fighting and persecuting them: 'Do not turn me away from my intention, while you sophistize ten thousand times ten thousand, you hang down punishments and threaten death itself.' 'I hated those committing transgressions.' 'Committing transgressions,' says those sinning; for every sin becomes an offense and a transgression of the divine law.

And the habit of the brothers calls those who have denied Christ 'transgressors'; it is fitting to hate enemies of the Savior with intensity. Therefore, the word says, regarding one wishing to be without fellowship with them: 'If any man named a brother sins with other sins and is an idolater, let him not eat with such a one' (1 Corinthians 5:11). For the apostle does not write this concerning the completely Gentile ones, for he marks in his own epistle: 'If any one calls you of the unbelievers and you wish to go, eat everything set before you without examining' (1 Corinthians 10:27). … he forbids eating with a so-called brother who is an idolater, which clearly signifies that one has stepped away from Christianity in order to worship idols. And these, those committing transgressions, must be especially hated, not because they happen to be humans, but because they are such things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God made man straight, and crookedness of heart is far from one shaped by virtue.
comments.comment: A crooked heart did not cling to me. It is written in Ecclesiastes: God made man straight (Eccl 7:29). If he has not become straight by being shaped according to virtue from the beginning, all wickedness and crookedness of morals is far from him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil turns away from everyone who guards the command not to give him a place, but Judas gave him room and Satan entered him.
comments.comment: When the evil one turned away from me, I did not know it. The evil devil turns away from everyone guarding the command: 'Do not give place to the devil' (Eph 4:27). Judas, therefore, since he did not guard himself to provide a place for him, did not turn away from him, but rather, having first cast into his heart impious thoughts, Satan entered into him the whole of Judas and worked his evils, so that Judas would feel and know that the evil one was acting in concert with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's words about the evil one turning away, with the example of Judas.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who sings has no crooked heart for the evil one to work in, so he does not perceive the evil one's presence.
comments.comment: For according to wickedness, he himself who received the evil one has been shaped, but he who now sings, not having a crooked heart in him, the evil one is able to work; he is filled with God and those of God, as one not having the evil one having a place with him turns away from him. He sings, therefore, saying, 'When the evil one turned away from me, I did not know it,' because he did not perceive his presence; for it was not a thought, but a work of his that he had with me. And perhaps, desiring also to present his excellence, he led forward such a voice, as is the custom of the magnanimous who despise the weak and say nothing about them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinners of the earth are the flesh, which is at enmity with God, and the city of the Lord is the righteous man's own soul.
comments.comment: And if we must also explain the slaughtering, and with it the righteous man’s power in all things, we must say that when he says, “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 101:8), by “earth” he meant figuratively the flesh, whose “mind” “is enmity against God” (Romans 8:7), and by the city “of the Lord” his own soul, in which there was “a temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:16), since he had received a right opinion and conception of God, one admired by all who saw it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's sinners of the land and city of the Lord as the flesh and the soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The morning stands for diligence, and removing the wicked is lawful, if only by separation until they repent.
comments.comment: The morning shows the diligent one, as God sends the prophets with diligence, saying, “Rising early, sending” (Jeremiah 7:25). The removal of the wicked is lawful: “Remove the wicked from among yourselves” (1 Corinthians 5:13). And this has not ceased even among us, even if it happens as a punishment. For the worthless are separated, even if not by death, until repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's 'early' and the removal of the wicked.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Sins start in the passions of the flesh, so when the body's members are put to death the soul stirs no more toward lawlessness.
comments.comment: For the soul holds the starting points of the evils that are in it from the passions of the flesh. If no one is able to kill all the sinners of the earth in the manner spoken of, he will destroy from the city of the Lord all those working in lawlessness. For when the members upon the earth are put to death, the body being subdued and led away as a slave, the starting points of the sins from the flesh are no longer those which stir up in the soul thoughts rushing toward the practice of lawlessness for the sake of pleasure.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Everyone who asks God for good things is poor, and David, though a king, pours out his petition because he lacks what only God gives.
comments.comment: Everyone asking for something, who does not possess what he asks for by coming through the asking, is poor (Psalm 102:1). Everyone praying to God asks for a participation in good things, which he is not able to have from himself; therefore, all are poor toward God. Even if David was great and a king, in the things given from God he was poor; therefore, knowing himself lacking many or all of the things provided by God, he is filled with dejection so as to be greatly disheartened. Then, having been thus disposed, he pours out his petition before the Lord, asking from the one who gives good things to those who ask him. For the one who asks not these things but the things of the temporal has no boldness to pour out his petition before the Lord on account of a passionate intention.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm is called a prayer of the poor who pours out his petition before the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Prayer is entreaty and petition is the specific request, and the saints' loud cry is the intensity of understanding, not utterance.
comments.comment: Prayer indeed expresses entreaty toward God and supplication, but petition expresses the request regarding which he desires to be granted to the one praying (Psalm 102:1). These indeed are the truly good things, which it is fitting to give to God and beneficial for the askers to receive. If it is said regarding the cry of the saints praising God and praying to him with a loud voice, that it is not the cry in utterance but the intensity of understanding.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turns his face from some who pray when they ask what does not befit him, are not yet ready to receive it, or ask for things that lead to sin.
comments.comment: But God turns his face away from some of those praying, in more ways than one (Psalm 102:2): either from those who ask without entreating to receive what it befits God to grant and is profitable for them to receive, or because, while they ask what it befits God to provide, they do not yet have the time to receive these things profitably; and there are also those who deem it worthy to obtain certain things for sinning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God may hide his face from those who pray.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker is like Solomon praying beforehand for the people's coming affliction, asking in his own person not to be overlooked.
comments.comment: What is said is similar in force to Solomon’s prayer, interceding beforehand about the coming affliction of the people, so that they might be heard when they pleaded in it—except that the one speaking says in his own person what belongs to all: he asks not to be overlooked by God, the very thing Israel was in danger of suffering because of its own wickedness, and he speaks also of the long affliction (Psalm 102:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The bones of the inner man are the strengths of the soul, which freeze under the burning of passions, and the heart dries up with no joy.
comments.comment: … It is often said that the bones of the inner man are the strengths of the dogmas and the powers of the soul, and they are frozen by the burning of the passions of the soul. And he says that his heart has become dry, with nothing cheerful or upon which he has acquired joy. For it has become in the coming circumstances such that it is no longer possible to feed the bread which is appropriate and fitting to his most precious essence. For to receive this bread is impossible without being surrounded and clouded by those from without. He says, moreover, that this bread has not been nourished and he has forgotten that he once tasted it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Remembering heavenly things makes one forget even to eat.
comments.comment: Similar to this is what is said by David, that 'I forgot to eat my bread' (Psalm 102:4). For the memory of divine and heavenly things brings forgetfulness to those who are being overwhelmed by them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist forgot to eat his bread.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God will have compassion on Zion at the time of the resurrection and the Savior's coming, which means the renewal of piety, not an earthly city.
comments.comment: For you will have compassion on those who have suffered, since you are God, the compassionate, and long-suffering, and full of mercy, and true. And there will be a time in which the things promised concerning Zion will be fulfilled; but who is not the most blessed and most desired time, the time of the resurrection, O Lord? And I prophesy this in these words of God, of Him, the Lord... and of our Savior Jesus Christ, the theophany into men being the cause of the rebuilding of Zion. Once having become so, do not suppose for me the city upon the earth, nor consider the earthly Jerusalem to be signifying it, but rather the renewal of the citizenship of piety.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He came first to the lost sheep of Israel, and with his own he will give life to the whole world.
comments.comment: Why has he remembered Zion alone? (Psalm 102:13) For what previously had not come except toward the lost sheep of Israel. For having come into the world once for his own (for his people were being used through the fathers), he will not present any of those in the world, but with his own he will vivify the whole world.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The set time is made by the entreaty of God's servants and his pity, and it was fulfilled when the Savior came to take away the world's sin.
comments.comment: The time is made by the entreaty of God’s servants and God’s pity, not by any other cause such as has been fabricated among the Greeks about fated times (Psalm 102:13). This is the time about which he himself says through Isaiah, “At an acceptable time I heard you” (Isaiah 49:8). Paul also writes that this time was fulfilled when the Savior came, saying, “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Corinthians 6:2). For properly the Savior’s descent also happened, he having shone forth at the consummation of the ages. For since the Savior came to take away the sin of the world, it was not fitting that so great a one should come and suffer for few sinners. When the time stood apart in which it is said, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and there was no longer a righteous person on earth who understood and sought after God, he came who by the grace of God tastes death for everyone on behalf of all of them. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the set time to favor Zion as the time Christ came.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When every help through their own kind had failed, the Savior came at the fitting time to heal every disease, and this is the time to have mercy on Zion.
comments.comment: Every remedy and help brought to them [the human race] through their own kind had failed against their incurable diseases. So after all those things, the Savior came, as was fitting, healing every disease and every sickness, so as to remove even their deadness and death. For this truth, then, the Savior shone forth in the time of Augustus, when the time had been fulfilled, since the salvation of human beings was being accomplished suitably (Ps 102). About this the present word also says: "For it is time to have mercy on Zion, O Master, and you, having risen up through yourself, will have mercy on her" (the title of Psalm 102 [103]).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who first fear the Lord's name come to faith in him and in Christ, and those who fear his glory more become kings who reign.
comments.comment:
When the fearing of the name of the Lord is being brought in, and the fearing of the same Lord having been perfected (for there is no lack to those fearing him), they begin even with piety, believing in his name. For after the faith into his appellation, they believe in God himself and in his Christ, a faith reckoned as righteousness, through which everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ will be born from God. And it is perfect to be born from God; therefore also sinlessness follows the being born from him.

And the Gentiles, having feared the name of the Lord, having surpassed the Gentiles, being intellectually kings by having received foolishness to reign for an eternity, fear the glory of the Lord more than his name, as it is between those fearing the name of the Lord and the Lord himself, those fearing his glory are kings reigning accordingly; as Paul writes to the Corinthians, 'For you reigned without us; and indeed you reigned, so that we also might reign with you.' (1 Cor 4:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ built Zion at his first coming, as the church, and will appear in his glory at his second, when we behold his glory.
comments.comment:
And perhaps according to the first visitation the Lord built Zion, but according to the second he will appear with his glory.

And not only thus: the Word having become flesh and having tabernacled among us (John 1:14), he built the church spiritually, called Zion; and he will appear in his glory, so that having tabernacled among us, we might behold his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Lord builds Zion and appears in his glory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be created in Christ is a change of form, not of substance, so a created people comes to know the one God and praises him.
comments.comment: For when anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; and in this Christ, the two—the one from circumcision and the one from the Gentiles—are being created into one new man. For the term 'creation' signifies not a change of substance but a change of form or a transformation. According to this, the meaning of 'O God, create in me a clean heart' (Ps 51:10) is expressed. … Thus, a people being created will praise the Lord, coming to the knowledge of the one God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that a people is created to praise the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord came down from his holy height without ceasing to be holy or high, and he looks down on the earth by his power, not by being in a place.
comments.comment:
The reason for the people being created and praising the Lord is presented in the fact that He descended from His holy height. Because He has taken the form of a servant and has descended to us even unto death, He descended from His holy height, never ceasing to be holy or to be high (Psalm 102:19). Incorporeal and spiritual essence, rather, is how the Lord exists; He is not in a place, for the incorporeal is not limited by place, being uncircumscribable and beyond boundaries. Since He has become accustomed by power to all that comes from Him and is governed by Him (for He was in the world, and the world came through Him), He works within the better and more excellent parts of the world.

If it is said according to 'He who dwells in the heavens' (Psalm 2:4) and 'Our Father who is in heaven' (Matt 6:9), we do not consider Him as being contained by places, but we set forth that He exists by an unutterable power toward His own works; therefore, it is said that He is in the heavens, which are the different parts of the world. For indeed, the thought of all things holds this kind of concept. Since God, not being in heaven in the manner spoken of, looks down upon the earth because of those having been made to be provided for by Him here, it is most correctly said, 'The Lord looked down from heaven upon the earth' (Psalm 102:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God can be said to look down from heaven though he is not in a place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those weighed down by the bonds of wickedness groan in repentance, and the Lord looking on the earth looses them and the sons of the dead.
comments.comment: He immediately brought forward, saying, 'Of those who hear the groans of the bound.' For those bearing the bonds and the shackles of wickedness groan out of repentance. For one used to doing evil with pleasure, he took it lightly and willingly bore the consequences following it; but others have withdrawn from the acts of wickedness, being weighed down by the hand of that evil, having been bound by it; therefore they also groan toward Him who is able to loose the bound. And the Lord, looking upon the earth, also looses the sons of the dead—that is, those born from those who practiced the sin leading to death and because of this have died. … And it is possible to use these two verses for those bound in persecutions because of the word of Christ, and for the sons of those dead through the witness of the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the groaning prisoners are and how the Lord looses them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul that contemplates is Zion, to which teachers announce the Lord's name and praise in Jerusalem, which profits by seeing peace.
comments.comment: For the contemplative soul, being Zion, will see those announcing to her the teachers of the name of the Lord, and announcing also His praise in Jerusalem, which by seeing peace profits through thought. If Zion and Jerusalem were to accuse the church because of seeing the greater things and seeing peace in the harmony and the concord of the dogmas, it would follow rightly that in this so-called Zion the name of the Lord and His praise should be announced in this so-called Jerusalem.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who answers God is the poor man who does not despair and pours out his prayer, answering by walking strongly in virtue rather than by voice.
comments.comment: Who answered Him in the way of His strength? The word does not agree. Does he not say of the people being created, to praise the Lord? Rather, he considers the one who, being poor by predestination, is not despondent and pours out his prayer before the Lord, to be the one answering, not with voice and utterance, but walking strongly in the way of His strength and with rectitude the way of virtuous deeds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To ask not to be taken in the half of days is to ask for time to become perfect in virtue, since fullness of days is spiritual, as with Abraham.
comments.comment: Because I need time to be perfected in these things, I beseech your goodness to announce to me the brevity of the days of my life which are stretching out toward my life in the flesh, lest I may not be able to grant myself to be perfected by a short prayer; and may you also deem me worthy of this, not to raise me in the half of days. But he is brought up in the half of days who has not fully nor as he ought fruited here according to virtue. And this is not measured in a chronological interval, because then I receive a full number of days according to Abraham, so that I may be perfected with the knowledge of the truth and of the virtues. For then take me up, so that when the true light has shone upon me, I may become full of all days, having done those things according to virtue and having thought, lest it happen through all things to exceed the time of my life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul applies these words to Christ, and 'at the beginning' shows the earth was founded by the Lord through whom all things came to be.
comments.comment: We previously noted as being toward Christ those words foretold by Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Psalm 102:25). For the Psalmist does not say such a thing: 'And you, at the beginning, Lord, founded the earth,' that is, you have made it to stand, in agreement with 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.' The thing lying 'at the beginning' is able to refute the glory of all those saying the earth is an element, as if everything came from it and nothing existed before it. For it appears not to be a beginning, but rather that there exist foundations of it according to certain pre-conceived beginnings. It is also said to Job by the Lord, who founded the earth: 'Where were you when I was founding the earth?' But the Lord, through whom all things came to be, is founding the earth; and concerning the Father it is said, 'God founded the earth in wisdom.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Creatures are called the works of God's hands, as a craftsman's works show he made them, and unlike them God does not change.
comments.comment: Regarding those called creatures. For just as the works produced by the hands of craftsmen among us demonstrate truly that they have made these things, so it is demonstrated that the works of God are properly the creatures, because they are called the works of His hand. But since the creatures are being changed because they produce the form of this world, you likewise remain not naturally changing or transforming. For this is a property of creatures, that essence itself begins to derive from them by way of a process.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Things under necessity grow old as time passes, but the Ancient of Days is old in being before all time, while the heavens' age is within time.
comments.comment: Furthermore, he says, 'And all shall be worn out like a garment' (Isa 51:6), referring to all things that are under necessity. For having taken a temporal beginning in their becoming, they grow old as much time passes by. But see that you are not deceived hearing in Daniel the 'Ancient of Days' (Dan 7:9). For there, it does not signify having become old through a multitude of days, but that he is ancient and old of days; as it is possible in the Psalms to say, 'He who exists from before the ages' (Psalm 55:19). Thus also, 'Before the days,' that is, before all time, he is ancient and old. But the oldness of the heavens signifies not that they are before time, but that they are within time.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heavens are not worn out but rolled up like a waistband and changed once their use is over, while the Lord, always the same, neither began nor will end.
comments.comment: Therefore, they are not being worn out like a garment, but they will be rolled up, and like a waistband they will be rolled up by Him who made them, in order to be changed and re-elementalized. Their growing old and being rolled up signifies that the necessity which they contributed to the adornment of the present has passed away. For just as a waistband is rolled up after fulfilling its need, so too, when the heavens will again undergo re-elementalization with the earth after they have passed away, according to the one saying, 'Heaven and earth will pass away' (Matt 24:35), it is rightly said that they are being rolled up like a waistband. To their rolling up, he adds, 'And they shall be changed.' And in Isaiah it is said, 'The heaven shall be rolled up like a scroll' (Isaiah 34:4). Because of these things, he says, in identity, since these things are not remaining, the eternal things shall not fail. But for You, O Lord, having always the same and the like, You neither began nor will end.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the heavens changing like a garment while the Lord stays the same.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His ages are not counted as time, and his being never ends.
comments.comment: Your ages will not end, for your generations are from age to age (Psalm 102:24). But one should not take the ages of the wills chronologically, for time is not spoken of in this way. Nor does His being end, since His nature remains incorruptible, being alone possessing immortality.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: None of us says there is change in God, in deed or thought, for he stays the same while governing changeable things by their nature.
comments.comment: If he [Celsus] had read the words of the prophets, David saying: “But You are the same” (Psalm 102:27), and Malachi, I think: “And I have not changed” (Malachi 3:6), he would have seen that none of us says that there is change in God, either in deed or in thought. For, remaining “the same,” He governs changeable things according to their nature, and His Word chooses that they be governed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'thou art the same' as God's unchangeableness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Children are spiritual, not only of the flesh, as the sons of the prophets and Paul's sons show, and they will dwell with him forever.
comments.comment: One must not take 'sons of God' entirely according to the flesh, but according to instruction and the imitation of a way of life. For in this way some were called sons of the prophets, because they had perhaps become like them according to the prophetic manner. And Paul, a slave of Christ, has sons: Silvanus and Timothy and those near to them. And it happened that those benefiting from these were their seed. The children previously mentioned will dwell with Paul in the heavenly tabernacles, as will those being directed with them and their seed forever.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the children of God's servants are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because a person is made of soul and body, he can speak of his own soul as though it were another, as the rulers and people of a city together make up the city.
comments.comment: Others say that the composite man often speaks of himself as if he were others, saying, 'My soul' or 'My body.' And Paul, indeed, uses this practice, sometimes saying, 'I call God to witness upon my soul,' and sometimes implying, 'My body.' They say this by taking the parts as we say a people, rulers, and overseers of a city are not always different from the city itself (for it is filled from among them), but are a different rank of the whole city (for the rulers alone are not the city, nor the councilors privately, nor the people by themselves), but together they are the city—not so, even if the composite man is not another from the soul and the body (for from these two he is composed), but the soul of the whole is called as another of it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist rouses every rational power within him, since it is good activities that bless the Lord's name.
comments.comment:
Thus, the one who exhorts his own soul to bless the Lord is not 'uncomposite.' … Within it, he calls upon every rational power of man. …

Through which we bless the name of the Lord. For the holy name blesses not powers, but good activities. Even the Savior says to those partaking of virtue and divine knowledge: 'The kingdom of God is within you' (Luke 17:21), saying only once: 'Seek the foundations of faith and virtue within yourselves, being rational and having become according to the image of God; seek not the good outside yourselves.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sins are diseases of the soul, and God redeems the life from corruption so that it lives in incorruption.
comments.comment: Sins are diseases of the soul. For he says, 'My soul, what harm hast thou done to thee?' (Psalm 103:3; LXX 102:3b). He redeems life from corruption, so that you may no longer live a life according to corruption and passion, but in incorruption, loving the Lord Jesus. And providing you an incorruptible body in the resurrection, he redeems your life from corruption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what healing diseases and redeeming life from corruption mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God crowns a person with mercy and compassion, a crown made from the almsgiving and compassion that person has shown.
comments.comment: And he crowns you also in mercy and compassion, the material of this crown being almsgiving and compassion. Just as others receive the crown of righteousness and the incorruptible crown of glory, woven from righteousness and upright glory, so also you, through mercy and compassion which you have worked, shall be crowned, according to 'Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy' (Matt 5:7).
comments.selected_reason: Says what the crown of mercy is made of and why it is given.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God crowns us by his own mercy and compassion and not for our own striving, since we are saved by grace.
comments.comment: And not thus is the better: not so much that I shall be emboldened in the struggling, but because you are being merciful and pitied by the Lord, you shall be crowned, the Lord returning to your intellect the crown of graces. For by the grace of God and not of our own works we are saved, and we do not deserve sufferings in this present time for the sake of the glory to be revealed to us; so also he crowns us, not looking toward our own striving, but toward his own mercy and compassion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God fills the desire of those who ask, since longing for good things is itself a way of asking.
comments.comment: And fill your desire also with good things. For he gives good things to those asking him. Since even the desiring of good things happens to be asking for them, giving to you all things, he fills your desire with good things through longing; for every desire of the righteous is good.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God fills desire with good things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eagle is said to renew itself in old age by going to a spring, which the psalm's words about renewed youth point to.
comments.comment: Having grown old, the eagle's eyes grow dim and his wings grow heavy; he goes to a spring and, as he rises into the air, his wings are scorched by the sun, and he looks up, and having immediately descended to the spring for a third time, he is baptized and renewed; therefore they say he points to the psalm: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's' (Psalm 103:5).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the old tradition about the eagle that lies behind the verse's picture of renewed youth.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: As an eagle sheds old feathers and grows new wings, so a person grown old through wickedness is renewed and lifted up toward heaven.
comments.comment: And this shall be to you, your youth being renewed according to the eagle. For just as this old feather is cast off, and immediately it grows new wings, so also you, having grown old through wickedness, are renewed from your antiquity, and your youth comes in completion, and those who once used strong wings are not so, but now being clothed with new ones, you may be lifted up into heaven toward all those who have waited for God. For those waiting for the Lord shall change strength, they shall become wing-bearing like eagles, they shall run and shall run the course.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the eagle's renewal as the believer's renewal from the age of wickedness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Made in God's image, one who has cast away virtue through heedlessness still has the power to grow wings and rise again, if he wishes.
comments.comment: And since you are becoming according to the image and likeness of God and have become fit to enter into the essence in advance of the good, but having flown away from heedlessness, you cast away virtue both practical and intellectual; without which, being suspended, you would rise to the height, know that you have the power to grow wings, if you should wish it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does judgment for those wronged by the devil by sending his Son to free them and to cleanse them from every injustice.
comments.comment: Father of mercies and alone good is the Lord, who performs acts of mercy, showing compassion to all, doing good (Psalm 103:6; LXX 102:6). God also, toward those being wronged by the devil and by wickedness, making judgment, sent his only Son to heal and to set free those being oppressed by Satan, redeeming souls from bondage and from injustice, having torn the handwriting of our debt and having nailed it to the cross. The one holding us, the devil, had made us debtors, through whom we were practicing, having set up the handwriting of our debt for him. We were rescued from all our injustice, God making judgment for those being wronged, so that through the blood of his Son Jesus Christ we might be cleansed from all injustice, not only the injustice by which we were being wronged but also the injustice which we were practicing. From here we learn, according to the exhortation of Paul, the difference between being wronged and doing wrong. For to those being wronged God performs judgment, doing them good, but to those doing wrong he brings punishment, so that they do not inherit the divine promise: For those who do wrong shall not inherit the kingdom of God (Psalm 103:6/1 Cor 6:9).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse's judgment for the oppressed is worked out in Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The song glorifies God's mercy and justice, since by mercy he will rescue his people.
comments.comment: A thanksgiving had to follow the preceding prophecy. This has also been arranged through this song: the mercy of God and the judicial righteousness are glorified, because through mercy he will rescue the people from those who wrong them …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The law is an image of spiritual things, and it was Moses, taught by God, who knew the way from bodily rites to their truth.
comments.comment: This law bears an image and a type of the intelligible and spiritual, as if it were to move from the sensible things to the spiritual and original ones by a way of analogy. And the Lord will teach such transitions—fittingly, concerning these transitions it is said, 'He made known His ways to Moses' (Psalm 103:7). For who else besides Moses, having learned from God how to ascend from the sensible circumcision and bodily sacrifice and the other shadowy things to the truth, knew this way? For He made known His ways to him.
comments.selected_reason: Says what God's ways made known to Moses are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: We can take courage that God will not stay angry with us to the end, for having sinned.
comments.comment: Therefore, we also take courage that He will not be angry with us for having sinned, in order to complete and destroy this. For this was 'He will be angry unto the end,' that is, to remain in anger as an end, and the anger toward the gods is destruction. He does not become angry unto the end, nor does He remain for an age.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy starts on earth and lifts the pious to the heavens, and virtues are like sunrises and sins like sunsets without light.
comments.comment: But the mercy of God takes its beginning upon the earth, according to what was said: 'The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord' (Psalm 33:5; LXX 32:5). If mercy, beginning from there, becomes directed toward the pious, it lifts them up and suspends them upon the height of the heavens: 'For great is your mercy, O Lord, unto the heavens' (Ps 36:5). For ascending into the kingdom of heaven happens more by the mercy of God than by anything else. And the saving virtues appear to be sunrises, while sins are sunsets, entirely deprived of light. Since no one can exist in both virtue and wickedness, he who has associated himself with the aforementioned sunrises, as if to dwell in them, is like the one in Eden, planted by God according to sunrises.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God's mercy reaches from earth to heaven and what removing sins is like.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evils are far from the virtues, and Jesus, who gives remission of sins, removes the evils from those rising toward paradise.
comments.comment:
Having been distanced from paradise, the previously spoken evils of the interpreted Easts hold such a distance from himself. For the evils are far from the virtues.

But as one in the Easts has the previously spoken evils distanced from him by God, so he who is in them, desiring to sin by himself and not from God, is not distanced from the Easts, but is cast out of paradise. But even after these things have happened through disobedience to the divine commands, Jesus comes upon the evils according to 'Make way for him who is stepping upon the evils, the Lord is the law to him' (Psalm 68:4), and he will not stay there long, but coming to the pain, saying 'With me you shall be in paradise.' For providing a remission of sins, he removes the evils from the rising toward paradise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God pities those who fear him beyond measure and counts them as his sons, because he knows how each was made and took flesh himself.
comments.comment: God excessively and super-abundantly pities those who fear him (Psalm 103:13; LXX 102:13), having set them into the rank of his sons, making known to each of us the creature. For he did not create anything hating, but knowing the hearts of men, he fashioned them individually as he saw fit for each of us. And we have power and a starting point, and these he gives upon us having them by energy to become his sons. It is possible to grasp that he himself knows our creature and thus: let him take experience of our creature; having become flesh, he assumed a natural disposition so as to consider us sons of himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Our faults are sicknesses but not unto death, and God, who knows how we were formed, forgives them in love.
comments.comment: Our faults are something like this: they are admittedly sicknesses, but not to the point of death and the ruin of the soul. The Judge does not examine too strictly, because ‘he knows how we were formed’ (Psalm 103:14), and he was not unaware of the weakness of our nature. So he grants forgiveness out of his innate love for humankind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God, who knows our frame, forgives our faults.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: In asking God to remember that we are dust, we name the weakness of the outward man, whose days in the flesh are short.
comments.comment: Not as a creator of our nature did he create the weakness. For even if not all our construction is from dust (for we have a spiritual nature in ourselves, becoming an icon and likeness of God), but rather in supplications toward God, deeming him a gatherer and benefactor, we say that he brings forward the lesser and weaker of those in us: 'Remember, Lord, what dust we are; therefore help our weakness and our poverty' (Psalm 103:14; LXX 102:14). Following 'Remember, Lord, what dust we are,' it forbids not the inner man, but the outer things lying ahead. For according to the present and after the flesh, we have certain days that complete the extending time of the life after the flesh, surpassing it like a parching meadow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The glories, honors and prosperities of this life depart like a flower and grass and wither as if they had never existed.
comments.comment: Isaiah says: 'All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the grass; the sun rises and withers the grass, and its flower falls' (Isa 40:6-8). These things represent the glories, honors, and all the prosperities existing in this life which seem to those living in the flesh to be abundant, yet they depart like a flower and grass, and wither as if they had never even existed (Psalm 103:15-16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the grass and flower as the passing glories of this life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy and righteousness reach from age to age those who guard his covenant, who are to remember his commandments in order to do them.
comments.comment: Thus, the mercy of God toward those who fear Him is indescribably extended from age to age (Psalm 103:17; LXX 102:17-18). For He does not sometimes show mercy and sometimes not; for being good by nature, He always shows mercy. Moreover, righteousness is the spouse of this mercy; it is not limited by time, but extends to all generations, remaining upon the sons of sons and through all succession, so that He may always have this righteousness with those who guard the covenant of God from age to age, who are also inscribed as heirs of the coming promises through their doing of good. For those guarding it will also remember the commandments of God by doing them. For these are given not as a mere memory, but a memory for the purpose of doing. And regarding that which they are given for the purpose of doing, the Savior also establishes, saying: 'He who has my commandments and does them, he is the one who loves me' (John 14:21). For the promises are the reward and inheritance not of their memory alone, but of their doing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains God's lasting mercy and what remembering his commandments means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though God is not in a place, he is said to dwell in heaven by his plan, with the throne of his rule over all.
comments.comment: And in other places it has been said that God is not in a place, but it is said that He dwells in heaven through a certain following and economy. Accordingly, it has been said that they have prepared for Him even here in heaven, that is, they have established the throne of His kingdom and His rule, not only of those in heaven, but of all, holding and dominating universally (Psalm 103:19; LXX 102:19). One should not regard the prophet as a man, but rather the Holy Spirit within him, commanding the angels regarding the things at hand; for all His angels (meaning the Lord's) say, 'Bless Him' (Ps 103:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the throne prepared in heaven means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The majesty God puts on is the virtue of those who succeed, and the Father clothes himself in the virtues of those who strive for him.
comments.comment: He clothed himself in majesty, and to those in greatness and those who exalt themselves, he gives the appropriate thing; but in confession, he gives to all a harmonious symphony concerning them. For the name of confession signifies also the symphony that is in words. But if you wish him to be clothed in another kind of confession according to repentance and in thanksgiving, it is not for sinners. Corresponding to this signified thing, he will also clothe the virtue of those who succeed, which is called majesty. And just as the Savior says, 'I am naked, and you clothed me' (Matt 25:36), this shows what his clothing and covering becomes: the practice of those living according to him; so also the Father will clothe himself in the virtues of those who strive concerning him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, whose essence cannot be grasped, puts on light as a garment, which stands for the sharpest knowledge, as Paul says he dwells in unapproachable light.
comments.comment: Just as one who puts on a sensible garment is covered from every side, so God, being filled with knowledge from every side, as his essence turns out to be ungraspable, puts on light as a garment, signifying even here the most sharp-witted knowledge of the light. Agreeing with this concerning God, Paul writes that he has an unapproachable light, or dwells in unapproachable light (1 Tim 6:16). For in this very expression, it is said that the whole is the knowledge of God, and for this reason, that it is difficult to understand for the intellects, that he dwells in unapproachable light.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God covers himself with light as with a garment.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God roofs the air with waters in the clouds, and in the mind he calls the intellectual essence 'heaven', roofed with the powers of the soul.
comments.comment: He roofs the air above us and the wind toward the ether with waters according to the swirling of the clouds. And toward the intellect: he calls the intellectual essence 'heaven,' being stretched out and made simple upon the canopy of the mind, he who roofs the intellectual and divine things with waters, the heavenly things of the soul, that is, its powers which happen to be above the sensible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heaven is no sphere but roofs the earth, stretched around it.
comments.comment: The heaven is not a sphere encircling the whole and running around it, but it roofs the earth, stretched around it, being roofed from above by waters with a stable and fixed standing (Psalm 104:2).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what shape the psalm gives the heavens.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: That the earth, the heaviest element, stays fixed above the waters shows God's power and not the nature of the elements.
comments.comment: He speaks of the wonder of the foundation as a proof of God's power: that the earth, being the heaviest element, has been fixed above the waters and remains unmoved forever, since the abyss beneath it can neither support nor establish it, but covers it like garments, so that its seat is ineffable and belongs to God's power, not to the nature of the elements (Psalm 104:5-6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the earth's standing fast above the waters shows God's power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The abyss goes with God's unsearchable judgments, which cannot be grasped.
comments.comment: You will find the abyss lying upon ungraspability, and in 'Your judgments, O Lord, are many' (Psalm 36:6), for his judgments being unsearchable, there is no grasping of them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The prophet's words that the abyss is God's covering show the depth of the teachings about God, which are beyond those without the Spirit.
comments.comment: And to show that the knowledge of God reaches human beings rarely and is found in very few, Moses is recorded to have entered “into the thick darkness where God was” (Exodus 20:21). And again it is said of Moses: “Moses alone shall come near to God, but the rest shall not come near” (Exodus 24:2). And again, to present the depth of the teachings about God, a depth beyond the grasp of those who do not have the “Spirit” who searches all things, and searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10), the prophet said: “The abyss, like a garment, is his covering” (Psalm 104:6).
comments.selected_reason: Says what the abyss as a garment shows about God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The thunder is the word sounding loudly in providence, and the fear it brings may be taken of the waters or of all living creatures.
comments.comment: Hearing the sound of thunder—that is, the word being made loudly according to providence—they shall fear. It is fitting that these things should be said concerning the visible things and the waters. It is possible to take 'From the sound of thunder they shall fear' (Psalm 104:7) not concerning the waters, but concerning men, rather concerning all living creatures, as it might happen that a thunder, of the invisible and unseen divinity, is perceived.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the thunder is and whom it frightens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's power gives the springs, keeps the mountains in place and sends the rain, which is the Son's work from the upper rooms of the air.
comments.comment:
The earth gives springs of water that gush up from the beginning, and these too by God's power; and he says that they often dry up and go into hiding by the fear of God, which is said more clearly in Psalm 73 (74):15: "You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up other rivers" (Psalm 104:10). He also marvels at the position of the mountains, raised up unmoved above the plains and not dragged down by the appointed force to cover what lies beneath, according to: "They will say to the mountains, 'Cover us'" (Hosea 10:8) (Psalm 104:13; LXX 103:13).

He calls the air the upper rooms of God, as if the whole world were one house. And he says the rain is the work of the Son, from which the earth receives its fruitfulness (Psalm 104:13).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalm glorifies God by naming each creature, and since he made the animals he provides their food and drink.
comments.comment: Through every word the preceding psalm glorifies and doxologizes God, remembering each of the creatures; and God, accepting his providence in the things set forth, marvels and considers his goodness with wisdom, caring for the endurance of the irrational animals. And rightly; for if he himself has made them, he is the provider of both their food and their drink.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spirit-bearing men are watered from the heavenly things of God, sharp contemplations of the truth, and so the earth is satisfied from the fruit of his works.
comments.comment: And by ascent you shall understand the words having been fully returned; for the spirit-bearing men are they. They are watered from the heavenly things of this God, being filled with the gifts of the Spirit, the word of wisdom, and the following things which are innumerable. And the heavenly things of God, from which the words water, are sharp and surpassing contemplations of the truth, being called heavenly because they have not ascended beyond themselves. 'The earth shall be satisfied from the fruit of your works.' For he is... Let the earth blossom with grass for pasture and a fruitful tree producing fruit, and the following. And by ascent from Jesus, having much fruit during the visitation, the whole earth is satisfied, receiving those things having been made by Jesus in such a paradoxical way. For this is the fruit of his works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The letter of Scripture is a meadow for the most irrational, and those who rise beyond it say that the Lord has prepared a table before them.
comments.comment:
Even in his super-natural and most high words, it is not possible to provide a meadow for those who are the most irrational.

The discourse concerning sensible things and the letter of the scripture is the meadow in this, but even the more ethical ones will not be able to partake, each of them saying of such things: 'Into the place of clover, there he pitched his tent' (Psalm 23:2).

Having once surpassed such a state, being no longer slaves of men but having become men, they will say again, each of them: 'You have prepared a table before me' (Ps 23:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: From the bodily stories of Scripture a beautiful spiritual word is brought forth, and God's teaching is food, vine, oil and bread to the inner man.
comments.comment:
From these, it is possible to take a word ascending through some analogy to the intelligible. And the beautiful word is brought forth from the earth by nourishing the endos and the man in secret; and from the bodily narratives of the scripture, the mystical word is brought forth beautifully because of the historical things said of the earth.

And the face of the inner man is appeased and made bright by the oil of the nourishing divine light, which alone dissolves diseases and the pains of the soul, differing from the attributed intellect. For the word of God is like the vine, so also the oil is; for he says, 'as an olive tree flourishing in the grove of God' (Psalm 52:8). For his teaching, by a diverse relationship, is both vine and oil and bread.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The vine and the olive were named first because they serve our life most, and the vine reminds us that Christ is the vine and we are branches.
comments.comment: But first, as we said, the things more essential to our life were deemed worthy of mention, all that were going to receive man with their own fruits and prepare for him an abundant way of life: the vine producing wine that was going to gladden the heart of man, and the olive providing fruit able to make the face cheerful with oil (Psalm 103:15 (104:15)). How many things came together at the same time, brought forth urgently by nature? The root of the vine; the branches around it, flourishing and great, spread above the ground; the shoot, the tendrils, the unripe grape, the clusters. A vine seen with understanding is enough for your sight to produce in you a reminder of nature. For you remember clearly the image of the Lord, that he calls himself the vine, and the Father the vinedresser, and he called each one of us, having been grafted into the Church through faith, branches (John 15:1-2). And he summons us to abundant fruit, so that we may not be condemned for uselessness and handed over to the fire.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Weaker souls, called swine, flee to the rock on which Jesus founds the church, which is the confession of faith.
comments.comment:
But those souls that have arrived at this state and are weaker, called swine, flee to the rock upon which Jesus founds the church as an unconquerable fortress; and this is the confession of the faith. And in Proverbs it is said, 'And the swine, a people not strong, made their dwellings in rocks' (Prov 30:26). It is nothing wonderful that the rock is spoken of both singularly and plurally, meaning Christ who is simply the rock, and who is also spoken of as rocks according to various thoughts.

It is suggested by scripture that 'Rock is a refuge for the hyenas,' as perhaps there is a synonymy between the hyena and the swine.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'As' in 'As your works have been magnified' marks truth and not likeness, for all that comes about in God's wisdom, which is Christ, is great.
comments.comment: The fact that the 'As' the simile here written is a demonstrator not of likeness but of truth, just as also in the phrase 'As God is good to Israel,' for he does not say God is like good, but truly good. And in the present passage then, that the works of God are magnified, is signified by the 'As' in 'As your works have been magnified, O Lord' (Psalm 104:24; LXX 103:24). For everything that comes about in wisdom is great of God. And the wisdom of God in which all things came into being is the Lord; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Among the creeping things of the sea there is a wise order, since each kind of fish keeps its own region without walls or boundary stones.
comments.comment: This is the great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number, small animals with great (Psalm 103:25 LXX). Yet among them there is a wise and orderly arrangement. We cannot only find fault with fish; there are also things in them worth imitating. How is it that each kind of fish, having distributed to itself the region suited to it, does not encroach upon the others, but remains within its own boundaries? No surveyor among them divided up their dwellings; they are not marked off by walls; they are not separated by boundary stones; yet what is useful for each has been assigned to each automatically. This bay feeds certain kinds of fish, and that one others; and the kinds that multiply here are not found among others. No mountain rising with sharp peaks separates them, no river cuts off their passage, but there is a law of nature that allots to each its way of life equitably and justly according to what each needs.
comments.selected_reason: Shows the wise order among the creatures of the sea that the verse names.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The great and wide sea stands for the distractions and confusion of this life, and those who dart about for nothing needed are like the fishes.
comments.comment: The Psalmist, pointing out to us with fine wit the distractions of this life and the bitter flood and confusion of affairs within it, sings: ‘This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number, living creatures small and great’ (Psalm 104:25). For we must surely liken to fishes those who at times dart this way and that for nothing needed for their good, and gather only such things as prove them fleshly and set them to endure pointless toil.
comments.selected_reason: Reads the great and wide sea as the confusion of this life.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: God laughs at his opponent because his cunning is futile and easily caught, as he did to the Egyptians.
comments.comment: God is said to mock him [leviathan], that is, to count his cunning as nothing. For God laughs at everyone who opposes him because of its futility, and counts it as play because of how easily it is caught, as he says about the Egyptians: "How many things I have mocked against the Egyptians" (Exodus 10:2) (Psalm 104:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for God to play with or mock the creature.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Another reading takes these words to be about rational beings who hope in God and gather what he gives in due time.
comments.comment: Another says that he speaks only concerning the rational beings. For to hope and to have expectation toward God, this is hinted at. And they hope to find this at an opportune time, being freed from every deficiency and disease. For when this is given, they will gather it, hastening so much to receive it, so that it may be fed into a basket. And there will exist for them the kindness that is upon such straightness, as He is opening for them the hand of your words and the wisdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some read these verses of food, which creatures rejoice to have and are troubled to lack.
comments.comment: Others have taken the preceding words about the food supplied to living creatures. For when this is present, it flourishes and rejoices; when it is absent, it is pressed by want and thrown into confusion by the lack of necessities (Psalm 104:29-30; LXX 103:29-30).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When God turned away his face after Adam's transgression humanity was troubled and went back to dust, but through the Word made flesh and the Holy Spirit we are created anew.
comments.comment: And somewhere the inspired David sings of the creatures on earth to God, the Savior of all: “When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; when you turn away your face, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust; you will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:28–30). For in Adam, because of the transgression, human nature suffered the turning away of the divine face; and so it was all but thrown into confusion and troubled, went back to its own dust, and was brought down into death and corruption. But since the Only-begotten Word of God has become like us, and we have been enriched with a share in the Holy Spirit, we are being reshaped to what we were in the beginning and, as it were, created anew. For we have been called to newness of life (Romans 6:4), escaping the power of death.
comments.selected_reason: Applies the turning away of God's face and the sending of his Spirit to Adam's fall and our new creation in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit gives life through the life it works, with the Father as source, the Son as worker and the Spirit as the one shared in.
comments.comment: This is the work of Christ, who also says that he is the resurrection and the life, and has promised to raise all, and when he was present, he gave life to those he wished (Ps 103:31). So what is said belongs to the Father as the source, to the Son as the worker, and to the Spirit as the one who is participated in and, as it were, brought in through the Son into the life of all things, according to: "He will give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you" (Romans 8:11). The Spirit, then, is life-giving through the life it works, and deifying through the participation it grants; and the human spirit is named after it, according to its formation by it (Psalm 104:30).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God rejoices in his works and in all who hope in him, as at the first creation, by accepting those who have perfected virtue.
comments.comment: God, providing eternal glory to his own works, rejoices in all that hopes for him. For just as having made all things very good in the beginning (Gen 1:31), he rejoiced in the inhabited world, and he rejoiced in the sons of men when there was not yet transgression, so He would rejoice at the perfection and restoration of the ancient order of his works, not out of the joy of God being not impassible (for the divine is impassible) but out of the acceptance of those having perfected perfect virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what way God rejoices in his works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's glory is eternal, and the fear and trembling of creation show its subjection to him.
comments.comment:
Eternal is the glory of the one who keeps his works forever; and since the glory is eternal, the things that glorify are eternal (Psalm 104:31).

The greatness of the glory is shown by the fear of creation, and the fear reveals the subjection. Thus the psalm says that the sea was subjected by being afraid. For what fears is subjected; and the subjection of the earth is the trembling at the oversight of God, and the smoking of the mountains is like burning, which was also seen bodily happening on Mount Sinai (Psalm 104:32).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the fear and trembling of creation show God's glory.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: When God looks upon a person the material world trembles as if about to pass away, and God smokes out the proud evil powers he touches.
comments.comment: If you wish to handle these things spiritually, consider how, when God looks upon you according to 'Look upon me' (Ps 103:6) and 'The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Psalm 34:15), the earth does not stand firm but trembles as if darkening, as if the material existence were to be cast away and pass away. But God, touching the evil powers because he sees the called ones in their pride, smokes them out, entering into them with a breath, as if into the punishment by fire.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To sing to the Lord is to have his presence in thoughts and deeds and not only in voice, and so to speak in a way that is sweet to him.
comments.comment: Sing to the Lord, having the presence of the one existing not in voice but in thoughts; and I will sing also in perfect deeds to God, since I have the presence of the one existing, in which I partake of the one existing before the ages and who said 'I am the Being' (Ex 3:14).
