And conversing in a way pleasing and acceptable to God, I will say, 'Let my conversation be sweet to him.' For he himself says, having accepted the church, 'Your voice is sweet' (Song of Solomon 2:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Life is for singing God's praise, so death, which silences the hymn-singer, is terrible, and we pray that all our actions may be a hymn in which God rejoices.
comments.comment: This is the gain of life, and it is for this that life itself is worth living. That is why death is terrible, because it silences the hymn-singer. Death is destruction, because in death no one remembers you, and life alone is true existence, because the living, he says, will praise you. For we have our being in union with the one who is, and separation from him is corruption. May my meditation be sweet to him, and I will rejoice in the Lord. It is worth praying that God may take pleasure in our hymns, and that joy may be ours through our hymns. And if this could be so through our whole life, so that all our actions were a hymn to God, God would rejoice in us as he rejoiced from the beginning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist sings as long as he lives and why death is terrible.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who keep examining the truth and practicing virtue seek God's face, desiring to see him with a pure mind.
comments.comment: Just as according to the history of Samuel ministering continually in the tent of meeting, he saw the face of God, so also those who continually and without interruption examine the dogmas of truth and having practiced the virtues, seek the face of God, desiring to see him with a pure mind. For the face of God is the exact imprint of the hypostasis, being an icon of the invisible God; therefore also the one seeing it immediately sees God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to seek God's face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God has given law-giving and precise commands from his mouth, and his judgment reaches all, the seed of Abraham and Jacob and those chosen from the nations.
comments.comment: As for his mouth, to perceive his word, he has given you instructions and commands judged to be both law-giving and precise. Having said 'slaves of God from Abraham' because of the bringing in of the race from Abraham, and 'the chosen ones from Jacob' because they are his and bear his name, and 'an election from the nations' then received into an inheritance, their own Lord and God, he says that his providential judgment is such toward all men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God governs the world by his judgments, so nothing happens apart from his providence.
comments.comment: We must not be ignorant, he says, that he is the Lord our God, whose providence governs the whole world by divine judgments, so that nothing happens without judgment or apart from his providence (Psalm 105:7; LXX 104:7).
comments.selected_reason: Says what it means that his judgments are in all the earth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'A thousand generations' is not said of a multitude but by appropriation to the unit.
comments.comment: The number of a thousand generations is not said according to a multitude, but by the appropriation toward the unit, just as also in 'When the thousands are increasing', and 'What is good to me is the law of your mouth, surpassing thousands of gold and silver' (Psalm 119:72; LXX 118:72).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abraham rejoiced to see Christ's day when God appeared to him at the oak of Mamre, and these truths were to be announced to the nations.
comments.comment: We have become such [partakers of Christ] through being made worthy of the appearance of the Son of God; for He is the Christ, the one who also spoke to them, and He himself, the Savior, teaches in the Psalms that Abraham your father rejoiced to see my day (John 8:56), and did rejoice. When did he not look up with his eyes and stand before God at the oak of Mamre? For then the Scripture says, 'God appeared to Abraham.' And these things, even if they are few, were necessary to be announced to the nations by those commanded there to do this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Brief' is said of size, 'few' of number.
comments.comment: 'brief' instead of 'few.' For the brief lies in respect to magnitude, but the few is arranged in respect to numbers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Spirit anointed them invisibly.
comments.comment: They were christs, having received the anointing through the Spirit invisibly, or having become chosen ones.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who teach the word of Jesus soundly are also called christs, as this verse says, because the one Christ has come.
comments.comment: And if anyone longs to see many bodies filled with a divine spirit, serving, as that one Christ did, the salvation of men everywhere, let him consider those who everywhere teach the word of Jesus soundly and with an upright life. The divine Scriptures call them christs too, in the verse: “Do not touch my christs, and do my prophets no harm” (Psalm 105:15). For just as we have heard “that antichrist is coming,” and have learned no less that there are “many antichrists” in the world (1 John 2:18), in the same way, knowing that Christ has come, we see that because of him many christs have come into being in the world. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'anointed' of this verse as those who teach the word of Jesus soundly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Joseph, sold as a slave and put in fetters, shows that the labors of self-control are repaid, and the iron is the hard onset of such sweat.
comments.comment: But the wondrous Joseph was unshaken. He did not have the loose, undisciplined ways of youth, nor was he afraid because he was a foreigner and a household slave; for he had been forced into both by his brothers when they sold him to the Ishmaelites (Genesis 37:28). And since he was stronger alike than that most loathsome pleasure and than the stirrings toward lewdness, the wretched woman slandered him and turned the charge round against the young man (Genesis 39:17–19). He would not yield to her demands, and she branded him an assailant. From then on the young man was a prisoner (Genesis 39:20); yet by divine grace he was kept safe, and at once he won, as the wage of his self-control, rule over the whole land of the Egyptians (Genesis 41:41). So even if this course brings labors, even if heavy sweat lies before the glories of self-control, it counts for little with one who has chosen to love God wholly. For he will have, yes, he will have praise to match it and rewards of equal weight. That is why the inspired David too marvels at the most praiseworthy young man for what he suffered in this cause, saying, ‘Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters; his soul passed through iron’ (Psalm 105:17–18). By iron, I think, he means the hard and unbreakable onset of such sweat, through which one may hold sin in check and depart from all filth, and indeed attain the holy and most pure life, I mean the life of the Gospel, the life in Christ, …
comments.selected_reason: Tells why Joseph's fetters and iron are praised: the labor of self-control.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: Joseph's feet were humbled but not his soul, for he held fast until the word of God came, and then he became a nourisher of all.
comments.comment: they humbled his feet alone, not binding his soul in shackles, but the soul having been made free from iron. For they, being surrounded by shackles, bear the affliction, having the soul bowed down by iron. But he endured this not unto all things; for he limits the end of the affliction, saying that he had held it fast until the word of God passed through; according to which, having been transferred from the prison, he became a fosterer and nourisher of all, having grasped the word of the Lord, kindling it to boil in the spirit and being filled with the divine light, with which also he is able to give the exhortation saying, 'Do not quench the Spirit' (1 Thessalonians 5:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the feet in fetters and the soul made free: Joseph endured until the word of God passed through.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sends guides to those too weak to leave harm by themselves, Moses by the law and Aaron by the priestly word.
comments.comment: since not all are able to depart from the harmful ones by themselves and through themselves, God sends to those who are thus weak the ones capable of being guides and leaders of the way that carries toward the good. And the law of God through Moses and the high-priestly word through Aaron are not the same; the one forbidding the deeds, the other ministering to God on our behalf and distributing the graces from Him to us; they are the leaders whom they say, 'Let us flee Egypt.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God sent both Moses and Aaron.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm names the plagues in no strict order and not all of them, since God's power shows even in those it names, and each fell on Egypt alone.
comments.comment: He uses the order of the plagues indifferently and does not list them all, because, I think, the power of God is shown even from the wonders that are mentioned one by one. What is needed is that God's power be made known, not that a complete record of events be produced. He says the frogs were not simply produced on the earth, but in the houses, and in the most prominent parts of the houses, and in their innermost rooms, so that their onslaught was unhindered and most violent, and no one, not even the most powerful, could stop them (Psalm 105:30). It was also extraordinary that the gnats and the dog-fly were poured out over the whole land and stopped at the borders without going further, so that the punishment was clearly being carried out against Egypt alone. That is why the turning of the waters to blood also stopped at the borders, and the streams flowing into the neighboring country were no longer such, because the punishment was against the Egyptians, taking away the abundance of the river (Psalm 105:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm lists the plagues freely and what the frogs and the waters showed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: With their salvation came abundance, since the Egyptians gave costly things to those leaving, and all departed unharmed.
comments.comment: Along with the salvation that was given, he also speaks of the abundance that came from God's power, which led the Egyptians to provide many costly things to those who asked and were about to leave the country (Psalm 105:37). It was also a great thing that they departed unharmed, every one of them, from a country that was suffering the worst plagues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the silver and gold and the unharmed departure.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Silver and gold mean good works, words and knowledge; without them the weak cannot leave Egypt.
comments.comment: It happens through good works, every kind of word, and all knowledge, in silver and gold, and outside of Egypt by God. For it is impossible for one being weak and lacking the aforementioned silver and gold to come out of Egypt.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The voice is that of those before the Savior's coming, asking to be remembered in the good pleasure of his people, since the prophets longed to see Jesus.
comments.comment: The set-forth voice is especially holy of those before the coming of the Savior, entreating that the Lord might remember them in the good pleasure of His people (Psalm 106:4-5; LXX 105:4–6), since He was well-pleased in His beloved Son to save, judging His people and the world; thus he says, showing Him: 'This is my beloved Son in whom I am well-pleased' (Matt 3:17). Because the divine prophets, desiring to see and hear the things happening and being spoken concerning Jesus by the eye of the mind, are worthy that their memory be made in the salvation according to the good pleasure.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is the salvation of God who has visited us, and we are to become his chosen ones and be glad in the feast of the believing nation.
comments.comment: And Christ is often called the salvation of God, as also in Ezekiel: 'For all flesh is the salvation of our God' (Isaiah 40:5). This visitation, the father of the baptizer making manifest concerning God, says: 'Through the bowels of the mercy of our God, in whom he visited us, the sunrise from on high' (Luke 1:78). Having visited us in His salvation, it will be for us to become His chosen ones and to behold in the goodness of His chosen ones the joy being fulfilled, and to be made glad in the divine feast of the nation being completed from all those believing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the visiting salvation and the gladness of God's chosen as Christ's coming.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The church from the Gentiles has the inheritance, and those who attend to the law spiritually are praised with it by God and the holy powers.
comments.comment: And may it be accomplished for us also to be praised with His inheritance, for it is for us as heirs to have the inheritance. Who is this church from the Gentiles, saying, 'Let them depart from me, and I will give you the inheritance of the Gentiles' (Psalm 2:8)? For spiritually, remaining according to the Gospel, those attending to the law are praised with the aforementioned inheritance. And they are praised by God and by the holy powers, receiving those who hasten to be well-pleasing to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who repent confess that they sinned like their fathers, and that, held within God, they were beaten by passions and toil.
comments.comment:
And the divine men, taking up also the countenance of those who repent of those on whom they acted wickedly, and teaching how they must repent after the sins, saying, 'We have not sinned, but we have sinned like our fathers'—calling their fathers the ancestors and those who came before, or those who begat them in wickedness—will not say everything when confessing, saying, 'We have turned away' …

We have acted perversely and done wrong. And even regarding those who are counted among those who repent, they do not appear to have been pious. For we were not made outside of the divinity, but being contained by it, we were defeated by passions and hard toil, and we sinned and did other things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He showed his power even when they provoked him.
comments.comment: And when they provoked him bitterly as they went up at the Red Sea, even then he made known to them his power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because Jesus rebukes the tossing sea into calm, he is shown to be God, the one who rebuked the Red Sea, and the Son of God.
comments.comment: God, who rebuked the Red Sea, is praised by all. If even Jesus, when the sea is tossing, rebukes the sea, so that from a storm a calm becomes, He is proven to be God, He who rebuked the Red Sea, and He is the Son of Him. But because God rebuked the Red Sea, the ancient sea becomes dry, as if it were to be passable, and the abyss is no longer called by the abundance of the waters.
comments.selected_reason: Shows from the rebuke of the Red Sea that the one who rebukes sea and storm is God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God first showed kindness, granting what they asked, and when they did not profit he used the fitting medicine of punishment.
comments.comment: When they tested God in the waterless place, he, who cannot be tempted and bears no grudge, did not repay them, but gave them their request. … But when they angered Moses and Aaron in the camp, then the earth opened and swallowed them. For the servants were not to be despised. But since kindness and severity are both with him, according to the words, See then the kindness and the severity of God, he first gave them the things of kindness. And when they did not benefit from it, he accordingly treated them with the fitting medicine of punishment.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Dathan's company angered Moses and the earth swallowed them, while Korah's company, who dared offer strange fire, angered Aaron and a flame consumed them.
comments.comment: So the followers of Dathan and Abiram angered Moses by saying, Has God spoken only through Moses? Has he not spoken through us as well? (Numbers 12:2). And Korah and his company, who dared to bring strange fire and offer sacrifices to God in the place of the priests, angered Aaron. But those who spoke against Moses—Dathan with his whole family—the earth opened wide and swallowed, and it covered the company of Abiram. And Korah and those with him who were about to offer their censers, a flame came out from the tabernacle and consumed them.
comments.selected_reason: Tells who Dathan, Abiram and Korah were and how each company was destroyed.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The calf was modelled on the Apis of Memphis, and the people worshiped it and other carvings.
comments.comment: And they made a calf in Horeb, having a vision of the Apis brought from Egypt in Memphis. Therefore, they worshiped this calf and other carvings, being bound to the drama of polytheism. Immediately, indeed, having made a calf, they were showing many, saying, 'These are not your gods, Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt.'
comments.selected_reason: Says where the golden calf came from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Justice decreed destruction, but love for humanity left room for Moses' intercession, because of his holiness, God's care for the world and the promise to the fathers.
comments.comment: According to justice, the decree was destruction; according to love for humanity, there was the concession of being saved. The intercession made room for the concession, both because of the holiness of the one interceding and because of the providence over the world by which the intercessor pleaded, so that the grace of God toward Israel might not be thought incomplete, and because of the memory of the fathers and the promise made to them, which Moses recalled as he pleaded. For according to their impiety and the foreknowledge of their whole wickedness, they would have been destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses' standing in the breach turned away the decree.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The dispute about the land fought against God's promise and came from cowardice, which despairs of success.
comments.comment: The dispute about the land was older than the rebellion of Korah and Dathan, but greater and more impious, since it fought against the promise of God and was not striving about the worship of God. So it is fittingly joined with the impiety toward God mentioned before, since it came about through cowardice just as that one came about through faintheartedness. Cowardice produces despair of success, just as faintheartedness, because of Moses' separation, produced despair of Moses' return.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God disciplines to set people right, so he first relaxed punishment, as at the Red Sea, and punished more harshly the whole people's refusal of the land, since they went on testing him.
comments.comment: But God brings events upon us by the ways of discipline. The end of discipline is the setting right of the human being toward the upright, with the Spirit in leadership and the flesh in obedience. For this reason he postponed the supply of pleasant things, training the desire for them to be subjected to the mind that follows the will of God. And he led them into dangers, exercising them to endure what would otherwise be avoided, through hope in God, which is fitting for those who think rightly. And since human beings are rather fleshly in their present condition, at first he relaxed the punishment for the disobedient and small-souled, but later he punished them to bring about a turning back. So then, when they were afraid at the Red Sea and spoke against him, he did not punish them; but at the promised land he punished those who did not have the courage to follow him into it. For this was plainly a proof of unbelief. Those who had seen with their own eyes such great and such numerous wonders had every right to be confident in everything through the power of the one who had saved them. And indeed, although the making of the calf was more impious, he punished it less severely, in partial measures; but he punished with the death of the people more harshly in the disobedience of the whole people of that time concerning the possession of the land, because they had not been brought to their senses by the earlier punishment and they persisted to the utmost in testing God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God punished the refusal of the promised land more harshly than the calf.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalm names the idolatry but not its cause, the fornication that drew them into fellowship with what they worshiped.
comments.comment: He did not name the cause of the idolatry, which was the fornication that drew them into fellowship with the object of worship—for that was connected with gluttony—but he accuses the result, for the sake of which the law also forbade intercourse with foreign women, so that they would not be led by affection for the women into fellowship with impiety (Psalm 106:28; LXX 105:28). And that is exactly what happened. For it drove them to such folly that they were initiated into the rites of Beelphegor and defiled themselves with sacrifices performed for the dead.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: At Shittim the people who had eaten bread from heaven shared the idolaters' meals and slid into apostasy and dancing with women.
comments.comment: And what happened to the people of old after this? In what way did they stumble? They were defiled at Shittim, they served idols, they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; Psalm 106:28). See, then, how those baptized in the cloud and in the sea, though they had eaten the bread from heaven and drunk the spiritual drink, became entangled with the idolaters. Because they shared meals with them and touched the table of the idols, they were at once easily carried away and slid into apostasy, and they danced with women: “And the people who understood were entangled with a prostitute,” in the words of the prophet (Hosea 4:14). For this is what is meant by “they rose up to play” (1 Corinthians 10:7).
comments.selected_reason: Tells what happened at Baal of Peor and how it came about.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prayer for gathering from the nations is added so that they may find firm salvation from God, always give thanks and boast in him.
comments.comment: He shows that the return through the mercy of their captors will not be unshaken, by adding a prayer about the gathering together from the nations and ending with it, so that they may find the firm and immovable salvation that comes from God himself, and may give thanks always to the one who saved them, and may have their boasting in God (Psalm 106:46-47; LXX 105:46-47). And it is necessary to await the mercy that comes after the present disobedience, as the apostle says, so that they may dance before God all their days, making supplication, as Zechariah foretells.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalm praises God's mercies to men, and those wandering in the desert had no guide to follow and no well-ordered city to dwell in.
comments.comment: The following psalm, its praise being of the divine benefits and mercies toward men that have been done, has the sequence arranged. … Psalm 106:1: Those upon whom the surrounding tribulations fall (without any of them bringing this upon themselves), knowing that the good God has these things, says the following verses. … Psalm 106:4: Therefore also, being in the desert, we wandered, not having a guide and a leader to follow, finding either a city well-arranged after the holy law in which we were able to dwell without departing from it, but virtue and the wisdom of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Jews, once freed from Egypt by crying to the Lord, will again be delivered if they seek the freedom Christ gives.
comments.comment: He says these things were spoken about the Jews, who long ago were set free from their sojourn in Egypt by crying out to the Lord, and who now will suffer the same thing and be delivered from their manifold wandering, if they cry out to the Lord and long to obtain the perfect freedom that comes through Christ himself.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly whom the wanderers who cried to the Lord stand for.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The prisoners in darkness are the same people, so the words are allegory: Israel is covered by death, bound by humiliation and held by slavery, and Christ is the Savior who sets the prisoners free.
comments.comment: This allegory is also about the same people, which is why it is especially clear that these things are spoken allegorically. For if they are taken literally, it does not fit that the same people wander in the desert and are bound in a dark prison. It is clear according to Isaiah, who says to those in bonds, "Come out," and to those in darkness, "Be uncovered" (Isaiah 49:9). Concerning this Zechariah also says, "By the blood of his covenant he sent out prisoners from a pit having no water" (Zechariah 9:11). Christ, then, is the Savior from the Father, and the Father is Savior through Christ. Israel is now covered by death, bound by humiliation, and constrained by the necessity of slavery. For “shadow” is what covers, “poverty” is the humiliation, and “iron” is the necessity. Being cast out to this very thing, they are appointed for the nations into a land of nations poor from the beginning, about whom the twenty-first psalm says, "The poor shall eat and be filled" (Psalm 21 (22):26) (Psalm 22:26).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: While men were still walking in lawlessness God took hold of them, as he took hold of the thief who repented on the cross.
comments.comment: While they were still walking in the way of their lawlessness, God took hold of them, because through a multitude of impieties having been humbled, they were held by those from whom he raised them. And see if you are able to apply this to the thief who repented on the cross; for while he was in the way of lawlessness (for he was condemned by robbery) and having been humbled by punishment because of his lawlessness, he was taken hold of by the one saying to him, 'Today you shall be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear example of the verse in the thief on the cross.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Loathing all food is a sickness of body or soul that refuses spiritual food too, and the gates of death are the sins toward death, from which those who cry to the Lord are saved.
comments.comment: Generally also, both upon the body and upon the soul, for what sickness of the emaciated one he abstains from all nourishment, both bodily and spiritual; but those having the health of the soul hunger and thirst for righteousness. And the gates of death are the sins toward death. These they approach before coming to him, having a life-giving breath and power, I mean indeed the thought concerning God; therefore, in their being afflicted, they cry out to the Lord, and he saves them from all the constraining necessities that hold them. And if they had not cried out to the Lord, they would have perished even until death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's Word heals people from lives of vice, as the many who have become self-controlled testify.
comments.comment: Among the Greeks there was one Phaedo, and I do not know whether a second, and one Polemon, who turned from a dissolute and utterly wicked life and took up philosophy. But with Jesus it was not only the twelve at that time; it has always been many times as many, who have become a company of the self-controlled and say of their former lives: “For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to all kinds of desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another; but when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Saviour appeared” (Titus 3:3–4), then “through the washing of rebirth and renewal of the Spirit, which he poured out on us richly” (Titus 3:5–6), we became what we are. For God “sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their corruptions” (Psalm 107:20), as the one who prophesied in the Psalms taught.
comments.selected_reason: Shows in plain terms how God's Word heals people.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One should declare the Lord's works from one's own experience of his goodness.
comments.comment: And he proclaims in gladness the works of him, everyone announcing those things having happened to himself and having had experience of his goodness, not simply recounting those things having happened to others.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what it is to declare the Lord's works.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The storm at sea pictures the people tossed up and down by a divine command until they are humbled and bewildered.
comments.comment: Having allegorized wandering, famine, thirst, darkness, and chains as the evils of the Jews, he now uses a maritime allegory as well. He brings the disturbances at sea, the changes from these into calm, and salvation even to a calm harbor into the same picture as their labors. And he shows that the rest which will succeed the labors came when their former calm was stirred into waves not without God, but by a divine command. It is as though the command raised a squall and stirred up with waves their former fair sailing. By these waves they are lifted up to a height as the waves crest, and brought down as the waves fall away, as tends to happen at sea: they are humbled, thrown into confusion, and bewildered to the point of losing their wits.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sea-storm of the psalm as a picture of the people's trouble.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Going up to heaven and down to the abyss is a figure of speech, as the Scripture often uses.
comments.comment: And the saying of ascending as if to heaven and descending as if from the abyss is said by hyperbole. For indeed in such a way there are countless examples in the Scripture; for concerning the cities of Israel, the enemies, whatever they had been walled up as if to heaven because they had been walled up with high walls, and 'I shall be made white as snow' (Ps 51:7) is said in the same way.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse speaks of mounting to heaven and going down to the depths.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sea stands for the life of men and their polity, and its waves for what happens to a man.
comments.comment: And according to allegory, often the life of men and their polity is called a sea. Here, waves are able to signify what happens to man. And he says that regarding the judgments happening to him, 'it ascends even unto the heavens' and 'it descends even unto the depths' (Psalm 107:26).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God quiets the winds the storm-tossed people reach the harbor of rest through mercy, and for this they give thanks in the church and the seat of the elders.
comments.comment:
Then they experience a change when the wind dies down, whenever God commands this too, and he releases the violence of the winds into a gentle breeze and quiets the sound of the waves. There they will have the joy that comes from the wilderness, and they will obtain the harbor they long for as a resting place. For these things it is fitting to give thanks to God, and in the church of the people and in the seat of the elders to sing hymns to him who handed the nation over to the waves because of sins, as has been said, but by mercy transferred them to good things. And the mercy itself shows that they had been brought forth from sins. For those who are shown mercy are not worthy of good things, but are pitiable because of their evils.

This matter is not common in the way it often happens at sea, where the good are storm-tossed and shipwrecked, as Paul was, and the wicked are carried along by fair winds. The things that happen are common to both, so that when they are tested in the same circumstances they may reveal the difference in their disposition, which will later come to an upright and righteous recompense, witnessed beforehand by their very works. So the word is not about those who sail the sea, but about the people who are storm-tossed because of sin and will come to a harbor through mercy (Psalm 107:30). For them there is a church of the people for confession and a seat of elders for the hymn of God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The flock are the gentle and well taught, and the mouth of lawlessness is shut when it cannot speak of God's plan.
comments.comment:
Others say:

They are livestock that are in the so-called sheep, which possess abundance and greatness because of their perfected gentleness and learning (Psalm 107:41). But also, if she does not possess the capacity to speak of the divine economy of God, it will shut her mouth. And you will perceive the devil as lawlessness, and all that is established according to it, as those speaking lawlessly with an enclosed mouth (Psalm 107:42).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ has shut the mouth of sin, since he suffered for us and our penalties should not be demanded of us again.
comments.comment: And he shuts the mouth of the sin, according to what is hymned in the Psalms: ‘And every lawlessness will stop up its mouth’ (Psalm 107:42); having been told to cry down against those who have sinned from weakness, and have been justified in faith. For ‘God is the one justifying; who is the one condemning?’ (Romans 8:33) And Christ having suffered for us, how was it consistent that the penalties for our own trespasses should still be demanded of us ourselves?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: God's glory is the practical and contemplative life, and those walking in the light sing to him.
comments.comment: His glory is the practical and contemplative life, through which it is divided toward moral and intellectual virtue. Those who raised up the true light, having risen toward the Lord, walking decorously as in the day, striking the harp and striking the lyre, sing to the all-wise God, offering up their hymns rhythmically and harmoniously.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's mercy and truth are magnified as high as heaven and the clouds, for the ministry of Moses and the prophets begins in shadow and ends in truth.
comments.comment: His mercy is magnified as that of the heaven, beginning from the earth; for the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord (Psalm 108:4). The end holds those who began to receive mercy from the earth to reach the heaven, in order to inherit the kingdom of the heavens. And his truth is also magnified in the clouds serving the spiritual, to Moses and the prophets, since their ministry begins from the shadow and ends in the truth, just as they also worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:24), as do the apostles and all the disciples of the Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the mercy above the heavens and the truth unto the clouds mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His glory spreads over the earth through those bearing the heavenly image.
comments.comment: Because of the lifting up of God in those who carry the image of the heavenly, and because of this, called heavens, his glory extends over all the earth that is able.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is lifted toward the heavens; his glory is on earth.
comments.comment: … as God is being lifted up toward the contemplative natures of the world, which are called heavens, His glory is found upon the practical earth, which is called earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The beloved are rescued by God's right hand and the speaker's intercession, and the Lord lifted on the cross divided men's works, justifying some and rejecting others.
comments.comment: Not otherwise are those worthy of being loved by you to be rescued from the enemies holding them or those surrounding them, than by you saving with your right hand and by me interceding for them (Psalm 108:6). An oath is interpreted as a symbol of work (Psalm 108:7-9). The Lord, having been lifted up on the cross and having ascended, divided the works of men as to justifying some and rejecting others; for He is a just judge. … Therefore, even the place near the surface, because it is called a valley below due to the human bodies dwelling in it, is called the measurement of the dwellings of the souls inhabiting it, to provide for both the things below and these things. Indeed, He sent the heralds of truth into all the nations, so that the gospel of justification might be proclaimed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Gilead, Manasseh and Ephraim are those who migrate from evil to truth, leave forgetfulness for memory, and bear fruit, and Judah is the one who confesses.
comments.comment: Gilead is interpreted as migration, Manasseh as being from oblivion, and Ephraim as fruitfulness. The Savior says, 'My Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine,' meaning migrating from evil to truth, or from evil to virtue, or from earth to heaven; and mine also is the one who has surpassed all the oblivion of good things and has come from it. For he who comes from oblivion into memory is Manasseh, that is, having left and abandoned the oblivion by which the good things of God were forgotten. But also the great fruitfulness of the believing nations has become a covering and a perception of the Savior; for as Paul writes to those who were benefited by him, saying they are his joy and crown (1 Thess 2:19), so also the Savior has a perception, a crown being woven for him by those bearing up righteousness and truth. And Judah is his king, not by his ruling, but by the king being made his own. Such is David, or perhaps everyone who confesses for the things he accomplished is Judah, interpreted 'confession.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the names of the verse by their meanings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sandal on Edom means the Savior's journey over the earth and earthly things in the flesh with which he is clothed.
comments.comment: Moab, however, because of being a punishment for those handed over to him by the Lord, is the lion of the saying of hope. And the lion often signifies punishment among the prophets. Since punishments fall upon a good intention, they bring good hope. … 'Upon Edom I will extend my sandal' (Psalm 108:9). If the face saying these things were the Savior's, since Edom is translated into the earthy, he will say to make a journey upon the earth and earthly things; for the sandal is a symbol of a covered journey. For of old he used a bare journey, creating and providing, but now with the flesh with which he is clothed, which is also his sandal. And since some shod the gospel with the preparation of peace (Eph 6:15), this sandal also, spread everywhere, was extended upon Edom in both the ways mentioned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God stands at the right hand of the holy man but the devil at the right hand of the sinner such as Judas, so the verse and the priest's case differ.
comments.comment: … Not all have the same right hand, but the serious man has the intelligible things and the things of virtue, while the worthless man has the sensible things and the things of evil; on the right of the holy one God stands, but on that of the sinner the devil. … But perhaps someone will object, saying: 'And concerning Jesus the great priest, who is holy, it has been said: And the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him' (Zech 3:1). But the objector did not attend to the difference of the words; for concerning Judas it is written: 'Let the devil stand at his right hand' (Psalm 109:6; LXX 108:6), but concerning the great priest: 'And the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him'; for he stands fighting and opposing at the right hand of the holy one, even if he is not able to overthrow the one at whose right God is; but at the right of Judas he stands as in his own place.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Satan stands at the right hand.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A prayer becomes sin when its sender fails to obtain what he asks, as Judas failed to destroy the Savior's word.
comments.comment: Therefore he is worthless, and what follows also shows his wickedness, with the Savior praying that the prayer of Judas become sin. Prayer becomes sin to the one who sends it up whenever he fails to obtain what he asks. For he prayed, in a manner betraying the teacher, that his word be destroyed and all the disciples and believers be scattered, but he failed. For his word ran, and those believing in him, increasing daily, filled the whole inhabited world. And in another way prayer becomes sin to someone whenever he deems it worthy to receive from God not what he ought but what does not profit him, and for this reason, since he asked neither what befits God to give nor what is profitable to him, God judged him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a prayer can become sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He was enlightened only a few days before he betrays the truth.
comments.comment: A few days, being enlightened, before he betrays the truth. Being enlightened by the true light, and receiving also the oversight of this instead of himself, becoming a teacher who both remained and progressed in the truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The whole psalm prophesies about Judas, and 'let another take his office' shows that another was chosen in his place.
comments.comment: If we must also set out an argument about Judas that will put them to shame, we shall say that in the Book of Psalms the whole of the hundred and eighth Psalm (Psalm 109) contains the prophecy about Judas. It begins: “O God, do not pass over my praise in silence, for the mouth of a sinner and the mouth of a deceiver have been opened against me” (Psalm 109:1–2). It is also prophesied in it that Judas cut himself off from the number of the apostles because of his sin, and that another was chosen in his place (Acts 1:25–26); and this is shown in the words, “And let another take his office” (Psalm 109:8).
comments.selected_reason: Shows plainly how 'let another take his office' was fulfilled when another apostle replaced Judas.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The betrayer's 'fathers' are those who begot his betrayal: the givers of silver, Satan who put it in his heart, and the rulers of this age who crucified the Lord.
comments.comment: The fathers of Judah, who begot him through betrayal (Psalm 109:14; LXX 108:14a), and those who are able to do this through the giving of silver, and what Satan, having cast it into his heart, incited him to betray the Lord; and those having the wisdom of this age, the rulers concerning whom Paul says, 'For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory' (1 Cor 2:8). And he put him to death, because he became the one handed over unto death (Psalm 109:16; LXX 108:16c).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judas was foreknown as the betrayer yet was the cause of the betrayal, because he could have remembered to show mercy and did not.
comments.comment: If you observe what is written in the psalm, you will find that, just as he was foreknown as the one who would betray the Saviour, so he was also the cause of the betrayal, and because of his wickedness deserved the curses spoken in the prophecy. For let him suffer these things, it says, “because he did not remember to show mercy, and persecuted a poor and needy man” (Psalm 109:16). So he could have remembered “to show mercy” and not persecuted the one whom he persecuted; but though he could, he did not do so, and betrayed him instead, so that he deserves the curses pronounced against him in the prophecy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalm's curses fall on Judas.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is shown mercy on our behalf as poor and lowly, sharing a nature disturbed by evils.
comments.comment: The mercy he asks for is the mercy shown to human beings, on behalf of human beings. He is not himself in need of mercy, since he lightens the terrors of the worthy, being good in giving freely and not measuring out an equal return. But all things come to Christ, and he is shown mercy on our behalf. Insofar as he is us, he is pitied as poor and lowly. He is pitied as being in disturbances, insofar as he shared in the nature that is disturbed by evils.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose mercy is asked and why Christ is called poor.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ speaks as the slave to the Father, asking mercy for his body, the disciples, and speaks of human life as passing like chaff and locusts.
comments.comment: He who is clothed in the form of the slave speaks as to the Lord the Father (Psalm 109:21-23; LXX 108:21–23). And he says to the Lord how he will do mercy with him, benefiting those who are his body; for the things happening to his body are reckoned to himself. Therefore he says, 'Do with me for the sake of your name, since in this I have come to those whom you sent, saying, I have come in the name of the Father; because of this name do it, for your mercy is good, benefiting and full of goodness; do it, since also my heart is troubled within me.' You say 'heart,' and the apostles are his equal-souled ones, the lesser ones having become believing ones who were found to be his body. Since the disciples were not scattered having been scandalized in that night, but Judas and the crowd of the Pharisees stood over to hold him, it happened that their being troubled was his heart. But even if his heart was troubled, he did not depart from him, being contained by him and dwelling in his disciples. But also everyone whose heart is being troubled from thoughts or suffering, doing nothing and saying nothing according to the trouble, says, 'My heart was troubled within me.' Since, indeed, the Savior is to live always among men (for indeed he was taken up after the resurrection into the heavens), he speaks concerning human life as not permanent nor standing, like a shadow in its vanishing: 'You were cast away from me like a chaff.' For just as the chaffs are scattered away through weakness of nature. … They are tossed about; not that I, having taken on a weak life through men, was quickly driven out of weakness to be crucified, but having been taken up after the resurrection. It is possible also to say concerning all the disciples as it is said concerning Him, 'I was tossed about like locusts' (Psalm 109:23), since, being persecuted and tossed about by those desiring evil, they are not humbled but are carried away flying upward. And all the martyrs, having been tossed about like locusts, having left the things below, pursue the prize of the high calling.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is pitied as stirred up, weakened by fasting and mocked by his enemies, taking these from us.
comments.comment: He is pitied as going into obscurity, insofar as his bodily manifestation was interrupted. He is pitied as one stirred up and lifted up like one of the lightest things, insofar as he handed himself over to those who seized him. He takes upon himself from us the weakness from fasting and the squalor from lack of washing, placing nothing between us and himself. And he calls the mockery from his enemies, which he now has through us who are reproached in his name, mockery upon these things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fasting, weakness and mockery of the verses as Christ's.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Lord stands at the right hand of the poor because Christ became poor for all, and the right hand is where all things are done rightly.
comments.comment: Giving the reason for confessing and praising Him, He brought it so that He might stand at the right hand of the poor; it is evident regarding Him who became poor for all, that through my poverty they might become rich. He stands at the right hand of Him who does all things rightly and thinks all things rightly. Again, the God, having set the pretext of standing at His right hand, says, 'To save my soul' (Ps 109:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemies who are made his footstool are those the Father wills to change through repentance, so that they rise from footstool to throne.
comments.comment: But those who have rushed toward wickedness and malice are enemies of the Word and the truth. But the Father also wills these to be changed through repentance, making them followers of the path and the feet of the Word, since having become his footstool, they fall from his feet; but with a turning toward virtue and wisdom, becoming more mobile, they themselves shall become a throne from being a footstool. Therefore Paul says, 'For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet' (1 Corinthians 15:25). And there God says, 'Until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet' (Ps 110:1). For he indeed sits at the right hands of the Father reigning, while the enemies oppose him. But having set for them the beginning of benefit by subduing them and making them his footstool, he raises their desiring hand, so that they themselves might be counted among the right-handed, no longer in the wickedness through which they happened to be on the left; so that in the end, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and all the rational beings, having been perfected, become toward the Father and the Son of God, all things becoming in all things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the footstool means and what the Father wills for the enemies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father says 'Sit at my right hand' to his only-begotten Son alone, not to any of the born.
comments.comment: And indeed the apostle, having followed this thought, has said: 'For which of the angels did he ever say, Sit at my right hand?' (Hebrews 1:13) saying only once. Not to any of the born, but to his only-begotten Son alone: 'Sit at my right hand,' since he himself is alone the only-begotten who is in the bosom of the Father.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord Jesus, having fulfilled the economy and ascended, hears 'Sit at my right hand,' which is not said of a place but of reigning together with the Father.
comments.comment: Having fulfilled the economy, both having been raised from the dead and having been taken up into heaven, the Lord Jesus says, 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet' (Psalm 110:1), that is, the Father. Paul, therefore, says that after this ascension, the voice was spoken through Him to say, 'Having made a cleansing of sins, He sat in the right hand of majesty in the high places.' For to which of the angels was it ever said, 'Sit at my right hand?' (Hebrews 1:13). The Lord, therefore, who is the Father of all those having been brought forth with Him, says to the Lord of creation, 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.' And the Father says to the Son, as if a father to a son and a son to a father, for He does not converse using speech; for He is His own thought, truth, wisdom, and word. And the Lord of the Lord sits in the right hands. It is not locally, in the body, that He says these things, as if we were seeking the right hand in a place. Rather, those partaking of God are indeed in the right hand, since God is holy and good; no one else will be counted holy, reigning with the Father. For the 'Sit at my right hand' declares the co-reigning of the Son toward the Father. If it is regarding the rational beings: those having wisdom and the most keen virtue are thrones of God; and in these, the Savior sits at the right hand of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David calls his own descendant Lord because Christ is David's son in the flesh and Lord by nature, one Christ and Son.
comments.comment: “And he said to them: How do they say the Christ is David’s son? For David himself says in the book of Psalms: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right until I put your enemies as a footstool of your feet. David therefore calls him Lord, and how is he his son?” (Luke 20:41–44) (Psalm 110:1) You hear how in these Christ himself tries to show that even if the Word became from David’s seed according to the flesh, yet even so he is by nature Lord, as Son and God. For if, he says, he is David’s son, how does David name him Lord? But he neither denies in these the birth from David’s seed according to flesh, nor dismisses being Lord by nature himself; rather he says both are present, even if from both he wills the one to be shown. So there is truly one Christ and Son.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why David calls his son Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The Word is exalted not into a foreign dignity but into what he was, and so is seated with the Father.
comments.comment: “Therefore, having been exalted by the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he poured out this which you see and hear. For David did not go up into the heavens; yet he himself says: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right until I put your enemies as a footstool of your feet.” (Acts 2:33–35) (Psalm 110:1) In these we may behold the whole mystery of the Only-begotten’s becoming human. For existing in the form and equality of the Father, the God-Word from him—the all-powerful right hand and all-working hand—is said to have been emptied (Philippians 2:6–9) because of the human, yet is exalted again not into a foreign dignity and not by crossing into what had not long belonged to him, but into what he was; and the Word, having appeared, is for this reason also co-seated with God and Father.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: The divine king's mighty authority goes out from Jerusalem over all the world, and all will obey.
comments.comment: He makes clear that the mighty authority of the divine king will be sent out over all the world, beginning from Jerusalem, according to the words: I was established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain (Psalm 2:6) (Psalm 110:2; LXX 109:2). And all will obey and serve.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rod of strength sent out of Zion means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His unfading prime, proper to eternal life, is compared to morning dews.
comments.comment: The perpetual and unfading quality of his prime, proper to eternal life, is compared to morning dews, just as the life that was dissolved was compared to a shadow that declines (Psalm 110:3; LXX 109:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the dew of his youth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The kingdom's beginning is not in chance events but in the brightness of the saints, lit by the true light, in the day of his power.
comments.comment: … the name of the beginning, 'kingdom,' here signifies not as with the Savior in the day of his power, but after the resurrection in which he rose from the dead; for if he was crucified out of weakness, but lives by the power of God. It signifies the beginning kindred to him which is coming, through which he holds and rules (that is, the day of his power), not in things happening by chance, but in the brightness of the saints through which they possess light, being illuminated and made bright by the true light, as one might say, 'Let the brightness of the Lord our God be upon us.' If, however, he says 'beginning' regarding those who are beginning, according to what is signified, it is said that God prevails over every beginning, and his beginning was made at his own time; and you do not say thus, but rather those who are beginning are under him in the day of his power, when the sun of righteousness shines (Mal 4:2). For he himself says concerning those being ruled by him toward the Father, 'I want that where I am, they also may be, that they may see my glory' (John 17:24).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Begetting from the womb differs from making with hands: the Son is the only-begotten offspring, while creation is the work of God's hands.
comments.comment:
Let us see also what this very word [from the womb before the dawn I begot you] intends. And it must be said that God is indeed simple and undivided; and even while he is thus, if the divine Word wishes to truly present himself as a maker, from whom we are, he says, speaking of his hands, that the heavens and the rest of creation are the work of his hands. … if we mean not the adoptive ones but the genuine ones, since some are truly sons and others are adoptive and placed; if we do not mean the placed ones but the genuine ones, we say they are the offspring of the womb of those who bore them. And God, wishing to present a genuine Son and the only-begotten from himself, remembers the womb.

But just as he makes it with hands in a God-befitting way, so also we hear 'to have been begotten from the womb.' But the works of the hands are many, while the only-begotten offspring of the womb is one; therefore, it is not to be said of God that creating and begetting are the same, as some say. For all things were made through the Word and in wisdom (John 1:3), and the wisdom and the Word were not through something, but were begotten from God. Therefore, begetting is not the same as making; for if there were no difference, nothing would prevent saying: 'My hands made you, and the heavens are the work of my womb.'

… But the Father does not say these things to the Son in ignorance, but so that we might know the intimacy of the Father toward the Son and of the Son toward the Father, these things were written.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He is a priest forever because he lives forever, and Melchizedek, whose death is not recorded, is his type.
comments.comment: He is an eternal priest because he lives eternally, a priesthood made secure as if confirmed by an oath (Psalm 110:4; LXX 109:4). Melchizedek is a type of him, whose death is not recorded as a sign that death does not even exist for him. Having just been shown as king, he is now also displayed as priest, which is impossible in Israel and under the law. And this too was prefigured in Melchizedek.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the eternal priesthood and Melchizedek.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God swears without change, and the Savior's priesthood is not of Aaron's order, which was changed, but eternal and without end.
comments.comment: As for us, the Savior defines the Yes as Yes and the No as No; moreover, God, being truthful, is said to swear, without using an unchangeable or a changeable method. Therefore, 'The Lord has sworn and will not repent' (Psalm 110:4; LXX 109:4), since the gifts and the calling of God are unchangeable; and the greatest calling is that of the Savior, into priesthood and an unchangeable gift, a priesthood not according to the order of Aaron but of Melchizedek unto the age. … For the priesthood of Aaron, lying ahead until a time of correction, was transferred, as Paul says, 'When the priesthood is changed, there is a change also of law by necessity' (Heb 7:12). But the covenant made toward the Savior is eternal, preserving the priesthood without transgression, being able to save those coming to God through him into perfection, the one who lives always to intercede for them. … Likewise also the spiritual sacrifices, a sacrifice of praise and of righteousness, he offers to the Father on our behalf, but he has also offered himself as a sacrifice for all, for the salvation of those being saved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the oath and why Christ's priesthood differs from Aaron's.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No scribe or Pharisee served in Melchizedek's order, for Melchizedek and his priesthood were a type of Christ.
comments.comment: If you knew the “God-breathed scriptures,” senseless Pharisee (2 Timothy 3:16), and the holy prophets’ voices, you would have remembered blessed David saying to Christ the Savior of all: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” (Psalm 110:4) Tell me, then: which of the scribes or Pharisees has served God “according to the order of Melchizedek”? None at all. Even Abraham our forefather, root of Israel’s line, was blessed under Melchizedek’s priesthood. Melchizedek and his priesthood were a type of Christ the Savior of all, who has become our high priest, bringing near to God the Father all who have believed in him and perfecting them into sanctification through worship beyond the law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Melchizedek honored God with bread and wine, imitating the Christ to come, and Christ's priesthood is of his order, not of Aaron's bloody sacrifices.
comments.comment: So Melchizedek was a righteous man and truly bore the image of God in himself. Moved therefore by prophetic spirit, he understood the offering that was to be brought to God by Christ, and he honored God with bread and wine, imitating the Christ who was to come. Since in the synagogue of the Jews the order of Aaron offered sacrifice to God—not bread and wine, but calves and lambs, glorifying God with bloody sacrifices—God cried out to Jesus, who was to be born from the virgin Mary, saying: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4; LXX 109:4), not according to Aaron, who served with bloody sacrifices, but according to the order of Melchizedek, bringing the offering of the nations in bread and wine perpetually.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the order of Melchizedek was.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The Son is at the Father's right hand and the Father at the Son's, not in a place, and the Father crushes the powers of darkness at his right hand.
comments.comment: As the Father says, 'Sit at my right hand, my Son' (Psalm 110:5; LXX 109:5), now it is said, 'The Lord is at your right hand' (Psalm 110:5; LXX 109:5), so that it might be manifest not locally that the Son is at the right hand of the Father. For behold, both he is at the right hand and his Father is at the right hand, which is impossible if one thinks of 'at the right hand' locally. Just as the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father, so the Son is at the right hand of the Father. And the Father of the Son crushes the intelligible kings at his right hand on the day of his wrath, who are found to be nothing other than rulers and powers and cosmocrators of the darkness. … His enemies will cease to be enemies after being crushed, as every such authority and power is being abolished by the Lord. The day of the Lord, the time of the judgment of all, is spoken of in the Scriptures.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the right hand is not a place.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God fills the dead with corpses so that those fallen may rise to life, and the Savior reigns over the crushed rulers as head.
comments.comment: When these things are thus fulfilled, God will fill the dead with corpses, not being empty or a non-participant of His fullness regarding those fallen from salvation, so that they might rise into eternal life. For the saints themselves have not received life from the fullness except for the fall and resurrection of many, casting down and making to fall those having a bad standing who seem to be established through wickedness and impiety, in order to raise them to a resurrection of life, so that they might serve Him as Head, after the bad kingdoms have been crushed as heads of many, who are called to be poured out because of wickedness. For since not only those but He himself has the head, that is, the king, first upon the earth that exists, having crushed the rulers of the nations upon evil, He himself legally reigns over them, being the Head of every man according to the inner human and of the blameless church.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The brook in the way is trial, which Jesus received in human life, and so he lifts up his head as King of heaven and earth.
comments.comment: The cause of all these things was established by Him having become one who is plucked from a streamlet in the way of the human life. For this the last verse alludes to, saying, 'From a streamlet in the way water is drawn'; because of this, He will lift up the head. Ps 109:7 A streamlet signifies trial in many places, and to draw from it is to receive it. Jesus has been tested, having become for salvation in the way of men, as the apostle says writing: 'For He himself has suffered having been tested, He is able to help those being tested' Heb 4:15; and having been shown to be King, authority being given to Him in heaven and upon the earth, He will lift up the head, a ruler not only of those upon the earth but also of those in the heavens, having been ordained by the Spirit so that every knee should bend to Him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the brook in the way and why he lifts up the head.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Walking the road and drinking from a stream symbolize lowliness, as when the Lord asked the Samaritan woman for water.
comments.comment: For it is clear that Christ was exalted even before the exaltation that came from human beings, since he was in the form of God and came down from heaven. Walking on the road and drinking water from a stream are symbols of lowliness. And we see the Lord traveling on foot and asking the Samaritan woman for water to drink.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the brook in the way as lowliness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalm is composed through the twenty-two Hebrew letters, which invites the study of letters and of the law.
comments.comment: In the present psalm the hymn is spoken in brief form, and the first sounds of the verses proceed through the twenty-two letters of the Hebrews according to the Hebrew language, from the first to the last, that is, from Aleph to Thau. Such a composition has grammatical elegance and invites one to a knowledge of letters and the learning of books. In this way the psalms immediately and clearly urge one to the study of the law, since Moses also commanded this from of old and ordered that they appoint teachers of letters and teach the law to children, because they had learning through hearing, not wisdom through the Spirit, as those who are perfected in Christ do (Ps 111:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the psalm's alphabetical form and what it teaches.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To confess with all one's heart is to love God with every power of the soul and to praise him among the upright, not anywhere or with anyone.
comments.comment: And the saint, about to proclaim the things having happened concerning the salvation of all by the Lord, pre-announces the voices set forth. And everyone confesses with all his heart, and he alone who has loved God with all his heart, soul, and mind; and, having turned away all his loving power toward God, he loves God with all his heart; and, having consumed all his hymnographic and eucharistic power toward God, he confesses to him with all his heart in the assembly of the important ones, not in a random place or with random people. It is possible to read 'With all his heart' as follows: 'In the counsel of the upright and in the assembly, the great works of the Lord' (Psalm 111:1-2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what confessing with the whole heart means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's works are great because the Creator is great, and every work was sought out for his wills, so that none is without purpose.
comments.comment: Generally and broadly called the will of the Lord, the things concerning his works in part are his individual wills. If not all things he willed, he did; the creation extends broadly to his will, the individual works being fitted to the specific wills. Therefore, since the Creator is great, his works are also great, most accurately fitted to the harmony of his wills; for they do not happen as they chance, but they happen as having been sought out for all the wills. Therefore, of the works having been sought out, let no one say 'to what purpose?' For all things were created for their need; therefore, all the works of God are very good. … And if one calls virtues the will of God because he will do all my wills, he will say great works have been sought out for all the wills of God, namely the activities according to virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wonders done through Moses, the prophets and Jesus, such as healings and resurrections, are signs of the will of God.
comments.comment: Since things happening paradoxically and marvelously (some through Moses and the prophets, others through Jesus our savior) are spoken of, the preceding words are also spoken of these. For the resurrections of the dead, the cleansings of lepers, the sight of the blind, and things similar to these, Jesus performs symbolically through them, manifesting the healings of his own humanity, which are always previously the will of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives food to those who fear him in wonderful ways, as with Daniel in the lions' den and Elijah fed by ravens.
comments.comment: … And indeed he gives food without exception to those fearing him with a certain paradoxicalness, just as Daniel found the best in the lion's den in Babylon; from Jerusalem, the transport of Habakkuk was brought to Babylon, carrying food to Daniel. But also, having commanded the ravens to bring bread in the morning and meat in the evening to Elijah (during a time of much famine), he nourished him who feared the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the examples of Daniel and Elijah for the food given to those who fear him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The old covenant gives way to the new, which has no successor, and God's covenant is remembered for eternity.
comments.comment: And of his old covenant, when the time of correction having been given, the end is taking up, he shall be remembered for an eternity during the age of the new covenant according to the gospel, which remains without a successor. Therefore also, to the people, he appropriated his own blood; through the bath of regeneration and the renewal of the spirit, Jesus gives the power of his works, making manifest to them what power he has commanded them to work, the people, and the words of the things that have happened. His covenant shall be remembered for an eternity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, not satisfied with the fullness of the nations alone, will show his works' power to Israel so that they too may be saved.
comments.comment: … But since God is good, not being satisfied with only the fullness of the nations entering into the pure and glorified inheritance, he is remembered for an eternity of the covenant toward the sons of Israel through their fathers. He will announce to the Israelite people the power he made his works, so that, having seen the power of the economy, they also might be saved, after the fullness of the nations has entered, receiving from God the inheritance appropriated and confirmed to the nations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The works of God's hand are truth and judgment: judgment that chooses good and flees evil, and truth that Christ gives through the Holy Spirit.
comments.comment: When calling the Father, we find the Lord, as 'The high hand has done all these things' (Ps 118:74). For the Word—through whom all things were made and in whom all things exist, which the Father made—is His hand creating the all. But also in a strong hand, having brought the people out of Egypt, God accomplished this in the same Son, as one of the apostles writes: 'Jesus, having saved a people once out of Egypt, twice destroyed those who did not believe' (Jude 1:5). And since other scriptures also say that God has made all things by one hand, such as the one saying 'The heavens are the works of your hands' (Psalm 102:25), and the one announcing 'The hands did not create all the host of heaven' (Isaiah 45:12) (this is consistent with the one who said 'Your hands made me and fashioned me' Ps 139:13), someone might rightly seek and find the Holy Spirit being called the hand of God; from which it is shown that the Holy Spirit is creative, in the Son and Holy Spirit of the Father, having worked the heavens and having created the host of heaven. … Among these works of the hand of God in all the saints, truth and judgment are found, happening to be truth. For He gives through the Holy Spirit a practical power, and judgment is that which judges and, with examination, defines, so that one must choose good and flee evil; but truth is what Christ gives through the Holy Spirit, namely a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge. The knowledge of truth and moral virtue are works of the hands of God, being truth and judgment; therefore, following this, all His commandments were brought forth, not spoken so as to be believed merely, but because of the immovable and certain, as it is written, 'I will give you an eternal covenant, the faithful things of David' (Isaiah 55:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To say the commandments are faithful means they are certain, for God is faithful not by sharing in faith but by having certainty.
comments.comment: It should be noted that to believe often signifies the certain, as it is said: 'All his commandments are faithful' (Psalm 111:7). And he interprets their faithfulness saying: 'established unto the age of ages.' And again: 'the word is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.' And again: 'God is faithful and there is no injustice.' For God is not faithful from participating in faith, but from having certainty.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'faithful' means when said of the commandments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's commandments are faithful and cannot be overturned, and they are made in truth and rectitude, for truth is godly doctrine and rectitude is its perfect guarding.
comments.comment: These faithful commandments stand for ever and ever because they are of God and cannot be overturned. Concerning them, indeed, the Savior says, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away' (Matt 24:35). But do not err by thinking that the things set forth concern the commandments which are according to the shadow. For those passed away until a time of correction was given. For concerning the spiritual laws according to Him, it is necessary to hear the things set forth, as the coming thing teaches thus: 'Having been made in truth and rectitude.' … For they become understood in truth according to the doctrine of godliness. But they are also completed in rectitude with the best of guarding, as the work of the hands of the Lord, and these being found to be being accomplished in each godliness, are truth and judgment. But take hold of judgment for the sake of rectitude, to direct the soul toward practical and ethical virtue, and judgment is to be critical of things to be done and not to be done.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the commandments are sure and what truth and uprightness mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls things faithful to mean certain and unshakeable, as the commandments of the spiritual law are.
comments.comment: Many scriptures signify the certain and unshakeable through the faithful. For that which is said about God: 'All his commandments are faithful, established for an age of ages' (Ps 111:7–8), and that: 'I will give you the faithful blessings of David' (Isa 55:3), and even that: 'I will raise for myself a faithful priest' (1 Sam 2:35), declare the certain and unchangeable, of the commandments of God existing faithful according to the spiritual law because of the unchangeable, and of the commandments according to the shadow of the law being transferred from the letter to the spirit and from the shadow to the truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sent redemption as the Son of Man gave his soul as a ransom, and his name is holy to the saints but fearful to those who sin.
comments.comment: As God sent redemption to his people (Ps 110:9ab: He has sent redemption to his people; there is nothing else to the one saying), the Son of Man came to give his soul as a ransom for many. By the same precious grace of God, having tasted every death, we were redeemed from our ancestral vain conduct. For Christ has become to us as wisdom and righteousness and sanctification from God, and also as redemption, saying, 'I was sent to proclaim liberty to the captives' (Luke 4:18). For the redeemer and benefactor of all has released from captivity those held by the devil and by wickedness, forgiving the sins and impieties of those fleeing to him. But his goodness was not satisfied with merely redeeming the captives and their heirs, those of his own father, but he set them as co-heirs of himself, having enjoined upon them an eternal testament, so that possessing it with brevity and perfect readiness, they might receive an immortal inheritance according to the eternal and incorruptible promises. … His name, he says, is holy to the saints, but fearful to the unholy (Psalm 111:9; LXX 110:9c).
