For just as the fountain of holiness makes those participating in it become saints, so it is fearful to those who sin by bearing it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the redemption sent to his people is and why his name is holy and reverend.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Doing righteous things begins the good way, and the fear of God is the beginning and cause of wisdom.
comments.comment: As the doing of righteous things is the beginning of the good way (for this is the contemplation of truth) (Psalm 111:10; LXX 110:10), so the fear of God is the same beginning and introduction into the wisdom of God, which is called the same as the contemplation of truth, which to the practically righteous belongs. For as the doing of righteous things leads toward the good way, so this fear of God leads toward wisdom. The name 'beginning' can be here, not instead of an introduction, but as being a cause, since the fear of God is that which is called the cause and the beginning. And the struggle with this wisdom is understanding.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Goodness belongs to those who do it, and since the one praised is immortal, his understanding never ends.
comments.comment: Goodness is not for those who have merely thought about doing it, but for those who are actually doing it. For those who practice understanding, no benefit will be other than that of virtue, from whose benefit they learn the goodness of it. … Regarding all that has been theologized in the present Psalm, it is said that the end of it is that his understanding remains. For this is a fitting end for those who theologize: to say that his understanding (clearly of the one theologized about) remains forever. Since the one being praised is immortal, it is necessary that his understanding also be without end, as it lasts for all the ages.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the good understanding of those who do his commandments and the psalm's ending.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessed man does the good for its own sake, not for glory, punishment or reward, and his seed sown in good land bears fruit a hundredfold.
comments.comment: He who does not act for the sake of anything else, but through human glory, or to avoid falling into the punishment that entices sinners, or for reward, but by choosing and acting for the sake of the good itself—for such a one will truly be blessed (Psalm 112:1; LXX 111:1bc). The seed of the blessed man, who has the fear of the Lord, sows into the good land, his diligent and beautiful heart; it is possible for him to bring forth a hundredfold fruit (Psalm 112:2-3; LXX 111:2,3). For those sowing the seeds of evils sow into the flesh, which is their weak and earthly existence (and so they reap corruption from the flesh), but those sowing into the Spirit, the powerful seed, they sow and reap into eternal life. For each of the imperfect and sinful, the Word commands: Sow for yourselves into righteousness, reap for yourselves into the fruit of life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is truly blessed and what his seed is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who turns Jesus's words into works builds his house on the rock and fills it with the glory of truth and every knowledge.
comments.comment: He who has heard the words of Jesus and turned them into works builds his house upon the rock, laying down the foundations of his life, both in thought and action, upon the unshakable Word of God. Each one who fears the Lord has built such a house upon having willed to do what is in the commands of the Lord (that is, to have intensely willed the words of Jesus), filling it with the glory of the notions of truth and the wealth composed of every word, every knowledge, and every working good. Thus, the promise of his righteousness extends into the age of ages.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wealth and glory in the God-fearer's house are not of a sensible house but of the mind, adorned with every virtue.
comments.comment: And regarding the saying about 'the one fearing the Lord and desiring his commandments exceedingly' (Ps 112:3): 'wealth and glory in his house' is not spoken concerning a sensible house or glory; for many fearing God do not have either human glory or a wealthy house, like Elijah, like Elisha and those similar. Of the 'one being rich in good works' and 'in every word and in all knowledge' (1 Tim 6:18), as Paul writes, he is having wealth and glory in the house of the intellect and being adorned through all virtues in his way of life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the wealth in the house means, with Elijah and Elisha as examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Until' does not mean he is moved after his enemies are gone, just as Mary remained a virgin until she bore her son.
comments.comment: But do not think because it is said chronologically, 'Until he goes against his enemies, he is not shaken,' that what is shaken after the destruction of the enemies is not the same. For how could he be moved, the one who, having the enemies removed, did not suffer this while threatening and looming over them? For it is customary in the Scripture to use such a way in many places; for regarding Mary, the Gospel says she remained a virgin until she bore her firstborn son, and so on. Since it is proper to show that the birth of Jesus came from a virgin without marriage, it fittingly speaks this way where there was room for doubt: had the virgin perhaps undergone corruption? He also said 'she conceived'; to remove this doubt, he says she remained a virgin until the childbirth. For if she is said to have been a virgin until she gave birth, then she did not conceive by a man the child she brought forth while still a virgin. In the same sense God says, 'I am, I am, and until you grow old, I am' (Isa 46:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'until' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All the righteous say 'God is my horn.'
comments.comment: He says, 'God is my horn.' For all the righteous say this, being confident: 'In you we horn our enemies.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessed man's righteousness extends into the age to come, where his horn, the kingdom, will be exalted.
comments.comment: He says that the righteousness of the one being blessed is not quenched, nor does it stop at the present, but it extends further into the age to come. In that age his horn will be exalted in glory (Psalm 111 (112):9)—that is, the kingdom of which he will be deemed worthy when he obtains the saving promises (Ps 113:16). For Scripture customarily calls the kingdom a horn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the righteousness that endures and the horn exalted.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Wealth scattered as the Lord prescribes remains, and wealth guarded is lost.
comments.comment: Wealth, when scattered in the way the Lord prescribes, naturally remains; when held together, it is alienated. If you guard it, you do not have it; if you scatter it, you will not lose it. For he scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever (Psalm 112:9, LXX 111:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what dispersing and giving to the poor does for one's wealth.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The name of the Lord is to be praised in every rising and setting, for the sun of righteousness rose for Israel and for the believing nations.
comments.comment: … Perhaps also regarding the sun of righteousness, if it is in some rises according to which it rises. These have a relationship (or are themselves) to the rises in which paradise is planted. If they have a harmony in these rises, it is fitting to praise the name of the Lord according to the rises by which it rises and the settings. For he was able for Israel, but he rose for the believing nations. Since not with unwise and unjust judgment he was able to rise for those also, having received providence's judgments everywhere and all things from the Lord: Praise his name; the Lord is high above all nations, his glory is above the heavens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord is high above all nations as king, and, with a deeper mind, above all believing nations who praise him with a pure life.
comments.comment: And the words being taken more simply declare that as God of all things he provides, being high above all nations as a king, and having his glory in the heavens ruling also the rational ranks there. But with a deeper mind, the Lord is high above all believing nations, being praised by them with pure life, practical and contemplative life. And upon the heavens, which no longer bear the image of the swine but the heavenly, his glory reaches, just as he announces it to his own disciples: for the heavens declare the glory of God (Ps 19:1). For certainly some declare it. If you are able to say the glory of the Lord, the radiance of his glory, the Lord and our savior, you would follow what was said to the one being illuminated: And the glory of God has shone upon you (Isaiah 60:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Holy One is incomparable among created things, for no one is like him since he is alone.
comments.comment: And through the coming words, foreseeing the God of all, we learn, regarding how incomparably the Holy One is compared to all created things, he says: Who is like the Lord our God? (Psalm 113:5-9; LXX 112:5-9). For there is no one like him, since he is alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Saying 'Who is like our God?' of the Father does not exclude the Son, for the divinity of Father and Son is one.
comments.comment: He is both maker and provider of all things. These things he says, not separating the Son from the Father or the Father from the Son; for the divinity is one, and there is no other God besides the Son and no other the Father. In Isaiah, indeed, concerning the Father, it is said: 'In you is God, and there is no God besides you; for you are God, and we are not afraid' (Isaiah 45:14). For if there were another God in the Son who is beside him, how could he subsequently bring forth: 'And there is no God besides you?' and immediately: 'For you are God, and we are not afraid, the God of Israel is Savior'? Therefore, even concerning the Father, when it is said, 'Who is like our God, the Lord?' (Psalm 113:5), the Son has not been excluded; but even concerning the Savior, the Father has not been set apart from the one divinity of Father and Son.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God dwells on high and providentially looks down on all lowly creatures, on earth and in heaven.
comments.comment: Who says: 'Who is the Lord our God, the one dwelling in the heights and looking down upon the lowly things?' For all lowly creatures and works are toward God, not only those upon the earth but also those in the heavens. And he sees these lowly things providentially.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that he dwells on high and beholds the lowly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God from on high makes the poor rich and makes rulers of the submissive, and these changes exist for benefit.
comments.comment: He ascends also to the providence according to men, and this, while remaining in discussion concerning God of all things, is that He Himself from on high makes the poor rich from the needy, from the submissive makes rulers, from the sick makes rulers healthy, and also the reverse. It is evident that these things, both being actually so and being seen and understood, exist for benefit, according to that which was said by the Holy Spirit: 'The Lord establishes kings and removes them' (Daniel 2:21), and 'Through me kings reign' (Proverbs 8:15), and 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap' (Psalm 113:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God lifts the poor and needy from poverty, seats them with the rulers of his people, and so raised the Gentile people to sit with Israel's rulers.
comments.comment: For he sees the poor man cast down upon the earth and the needy man upon the refuse, and he raises them up from those standing in evils of want and poverty; and not merely to raise and make stand, but strengthening their goodness, seating them with rulers, preparing them to be equal to them. And he will seat them not with simple rulers, but with the rulers of his own people. … It can also be said concerning the people from among the Gentiles, for whom the prophecy is: 'For this the poor people shall bless you'. Therefore, having raised this poor and needy people from the lowly things and from the refuse of Greek customs, he will seat them with the rulers of Israel, being their people. And the apostles are the rulers of the Hebrew people, whom we say are sitting on twelve thrones to judge the twelve tribes of Israel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the poor raised from the dust are and who the princes are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The barren woman is the church from the Gentiles, now with more children than she who has a man, and every soul inhabited by God becomes a mother rejoicing in the Word's offspring.
comments.comment: And a woman, formerly dwelling in barrenness, will become a mother having borne many children. … And the church from among the Gentiles, formerly barren, is called into joy, saying: 'Rejoice, barren one who does not bear children; break forth and cry out, you who do not labor in childbirth; for many more are the children of the desert than of her who has a man' (Isa 54:1). For truly, the church from among the Gentiles has become very much with children, more than she who has a man. The law of the man is the assembly of the Jews. Every soul, through chastity, is inhabited by God as a child in the church of the living God, a mother working out thoughts and words to rejoice in the offspring produced by the Word of God dwelling within her. This also happened according to the history of the Scripture. For instance, Anna, the mother of Samuel, is called a mother inhabiting the church, a mother having become such from children, rejoicing in children. And concerning Sarah and Rebekah and Elizabeth, and before this mother, the one born to Samson, someone says wisely concerning each of them what inhabited her: a mother of children, rejoicing (Psalm 113:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the barren woman and joyful mother are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Barrenness is good when she gives up evil lovers and takes seed from God, becoming a many-child mother in the house of her husband.
comments.comment: When the succession of children is thus divided in two, it is a blessed thing to undergo barrenness, she who was giving birth destructively from the invisible evil lovers; for this barrenness is for the sake of good, as she takes up the seed from God, from which a generation of offsprings shall be saving, as the result of the bride having been blessed and having become a many-child dwelling in the house of the husband, concerning whom it is said thus in the Psalms: 'To her who dwells barren in the house, a mother of children rejoicing' (Psalm 113:9); and in another scripture, after barrenness, being a child and many-child is brought forth: 'A barren woman has borne seven' (1 Samuel 2:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Judah is confession and Israel is the mind seeing God, who after becoming God's sanctuary is perfected by the vision of truth and comes under his authority.
comments.comment: For Judah is confession, but Israel is the intellect seeing God. Previously, it was not fitting to confess, but now, since one has become a sanctuary of God, and His holy temple is being constructed, thus, having been perfected through the vision of the truth, Israel shall be shown to have come under the authority of God in order to be able to reign under Him, about to experience blessedness, seeing God with a pure heart (Psalm 114:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Judah and Israel stand for in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The leaping mountains are the holy powers rejoicing over Israel's salvation, a multitude turning from wickedness to virtue.
comments.comment: It is a custom in Scripture to call holy [powers] mountains such. Thus also David lifts up his soul, asking, 'From where will my help come?' (Psalm 121:1); and again: 'The mountains leap like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock' (Psalm 114:4) concerning the salvation of Israel. For if angels rejoice over one repenting, how much more over such a multitude traveling from wickedness to virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the skipping mountains and hills are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The nations mock 'Where is their God?' because their gods stand in places, but our God is in the heavens not by place but by majesty, outside all things and in them by providence.
comments.comment: 'Where is their God?' the mortals say, when You, Lord, are doing us good. For they have local gods established in places, and they mock You by this, saying, 'Where is their God?' Perhaps they say this mockingly, thinking we have no God. But even if those wandering say this, we do not hold the precise opinion that our God is in the heavens above, but we think of Him not locally, but with a superabundance of majesty. For if He were in a place, He would be prevented from being elsewhere. And there is also a cause for all the heavens and upon the earth, since whatever He willed, He made, surpassing all things. Therefore, He is not contained by all things, but is also outside all things and exists in them according to the logic of creation and providence. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mockery 'Where is their God?' and in what sense God is in the heavens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Creation alone comes into being by the will of God, but the Son is not a work of will: he is the exact imprint of God's hypostasis, and is himself the will of the Father.
comments.comment: But if all the heavens and those in them, the earth and all that is in it, should come into being as the essence of God's will, some are very impiously thinking and suddenly snatching away the substance of the Son, the will of the Father, making him a will of those in the heavens who are substantial. But let the impious hear how creation alone was subject to the will of God. For it is fitting for the Maker that he wills to create (God and James agree in writing: 'Having willed, he brought us forth,' Rom 8:28 as he says in the word of God, a word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his own creatures and works) that the will of God be the cause. But the Son is neither a creature nor a work; he is a generation not of essence, but of will. For if he were a son of will, he would be an image and a character of God's will; but the divine words say he is the exact imprint of his hypostasis and an image of the invisible God. If the Son is not the exact imprint of the hypostasis and an image of the invisible God, then it is fitting that the Only-begotten be a generation of the essence of the invisible God and of his hypostasis. For indeed, those being born by the word of truth, they are such; and the Word and the Truth himself is the Only-begotten of God. Since he is not brought forth by a word of truth, he himself is the will of the Father; for in the same way that wisdom and truth are, so also the will of God is. Indeed, it is the same in wisdom and in will to do all things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Worshippers of lifeless things justly become like them, which to them is no curse but something worth praying for.
comments.comment: But it is also just that those who worship lifeless things as something better and consider them divine should become like them. And this would not rightly appear to them as a curse, but as something worthy of prayer: to become gods, just as they suppose, and to possess what they admire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why those who trust in idols become like them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Israel, those who have the mind to see God, hopes in the Lord, the priest hopes in a greater Lord, and those who fear the Lord call on him as helper and defender.
comments.comment: All the perceptive race has the mind to see God (Israel signifies by chance the church of the living God) Ps 113:17 and hopes in the Lord, whereas all other men hope for nothing. And the one who is among those healing the divine, by chance being a priest, hopes in a greater Lord and in a hope witnessed by Israel; for of those who have ascended above by contemplation and practice, the hope is greater, asking more greatly to have him as a helper and a defender. But also all those fearing the Lord (these are not the proselytes and those added to the law from the Gentiles) hoping themselves in the Lord, call upon him to be a helper and a defender Ps 113:20-21.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God remembers those who remember him, turns toward what is blessed, and gives blessings in proportion to faith, so that the small receive them along with the great.
comments.comment: For God remembers all of those who have remembered him. … For the one forgetting the divine law immediately forgets also that which was given to him; but when a god remembers something blessed, he immediately turns toward it, giving spiritual and heavenly blessings according to the proportion of the greatness of faith, just as he gives the other gifts. Stand firm, for it is necessary for the small ones to receive blessings along with the great ones, among those alone fearing the Lord, and upon all the mentioned ranks, so that you may not differ in these things, where some are great and others small.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Beyond the visible heavens there is a heaven that is God's own, in which God alone is; it is not a place, and one must not think of it as a local heaven.
comments.comment:
Blessed are we by the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Psalm 115:15). … But he who wishes to contemplate these things more deeply will say that something is exceptionally said in the Scripture, a heaven characterized for God, in which God alone is; but I speak of God concerning the Trinity.

This heaven, far from being a place, is a property of essence for the created things, as these things are in the heavens. … No one has ascended into this heaven except the one descending from heaven, since having been sent from there, he has come, saying, 'I have descended from heaven.' But also the Holy Spirit was sent from this heaven, which Peter says: 'Truly it has been announced to us through those who evangelized us by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven' (1 Peter 1:12). … For the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are thus. But stand firm, lest you carry the thought concerning these things down to sensible things, supposing a local heaven and a movement occurring there by transport …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those deadened by sin do not praise God, nor does anyone in Hades confess him, but we who live and share eternal life praise him.
comments.comment:
None of those deadened by sin praises God (for a beautiful praise is not in the mouth of a sinner, Psalm 115:17), nor do those descending into the tropical [figurative] Hades become those who die the death following sin (for there is no one remembering God in death, Psalm 6:5), nor anyone in Hades confessing himself.

Therefore, since they do not praise Him, we who live and partake of eternal life praise Him, concerning which the Savior says, 'And this is the eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and whom you sent, Jesus Christ' (John 17:3).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason the dead do not praise and the living do.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord protects those who are childlike until the time of struggle, and when he sets one against a struggle he humbles that one and then saves him with strength and armor.
comments.comment: The Lord himself protects those who, according to the commandment of Jesus, are childlike in turning and becoming, so that enemies do not attack them before the time of struggle. Just as He protects those who are such children, He humbled me, having set me against a struggle, as if I had ascended far above the age of children, and instead of being tested by many strong things, He made me; and just as He humbled me, so also He saved me, having clothed me with a strength surpassing the struggle and an invincible panoply.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Lord keeps the simple and helps those brought low.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Words about God must be led by faith and not by demonstration, as first principles are accepted unexamined in every discipline, and the speaker believes in the land of the living and therefore speaks of it.
comments.comment:
I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was humbled exceedingly; but I said in my ecstasy, “Every man is a liar.” Let faith lead the words about God—faith, and not demonstration. … For the first principles of every discipline must necessarily be unexamined by those who learn them; otherwise it is impossible for those who dispute about the first things to advance by method and order to the end. … So then, the mystery of theology also seeks assent from unexamined faith. For one must believe, it says, that God exists—not investigate, nor dispute what he is (Hebrews 11:6). …

Now the psalm in hand seems to me to have a sequence of thought that follows the thought of the preceding psalm. For there he said, “I will be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 114:9 LXX; Psalm 116:9 Hebrew). Since, then, he speaks about a land not seen, as one who knows it clearly, he gives the reason for his determination about things unseen, saying: “I believed that there is a land of the living; therefore I spoke, that I will be pleasing to the Lord in it” (Psalm 115:1 LXX; Psalm 116:10 Hebrew).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why faith comes before speech, in terms any reader can follow.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: A soul that speaks without faith babbles in vain, and faith is made perfect by humility, so that the one who measures God by his own mind cannot say 'I believed, therefore I spoke.'
comments.comment: In general, a soul that comes to speech without faith will babble in vain, driving its words forward with nothing beneath them. The beginning of rational discourse, then, is faith firmly established in the heart of the speaker. Next, he goes on to show how it is possible for us to accomplish faith perfectly, saying: “I was humbled greatly.” For the one who has not humbled his own mind, who does not say in imitation of the Apostle, “Brothers, I do not consider that I have yet laid hold of it” (Philippians 3:13), but instead pondering the comprehension of God’s essence, measuring out what cannot be reached with his own reasoning, and reckoning God to be only as great as his reasoning has encompassed—in short, the one who makes his own mind the measure of all things, not reckoning that it is easier to measure out the whole sea with a small cup than for the human mind to grasp the unutterable majesty of God—such a person is puffed up in vain and lifted up by the emptiness of his own mind. He cannot say, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” because he cannot add what follows: “I was humbled greatly.” For he lives with conceit and boastfulness, and exults in empty words, because he does not possess the strength that comes from faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'I was humbled greatly' follows 'I believed, therefore I spoke.'
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Belief comes first and speech follows, and the one who has believed and spoken great things is greatly humbled by seeing the greater one above himself, as John was before Jesus.
comments.comment:
Regarding this word, the Apostle says to the Corinthians, 'Having this, we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed, therefore I spoke; and we also believe, therefore we also speak' (2 Cor 4:13). … 'I believed, therefore I spoke' is in accord with the heart, for it is believed in the heart unto righteousness, but with the mouth it is confessed unto salvation; for he says, 'If you confess the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom 10:9). For by this one is immediately brought to the heart, for it is believed in the heart unto righteousness, and the following. You will also receive this understanding, and 'If you do not believe, you will not understand' (Isaiah 7:9); for first one believes, if he understands, and after this he speaks, as the Psalm says, 'I believed, therefore I spoke.' When, having believed, I spoke exceedingly and great things, then, seeing nothing of myself, I was greatly humbled. Such is that which is said by John concerning Jesus.

Regarding the saying, 'That He must increase and I must decrease,' John was not diminishing in terms of actual magnitude, but was comparing himself to the superiority of Jesus's teaching and way of life (John 3:30). He who said, after speaking from the beginning, that he had believed, 'I have become exceedingly humbled,' did not suffer this by a subtraction of honor, but by seeing the greater and above himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who is not helped by faith but speaks from his own resources is a liar, and the Psalmist spoke this in an ecstasy, either of amazement at finding no truth in men or of the pretended madness before Achish.
comments.comment: Then he does not humble himself alone, but with himself all humanity that is akin to him and shares his nature. “I said in my ecstasy,” he says, “Every man is a liar” (Psalm 115:2 LXX; Psalm 116:11 Hebrew). So the one who is not helped by faith, but comes to speech from his own resources, trusting in human preparations for grasping the truth, is a liar, falling far short of the truth. And he says he spoke this word in ecstasy. What is the ecstasy? Either that, after looking around at human nature and searching carefully whether there is any truth among human beings, he could find it nowhere without help from God, and being struck with amazement at the strangeness of the matter, he cried out, “Every man is a liar.” Or it was in that ecstasy which he feigned before Achish, pretending epilepsy and derangement, when he saw that he had come to the necessity of lying about himself and inventing things that were not, in order to escape the danger from the enemies—then he said, “Every man is a liar.” Even if not by choice, nor for the harm of neighbors, still in every case he took refuge in lying because of some circumstantial causes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'ecstasy' of this verse may be and why every man is called a liar.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Sophistical arguers say that if every man is a liar and David is a man, then David lied, and so he cannot be believed whatever he declares.
comments.comment: The Prophet does not, however, fall into his own trap, as some of the sophistical arguers try to refute him, saying that the Prophet has fallen into the refutation by reversal. For if every man is a liar, and David is also a man, then clearly he too was a liar. And if he was a liar, he must not be believed in what he declares. But if this statement is not true, and not every man is a liar, then we will release David from the charge of lying. And if he does not lie, let us believe him in what he declares; but by believing him, we will again be driven around into the necessity of disbelieving. So if David speaks truth, he dissolves his own statement, since he is a man and does not lie. But if he lies, he has from that very fact the reason not to be believed—for who will pay attention to a liar? So since he once declared that every man is a liar, let David lie in order to confirm his statement; or if he himself speaks truth, he has destroyed his own declaration.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The saying does not hold for the one who has risen above the passions of the flesh and become like a god through virtue; it is a warning to those still mixed with the flesh by their passions.
comments.comment:
But these are the games of people who jest and delight in the twists of words at the expense of the inexperienced. The truth is not like that. For those are called men who are still held by human passions. But the one who has already risen above the passions of the flesh, and through the perfection of his mind has passed over to the state of the angels—when he speaks about human things, he clearly exempts himself from the rest. For the one who said, “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High; but you die like men’” (Psalm 82:6-7, LXX 81:6-7), is truthful. “You are gods.” And certainly if to anyone else, this title is fitting also for David. For he too is a son of the Most High, made akin to God through virtue, and he does not die like a man, but having God living within himself.

“I said in my ecstasy,” he says, “‘Every man is a liar’” (Psalm 116:11, LXX 115:2). Let those hear this who are mixed together with the flesh through their passions, yet exalt their own minds above the things beyond the world. Let it be the common aim of all who lay claim to piety to tear down their reasonings and the height of their heart that is lifted up against God.
comments.selected_reason: Answers the puzzle of how David can say every man is a liar.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Man is empty and false, moving in an image of life, not truth.
comments.comment: For man is empty and a falsehood in his being and non-being, because even when he seems to be, he is not, but he moves about in an image of life rather than in truth (Psalm 116:11).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The saying 'every man is a liar' was spoken by one who was a god and not merely a man, for if a man were thus a liar, 'every man' would no longer be true.
comments.comment:
Similar to this is also 'I said in my ecstasy: every man is a liar' (Psalm 116:11); for he was a god, as we have demonstrated, the one saying these things. For if a man were not thus, if he were a liar, then 'every man' would no longer be true.

Not a liar, but speaking the truth, yet he is not a man himself, who is called a man through excellence beyond human measure, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy, are you not men, as these also walk?' (1 Corinthians 3:3). For their malice was not practiced by them by chance, but with care and deliberation; for this reveals what is in the heart (Luke 6:45). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In answer to what he can give back to the Lord, he offers his whole life, taking the cup of salvation as the contest for piety even to death and paying his vows before all the people.
comments.comment:
“What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given back to me? I will take the cup of salvation” (Psalm 116:12-13, LXX 115:3-4). Coming to awareness of the countless gifts from God—that he was brought from non-being into being; that, formed from the earth, he was honored with reason, in which he is also able to bear the image of the heavenly one; and then, looking also to the plan for the human race, that the Lord gave himself as a ransom for us all—he is at a loss, and searches among all that he possesses for what worthy gift he might find for the Master.

“What then,” he says, “shall I give back to the Lord?” Not sacrifices, not whole burnt offerings, not the service of the legal worship, but my whole life itself. And for this reason, he says, “I will take the cup of salvation,” meaning the suffering in the contests for the sake of piety, the standing against sin even to death. And this would be what the Savior himself taught in the Gospels: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); and again to the disciples, “Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). He was indicating the death he accepted for the salvation of the world.

For this reason, he says, “I will take the cup of salvation”—that is, thirsting, I come to the perfection through martyrdom, counting not as pains the tortures brought on in the contests for piety, but as rest for soul and body. “I will offer myself,” he says, “as a sacrifice and offering to the Lord, since I consider all things too small for the worth of my benefactor. And these promises I am ready to pay before all the people, who are my witnesses. For I will pay my vows in the presence of all his people” (Psalm 116:14, LXX 115:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the cup of salvation' and 'what shall I give back' mean.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The cup of salvation in the Psalms is the martyr's death, which is why it is followed by 'Precious before the Lord is the death of his holy ones.'
comments.comment: 'What shall I render to the Lord for all he rendered to me? The cup of salvation I will take, and call on the Lord's name.' The 'cup of salvation' in the Psalms is the martyr's death — which is why 'I will take the cup of salvation' is followed by 'Precious before the Lord is the death of his holy ones.' Precious then comes death to us, God's holy ones — not the common, as it were idle death of godliness, but a choice one: through Christianity and godliness and holiness. 'Can ye drink the cup that I drink, or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?' (Mark 10:38) And elsewhere: 'I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!' (Luke 12:50) Consider whether the baptism after martyrdom, as the Savior's cleansing came to be for the world, itself comes to be for many unto healing. For as those who served the Mosaic altar were deemed to minister forgiveness of sins through blood of goats and bulls, so the souls of the beheaded for Jesus' testimony, not idly attending the heavenly altar, minister to prayers forgiveness of sins. And as Jesus Christ the High Priest offered himself a sacrifice, so the priests whose High Priest he is offer themselves a sacrifice — seen by their own place at the altar. But of priests, the blameless offering blameless sacrifices healed the Divine; those stained with blemishes, which Moses recorded in Leviticus, were fenced from the altar. Who is the blameless priest offering a blameless victim but he who holds the confession and fills every number the martyrdom-word requires (Psalm 116:12–15)?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who die with Christ will receive and bravely drink the cup of a saving death.
comments.comment: …those who die with Christ and carry His death in the flesh, and who recognized how well to give thanks, will receive the cup of such a saving death, and he who receives it will drink it blamelessly, if he calls upon the name of the Lord to drink it bravely.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Psalmist calls the sacrifice of praise a cup of salvation.
comments.comment: So, very much in keeping with the law, the inspired David too, striking up the spiritual lyre, says: ‘I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord’ (Psalm 116:13), and so expressly calls the sacrifice of praise a cup of salvation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The hearers are exhorted not to be terrified by death, for it is not corruption but the starting point of life and a passage to honor.
comments.comment: Then comes an exhortation to the hearers not to be terrified by death. “Precious before the Lord,” he says, “is the death of his holy ones” (Psalm 116:15, LXX 115:6). Do not shrink from the good contest, you people, and do not be cowardly before death. For it is not corruption, but the starting point of life; it is not utter destruction, but a passage to honor.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The death of the holy ones is precious because a soul purified and crowned stands before the Judge in radiance, while human birth comes through dishonor, so one should not lament their departure.
comments.comment:
Among people who love wealth, certain little stones that gleam with bright colors have by nature come to be called precious. But truly precious before the Lord is the death of his holy ones. When a soul purified in its life, free from the defilements of the flesh, having no spot or wrinkle, glorified by the contests for the sake of piety, and having bound on the crown of righteousness, outshining all these things by the beauty of virtue, stands before the Master and Judge of all things, possessing a radiance from grace more brilliant than any costly stone—how is the death of such a person not precious before the Lord?

Let us not, then, lament the departures from this world of holy men, but rather their births and their entrances into this life. For the entrance into this world comes through the dishonor of filth and stench, things whose very sight not even one of those presiding over our life could easily endure. For through such things the passage of fleshly birth has been ordained by the necessity of nature. But the departure and release from here is precious and glorious—not for all people, but for those who have passed through this life in holiness and righteousness. Precious, then, is the death; not precious is the birth of human beings. For it is sown, he says, in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption (1 Corinthians 15:43). Compare, then, death with birth, and stop lamenting for the one who is being released from dishonor.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the death of the holy is called precious.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Under the old law corpses were abominable, but the remains of those who die for Christ are precious, so one should not prefer the corruptible life to the incorruptible.
comments.comment:
When they died in the Jewish manner, the corpses were abominable. When death is for Christ's sake, the remains of his holy ones are precious. Before this, it was said to the priests and the Nazirites: “You shall not be defiled by any dead person,” and, “If anyone touches a corpse, he shall be unclean until evening,” and, “He shall wash his garments” (Leviticus 21:1; Numbers 19:11, 19). But now the one who touches the bones of a martyr receives a certain share of sanctification from the grace that attends the body. Precious, then, before the Lord is the death of his holy ones (Psalm 116:15 [LXX 115:15]).

Do not prefer the most dishonorable things to the most valuable, and do not become bad traders, preferring the corruptible life to the incorruptible and blessed state. For apart from the sufferings of dishonor to which most lovers of pleasure are subject, the needs of life also bend down the soul's greatness and, as it were, enslave it, dragging it down into the service of the flesh. And where there is slavery, there clearly is also dishonor. We must therefore flee the life to which dishonor is naturally attached.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The precious death is that of the holy ones who die to the world and live to God, like a sacred offering.
comments.comment: And perhaps our godly David sings of something like this when he says: ‘Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.’ (Psalm 116:15) For the death of the holy ones will be like a sacred offering to God; and surely I do not mean the death of all who live in the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The speaker is the Lord's servant by nature and the son of his handmaid, and since the Lord loosed his bonds, he will offer not animals or incense but his own glorification of God from the altar of his own mind.
comments.comment: “I am doing nothing great,” he says, “in giving myself back to you, the Master. For since I am your servant, I bring to you your own possession. For what has been created is altogether the servant of the Creator. So I am a servant not only by choice, but also by nature. For I am the son of your handmaid, whom the enemy led away when she was an infant and a mere child, and, separating her from your service, made her a slave of sin. But I turn back and run again to the Master from the beginning, and I acknowledge my ancient servitude. You have broken my bonds (Psalm 116:16 [LXX 115:16]). Since you freed me from the bonds of sin, descending into Hades and releasing humanity, which was a prisoner of death and held in the inescapable prisons of Hades, for this reason I will sacrifice to you—not four-footed animals with divided hooves and chewing the cud, nor clean birds, nor fine flour mixed with oil, nor transparent frankincense, nor that incense of compound spices (for these are offered to you, the Master, from the earth). But what is my own possession and the offspring of my own heart—your glorification—I will offer up from it, as from an altar of my own mind.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'son of your handmaid' and why the sacrifice offered is praise.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Release from the bonds of Hades is needed so that we may be ministers in the heavenly church.
comments.comment: There is need of release from the bonds of Hades, so that the God of the living and not of the dead may be our God, and we may be his ministers in the heavenly church, to which we return as we flee the bonds of death (Psalm 116:16-19).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sacrifice of praise is better than ten thousand burnt offerings, a confession from the heart open to all, to be paid publicly before all the people and not in a hidden corner.
comments.comment: And I will offer to you the sacrifice of praise, more honorable to you than ten thousand whole burnt offerings—to you, the self-sufficient and perfect God, who do not demand bodily sacrifices, in which the wealthy have the advantage, but rather the confession that comes from a sincere disposition and heart, which is equally available to all who desire it. “I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people” (Psalm 115:8 LXX; Psalm 116:14 Hebrew). When I offer you praise, I will not do it secretly, in some hidden corner, as if ashamed and fleeing the reproaches of the ungodly. No, I will perform a public sacrifice, taking the whole people as partners in the worship. And the place appointed for our sacrifice will be the very center and most conspicuous parts of Jerusalem.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sacrifice of praise is public and available to every worshipper.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Vows must be paid in the midst of Jerusalem, which is the Church of God, because even under the old worship only one altar was appointed.
comments.comment: Listen, you who abandon the Church and gather in ordinary houses, you wretched fragments torn from the precious body: vows must be paid in the midst of Jerusalem—that is, in the Church of God. For even under the old worship, no one was permitted to set up a private altar; one altar alone was appointed for those who chose to sacrifice. But you raise up an altar against the altar of the fathers, and you kindle alien fire upon it, not even being corrected by the ancient example. You draw in people whose minds are corrupted, and you defile yourself along with them. May you flee from imitating those people, you people of the Lord, and do not be separated from the portion of those who are being saved. Remain in the faith, being perfected in the commandments of the Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: After the shadow ended, God's mercy reached all nations, and the truth of the Lord, being eternal, remains forever.
comments.comment: The word concerning salvation is not complete unless the memory of the saved is also taken up. For having said in that psalm as the end of the shadow approaching, 'I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving' (Psalm 116:17), he immediately calls all nations into eternity, just as these also offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving through the ages, after one nation and people has been cast away, since a sinful nation and people having become full of sins is tossed about. But after this nation and people has been cast away, the mercy of God has reached all, as a certain and strong thing for His mercy to become upon us. And because this has surpassed, 'The truth of the Lord remains forever' (Ps 117:2). … For the truth accepted the shadow as an end and a lot, limiting it, but the truth itself, being eternal, will receive nothing that is nothing above it, but itself above all, in an incomparable excess. For indeed, as with a cause, He has given that the remaining truth remains forever.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Truth shone on the human race and calls all nations and peoples to thank the Father, whose mercy and truth remain.
comments.comment: Truth is spoken of in the Savior and in the psalm where God sent His mercy and His truth and rescued my soul from the midst of troubles (Psalm 57:3). Thus truth and the hope of the nations are one; therefore, having shone upon the human race, it calls all the nations and all the peoples, teaching them to give thanks to the Father who strengthens His mercy and makes His truth remain unto the age.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the call to all nations and the lasting truth and mercy of this psalm fit together.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is good and wills the repentance of sinners, and his mercy is inseparable from him and found by all who have experienced his goodness, from the beginning until now.
comments.comment: Since God is good and wills the repentance of the sinner rather than his death, you who are responsible for sin, by performing confession through repentance upon him, you will have him forgiving those for whom you confess. For His mercy is found inseparable from Him unto the age, since it is always so; in His mercy, not only now but also formerly from the beginning, all those having experience of His goodness confess to Him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why thanks and confession are due to God for his lasting mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A righteous man in affliction does not ask to be outside it but to bear it bravely, like an athlete who asks the trainer to help him through the contest rather than end it.
comments.comment: A righteous man having become in affliction does not so much entreat to be outside of it, but how to bravely and cheerfully bear it (Psalm 118:5-9; LXX 117:5-9). For indeed the one being distressed in the stadium against opponents does not wish the contest to pass by him, lest he become exhausted, but entreats the trainer to cooperate with him, so that, enduring the things brought by the adversary with hope of victory and crown, the things through which the crown is awarded may seem gentle to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist asks of God when he calls on him in distress.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words about not fearing man may be said of mortal enemies, and 'I also shall see my enemies' of invisible ones, though the devil too is called a man.
comments.comment: And it is possible to say different things concerning mortals, 'I shall not fear what man shall do to me' (Psalm 118:6; LXX 117:6), but concerning invisible enemies, 'I also shall see my enemies' (Psalm 118:7; LXX 117:7); for some enemies are even the men who rise up against us, waging war against us and setting themselves against us lethally. And if 'I shall not fear what man shall do to me' is also referred to the devil, on account of 'An enemy, a man, did this' (Matt 13:28)—for it is clear that he did the sowing of the tares—and 'But you are man and not God: visit' (Ezek 28:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He hopes as one who will obtain help, and neither Israel nor the church from the nations feared the plots of men, for those who took courage in God conquered their adversaries.
comments.comment: He takes courage as one who has been heard, and he hopes as one who will obtain help. He is strengthened by hope so as not to fear the plots of men, nor to marvel at their powers, but to foresee their fall. These things long ago concerned Israel when the other nations pressed upon it—the word is spoken hyperbolically—and after these things they concerned the church from the nations, warred upon by the uprisings of the unfaithful. For those who had believed in each nation endured the disturbances and dangers from those who did not believe, but nevertheless both these and those, having taken courage in God, conquered their adversaries (Psalm 118:7-9; LXX 117:7-9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Trusting in the Lord is simply and properly good, not merely better than trusting in man, who is easily corrupted, double-minded and may harm the one who trusts in him.
comments.comment:
'It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man' (Psalm 118:8; LXX 117:8), and the following: it is not that trusting and hoping in the Lord is good only when compared with trusting in man and hoping in rulers. For this is simply and properly good.

But to trust and hope in man and ruler is not good; rather, such instruction is brought to those who are eager to trust in man and hope in a ruler, that they may learn to trust in the ever-abiding and strong and almighty God, and not in mortal man, easily corrupted.

And sometimes he is also double-minded in intention; for instead of helping, sometimes he will also greatly harm the one who trusts in him; therefore blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord, remaining unashamed, according to 'In you, Lord, I hoped; let me not be ashamed unto the age' (Psalm 31:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense it is 'better' to trust in the Lord than in man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who fight God's servants rely on human power, but those of Christ resist visible and invisible enemies by the Lord's name alone.
comments.comment: Those who make war on those who serve God are lifted up by human power and human authorities, but those who have chosen the worship of God are encouraged by God's help and find it stronger than every strength. And most conspicuously, those of Christ defend themselves against both visible and invisible enemies through the name of the Lord alone (Psalm 118:10-11; LXX 117:10-11).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The promise that all the nations surrounded one man is impossible unless said hyperbolically, so it can be understood of evil spirits and sophistic reasonings, which the one armed with God's name overthrows.
comments.comment:
If it is not said hyperbolically, what is promised is impossible; for how did all the nations surround one man dwelling in Judea, warring as they surrounded him, and he defended himself against them in the name of the Lord?

For it becomes weapon and shield and fortress to the one who wears it.

But consider whether it is not possible to understand the things set before us similarly to the 'In the mornings I slew all the sinners of the earth' (Psalm 101:8; LXX 100:8), by the serious man being surrounded by evil spirits suggesting the titillations of the flesh and the other passions with all the works of the flesh, and moreover godless words refuting with sophistic cleverness the doctrines of the truth.

But the well-strung and strong one, armed with the appellation of God, shall overthrow all the nations, turning them to flight, and sometimes even destroying them.

For the one who instead of weapon and sword used the name of God shall cut off the passionate impulses along with the troubled reasonings …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how 'all nations compassed me about' can be understood and what the name of the Lord does.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bees that surround him are false doctrines, while the true bee is the Church that honors the wisdom of God, and those who surround the wise one were burned like fire in thorns and he cast down their reasonings.
comments.comment:
They have surrounded me like bees surround wax, and the following: the genus of wax-makers is similar to bees; for although they are greater than bees in size, they do not deceive the unreasoning ones as bees do; nor do they make honey or mold wax, nor do they have a sting to repel those attempting to harm the wax. But eating the honey from the opposite, they wage war against the bees, just as those having used their own sting to safely destroy the wax-makers as having defiled their fruit.

The honey-making and wax-molding bee is not an allegory, but the Church which has honored the wisdom of God, whose labors, though not of a precious or glorious kind, are offered by kings and laymen for health; even though she is weak in strength, her preaching is not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but she possesses the sting in the demonstration of the spirit and power of God, having the word of faith, just as she destroys heresies like wax-makers, dividing them by the reproof of the truth. And one is the bee that has honored the wisdom, but many are those that depart from honoring the wisdom of God—not bees, but those who are like bees; he is not sinning, saying they are wax-makers surrounding like wax to consume the honey and having been burned like fire in thorns. For those from the heresies and the fire of shameful things and desires escape, as Paul says, 'For what is shameful to speak of is made known by them' (Ephesians 5:12). And the Gospel interpreted the thorns as pleasures.

However, even if they surrounded the wise one like wax, bees, and were burned like fire in thorns, they did not defend themselves by the name of the Lord alone. For he did not only remain undefiled, but he also cast down all their sophistical reasoning, and every high thing boasting itself against the knowledge of God, since his works are not fleshly but are powerful in God, not being defeated by the approach of God. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord becomes salvation for us in relation to us and not in his own being, for he is eternal, and to us he has become wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption.
comments.comment:
The Lord becoming salvation does not receive a beginning of being; for he is both eternal and everlasting. …

Regarding those being saved, God submits to the mind these things said by the one declaring that all things have become Christ; for it has not become that God is Word, not truth, not wisdom, not Son, but he has become to us wisdom, not merely having become wisdom, but this himself to us is righteousness and sanctification and redemption. For the reference to these things having become to us simply and eternally is said according to the relation toward us; thus God has made him both Christ and Lord, Christ meaning king and priest to those who reign and to those for whom he offers the sacrifices, but also to those who wish to serve him as Lord, and in general, the things said concerning him are not thought to be impieties.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dwellings of the righteous are the eternal dwellings of the promised good things, where there will be a voice of joy and confession, with sorrow and sighing fleeing away.
comments.comment: You will understand the dwellings of the righteous, which are alone with the Father according to the fulfillment of the promises, concerning which the Savior says: 'When Mammon departs' (meaning that), 'they will receive you into the eternal dwellings' (Luke 16:9). In these dwellings all the righteous are rejoicing; for they have attained the promised good things. Thus it is well said, 'A voice of joy and confession in the dwellings of the righteous' (Psalm 118:15; LXX 117:15b), with sorrow and sighing fleeing away. And if you say that even the bodies of the righteous, their dwellings, will be returned to them incorruptible and spiritual, you will not dispute that in these dwellings of theirs there will also be a voice of joy and confession. A voice of joy and salvation is brought forward, as the righteous rejoice in the aforementioned dwellings having received the eternal salvation, not different from eternal life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'dwellings of the righteous' are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The right hand of the Lord makes the one who shares in him strong, and he lifts him up so that he does not die the evil death but lives to recount the Lord's works.
comments.comment: He has thus made power for those partaking of him, as it is possible to say, 'I can do all things in Christ who strengthens me' (Phil 4:13). He thus lifts up and exalts the one partaking, as one having been strengthened by the right hand of the Lord more brightly and more greatly, and to say a second time, 'The right hand of the Lord made power' (Psalm 118:16; LXX 117:16). Therefore he says, 'I shall no longer die, he who follows the evil death, but I shall live' (Ps 118:17), partaking of the life opposite the evil death, in order to recount the wonderful works of God that have become in me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who is educated by the Lord's discipline does not fall into the death that holds those who sin, for that death meets the uneducated.
comments.comment: Understand this (Psalm 118:18; LXX 117:18-20): he who is being educated by divine discipline and most profitably by the Lord does not fall into the death that holds those who sin. For death encounters those who are uneducated, but he who is being educated by the Lord, having excellent thought and practice, is not handed over to the death that receives those handed over to the passions of dishonor and unproven mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the Lord can chasten without giving over to death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gates of righteousness are the individual virtues, which one enters and passes through by confessing what has been done, and beyond them another gate, of the truth, is reached by those who have perfected righteousness.
comments.comment: When the name of righteousness is being accused against every moral virtue, its gates—the private virtues—must be spoken of, into which those who are through asceticism and care for them enter, knocking at them. And they enter upon confessing those things which they have done outwardly, being of the gates of righteousness. He says 'into them' and not 'through them'; for one must not bypass the activities of the virtues, but must travel through them. But having entered into the gates of righteousness and having confessed within them, another gate is shown to be superior and more honorable, the one according to the theory of the truth, into which those having perfected righteousness enter, so as to be called righteous as a nickname from it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The gates were formerly the law and the prophets, but now the gate is faith, and those who walk the good ways of the saints find cleansing for their souls.
comments.comment: The gates were formerly the law and the prophets through which Israel entered toward God (Psalm 118:19-20; LXX 117:19-20), but now the gate is faith, through which we are more closely brought near, being testified to by the law and the prophets. Into this understanding one should take also that which is said in Jeremiah: 'Stand in the paths and ask for the ancient well-trodden ways of the Lord, and examine what is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find cleansing for your souls.' For if someone stands here in the many paths—I mean the private virtues—he will examine those worn down from eternity by the saints, in order to know who, after this, according to the theory, is the good way; he who walks finds cleansing for his soul, having cleansed it through obedience to the truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the gates are that the psalmist asks to have opened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'gates of righteousness' are the gates of virtue, which open readily to anyone who pursues the deeds of virtue.
comments.comment: And it is not unlikely that “gates that open of their own accord” was said by some who were hinting at and expounding the words: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may go in through them and give thanks to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall go in through it” (Psalm 118:19–20). … “gates of righteousness” is the same as “the gates of virtue”; and these open readily to anyone who pursues the deeds of virtue. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the gates of righteousness are, in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He will praise God at once for hearing him and bringing salvation.
comments.comment: I will praise you immediately having opened to me the gates of righteousness, and I thank you that you heard me and received the petition and provided salvation (Psalm 118:21; LXX 117:21).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Church of Jews and Greeks makes one corner of two walls, one built from the Jews and one from the Gentiles, with Christ as its head.
comments.comment:
For how did the two walls not join and complete one single corner: the one being built from the Jews coming to the gospel, and the other from the Gentiles who believed? For when the Church of both Jews and Greeks was gathered, Christ having become its head, He completed one corner, with all those joined to one building in one faith, all people from the two peoples being created into one new man Eph 2:15.

This stone, thus announced as the cornerstone, chosen, precious, which God placed in the foundations of Zion, no longer to be shamed by any sin, having become pure for everyone believing upon it. Those coming to the immortal living Word, living themselves, are being built up as hidden stones, so that a spiritual house may be composed and an intelligible altar, upon which the sacrifice of praise is offered and all things being like it are spiritual.

May we also, living, become holy stones, rolling upon the earth of God, so that, having been built up on the foundation of the apostles and prophets of Christ Jesus Eph 2:20, we may be completed as a temple and a spiritual house, so that God may dwell in us. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the corner of two walls means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David marveled at the corner, the meeting of the two peoples in one, which saves those within it but crushes those who remain outside.
comments.comment: Blessed David marveled at this corner (Matthew 21:42) — that is, the meeting of the two peoples into one — saying, “This was from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Psalm 118:22–23) So the stone is saving for the corner made by him, but crushing and ruin for those who remained outside this intelligible and spiritual concurrence. For some, Christ is “a rock of stumbling and a stone of scandal.” (1 Peter 2:8)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The day the Lord has made is the day under the sun of righteousness, in which those lit by the true light rejoice as sons of light and truth.
comments.comment: For every day of sensation occurring under the sun, the sun may rise over the earth; the day shown under the sun of righteousness being the Lord was constructed, which they also, showing to one another, being illumined by the true light, say: 'This is the day which the Lord has made' (Psalm 118:24; LXX 117:24); hence let us rejoice and be glad in it, as walking becomingly in the day; for we are no longer of night and darkness but sons of light and truth, having the faith of Abraham who rejoiced to see the day of the Lord (John 8:56), and rejoiced at having seen it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the day which the Lord has made' is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who has a conception of God asks to be saved and to prosper, since God saves and directs a man's steps.
comments.comment:
The one who has a conception of God takes forethought for all things from him, and demands both to be saved and to prosper; for God is a God of saving, and by him the steps of a man are directed (Psalm 37:23; LXX 36:23).

Hence also in the first psalm the one being blessed prospers in all things whatsoever he does (Ps 1:3), using God as guide of the way leading to blessedness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who came before him came as servants of the Lord, but this one who comes in the Lord's name is blessed, and the prophets who announced him say they bless him from the house of the Lord, from the Father's bosom.
comments.comment:
'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Psalm 118:26; LXX 117:26). And the Evangelists took this voice to be a prophecy concerning Christ; for he is truly the one who comes authoritatively and in the name of the Lord. …

Though all the men before him together with angels came as servants of the Lord—indeed each said 'Thus says the Lord,' and each of the angels says to the one to whom he comes, 'The Lord sent me'—yet this one who comes in the name of the Lord is blessed.

Hence each of those who announced his sojourn beforehand says: 'We have blessed you from the house of the Lord' (Psalm 118:26; LXX 117:26).

For the one coming is from the house of the Lord, from the Father's bosom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'he that cometh in the name of the LORD' is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's coming is an appearing and not a change of place, for the invisible one took the form of a servant and was seen, and he always comes and sojourns with men without being moved.
comments.comment:
For it is added immediately: 'God is the Lord, and he has appeared to us' (Psalm 118:27; LXX 117:27). For his coming is not to change place but to appear, previously unseen.

For existing invisible by being the image of the invisible God (Col 1:15), having taken the form of a servant (Phil 2:7) and become the Word flesh (John 1:14), he was seen, that thus manifested he might lead by this contemplation unto also beholding his glory, 'glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth' (John 1:14).

For those who have completed this initiation say: 'Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer' (2 Cor 5:16).

And it is well said 'the one coming,' but not 'the one who came'; for he always comes and sojourns with the race of men, even if not through flesh; not moved nor changing place himself—for he is unchangeable and unalterable, filling heaven and earth with divine presence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'he has appeared to us' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm hymns the manifestation of the Lord, who ruled over us for life and over his adversaries for punishment.
comments.comment: He clearly hymns the manifestation of the Lord, through which salvation is restored to all, calling him God according to the Father's name and Lord according to the Son's name, because the Lord is God and God is Lord. And having appeared as Lord, he ruled over us for life, according to the words, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living (Romans 14:9), and over his adversaries for punishment, according to the abolition of every authority and power (1 Corinthians 15:24) (Ps 117:27a; Ps 117:27bc).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The command to keep a feast up to the horns of the altar shows those who present themselves as a living sacrifice, a multitude filling the altar up to the angels.
comments.comment: He commands the establishment of a feast through a multitude of sacrifices placed on the altar, up to its horns and its other projections. But as the word advances to our sacrifices, it reveals those who, according to the type of Christ, present themselves as a living sacrifice, a sacrifice truly pleasing to God (Psalm 118:27). Their multitude fills the altar up to the highest height that is joined to the heavenly angels, through the same power that both holds up the heavenly things on high and lifts up the things on earth in the manner of an altar, receiving those who approach God (Psalm 118:27).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'horns of the altar' as a living sacrifice.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To do what is necessary and think the truth is to keep a feast up to the horns of the spiritual altar, especially for those who have cast off oldness and become a new planting.
comments.comment:
In these things, not finding them, establish a feast extending until the horns of the spiritual altar, from which, having taken a coal with tongs, the other of the seraphim is sent to the prophet to cleanse him and to take away his iniquities and his sins. But to whom is it commanded to establish a feast—the teachers and priests? Perhaps you will even say to the angels. But to do what is necessary and to think the truth is a feast established according to the guidance of God. This has especially much room among those who have cast off oldness in order to become a new planting.

And since the Passover is fulfilled in the month of the new moons, it is possible to conceive that anyone passing from wickedness and the sensible things to virtue and the intelligible things, being renewed, prunes, so as to celebrate and to bring forward spiritual sacrifices, as those showing the altar to be royal by its horns. And if these things were said concerning our feast of the weeks, they would not be lacking truth (Psalm 118:27).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who thanks God for his many blessings says that God is his God, exalts him, and exhorts others to confess to the Lord who is good and whose mercy lasts forever.
comments.comment: He who is thanking God through the Psalm for having made such great and so many blessings proclaims: 'You are my God, and I will confess to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you' (Psalm 118:28). Glorifying, theologizing you, I say: 'You have done wonderful things in me; for having exalted me and having made strength, so that I might not die but living, I might recount your works.' And second, I will confess that you heard my petitions and became my salvation. Having learned through experience your great mercy and your goodness, and exhorting others, I say to many, proclaiming: 'Confess to the Lord, what is good, what has mercy extending into the age, according to how he shows mercy by his much goodness' (Psalm 118:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist closes with praise and a call to give thanks.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Blamelessness here means doing what lay in one's power, since God does not demand the impossible but supplies what is lacking through Christ.
comments.comment: These were those who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, but chose the law and the journey in it. He does not say that blameless means entirely free from falling into blemishes and sins. For that was reserved for Christ and for those who share in Christ through him. But for those others, blamelessness was judged in what was within their power, by pardon from God and not by exactness concerning the commandments. For God does not demand what is not possible, but he legislates to expose what is lacking, and he concedes what is weak, since he knows it, and provides salvation through the participation in Christ, the powerful God, which was then still to come. So blamelessness befits us who live according to Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'blameless' means in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The blessing belongs to those who actually go on the way, seeking God through good works and right understanding, not to those who hear the teaching and then stumble.
comments.comment: Blessed then are those searching out his testimonies and seeking him with all their heart, turning away from all human haste and approaching him through good works and right understanding. But the blessing is not for those who have gone away, but for those who are going; even though those working lawlessness in his law have not gone, it is evident that they have never attempted to test the divine law as if it were among them; for whoever sins lawlessly, lawlessly he shall perish. Nor are they those who have never heard the divine teaching; for those who, after being initiated into this, stumble, are said to have sinned against the law and to be transgressors of it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Stumbling-blocks stand in the way of virtue, so the psalmist asks God to take them away and prepare the road.
comments.comment: Since there were very many oppositions to virtue, like stumbling-blocks on a road, he asks for their removal (Psalm 119:5; LXX 118:5). For in this way a road is prepared when the hindrances are taken away, according to the words, Cast the stumbling-blocks out of the way of my people (Isaiah 57:14). For example, for the divine David a stumbling-block was the woman and the untimely encounter with the sight; for another it was food seen for pleasure, as for Esau; for another it was glory, as for Saul; for another it was a possession, as for Ahab (Psalm 119:6; LXX 118:6). Against all these things there is need of God, who prepares the way, so that he may cast these things off and preserve the love of what is good, drawing off the more violent impulses of the will and, as it were, drying them up because of the inclination of nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer that his ways be directed, with examples a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those joined to the Spirit and not turned to the flesh will not be ashamed.
comments.comment: But for us who look to the divine Spirit, there will be no shame, when we see ourselves joined to him everywhere and in no way shifted toward the flesh, nor brought down by a fall from on high.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
