comments.capsule: One who keeps all the commandments, not one only, will not be ashamed, and though left a little while to be tested, he asks not to be forsaken utterly.
comments.comment: Then I shall not be ashamed in keeping all your commandments; not on one thing, but on all (Psalm 119:6; LXX 118:6). For according to those commandments I do not look, I shall be ashamed (Psalm 119:8; LXX 118:8b). For I am often abandoned for a little while for the sake of testing and my trial, having bravely endured circumstances to be benefited. But immediately, with your helping, having run the race, I shall be crowned; therefore, so that I may not be defeated by those striving mightily, do not leave me exceedingly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks for understanding and promises to keep the statutes, fearing the ignorance that leads even zealous people astray.
comments.comment:
He asks for understanding, he says, and promises that it will not be without fruit. For I will not only learn, he says, but I will also keep your statutes (Psalm 118:7-8, 119:7-8) (Psalm 119:8).

Aquila says, “Do not let me go astray in ignorance.” Using his desire for the law, he fears the lack of understanding that turns many people’s zeal to the opposite. Even in what they think they are doing rightly, they have stumbled, as Solomon says: “There is a way that seems right to people, but its end goes down to the bottom of Hades” (Proverbs 14:12).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's words hidden in the heart shape the mind and purpose, so that one is without sin before the God who sees the hidden.
comments.comment:
He who does not receive the words of God from above and hides them in his heart, so that having made his mind and purpose according to these, is without sin before God who sees the hidden, not only not committing adultery but not even reaching for the shameful thing (Psalm 119:11; LXX 118:11).

The Son also agrees with what is set forth: if, having received the word of my commandment, you hide it with yourself, your intellect will obey wisdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Understanding comes from divine illumination, not from memory alone.
comments.comment: For understanding does not come immediately from memory but from divine illumination. The statutes are the things that can make righteous (Psalm 118:12, 119:12).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a short, clear reason for asking God to teach.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks for the blessed life so that, living by it, he may keep God's words, since whoever remembers the commandments also keeps them.
comments.comment: So that I may not be glorified for nothing having had your judgments performed, repay me the divine and blessed life, so that living according to it I may keep your words; for after remembering them, to keep them following (Psalm 119:17; LXX 118:17). To this end you will take that which was said by Jesus: 'He who holds my commandments and keeps them' (John 14:21/21); for he who remembers them also keeps them, doing them as well. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only through the Holy Spirit can one see the depth beneath the wording of the law, which is why David prayed to have his eyes unveiled.
comments.comment: There is no other way to see the depth beneath the spare wording of the law except through the Holy Spirit alone; for it is the Spirit who searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). By “the depths of God” we say is meant the knowledge stored up like treasure in the sacred writings. That is why the inspired David made his prayers to God, saying, “Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive Your wonders out of Your law” (Psalm 119:18). And the Savior Himself regarded with no small admiration the one who rises from knowledge of the law to spiritual knowledge, that is, the knowledge of the gospel. For He said, “Therefore I tell you that every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52). The old are the things in the law; the new are the things in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist asks for when he asks God to open his eyes.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet would not have prayed to have his eyes uncovered if the law held no hidden meanings.
comments.comment: Moreover, if the law of Moses had contained nothing written in it to be made known through hidden meanings, the prophet would not have said to God in his prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). But as it is, he knew that a “veil” of ignorance lies upon the heart of those who read but do not understand what is said figuratively (2 Corinthians 3:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Pride, the mother of lawlessness, makes people refuse God's commands, and God will rebuke them for it.
comments.comment: Pride is the mother of lawlessness. Because of it they refuse to obey God’s commands, like the disobedient people who say, “We shall not be mastered, and we will not come to you any longer.” He says this to show his own eagerness before God for obedience to the commandments. Because God understands them to be guilty, he will rebuke those who are disobedient and unsubmissive through pride (Psalm 118:21, 119:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the proud are and why they are rebuked.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The reproach is removed when those who once reproached him come to know the truth and themselves seek God's testimonies.
comments.comment: Since some reproach and belittle me for seeking your testimonies (Psalm 119:22; LXX 118:22), you have removed the reproach and the belittling from me. How could these be removed? For the coming knowledge of the truth of those formerly reproaching and belittling me; and if this exists, they themselves will seek your testimonies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dishonor to fear is shame before God, and the one devoted to the Scriptures is not turned from them even when great and proud people mock him.
comments.comment: He prays to escape true dishonor in the sight of God, which the Lord shows to be most fearful, saying that those who put him to shame will be put to shame (Psalm 119:22; LXX 118:22). Showing the opposite of this, this man of the law says here that though he is mocked by great and proud people, he does not turn away from the study of the sacred oracles and from correction by them (Psalm 119:23; LXX 118:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what true shame is and how the psalmist stands when mocked.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist brings his soul down to the ground in humility, and asking God for the good life, not claiming it as his own power, is itself a mark of that humility.
comments.comment: What he himself says is a sacrifice to God—a broken and humbled heart—he now says he has fulfilled by bringing his soul down as if to the ground and humbling himself willingly (Psalm 119:25). About the unwilling humiliation he says, “Our soul was humbled to the dust; our belly clung to the earth” (Psalm 43:26 (44:25)). So having brought himself forward as humbled as is fitting, he seeks from God as recompense a lawful way of life and life according to God’s word. And this very thing is also a mark of humility: not to place the good life in one’s own power but to seek it from God (Psalm 118:25, 119:25).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my soul cleaveth unto the dust' as humility.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist declared in diligent practice the ways of virtue that lead to God, and God heard him.
comments.comment: Another scripture says, 'I have declared your ways' (Psalm 119:26; LXX 118:26), meaning: the ways that lead to you are not other ways of virtues, O Lord; I have declared them practically with diligent intention and in appropriate works, and you heard me; therefore, toward those who obey I say, 'Teach me your statutes' (Psalm 119:26).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Doing all things in God's sight, he asks for revelation, and by speaking of divine righteousness he will also help others.
comments.comment: It is a great thing to do everything as in the sight of God, and to say these things and recount them, and to ask for revelation about them that corrects or confirms (Psalm 119:26-27; LXX 118:26-27). And he will also gain benefit for others by speaking from more divine understanding and proclaiming the wonderful kindness of God that is stored up for those who act in holiness. For the one who teaches about righteousness also teaches about its end, which is stored up for it—something wonderful and unexpected, because God rewards greatly and beyond what is deserved. Paul also spoke about self-control and righteousness and the coming judgment, so that the governor became afraid (Acts 24:25). Instead of “I will meditate,” Aquila says “I will converse,” and Symmachus says “I will explain” (Psalm 118:26-27, 119:26-27).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Having turned from ignorance and come to the law by faith, a person asks the teacher to turn ignorance away and show mercy by his knowledge.
comments.comment: He who will turn away from the way of unrighteousness and approaching the law of God wants to be perfected and established toward God, who brings the ends of good things (Psalm 119:29; LXX 118:29). For as one having hated ignorance has had a longing for the opposing knowledge, so one who has turned himself from ignorance and approached by faith asks the teacher: 'Turn ignorance away from me and have mercy on me by your knowledge.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer to be rid of the way of lying.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the heart leans toward evil from youth, God must move it toward righteous commands.
comments.comment: Since the human heart lies intently upon evil from youth, God is needed to move it toward righteous commands—that is, to lead our faculty of choice by dispensations and deeds, and by the illumination of the divine Spirit (Psalm 118:36, 119:36).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks God to incline his heart.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Vanity is the mind's disordered contemplation of things that do not exist, and turning from it lets a person live in God's way, which is life.
comments.comment: Vanity is the madness about sights, the contemplation of things that do not even exist, and also the disordered imagination in the mind. Paul clarifies this when he says, “In the vanity of their mind, being darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God” (Ephesians 4:17-18). See how it is called vanity of mind when someone has a mind and does not use it for the contemplation of realities, but hands it over to Satan who binds it. So praying for this he says, “Turn away my eyes from seeing vanities” (Psalm 118:37, 119:37). For this is the grace of God. In this way, having turned away from such contemplation, he will be able to live in the way of God, walking in it and being made alive by it. For the way is at the same time life. Therefore the Savior says, “I am the way and the life” (John 14:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'vanity' means and what the prayer gains.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: For those taken out of worldly life it is perilous even to look back, so the psalmist pleads for his eyes to be turned from vanity, the empty delight of temporary things.
comments.comment: For it is wholly hard to choose to be sick again with the things from which one would go out; so that for those once taken out by the power of God from a worldly way of life, it is very perilous even only to look toward it, and as it were to go toward a remembrance of faults, sending the mind into the love of them. And so the divine Singer pleaded, saying: 'Turn away my eyes from seeing vanity.' (Psalm 119:37) For vanity in truth is the distraction of this life, and the empty delight of the temporary things, from which that we should stand apart and to leave, and for the one who has chosen in truth to walk straight to refuse even the mere looking as still in thoughts and with pleasure, one may learn easily from here too.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The psalmist is not conscious of sin but fears a suspected reproach, trusting that God's judgments are full of kindness.
comments.comment: The voice is not one who is conscious of sin, but of one suspecting, as in 'From my secret things cleanse me' (Psalm 19:12). But I am confident in what you will remove, the suspected reproach, being convinced of what your judgments are, being full of kindness and love for mankind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever wants to live in the Son, God's righteousness, speaks this verse.
comments.comment: And since the Son is the righteousness of the Father, the one who wishes to live in the Son says this: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in him from faith to faith” (Romans 1:17) (Psalm 118:40, 119:40).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: We must seek the Lord's mercy and salvation, and so answer those who reproached us as lacking them.
comments.comment: … he [the Word] himself is both mercy and salvation of the Lord (Psalm 119:41-42; LXX 118:41-42). Therefore, it is necessary for us to seek the mercy of the Lord, the salvation according to his mercy. … We answer those who previously reproached us as lacking the mercy and salvation of God (Psalm 119:41).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks for an interpretation of the truth so that he can answer those who wander, and the law once kept as a shadow is kept for the good things to come, forever.
comments.comment:
I ask for insights, not merely such words; even if I sometimes fall into difficulties regarding providence and similar matters, I do not wish to give an answer that merely resolves the contradictions of those who wander, but rather, since you have opened my mouth with your own goodness, give me an interpretation of the truth through your word, so that the word of truth may not be entirely torn from my mouth, but that I may be able to speak somewhat regarding the unanswerable ones, saying: 'I have erred concerning your judgments, your examined and tested words; how do you judge and provide for men?' (Psalm 119:43).

Do not let the word of truth depart vehemently from my mouth. For indeed, keeping your law will not only happen in this age but unto the age, the words of Jesus not passing away. We therefore keep God's law according to the image of things, previously kept by the Jews according to a shadow, to be kept for us according to the future good things unto the age of ages (Psalm 119:44).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The promise of true life is the only thing that can comfort us in afflictions.
comments.comment: He says that the only thing sufficient to comfort us in afflictions is to have the promise of true life. Bring this to completion for us. For if we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all people, because we are afflicted now and have no hope of the life to come (Psalm 118:50, 119:50; 1 Corinthians 15:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what comforts the psalmist in affliction.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist grieves for those who sin against the law, since the members of one body suffer together and it is fitting to mourn sinning brothers.
comments.comment:
Regarding the heterodox who boast against the law by slandering it (Psalm 119:53; LXX 118:53), I was intensely occupied with its keeping, and how much I was shaken in my assent to it, not enduring the slander.

Since of the sinners some sin lawlessly, not even attempting the beginning of laws, and others transgress it while in law, discouragement seized me from the sinners who abandon God's law; for if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it. And it is fitting to be grieved for our brothers who sin, what kind of people they are, and not to be divided against this holy one (Psalm 119:53).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist is horrified at those who forsake the law.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lawlessness horrifies the godly, who foresee punishment.
comments.comment: To the sinner, godliness is a ridiculous character; but to the godly person, lawlessness is horrifying, because he foresees the terror of punishment (Psalm 119:53; LXX 118:53).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist's only comfort and gladness are God's judgments and commandments sung in melody, like a stranger's longing for home.
comments.comment: “To me,” he says, “the only comfort is to look at your judgments, and my gladness is your commandments taken up in song and leading to joy through melody” (Psalm 119:54; LXX 118:54). And I considered this the only good, as in a foreign and alien dwelling that can have no true good, because for the stranger the things at home are longed for, and before the return to them everything is painful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'songs in the house of my pilgrimage'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The ropes are evil thoughts and powers, and the righteous man who bears patiently what sinners do to him, or stays sober against their deceptive words, does not forget God's law.
comments.comment: And what are the ropes, namely the evil thoughts and the evil powers that subvert these, which they undertake to cast down the standing against God? But the zeal of those surrounding the righteous with ropes is unceasing, those who with rapid zeal remember the law. The same circumstances occurring to the righteous through the sinners can also be ropes for them; but the righteous, bearing these patiently, does not forget the law of God. And those who entangle ropes into sin through deceptive words; but if one remains sober, he does not forget the law of God (Psalm 119:61).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's kindness comes to those who serve him and stand in faith, and the added 'According to your word' shows that it comes with reason, not by chance.
comments.comment:
If there is not kindness and severity concerning God according to the apostle, the kindness becomes for those standing in faith, but the severity for those having fallen away from it. Since the saint was confirmed in faith, 'Kindness, O God, you have done with your servant,' he says; but he says, wanting to present not as occurring by lot with someone the kindness of God, but with the one serving him, whoever this may be.

And the added 'According to your word' (Psalm 119:65; LXX 118:65) signifies that the Lord's kindness comes to someone with reason and rational cause.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Instruction is the ethical virtue and knowledge the intellectual virtue, and the psalmist, having believed the commandments, asks God to teach him both.
comments.comment:
Therefore also, wishing to know the rational and wise aspect of it, he deems no other worthy to become his teacher concerning it, that with it he may also learn instruction and knowledge—calling instruction the ethical, and knowledge the intellectual virtue.

And in Proverbs the 'Take instruction and not silver, and knowledge above tested gold' (Prov 8:10-11) is to be referred to practical and theoretical benefit. … Since rightly and wisely approaching your commandments I believed them so as to keep them, stretch out wisdom to me, having taught me kindness and instruction and knowledge.

In agreement with these is the 'If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant her to you' (Sir 6:37).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'good judgment and knowledge' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Affliction comes either for sin or for testing, so having accepted humiliation for his transgression, the psalmist asks to be taught by God alone, looking to God's kindness and not his own worthiness.
comments.comment:
For even if the manner of bringing such things is twofold—for to some through sin, to others for testing and manifestation they are brought—giving himself the lesser of these, he said he had transgressed.

But nevertheless, he says, I kept your word, that just as having transgressed I was humbled, so having accomplished and kept your word I may be released from humiliation. … Not looking to my worthiness (for I transgressed) but to your kindness, since being kind you have kindness, I deem it worthy to be taught by no other than yourself your ordinances.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist was afflicted and what he asks.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though deceivers slandered the commandments, the psalmist searched them out with his whole heart, so that seeing their beauty he might condemn the slanderers.
comments.comment:
With many deceivers despairing against your commandments and saying myriads of things seemingly for their slander and overthrow, much injustice has come upon me.

But even if the things they said seemed terrible, able to turn away the uninstructed from them, yet I, intensifying my zeal and desire for them, searched them out with my whole heart, so that having beheld their beauty from the much and intense searching of them, I might utterly condemn those who slander them.

And one oppressed and wronged by certain proud and powerful men in the affairs of life might also say these things; for 'from your commandments,' he says, 'I shall be able to learn that it is more worthless to wrong and deprive than to be wronged and deprived.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the psalmist answers the lie told against him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those given the guileless milk of instruction did not digest it, so it curdled in them, while the psalmist, meditating on the law, sought to understand it.
comments.comment:
For since, having been given to drink the rational and guileless milk by the instructors, they did not digest nor concoct it, curdled and hardened in them, their heart was curdled.

But even if those suffered this by themselves, I, having your law through meditation, was eager to understand it, with the understanding of it loosing not only the mist but also the thickness of the material disposition.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the fat, curdled heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law of God's mouth is better than thousands of gold and silver, which stand for the word and the mind found in worldly philosophers.
comments.comment: Regarding the mediator, the prophet says to him that the law of the divine mouth is good above all the pleasures of the world, which he showed through thousands of gold and silver. For contemplation, it must be said that silver stands for the word, and gold stands for the mind; for many thousands of such silver and gold are found in those who philosophize about the things of the world and heresies. Above all these things, the law of the mouth of God is good to the lover of the wisdom and truth of God, for those who attend to it alone receive the proper benefit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, and the law of God's mouth is better than gold and silver.
comments.comment:
'Your mouth's law is more precious to me than ten thousands of gold and silver' (Psalm 119:72), and 'Take instruction and do not forsake knowledge, which is tested above silver' (Prov 8:10); for wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, and every precious thing is not of equal value to it. Therefore it is also said to companions concerning it to Job: 'The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equaled to it' (Job 28:19).

But these things are not said by comparison, but with respect to men's choice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law is worth more than gold and silver.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not shape a human being like a craftsman but completes him by his power, so the request is for the understanding that makes his commandments known.
comments.comment: God does not fashion a human being in the manner of a modeler, even though he is said to fashion, but such as a modeler would produce, he completes by the power that works such a shaping. And the present fashionings must be referred back to that first fashioning, as in “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5) (Psalm 119:73; LXX 118:73). So also Job says, “You fashioned me as clay” (Job 10:9), indicating the clay-fashioning in Adam upon himself. The request in the making is a thanksgiving, very fittingly the request for the intellectual power that makes the commandments understood. About this Paul also says, “Think about what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding in everything” (2 Timothy 2:7). The request is fitting as addressed to the Creator, as if to say: Care for your own workmanship, and perfect the living being that is intellectual by understanding. And what you prepared for your own kinship, make your own through your knowledge of your wishes. Since from the beginning the human being needed a command, by which his mind was set without need of many commands, and indeed having fallen away from that one, he needs more commands to fill the greater lack.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'thy hands have made me and fashioned me' means and why understanding is asked.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The God-fearing rejoice at others' progress, as heaven does at penitents.
comments.comment: Therefore they [those who fear God] desire all to progress and to have benefit, and they rejoice over those things pleasing to God, imitating those in heaven who rejoice over the benefit of the penitents.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Without many hardships a person cannot be firmly fixed in virtue, so the psalmist praises God's confirming providence and asks for rest from labors.
comments.comment: For without training in many evils and the help of God that comes beyond hope, a person cannot be firmly fixed in virtue. For those without contest are easily shaken when a struggle comes. Therefore, having recognized in himself the firmness that comes from many hardships, he hymns the confirming providence of God. Then he asks for rest from labors, saying, “Let your mercy come to comfort me, according to your word to your servant” (Psalm 119:76).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist accepts affliction as right.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The soul that longs for God's salvation and continues in hope becomes one with his word, for 'soul' names a relation to the body rather than its essence.
comments.comment: 'My soul fails for the salvation of God, but the end of faith shall bring salvation'; for there remains no soul, setting aside the state through which the soul used to exist, but desiring the salvation of God and continuing in hope, the spirit and mind becoming one with his word. For the name of the soul does not declare its essence, but the relationship toward the communion of the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's word is spiritual dew cooling the flame of the passions.
comments.comment: The word of God is a spiritual dew (Psalm 119:83; LXX 118:83a), since dew and rain are often called; it cools my unbridled flame from passions and makes my flesh weak, as to bear the death of Jesus in it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Under affliction the righteous may seem like dead wineskins, yet the psalmist did not leave the God-taught righteousness, as Joseph kept his self-control.
comments.comment: Perhaps the righteous become dead rather than living under their afflictions, so as to resemble wineskins rather than human beings, losing their breath like settling frost, but choosing what is warm and active, as he says elsewhere, “They set me in dark places like the dead of the age” (Psalm 142 (143):3) (Psalm 119:83). But even in such things, he says, I did not stand away from the God-taught righteousness, just as Joseph guarded his righteous self-control.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Many try to interpret Scripture, but few have God's grace for it, since a word cannot be strong and saving in an unlawful soul.
comments.comment: Many attempt to interpret the divine writings of the Church and those outside it, both heretics and Jews and Samaritans (Psalm 119:85; LXX 118:85), but not all speak well; for rare is the one possessing the grace from God for this, speaking of many things promised, but living not well and unlawfully. If they say anything, it is wandering and babbling; for a word cannot be vigorous, strong, and salutary in an unlawful soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Commandments' here means God's promises, which he trusts.
comments.comment: He calls promises commandments. Trusting, he says, in your promises and their truth, I seek help from you, my God (Psalm 119:86; LXX 118:86).
comments.selected_reason: Explains a word in the verse.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To live according to the word of God is to live with piety, not simply this sensory life, and one who has this life will guard God's testimonies.
comments.comment: Those pursuing righteousness and the teaching of Christ will healthily speak the aforementioned word (Psalm 119:87; LXX 118:87a), and all the prophets also. And to be accomplished is in the earth, not the common dying, but that which was called into the material existence as earth, to come to an end in order to be done according to it. To live according to the word of God is to live with piety (Psalm 119:88; LXX 118:88), not simply this sensory life. For having obtained this, he will be in well-being, as to guard the testimonies of the mouth of God testified and demonstrated by the word of God, which are in His mouth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He asks for the present life, not as an end but so that, having survived, he may keep God's commandments and obtain eternal life.
comments.comment: He asks not to be handed over to the hands of those plotting against him unto death, asking for life—not yet the life eternal but the present one (Psalm 119:88; LXX 118:88). He does not ask for this as an end, but as something that will contribute to a good end, because, he says, having survived, I will keep the commandments of God, through which it is possible to obtain the life eternal (Psalm 119:93; LXX 118:93).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks to be quickened.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The day keeps its regular course by God's ordinance.
comments.comment: The day remains by Your ordinance (Psalm 119:91; LXX 118:91a), as to circle regularly and uniformly according to the annual cycles, the day not deviating, never having toward night an ordinance of inequality or inequality. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous alone live, even if they seem to die, because righteousness is the life in them, while the unjust, lacking it, are like things moved from outside.
comments.comment: “I will follow your laws,” he says. “For I will have life in them, just as you have said to me: ‘The person who does them will live in them’ (Leviticus 18:5).” Therefore the righteous person alone lives, even if he seems to have died, and the unjust are dead even if they appear to live. For the former have the constitution of life in themselves, namely righteousness, while the latter, not having this, resemble lifeless things moved not by themselves but from outside, because their vital principle is outside, and they have not one life in themselves. Therefore the Lord, being himself the righteousness that truly is, declares himself to be the life, and says that those who do not share in him do not have life in themselves. And the death of the Savior is not only life, but also life-giving for human beings, becoming the release from death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to have life in God's precepts.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist surpassed even his teachers through intense practice.
comments.comment: All good things in a person come through practice, and so he was extended along with the intensity of his practice, so that through it he surpassed the elder, the young man, and the disciple—surpassing his teachers.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whoever turns from every wicked way restrains his feet to keep God's words.
comments.comment: Turn away from evil and do good; for he who turns away from evil from every wicked way restrains his feet, so that having done good, he may guard the words of God (Psalm 119:101).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The law is a lamp for those walking in the night before the sun of righteousness rises, and to swear is to hold something unchangeably without transgression.
comments.comment:
The law is a lamp to those walking in the night before the rising of the sun of righteousness (Psalm 119:105); just as the night has passed and the day has approached, they are illuminated not by a lamp but by the sun of the true light, so that it is possible to walk decorously during the day.

And to set it here and to define firmly signifies to stand fast, and to swear is not merely to name God, but to set this thing unchangeably and to guard it without transgression, performing the work of an oath by power (Psalm 119:106).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lamp image and the oath in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Humble, he asks the salvation God promised to those who love him.
comments.comment: Presenting himself as humble and obedient, he asks for the salvation that comes from this, from God who gives grace to the humble and has promised mercy to those who love him (Psalm 119:107; LXX 118:107).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Staying in the law amid dangers and plots, without being drawn into anger or revenge, proves zeal, as David did not avenge himself on Saul.
comments.comment: It is a greater proof of eagerness to pass through dangers and not stand away from the law, and to be in the midst of plots and not be dragged away from righteous things by anger and irritation toward those plotting against him (Psalm 119:109-110; LXX 118:109-110). Thus Saul’s plot did not lead David astray into avenging himself, even where that might have seemed fitting.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the psalmist's steadfastness shows, with David as example.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He takes the law as his lasting inheritance, living in it gladly, not under compulsion.
comments.comment: He intensified the demonstration of his zeal for the law when he said he had set the law as his own inheritance, choosing to live in it not for a time but forever, not as under a yoke of necessity but holily in gladness of soul. For what is done with gladness is lasting and hard to overturn.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'taken as an heritage for ever'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The greatest proof of loving the law is hating those who have turned aside from it, as God is said to hate those who work lawlessness.
comments.comment: Even if they are not hateful insofar as they are human, it is not unworthy of God that such people are said to be hateful to God, according to the words: “You hated all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 5:6 (5:5)) (Psalm 119:113; LXX 118:113). So the greatest proof of loving the law is hating those who have turned aside from the law. For this reason Jehoshaphat’s friendship with such a person became a reproach through the prophet, because he loved the one hated by God (2 Chronicles 19:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The apostate from God's ordinances is made worthless by God, like grape-pressings or dross, so the psalmist is stirred to love the divine commands.
comments.comment: He shows an imitation of God. If every apostate from the ordinances is made worthless by God for his vain thoughts, then to him also they appear no more valuable than grape-pressings or dross. Therefore he is stirred up to love of the divine commands, taking the vanity of the wicked as an encouragement to care for what is good.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Asking God to be surety is asking him to fill what is lacking, as a guarantor steadies debtors.
comments.comment: He longs for what is lacking to be filled up by God’s forbearance, since God waits for the good work that is still to come, as if guaranteeing that it will be fulfilled—just as those who guarantee debtors do so to keep them from falling badly into deceptions (Psalm 119:122; LXX 118:122).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what asking God to be 'surety' means, with the alternative renderings.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist who has learned God's ordinances and spends time with them always seeks more, so that knowledge of the testimonies keeps rising through progress.
comments.comment:
Not as if, not having attained the petition, he approaches it again, but as having learned the ordinances of God according to a prior worthiness; as one who is spending time with them, desiring to contemplate them more greatly, he needs and always does this, so that he may reach the goal of their understanding (Psalm 119:125; LXX 118:125).

Since, however, regarding the learning of the ordinances, various things are becoming different, I will say this also concerning the knowledge of the testimonies: that through progress, their knowledge is always becoming ascended for the one spending time with their comprehension (Psalm 119:125).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He values God's commandments above the gold and gems that others admire.
comments.comment: Others, he says, admire gold and precious stones, but I, knowing the divine commandments to be the only wonderful and beautiful thing, hold to them and guard them more than any treasure (Psalm 119:129).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist loves the commandments above gold.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ makes the words of the law and the prophets manifest by fulfilling the prophecies and uncovering the law as spiritual, not letter and shadow, and so enlightens the nations.
comments.comment: He [Christ] who has come to fulfill the law and all the prophets, making manifest the words contained in them (Psalm 119:130; LXX 118:130), does this by fulfilling the prophecies, and does this by uncovering the law, so that it is seen no longer as letter and shadow but as spiritual. For thus the manifestation of the divine words that has occurred will prove the prophet intelligent, and will enlighten those called after Israel from the nations, babes, because late and at last they received the birth from faith.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the entrance of God's words gives light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The oracles must be opened, as the Lord opened the disciples' minds, which drives away deception.
comments.comment: The oracles need to be opened. Therefore the Lord opened the mind of the disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and the understanding given through the words drives away the deception that comes through pleasure or glory (Psalm 119:130; LXX 118:130).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: David's prayer to be delivered from the slander of men calls the demons men, because of their rational nature.
comments.comment: And blessed David also prays, saying: ‘Deliver me from the slander of men’ (Ps 119:134) — calling the demons ‘men’ as well, because of the rational element of their nature. But the Savior also, in the Gospels, called ‘an enemy, a man’ the one who sowed among us the tares of evil (Matt 13:28).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Sound teaching is hard amid troubles.
comments.comment: He asks for this because precision about sound teaching is difficult amid disturbances and griefs (Psalm 119:134; LXX 118:134).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks to see the shining of the Savior's face, since seeing him is seeing the Father, and learning God's ordinances means walking in them by grace.
comments.comment: He is worthy to see and learn the shining forth of the Savior this time, saying to the Savior about it, 'Let your face shine, so that whoever seeing you may see you' (Psalm 119:135; LXX 118:135). For he himself says about himself, 'He who has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). For since this exists, he says, it will be possible for me to learn your ordinances. And to learn that is to walk in them, not according to the flesh but according to grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer 'make thy face to shine' and what learning the statutes means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's judgment is upright because he is just, and his commandments, old and new alike, are truth and righteousness.
comments.comment: Therefore your judgment is straight, because you are just, judging all those who received your judgments straight according to the canons of righteousness, since I commanded truth and righteousness intensely (Psalm 119:137-138; LXX 118:137). For I commanded your divine writings to men, not only the new ones but also the old ones, being just according to ethics and truth, that is, being precise according to the view of things according to which I commanded us to make judgments, so that we might judge the great and the small, judging a just judgment intensely, they are truth and righteousness (Psalm 119:138; LXX 118:138).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous are enemies of injustice and forgetfulness.
comments.comment: See the enmity that the righteous have (Psalm 119:139; LXX 118:139). This was enmity toward their injustice and their forgetfulness of the law.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: One burning in spirit for God's word is amazed in heart when Jesus makes the Scriptures clear, as the Emmaus disciples said their hearts burned.
comments.comment: Therefore that word so ignited is made to him intensely loved by something, making him a servant of God burning in the spirit (Psalm 119:140; LXX 118:140). Such a person, when the Scriptures are made clear by Jesus, is amazed in heart, as saying according to the Road to Emmaus, 'Did not our heart burn within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?' (Luke 24:32).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, youngest and despised among Jesse's sons, received the kingdom because he had not forgotten God's ordinances, and so may the despised learner and the nations called after Israel.
comments.comment: According to the history, the words can be referred to David speaking about himself. For he was the youngest of all the sons of Jesse, and also despised. When all his brothers were taken by their father to the feast that Samuel had prepared, David was with his father’s sheep and was not taken to the banquet. Yet although he was younger and despised, he himself received the kingdom by God’s decision, since he had not forgotten the ordinances of God. The one who is being instructed in the divine words is also younger and despised because he humbles himself. And the people called from the nations after the elder and firstborn Israel could also speak this verse.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who 'small and despised' can be, with David as the example.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He is despised for remembering God's ordinances.
comments.comment: For those from circumcision despise him [the people called from the nations], because with unforgetting memory he keeps the ordinances of God (Psalm 118:162 [119:162]).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is the unchanging source of righteousness, and his word is truth forever.
comments.comment: For he is unswerving and unchangeable, never having or not having righteousness, being the source and generator of it (Psalm 119:142; LXX 118:142); and his word is truth, being truth to those hearing for all eternity, not being such a human word; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God's righteousness and law are called everlasting and true.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's testimonies are lasting, useful righteousness, justifying all who draw near.
comments.comment: I have given you testimonies not for a short time, but they prove to be useful righteousness for eternity, justifying the one who possesses them by drawing near to them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unseasonable time is the night of this present age, and one who meditates on God's commandments there is lifted toward the true light, no longer in the night but in midday.
comments.comment: First, in an unseasonable time—that is, what is called night in this present age, often called day as if for the coming age, according to 'The night has passed, and the day is near' (Romans 13:12)—but the perceptive powers of his eyes, acting as eyes, reach forward toward the righteousness coming from the rising of the sun. Therefore, having been enlightened and finding himself in the light, he meditates on the commandments of God, which cause him to fly to be lifted up and to approach the true light nakedly, so that he may find himself no longer in an unseasonable time, but in a peak and midday light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All God's ways are truth because they lead to Christ, who is the way, the truth and the life.
comments.comment: Another scripture says: 'And all your ways are truth' (Psalm 119:151; LXX 118:151), clearly meaning those paths leading to Him; for the end of all these ways is He who said, 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). He who has reached the goal of these ways is in truth, having both it and its Father within himself. And since He also approaches the sinners in another way, He is near to them; and all His ways are truth, for as one travels them, He performs the examination and judgment of their affairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God is near and what makes his ways truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's testimonies cannot be shaken because his word is wisdom and his Son is their foundation.
comments.comment: The testimonies were established by God so that no one would be able to shake or overturn them; for your word is wisdom, and your Son is their foundation. Therefore, presenting their unassailable and unshakeable nature, He says, 'My words will never pass away, even if heaven and earth pass away' (Matt 24:35).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the testimonies are founded for ever.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'The beginning' here is the truth of God's words.
comments.comment: Often, when 'the beginning' is taken in a certain sense, we say the beginning is the truth of the words of God, as that which is first.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Truth is the beginning of God's words, for Christ is the truth and the Father's word is truth.
comments.comment:
… If the beginning of those bearing them is the truth itself and they become so because of it, and if God's words also bear toward the truth (for they are spoken because of it), it is rightly said that their beginning is the truth. … And because of this, it is right to say that the truth is the beginning of God's words.

And what is it? Since the Lord says, 'I am the truth,' the word of God is also that itself; he says to the Father, 'Your word is truth,' who becomes with each prophet. … Just as the truth was the beginning of your words, so all your judgments of justice are found indestructible and shown forever (Psalm 119:160).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, pursued by Saul without cause, was kept from revenge by the fear of God, which guards everyone in the wars of princes.
comments.comment: The saying also has David’s own particular meaning: when he was pursued by Saul without cause and out of envy, his fear of God restrained him from taking vengeance. But it extends also to the common case, that there is no other way to escape wars of princes unharmed unless one is guarded by the fear of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the fear of God guards the persecuted, with David as example.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The righteous man, enlightened in a day without night, praises God sevenfold, and awaiting the Savior he loves the commandments with a pure practice and a contemplative hope.
comments.comment:
… Throughout his life, the righteous man, being enlightened, will be in a perfect day not intercepted by night and will praise God sevenfold (Psalm 119:164; LXX 118:164), having become transcendent to be separated from the world that has become in days of exile, even having been in God's paradise, having contemplated the word of God's creation and providence, will confess the judgments of the justice of God, according to the judgments of each varied creation and providence. If he also awaits the Savior, as it is said, 'All flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Psalm 119:166; LXX 118:166), following this he loves the commandments of God.

And he has expected salvation, so that both his practice is pure and his expectation is contemplative, always expecting and contemplating that God has come to seek and to save the lost.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The great peace of those who love God's law is the tranquility of the soul, the fruit of the Spirit.
comments.comment: And we have in the divine writings things said concerning peace of the kind according to the soul, concerning which it is said: 'great peace is in those who love you, and there is no stumbling block in them' (Psalm 119:165). And this, being the tranquility of the soul, is the fruit of the Spirit: 'for the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace' (Gal 5:22). From this they are blessed, concerning whom it is said: 'blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God' (Matt 5:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the great peace of those who love the law is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist asks to be rescued according to God's word, offers a hymn of thanks once taught, and utters the word of righteousness by works as well as by voice.
comments.comment:
He prays for such a worthy condition to be tested, certain and unshakeable, as if to enter before the Lord. 'And I will know if my worthiness enters before you, if I am rescued by you according to your word and your wisdom' (Psalm 119:170; LXX 118:170). For He, being above all passions, irrational and the evils working from irrationality, having departed from them, is rescued by God according to His word.

'Oh that you would teach me, so that I might act from it and know them clearly; I would bring to you a thankful hymn from my lips, O Lord, of your man' (Psalm 119:171; LXX 118:171). …

'Your various commandments are instructions; they all possess the virtues of those who are wise, the general virtue being to follow the particular virtues, as one possessing the one perfectly possesses all' (Psalm 119:172; LXX 118:172). 'I utter your word with my lips toward your man' (Psalm 119:172). But the word concerning righteousness is uttered principally not by voice alone, not by merely bringing it forth, but also by works and by practical intention, being corrected according to the right word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Longing for eternal salvation, the psalmist says he will live again and praise God, and this points to Christ, who by his suffering and death redeems the suffering and the dying.
comments.comment:
After the gift of wisdom he asks again for salvation from dangers. This too is a reward for his willing zeal for the divine law (Psalm 118:173 [119:173]) (Psalm 119:174-175; LXX 118:174-175).

So then he was truly saying just now that he awaited eternal salvation, and now also, longing for it, he has made this the goal of his study of the law. For he says that he will live again and praise God, helped toward this by his all-wise judgments (Psalm 119:175). This is Christ, who comes down in place of human beings to the saving death for human beings, and by his suffering redeems those in sufferings, and by his death redeems the dying. And in accordance with this there follows, “My soul will live,” and what comes after (Psalm 118:175 [119:175]).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer for salvation and life.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's hand means his care for those being saved, and remembering his judgments turns one from the death that follows sin, so that the soul lives and praises.
comments.comment:
'Let your hand be done to save me' (Psalm 119:173) does not signify here the generation of it according to essence, but the relation toward the ones being saved. … The path of the one longing for the salvation of God is the one who has the study of the law as his desire, pre-sounding his arrival here. By 'law' he calls here the ancient and divine Scripture.

'Since remembering your judgments and being set apart, I turn away from the death that follows sin' (Psalm 119:175; LXX 118:175). … Since remembering your judgments, I turn away from the death following sin by not sinning; my soul shall live, having worked out those of life and praising the thankful ones, through which you provide it with immortal life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lost sheep is the human race gone astray through Adam, and the psalmist speaks as part of that sheep, asking to be sought because he has longed for God's commandments.
comments.comment:
Having lost a sheep from the hundred, the Savior comes seeking it, having left the ninety-nine in the wilderness; the human race has gone astray through Adam's transgression. The human race is the lost sheep from the hundred, while the rational things that do not stumble remain part of creation in the desert, staying high in virtue and truth, except for man who has gone into error.

Therefore, like the sheep, but rather a part of it, the Psalmist says: 'I have gone astray; seek me, your servant; for you came to seek and save the lost; seek me so that you may find me ready for this; for I have longed for your commandments' (Ps 119).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the lost sheep is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Jerusalem temple had fifteen steps on which the odes were sung, and the steps stand for stages of progress in knowing God.
comments.comment:
It is to be understood that he in the Jerusalem temple has fifteen steps, and standing on each of them, those appointed to sing hymns were saying an ode. Therefore, the number of odes coincided with the steps. The arrangement concerning the odes and those singing them on each step of the temple lies in the Chronicles.

You shall understand the temple of God to be a holy, intelligible, and spiritual thing—the theology—and the steps to be the stages of progress.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the idea of the psalm as a song of steps.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist laments because he longs to depart and be with Christ.
comments.comment: “Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged” (Psalm 119:5 LXX). For he has a desire to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). So he is distressed at the prolonging of this sojourning as an obstacle to joy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist laments his long sojourning.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Hostility to the righteous has run from Cain through this whole age, and Israel's sojourning in a foreign land has been the longest of all.
comments.comment:
This was so immediately after the first apostasy of the human being, when Cain by deceit struck down his brother, and it is so throughout the whole present age, as is shown in other cases and in the present matter. So the person who looks to God, worn down and afflicted by this, asks for salvation from him. He does not foresee the cessation that will come then, when he is brought up to dwell in the peaceful city, with good and bad alike sharing its citizenship (Psalm 120:5; LXX 119:5).

Another passage also indicates the foreign land in one respect, into which Israel fell and sojourned, and that his sojourning was extended to the greatest length. Prophesying in lament he brings this out so that it reaches also to the present condition; for this is the longest sojourning (Psalm 120:5).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The good keep peace with everyone as far as they can, but the wicked abhor godliness and are not softened by kindness.
comments.comment: For the good and godly keep peace as far as depends on them and with all human beings, whenever there is no need of judicial punishment such as God commanded against the Canaanites and Amorites, forbidding friendship with them (Psalm 120:7). But the wicked and those who do not know God would never enter into friendship with the good; rather they abhor godliness, and they do not receive kindly anything good from the godly, nor are they tamed by their kindness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'I am for peace' and why the others are for war.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The mountains are heavenly powers, but help comes from the Creator.
comments.comment: He calls mountains here the invisible and heavenly powers. And while he awaits help through them, he says that the help does not originate from them but from the Creator (Psalm 120:1b-2 [121:1b-2]).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hills are and where the help really comes from.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The mountains are the prophets, and whoever gives his mind to their words lifts his eyes to them and finds his help from the Lord who made heaven and earth.
comments.comment: The mountains are the prophets—Moses and those after him. And the Scripture makes this clear: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Psalm 121:1). The one who gives his reasoning mind to the words of the prophets lifts up his eyes to the mountains, seeing that his help will come from the words understood in the prophets, from the Lord who made heaven and earth and filled the pure heart of the prophets with mysteries.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hills are.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One who goes up to the second step is transformed toward perfection and lifts the eyes of the mind to the height.
comments.comment:
He who has ascended to the second step of the temple begins to be transformed into perfection, no longer thinking of something lowly. Therefore, he says he has lifted the eyes of the intellect toward the height. Thus, the ode of the second step has attained a familiar number. For the one hundred and twentieth limits the perfection of human life.

Indeed, it has been said concerning men after the flood: 'Their days shall be one hundred and twenty' (Gen 6:3). Thus also Moses, the great hierophant and servant of God, having perfected human life into one hundred and twenty years, describes his own life, setting forth his own life as a pattern for those under him who receive the laws.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The servant who serves God with the mind finds shade, and the promise that the sun will not strike him is not literal, since the righteous bore the heat of the senses but not the heat of sin.
comments.comment: And the servant who serves God intellectually is there, obtaining shade and rest, having escaped the heat of life: 'a wise son was saved from the heat' (Proverbs 10:5), not being consumed by the heat, according to those in the parable who did not receive the seed into depth and fell by the flame of sin. This promise is said to David in the Psalms: 'the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6), which according to the literal sense we do not find. For he himself, being righteous, was labored upon by the heat of the sensible, but was unlabored upon by the heat of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the promise about the sun by day can be true of the righteous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The burning of the sun stands for worldly cares, tribulations and persecutions.
comments.comment: The natural thinker hears, 'The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6). He calls the worldly cares a burning; and those being dried up by it he calls hay; but the Savior, through the parable, indicates the tribulations; and he called the persecutions according to the word a burning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The going out that God guards is a going out from the sensible to the intelligible and spiritual.
comments.comment: It can also be strongly understood regarding the exodus: the exodus of God guarding from evil for one turning away from evil, and likewise the exodus of one guarding the doing of the good, an exodus from the sensible toward the intelligible and spiritual. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One who has begun the ascent to the temple does not turn back, but hastens upward toward what he has been shown.
comments.comment: He who stretches himself forward toward those before him does not forget them, nor does he run back again. For he who hastens toward the prize of the higher calling goes toward the higher things. Therefore, having begun the ascent toward the temple, he does not return after having traveled; having ascended to the third degree, he does not even depart from the flight of the soul, but, having received a vision, he hastens toward that which he is being urged to lead the entrance of, being in good spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist rejoices at the angels' word of Jerusalem's lasting dwelling, and "as a city" means its people are united to one another, with the Lord as its wall.
comments.comment: It is a joy to hear what is said by the angels, clearly the ones who speak to the prophets and who, as it were, lead the herd of Israel. Such is the one made known through Zechariah, interceding for fallen Jerusalem and speaking of her future dwelling (Psalm 122:1; LXX 121:1b). The psalmist says that he rejoiced when he heard these things, and that he foresaw the secure dwelling in the holy city and, as it were, perceived the matter as present prophetically. For this is what “Our feet were standing in the courts of Jerusalem” means (Psalm 121:1b-4 [122:1b-4]) (Ps 122:2). The standing of feet is the immovable dwelling which the holy prophets also proclaim. The opposite of this was when, according to the history, God shook the foot of Jerusalem from its own land. So the psalmist speaks of the rebuilding of the city, seen by him as also by Ezekiel, and says that the building is of a city united—not, clearly, in the customary way of walls uniting it, but of the inhabitants united to one another. Therefore he did not say “city” but “as a city” having its joining together at once. For neither Ezekiel nor Zechariah declares that it will be inhabited under walls, but unwalled, and that its wall will be the Lord, since God is the guardian and holder together of the unity of the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains "builded as a city" as a unity of people rather than of walls.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those whose souls stand firm in the courts of Jerusalem long to rise to the temple, and the vision of peace becomes a city built by the Lord, set on a height.
comments.comment: Those having firmly established the feet of their own souls previously in the courts of Jerusalem (Psalm 122:2; LXX 121:2–4), have a desire also to ascend to the temple. And the most sharp-witted theology is the temple, while the partial contemplations are the courts of the vision of peace, the specific virtues that occur. The vision of the aforementioned peace, having begun to be transformed, becomes as a city built by the Lord, and its participation consists of the same aforementioned courts, in which the feet of the firm ones are standing. And it is not a low-lying thing, but exists in some height, so that the citizen who wishes to become of it does not descend, but ascends toward it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tribes were united not by walls thrown around them but through themselves, and their going up bears witness to Israel and gives thanks for the promise fulfilled.
comments.comment: He interprets the unity as being through the inhabitants themselves, saying, “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (Ps 122:4). Not because walls were thrown around them were they united, but because they themselves were united through themselves. It is a testimony to Israel, clearly witnessing to the truth of the promises, and to give thanks to the name of the Lord, because confession of grace is owed by the beneficiaries to the one who fulfilled the wonderful promise.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the tribes go up and give thanks.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The saved ascend as the Lord's watchers, and the church of David is where thrones for judgment stand, on which the apostles sit judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
comments.comment: And indeed, the various ranks of the saved, having the choice of confession, ascend there as watches of the Lord, having been well testified by the Lord to ascend and having confessed, and they increase in zeal and progress, doing these things, Israel. David the savior has said many things (Psalm 122:5; LXX 121:5); therefore, because it is from the seed of David, it is according to the flesh, and because it is sufficiently by hand, it is so; for David is interpreted as being 'capable by hand.' For how is he not capable by hand, he who performs wondrous powers? This is the church of David, in which thrones are seen for judgment, upon which the apostles sit judging the twelve tribes of Israel. For the faith and the citizenship of each apostle is a throne of his kingdom, judging and condemning those who have not conformed to what is prophesied in the divine scriptures, nor believed in those whom he made and taught with words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thrones of David's house are a shared kingdom of the godly, upheld by Christ, who gave the apostles twelve thrones to judge Israel.
comments.comment: He says that thrones of the house of David were established in her, since Daniel also prophesies a kingdom over all things. It is not the rule of some one person or of a single ruler, but a common kingdom for the best and most godly, through whom the kingdom of David is set upright by the grace of Christ, who gave to the twelve apostles the right to sit on twelve thrones and judge Israel.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the thrones of David's house are, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whoever loves Jerusalem prospers by bearing both virtue and the contemplation of truth.
comments.comment: And according to contemplation (Psalm 122:6-7; LXX 121:6-7), he who bears spiritual fruit because of loving Jerusalem will be in much prosperity and well-being, bearing not only the acts of virtue but also the contemplation of the truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jerusalem, using the power that comes from God, has subdued her opponents, so peace and tranquility follow in her high towers.
comments.comment: Jerusalem, because she reigns with power, has become peaceful, having previously been at war with enemies whom she overcomes by her might, finding tranquility in her high towers. For the great towers in the walls are being constructed for the purpose of watching for the coming enemies.… Therefore, Jerusalem, having used her own power which is from God, has subjected those who oppose her; she will make peace, and tranquility will follow in her high towers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the peace of Jerusalem in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The high towers are those who watch for enemies and cast them down, and the one born from God has brothers and neighbors who share his righteousness and faith.
comments.comment: If, however, in allegory, the high towers are those who, through the height of the commonwealth and the vision of the truth, not only watch for the enemies coming for war but also cast them down from on high in reproofs. According to the vision, he who is born from God, doing righteousness and believing that Jesus is the Christ, has brothers who perform the same things and believe, and neighbors who approach through the doing of righteousness and the faith of Jesus Christ.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Peace is spoken for the brothers and neighbors, and seeking the good of Jerusalem means keeping the divine commandments and rightly understanding the true faith.
comments.comment: But since of both these ranks, of his brothers and of his neighbors, I say that Jerusalem, who is to be given, says she speaks peace and is peaceful (Ps 122:8,9), I wish for them, both the brothers and the neighbors of the fatherland, but since they seek the goods of the Lord their God, seeking the truly good things for Jerusalem. For he says concerning the one who began to ascend (Ps 122:2), since seeking the good things for Jerusalem, the keeping of the divine commandments and the right understanding of the true faith.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The eyes lifted to God are the soul's enlightened eyes, and without the mind of Christ a person cannot see rightly.
comments.comment: … I say that there are eyes of the soul which are enlightened, concerning which the apostle writes, "the eyes of your heart having been enlightened" (Eph 1:18). Concerning these it is said, "To you I lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in heaven" (Psalm 123:1). Of these eyes is the beginning of seeing. If anyone does not have the "mind of Christ," he is not able to see rightly, if he has not been enlightened by the true Light.
comments.selected_reason: Says what lifting the eyes to God means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Our eyes are not on the hands of those masters but turn to the Lord our God for mercy.
comments.comment: It is possible for slaves having eyes to take into the hands of masters the nations which are being managed under the angels, according to how the nations stood according to the number of the angels of God; but the circumcision assembly having eyes, a little girl into the hands of the mistress, a little girl because she is called a spirit of slavery; but her mistress, calling the unblemished and spotless church of God, no one stumbles. But we do not have our eyes in the hands of those masters, but we approach to the Lord our God for mercy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As Mount Zion is unshakable, so those who trust in God stand immovable, for the Zion meant is the heavenly one, the Church, and trust in him is where being lifted up begins.
comments.comment:
Just as the mountain of Zion is unshakable and immovable (for the Word of God is it), so also those trusting in God have an immovable standing, imitating Him as they hasten to be. For the upcoming text is not said regarding the sensible mountain, similarly to all those mountains that are steadfast, but regarding that mountain about which the Spirit commands the prophet, saying, 'Ascend upon a high mountain, O you who preach Zion.' For Zion, being interpreted as the watchtower of the holy Church's contemplation of good things, is the high mountain; and regarding the mountain of the heavenly Zion, it is said, 'But you have come to the mountain of Zion and to the city of the living God, Jerusalem the heavenly' (Hebrews 12:22). Let us therefore establish the trust toward God, so as to chance upon both blessedness and the other promises, as the prophecy exhorts us: 'And having trusted in the Lord, He will lift you up upon the good things of the earth' (Isaiah 58:14). For the beginning of being lifted up upon the good things of the earth of the living and gentle ones is to have trusted in Him.

As for the Church, it is seen being enriched in the 'Shine, shine, Jerusalem, Jerusalem built as a city.' Therefore, he who thinks perfectly and genuinely that the things of the Church will dwell in it forever will not be shaken, nor will he be removed from this habitation, having received the things to be practiced and thought about with certainty and immovability. And it will be said specifically that he dwells in it forever, the living one and the believing one in the Lord, who shall not die forever, having here received the pledge of eternal life. But if he should ever become negligent, as if it were possible through attention and desire for the good, the habitation will be moved; for this reason it says in Proverbs, 'A righteous man will not be moved forever' (Proverbs 10:30).…
comments.selected_reason: Explains why those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord becomes a circle around his people, not by enclosing them in a place but by being shared with them now and in the age to come.
comments.comment: And with these the announcements can be made, placing around those who fear the Lord the mountains that surround Jerusalem. But greater than the security of the mountains exists for the people dwelling in Jerusalem, through whom especially the one dwelling in it is not shaken for ever, the Lord becoming a circle around him. And the Lord becomes a circle not locally and bodily enclosing some within, but being participated in by them and being with them over all, not only in the present age but also in the coming one.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Lord is round about his people.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ will not let evil demons corrupt good subjects but will free them from a harmful slavery.
comments.comment: But he will not allow good subjects to be corrupted by evil demons. Rather, after the good have toiled a little under them, he will free them from a harmful slavery that does not dare to come upon those who are ruled by God (Psalm 125:3; LXX 124:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the rod of the wicked not resting on the righteous means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The rod of the wicked does not rest on the righteous, whose hands the Lord would have lifted piously toward righteousness, and God does good to the upright in heart.
comments.comment:
Regarding the rod, indeed there is a purpose to strike, to stretch out the hands of the righteous against lawlessness; but the will of the Lord is for the righteous to stretch out their hands toward righteousness, lifting them up piously without anger or inner deliberation (Psalm 125:3; LXX 124:3). Good are those who have been benefited in mindset by virtue, and upright in heart are those who truly and rightly think the things of piety.

… For those dwelling in Jerusalem unto the age, unshaken, being at once practical and knowing, are good and upright in heart.

And God does them good, giving good things to those who ask him—an addition of faith and of the remaining virtue, with participation in divine gifts, furnished for leading them also into the heavenly promises and the kingdom of heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the righteous do not put forth their hands to iniquity, and who the upright are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To lead away means to hand over those who chose uncleanness, so those on crooked ways are shown openly, while peace is given to Israel, the one who has a mind.
comments.comment:
… 'He shall lead away' means 'he shall hand over': those who chose to have desires unto uncleanness and unto passions of dishonor and unto a reprobate mind, to do the things not fitting.

And he also said in the psalms: 'And I sent them away according to the devices of their hearts; they shall walk in their devices' (Psalm 81:12).

He shall lead away, then, those who turn aside into crooked ways with the workers of iniquity, that it may be shown openly who they were, being hidden—seeming not to do iniquity, though disposed according to it.

… But the peace surpassing all mind (Phil 4:7), given with divine grace by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, shall be to everyone and only to the one having a mind, being Israel, with the hymnist praying.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "lead them forth" means and who receives peace.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To sow in tears is to sow virtue with pains, so as to reap in joy.
comments.comment: … In this morning, 'sowing in tears', sowing the seeds of virtue with pains, sowing into the Spirit with sweat, so that you may 'reap eternal life', and having 'sown in tears you may reap in joy' (Psalm 126:5) and come 'rejoicing', bringing the sheaves of the seed.
comments.selected_reason: Says what sowing in tears and reaping in joy mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm, the eighth song of ascents, is inscribed to Solomon, a symbol of the truly peaceful Lord who is our peace and builds the house of God.
comments.comment:
… Eighth song of ascents; riddling the mysteries of the resurrection of the Lord in the ogdoad, it is inscribed to Solomon—to the one born from the seed of David according to the flesh, the truly peaceful one.

For he is our peace, of us who are being saved, saying: 'My peace I give to you' (John 14:27).

To the one bringing about the dissolution of every enemy and foe, making peace, and founding and building the house of God—whose symbol Solomon, born of David, bore, who built the temple of God in Judea, much peace having come in his days.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
