comments.capsule: Human effort is vain without God, yet we should neither take the whole credit ourselves nor leave everything to him and do nothing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "they labour in vain" does and does not mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Solomon, who built the temple, points to the true Solomon, Christ, so the building is made and guarded by God, while human buildings and night watches fall into vanity.
comments.comment: Solomon is inscribed on the song, because he built the temple (Psalm 127:1; LXX 126:1-2). But it signifies the true Solomon, our Lord, the cause of the true and peaceful building. For this reason the building is shown to be made by God, and its guard is secure because it is guarded according to God. And this is fitting, because the buildings and guards made by human beings fell into vanity: the night watches of those who keep guard, and the diligent and laborious care by day. For this reason human things, being such as they are, came first, so that divine things alone might be recognized as having what is sure and unchangeable. Just as righteousness came through the law, so that God's righteousness might be seen after it as having what is genuine and alone true, and true life after the life that was in shadow and image.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the house and the city can be kept only by the Lord.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's rest, like sleep, is given out of love.
comments.comment: "When he gives sleep to his beloved ones." He has indicated the rest from God that is like sleep and will be given out of love.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The saints are the arrows of the Mighty One, used against the ungodly.
comments.comment: "For I have stretched you, Judah," he says, "for myself as a bow." Here too he calls the remaining saints the arrows of the Mighty One, for the defeat of the ungodly and those who are violent with injustice (Psalm 127:4; LXX 126:4a).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sons of those building the Lord's house build with one hand and fend off its opponents with the other, and the man whose desire is fulfilled from the arrows speaks boldly before his enemies.
comments.comment:
Next, through the spoken words, we understand that the sons of those stretching themselves out to build the house of the Lord hold stones and swords and other weapons, as with one hand doing the work of the building, and with the other throwing stones to hinder those wishing to stop the construction of the divine house.

For the divine teachers strive in each soul being educated to build for God and to fight against thoughts and evil powers attempting to obstruct the growth of the building. He blesses the man who, because he has preserved that which remains according to the image of God, has had his desire fulfilled from the arrows of the Mighty (Psalm 127:5; LXX 126:5). For having been directed toward the desire of good things by them, he has been shown blessed. And possessing unashamed and undaunted boldness in the gate of the beneficial entrance, he speaks without being shamed by the enemies, who were striving to be obstacles to the fulfillment of desire and to the building.

And it is no wonder that he has blessed a man singularly; he has blessed in the plural, that those speaking in the gate shall not be shamed; for the word is not about one, but about everyone who has fulfilled his desire from the arrows (Psalm 127:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the arrows and the speaking in the gate in terms of building and defending God's house.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ways in are many but perfection is one, and fearing the Lord means turning away from evils and so being ready to walk in his ways.
comments.comment: The paths of entrance are many and various, and the lives of those who begin are of many kinds, but there is one perfection that reaches the height (Psalm 128:1; LXX 127:1). He characterizes those who fear the Lord by saying next what sort of people they are: "Those who walk in his ways." For those who do not do this do not fear the Lord. The fear of the Lord is a turning away from evils, and the one who has turned away from evils is ready for the divine ways.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what fearing the Lord and walking in his ways involve.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Since many who feared God stayed childless, the wife is the wisdom living with the blessed man, who gives birth to works, words and divine thoughts.
comments.comment: To be called blessed, as the Psalmist says: 'Blessed are you, and good shall it be to you; your wife as a vine growing straight in the trellises of your house, your sons as young olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall be blessed the man who fears the Lord' (Psalm 128:1-4). This, according to history, is not without contradiction, for many who feared God remained childless, or remained so until old age, according to Abraham and the father of John, Zechariah. Therefore, what he says is this: the opinion and the faith which the blessed one received, a wife is living with him, able to give birth to works, words, and divine thoughts. For it is said: 'Wisdom gives understanding to a man' (Proverbs 10:23), and the wise man says concerning her: 'I became a lover of her beauty' (Wisdom 8:2), making the wisdom evident, and 'I led her to a union with myself' (Wisdom 8:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who loves the Lord as perfect will eat the heavenly bread, while 'the labors of your hands' are the soul's practical powers.
comments.comment: …  He who does not fear the Lord eats the labors of his fruit, but he who loves him as perfect will eat the bread, the heavenly one, according to 'Blessed is he who eats bread in the kingdom of heaven' (Luke 14:15). And he says 'fruits' here, so that it might be in some way 'He shall eat the labors of your hands,' that is, of the practical powers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A gift of God is given to the one who fears him, a companion grafted into the true vine, and his sons are like olive shoots crowning his table, which the ungodly do not have.
comments.comment:
To the one fearing the Lord, a gift of God is given, a partner and a companion, not a woman by chance, but one grafted into the true vine.

Who can find a woman of worth, a good wife, and a woman of manly strength? Such a thing is more precious than costly stones. Just as the opposite of evil is good, and the wrath of God is a spouse in a harsh manner, so also sons from God are given to the one fearing the Lord; they are not like many sons, but like young olive shoots surrounding and crowning his table. You will also understand these from the perfection of the one saying, 'But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God' (Ps 52:8). For the offspring of such an olive tree are called like young olive shoots. If anyone says that those not fearing the Lord often possess much in the property of children and in the prosperity of a wife, we will say that the present beatitude does not simply promise a wife and children, but all of this is depicted as a woman in a vineyard and children as young olive shoots; such things are not the lot of the ungodly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wife and sons here are not a literal woman and bodily children, since many who fear God have had neither, so their spiritual sense must be sought.
comments.comment: … Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, since the wife accompanying you is fertile, finding herself like a vine rejoicing with fruits (Psalm 128:3). But also your offspring are not weak or female, but strong sons being around your table, bearing the food of light like young olive shoots. And your spiritual table exists, full of all those who nourish mind and soul. Be having in these things a blessing from the Lord; no one else, but the God-fearing shall receive from the Lord. This is shown through 'the Man' and 'every man.' Therefore, regarding the present things, one ought not to take them as being about a sensible woman and bodily children, since many having obtained the fear of God have possessed neither wife nor children. If, then, the things of the word are not entirely literal, the spiritual sense of the things expressed must be sought by every one existing in piety.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the vine-like wife and olive-shoot sons are to be read spiritually.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only one who has driven off his enemies many times, strengthened by the Lord, can say they have not prevailed against him.
comments.comment: By ascent you will understand thus: those being captured by the enemy in a single blow would not say this, but the one alone, driving the enemies into flight anew until old age, becoming always a victor and a triumphalist over them (Psalm 129:1-4; LXX 128:1-4). And he brought forward the proof of having fought them many times: 'For even I was not able; for He was strengthening me, the Lord, who crushes the enemies.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one fighting from his youth is strengthened by Christ and never overturned by the devil and his allies, who cannot trample him, since Christ gave authority over the lion and the scorpion.
comments.comment:
The 'from my youth' is able to show that he is strong and being strengthened by Christ, from whom I have cast off old age, having cast away the old man with his deeds; having clothed himself with the new man, fighting against the aforementioned enemies, he was never overturned by them, but conquering unceasingly and steadily, and turning them to witness for Israel.

And the boast is not small, to be fought against by the devil and those around him, who do not possess this strength; for they are his friends and obedient ones. And everyone alone says, 'For indeed you were not able to trample upon me, having received authority from the Word of God, upon the lion and the scorpion, and to trample the lion and the dragon' (Luke 10:19). For having escaped all such things, the God crushing Satan under his feet, he says, 'Many times they have fought against me from my youth, and indeed they were not able; but I was able against them, being strengthened by the Lord. The sinners have stretched out their necks upon my back, they have lengthened their lawlessness' (Psalm 129:1-3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is dangerous to face the enemies and be harmed through sight and the senses, so the one who hastens to God turns away from wickedness and keeps sinners behind him.
comments.comment:
It is a stain and very dangerous to have the enemies before one's face, having them sufficiently according to thought, and to harm and destroy them merely through seeing and through the senses, those whom we have perceived of them; it is proper to always turn away from them, casting them upon the back. For he who hastens toward God and virtue turns away from wickedness.

For if the sinners have stretched out their necks upon the face and before one, they have harmed the heart, timely casting it into evil thoughts, and the sight through destructive spectacles, and the other senses harming through those things belonging to them. But he has the sinners behind, the one forgetting those behind, and stretching out himself toward those before, and going behind the Lord God;…
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinners weave sin upon sin like a long rope, and the righteous Lord cuts off the necks of those who will not submit to his good yoke.
comments.comment: The lengthening of their lawlessness reveals the persistent wickedness of sinners who weave a series of sins like a rope, and by adding to those who have already received, they lengthen their lawlessness. The word weighs such people down: 'Woe to those who pile up sins,' as with a long rope and as with a heavy yoke, subduing their lawlessness. For their hands weave injustice, and as adding sin upon sin, they lengthen their own lawlessness. The Lord is righteous and has cut off the necks of sinners. The righteous Lord cuts off the neck of those who do not submit to his good yoke.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lengthened lawlessness and the Lord cutting it off.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wise of this world are like dried stubble that withers before it can be reaped, and those who hate Zion are burned like the weeds sown among the good seed.
comments.comment: And the wise of this world are themselves like stubble, having only their promise until this present life; and they are a heap of roofs for those who through them act and think that they have surpassed all. Therefore, it is a dried-up stubble, not casting its roots into the soil (that is, the sensible things), nor hastening toward a spiritual planting instead of stubble. Before they are even cut, they dry up, not filling the hands of the one harvesting this stubble, because they have unbelief. For the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, and 'he who does not believe is condemned' (John 3:18). Not only hands, but even the bosom of himself the harvester of this stubble will not fill, by not receiving them first into the bosom of Abraham, and then thereafter into the bosoms of the harvesting angel;… He [the Savior] himself also cleanses his threshing floor, having the winnowing fan in his hand to gather the wheat into the granary, but the chaff to burn with unquenchable fire. And who are those who hate Zion? They become not stubble, but like stubble, the weeds sown among the good seed by the evil one and being burned in the future.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Finding no one able to help, he cries to God out of the depths, confessing where he has fallen, for God will raise him from the depth of wickedness.
comments.comment: Not as one ascending, but finding no one able to help, he cries to God. Along with confessing where he has fallen, he says, 'Out of the depths I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice; for having heard, you will raise me up from the depth of wickedness and the deepest pit' (Ps 130:1-4). This expression agrees with what is said by him later: 'If iniquity be observed, Lord, Lord, who shall stand?' (Psalm 130:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what crying out of the depths means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One may cry from the depths of earth, feeling far below heaven and God, and a holy person prays for heavenly things, enlightened by the Spirit who knows the depths of God.
comments.comment: It is possible even for one dwelling in the earthly place, through human life, to send up this prayer, feeling himself far below both heaven and God; for heaven is high and earth is deep. It is also possible for the one praying to be holy according to what was previously stated. For he does not send up the prayer concerning small and earthly things, but large and heavenly things. He does not send up the prayer from a psychic discourse concerning them, asking for them, but being enlightened by the Spirit, searching all things, and knowing and contemplating the depths of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The depths may be the waters of afflictions, and the repeated words show one who clings to his prayer.
comments.comment: The cry "out of the depths" could mean out of the waters of afflictions that have poured around him. The endurance and the repetition of the same words belong to one who clings and hangs on and does not wish to let go of his supplication because of his desire (Psalm 130:1-2; LXX 129:1b-2). For this reason he says, "Hear my voice, and let your ears be attentive."
comments.selected_reason: Explains the depths and the repeated plea in plain terms.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: If God marked iniquities no one would stand, since all have sinned, so we need the propitiation that comes from him, which is the Savior, Jesus Christ.
comments.comment:
Observe, examining iniquities; for if he were to do this, no one would stand. For all have strayed, all have sinned. Therefore, since no one stands before the judgment from you, there is need of the propitiation from you, being propitiated for the salvation of all.

And what is the propitiation, the Savior? John writes: 'And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, a righteous Lord Jesus Christ' (1 John 2:1); and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, not only concerning ours but also concerning the sins of the world. But also Paul: 'For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood' (Romans 3:23-25), and the following. A symbol of this propitiation was constructed in the law, concerning which also now the one praying to God says: 'That from you is the propitiation'; from you, as a generation from the only good Father, is the propitiation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one could stand if iniquities were marked, and where forgiveness comes from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Israel, the discerning mind, should hope in the Lord in bright times and dark, for he redeems him from all his iniquities, however many.
comments.comment: Always and at all times it is necessary to hope in the Lord, not only the one standing openly but also the one standing in gloom. From the morning watch, the one with the bright things present, and until night, the one with the dreary and darker things surrounding; and what is from the morning watch, the rising of the true light and making the beginning of a mental day, the discerning mind, Israel, called by the Hebrew voice, let him hope in the Lord (Psalm 130:6-8; LXX 129:6-8), expecting from him an addition of the bright things and a deliverance from the gloomy things, what is from him as in a fountain and from him the mercy which those hoping in him need; but also much redemption from him, the propitiation from him is not another; for he himself from all iniquities will redeem him. For even if the iniquities of Israel are many, from all he will redeem him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the watching for the morning and the hope of redemption.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David, perfected in gentleness, asks for the land of the gentle.
comments.comment: David, having perfected gentleness, says the following: 'Remembering me,' he says, 'upon these things you will give me an inheritance, the land of the gentle' (Psalm 132:1; LXX 131:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David declared gentleness worthy of God's remembrance, and the Savior told us to imitate his gentleness.
comments.comment: … And holy David too declared it [gentleness] worthy of God’s remembrance, saying: ‘Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness’ (Ps 132:1). But the Savior Himself commanded us to become imitators of His gentleness, saying: ‘Learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matt 11:29).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: God's command showed David the place, the threshing floor of Ornan where he built the altar, and God made a visitation there through the presence of the angel.
comments.comment: The place did not become clear to David from the matter itself by his own forethought (Psalm 132:6; LXX 131:6). For this reason he says, "We heard and we found," because a command of God pointed out the threshing floor of Ornan, on which he built the altar to turn away the death that was destroying the generation of the Hebrews (Psalm 132:8; LXX 131:8). And having loved the discovery exceedingly, as one who had come to know what he had long desired, he rejoices in the matter and loves the worship there. There, he says, God also made a visitation, because the glory of God became manifest through the presence of the angel (Psalm 132:9; LXX 131:9).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Virgin is the ark gilded within and without, and the Lord is bidden to arise to raise the fallen race.
comments.comment: … Arise, O Lord, into Your resting place, You and the ark of Your holiness (Psalm 132:8). For truly the most holy Virgin is an ark, gilded within and without (Exodus 25:11), who received the whole treasure of holiness. Arise, O Lord, into Your resting place (Psalm 132:8). Arise, O Lord, from the bosom of the Father (John 1:18), to raise up the fallen race of the first parent.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The time of Solomon is foretold, when the ark is set in the temple and a cloud fills the house.
comments.comment:
In the same way, he says, he foretells the time of Solomon, in which the ark is moved from the tent and set in the temple, and divine glory appeared and a cloud filled the house.

These things, he says, we see happened in Solomon's time according to David's words (Psalm 132:10; LXX 131:10).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Priests put on righteousness and rejoice because of David, from whose seed Christ took the form of a servant.
comments.comment: Who is the cause of them [the priests and saints] putting on righteousness and rejoicing? It is David, the holy one, who is capable by hand. For the Lord brought forth for David his servant. He who became God's servant according to the flesh from the seed of David, having taken the form of the servant, emptied himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The favor is toward David, but its benefit passes to his descendants, as the Lord spared Solomon and Hezekiah for David's sake.
comments.comment: For the favor is toward David, even if the benefit extends to those after him (Psalm 132:10; LXX 131:10). Just as it is said directly to Solomon that because of David he would not fall entirely from the kingdom, so also the sparing for David's sake passed to his descendants, just as it is said to Hezekiah: "I will shield this city for the sake of David my servant" (2 Kings 19:34).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "for thy servant David's sake" means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is asked not to turn away the face of his Christ, and the oath to David guarantees it.
comments.comment: … intending by your grace to shine upon men the face of your Christ, O Lord, do not turn it away, so that they may remain unhidden from his appearance, having been benefited. The cause of the certain fulfillment is the one having brought forth, saying, 'The Lord swore truth to David and will not deny it' Ps 131:11.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fruit of David's womb sitting on his throne is fulfilled in the Lord, since God's oath is truth, as Gabriel told Mary.
comments.comment: The 'certainly shall be' regarding what was sworn in truth to David, concerning the coming of the Lord, is that the fruit of the womb of David shall sit upon his throne Ps 131:11. He will fulfill it as he swore; for the oath of God is truth, according to what was said by Gabriel to Mary concerning him being genealogically from David: 'And God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever' Luke 1:32; Ps 131:12-13.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who sits on David's throne and why the oath holds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earthly Zion cannot be God's resting place for ever since the earth passes away, so Zion is the Church, which he desired as his dwelling.
comments.comment: If someone takes the earthly Zion, how could he understand 'that my resting place for ever and ever' Ps 131:14, since passing to the end of this age, the heaven and the earth pass away? For if the whole earth passes away, then the Zion which is upon the earth will also pass by. Regarding the spiritual Zion, concerning which it is written, 'Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion' Ps 87:1, that is the most holy Church, which he desired for a dwelling place for himself, he who said, 'I will dwell, what I have desired' Ps 131:14.
comments.selected_reason: Explains which Zion is meant by "my rest for ever".
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord dwells with us where one faith and true piety are proclaimed, which is what "here" means.
comments.comment: … For in this way we believe that the Lord will dwell with us, as he says, "I will dwell in them and walk among them" (2 Corinthians 6:16), and, "Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her" (Psalm 132:14). And where is "here," except where one faith and true piety are proclaimed?
comments.selected_reason: Explains where the Lord's dwelling is.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God blesses the poor and fills them with bread, so that each, being the seed of the righteous, is not diminished.
comments.comment: Another text instead of 'the widow' says 'the huntress' and says: 'The unprotected and the brave guardian they do not have, I will bless all the poor to whom he provides an abundance of bread,' he says, 'I will fill her poor with bread' Ps 131:15, since each of such poor people, being the seed of the righteous, is not diminished by bread.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Beyond the earlier gifts of food and priestly salvation, which later failed, God brings the horn of David, a lamp whose light reaches the whole world.
comments.comment: To the earlier and brief gifts he brings the greatest one, which preserves all of them. For from the beginning he gave an abundance of food, which one translator calls "prey" and another renders as "grain." And he promises to make the inhabitants free from want. Concerning priests and holy ones he has made a decree that they be saved and attend to the sacred hymns. But when all these things had already been corrupted—the nation unable to enjoy the good things of the land because it had fallen under the power of the Romans, the priesthood failing, and all the joy in the temple dissolved—the great power arose there, the horn of David, which gores every power of enemies, a beautiful lamp shining with heavenly light for David and for his offspring, who, having begun there, sends out his radiance to the whole world, as the prophet Simeon says: "A light for revelation to the nations and for glory to your people Israel."
comments.selected_reason: Explains the horn and the lamp in terms of Christ's light.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The priests are clothed with salvation, which is Christ, who came to seek and save the lost.
comments.comment: 'I will clothe the priests of this Zion with salvation' (Psalm 132:16). Christ has come as salvation for all, to seek and to save the lost (Lk 19:10). Regarding the presence of salvation and the clothing of it, it is written: 'Let my soul rejoice, for you have clothed me with a garment of salvation; they shall rejoice, and those who are holy of him shall rejoice in divine joy' (Isaiah 61:10).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what clothing the priests with salvation means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The horn is the kingdom raised up by God in David's house, and John was the lamp prepared for Christ.
comments.comment: There, in Zion, I will cause a horn to rise up for David (Ps 132:17). This horn of the kingdom is raised up by God in the house of David, according to what was said by the righteous: 'Raise up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David' (Ps 132:17).… And John, until the law and the prophets, is a lamp being prepared for his own Christ, concerning that Savior. There is that lamp which is kindled and shines: 'Did you not desire to rejoice at the right hour in his light?'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: John the Baptist was a lamp going before Christ, as God the Father foretold.
comments.comment: … Or do you not know that for those under the law in Judea the inspired Baptist was a kind of lamp going before Christ, and that God the Father spoke of him beforehand: ‘I have prepared a lamp for my Christ’ (Psalm 132:17)? The Savior himself also bore witness to this, saying of him to the teachers of the Jews: ‘He was the lamp that burns and shines, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light’ (John 5:35).
comments.selected_reason: Says who the lamp prepared for the anointed is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: His enemies will be clothed in shame, while holiness blossoms upon Christ, the flower from the root and the flower of the field.
comments.comment: These things being theologized concerning the one who came from the seed of David according to the flesh, his enemies shall clothe themselves in shame… Therefore also upon him his holiness shall blossom, as it is said in Isaiah: 'And a flower shall ascend from the root' (Isa 11:1)… For this blossoming sanctifies those passing by it, which is the very holiness of God, a flower, or rather to say, 'I am a flower of the field, a judge of the valleys' (Song of Solomon 2:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Unity is what is good and pleasant, since the Church is our house.
comments.comment: … For what is so "good," as the Psalmist said, or what is "pleasant," except "for brothers to dwell together in unity" (Psalm 133:1)? Our house is the Church, and our mind should be the same.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the good and pleasant dwelling together as unity of mind in the Church.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the head, so the ointment on him flows down to his body, the church.
comments.comment: …  Therefore, since Christ is “the head of the church” (Ephesians 5:23), so that Christ and the church are one body, “the ointment upon the head” has come down “upon the beard,” the marks of the full-grown man, the beard “of Aaron”; and this “ointment,” “coming down,” has reached “to the hem of his garment” (Psalm 133:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the ointment, the head and the beard as Christ and his body.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Aaron's beard is a symbol of manhood, and the oil of Christ's name descends from the priestly head to those who have grown into manhood.
comments.comment: … The beard is a symbol of manhood. The oil descends from the beard of Aaron onto the shoulder of his garment (Psalm 133:2; LXX 132:2). Aaron represents the shadow of priesthood. His head, the original, is filled with the divine oil of the name of Christ, regarding which it is said, 'Myrrh, your name.' This oil descends upon the beard of each who is able to say, after surpassing the shadow, 'I have become a man,' opposing the infant. Such a man becomes an imitator having become like Him, regarding which it is written, 'Behold, a man, whose name is Dawn, and a man comes after me' (Zechariah 6:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The oil descends only on the high priest's beard and garment, which is the Lord's body, and the mountains of Zion are the Church's high doctrines.
comments.comment: However, even if the oil descends upon Aaron's head, it does not descend upon a random beard but upon the high-priestly one, and from there onto the shoulder of the high-priestly garment. Aaron's tunic does not merely bear a type, for it is the Lord's body, born of the Holy Spirit, according to what was said concerning the Virgin: 'For that which was born in her is of the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 1:20). Regarding the mountains of Zion, you shall perceive the divine and universal Church, which is the high doctrines of truth, the ornaments of the soul, having seized the being of Mount Zion (Psalm 133:3; LXX 132:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dew from heaven makes clear that the gift is heavenly and not human, given only from above.
comments.comment: The ointment was also a parable of a divine matter, but what comes from God is made more evident by the parable of the dew that comes down from heaven upon the mountains. For the gift and the good are heavenly, not human, and do not appear among human beings apart from the gift from above.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the ointment and the dew as a gift from above.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The dew on the mountains is spiritual, coming down from the light of the one who came as light into the world.
comments.comment: Upon these mountains descends a spiritual dew, regarding which Moses said, 'And I will come down as dew' (Deuteronomy 32:2), and in the prophet, 'For the dew from you is its essence' (Isaiah 26:19). From this heavenly dew, the habitation of the blessed shall be from heaven. This spiritual dew does not descend from random clouds, but from the celestial light of the one saying, 'I have come as light into the world' (John 12:46). For this light both dews and shines from above, and makes things to become in most piercing brightness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the dew on the mountains of Zion stands for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's servants bless him by approaching him through wisdom, standing firmly in his courts, which are the God-breathed writings and the doctrines of truth.
comments.comment: All the servants of the Lord bless the Lord (Psalm 134:1; LXX 133:1), not having stepped far from Him but approaching Him through wisdom. Therefore they have stood in the court of the Lord, firmly established in Him. And they have stood in the courts of our God. The courts of God are where those who fear Him stand, the God-breathed writings and the doctrines of truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the servants are and what "the house of the Lord" means here.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm foretells the saints' hymns that will never cease, since their bodies will not tire or sleep.
comments.comment: He signals beforehand the work of hymns that will take place at the gathering together of all the saints, when neither day nor night will it cease, since sleep itself will not prevail in the power of the incorruptible and untiring bodies of that time (Psalm 134:1-2; LXX 133:1-2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the night-time blessing as unending praise.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Hymns are the end of good things and tell God's works and gifts, sung by attendants who stay near.
comments.comment: … Hymns are the end of good things, and the subject matter of hymns is the works of God, his gifts and benefits (Psalm 135:1-2; LXX 134:1-2). Those who hymn are not strangers standing far off, but attendants who remain near, just as David appointed the singers to remain for this purpose. …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms what the praise of the psalm is about and who offers it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Those who go up with songs and praise will stand in the house of the Lord with right thought and sound practice, and the courts of God are the old and new Scriptures.
comments.comment:
It is not a temple for those ascending into it to follow the songs of the ascents and praise God joyfully. Therefore also 'Alleluia' is written upon the psalm, the superscription signifying that the living God must be hymned (Psalm 135:1-3; LXX 134:1-3).

How will it not be that all those having ascended the ascents with songs and hymns will stand in the house of the Lord with right thought and unassailable practice, being His servants in the house of the Lord, and hymning Him in the courts of our God? But the courts of God are the old and new Scriptures, the theologies according to their parts, or the many dwellings in the promises in the house of the Father. And to praise first according to the introductions His name, so that they might serve the Lord and serve Him sincerely. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The chief of God's benefits is making humans his own, as he made the Hebrews his own people above all nations, though in creation he is God of all.
comments.comment: … One might say that a great benefit, and the chief of all benefits from God, is the making of humans his own, just as he made the people of the Hebrews his own and set them as exceptional for himself beyond all the nations at that time, placing them as something more and superior, inasmuch as the God of all is his own God to them in intimacy, though in creation he is God of all (Ps 134:3-4; Psalm 135:6-7; LXX 134:6-7). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words what it means that the Lord chose Jacob for himself.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Read as allegory, the clouds rising from the end of the earth are the Gospel's call to the lowest of men, and the lightnings become a rain that enlightens and waters those who ask.
comments.comment: … And toward allegory, if there are certain spiritual clouds, they signify a mental and invisible rain flowing. And these rise from the end of the earth, since the Gospel does not call those from great, rich, philosophical, oratory rulers, but from men thought to be the lowest, the unlettered and the laypeople. But He has also made the bright flashes of theories and the justices into a rain, to enlighten and to water those asking for these things in harmony with what is set forth. And He brings forth winds from their treasuries, which some signify better breaths and intellectual, transcendent natures. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wonders done for Israel are traced back to the creative power that lifts the clouds, sends lightning before rain and brings the winds from an unseen source.
comments.comment: … Remembering the wonders that happened around Israel—things not done by the nature that appeared at the beginning, but by a will beyond nature, some heavenly, such as fire and hail and darkness, some earthly, such as frogs and locusts and gnats and the punishing power against the firstborn, and some done in the sea and the deep, such as the things at the Red Sea—he brings them back to the creative authority, joining these to those as having come from the same power, saying that he is the one who once for all lifts up clouds from the ends of the earth and flashes forth lightnings as the prelude of rains and sends out winds from an unseen source (Psalm 135:7). They are not known where they are before they blow. He says that the unseen and unknown origin of the winds is God's treasury, the winds being understood to be stored away somewhere continually, as in the treasuries of bodies. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the psalm joins the plagues in Egypt to God's rule over weather and creation.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The wonders made God known to all the earth and, through memory, to all time.
comments.comment: … He indicates that the wonders did not happen for Israel alone, but for the knowledge of God through all the earth and all time—not only while the works were being done was the doer known, but also afterward through memory. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The memorial belongs to the former generation of the Hebrews as a type of the calling of the Gentiles, and God has mercy on His people because He grants the appeal of His servants.
comments.comment: … This memorial is from the former generation of the Hebrews as a generation of the calling of the Gentiles, concerning which it is written, 'The coming generation shall declare to the Lord' (Psalm 135:13-14; LXX 134:13b-14). And these things shall remain, as God has mercy on His people and calls upon His servants. For having responded to the intercession and the appeal of His servants on behalf of the people and themselves, being sent up, He was comforted, that is, He granted the appeal. Therefore also He has mercy on His people. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To shame the falsely named gods the psalm calls them idols, shown false by their material, their human workmanship and the lack of any spirit of life in them.
comments.comment: … Above, then, he called them gods according to the custom of the nations, though they are not gods. Now, to shame the falsely named gods, he calls them idols, discrediting them by the material, because they are silver and gold, and by the workmanship, because they are made by humans, and by the lifelessness along with the vanity of the likeness of souls, because there is no spirit of life in them. All these things carry the open discredit of the worship and the open refutation of the demons, that those whose likenesses are such things are not gods. For the likeness of God is divine; therefore the human being who is an image is the divine one, not the one deprived of the Godhead. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the psalm mocks idols.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Lord is blessed from the heavenly Zion, the city of God, and the soul with knowledge and perfect virtue may also be called Zion and Jerusalem.
comments.comment:
… 

But those previously mentioned do not merely bless, but he is also blessed, not from a chance place but from the heavenly Zion, dwelling in the city of God, who gives the heavenly Jerusalem and the church which has no house or wrinkle, unlike Jerusalem, to see the peace which Jesus gives, saying, 'My peace I give to you' (John 14:27). But even if he is blessed in Zion by another thought, God is not thus in it and from it. Let these things also be said concerning the soul through knowledge and perfect virtue, being called Zion and Jerusalem. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every verse carries the refrain 'For his mercy is unto the ages' because God always has mercy and never has none.
comments.comment: … The present psalm, being called forth for thanksgiving, commands to confess to the Lord, who does much in kindness and goodness (Psalm 136:1-3; LXX 135:1-3). Therefore, in every verse, a hymn-like phrase is selected: 'For his mercy is unto the ages.' For since he neither ever has mercy nor ever does not, but always has mercy, it is fitting that those who hymn say, 'For his mercy is unto the ages.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the same refrain closes every verse of the psalm.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those called gods are such only by taking part in divinity, but the Savior is God by essence and so makes gods of those who partake of him.
comments.comment:
… Of what gods is he, concerning whom it is said? If he is not God to them, then the Word of God did not become toward them according to the scripture saying, 'I am God'. For this one truly it is fitting to be called God; so do not worry even about those who are called gods around Abraham (Exodus 3:6; 'God of Abraham, and God of Isaac, and God of Jacob'; for this one truly it is fitting to be called God). According to this, the meaning of divinity and angels and divine powers is said to be 'gods,' as the apostle says, 'As there are many gods and many lords in heaven and on earth' (1 Cor 8:6), so all those called gods with the Trinity are such by participation of divinity.

But the Savior is not thus, but is God by essence; therefore he makes gods of those who partake of him. He has been said to be the only-begotten God; for he himself alone is the true God from the true God, being God according to the same nature as the Father, being consubstantial with the one who begets him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words 'God of gods' and 'Lord of lords' show that the Scripture knows of gods and lords, some so called and others truly such, as Paul also teaches.
comments.comment: Such, too, are the things that the divine words teach us to examine and to hold about the Lord and lords. In one place they say: “Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy is for ever; give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is for ever” (Psalm 136:2–3); in another, that God is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Timothy 6:15). The word knows of gods, some of whom are so called, while others actually are gods, whether they are so called or not. Paul teaches the same about lords too, both those who are and those who are not, when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'God of gods' and 'Lord of lords' mean in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: He who is God of gods and Lord of lords alone does wonders, and the heavens are made firm in understanding and the earth is strengthened upon the water to bear fruit.
comments.comment: If he is God of gods and Lord of lords, he is of those in heaven and on earth having a relationship to the holy principalities and powers and lordships (Psalm 136:2-6). For it was written that he alone does wonderful things; for the Father, remaining in the Son, does the works. But also, while making the heavens in understanding and strengthening the earth upon the water, it must be confessed again. And what is set forth agrees: God in wisdom founded the earth, and prepared the heavens in prudence. Understanding and prudence are through which the heavens are prepared and strengthened; who is like the wisdom through which all things came to be, concerning which the theologian says Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God. For also those bearing the image of the heavenly become intelligibles, being heavens. Such things are prepared in the revealed understanding and prudence of God. And the earth is strengthened upon the water, receiving the seed cast under Jesus in order to bear fruit. For in the flowing and temporary things of life, they allegorically strengthen and provide firmness upon the water to bear fruit most fully (Psalm 136:5-6). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God made the sun to rule the day and the moon and stars the night, and these serve the order and the very life of man.
comments.comment: … Having made great lights alone, by saying: 'Let there be lights in the expanse of the heaven'; he arranged the sun for the dominion of the day and the moon and the stars for the dominion of the night, just as it is said in the creation to have become the sun for the beginnings of the day and the moon for the beginnings of the night and the stars. And these things contribute not a little to us for the order of life and for life itself: the elements nourishing fruits, without which one cannot live; showing us seasons, marking hours, representing the courses of day and night, guiding the travelers of earth and sea, providing ten thousand other uses. If you see how unto the age is his mercy (Psalm 136:7-9). …
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain words what the lights are for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sun and stars rule the day and night without making them, since day and night are older than the lights, and the sun brings day by dissolving the darkness.
comments.comment: … But let them be, Scripture says, also for days—not so as to make days, but so as to rule over the days. For day and night are older than the creation of the lights. The psalm shows us this when it says: He set the sun for authority over the day, the moon and stars for authority over the night (Psalm 135:8-9 LXX; Hebrew 136:8-9). How then does the sun have authority over the day? Because it carries light in itself, and whenever it rises above our horizon, it provides day by dissolving the darkness. So no one would go wrong in defining day as the air illuminated by the sun, or in defining day as a measure of time in which the sun spends its course in the hemisphere above the earth. …
comments.selected_reason: Clears up what it means that the sun and moon 'rule' day and night.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Read allegorically, the firstborn of Egypt are struck down for Israel's benefit, and God leads the mind that sees Him out through His word and wisdom, His arm and mighty hand.
comments.comment: … Regarding what belongs to the tropical Egypt while the world exists around the earth, these things, appearing to be firstborn, are struck down by God for the benefit of Israel. For when these are struck down, the mind seeing God is led out from it by God. And God leads Israel out from the middle of the allegorically called Egypt through His word and His wisdom, which is named His arm and His mighty hand. And these things are said concerning Christ, since according to the Epistle of Jude, Jesus is the one who saved the people out of Egypt. A mighty hand and a high arm should be said to express His paradoxical energy and power. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God divided the Red Sea so each tribe had its own way through, and for the mind life is a sea of passions through which the word of God makes a dry way.
comments.comment:
… God divided the Red Sea into not one division but into many, so that it might be driven out from the middle of it by God, while Israel walked as on dry land (Psalm 136:13; LXX 135:13–15). It is given into twelve divisions according to the twelve ways, so that each tribe of Israel might have its own passage to pass through.

And these things are indeed according to the literal sense; but for the intellect, the life of man is often like a sea placed before us, filled with waves and much saltiness and turbulence, yet the word of God provides us a way through, rising up and piercing the storms laid upon us from passions, so that we might have a way through once the moisture of all those passions has been dried up by God, while the intelligible Pharaoh and all that from demons and unclean spirits are being sunk in it, his power being fulfilled as if he were scattering them like the most worthless dust into the sea of God. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives the literal sense of the crossing and then what it means for the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Babylon is read as a symbol of what shames those who do evil, so its king is struck down with the king of the Amorites and the land is given to Israel to inherit.
comments.comment: … But also, since Babylon is interpreted as a symbol of that which brings shame upon those doing evil, accordingly the king of this Babylon will be struck and killed along with the king of Zion among the Amorites, so that the land may be given to Israel. They ruled it badly through sophistry and through a wearying life, meddling in the nature of things and appearing to rule it; but their interpreted land being taken away, it is given as a possession to Israel to inherit it, becoming a true servant of the cause of all things. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The feeding in the desert and the fall of the Amorite kings show God's mercy, for he gave their land to the Hebrews once the Canaanites had come to the fullness of their sins.
comments.comment: … No less than the subduing of those who warred against them, the feeding in the desert and the guiding of them without want, and the destruction of the kings of the Amorites, he sets down as a demonstration of God's mercy, who gave their land to the Hebrews as a good land to dwell in (Psalm 136:16-22; LXX 135:16, 22). And this was the treasuring up for the righteous of the wealth of the impious. For they would not have perished otherwise, had they not come to the fullness of their sins, as God said to Abraham. And Moses says that Israel did not take possession of their land because of his own righteousness, but because of their lawlessness and because of God's love for the fathers. So against those the destructive judgment was just, while toward these the beneficent gift was loving, and the piety of the fathers became a preparation for sharing in that love. For in this way the things from God are shown forth justly and well and fittingly for the world. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In 'food to all flesh', 'flesh' means all mortal creatures that live by being fed.
comments.comment: … The term 'flesh' being homonymous signifies many things, as it stands for the God-breathed writing itself. For when it is said in the Psalms, 'To give food to God to all flesh' (Psalm 136:25), it stands for all mortal animals being sustained by food in living, as also in: 'All flesh is gathered according to its kind'. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the people of Jerusalem grieved God they fell under the Babylonians, and singing sweet hymns in the ears of foreigners seemed shameful, so they wept and hung up their instruments.
comments.comment: … For when those who lived in the holy city, I mean Jerusalem, dared through the running-away toward anything out of place to grieve the Savior God of all, they came under the hand of the Babylonians, who, having taken them as captives of the spear, commanded them to serve (2 Kings 25:1–11). For it was a necessity to yield to those who ruled, even them not willing.  …  But it seemed somehow shameful to those who wished to strike up and to fulfill the customary things, to love to put so sweet a sound into the ears of the foreigners, and already as it were to throw into the air the melody most sweet and most clear to themselves, the Babylonians sometimes smiling down, and being wholly burdened at the songs through instruments. That is why they also said: 'By the rivers of Babylon there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion' (Psalm 137:1); in which, according to the laws and customs of the Jews, the sacrifice of praise was brought with strings and instruments being completed, and charming with the songs those who came to the divine temple. And when they were bound tight in a stranger's yoke of slavery, lamenting they say: 'On the willows in the midst of it we hung our instruments.'
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: The captives are in a desert like prisoners taken from their cities, and hang up their instruments.
comments.comment: … He makes clear that they will be in a desert, like the condition of captives after their removal from their own cities (Psalm 137:1-2; LXX 136:1, 2). For this is what it means: "On the willows we hung up our instruments" (Psalm 137:2; LXX 136:2). …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Captives carried off to Babylon would not hymn God even when asked, but hung up their instruments and wept by the rivers.
comments.comment: … Enemies, we are told, once came against a great and holy city in which God was worshipped, and dragged off its inhabitants as captives, singers of hymns and those who spoke of God, to their own country, which was Babylon. And those who were carried there were not willing to hymn God, even when their masters asked them (Psalm 137:3), or to sing psalms in a profane land. Instead, now idle, they hung their musical instruments on the willows, and they themselves wept by the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137:1–2). …
comments.selected_reason: Tells the setting of the verses in plain words.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The captives' hanging of instruments on the fruitless willows and their captors' plural 'songs' are read as a broken, discordant song, whereas Zion's song is one.
comments.comment:
… Having said, 'Sing to us a hymn from the songs of Zion,' they were mocking. They said, 'Even upon the rivers of Babylon there we sat and wept' (Ps 137:1). 'Having reached Babylon and its unstable currents called rivers, we sat; we no longer desired to depart, taking memory of their own fatherland. This happened by us remembering Zion; we no longer desired to depart before Babylon.'

Then he says, 'Upon the willows in the midst of it we hung our instruments' (Ps 137:2), the musical instruments, the instruments of the new song. And the willows are a plant that is fruitless, deceiving men. They say that if its flower is rubbed into water and drunk, it makes the castrated ones lustful. For this reason the poet said the willows are 'fruitless,' because they castrate the men in a certain way. The instruments, therefore, that is, the bodies, were hanging from the willows, the branches of impurity.

Then they, as if performing a circumcision, were saying, 'Sing to us a hymn from the songs of Zion,' saying 'songs' in the plural more insolently. For one song is that of Zion and one hymn; for it is said, 'O God, I will sing to you a new song' (Psalm 144:9), one song. These, therefore, since the discordant one makes many songs, are saying this in a broken way; it is said discordantly, 'Sing to us a hymn from your songs' (Ps 137:3).

Then they, knowing that they are saying the songs in the plural badly, say: 'How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?' (Ps 137:4). 'In a foreign land we are yours' (Ps 137:4). So it is a broken song and a thing to be blamed. And if he says, 'with the singing not to be allowed,' it signifies a broken song, a psalm not being properly brought forth. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The willow is fruitless, so hanging the instruments on it shows the songs lay idle, and under a foreign yoke outside the holy land they thought it fitting no longer to sacrifice.
comments.comment: … marking by this very thing that they were idle in songs. For the willow is a fruitless plant, or rather a fruit-destroying one; for it is said so by the poets among the Greeks. The instruments of song were then laid up toward idleness and fruitlessness; and crying out the occasion of this ease they say: 'How shall we sing the Lord's song on a foreign land?' (Psalm 137:4) … For they thought it fitting for themselves no longer to sacrifice, being housed outside a holy land, and acting for the time no longer under God, but yoked as it were to another and having fallen under the tyrannical hand; yet to those who still lived in the holy city, and had obtained the glory of the holy liturgy, they assign the worship, using, clearly, a right reasoning toward the examination of what is fitting and needed. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: In spiritual worship a foreign land is a foreign soul, and they guarded against carrying the divine things into it, as Christ says not to give what is holy to dogs.
comments.comment: … And according to the spiritual worship, they considered the foreign souls a foreign land, and they guarded against bringing out the divine things among them, as things being moved from their own place into a foreign one, as the divine mouth of Christ says: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before the pigs." Such was Herod, who wanted to see the signs of Christ, not seeking this for reverence but for pleasant spectacle, and therefore he did not obtain it.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: He will not treat another land as equal to Jerusalem or the profane as equal to the holy, so they prayed toward Jerusalem, and remembering the holy city is the highest gladness.
comments.comment:
"I will not use another land like you, O Jerusalem," he says, "nor will I place the unclean on an equal footing with the clean, nor will I consider the profane as comparable to the holy; but even when I am outside your dwelling, your longing will approach me (Psalm 137:4-5; LXX 136:4, 5). And whenever I might depart from this, all my strength would depart as well." For this reason they also made their prayers while looking toward Jerusalem, and they received the power of their prayers there, according to the prayers of Solomon and the divine promises—just as it is necessary for us to look toward the heavenly Jerusalem (Psalm 137:6; LXX 136:6).

For it is not just for the instrument of words to be vigorous when it is not directed toward what it ought to be. Therefore the blessed men devoted their whole life to the care of hymns, saying, "I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will psalm to my God as long as I exist" (Psalm 145:2 (146:2)) (Psalm 104:33; LXX 103:33). And the city was precious to them because of the worship of God established in it, just as it was said before: "For the sake of the house of my God I sought good things for you" (Psalm 121:9 (122:9)).

For the highest and purest gladness is placed in remembering the holy city. In this way the gladnesses that follow will also be good, just as the Lord introduces the sacred foods to us before the common and bodily ones. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms the singer's loyalty to Jerusalem in a strange land.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Edomites, brothers and neighbors of Israel, kept the ancestral hate, and the evils foretold for them are those David asks the Lord to remember.
comments.comment: The word is toward those from Edom and Esau the brother of Jacob, foretelling an excess of evils for them (for this is the “you will be drunk and you will pour out” (Lamentations 4:21)), about whom David also says: “remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, those saying: empty, empty, until the foundation in it.” (Psalm 137:7) For being brothers and neighbors, they preserved the ancestral hate. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What is prayed for is the just judgment that repays the Babylonians as they acted, and the infants dashed on the rock are the seeds of wickedness crushed by Christ the rock.
comments.comment: … The just thing is what they pray the Babylonians receive, namely what they have done (Ps 137:8). For this is the holy judgment according to the words, "The Lord is known as making judgments; in the works of his hands the sinner was caught" (Psalm 9:17 (9:16)). He declares blessed the one who will be able to do this, through whom God reveals the just judgment and turns plundering back upon those who plundered, and killing back upon those who killed. For the ministry belongs to God, and blessed is the one who ministers to God. But it must also be accompanied by knowledge and one's own deliberate choice. So he does not bless Cyrus, the king of the Persians, who conquered the Babylonians, because Cyrus did not know for whose sake he was receiving the strength against them, nor did he know the God who gave it—"For you did not know me," he says (Isaiah 45:4)—nor did he understand that he was being advanced to power for the release of Israel, as the prophecies through Isaiah have it. Rather, the declaration of blessedness will turn to those who repay Babylon in kind, and upon the one who dashes her infants against the rock and kills them. For truly, the first blessedness was never to have seen Babylon at all, nor to have been in the confusion of her evils. But if someone once found himself in her, having fallen away from better things, he would still be blessed if he should do what he suffered, and should take the Babylonians captive in return, and should lead the very souls of the Babylonians to the fear of God. And if he should not allow their infants to grow up but should crush them against the rock, he would be more blessed than many. You would not be wrong to say that the infants of Babylon are the seeds of wickedness and the beginnings of sins of confusion, which the one who is blessed in these things will be eager to destroy by the saving Word—for the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4)—so that they do not grow or proceed to deeds. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains both the justice of the prayer and how the harsh closing verse can be read.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The infants of Babylon, which means 'confusion', are confusing thoughts newly arising from wickedness, and the one who dashes them against the rock of the word is blessed.
comments.comment: … So too we understand the text in the hundred and thirty-sixth psalm, which runs thus: “O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the recompense with which you repaid us; blessed is he who will seize your infants and dash them against the rock” (Psalm 137:8–9). For the “infants of Babylon”, a name that is interpreted “confusion”, are the confusing thoughts arising from wickedness that have just sprung up and are rising in the soul. The man who seizes them, so as to break their heads against the firmness and strength of the word, dashes “the infants” of “Babylon” “against the rock”, and for this reason becomes “blessed”. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: After the prayer for Israel comes thanksgiving, because the Word's manifestation has spread the worship of God from one nation to the whole world while keeping the promises to Israel.
comments.comment: So the arrangement of these songs followed the same order. After the prayer for Israel came thanksgiving, and hymns were proclaimed beforehand, and acts of worship toward God. For by his mercy and truth, because of the glory of the word of God above every name of his—that is, what has now been accomplished—God is glorified in the name of the Word as he was never glorified before. Before the manifestation of the Word, the worship of God occupied only a portion of the earth. He was hymned as maker of all things, and he was proclaimed as the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, but all of this had its knowledge and honor only as far as the Hebrew nation. But when his living oracle appeared, coming forth from God and revealed to the world through a body, then every nation and the whole inhabited world runs together to the worship of God, serves the name of the Word, and glorifies God in the presence of the Word. Now worship has increased among the nations according to mercy, and it is preserved for Israel according to the truth of the promises. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the move from lament to thanksgiving and what the glory of the word means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The singer confesses on God's mercy and truth, which rescued him and keep him from wandering, and worships because God's word is magnified in him until every tongue confesses Christ.
comments.comment:
… Let my confession be upon your mercy and your truth, since, having been often shown mercy and having seen the truth which was enlightened in me by you, I was rescued from all evil and from its related deception, you providing remission of sins through your mercy and keeping me from all wandering through your truth. …

But since you have magnified the word given to me by you, depending on it through your presence as if it were your own wealth, I will worship toward your holy temple and I will confess your name, giving thanks that your word is being magnified in me; for then it is magnified in me, and since I am progressing by it, I hasten toward its perfection. …

When is this fulfilled? When every knee shall bow in the name of Jesus, both heavenly and earthly and under the earth, every tongue confessing what the Lord Jesus Christ is, to the glory of God the Father, announcing to his brothers who have come to be the Son's likeness the greatness of the Father's presence; for he has not come alone in the name of the Father, so that the holy name of God might be magnified above all. We learn to say in prayer, 'Hallowed be your name.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse shows God's favor and the power given to souls who ask in Christ's name.
comments.comment: … He shows the great favor and the swift obedience, and the supply of power given to souls in the name of Christ (Psalm 138:3; LXX 137:3). For Christ says, "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:14). And the apostle says that the supply of the Spirit comes to those who believe. …
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse to prayer answered in plain terms.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one who prays unceasingly, by spirit and mind, has God as a listener each day and a guardian who does not delay or despise him.
comments.comment: … The one who prays unceasingly and performs this by spirit and mind: 'I will pray, saying, by spirit, and I will pray also by the mind,' having God as a listener on each day, concerning whom it has been written, 'and the ears of the Lord are toward the righteous, and to their supplication' (Psalm 34:15). For one possesses God as a guardian who does not delay nor despise him, but watches over him in his provident power. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of God's mouth call the peoples, and the verse puts 'kings' where 'peoples' stood, for those who confess the Lord are called to reign as a royal priesthood.
comments.comment:
… Because of setting the mind on earthly things and seeking the lower and temporal things, making a profit, the peoples of the earth—about which the prophecy says here—the reason for wanting all the words of your mouth that you spoke in the law and in the prophets concerning their calling is this: for even if they are not hearers of your oracles, it is not by their power that their faith was foreknown. Therefore also I desire to reach them with diligent and musical recitation in your ways, namely, the Scriptures, so that one traveling through them by continuous study and reading might diligently proclaim the meanings from them. …

All these things shall be made perfect, since also the glory of the Lord which performs these things is great, concerning which it is said toward Jerusalem: 'And the glory of the Lord has risen upon you, and all flesh shall see the salvation of our God' (Isaiah 60:1), since the glory of the Lord shall be seen. And who then is this, the savior, being a radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his hypostasis? It is brought here instead of 'Peoples' as 'Kings': 'Let all the kings of the earth confess to you, O Lord' (Psalm 138:4). And both expressions have harmony with the concept of being called to reign, the peoples confessing to the Lord being set as a royal priesthood and a holy nation (Ex 19:6); and toward some of them it is written, 'And you have reigned, so that we also may reign with you' (1 Corinthians 4:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's greatness is shown through his providence, as the seraphim hymned it when they cried that the whole earth is full of his glory.
comments.comment: … Let the providence of God be hymned, because God is great and his greatness is revealed through providence. Just as through the seraphim the glory of God in his present providence and economy was hymned when they cried out, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory" (Isaiah 6:3) (Psalm 138:5; LXX 137:5; Ps 137:6). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'great is the glory of the LORD' refers to.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The nations, once the more dishonored part, are not overlooked, for all things are lowly before God, so he extends his benefits even to the smallest.
comments.comment: … Because, he says, the human creation enjoys the gift of God, and the lesser and formerly more dishonored part of it—the nations—is not now overlooked either. For to God all things are lowly, even the highest, so that these too are known by him from afar, because they cannot draw near to the unapproachable height of God. Since all things are small before God, it is no wonder if he extends his benefits even to the smallest—that is, to those who had no hope and were without God in the world, whom the apostle calls "those who are not" (1 Corinthians 1:28). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the LORD 'hath respect unto the lowly' in plain words.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The high Lord sees someone among the lowly and does not know him as one far away.
comments.comment: … Even if the High Lord sees someone among the lowly, He is high to the heavenly and is of a nature that has ascended far above, but He does not only know these things from a distance as being far from Him by a change of existence. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalm turns to Israel, caught in afflictions but to be restored, and God will repay on behalf of the wronged nation and rescue it from its oppressors.
comments.comment: … He brings in the second part, the portion of Israel, which has been caught up in afflictions but will be restored to salvation. Through this your enemies are struck by God, and they themselves will obtain salvation from God. "The Lord will repay on my behalf." For he will repay on behalf of the wronged nation, so as to rescue them from the hands of those who oppress them (Psalm 138:8; LXX 137:8c). …
comments.selected_reason: Says whom the verses on trouble and the right hand concern.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: We ask not to be overlooked, since we are his works.
comments.comment: … Even if, he says, we do not produce fruits worthy of your love, yet because we are your works, we ask not to be overlooked (Psalm 138:8; LXX 137:8c). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plea 'forsake not the works of thine own hands'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God does not come to know my thoughts when I reason, for he foreknows things and so also thoughts.
comments.comment: … Similar to this is what is said by David: 'Lord, you have tested me and known me; you knew my seat and my rising; you understood all my thoughts from afar' (Psalm 139:2). For it is not that when I reason, you come to know my thoughts, but rather you exist as a foreknower of things, and so also of thoughts. …
comments.selected_reason: Says clearly what it means that God understands my thought from afar.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist, thinking of God as holding both beginnings and ends, says the Lord has made all things, the ends and the ancient.
comments.comment: … And the boundaries of the world are also called 'ends'; as it has been said: 'An infinite ocean and the worlds with it are driven by the same reins of the Master'. The psalmist, having a concept of God as encompassing both the beginnings and the ends and altogether all things happening under him, was saying: 'Behold, You, Lord, have made all things, the ends and the ancient' (Psalm 139:5). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's knowledge of all things about me goes with his forming me from clay, and he laid his hand on me not only to make me but to improve, guard and lift me.
comments.comment:
… And it is nothing wonderful if He knew all things concerning me, He says (Psalm 139:5; LXX 138:5); for knowing all things, He does not merely observe them, but also the beginnings and the ends of them, and the causes by which they came to be, and what will be about them after the cosmic variety. Having formed me possessing the knowledge of all things, You placed Your hand upon me, which is said first. Having placed Your hand upon me, and having formed me from dust and clay as a man, it is as if one of the wise said this: 'Your hands made me and formed me,' and likewise, 'Remember what clay You formed me from.'

And it is also not so; having formed me, You were not satisfied with having made me, but You also placed Your hand upon me in order to improve and guard me and to lift me up by it. Therefore, let him who understands this gift and advises others be careful, saying, 'Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that He may lift you up in due time' (1 Pet 5:6), so that, being secured by it, you may not have any insolence or scheme occur. For no one snatches from the hand of the Father; for the invisible enemies only tear apart those who have been cast away from it. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'laid thine hand upon me' means: God formed and then keeps the one he made.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse sets soul and body together under one formation, for God knows the soul's properties from its forming and the work is not divided.
comments.comment: … Here he appears to place soul and body together as one, arranging both under a single formation, because he says that God has knowledge of the soul's properties from its formation (Psalm 139:5; LXX 138:5). Just as another has said, "He who formed the spirit of man within him" (Zechariah 12:1). For the work is not divided. Even if the making of the soul is more beautiful than that of the body, it is not as if made by hands according to the shaping of matter, but inspired according to its subsistence from divine power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Soul and body are brought together into one, sharing a single name, and the apostle includes the body in calling the man the image of God.
comments.comment: At any rate, he [the psalmist] brings both [soul and body] together into one, just as they also share a single name, the combined thing being called sometimes soul and sometimes flesh. So too when the apostle calls the man the image of God because of the inbreathing that came to him from God and did not come upon the woman, he clearly includes the body together with the soul, insofar as the male is distinguished from the female. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Knowing oneself is hardest, yet it teaches God's wisdom as heaven and earth do, so knowing myself taught me his greatness.
comments.comment: … For truly it seems to be the most difficult thing of all to know oneself. … And yet it is no more possible to know God from heaven and earth than from our own constitution, at least for the one who examines himself intelligently. As the prophet says, 'Your knowledge became wonderful from me' (Psalm 138:6 (LXX; Hebrew 139:6))—that is, by learning to know myself, I was taught the surpassing greatness of the wisdom in you. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words why knowledge of God is 'too wonderful' and how self-knowledge leads to it.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Because God's judgments are deep, even David, to whom the hidden things of wisdom were revealed, cannot reach his knowledge, as Ecclesiastes also says of wisdom.
comments.comment: … For because the judgments of God have deep knowledge, the blessed David teaches, to whom 'the obscure and the hidden things of wisdom' are revealed, saying: 'Your knowledge has been marveled at beyond me; it has been strengthened, I am not able toward it.' (Ps 139:6) And another says concerning wisdom: 'I said, I will act wisely, and it was removed far from me beyond what it was. And a deep depth: who will find it?' (Ecclesiastes 7:23-24) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Having understood God's knowledge of all things, the singer marvels and cannot reach it, as Ecclesiastes and Paul also say of the depth of God's wisdom.
comments.comment:
