… Having understood how You have knowledge of all things, I have come to a marvel. But even if, having understood, I marveled at Your knowledge, it is not that my will understands it on my behalf, having been made by You.

It has been strengthened so that I might not be able to reach it. This is consistent with what is in Ecclesiastes: 'I said, I will be wise, but wisdom has departed from me, and it was made far from me, beyond my reach; who can find it?' (Ecclesiastes 7:23-24). And also Paul left the same voices, saying: 'O the depth of the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable are his ways!' (Rom 11:33). And he himself says this, since he is not able to reach the knowledge of God having been strengthened beyond him. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is present in heaven, in Hades and in the sea, not dwelling in any place but entering into all things by his creative and providential care.
comments.comment:
… He indeed says toward the one being theologized about: 'If your spirit has filled the inhabited world, where shall I go from it? But since your face also observes and looks upon all things, where shall I flee from it? For ascending into heaven, with you present, I receive a vision; if I become in Hades, I see you present' (Psalm 139:7; LXX 138:7-12). And if in heaven and in Hades your presence is known, and in the intermediate places it is evident that you are there; 'Do I not fill the heaven and the earth?' says the Lord, as the prophet says (Jer 23:24). But also in the sea itself, he manifests himself to those seeking him, as the following word presents.

Therefore also, one of the theologians says to one of those listening: 'And he shall know by intellect what God is in the heaven above and on the earth below, and there is nothing besides Him.' But He presents Himself everywhere, not locally dwelling, but creatively and providentially entering into all things. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: David's 'Where shall I go from your Spirit?' shows the Spirit exists and fills all things, as the face and right hand of God do, and God says the same of himself and his Spirit.
comments.comment: … “For where shall I go from your Spirit?” says David (Psalm 138:7 (Hebrew 139:7)), since clearly he exists, and fills all things, and stands in divine dignity. For what he said about the Spirit, he also says about the face of God and about his right hand, saying next: “And from your face where shall I flee? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend to Hades, you are present; if I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Psalm 138:7-10 (Hebrew 139:7-10)). And the voice of God says this about himself and the Spirit: “I am in your midst, says the Lord, and my Spirit stands in the midst of you” (Haggai 2:5). …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Jonah, who fled to the sea, found God's power at work in the waves and the sea-monster, which received him and kept him safe without corruption.
comments.comment: … This is just what appeared in the case of Jonah, when he fled to the sea and found God's power at work both in the movement of the waters, stirring up waves, and in the nature of the creatures: the sea-monster received him and did not crush him, and he was kept safe inside the sea-monster and suffered no corruption (Psalm 139:9-10; LXX 138:9-10). …
comments.selected_reason: A concrete example of the hand that leads even at the uttermost parts of the sea.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God is not in a place but moves through and exists in all things by his creative and providential presence, so no distance takes the singer from his spirit.
comments.comment: … Therefore, God is not in a place; for if he is everywhere, not passing from one place to another, nor being limited by each one, nor being circumscribed by all the places, it is evident that by a creative and providential presence he moves through all, upon all, through all, and exists in all, according to apostolic philosophy (Psalm 139:9-10; LXX 138:9-10). 'I searched,' he says, 'whether by using the wings of thought I might have become far beyond the sea and the ocean itself at the ends, whether I would be able to go from your spirit and flee from your face, and there also to have seen your active and providential hand, and that very right hand of yours surpassing, working; as this very thing, that to have dwelt with me, would be established for me in a predicted sequence at the ends of the sea, your hand guiding me and holding me with your right hand.' For even if the ocean is boundless, yet even the worlds with it are driven through by the commands of the Lord; for all things having been made toward him, whatever they ever are, are straightened for me by the commands of his own providence (Psalm 139:9-10). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Darkness cannot hinder the knowledge of God, for to men night differs from day, but to the Lord all things are lit and manifest, and he makes hidden deeds known when needed.
comments.comment: … But even beyond these things, he says something else in the 'I said: therefore darkness shall overpower me,' instead of 'hide me.' But even this, teaching again that the knowledge of God cannot be prevented, he says: 'The darkness shall not be darkness from you, and night shall be enlightened as the day' (Psalm 139:12). For to men, indeed, the night makes a difference from the day, but to you, O Lord, even these things are enlightened, instead of 'they become manifest'; which is also what the apostle makes manifest, saying: 'all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him' (Hebrews 4:13). And in Daniel it is said: 'knowing all things in the darkness, and the light is with him' (Daniel 2:22), which is our Savior, who 'enlightens every man' (John 1:9). Therefore, everything is manifest to him... and the deeds of men, those happening in secret and in darkness, he makes manifest when it is necessary. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words why darkness hides nothing from God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To God night is lit as day, and the righteous man applies this to teach those with a wrong opinion that no one can flee from God, as Cain and the sinner in Sirach wrongly thought.
comments.comment:
… For among us, those using the distinction see the difference between night and day, and those seeing in the day, but in the night they neither see nor are seen; but with God, the night is illuminated as the day, seizing for himself those in darkness and night as those in light and day, since the night is illuminated as the day by God himself.

The righteous man applies all these things to himself, having intended to teach those having wrong opinion about God that it is not possible to flee from God. For are those thinking these things about God, to say even the God himself, 'Will someone not be hidden in secret places, and I will not find him?' (Jeremiah 23:24), for God is approaching all, and I am not God from a distance. Cain has become a father of this ill-reputation, having said to God, 'If you cast me out from the face of the earth today, and from your face I will be hidden' (Gen 4:14).

And another, through surpassing foolishness, sinning in a dim and gloomy place and night, says, 'Darkness covers me from every side, and the walls cover me; who sees me?' (Sirach 23:18); 'The Most High will not remember my sins' (Sirach 23:18), saying only once, 'Since in darkness and in the midst of the gloom I sin, with no one present, I elude everyone, and even the Most High would not know my sins.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Darkness is held by choice, not by nature, so the one passing from ignorance can say night shall be as day, and God who knows my hidden things and formed me in the womb is wondered at with fear and thanks.
comments.comment:
Lest I become a son of night and darkness, having striven to be a son of darkness through whom I act and think wickedly; rather, since the darkness is not darkened by it, God who illuminates all things says: The God who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness,' who shone in the hearts of men for the illumination of the knowledge of Christ, says night shall be as day, of the one passing from ignorance and wickedness saying, 'I am not a son of darkness and night but of light and day.'

For this reason night shall be as day, since its darkness is not so, nor its light. For since darkness is held by choice and not by nature (for no one is evil by creation), so also it holds virtue; and finding no place of flight, having turned to himself, he says: It is no wonder that, having become evil, I cannot be far from you, since I have even possessed my own kidneys, God who examines kidneys and heart; for if you are a knower of my hidden things, having possessed even my kidneys, in whatever part of the world I may be, you have knowledge of my presence; for if you even took hold of me from my mother's womb, having formed me in the belly and laying your hand upon me. Since, because of all the aforementioned things, you were fearfully wondered at (for with fear I have marveled at all things concerning you), I say, turning toward thanksgiving: I will confess to you what I fearfully wondered at (Psalm 139:14-15; LXX 138:14b,15). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The kidneys, which separate out what is harmful and distribute what is useful, stand for the mind's discernment, and the saints' kidneys are the discernment they offer to God.
comments.comment: … The kidneys, again, would be a type of the activity of discernment within the mind, by which one rejects what by nature does harm, and counts what is beneficial as worth choosing and taking. And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good; keep away from every form of evil’ (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). So since the kidney is a part of the body that discerns (for it separates out what is surplus very well, lets what is wholesome and useful into the body, and distributes it with art to the parts that should receive it, and in the right amount), we must with good reason take the kidneys to mean the discernment of the mind. Holy, then, and an offering dedicated to God are the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they have in the mind. For those who cleave to God are approved and exact money changers: they always reject what is worthless as counterfeit, but they are accustomed to honor with their excellent verdict whatever leads to benefit. It was in this way, I think, that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out to God: ‘For you have taken possession of my kidneys, O Lord’ (Psalm 139:13). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God possessed the kidneys.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: God has possessed the kidneys of the one who has reached purity in temperance, and that man says God's works are wonderful and his soul knows it intensely.
comments.comment: … God has possessed the kidneys of the one who has accomplished purity in temperance. He, therefore, being idle in celibacy, having inscribed his own kidneys to God, says: You have possessed my kidneys, Lord; with the achievement of knowing all his wonderful works of creation, providence, and paradox, he says: 'Wonderful are your works,' and my soul knows it intensely. The 'intensely' refers to the knowledge of the soul or to the wonders. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's work in secret is invisible even to students of nature, since no one can see how blood becomes bone, and my being is not hidden from him even in the lowest parts of the earth.
comments.comment:
… He says: 'You have done in secret so that no one knows the combination of this; nothing of it is hidden from you' (Psalm 139:15). For how can those who are your handiwork not be like the soul of the body? And it is said also to those discussing the nature and generation of animals that the transformation of blood into bone is invisible and incomprehensible, even though I say that others observing the generation of flesh and nerves see how they are.

And the scripture of Ecclesiastes establishes this, not saying 'as a bone in the belly of the pregnant' (Eccl 11:5), but 'you shall not know the works of God.' And my hypostasis was not hidden from you, having reached the lowest parts of the earth; for neither the soul having been created in water, nor even the body having been decomposed and dissolved into the earth, escapes your vision. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who study animals could not explain how bone forms, which is why the Psalm says that what God made in secret was not hidden from him.
comments.comment: … Those who have dealt with the nature of animals have spoken of a certain way and a sequence of change for each part; concerning 'bone' they did not have the power to say. … They say that blood is composed in such a way: when food is presented and digested—when it becomes through being sent to be processed—the food changes into blood; and that which is rejected must be cast out, it is not decomposed into the composition of the thing eaten, but is cast off as waste. But when it has been absorbed, then, through a change occurring successively, it is decomposed into blood. Then they say that from the blood, having become thick and congealed, flesh is made, and from the wastes of the food, hair, nails, and such things are made, which are as wastes. But concerning the generation of 'bone', none of them found it, so that this was as 'your judgments are a great abyss' (Psalm 36:6). Such a thing is also what is said in one of the Psalms: 'My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret' (Psalm 139:15). And 'which you made in secret', he says this, that its genesis is hidden; and 'was not hidden' this was 'from you'. Therefore, take this for an illustration. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a concrete picture of what 'made in secret' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God knows my very being and the composition of my bones, wrote me in his book, and fixes the time and number of days for each human being, none lacking.
comments.comment: … You know my very subsistence, he says, and the composition of my bones is your work (Psalm 139:15-16; LXX 138:15-16). In the hidden place of my mother's womb, as if within the earth, you knew me as one intricately wrought even before I was formed. And I am written by you as in a book, and every human being who is fashioned is measured by a fixed time and a set number of days (Psalm 139:16). This is indeed the wonder of the order and precise symmetry: that the production of life is brought to completion with not a single day lacking. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words how God knew and recorded the unformed person.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Looking with prophetic eyes, the singer sees the Lord's birth from the virgin as unworked, and the resurrection of the dead as written in God's book.
comments.comment:
… Through these things extended, having theologized with prophetic eyes, he says he has seen the Lord's visitation, that it has come from the virgin. For having been born from the virgin Mary, the birth is unworked, not composed from a studied combination of labor, but existing from the Holy Spirit. Some understand this as what was said in Daniel concerning the stone being cut out without hands (Dan 2:45).

This being made manifest unworked, subsequently salvation for all shall come to be, as if it were written of them in the book of God to become worthy. But since that also can be unworked—being of a nature to receive labor yet not having had it—it is possible to speak concerning all those who are about to exist, the Maker of God, and especially concerning the resurrection of the dead, of which the said thing is the anchor. Since my hypostasis is in the lowest parts of the earth, and not to always have such a thing, I say I have pre-conceived this with faith and hope, that the resurrection of the dead will be: 'Your unworked thing my eyes have seen, and upon your book all are written' (Ps 94:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The things written in God's book include all darkness and grief, and those written there will shine like the sun and be raised in incorruption and glory.
comments.comment:
They shall be written: all things happening to them in all things, and all darkness, and all grief, and pain, and the sighing happening from the feet, but in a bright day they shall shine forth like the sun in the kingdom of their own Father. For it is said, 'They shall be made as the Day' (Ps 139:16), so that they are no longer in the darkness of their creation, being sown in corruption and in dishonor, but in light and in a day standing together, being raised in incorruption and glory.

But since they are not made such as the day, and since all things happening in all things are written in the book of God, God will be in them, and there is no one among them of the evil ones or worthy of being despised. Perhaps the multitude and the 'who' and the 'no one' will vanish; for because of a great perfection and for the sake of oneness and identity, having restored the number, there shall no longer exist a 'who' or a 'no one' among them, having understood all things into the unity of the Spirit. The 'who' and the 'no one' shall no longer be among them. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's eyes see all hidden things before they are done, and his friends, such as Abraham, Moses and the apostles, are highly honored and rule strongly with Christ.
comments.comment:
… A scripture is brought forward: 'My unformed eyes saw you' (Ps 139:16). And let this itself be understood likewise: 'You understood my thoughts from afar,' instead of 'the unformed of my thoughts'; before anything is accomplished, your eyes, seeing all hidden things, are full. And the Gospels are full of such things. They are friends of God, having come to be from faith and virtue. For it is said concerning Abraham: 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness, and he was called a friend of God' (Gen 15:6); and concerning Moses it says: 'God spoke to him mouth to mouth, face to face, as if one were speaking to his own friend' (Exod 33:11). But even the greatest of the prophets has not become such a friend of God. And toward the apostles, indeed (they possess this friendship), Jesus says: 'I say to you, my friends' (Luke 12:4).

And these rulers, receiving authority from the King Christ over more than ten cities or more than five cities, are very strong as they co-reign with Christ. And it is said also by another meaning: their rule is strong because the reasons for it are friends of God. For those who are highly honored, friends of God, through a multitude of contemplations and good activities which they have, shall be multiplied beyond the immaterial, that is, beyond the sensible and the bodily. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The singer did not think the righteous few, for looking at all who have existed from eternity he saw they are many, and the resurrection will show them together.
comments.comment: … I did not think, he says, that the righteous were few, even though at any given time only a small number are found. Rather, I looked to the whole multitude that has existed from eternity, and I saw that they are many and greater in number, whom the resurrection will display all together—and especially now, when they have increased into a multitude at the coming of Christ, according to the words, "The whole earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord," and "I will give thanks to you in the great church; in a heavy people I will praise you" (Psalm 35:18). …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of the thoughts 'more in number than the sand'.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: To honor the friends of God is also to hate his enemies with a perfect hatred, not for another's sake but because they turn the deceived away from the truth.
comments.comment: … it is to accept and honor the friends of God and to hate those who hate him, and to count as enemies the impious and those who think foolishly concerning God. For how are those who turn the deceived away from the truth not enemies of God, since God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim 2:4)? And perfect hatred exists against such people, not for the sake of another, but because one hates them as enemies of God. And just as someone has perfect love toward the good, not for the sake of another but desiring it for its own sake, so the one hating those diverse from God does so not for the sake of another but because they are enemies of God, raging against them according to the one saying the prophet, 'I have envied with zeal for the Lord Pantokrator, whom the sons of Israel have forsaken' (1 Kings 19:10). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'perfect hatred' of God's enemies means in this passage.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hatred of the demons helps toward salvation, and the one who hates enemies with perfect hatred sins neither in deed nor in thought.
comments.comment: … Hatred against the demons contributes greatly to our salvation, and is fit for the working of virtue; but we cannot nourish this in ourselves as some good offspring, since the pleasure-loving spirits destroy it and call the soul back again to friendship and familiarity; but this friendship — or rather, this hard-to-heal gangrene — the Physician of souls heals by abandonment; for He allows us to suffer something fearful from them by night or by day, and again the soul runs back to its original hatred, taught to say to the Lord, according to David: ‘I have hated them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me’ (Ps 139:22). For he hates the enemies with perfect hatred who sins neither in deed nor in thought; which is the proof of the first and greatest dispassion. …
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Since the righteous are precious to God and the wicked are headed for destruction, the singer asks to be cleansed even of evil done through ignorance and led by good deeds.
comments.comment: … Since righteous men are precious in your sight and are laid up for eternal glory, while the wicked are destined for destruction, I beseech you that I may be cleansed from all wickedness by the cleansing that comes from you, who are able to purify us even when we fall into evil through ignorance (Psalm 139:24). I pray that you cleanse me, he says, from every evil that leads to destruction and lead me through good deeds, for which eternal life will be given. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prayer 'search me and lead me' in plain terms.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The evil man is treacherous and deceiving, the unjust man worse, and they hide iniquity in the heart, prepare wars all day and sharpen the tongue like a serpent.
comments.comment: … An evil man is a treacherous and deceiving man; but an unjust man is one who has ascended above this in wickedness, as if through craftiness and mischief, hastening the rational nature from virtue into wickedness, attempting to transfer it by some craft. Desiring to be saved from both, the one declaring the things set before him prays to God, since they reckoned iniquity against him, hiding it in their own heart, so that through remaining hidden, what such people are, they might be able to ensnare him, standing hostilely and against him for the sake of the duration of his life. Therefore, if it is said, 'All the day they prepared wars,' having no time of peace and rest, instead of a sword they have sharpened the tongue of themselves upon the deceiver, and being able to wound, they utter a word imitating the serpent who corrupts in his craftiness. And under their own lips, that is, their speech, they have thoughts made to be cast into them by evil powers because of the harmful and venomous nature of what are called 'darts.' And it is possible also concerning the devil and the other invisible enemies to grasp these things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms the kinds of enemies the psalm describes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The singer asks to be kept from the sinner's hand, whether the devil, unjust men or evil angels, who hide ropes of deceptive wisdom to trip those walking rightly.
comments.comment:
… The hand of a sinner, the sinful practice, prays to be guarded from by God acting as a watchman. And besides this, it is worthy that he also be rescued from men who intend to do wrong by their choice, since they have reasoned through deceptive words and thoughts to trip up the steps of those walking toward progress in greater things.

It is possible in these things to catch the sinner, the devil, and unjust men, or rather his evil angels, or those who work men toward iniquity of soul. For they possess a deceptive wisdom, which they do not bring forth openly but hide like a snare under their sophistical words. But also their complex ropes of wickedness, which are composed and entwined by their sophistical words, stretch out to catch the feet of those walking rightly, calculating through these ropes to trip the steps of those who unthinkingly follow a path that someone has worn down.

Obstacles and stumbling blocks are, if they are thoughts, being cast against those intending to walk well and according to virtue. But he who has known himself, that he is not self-sufficient to remain harmless before so many dangers, flees to God and requires power; therefore he also announces those surrounding him. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who calls the Lord his own God asks to be heard, and the power of salvation, found in living by the Gospel, covers his mental head in the day of war.
comments.comment:
… He who is mastered by practice and thought will say practically to Him, 'My God, are you?' and it is worthy that he asks how his voice of petition might be heard, receiving it unto his own. For he truly says, 'O Lord of all, and You are my Lord, and I am your servant; therefore You are the power of my salvation.' For of the truly and attainable salvation of yours, man's power exists to have an impossible salvation if he has not become in you. And my salvation is the likeness according to the image and the likeness that has become yours, to partake of your holiness through which also salvation exists. …

One possesses the power of salvation by living and acting according to the Gospel. The power of my salvation, O Lord, has overshadowed my head on a day of war, specifically my mental head. I am convinced, therefore, that nothing is difficult against the invisible enemies during the day, that is, during the temporal extension of this life. The testimony that the head is mental is found in 'The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous' (Proverbs 10:6) and 'The eyes of the wise are in his head' (Ecclesiastes 2:14). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever is drawn from desire into the act becomes the devil's instrument, so one prays not to be handed over to the sinner but to be held back by the better thought.
comments.comment:
… The sinful devil takes those who perform sin, making them his instruments. It is not clear, however, if one is mastered by a certain shameful desire. For if someone is drawn from desire into practical sin, he immediately becomes the devil's instrument; but if, having looked at a woman with desire, one stops in thought to prevent the fulfillment of the desires, he will not become the intended sinner. Therefore, one prays to the Lord that from desire alone, without being drawn into the action of the desire, he may not be handed over to the sinner, nor proceed further being conquered by it, but rather always be prevented by the better thought from You. It is also said: since all good desire is present to me as a righteous man, let me not be such as to fall from such desire and be handed over to the sinner having acted sinfully.

‘Lest through many of my thoughts I may be able to sin, do not leave me, guarding me in the shelter of your wings and under your strong hand’ (Psalm 140:8), so that no one may seize or lift himself up arrogantly against me as one caught by him. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is worthy of God that lawlessness be given no proud thought against righteousness, for when injustice succeeds it grows into blasphemy against God.
comments.comment: … What is said is worthy of God: that lawlessness be given no proud thought and no exaltation against righteousness, and that their bitter and destructive purpose not come to fulfillment nor be permitted to prevail over those against whom they hold their bitterness (Psalm 140:8). For when injustice succeeds, it becomes far more grievous and grows into blasphemy against the God of righteousness. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the prayer 'further not his wicked device' asks.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The wicked will fall an incurable fall and be driven from the earth to destructive punishments.
comments.comment: … And they will fall a fall—not the kind the righteous fall when they fall and rise again, but the incurable kind that no longer comes to resurrection (Psalm 140:10). They will depart into obscurity, unable to become established on the earth, but driven out from it into destructive punishments. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'that they rise not up again' means.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Judgment' is the examination of deeds and intentions and 'justice' is repayment according to merit, and the poor and the needy differ as one fallen from wealth and one who has only what toil provides.
comments.comment: … He [the psalmist] says 'judgment' is the examination of deeds and intentions, and 'justice' is the repayment according to merit. And even if the same subject is signified by both words in a parallel way, examine it yourself. The same must be said concerning the poor and the needy; for indeed, both names applied to the same thing must be taken according to different matters, such as being 'poor' if one has fallen greatly from wealth (for the rich have become poor and hungry), but 'needy' being one who has the necessary things for living through toil rather than through property. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous confess God's name and the upright dwell in his face, in the likeness of the image of the Son, which is to be understood in a God-befitting and not a local way.
comments.comment:
… The righteous confess either that they have not fallen into such things themselves, or that those who disregarded them and caused them much harm were subjected to such burdens by the judgment and justice of God. Regarding the confession of the righteous, the upright—others of the righteous—will dwell in the face of the Lord; those who confessed by the name, the righteous, confessed. Others of the righteous, the upright, if not entirely in hypostasis, but in thought only, being righteous in one who performs moral virtues, and upright in one who has possessed the contemplation of truth.

Perhaps one who sometimes performs praiseworthy things may be called righteous, but while the practical man of the righteous confesses by the name of God, the upright one has acquired a city and a house through contemplation, dwelling in the face of God. For the exact imprint of the hypostasis has been shown to be the face of God, Him dwelling in this face, concerning which it is said everywhere, 'If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation' (2 Cor 5:17). …

They [the upright] dwell in the likeness of the image of your Son, so that your Son may be found in them, the fulfillment of what the Savior said concerning such things: 'I am that I am, and they shall be with me, to behold my glory.' And this is to be heard not locally but in a God-befitting manner. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Pressed by darkness, one must cry out to the only one who can bring dawn out of evening and day out of night.
comments.comment: So now a person needs intense crying out, because he has been pressed in by darkness and weighed down by the evils that surround him. He cries to the only one who can give light, who can show dawn out of evening and day out of night, and who can bring about a change from these evils (Ps 140:4-5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the urgent cry of 141:1: pressed by darkness, he calls on the one who alone can turn night into day.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: If morning is the life to come, the present life is evening for the light of the good that remains and night for wickedness.
comments.comment: If by morning we understand the life that is coming, the life of rest and glory for the righteous, then let us understand the present life as night and evening—evening because it retains something of light through the remaining knowledge of the good and because of the gifts from God, and night because of the darkness of wickedness and the domination of the world-rulers of darkness (Psalm 141:2; LXX 140:2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The evening sacrifice is offered by one who has hurried to complete it, after the morning sacrifices of the law and the knowledge of God learned at noon.
comments.comment: … This sacrifice is offered by one who, having hurried to complete it, reaches the evening, while the one sacrificing in the morning offers according to the law the sacrifices that present the sensible things. But at noon, after this, he who has learned what is said by the Lord, 'You desire sacrifice, not burnt offerings, but the knowledge of God' … And above all, an evening sacrifice is to be heard, the offering of the hands previously mentioned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Our altars are the ruling mind of each righteous person, from which prayers from a pure conscience rise as fragrant incense.
comments.comment: … our altars are the ruling mind of each righteous person, from which there truly and spiritually rises fragrant “incense”: “prayers” from a pure conscience. That is why John says in the Revelation: “The incense is the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8); and the Psalmist: “Let my prayer be as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the incense of the verse is: prayer from a pure conscience.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The usual prayer is owed three times a day, and the last of the three is the one shown by 'the lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.'
comments.comment: … the customarily-named prayer is part, owed no less than thrice daily — clear from Daniel, praying thrice a day with such danger hanging over him. And Peter going up to the roof to pray at the sixth hour, … exhibits the middle of the three prayers: with before it the one spoken by David, 'In the morning You shall hear my prayer; in the morning I shall present myself to You and watch' (Psalm 5:3); and the last shown by 'The lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.'
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the evening sacrifice of the verse fits the three times of daily prayer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The posture of the body in prayer, the lifting of holy hands, is taken from this verse.
comments.comment: The condition must be laid upon the soul, the figure upon the body. … and the figure in the 'lifting holy hands' — which I take him [Paul] to have received from the Psalms, running thus: 'The lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.' (Psalm 141:2)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The tongue is the demon's best tool against us, so the prophet lifts his hands to God and asks that a guard be set over his mouth.
comments.comment: He [the demon] is accustomed to harm us from every direction, but especially through the tongue and through the mouth. For no instrument is so well suited to him for deceiving us and destroying us as an undisciplined tongue and a mouth without doors. From here come most of our falls; from here come our serious accusations. … And again elsewhere, showing that along with our own effort we need help from above even before our own, the prophet lifted his hands to God and said: "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice. Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of enclosure over my lips" (Psalm 141:2-3). … Do you see how each one fears these falls, and laments them, and counsels, and prays that the tongue may enjoy great protection?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks for a guard on the mouth, and that help from God is needed along with our own effort.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: A guard on the mouth is asked for by one who knows when to speak and when to be silent, so that nothing comes out unseasonably.
comments.comment: May I also not fall into these things, O Lord; a guard to my mouth and a door of restraint around my lips. … For it is not advantageous for all to speak, nor even to be silent; for to the one able to open the mouth with the word of God, silence is not fitting, but to the one who brings forth a word that is idle and to those condemning words, silence will be for good. … For the one possessing the knowledge of the time to speak and the time when it is not necessary to speak, would ask that a guard and a door be present to his mouth and his lips from God, so that he might not bring forth anything unseasonably …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the guard and door on the lips as knowing the time to speak and the time to keep silent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who excuse their lawless deeds with pretexts are worse than those who act without covering.
comments.comment: Men make excuses for their sins alongside those who practice lawlessness. For if my heart were kept by your guarding, I would not be joined with the chosen ones among men who practice lawlessness. And these chosen ones are those who use pretexts upon which they act wickedly, being worse than those without pretexts who lawlessly act without covering.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He shuns wickedness, for a friend's wounds are better than enemies' kisses.
comments.comment: He speaks, then, against wickedness, wanting to be pure from it and a stranger to those who live in it. For the wounds of friends are more trustworthy than willing kisses of enemies (Proverbs 27:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness' through Proverbs: a friend's wounds are better than an enemy's kisses.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: His prayer here becomes a request that false doctrines and evil dispositions be overthrown and destroyed.
comments.comment: Understand also this: what else are the chosen ones who practice lawlessness but those in good will, or false doctrines and evil dispositions, whom you would deem worthy of having your own prayer become a means to be exposed and cast out? (Psalm 141:5; LXX 140:5c–8a). For in these things his prayer becomes nothing other than a request to God for their overthrow and destruction.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked mock prayer and what is holy, and a man dies like a clod breaking apart.
comments.comment: They mock what is good, he says, and disparage what is by common agreement the most beautiful thing of all—prayer—twisting it to suit their own will. And this, he says, will destroy them, uprooted from the earth, as if dug out, with a rock pushing through and dislodging their rooting. They made my words a laughingstock and a pleasure, mocking what is holy because they delight in what is unholy, and because their long habit in these things has cut off their asking for what is good and truly lovely and delightful. Second, he speaks of the sorrow of death, describing the dissolution of a human being: like a clod of earth breaking apart, he is scattered (Psalm 141:7).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sinner's harmonies lie in the region of sin and of the dead, and of him it is said his bones were scattered.
comments.comment: Our bones were scattered beside Hades. What bones of the speaker were scattered beside Hades? If you see for me the one who has sinned, and you see his harmonies in the region of sin, in the region of the dead, in the region of vice, you will say of such a one that his bones were scattered.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The scattering of the bones is spoken of in the plural, but the saving turn to the Lord in the singular: not 'our eyes' but 'my eyes.'
comments.comment: But this has not arisen from inattention alone, but it is also possible for the eyes of the soul to be lifted toward the Lord, who is able to gather together into himself the things scattered by the adversary … And also, to speak in the plural regarding the dispersion (for 'our bones were scattered'), while the saving thing is spoken of in the singular; for it is not said, 'O Lord, Lord, our eyes are toward you,' but 'my eyes.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lord and God, joined as two, show that God is understood in the Lord and the Lord in God, as Paul sets out one God and one Lord.
comments.comment: The unity of the dyad is beautiful when it places the Lord and God in such a relation, but for those who have learned the perfect things, the comprehension of the dyad in the unity is more revealing. Paul presents this when he expounds one God and one Lord, and unites the two, who are two, so that God is understood in the Lord and the Lord in God. In this way the properties of the divine and lordly essence are seen in identity, proceeding from the Father to the Son according to what is divine, and led back from the Son to God according to what is lordly (Ps 141:8).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalmist fixes his eyes on the Lord and asks that his soul be saved from the snare and from the stumbling blocks of those who work lawlessness.
comments.comment: Toward you, O Lord, are my eyes, hoping in you; therefore do not let my soul fall, lest it fall down to the pit (Psalm 141:8; LXX 140:8). … not only will my soul not be destroyed, but it will be saved, you guarding me from the snare in which he established it for me. And not from this alone, but also from the stumbling blocks of those working lawlessness, guard me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since a bodily separation from the wicked is impossible, the safeguard is to turn aside from them spiritually and not be entangled with them.
comments.comment: Symmachus says: 'Let the lawless fall into their own nets.' Let their schemes, he says, turn against them and not against us who are innocent. But I, he says, will turn aside from mixing with the wicked, until I am able to escape them altogether. For this is the safeguard against being harmed by them at all: not to come near them or be entangled with them. Jeremiah also says this: 'It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth; he will sit alone and be silent' (Lamentations 3:27-28). But for us now the separation from the wicked is spiritual, because a bodily separation is impossible, since we would have to go out of the world, as Paul says.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Let the wicked fall into their own nets': their schemes turn on them, and the righteous keep apart from them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The goal is not escape from enemies but to offer thanks to God.
comments.comment: He does not set as the goal the escape from the siege of enemies, but something still more beautiful: to offer thanks to God (Ps 142). For this is indeed the highest goal.
comments.selected_reason: Says what the freed soul is for in the last verse: thanks to God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: David, though a king, counted life like a prison and longed to be delivered from it, not being held in any prison of the senses.
comments.comment: … and even the blessed David, looking toward those things and though being king, considering life to be like a prison, sang to God: 'Bring my soul out of the prison' (Ps 142:7). For he was not being guarded in a sensible prison. There is also the thought from what is approaching, as he desired the deliverance from here; for he says: 'The righteous shall wait for me, until I am repaid' (Psalm 142:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prison of the verse as this present life, and the wish for deliverance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some say the psalm is titled 'when his son pursued him,' but not all versions have it.
comments.comment: Others say the psalm is not without a title, but is inscribed: 'A Psalm of David, when his son pursued him.' This is not found, however, in all the versions. But what is said is not foreign to it; and nothing prevents these words from having been spoken about the persecution by Saul (Psalm 143:8; LXX 142:8ab).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God does not enter into judgment with the one who believes in Christ, for judgment comes to those who loved the darkness or do evil works.
comments.comment: By the grace through the faith of Jesus Christ, having the righteousness that was revealed apart from law, being testified to by the law and the prophets. Perhaps, since the one believing in him is not judged, he receives from him perfect faith so that he might happen not to be judged. For judgment comes to those who loved the darkness more than the light or to those who do evil works. Surely, if God listens to someone in his own righteousness, he does not enter into judgment with him; for he happens to be his servant, doing all these things commanded to him (Ps 142:3b–4a).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No living thing is justified before God, for all are found lacking when they stand toward God.
comments.comment: A pure person is not entirely contrary to the Lord. … and by the Psalms: 'No living thing shall be justified before You' (Psalm 143:2). For he did not say, 'no one is justified,' but rather, 'before You.' For you will find that all are lacking when they are toward God, and they do not possess righteousness in excess.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'before You': all are lacking when measured toward God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To be brought low to the earth is to live observing and thinking of things below, while those whose heart is in heaven are lifted up.
comments.comment: To be brought low to the earth is to have the life of someone observing the things below and thinking the things upon the earth. Just as the life of those having their heart in heaven is tossed about and lifted up, so the one hoarding on the earth and having his mind about sensible things is brought low, having his life toward the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it is to have one's life struck down to the ground.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The spirit of man despaired for lack of help, like a dead man of the age.
comments.comment: He says, 'In the dark ages' (the rulers of this darkness rule there), 'as the fallen one, to be made like the dead of the age.' … Therefore also the spirit called the spirit of man, being with him, despaired for the sake of help.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since the Holy Spirit does not remain where sin is, the one who says the enemy pursued his soul prays not to be abandoned.
comments.comment: And since the Holy Spirit does not remain where sin is, having said, 'The enemy pursued my soul' (Psalm 143:3; LXX 142:3), and the following, let him be careful not because of these things to abandon him then as a spirit present with him, as it is the same as the one proposed: 'Turn not your face away,' and the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unclean spirit does not pass through parched souls, and the Lord will rain on them so they have springs of living water.
comments.comment: This parched earth and the adjacent souls, parched places, the unclean spirit does not pass through, finding no rest or repose with them. But even if they happen to be parched by the drying up of foul waters, they do not pursue the Lord to find him on the straight path, who will also rain upon them as a preceding rain and as a dry rain. Therefore they shall be in waters, having springs in them of living water changing into eternal life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who has the Spirit is not cast out at once for sinning, but the persistent sinner is.
comments.comment: Do not drive me away from you. For no one who is in God and possesses the Spirit is immediately cast out for sinning, but he who persists in sinning is like a craftsman preparing a tool; for then such a person will be cast out from the divine face and be deprived of the Holy Spirit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Illuminated at the day's start, the psalmist asks to hear of God's righteousness so he can progress to seeing it.
comments.comment: In the beginning of the day being illuminated by you, and having begun to shine like the rising of the sun, let me hear of your righteousness … I am not speaking about it as my own state or hearing. For then, having been benefited by the hearing about it, I will be able to progress as to seeing it with longing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous do not yet receive perfect mercy but await the morning of the Master's appearing.
comments.comment: Or, according to the whole theme of the life of the righteous, he does not yet receive the perfect mercy now, but awaits the future appearing from heaven that announces the morning, when the Master will shine upon the righteous, appearing from heaven (Psalm 143:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'morning' of the verse as the Lord's appearing, when the righteous receive his full mercy.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one who has walked the former ways of Moses and the prophets asks the father of the way to make it known, and the Savior says 'I am the way.'
comments.comment: Perhaps also the former ways, Moses and the prophets, having been walked by someone … after the journey in them, seeking the good way, he will say to the father of this way alone to the one knowing the way, 'Like a son, make known to me the way in which I shall walk.' Therefore also, having been acknowledged by the father, making itself manifest, he says to the worthy, 'I am the way; for no one comes to the Father except through me' [John 14:6].
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The leader of evil is called 'the enemy' in the singular and his army 'enemies' in the plural, and he is rescued by fleeing to God alone.
comments.comment: Being pursued by a single enemy, as if being finished, he prays now to be rescued from a multitude of enemies Ps 142:9. But they do not fight with different words; for he called the leader of evil, the enemy, singular, but his army he called enemies in the plural. And it is most just to be rescued from the enemies, since he fled to no one but to him alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To know God's will is not what sanctifies and blesses, but to work and do it.
comments.comment: 'Teach me,' he says, 'not only to know but also to do your will' … for it is not the knowing of it that is sanctifying and making blessed, but it being worked and being done. Therefore also the Savior says, 'Not everyone saying to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist asks to be taught to do God's will, not just to know it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Learning the divine will is the Holy Spirit's guidance into the straight land, which is the good and pure heart in which Jesus bears fruit.
comments.comment: And what is this learning of the divine will, the following word signifies: what is the guidance of the Holy Spirit into the straight land. For the one having learned the will of God in moral virtues will be guided by the gift of God by the Holy Spirit who works upon all truth. And the straight land is the good and pure heart in which Jesus will bear fruit, the seed of the gentle ones. And it can also be thus: 'Teach me to do your will,' not merely formally but spiritually, fulfilling your law, which happens to be not other than your will; and having progressed to this and having been guided by the Holy Spirit into the straight land, one articulates the remaining truth face to face.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'land of uprightness' as a pure heart guided by the Spirit into obedience.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some texts have 'Your Good Spirit' for 'Your Holy Spirit,' showing that the holy is good and the good is holy, as the Father is.
comments.comment: In some texts it is carried instead of 'Your Holy Spirit' as 'Your Good Spirit'; from which it is presented that the holy is good and the good is holy, and 'good' is not by participation in goodness but is good by essence, such as also the holy is. And such is the Father; for indeed it is said concerning him, 'Holy Father,' and 'No one is good except God.' And the Son, being from the good and the holy, is said to be good and holy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The pious give up their own will and wish to have God's will, turning their will into action; God's wills are the virtues.
comments.comment:
Each of those having a pious disposition, having denied human will, wishes to have the will of God, saying, 'Teach me to do your will, O my God, for You are God' (Psalm 143:10). Therefore, he who does the will of those fearing Him transforms his own will into action, he who wishes to have God as his will, revering Him.

And there is no difference, in the plural or the singular, between 'wills' and 'the will'; for His wills are the virtues according to each kind, but His will in general is the universal and common virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'You will make me live' points to future time, since we shall live perfectly when Christ, our life, is revealed.
comments.comment: It is fitting, therefore, that 'You will make me live' inclines toward future time, since here, just as we possess other good things only partially, we shall live perfectly when Christ, our life, is revealed; for he is the righteousness of God, in whom the one who approaches him will live.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The name of goodness becomes the occasion of God's salvation, as Paul says.
comments.comment: He asks that the name of goodness become for him the occasion of God's salvation, according to the apostle who says: 'To the praise of the glory of his grace' (Ephesians 1:6) (Psalm 143:11; LXX 142:11).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Hands trained for war strike the evil men and demons who protect wickedness.
comments.comment: Regarding such wars, it is as if the fingers and hands of a man were skillfully touching the defenses, through which one might strike and wound the evil men and demons who are protectors of wickedness and false knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints give thanks to God, knowing him as the cause of the good things; so David blesses God after fighting his enemies.
comments.comment: Since everything that is good and useful comes from God to men, what do the saints possess concerning such things? They give thanks to God, knowing him to be the cause of the good things. Behold, even David, having experienced fighting his enemies in military matters, those invisible diverse ones who are overturned and cast down, bless God, becoming a teacher to himself of that knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the psalmist begins by blessing God: he is the cause of all good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse does not say man knows God but that God is known and thinks of man; the Son shows the Father to those prepared.
comments.comment: For it is not said, 'What is man, that he should know you and think about you,' but, 'That you were known and you think about him.' For the Savior makes himself manifest to those prepared for this, and by this it is said that they know him. Having been known also according to spiritual contemplation, having been seen, he shows also the Father to be seen by the same. For 'He who has seen me has seen the Father,' and 'No one knows the Father except the Son and whomsoever the Son wills to reveal.' Since, therefore, the Son, possessing the Father within himself, shows Him to be seen by the same, so also the Father, possessing the Son within himself, reveals Him to him who wishes to have knowledge not through flesh and blood but from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording of the verse: man is known by God, and the Son and Father reveal each other to those prepared.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the body a man is nothing, like a shadow, but his immortal soul knows the cause of all things.
comments.comment: The composition of men from a corruptible body and an immortal soul, joined together, possesses according to the immortal and spiritual soul a thought and knowledge of the cause of all things; but according to the body, it is nothing, being like the moving and bright shadow of a man's daily life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's contrast: man's body is a passing shadow, his soul knows the cause of all.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: This psalm speaks of the body's weakness, and Psalm 8 of man's greatness, 'a little less than the angels.'
comments.comment: If he had observed according to the soul and according to the intellect, he contemplated the greatness of human nature, which the hymnographer teaches on both sides, saying: 'What is man, that you take thought of him? Man is made like vanity' (Psalm 144:3-4), which he has said regarding the weakness of the body as comparing it to divine things. But instructing on greatness, he says again: 'You made him a little less than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5).
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the psalm's words on man's weakness are balanced by Scripture's words on his greatness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bending of the heavens signifies the Savior's coming from Mary, who came down and overturned the invisible demons with their host.
comments.comment: And the following things are able to signify the coming of the Savior from Mary, who, having bent the heavens which are His handiwork, descended because He was to come forth from her. Since, therefore, having descended, He overturned the invisible demons who are harmful and filthy to men with all their host, through which they are called 'decaying' because they see themselves as arrogant and lofty.
comments.selected_reason: Reads 'Bow thy heavens, and come down' as the coming of the Savior.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The many waters are the diverse and discordant doctrines, and to be rescued from them and from strange sons is to be rescued from the devil and evil powers.
comments.comment:
Many waters are brought forth in vain, through which the impious and godless contend. For they wish to imitate through them the one who said, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and whoever drinks of the water I will give him shall become a spring of water welling up to eternal life' (John 4:14). And indeed, in these things Jesus gives as if it were one water; this is the Spirit which those believing in him are to receive.

The waters of the heterodox, through which they imitate the quenching given by the Lord, are many, because they are diverse and discordant and do not lead to a single end; for both the ends and the beginnings of their mindsets are different. 'Send therefore,' says the Psalmist, 'your poetic and protective hand, to bring me out and to rescue me from many waters and from the hand of strange sons' (Psalm 144:7; LXX 143:7). For the strange is commonly to be taken both in terms of sons and of waters. And it is possible to say that to be rescued from many waters means from the evil powers and from the devil, the king of all those in such waters; and to be rescued from the hand of strange sons means those working through men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ten commandments are the strings of the ten-stringed psaltery.
comments.comment: The ten-stringed psaltery is composed and joined by the energy of the ten commandments; for each of the ten commandments is a string musically composed in the whole instrument.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the ten-stringed instrument of the verse as the ten commandments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The kings saved by God possess the kingdom, and God did not cease to give salvation but always has given and will give it.
comments.comment: 'And kings, he says, you shall perceive, and those who rule perceptibly the nations and the inhabited world' (Psalm 144:10; LXX 143:10). For if a king is not saved by much power, the kings being saved by God possess the kingdom. And also it is said of giving salvation to kings. Since they always have it from the one being saved, he did not cease to give salvation, but always has given, and will give, and gives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Strange sons use the sword of words, and their words are trimmed with smooth composition, a likeness of a temple but not a temple.
comments.comment:
For concerning the women of the church, Paul writes how they, praying with modesty and self-control, adorn themselves with the works of godliness, but not with the laying down of gold and pearls and elaborate hairstyles (1 Tim 2:9). Consider these things said and apply them to the heterodox. For their word is struck like swords.

Regarding the devouring and the stripping away of those who have not put on the armor of God. Those previously mentioned as speaking vanity, who are alien sons, use this evil sword. The divine thoughts may be their sons, having strength in youth but not in perfection, being like their daughters, whose words are beautified and trimmed with a smooth composition and the elegance of phrasing.

Therefore, they are a likeness of a temple but not a temple; for they do not have within themselves a divine mind like the words of the divine Scriptures; for a temple is where God is found in them who encounter them rightly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He exalts God by theologizing rightly, and he will bless God's name for ever, much more when he approaches the perfect good and knows God face to face.
comments.comment: He exalts God, the one theologizing rightly and truly, uttering great and high things concerning God (Psalm 145:1; LXX 144:1). He says regarding the faith set forth of him who became a child of Abraham through works and faith, that the God of all causes is not his God, but he confesses toward him, 'I am your God.' But he, having become a man of God by serving his God, fleeing every evil kingdom, is ruled by this God himself, and so he will be able to say, 'You are my king and my God.' Having the soul say immortal, he says, 'I will bless your name for ever and unto the age of ages.' And he blesses the name of God and his king, the one doing to wear it and saying and thinking the things belonging to the divine calling upon him, beginning to bless from the present age unto the doing of it as of the age; for if now, knowing in part and participating partially in the good, he blesses the name of the benefactor, much more he will bless when he approaches the perfect good and the face-to-face knowledge of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist stretches his praise beyond himself to all people and into the endless age.
comments.comment: Again he stretches his praises to a great length and does not stop at one person or his own person, but he will do the same for all people [...] into the endless age, if he too will one day see with those who run, showing that they share in the company of the righteous who have become a beginning for God, according to the apostle (Ps 145:1-2).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: In this life these words fit one man after another; in the life to come each one praises God continually and for ever.
comments.comment: In the present life these words could apply to one human being after another in succession, because as the earlier ones depart, there are others who take their place in their territory. For this reason we are all called by the name of Adam, as being those very ones, and God says, "I made the earth and humanity upon it," reckoning all as one (Isaiah 45:12). But in the life to come these things are true for each individual as well, as he praises God continually and eternally, and because it is not sufficient to praise for a short time, the worshiper adds, "Forever and to the age of the age" (Psalm 145:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'for ever and ever' of the praise: generations in this life, each person in the life to come.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Each generation that sees God's works praises them, and the power and wisdom by which he made them is his only-begotten Son.
comments.comment: Since everything God made remains forever, according to Ecclesiastes, each generation that sees his works praises them, seeing that they receive praise beyond all praise. And they declare your power, by which you brought them into existence. This is the wisdom by which you made all things, and your power and wisdom is your only-begotten Son; for Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why each generation praises God's works and declares his power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: 'Generation and generation' means believers from the circumcision and the Gentiles, worthy of praise.
comments.comment: And it shall be said also concerning those from the circumcision and from the Gentiles who have believed: 'Generation and generation shall praise your works' (Psalm 145:4; LXX 144:4), being rightly worthy of praise by his own word, just as he has seen the divine Creator with a divine gaze to be very beautiful.
comments.selected_reason: Says whom 'generation and generation' praising God's works includes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those instructed in God's holiness hymn him by works and right disposition, not bare speech.
comments.comment: Therefore, those who have been instructed in the holiness of God and also in his glory, they are transformed and they hymn him magnificently, not by bare speech, but before this by works and right disposition, thinking, acting, and speaking holily, gloriously, and magnificently.
comments.selected_reason: Explains speaking of God's glory as done by works and right disposition, not speech alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's holiness is the Savior himself, who sanctifies those who approach God.
comments.comment: The holiness of God is not another of the Savior; for he himself is the sanctification who sanctifies those approaching God, to whom it is said, 'You shall be holy, as I am holy' (Lev 11:44). The glory of this holiness is majestic.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who hear the Paraclete declaring speak of God's holiness and recount his wonders with precision.
comments.comment: The glory of the holiness of God is able to be: 'He will glorify' (that is, the Paraclete), what he will take from me and declare to you. Therefore, also those who hear him declaring, in giving the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, they speak of this holiness. And toward this they will recount his wonders, not merely what the holiness is, but penetrating the mystical word of his wonders, which occur at various times and are occurring, with precision and keen contemplation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Such things indicate fearful, strong divine activity.
comments.comment: All these things are alike in their human elements, but they are indications of divine activity that is fearful, strong, and destructive of humans (Psalm 144:5-6).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: They will speak of God's awesome acts through right understanding, with fear and reverence, as surpassing every human apprehension.
comments.comment: It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31), and 'Shout to God with a voice of joy' (Psalm 145:6; LXX 144:6), what the Lord is most high and awesome; they will say this in practice and through right understanding (for through this fear of God and exceeding reverence, they will say to him the power of his awesome things). And if they have been benefited, they will fear his greatness with virtue and sinlessness, and they will not say 'the power of your awesome things' but they will recount it after having known what is without experience and without limit; for they do not recount it as having described and limited it to the intellect, but as surpassing every human apprehension.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's justice can be his only-begotten Son, the redemption of the captives, in whom those who remember his goodness rejoice.
comments.comment:
And the mind judges them, so that the memory of your goodness shall be searched out, and they shall rejoice in your justice. The justice of God can be the only-begotten offspring of Him, upon which those having obtained the Wisdom born to us from God—justice and sanctification and redemption—rejoice.

For what was sent to proclaim to the captives the goodness of God has become redemption for those being set free from captivity, who, remembering the goodness of God that happened to them, search out its memory; but also having perceived how they were justified, it having become for them the work of the one redeeming and of the justice from God, they rejoice in this justice of God. And those who are to receive both all practical virtue and the justice having come through the faith of Jesus into all those believing are made manifest in the present word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the righteousness and goodness the verse sings of as Christ, who redeems.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: People make known that God holds dominion over all things, though humans cannot yet receive the greatness of his kingdom.
comments.comment: They make known that he holds dominion over all things, even if he does not yet reveal this, since humans are not yet able to receive it (Psalm 145:12). For humans are too small for the greatness of the divine kingdom to be shown in them; therefore he adds what is fitting for God (Psalm 145:12; LXX 144:12).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Word's kingship has no beginning and no end, for 'Lord' means reigning for the age and yet more, whatever ages are taken.
comments.comment: 'your kingdom is the kingdom of all the ages' (Psalm 145:13). This is said of the Word God. The Word has neither a beginning having kingship nor an ending; for 'Lord' means 'reigning for the age and upon the age and yet more'. … We take 'yet more' thus: even if you take another age, he reigns yet more; even if another, yet more; even if all ages, yet more he reigns; from which it is shown that his beginning is without end
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God holds and reigns over all he made through his word and wisdom, and reigning over all ages is the same as being King of the ages.
comments.comment:
All those whom God has made through his word and his wisdom, God holds and reigns; therefore God is almighty.

Since, therefore, even the ages, being part of all things, have come to be through God by means of the Savior according to the Scripture saying, 'Through whom also he made the ages, and over all of them he reigns,' and since the thing theologized by Paul agrees with these things: 'To the King of the ages, the incorruptible, invisible, only wise God' 1 Tim 1:17. For to reign over all the ages and to be the King of the ages is the same thing.

Consider if it is said of the Son, 'Your kingdom is the kingdom of all the ages,' reigning over Jacob, that his kingdom has no end; for reigning over all those having come through him, he holds and reigns for the ages. Therefore, just as the others who belong to the Father, so also the Almighty shares in the approachability. If not the Father is the King of the ages and the Son's kingdom is the kingdom of all the ages, it is fitting that his kingdom is also without beginning and without end, both before the ages and while reigning with them …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is Lord over all generations and faithful in all his words, and holy in his works as he gives holiness through communion with him.
comments.comment:
He rules over all generations, being Lord of those within time and generation, but reigning over those who have ascended beyond the temporal by looking at the unseen and eternal things. 'But God is faithful in all his words' (Psalm 145:13; LXX 144:13a). It is said not that they offer something from faith or by faith, but that it is fitting for the one who believes.

… For it is said, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away' (Matt 24:35). Regarding being faithful in his words and holy in all his works, imparting to them the holiness from himself: just as one is holy among those participating in his holiness, and the Savior is wise among the wise according to him, so the Lord is holy in all his works becoming holy through communion with him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God helps both those who fall in practice and those who are shattered, supporting some and restoring others.
comments.comment: Perhaps those who are in desires and bad thoughts without practice fall; but those who sin actively are shattered. However, he helps both sides, supporting some and restoring others. How does he support? By commanding each one, 'You shall not covet your neighbor's wife' (Ex 20:17), and the following, and 'Do not let beauty's desire overcome you' (Proverbs 6:25) by advising through a wise man. Those falling are those sinning in morals while being encompassed by Christianity, but those shattered are those turning away from it; those falling are those sinning in practice, but those shattered are those who embrace impious heresies of the ungodly.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'upholdeth all that fall' as God's help to those who fall and those who are shattered.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's opened hand is not a bodily hand but his creative power providing food.
comments.comment: When he speaks of the opening of God's hands as the provision of food for created things, he clearly is not presenting bodily hands but likening the creative power in this way (Psalm 145:16; LXX 144:16; Ps 144:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Thou openest thine hand' as God's creative power that feeds all things, not a bodily hand.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God provides, governs and judges in all his ways, and no one who lives earnestly according to virtue blames his providence.
comments.comment: In all his ways he causes to walk, providing and governing, judging, benefiting, granting, punishing; righteous he is found (Psalm 145:17; LXX 144:17a); 'for God is faithful, and there is no injustice' (Ps 144:17). If someone says his ways are the virtues (for those traveling practically and intellectually bring them to him), and in these he appears righteous. No one living earnestly and according to virtue blames providence, but if someone has stood foolishly outside his ways: 'A man's folly ruins his paths' (Proverbs 19:3), yet he blames God in his heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'righteous in all his ways': his ways are the virtues, and no one living well blames providence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those making progress pass from calling on the Lord's name to calling on him in truth, worshiping him in spirit and truth.
comments.comment:
It is said that He is near to those who call upon His name. Therefore, those making progress pass on to calling upon Him in truth; for calling upon the name of the Lord is more introductory for those who are perfecting themselves in calling Him. For Moses says, and Aaron among His priests, and Samuel among those calling His name, they called upon the Lord, and He himself heard them—those doing this sincerely and not by chance.

It is possible to say that those living according to the letter of the law call upon the name of the Lord, whereas those following the novelty of the Spirit call upon Him in truth, appropriately worshiping Him in spirit and truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'to all that call upon him in truth' as the calling of those who worship in spirit and truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Justice is interwoven with goodness, so that no painful thing in life, such as failed crops or disease, is outside righteousness.
comments.comment: For if, he says, love for humanity is not seen in all things, but many painful and destructive things accompany what is pleasant and saving—such as failure of crops, the birth of deadly beasts, and the onsets of diseases—yet none of these is outside righteousness, which is beautifully interwoven with goodness so that zeal for what is good is not corrupted by the unrebuked cheerfulness of those who break the law (Psalm 145:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the loving God also destroys the wicked: his goodness is joined with righteousness.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Whoever loves God with all his heart, soul and strength is guarded from the evil one and receives what God has promised.
comments.comment: He who wishes to be guarded by Him, so that by no means the evil one may deceive him, let him love God with all his heart and soul and strength.
