To those thus guarded by Him because they love Him, the things promised without falsehood are made favorable, concerning which it has been said, 'An eye has not seen and an ear has not heard, nor has there risen upon the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love Him' (Ps 144,19a).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'preserveth all them that love him' as being guarded from the evil one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mouth is the intelligible mouth, and all flesh hearing God's praises shall bless his name.
comments.comment: He says 'mouth,' not the sensible but the intelligible, as also in another psalm toward God: 'I will open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praises.' Yet, when His praises are being spoken, all flesh having heard Him shall bless His holy name.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the mouth of the verse as the intelligible mouth, and all flesh blessing God's name.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'All flesh' does not mean sensible flesh but the fleshy hearts on which the spiritual law is written.
comments.comment: And all that flesh blesses his holy name; concerning this it is said, 'Hear my prayer; unto thee all flesh shall come' (Psalm 65:2). And all flesh shall see his salvation. These things are not said concerning sensible flesh, but concerning the existing analogy to the fleshy hearts, concerning which God says, 'I will take away from them the stony hearts and I will put in them fleshy hearts,' in which the spiritual law has been inscribed, Paul saying about this, as it is not written on stone tablets but on fleshy heart tablets (2 Cor 3:3).
comments.selected_reason: Says what 'all flesh' means in the verse: fleshy hearts in which the law is inscribed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The title's names mean a feast (Angaios) and the memory of God (Zechariah), so the hymn belongs to one who does good and remembers God.
comments.comment: The hymn is not being sent up to God by those happening to be celebrating, but by the one who celebrates God through doing the necessary things and remembering him with proper and pious speech. For 'Angaios' is a feast, and 'the memory of God' are the interpretations of Zechariah. Everyone who does not work the practical virtues unceasingly, not even one but many feasts, is named Angaios in the Hebrew tongue; but also everyone who has suffered well through all things and has been benefited by the goodness of God, remembering him, is called Zechariah according to the Hebrew voice, interpreted as the memory, that is, of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praise is due to the upright, and to sing according to virtue means to act; no one possessing death can praise the Lord.
comments.comment: Praise, O my soul, the Lord. But when will this happen and how will you always do it? How does the release from sins approach through virtue and the rectitude of the knowledge of truth? For praise is due to the upright, not to the beautiful word in the mouth of a sinner. I will praise the Lord in my life; for as long as I live (and I live always the eternal life), I will praise. It is shown through the things set forth that no one possessing death, every soul sinning, is able to praise the Lord. I will sing to God my God, as long as I exist. And it is often interpreted that to sing according to virtue means to act. Therefore, a harmonious practice is promised to the Praise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The work of life and the benefit of existing is to be joined to true life and to the one who truly is.
comments.comment: He seems to teach that this is the work of life, this is the benefit of existing—if we are joined to true life and to the one who truly is (Psalm 146:2). For this is a provision both for true life and for existing eternally, … since we carry with us from this present life a provision for the life to come.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'while I have any being': the purpose of existing is to be joined to true life.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: No one can sing separated from the existing God and not becoming a being.
comments.comment: Such a thing is not possible: for as I possess a share in the one who says, 'I am the Being,' I sing with the one who has the desire for me, for no one can sing being separated from the existing God and not becoming a being.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Trust is not to be placed in rulers of this age, evil powers or the sons of men, for only the Savior is the cause of eternal salvation.
comments.comment: It is also not possible to divide trust thus: 'Do not trust in rulers who are of this age, nor in other evil powers (for they are falling and do not have the beginning), nor even in the sons of men; for salvation is not for them, they do not become salvation for mortals; for they are not able to provide it, nor do they have salvation from where they are, but they receive it from God' … For the Savior alone is the cause of eternal salvation, saying, 'Salvation is not from me.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'Put not your trust in princes': they cannot give salvation, which comes from God alone.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope in humans is wretched, but hope in God, a true helper, is blessed.
comments.comment: So hope in humans is wretched, but hope in God is blessed. For he is a true helper, eternal and holding power over all things (Psalm 146:5). In him is the authority, as from ungrudging wealth and boundless resources, to do great good easily.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the one who has God for his help is happy and trust in men is not.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The one helped by the God of Jacob has hope in the Lord who made all things, since if his works endure he himself is much more enduring.
comments.comment: But he is blessed not simply as God is a helper, but as 'God of Jacob is a helper' … being helped by the God who shakes the rulers and the authorities and the cosmic rulers of this darkness. For he who has the struggle against these, having shaken them regarding what has happened to them, is helped by the God of Jacob, the son of Jacob who is so called according to practice in his doing his works. Thus being helped, he has hope in the Lord God who in the beginning trusted the heaven and the earth, the sea and all things in them. For he did not only those things, but also all things in them he himself made. And if his works endure, much more he himself is enduring and powerful.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The truth of God's words and promises is confirmed, and he will bring the coming judgment and vengeance for those wronged.
comments.comment: Therefore, take courage, for the truth of both his words and the promises in the holy letters is confirmed, and he preserves his own promises for the whole age, so that his word and promises do not fail, as he promised to his own people. And what is the truth of the word? It is the coming judgment and the vengeance for those being wronged in the present life. For do not think, he says, that the pious are overlooked, nor that the blood of God-beloved men goes unavenged.  …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'which keepeth truth for ever': God keeps his promises, including judgment for those wronged.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives eternal food to those who hunger for righteousness, and judgment to the wronged, as shown by manna, Elijah, Joseph and Susanna.
comments.comment:
And they hunger and thirst for the things of this life, and He gives eternal food to those who are suffering, according to the Beatitudes: 'Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall themselves be filled' (Matt 5:6), and according to the prophetic word saying, 'Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger' (Isaiah 65:13).

If one wishes to perceive these things sensorially: He gave manna to those hungering in the wilderness, and nourished five thousand hungry men; and He gave also to Elijah and Daniel, the one through ravens, the other through the prophet Ambakum. And He made judgment for those being wronged: Joseph by the Egyptians, Susanna by the judges of Israel, and David being wronged by Saul and others more; the Scripture is rich with these examples.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'food to the hungry' and 'judgment for the oppressed' with the Beatitudes and examples from Scripture.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The broken and humbled are those laid low by wickedness, and the blind are those who cast away the seeing of the intellect, whose hearts God enlightens.
comments.comment:
Those being broken are the same as those who are humbled, differing only in thought; for they are hindered from acting and from running toward the truth, laid low by wickedness, they fall from the height of virtue and happen to be broken. It must be said that those laid low and broken are those sinning in practice, being blind ones who cast away the seeing of the intellect, so that they do not see the beauties of the dogmas of the truth.

Just as he released the laid low and straightened the broken, desiring the forgiveness of sins, so he enlightened the blind, having opened the eyes of their hearts, he himself about whom Paul writes: 'The God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has shone in your hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God' (2 Cor 4:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's blind and bowed down as people hindered by sin whom God raises and enlightens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who saw wickedly are no longer blind but see sharply, with the eyes that see God.
comments.comment: One should also take up what was proclaimed in the Psalms: 'The Lord makes the wise blind' (Ps 146:8), so that they might no longer be shown as blind but as seeing sharply, once the eyes of those seeing wickedly have been hindered and have fallen away from their own pupils—and these are the natural meanings—the eyes that see God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God loves the righteous but guards the proselytes from the Gentiles, who need his guarding lest they be lost.
comments.comment:
Since the word spoken refers to the memory of the righteous among the converts: those loved by the Lord are called righteous, those having been pleasing to him according to the Old Scripture; but converts are those called from the Gentiles upon the teaching of the Gospel. And what the intellect questions, it is to be heard from the Savior saying, 'Many prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear' (Luke 10:24). Among these righteous ones is Abraham, concerning whom it is written: 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness' (Gen 15:6).

… In addition to this, take care lest the proselytes who are coming now through godliness—though those who have passed through and been perfected in it are called righteous—should be lost; for God loves the righteous, but He guards the proselytes. For those who have arrived immediately by the word of truth, lest they may not be strong and firm, need the guarding of the Lord so that they may remain unhurt, whereas the righteous are made members of Him and loved by Him through perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'loveth the righteous' and 'preserveth the strangers' as God loving the righteous and guarding new converts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The widows and orphans taken up are souls that cast off the devil as their father.
comments.comment: But more allegorically, the souls that cast off the one who became their father, the devil, are orphans and widows being taken. Once these are taken, the way of the sinners, which is nothing other than wickedness, shall be destroyed by God (Psalm 146:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The widows taken up are those continuing in purity and reverence, and the orphans are the godly who leave their parents.
comments.comment: He will take up the orphan and the widow (Psalm 146:9)—not any widows, but those continuing in purity and reverence. Such is Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, whom the Gospel remembers (Luke 2:36). The Lord will take up such a widow through incorruptible prudence, along with her well-endured orphanhood, lifting them up and raising them by virtue, … It is possible to say of orphans being taken up that they are the godly who leave behind parents; such as Abraham, going out from the land and kindred and the house of his father at God's calling of him (Gen 12:1); and also James and John, having left Zebedee their father through the invitation of Jesus (Mark 1:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fatherless and widow of the verse as those who live in purity and who leave home at God's call.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Zion is the perfect soul, the church of the living God, whose God reigns forever.
comments.comment: Zion, the watchful and examining one of the truth, is the perfect soul, the church of the living God; your God shall reign forever (Psalm 146:10), the end of the kingdom shall not be delayed, his rule extending from generation to generation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Zion is and that God's reign extends through all generations.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A crushed heart, one without healthy thoughts and straight understanding, needs a physician who heals what is hidden.
comments.comment: And sometimes the name of the crushing signifies such a thing as not having healthy thoughts, not having straight understandings. This crushing of the heart needs a physician, and a physician who heals what is hidden; for it has been said: "The Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersals of Israel, he who heals the crushed in heart" (Psalm 147:2). These were crushed like wounds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not even the countless stars are outside God's knowledge, who knows each one's nature and power.
comments.comment: He is so great and so vast that not even the countless stars are outside his knowledge, but having been ordered by him, they are known to him precisely, since he distinguishes the nature and power of each one as by names that mark them off (Psalm 147:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'he calleth them all by their names': God knows each star's nature and power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's understanding has no number, being incomprehensible and a multitude of contemplations.
comments.comment: For since his understanding is deepest, because of its incomprehensibility it has no number. And if it is also said to have no number because of the surpassing multitude of the contemplations in it, you yourself will also understand.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'his understanding is infinite': it cannot be numbered because it cannot be comprehended.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God's strength and understanding are not a human power and wisdom that come and go, but his own offspring and fruit, great beyond number, and the understanding in which he made the heaven.
comments.comment: Strength then and understanding—even if we hear these in human terms, let us not think humanly about what kind of strength it is by which a strong man acts, and what kind of understanding it is by which a wise man deliberates, since he has power and wisdom that come and go. For as God he is not powerful and wise in that way, since he does not even have anything better or lesser in himself—such as power and what is filled with power, wisdom and what is full of wisdom—but he is entirely the most perfect, and for this reason he does not have power and wisdom that fill him, but full, proceeding from himself. Just as Solomon calls wisdom an offspring and presents wisdom-itself as having come from God, and by saying that the works of creation were made by wisdom he teaches that the begetter of wisdom is something greater than the direct work of creation. To him belongs the great superiority that has risen above any connection with created things by its presence to the one who creates, since it is impossible to conceive of anything greater than the greatest. So what is conceived as greatest, by having surpassed every relation to created things, is what belongs to the Father of wisdom and power. And so great is his strength and his understanding, as being from him and with him an offspring and fruit and son, not as an accident in him—concerning which it is said, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). Then, since this power is also wisdom, having the same name as the understanding in which he made the heaven, according to what was said, “To him who made the heaven in understanding” (Psalm 135:5 (136:5)), his strength and understanding are great beyond number, and the understanding of God is untraceable. …
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The Lord lifts the meek up to inherit a land high above, but humbles sinners who think of earthly things.
comments.comment: He also takes up the meek (Ps 147:6), lifting them up to where they inherit the land. But that land they inherit is high above. Therefore it has also been written, 'He will bring you up upon the good things of the earth,' and 'He will lift you up to inherit the land.' He takes up the meek, but he humbles the sinners as those who carry the image of the earth, thinking of low things and those upon the earth.  …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'The LORD lifteth up the meek' and casting down the wicked as the lifting of the meek to a heavenly land.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The psalmist calls for thanksgiving and confession, and his divine word surrounds the heaven with noetic clouds that pour a noetic rain.
comments.comment: For thanksgiving, awakening those who have received so many good things. 'Begin,' he says, 'in confession, hymning and glorifying him for those things on which he worked' (Psalm 147:7-8). And allegorically, his divine word surrounds the heaven with noetic clouds pouring down a noetic rain: for the heaven above rejoiced, and the clouds (surrounding him) rained down righteousness. From these noetic clouds he prepares rain for the earth, which Jesus spiritually sowed to bring forth fruit divided into one hundred and sixty and thirty, bringing up grass in the deserts …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The young ravens are believers from the nations, who call on the Lord and are given spiritual food as he feeds the simpler sheep and cattle.
comments.comment: …  He brings up and gives food to the simpler sheep and cattle of those having believed in Christ, which are being saved apart from men. But he gives food not only to these, but also to the high-flying ones, for he commanded the young ravens to call upon him. God gives food to these, since they call upon him, according to the perfect men, concerning whom it is said, 'They called upon the Lord, and he heard them' (Psalm 99:6). And you will understand the young ravens to be those from the nations who have believed and because of this call upon the Lord, so that he may give them spiritual food. For the raven is unclean and gloomy. Such are the evil demons and those who have added to impiety, of whom they were formerly sons, but having believed they obtained the heavenly food.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the beasts and young ravens of the verse as believers whom God feeds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bars of the gates are faith, hope and love.
comments.comment: He said it twice, “extol” and “praise,” with soul and body, “for He has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Psalm 147:13), which are faith, hope, love…
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The gates of Jerusalem are the introductory teachings, and her blessed sons act and learn to turn to the house of the Lord.
comments.comment: The gates of Jerusalem are the introductory teachings, with the destructive words lying upon them, or the representing ranks of Jerusalem, having the capacity to silence those who contradict (Psalm 147:13). 'For he has blessed your sons in you,' those who will act and will possess the capacity of thought; for because they become such sons of her, being blessed in her, they never cease to act, having learned to turn to the house of the Lord all the days of their lives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The children God has blessed are the faithful infants who nurse on the milk of Christ's teaching and praise him as soon as they believe.
comments.comment: … “He has blessed your children within you” (Psalm 147:13). These are the faithful infants who received the Lord with the branches, that is, with new fruits, who nurse on the milk of Christ’s teaching. For as soon as they believe in Him, they praise, they sing hymns, they give glory, as it is written: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have prepared praise” (Psalm 8:2; Matthew 21:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the children blessed in Jerusalem as newly faithful believers who praise God.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The prophecy that God's word will run swiftly is fulfilled in the apostles, whose sound has gone out into all the earth.
comments.comment: For, as was said in the prophets, who announced beforehand the preaching of the gospel, “The Lord gave a word to those who preach the good news with great power, the King of the powers of the beloved” (Psalm 68:11–12), so that the prophecy which says, “His word will run swiftly” (Psalm 147:15), might also be fulfilled. And indeed we see that the “sound” of the apostles of Jesus “has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4; Romans 10:18).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how 'his word runneth very swiftly' was read as the gospel spreading through the apostles.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one can withstand those whose hearts are kindled by lawless desires like a furnace.
comments.comment: No one will be able to withstand those who are burned by passions, since their hearts have been kindled like a furnace, like the light of fire, since all are committing adultery and are being burned by lawless desires. To these things, the coming of pain from the storehouses and cold from the heights, as carried in Job, is appropriate.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word of God, sent into the heart, will melt the snow and trials, and his breathing spirit makes them flow.
comments.comment: The provident Word of God, being sent, will melt the snow and those counted with it, but also when He breathes, His spirit will flow (for He says the south wind), turning into these things the ones forenamed of the snow and those near it (Psalm 147:18). And it is necessary even spiritually to hear these things: the clarifying Word of God, having been sent with concealment, will melt the mist, the crystal, and the snow, making them like a drink upon the watering place, but by His spirit, the spirit of this God breathing; but also the Word of God, being sent into the heart of those receiving Him, will melt the trials and make them invisible, those who, warming by the spirit, will courageously undergo such trials, will dissolve them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God sends his saving, creative word to Jacob, the one who supplanted the rulers of this darkness, and to Israel who sees God by the intellect.
comments.comment: To the one who has trampled and supplanted the rulers and the authorities and the cosmic rulers of this darkness, mystically called Jacob, He sends His word, which is salvific and creative, in order to make all the true doctrines of piety clear to him (Psalm 147:19-20). And after the victory having been achieved through insight and Israel having been shown to see by intellect God, His requirements and His judgments, He sent the Word to work all things determined and just. And upon these things, the greatness of the God's gift existing to the mortal, manifesting, He says: He did not do thus to every mortal, but only to Israel He performed the foretold things before the arrival of the Savior; however, the coming of Christ, the High Priest of truly good things, all mortals are filled with the divine Word (Psalm 147:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angels are those in the heavens, the powers above them, and the thrones are subject to the divine majesty, standing in the reception of God's glory.
comments.comment: The angels would be those in the heavens, and the powers are above even these, belonging to the highest places, being above the task of bringing messages to human beings, and having their blessedness in perpetual steadfastness with God alone (Ps 148:2). Such also are the thrones, which the apostle calls, the name indicating that God is seated upon them, and that they are subject to the divine majesty that is above creation, standing always in this and having their fixed and stable state in the reception of the divine glory.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the angels and hosts of the verse as the heavenly ranks that stand steadfast before God.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The sun is praised as a fine work of God, which keeps his laws and hymns its Maker with all its power.
comments.comment: We answer, then, that we do not wait for someone to command us before we praise the sun, we who have learned to speak well not only of those who are subject to God’s ordering but even of our enemies (compare Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:28). So we praise the sun as a fine work of God, which keeps the laws of God and hears the words, “Praise the Lord, sun and moon” (Psalm 148:3), and which with all its power hymns the Father and Creator of the universe.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the sun and moon of the verse are creatures who praise God, so Christians praise the sun as God's work.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lights of heaven and the water above are commanded to praise God, and are a hymn to their Maker.
comments.comment: The lights that shine in the heaven by day and by night, illuminating the heaven itself, the highest one—that is, the firmament according to Moses—and also the water above this, are commanded to praise God. It is clear that all these things are a hymn of God, displaying in their own beauty and power and activity the all-hymned nature of their Maker.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sun, moon, stars, heavens and waters of the verses as a hymn to God displayed in their beauty and power.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The psalm, naming the heavens of heavens, gives the idea of still more heavens.
comments.comment: We, however, are so far from disbelieving in the second that we seek also the third, the vision of which the blessed Paul was counted worthy to receive. And the psalm, naming the heavens of heavens (Psalm 148:4), has given us the idea of still more.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'heavens of heavens' as pointing to more than one heaven.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Heaven is neither Zeus nor God, since a being lower than God has risen above the heavens and the whole sensible nature.
comments.comment: So let the Persians call the whole circle of heaven Zeus. We, however, say that heaven is neither Zeus nor God, since we know that even one of the beings lower than God has risen above the heavens and above the whole of nature that the senses perceive. And this is how we understand the words: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We hope to reach the heights of the heavens and be with the waters above the heavens, praising the Lord while contemplating his invisible things.
comments.comment: For this reason we hope, after the toils and the contests here, to reach the very heights of the heavens. Having received, according to the teaching of Jesus, springs of “water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), and having made room for rivers of contemplation (John 7:38), we hope to be with the waters said to be “above the heavens,” which praise “the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the waters above the heavens as the place where the saints will praise God and contemplate him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son, the Word, is the immediate Creator, while the Father who commanded him is the Creator in the primary sense.
comments.comment: “He spoke, and they came to be; He commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 33:9; Psalm 148:5). We said that the immediate Creator, the one who as it were made the world with His own hands, is the Son of God, the Word, while the Father of the Word, by having commanded His own Son, the Word, to make the world, is Creator in the primary sense.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The deep was not judged rejectable by the psalmist but was received into the common chorus of creation, completing the hymn to its maker.
comments.comment: For not only does the water above the heavens fulfill its praise to God, as holding first place in honor because of the superiority it possesses from virtue, but, as it says, 'Praise him, also the things from the earth, dragons and all deeps' (Psalm 148:7). So even the deep, which the allegorizers cast away into the worse portion, was not judged rejectable by the psalmist, but was received into the common chorus of creation; and it too, according to the principles inherent in it, harmoniously completes the hymn to its maker.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why dragons and deeps are called to praise: even the deep joins the chorus of creation.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The Word crushed the evil powers signified by the dragons and abysses, who are not commanded to praise but only mentioned, while the fire and hail do his word.
comments.comment: If he says that the dragons were also named appropriately with the abysses, being more terrible than the creeping things upon the earth; and in another psalm, being called waters, it was said that dragons were in them, not other than the abyss named here. … It must be understood that evil powers are signified by these, as the Word of God crushed them, and through time has descended even unto the abysses. But observe, he says, how very strongly the Word does not command the dragons in the abysses to praise, but simply mentions them; for they are not worthy to praise God. They are called by necessity to obey the hymn being lifted up by all creation to the Lord, King, and God: fire, hail, snow, ice, wind of a storm, which do His Word (Ps 148:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Fire, snow, ice and wind would never subsist or act apart from the creative Word and his will, so they do not act independently.
comments.comment: All these things, existing around the air, were necessarily mentioned as parts of the whole cosmos and as subsisting through the Divine Word and serving Him. For apart from the creative Word, the whole cosmos would be moving aimlessly and without presiding over its days; neither snow, nor fire, nor ice, nor storm, nor wind would ever subsist, nor would they ever act apart from His will. Thus, these things doing His Word should not be heard as acting independently.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'fulfilling his word': the elements exist and act only through the creative Word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Kings and judges can mean those who examine things critically.
comments.comment: It is also possible to say of kings and rulers and judges, those living loftily and approaching things critically and investigatively, and the lower peoples who have believed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ages of the inner man are little children who have just received forgiveness, fathers expert in theology, and young men who are strong.
comments.comment: Concerning all those strolling in the streets of the highly-praised city, it is brought forward like a single dance in one of the Psalms: 'Young men and virgins, elders with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord' (Ps 148:12). Concerning the various ages of the inner man, and whom Jesus loved, he writes to the disciple: 'I write to you, little children, that your sins are forgiven you through his name' (1 John 2:12)—that is, the Savior—'I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning; I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have overcome the evil one' (1 John 2:13-14). He calls 'little children' those who have just received the forgiveness of sins, whatever age they might be according to the outer man; he names 'fathers' those who are expert in the theology from the beginning; and 'young men' those having strength, remaining unassailable with the word of the exhorting one remaining in them …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the young, the old and the children of the verse as stages of the inner man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Holy ones' means those from every nation, with Israel following.
comments.comment: And by saying “holy ones” he indicates those from every nation (Ps 148:14). Then, bringing in Israel by prophecy because it had drawn near from the beginning, he shows that its following comes after the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'all his saints' as people from every nation, with Israel coming after them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The only-begotten Word is the horn of the people, the horn raised up for David, which lifts up his people.
comments.comment: The only-begotten Word of God is the horn of the people, to whom the holy ones, when they call out, say: 'We gore our enemies with you.' Therefore also the Word was named one-horned, according to the glory of being one-horned. Concerning this it is said: 'There I will cause a horn to rise up for David, I have prepared a lamp for my Christ' (Psalm 132:17; LXX 131:17); … This, therefore, the horn says, will lift up his people, so that having been lifted up, it may become manifest to all the nations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the horn of his people' as the only-begotten Word, the horn raised up for David.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Song belongs to the holy, who approach God by an enlightened mind and a pure soul, not to sinners.
comments.comment: But it is for the holy alone to sing, not for the sinners, since: 'Not a beautiful song in the mouth of a sinner' (Sirach 15:9); for praise is due to the upright. And who are the holy whose song it is, or the discerning sons of Israel who have God in their mind, or those who are called the people approaching God? Those having an enlightened mind and a pure soul approach God by relationship and disposition, being near the exhortation of the one who said: 'Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you' (James 4:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Only those clothed with the new man attain newness of mind and serve by newness of spirit, not the letter.
comments.comment: Only those having clothed themselves with the new man are able to attain the newness of mind and to do the things of the new covenant, serving by the newness of spirit and not by the oldness of the letter. These same also fulfill the assembly of the holy, accomplishing the faithful and holy things of David and having the most holy righteousness toward God …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'new song': it belongs to those who serve in newness of spirit, not the oldness of the letter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy ones will rejoice in the glory that is to come, for the present sufferings are not worthy of the glory to be revealed.
comments.comment: The holy ones, having accomplished this, will rejoice in the glory that is to come and is eternal, even as they are called by that name from it (Psalm 149:5). For we reckon, as the apostle says, that the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that is about to be revealed to us (Rom 8:18). And it is possible to hear of the glory in which the holy ones boast, concerning which it is said: 'The glory of the Lord shall be seen' (Isa 60:1) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'let the saints be joyful in glory' as the coming glory, beside which present sufferings are small.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy ones, joined to God the Word as brides to the bridegroom, sleep together with glory and wisdom and rejoice at their beds without fear.
comments.comment: Therefore it is also written, 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.' Sleeping together with this glory and wisdom, the holy ones shall boast; for it is said, 'Whenever you sleep, let wisdom be with you'; appropriately to these things you say, 'Honor her, so that she may embrace you.' He who sleeps together with this is without fear and without care, and rejoices at his bed. Therefore all the souls of his holy ones, his brides, being joined together with God the Word, as a bride to the bridegroom of every rational nature, rejoice at their beds (Psalm 149:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word prophesied rest after death and exultation in it.
comments.comment: The word necessarily prophesied for those who have fallen asleep the rest after death and the exultation in it, according to the verse, “In peace I will lie down and sleep” (Psalm 4:9 (4:8)) (Ps 149:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'sing aloud upon their beds' as the rest after death of those who have fallen asleep.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: The holy ones carry two-edged swords, not killing as men do but cleansing every seductive fortification.
comments.comment: For praising with much truth, they glorify and highly exalt Him, having in their hands two-edged swords, although they are not killing according to men, but are ready to avenge every disobedience, since the weapons of their warfare are not fleshly but are powerful through God, by which they cleanse every seductive fortification through the utterance of high words being raised against the knowledge of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two-edged sword in the hand as a spiritual weapon that cleanses falsehood by words, not a sword for killing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy ones' words are more two-mouthed than any sword, cutting away the false and wounding hearers into the questions of the truth.
comments.comment: And it is also possible to call the two-edged swords in their hands 'two-mouthed'; for the holy ones do not possess each word as two-mouthed, but according to the living and active Word of God, they are more two-mouthed than any sword. Therefore also those using the words of truth do not only cut away the false and the superfluous by loosening sophisms, but they also wound the hearers into the questions of the truth. It is possible to call both types of two-edged swords in the hands of the holy ones found in these practices. And it is possible to call even an exhortatory word a two-edged sword, doing both: rebuking the one who receives it unto repentance, and avenging and punishing the disobedient unto the end.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy ones' vengeance is not destruction of the Gentiles but leads them to become fellow-citizens of the saints.
comments.comment: He does not say that the holy ones make vengeance that leads to destruction upon the Gentiles, but rather the vengeance that happens well upon them, just as the Gentiles and idolaters happen to be, so that, having cast off the life of the nations, they might become fellow-citizens of the saints and become members of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'vengeance upon the heathen' as a vengeance that turns the nations into fellow-citizens of the saints.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Reproaches are against the better peoples, who do not hate the reprover, but one who has despised the church is not to be reproved, for he will hate everyone who reproves.
comments.comment:
And also reproaches will be active among the nations, since the vengeance upon the nations is a greater evil than the reproaches of the people, but the reproaches are against the better peoples. For it is said: Reprove the wise, and he will love you; make known to the righteous, and he will add to the receiving. For the peoples will not hate those reproving them because they do not happen to be evil, even if they sin through inadvertence, as opposed to those having a hateful disposition toward those reproving them because of perfected wickedness. If it is therefore said, Do not reprove the evil, lest they hate you.

You will find this same interpretation also in the Gospel, understanding the word of the Savior as saying: If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone; and if he listens to you, you have gained your brother; but if he does not listen to you, take one or two, and if he listens to them, announce it to the church; but if he even despises even the church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector (Matthew 18:17). This one, having become evil, having despised through all, is not to be reproved; for he will hate everyone who reproves, if he happens to be unholy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The righteous do not take vengeance imprecisely but with written judgment, building true doctrine from the oracles and overthrowing false knowledge.
comments.comment: … But the righteous do not perform the vengeance and the reproaches or the making of the enclosure of bonds in an imprecise way, but with written judgment, bringing about the construction of true dogmas from the written oracles and the overthrow of pseudonymous knowledge. And I do not ignore that some of those who have explained this historically have taken the interpretation for the sake of a victory and trophies and hymns of praise to themselves against certain sensual enemies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the judgment written' as the righteous building true doctrine from the Scriptures and overthrowing false knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture calls a thing that excels in strength a firmament, so the firmament of God's power is his strong and unyielding power.
comments.comment: The name “firmament” is customary in Scripture for things that excel in strength. For example, when it says, “The Lord is my firmament and my refuge” (Psalm 17:3 LXX [Hebrew 18:2]), and “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:4 LXX [Hebrew 75:3]), and “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Psalm 150:1 LXX [Hebrew 150:1]). … But it is customary for Scripture to call what is strong and unyielding a firmament, as it often uses this word even of air that has been greatly condensed, as when it says, “He who makes firm the thunder” (Job 37:4 LXX [Hebrew 37:4]).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the firmament of his power': in Scripture a firmament is what excels in strength.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The comprehension of God through the divine Scriptures is a stronghold of the power of God, but it is not that power itself.
comments.comment: But also the comprehension of God through the divine Scriptures is a stronghold of the power of God, but it is not the power of God itself that exists. And you will perceive also this: whether the power of God is in men, or whether one partakes of the Holy Spirit: For you shall receive power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, to the apostles (Acts 1:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who keeps the power given to him praises God, from whom the power is, and the all-ruling powers praise him upon his powers.
comments.comment: Words are spoken by the Savior, and 'You indeed shall sit in the city,' as if you would not put on power from the height. Therefore, if anyone firmly preserves this power given to him, watching over it with care, becoming in its stability a part of it, he praises God, from whom this divine power is, and he says, 'I am able to do all things in Christ who strengthens me' (Phil 4:13). Since they are ruled by the Savior of power, and in the stability they praise him, understanding that the all-ruling powers—through which he royally creates, provides, benefits, and corrects—they praise him upon his powers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wise man praises God according to the multitude of his unsearchable judgments, which are infinite and incomprehensible.
comments.comment: He who is the unsearchable judgments of God and the unsearchable ways of him, the wise man, knowing according to the multitude of the unsearchable judgments, will praise him (Ps 150:2b); not because of the incomprehensibility of the judgments and the ways, as it says, 'O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, and your wisdom was wondered at by me' (Rom 11:33); I was strengthened, yet I am not able toward it. For I cannot contemplate the multitude of it; it becomes stronger than me, as if I were not able to assist it, being infinite and incomprehensible.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who is not ashamed of Jesus praises him in a trumpet by proclaiming theology boldly, and the resurrection of the dead is signaled by a trumpet.
comments.comment: He who is not ashamed of Jesus and his words, clearly and loudly bringing forth the things of theology with boldness, praises him and his Father in a trumpet; for even the heralds of the truth have the command to proclaim the teaching more boldly and clearly, having as a trumpet to lift up their voice. For words are indeed spoken to them, 'Sound the trumpet in the trumpet, proclaim in Zion in my holy mountain' (Joel 2:1). But also the resurrection of the dead, which becomes fearful to all those rising, is signaled by a trumpet, for he says, 'The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible' (1 Cor 15:52), and in another epistle, 'With the voice of an archangel and in the trumpet of God he shall descend from heaven' (1 Thess 4:16), in order to raise those who have slept in Christ. As the command of the resurrection being revealed to all, in order to raise the righteous and the unrighteous, is made known by the loud voice of the instruments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the sound of the trumpet' as bold proclamation of the truth and the trumpet of the resurrection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is praised with the psaltery in spirit and mind, and with the lyre through every power of the soul and every action of the body.
comments.comment: Praise him with psaltery and lyre. What is the psaltery and the lyre, and what difference is said to be held between them in what was said before? God is to be praised, singing in spirit and mind; for this is the psaltery; for the spirit and the mind are held together from above by God through the loftiness of dogmas. And he is to be praised also with lyre; through every power of the soul and sensation, with strings stretched, they are struck in order. For the soul was given as a lyre in those things previously read. If, however, through every activity of each member, it is struck as an alien lyre, no one would err in praising God through every action of the body.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the psaltery and the lyre as praise in spirit and mind and through every action of the body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The timbrel is the body, which the soul will take up at the resurrection, so that it dances with the powers in an incorruptible, spiritual body.
comments.comment: Those carrying about the death of Jesus in the body, through which the flesh was killed, praise him with a timbrel (Ps 150:4). It has been interpreted before that the timbrel is that which was destined to be the one among the young women, the timbrel-players. For this is the body, which the soul will take up at the resurrection; it is a young woman playing the timbrel in announcing the minds of God in the standing of the heavenly ones with the myriads of the celebrating angels, as this is made manifest through the approaching word sounding, 'Praise him with timbrel, and also with dance'; for the soul dances with the powers and with all the higher creation after the resurrection, instead of a corrupt and weak and dishonorable and psychic body, having taken up an incorruptible, powerful, glorious, spiritual body.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Praising with loud cymbals means commemorating the Lord with the voice through theology, not with a voice only and no thought.
comments.comment:
I think it is made manifest through the praising him with loud cymbals (Ps 150:5) that it is necessary also to commemorate the Lord with voice according to utterance through theology. And there appears to me to understand this from the word of the apostle writing thus: 'I have become a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal' (1 Cor 13:1); … Having only a voice without possessing thought, so that the one speaking seems to be a barbarian, having sense of voice and sound only, he becomes to himself a bronze clanging or a resounding cymbal, striking and only making a noise in his hearing. Let us therefore glorify God, and imitating the perfect and righteous men in speech. For it is said concerning each of these: the discourse of a pious man is wisdom throughout; likewise, the mouth of the righteous shall meditate on wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment, the law of God being in his heart; that is to say, he praises God also with mind and tongue and mouth.

But the cymbal sounds well if it has a careful and well-modulated voice clearly signifying things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the loud cymbals as speaking of God with mind as well as voice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God imparts the breath of life, which makes blessed and sanctifies, to those who believe in the one he sent and rise above sensible things.
comments.comment:
For assisting our weakness, He imparts to us the notion of divine breath, just as it has been written concerning the first man: He breathed into his face the breath of life, and he became a living soul (Gen 2:7). For life and the fountain of life is the one who said, 'I am the life' (John 14:6), and concerning life it has been said to the Father, 'From you is the fountain of life' (Psalm 36:9).

This breath of life, which makes blessed and sanctifies, coming into the man, shall prepare his soul to live, or to say thankfully, 'My soul lives in him.' This gift alone all shall enjoy who has received the word of Jesus and has believed in the one who sent him to the Father. For the Savior says, 'The one hearing my words and believing in the one who sent me has eternal life' (John 5:24). God offers this breath to those who have ascended far above the sensible things and tread upon them, called His people, just as the prophet says concerning him: 'Thus says the Lord God who made the heavens and established the earth, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it' (Isaiah 42:5); it is evident what is the earth. And it is said also toward something ancient: 'And the breath of the Almighty is the one teaching me' (Job 32:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'every thing that hath breath' as the breath of life God gives to believers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
